exp.79:4:
It says that God gave his people tears to eat and tears to drink in great measure. It is an image: the weeping is so constant that it seems to be their daily food and drink.

The psalmist speaks on behalf of all Israel, in a communal prayer. The people suffer, feel that God is far away, and ask how long this will last. Their neighbors mock them. The psalm does not say exactly what the historical moment was, and scholars have understood it in different ways. Even so, the people cry out to God and ask him to restore them.

Today we can learn to weep honestly before God. If you are going through a painful season, you do not have to pretend to be strong: you can tell him what you feel and ask him to show you his face again.
exp.70:11:
The explanation says that the psalmist asks God not to stay far from him and to come quickly to help him. The words "to come quickly" and "to help" are the meaning of the verse itself, so they can be kept as they are. The sentences explaining the old word and the word for "help" are removed, since "make haste" and "for my help" in the verse already carry that meaning.

The one speaking is an elderly believer, as can be seen in other parts of the psalm (verses 9 and 18). The psalm does not say who wrote it. His enemies say that God has already abandoned him and that no one will defend him. For that reason he cries out with urgency, and then says that he will keep waiting for and praising God.

When you feel alone or surrounded by criticism, you can pray sincerely and without hesitation: "My God, do not be far from me; make haste to help me." God is not offended by your urgency. And even if the answer takes time, you can keep trusting and praising him.
exp.118:35:
This verse is a prayer. The psalmist asks God to turn the desires of his heart toward his decrees, that is, the teachings and commands of God, and to keep him from covetousness, which is an excessive desire to gain more money or possessions. The word "incline" here means to direct or to turn.

The speaker is the author of Psalm 119, whose identity is not known for certain. Here he loves God's law and recognizes that he needs help to obey it. Earlier he asked for understanding and guidance; now he asks that his eyes not be fixed on empty things. His heart needs to be directed by God.

For today: ask God each morning to put in you a hunger for his Word. When you feel the desire to have more, stop and pray: "Lord, turn my heart to you."
exp.93:15:
Here the psalmist asks two similar questions: who will stand up on my behalf against the evildoers? Who will defend me against those who practice wickedness? The ones who do harm on purpose are the people the verse calls the evildoers, and the second question refers to the workers of iniquity, meaning those who practice injustice. Both questions look for a defender.

The one speaking is a believer from Israel, whose name the psalm does not give. He is suffering because of the injustice of powerful people. Earlier he said that God will not abandon his people, and then he answers his own question: God was his help and his support when he felt his foot slipping.

When you feel alone in the face of injustice, do not keep your pain silent: bring it to God in prayer, as the psalmist did. And also seek out people of faith who will walk with you, because God often sustains us through his mercy and through his people.
exp.54:1:
It says that David asks God to pay attention to him and answer him.

David speaks, and the title calls it a "Masquil," a term that many understand as a poem for teaching or meditation (its exact meaning is uncertain). His following verses say that an enemy and wicked people who threaten him oppress him. That is why his heart is full of fear. The Psalm does not fully clarify the exact moment of his life, and several possibilities have been proposed.

For today: you do not need to pray with beautiful words. If you are distressed, you can tell God everything you feel, even with weeping or despair. He invites his people to come near with sincerity.
exp.73:13:
It says God crushed the heads of Leviathan, a sea monster, and gave him as food to the people who live in the wilderness. "Brakest" means you broke and smashed him in pieces. The verse's wording for the people is not settled: some think of creatures of the desert, others of people who live in dry regions. It is not certain, and the language is poetic.

The psalmist, named Asaph, prays in a moment of national distress, probably after the destruction of the temple. He remembers God's ancient victories over chaos and over Egypt, which many see represented in Leviathan, and asks him to act again.

For today: when your problems feel enormous, remember what God has done before. Pray honestly, as Asaph did, and trust that the God who defeated monsters is still your king.
exp.118:169:
This verse is a simple request: the psalmist asks that his prayer come before God and that God rescue him according to what he has promised. The word "word" here means a promise or a word given. "Deliver me" means take me out of, rescue me from what oppresses me.

The speaker is the author of Psalm 119, a believer who loves God's law. We do not know with certainty who wrote it. He has just said that he has kept God's commandments and that he lives with God as his witness. He is in the midst of difficulties, but his plea does not rest on his own merits, but on the faithfulness of God. Furthermore, he already anticipates that he will praise God when he is helped.

Today we can pray with confidence, relying on the promises of the Bible. Before asking for help, look for a promise of God that relates to your need, and present it in prayer with humility and hope.
exp.20:8:
This verse says that God will make the enemies of the king like a blazing furnace in the time of his anger. "Shalt make them" means that he will destroy them, and "anger" is an intense wrath. The fire will consume them, that is, it will finish them off completely.

It is a psalm of David, which speaks of the king and of God. The king gives thanks because he trusts in the Lord and God sustains him. It uses strong, poetic language, typical of the Old Testament, to show that those who oppose God's purpose will not prevail. Some also read it as a reference to the Messiah, the ultimate King.

Today we can rest in the fact that God is just and we do not need to take revenge. When someone harms us, we can entrust the matter to God, pray, and keep trusting in him, as the king of the psalm does.
exp.115:8:
It says that the psalmist will walk before God, that is, he will live each day aware of his presence and wanting to please him. The phrase "I will walk" speaks of a daily life, not of one special moment. The phrase "the land of the living" refers to this present life, where there is life, in contrast with death and the grave.

The speaker is a believer who came very close to death, with tears and danger, and who cried out to God. God delivered him, and now he responds with gratitude. The verses before say that God delivered his soul from death, his eyes from tears, and his feet from falling. The text does not say exactly what the crisis was, so it is not right to invent it.

For today: when God helps you in a difficulty, do not stop at relief. Respond with a life of gratitude: pray, obey, and do what is right even in everyday matters, as one who lives before God.
exp.145:3:
When a person dies, it says, their spirit leaves them and their body returns to the earth from which it was formed. The word "returneth" in the verse means "returns," and the phrase "perish" means that their plans and projects come to an end that very same day.

The psalmist encourages himself to praise God all his life. For this reason he warns that one should not put trust in princes or in any human being, because they cannot save. They are mortal, and their plans end with them. The author is not identified with certainty in the text. Right after this, he contrasts it with the happiness of the one who hopes in the eternal God, the creator of everything.

For today: respect and value people, but do not place your final trust in leaders, money, or human plans. When you feel pressured by someone with power, pray and rest in God, who never dies or fails.
exp.47:9:
Its praise, like its name, reaches to the ends of the earth. It says that God's fame is as great as his name: his praise reaches the farthest corners of the land. "Praise" in this context means exactly what the verse says. The "right hand" is a symbol of power and action, so his mighty hand always acts with justice, never bending anything.

This is a psalm of the sons of Korah, sung by God's people in Jerusalem. The speakers are the gathered worshipers in the temple, who recall what they had heard about God and now see with their own eyes his protection over the city. Scholars do not agree on exactly which event is being celebrated, so it is best not to state that with certainty.

For today: when everything seems unfair or confusing, remember that God acts with justice. Take a moment to praise him for something concrete he has done in your life, and trust that his hand is still working for good.
exp.118:58:
The psalmist says that he stopped to think calmly about how he had been living. Examining his ways means looking closely at his conduct and his direction. He then turned around and changed course. The laws of God are the teachings of God, which bear witness to his will and to who he is.

The one speaking is the author of Psalm 119, a believer who loves God's Word. We do not know with certainty who wrote it. He has just said that God is his portion and asked for mercy. His reflection leads him to obey at once, as the next verse shows.

For today: set aside a quiet moment this week, preferably with your Bible open, and ask yourself whether there is some habit or decision that is pulling you away from God. Ask him for help and take one concrete step to set your course right.
exp.16:0:
David asks God to listen to him. He tells God to pay attention to his cry, that is, his call for help. He asks that God hear a prayer that comes from honest lips, that is, one spoken with sincerity and without deceit. Here the word for right means a just cause: David presents his case as someone who seeks to have justice done.

The speaker is David, and the psalm bears his name. The text does not state the exact occasion, but the verses that follow show that he faces enemies and trusts that God knows his heart. For that reason he approaches God as a just judge.

For today: when you pray, do it with honesty. You do not need to dress up your words or pretend. Tell God sincerely what you feel and what you need, and trust that he hears and judges with justice.
exp.37:5:
He says the psalmist is bent over, like someone carrying an enormous weight. Being bent over means walking with the head down, and being very low in spirit means being deeply cast down. And all of this happens "all the day long," without rest.

David speaks here, according to the title of the psalm, which calls it "a psalm of David, to bring to remembrance." He suffers because of his sin and because of a painful illness. He sees both things joined together: his guilt weighs on him like a burden, and his wounds consume him. We do not know exactly what illness it was, and scholars interpret it in different ways.

For today: when the weight of guilt or pain bows down your spirit, do not hide it. Speak about it honestly with God, as David did. He does not reject a broken heart, and confessing is the first step toward rising up again.
exp.89:10:
Who really understands how strong God's anger is? The second part says that his indignation is as great as the reverent awe that he deserves. "According as thy fear" means that his anger matches his greatness. The question suggests that almost no one fully understands it.

The psalm is traditionally attributed to Moses, although some scholars debate this. It speaks on behalf of the people and reflects on how brief and fragile life is in contrast to an eternal God. It connects death with God's judgment on human sin. This verse prepares the prayer that follows: asking for wisdom to number our days well, and asking for compassion.

For today: do not take God or sin lightly. Live with reverence, but also with trust, and ask him each day for wisdom to use your time well and to return to him in humility.
exp.136:7:
It says that Babylon, here called "daughter of Babylon," will be destroyed. And it calls happy (blessed, fortunate) the one who pays her back with the same harm she inflicted on God's people. The phrase "who art to be destroyed" can be understood as "doomed to be destroyed."

It speaks as an Israelite exiled in Babylon, after Jerusalem had been laid waste. His grief is very deep and he calls for justice. It is a psalm of lament, and it expresses human anger with raw honesty. The Bible records it as it is, without saying that we should imitate that vengeance. Some see here a prayer that leaves judgment in God's hands.

For today: when pain and anger overwhelm you, bring them to God honestly, rather than taking revenge yourself. Then ask him to guide you toward justice and forgiveness, as Jesus taught (Matthew 5:44).
exp.3:5:
Many people, it says, are looking for someone to show them something good, someone to give them hope. But the speaker turns to God and asks him to lift up the light of his face upon us. It is a way of asking for his favor, his nearness, and his blessing, the way someone looks at you with kindness.

The psalm is attributed to David and is said to come from a time of distress, surrounded by people who doubted him or criticized him. The verses that follow show that, even so, he finds joy and sleeps in peace. It is thought to have been written as a prayer for the night, although we do not know the exact circumstances with certainty.

When the world offers you quick answers for being happy, pause and seek God first. Before you sleep, bring him your worries and ask for his presence. His peace is worth more than any harvest.
exp.26:4:
This verse says that God will protect those who trust him when troubles come. The "pavilion" and the "tabernacle" are God's tent or dwelling, and the "secret place" is the most hidden and safest spot. "He will set me up upon a rock" speaks of a firm place, out of reach of danger.

David speaks here, according to the psalm's heading. He is surrounded by enemies and threats, yet he says he is not afraid. His greatest desire is to stay close to God and to gaze on his beauty. His confidence comes from that closeness. Scholars debate whether the "tabernacle" is a physical place or an image of God's protection; both readings fit.

For today: in your hard days, before looking for a thousand ways out, draw near to God in prayer and in his Word. There you can find rest and firmness, even if the problem has not yet been resolved.
exp.6:13:
The explanation says the wicked person is like a pregnant woman: he began with wickedness, carried it inside him like a heavy load, and in the end gave birth to a lie, that is, something empty and deceptive. His evil plan does not produce what he expected.

David speaks in this psalm. According to the heading, he wrote it concerning Cush, a Benjamite, and we do not know for certain who he was or exactly what happened. David feels persecuted and asks God to judge him with justice. Here he describes how evil is planned, grows, and ends in failure. The verses that follow show that the wicked man falls into his own trap.

For today: do not feed thoughts of revenge, envy, or deceit, because they grow inside you and bear bitter fruit. Hand your offenses over to God and trust that He does justice.
exp.118:112:
The section begins with "Samech," which is the name of a Hebrew letter. Psalm 119 is arranged according to the Hebrew alphabet, and each section starts with one letter. The psalmist then says that he hates "vain thoughts," that is, divided, uncertain ideas that waver between obeying God and not obeying him. The Hebrew word can be understood in several ways. In contrast, he states that he loves God's law.

The author does not name himself in the psalm. Tradition attributes it to David, but this is not certain. He speaks as someone faithful who faces pressure from wicked people, as seen when he says: "Depart from me, ye evildoers." Earlier he expressed his joy in God's testimonies and his desire to obey always. Here he draws a clear line between what he rejects and what he loves.

For today: when thoughts of doubt, envy, or resentment come to you, do not let them stay. Replace them by reading a verse and praying with it, so that your mind is filled with what God says.
exp.67:15:
Why do you look so proudly at the high mountains, like those of Bashan? They have no reason to boast, because God chose another mountain, Zion, to live there. Here, looking with envy or arrogance is what is meant by the phrase about the mountains rising up. The place where someone dwells or reigns is the seat God has chosen. God promises to stay on that mountain forever.

The psalm is by David, a song of victory when God leads his people and defeats the enemy kings. Bashan was a mountainous and imposing region. Many understand the mountains as rivals competing with one another, but God chooses the humble place, not the greatest one. Some think it refers to the bringing of the ark to Jerusalem, though the text does not say so with complete clarity.

God does not choose by appearance or by size. You do not need to compare yourself with others or compete to get his attention. He draws near to the hearts that receive him, even when they feel small. Offer him your life today as his dwelling place.
exp.49:15:
This verse says that God speaks to the wicked person and firmly asks what right he has to talk about his laws or to repeat his covenant with his mouth. The verse's own words "declare" and "covenant" are the ones to note here: "declare" means to tell, explain, or recite, and "covenant" is the agreement God made with his people. The question points out that speaking about God with the lips is not enough if one's life does not support it.

In this psalm, which is attributed to Asaph, God himself speaks as the judge of his people. First he rebukes those who offered sacrifices only out of habit, and then, beginning with this verse, he confronts those who knew the law but lived in theft, adultery, and deceit. The verses that follow explain the problem: they rejected correction and despised his words.

For today: before speaking about faith or teaching others, it is wise to examine whether our lives are going in the same direction. If something appears that God corrects in us, we can accept it with humility and ask him for help to change.
exp.121:7:
This verse says that the psalmist, out of love for his family and friends, will declare peace over Jerusalem. "Brethren" can refer to relatives or to the whole people of Israel, and "companions" are close friends. The phrase "I will now speak peace concerning you" means "I will now say, Peace be within you," as a blessing.

It is a psalm of ascent, one of those sung on the way up to Jerusalem for the feasts. The title attributes it to David, though some scholars debate its authorship. The one speaking is a pilgrim glad to have arrived in the city where the temple stood. His desire for peace comes from loving his community and wanting its good.

Today we can pray and speak words of peace over our church, family and friends. This week, bless someone with whom there is tension, and do it out of love for people, not out of obligation.
exp.24:5:
It says that David asks God to remember his tenderness and his goodness. The "tender mercies" are the displays of compassion, that affection which is moved by suffering. The "lovingkindnesses" are his faithful love that forgives and helps. And "ever of old" means they come from long ago and never run out. When it says "remember," it does not mean that God forgets; it is a way of asking him to act according to his character.

The psalm is attributed to David. It is a prayer from someone who needs guidance, forgiveness and help. Earlier he asked God to teach him his ways, and then he begs him not to remember the sins of his youth. That is why he bases his request on God's mercy and not on his own merits.

For today: when you fail or do not know what to do, pray leaning on God's goodness, not on how good you have been. Speak to him with confidence and ask for forgiveness and direction.
exp.17:46:
It says that God is the one who takes up the cause of David and brings justice. "Avengeth" here means that God sets right what is wrong and defends the one who suffers injustice. "Subdueth the people under me" means that God put nations under his authority.

David, king of Israel, speaks. This psalm is his song of thanks after God delivered him from his enemies and from Saul. David does not claim the victory for himself, but praises God, whom he calls his rock and his deliverer. Some understand this only as the story of David, and others also see a look forward to the Messiah.

For today: when you are hurt or mistreated, do not carry the desire to get even yourself. Hand that pain over to God in prayer, trust that He is just, and ask Him for help to act with kindness while you wait.
exp.17:49:
He gives great deliverance to his king, and shows mercy to his anointed, to David, and to his descendants forever. That is, God gives great victories to his king, and shows mercy, meaning faithful love, to the one he has chosen and set apart to rule. That kindness reaches David and his descendants forever.

David speaks at the end of a psalm of thanksgiving, after being rescued from his enemies, among them Saul, according to the psalm's title. He refers to himself in the third person. He ends by praising God and recalling his promise to preserve his line. Many Christians also see here a sign pointing to Jesus, a descendant of David, although the psalm speaks first of David.

For today: when God helps you through a difficulty, do not keep it to yourself in silence. Write it down, tell it, and give thanks. Remembering his past help strengthens your confidence that he will remain faithful tomorrow.
exp.118:106:
It says that the writer is suffering greatly and asks God to give him new life, that is, to revive and sustain him, according to what God has promised in his word. "I am afflicted very much" means "I am very distressed." "Quicken me" means "give me life, restore my strength." "According unto" means "in accordance with."

The speaker is the psalmist, who is not identified with certainty. This psalm celebrates God's law, and this section (the letter Nun) comes after saying that God's word is a lamp to his path. Many believe he was suffering persecution or danger, since he says his life is "in his hand." Even so, he does not abandon God's law.

For today: when you are downcast, do not remain alone with your pain. Pray honestly and look in the Bible for specific promises. Tell God how you feel and ask him to lift you up according to what he has said.
exp.5:1:
David begins by asking God to have mercy on him. He says he is weak, without strength, and asks to be healed. The phrase about his bones means that his bones are shaken; it is a way of saying he feels pain and trembling deep within his body.

David is the one speaking. He has just asked God not to rebuke him in anger. He seems to be suffering greatly, both in body and in spirit, and he feels that God is disciplining him. The psalm does not say exactly what the cause was: it may be an illness, distress, or guilt, and scholars understand it in several ways.

When you feel weak, you do not have to pretend that you are fine. You can speak honestly to God, rely on his mercy, and ask him for help in your own simple words.
exp.34:17:
This verse says that the psalmist promises to give thanks to God and to praise him in public. "Give thanks" here does not mean admitting sins, but acknowledging and declaring what God has done. The "great congregation" and the "much people" refer to a large gathering of people who worship God.

David is speaking, according to the title of the psalm. He is surrounded by enemies who hate him without cause, mock him, and show their teeth in rage. He cries out to God, asking for rescue. In the midst of that suffering, he promises that when God delivers him, he will not keep it quiet, but will tell it before many.

For today: when God helps you through a difficulty, don't stay silent. Tell what he did in your church or with your family. Your testimony can encourage others who are suffering today and show them that God does hear.
exp.76:2:
The explanation says that the psalmist remembered God, but instead of feeling relief, he cried out and complained. His spirit grew faint, meaning it was weakened and he felt without strength. "Selah" is a pause or musical marking whose exact meaning is not known for certain; it probably invites the reader to stop and reflect.

The one speaking is Asaph, or someone from his group of musicians, in a psalm addressed to the choir director. He is passing through a night of distress and finds no comfort. It is striking that remembering God, at that moment, increases his pain. Later the psalm shows that little by little he recalls God's past works.

For today: when you are discouraged, do not pretend or keep silent. You can bring your honest complaints to God, even if you do not feel comfort right away. Praying with honesty is also faith.
exp.4:1:
It says David asks God to listen closely to his cry, that is, to his cry for help. The phrase that means "pay attention" is rendered here as "listen," so that the request is clear: "Hearken" in the verse above. He addresses God as "my King and my God," acknowledging that God is his authority and his Lord. And he states that he will pray to God, because he trusts that God does hear.

The one who speaks is David, according to the heading of the psalm. It is a prayer, probably sung in worship. The word that appears in the heading only here is uncertain, and no one knows its meaning for sure; some think it refers to a wind instrument, but this is uncertain. David prays because he faces wicked and deceitful people, as the following verses show.

For today: when you feel distress, you do not need to have perfect words. Speak to God with sincerity, as to a King who rules and a Father who listens. Praying is the beginning of trusting.
exp.118:144:
The psalmist says he prayed with complete sincerity, with his whole being. The word "cried" means he spoke to God aloud and with urgency. He asks God to answer him and promises that he will keep God's statutes, that is, that he will obey God's instructions. The Hebrew letter heading is simply the name of a letter of the alphabet, because this psalm follows the order of the alphabet.

The one speaking is the author of Psalm 119, whose name we do not know for certain. He is going through affliction and distress, but he loves God's Word. Earlier he asked for understanding in order to live. Here his prayer becomes intense, and in the verses that follow he rises early to cry out and to wait on God's word.

For today: when you pray, do not stop at quick phrases or out of habit. Speak to God honestly about what weighs on you, and ask him for help to live out what he teaches. Prayer and obedience go hand in hand.
exp.110:7:
They say that God's commandments, mentioned in the previous verse, stand firm forever and ever. "Stand fast" means held up, secure, not moving. "Done in uprightness" means they are just and right. They were made in truth, that is, they do not deceive or fail.

This psalm is a song of praise, and no one knows for certain who wrote it. The author speaks in the midst of the community of God's people, remembering his works: the inheritance he gave them and the redemption he sent. All of this shows that God is faithful and that his covenant does not change.

Today we can build our lives on the Word of God, even though opinions and fashions change. When you have to decide something, ask yourself what the Bible teaches. What God has said is firm and will not fail you.
exp.137:2:
It says that when David asked God for help, God answered him. And it also strengthened him inwardly, in the deepest part of his being. Where the verse speaks of God giving him strength in his soul, the wording shows God gave him courage and strength within himself.

David speaks in a psalm of thanksgiving. He has just said he will praise God with his whole heart for his mercy and his truth. Here he recalls a specific moment when God answered him. We do not know exactly what situation he is referring to. Afterward, he hopes that even the kings of the earth will acknowledge God.

Today, when you pray in the middle of a difficulty, do not depend only on the situation changing. God often responds first by giving you inner strength to keep going with peace and courage. And afterward, remember to thank him for those answers.
exp.105:20:
This verse says that the people of Israel forgot God, who is called here "the God of their salvation," meaning the God who saved them or set them free. Here "salvation" refers not only to being well, but to rescue and deliverance. And that God had done mighty deeds in Egypt.

The psalmist is going over Israel's history to acknowledge the people's sins. Just before, he mentions the golden calf at Horeb (another name for Mount Sinai), and just after, he recalls the wonders in Egypt, in the land of Ham, and at the Red Sea. The psalm is a confession: it shows God's faithfulness in contrast to his people's poor memory.

For today: don't let routine or worries erase what God has already done for you. Write down a few times when he helped you and thank him for them this week.
exp.135:10:
This verse praises God because he brought the people of Israel out from among the Egyptians. Some old words need explaining: the word "brought out" is the same as "brought out," and "mercy" here means his faithful, steadfast, loyal love for his people. The phrase "his mercy endureth for ever" is repeated in every verse of the psalm.

The psalm is a song of praise, probably sung by the community, perhaps in the worship of Israel. We do not know for certain who wrote it. Here the exodus is remembered: after striking down the firstborn of Egypt, God freed his people from slavery. The people repeat God's mercy as a response to what he has done.

For today: when you feel trapped in a difficult situation, remember the times God helped you. Recalling his faithfulness in the past strengthens your trust. Write down today one thing for which you can say, "His mercy endures forever."
exp.23:9:
This verse answers the question, "Who is this King of glory?" The answer is "the Lord of hosts," that is, God who commands all the armies, both of heaven and of earth. He is called "the King of glory" because his greatness and honor are perfect. "Selah" was probably a pause to stop and meditate, although its exact meaning is not entirely certain.

This is a psalm of David, sung as a dialogue. Some think it was used in processions when the ark was carried toward Jerusalem, but this is not known for certain. Some voices ask questions and others answer, while the gates are called to open to receive the King. The purpose is to call the people to recognize who God is.

Today we can open the "gates" of our heart and of our plans. Before facing a problem, pause for a moment and remember that the mighty God is the King of your life. Hand that matter over to him with confidence.
exp.144:15:
It says that God opens his hand, like someone who gives generously, and fills with blessing every living thing. The word "fills" means to fill completely, until there is more than enough. In other versions the verse is read as God "satisfies the desire of every living thing," and that idea also fits the text. No one is left outside his care.

This psalm carries the heading "A psalm of praise, by David." The one speaking is the psalmist, who praises God as a kind King. The verses before this one say that God upholds those who fall and gives food in due season. The verses after it affirm that he is righteous, merciful, and near to those who call on him sincerely. So this verse shows his generous provision.

Today we can recognize that everything good comes from the open hand of God. Before you eat, or at the end of the day, write down three things you have received and thank him simply.
exp.41:1:
This verse says the person feels a deep need for God, like someone who is very thirsty. It calls him "the living God," that is, a real and present God, not an idea. The phrase "appear before God" means "come before God" or "be in his presence."

The one speaking is a psalmist, probably a Levite from the sons of Korah, who served in worship. He seems to be far from the place of worship, sad, and surrounded by people who mock his faith. The verses that follow show that he remembers with longing when he used to go with the crowd to the house of God. We do not know for certain where he was or at what exact moment he wrote this.

For today: when you feel dry or far from God, do not hide it. Tell him honestly that you need him. Seek his presence in prayer, in the Word, and in the company of other believers, because that thirst is also an invitation to draw near.
exp.97:8:
This verse says that all creation rejoices before God, because he comes to govern the earth. The words "came" and "will judge" mean that God arrives to set things in order. "Judge" here does not only mean to condemn, but to govern and put right what is crooked. He will do it with righteousness and with uprightness, that is, in a clean way and without favoritism.

Psalm 98 is a song of praise. No one knows for certain who wrote it; its heading simply calls it a psalm. The people of Israel invite the seas, the rivers, and the mountains to celebrate their King. They rejoice because his rule will be good, not abusive. Some read it as a hope for the future, and Christians connect it with the coming of Christ.

Today you can rest in the knowledge that God sees every injustice and will correct it. When something seems unfair to you, bring it to him in prayer, and treat others with righteousness yourself.
exp.121:6:
The verse says there should be peace and security within its outer walls, and tranquility within its palaces. The word "walls" here refers to the city's defensive wall, the outer wall that protected Jerusalem. "Prosperity" means calm and security, without threats. It is a wish for blessing on the whole city, from its defenses to its most important houses.

It is a psalm of ascent, a song of pilgrims who went up to Jerusalem. The title attributes it to David. The one speaking is a joyful pilgrim who prays for the city where the temple stood and where justice was administered. His reason is love for God's people and for the house of the Lord.

Today we can pray for the peace of our church, our family, and our city. Ask God for tranquility in your home, and work for peace with those around you.
exp.67:6:
This verse reminds us that God himself went before his people when Israel was walking through the wilderness. The phrase "went forth before" means that God guided them like a shepherd or a captain. "Selah" is a word that appears in the Psalms; its exact meaning is not known for certain, but many believe it invites the reader to pause and meditate.

The one speaking is David, according to the title of the psalm, and he sings praising God. He looks back to the time of the exodus, when God brought Israel out of Egypt and led them through the wilderness to Sinai, as the following verses say. Earlier, the psalm had already shown God as the father of the fatherless and the defender of widows, that is, a God who cares for the weak.

For today: when you find yourself passing through a "wilderness," remember that God does not send you alone. Pause, as the Selah asks, and think about the times he has guided you before.
exp.61:0:
This verse says that David's soul rests in God and in Him alone. Words such as "truly" and "waiteth" in the King James wording point to a quiet, settled trust, a heart that is still and free of complaint or anxiety.

The one speaking is David, and the psalm is addressed to the chief Musician and to Jeduthun, a name tied to the music of worship in Israel. The verses that follow show David facing enemies who attack him and want to bring him down. It is not known with certainty at what exact point in his life he wrote it. Even so, in the middle of the threat, he chooses to trust God.

For today: when you feel pressured, before rushing from one side to the other looking for a way out, take a few minutes to quiet your heart before God. Tell Him what worries you, hand it over to Him, and rest in the knowledge that He cares for you.
exp.26:13:
It says that we should wait for God with patience and trust. "Wait" and "wait" mean the same thing here: counting on Him to act. The call to "be of good courage" is an invitation to be brave, and "let your heart take courage" means that the spirit should grow stronger. Repeating "wait on the Lord" stresses how much this matters.

It is spoken by David, according to the traditional heading of the psalm. He is surrounded by enemies and false accusations, and he asks for protection. Even so, he trusts that he will see the goodness of God in the land of the living, that is, in this life. At the end he encourages himself, like someone speaking to his own heart.

For today: when you are tired of waiting for an answer, do not stay alone in anguish. Set aside a few minutes each day to pray, to remember how God has helped you before, and to say to Him sincerely: "I trust in you, give me strength today."
exp.25:5:
This verse says the psalmist will wash his hands "in innocency," meaning with a clear conscience, and that he will go around God's altar to worship him. The name of God is "Jehovah," which today is sometimes written "Yahweh" or "the Lord."

David is the speaker, according to the traditional heading of the psalm. He asks God to examine him and declares that he has kept away from false and wicked people. Washing one's hands was a sign of purity before approaching the altar, and some believe that going around the altar refers to a procession of worship. The exact details are not known with certainty.

For today: before worshiping, examine your heart. Ask God to forgive you, step away from whatever defiles you, and come to him with sincerity.
exp.65:7:
Psalm 66:8 says that all the peoples should praise our God. "Bless" means speaking well of Him and giving Him thanks. "Make the voice of his praise to be heard" means that the praise should not be quiet or hidden, but should be heard openly.

The psalmist speaks on behalf of the people of Israel. He has just recalled how God turned the sea into dry land and how they crossed the river on foot, probably alluding to the Red Sea and the Jordan. He then invites the nations to join in, because God rules with power and cares for His people, even when He tests them, as silver is refined.

For today: when you remember how God helped you, don't keep it to yourself. Tell someone this week, or thank Him out loud, so that others will also be encouraged to trust in Him.
exp.6:14:
He dug a pit and deepened it, and then he himself fell into the hole he had made. The word "ditch" in the verse refers to a hole dug as a trap, and the passage pictures the harm someone plans against others coming back on that person.

David speaks in a psalm where he asks God for help against an enemy who is pursuing him. The heading names a man from the tribe of Benjamin, but nothing is known for certain about who he was. The verses before this one describe the wicked person as one who carries within himself wrongdoing and gives birth to falsehood. David trusts that God is just and ends by praising him.

For today: do not repay evil with evil or set traps against anyone. If someone harms you, leave it with God, who is just, and take care that your own heart does not fill with deceit.
exp.56:2:
He says that God will answer from heaven and rescue David from the shame and the attack of the one who pursues him. The word "Selah" is a pause, perhaps musical or for reflection; its exact meaning is not certain. God will send his mercy (his faithful love) and his truth (his faithfulness).

David speaks in a psalm that, according to its heading, he wrote when he was fleeing from Saul and took refuge in a cave. He is in real danger, surrounded by enemies whom he compares to lions. Even so, he does not rely on his own strength, but trusts that God will act on his behalf.

Today, when you feel pursued, pressured, or unfairly treated, you can pause, as in the "Selah," and remember that God is faithful. Tell him honestly what you feel, and trust that his love and his truth will sustain you, even if you cannot yet see the way out.
exp.102:18:
He says that God established his throne in the heavens, meaning that his authority is firm and does not depend on anyone. "Established" means he set it up with certainty. And his kingdom "rules over all": his government reaches everything that exists, people, nations and powers.

This psalm is attributed to David. He praises God for his forgiveness and his mercy toward those who revere him and keep his covenant. After speaking of that close love, David lifts his gaze and recalls that this compassionate God also reigns over all. That is why he then invites the angels and all creation to bless him.

For today: when you feel that the world or your life is out of control, remember that God is still on his throne. Give him your worry today in prayer and trust that his goodness and his power work together.
exp.117:28:
This verse invites us to give thanks and honor to the Lord, for two reasons: because he is good, and because his mercy lasts forever. The explanation of the word "mercy" here is that it speaks of his faithful love and his compassion, which never wear out or come to an end.

Psalm 118 is a song of thanksgiving. The speaker seems to be someone who was rescued from a great danger and now celebrates with the people in the temple. The psalm begins and ends with this same phrase, like a frame. The Bible does not say for certain who wrote it or what exact moment it refers to. The verses before this one speak of offering sacrifices on the altar as a sign of gratitude.

Today, we can begin or end the day by naming out loud three good things God has done for us. Even on hard days, remembering that his mercy does not end helps us to trust and to be thankful.
exp.144:9:
This verse says that everything God has made should give Him thanks and honor. "Praise" means to speak highly of Him and acknowledge His goodness. "Saints" are the people who belong to God and are faithful to Him. "Bless" means to speak well of Him and acknowledge His goodness.

It is a psalm of praise that tradition attributes to David. He has just spoken of the goodness of God: slow to anger, great in mercy, good to all. So now he invites creation and God's people to respond. The verses that follow show how: by speaking of His kingdom and His power.

For today: do not keep your gratitude silent. This week, tell someone one specific thing God has done for you, and give thanks to Him out loud. In this way your life also becomes a song of praise.
exp.77:7:
This verse asks that children not repeat the bad example of their parents. It describes them as a generation that was stubborn and obstinate, and rebellious. It says they did not set their heart aright, meaning they did not prepare or direct their heart toward God, and that their spirit was not faithful to Him.

The speaker is the psalmist, Asaph according to the title of the psalm. He is teaching the history of Israel so that each generation will tell the next the works of God. The purpose is that they trust in Him and keep His commandments. The following text gives an example: the men of Ephraim, although they were armed, turned back in the day of battle because they did not keep God's covenant.

For today: it is not enough to inherit a faith; the heart must be prepared. Set aside a moment each day to pray and read the Bible, and tell someone younger what God has done for you.
exp.101:25:
It says that the earth and the heavens, which seem so firm, will one day come to an end, like a garment that wears out with use. God, by contrast, remains forever. "Change" here means to exchange one thing for another, as when a person changes their clothes. "Perish" means they will cease to exist in the form we know them.

The psalmist is afflicted and weakened, and feels that his life is being cut short (verses 23-24). In his suffering, he looks to God, who is eternal. Some believe the psalm was written by someone in exile or in hard times, but this is not known for certain. Hebrews 1:10-12 quotes these words to speak of the greatness of Christ.

When you feel that everything around you is changing or wearing away, such as your health, your work, or the things you counted on as secure, remember that God does not change. You can rest your life on Him, and today pray with confidence, handing over to Him whatever worries you.
exp.129:1:
This verse is a prayer. The person asks God to hear them. "Hear my voice" is a plea for God to pay attention. "Let your ears be attentive" means that God should not be distracted, but should listen closely. A "supplication" is a request made with humility and need.

The psalm is called a "song of ascents," meaning a song that, according to many, was sung when going up to Jerusalem, although the exact meaning of the title is not known for certain. The one speaking does not identify himself; he cries out from "the depths," a place of distress, and the psalm shows that he is aware of his sins and waits for God's forgiveness.

For today: when you feel overwhelmed or guilty, do not turn away from God. Speak to him honestly, without pretense, and ask him to listen to you. He invites the needy to draw near.
exp.74:1:
He says that God himself promises to judge with justice, without bending anything. "When I shall receive the congregation" sounds strange today; the wording points to a set time or appointed moment. God does not act out of haste or human pressure, but in his chosen time. The idea of judging "uprightly" means with justice and without favoritism.

In this psalm of Asaph, the people praise God because his name is near. Here God himself seems to be speaking, and interpreters understand it this way. He answers a world that is shaking: he holds up the pillars of the earth and warns the proud not to lift themselves up, which means boasting of power.

Today, when you see injustice and feel that God is slow, remember that his timing is not ours, but his justice is certain. Trust, do not seek revenge, and keep doing what is right with humility.
exp.80:5:
He says God took the weight off Israel's shoulders. The "burden" was the hard labor they carried in Egypt. The "pots" are, according to many scholars, baskets or containers used for carrying bricks or clay; the Hebrew word can also refer to a work basket. So God freed them from slavery.

The one speaking here is God himself, within a psalm of Asaph that was sung at an Israelite festival. God reminds his people how he rescued them from Egypt, and he does so to invite them to listen to him and to remain faithful to him. After the reminder comes a call: "Hear, my people".

For today: when you feel overwhelmed, remember the times God has already delivered you. That grateful remembrance helps you trust him and listen to his voice, instead of looking for relief in other things.
exp.9:4:
The wicked man prospers in his wrongdoing at all times, and he is not troubled by God's judgment, as if it were far removed from his sight. The words that would need explaining here are rendered in the verse above, so we simply note that the wicked man scoffs at those who oppose him, snorting disdainfully and mocking them.

The speaker is the psalmist, who complains before God as he sees the wicked seem to get away with their schemes. The verses around this one show his arrogance: he does not seek God and thinks nothing will bring him down. Some scholars see here a single anguished statement; what matters is that the psalmist describes what he sees and then presents it to God.

For today: when you see injustice seem to triumph, do not let yourself be carried away by bitterness or envy. Tell God honestly what hurts you, and trust that He sees and judges with justice, even if not in the time you expect.
exp.54:3:
His heart is in great pain inside him, and terrors of death have come upon him. "Heavy with pain" means full of sorrow, and the fear arrived all at once, like a weight that crushes him.

The one speaking is David, according to the title of the psalm, though it is not known for certain at what point in his life he wrote it. He is asking God for help because enemies threaten him with rage and oppress him. The psalm also speaks of a painful betrayal by someone close to him, and that is why his anguish is so deep.

For today: when fear or pain overwhelm you, do not hide it or deny it. Tell God honestly, as David did. Prayer does not require beautiful words, only an honest heart that comes to God to be heard and held up.
exp.39:4:
God has done many wonderful things, and his thoughts and plans toward us are so many that they cannot be counted. The psalmist wants to announce them and speak of them, but words fail him; he cannot tell them all.

The one speaking is David, according to the title of the psalm. He has just described how God brought him out of deep distress and gave him a new song. His praise comes from gratitude. Later, the psalm speaks of obeying God from the heart rather than simply offering sacrifices.

For today: make a habit of giving thanks. This week, write down each day one good thing God has done for you, even if it is small. Over time you will see the list grow, and your trust in him will grow with it.
exp.89:13:
Here the psalmist asks God to fill him with his mercy, that is, with his faithful love and goodness. The phrase "early" in the verse means soon, without delay. The line about being satisfied means being filled completely, as someone who eats until fully content. The expected result is to sing and rejoice all our days.

This psalm is traditionally attributed to Moses, although some scholars debate whether he wrote it. It speaks in the plural, on behalf of the people. It acknowledges that life is brief and that sin and suffering weigh heavily. After asking for wisdom, the people cry out for relief and hope that the morning of God's mercy will arrive soon.

For today: before the workday or worries of the day are over, begin by seeking God so that he becomes your satisfaction. Ask him to let his love fill your emptiness, and give thanks for one specific thing. In this way, joy does not depend only on circumstances.
exp.36:29:
The person who is righteous, the one who lives uprightly before God, speaks with wisdom and expresses what is just. The word "speaketh" in the verse means to say something aloud. "Judgment" here does not mean punishment but good discernment: knowing how to tell right from wrong.

This is a psalm of David, written as counsel for anyone who becomes troubled when they see the wicked prospering. David encourages trust in God, who cares for his own. The following verse explains where that wisdom comes from: the law of God is in the heart of the righteous. What comes out of the mouth reflects what is within.

For today: before giving an opinion, offering advice, or answering in anger, take a few minutes to read the Bible and pray. If your heart is filled with the word of God, your words will be wiser, steadier, and more useful to others.
exp.72:2:
This verse says that the psalmist felt envy toward the foolish, that is, toward people who are senseless and live without taking God into account. He also calls them the wicked, those who do not honor God. What troubled him was seeing them flourish, enjoying well-being and success. Here, prosperity means peace, comfort, and a good life.

The psalm is attributed to Asaph, a musician and worship leader in the temple. He speaks honestly about an inner struggle: he nearly lost his faith on seeing that the wicked were doing well. That is why in verse 2 he says his feet had almost slipped. Later, when he enters God's sanctuary, he will understand things differently.

When you see others doing well even though they live badly, do not become bitter or compare yourself with them. Tell God what you feel, as Asaph did, and look at life from God's perspective, who sees beyond what seems true right now.
exp.10:6:
Psalm 11:7 says that the Lord is righteous and therefore loves righteousness. "His countenance doth behold the upright" means that God looks upon people of integrity with favor, closeness, and approval. The verse's picture of God's face turned toward the upright speaks of enjoying his presence and his favor.

The psalm is by David. It seems someone was advising him to flee from his enemies out of fear, but David answers that he trusts in the Lord. The verses before this one speak of judgment on the wicked. This last verse ends with hope: God is not indifferent, and those who live uprightly are under his loving gaze.

Today, when injustice seems to be winning, do not lose heart or change your principles. Do what is right even when it costs you, and remember that God sees your life, values your integrity, and is near to you.
exp.106:8:
He gave food and drink to those who were thirsty and hungry in a deep way. The phrase "satisfieth the longing soul" means that he fully met their need, filling them until they had enough. The word "hungry" in the verse refers to someone in need or lacking what they require. The word "soul" here refers to the whole person, with their desires and needs. "Filleth the hungry soul with goodness" speaks of an abundant provision, not a meager one.

The psalmist calls on those whom God rescued to give thanks. Earlier he speaks of travelers lost in a desert, with no city to live in. God guided them along a straight path to an inhabited place. This verse is the reason for his praise. We do not know with certainty who wrote the psalm; many place it after the return from exile, though this is debated.

When you feel an emptiness or a need, bring it to God honestly in prayer. He knows your real lacks. Then, like the psalmist, thank him out loud for a specific way in which he has sustained you.
exp.118:3:
God himself commanded, with firmness, that his commandments be kept carefully and completely. "Commanded" means that God gave a serious order, and "kept diligently" means obeyed with attention, not halfway.

Psalm 119 is a long poem in honor of God's Word. We do not know for certain who wrote it; tradition attributes it to David, but others dispute this. The one speaking is someone who loves God's law. At this point, after speaking of the blessing of obedience, he recognizes that God does not suggest but commands. Then he expresses his desire to be steady.

Today we can take obedience seriously, but without fear. If God asks something of us, it is for our good. Choose one command from the Bible that you have neglected and ask God for help to keep it this week.
exp.0:1:
The explanation says that the happy person not only avoids the wrong path but finds joy in God's teaching. The word "but" here is rendered "rather" or "on the contrary." "Law" in this verse means God's instruction or teaching, not only rules. "Delight" is joy and deep pleasure. "Meditate" means going over the words slowly, thinking about them, and "day and night" indicates constancy.

Psalm 1 is the gateway to the book of Psalms. Its author is not named in the text. A wise person, in the style of wisdom literature, contrasts two paths: that of the righteous and that of the wicked. The following verses show the fruit of that life, like a tree beside the water, in contrast to the wicked, who are like chaff driven away by the wind.

Set aside a few minutes each day to read a Bible passage slowly. Repeat one phrase during the day and ask God to help you live it, not out of obligation, but out of delight.
exp.77:68:
This verse says that God built his sanctuary as a high, firm, and lofty place, like the earth that he set in place to last forever. The phrase "like high palaces" in the King James wording conveys the idea of a height or an elevated mountain. The word "established" means that he laid firm foundations.

The psalm is attributed to Asaph, and it reviews the history of Israel to remember the people's failures and God's faithfulness. Earlier, God left the tabernacle at Shiloh, in the territory of Joseph and Ephraim, and chose Judah and Mount Zion. Many understand the "sanctuary" to refer to the temple in Jerusalem; others see it as God's presence there. The text emphasizes that God is the one who chooses and builds, not the merit of the people.

For today: you can rest in the fact that what God establishes does not depend on your strength or your perfection. Even when you fail, he remains firm. Entrust your life to his faithfulness and seek to stay close to him.
exp.147:10:
This verse continues a list of those who should praise God. It names the kings of the earth, all peoples, the princes (rulers), and all the judges. In other words, it calls on both those who hold power and ordinary people.

The psalmist, whose name is not given, invites all of creation to praise God. First he calls on the heavens, then on the earth: mountains, trees, animals, and finally all people. Rulers are mentioned because they are often thought to be the most important, but here they stand on the same level as everyone else: they are creatures who must honor the Creator.

For today: if you have some authority, at work, at home, or in your community, remember that your position does not make you superior before God. Use it with humility, serving others, and praise God with sincere gratitude.
exp.33:18:
The verse says that the one who lives in righteousness before God (the "righteous" person) suffers many afflictions, but that the Lord rescues him from all of them. "Troubles" here means problems, pains and hardships, not sins.

The psalm is attributed to David. Its heading says he wrote it after escaping from Abimelech, when he pretended to be insane to save himself. He speaks from his own experience and wants to encourage others who suffer. The nearby verses speak of a God who is close to the brokenhearted. How and when that deliverance comes, the text does not detail.

Being faithful to God does not free you from problems, but it does not leave you alone in them either. Today, when something weighs on you, bring that problem to God in prayer and trust that he sustains you, even if the way out takes time.
exp.24:4:
Here the speaker asks God to guide him along the path of truth and to teach him. The phrase "lead me by the hand along the way" is what the speaker is asking for: to be guided step by step, as one would be led by the hand. The idea of being rescued and cared for by God is what the speaker finds in God as "the God of my salvation." To wait on God means to trust him and to wait for him patiently. He has done this all day long.

This is a psalm of David, according to its traditional title. Earlier, he says that those who trust in God will not be put to shame. Later, he asks forgiveness for the sins of his youth. He presents himself as someone humble, who knows that he needs direction and mercy.

Today you can begin the day by asking God to teach you and guide you in your decisions, large or small. Then trust him patiently, even when the answers take a while, because he is your saviour.
exp.134:10:
It says that God defeated Sihon, king of the Amorites, Og, king of Bashan, and all the kingdoms of Canaan. The Amorites are the Amorites. Sihon and Og are concrete examples of the "mighty kings" mentioned in the previous verse.

The psalmist calls the people to praise the LORD and recalls his works: first the deliverance from Egypt, and then the victories on the way to the promised land. Sihon and Og were defeated before Israel entered Canaan, according to the books of Numbers and Deuteronomy. The psalm does not say who wrote it. Its purpose is that Israel remember the land was a gift from God, not an achievement of their own.

For today: when you face something that seems too big, remember what God has already done for you and for his people. Write down three moments when he helped you and give thanks for them. That remembrance strengthens confidence for the present.
exp.33:11:
This verse asks a question to stir up interest: who truly wants a long and good life? The word "desireth" here means wanting something eagerly, and "see good" means enjoying what is good, living in well-being.

The one speaking is David. This psalm, according to its heading, was written after he escaped a danger before King Abimelech. Like a teacher with his students, he calls them "children" and teaches them the fear of the Lord, that is, living with reverence and trust in God. The question prepares the instructions that follow about how to live.

For today: before looking for a good life, ask yourself what you are willing to take care of. Today, try to speak without lies or hurtful words, and seek peace in your home or at work. God guides the paths of those who seek him, though he does not promise that everything will be easy.
exp.101:11:
It says God is eternal: "you will endure" means that He does not come to an end or change. "Your memory" refers to his name, that is, to what He is and to how He is remembered. This will remain so from one generation to another, without interruption.

The psalm is the prayer of a person in distress, who feels weak, like a passing shadow and dry grass. It is not known with certainty who wrote it. Many think it was someone from the people of Israel in difficult times, with Zion in ruins. In contrast to his frailty, the psalmist looks to God, who does not grow weak. From this comes his hope that God will have mercy on Zion.

For today: when you feel tired, fragile, or without strength, do not look only at your situation. Remember that God remains the same and you can rest in Him. Today, say to Him in prayer: "Lord, I pass away, but you remain."
exp.118:133:
Here the psalmist asks God to free him from the oppression of violent people. "Deliver me" means to rescue me, to set me free, like someone who pays to bring another out of a difficult situation. And he promises that, if God delivers him, he will obey God's commands. "Will keep" means to carry out and maintain faithfully.

The speaker is the author of Psalm 119, a long psalm in honor of God's Word. We do not know with certainty who wrote it. He feels pressed on by people who mistreat him, and at the same time he desires to live faithfully to God. Earlier he asked that God would direct his steps, and afterward he pleads for God's favorable face and grieves because others despise the law.

For today: when you face injustice or pressure, pray with confidence, but also ask for a heart willing to obey. May the difficulty not draw you away from God, but bring you closer to his Word.
exp.117:16:
The speaker says they will not die now, but will remain alive. And the reason they want to live is to tell, that is, to proclaim to others, what God has done.

The psalm is a song of thanksgiving, and the speaker is someone who has been rescued from a great danger. The verses that follow say that God disciplined them severely, but did not let them die. It is not stated with certainty who the speaker is: it could have been a king, or the whole people speaking as one voice. Christians also read this psalm with Jesus and his resurrection in mind.

If God has sustained you through a trial, your life is a gift with purpose. Think of one specific help God gave you and tell it this week to someone who needs encouragement.
exp.97:1:
This verse says that the Lord has made known his salvation, a word that here means his rescue. It also says that he has openly shown his righteousness before all the nations. God did not act in secret; he did it in full view, so that everyone could see it.

The psalmist invites the people to sing a new song for the wonders God has done in saving them. The verses that follow say that God remembered his mercy and his faithfulness toward Israel. The psalm does not clearly say which specific deliverance it has in mind, and some connect it with the return from exile. Even so, its message reaches to the ends of the earth.

Today you can note one concrete way in which God has helped or sustained you, and share it with someone this week. In this way, your simple testimony also shows his goodness.
exp.99:3:
This verse invites us to come before God with thankfulness and praise. "Thanksgiving" here means gratitude, that is, giving thanks for what God has done. The gates and courts were the entrances and open spaces of the temple in Jerusalem. "Bless his name" means speaking well of God and honoring him.

The psalm does not say who wrote it; its heading describes it as a psalm of praise or thanksgiving. It seems to be addressed to the whole people, who gathered to worship. The verses before it remind us that God is Creator and Shepherd of his people, and the verse after it gives the reason for the praise: God is always good and faithful.

For today: before you pray or attend church, take a moment to give thanks for specific things. In this way your heart comes near to God grateful, and not only asking.
exp.103:33:
He says that meditating on God and speaking of him is sweet and pleasing to the psalmist. "My meditation of him shall be sweet" means that his thinking about God will be pleasant and delightful. "Speaking of him" can also be understood as meditating or reflecting on God. That is why he concludes: "I will be glad in the Lord," that is, he will find his joy in God.

The one speaking is the psalmist, although the psalm does not give his name. The whole psalm celebrates God as Creator who sustains the earth, the seas, the animals, and people. After looking at so much greatness, the psalmist responds with praise and offers his thoughts to God. The verses that follow ask that evil be removed and return to worship.

Today we can set aside a few minutes each day to think about God and talk with him, perhaps looking at something of his creation, and thank him simply. In this way joy does not depend only on circumstances, but on knowing him better.
exp.88:24:
This verse says that God will extend the power of King David over the sea and the rivers. "Hand" and "right hand" speak of authority and strength. "The sea" is the sea itself, and the rivers can represent distant lands and peoples. In other words, his rule would reach very far.

Here God speaks, recalling the promise he made to David. The psalm is a prayer by the singer Ethan the Ezrahite, who remembers this covenant. Many understand that the sea and the rivers mark the boundaries of the kingdom, from the Mediterranean to the Euphrates. Christians also see in this a sign of the reign of Jesus, a descendant of David.

For today: when your problems feel as vast as the sea, remember that God is faithful to his promises. Trust that Christ reigns over everything that surrounds you.
exp.72:12:
This verse says that the psalmist feels it was pointless to keep his heart pure and his hands clean. "Cleansed my heart" refers to seeking an honest and sincere life before God. "Washed my hands in innocency" is an image of living without doing wrong. "In vain" means "to no profit." He wonders whether it was worth it.

Asaph, the author of the psalm (as the heading indicates), speaks. He is tired and confused because he sees that the wicked prosper, mock God, and live without trouble, while he suffers even though he tries to obey. It is an honest complaint, and the psalm does not stop there: later, when he enters God's sanctuary, Asaph understands the situation better and recovers his confidence.

For today: when you feel that doing what is right does you no good, do not hide that doubt. Bring it to God honestly, as Asaph did, and seek his presence before drawing conclusions.
exp.7:2:
Here the psalmist looks up at the sky at night and is filled with wonder. He says the heavens are the work of your fingers, a poetic way of saying that God made them with care and skill, like a craftsman. The moon and the stars did not make themselves: God ordained them, that is, set them in their place.

The speaker is David, according to the psalm's title. He is praising God, and this verse sets up the great question that follows: if the universe is so vast, why does God pay attention to human beings? Some think David wrote this at night, perhaps while tending sheep, but the text does not say so.

For today: spend a few minutes looking at the night sky, without screens or hurry. Let its greatness remind you that God is greater than your problems, and yet he knows you and cares for you.
exp.101:23:
He says that someone, in distress, begs God not to take his life when he is only halfway through his days. He does this by recalling that God has no end: "thy years are throughout all generations" means that God lives through all generations, forever. Here "take away" means ending a life before its time.

The psalm is the prayer of a afflicted and weakened person, who feels that God has shortened his strength and his days. The heading presents it as a prayer of one who is afflicted. It is not known with certainty who wrote it; some connect it with the exile or with the ruin of Jerusalem, but that is interpreted in several ways. What is clear is that it contrasts human frailty with the eternity of God.

For today: when you feel weak or fear that your life is fading, pray with sincerity, as this psalmist did. Your life is short, but God remains, and you can rest in Him.
exp.50:9:
This verse is a prayer. The speaker asks God to do something new inside him. "Create" is the same word used for creation: something only God can do. "Clean" means pure, without stain. "Right" means firm and faithful. "Renew" means to make new again.

According to the heading of the psalm, David wrote it after the prophet Nathan confronted him about his sin with Bathsheba. Some scholars debate whether the heading is original, but many accept it. David does not defend himself; he acknowledges his guilt and asks for forgiveness. He knows the problem is not only what he did, but also his heart.

For today: when you fail, do not hide or make excuses. Pray sincerely, asking God not only to forgive your mistakes, but also to change your desires from within.
exp.77:65:
It says that God struck his enemies "in the hinder parts," meaning he made them flee and wounded them from behind. He also gave them "a perpetual reproach": a lasting shame that would not be easily forgotten. The phrase "hinder parts" is an old expression; some think it refers to a humiliating defeat and others to a physical wound.

The psalmist, Asaph, reviews the history of Israel. Earlier, God let the Philistines defeat his people because of their unfaithfulness, and the ark was captured. Then God awoke as someone rises from sleep, that is, he acted with power. That image describes how the people saw it; God does not sleep. Afterward came the choosing of Judah and of Zion.

For today: even when God corrects his own, he does not abandon them. When you feel defeated, trust that he can act and give you a new season.
exp.120:5:
God protects his people both by day and by night. The sun stands for the strong heat of the day, and the moon for the dangers of the night. It is a poetic way of saying that no hour falls outside God's care.

This is a psalm of pilgrimage, one of those sung while climbing up to Jerusalem. It is not known with certainty who is speaking: it may be a single pilgrim encouraging himself, or someone blessing him. The roads were long, with burning sun and unsafe nights. That is why the psalm insists that the LORD is your keeper and shade, and that he never sleeps.

Today, when you feel tiredness or fear, whether in heavy work or in a sleepless night, pray and rest. God remains awake and watching over you.
exp.90:13:
This verse says that God promises to deliver and set on high the one who has set his love upon him, that is, the one who loves God and clings to him with all his heart. The phrase about setting him on high means that God will place him in safety, in a secure place. The phrase about having known his name means knowing God truly and trusting in his character, not merely knowing his name.

In this psalm, the one speaking now is God himself. Earlier the psalmist was speaking, but in verses 14 to 16 God answers with personal promises. He gives them to the one who trusts in him, after describing dangers such as the lion and the serpent. Scholars understand those animals as images of threats of every kind.

For today: when you face fear or pressure, do not begin only by asking how to escape, but draw nearer to God. Spend a few minutes in prayer and remember how faithful he has been to you. Trusting him is the foundation of his promise.
exp.34:14:
It says that when David stumbled or suffered, his enemies rejoiced and gathered together against him. They were despicable people, lowly folk, whom he did not even know well. They tore him to pieces, that is, they attacked him with words and mockery, and they never stopped.

David speaks (as the heading of the psalm indicates) and cries out to God asking for help. He recalls earlier that he prayed, fasted, and wept for these same men when they were sick, as if they were his brother. Now they repay him with mockery and betrayal. Scholars do not agree on the exact moment in his life to which it refers.

For today: if someone answers your goodness with evil, do not let that harden your heart. Bring your pain honestly before God, as David did, and keep doing good, trusting that God sees and defends.
exp.48:13:
They go to the grave like sheep, and death leads them and consumes them as if they were its pasture. The upright will have dominion over them, that is, they will rise above them, in the morning, perhaps a new day of justice. Their outward appearance and their luxury come to an end in the grave. The Hebrew of this verse is difficult and is translated in several ways.

The speaker is a wise man, a psalmist of the sons of Korah. He is encouraging those who feel intimidated by rich and powerful people. He reminds them that no one escapes death, and in the next verse he declares his hope that God will redeem him.

For today: do not envy or admire someone who boasts of money or fame. Invest your life in what lasts, trusting in God, who can indeed rescue you from death.
exp.91:0:
This verse says that it is good to give thanks to God and to praise him, and to sing psalms to his name. "Lord" is the name of God, and "most High" presents him as the greatest, above all things. The title says it is a song for the sabbath day, the day of rest. The word "unto" is an older way of saying "to."

Context: we do not know with certainty who wrote this psalm; the title only says that it is a song for the sabbath. The one speaking is a worshiper who invites everyone to recognize that praising God is a good and fitting thing. In the verses that follow, he speaks of singing in the morning and at night, with musical instruments.

For today: set aside a moment each day, even a brief one, to thank God aloud or in song. You can begin the morning by remembering his goodness and end the night by remembering his faithfulness.
exp.118:18:
It says that the psalmist feels like a "stranger" on the earth, that is, a foreigner, someone who is just passing through and does not belong here. That is why he asks God: "hide not thy commandments from me," that is, do not conceal your instructions from me.

The author of Psalm 119 speaks, though his name is not known for certain. He loves God's law and has just asked him to open his eyes to see his wonders. As a stranger, he does not know well the way of this world and needs God to guide him. Some think he also speaks of living surrounded by people who do not follow God, although the text does not say this directly.

For today: if you feel out of place for following Jesus, do not lose heart. Read the Bible each day and ask God, "Show me the way." He is your guide in a foreign land.
exp.33:7:
The psalmist invites: "O taste and see that the Lord is good." The word "taste" means to try or sample, and "see" means to look and notice for yourself. "Blessed" means happy or favored. The person who trusts God finds that he is good, and that is why they are happy.

It is David who speaks. The title of the psalm connects it to a time when he escaped a great danger. He tells how God heard him and delivered him from his troubles. That is why he invites others to test it for themselves, not just to believe it secondhand.

Today we can take a concrete step of trust. Before deciding something difficult, pray and hand your worry over to God. Then calmly notice how he sustains you, even if he does not resolve everything right away.
exp.77:16:
Despite all the good things God had done, the people kept sinning against Him. The Hebrew-style phrasing shows that this was not a single lapse but a continued pattern. The rest of the verse names the desert as the place of this rebellion and God as the One they provoked.

Asaph wrote Psalm 78 to retell the history of Israel and teach the new generations. Just before this verse, he recalls how God opened the rock and gave abundant water in the desert. Even so, the people doubted and demanded food, as if God could not take care of them. Asaph wants his listeners to learn from that mistake and not repeat it.

For today: when we remember how God has helped us in the past, it is easier to trust Him in difficult times. You might write down some things God has done for you and read them when you feel doubt or fear.
exp.103:7:
The verse says that when the waters withdrew, the mountains rose and the valleys sank, each in the place God had prepared for them. "Founded" means that God gave them a firm base and a fixed place. Some scholars think the text speaks of the waters fleeing, and others of the mountains rising; the general sense is the same: God orders creation.

The psalmist praises the Creator with a poetic hymn about creation. The verses before describe the waters covering the earth and fleeing at the voice of God. It is the language of worship, not a scientific report; many connect it with the account of the third day in Genesis 1.

For today: if God knows how to give each mountain and each valley its place, he can also bring order to the chaos in your life. Hand him that confusing situation today and trust that he has a place and a purpose for it.
exp.21:3:
This verse says that the ancestors of Israel trusted in God and that He rescued them. "Trusted" here means placing their hope in God, and "delivered" means saved or brought out of danger. The repetition of "trusted" emphasizes that their trust was steady.

The speaker is David, according to the heading of the psalm. He feels abandoned, crying out day and night without receiving an answer. In the midst of that pain, he remembers the history of his people to sustain his faith.
