Christians also read this psalm as a foreshadowing of Jesus' sufferings on the cross, which begins with the same words: "My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?"

When you feel that God is silent, do not stay alone with what you feel. Remember how He has been faithful before, in the Bible and in your own life, and let that strengthen your trust.
exp.74:9:
This verse says that God will take away the power of the wicked and lift up those who live in righteousness. In the Bible, the "horn" is an image of strength, power and dignity, like the horns of a bull. To cut off the horns is to end that power, and to be "exalted" means to be lifted up and honored.

The psalm is a song of Asaph. Here it seems that God himself is speaking, though some read it as the voice of the psalmist joining in God's decision. Earlier the psalm spoke of the cup of judgment that God makes the wicked drink, and for that reason the psalmist promises to praise the God of Jacob. It is a psalm of trust that God governs with justice.

For today: when you see unjust people seem to prosper, do not become bitter or seek revenge. Keep doing what is right and trust that God knows when and how to set everything in its place.
exp.144:4:
This verse says that the psalmist will speak of how glorious and splendid God is, and of the wonderful works He has done. The words about splendor and beauty describe a radiance and grandeur that impress the one who sees them. In other words: "I will speak of your splendor and of your amazing works."

The one speaking is David, according to the title of the psalm. It is a song of praise. It comes after saying that each generation will tell of God's works, and here David says that he himself will also do so. He not only encourages others; he personally commits himself to speaking of God.

For today: think of something concrete that God has done in your life, or something about Him that has impressed you, and tell someone about it this week, whether a family member or a friend. Praising God is not only singing; it is also simply recounting what He has done.
exp.17:23:
It says that God gave David what was due to his upright life. The words "pagóme," meaning "paid me" or "rewarded me," and "justicia," which speaks of living in a right way, along with "limpieza de mis manos," a way of saying his actions were pure and without guilt in God's sight, are the wording behind this verse. In the version you are reading, these ideas appear as "recompensed me," "righteousness," and "cleanness of my hands."

David is the one speaking, in a psalm of gratitude for being delivered from his enemies, including Saul. He does not say he never failed, but that he was faithful to God in that conflict, without taking revenge on his own. Some understand this as a defense in that specific situation, not as a claim of perfection.

For today: try to live with integrity even when no one sees you, and trust that God sees your motives. Do not expect automatic rewards, but rest in the fact that God is just and cares for those who obey him sincerely.
exp.121:1:
The explanation says that the pilgrims have already arrived in Jerusalem and are standing at its gates. The word "stand" sounds like something in the past, but it expresses the joy of having finally arrived. The name "Jerusalem" appears here in its older spelling form.

This is a "song of ascents," a song the Israelites sang as they went up to Jerusalem for the festivals. The title attributes it to David. The one speaking is a pilgrim who had been glad when he was invited to go to the house of the LORD. Now he celebrates that his journey has reached its goal. Some think the psalm was sung while on the road, and others think it was sung once they were already in the city.

Today we can value the moments of gathering with other believers to worship God. If someone invites you to church, go with joy, without seeing it as a burden. There you also receive encouragement and give thanks together.
exp.131:14:
It says that God will bless abundantly what Zion needs to live. "Provision" means supply, food and sustenance. "Satisfy" means that he will give until people are full. So God promises that the poor of Zion will not lack bread.

Here God speaks, according to what the psalmist recalls of his promise. The psalm celebrates that God chose Zion (Jerusalem) as his dwelling, and that he promised David and his descendants a lasting reign. Therefore, where God dwells, his care and provision also come. The following verses speak of salvation for the priests and joy for the people.

For today: God is concerned with concrete needs, such as our daily bread. Trust in his care, and be also part of the answer: share what you have with those in need in your church or your neighborhood.
exp.118:101:
This verse says that the psalmist did not turn away from God's "judgments," that is, from his righteous decisions and standards. And it gives the reason: because God himself was his teacher. "I have not departed" means "I have not gone away from" or "I have not strayed from." What he did, he did because God had taught him.

The one speaking is the author of Psalm 119, a psalm that celebrates God's law. We do not know for certain who wrote it. The verses around this one show that his obedience gave him understanding, kept him from walking in evil, and made him love God's words as something sweet. Here he recognizes that his faithfulness was not his own merit, but the fruit of divine teaching.

For today: before reading the Bible, ask God simply to teach you. Then choose one lesson you read and put it into practice this week. In this way, learning and obeying go hand in hand.
exp.85:13:
It says that proud men have risen up against the psalmist. A group of powerful people, who agreed on it in secret, seeks to take his life. A band of violent men who join together to do harm is what the words point to, and "they have sought after my soul" means that they are going after his life. And "have not set thee before them" means that they do not respect God or think about him.

The speaker is David, according to the title of the psalm, though some scholars think it may have been written by someone else in David's style. It is the prayer of someone in danger. Earlier he thanked God for having delivered him, and now he tells God his present trouble. Right away he recalls what God is like: merciful, slow to anger, and faithful.

For today: when someone treats you unjustly, tell God about it honestly. Remember how he has helped you before, and trust his character.
exp.49:1:
This verse says that God has shown his light and his glory from Zion, which it calls "the perfection of beauty." "Has shined" means that he shone forth, becoming visible. Zion was the mountain of Jerusalem, where the temple stood.

The psalm is by Asaph, a Levite in charge of the music in worship. Here he presents God as a Judge who calls the whole earth, from the rising of the sun to its setting. He shows his glorious presence in Zion before speaking to his people. The verses that follow say that he will come with fire and a tempest to judge. Some think that the beauty of Zion comes from God's presence, not from the place itself.

For today: God is beautiful and also holy, and he deserves reverence. Before asking him for something, take a moment to admire who he is. Then examine your heart honestly, because he desires a sincere life, not just ceremonies.
exp.17:16:
He delivered me from my strong enemy and from those who hated me, for they were too strong for me. That is, they were stronger than he was, so he could not save himself alone. The verse's wording "delivered me" and "hated me" carries the same meaning as the explanation's point about rescue and hatred.

David speaks, according to the psalm's heading, and he sings it when God rescued him from his enemies and from Saul. Before that, he describes the deliverance with powerful images: deep waters, the earth shaken, and the wind of God. These are poetic figures to show that God intervened with great power. Then David recalls the difficult day when he was attacked, but the LORD was his support.

For today: when you feel overwhelmed by a problem or a person, you are not alone. Pray sincerely, ask God for help, and trust that he can sustain you, even when your own strength falls short.
exp.134:5:
This verse says that God does whatever He decides, and no one can stop Him. His power reaches everywhere: the heavens, the earth, the seas, and the deep places (the depths of the ocean, which the ancients regarded as mysterious and unreachable).

The psalm is a song of praise addressed to the people of Israel, probably sung in the temple. We do not know for certain who wrote it. The psalmist recalls that God chose Israel and is greater than all false gods. He then gives examples: the rain, the winds, and the deliverance from Egypt.

For today: when you feel that everything is out of control, remember that God still reigns. You can pray with confidence, knowing that your problems are not bigger than He is.
exp.108:6:
It says that when this person is judged, the result will be that he comes out condemned as guilty. And that even his prayer, instead of helping him, will be counted as one more sin.

The phrase that describes him as coming out wicked means that he is declared to be a villain. The phrase about counting as sin means that his prayer is to be counted as sin.

The speaker is David, or so the psalm presents him. He complains that good was repaid with evil and love with hatred. This is an imprecatory psalm, that is, a prayer that calls for justice in very harsh words against an enemy. Some understand that David is quoting the words of his accusers, but others think they are his own cry. This cannot be stated with complete certainty.

For today: when someone hurts you, bring your pain to God honestly and leave justice in his hands. Jesus also taught us to pray for those who persecute us (Matthew 5:44).
exp.45:7:
It says that we should come and look carefully at what God has done. "Come" in the text is the same as "come," and "see" is "look." "Desolations" are destructions, places left in ruins. The text invites us to recognize the hand of God in what happens in the world, even in the midst of destruction.

Psalm 46 is a song of the sons of Korah, addressed to a people facing chaos, nations in conflict, and earthquakes. Here the psalmist speaks, inviting the community to observe. The following verse clarifies that God also brings wars to an end. Some understand the "desolations" as judgment on the nations; others, as the end of violence itself.

When everything seems uncertain, pause and remember how God has been faithful before. Write down one of His works in your life and thank Him, trusting that He still takes care of you.
exp.41:3:
It says the psalmist remembers past times and pours out his heart before God. "I pour out my soul in me" means that he unburdens himself in deep sorrow. He recalls going with the crowd to the house of God, with voices of joy, praise, and festival. "I went with them" means that he walked among the great throng of pilgrims. Some translations read this passage differently, since the Hebrew is difficult.

The speaker is a believer who, according to the psalm's title, belongs to the sons of Korah, Levites who served in worship. He is far from the temple, perhaps in the north, near the Jordan and Hermon, as the following verses indicate. He feels alone, and others mock his faith. Remembering the worship of the past increases his pain, but it also awakens his hope.

When you are sad, do not hide your pain. Tell God honestly, and remember how He sustained you before, or seek the support of your community of faith.
exp.64:9:
This verse says that God cares for the land through the rain. He makes the furrows, that is, the lines the plow opens, fill with water. He also sends the water down the channels that the land itself forms. "Thou makest it soft with showers" means the rain softens the hard ground. The "springing" are the new shoots of the plants, and God blesses them by making them grow.

It is a psalm of David, a song of thanks to God. Before this, the psalmist praises God for forgiving and for his wonders. Here he celebrates him as the one who provides the harvest. In Israel life depended on the rain, so seeing the grain grow was seeing the hand of God.

For today: before eating, think about all that was behind it, such as the rain, the soil, and the work of many people. Give thanks to God from the heart, for he continues to sustain life every day.
exp.24:2:
This verse says that no one who waits on God will be left ashamed or humiliated. "Ashamed" here means being put to shame or left disappointed, rather than being unable to grasp something. The ones who will be put to shame are those who turn against God "without cause," that is, without any just reason, out of pure treachery.

David speaks in this psalm, and he does so in a moment of need. He had already asked that God not allow his enemies to rejoice over him. Now he expresses his confidence: God does not leave in shame those who trust in Him. Then he asks Him to teach him His ways. We do not know with certainty what situation he was living in when he wrote it.

For today: when you are waiting for an answer, a change, or a way out, do not lose heart by thinking that God will leave you in shame. Pray honestly, ask Him for direction, and keep doing what is right while you wait.
exp.34:9:
This verse says that David wants to praise God with his whole being, even with his bones, that is, with every part of his body. He asks, "Who is like you?" because God rescues the afflicted from someone stronger than they are, and the poor and needy from the one who plunders them, that is, from the person who robs or abuses them. "Needy" means in need. "Salvation," in the verse before, means deliverance.

David speaks here, according to the title of the psalm. He is being hunted by enemies who attack him without cause, and the text that follows speaks of false witnesses. He asks God for help and promises to praise him when he is delivered. Scholars debate which exact moment in his life the psalm refers to.

For today: when you feel weak in the face of injustice, bring your complaint to God honestly. And when he helps you, do not keep it to yourself: give him thanks in concrete ways, with your words, your time, and your life.
exp.32:14:
He fashions the heart of every person, and he also takes note of everything they do. The word "fashions" speaks of God shaping the inner being of each human, that is, their mind, their will, and their feelings. "Considers" means he watches closely and understands. The "works" are the actions and decisions of people.

This is a psalm of praise, and tradition ascribes it to David, though the text does not say so. Before this verse, the psalmist tells us that God looks down from the heavens on all of humankind. Afterward, he warns that neither a king, an army, nor a strong horse brings true salvation. The idea is that God sees everything, and for that reason trust can be placed in him alone.

For today: you do not need to pretend before God, because he knows your heart. Bring him your fears and your decisions with sincerity, and trust his care more than your own strength or resources.
exp.110:5:
It says that God showed the strength of what he does by giving his people the land of other nations. "Showed" means he made it known through clear deeds. An "inheritance" is a property received as a gift, not as payment. "The heathen" are the peoples who were not Israel.

The psalm is a song of praise, and no one knows with certainty who wrote it. The author invites us to remember what God did for Israel. It probably refers to when the people received the land of Canaan, after leaving Egypt. This fits the nearby verses: God is faithful to his covenant, he cares for those who fear him, and his works are true and just.

For today: when you doubt that God will keep what he promised, think back on what he has already done in your life and in his history with his people. Write down three things you have received as a gift from him and thank him for them today. That strengthens confidence for what lies ahead.
exp.76:10:
Here the psalmist decides to remember what God has done. "I will remember" is the wording of the verse, and "wonders of old" refers to the mighty acts of God in the past.

The one speaking is the author of the psalm (the title attributes it to Asaph), in the middle of deep distress. He asks whether God has stopped being merciful. Then he decides to change his focus: instead of sinking into doubt, he looks back at what God has done. The verses that follow connect him with the history of Israel, although the psalm does not detail his exact crisis here.

When you doubt that God hears you, make a deliberate effort to remember. Write down three moments when God helped you, or your family, and thank him for them. Remembering does not erase the pain, but it strengthens trust.
exp.24:8:
The verse says that God guides the humble in what is right and teaches his way to the meek. "Will guide" means he will set them on the right path. "Judgment" here is understood as what is just, what is upright, the right way of acting. "Way" is the path or course of life. The "meek" are those of a gentle heart, who do not force themselves on others.

David is said to speak, according to the psalm's heading, though some scholars debate details of its origin. He asks forgiveness for the sins of his youth and trusts in God's goodness. He has just said that God teaches sinners the way, and here he explains who truly learns: the humble who recognize their need.

For today: before making an important decision, pray sincerely and admit that you do not know everything. Ask God to teach you, and listen with a willingness to change course, by reading his Word and accepting wise counsel.
exp.88:14:
It says that those who know how to praise God with joy are happy and blessed. "Praising you" means celebrating him with shouts of joy, the way a king is acclaimed. These people will walk "in the light of your face," that is, they will live under God's favor and nearness, without getting lost in the darkness.

The psalm was written by Ethan the Ezrahite, according to its heading. First it celebrates God's power, justice, and faithful love. That is why the people can praise him with confidence. Later the psalm turns painful, because Israel feels that the promises seem distant. Even so, this verse reminds us where true blessedness is found.

For today: before asking God for something, take a few minutes to thank him and praise him for who he is. That helps you walk through the day more aware of his presence.
exp.108:18:
He says the curse should be upon that person like a garment that covers him completely, and like a belt that is tied around him and surrounds him every day. The image is that the evil he chose would stay with him always and he could not take it off.

The one speaking is David, according to the title of the psalm. He is distressed by enemies who accuse him falsely and repay his kindness with hatred. This passage is a prayer of complaint and a plea for justice. Scholars debate whether these verses quote the words of his enemies or express the psalmist's own desire. In either case, he hands the matter over to God and does not take revenge.

For today: when you are wounded unjustly, do not seek revenge. Tell God honestly what you feel and trust that He does justice. Ask Him also to guard your heart, so that you do not clothe yourself in bitterness, but in blessing.
exp.132:0:
This verse says that it is a very good and pleasant thing when brothers and sisters live together in unity. The phrase "song of ascents" most likely refers to the songs sung on the way up to Jerusalem, and the idea of living together in harmony and togetherness means getting along in peace and agreement. "Pleasant" means enjoyable and agreeable.

It is attributed to David, although some scholars debate that authorship. It was one of the songs the Israelites sang when they went up to Jerusalem for the feasts. The verses that follow compare unity to the anointing oil on Aaron and to the dew of Hermon: something that blesses, refreshes, and gives life. "Brothers" can refer to family or to the whole people of God.

Today we can nurture unity in the family, the church, or the workplace. It means seeking peace, forgiving quickly, and speaking with respect, even when we think differently.
exp.102:9:
This verse says that God does not treat us as we deserve. "Iniquities" and "sins" are our wrongdoings and failures. "To repay" here means to give the punishment that is due. And the old form of the word "to" is written differently in older texts. In other words, God does not give us the full punishment our failures would deserve.

The speaker is David, according to the title of the psalm. He is praising God and encouraging himself to remember God's benefits. The verse before this one says that God is slow to anger and abounding in mercy. The verses that follow explain how far he forgives: as far as the east is from the west.

Today we can live with gratitude instead of fear. When you fail, do not hide from God or sink into guilt. Come to Him, acknowledge your mistake honestly, and receive His forgiveness. Then treat others with the same patience that God has shown you.
exp.59:7:
It says God treats Israel's neighboring peoples as his own possessions. Moab would be the basin in which he washes his feet, that is, a humble servant. Casting out the shoe over Edom may indicate that he takes it as property or rules over it. To the Philistines, he says to shout for joy, and many read this as mockery: the triumph belongs to God, not to them.

The speaker is God, according to the promise that David recalls in this psalm of lament. Israel had suffered a defeat and asked for help. God responds by recalling that the land and the tribes are his, and that he decides the outcome. Scholars discuss some details, such as the gesture of the shoe.

For today: when you feel defeated, remember that God still governs. Pray with confidence, for your hope is not in your own strength, but in his promise.
exp.30:12:
Here the psalmist tells how he heard the insults and slander of many people. Fear was everywhere around him, because his enemies gathered together to make plans in secret, and even thought about how to take his life. "Slander" here means a public attack on someone's reputation or honor. "Devised" means that they were making plans.

The one speaking is David, according to the title of the psalm. He is in a moment of deep distress: he feels rejected by neighbors and acquaintances, forgotten like a dead man. We do not know for certain which episode of his life is meant, and scholars have connected it to different stages of persecution.

For today: when you feel surrounded by criticism or rumors, do not hide your fear. Tell it to God honestly, as David did. And notice what follows: he goes on to say, "But I trusted in you." You can pray sincerely and, even with fear, choose to trust.
exp.115:14:
It says that the death of God's faithful ones is "precious", that is, valuable and dear to him. "Saints" means those who belong to God, his devoted ones. The name of God is "the Lord". It does not say that death is pleasant, but that God does not look on it with indifference.

The psalmist thanks God because he rescued him from a situation close to death (vv. 3-8). Now he promises to fulfill his vows publicly, in the midst of the people. In that atmosphere of gratitude, he affirms that God cares for his own even when they die. It is not known with certainty who wrote this psalm; what matters is his trust in God.

If today you are suffering over the loss of a believing loved one, or you fear death, remember that God is not far off or indifferent. You can bring him your pain with confidence, knowing that he values each one of his children.
exp.83:3:
It says that those who live in the house of God are happy and blessed, because there they spend their lives praising him without stopping. The word "blessed" in the verse above is a word that also means happy. "Selah" is a Hebrew word whose meaning is not certain; many think it invites the reader to pause and meditate.

The psalmist, a believer from Israel (the title attributes the psalm to the sons of Korah, who served in the temple), expresses his deep longing to be in the courts of God. Earlier he spoke of the little birds that find a nest near the altar, and now he admires those who live always close to God.

Today we can look for a moment each day to be close to God with praise and prayer, and not only on Sundays. In this way our homes and our hearts can become places where God is welcome.
exp.123:5:
The explanation says that God deserves praise because he did not let the enemies devour us. The word "blessed" means praised or worthy of thanks, so the opening phrase of the verse is shown as the key idea. The prey, the animal that was hunted, is described as us, and the enemies are shown as a wild beast ready to swallow its victim.

It is a psalm of David, sung by the people of Israel. They had faced an enormous danger, but the text does not say exactly what it was. Earlier they speak of waters and torrents that nearly swept them away; later, of a bird that escapes from a trap. They acknowledge that they were not saved by their own strength, but because the Lord delivered them.

When you go through a difficulty and come out ahead, do not credit it only to your own effort or to luck. Stop and thank God with a sincere prayer. Remembering his past rescues also helps you trust him in the problems you still face.
exp.58:4:
David asks God to rise up and act. Saying "awake" does not mean that God is sleeping, but that he should step in. "Visit" means coming to set things in order, and "nations" are the peoples of the earth. He asks that there be no mercy for those who rebel and do wicked deeds. "Selah" seems to mark a pause in the song, though its exact meaning is not certain.

The title of the psalm connects it to David at the time when Saul sent men to watch his house in order to kill him. David feels surrounded and unjustly pursued, and he cries out to God as a just judge.

Today, when you suffer an injustice, you can tell God honestly what you feel and ask him for justice, instead of taking revenge yourself. Hand him your case, and also ask him to examine your heart so that you keep acting with uprightness.
exp.139:3:
Here the psalmist asks God to watch over him and to rescue him from wicked people. A man who lives without regard for God is one who has no reverence for him. Someone who harms others with violence or with words is one who hurts people, whether by force or by what he says. To make someone stumble, or to push him off his path, is to trip him up and turn him away from the way he is walking.

The psalm is attributed to David and speaks from a place of danger. His enemies plan evil, stir up quarrels, and wound with their words like poisonous snakes. Then he says that they have set traps for him. Scholars do not agree on which exact moment in David's life the psalm describes, so it is better not to claim more than the text itself says.

For today: when someone treats you with malice or tries to make you fall, do not first give in to the urge for revenge. Speak to God honestly, as the psalmist did, and ask him for protection and wisdom to keep walking in what is right.
exp.6:0:
This psalm begins with a heading: a "Shiggaion" of David, a Hebrew word whose meaning is uncertain; it may indicate an emotional song or one with a passionate tone. David sang it to the Lord because of the words of Cush the Benjamite. Then he prays: "in thee do I put my trust," and asks to be saved and delivered from those who persecute him.

David speaks here in a time of accusation and persecution. We do not know for certain who Cush was, since he does not appear in any other biblical account; some think he was a follower of Saul from the same tribe of Benjamin, but this is only a guess. The verses that follow show that David also defends his innocence before God.

When you feel cornered or unjustly judged, you can begin as David did: by telling God that you trust in Him. Then, honestly lay your situation before Him and ask for help and justice.
exp.17:1:
David uses many images to describe God: rock, fortress, deliverer, strong one, shield, refuge. The phrase "the horn of my salvation" in the verse means the power that saves me, and the horn of an animal was a symbol of strength. He also says "in whom I will trust," that is, I will place my confidence in God.

David speaks at the end of his life, according to the heading of the psalm, on the day God delivered him from all his enemies and from the hand of Saul. This song also appears in 2 Samuel 22. He looks back, remembers years of danger and flight, and responds with gratitude, acknowledging that God was his protection.

For today: when you feel fear or pressure, do not rely only on your own strength. Name what God has been for you, as refuge, help, or strength, and tell him so in prayer. Remembering his past faithfulness strengthens confidence to face what lies ahead.
exp.7:1:
God receives praise and strength even from the youngest children, including infants still nursing. With that praise he set up a firm defense, to silence those who oppose him. The phrases quoted from the old wording are not in the verse you are reading, so they need no explanation here, though the idea is that God's enemies and those who seek revenge are the ones he restrains.

David speaks in prayer and praise, amazed at God's greatness, which is seen in the heavens. It is striking that, alongside such greatness, God uses something as weak as a child's voice. Jesus quoted this psalm in Matthew 21:16, when the children were praising him in the temple. Scholars explain in several ways what this "strength" is; what is certain is that God's power does not depend on human strength.

Today, do not despise simple faith. God can work through what is small, so praise him sincerely and value the faith of children.
exp.148:6:
This verse says that the faithful will have two-edged swords in their hands to carry out judgment on the nations, that is, on the peoples of the earth, and to bring punishment upon the nations. The word "vengeance" here means applying justice or repayment, not a simple personal grudge.

The psalmist does not identify himself, and the psalm is a song of praise to God for his victory. The faithful sing, and at the same time the image of the sword appears. Some understand it as a reference to a real war of Israel; others see symbolic language about God's final judgment. Interpreters do not fully agree. What is clear is that justice belongs to God.

For today, do not use this text to justify violence. Rather, trust that God will correct every injustice in his time, and in the meantime respond to evil with peace, truth, and praise.
exp.103:16:
This verse says that the birds make their nests in the trees that God planted, and that the stork builds its house in the fir trees. The explanation of the word "make their nests" is simply that they build nests. The Bible translation the explanation was written for renders a Hebrew term that others translate as "cypresses" or "firs," so the exact tree is not entirely certain.

The psalmist, who is not named in the text, praises God as Creator and sustainer. He has been speaking of the cedars of Lebanon full of sap, and now he shows how those trees serve as a home for the birds. The pspsalm celebrates that God cares for all his creation, not only for people.

For today: God provides a home even for a stork, so you can trust that he also cares for you. Take a moment to observe nature and give thanks for its daily care.
exp.115:17:
This verse says that the psalmist will fulfill, right now, the promises he made to God, and he will do it in public, in the presence of all the people. "Vows" are solemn promises made to God, often in a moment of distress. "I will pay" means to carry out what was promised.

The psalmist is not identified with certainty; tradition is not clear about who wrote it. He speaks as someone who cried out to God in a situation of death or affliction and was delivered. Now he responds with gratitude, offering praise in the temple, in Jerusalem, alongside the community of faith.

For today: if at some difficult moment you promised God something, such as serving him more or being more generous, do not forget it. Keep your word with gratitude and, when you can, tell your church what God has done for you, to encourage others.
exp.59:10:
It says: "Help us against the enemy, for the help that comes from men is worthless." Here "help" is help in a moment of danger, and "worthless" means useless or without value.

David speaks, or the people through him, in a psalm written after a military defeat. The verses before this one show that they felt God had rejected them and no longer went out with their armies. Even so, they do not turn away from Him: they ask God himself for help. The exact details of the battle are understood in different ways.

For today: when you feel without strength or without a way out, go first to God with sincerity. You may seek advice and help from other people, but do not place your final hope in them. Tell Him with confidence what you are feeling and ask Him to sustain you.
exp.118:152:
This verse is a prayer. The psalmist asks God to look upon his suffering and rescue him. "Resh" is the name of a Hebrew letter: the psalm is written as an acrostic, and each section begins with a letter of the alphabet. The word "affliction" means pain, distress or suffering. His reason for asking for help is that he has not forgotten God's law.

The author of Psalm 119 does not name himself, and we do not know for certain who he was. He speaks like someone who is suffering, perhaps through mockery or persecution, yet who still trusts in God's word. Just before this, he said that God is near and that his commandments are true. That is why he dares to ask for help.

When you are going through a hard time, pray honestly. You do not have to pretend that you are fine. Bring your pain to God and remember what He has already said in His Word. That strengthens trust.
exp.103:2:
He says God builds his "chambers," that is, his elevated rooms, upon the waters that are above. The clouds are like his chariot, his riding carriage, and he moves forward upon the wings of the wind. These are poetic images meant to show that all of nature is at the service of his greatness and his nearness.

The one speaking is the psalmist, who addresses himself: "Bless the Lord, O my soul." The psalm is a hymn of praise to God as Creator. Many believe it follows the order of creation in Genesis 1, although that is interpreted in different ways. The author does not name himself in the text.

For today: when you see clouds or feel the wind, let them remind you that God governs what seems out of control. Take a moment to thank him and to entrust to him what worries you today.
exp.115:3:
It says that when the psalmist was in terrible distress, he called on God by name and asked him simply: "deliver my soul." To call upon the name of the Lord means to cry out to God for help. To deliver means to rescue or save. "Soul" here refers to his life, to himself, not only to his spiritual part.

The speaker is a believer who came close to death, surrounded by pain and fear. We do not know for certain who wrote it or what the exact situation was; some think of a king like David, but this is not certain. What matters is that, in his trouble, he turned to God. The verses that follow show that God heard him, was merciful, and saved him.

For today: when you are distressed, do not wait until you have beautiful words. Pray sincerely and briefly, as this psalmist did: "Lord, deliver me." God hears those simple prayers.
exp.67:13:
It says that when God, the Almighty, scattered the enemy kings in that land, the place turned white like when it snows on Salmon. "Almighty" means the All-powerful. "Turned white" means it became white. Salmon was a mountain near Shechem, but it is not known for certain what the image shows: it may be real snow, scattered bones, or simply purity after the victory.

David wrote this psalm as a song of victory. He remembers how God went with his people and defeated kings who attacked them. The verses before it speak of kings fleeing and of spoil being divided. Interpreters explain this verse in various ways, because it is a difficult poetic image.

For today: when you face something that seems bigger than you, remember that God is still the Almighty. Trust in Him and give thanks for the victories He has given you.
exp.78:7:
It says the people ask God not to hold against them the faults of their ancestors or of earlier times. "Old iniquities" means old sins; "old sins" is the phrase to use here. "Let your mercy come quickly to meet us, before it is too late" is what "let your tender mercies speedily prevent us" means. "Brought very low" means very down and without strength.

The psalmist speaks, whether Asaph or someone from his line, on behalf of Israel. Jerusalem and the temple had been destroyed, probably by the Babylonian invasion, though the psalm does not say so precisely. The people acknowledge their sin and, in despair, cry out for forgiveness and help.

For today: when you feel without strength because of mistakes from the past, do not hide from God. Come to Him honestly, admit what you did, and trust in His mercy, not in your own merits.
exp.116:0:
This verse is an invitation for all nations and all peoples to praise God. The word "praise" means to commend, honor, and celebrate someone for who they are. "The Lord" is God's name in the Old Testament. The repetition, "all ye nations" and "all ye people," stresses that no one is left out.

It is the shortest psalm in the Bible. No one knows for certain who wrote it. The speaker is an Israelite who invites the other peoples to join Israel's praise. The reason appears in the next verse: God has shown his mercy and his truth endures forever. Paul quotes this psalm in Romans 15:11 to show that non-Jews are also called to praise God.

For today: do not keep your gratitude to yourself. Tell others, of any background, the good things God has done for you, and invite them to know him.
exp.103:1:
He says that God wraps himself in light as one puts on a cloak. He also says that God stretches out the heavens as one spreads out a curtain or a tent. Here "curtain" refers to the cloth of a tent. It is poetic language: it describes God with images we can grasp.

The psalmist speaks in praise and encourages himself. The psalm does not say who wrote it; tradition has attributed it to David, but the text does not confirm this. It comes from reflecting on creation, and many scholars see in it echoes of the account in Genesis 1, though this is interpreted in different ways. Its purpose is to show the greatness of God.

Today, before asking God for things, we can pause to look at the sky, the morning light, or the stars, and give thanks. Praising God for who he is reminds us that he is greater than our problems.
exp.17:42:
Here David says that God rescued him from the struggles and conflicts of the people. He made him the head of the heathen, that is, the leader of nations. Even a people he had never known ended up serving him. "Thou hast delivered me" is the same as saying "you have delivered me," and "thou hast made me" means "you have made me."

David speaks in this psalm of thanksgiving, written after God saved him from his enemies and from Saul. He looks back and recognizes that his victory and his reign came from God, not from his own strength. Some scholars also see here a look toward the future kingdom of the Messiah, though this is interpreted in different ways.

For today: when God brings you out of a problem or opens a door you did not expect, do not credit it only to your own effort. Stop to thank him, and use that position to serve others with humility.
exp.102:11:
This verse says that God has put our rebellions, that is, our offenses against Him, as far from us as the east is from the west. Those two directions never meet, so the image speaks of a distance that cannot be measured. The word "transgressions" refers to deliberately disobeying God.

This is a psalm of David, according to its heading. He praises God and remembers His benefits. Just before, he speaks of divine mercy, and just after, he compares God to a tender father who knows our frailty: we are dust.

For today: if you have repented, do not keep carrying guilt that God has already forgiven. Come to Him with confidence, and let His forgiveness give you freedom to begin again and to treat others with grace.
exp.77:20:
It says that God heard the people's complaints and became very angry. "Was angry" means he was filled with righteous anger. The "fire" and the "wrath" are images of his judgment. "Jacob" and "Israel" are names for the same people, the descendants of Jacob. "Salvation" in the following context means deliverance.

The psalmist, Asaph, recalls the history of Israel in the wilderness after leaving Egypt. The people had seen God open the sea and bring water out of the rock, yet they still doubted that he could give them bread and meat. Their sin was not being hungry, but challenging God and distrusting him, despite what he had already done for them.

For today: when difficulties come, let us remember how God has helped us before. We can bring our needs to him honestly, but trusting that he is faithful, rather than doubting his goodness.
exp.15:7:
David says that he keeps God always present, as someone who has him before his eyes all the time. Because God is at his right hand, in the place of helper and defender, he will not be moved, meaning he will not fall or stagger.

David speaks in a psalm that expresses complete trust in God. He has just said that God is his inheritance and his counselor, even at night, and that his life is in good hands. The New Testament quotes this psalm in Acts 2, applying the following verses to the resurrection of Jesus; some see in David a voice that points to Christ.

For today: before you begin your day, take a moment to set God before you, in prayer or with a verse. That awareness of his nearness gives you steadiness when pressures come.
exp.104:44:
This verse says that God did all that came before it so that his people would keep his statutes, that is, his commands, and obey his laws. The word "observe" here means to carry out with care and attention, which is how the King James reads "observe his statutes." "Praise ye the Lord" closes the psalm with praise.

Psalm 105 is a song of thanksgiving that recalls the history of Israel: the promise to Abraham, Joseph in Egypt, the exodus, and the entry into the land. It is not known with certainty who wrote it; part of it also appears in 1 Chronicles 16. The verse shows the purpose of the deliverance: God not only rescued his people, but called them to live in thankful obedience.

For today: obedience to God can come from gratitude, not from fear. Today you can remember how God has cared for you and choose one concrete act of obedience, such as forgiving, being honest, or giving time to his Word, as a response of gratitude.
exp.95:8:
This verse invites us to bow down and worship God with reverence. "Bow down" means to bend low or prostrate oneself. The phrase "in the beauty of holiness" can be understood as the beauty of the holy place or as the beauty of God's holiness; the phrase allows both readings. "Fear" here speaks of reverence, a deep respect before God. And "all the earth" shows that the call is for all peoples.

The psalm is a song of praise, and it is not known with certainty who wrote it. It speaks to the nations and encourages them to give God the glory he deserves, bring offerings, and come into his courts. Then it announces that the Lord reigns and will judge with righteousness, so all creation can rejoice.

For today: before you pray or sing, pause for a moment. Set aside your phone and your hurry, and acknowledge who God is. Let your worship come from a humble and grateful heart, not from habit.
exp.1:0:
Why do the nations rage, and the peoples plan things that will never succeed? This verse asks the question with a sense of amazement. "Rage" here means stirring up and rebelling together as a group. "Vain thing" means something empty that will never reach its goal.

The psalm does not say who wrote it. The New Testament, in Acts 4:25, attributes it to David. The one speaking seems to be the psalmist, who sees rulers joining forces against God and against his anointed one, the king chosen by God. Christians also read it as a reference to Jesus, the Messiah.

Today, when we feel pressured by powers or ideas that oppose God, we can remember that his plans do not fail. In this way we can trust in him and not live in fear.
exp.6:8:
Here David asks that God bring the evil of the wicked to an end and that he keep firm the one who lives uprightly. "The unjust" are those who act wrongly, and "wickedness" is their evil. The heart and the inner parts are the deepest place of a person: thoughts and strong feelings. God sees the whole heart, not only outward appearances.

David speaks in a psalm of complaint, when someone accuses him unjustly (the title mentions Cush the Benjamite). He does not take justice into his own hands, but appeals to God as judge. His request to be judged according to his righteousness refers to this particular accusation, not to a claim that he is perfect.

For today: when you are treated unfairly, bring your case to God in prayer. Ask him to examine your heart first, and trust that he sees what no one else sees.
exp.106:23:
They say that those who travel by sea have seen up close what God does.

The psalmist speaks to the whole people of Israel who have been rescued by God. In this part of the psalm he describes the sailors and merchants. Further on he tells how a storm frightens them and then God saves them. For this reason the psalm calls for giving thanks and praising him with joy.

For today: in life's storms, such as an illness, a debt, or a loss, do not only look at the problem. Ask yourself where God has sustained you. Write down those experiences and give thanks for them; in this way your trust will grow.
exp.117:27:
This verse is a personal declaration of faith. The speaker says, "Thou art my God," and promises to praise him and to exalt him. "Exalt" means to lift someone up to the highest place, to acknowledge their greatness.

Psalm 118 is a song of thanksgiving after a great deliverance. The one speaking seems to be someone who was rescued and now enters the temple among a crowd that is celebrating. Many think it is a king or a leader, although the text does not say so with certainty. The verses before it speak of blessing and of bringing offerings to the altar, and the one that follows invites everyone to give thanks because God's mercy endures forever.

For today: do not wait until you feel perfect to give thanks. Spend a few minutes saying to God aloud, "Thou art my God," and name something specific in which you have seen him help you.
exp.44:2:
He says the king should gird his sword on his thigh, that is, wear it at his side, ready to act. He calls him "mighty" and speaks of his "glory" (his honor and greatness) and his "majesty" (his dignity as king). To "gird up" means to fasten on or put on.

This psalm is a wedding song for a king. The author, a Levite from the sons of Korah, speaks with joy and addresses the king directly. Interpreters understand it in different ways: some see a king of Israel at his wedding, and others see a look toward the Messiah. The New Testament applies nearby verses to Christ (Hebrews 1:8-9). The sword here appears alongside truth, humility, and justice.

For today: true strength goes together with truth, humility, and justice. Ask God that your character be both firm and kind.
exp.27:0:
David speaks to God with urgency: "To you I will cry, O Lord, you are my rock." He asks God not to pretend he doesn't hear, that is, not to ignore him or keep silent. He fears that if God leaves him alone, he will end up like those who "go down into the pit," a way of speaking about those who are already dead.

The one speaking is David, and he writes this psalm as a prayer in a moment of distress. The following verses show that he lifts his hands toward the temple and asks not to be counted among the wicked, who speak of peace but hold evil in their hearts. We do not know with certainty what exact situation he was living through.

For today: when you feel that God is silent, do not turn away from him. Keep praying honestly, even with fear, and keep leaning on him as your strength.
exp.12:4:
It says that, despite his distress, the psalmist chooses to trust in God's mercy, that is, in his faithful and kind love. It also states that his heart will rejoice in God's salvation. Here the word for rescue means deliverance, not only good physical condition.

The psalm is traditionally attributed to David, according to its title, although some scholars debate details of its origin. It comes from urgent pleading for help: he feels forgotten, surrounded by enemies, and close to death. This verse marks a turning point. Without the situation having changed yet, he moves from lament to trust, and the next verse announces that he will sing.

For today: when you are worried, you can decide to trust before you see the solution. Speak to God honestly about your pain, and then write down a few times when he has been faithful to you. That remembrance can sustain your joy while you wait.
exp.20:3:
This verse says that the king asked God for life, and God gave it to him, and also granted him length of days, that is, a long life, forever and ever, which means for a long time or for eternity.

This psalm is by David, and it speaks of the king's joy over the victories and blessings God gave him. It is a prayer of thanksgiving. Some understand "forever and ever" to refer to a lasting dynasty, and others see here a promise that points to Christ, the eternal King. Both readings are possible.

For today: when you pray, do it with confidence, because God hears. And do not forget to thank him for what he has already given you, especially for life and for the hope of eternal life in Jesus.
exp.115:11:
Here the psalmist asks himself: "What shall I give to God for all the good he has done for me?" The explanation's quoted word "pagaré" does not mean that a debt can be paid off to God, but that he is seeking how to respond with gratitude. "Benefits" are the favors and blessings received.

The speaker is a believer who was delivered from great distress, perhaps close to death (as the psalm indicates). It is not known for certain who wrote it. After the question, he answers it himself: he will lift up the cup of salvation, call on the name of the Lord, and fulfill his promises before all the people. His gratitude is public and concrete.

Today we can make a list of the times God helped us and respond with actions: pray with thankfulness, keep what we have promised, and tell others what He has done for us.
exp.135:8:
This verse says that God made the moon and the stars to rule the night. "Rule" here means govern or have authority over: just as the sun marks the day, the moon and stars mark the night. After naming it, the people repeat: "for his mercy endureth for ever," that is, his faithful love never comes to an end.

It is a song of praise that was sung together in community, with a refrain repeated in every verse. We do not know with certainty who wrote it. It first recalls creation and then moves on to Israel's deliverance from Egypt. In this way it joins two ideas: the God who orders the universe is the same God who cares for his people faithfully.

For today: when night comes, whether it brings tiredness or worry, look up at the sky and remember that God holds everything together with order and care. Give thanks for a mercy that does not depend on your mood or your circumstances.
exp.26:11:
Here David asks God not to let him fall into the hands of his enemies. The words about wanting and whims are not needed in English, and the old spelling of the preposition is nothing a modern reader would notice, so I have left those out. The verse says that false witnesses have risen up against him, people who lie in order to accuse him, and people who breathe out cruelty, meaning people who are full of violence and wickedness.

David, the traditional author of the psalm, speaks here in the middle of great pressure. Earlier he had said that the Lord would take him up even if his father and mother forsook him, and he asked for guidance along a straight path. Afterward he confesses that he would have lost heart without his hope in the goodness of God. It is not known with certainty at what exact point in his life he wrote it.

For today: if someone accuses you unjustly, do not strike back or sink into fear. Lay your case before God honestly, ask him for direction, and keep doing what is right while you wait for his help.
exp.13:4:
They suddenly became filled with a great fear. The sentence says the wicked, who felt secure while they abused others, were overcome by enormous dread. The reason given is that God is not with them but is with "the generation of the righteous," meaning those who live uprightly and trust in Him.

The speaker is the psalmist, David according to the title of the psalm. He has just described those who oppress the poor and consume his people as if they were bread, without taking God into account. This verse shows that their apparent power collapses when God acts on behalf of His own.

For today: if you suffer injustice, do not lose hope. Keep doing good and trust that God is with you, even when evil seems to be winning.
exp.88:18:
Psalm 89:19 says that God spoke in a vision to his holy one, someone faithful to him, and announced that he had placed help on a mighty man. "Exalted" means lifted up to a place of honor. God chose someone from among his people to give him strength and authority.

The author of the psalm is Ethan the Ezrahite, and he recalls the promise God made to David. The verses that follow show that the chosen one is David. Some think the "holy one" is the prophet Nathan, but this is not certain, and others understand it in a more general way. The people are in a difficult situation and rely on this ancient promise.

For today: God often helps his people by calling and strengthening ordinary people. If you are given a responsibility that is greater than you, trust that God sustains you. Ask him for strength and do not depend on yourself alone.
exp.118:110:
It says the psalmist has taken God's teachings as his inheritance, that is, as a treasure that belongs to him and that never runs out. "Thy testimonies" are the words and commands by which God makes his will known. "For ever" shows that he does not intend to let them go. And the reason is simple: those words bring joy to his heart.

The one speaking is the author of Psalm 119, a believer who loves God's law. It is not known for certain who wrote it. Earlier he says his life is in danger and that the wicked have set traps for him, but he did not turn away from God. After feeling threatened, he finds in the Word something more valuable than any material good: a secure inheritance and a source of joy.

For today: when everything seems uncertain, treat God's Word as your greatest riches. Set aside a moment each day to read it calmly, and write down one promise that brings you joy so you can remember it through the day.
exp.21:17:
It says that the enemies divide up the clothing of the one speaking, as if he had nothing left. "They divided" describes sharing it out, and "cast lots" means they used a drawing of lots, like dice, to decide who would keep the most valuable garment.

It is a psalm of David, written in a moment of extreme anguish. He feels surrounded, mocked, and without strength, and he cries out to God. The writers of the Gospel saw this verse fulfilled at the cross, when the soldiers divided Jesus' clothing (John 19:23-24). For this reason many Christians also read this psalm as a prophecy of Christ.

For today: when you feel stripped bare or ignored, remember that Jesus went through that too. You can speak to Him honestly, because He understands your pain and does not leave you alone.
exp.30:10:
David says he is looked down on by everyone. His enemies mock him, and his neighbours despise him even more. Those who know him well are filled with dread and keep their distance, and people who see him in the street turn and run from him, as if he were something catching.

The psalmist, traditionally David, speaks out of deep distress. He is sick and worn out, and he admits that part of his suffering comes from his wrongdoing. Commentators do not agree on the exact situation he was in; the text does not say. What we do see is that he feels alone and forsaken, and still he cries out to the LORD.

For today: when rejection or loneliness weighs on you, do not shut yourself away. Tell God honestly what you feel, as David did. He listens, and you can also look for a trusted person who will stand with you.
exp.6:12:
God is the one who appears here as a righteous warrior. The psalmist says that God has his deadly weapons ready and has made his arrows against those who pursue harm, that is, against those who do wrong without repenting.

David prays to God while someone pursues him unjustly. The title of the psalm mentions Cush, a Benjamite. David does not take justice into his own hands but describes God as the judge. These images of war are poetic language to show that God does not ignore wickedness and that his patience has a purpose: to give time to turn back to him.

When someone treats you unjustly, hand your pain over to God instead of seeking revenge. He sees and will judge with justice. And remember that this same patience of God invites all of us to repent.
exp.145:5:
This verse says that Jehovah, the God of Jacob, is the one who made heaven, earth, the sea, and everything in them. It also says that he "keeps truth forever," meaning that he is faithful and always fulfills what he promises.

The psalm does not say who wrote it. The author addresses himself and his people in praise. Before that, he warns against trusting in the powerful, because they are mortal: their breath departs, they return to the earth, and their plans come to an end. Then he shows whom we can truly trust: the Creator. After this, the psalm lists how God helps the oppressed, the hungry, the prisoners, and those who have fallen.

For today: when you are afraid or unsure whom to turn to, remember that God made all things and does not change in his faithfulness. Pray with confidence and lean on his promises, while still acting wisely and helping others.
exp.20:10:
The explanation says that the enemies of the Lord planned to do harm against God and devised clever schemes to achieve it, but those plans will not succeed. The verse says they "imagined a mischievous device." The explanation says it "imagined" means they came up with plans or set up plots, and "they are not able to perform" means they will not be able to carry them out.

This is a psalm of David, which is usually read as a song for the king and his victory. It speaks to the Lord and trusts that He sustains the king. The surrounding verses describe, with strong images, the judgment on those who oppose God. Many believers also see it pointing to the Messiah, though this is interpreted in different ways.

For today: when wickedness seems very organized and powerful, do not lose hope. Bring your concerns to God in prayer and keep doing good, trusting that unjust plans do not have the last word.
exp.105:27:
They joined themselves to Baal-peor, a false god of the Moabites. To join oneself to something means to attach yourself to it or stick close to it. They also ate "the sacrifices of the dead," which probably refers to offerings made to lifeless idols. Some think it may also point to rituals involving the dead, but the text does not make this completely clear.

The psalmist reviews the history of Israel to remind us how many times the people were unfaithful and yet God was patient. This happened in the wilderness, at Peor, according to Numbers 25. There the people mixed themselves with the customs of Moab, and a punishment came, which the psalm speaks of next.

Today we can ask ourselves what things we stick to without realizing it. No one turns away from God all at once; it almost always starts with small compromises. Let us be careful about who and what we join ourselves to, and let us return quickly to God, who forgives the one who repents.
exp.60:1:
The explanation says that David calls out to God from a very distant place, "the end of the earth," meaning the far edge or border of the world. He does this when his heart is overwhelmed, that is, when he feels weak and without strength. He asks God to lead him to a rock that is higher than he is, a firm and elevated place, higher than he can reach on his own.

The speaker is David, in a psalm for the choirmaster. It is not known with certainty when he wrote it. Some think it was while he was fleeing from Absalom, but that is an interpretation. What is clear is that he feels far away, tired, and threatened, and he remembers that God has been his refuge.

For today: when you feel worn out or far from everything, do not wait until you have the strength to pray. Cry out to God just as you are and ask him to lead you to a place of safety greater than your own strength.
exp.73:8:
The explanation says that the people no longer see God's signs, that is, the visible tokens of his presence and his work. There is also no prophet, someone who speaks on God's behalf, and no one knows how long this suffering will last. "Signs" can be miracles, symbols of worship, or divine guidance.

The psalm is spoken by a psalmist named Asaph (the title says so, though scholars debate whether he himself wrote it or his descendants did). He prays after an enemy has destroyed the sanctuary. Many connect this with the fall of Jerusalem in 586 B.C., but this is not certain. What is clear is the pain of feeling abandoned and without answers.

When you feel that God is silent and you see no way out, do not pretend to a strength you do not have. You can bring your confusion to him honestly, as the psalmist does, and keep crying out to God.
exp.36:17:
Verse 18 says that God knows well the lives of the blameless, meaning people who are upright and honest, not without flaws, but with a sincere heart toward Him. Here "knows" means that God cares for them and takes charge of them. Their "inheritance" is what is received as a legacy, and the verse promises that it will last.

This is a psalm of David, already an old man, that encourages readers not to envy the wicked who seem to prosper. Earlier it says that the little the righteous person has is worth more than the great wealth of the wicked, and later it promises that God will sustain them in difficult times. There are differing views on whether the words "for ever" refer only to the promised land or also to eternal life.

For today: when you feel insecure because of scarcity, or because you see others doing better without living with integrity, remember that the Lord knows each of your days. Keep doing what is right and trust that He sustains you.
exp.69:3:
It says that all who seek God can be filled with joy and gladness in Him. It also says that those who love his salvation (his deliverance, his rescue) should keep saying continually: "Let God be magnified," that is, recognized as great and worthy of honor.

David speaks here, according to the title of the psalm, in a time of great pressure. His enemies pursue and mock him. Even so, he asks that those who seek God not lose their joy. The next verse shows that David himself is still in need and pleads with God to hurry.

For today: even in the middle of a problem, we can choose to praise God. Before you state your need, take a moment to say: "God, you are great." That does not deny the pain, but it reminds you in whom you trust.
exp.38:1:
David says he became completely silent. Where the verse says he was "dumb with silence," this means he stood there mute, saying nothing at all. "I held my peace" means he kept quiet. The phrase "even from good" means he refrained from speaking even good things. The phrase "my sorrow was stirred" means his pain became agitated and grew, instead of settling down.

David speaks in the first person. He had decided to guard his tongue so that he would not sin while a wicked man was near and attacking him. That is why he put a restraint on his mouth. But keeping everything inside hurt him even more. The next verse shows that his heart burned and that he finally spoke, but addressed to God. Some think the silence was wise, others that it was excessive; the text only describes his struggle.

For today: when you are hurt or angry, think before you speak. But do not shut yourself in with your pain. Bring it to God in prayer with complete honesty.
exp.64:2:
The explanation says that the words of wickedness, that is, the accusations and sins that weigh on us, overcame us or overwhelmed us. Overcame means they were stronger than we were. But God will forgive our rebellions, that is, our disobedience against Him. The idea of forgiving can also be understood as covering over or atoning for the guilt.

David speaks, or a psalm sung in his name, within a praise gathered in Zion. The people come to God with prayer and with vows fulfilled. Before speaking of dwelling in His courts, he humbly acknowledges that no one can draw near on the basis of their own merit. Some understand the words of iniquities as voices of guilt or of enemies; the text does not specify.

For today: when guilt or negative voices overwhelm you, do not hide from God. Bring Him your failures honestly and rest in the fact that He offers forgiveness, so that you can draw near to Him with gratitude.
exp.90:15:
God says he will give the one who trusts in him a long and satisfied life. The word for "satisfy" here means "to fill" or "to leave satisfied." Healthy wellbeing is not what is meant by the word "salvation" in this verse; it refers to God's deliverance itself, not only good physical condition. The promise is that such a person will see God's salvation.

Near the end of this psalm, God himself speaks. Before this, the psalmist spoke of protection; now God responds with promises for the one who loves him, knows him, and calls on him. Some understand "long life" as a literal promise; others understand it as an expression of a full life under God's care. Believers have debated how to apply it, because there are also faithful people who die young.

Today you can trust that a life with God is a complete life, no matter how many years it lasts. Each day, pray and place your plans in his hands, and look for his help in everyday matters, thanking him for it.
exp.11:1:
They tell lies to their neighbours. Flattering lips are lips that praise with smooth, false words, to please someone or to deceive them. A double heart means saying one thing outwardly and thinking another thing inwardly. Each one speaks this way with his neighbour, that is, with the person who is near him.

David cries out to God in this psalm, and he feels almost alone in an environment where loyalty and compassion seem to have disappeared. We do not know with precision at what point in his life he wrote it. Afterward, the psalm contrasts these false and proud words with the words of God, which are pure and trustworthy. God promises to act on behalf of the humble.

Today we can examine our own words: do I praise someone only to look good or to gain something? Let us ask God for a sincere heart, and let us speak with truth and kindness, without manipulating others.
exp.37:9:
My heart pounds and races, and my strength has left me. As for the sparkle in my eyes, it has also faded away from me. The source describes the speaker's heart as full of anguish. The word for "anguished" means distressed and pressed down by pain. The phrase about strength leaving him means that his energy has abandoned him. Then, the verse says the light of his eyes is gone, which can be understood as his eyes being dulled by exhaustion and weeping, or as him having lost the spirit and clarity to see his life.

The one speaking is David, according to the heading of the psalm, which calls it a prayer for remembrance. He is suffering because of his own sins, from an illness that is wearing him down, and from the desertion of his friends. Scholars do not know with certainty what the illness was or exactly when it happened. Even so, in the middle of his pain, he speaks to God with complete honesty.

For today: when you feel without strength and without spirit, do not hide it. Tell God exactly how you are, as David did, and ask someone you trust to walk alongside you.
exp.142:3:
The explanation says the psalmist felt a very strong distress deep within his being. Being "overwhelmed" means he felt weighed down and crushed. The word "desolate" in the verse describes how he was so struck down that his heart could barely respond at all.

The one speaking is David, according to the heading of the psalm. He is being pursued by an enemy who has left him fallen and in darkness. Even so, he does not claim his own merits; he asks that God not judge him according to what he deserves, because no one is righteous before Him. Some scholars connect this to his flight from Absalom or from Saul, but the text does not say so with certainty.

For today: when your spirit breaks, do not pretend to strength. Tell God honestly how you feel. Then, as David does in the next verse, remember what God has done before and stretch out your hands toward Him.
exp.138:18:
The explanation says that the psalmist is certain that God will act against the wicked. A person who lives without respect for God is described here, and those who seek to shed blood, that is, the violent, are described as well. For this reason he asks these men to depart from him.

The one speaking is David, according to the title of the psalm. He had just been praising God because God knows him completely and has cared for him since before he was born. Now, seeing the evil in the world, he cries out for justice. It is strong language, typical of the psalms of lament, and it should be read together with verse 23, where he asks God to examine his own heart.

For today: when injustice hurts you, do not take revenge. Bring your pain honestly to God, and also ask him to search your heart, so that he may guide you and free you from every wrong path.
exp.88:25:
He says that the king chosen by God will call him "my Father." He will also acknowledge him as "my God" and as "the rock of my salvation." The word "salvation" here means deliverance and protection. The "rock" is an image of a firm and secure refuge.

God speaks here, recalling the promise made to David (2 Samuel 7). He assures him that his descendant will have a close relationship with Him. The psalm celebrates that covenant, although later the psalmist complains because it seems to have been broken. Many Christians see in these words a foreshadowing of Jesus, the Son of David, although the original text first spoke of the king of Israel.

For today: when you feel insecure, return to God as to a close father and as to a firm rock. Say it in your own words: "You are my Father and my refuge." He sustains those who trust in Him.
exp.29:0:
This verse is the title and the first verse of the psalm. David says he will praise God, that is, lift Him up and speak well of Him, because God has raised him up from a low place. He also thanks God for not letting his enemies laugh at his fall. The word "extol" in the verse is an old way of saying "praise" or "lift up," and here it means the same thing as the first clause, "I will extol thee."

The speaker is David, and the title says the psalm was sung at the dedication of the house. It is not known for certain what house is meant: it could be the temple, David's palace, or a place of worship, and scholars interpret it in different ways. The verses that follow show that David had gone through a serious illness and that God healed him.

For today: when God brings you out of a trial, do not forget it. Take some time to thank Him aloud or in writing, and tell someone what He has done for you.
exp.15:5:
It says David feels his share in life fell to him in a very good place. The "measuring cords" were the ropes used to measure out land when it was divided; the phrase "in pleasant places" means his portion came to a pleasant spot. The "inheritance" is what a person receives as his share. He calls it beautiful.

David speaks in a psalm that tradition attributes to him. He has just said that the Lord himself is his portion and his cup, that is, his greatest treasure. So rather than speaking mainly about land, he expresses gratitude for what God has given him. He sets this against those who follow other gods and only gather sorrows.

For today: instead of looking at what others have, make a list of what God has given you: people, opportunities, peace. Give thanks for your "share," knowing that having Him is the best inheritance.
exp.49:18:
This verse says that the person was speaking in ways that did harm and used their words to deceive. "Giving the mouth to evil" means devoting what one says to hurtful purposes, and "framing deceit" means putting lies together with care, like someone building them piece by piece.

Here God himself speaks, calling his people to account. He addresses the wicked who keep the outward forms of worship but despise his word, who keep company with thieves and adulterers, and who slander their own brother. God reminds them that his silence was not approval; that is why he now confronts them.

For today: our words matter as much as our religion. Before you speak, ask yourself whether what you are about to say is true and whether it helps or hurts. Ask God to guard your tongue, including in chats and on social media.
exp.91:9:
It says God will lift up and strengthen the psalmist. "Horn" in the Bible symbolizes strength, power and dignity. The "wild ox" of the King James wording most likely refers to a powerful wild animal, a strong creature whose exact identity is debated. "Fresh oil" speaks of a new anointing, a sign of blessing, joy and renewal.

The one speaking is the psalmist, who praises God for His faithfulness. He has just said that God is the Most High forever and that his enemies will perish. Now he contrasts the two: while the wicked fall, God lifts up the one who trusts in Him. Afterward the image of the righteous person who flourishes like a palm tree will follow.

For today: when you feel weak or tired, do not depend only on your own strength. Ask God to renew you, and trust that He knows how to lift up his own in His time.
exp.59:2:
He says that God has allowed his people to go through very hard things. "Hard things" are painful trials. "The wine of astonishment" is an image: it is like a cup that, when drunk, makes a person stagger, like someone dizzy who cannot keep their footing. The phrase "to make us drink" means to make us experience it or go through it.

The verse is spoken by David, or the psalm is written in his name, after a defeat or a national crisis. The heading mentions wars against Aram and Edom, and the psalm describes a nation shaken and bewildered. David acknowledges that God is above everything, even hard times, and that is why he asks him to help them again and heal them.

For today: when you go through a season that leaves you staggering, do not keep your pain silent. Bring it to God honestly, as this psalm does, and ask him for help and steadiness.
exp.71:2:
This verse says that the mountains and the hills will bring peace and justice to the people. It is a poetic image: the whole land seems to take part in a good kingdom. "Bring" here means to yield or produce, and "hills" are smaller rises than mountains.

The psalm bears the heading "For Solomon," and it may be understood as a prayer for him or as something he wrote; scholars do not agree. It asks that God give his justice to the king, so that he will care for the afflicted and the poor. Many Christians also see here a look toward Christ, the perfect King. Here peace springs from justice.

For today: true peace is not only calm, but that no one is treated unjustly. You can ask God for wisdom and concretely help someone who is vulnerable: defend them, walk with them, or treat them justly in your work, your home, or your community.
exp.75:1:
He says that God has his house in Salem and his dwelling place in Zion. "Tabernacle" here refers to his shelter, the place where he lives, and "dwelling place" is his home. "Salem" is an old, short name for Jerusalem; Zion is the mountain where the city of David stood and, later, the temple. The verse shows that God makes himself present among his people.

The psalm is a song of Asaph, a musician and Levite from the time of King David, or of his group of singers. It celebrates a victory that God gave to Jerusalem. It is not certain which episode it speaks of; some think of the defeat of the Assyrian army, but the text does not make this clear. The central point is that God, who dwells in Zion, is the one who protects the city.

Today we can remember that God is not distant. When you feel fear or weariness, take a few minutes to pray and to remember that he dwells among his own and cares for them.
exp.73:14:
This verse says that God caused springs and streams to flow to give water to the land, and that he also dried up mighty rivers with violent currents. The word "mighty" refers to rivers that run with great force. God rules over the water that gives life and also over the water that threatens.

The psalm is by Asaph, or by his group of singers, and it is a prayer of the people in a time of pain. The temple has been destroyed and the enemies mock. It is not known with certainty whether it speaks of the fall of Jerusalem or another crisis. To encourage themselves, the psalmist recalls what God did in creation and in the exodus, when he divided the sea and dried up the Jordan. Interpreters see these images both as historical memory and as poetry about God's power.

For today: when you feel that a problem is sweeping you away like a raging river, remember that God has already shown his power. Pray honestly and trust in his care.
exp.118:124:
The explanation says the psalmist presents himself as God's servant and asks for understanding. The "testimonies" are the teachings and commands God has given, which bear witness to his will. He wants to grasp them, not merely to know them by heart.

The speaker is the author of Psalm 119, a long psalm that celebrates God's law. We do not know for certain who wrote it. Here it is said that his eyes "grew weary" waiting for God's salvation, meaning he is tired of waiting. As a servant, he demands nothing; he relies on God's mercy. Shortly afterward he speaks of the law being despised around him.

For today: before opening the Bible, ask God humbly to give you understanding. Then read slowly, ask yourself what it teaches you, and consider what you can put into practice that same day.
exp.73:9:
