It says the people ask God how much longer he will allow the enemy to humiliate them. The one who oppresses and makes others suffer is the adversary; to insult and shame someone is to reproach them; to speak with contempt of God is to blaspheme. The one who prays asks whether this will last forever.

The psalm is spoken by Asaph, or perhaps by a group of his descendants, on behalf of Israel. It is a psalm of lament. It seems to have been written after the temple and the places of gathering were destroyed, although scholars debate whether it refers to Babylon or to another moment. The people feel without prophets and without answers, yet they still cry out to God.

For today: when you feel that evil is advancing and God seems silent, do not hide your pain. You can ask him sincerely, "How long?", and at the same time remember, as the psalmist does afterward, that God is still king.
exp.74:8:
This verse says that the psalmist decides to proclaim always what God does and to sing praises to him. "I will declare" means to tell or announce publicly. "The God of Jacob" is a way of naming the God who made a covenant with Israel and was faithful to Jacob, despite his failures.

The one speaking is the psalmist, in a psalm attributed to Asaph. He has just said that God is the judge who brings some low and lifts others up, and that the wicked will drink the cup of his judgment. In the face of that justice, the psalmist responds with praise. Some translations suggest the "I" of the following verse could be God himself, but here the one singing seems to be the psalmist.

For today: when you see injustice or feel impatient, do not stop at complaining. Choose to speak and sing of God's faithfulness, trusting that he judges with justice in his time.
exp.118:81:
Your eyes grew tired, the psalmist says, worn out from looking and waiting. While his gaze stayed fixed on God's word, watching for his promise, he asked: "When will you comfort me?" "Worn out" means weakened or used up from waiting for so long.

The one speaking is the author of Psalm 119, who is not identified with certainty. He is suffering, and the verses that follow mention that he is being persecuted. Even so, the section marked by the letter Kaph shows that his soul longs for God's salvation and hopes in his word. He does not hide his weariness; he tells God about it honestly.

When you are tired of waiting for an answer, you can be honest with God and ask him: "When?" Doing so is not a lack of faith. Keep reading his word, for it was there that the psalmist found strength not to let go while the comfort was on its way.
exp.6:2:
Here David speaks with God and says: "if I have done this, if there is wickedness in my hands...". The "hands" stand for his actions. "Iniquity" means wickedness or injustice. It is the opening of an oath: David places himself before God and accepts being judged if he is guilty.

David speaks in a psalm with the heading "Shiggaion," a word of uncertain meaning, perhaps an emotional song or a lament. He sang it concerning the words of Cush, a Benjamite. We do not know for certain who he was or what he said, but it seems he accused David unjustly. David feels pursued and, instead of seeking revenge, brings his case to God, the righteous judge.

For today: when you are falsely accused, do not hurry to defend yourself in anger. Ask God to examine your heart. If you are guilty, correct yourself; if you are not, rest in the knowledge that he knows the truth and does justice.
exp.105:0:
"Praise the Lord" is the opening phrase, which means "praise the Lord" (to God). It invites us to give thanks because God is good and because his mercy, that is, his faithful love and compassion, endures forever. The phrase "Praise ye" is an older way of saying "praise," and "the Lord" is the name of God.

Psalm 106 does not say who wrote it. It is a prayer of the people of Israel that honestly remembers their failures and God's patience throughout their history. That is why it begins with praise: before looking at the mistakes of the past, it affirms who God is. Some scholars think it was sung in worship at the temple, but this is not certain.

When you have difficult days or feel like you are failing, begin your prayer by remembering that God is good and that his mercy does not run out. Give thanks for one concrete thing today, and you will see how your way of looking at your problems changes.
exp.58:12:
Here David asks God to bring an end to his enemies "in wrath", that is, with his righteous anger, until they no longer exist. The word "consume" means to destroy them completely. The goal is that they will know that God rules over Jacob, that is, over his people Israel, and that his authority reaches to the farthest corners of the earth. The word "Selah" is probably a pause for reflection, although its exact meaning is not known with certainty.

The title of the psalm connects it to the time when Saul ordered David's house to be watched so that he could be killed. David prays as a persecuted man, with lies and threats all around him. It is a prayer of distress, written in strong language, that places justice in the hands of God.

Today, when someone wounds us or slanders us, we can bring that sincere pain to God in prayer, instead of seeking revenge. He is the righteous judge, and Jesus also taught us to pray for those who harm us.
exp.77:8:
The explanation says that the men of the tribe of Ephraim, although they were well equipped with bows and arrows, drew back and fled when the time came to fight. "Armed, and carrying bows" refers to those who fight with the bow. "Turned back in the day of battle" means that they fled.

The speaker is Asaph, the author of this psalm, who teaches the children the history of Israel. He wants the new generation to trust in God and not repeat the mistakes of their fathers. Commentators do not agree on which exact battle is meant; some think it is a general picture of Ephraim's unfaithfulness. The verses that follow say that the real failure was spiritual: they forgot the covenant and the works of God.

Having good resources is not enough if the heart forgets God. Remembering what He has done for you gives you firmness when your day of trial comes.
exp.74:7:
It says that God holds a cup of judgment in his hand. The wine is deep red and full of a mixture, meaning it has been blended with spices, which made it stronger. God pours it out, and the wicked will have to drink down to the dregs, the bitter sediment at the bottom. No one is left out: every wicked person on earth.

It is a song by Asaph. God speaks first, and then the psalmist. The verses before say that no human power lifts up or brings down anyone; only God is judge. The cup is a common image in the Bible for divine judgment (for example, Isaiah 51:17). The psalmist trusts that God will set injustice right, and he praises God for it.

For today: you do not have to take revenge or despair in the face of injustice. You can trust that God is a just judge, in his own time. In the meantime, live with humility and uprightness, and praise him.
exp.80:12:
This verse expresses the longing of God. The phrase "Oh that..." shows a deep desire and also sorrow. God says that he would have delighted in his people listening to him and walking in his ways, that is, living as he had taught them.

The one speaking is God himself, in a psalm that is attributed to Asaph and was sung at a festival in Israel. God recalls how he delivered them from Egypt, but his people would not obey him and followed their own plans. Then God left them to the stubbornness of their hearts. The following verses say that obedience would have brought protection and victory over their enemies.

For today: God does not ask for obedience out of whim, but because he desires our good. Today you can choose one specific thing you know God is asking of you, and do it with confidence that he cares for you.
exp.43:13:
You let us become a byword among the nations, a thing people speak of when they describe misfortune. Shaking the head was a gesture of mockery and contempt: people shook their heads as they watched Israel fall. The nations and peoples in view are the neighboring nations.

The psalm is a lament from the people of Israel, voiced by a singer from the sons of Korah. They have suffered military defeat and humiliation, yet they feel they have not abandoned God. No one knows with certainty which battle is meant; interpreters have placed it in various periods. What matters is that the psalmist speaks to God honestly, without hiding his pain.

For today: when you feel ashamed or misunderstood, do not keep your pain silent. Bring it to God in prayer with sincerity, as the psalmist did, and trust that He listens even when you do not understand what is happening.
exp.142:1:
It says that David asks God not to bring him into strict judgment. The reason is that no one among the living can be declared righteous or free from guilt before God. A "servant" is someone who serves God. "Shall be justified" means he would be declared innocent or in the right.

The psalm carries David's name, although some scholars debate the exact circumstances in which it was written. The one speaking is distressed: an enemy pursues him, and he feels like one among the dead. Even so, he does not ask for help by claiming to be perfect. First he appeals to the faithfulness and justice of God, and he acknowledges that he needs God's mercy.

For today: when you ask God for help, do it with humility, without presenting your merits. You can trust in his mercy, not in your perfection. That frees you from pretending and allows you to come near to him with sincerity.
exp.140:1:
David says he wants his prayer to reach God like the fragrance of incense, which rises and is pleasing. He also asks that the lifting up of his hands be received like the evening offering.

David speaks in a psalm of crying out. He is in distress and asks God to hurry and hear him. In Israel's worship, incense and an evening offering were presented, and David uses those images. Scholars debate whether he was far from the sanctuary or was speaking symbolically, and the text does not make this clear. Right after this, he asks God to guard his mouth and his heart.

For today: before you pray, set your heart in order. Pray with sincerity, without rushing, and ask God to also watch over your words and your desires.
exp.104:30:
This verse recalls that God spoke, and plagues came upon Egypt: swarms of flies and gnats throughout its land. The word "territory" in the verse refers to the land or borders of the nation. Some translators understand the insects here as gnats or other small biting insects, since the Hebrew word is uncertain.

The psalmist tells the story of the people of Israel in order to praise God. This psalm reviews how God cared for his people and brought them out of Egypt, where they had been enslaved. The plagues were God's answer to the hardness of Pharaoh, who did not want to let Israel go. Here it is emphasized that it was enough for God to speak for everything to happen.

For today: you can trust that God's word has real power. If he was able to free his people from such great oppression, he can also work in your difficult situations. Pray with confidence and wait on him.
exp.35:5:
God's righteousness is firm, high, and immense, like the greatest mountains (the phrase "mountains of God" is a way of saying "enormous"). His judgments, that is, his decisions and the way he governs, are deep like an abyss, hard to fully measure. And God cares for and sustains both people and animals. "Preserves" means that he keeps them and maintains their life.

David speaks, according to the title of the psalm. Before this, he described the wicked person who plans evil even in bed and does not reject it. In contrast, David looks to God: his love reaches to the heavens. He then goes on to say that those who take refuge in God find shelter and joy.

For today: when you see injustice or do not understand what is happening, remember that God is just and cares for everyone. Trust in him and rest under his protection, even when you do not see all the answers.
exp.29:1:
It says the psalmist asked God for help with a sincere cry, and God healed him. "I cried out" means he called aloud, with urgency. "You healed me" can refer to a physical illness, but in the Bible it is also used for a broader restoration.

Notice that it says "O Lord my God": he speaks with confidence, like someone who knows God closely.

The psalm is spoken by David, according to its title. He is thankful because God brought him up from a situation close to death and did not let his enemies gloat over him. The title mentions the dedication of the House, but scholars do not agree on how it relates to David's life. It is a song of gratitude after the crisis.

When you are in need, speak to God without fear or pretense. And when He helps you, do not forget it: thank Him out loud and tell others about it.
exp.55:5:
It says that the psalmist's enemies gather together in a group, hide themselves so they cannot be seen, and watch closely every step he takes. Their aim is to take his life. "When they wait for my soul" means they are lying in wait, ready to kill him when they get the chance.

The psalm is spoken by David, according to its heading, at the time when the Philistines seized him in Gath. He is surrounded by people who watch him and wish him harm. Yet in the verses around it he declares that he trusts God and will not fear what man may do to him. The psalm mixes real fear with faith.

For today: when you feel watched, criticized, or stalked, do not deny your fear. Tell it to God honestly, and, like David, choose to trust Him. God sees every step you take, including the steps of your enemies.
exp.63:4:
They encourage one another in their evil plan. An "evil design" is an unjust and wicked purpose. "Snares" are traps, like the ones set to catch animals. They hide their traps and think, "Who will see them?" They believe no one will discover them.

The speaker is David, according to the psalm's title, though it is not known with certainty when he wrote it. He cries out to God for protection from enemies who attack with words, slander, and secret plans. The following verses show that, although they feel hidden, God sees them and suddenly acts against them.

For today: if someone has harmed you in secret, or if you feel the temptation to act behind people's backs, remember that nothing is hidden before God. You can hand him your pain and trust in his justice, without seeking revenge. And examine your own heart so that you live with integrity, even when no one sees you.
exp.51:5:
This verse says that the righteous will see the fall of the wicked. They will feel reverent fear before the justice of God, and they will laugh at him. That laughter is not cruel mockery, but the recognition that trusting in oneself is foolishness.

David writes this psalm after Doeg the Edomite informed on the priests of Nob to Saul, as the heading of the psalm indicates. David speaks of that man's deceitful tongue and trusts that God will do justice. Scholars understand the tone of that laughter in different ways: for some it is relief and approval of God's justice, for others it is a warning.

For today: do not place your security in money or in your own cleverness. Trust in God and guard your words. When you see injustice, wait on Him without becoming bitter.
exp.44:4:
It says the king's arrows are sharp and accurate. Arrows are what the verse calls "arrows," so the word itself is not a problem. With them the peoples fall defeated at his feet, and the arrows reach the heart of those who oppose the king. It is language of war to show that his power does not fail.

This psalm is a song for a royal wedding. The author, a poet of Israel, addresses the bridegroom king and praises him. But the text goes beyond a human king: the verses that follow call him "God" and speak of an eternal throne. That is why the New Testament applies this to Christ (Hebrews 1:8). His victory is described with truth, humility, and justice, not with simple violence.

For today: you do not need to defend Christ with harshness or pride. Trust that his kingdom advances through truth and justice. Make sure your treatment of others reflects that same humility.
exp.127:2:
It says that the wife of the man who fears God will be like a vine bearing much fruit within his home, and that his children will be like young olive shoots around his table. A "vine" is a grapevine. Its meaning is that of a home full of life, abundance and a united family.

This is a song of ascents, that is, a song sung by pilgrims going up to Jerusalem. The author is not named. A man who honors God and lives from his own labor receives the promise of a blessed family. It is a poem of wisdom, not a guarantee for every case, since the Bible also shows families who suffer.

For today: value your family table. Set aside a regular time, without screens, to eat together, thank God, and listen to your loved ones. In this way you care for what God has given you.
exp.118:8:
This verse asks a question: how can a young man keep his way clean? And it answers at once: by taking heed to God's word. The word "way" means a person's daily conduct, and "cleanse" means keeping it pure. "Beth" is just the name of the second letter of the Hebrew alphabet; each section of this psalm begins with a letter of the alphabet.

The psalm does not say who wrote it. Some attribute it to David, but that is uncertain. The speaker loves God's law and desires to live by it. Here a new section begins, and earlier the speaker had promised to praise God and keep his statutes. Then he says he seeks God with his whole heart and keeps his word so as not to sin.

For today: it is not enough to want to be clean; you need to fill yourself with the Bible. Choose a short passage each day, read it slowly, and ask God for help to put it into practice in one concrete decision.
exp.118:126:
The psalmist says he loves God's commandments more than gold, even more than the finest gold. "Therefore" points back to what has been said before. The "very pure gold" in this verse refers to refined gold, the most precious thing people of that time knew.

The one speaking is the author of Psalm 119, a poem in honor of God's law; no one knows for certain who wrote it. He presents himself as a servant of God and asks for understanding. He feels that it is a time to act, since people have set the law aside. That is why his love for the Word stands out even more: he loves what others have pushed aside.

Today we can ask ourselves what holds first place in our hearts. A simple idea: before checking your phone in the morning, read a passage from the Bible and ask God to teach you to value it more than money or success.
exp.128:1:
It says that the people have suffered greatly and for a long time, from their beginnings. But it also says that their enemies never managed to defeat them completely. "Afflicted" means oppressed, attacked, or put in distress. "Prevailed" means that they won or gained the upper hand.

Israel speaks as a people, in a song that was probably sung when going up to Jerusalem. It looks back and remembers its sufferings, which the psalm compares to a field plowed upon their backs. The "from my youth" is usually understood as the early days of the nation, such as the slavery in Egypt, although the psalm gives no exact details. In the end, the psalmist acknowledges that God is righteous and has cut the cords of the wicked.

Today we can look at our past difficulties and recognize that, although they hurt, they did not destroy us. Today, in prayer, you can thank God for a difficult situation in which He sustained you, and ask Him for confidence for the one you face now.
exp.96:3:
It says that God's lightnings lit up the whole world, and the earth, seeing them, trembled with awe. The word the verse uses for "lit up" means that they gave light. The old spelling of "saw" is now written as "saw" in modern usage. The word for "trembled" means the earth shook, that is, it trembled. These are poetic images of God's power.

It is a psalm of praise, and the text does not name its author. The psalmist describes God as King who appears with clouds, fire, and lightning, in the style of the appearance on Mount Sinai. Earlier he speaks of God's throne being founded on justice, and afterward he says the mountains melt before Him. Scholars understand these images as poetic language, not as a literal description.

For today: God is not small or distant. When you feel afraid, or when it seems that evil is in charge, remember that his throne stands on justice. Respond with reverence and trust, and place your concerns in his hands.
exp.79:13:
This verse is a prayer of request. The psalmist asks God, called "God of hosts" (that is, God with all power), to return, to look down from heaven, to behold, and to visit his vine.

The one speaking is a psalmist, who prays on behalf of the whole people of Israel. Israel is compared to a vine that God planted. Now that vine is damaged: its hedges have been torn down, and passersby and wild animals ravage it. The people suffer and cry out, asking God to restore them.

When you feel weak, wounded, or unprotected, you can speak to God honestly, as this psalmist does. Tell him frankly what hurts and ask him to draw near. He invites his people to cry out with confidence.
exp.5:6:
The explanation says the speaker's eyes are worn out and weak from so much crying and suffering. The word "consumed" means worn away, like something gnawed away little by little. "Grief" here is understood as sorrow, affliction, or deep anguish. The phrase "waxeth old" means they have grown old and tired. His "enemies" are those who cause him suffering.

The speaker is David, according to the psalm's heading, though we cannot know with certainty what situation he was living through. He is sick or deeply distressed, feels that God is displeased with him, and spends the nights weeping. He asks God for mercy. Besides this, there are enemies pressing against him. At the end of the psalm, his spirit changes because he trusts that God does hear him.

For today: you do not have to hide your pain or pretend to be strong before God. Tell him honestly about your weariness and your tears, as David did. God invites us to pray this way, and often honest prayer brings relief and hope.
exp.67:25:
This verse is an invitation to praise. "Bless" means speaking well of God, giving thanks, and acknowledging who he is. "In the congregations" means gathered together as a group. "Descendants of Israel" refers to the offspring of Israel, that is, the people of God. Also, "you all" is an older way of saying "you."

The psalmist, David according to the title, speaks to the people. He has just described a procession toward the sanctuary, with singers, musicians, and young women playing tambourines. Now he calls everyone gathered to join in praise. The following verses mention the tribes present: Benjamin, Judah, Zebulun, and Naphtali. Scholars debate which exact historical occasion this procession refers to.

For today: do not praise God only in private. Take part with other believers, sing, give thanks, and encourage others to do the same. Shared praise strengthens the faith of everyone.
exp.81:1:
This verse is a rebuke in the form of a question: "How long will ye judge unjustly, and accept the persons of the wicked?" God asks those who are supposed to do justice how much longer they will keep judging wrongly. To "accept the persons of the wicked" means to favor the wrongdoers, treating them with partiality. The word "Selah" seems to be a pause or musical signal, and its exact meaning is not known for certain.

God himself speaks, in a psalm of Asaph. He stands among "the gods," a term that is explained in several ways: human judges or rulers, or spiritual beings. Many believe they are the judges of Israel. God confronts them because they were leaving the poor, the fatherless, and the needy without protection, as the following verses say.

For today: if you have any authority, at work, in the family, or in the church, treat everyone with justice, without favoring those who have power or money. And boldly defend the one who has no voice.
exp.104:29:
It says the land of Egypt was filled with frogs throughout the whole country, and that they even reached the king's chambers, that is, the private rooms of the palace. The word "brought forth" means that the land produced them in great numbers. Not even the most protected place of the pharaoh was free from this plague.

The psalmist recalls the plagues of Egypt within a psalm that praises God for his works on behalf of Israel. It tells how God kept his promise to Abraham and brought his people out of slavery. This is the second plague according to Exodus 8. The text shows that God has authority over nature and over the most powerful rulers.

For today: no human power stands above God. If you face injustice today, or people who seem untouchable, you can trust that God sees and still governs. Pray with patience and do what is right, while continuing to wait on him.
exp.64:11:
God's rain falls drop by drop on the pastures of the wilderness, that is, on the open fields where nothing is planted. The explanation of "drop upon" is that the rain falls gently, letting its water soak down. The places for grazing are the pasturelands. The hills, which "rejoice on every side," are wrapped in joy, as if they were dressed for a celebration.

This is a psalm of David, a song of praise to God for his care of the earth. Earlier it speaks of the rains that soften the furrows and bless the new shoots. Here the poet describes creation as if it were glad over God's provision. This is poetic language, not a literal claim that the hills have feelings.

For today: learn to see God's hand in everyday things, such as rain, bread, or work. Before starting the day, give thanks for one concrete provision, even if it seems small. Gratitude grows when we notice it.
exp.105:31:
It says that the people of Israel once again provoked God's anger at the waters of Meribah, and that things went badly for Moses because of them. The phrase "they angered him" means they made him angry, and "it went ill with Moses" here means that he suffered harm and a painful consequence.

The psalmist reviews Israel's sins to remind us of God's faithfulness despite the people's rebellion. This episode is connected to Numbers 20, when the people complained for lack of water. Moses, under pressure, spoke in anger and did not honor God as he should have (v. 33). For this reason he did not enter the promised land.

Our complaints and attitudes can affect those who lead us or walk with us. Before we voice complaints, it is good to pray and trust God. We can also support our leaders with patience and gratitude, rather than burdening them with our distrust.
exp.105:30:
It says that Dios counted Phinehas (Finees) as righteous for his action. Here "counted" is the word the verse uses: it was counted unto him for righteousness. This would be remembered from generation to generation, forever.

The psalmist reviews Israel's sins in the wilderness. At Baal-peor the people fell into idolatry and immorality, and a plague came. Phinehas acted out of zeal for God, and the plague stopped (Numbers 25). The psalmist does not say who wrote this psalm, and it cannot be known with certainty. What stands out here is that God valued Phinehas's faithfulness.

For today: God notices those who take his holiness seriously and act with courage and obedience. We do not imitate the violence of that moment, but his loyalty to God. Ask yourself today where God is calling you to be firm and faithful, even when others are not.
exp.37:14:
This verse says that the psalmist placed his hope in God and is sure that God will answer him. "Hope" here means he trusted and waited patiently. "You will answer" means that God will act and will not leave him without a reply. He addresses God as "O Lord my God," with a very personal confidence.

The speaker is David, according to the heading of the psalm. He is sick, feels guilt for his sin, and suffers because enemies mock him. In the verses before this one he stays silent, like a deaf man or a mute, and does not defend himself. Instead of answering his accusers, he leaves his case in God's hands.

For today: when others attack you or you feel wounded, you do not have to answer everything or defend yourself at all costs. You can be silent, pray sincerely, and trust that God hears and responds, even if in his own time.
exp.16:2:
God says that he examined David's heart, visited him at night, and tested him, the way metal is refined by fire. And God found no wrongdoing in him. David states that he has decided his mouth will not go beyond what is right, meaning he will not speak more than he should or say hurtful things.

David prays to God when he faces enemies and asks that God judge his case with justice. He does not claim to be perfect. His point is that there is nothing hidden or deceptive in his prayer. Some believe that "at night" refers to moments of quiet and reflection, though the text does not make this clear.

Today you can pray with sincerity, inviting God to examine your heart. Before you speak in anger or criticize others, decide to guard your words, and ask God to help you keep that decision.
exp.72:14:
This verse says that the psalmist holds back before speaking. If he were to say out loud what he has been thinking, that there is no point in living a pure life, he would be unfaithful to God's people. The phrase "I will speak thus" means that he would say such things. To say he "would have betrayed" them, or "would have been faithless," is the sense of the verse. The "children of God" are the generation of the faithful.

The speaker is Asaph, or the author of the psalm, who is confused. He sees that the wicked prosper while he suffers even though he is upright. He feels that his righteous life was in vain. But he realizes that saying it in public could discourage other believers. Some understand that this is where his change of attitude begins, before he reaches the sanctuary.

For today: when you have doubts or pain, be honest with God, but guard your words with others. Try not to spread discouragement, and seek God's presence and your community of faith to regain perspective.
exp.17:21:
He says that David kept all of God's decisions and commands in view, and never set them aside. "Judgments" are God's just decrees or rules, and "statutes" are his laws and commandments. The phrase "did not put away from me" means "did not reject them."

He speaks in a psalm of thanksgiving for having been rescued from his enemies, among them Saul. Here he does not claim to be perfect; he speaks of his general faithfulness to God in that conflict. He himself acknowledged his sins elsewhere, as in Psalm 51. Here he describes a heart that kept seeking God and that God looked after.

For today: keep God's Word in view. Read a passage each day and ask yourself what concrete change it calls for. That way, when pressures come, you will already know which path to follow.
exp.31:6:
It describes God as a secure place where David can hide. He trusts that God will look after him when distress comes, that is, suffering and affliction. He also pictures God surrounding him with songs of deliverance, as if on every side he heard joy over having been rescued. "Selah" is a Hebrew word whose exact meaning is uncertain; many think it invites the reader to pause and reflect.

David speaks, according to the psalm's title. He has just told how he kept his sin hidden and suffered, but when he confessed it, God forgave him. So now, filled with relief, he expresses his trust in God as his protection.

When you fail, do not hide from God or carry the guilt alone. Tell him everything honestly, trust in his forgiveness, and rest in him as your refuge. His care brings peace and even the desire to sing.
exp.33:5:
This verse says that a poor man, humble and in need, asked God for help with a sincere cry. God heard him and rescued him from all his distresses, that is, from his afflictions and hardships.

The psalm is attributed to David, and its heading connects it to the time when he pretended to be insane before Abimelech in order to escape (1 Samuel 21). Here David speaks of himself with humility, as this poor man, and bears witness to what God did for him. The verses that follow invite others to trust the Lord. Some think the "poor man" also represents any humble person who seeks God.

Today, when you feel weak or without a way out, you do not need perfect words. Speak with God sincerely, tell him what worries you, and trust that he listens. Then share with someone else how God has helped you.
exp.103:4:
He says God set the earth on its "foundations," an old word meaning bases or footings. It is a poetic image: the earth is pictured as a well-built house. He adds that it "should not be removed for ever," meaning it will not be shifted or fall. He speaks of the stability God gave the world.

The psalmist praises God as Creator. We do not know with certainty who wrote it. Earlier he describes God with grand images: the clouds are his chariot and the wind his wings. Then he recalls that the waters once covered everything, but they fled at the sound of God's voice. This is the language of poetry, not a scientific explanation. Many understand that "for ever" stresses that the order of creation depends on God, rather than meaning that nothing will ever change.

For today: when everything seems to be shifting and nothing feels firm, remember that the one who holds the earth can also hold you. Rest in him and give him thanks today.
exp.102:6:
He made known his ways to Moses, meaning his manner of acting and his purposes. And to the children of Israel he showed his deeds, that is, what he did for them.

David speaks here, according to the title of the psalm, praising God and encouraging himself to remember his benefits. The verses before this one speak of justice for the oppressed. The next one shows what God revealed of himself: he is merciful, slow to anger, and great in kindness. Many readers see here an echo of Exodus 34:6-7, when God made himself known to Moses.

Today we can remember that God is not a distant mystery, but lets himself be known. Set aside a few minutes this week to read how God acted in the Bible and in your own life, and give him thanks for his patience and mercy.
exp.127:4:
This verse is a blessing. "The Lord shall bless thee out of Zion" means that God shows you his favor from his holy mountain, where the temple stood. "Thou shalt see the good of Jerusalem" means that you will enjoy the prosperity and peace of God's city all the days of your life.

Psalm 128 is a song of ascents, probably sung by pilgrims going up to Jerusalem. We do not know for certain who wrote it. It seems that a priest or leader speaks these words to the one who fears God, after describing a united family full of blessing. The personal blessing is joined to the blessing of the whole people.

For today: God's blessing is not only for me and my household. We can also pray for the good of our church and our community, and work for it. Living with reverence for God turns us to look beyond ourselves.
exp.118:156:
This verse says that the psalmist has many opponents who pursue him and treat him as an enemy, yet even so he has not turned away from God's testimonies. That word refers to God's commands and teachings, which bear witness to what God wants and to what kind of God He is.

The one speaking is the author of Psalm 119, a believer who loves God's law. We do not know for certain who wrote it or who his enemies were. Earlier he has said that the wicked do not seek God, and he asks God to revive him, that is, to give him new strength and life. Then he grieves when he sees those who disobey.

For today: when you face pressure, mockery, or rejection because of your faith, do not depend on the opinions of others. Read the Word every day, ask God to strengthen you, and stand firm in what He has said.
exp.40:1:
It says that God protects and gives life to the person who is generous to the poor. "Keep" means to watch over and protect. "Blessed" means happy and favored. The last part, "thou wilt not deliver him unto the will of his enemies," is a request: that God not let his enemies do whatever they want to him. Some translations render these phrases as promises ("The Lord will preserve him") and not as wishes.

The psalm is traditionally attributed to David. He speaks about the one who cares for the weak and about how God looks after him in hard times. Later he speaks of sickness, of enemies, and of his own sin. Scholars do not agree on the exact time when he wrote it, so it is best not to claim a date.

Today, we can notice someone in need near us and help them in a concrete way. Even so, this is not a guarantee that we will never suffer. It is an invitation to trust in God's care.
exp.118:168:
The explanation says that the psalmist asks God to let his cry, that is, his cry for help, come before Him. He also asks for understanding, meaning comprehension and wisdom, according to God's word. The Hebrew letter "Tau" is the last letter of the Hebrew alphabet; the psalm is arranged by letters, and this one opens the final section.

The speaker is the author of the psalm, who is not named with certainty. He is someone who loves God's law and tries to live in His presence. In earlier verses he has already said that he keeps God's commandments. Now he asks for help to grasp more, and then he also asks to be delivered, which suggests he is going through some difficulty.

For today: before reading the Bible, pray simply and ask God to give you understanding. Read with humility, ready to obey what you discover, and not only to know more.
exp.135:21:
The explanation says that God gave the land as an inheritance to Israel, whom it calls "his servant." The word "inheritance" here refers to a property that is received as a gift and passed on to one's children. "Mercy" in this verse translates a Hebrew word that speaks of a faithful, steadfast love, one that keeps what has been promised. And "forever" is repeated in every line.

It is a psalm of praise, almost like a song with a refrain, in which the people respond: "his mercy endures forever." It recalls the history of Israel: God brought them out of Egypt, guided them through the wilderness, and gave them the land after defeating kings such as Sihon and Og. It is not known with certainty who wrote it, but it was sung in the worship of the people.

For today: remember the times God has sustained you and give him thanks by name. What you have is not only your own achievement, but also a gift of his faithful love.
exp.61:4:
This verse says that the psalmist speaks to his own soul. He asks it to wait and to rest quietly in God alone, because his expectation comes from Him. The word "wait" here means being still and calm, trusting. "Only" stresses that he does not look for rest in anyone else.

The psalm is attributed to David. Earlier, he describes people who plot against a man to bring him down from his position. They speak sweetly, but inwardly they desire harm. Faced with that betrayal, he does not respond with fear or revenge. He tells himself that his security is in God, whom he calls his rock and his refuge. It is not known with certainty to what exact moment in his life it refers.

When someone criticizes or betrays you, speak to yourself with calm. Before reacting, pray and remember that your hope does not depend on what people think, but on God.
exp.57:7:
It says that the wicked should pass away like a snail that melts into its own slime, and like a child born dead that never gets to see the light of the sun. Those are harsh images, asking that the power of the unjust come to an end soon.

David cries out to God against judges and rulers who speak of justice but commit violence (vv. 1-2). This is an imprecatory psalm: a cry of pain that leaves the punishment in God's hands, not our own. The images are poetic and strong, not instructions for acting.

Today, when you see injustice, you can bring your anger to God honestly, instead of seeking revenge. Ask him to put an end to evil and to free you from bitterness, trusting that he judges with justice.
exp.68:32:
It says that God hears the "poor" and needy, that is, the poor and those in need. It also says that he does not despise "his prisoners," that is, those who are held captive or bound, whether by imprisonment, oppression, or suffering. God does not ignore them.

The speaker is David, according to the title of the psalm. He is going through a deep distress: he is rejected and accused without cause. Even so, at this point in the psalm he moves from lament to praise, because he trusts that God does attend to those who suffer. The verses that follow call all of creation to praise God. Some understand "prisoners" to refer also to exile, but that is a possible interpretation, not a certain one.

For today: if you feel small, trapped, or ignored, speak with God honestly. He hears you, and your situation does not make you any less valuable in his eyes.
exp.39:11:
It says that the psalmist feels surrounded by evils so many that they cannot be counted. His own wrongdoings (his sins) have overtaken him, and they weigh on him so heavily that he cannot lift up his eyes. They are more than the hairs of his head, and his heart fails him, that is, he is left without courage or strength.

David is said to speak, according to the heading of the psalm. He has just praised God for having rescued him and has publicly told of his faithfulness. But now, humbly, he acknowledges that he still needs mercy. Some think the "evils" are outside troubles and the "wrongdoings" his guilt; scholars do not agree on how the two are related.

Today we can learn that thanking God and asking him for help do not contradict each other. If you feel overwhelmed by your mistakes or by your problems, do not hide. Bring them to God with sincerity, trusting in his mercy.
exp.148:7:
The explanation says that God's people will take part in the judgment on the nations: kings will be bound with chains (iron rings for the feet), and nobles, that is, the important leaders, with iron chains. It is an image of authority falling on the powerful.

It is a psalm of praise that invites Israel to sing to its King. The psalmist joins worship with the image of a double-edged sword. Interpreters understand it in several ways: as military victory in Israel's history, or as God's final justice that will be fulfilled in the end. The text does not say that the people should take revenge on their own.

Today, as Christians, we can trust that God will judge every unjust power with justice. So we can let go of resentment, pray for those who wrong us, and live with hope, leaving justice in God's hands.
exp.104:21:
The explanation says that Pharaoh placed Joseph in such a high position that he could correct and govern the princes of Egypt as he saw fit, and even teach wisdom to the elders, the most experienced counselors. The phrase "to his great men" refers to the nobles and officials of the king.

The psalmist is not speaking about himself, but recalls the story of Joseph, who went from prison to governing Egypt (Genesis 41). The psalm reviews how God cared for his people from Abraham onward, in order to encourage Israel to give thanks and trust in him. Some understand "at his pleasure" as the authority delegated by Pharaoh, not an unlimited power.

For today: God can raise up people who are humble or mistreated and give them wisdom to serve. If you are in a difficult season now, remain faithful; and if God gives you responsibility, use it with wisdom and humility.
exp.108:13:
The verse asks that God not forget the sins of an enemy's ancestors: that the wickedness of his fathers and the sin of his mother remain before the Lord and not be wiped out or forgiven.

The one speaking is David, or a psalmist speaking in his name. He feels falsely accused and attacked without cause by someone cruel, who hunted down the afflicted and the poor. It is an imprecatory psalm, that is, a prayer of complaint and a plea for justice, very raw and painful. Many scholars point out that God himself teaches in other passages that each person answers for his own sin (Ezekiel 18:20).

For today: when you are wounded, you may bring your pain to God with complete honesty, but leave justice in his hands. Jesus teaches us to pray for those who persecute us.
exp.55:11:
The explanation says that David feels bound to God by the promises he made to him. Vows are solemn promises spoken to God, often in moments of danger. Giving praise to God means thanking him and honoring him as an offering. In other words: "God, I have what I promised you still pending, and I will fulfill it by giving you thanks."

David speaks, according to the title of the psalm, when the Philistines seized him in Gath. He is surrounded by enemies and afraid, but he decides to trust in God. Before seeing the complete deliverance, he already promises to give thanks. Afterward he affirms that God rescued him from death and from falling, so that he may keep living before him.

For today: if in a difficulty you made a sincere promise to God, do not forget it. Keep what you said and, in addition, thank him with concrete words, for he sustains you in the trial.
exp.62:8:
This verse says that those who wanted to destroy the psalmist's life will end up in the deepest part of the earth. It is a way of speaking about death or total defeat, perhaps the grave or Sheol. The words "But" and "sought my life to destroy it" mean that they sought to take his life away.

According to the heading, David wrote this psalm in the wilderness of Judah, pursued by enemies. Some think he was fleeing from Saul, and others from Absalom; it is not certain. After praising God for his help, David trusts that injustice will not have the final word.

For today: when someone harms you, you do not have to take revenge. You can hand your pain over to God, stay close to Him in prayer, and trust that He will do justice in His time. In the meantime, seek His protection and avoid resentment.
exp.36:34:
It says that the psalmist saw a wicked man in great power and prosperity. "Exalted" means very high, admired and successful, and "spreading himself" describes him stretched out like a green bay tree, that is, a leafy tree, strong and full of life. The image shows that the wicked man seemed stable and flourishing.

This is a psalm of David, already elderly, who gives wise counsel to someone troubled by wicked people who prosper. The psalmist recalls what he himself observed. But the next verse shows the outcome: that man passed away and was no longer found. Some translators explain the green bay tree in other ways, as a native and vigorous tree, but the central idea is the same.

For today: do not measure your life by the apparent success of others. When it bothers you to see that someone dishonest is doing well, remember that what is visible does not last forever. Keep trusting God and practicing integrity, even when it seems it does not benefit you.
exp.27:2:
David asks God not to drag him away together with the wicked, that is, not to treat him as they are treated or bring on him their same punishment. Describing these people as those who greet their neighbors with peace while keeping evil in their hearts, the explanation shows their outward kindness hiding inner harm.

David speaks in a psalm of pleading. He cries out to God with his hands lifted toward the temple, fearing that he might end up like those who go down to the grave. He is concerned about the judgment that will come upon those who do harm, and he asks to be set apart from them.

For today: ask God to keep you from hypocrisy, beginning with your own heart. Make sure your kind words are sincere, and when false people surround you, pray that you will not take on their ways.
exp.104:15:
He called for a famine upon the land: that is, he brought a great shortage over the whole region. "He broke the whole staff of bread" means that he took away or broke the basic supply of food, the staff of bread, as it used to be called. Without bread, the people had nothing to eat.

The psalmist, who is not named with certainty, reviews how God cared for Israel in its history. This verse speaks of the famine in the time of Jacob and his sons. The verses that follow show that God used that hunger and the story of Joseph, sold as a servant, to preserve his people. Some see God here as the direct cause; others see him as the one who permits and directs events for his purpose.

Even in times of scarcity and injustice, God may be caring for you in ways you do not yet see. Trust in him, and share your bread with whoever is in need.
exp.23:1:
It says that God is the one who set the earth in its place. "Founded it" means he established it the way a house is built on a foundation. "Upon the seas" and "upon the floods" is poetic language: the ancients saw the waters as vast and powerful, and the psalm says God mastered them. "Established it" means he made it firm.

It is a psalm of David, probably sung in worship, perhaps in a procession toward the temple; we do not know the occasion for certain. The verse explains why the earth belongs to the Lord: he made it. That prepares the next question: who may draw near to a God so great?

For today: when you feel your life is unsteady, remember that the God who holds the world up can also hold you up. Trust in him and live with clean hands and a sincere heart.
exp.87:16:
What it says: The psalmist feels that his problems and fears surround him on every side, like a flood that does not stop. He feels that they close in on him all together, leaving him no way out.

Context: Psalm 88 is written by a man, traditionally attributed to Heman the Ezrahite, who has been suffering for years, perhaps through illness or abandonment. It is a very unusual psalm, because it has almost no words of hope and ends in darkness. Even so, it opens by calling God "the God of my salvation." Some think that what the psalmist feels is God's anger, though the exact cause is not explained.

For today: If you feel overwhelmed by difficulties, you can pray honestly, without pretending to be strong. God allows us to speak to Him even from the darkest pain, and He also invites you to seek the company of people you trust.
exp.50:10:
The explanation says that the one who prays asks God not to cast him away from his presence or take his holy spirit from him. "Cast away" means to expel or drive off, so it can be rendered as "cast me out," which the verse itself already uses. "Your holy spirit" refers to God's presence and work in a person's life. "Salvation," in the following verse, means deliverance.

According to the heading of the psalm, David wrote it after the prophet Nathan confronted him about his sin with Bathsheba. David does not justify himself; he confesses his guilt and pleads for forgiveness. His greatest fear is not punishment but losing closeness with God. Scholars discuss how "spirit" should be understood here in the Old Testament period, but clearly the psalm speaks of the presence of God.

For today: when you fail, do not run from God out of shame. Come to Him sincerely, acknowledge your mistake, and ask Him to restore your relationship with Him.
exp.66:0:
This verse begins with a musical note: the psalm was meant for the choir director, with stringed instruments ("Neginoth"). Then the psalmist asks that God have mercy on us, bless us, and cause his face to shine upon us. "Cause his face to shine" means that God would look on us with pleasure and favor. "Selah" was probably a musical pause or a moment to reflect, though this is not known for certain.

The psalm does not say who wrote it. It speaks in the words "us," that is, the people of Israel praying and singing together. Its request recalls the blessing of Numbers 6:24-26. But the following verse shows the purpose: that God's way and his salvation may be known among all the nations.

For today: when you ask God for a blessing, also ask yourself how you can help others come to know him. His blessings are not only to be kept, but to be shared generously and as a witness.
exp.15:0:
It says David asks God to keep and protect him, because his trust is placed in Him. Where the wording "keep me" appears, the sense is simply "protect me, care for me." The title word that appears at the start of the verse in the King James Version is a Hebrew word whose meaning is uncertain; some think it indicates a precious or valuable poem, and others a song for meditation. No one knows for certain.

The one speaking is David, king of Israel, in the form of a prayer. The title does not say when he wrote it, so we do not know what situation he was living through. But it is clear that he feels in danger or in need, and so he runs to God as his refuge. Afterward, the psalm goes on to speak of his loyalty to the Lord.

For today: when you feel fear or uncertainty, make this line your simple prayer. Before looking for other ways out, say: "Preserve me, O God, for in you I put my trust." Trusting does not mean not feeling fear, but bringing that fear to God.
exp.85:2:
Here David asks God: "Be merciful to me," that is, "have compassion on me, do not treat me according to what I deserve." He says he cries out to God "all day long," meaning he does not stop seeking him at any time.

It is a prayer of David. Before this, he says he is afflicted and in need, and that he trusts in God as his servant. Then he recalls that God is good, ready to forgive, and abundant in mercy toward those who call on him. The text does not say exactly what his problem was, so it is better not to invent one; we only see that it was a real and urgent need.

For today: do not wait until everything is settled before you pray. You can speak with God throughout the day, at work, on the road, or at home, with simple words like "Lord, be merciful to me." He invites those in need to come to him with confidence.
exp.80:2:
This verse calls for the trumpet to be blown at the new moon, on the appointed day, which is the day of our solemn feast. A "solemn feast" means a special celebration, set apart for God. The trumpet was an instrument that called the people to gather and to rejoice.

It is a psalm of Asaph, a musician in the worship of Israel. Here the psalmist calls the people to sing with joy, and reminds them that these feasts are an ordinance that God gave to Israel, tied to the departure from Egypt. Scholars debate which exact feast is meant: some think of the Feast of Trumpets or the Feast of Tabernacles, but the text does not specify.

For today: set aside fixed times to stop and praise God with other believers. Do not wait until you feel like it; make gratitude a habit, remembering what God has done for you.
exp.138:17:
Psalm 139:18 says that God's thoughts toward us are so many that, if anyone tried to count them, they would outnumber the grains of sand. The explanation notes that the thoughts keep increasing without end. The phrase "when I awake, I am still with thee" can be understood in two ways: when the psalmist wakes up, he is still with God and still thinking of him; or, having been counting so long, he falls asleep, and on waking he finds that God is still there, watching over him.

The speaker is David, according to the title of the psalm. He is meditating on how God knows him completely, from before he was born. His amazement and praise arise from seeing how much attention he receives from God. Then the tone changes and he asks for justice against the violent.

For today: when you feel forgotten or insignificant, begin the day by remembering that God thinks of you and is with you. Thank him aloud for one specific thing.
exp.77:64:
It says that the Lord, after seeming silent and inactive, suddenly rose up. He is compared to someone who wakes from sleep, and to a strong warrior who shouts with spirit after drinking wine. The word "young men" is not used here; the explanation of the comparison is simply that it is a figure of speech: God does not sleep or get drunk, but this is how it appears from the human experience.

The psalm is by Asaph, and it reviews the history of Israel. It recalls how the people rebelled and how God allowed the Philistines to defeat them at Shiloh. Then the Lord acts against the enemies. Some understand the image as bold but poetic; others see it as a way of expressing that God's silence is not absence.

For today: when you feel that God is slow or silent, do not conclude that he has abandoned you. Keep trusting, and examine your heart with humility, for God acts in his own time.
exp.36:5:
He says that God himself will bring your righteousness to light, that is, your good conduct and your innocence, and that it will be as clear as the light of the morning. "Shine forth" means to show or make visible. "Judgment" here refers to your just cause, and "noonday" is midday, when the sun shines brightest and nothing remains hidden.

It is a psalm of David, already an old man, that encourages God's people. Many saw that the wicked were prospering while the faithful suffered slander or injustice. David advises trust, committing the way to God, and not becoming angry. The promise is that God will defend the one who entrusts himself to him, even though he does not say when or how.

When someone judges you wrongly or treats you unjustly, there is no need to defend yourself with resentment or revenge. Do what is right, pray, commit the situation to God, and wait in peace. He knows how to reveal the truth in his own time.
exp.88:49:
This verse is a prayer. The psalmist asks God not to forget the shame and mockery that his servants suffer. The word "disgrace" here means insult, dishonor, or contempt. The phrase "bear in my bosom" means he carries it deep inside, like a personal weight, and it comes from the mockery of "all the mighty people," that is, of neighboring nations.

The one speaking is the author of the psalm, identified as Ethan the Ezrahite. He speaks on behalf of Israel. The psalm celebrates God's promise to David, but it ends in lament, because the kingdom seems fallen and the enemies mock the anointed king. That is why it asks where God's former mercies are.

For today: when you feel ashamed or mocked for following God, do not keep it silent. Bring it to God in prayer with honesty. And like the psalm, end by blessing God, trusting that He remains faithful.
exp.125:1:
It says that when God sets them free, the people will be filled with laughter and songs of praise. Where the wording is "shall be filled," the sense is "will be filled completely." The "nations" are the neighboring peoples, who will see what happened and acknowledge that the Lord acted on behalf of his people. "Among these" refers to the Israelites.

It is a song of ascents, probably one of those sung on the way up to Jerusalem. The people of Israel speak, remembering or hoping for the return from captivity. Many connect it with the return from Babylon, though the text does not say so with certainty. The verses that follow show joy over what has already been experienced and also a prayer asking for further restoration.

Today, when you go through a hard season, remember what God has already done for you and tell others about it. Your testimony of gratitude can encourage someone else and show them that God is still at work.
exp.17:12:
The explanation says that God made his voice heard from the heavens like thunder. "The Highest" is another name for God, showing that he is above all things. The phrase "gave his voice" is an older way of saying it. Along with the thunder came hail and "coals of fire," an image of lightning and embers that accompany a storm.

David speaks in a song of thanksgiving for having been rescued from his enemies and from Saul (as the title of the psalm indicates). He uses poetic, stormy language to describe how God acts with power on behalf of the one who calls out to him. It is not known whether he remembers a specific storm; many understand it as an image.

For today: when you feel your problems are too large, remember that God is greater. Call out to him with confidence, because he listens and can act on your behalf.
exp.118:122:
He says that the psalmist's eyes grew tired, almost worn out, from looking and waiting so long. He was waiting for "salvation," which here means rescue or deliverance from God. He also waited for "the word of your righteousness," that is, God's word or promise, which is just and true. The word "failed" means that his eyes grew weak and were spent.

The speaker is the author of Psalm 119, a believer who loves God's Word. At this moment he feels surrounded by oppressors and proud people, and so he asks for help. His waiting has been long and painful, but he has not stopped trusting. Then he asks for mercy and teaching. It is not known for certain who wrote this psalm.

Today, when an answer from God seems slow, you can honestly tell him that you are tired. But keep looking toward Him and lean on His written promises. Read one promise from the Bible today and repeat it in prayer.
exp.39:1:
He says that God drew the psalmist up out of a "pit of misery," that is, a pit or hole of anguish, and out of the miry clay, a mud in which one sinks. Then God set his feet upon a rock, a firm stone, and "established my goings," that is, made his path secure so that he could walk safely.

The speaker is David, according to the title of the psalm. He had waited patiently for God, and God heard him. The writer uses images of mire and rock to describe a difficult situation from which he could not get out on his own. The text does not say exactly what that distress was, so it is not wise to invent it. His rescue ends in a new song of praise.

For today: if you are caught in a heavy situation, keep crying out to God with patience. He can give you firmness and direction. When he rescues you, tell others about it to encourage them to trust.
exp.108:23:
He says that the psalmist's knees are weak because he has gone a long time without eating. His body looks thin and without strength. Here, "fatness" means body fat, that is, he has lost weight. "Faint" means worn out, without strength.

The text speaks of David, according to the title of the psalm, though some scholars think the words may later have been used by others who were suffering. He is being accused and attacked with lies by people he had previously treated with kindness. His fasting seems to show distress and a plea to God; the Bible does not say exactly how long it lasted. Shortly afterward he mentions the mockery of his enemies and asks God for help.

When pain leaves you without strength, you do not have to pretend that you are fine. You can bring your weariness and anguish honestly before God, as the psalmist does, and ask for his help and his mercy.
exp.33:19:
He watches over the righteous completely, like someone who guards every bone of their body so that none of them is broken. "Keepeth" means protects or takes care of. The picture is of total protection, not necessarily a promise that there will never be any wounds.

David wrote this psalm, which recalls the time God rescued him from a great danger. It speaks of the many troubles the righteous suffer, but also of God's help in all of them. In John 19:36, the evangelist quotes this line when he tells how Jesus' bones were not broken on the cross. In this way, the verse finds a deeper fulfillment in Christ.

For today: even when you go through trials, God does not let go of you or forget you. Trust that he cares for you in every detail, and bring to him in prayer today whatever hurts you or worries you.
exp.105:4:
It says that the psalmist asks God to remember him and save him, with a purpose: to see the good of the chosen ones, that is, of the people God chose. He wants to rejoice in the gladness of your nation, the people, and to take pride in them, together with your inheritance, the people who belong to God as a possession.

The one speaking is a psalmist, whose name the text does not give. He speaks on behalf of the people of Israel. He asks for God's help, but not only for himself; he wants to share in the good of everyone. Right after this, the psalm confesses Israel's sins from the time of their ancestors in Egypt. That is why his plea is humble.

For today: when you ask something of God, include others in your prayer. Seek to be part of a community of faith, and sincerely rejoice in the good that God does in the lives of others.
exp.77:59:
This verse says that God abandoned the tabernacle at Shiloh, the sacred tent where he had lived among his people. "Abandoned" means that he withdrew his presence from that place. The tabernacle was the tent of worship, and Shiloh was the town where it stood for many years.

The psalm is written by Asaph, who recalls the history of Israel. Before this verse, the people had provoked God with their idols and their high places of false worship. Afterward, the text speaks of the defeat and the loss of the ark, which many understand as what happened in 1 Samuel 4. Asaph recalls this to show the danger of unfaithfulness.

For today: let us not take God's blessing for granted while we live in any way we please. Having religious things is not enough; God seeks a faithful heart. Let us examine whether anything occupies the place that only he should have, and turn back to him with humility.
exp.84:2:
It says that God set aside all his "saña," which is his strong anger, and turned away from the burning of his wrath. It is a poetic way of saying that God stopped punishing his people and returned to treating them with favor.

The psalmist speaks on behalf of the sons of Korah, a group of musicians in worship in Israel. He remembers how God restored his people, probably after the exile, although the psalm does not give all the details. Looking back at that past gives him confidence to ask for help in the present, as the following verses show.

For today: when you feel weighed down by mistakes or difficulties, remember the times God has already forgiven you and lifted you up. That memory can give you courage to pray again with confidence and wait for his mercy.
exp.68:5:
Here David asks God that his suffering would not bring shame on those who trust in the Lord. Being "ashamed" and "confounded" means being humiliated, as if their hope in God had been in vain. "Those who wait on you" are those who trust God patiently, and "those who seek you" are those who want to live close to Him.

The psalm is attributed to David, who speaks out of deep distress. He has many enemies without cause, and he acknowledges that he is not perfect, saying, "You know my foolishness." Even so, he is concerned that his fall or his pain might discourage other believers. Some also see in this psalm a foreshadowing of Christ, because the New Testament quotes parts of it.

For today: when you go through trials, remember that the way you respond can encourage or discourage others. Ask God that your life, even in weakness, may be a witness that He is faithful.
exp.146:18:
He declares his word to the people of Jacob, that is, to Israel. Here "declares" does not mean accuse; it means announce or make known. "Statutes" are his rules or laws, and "judgments" are his just decisions, his ordinances for living well. "Jacob" and "Israel" are two names for the same people.

The author of the psalm is not known with certainty; it is a song of praise to God. Before this, it speaks of God's power over nature: the ice, the cold, the wind. The same word that melts the ice is the one God gave to Israel. The psalmist marvels that the Creator of all also drew near to his people to speak to them. The following verse says that he did not do this with other nations.

Today we can value the Bible as a gift, not as a burden. God spoke so that we might know him. This week, read a passage with gratitude and ask him to soften your heart through his word.
exp.118:145:
Here the psalmist says to God, "I cried unto thee," that is, he called out for help with loud, urgent pleading. He begs God to save him and promises to keep God's testimonies, meaning to obey and honor his commands and teachings.

Psalm 119 celebrates the law of God. It is not known for certain who wrote it, though many attribute it to David. The speaker is in distress, perhaps persecuted, and seeks God with all his heart. This verse belongs to the section of the psalm where the cry for help and the hope placed in God's word come together.

For today: when you are in trouble, pray sincerely and without hiding your need. But let your prayer not be only a request for relief. Ask God to help you also live as he teaches, and decide to obey him.
exp.64:1:
This verse says that God hears prayer, and that for this reason every person can draw near to Him. "Flesh" is an old way of saying "human being." "Unto thee" means "to you." That is: God hears, and all human beings are invited to come to Him.

The speaker is David, or the psalm is attributed to him, and he directs it as a song of praise in Zion, where the place of worship was. Earlier he speaks of fulfilling vows, or promises made to God. Then he acknowledges that guilt weighs heavily, but that God forgives rebellions. Some think that "all flesh" includes even other peoples; the text does not spell this out.

For today: pray with confidence, without waiting to have a perfect life. If you feel guilt, bring it to God with sincerity, remembering that He hears and forgives. Today, set aside a few minutes to speak with Him without rush.
exp.3:0:
This verse opens with a musical note: it is for the choir director, with stringed instruments (Neginoth), and it is a psalm of David. Then David asks God to answer when he cries out. He calls him "God of my righteousness," that is, the God who defends what is right in his cause. He says that God gave him room in distress, meaning God gave him space and relief when he felt hemmed in. That is why he asks for mercy and for God to hear his prayer.

David is probably speaking during a time of opposition, since in the verses that follow he confronts those who stain his honor and love lies. The psalm does not say with certainty what exact situation he was facing, and some think of Absalom's rebellion, but this is only a guess.

For today: when you feel pressed down by pressure or injustice, remember how God helped you before and pray with that confidence. Ask him for help honestly, without pretending to be strong.
exp.88:48:
Here the psalmist asks God where his former lovingkindnesses are, that is, those past demonstrations of goodness and faithfulness. He reminds God that he had sworn to David, by his truth (his faithfulness), that David's descendants would reign. "Swarest" means that God made a solemn promise.

Psalm 89 is attributed to Ethan the Ezrahite, according to its heading. It first celebrates God's covenant with David. But at this point, the people seem to be suffering defeat and mockery, and the anointed king appears humiliated. That is why the psalmist, with pain and sincerity, asks for an explanation. Interpreters do not agree on the exact moment in history this refers to.

For today: when you feel that God is slow or that his promises seem distant, you can tell him so honestly, as the psalmist does. Praying with questions is not a lack of faith; it is bringing your pain to the God who remains faithful.
exp.73:6:
They have set fire to the holy places of God. The "sanctuaries" are the places set apart for Him. To "defile" something means to treat as common what is holy. "The dwelling place of thy name" is the place where God had chosen to be worshiped, and "casting down to the ground" means they tore it down completely.

The one speaking is the psalmist, called Asaph, who cries out to God on behalf of his people before a great destruction of the temple. Scholars do not agree on whether this refers to the fall of Jerusalem in 586 B.C. or to some other moment of attack. What is clear is his pain and confusion, for he asks why God allows this.

For today: when you see something you love being destroyed, do not keep your pain silent. Bring it honestly to God, as the psalmist did, and remember that He is still King.
exp.134:1:
This verse continues the call to praise. It speaks of "ye that stand in the house of the Lord," meaning those who served or gathered in the temple, and of those who stood "in the courts of the house of our God," the open courtyards that surrounded the sanctuary. The name of God appears in the verse as "the Lord," and the "courts" are the spaces where the people gathered.

The psalm does not say who wrote it. The speaker is a psalmist who invites God's servants to praise him. It was probably sung in temple worship. The reason he gives next is that God is good and chose Israel as his people.

For today: if you belong to a church or faith community, do not simply attend. When you meet with other believers, praise with your mind and your heart. Today, give thanks to God for one specific kindness you have received.
exp.102:5:
This verse says that God does what is right and defends the cause of all who suffer violence or abuse. "Suffer violence" means being oppressed, mistreated, or treated unjustly. The words "does justice and right" mean that God acts to put wrong things right and to protect the weak.

The speaker is David, according to the heading of the psalm. He praises God and encourages himself to remember God's benefits: forgiveness, rescue, and care. After speaking of what God has done for him, David looks around at others and shows that God also cares about the oppressed. Then he recalls how God made himself known to Moses and to Israel, as a compassionate God.

For today: if you suffer injustice, you can pray with hope, because God sees. And if you have the opportunity, defend someone who is being mistreated, imitating the heart of God.
exp.108:19:
This verse asks that what has been said in the verses before it, the curse like a garment, be God's answer to those who slander the one speaking. "Reward" in the verse means a payment or what is deserved, and the phrase about speaking evil against the soul means they are speaking evil against his life or his person.

The one speaking is David, according to the title of the psalm. He is being falsely accused by people he had treated with kindness. Instead of taking revenge himself, he hands the case over to the Lord. This kind of psalm is called imprecatory. Some read it as a cry for justice, and others point out that Jesus taught us to love our enemies.

For today: when you are hurt by unjust words, do not repay evil with evil. Tell God everything honestly, even your pain and your anger, and leave justice in his hands. Then also ask him for a heart free of resentment.
exp.32:13:
This verse says that God, from the place where he reigns, looks closely at all the people who live on the earth. The phrase "the place of his habitation" is an old way of saying the place where God sits as King, that is, heaven. "Those who live on the earth" are the people who dwell on the earth.

Psalm 33 is a song of praise. It does not say who wrote it, although many versions connect it with David because of its link to the psalm before it. The psalmist invites the people to praise God because he is faithful, he is the Creator, and he rules over the nations. Here he reminds us that no one escapes the gaze of God, neither kings nor mighty armies.

For today: if God sees everyone, he also sees you. You can rest in the knowledge that your life, your struggles, and your prayers do not go unnoticed by him. Trust in his care, and not in your own strength.
exp.77:9:
The explanation says that the children of Ephraim did not keep the covenant God made with his people, and that they refused to live according to his law. "Keep" here means to fulfill and obey. "Walk in his law" means living day by day according to his commands. It was not an oversight but a decision: "they refused."

This is a psalm of Asaph, which teaches the children of Israel by using the history of their people. It wants the new generation not to repeat the mistakes of their ancestors. The following verses explain the root of the problem: they forgot the wonders that God had done in Egypt. Some think Ephraim represents the northern tribes, although the exact detail is debated.

For today: remembering what God has done in your life strengthens obedience. Write down his answers and keep them, so that you do not live forgetting his faithfulness.
exp.118:2:
The explanation says that those who walk in God's ways do not practice wickedness. "Iniquity" means injustice or wrongdoing, and "walk in his ways" means living according to what God teaches. It does not speak of people without faults, but of those whose life has a direction guided by God, and this shows in the fact that their conduct is not ruled by evil.

The psalm does not say who wrote it; tradition attributes it to David, but this is not certain. It is a poem that praises God's law, and each group of verses begins with a Hebrew letter; this section is marked by the first letter of the Hebrew alphabet. The speaker admires those who obey and, in verse 5, confesses a desire to be like them.

Today we can ask ourselves each day: "What path am I following?" Reading the Bible and praying in the morning helps guide our decisions, and so wickedness gradually loses its place, without our having to pretend to be perfect.
exp.108:24:
Here the psalmist says that he has become a source of mockery and shame to his enemies. When they looked at him, they shook their heads, a gesture of contempt that showed they saw him with scorn and without compassion.

The one speaking is the psalmist, traditionally identified with David, though the text gives no further details. He is weak, sick, and surrounded by accusers. He has fasted, he is very thin, and he feels like a shadow that is fading away. In the midst of that rejection, he does not take revenge: he cries out to God and asks for help according to his mercy.

For today: when others despise you or judge you, you do not have to respond with bitterness. You can bring your pain to God honestly, ask for his help, and trust that he sees what others do not understand.
exp.118:98:
He says the psalmist has more understanding than all his teachers, and he gives the reason: because he meditates on God's decrees. The word "decrees" refers to the commands and teachings God gave so that his people would know them. The word "teachers" refers to those who instruct. The word "meditation" here means thinking about something again and again, with attention.

The speaker is the author of Psalm 119, a believer who loves God's law and keeps it in mind all day long. It is not known for certain who wrote it. He does not claim to be wiser by his own ability; his advantage comes from devoting time to God's Word. In the verses that follow, he joins that understanding to obedience.

For today: set aside a few minutes each day to read a passage of the Bible and go over it calmly. Ask yourself what it teaches you about God and how you can put it into practice. In this way you will grow in wisdom, without looking down on those who teach you.
exp.104:27:
He sent darkness over Egypt and made it dark.
