The final phrase, "they rebelled not against his word", is difficult: some understand that Moses and Aaron obeyed what God commanded them; others, that the darkness itself carried out God's order. There are translations that say the opposite, that Egypt did rebel. For that reason it is wise to read it with caution.

It is a psalm of praise that recalls the history of Israel. The author reviews how God kept his promise to Abraham and freed his people from Egypt through Moses and Aaron. The plagues are told here to show the power and faithfulness of God. Egypt is also called by another name in the psalm.

When God asks something of you, simple obedience is an act of trust. Moses and Aaron did not understand everything, but they obeyed, and God worked through them.
exp.117:15:
The explanation says that this verse speaks of the right hand of God being raised high, that is, that God is great and powerful. And that same hand does mighty deeds, which means acts of power and victory. The "right hand" is the hand of the Lord, a symbol of strength and action. The name of the Lord is the name the verse refers to.

The psalmist speaks on behalf of a people who give thanks. He has passed through a great danger and God has rescued him. For this reason there are songs of joy in the tents of the righteous. The verses that follow say that he was severely punished, but not handed over to death. It is not known with certainty whether a king or the whole people is speaking; it has been understood in both ways.

For today: when God helps you through a difficulty, do not keep it to yourself in silence. Make a list of what He has done for you and tell someone about it, to encourage their faith.
exp.44:15:
This verse speaks to the king and promises him that, instead of his ancestors, he will have children. They will be princes, that is, rulers with authority, throughout the whole earth.

Psalm 45 is a royal wedding song. The psalmist addresses the king on the day of his marriage, and at this point speaks to him with blessing and hope. The children will continue his line and his work. Christians often also see here a reference to the Messiah, and the New Testament applies part of this psalm to Christ (Hebrews 1:8-9). Some scholars read it first as a psalm for a king of Israel in his own time.

For today: what we do in faith can bless those who come after us. We can dedicate time to teaching, praying, and setting a good example for children, young people, or brothers and sisters, trusting that God can use that seed beyond our lifetime.
exp.21:16:
He says that the one speaking is so thin and worn down from suffering that he could count all his bones one by one. Meanwhile, others look at him fixedly, like spectators.

It is a psalm of David, a prayer of distress. He feels surrounded by enemies, weak and humiliated, yet he keeps crying out to God. The New Testament connects this psalm with the cross of Jesus, since the Gospels mention the dividing of his garments, and Jesus quoted the opening of the psalm. Christians often see here a foreshadowing of Christ's suffering, although the psalm also expresses David's real experience.

When you feel exposed, weak, or judged by others, do not hide your pain. Bring it to God honestly, as the psalmist did, and trust that He does not turn away from you.
exp.106:0:
The psalmist calls us to praise, that is, to give thanks and speak well of the Lord, the name of Israel's God. He gives two reasons: God is good, and his mercy endures forever. The word "mercy" translates a Hebrew term that speaks of faithful love, of a kindness that does not break.

This psalm does not say who wrote it. Many believe it was composed after the return from exile, because it speaks of people gathered from the lands, though this is understood in several ways. The speaker calls the redeemed to sing, those whom God rescued from distress, so that they will acknowledge what he has done for them.

Today you can note three things in which you saw God's goodness this week and thank him for them in prayer. In this way you remember that his love does not depend on your circumstances.
exp.43:24:
The explanation says that the people are completely brought down and humbled. The phrase "bowed down" means crushed and weighed down by the weight of suffering. The phrases "to the dust" and "cleaveth unto the earth" paint a picture of someone lying flat on the ground, without strength to rise. "Belly" here refers to the whole body.

This psalm is a collective prayer of the people of Israel, traditionally attributed to the sons of Korah. They speak in the plural, "our soul." They have suffered defeat and the mockery of their enemies, yet they feel that they have not abandoned God. Scholars do not agree on the exact historical moment when it was written. What is clear is an honest cry, one that tells God what hurts.

For today: when you find yourself on the ground, do not pretend to be strong. Speak to God with sincerity, as this people did, and seek the support of your community of faith. Crying out is also a way of trusting.
exp.138:9:
It says that even if a person goes to the farthest place, God does not leave them alone: his hand guides them, and his right hand, that is, his right hand, holds them firmly. The word "hold" in the verse means "to take hold of" or "to grasp firmly." God's hand both guides and holds.

The psalm is spoken by King David, according to its title. He reflects on how God knows him completely and is present everywhere. The verses before this one mention the heavens, the depths, and the farthest edge of the sea as places one cannot escape from God. Here the tone is not one of fear but of comfort: God's presence accompanies.

For today: when you feel far away, lost, or in an unfamiliar place, such as a new job, an illness, or a move, pray with confidence. Ask God to guide you, and remember that he holds you even when you do not feel his closeness.
exp.8:0:
The note at the start of this verse was for the choir director: it was to be sung "to the tune of Muth-labben," which probably names a familiar melody or musical theme. Its exact meaning is unclear, and scholars explain it in several different ways. Then David promises to praise the Lord with his whole heart, meaning with complete sincerity, and to tell of all his wonderful works, that is, the astonishing things God has done.

David is the one speaking. He writes a song of thanksgiving, and the verses that follow show that God had rescued him from his enemies. That is why his praise grows out of what he remembers and has lived through.

We can do the same today: write down, or tell someone, one specific thing God helped you with this week. Recalling his works out loud or in writing strengthens faith and leads us to give thanks with our whole heart, not only with words.
exp.80:1:
This verse invites the people to begin the festival with music. The phrase "Take a psalm" is like saying: start singing. To "bring hither" means to bring here, and it points to the instrument, the timbrel, a percussion instrument similar to a tambourine. The harp and the psaltery were stringed instruments, and the word "pleasant" speaks of a sound that is agreeable to hear.

The psalm is of Asaph, a musician of the temple. Here it seems to speak to Israel before a special feast, perhaps one of those celebrated at the new moon, as the verses that follow suggest. It calls them to worship God with joy, remembering that He is their strength. Scholars do not agree on which feast exactly it was.

Today we can give praise a real place in the week. Singing to God, alone or with family, with eagerness and gratitude, reminds us that He is our strength, especially on difficult days.
exp.77:49:
He opened a way for his anger, as one who lets free passage to something that was already coming. He did not prevent them from dying, but handed them over to the plague or pestilence. The Hebrew-style phrase "spared not" means he did not hold back their soul from death. The verse speaks of the plague that reached the people in Egypt, after the ones that fell on the livestock.

The psalm is by Asaph, and it recalls before Israel the story of the plagues of Egypt and the departure of the people. Its purpose is to teach new generations not to forget what God did, nor to repeat the rebellion of their ancestors. Some understand the pestilence as a separate plague; others understand it as a general description of the judgment on Egypt.

For today: do not take lightly the holiness of God or his patience. He is just, and he also rescues his people, as sheep. If you hear his voice today, do not harden your heart; trust in his care and obey him with humility.
exp.114:8:
This verse is a direct invitation to the people of Israel: trust in the Lord, because he helps and protects them like a shield. The name of God appears in a form that your reader does not see here, and the word "shield" speaks of protection in the midst of danger.

The psalm speaks first about idols, which have hands, feet and a mouth but cannot do anything. Then comes this call, which is repeated to Israel, to the house of Aaron (the priests) and to those who fear God. It is not known with certainty who is speaking; many think it is a voice that leads the people in worship, like a song in which one part answers another.

Today we can ask ourselves where we place our trust: money, work or our own plans. When worries come, we can pray and say: "Lord, you are my help and my shield."
exp.118:118:
This verse says that God removes the wicked from the earth the way dross is removed, which is the waste that comes off metal when it is melted down. What has no value is set aside and destroyed. That is why the psalmist says he loves God's decrees, that is, God's teachings and commands. The phrase "God burns them away" means that God puts an end to them.

The one speaking is the author of Psalm 119, a believer who loves God's Word. He has just said that whoever turns away from God's laws deceives himself. Seeing how God deals with evil, he feels reverence and wants to follow God more closely. Right after this, he says that his body trembles before God.

Today we can learn that God's Word is what endures and has true worth. Before deciding something important, ask yourself whether it agrees with what God teaches, and choose to love his Word with reverence.
exp.68:28:
This verse says that the one speaking feels afflicted and in pain, that is, humbled, poor, and deeply troubled. Even so, he trusts that God's salvation will rescue him. The explanation of the older wording is that "salvation" here means deliverance or rescue, and the phrase about being set up on high means being lifted to a safe place.

The one speaking is David, according to the title of the psalm. He is being attacked and rejected unjustly, and shortly before this he asked for justice against his enemies. Here his focus shifts: he stops speaking about them and returns to trusting God. He then promises to praise God with songs, and says that this pleases God more than a sacrifice.

For today: when you feel hurt or without a way out, do not wait until everything is resolved before coming close to God. Tell Him honestly how you are doing, ask for His help, and trust that He can lift you up. Praising Him in the middle of pain also strengthens hope.
exp.61:9:
It says that we should not place our trust in violence or in robbery, nor let ourselves become full of pride. The word about taking things by force is rewritten here as the verse's own wording: it speaks of trusting in oppression and of becoming vain in robbery. The phrase about not thinking oneself so important is handled by the verse's "become not vain," so the sentence about it is removed. And if riches increase, we should not set our heart on them.

It is a psalm attributed to David. He himself trusts that only God is his rock and his salvation. Earlier he says that people, whether rich or poor, are as fragile as a breath. Then he affirms that strength and steadfast love belong to God. For this reason, nothing that the world offers as security compares with Him.

We can be thankful for what we have and work with honesty, but without resting our peace on money or power. If things are going well for you today, use your goods generously and remember that your true security is in God.
exp.73:21:
The explanation says the psalmist asks God to rise up and defend his own cause, that is, his honor and his people. The word "plead" means to defend someone the way a lawyer does. The "foolish man" is the fool who lives as if God did not matter. The "reproacheth" means insults or mocks. The request is that God remember that this mockery happens every day.

It is a psalm of Asaph, or of someone from his group of singers. It probably reflects Israel's anguish after the destruction of the temple, although scholars do not agree on the exact moment. The people feel humiliated and make their request by relying on the covenant God made with them.

When you see mockery against God or injustice that hurts you, bring it before him in prayer with sincerity. Do not take revenge or become bitter; trust that God defends his name and cares for those who suffer.
exp.14:1:
This verse begins to answer the psalmist's question: who may live near God? It says that this is the person who "walketh uprightly," that is, who lives honestly and wholly, without a double life. It also "worketh righteousness," meaning they do what is right toward others. And "speaketh the truth in his heart," which means that sincerity is not merely on the lips but springs from within.

David wrote this psalm, and the dwelling place and the holy hill speak of the place where God was present among his people. The question does not seek a checklist for earning God's favor, but to show the character of someone who truly loves him. The verses that follow make it clearer with examples of how to treat one's neighbor.

Today you can ask yourself: do what I think, what I say, and what I do agree? This week, choose a situation where it would be easy to exaggerate or pretend, and decide to be sincere.
exp.52:3:
This verse asks a question with a tone of rebuke: do the people who practice wickedness not understand? It says they prey on God's people as naturally as someone eats bread, without a second thought. And it adds that they do not call on God or seek him.

The phrase "workers of iniquity" means people who practice wickedness.

The author is David, according to the title of the psalm, although some scholars think it was adapted later. He speaks with pain, because he sees corrupt people who oppress believers and live as if God did not exist. It is nearly the same as Psalm 14, and the psalm ends with the hope that God will rescue his people.

For today: when you see injustice, do not lose hope. God sees and acts. Also guard your own heart: live each day in prayer, and treat others with justice and respect.
exp.39:0:
David says he waited for God with patience, that is, without giving up or despairing. "Patiently" here does not mean accepting things with sadness, but enduring with steadfastness. Then God bent down toward him, like someone who stoops to listen closely, and heard his cry, his plea for help. The words "To the chief Musician" were a note for the director of the singers.

David is the speaker, according to the psalm's heading. The verses that follow tell that God lifted him out of a pit of misery and mire, and gave him a new song. Interpreters see a difficult situation here, but the text does not say exactly what it was.

For today: when you pray and the answer is slow in coming, keep waiting with confidence. Meanwhile, remember that God listens to you closely, and write down the times he has already helped you to strengthen your faith.
exp.83:7:
This verse is a simple and direct prayer. The psalmist asks God to hear him. He calls him "O Lord God of hosts," meaning the Lord who has power over all things, and also "God of Jacob," the God who cared for Israel from its ancestors. "Selah" is a word that probably marks a pause for reflection or praise, though its exact meaning is not known for certain.

The one speaking is a pilgrim on the way to the temple in Zion (Jerusalem). The journey is long and hard, and it even passes through a place of dryness, a valley that can be understood in several ways, such as a dry valley or a valley of tears. Even so, he longs to be close to God, and so he prays with confidence.

For today: when the road grows tiring, speak to God honestly. Ask him to hear you and to sustain you, and trust that he draws near to those who seek him.
exp.106:9:
It tells of people who lived in complete darkness, in "the shadow of death," an expression for extreme danger and deep anguish. They were "imprisoned," that is, shut in, and bound with "irons," or chains of metal. Their affliction was like a prison.

The psalmist calls us to praise God for his mercy. This is the first example of several groups he rescued. The verses that follow explain that this imprisonment came from rebelling against the words of God. Even so, the psalm does not end there: God hears them when they cry out. The psalm does not say who wrote it, and many see it as a song for the people after returning from exile.

For today: if you feel trapped in darkness, whether because of your mistakes or difficult circumstances, do not think there is no way out. Cry out to God sincerely, and remember how faithful he has been before.
exp.71:10:
It says that all kings will bow down before this king and that all nations will serve him. The old wording "shall fall down before him" is an older way of saying "will bow down before him." The word "nations" means peoples or nations.

This psalm is attributed to Solomon, though the heading can also be understood as "for Solomon." It is a prayer for the king of Israel, asking that he rule with justice. The verses that follow show why he deserves honor: he cares for the poor and the afflicted. Many Christians also see here a foreshadowing of Christ, the perfect King, although the psalm first describes a king of Israel.

Today, this verse invites us to ask whom we truly serve. If Jesus is King, his way of ruling should shape ours: serving with humility and paying attention to the needy whom no one else attends to.
exp.108:12:
He says that this man's descendants should be cut off, as a tree is cut down, and that in the following generation his name should be blotted out. "Posterity" means children and descendants. "Cut off" means cut down. "Blotted out" means scraped away or erased completely.

David speaks in a psalm of complaint. A wicked man was accusing him with lies and repaying his good with hatred (vv. 2-5). These words are a cry for justice, and a very harsh one, and in the culture of that time erasing a name was the worst loss. Some believe David is quoting what his enemies say against him, but others see it as his own request. There is no certainty.

For today: when you are hurt, do not seek revenge. Bring your pain to God with sincerity, and let him judge. Jesus also taught us to pray for those who harm us (Matthew 5:44).
exp.88:39:
He says that God has broken down the defenses of the anointed king. "Broken through" means making breaches, tearing openings in a wall; the "walls" are the barriers that protect; the "strongholds" are the fortified cities or castles. The speaker feels that God himself left his king defenseless.

Psalm 89 is attributed to Ethan the Ezrahite. First it celebrates God's promises to David, and from verse 38 on it laments that everything seems to have collapsed. Many think it reflects a defeat of the kingdom of Judah, but the psalm does not say exactly when it happened. The psalmist does not hide his complaint: he speaks frankly to God, because he trusts that he is the one who can answer.

For today: when you feel that your defenses have crumbled and you do not understand God, do not stay silent or pretend. Bring your pain to him honestly, remembering his promises, as the psalmist did. A sincere complaint can also be a form of faith.
exp.88:28:
God says he will keep the line of David alive forever, and that his throne will last as long as the heavens. "Seed" means descendants, children, and heirs. "The days of heaven" is an image of something that endures, like the sky above us.

Here God speaks, according to the psalmist Ethan the Ezrahite, recalling the promise God made to David (2 Samuel 7). God affirms his covenant with the royal house. The verses that follow say that if the children turn away, there will be correction, but the promise will not be cancelled. Many Christians see in this a foreshadowing of Jesus, a descendant of David, whose kingdom does not end.

For today: when everything seems unstable, trust that God keeps what he promises. Pray today, thanking him for his faithfulness, and obey him in one concrete decision.
exp.54:14:
Here the psalmist asks that death overtake his enemies suddenly. The word rendered "hell" in the earlier text refers to the place of the dead, the Hebrew word Sheol, which usually names the realm of the dead. The phrase "go down quick" suggests a sudden fall, perhaps like the event in Numbers 16. He says that wickedness is in their dwellings and among them.

David, or whoever wrote this psalm, is wounded by the betrayal of a close friend, someone with whom he shared closeness and worship. It is a prayer of pain, called an imprecatory prayer. He does not seek revenge with his own hands, but brings his complaint before God. Then he says that he will call on God and that God will save him.

When someone brings you pain, do not hold onto it or take revenge. Tell God honestly what you feel and entrust justice into His hands. Jesus also taught us to pray for those who hurt us.
exp.101:7:
It says that all day long the enemies of the speaker insult him and humiliate him. To "reproach" is to dishonor or insult someone in public. Those who are most angry with him have banded together, that is, they have agreed as a group to set themselves against him.

The psalm carries a heading that describes it as the prayer of one who is afflicted and pours out his complaint before God. It is not known for certain who wrote it. The one speaking is alone, sick or crushed in spirit, and feels rejected. For that reason he is compared to lonely birds of the desert. He also feels that he suffers under the anger of God, though at the end of the psalm he remembers that God endures forever.

For today: if you feel attacked or alone, do not keep your pain to yourself. Tell it to God honestly, as this psalmist does. Praying this way is not a lack of faith; it is seeking refuge in the One who does listen.
exp.12:5:
It says that the psalmist promises to sing to God, that is, to praise him with joy, because God has dealt well with him. The word "Jehovah" is the name of God, and "has done me good" means that he has treated him with generosity and care.

The one speaking is David, according to the psalm's heading. He began the psalm in anguish, asking how long, and feeling forgotten and threatened by his enemies. But he ends by changing his tone: he trusts in God's mercy, and his heart rejoices in his salvation, which here means deliverance and rescue. His song is born from trust, even though the difficult situation may not yet be over.

Today we can imitate that step: even in the middle of a struggle, pause and remember, aloud or in prayer, three good things God has done for us. Giving thanks helps us see hope.
exp.101:24:
He says that God laid the foundations of the earth long, long ago, and that the heavens are the work of his hands. The word "of old" means "from the beginning" or "long ago." Where it says "hast laid," the sense is that he set it firm, like someone building a house from its base.

The psalm is written by a person who is deeply distressed, weak, and afraid of dying young. He feels drained of strength and begs God not to cut his life short in the middle of his days. Then he looks toward God and remembers that God is eternal. The verses that follow say that the heavens and the earth will wear out like a garment, but God does not change. Scholars do not agree on who the author was.

When your life feels fragile or uncertain, remember who holds everything up. What worries you today is small compared with the God who made the heavens and does not change. You can pray with confidence and rest in him.
exp.35:10:
This verse is a prayer. The psalmist asks God that the proud person not reach him or trample him, and that the hand of the wicked not make him stumble or drive him from his place. The "foot of pride" is the arrogance of someone who wants to humble others. The "wicked" are those who live without reverence for God. The word "remove" here can be understood as pulling someone away or forcing them out of their place.

The speaker is David, according to the heading of the psalm. He comes after praising God's goodness, the source of life, and his faithfulness. That is why his request grows out of trust: whoever knows God's love knows where to turn when a threat appears. The following verse shows the fall of the wicked.

For today: when you feel pressured by the pride or injustice of others, before you respond in anger, pray with this verse. Remember who your refuge is and ask him to keep you steady.
exp.83:10:
It says that God is like the sun and like a shield. The sun gives light, warmth and life; the shield protects from danger. It also says that the Lord gives grace, that is, his favor and kindness, and glory, which is honor and dignity. And it promises that he will not withhold good from those who walk uprightly, that is, from those who live with sincerity and righteousness.

This psalm was written by a son of Korah, a worshiper who longs to be in the temple. He speaks with joy of God's presence and prefers one day near him to a thousand far away. For that reason he declares who God is: his light and his protection.

For today: trust that God cares for you, even when you do not understand everything. Try to live with honesty in small things, at home and at work. This is not a bargain to earn blessings, but a life of closeness to God, who gives what we truly need.
exp.18:13:
Here the psalmist asks that what he says with his mouth and what he thinks in his heart be pleasing to God. "Acceptable" means agreeable, well received. "Meditation" refers to the deep, quiet thoughts of the heart. He calls God "my strength", that is, a firm and secure refuge, and "my redeemer", that is, the one who rescues and sets him free.

David is said to be the speaker, according to the heading of the psalm. Earlier he praised God for creation and for his Word. Then he acknowledged that he does not always see his own faults, and he asked to be kept from pride and rebellion. This verse closes the psalm as a humble prayer.

Today we can make this prayer a habit. Before speaking, writing a message, or answering in anger, we can pray briefly: "Lord, may what I say and think please you." In this way we let God watch over our words and thoughts.
exp.37:1:
David says he feels that God has struck him with force. The "arrows" are arrows, and the "hand" speaks of the weight of God's punishment. The words "came down" and "has fallen" show that the blow came from above and weighs heavily on him. This is the language of poetry, not of literal wounds.

David speaks in a prayer of pain. The heading says "to remind," so it seems to be a cry to be remembered before God. The verses that follow connect his suffering with his sin, which weighs on him like a burden. Scholars do not know for certain what illness or situation he was living through; the text does not say.

For today: when you feel the weight of your mistakes, do not hide them or run from God. Bring them to Him with honesty, as David did, and ask Him for mercy. He invites the broken to come close to Him.
exp.136:8:
This verse says that the one who takes the children of Babylon and dashes them against the rocks will be happy. "Happy" means joyful or blessed. "Dashes" means striking with violence. It is one of the harshest lines in the whole Bible.

It is spoken by an Israelite exiled in Babylon, with the pain still fresh from the destruction of Jerusalem. It is a psalm of lament, not a command from God. It expresses the desire for justice and revenge of a wounded people, who had seen similar things (2 Kings 8:12; Nahum 3:10). Some see here an honest prayer that leaves vengeance in God's hands; others see an example of raw human grief. Christians often read it in the light of Jesus, who taught love for enemies.

For today: bring your anger and pain to God with sincerity, but hand justice over to Him and ask Him for a heart free of revenge.
exp.112:3:
The explanation says that the Lord is far above all the peoples of the earth, and that his glory is greater than the heavens themselves. "High" means lifted up, supreme. "Nations" means all peoples, not only Israel. The idea is that no one and nothing compares with God in greatness.

Psalm 113 is a song of praise, and it is thought to have been sung at Jewish festivals, such as Passover, though we do not know who wrote it. The verses before this one call people to praise God in every place and at every time. Then the psalm shows something surprising: this God, so high, bends down to look upon the humble and the needy.

When you feel small or worried, remember that God rules over all and yet draws near to you. Praise him today, thanking him for his greatness and his care.
exp.105:19:
It says that the people of Israel exchanged their glory, that is, the glorious God who had brought them out of Egypt, for the image of an ox that eats grass. The word "changed" in this sentence means "exchanged." "Their glory" is understood to mean God himself. The image is the golden calf. It is a strong contrast: the eternal exchanged for something that only eats grass.

The psalmist, whose name is not given, reviews the sins of Israel in the past. He recalls the episode at Horeb (Mount Sinai), when the people made a calf (Exodus 32). He tells it to confess that they and their fathers have been unfaithful, and to praise the patience and mercy of God.

Today we too can exchange God for lesser things: money, success, or approval. Ask yourself honestly what occupies first place in your heart, and return to God with gratitude, remembering what He has done for you.
exp.17:31:
It is God who girds me with strength for battle, like someone tying a belt around the waist before a fight. He also makes my way perfect, meaning He makes it straight, secure, and without fault.

David, the king of Israel, speaks. He wrote this psalm on the day God delivered him from his enemies and from Saul. He looks back and acknowledges that he did not triumph alone. The verses before this one present God as shield and rock, and the verses that follow show Him giving David swiftness and skill in battle.

Today we can remember that the strength to face our struggles does not come from ourselves alone. Before a difficult day, you can pray: "Lord, gird me with your strength and guide my steps." And at the end of the day, give thanks to God for what He has done.
exp.31:7:
The explanation says that God promises two things: to give us understanding and to teach us the right path. The phrase "I will guide you with my eye" is not a threatening watchfulness, but attentive care, like a guide who never loses sight of you. "Understanding" here means God giving us wisdom to grasp what is right.

This is a psalm of David, written after he confessed his sin and was forgiven. Many scholars see in verse 8 the voice of God answering the psalmist, though some think it is David who is teaching others. In either case, the contrast is clear: God guides with closeness, not like a mule that needs a bridle.

Today we can seek God's guidance with humility, before life forces us to pull back. Pray asking for direction, read his Word, and listen to the counsel of mature believers, trusting that God cares for you and never loses sight of you.
exp.40:6:
All who hated me would whisper together against me; against me they would plot my harm. They muttered, that is, they spoke in secret, and they imagined the worst about his situation. The word "hate" here means to despise, and "plot" means to imagine or wish evil things for him. What they say comes in the next verse.

The psalm is spoken by David, according to its heading, though some scholars think the poem may have had a different later use. He is sick and weak, and those around him take the opportunity to wish him dead. Some visit him with false words, and even a close friend betrays him. His pain is twofold: the illness and the disloyalty.

For today: when someone speaks badly of you behind your back, do not answer with revenge. Do what the psalmist does: bring your pain to God honestly, trusting that He sustains you and knows the truth.
exp.0:3:
This verse compares the wicked to chaff, which is the light outer husk of the grain. When wheat was threshed, it was tossed into the air to separate it, and the wind carried that chaff away, since it had no weight or value. The phrase "not so" means that the wicked do not share the situation of the tree in the previous verse: they have no roots and no steadiness.

Psalm 1 is a wisdom poem. It is not known for certain who wrote it, though it is traditionally associated with David. It contrasts two paths: that of the righteous, firm like a tree beside water, and that of the wicked, unstable and without fruit. Its purpose is to invite the reader to choose well.

For today: let us ask ourselves what we are rooted in. When we give time to God's Word, whether by reading it, thinking about it, or praying over it, our lives gain firmness against pressures. Without roots, any wind of opinion or trouble sweeps us along. We can begin with a daily, steady moment of reading.
exp.1:11:
Kissing the Son was an ancient gesture of respect and submission to a king. The verse calls people to humbly submit to the Son, so as not to provoke his anger and be lost on the way.

The psalmist speaks to kings and rulers who rebel against God and his chosen king. First we hear God's voice, and now the psalmist gives a warning with hope. Christians see Christ as the Son in this verse. The Hebrew word for "Son" in this verse is hard, and some translations render it differently.

Today, instead of doing things your own way, hand Christ your plans and your fears. Trusting him brings rest and security.
exp.46:8:
The explanation says that the rulers of the nations gather together with the people of the God of Abraham. The reason is that "the shields of the earth" belong to God. Shields were the protection of a country, and here they stand for the leaders and rulers who defend their people. As for the word "exalted," it means lifted up, placed on high.

The psalm was written by the sons of Korah, probably to be sung in the worship of the people of Israel. It invites us to praise God as King of the whole earth, not only of Israel. Some believe it speaks of a future time when the nations will join together with God; others think it celebrates a specific victory. The text does not fully make this clear.

Today we can remember that no human leader or power is our final protection. Pray for your authorities, but place your security in God, for He is above all of them.
exp.20:4:
He says the king has great glory because of God's salvation. Here "salvation" means deliverance, that is, the victory God gave him. Furthermore, God laid upon him honour and majesty, that is, dignity and splendour recognized by all.

This psalm is by David, or at least it is attributed to him. It is a prayer of thanksgiving for the king, after a victory or a blessing from God. David acknowledges that his glory does not come from his own strength, but from God. Many Christians also see here a prophetic look toward Christ, the ultimate King, though this is interpreted in different ways.

For today: when you receive some achievement or recognition, remember where it comes from. Give thanks to God instead of boasting. What good you have is a gift from him, and that gives you humility and joy at the same time.
exp.101:16:
The verse says that God has heard the prayer of the destitute and has not rejected their plea.

The psalm begins as the prayer of someone in distress who pours out a complaint before God. We do not know with certainty who wrote it. Some connect it to the time of the exile, but this is debated. Here the psalmist trusts that God will raise up Zion, and that this act of mercy toward the weak will be remembered by future generations.

Today, if you feel alone or without strength, you can pray without fear of being ignored. God does not despise the one who cries out with sincerity. Tell Him simply what you carry inside, and trust that He listens.
exp.118:99:
The explanation says that the psalmist has more understanding than the elders, not because he has more years, but because he has obeyed God's commandments. "Elders" are the older people, those who were presumed to have great wisdom. Keeping means putting into practice and obeying, not merely preserving.

Psalm 119 is a long prayer in the form of a poem, and no one knows for certain who wrote it. The speaker loves God's law and meditates on it all day. In the verses nearby he says that he is wiser than his enemies and his teachers. He does not boast; he acknowledges that God himself taught him (v. 102).

For today: wisdom does not depend only on age or study, but on putting into practice what God says. This week, choose one teaching from the Bible and obey it in a concrete situation. As you practice it, you will understand it better.
exp.78:9:
The explanation says that the nations mock and ask, "Where is their God?" For this reason the psalmist asks that God act justly in full view of everyone, bringing judgment on the blood of his servants that has been poured out. Here "revenging" means justice that sets wrong right. The "heathen" are the nations that do not know God.

A group of Israelites, or a voice from the people, speaks after a great destruction. Psalm 79 opens by lamenting that foreigners invaded the land, defiled the temple, and killed many people. Many link it to the fall of Jerusalem, though the psalm does not give the exact date. The people acknowledge their sins, but they also cry out because the name of God is being dishonored.

For today: when you suffer injustice or mockery because of your faith, bring your pain honestly to God and leave vengeance in his hands. Ask him to honor his justice and his name, and to give you a heart that does not repay evil with evil.
exp.77:52:
He led them on safely, so that they did not fear, and the sea covered their enemies who were chasing them. The explanation of the Hebrew-style phrasing is not needed here since the reader sees the verse as written. It refers to the crossing of the Red Sea, when the people passed through and the Egyptians were overwhelmed by the waters.

This psalm is a poem by Asaph that reviews the history of Israel. It wants the new generations to remember what God did and not repeat the disobedience of their ancestors. Here the moment of deliverance is recounted, just after the plagues, as evidence of God's care for his people.

For today: when you face an uncertain path, remember how God has sustained you before. Write down three moments when he took care of you and thank him for them. That remembrance helps you trust and walk with less fear.
exp.32:8:
God created everything simply by speaking. "He spake" and things came into being; "he commanded" and they stood firm. Phrases like "was done" and "stood fast" describe things coming into being and holding their place. His word does not need help to accomplish what it says.

The psalm does not say who wrote it; tradition ascribes it to David, but this is not certain. It is a song of praise to the people of God. First it speaks of the sea gathered together as in a storehouse, and so it calls the whole earth to fear the LORD. Then it shows that this same God frustrates human plans that oppose him, while his purposes remain.

When your problems or the powers of the world seem greater than everything, remember who speaks and things come into being. Trust his word, pray calmly, and rest in the knowledge that his plans do not fail.
exp.106:39:
It says that God humbles proud rulers. "Contempt" means scorn or dishonor. "Princes" are the leaders or nobles. God allows them to go astray and wander, that is, to be lost, without direction and without a path to follow.

The psalmist praises God for how he cares for his people and rules over all. In this psalm it shows that God changes circumstances: sometimes he blesses, sometimes he corrects nations. Here we see that no powerful person is above God. The verse that follows shows the contrast: God lifts up the poor. This same verse also appears in Job 12:21 and 24, with very similar words.

For today: if you hold any office or influence, exercise it with humility and justice, knowing that you answer to God. And if you feel small or overlooked, trust that God sees and can lift up the humble.
exp.138:1:
It says that God knows everything I do, even the most ordinary things: when I sit down and when I rise up. He also understands my thoughts from afar, that is, he knows them before I express them, and even before I fully understand them myself. Here the word "understandest" means that God comprehends, not merely that he knows.

David speaks, according to the title of the psalm, and addresses his words to God in prayer. He does not present God as a watchman who accuses, but as someone who has examined him and knows him thoroughly. The whole psalm meditates on how near God is to us, in every moment of life.

For today: you do not need to pretend before God. When you are confused, tired, or do not know how to express what you feel, speak to him honestly. He already understands your heart and receives you with love.
exp.74:4:
It says we should not be proud or arrogant. The image of "lifting the horn" is one of strength: an animal raising its horns to show off its power. Holding the neck "stiff" means speaking with pride and without humility. To be puffed up means to fill oneself with vanity.

In this psalm of Asaph, God seems to be the one speaking in these verses (some think it is the psalmist, and this is not entirely clear). He declares that he holds up the world when everything is shaking. So he warns the foolish and the wicked not to boast. A person's rise or fall does not depend on other people, but on God, who is the judge.

Today: when you succeed, recognize that everything is a gift from God. Speak with humility and treat others without superiority, because your worth does not depend on showing off.
exp.2:5:
This verse says that the speaker will not be afraid, even though thousands upon thousands of people surround him, ready to attack. The phrase "ten thousands" is a way of saying a huge number. "Have set themselves against me round about" means that they surround him in order to attack.

The title of the psalm attributes it to David, when he was fleeing from his son Absalom. Here he speaks of a real threat. His calm comes from what he said before: he cried out to the LORD, received an answer, and slept peacefully because God sustained him. His courage does not come from his own strength, but from his trust in God.

For today: when you feel that problems surround you, do what David did. Before you worry, pray sincerely, and remember how God has sustained you at other times. That memory helps you rest and face the day with more peace.
exp.63:5:
This verse describes wicked people who seek out evil with great care. The phrase "they search out iniquities" means they look for ways to do wrong and work out every detail. The inward thought and heart of such people are "deep," meaning they are hard to see into or understand. Some translators take this to mean that their intentions are very well hidden.

David prays to God because he is attacked with words and with hidden traps. The wicked feel secure and say, "Who shall see them?" But the psalm goes on to show that God does see, and that in the end He acts. Although the text gives no further details, the tone is that of a righteous man crying out for protection.

For today: when someone plans evil against you in secret, do not despair. Commit your situation to God in prayer, trust that He sees what is hidden, and avoid answering with deceit or revenge.
exp.77:12:
He divided the sea and led the people through it, and the waters stood still and piled up together, like a heap or a wall. The explanation of "the sea" and "made them pass" and "and" has been removed, since those are wording from the original text that does not appear in the verse your reader sees.

The speaker is the psalmist Asaph, who in this psalm recalls Israel's history in order to teach the new generations. He does so because their ancestors forgot God's wonders and rebelled. Here he remembers the crossing of the Red Sea, after the signs in Egypt. It is a reminder that God did keep his word and deliver his people.

For today: when you face something that seems like a dead end, call to mind what God has already done in your life and in his Word. Remembering his faithfulness strengthens trust and keeps fear from having the final word.
exp.20:1:
This verse says that God gave the king what he most desired and did not refuse the request he made in prayer. The phrases "thou hast given him" and "hast not withholden" are two ways of saying the same thing: God answered.

"Selah" is a word that probably marks a pause for reflection or a musical moment, though its exact meaning is not known for certain.

This is a psalm of David, addressed to the chief musician to be sung. The king gives thanks for a victory or a blessing received. Many believers also see here a look toward Christ, the King who was to come, though scholars interpret this in different ways.

For today: when God answers a prayer, do not take it for granted. Pause, as the "Selah" invites, and give thanks in a concrete way. Ask also with a heart that desires what pleases God, because He delights in hearing His children.
exp.106:2:
This verse says that God gathered his people from every part of the world: from the east, from the west, from the north, and from the south. The words "from the north" and "from the south" are explained as the translation of an old word for the north and of the phrase that many understand as the south, though others think it refers to the Mediterranean Sea, to the west. The term for "gathered" means brought back together.

The psalmist calls those who have been rescued from oppression to praise God. He most likely has in mind the people of Israel who returned from exile, although the psalm does not name its author or give the exact date. Then he describes people who were lost, hungry, and thirsty, and whom God rescues. It is a song of thanks for God's faithfulness.

For today: if you feel far away, lost, or alone, remember that God knows how to seek out and gather his own. Give thanks for someone or something through which he has rescued you, and seek to draw near to a community of faith, where others also celebrate his mercy.
exp.49:17:
He says that this person, upon seeing a thief, did not reject him but joined him and ran alongside him. Moreover, his "share" or companionship was with the adulterers, that is, he shared their way of living. Here "share" means taking part or close association.

God himself speaks in this psalm of Asaph. He addresses the wicked one, someone who claims to know God's law and repeats its words, but lives differently. God confronts him because his religion is only on the lips: he despises correction and makes himself a friend of sin.

For today: it is not enough to talk about faith if our friendships and habits contradict what we say we believe. Let us ask God to show us where we have grown accustomed to what He rejects, and give Him one concrete step of change today.
exp.149:0:
This verse begins with "Praise ye the Lord," which means to praise God. It then invites people to praise God "in his sanctuary," which can be understood as the temple in Jerusalem or the place where God is present. It also says "in the firmament of his power," a phrase that many understand as the heavens or sky, where his power is seen. The word "praise" here means to give praise.

This is the first verse of the last psalm, which closes the whole book of Psalms with a call to praise. The author is not named. The speaker invites everyone to praise God, both in the place of worship and throughout all of creation. The verses that follow explain why to praise him and with which instruments.

For today: do not wait until you feel perfect to praise God. Today, at home, at work, or in church, set aside a few minutes to thank him for something specific he has done for you, and do it in your own words or with a song.
exp.79:15:
It says that God's vineyard, which is his people, is burned with fire and cut down. Then the phrase "they perish at the rebuke of thy countenance" is usually understood as a reference to the enemies who burned it, who fall under God's judgment. "Cut down" means ruined and laid waste. "The rebuke of thy countenance" speaks of God's stern gaze that judges.

The speaker is the psalmist, on behalf of Israel, in a prayer of lament. The people are compared to a vineyard that God planted, and now it lies in ruins. We do not know with certainty which historical event is in view; some think of the fall of the northern kingdom, but this is not certain.

For today: when everything seems burned and destroyed, we can speak to God with sincerity and ask him to look upon us again. He can restore what seems lost, and our hope rests on his mercy.
exp.107:9:
Here the psalmist asks who will bring him into a well-defended city and even into Edom (Idumea). A "fortified city" is a city with strong walls. It is a question that shows how very difficult the task seems.

This psalm is attributed to David and joins parts of Psalms 57 and 60. God has promised lands and victory, but Edom still seems out of reach. So, after speaking with confidence, the psalmist acknowledges that he needs God, who will lead him and go out with his armies. The next passage says that the help of man is worthless.

For today: when a goal looks like a walled city, remember God's promises, but do not trust only in your own strength. Ask Him to guide you step by step and to go with you.
exp.93:18:
This verse says that when the psalmist's mind was filled with worries and troubling thoughts, God's comfort brought joy back to his soul. "Many thoughts" are many worries going around inside. "Comforts" are the consolation and encouragement that God gives.

The speaker is the psalmist, whose name the text does not give. He lives in the middle of injustice: later he speaks of corrupt judges who attack the righteous. Before this verse he recounts how God helped and upheld him when he felt his foot slipping. Here he describes how God also sustained him inwardly, in the midst of distress.

When your mind is filled with worries, do not face them alone. Bring them to God in prayer and read his promises in the Bible. He can calm your heart, even if the situation has not yet changed.
exp.105:42:
This verse says that God rescued Israel many times. Yet the people rebelled against his counsel, that is, against his guidance and his instructions. Because of this they ended up brought low, cast down and impoverished, on account of their iniquity. Their iniquity here means their sin and their folly in disobeying.

The psalmist goes over the history of Israel, from Egypt to the time of the judges. He does it as a confession: he acknowledges that the people repeated the same mistake again and again. The psalm does not hide the guilt, but the next verse shows that God still looked on their distress, heard their cry, and remembered his covenant with compassion.

For today: when you notice that you are falling back into the same thing, do not stay in shame or carry on alone. Acknowledge your mistake honestly and listen again to God's guidance. He remains patient and merciful toward whoever cries out to him.
exp.96:4:
It says that the hills, which seem firm and impossible to move, melt like wax when God appears. The name "Lord" is the name of the God of Israel, and "the Lord of the whole earth" presents him as the owner and ruler of the whole world.

The psalm does not name its author. It is a song of praise that celebrates God's reign, using images of fire, lightning and trembling, similar to those of God's appearance at Sinai. It is poetic language: it expresses that nothing created can withstand his presence. The verses that follow contrast him with idols, which can do nothing.

Today we can remember that no problem, however large it may seem, is a mountain before God. When something frightens you, pray and hand it over to the One who rules the whole earth, and trust that his power and his justice are greater.
exp.9:10:
He says in his heart: "God has forgotten everything, he has hidden his face so as not to look, and he will never notice what I am doing." The phrase about hiding the face means that God does not want to see, or cannot see. The words "he will never see it" are what the wicked man convinces himself of.

The psalmist, who does not identify himself in this psalm, is describing a cruel man who traps the poor like a lion in its den. What the wicked man says is a lie that serves to make him feel free of guilt. Right after this, the psalmist prays that God will rise up and not forget the humble, showing that he does trust that God sees.

When someone acts wrongly and no one seems to notice, or when we suffer and feel that God is silent, let us remember that his silence is not absence. We can bring our complaints to him honestly, as the psalmist did, and trust that he sees.
exp.49:16:
He says the wicked person speaks of God's laws, but in truth does not want to be corrected and sets aside His words. Here "instruction" means correction or discipline, not only a painful punishment. "Cast behind" means deliberately ignoring something, like someone who refuses to look at it.

God is speaking, addressing those who claim to be His people. After inviting the faithful to call upon Him, He rebukes the one who talks about the law but lives in another way. The verses that follow show that contradiction: he keeps company with thieves and adulterers, and uses his mouth for evil and deceit.

Today it invites us to examine whether our words about faith match our lives. We can ask ourselves: do I humbly accept it when God, or someone wise, corrects me? Listening to their correction is part of a sincere faith.
exp.99:1:
This verse invites us to serve God with gladness. To serve means to obey and worship him. The verse says "come before his presence," and the word "presence" names the place where a person stands before someone with respect. Joy shown openly is what the verse calls gladness. In this way, we are called to come before God with a cheerful heart.

The psalm is a song of praise, and the text does not say who wrote it. It is addressed to all the earth, not only to Israel. The verses that follow give the reason for this joy: the Lord is God, he made us, and we are his people, like sheep that he cares for. It was probably sung when people entered the temple.

For today: before your tasks, your work, or serving in your church, pause for a moment and give thanks to God for who he is. Serving from gratitude, and not from obligation or weariness, changes the spirit in which you do things.
exp.106:38:
This verse says that some people, after prospering, are once again reduced and brought low. The word translated as "minished" means made smaller or left with less than before; "brought low" means knocked down or discouraged; and "sorrows" refers to deep distress. The cause is oppression, misfortune, and pain.

The psalmist, who is not named, praises God for his faithfulness. In this passage he remembers that God blesses his people with harvests and children, but may also allow times of difficulty. The verses that follow show that God lifts up the poor and humbles the powerful who oppress. Some scholars see here a general warning about how circumstances change; others see it as a reference to judgments upon the people.

For today: do not place your security in what you have, because everything can change. Give thanks to God in good times, and trust Him when trials come, for He is still the one who lifts up the fallen.
exp.111:9:
The wicked will see the blessing and honor of the righteous, and it will fill them with anger and bitterness. Their envy and rage leave them consumed and undone inside. What the wicked desire and plan will not come to pass.

The psalm does not name its author. It is a wisdom poem that describes the person who fears God, who is generous and steadfast of heart. The whole psalm contrasts the life of the righteous, which endures, with the life of the wicked, whose plans fade away. This verse closes that contrast.

For today: do not envy those who prosper by doing wrong, and do not live with resentment. Instead, cultivate a generous heart that trusts in God. Envy consumes us from within, but trust in Him gives us peace and firmness.
exp.88:46:
Remember how short my time is. The psalmist asks God to keep in mind that human life is brief. Then he asks: "wherefore hast thou made all men in vain?" That is, if life is so short and empty, what was the point of creating us? The phrase "all men" means human beings.

The author presents himself as Ethan the Ezrahite, according to the title of the psalm. Earlier he praised God's promises to David, but now he sees the king defeated and humiliated. He is distressed and honestly challenges God: where is your promised faithfulness? Some think he speaks on behalf of the king and others on behalf of the whole people.

For today: when life feels brief or confusing, do not keep quiet. Bring your questions to God in sincere prayer, and remember that He remains faithful even when you do not yet understand.
exp.16:1:
David asks God to be the one who pronounces judgment in his case. The phrase "from before your face" means "from your presence." "Judgment" is the verdict or the just decision. "Uprightness" is what is correct and right. David wants God's eyes to look upon what is just.

David speaks in a prayer, probably in the face of accusations or injustice, though the psalm gives no exact details. He does not turn to people to defend himself, but to God. That is why he says his prayer comes out "without deceitful lips" and that God has tested his heart. He trusts that God sees what is hidden. He does not claim to be perfect, but to be sincere before God.

When you feel judged or misunderstood, bring your case to God honestly. Ask him to examine your heart, correct whatever needs correcting, and give you peace, even when others do not understand you.
exp.65:18:
What it says: The psalmist states with confidence that God did hear him. The word "But" introduces the contrast, and "verily" shows firmness. "Attended" means that God paid attention and answered. "Prayer" refers to a request made out of need and pleading.

Context: The speaker is the psalmist, whose identity we do not know for certain. After praising God for his works, he gives personal testimony. In the verse before, he says that God does not listen to someone who holds wickedness in the heart. Here he contrasts: he cried out with sincerity, and God heard him. He ends by blessing God for his mercy.

For today: Before you pray, ask God to examine your heart and help you let go of whatever keeps you from him. Then pray with confidence and sincerity. God does not look for perfect prayers, but for honest hearts that come to him with humility.
exp.31:9:
It says that those who live without God and reject his guidance suffer many sorrows, while those who trust in the Lord are surrounded by his mercy. The word "wicked" refers to someone who lives without taking God into account. Trusting in the Lord means relying on him and depending on him. The word "surrounded" means encircled, like a protective wall.

It is a psalm of David. He speaks after confessing his sin and receiving forgiveness. In the verses before, God promises to teach him the way and asks him not to be stubborn like a mule, which only obeys when pulled by the bit. This verse sums up the contrast between resisting God and trusting in him.

Today, when you know that something does not please God, do not wait until pressure forces you to change. Confess it soon, trust in him, and obey calmly. His mercy will surround you.
exp.118:76:
The explanation says the psalmist asks God that his mercy, that is, his tender and compassionate love, may come to him so that he may live. He does not ask to live on the basis of his own merit, but by God's goodness. And it explains why: God's law is his delight, that is, his joy and gladness.

The speaker is the author of Psalm 119, a believer who is suffering. Earlier he acknowledged that God was faithful even when he afflicted him, and now he asks for comfort. Later he mentions proud people who slander him. We do not know with certainty who wrote it or what his exact situation was; the text only shows someone wounded who clings to God.

For today: when you are tired or hurt, ask God for his mercy with confidence. Spend a few minutes reading his Word, not as an obligation, but looking for comfort and joy in him.
exp.67:0:
This verse opens with the heading of the psalm: it is addressed to the director of the musicians, it is by David, and it is a song to be sung. Then comes a cry: that God would rise up, that his enemies would be scattered, and that those who hate him would flee before him. The words "let God arise" are a plea for God to act with power.

David is named as the author in the heading. Many believe this prayer is connected to the ark of the covenant, because it resembles the words of Moses in Numbers 10:35. However, the exact occasion of the psalm is not known for certain. It is a song of confidence that God defends his people.

Today we can pray with this same confidence when we face injustice, fear, or pressure. Instead of taking revenge, we ask God to act, and in the meantime we try to live with honesty and hope, knowing that he cares for his own.
exp.135:5:
This verse praises God for having "stretched out the earth above the waters." "Stretched out" means that he spread it out or set it firmly in place. "Mercy" here is his faithful love, the kind that never fails. Each line of the psalm repeats that this love lasts forever.

The psalm is a song of praise from the people of Israel, probably used in worship, where one group recited what God had done and everyone answered with the refrain. It speaks of creation as proof of God's goodness. The image of the earth above the waters reflects how the Israelites saw the world; it is not a scientific explanation but poetic language about the order God gave to creation. Afterward the psalm goes on to the sun, the moon, and the history of Israel.

For today: when you look at the solid ground beneath your feet, remember that God sustains your life with faithfulness. Give thanks to him today for one stable thing he has given you.
exp.23:0:
The explanation says that everything belongs to God. "Jehovah" is the name of God. "Its fullness" means everything that fills the earth: its resources, its creatures, its riches. "The world and those who dwell in it" includes all people, not just one nation.

The title says this is a psalm of David, and the text presents it that way. It is a song of praise that was sung in the worship of the people of Israel. The following verses give the reason: God made the earth and sustains it, so it is his. Then the psalm asks who may approach God on his holy hill. Some think it was used in processions toward the temple, but this is not certain.

For today: if everything belongs to God, what we have is not truly ours but a trust from him. We can live with gratitude and generosity, caring responsibly for our money, our time, and creation.
exp.67:2:
This verse says that righteous people, those who live in friendship with God and in obedience to him, will be filled with joy. They will rejoice in his presence, and their gladness will be so great that they will even leap with delight.

David wrote this psalm, and it begins with a prayer that God would rise up and defeat his enemies. The wicked vanish like smoke or like wax melting before the fire. Against that outcome, the verse shows a contrast: while the wicked flee from God, the righteous rejoice in him. Afterward, the psalm invites them to sing to him, because he cares for orphans and widows.

For today: when you face injustice or fear, remember that God cares for you. Take a moment to thank him aloud or in song, and let your joy rest in him rather than in your circumstances.
exp.33:9:
The explanation says that even the young lions, which are strong and are hunters, can go through need and hunger. But those who seek Jehovah (the Lord) will not lack any good thing. "Lack" means that what is necessary was missing from them.

David is the speaker. The title of the psalm connects it with the time when he pretended to be mad before Abimelech and escaped. He praises God for delivering him and encourages others to trust. The verses that follow go on to teach the fear of Jehovah. "Any good thing" does not promise that we will have everything, but that God takes care of what we truly need.

Today, when you feel that something is missing, do not rush first to rely only on your own strength or cleverness. Set aside a few minutes to seek God in prayer, tell Him your need, and trust that He will take care of you, even if He does it in a different way than you expected.
exp.5:9:
The explanation says that those who oppose the psalmist will be humiliated and greatly frightened. The word "be sore vexed" in the verse above means to be deeply troubled or filled with fear, and "suddenly" means all at once, without warning. It also says that they "return," that is, they fall back defeated, without achieving their purpose.

The psalm is spoken by David, according to its title, and he is distressed, weak, and full of weeping. Earlier he asked God for mercy. Now, sensing that God has heard him, his spirit changes and he trusts that God will act on his behalf. Some understand these words as a petition and others as a declaration of faith. Both readings are possible.

For today: when you feel attacked or unfairly treated, bring your pain to God in sincere prayer and not to revenge. Trust that He does justice in His own time, and also ask for a heart free of resentment.
exp.136:4:
It says that the one speaking swears never to forget Jerusalem. If he forgets her, he asks that his right hand be made to forget, that is, that it lose its skill or its strength. The right hand is the hand used for doing things. Some scholars believe the phrase is incomplete in the original text, which is why it is understood in several ways, but the central idea is clear: an oath of loyalty.

The one speaking is an Israelite exiled in Babylon after the destruction of Jerusalem. His captors ask him to sing joyful songs of Zion, but he feels pain and does not want to treat his faith as entertainment. For this reason he promises to keep the city of God in his heart, even in a foreign land.

For today: do not let noise, tiredness, or pressure make you forget what matters most in your faith. Choose a simple habit, such as praying each morning or reading a psalm, to keep your memory of God and his people alive.
exp.124:0:
They that trust in the Lord are like Mount Zion: firm, unmoving, forever. The title of the psalm is "A Song of degrees"; it is thought these were songs sung on the way up to Jerusalem, though their exact meaning is debated.

The psalmist does not name himself, and the text does not say who wrote this song. It was probably sung by pilgrims going up to Jerusalem. The verses that follow explain the image: just as mountains surround the city, the Lord surrounds his people. The psalm reminds them that the oppression of the wicked will not last forever.

For today: when you feel unsteady because of problems or fears, remember that your security does not depend on your own strength, but on the One in whom you trust. Take a few minutes today to tell God your worry and to entrust it to Him.
exp.131:15:
This verse says that God himself will clothe the priests with salvation, a word that here means rescue and complete well-being. It also says that his saints, the faithful people who belong to him, will shout aloud for joy. "Shout aloud for joy" means they will sing with gladness.

The one speaking is God, in answer to the prayer of the psalmist. This is a song of the pilgrims who went up to Jerusalem. God promises that Zion will be his resting place, that he will give bread to the poor, and that he will care for the line of David. The priests and the people receive those blessings. Some see here a hope that is fully fulfilled in Christ, but the psalm speaks first of Zion.

Today we can remember that salvation and joy are not manufactured by our own effort, but are given by God. When you go to church or pray, ask him to clothe you with his salvation, and thank him with a simple song.
exp.75:10:
This verse invites us to make promises to God and to keep them. It also asks that all who live near Him bring gifts or offerings to Him. Keeping what has been promised is what it means to fulfill a vow, and the gifts are offerings brought to Him. The one being addressed is the one who deserves deep respect and reverent awe, because He is powerful.

The psalm is a song by Asaph, or dedicated to his group of singers, that celebrates God as judge and savior. Earlier it speaks of how God defends the meek and of how even human fury ends up honoring Him. Afterward it says that God humbles princes and kings. For this reason, the psalmist calls for a response of reverence and faithfulness.

For today: think of some promise you have made to God, such as prayer, service, forgiveness, or giving, and take one concrete step today to keep it, with gratitude and respect.
exp.36:18:
It says that righteous people, those who trust in God, will not be left in shame when hard times come. Even in seasons of hunger, they will have enough. The phrase "evil time" refers to periods of difficulty or calamity, and "satisfied" means content, well fed.

This is a psalm of David, written as wise counsel, probably by someone already advanced in years (v. 25). It seeks to encourage those who see the wicked prosper and feel envy or anxiety. The nearby verses contrast the righteous, whom the LORD upholds and whose way he knows, with the wicked, who will perish. It is a general promise of care, not a guarantee that the righteous will never suffer.

For today: when the economy or life becomes hard, do not copy the dishonest shortcuts of others. Remain honest and generous, and trust that God sustains you, step by step, even when the path is short on resources.
exp.53:3:
This verse says that God is the one who helps the one who speaks. The phrase "the Lord is with those who uphold my life" means that God is on the side of those who support and care for him. It can also be understood that the Lord himself is the one who sustains his life. Both readings are possible. "Behold" is a way of saying "look" or "see."

David speaks, according to the title of the psalm, which places him in the time when the Ziphites went to tell Saul where he was hiding. He feels surrounded by hostile people who do not take God into account. For this reason he prays asking for help and, in the midst of danger, affirms his confidence that God is with him.

For today: when you feel alone or under pressure, remember in prayer that God is your help. Tell him sincerely what you are facing, and also give thanks for the people God places at your side to uphold you.
exp.58:3:
It says that David's enemies run and get themselves ready to attack him, even though he has done nothing wrong. The phrase "get ready" here means that they arrange and organize themselves for the attack. That is why David asks God to "awake", that is, to act and make himself present, to come to meet him and see what is happening.

David speaks, according to the psalm's heading, when Saul sent men to watch his house in order to kill him (1 Samuel 19). He feels surrounded and accused without reason. He does not say that he is perfect, but that he has done nothing that justifies this attack. For that reason he appeals to God as a just judge.

For today: when you are treated unfairly, do not keep your anger to yourself alone. Tell God honestly what you feel, ask him to see your situation, and trust that he defends the truth.
exp.118:11:
It says that God is worthy of praise, and for that reason the speaker asks him to teach him his decrees, that is, his laws and rules. "Blessed" here means praised or worthy of being blessed. "Lord" is the name of God. "Teach me" expresses a desire to learn, not just to know facts.

Psalm 119 is a long poem in honor of God's Word. It does not say who wrote it; tradition attributes it to David, but this is not certain. The speaker has already sought God wholeheartedly and has kept his words so as not to sin. Now, with humility, he acknowledges that he needs God himself to instruct him.

Before opening the Bible, we can pray with this same attitude: praising God and asking him to teach us. In this way we read not only to know more, but to know him and obey him with a willing heart.
exp.76:15:
It says that even the waters of the sea, when they saw God, were filled with fear and trembled. The word for "saw" in the quoted phrase is not in your verse, so it is left out here. "Depths" are the deep parts of the sea. It is a poetic way of saying that all of creation recognizes the power of God.

The speaker is the psalmist Asaph, in a moment of distress. To find comfort, he remembers what God did for his people. Many understand this to refer to when God opened the Red Sea and freed Israel from Egypt. The psalm describes this with images of storm, thunder, and trembling, though these are poetic words.

When you feel that your problem is too big, remember what God has already done in your life and in his Word. If the sea trembles before him, your situation is not beyond his control. Trust and rest in him.
exp.16:9:
They are shut up in their own fat: they speak proudly with their mouth. Here it says that David's enemies have hearts that have become hard and unfeeling, as if covered in fat. Fat stands for people who are prosperous and feel so secure that they no longer listen to anyone, not even to God. Their words are spoken with pride and arrogance. Some readers understand that the fat shuts off their compassion, while others understand that it shuts their mouth to the truth; the general meaning is the same either way.

David prays for protection. Violent men surround him and pursue him, and he cries out to God as to one who watches over him as the apple of the eye. The text does not specify at what exact moment of his life he wrote this.

For today: when you have to deal with arrogant or hard-hearted people, do not answer them with the same pride. Bring your situation before God in prayer, and guard your own heart so that it does not harden through comfort.
exp.145:1:
It says that the psalmist commits to praising God throughout his whole life. The phrase "I will praise the Lord" is rendered here as "I will praise the Lord," and "I will sing praises" means singing hymns of worship. "While I live" means "while I have any being." It is not a passing wish but a decision for a whole lifetime.

The psalm does not clearly say who wrote it. The speaker begins by encouraging himself: "Praise the Lord, O my soul." Then he moves to a personal promise. What follows gives the reason: one should not place trust in rulers or in human beings, who die and whose plans die with them. Only God is worthy of a trust and a praise that last forever.

For today: when you feel your hope resting on leaders, money, or people, stop and praise God with a song or a prayer of gratitude. Do this every day, even in hard times, to remember in whom you truly trust.
exp.143:10:
Here the psalmist asks God to rescue him and free him from the power of "strange children," that is, foreign people or those who are outside of God. Of them he says that their mouth speaks vanity (empty and false words) and that their right hand is a hand of falsehood. This suggests that their promises and oaths cannot be trusted.

The one speaking is David, or a psalmist speaking in his name. He has just praised God for having delivered him from the evil sword. Now he asks for help again in the face of deceitful enemies. Afterward he asks for peace and prosperity for the people: strong children, safe homes, and abundant harvests.

For today: when false words or promises that are not kept surround you, you do not have to defend yourself alone. Pray sincerely, ask God for wisdom to discern, and keep your own word firm and honest.
exp.22:3:
What it says: The speaker affirms that, even if he passes through a dark and dangerous place, he will not be afraid, because God goes with him. The phrase "the valley of the shadow of death" can mean a very dark valley or a situation of serious danger. The shepherd's tools were used to defend and guide the sheep. To give courage means to encourage and comfort.

Context: This is a psalm of David, traditionally attributed to him, who was a shepherd before becoming king. It speaks in the first person and compares God to a careful shepherd. Up to this point, the shepherd led him to rest; now he accompanies him in the difficulty, and the psalmist shifts from speaking about God ("he") to speaking to him directly ("you").

For today: When you face an illness, a loss, or great uncertainty, pray saying to God: "You are with me." Your comfort does not depend on the valley disappearing, but on the fact that you do not cross it alone.
exp.76:1:
It says that the psalmist sought the Lord when he was in great distress. His "sore" (his pain or wound) "ran in the night," that is, it kept flowing without stopping, like an open wound or like someone who stretches out a hand without rest, as it can be translated. "Refused comfort" means that he would not allow himself to be comforted.

The one speaking is Asaph, or a singer of his line, and the psalm is dedicated to Jeduthun, a music director of the temple. It is not stated with certainty what his exact problem was. We see a sincere, deeply distressed believer who prays and yet does not feel relief right away.

Today, if your heart is not soon comforted, do not think your faith is weak. Keep seeking God honestly, even at night, and tell him everything just as you feel it.
exp.17:43:
It says that as soon as the foreign peoples heard about David, they submitted to him. The phrase about them obeying him at once speaks of a quick obedience. The sons of strangers are people from other nations. The word translated "lied to me" in the Hebrew is understood to mean that they pretended or flattered: they submitted outwardly, out of fear, not from sincere loyalty.

David speaks in a song of thanks to God for having delivered him from Saul and from his enemies, and for having made him king.
