He acknowledges that his victory and his fame come from God, not from his own strength. Some think the psalm also looks forward to the Messiah, but that is an interpretation.

For today: God can give us respect or success, but people sometimes applaud us without sincerity. Let us not place our security in flattery, but in God, our rock, and let us thank him for what he gives us.
exp.9:8:
He lies in wait in hiding, like a lion in its den. His goal is to catch the poor. Lying in wait means watching in secret in order to attack. Seizing means taking by force. The lion's hiding place is its den, and the net is the trap where the helpless one falls.

The psalmist speaks to God in the middle of his pain. He describes a cruel man who takes advantage of the humble while it seems God does nothing. For this reason the psalm ends by asking God to rise up and do justice. Some scholars see Psalms 9 and 10 as one unit, but this is not certain.

Today we can open our eyes to those who take advantage of the weak, as in scams, abusive debts, or deceit. We should not stay silent. We can protect someone vulnerable, speak out against injustice, and pray with confidence, because God sees the poor.
exp.140:7:
It says that David looks to God with his eyes fixed on Him, because he trusts in Him. "Therefore" means "so" or "but," in the sense of "then" or "yet." "My eyes are unto you" means that he directs his attention and his hope toward God. "Leave not my soul destitute" is a plea: "do not abandon me, do not leave my life without protection."

The speaker is David, in a time of danger, surrounded by wicked people who set traps for him. The verses before this one are difficult and are interpreted in various ways, but they show that judgment is in God's hands. That is why David stops looking at his enemies and looks to God. Then he asks to be kept from the snares they laid for him.

For today: when you feel pressure or fear, decide where to look. Before you react, make a short, sincere prayer: "In you I trust, do not let me go."
exp.37:15:
David prays to God and explains why he asked for help: he did not want his enemies to laugh at him. When his foot was slipping, that is, when he began to fall or fail, they were puffed up with pride and gloated over him.

The speaker is David, in a psalm of lament. He is sick, suffers because of his sin, and feels surrounded by people who rejoice at his fall. So he waits on God and trusts that he will answer. Some understand the slipping as a moral fall and others as an illness or weakness; the text allows both ideas.

When you feel weak or have failed, do not hide or sink into shame. Speak with God with complete honesty, as David did, and trust that he hears you and holds you up, even when others mock.
exp.115:13:
The speaker says that he will now fulfill the promises he made to God, and he will do so in public, in the presence of the whole community of believers. "Vows" are solemn promises made to God, usually in times of distress. The Lord's name is what he calls on in the verse.

The one speaking is a psalmist, whose name is not given. God rescued him from a serious danger, perhaps from death, and for that reason he gives thanks. Some think the psalm was sung in the temple during a thank offering. This cannot be affirmed with certainty, but it fits the tone of the psalm.

When God helps us, gratitude should not stay only in words. We can keep what we promised, serve others, testify to what God has done, and praise him together with our church, so as to encourage others to trust in him.
exp.146:6:
This verse is an invitation to sing to God with thanksgiving and joy. The word "sing" is the same as "sing" in the verse, and "Lord" is the name of God used in this verse. Praise is expressing in words and music how much God is worth. The harp was a stringed instrument widely used in Israel for worship.

The psalm does not say who wrote it, so its author is uncertain. The speaker calls the whole people to worship. The verses before explain why: God is great, wise, lifts up the humble, and puts the wicked in their place. The verses that follow add that he cares for creation, sending rain, making the grass grow, and feeding even the young ravens.

For today: when you see the hand of God in everyday life, such as food, rain, or another day of life, respond with a song. It can be in church or at home, with an instrument or without one, but with a grateful heart.
exp.41:10:
The psalmist speaks to himself: "Why are you so downcast, my soul, and so disquieted within me?" He answers himself: "Hope in God." Soon he will praise him again, because God is his health and his God. To be cast down means to be discouraged; to be disquieted means to be troubled.

The one speaking is a psalmist, probably a Levite, who feels far from the temple and from God. He suffers under the oppression of enemies who mock him: "Where is your God?" Even so, he does not hide his pain. He expresses it honestly and, at the same time, encourages himself to trust. This same refrain also appears in verse 5 and in Psalm 43:5.

For today: when discouragement overwhelms you, be honest with God about what you feel, but do not let yourself be guided only by your emotions. Speak to your soul, remember who God is, and pray with hope. You can say: "I shall yet praise him."
exp.23:7:
This verse answers a question: who is the King of glory who is about to enter? The answer is Jehovah, the strong and mighty one, mighty in battle. The words describing him as a God who defeats his enemies and is never overcome by anything are drawn from "strong and mighty" and "mighty in battle" in the verse.

This psalm is attributed to David and seems to be a processional song. Many believe it was sung when the ark of the covenant, the sign of God's presence, was carried up to Jerusalem, though it is not known for certain when it was first used. It seems to be a dialogue: some call out from the gates and others answer. The gates are pictured as if they must open before the King.

For today: when your struggles feel bigger than you are, remember who the King is who walks with you. Open the gates of your heart and of your worries, and trust that the Lord, strong and mighty, fights for his own.
exp.102:19:
The explanation says that the angels praise God. They are described as "mighty in strength," that is, very strong. They carry out his word, meaning they fulfill it and put it into effect, and they do so by obeying the voice of his word, which means attending right away to what God commands. "Bless" here means to praise and acknowledge how good God is.

The speaker is David, according to the heading of the psalm. He has already encouraged himself to bless God for his forgiveness and mercy. Now he calls the whole universe to join in: first the angels, then the heavenly hosts, and all creation. The reason is that God rules over everything from his throne in the heavens.

For today: the angels obey God promptly and joyfully. We can ask him to help us obey in the same way, without delay or complaint, and make that obedience a way of praising him in our everyday lives.
exp.92:2:
It says that the rivers raised their voice with force: their sound and their waves grew like a roar. "Raised" means "lifted up," and "waves" are the water's surges or currents. It is an image of forces that make a great noise and seem overpowering.

The author is unknown; the psalm is a song of praise to God as King. Turbulent waters often represent chaos or threatening powers in the Bible, and some see them as restless nations, although the text does not say so clearly. The next verse responds: God is mightier than all that noise. Thus the psalm encourages trust that his throne does not move.

When problems make a lot of noise in your life, remember that they are not the strongest thing. Breathe, pray, and rest in the fact that God reigns and remains steady.
exp.49:5:
This verse says that the heavens publicly proclaim God's righteousness, because God himself is the judge. The word "declare" here means "make known" or "reveal to all." "Selah" is a word that appears in the Psalms; it probably indicates a pause for reflection, though its exact meaning is not certain.

The psalm is by Asaph. It presents God as the one who calls his people to account, with the heavens and the earth as witnesses. He gathers those who made a covenant with him through sacrifice. Afterward he will tell them that their problem is not the sacrifices themselves, but a heart that performs the outward acts and neglects everything else.

For today: God sees beyond our religious practices. Before judging others, we can ask ourselves honestly whether our faith is sincere: whether we truly love him and live with justice and gratitude in our everyday lives.
exp.70:10:
This verse repeats what the psalmist's enemies are saying: "God has forsaken him. Pursue and seize him, because no one is going to deliver him." The words "pursue" and "seize" in this verse are the translations that match the commands of the enemies.

The one speaking is an older believer who prays to God in fear. The psalm does not say with certainty who wrote it. His enemies conspire against him and take advantage of his weakness. They think that, since he is old and without strength, God has already left him alone. The psalmist answers them by asking God for help.

For today: when others make you feel that God has abandoned you, do not accept that lie as truth. Bring that pain to prayer, as the psalmist did, and ask God to sustain you. Also seek the support of trusted brothers and sisters.
exp.91:10:
This verse says that the psalmist will see with his own eyes and hear with his own ears what happens to his enemies, to those who rose up against him, to the wicked, that is, to those who do evil. It is an expression of trust that God will act with justice.

The one speaking is a psalmist who praises God for his faithfulness. He has just said that those who work iniquity will be scattered, and that God will strengthen him and anoint him with fresh oil, a sign of blessing and joy. Right after this, the psalm speaks of the righteous who flourish like the palm tree. Some understand that the psalmist expects to see God's justice at work in his own life, and others read it as a more general hope.

For today: when you are wounded or treated unjustly, do not let bitterness take root or seek revenge. Hand the matter over to God, trust that he is just, and keep doing good while you wait.
exp.84:3:
The verse says "Turn us, O God of our salvation, and cause thine anger toward us to cease." In this prayer, the words "turn us" mean "restore us" or "bring us back to yourself." "Our salvation" means "the God who saves us." "Cause thine anger to cease" is a request that he no longer be angry with his people. It is a simple and humble prayer.

The psalmist speaks together with the people of Israel, in a collective prayer. First he recalls that God already forgave them in the past. But now they seem to be going through hardships, and they ask God to renew them. It is not known with certainty at what exact moment in history it was written; some connect it with the return from exile, but this is not entirely certain.

For today: when you feel far from God or are going through a hard time, you can pray with confidence. Remember how God has forgiven you before, and ask him to draw you close to himself again.
exp.67:10:
This verse says that the Lord gives a word, that is, a message or command, and that many women proclaim it. The ones who carry good news are the ones who announce it, and a great company means a large crowd. In the original the form is feminine, which is why the verse speaks of women.

This psalm is attributed to David and praises God as King who delivers and cares for his people. Here a victory is remembered: God speaks and his people proclaim it. Some think it refers to the women who sang and announced Israel's triumphs, as in Exodus 15 and 1 Samuel 18. The verses that follow speak of kings who flee and of spoil being divided.

For today: God continues to give his word and uses all kinds of people to share it. Think of someone who needs good news, and tell them, in simple words, what God has done for you.
exp.30:16:
The explanation says that David asks God not to let him be put to shame, because he has already called upon him in prayer. Here "put to shame" means to be embarrassed or humiliated. The wicked, by contrast, are to be brought to shame. The phrase about them being silent in the depths refers to their being silenced in Sheol, the place of the dead. Some understand this as a wish that the wicked be silenced, not as a personal desire for revenge.

The one speaking is David, who feels pursued and falsely accused. Earlier he said that his times are in God's hand, so he trusts that God is in control of his life. He asks for help because his enemies speak lies against him.

For today: when you feel unfairly attacked, pray honestly and leave your cause in God's hands. There is no need to respond with resentment; trust that he cares for those who seek him.
exp.118:33:
He asks God for understanding, that is, the insight to grasp what his law means. He promises that if God gives it to him, he will keep the law, that is, obey it, and he will observe it, which means carrying it out with care. He will do this with his whole heart, with sincerity and not merely on the outside.

This psalm, Psalm 119, is a long poem that praises God's word. The text does not say who wrote it, so no one can be sure. The one speaking is a believer who loves God's law and recognizes that he needs help to understand it. Earlier he asked to be taught, and afterward he asks to be guided and for his heart to turn toward God and not toward greed.

For today: before you read the Bible, ask God to help you understand it and put it into practice. Then choose one specific teaching and live it out this week.
exp.17:32:
He makes my feet light and sure, like those of the deer, which run and leap over hard ground without falling. He also says that he sets me upon my high places, that is, on high and firm ground.

David is speaking, and the psalm places it on the day the LORD delivered him from his enemies and from Saul. He looks back and recognizes that he did not win by his own strength. He uses the image of the deer and of the high places to speak of stability, security, and victory. Some understand the high places as places of refuge; others, as a position of authority.

Today, when the road is steep or slippery, you can ask God for firmness in every step. You do not have to see the whole path to trust that he holds your feet. Give thanks for the places where he has already made you stand firm.
exp.70:1:
The explanation says that the psalmist asks God to deliver him from danger and rescue him in accordance with his righteousness, that is, in keeping with God's faithful and upright character. "Incline thine ear" is a way of asking God to listen to him with attention. "Cause me to escape" means "get me out safely."

The psalm does not say who wrote it. Tradition attributes it to David, though this is not certain. The one speaking seems to be someone who has trusted God since youth and now faces violent enemies. That is why he calls God his rock and fortress, and asks for a secure refuge.

When you are in trouble, you can pray simply and honestly: "Lord, listen to me and help me." You do not need perfect words. You can rely on the fact that God is just and faithful, and return to him again and again, like someone coming back to a familiar place of shelter.
exp.89:11:
He says we ask God to help us understand how short our days are, so that we may live with wisdom. "To number" here means to value, to take seriously. The phrase "let us bring to the heart" means that this wisdom reaches the very depths of our lives. The phrase "teach us so" is a prayer: "Lord, teach us this way."

The title of the psalm calls it "a prayer of Moses, man of God," although some scholars debate when it was written. Moses speaks on behalf of the people. He has just spoken of the brevity of life, the weight of sin, and the holiness of God. That is why he asks for help to live with meaning, and then pleads for mercy and joy.

For today: do not assume you have plenty of time. Today, before the day ends, choose something important, such as praying, forgiving someone, or spending time with your family, and do it with gratitude, remembering that each day is a gift from God.
exp.77:28:
It says the Israelites ate until they were full. The verse's "so they did eat, and were well filled" makes clear they were satisfied, and "for he gave them their own desire" means that God gave them what they were asking for. The meat and birds that fell near their tents were the answer to their craving.

The psalm is written by Asaph, who reviews the history of Israel to teach the new generations. He recalls how the people, in the wilderness, tested God and demanded meat out of whim, not only out of need. God gave it, but the following verse shows that this granting came with judgment, because their hearts remained set on the craving.

For today: not everything God allows us to obtain is a sign of his approval. Before insisting on something, it is good to ask ourselves whether we are asking for it with trust and gratitude, or only on impulse. Let us first ask for a heart that desires what pleases God.
exp.44:12:
She is the king's daughter, that is, the royal bride, and the verse says she is very glorious ("all glorious") within, and that her clothing is made of fine cloth with threads of gold. These words can be understood as "within the palace" or as "in her inner self," and scholars do not agree on which reading is best.

This psalm is a royal wedding song. The poet first speaks to the king and then to the bride, to celebrate their union. It is not known with certainty which king was in mind. Many Christians also read it as an image of Christ and his people.

For today: take care of your inner life more than your outward appearance. Set aside time for prayer, honesty, and sincere love, because true worth is formed within.
exp.59:5:
Here it says that God spoke from his holy place, perhaps his temple or his holiness, and promised something. For that reason the one speaking rejoices. God says he will divide Shechem and measure out the valley of Succoth, two regions on the east and west of the Jordan. "Divide" and "measure out" are like dividing up the land that belongs to him.

The one speaking is God, quoted in this psalm of David. Israel had suffered a military defeat and was asking for help. God answers by reminding them that the land is his and that he decides its future. Some think "by his sanctuary" means "by his holiness," as a firm promise. Both readings are possible.

For today: when you feel defeated, remember what God has already said in his Word. His promises are more secure than your circumstances. Before acting out of fear, listen again to what he declares, and let that restore your joy and confidence.
exp.144:17:
Says that God is very near to all who call upon him, but especially to those who do so in truth, that is, with sincerity and honesty, not merely with words. To call upon God means to ask him for help and to acknowledge him as Lord. God is the name given to him here. Plus, there is the old way of writing a word that appears in the verse.

This psalm is a song of praise attributed to David. He celebrates the greatness and goodness of God, who cares for every living thing, is righteous and merciful. After speaking of how God provides, David shows that God also draws personally near to those who seek him. The verses that follow say that God hears their cry and saves them.

Today, you can speak with God without fear and without complicated formulas. Pray honestly, telling him what you feel and what you need, trusting that he is near and that he hears you.
exp.134:15:
This verse describes what the idols of the nations are like. They have mouths, but they cannot speak; they have eyes, but they cannot see. They look like people, but they are only lifeless figures. The words "have" and "not" show the contrast between appearance and reality.

The psalm is a song of praise, and no one knows for certain who wrote it. It speaks on behalf of the people of Israel, who are called to praise the LORD for his greatness and his care. By comparing the living God with idols made of silver and gold, the work of human hands, the psalmist wants to remind us that only God acts, listens, and guides his people. A very similar passage appears in Psalm 115.

Today we may not carve statues, but we can still place our trust in things that do not respond: money, fame, success, or approval. Ask yourself where you put your trust. Only God hears you when you pray and truly walks with you.
exp.8:7:
This verse says that God will judge the whole earth and all the nations in a fair and upright way. "Uprightness" means that he never bends anything or favors anyone; his decision is always clean and true.

David is the one who sings this psalm, according to its heading. He thanks God because he rescued him from his enemies. Just before the verse, he speaks of the oppressors vanishing, while the LORD remains forever on his throne. Then he says that God is a refuge for the poor and the afflicted. In this way, God's judgment is presented as good news for those who have been mistreated.

For today: when you feel that someone has treated you unjustly, do not carry only the desire for revenge. Entrust the case to God, pray with sincerity, and keep acting honestly, trusting that he sees everything and judges rightly.
exp.33:14:
This verse says that God takes care of the righteous. The phrase "the eyes of the Lord" means that God watches them with close attention, and "his ears are open" means that he listens when they ask for help. "The Lord" is the name of God, and "the righteous" are the people who seek to live according to what God wants. "Cry" is a shout asking for help.

According to the heading of the psalm, David wrote it when he pretended to be mad before Abimelech and was saved. Here David teaches others what he learned: God cares for those who trust in him. Earlier he speaks of guarding one's words, turning away from evil, doing good, and seeking peace. Afterward he contrasts this with God's judgment against those who do evil.

For today: when you feel alone or distressed, pray with confidence, because God sees you and hears you. And try to live with honesty, doing good and seeking peace.
exp.118:74:
Here the psalmist says that he knows and acknowledges that God's decisions are just. The words "judgments" and "righteousness" speak of God's decisions and of his way of acting, which are upright. He also affirms that, if God afflicted him, he did so faithfully, that is, in accordance with his loyalty and his character. "Afflicted" means that he brought him through suffering or hardship.

The speaker is the author of Psalm 119, a psalm that exalts God's law. We do not know with certainty who wrote it or what his exact affliction was. This verse appears in the section where he asks for understanding, and then he asks for comfort. He acknowledges the pain, but he does not accuse God.

For today: when you go through a trial, you can tell God honestly what you feel and, even so, choose to trust that he is faithful. Ask him for understanding and comfort, as the psalmist did.
exp.77:29:
They had not yet turned away from what they craved. The word "food" is the meaning of the word rendered "meat" here, and "to turn their desire away" means they had not set aside their craving. They still had the meat in their mouths when what follows took place.

The psalmist, Asaph, reviews the history of Israel to warn the generations to come. He recalls when the people, in the wilderness, asked for meat with greed, and God sent quail (Numbers 11). While they were eating, God's judgment came upon many. The psalm shows how patient God was and how stubborn the people were.

Today we might ask what desires we are feeding without asking God. Having what we long for is not always a blessing. It is wise to ask with humility, to give thanks for what God already provides, and to learn to say, "Your will be done," rather than demanding what we fancy.
exp.76:14:
It says that God freed his people with his "arm," a way of speaking about his power. The word "redeemed" means that he rescued them and made them his own. It mentions the sons of Jacob and of Joseph, that is, all of Israel. "Selah" is a pause or musical signal, probably to stop and meditate.

The speaker is the psalmist Asaph, who is distressed and full of doubts. In the middle of his pain he decides to remember what God did before. Here he thinks of the deliverance from Egypt, which he then describes with the sea, the clouds, and the thunder. Some think that mentioning Joseph recalls the northern tribes, but this is not certain.

For today: when you feel tired or confused, pause and remember how God has sustained you before. Write it down or tell it to someone. Remembering his past faithfulness can give you hope for what you are facing now.
exp.34:24:
This verse is a prayer that the enemies will not get their way. The words "Ah, so would we have it" express satisfaction, like saying "Just what we wanted!" The words "We have swallowed him up" mean "We have destroyed him!" David asks that his adversaries not be able to think or say that.

David speaks as one who feels unjustly persecuted by people he had once treated with kindness. He does not take revenge with his own hands, but appeals to God as a just judge. He asks that his cause be defended and that the mockery of his enemies not have the last word.

For today: when someone treats you unjustly or rejoices at your fall, do not sink into bitterness or revenge. Bring your cause honestly before God, and trust that He sees, judges with justice, and cares for you.
exp.118:171:
It says the psalmist will speak, that is, sing or tell, what God has said. The "sayings" are the words or promises of God, and the reason given is that all of God's commandments are righteousness, that is, they are right, correct and good, without error or evil.

The one speaking is the author of Psalm 119, who is not identified with certainty, although tradition attributes it to David. It is a poem that praises the Word of God. Here, after asking for teaching and help, the writer promises to respond with praise. He speaks because he has learned to trust that what God commands is just, even in the midst of difficulties.

Today we can do the same: instead of keeping the Bible only for ourselves, we can share simply with others something God has taught us. It can be in a conversation, a family prayer or an encouraging word to a friend.
exp.90:10:
He tells us that God will give orders to his angels to watch over the person who trusts in him, in all his ways, that is, in his daily life.

The psalm does not say who wrote it, and scholars have no certain agreement on this. In these verses, someone speaks to the one who has made God his refuge. That is why the promise is tied to the trust expressed in the verse before. When the devil quoted this passage to Jesus in the desert, Jesus answered that God should not be put to the test (Matthew 4:6-7).

Today we can live with calm, knowing that God cares for his own, even when he does not explain how. Trusting is not taking risks without thinking, but walking with prudence and praying each morning, handing our steps over to God.
exp.87:4:
The explanation says that the psalmist feels like someone abandoned among the dead. "Free" here does not mean happy, but set apart or cast aside, like someone who no longer counts. The ones who are "slain" are those who died in battle or by violence, and "lie" means that they are stretched out. It says that God no longer remembers them and that they are "cut off from his hand," that is, they no longer receive his care.

The one speaking is the author of the psalm, attributed to Heman the Ezrahite, although some details of the title are debated. He is very sick or suffering greatly, and he says so with painful honesty. It is one of the few psalms of lament that end without a clear word of hope. Even so, he speaks to God.

For today: when you feel forgotten, do not pretend to be fine. Tell God exactly what you feel. Praying with sincerity, even in the darkness, is already an act of faith.
exp.96:5:
This verse says that the heavens "declared" — that is, announced and made known publicly — that God is righteous. And because of this, all peoples were able to see his glory, that is, his greatness and his power. The old way of saying that they clearly noticed it is that they "saw" it, and the explanation of that word has been left out here.

The psalmist does not speak of a single figure, but sings of God as King over all the earth. Before this, he describes lightning, earthquakes, and mountains melting like wax, poetic images of the presence of the LORD. Afterward, the psalm contrasts those who worship idols, who are put to shame, with Zion, which rejoices. Many understand this as poetic language, not as a literal account.

Today we can look at creation, the sky, starry nights, or a storm, and remember that God is righteous and great. When the world seems unjust, this invites us to trust that he governs with righteousness.
exp.65:4:
It says he invites everyone to come and look carefully at what God has done. The word "terrible" does not mean something bad; it means something that causes awe and reverence because of his greatness. "The children of men" are all human beings. God acts in striking ways on behalf of his people and before the world.

The psalmist calls the whole earth to praise God. The verses that follow recall how God opened the sea and the river, a memory that many understand as the exodus from Egypt and the entrance into the promised land. It is not known with certainty who wrote this psalm or on what exact occasion it was sung.

Today we can take time to remember what God has done in our lives and in the history of his people. Write it down, share it with someone, and let that remembrance lead you to trust and to worship with reverence and joy.
exp.90:14:
This verse shows God's answer to the one who trusts in him. It says that when the person calls on him, he will answer. It also promises to be present in distress, that is, in affliction and hardship. "Rescue" would mean to save or bring out of danger, and "honor" here means to give dignity and respect to that person.

In this part of the Psalm, the one speaking is God himself. Before, the psalmist spoke about the believer; now God responds with promises to the one who has set his love on him and knows his name. The earlier verses use images of danger, such as lions and serpents, to speak of threats. Scholars debate whether the psalm refers to a king, a priest, or any believer.

For today: when you feel fear or pressure, pray sincerely, even with few words. Do not promise yourself that there will be no pain; you can, however, trust that God accompanies you and sustains you in the midst of it.
exp.103:26:
It says that all creatures, both those of the sea and those of the land, depend on God to live. "Looking to you" means they look to Him as their provider. "In due season" means "at the right moment." "Give them their food" refers to the daily sustenance God provides.

The psalm does not say who wrote it. It is a hymn of praise to God as Creator. The psalmist moves through creation: heavens, waters, mountains, animals, and the sea. He has just spoken of the sea, with its fish and the "leviathan," which is probably a great sea creature. His purpose is to show that every living thing depends on God each day.

For today: if God cares this way for the animals, you can trust that He also cares for you. Today, thank Him for your food and for what you need, and wait for His timing with patience, without forgetting to work responsibly.
exp.50:7:
He says David asks God to let him hear words of joy and gladness again. The "broken bones" are bones that have been crushed or shattered, a way of speaking of the deep pain of his soul and body. The phrase "that the bones... may rejoice" means that they will be glad and feel rest again.

It is part of the prayer of repentance that, according to the heading of the psalm, David prayed after the prophet Nathan confronted him about his sin with Bathsheba. He speaks with the weight of guilt and asks for forgiveness. Some understand the crushed spirit to come from God's discipline; others, from the anguish of his own conscience. Perhaps it is both.

For today: if you carry guilt, do not hide it. Bring it to God honestly and wait for his forgiveness, which restores the peace and joy that sin takes away.
exp.107:11:
What it says: The psalmist asks God for help in the middle of a crisis. The word "help" means aid or assistance, and "trouble" is a great distress or hardship. The phrase "for vain is the help of man" means that the salvation or help a human being can give is empty and unreliable; it cannot be trusted. Other versions read it this way too.

Context: David speaks, according to the psalm's heading, and he gathers parts of other psalms (Psalms 57 and 60). Israel had suffered a defeat and felt that God had abandoned them. Even so, David recognizes that only God can lead them to victory against enemies such as Edom, and so he ends by saying: "Through God we will do valiantly."

For today: When you find yourself in trouble, do not place all your hope in your own resources, your connections, or your plans. Ask God for his help first, and then take the steps you can, trusting that he sustains your efforts.
exp.103:28:
It says that all creatures depend on God at every moment. When God "hides his face," that is, withdraws his care and favor, living beings are "troubled," that is, they are frightened and bewildered. If he takes away their breath, which here is the breath of life, they cease to exist and return to the dust from which they came.

This is a psalm of praise to God the Creator. The psalmist considers the sea, the animals, and the earth, and acknowledges that all of them wait on God to receive their food. The verses before speak of his generous provision; the verses after say that God sends his breath and renews the earth. Life is not one's own: God gives it and sustains it.

For today: every day we breathe and eat because God sustains us. Today you can thank him for something simple, such as the air or your food, and humbly entrust him with your concerns, remembering that your life is in his hands.
exp.15:10:
It says that God will teach the one who speaks the path that leads to true life. The phrase "fullness of joy" means complete joy, joy that fills a person entirely. "With your presence" means being in the presence of God. "At your right hand" is his right hand, the place of honor and power. There are pleasures and goodness there that never end.

It is a psalm of David. He speaks with confidence because he has made God his refuge. The verses before it speak of not being left in the grave. In Acts 2, Peter applies this psalm to the resurrection of Jesus. Some read it first as David's hope, and others see in it above all a prophecy of Christ. Both readings have been held among Christians.

Today, before seeking joy in passing things, you can seek it in the presence of God. Set aside a few minutes each day to pray and read his Word, asking him to guide you on the path.
exp.29:4:
The explanation says that God's anger lasts only a moment, but his favor lasts a lifetime. "Anger" here means wrath or displeasure; the phrase about his good pleasure is understood as his favor or goodwill toward his people. Weeping can stay like a guest for the night, but joy comes with the morning.

David speaks here, according to the psalm's title, which connects it to the dedication of the house. He gives thanks because God rescued him from a situation close to death. The verses that follow show that he had felt very secure, and that when God hid his face, he was troubled. Scholars do not agree on which exact episode in his life this refers to.

For today: if you are going through a season of pain or correction, do not take it as the end of the story. Speak to God honestly, trust in his goodness, and remember that his favor lasts longer than your sadness.
exp.118:15:
The explanation says that the psalmist will find his joy in God's statutes, that is, in God's instructions and commands. The word "delight" is used here to mean finding pleasure and enjoyment in them. He also promises not to forget God's word, meaning he will keep it always present in his mind and in his heart.

Psalm 119 is a long poem that praises God's law, and this verse belongs to the section called Het (in the Hebrew tradition, each section begins with a letter of the alphabet). We do not know with certainty who wrote it; tradition attributes it to David, but others think of a later author. The speaker is someone who loves God and finds more value in His Word than in any riches.

For today: instead of reading the Bible only out of duty, ask God to help you enjoy it. Choose one verse each week, read it calmly, repeat it during the day, and ask yourself what it teaches you about God.
exp.37:19:
The verse says that those who repay good with evil are his enemies. They criticize him and oppose him precisely because he tries to do what is good. Repaying evil for good means answering with harm someone who has done good to you. "Are mine adversaries" means that they stand against him or act against him.

The psalm, according to its heading, is spoken by David during a time of great suffering. He feels sick, guilty because of his sin, and surrounded by adversaries. Even so, he distinguishes between his own failure, which he humbly acknowledges, and the unjust hostility of those who attack him without cause. For that reason he asks God not to abandon him.

Today this can encourage us when doing what is right brings mockery or rejection. We will not always be understood. We can honestly examine our hearts, keep doing good, and bring the pain of injustice to God, trusting that He is near.
exp.43:23:
This verse is an honest cry to God. The people ask why God "hides his face," that is, why he seems to turn away his gaze and his favor. They also ask why he seems to forget their affliction and their oppression, which means the mistreatment and the unjust burden they suffer.

The one speaking is God's people, speaking on behalf of all of them. Many scholars think it is a psalm of national lament, written after a defeat or persecution, though the exact time is not known for certain. They say they remain faithful and yet they suffer. That is why they cry out so boldly.

For today: when you feel that God is far away, do not silence your pain. Tell him honestly, as this psalm does. Praying with hard questions is also an act of faith, because you are still seeking him.
exp.114:14:
It says that those who trust in God are blessed by Him, and that this God is no ordinary one: He is the Creator of heaven and earth. "Ye are blessed" means "you are blessed." "Lord" is the name by which many Bibles render God's personal name.

Psalm 115 contrasts the living God with the silent, lifeless idols of the nations. It was probably a song for the people's worship, perhaps sung by several voices, although we do not know with certainty who wrote it. The verse before promises blessing to those who fear God, from the small to the great. Here it is stated that this blessing comes from the One who made everything that exists, not from a statue without power.

For today: when you feel that your resources or your future are small, remember who blesses you. Before you worry, take a brief moment to pray, giving thanks to the One who sustains all things and cares for you and your family.
exp.135:22:
The explanation says that God did not forget his people when they were brought low and in a very humble situation. Being brought low means being fallen, defeated, or without strength. "Remembered" here means that God acted on their behalf, not merely that he called them to mind.

This psalm is a song of praise that the people of Israel sang, repeating in each verse that God's love is forever. The speaker is the believing community, recalling what God did: creation, the deliverance from Egypt, and the land they received. Here they remember that God helped them in difficult times. It is not known with certainty what exact moment is in view.

When you feel fallen or abandoned, remember how God has sustained you before. Write down three moments when you felt his help, and thank him for them today.
exp.17:11:
This verse describes an impressive storm. It says that, before the brightness that comes from God's presence, the clouds part or break open, and hail and burning coals fall. "Brightness" refers to a very intense light, and the "burning coals" are glowing embers of fire, an image of lightning or of judgment.

David speaks here, giving thanks to God for rescuing him from his enemies and from King Saul (see the title of the psalm). To describe how God delivered him, he uses images of storm, fire, and wind. These are poetic figures that show God's power, not a literal account of what happened.

For today: when you feel trapped or without a way out, remember that God is greater than any threat. Pray with confidence, knowing that He listens and can act on your behalf.
exp.146:14:
This verse says that God sends his command to the earth, and that this word travels with great speed. The old word for "swiftly" means "quickly" or "right away." The idea is that when God speaks, his word is fulfilled without delay, and nothing can stop it.

The psalmist, who is not named in the text, praises God for caring for Jerusalem and his people. Earlier he speaks of peace, protection, and abundant wheat. Then he speaks of snow, frost, and ice. In this way he shows that the same word of God sustains the life of his people as well as the forces of nature. Many understand that this "word" is his creative command; others also see in it his law.

For today: trust that God continues to act through his word. When you feel anxious or lost, read the Bible calmly and ask God to guide you. His word can reach your life with power and at the right time.
exp.76:17:
The explanation says that the sound of God's thunder was heard everywhere, that the lightnings lit up the world, and that the earth shook and trembled. The phrase in the verse about the sound spreading is rendered as "went around about" in the source, meaning the sound spread all around. The word for trembling in the source means that it shook violently, that is, it was shaken with force.

The one speaking is the psalmist Asaph, who is distressed and remembers God's works in order to trust again. He describes, in poetic language, God's power in freeing his people in the exodus. The verses that follow speak of the sea and of Moses and Aaron. Many understand that it alludes to the crossing of the Red Sea, although the psalm uses storm imagery and does not give all the details.

When you feel weak or afraid, remember how God has acted before. His power is greater than your problem, and you can trust him again with calm.
exp.95:5:
This verse says that around God there is praise and splendor, and that in his sanctuary are found his power and glory. The word translated as "majesty" in the verse above means greatness and wonder. The word for "strength" means power or might. A sanctuary is the sacred place where God was worshiped.

The psalm does not say who wrote it, and scholars have attributed it in different ways. The speaker invites all the nations to worship the LORD. Before that, the psalm contrasts God with idols, which do nothing, while the LORD made the heavens. This verse shows why God deserves worship: his presence is majestic and strong.

For today: before you pray or go to church, pause for a moment and remember who God is. His greatness can change your mood, calm your fears, and lead you to worship with more sincerity, without rushing.
exp.65:19:
The psalmist gives thanks to God because he did not reject his prayer or take away his mercy. The verse's word "Blessed" means praised or worthy of thanks. "Turned away" means set aside or refused. In other words: God listened, and his goodness never left him.

The speaker is a worshiper who has experienced divine help. Shortly before, he says that God heard the voice of his plea and that, had he cherished wickedness in his heart, the Lord would not have listened to him. The psalm ends with this simple thanksgiving. Some versions attribute the psalm to David, but the text does not say so with certainty.

For today: before you pray, examine your heart honestly and confess what you need to. Then pray with confidence, and when God answers, do not forget to thank him aloud, as the psalmist did.
exp.117:9:
The psalmist says that all the nations surrounded him, but that in the name of the Lord he defeated them. "Surrounded" here means encircled for an attack. "Destroy" in this verse means to destroy or overcome. The Hebrew verb can be translated in several ways, but the underlying idea is the same: the victory comes from God.

The speaker may be a king of Israel or the whole people speaking as one voice. Interpreters do not agree. It is a psalm of thanksgiving for being delivered from enemies. The verses before it say that it is better to trust in God than in men or princes.

When you find yourself surrounded by pressures or problems, do not rely only on your own strength or on other people. Pray, ask God for help, and take the next step trusting in him.
exp.65:5:
It says that God turned the sea into dry land, and that the people crossed the river on foot. The sea was turned to dry ground means that the water parted and left firm ground. Then they rejoiced in him means that, in that very place, the people celebrated with joy what God had done.

The psalmist invites all the nations to see the works of God. He recalls the crossing of the Red Sea and probably also the crossing of the Jordan, though some think he speaks only of the Red Sea. He speaks on behalf of the people of Israel, who revisit their history to praise God.

For today: when you face a situation that seems closed off, remember what God has already done for you and for his people. That helps you to trust, and to thank him out loud, without waiting for everything to pass.
exp.146:0:
This verse calls people to praise JAH, a short form of God's name (Jehovah or Yahweh). It says that it is good to sing psalms to him, that is, songs of worship. It also says that praise is pleasant, and that it is fitting and appropriate.

The psalm does not say who wrote it. It seems to be a song for the people of Israel gathered together, and many think it was sung after the return from exile. The verses that follow suggest this: God builds Jerusalem, gathers the scattered, heals the brokenhearted and binds up their wounds. Praise springs from what God does for his people.

For today: when you are tired or hurt, do not wait until you feel better to praise. Sing to God, even if it is a simple song, and remember that he cares for the brokenhearted.
exp.50:6:
Here the psalmist asks God to cleanse him from his sin. Hyssop was a small plant used to sprinkle blood or water in purification rites. The word "whiter" in this verse means made clean, pure. He knows he cannot cleanse himself, and so he asks God to do it.

The psalm carries a heading that links it to David, after his sin with Bathsheba and after the prophet Nathan confronted him. This is how the tradition understands it. David speaks with grief and acknowledges that his heart needs to be changed, not just his behavior. God desires truth in the inward being, not only outward rituals.

Today we can come to God with honesty, without excuses, and ask him for forgiveness. We do not have to pretend that we are fine. Take a moment to tell him simply where you have failed, and trust that he is faithful to cleanse and renew your heart.
exp.101:2:
It says that the life of the one speaking is fading fast, like smoke that drifts away into the air. It also says that his bones burn like a firebrand, which is a half-burnt stick still glowing with embers. It is a way of saying that he feels deep pain and exhaustion, both inside and out.

The one speaking is a troubled man who prays before God. The heading of the psalm calls him the poor one in distress. No one knows for certain who wrote it. Some connect it with the exile, but that is an interpretation. What is clear is that he is suffering greatly and holds nothing back: he pours out his lament before God.

For today: when pain wears you down, do not pretend to be strong. Speak to God with complete honesty, in your own words. The Bible shows that He listens to the honest cry.
exp.110:4:
He says that God gave food and provision to those who fear him, that is, to those who respect him and honor him with reverence and trust. The phrase "gave provision" in the original wording is an old way of saying "gave food, provision," and so it is simply rendered here as "gave food and provision." He also affirms that God will always remember his covenant, that is, the solemn promise he made with his people.

The psalm does not say who wrote it. It is a song of praise that invites us to remember what God has done. First it speaks of his works and his mercy; afterward it mentions the inheritance given to his people. Many believe it refers to God's care for Israel, such as the manna in the wilderness, although the text gives no exact example.

Today you can rest in the knowledge that God cares for you. When you feel want or fear, remember his past faithfulness and give thanks for it. Trust that he keeps what he promises.
exp.139:4:
This verse uses the image of a hunter. The proud, that is, the arrogant, have hidden a snare and cords for the psalmist, have spread a net beside the path, and have set traps for him. The word "snare" refers to a knotted cord used to catch, and "path" is the way along which he walks. "Selah" was probably a musical or reflective pause; its exact meaning is not certain.

The psalm is spoken by David, according to its title, although some scholars debate its origin. He cries out to God because violent and deceitful people, with venomous tongues, want to bring him down. He describes their plans as hidden traps. That is why he asks for protection, and right away he confesses that God is his God.

Today we sometimes face criticism, gossip, or deception that we do not see coming. This psalm invites us not to respond with revenge but to pray honestly: to tell God what we feel, to ask him for wisdom to walk carefully, and to trust that he cares for our lives.
exp.30:23:
The explanation says that all who wait on God should be brave and let their hearts be filled with encouragement. "Be strong" means to be strong and not give up. "Hope in the Lord" means to trust the Lord and wait for his help. The inner strength and courage that the verse promises are what it calls the strengthening of the heart.

This psalm is attributed to David. He speaks after having gone through a very great distress. He says that in his haste, that is, in his affliction and trouble, he thought God had left him. But God heard his cry. For that reason, at the end, David encourages other believers to trust as he did. It is not known with certainty at what exact moment of his life he wrote it.

When you are tired or afraid, remember how God has helped you before. Pray sincerely, and encourage another person who is going through a trial, telling them that God does hear.
exp.60:2:
What it says: David speaks to God and reminds him of something he has already experienced. God has been for him a "shelter," that is, a safe place to take cover. He also calls him a "strong tower," a high, sturdy tower where a person is safe when the enemy comes near. "In the face of the enemy" means right in front of the threat.

Context: David speaks in a moment of distress. He says he calls out from "the end of the earth," and it is not certain whether he means a real faraway place or a feeling of being far away and without strength. His heart is faint, but he leans on what God has already done for him.

For today: When you are afraid or tired, remember the times God helped you. Write them down and give thanks for them. That memory will give you courage to ask for help again with confidence.
exp.87:5:
He says that God himself has laid him in the lowest pit, that is, in a dark grave, in the lowest depths. "Thou hast laid me" means "you have laid me." "In the deeps" refers to the depths. These are images of the grave, of the place of the dead, and of an anguish that seems to have no way out.

The speaker is a man named Heman the Ezrahite, according to the title of the psalm. He is very sick or suffering terribly, and he feels forgotten, rejected by his acquaintances, and under the wrath of God. This psalm is very unusual because it almost never ends with hope. Even so, the author keeps speaking to God, whom he calls "God of my salvation" at the beginning.

When you are in your darkest pit, you do not have to pretend to be strong. You can tell God with complete honesty how you feel. Praying in pain is still praying in faith.
exp.56:10:
This verse is a prayer of praise. The word "Be exalted" is an old way of saying "be lifted up" or "be raised high." David asks that God be recognized as the greatest, above the heavens, and that his glory, meaning his greatness and his beauty, fill all the earth.

The one speaking is David. The title of the psalm places him when he was fleeing from Saul and hiding in a cave. Even so, in the middle of danger and fear, he ends his prayer by looking to God and not to his problem. This same verse is repeated as a refrain in verse 5.

For today: when you are distressed, before asking for a solution, take a few minutes to praise God. Tell him out loud who he is and how much mercy you have seen in your life. That does not erase the problem, but it puts it in its proper place and gives you back hope.
exp.118:49:
This verse says that the psalmist finds comfort in the middle of his suffering. The reason is that God's word has given him life. "Your promise" in the older wording refers to what God has said, his promise. The word "quickened" means that God has restored his life and strength.

The speaker is the author of Psalm 119, who is not identified with certainty. He is someone who suffers because the proud mock him. Just before this, he asks God to remember the promise he gave him. Afterward, he says that he did not turn away from God's law and that remembering God's past works comforted him.

When you are going through a hard time, do not wait until you feel better to seek God. Read a promise from the Bible, repeat it calmly, and bring it into prayer. God can give you encouragement and hope through his word.
exp.36:9:
It says the wicked person will not last long. "In a little while" is rendered here as "within a short time." If you look for them where they used to be, you will no longer find them. "You will look carefully at his place" means "you will look at the spot where he was." "He will not be there" is an older way of saying "he will be gone" or "he will no longer be there."

This is a psalm of David, written as wise counsel, probably by a man who was already advanced in years (v. 25). It speaks to someone who becomes frustrated when they see wrongdoers prosper. First it asks them to let go of anger, and then it reminds them that those who wait on God will inherit the land. The words are poetic: they affirm that injustice does not have the final word.

Today, when it bothers you to see an unjust person seem to get away with things, do not let anger push you into responding wrongly. Pray, do good, and trust that God governs with justice, even when his timing is not yours.
exp.138:4:
He says that God surrounds the person on every side: behind and before. The word translated "beset" is an older one that means God has hemmed him in, guarded him, or placed him under his care, like someone who surrounds a city with walls. Laying "thine hand" upon someone can be understood as protection and care, though some also see it as God's control over a person's life.

David speaks, according to the title of the psalm. He is amazed that God knows him completely: his ways, his resting and even his words before he speaks them. The verses that follow show that he cannot escape God's presence. The tone is one of wonder and trust rather than fear.

For today: when you feel insecure about the past or the future, remember that God is on both sides of your life. Say to him in prayer: "Lord, you watch over me behind and before; today I rest in you."
exp.126:4:
It says that the man who has many children, compared to arrows that fill his quiver (the case where arrows are kept), is happy. The word for "fill" in the verse is "full," so the phrase "his quiver full of them" stands for a quiver filled with arrows. A man who has his quiver full in this way will not be ashamed when he speaks with his adversaries in the gate, that is, at the entrance of the city.

The psalm is titled "A Song of Ascents, for Solomon," although it is not known for certain whether he wrote it. It was a song for pilgrims. In that time, the city gate was the place where legal and public matters were handled. A large family gave support and backing. Some think it also refers to the protection and honor of the family.

Today we can see children, or the people God places in our care, as a gift and not as a burden. Give them your time, teach them to trust in God, and support them with love. Those who have no children can also care for and strengthen others.
exp.148:2:
This verse invites God's people to praise his name with dance and music. The word for group dance refers to people moving together in a circle with joy. The instrument named in the second part is a small hand drum, like a tambourine. The harp accompanies the singing. In this way, praise is expressed with the body, the voice and the instruments.

The author of the psalm is not named; it is a song of praise that calls Israel to celebrate God as its Maker and its King. It is addressed to the congregation of the saints, that is, to the faithful people. The reason for the celebration is in the verses that follow: God takes pleasure in his people and lifts up the humble. Praise is given because God is good and near.

For today: do not be ashamed to express your gratitude to God with joy. Put on a song of praise, sing it at home or in your church, and let your heart rejoice in him.
exp.39:10:
Here the psalmist asks God not to hold back his compassion and to let his faithful love and truth keep him continually. Words like "withhold" carry the same sense as the verse above. "Mercy" is God's faithful, loyal love, and "truth" is his faithfulness, which never fails.

The psalm is spoken by David, according to its title, though some scholars debate how it was originally used. Earlier, he tells how he publicly proclaimed God's righteousness and faithfulness. Now, surrounded by troubles and his own guilt, he begs for help. He rests on the very thing he had just proclaimed: the character of God.

For today: when you feel overwhelmed by problems or failures, pray by remembering how God has been faithful to you. Do not trust in your own strength, but in his mercy, and ask him to sustain you today.
exp.25:8:
David asks God here not to place him in the same group or the same fate as sinners. The phrase "gather not my soul" means "do not gather me" or "do not count me" among them. "Men of blood" are violent people, who shed blood. "My life" repeats the same idea: he does not want to share their fate.

The speaker is the psalmist, traditionally David. He has just said that he loves the house of God and wants to give thanks to him. For that reason he rejects the path of those who do harm and accept bribes. The verses that follow show that he seeks to live with integrity, though he also asks for mercy, because he knows he needs it.

For today: be careful about whom you join in your decisions, your friendships, and your work. Ask God to guide you to live with honesty, and rely on his mercy when you fail.
exp.108:30:
It says that God places himself beside the poor person, at his right hand, that is, as his defender and protector. His purpose is to save the life of the needy one from those who condemn him or accuse him unjustly. To rescue his life means to deliver his life. Those who judge him are the accusers or judges who treat him with injustice.

The one speaking is the psalmist, traditionally identified as David. He is being slandered and attacked, and he feels alone and vulnerable. Shortly before, he calls himself poor and needy. The psalm closes with praise, confident that God will defend him. Interpreters differ on how to understand the harsh wishes against his enemies, but all see here a closing note of hope.

If today you feel judged or without a voice, you can pray with confidence: God is at your side. And you can imitate him by defending, with respect and truth, anyone who is treated unjustly.
exp.26:6:
This verse is a simple and direct prayer. David asks that God hear his voice when he cries out to Him. He also begs for mercy, that is, compassion and kindness he does not deserve, and he asks for an answer. The word "cry" means to call out loudly, with urgency.

The one speaking is David, according to the traditional title of the psalm. Up to verse 6 he spoke with great confidence in God's protection. Here the tone changes: it moves from certainty to pleading. Although he trusts, he still faces enemies and needs real help. The psalm shows that faith and crying out can live side by side.

For today: you do not need to pretend to be strong before God. You can be strong in faith and, at the same time, honestly ask Him to hear you and help you. Today, tell Him in your own words what worries you, and wait for His answer.
exp.67:18:
It says we should praise the Lord because every day he fills us with blessings. The phrase about being filled with blessings means that he gives good things in abundance, like filling a glass right to the brim. The phrase about the God of our salvation means the God of our deliverance, the one who rescues us and cares for us. "Selah" is a pause or a musical marking; its exact meaning is not certain.

The psalm is traditionally attributed to King David. This song celebrates God as powerful, surrounded by thousands of angels and present among his people. After recalling his victory and his gifts, David pauses to bless him for his daily care. Then he speaks of salvation and of the defeat of his enemies.

For today: begin or end your day by naming out loud three good things God has given you. In this way gratitude becomes a habit, even on difficult days.
exp.11:4:
This verse says that God hears the suffering of the poor and the needy. For that reason he promises to rise up and act, and to set them in safety from the one who treats them with arrogance.

David cries out to God in this psalm because lies and flattery are everywhere around him. The powerful boast that their tongue will make them prevail and that no one rules over them. Here God himself answers: he does not stay silent in the face of injustice. The psalm then says that his words are pure and trustworthy, like silver refined seven times. Some understand that the wicked of that time are meant by the phrase about this generation.

Today you can trust that God sees those whom no one listens to. And you can be part of his response: help someone in need, and use your voice to defend anyone who is treated unjustly.
exp.43:14:
This verse says that the person feels their dishonor every day, as something they always have before them. The "confusion" is a mix of shame and bewilderment, and "covered" means that it wraps around them, as if it hid their face.

The one speaking is the psalmist, on behalf of God's people. They have suffered a defeat and the mockery of the neighboring nations. What hurts them most is that they feel faithful: they say they have not forgotten God or broken his covenant. It is not known with certainty at what historical moment this happened.

For today: when shame or ridicule weighs on you, you do not have to pretend you are fine. You can tell God with complete honesty what you feel, just as this psalm does, and keep trusting him.
exp.118:102:
Here the explanation says that God's words taste very sweet to the one who speaks, sweeter than honey in the mouth. The word "taste" in the verse is the sense of flavor, the part that savors. The comparison is simple: just as honey gives pleasure when eaten, God's word gives joy to the heart.

The one speaking is the psalmist, who is not named in this psalm. Tradition has attributed it to several authors, but there is no certainty. He tells that he turned away from the wrong path and that God himself taught him. For that reason his obedience does not weigh on him; he enjoys it. That sweetness leads him to hate lies and to see the word as a light for his path.

For today: do not read the Bible only out of duty. Ask God to make it pleasant to you, and read slowly a short passage each day, thinking about the good that God tells you in it.
exp.88:10:
It says that everything belongs to God: the heavens and the earth. "The world and its fullness" means the inhabited earth and everything in it. God is not only the owner of all things; he also founded them, that is, he set them in their place from the beginning. The north and the south, mentioned in the verses that follow, are the directions the verse names together with the earth.

The psalm is written by Ethan the Ezrahite, according to its title. It praises God's faithfulness and his promise to David, while the people are going through a difficult time. Before recalling that promise, the psalmist shows God's power over the sea and over Rahab, a name that in the Bible sometimes stands for chaos or an enemy power (it is also used for Egypt). If God rules over everything, he can carry out what he has promised.

For today: when you feel that your life or the world is out of control, remember that nothing escapes God's hands. Pray with confidence and hand over to him what worries you.
exp.8:19:
This verse is a prayer. The psalmist asks God to put fear into the proud nations, so that they will recognize that they are simply human, frail and limited.

The word "nations" in the verse is the word for the peoples or nations of the earth. "Selah" is a word that probably indicates a pause for reflection, although its exact meaning is not entirely certain.

The speaker is David, according to the heading of the psalm. He has just praised God for judging with justice, and now he asks that God act again. He remembers the poor and the oppressed, and asks that the powerful stop believing they are invincible and be judged before God.

Today we can remember that no human power is absolute. If someone oppresses or intimidates you, you can pray with confidence, knowing that God sees. It is also a call to examine our hearts: do I trust too much in my own strength? Living with humility means recognizing that we depend on God.
exp.32:3:
This verse says that the word of God is right, meaning just and without deceit, and that everything He does is done in truth, that is, with faithfulness and without falsehood. The name of God is the LORD, and what He does refers to everything He accomplishes.

The psalm does not say who wrote it. It is a song of praise that invites God's people to celebrate with the harp, the lyre, and a new song. This verse gives the reason for praise: God can be trusted in what He says and in what He does. The verses that follow connect this to His love for justice and to creation through His word.

Today we can rest in the fact that God does not change or lie. When you doubt or feel confused, read the Bible and remember that His promises and His ways are firm. That can also lead you to give thanks to Him in prayer.
exp.106:19:
He sent his word and healed them, and he rescued them from the place they were headed, which was destruction. "Healed them" is the sense of the first phrase, and "rescued them" is the sense of the second. "Destructions" here refers to ruin or the grave, that is, to a fatal end.

The psalmist speaks to the community of Israel and recalls how God rescued them. Earlier, some had become so sick that they could no longer eat and were near death. They cried out to God, and he answered. This psalm follows a pattern: distress, cry for help, rescue, and praise. Some believe it speaks of physical sickness, while others read it as a general picture of any crisis; the text allows for both readings.

Today, when you feel weak or see no way out, call out to God honestly and do not stay silent. Then, when he helps you, do not forget it: tell someone about it and give thanks out loud.
exp.17:45:
This verse is a shout of praise. "The Lord liveth" means that God is alive and reigns forever. "My rock" is a picture of refuge and firmness. "Exalted" means lifted up and honored. "The God of my salvation" refers to the God who saves or rescues me.

David speaks, according to the psalm's heading, after being delivered from his enemies and from Saul. He has remembered how God protected him and gave him victory, and now he responds with gratitude. Some historical details of the psalm are interpreted in different ways, but the tone of thankfulness is clear.

For today: when God helps you through a difficulty, do not let it pass in silence. Take a moment to thank him aloud or in writing. Praising him reminds you that your security is not in yourself, but in him.
exp.56:9:
It says that God's faithful love is so immense that it reaches to the heavens, and that his truth, that is, his faithfulness to keep what he promises, reaches to the clouds. Mercy here means a loyal and compassionate love. Truth means that God is reliable and never fails. These are images of something without limits.

The speaker is David. The heading of the psalm places him when he fled from Saul and hid in a cave. Even surrounded by danger, David wakes up with praise and promises to sing among the peoples. His confidence does not come from his situation, but from who God is.

Today, when you feel small or threatened, remember that God's love is greater than your problem. Before facing the day, take a moment to thank him for one concrete example of his faithfulness in your life.
exp.145:7:
What it says: God gives sight to the blind, lifts up those who are bowed down or downcast, and loves the righteous, meaning those who live uprightly. "The Lord" is the name of God.

Context: This is a psalm of praise. It does not state with certainty who wrote it, and it is best not to claim otherwise. The psalmist encourages the people to trust in God rather than in powerful humans, because God made everything, is faithful, brings justice to the oppressed, and gives bread to the hungry. This line continues that list of God's care. Some understand the blindness literally, while others also read it as an image of helping people to understand; both ideas fit.

For today: When you feel tired or see no way out, bring your need before God with confidence. And you can be his hands, helping to lift up someone who is down today.
exp.36:22:
It says that God directs and steadies the steps of the good person. "Are ordered" means that they are arranged and guided by Him. "Delighteth in his way" means that God takes pleasure in that person's manner of life and cares for them.

The psalm is by David, and speaking from old age, he draws on his own experience. Earlier he contrasts the wicked, who does not repay what he owes, with the righteous, who is generous. Then he says that if the righteous person falls, God holds him up. David wants to encourage those who see that things seem to go well for the wicked, and to remind them that God does not abandon his own.

For today: when you have to make decisions or feel uncertain, pray each morning and entrust your plans to God. Walk with honesty and generosity, trusting that He guides even your stumbles and lifts you up.
exp.24:9:
All the paths of the Lord are full of mercy (kindness that forgives and helps) and truth (faithfulness; he does what he promises). This is for those who keep his covenant, that is, those who care for it and remain loyal to him, and his commandments, which are his instructions and teachings.

It is a prayer of David, according to the heading of the psalm. He asks for forgiveness and guidance, and he acknowledges his sin. Before this, he says that God teaches the humble, and afterward he confesses that his sin is great. For this reason he trusts that God is good.

For today: even when you do not understand the direction of your life, you can trust that God is faithful and compassionate. Obeying him humbly each day helps you walk in peace under his care.
exp.32:6:
This verse says that God gathers the waters of the sea together as a heap, and that he keeps the deep, that is, the deep waters, in storehouses. "Gathereth" means he brings together, and "heap" speaks of a mass gathered into one place.

Psalm 33 is a song of praise, and the text itself does not say who wrote it. It invites the righteous to worship God for his word and for his creation. The verses before it say that God made the heavens by his word. Here the psalmist shows that God also sets limits on the sea, which in ancient times symbolized what is great and frightening. The verses that follow call the whole earth to fear the Lord.

For today: when you feel that troubles are covering you like waves, remember that God rules even the deepest waters. You can hand him your fears with confidence, because what seems enormous to you, he has under control.
exp.62:5:
This verse says that the psalmist remembers God while lying in bed, and thinks about Him during the night watches. That expression refers to the periods into which the night used to be divided, that is, the hours of being awake. Bed is the place where one lies down to rest. To meditate means to think quietly and carefully.

The title of the psalm attributes it to David, when he was in the wilderness of Judah. Perhaps it was a time of flight and danger, though the text gives no further details. He thirsts for God and, even in the middle of difficulty, remembers that He has been his help and his support, as the following verses say.

For today: when you cannot sleep or worries overwhelm you, use that time to remember how God has helped you before. Thank Him for one specific thing and bring your restlessness to Him in a simple prayer.
exp.47:10:
It says that Mount Zion and the daughters of Judah, that is, the cities and towns of Judah, will fill with joy because of God's "judgments." That word does not speak only of punishments, but of his just decisions and of his acts to defend his people. Its wording in the verse above, "let mount Zion rejoice, let the daughters of Judah be glad," shows the same joy.

It is a song of the sons of Korah, sung by the people who worship in the temple. The whole psalm celebrates Jerusalem as a city protected by God. It is not known with certainty what exact event inspired it. Some think of a deliverance from enemies, but this is interpreted in several ways.

For today: let us learn to rejoice that God is just, even when we do not understand everything. When you remember how he has cared for you, thank him out loud and tell someone else about it.
exp.77:17:
They tested God in their hearts. They asked for food not only because they were hungry, but according to their craving or desire. Here, "tested" means putting God to the test, doubting whether he was able or willing to care for them.

The psalmist, named Asaph, recalls the history of Israel in the wilderness after leaving Egypt. God had already given them water from the rock, but they kept doubting. Asaph tells this so that future generations will learn to trust God and not repeat that lack of faith.

For today: when we go through need, we can ask God honestly, but without demanding that he act the way we want or doubting his goodness because of what he has already done. Remembering how he has cared for us before strengthens our trust.
exp.144:0:
Here David says he will extol God, that is, speak of Him with admiration and place Him in the highest position. He calls Him "my God" and "my King," and promises to bless His name, meaning to speak well of Him with gratitude. The phrase "for ever and ever" means without end, for all of life and beyond.

The title presents it as a psalm of praise by David. A king speaks here who acknowledges that there is another King above him. It is a poem of personal worship, though it also invites others to join in. In the verses that follow it explains the reason: God's greatness cannot be fully measured. Some scholars note that this psalm follows the order of the Hebrew alphabet, though there is no need to go into those details here.

Today you can begin the day by saying aloud a short phrase of gratitude to God, without waiting to feel perfect. Praise becomes a habit when you practice it, even on difficult days.
exp.118:25:
The psalmist says he told God everything he had done and lived through, and that God answered him. Then he asks: "teach me thy statutes," that is, your laws and rules. "My ways" refers to his manner of living, his steps and decisions. "Declared" here means to recount, to open the heart.

The one speaking is the author of Psalm 119, whose name is not known with certainty. He speaks of his soul being cleaved to the dust, that is, brought low and weak. In that state, he is open with God and seeks his guidance. Then he asks to understand the way of the commandments and for strength to go on.

Today we can do the same: speak with God honestly about our lives, without hiding failures or weariness. And after praying, open the Bible with a desire to learn, not only to be comforted. God hears us and also wants to teach us.
exp.108:29:
The explanation says that the psalmist promises to praise the Lord with all his strength, with his mouth and out loud. He will not do it in secret, but before many people. "I will greatly praise" means I will praise him or speak well of him. "Greatly" means with great intensity.

The psalm is traditionally attributed to David, according to its title, although some scholars debate its origin. He is distressed by false accusations and enemies who attack him. After asking God for help, he ends with confidence. The following verse explains the reason: God stands at the side of the needy and defends him from those who condemn him.

Today we can thank God out loud, even before we see the full solution. This week, tell a trusted person how God has helped you, or give thanks in your church or family. Praising reminds us that we are not alone.
exp.61:7:
This verse invites all the people to trust in God at all times, not only when everything is going well. The phrase "wait upon him" means to trust and rest in God. "Pour out your heart" means to tell him honestly everything we feel. The word "refuge" here refers to shelter and protection. The word "Selah" is one whose exact meaning is not known for certain; it probably indicates a pause to reflect.
