The speaker is David, according to the heading of the psalm. He has just said that God is his rock and his salvation. Now he encourages others to do the same. Afterward he warns that trusting in people, in violence, or in riches is useless.

Today you can take a moment of your day to speak with God without pretense, telling him your fears, weariness, and worries. He is a secure refuge, and he invites us to come near with confidence.
exp.142:5:
The explanation says that the psalmist lifts his hands toward God, as a sign of prayer and need. He compares his soul to dry ground, which waits for rain. "Selah" is a pause or musical marking whose exact length is not known for certain.

The psalm is traditionally attributed to David, though some scholars think it may have been written by someone else in his style. He feels persecuted and deeply distressed. In that pain he remembers what God has done before, and this stirs up his desire to seek Him. His spiritual thirst is real and deep.

For today: when you feel dry or weary inside, do not turn away from God. Remember how He has helped you before, and come to Him with sincerity. Tell Him how much you need Him, with your hands open, and hope that He will refresh you.
exp.2:4:
The verse says that the psalmist lay down, slept, and woke up alive and at peace, and he attributes this to the Lord, Jehovah, having upheld him. The word "upheld" means that God supported him and kept him steady, like someone holding up a person who cannot stand on their own.

The title of the psalm attributes it to David, when he was fleeing from his son Absalom. He was surrounded by enemies and in serious danger, and yet he was able to sleep. His calm did not come from the danger having passed, but from having already cried out to God and received an answer. That is why he can say afterward that he will not fear the thousands who surround him.

Today, when worry takes away our sleep, we can bring to God in prayer whatever troubles us before we go to bed. Entrusting the night to God, and trusting that he continues to care for us while we sleep, helps us rest with greater peace.
exp.104:24:
The verse says that God changed the attitude of the Egyptians toward Israel, so that they came to hate his people and to plot harm against those who served him. The old word for "hate" in the source means to hate, and the phrase about plotting means to plan harm. This psalm does not explain how that change came about; it simply attributes it to God's action.

The psalmist recalls the history of Israel in Egypt. After God made his people grow and become strong, the Egyptians felt fear and rejection. The author reviews these events to praise God for his faithfulness. Some scholars see here a way of speaking about how God allows difficult situations to accomplish his purposes, while others understand it in a more literal way. Either way, the psalm presents it as part of a plan that leads to deliverance.

When you face rejection or difficulty, remember that God is still at work even in what you do not understand. Trust that his care continues, even in the hardest times.
exp.18:7:
This verse says that the statutes of the Lord are "right," meaning correct and without deceit, and that is why they bring joy to the heart. It also says that his commandment is "pure," clean and free of any mixture of error, and that it "enlightening the eyes," that is, it gives clarity to understand and to see life in the light.

The psalm is attributed to David. First it praises God for what is shown in creation, such as the sun, and then it moves on to celebrate his Word. Here the psalmist uses several images to describe how valuable the law of God is for the life of his people.

For today: when you feel confusion or discouragement, read a passage of the Bible calmly and ask God to show you what to do. His Word can give you clear direction and a deep joy, even in difficult times.
exp.140:2:
David here asks God to set a guard, like a watchman, over his mouth. Picture a doorway with a sentry who decides what goes out and what stays in. A "guard" means a watchman or sentry, and the lips are the doorway through which words come out.

David prays to God in a moment of pressure. Surrounded by people who do wrong, he knows that his heart and his tongue could be pulled along with them. That is why, right after, he asks not to be drawn toward evil or to share in the pleasures of the wicked. His prayer is humble: he recognizes that he cannot control himself alone.

Today, before you answer in anger, gossip, or post something online, pray a short prayer: "Lord, keep watch over my mouth." Then wait a moment before you speak. Asking God for help makes us wiser and kinder.
exp.47:8:
The explanation says that God's people, gathered in the temple, pause to think calmly about his lovingkindness. The word translated "thought of" here can also be understood as "meditated on" or "considered"; some translations use that sense, and others prefer "remembered". "Lovingkindness" is his faithful, steadfast love.

It is a song of the sons of Korah, spoken together as a community. Jerusalem had been protected from enemies, and the people do not credit that to its walls but to God. Now, in the temple, they look back and give thanks. Scholars do not agree on which exact attack or event the psalm had in mind.

For today: before you worry about what is coming, pause, alone or with your church, and remember how God has cared for you. Write down three times he showed you his lovingkindness and thank him for them. This strengthens trust.
exp.61:10:
God has spoken once; twice have I heard this; that power belongeth unto God. This verse says that God spoke once, but David heard it twice, meaning he holds it very clearly: strength, or power, belongs to God. The words "once" and "twice" form a way of speaking that shows something is firm and certain. The word "strength" here means power and might.

The one speaking is David, according to the title of the psalm, although some scholars debate this. It follows from saying that people are as fragile as a breath and that one should not trust in violence, in robbery, or in riches. Then it shows where true power really is: in God, who is also merciful and just.

Today we can ask ourselves what we lean on when we are afraid: money, our own abilities, or what others think. Today, in your worry, repeat calmly: "That power belongeth unto God," and bring that burden to him in prayer.
exp.71:11:
He says the righteous king will rescue the needy person who cries out for help, and also the one who suffers and has no one to come to their aid. "Needy" describes someone who lacks what is necessary; "afflicted" describes someone who is oppressed or distressed; "help" means to assist or come to the aid of.

This psalm is a prayer for the king, and its title attributes it to Solomon, though some understand it as written by David or for Solomon. Earlier it speaks of kings and nations bowing before him. Here it explains why his authority is good: he is not only powerful, but protects the weak. Christians often see in this also a picture of the reign of Christ.

For today: do not ignore the person who is alone and without support. This week, help someone in need with something concrete, whether with your time, a visit, food, or by speaking up on their behalf.
exp.40:12:
This verse is a song of praise. It says that God, called here the LORD, the God of Israel, deserves to be blessed, that is, praised and recognized as good, forever. "Forever and ever" means for all eternity. The closing "Amen, and Amen" is a way of saying with firm conviction: "So it is, truly."

The speaker is King David, according to the traditional heading of the psalm. He has spoken of his illness, of enemies, and of the betrayal of a friend. Even so, he ends grateful because God sustained him. This verse closes Book I of the Psalms; many scholars think it is a final formula added when the book was arranged, though this is understood in different ways.

For today: even when you go through pain or disappointment, end your day giving thanks to God for one concrete way he sustained you. Giving thanks reminds you that you are not alone.
exp.74:5:
The explanation says that no promotion or position of honor comes from any direction on the map: not from the east, not from the west, not from the desert. Being "lifted up" means being raised to a high place, like a promotion or recognition. No person or nation achieves it by their own means alone.

It is a psalm of Asaph. In the verses nearby, someone warns the proud not to boast or to lift up their horn, an image of strength and arrogance. Some think God is speaking here and others think the psalmist is, and the text does not fully settle it. What follows explains the point: God is the judge, and he brings down one and lifts up another.

Today, if you receive an achievement, thank God for it and do not boast. If you lack recognition, trust that he sees and can lift you up in his time.
exp.62:9:
It says that the enemies of the psalmist will die in battle, by the sword, and that their bodies will be left unburied and will become food for foxes.

David speaks (as the title of the psalm indicates). He was in the wilderness of Judah, seeking God and thirsting for his presence. There were people who wanted to kill him. Some understand that this refers to the persecution by Saul, and others to the rebellion of Absalom; it is not certain. He trusts that God will do justice.

For today: when someone treats you unjustly, do not take revenge. Cling to God, as the previous verse says, and leave judgment in his hands. That gives you peace and frees you from bitterness.
exp.70:23:
The explanation says that the psalmist will speak of God's righteousness all day long, that is, constantly. The reason is that those who sought to harm him were put to shame and left confused. The words "sought to" mean tried or attempted. "Confused" means frustrated, with their plans undone.

This is the closing of a psalm by a believer who is now old (vv. 9, 18), who has gone through many trials and has been attacked by enemies. The tradition gives no author in the title, and many connect it with David, though this is not certain. Before this verse, he promises to praise God with music and with his redeemed soul.

For today: when God sustains you in a difficulty, do not keep silent. Think of a situation where He helped you and tell it today to someone. Speaking of his faithfulness strengthens your faith and encourages others, without any need to rejoice in another's misfortune.
exp.82:7:
Here it says that Assyria, a great power of that time, joined the alliance of nations hostile to Israel. The phrase about "the children of Lot" refers to Moab and Ammon, peoples descended from Lot, the nephew of Abraham, and the verse says that Assyria gave them support and strength. "Selah" is a pause, a call to stop and reflect.

Psalm 83 is attributed to Asaph. It is a cry for help: several neighboring nations conspire to wipe out the name of Israel. It is not known with certainty which historical moment it refers to, and scholars have interpreted it in different ways. Assyria appears here as a powerful ally who strengthens the threat.

For today: when you feel that difficulties are piling up and overwhelming you, follow the psalmist's example. Do not stay alone with your fear; bring it to God in prayer with sincerity, trusting that He is greater than any alliance against you.
exp.63:9:
The explanation says the righteous person will be filled with joy because of who God is, that is, in the Lord, the name of the Lord. They will also place their trust in him. "Shall glory" means they will feel proud and happy to belong to God. The upright in heart are those who live with sincerity, without duplicity.

The psalm is by David, who asks for protection against enemies who attack with words, slander, and hidden schemes. Before this verse, he describes how God brings down those wicked people and how people recognize what God has done. This verse is the closing: after God's justice, the faithful respond with joy and trust.

For today: when you face injustice or false criticism, don't stay only in anguish. Hand the matter over to God, trust that he sees everything, and look for concrete reasons to give him thanks. That trust brings joy, even while you wait.
exp.128:3:
He says that God is righteous and that he has cut the cords of the wicked. The cords are the ropes or straps that tied oxen to the yoke for plowing. So the psalmist pictures the Lord cutting the cords with which the oppressors held and mistreated his people, leaving them unable to keep doing harm.

Israel, the people of God, speaks through the voice of the psalmist. It remembers how they oppressed it from its youth, as if they had plowed its back with long furrows. Even so, they did not defeat it. This is a psalm of pilgrimage, and it was sung to remember that God was faithful in the midst of suffering.

For today: if you are going through an injustice or a burden that seems never to end, you can rest in the fact that God sees and is righteous. He knows when and how to break the cords that oppress. In the meantime, remember the times he sustained you, and trust that he will not leave you alone.
exp.88:20:
This verse says that God promises to sustain David with his power. God's "hand" and "arm" represent his strength and his help. The phrase "will be firm with him" means that he will stay by David's side without failing. The phrase "will strengthen him" means that he will give him the strength to carry out what he entrusted to him.

Here God speaks, recalling what he promised to David when he chose him and anointed him as king. The psalmist, Ethan the Ezrahite according to the title of the psalm, reviews that promise in order to rest on it. Later in the psalm, the situation of Israel seems to contradict it, and so the author asks God to be faithful to his word.

For today: if God has given you a task or a responsibility, you can trust that he will not leave you alone. Ask him for strength each day, and rest in the knowledge that his help is firmer than your own abilities.
exp.37:12:
The explanation says the author acted as if he were deaf and mute toward those who attacked him. He did not answer their words or defend himself. The sentence that explains the contrast of "but" and "as if" in the verse should be dealt with: here the verse states "as a deaf man" and "as a dumb man," which show that he acted this way on purpose and that it was not a real deafness.

David speaks, according to the psalm's heading, in a prayer of someone who is sick, alone, and abandoned by his friends. His enemies lay in wait for him with lies and deceit. Faced with this, he decides to keep silent and not fight. The next verse gives the reason: he waits on God and trusts that He will answer. Some understand this silence as trust, and others also as a certain weariness in the face of pain.

For today: when you are criticized or slandered, you do not always need to answer right away. You can keep silent, pray, and place your situation in God's hands, waiting for Him to act in His time.
exp.118:107:
Here the psalmist asks God to graciously accept the freewill offerings of his mouth. These are offerings that were not required but came from the heart: his praises, prayers, and thanks spoken with his lips. The word "judgments" means God's just decisions and teachings, so he also asks, "teach me thy judgments."

The one speaking is the author of Psalm 119, whose name we do not know for certain. He is suffering greatly and surrounded by enemies who set traps for him. Even so, he has promised to obey God and does not forget his law. His praise arises in the middle of his pain.

For today: praise God with your words even in difficult days, not out of obligation, but sincerely. And ask him to teach you to live as pleases him, opening your Bible with humility and a desire to learn.
exp.104:41:
He kept the promise he had made. "He remembered" does not mean he had forgotten, but that he acted on behalf of his people in keeping with his promise. "His holy promise" is his sacred word, given to Abraham, whom he calls "his servant."

This psalm is a song of praise that recalls God's works in the history of Israel. The author does not name himself in this psalm. It goes over the plagues of Egypt, the manna, the quail, and the water from the rock. All of this is presented as the fruit of God's faithfulness to his covenant with Abraham, and it leads to the entry into the promised land.

For today: when your faith grows weary of waiting, remember that God is faithful to his word. Take stock of how he has cared for you in the past, and trust that he continues to keep what he promises, even when his timing is not yours.
exp.65:11:
He says that God allowed other men to dominate and trample his people, as if they were riding over their heads. They went through extreme dangers, the kind of peril that is like passing through fire and through water. But in the end God brought them out into a place of abundance and rest. The words "wealthy place" mean a place of plenty and relief.

The psalmist speaks on behalf of the whole nation of Israel, giving thanks for a deliverance. It is not known with certainty which episode he has in mind; some think of the Exodus or of some other national crisis. The verses before this one explain that God tested them as silver is refined, and the verses that follow show the psalmist fulfilling his vows in the temple.

For today: when you go through a hard trial, remember that God can use it to purify you and that he does not leave you alone. Write down today one promise you made to God in a difficult moment, and fulfill it with gratitude.
exp.8:15:
This verse says that God makes himself known when he carries out justice. The wicked person is caught by the very thing he prepared: his own wrongdoing turns back against him. The word "snared" means he was caught, like an animal in a net, and the KJV's "snared" is the word used here. The words "Higgaion" and "Selah" are musical or meditative terms; their exact meaning is not known, but they seem to invite a pause and reflection.

David is the one speaking in this psalm. He is grateful because God defended him from his enemies. Earlier he spoke of nations that fell into the pit they had dug. Then he says that God does not forget the poor or their hope.

For today: when you see injustice, do not give in to revenge or bitterness. Trust that God sees everything and that he brings justice in his own time. In the meantime, try to live with honesty, and take a pause to meditate on his faithfulness.
exp.96:6:
Psalm 97:7 says that those who serve carved images and boast of their idols will be put to shame. The "gods," meaning everything people worship in place of God, are told to bow down before the Lord. Where the explanation comments on the old wording, I have rewritten it for the words of the verse your reader sees: "serve" for the first sense and "boast" for the second, with "bow down" for the third.

The psalmist, whose name is not given, celebrates that the LORD reigns over all the earth. After describing his power and justice, he declares that idols have no worth before Him. Some understand "the gods" as spiritual beings and others as simple false idols; the text allows both readings. Then Zion rejoices because of God's judgments.

Today we can ask ourselves what things take the place of God in our hearts: money, success, appearance, or approval. Ask God to help you put Him first, and trust Him more than those things.
exp.46:0:
This verse begins with a dedication: the psalm is for the director of the choir or of the music, and it comes from the sons of Korah, a group of Levites who served in worship. Then it calls all the peoples to clap their hands, that is, to applaud, and to shout to God, that is, to cry out to him with joy and a voice of gladness.

The psalmist invites people to celebrate God in public. The following verse gives the reason: the LORD is the Most High, the great King over all the earth. It is not known for certain on what occasion it was written; some think it was for a feast in the temple, and others connect it with a victory. His invitation embraces all the nations, not only Israel.

For today: do not keep your praise only to yourself. Today, in your church or at home, rejoice openly over who God is, without shame, because He reigns over everything.
exp.17:36:
David speaks here and says that he pursued his enemies, caught up with them, and did not stop until he had brought them to a complete end. The words "pursued" and "overtaken" in the verse describe chasing down and catching his foes, and "neither did I turn again till they were consumed" means that he did not return or give up halfway.

The psalm's heading presents David singing to God on the day the Lord delivered him from all his enemies and from the hand of Saul. It is a song of thanksgiving. Before and after this verse, David makes clear that the strength was not his own: God gave him the shield, upheld him, and girded him with strength for the battle. It is the language of war appropriate to a king of that time.

For today: when you face a struggle, such as a habit, a fear, or a problem that will not give way, do not leave it unfinished or rely only on your own strength. Ask God for strength, persevere, and then give him the thanks.
exp.72:25:
The explanation says that the psalmist's body and spirit may fail, that is, run out of strength. But God is his rock, something firm that sustains him from within, and his portion, the most precious thing he receives in life. And this lasts forever. The word "faileth" means that one grows weak or is worn out. "Whoring" here speaks of spiritual unfaithfulness toward God.

The speaker is Asaph, the author of this psalm. He had felt envy on seeing the wicked prosper and nearly lost his faith. Upon entering the sanctuary he changed the way he saw things. He acknowledges that God has guided him and that God remains his greatest treasure, even though not everything is explained to him.

Today, when you feel tired, sick, or confused, do not lean only on your own strength or on what others have. Spend a few minutes praying sincerely and telling God: "You are my rock."
exp.27:7:
God is said to be the strength of his people and also the refuge who gives power and salvation to his anointed one. A "stronghold" is a safe and firm place. "Salvations" is an old way of saying rescues, victories, and care. An "anointed one" is someone chosen by God for a mission, here probably the king.

The psalm is attributed to David. He has just seen that God heard his prayer and helped him, so he moves from asking for help to giving thanks. Here he speaks of "their" strength, looking at the whole people and the king who leads them. Then he asks God to save and care for his people like a shepherd. Some understand "anointed" as only David; others also see a hope that points to Christ.

For today: when you feel weak, do not rely only on your own strength. Before you act, pray and ask God to sustain you. Then give thanks for every help you receive.
exp.85:7:
He says that among all those called "gods," there is no one like the Lord, and nothing they do can compare with what He does. The phrase "there is none like you" means that God is unique. The word "gods" refers to the deities other peoples worshiped, and the psalmist places them far below the Lord.

It is a prayer of David, according to the heading of the psalm. He is in distress and asks for help, but before asking, he remembers who God is. He trusts that God answers, and so he speaks of God's greatness. Then he says that all the nations will acknowledge Him, and that He alone is God.

For today: when you feel overwhelmed, begin your prayer by remembering who God is and what He has done before. Looking at His greatness does not erase the problem, but it puts the problem in its true size and strengthens your trust.
exp.108:0:
This verse begins with a dedication: it is a psalm of David, given to the chief musician, that is, to the leader of singing in worship. Then David cries out: "Hold not thy peace, O God of my praise." It means: "God, you whom I always praise, do not remain silent or ignore me."

David is speaking, probably at a time of false accusations, as the verses that follow show. He does not defend himself with revenge of his own, but asks God to intervene. It is a sincere prayer from someone who has been wounded. The exact details of the situation are not known with certainty.

For today: when someone speaks badly of you without reason, bring that pain to God in prayer before you respond. You can praise him and, at the same time, honestly ask him to defend you and give you peace.
exp.134:7:
This verse says that God is the one who struck the firstborn of Egypt, both of people and of animals. The word "struck" means that he killed them. It refers to the last of the ten plagues, which is told in Exodus 11 and 12.

The psalmist, who cannot be identified with certainty, calls the people to praise the LORD. First he speaks of God's power over nature: clouds, lightning, and winds. Then he recalls God's power in history, when he delivered Israel out of Egypt. It is a grateful remembrance that God accomplishes his will and rescues his people, although the passage is harsh and shows his judgment on Egypt.

For today: when you feel trapped by something that seems stronger than you, remember that God has already shown that he can deliver. Praise him with gratitude and trust him, without taking this text as permission for violence.
exp.30:1:
Here the psalmist asks God to listen to him with close attention: "bow down thine ear" is like stooping down to hear someone better. He asks to be rescued "speedily," which means quickly or without delay. He also begs that God be for him "a strong rock" and "an house of defence," that is, a firm and safe refuge where nothing can reach him.

The psalm carries the name of David, though it is not known with certainty at what exact moment of his life he wrote it. It is clear that he faces a real danger: he speaks of hidden nets and of enemies. Before asking for help, he has already said that he has waited on God and trusts in his righteousness. His plea comes from trust, not from despair.

For today: when you feel pressure or fear, pray sincerely and ask God to be your refuge. You can say in your own words: "Lord, hear me, you are my safe place." Then rest in the knowledge that he cares for you.
exp.33:21:
This verse says that God rescues the lives of those who serve him. "Redeemeth" in the verse above means to set free or rescue by paying a price, and the word "soul" here refers to the whole person, their life. Those who trust in God will not be left to ruin, which is what "desolate" means: to be ruined, abandoned, or destroyed.

David speaks here, according to the title of the psalm, after escaping a serious danger before King Abimelech (in 1 Samuel 21 he is called Achish). That is why he praises God and encourages others to trust him. The verses before this one contrast the righteous, whom God watches over, with the wicked, who fall through their own evil. This verse closes the psalm with that hope.

For today: when you feel fear or pressure, bring your situation to God in prayer and keep doing what is right. Trusting God does not guarantee a life without pain, but it does mean that God sustains your life and will not leave you lost.
exp.118:138:
He says the psalmist feels a love for God so strong that it wears him down from within. "Zeal" is a passionate interest, and "consumed" means worn out or devoured. The cause is painful: those who oppose him no longer remember what God said, that is, they ignore it or set it aside.

The one speaking is the author of Psalm 119, a believer who loves God's word. We do not know for certain who he was. Earlier he said that God's testimonies are righteous and faithful, and later he will say that God's word is pure. That is why it hurts him to see others despise it. His pain comes from loving God, not from pride.

Today we can be concerned when God's word is ignored, but with humility and love. A good way to begin is to read the Bible each day and live it out with example and kindness, praying for those who have forgotten it.
exp.118:50:
The proud mocked the psalmist greatly, but he did not turn aside from God's law. The "proud" are the arrogant, those who think themselves superior and do not want to submit to God. "Law" here means the teachings and instructions of the Lord. Although they ridiculed him, he remained firm.

Psalm 119 does not say with certainty who wrote it; tradition often thinks of David, but this is not certain. The one speaking is a believer who suffers affliction and relies on God's promise. In the nearby verses he says that God's word comforts him and gives him life, that is, it gives him life and encouragement. That strength enables him to withstand the mockery.

If someone mocks your faith or your values, you do not have to respond with anger or give in. Seek comfort in the Word of God, remember his promises, and ask him for the courage to remain faithful with humility.
exp.48:4:
The explanation says that the psalmist has no reason to be afraid when hard times come, even though the wickedness of those who lie in wait for him surrounds him. Those who set traps or seek to harm through deceit are the ones who lie in wait; and wickedness or injustice is what they bring. Some translators understand the enemies as "those who pursue me"; others read the phrase as wickedness surrounding his heels, and it is not entirely certain which is the exact meaning.

The speaker is a wise man, perhaps a poet of the people, who says he will teach through a proverb and with the music of the harp. His question expresses not doubt but confidence. He then shows that those who trust in their wealth cannot save themselves or redeem others, but whoever trusts in God has a firm hope.

Today, when you feel fear because of threats, injustice, or crisis, remember where your trust is placed. Money does not fully protect you; God does sustain you. Pray and rest in Him.
exp.29:6:
It says that God, by his kindness and favor, made the psalmist's life firm like a mountain. But when God hid his face, that is, when the psalmist no longer felt God's presence and help, he was troubled, meaning he was very frightened and disturbed.

The psalm is spoken by David, according to its title, which mentions the dedication of the house (the text does not clearly say which moment it refers to). Earlier he said he felt secure and thought he would never fall. Now he recognizes that his strength did not come from himself but from God, and he realized this when he felt God's absence.

For today: when everything is going well, do not boast in your own strength. Thank God for what you have. And if one day you feel that God is far away and you are troubled, do what the psalmist did: cry out to Him with confidence.
exp.2:1:
Here David reports what his enemies are saying: "God will not save him anymore." The word "salvation" here means rescue or deliverance, not sickness. "Of my soul" means "about me" or "about my life." "Selah" is a pause, probably musical or for reflection; its exact meaning is uncertain.

David wrote this psalm when he was fleeing from his son Absalom, who had rebelled against him. It was a time of humiliation and danger. The people speaking believe that God has abandoned the king, perhaps because of his past sins, although the text does not say so. David does not argue with them but brings everything to God, and in the next verse he declares that the LORD is his shield.

Today, others may tell you that God has left you alone, or your own thoughts may tell you so. Those voices do not have the last word. Do as David did: pause, tell God what you are hearing, and remember who he is to you.
exp.104:43:
He says that God gave the Israelites the lands that had previously belonged to other peoples. The phrase "gave them" carries the sense of handing something over. "The labour of the nations" refers to what those peoples had worked on and built: crops, houses, vineyards, and cities. The Israelites received it as an inheritance, without having built it themselves.

The psalmist, whose name the text does not give, reviews Israel's history to praise God. He recalls that God kept the promise made to Abraham, brought his people out of Egypt, and then gave them the land of Canaan. The following verse explains the purpose: that they would keep his laws and obey him. The land was a gift, but it was also a responsibility.

Today we can recognize that much of what we have is a gift from God, not only the fruit of our own effort. That invites us to give thanks every day and to use what we have received in a way that honors God and blesses others.
exp.85:0:
David asks God to come close and listen to him. "Bow down thine ear" is a figure of speech: like someone who leans down to hear better a person who is speaking softly. The explanation says the psalm is a prayer of David, according to its title. The text does not explain the exact situation. The verses that follow show that he prays with confidence in God and cries out to Him all day, so he is going through a hard time and sees no way out except through God.

For today: you do not have to pretend you are fine in order to pray. You can come before God just as you are, tired, worried, or in need, and tell Him simply: "Lord, hear me, I need you." Doing so is an act of trust.
exp.46:4:
This verse says that God went up amid shouts of joy and the sound of a trumpet. The words "went up" are the ones quoted from the source, and "joy" is the great delight the verse describes. The name of the God of Israel is the Lord. It is like a celebration when a king arrives or takes his place of honor.

The psalm is an invitation from the sons of Korah, according to its heading, for all peoples to clap their hands to God as King. It may recall a victory or a procession toward the temple in Jerusalem. Some think it was sung when the ark was carried up to Mount Zion, but this is not certain. The exact place and occasion are understood in several ways. What is clear is that the people celebrate that God reigns over the nations.

For today: praise God with joy, not only out of habit. Before your worries, take a moment to sing or give thanks to Him, remembering that He reigns over all.
exp.67:21:
It says that the Lord promises to bring his people back, even if they are far away like Bashan, a region east of the Jordan, or hidden in places as deep as the bottom of the sea. There is no place so distant that God cannot reach it.

The psalm is by David and celebrates God as Savior and Judge. It comes right after speaking of God delivering from death and defeating his enemies. Here God promises to rescue his own. Some understand it to refer to enemies or to scattered Israelites; the text does not make this entirely clear, and scholars interpret it in several ways.

For today: if you feel lost, far away, or deeply sunk in a difficulty, remember that God knows where you are. You can pray with confidence, for he has the power to rescue you and bring you back.
exp.66:6:
It says we ask God to bless us, so that all the nations, even the most distant places, will respect him. "Fear him" here does not mean being afraid, but revering him, honoring him, and living in obedience. All the corners of the earth means every corner of the world.

Psalm 67 is a prayer or song of Israel, and no one knows for certain who wrote it or on what occasion it was sung. Some think it was used at times of thanks for the harvest, since the verse before it speaks of the earth giving its fruit. The central point is that Israel asks for blessing so that other peoples will come to know God.

For today: when you ask God for something good, also ask yourself how your blessed life can show him to others. Share generously, treat people well, and speak humbly about what God has done in you.
exp.117:18:
This verse is both a request and a promise. The speaker asks that the gates of righteousness be opened to them, meaning the entrances to the place where God is worshiped and where people live uprightly. They say they will go in and praise the LORD.

The psalm is a song of thanksgiving. The speaker has come through a hard trial; God corrected them, but rescued them from death. Many believe it refers to the temple in Jerusalem, and that a king or leader speaks on behalf of the people, though the psalm does not say so with certainty. Christians have also read in it a foreshadowing of Christ.

Today, after a difficult time, do not let gratitude pass by. Find a moment, alone or with your church, to enter into God's presence and give thanks for sustaining you.
exp.49:11:
He says that God does not need our food or our offerings. And if he were ever hungry, he would not ask anyone for it, because everything belongs to him. The phrase "the fulness thereof" means everything that fills the earth: its animals, its fruits, and its riches.

God himself is speaking, in a psalm of Asaph. He is correcting his people, who were offering sacrifices as if God depended on them, but were doing so in an empty way. God does not reject sacrifices as such. He asks for a grateful and sincere heart, as the next verse shows, which calls us to offer praise as a sacrifice to God.

For today: do not serve God in order to give him something he lacks, because he needs nothing. Come to him with gratitude, recognizing that everything you have comes from him, and live out that gratitude through prayer, praise, and sincere obedience.
exp.21:21:
Here the speaker promises to make known the name of God, that is, who God is and what he is like, to his "brothers," his family and his people. And he will do it "in the midst of the congregation," that is, in the gathering of the people, praising him in public.

This is a psalm of David. Before this verse, he cries out in despair, surrounded by enemies who are like dogs and lions. Suddenly the tone changes: after asking for help, he promises to praise God. The verses that follow explain why: God heard the afflicted man and did not abandon him. In the New Testament, Hebrews 2:12 applies this verse to Jesus.

When God helps you through a difficulty, do not keep the testimony to yourself. Tell your family or your church; your story can encourage others to trust God.
exp.118:68:
The explanation says that proud people invented lies to harm the psalmist. The phrase for this is rendered as "forged a lie," which means to fabricate or build a false accusation. "The proud" are the arrogant, those who think they are superior and do not submit to God. Facing this, the psalmist resolves: "I will keep your precepts with my whole heart," that is, he will obey God with complete sincerity, not halfway.

The one speaking is the author of the psalm, who cannot be identified with certainty. Some think of David, but this cannot be asserted. Earlier he acknowledges that he had gone astray until God humbled him, and now he trusts that God is good. He then contrasts his heart with that of the proud, whose hearts are dull and insensitive. Even while slandered, he holds fast to the Word.

Today, when someone speaks badly of you unjustly, do not answer with revenge or lies. Ask God for calm, examine your heart, and keep obeying him with integrity. Your faithful response is worth more than your defense.
exp.73:20:
This verse is a prayer. The psalmist asks God that the one who is "crushed," that is, the oppressed and humbled, not turn away ashamed, like someone who asked for help and did not receive it. He says that the one who is "troubled" and the one who is "needy," that is, the poor and those in want, will praise God's name when He helps them.

Psalm 74 is a lament of God's people, attributed to Asaph. It seems to reflect the destruction of the sanctuary by enemies, though it is not known with certainty whether the psalmist speaks of the fall of Jerusalem or of some other event. Here he appeals to God's covenant and to His faithfulness.

For today: if you are weighed down, you can bring your need before God with sincerity, without fear of being rejected. And when He helps you, do not forget to give Him thanks out loud.
exp.104:38:
He spread a cloud over his people to cover them, like a roof that gave shade and protection in the desert. And at night, instead of darkness, he set a fire that gave light. "Covering" means something that covers or protects; "give light" means to shed light.

It is a psalm of praise, written by an author who is not named in the text. It recalls how God brought Israel out of Egypt and cared for them in the desert. The verses before it speak of the departure; the verses after it, of food and water. The author wants the people to remember God's works and to remain faithful to him.

God cares for us by day and by night, in the light and in the dark. When you go through a difficult time, remember how he has sustained you before. Write down three occasions when God helped you and give him thanks for them today.
exp.54:8:
Here the psalmist asks God to "destroy" the plans of the violent and to "divide their tongues," that is, to confuse their words and counsel so that they cannot agree. The word "strife" means quarrel, fighting, or discord. He has seen violence and fighting throughout the city.

The psalm is attributed to David, and the text presents him as someone distressed, who wishes to flee to the wilderness. Some connect it with Absalom's rebellion and the betrayal of a close friend, but the psalm does not say so clearly. Some recall when God confused the languages at Babel, although that is only one possible connection.

When you see injustice, quarrels, or wickedness around you, do not carry it alone. Ask God to stop the evil and give you wisdom, and keep seeking peace with those around you.
exp.32:4:
God loves righteousness and justice. Here "judgment" means deciding rightly, doing what is correct. And the mercy he shows is his faithful, kind love, which fills the whole earth. God is not indifferent to good and evil, but his goodness also reaches everyone.

The psalm does not say who wrote it; some attribute it to David, but this is not certain. The speaker invites the righteous to praise God with a new song. The reason is that his word is upright and his works are true. The verses that follow show his power as Creator.

Today, when you see injustice or feel far from God, remember that he loves justice and that his goodness is present in the world. Thank him for one concrete sign of his mercy today, and try to treat others with justice and kindness.
exp.123:0:
The explanation says that the people of Israel should acknowledge out loud that, if the Lord had not been on their side, things would have gone very badly for them. The title "A Song of degrees" appears over several psalms; many believe these were sung by pilgrims as they went up to Jerusalem, although this cannot be known with complete certainty. "Now may Israel say" is an invitation to confess that truth together.

Here, according to the title, David speaks, although some scholars doubt that he wrote it. He invites the whole people to remember that they were delivered from enemies who seemed very strong. It is a song of communal thanksgiving, not only personal.

For today: think of some difficulty you came out of without understanding how. Instead of attributing it to luck or to your own strength, give thanks to God out loud, and better still, tell others in your church or family so as to encourage them.
exp.32:18:
This verse says that God watches over those who fear Him and hope in His mercy, and it gives a purpose: to save their lives from death and to sustain them when there is hunger. The phrase about delivering their soul means rescuing their life, the whole person. The phrase about keeping them alive means sustaining them and providing for them in times of scarcity.

The psalm does not name an author in the text itself; some traditions attribute it to David, but this is not certain. It is a song of praise for God's people. The verses before it say that neither the king nor the war horse brings true salvation. Only God can deliver, and so the people declare that they wait on Him.

For today: when money, work, or food runs short, do what is within your reach, but do not place your security only in that. Pray with confidence, ask God to sustain you, and remember that He cares for His own.
exp.133:2:
This verse is a closing blessing. It says that the Lord, the God who made heaven and earth, should bless the one who hears it, and that this blessing should come "out of Zion," that is, from Jerusalem, where the temple stood.

The psalm is a song of ascents, a song that was probably sung on the way up to Jerusalem, though scholars explain it in several ways. First, the servants who keep watch over the temple at night are encouraged to praise God. Here it seems that a priest or leader answers them with a blessing in return. It is a reminder that the God of Zion is not limited to one place: he is the Creator of everything.

For today: when your day ends, bless God for his care, even if you are tired or alone. And do the same for others: say to someone, sincerely, "May God bless you," remembering that the Creator of the universe also cares for you.
exp.35:7:
It says that those who take refuge in God will be fully satisfied. "Drink deeply" here means being filled completely, like someone who eats and drinks in abundance. The "fatness" of the house is the best and richest part of the food, and to "make drink" means to give someone water. "Your house" refers to the place of God's presence, and "the river of your pleasures" speaks of a stream of joy that God himself gives.

The speaker is David, according to the psalm's title. Before this verse, he contrasts the wickedness of the wicked with God's faithful love. Then he shows how those who shelter under his wings receive his provision. After that he says that the fountain of life is in God.

For today: when you feel emptiness or weariness, do not run first to other sources. Spend a few minutes in prayer and in reading the Bible, and ask God to fill you with his peace and his joy.
exp.94:3:
This verse says that God holds in his hand everything that lies deep within the earth, such as caves and chasms, and that the highest peaks of the mountains also belong to him. In other words, from the deepest places to the highest, everything is under his rule. "Theirs" in the old wording means "belong to him."

The psalm does not say who wrote it. It is a song of worship that invites the people to come before God with joy. This verse gives a reason to praise him: God is a great King and Creator, and nothing in creation escapes his care. The psalm then invites us to bow down before him.

For today: when you find yourself in a low place or facing an impossible mountain, remember that both are in God's hands. Before telling him your problem, take a moment to praise him for who he is.
exp.48:10:
The verse says that the rich, in their hearts, think their houses will last forever and their dwellings will pass from generation to generation. They even give their own names to their lands so that they will be remembered. "Their inward thought" is the same as what the verse calls their innermost thinking, and the word for dwellings refers to their homes.

The psalmist, one of the sons of Korah, speaks as a wise teacher who instructs everyone. He wants to remove the fear that people feel before the rich and powerful. He reminds them that both the wise and the foolish die and leave their riches to others. For this reason, the security that money gives is an illusion.

For today: ask yourself where you are placing your security. Enjoy what you have with gratitude, but do not make it your refuge. Invest your life in what truly lasts: trusting God, loving people, and living generously.
exp.105:22:
It says that God was about to destroy Israel because of their sin, but Moses, whom God had chosen, stood "in the breach," that is, in the gap of a broken wall. There he stood between God and the people to hold back God's anger and keep him from destroying them.

The psalmist recalls the history of Israel. He speaks of the sin of the golden calf at Sinai (Exodus 32), when the people forgot the wonders God had done in Egypt. The psalm confesses the people's failings and also shows God's mercy. Moses appears as an intercessor, and his prayers were heard.

Today we can pray for others with courage: for family, friends, or the community. For Christians, Jesus is the perfect intercessor (Hebrews 7:25). Our prayer matters, but we always rest in his mercy.
exp.79:14:
Psalm 80:15 speaks of Israel as a plant, a young shoot that God himself planted with his own hand, that is, with his power and care. A "shoot" is a young sprout. The phrase "that thou madest strong for thyself" means that God strengthened it and made it firm for his own purpose. Some translations read "son" instead of "shoot," and scholars debate whether this refers to the people or to a king.

The psalm is a communal prayer attributed to Asaph. The people are suffering: their vineyard has been trampled and burned by enemies. So they cry out to God, reminding him that they are his work, and they ask him to return, look upon them, and restore them.

For today: when you feel trampled or worn out, remember that God planted you and sustains you. You can pray with sincerity, relying on what he has already done for you, and ask him to renew you.
exp.20:6:
This verse says that the king will not be shaken or fall, because he trusts in the Lord and in the steadfast love of the Most High. The word "mercy" here refers to a loyal kindness, a love that does not abandon. The word "moved" means being moved from one's place, made to totter.

It is a psalm of David, or dedicated to him, that thanks God for the king's victories and blessings. The verses before it speak of glory and joy; the verses after it speak of defeated enemies. Here the reason for his firmness is explained: it lies not in his army, but in his trust in God. Many Christians also see in this king a foreshadowing of Christ, although the text speaks first of the king of Israel.

For today: when everything seems to be shifting beneath your feet, lean concretely on the character of God. Before you decide or worry, pray remembering that his love is faithful, and let that give you stability.
exp.87:9:
Here the psalmist asks God painful questions: Will you do wonders for the dead? Will the shades of the dead rise up to give you thanks? "Selah" is a pause for meditation. The old words for "will rise up" and "will you do" mean "will rise up" and "will you do."

The speaker is a man named Heman the Ezrahite, according to the title of the psalm. He is sick, alone, and rejected by his acquaintances. He has prayed every day and sees no answer. His questions do not deny faith; they are a cry for God to act while he is still alive. In that time, little was understood about life after death.

For today: if you are exhausted and without answers, you can speak to God with complete honesty, even with painful questions. Continuing to pray, even with tears, is a form of faith. God is not offended by your honesty.
exp.109:0:
It says that the LORD, that is, God, speaks to someone whom David calls "my Lord." He orders that person to sit at his right hand, the place of honor and authority. There he will remain while God makes his enemies a footstool for his feet, a low stool where the feet rest, a sign of complete victory.

David is the one who writes, according to the heading of the psalm. He speaks of a king greater than himself, to whom God gives a throne and a victory. The verses that follow present him reigning from Zion. Jesus quoted this verse to show that the Messiah is more than a descendant of David (Matthew 22:41-45), and the New Testament applies it to Christ risen. Some scholars think it was first sung at the coronation of the kings of Israel, but Christians read it as a promise fulfilled in Jesus.

For today: if Christ reigns, you can rest even when evil seems strong. Trust that God knows how to finish what he began, and live with patience and hope.
exp.105:46:
Here the psalmist asks God to save them and gather them from among the nations where they had been scattered. The word "gather" means bring back together. "Heathen" means peoples or nations. The goal of the request is to be able to give thanks to God's holy name and to triumph in his praise, not in themselves, but in praising God.

It is the closing prayer of a psalm that reviews Israel's failures from Egypt through the captivity. The author does not name himself, and from the mention of the captives he seems to speak from exile, though some think it was written later. He asks for help trusting in God's covenant and compassion, mentioned just before. The verses that follow close with praise.

For today: when you feel far away or scattered because of your mistakes, pray honestly and with trust in God's mercy. Ask him to restore you, and let your aim be to praise him, not only to get out of trouble.
exp.31:5:
It says that, because God forgives the one who confesses his sin, everyone who is faithful to God should pray to him while he can still be found. "Godly" here means someone who belongs to God and is loyal to him. The image of great waters is a picture of great troubles or dangers, and it promises that they will not reach the one who is near to God.

David speaks, according to the traditional heading of the psalm. He has just told how he felt inside when he kept his sin silent: dry and worn out. When he confessed it, God forgave him. Now he invites others not to wait and to seek God sincerely. Scholars debate which specific event he has in mind, and we cannot be certain.

For today: do not put off talking with God about what weighs on you. Tell him the truth of your heart today. His forgiveness is a safe refuge when the storms come.
exp.93:12:
It says that God gives calm and rest to the one he corrects and teaches, so that he does not lose heart when the hard days come. "Give him rest" means giving him peace and inner quiet. "Adversity" is suffering or hardship. Meanwhile, for the wicked, that is, the one who lives with his back turned to God, a pit is being dug, a picture that his fall is already being prepared.

The psalmist speaks to God and also to his people. He sees that the wicked oppress others and seem to get their way, and he asks when God will act. Here he answers with confidence: God corrects his children with purpose, and justice has not been lost. Some understand the pit as the punishment the wicked bring on themselves; others, as God's judgment. Both ideas fit.

When a difficult time comes your way, do not simply stand there looking at the injustice. Open the Bible, let God teach you, and rest in the knowledge that he has the last word.
exp.43:4:
The psalmist says that, with God's help, his people will defeat their enemies. To "push down" means to throw down with force, the way a bull drives with its horns. To "tread under" means to trample underfoot. "Through thy name" means with the authority and power of God, not with one's own.

The people of Israel speak in prayer. They remember how God gave them the land in the past, and it was not by their own sword or strength. For that reason they trust that God will also give them victory today. Later in the psalm the tone shifts to a lament, because the people suffer a defeat and do not understand why.

For today: before facing a difficult problem, recognize that your own strength is not enough. Ask for God's help, trust in Him, and give thanks to God for what you accomplish.
exp.118:146:
He says that the psalmist rose before the dawn and called out to God for help. The phrase that means he rose before the first light of day is rewritten here as he got up before the morning came. And his words about hoping in God's word mean that he placed his trust in what God has said and promised.

The speaker is the author of Psalm 119, a psalm that praises God's word. We do not know for certain who wrote it. Here we see a moment of distress: earlier he called out with his whole heart and asked to be saved. The verses that follow show that he also spent the hours of the night meditating on God's words.

For today: set aside a moment at the start of your day, even a brief one, to pray and read a verse. Before the rush of the day overtakes you, hand your worries over to God and affirm your trust in his promises.
exp.28:8:
This verse says that the voice of God is so powerful that it makes the deer give birth, or tremble in labor, and strips the forests bare of leaves. The thick, tangled woods are where the forests grow dense and wild. While the storm shakes nature, in the temple everyone who belongs to God cries out: "Glory!" Some translators understand that the voice makes the oaks twist and turn, and the phrase about the deer is interpreted in several ways.

It is a psalm of David that describes a great storm advancing like the voice of God, from the sea to the desert. David wants his people to see that the Lord governs all of creation, and that is why he praises him.

Today we can do the same: when faced with what frightens us or overwhelms us, instead of staying in fear, we can stop and say "glory" to God, remembering that he reigns and cares for his people.
exp.77:10:
They had forgotten what God had done. Instead of remembering, they forgot. "His works" are the actions of God, and "his wonders" are the miracles he had shown them.

The psalm is a poem by Asaph, which teaches the history of Israel so that the children can learn from the mistakes of their fathers. Before this verse it mentions the sons of Ephraim, who fled in battle and did not keep the covenant. Afterward, the psalmist recalls the miracles in Egypt and at the Red Sea. Interpreters explain the exact episode of the battle of Ephraim in different ways, because the Bible does not detail it here.

Today we can write in a notebook the times God helped us and reread them when we are afraid. Remembering his faithfulness strengthens trust and obedience.
exp.106:3:
This verse describes people who wandered without direction through a dry, empty region. "Solitary way" means an empty place, with no paths to guide them. "City to dwell in" refers to an inhabited city, where they could rest and find help. They were looking for a place to stay, but they did not find one.

The psalmist calls the redeemed of the Lord to tell their story. Earlier he speaks of those whom God gathered from all the lands. Here begins the first example of people who were rescued: travelers who were lost. Some connect this with the return from exile, and others see it as a general picture of any kind of need. The text does not specify. The next verse shows that they then cried out to God, and He delivered them.

For today: when you feel lost, without direction or without a place to rest, do not stay silent. Speak to God honestly. He listens to those who, being without a way, cry out to Him.
exp.103:30:
This verse expresses a wish and a prayer: that the glory of the Lord, that is, his greatness and honor, will endure forever. It also asks that God rejoice, or take delight, in everything he has made. The word "works" refers to his creation.

The psalmist is a worshiper who has just surveyed creation: the sea, the animals, the seasons. He sees that everything depends on God, who gives life and takes it away. After contemplating this, he responds with praise. He then says that God looks upon the earth and it trembles, and the psalmist vows to sing to him all his life. Some think that God's joy in his works recalls Genesis 1, where God sees that everything is good.

For today: take a moment to observe something of creation, such as the sky, a plant, or a person, and thank God for it. Let your admiration become a brief prayer of praise.
exp.104:34:
It says that the locusts and the caterpillars ate every plant and every fruit in Egypt. "Herb" refers to the vegetation and crops of the field, and "devoured" means they consumed it completely. Nothing was left to feed on.

The psalmist, who is not identified in this psalm, recalls God's works on behalf of Israel. Here he reviews the plagues of Egypt, especially the plague of locusts (Exodus 10). The purpose is to praise God and to remember that He cared for His people and freed them from slavery, while Pharaoh refused to listen to Him.

For today: when everything seems lost or scarce, we can remember that God has power over creation and cares for His own. It also invites us to obey Him promptly, before hardening our hearts as Pharaoh did.
exp.25:4:
It says the psalmist feels a deep rejection toward gatherings where people who do evil come together. The words "evildoers" and "wicked" refer to people who live in wickedness and without respect for God. The phrase "will not sit with" means that he did not join them or share in their way of living.

The tradition holds that David wrote this psalm. He asks God to examine him and defend him, because he says he has walked with integrity. Keeping God's mercy and truth in mind keeps him far from falsehood. Then that clean path leads him to worship at the altar with gratitude.

Today, let us think about who we spend time with and which conversations we keep following. This is not about looking down on people, since Jesus also drew near to sinners to help them. It is about not taking part in mockery, gossip, or deception. Let us ask God for wisdom to be kind but firm.
exp.36:33:
It says we should wait on God with patience and trust, and keep living according to his ways, that is, his commandments. In return, God promises to exalt you, which means lifting you up and honoring you, so that you inherit the land. It also says that sinners will be cut off like trees, and that the believer will see it.

This is a psalm of David, written as advice from an older man to people who suffer from injustice. The whole psalm encourages us not to become angry or envious of the wicked who seem to prosper. The verses nearby show the wicked plotting against the righteous, but also show that their success is temporary: they flourish like a green laurel and then vanish.

When injustice frustrates you, do not take revenge or become bitter. Keep doing what is right each day, and leave your waiting in God's hands, trusting that he acts in his own time.
exp.1:1:
This verse says that the kings and rulers of the earth band together to oppose God (the Lord) and his anointed one. "Anointed" means someone chosen by God and set apart for a mission, and the word is connected to "Messiah" or "Christ." The phrase "take counsel together" means they make plans together.

The psalm does not say who wrote it. The New Testament quotes it in Acts 4:25-26 and applies it to Jesus. In its original setting, it probably spoke of the king of Israel and the nations that rebelled against him. The verse describes a rebellion that seeks to throw off God's authority, which is why the next verse speaks of "breaking their bonds," that is, their chains.

Today we might ask ourselves whether we sometimes see God's will as a burden. This psalm invites us to trust that his rule is good and to place our plans before him with humility.
exp.89:6:
This verse says that human life is fragile because God is holy and just. "Consumed" means finished off or used up, and "troubled" means greatly disturbed, filled with dread. In other words, God's anger against sin leaves the human being feeling small and afraid.

It is part of Moses' prayer, according to the title of the psalm. He speaks on behalf of the people, who lived with the fragility of life and the consequences of their sin. The nearby verses compare life to grass that springs up in the morning and withers by evening, and they say that God keeps our faults in view. Some connect this with the wilderness, though the psalm does not specify it.

For today: do not take your sin lightly or think little of the shortness of your life. Each day, sincerely acknowledge your faults before God and ask him for mercy, because the same psalm ends by seeking his compassion.
exp.75:4:
It says the bravest and proudest warriors were stripped, meaning everything they had was taken from them. "They have slept their sleep" is a way of speaking about death or being defeated and left without strength. In the end, their hands, once full of weapons and plunder, were left empty.

Psalm 76 is a song of Asaph that celebrates God as the defender of Jerusalem (Zion). Many believe it recalls the defeat of the Assyrian army under Sennacherib, but the psalm does not name him, so this is not certain. What is clear is that God stopped a powerful enemy without His people having to fight.

Today, this invites us not to fear too much what seems stronger than us: problems, people, or systems. We can hand our worries over to God and trust that He has the final word.
exp.43:20:
It says that God would not overlook such a betrayal, because he knows even the most hidden things of the heart. The word that would be rendered "search out" here is explained as meaning "call to account" or "investigate," but that comment is not needed for the reader, so it is omitted. The question is rhetorical: of course God would find it out.

The speaker is the people of Israel, or a representative of them, in a psalm of lament. They are suffering defeat and humiliation, yet they affirm that they have not forsaken God. They do not claim to be perfect, but that they have not fallen into idolatry. They remind God that he sees their heart and knows that their complaint is sincere. Scholars do not agree on the exact historical moment when it was written.

For today: when you suffer without understanding why, you can speak to God with complete honesty. He already knows your heart, so you do not need to pretend. Bring him your questions and your pain, and also examine whether your heart remains faithful to him.
exp.108:9:
This verse asks that the children of a wicked man be left to wander without a fixed home, beg for food, and search for something to eat far from the ruins of their house. The verse's own words describe those who are continually wandering and begging, and seeking their bread out of their ruined places.

David speaks here, according to the heading of the psalm, and he is crying out to God for justice. He feels falsely accused and repaid with hatred for his love. These words are very harsh language, known as imprecatory. Some believe David is quoting what his enemies were saying against him (vv. 6-19); others think it is his own petition. Interpreters do not agree.

For today: when you are hurt, bring your pain and your anger honestly to God, instead of taking revenge. And remember that Jesus taught us to bless and pray for those who harm us.
exp.41:2:
This verse says that the psalmist has cried so much that his tears have become his food, as if he had no other bread, and that he does this without rest, day and night. Also, people keep asking him again and again, "Where is your God?", as if mocking his faith. "Bread" here means daily food.

The speaker is a believer, probably a Levite of the sons of Korah, according to the title of the psalm. He feels far from the house of God and from worshiping with his people. The verses that follow say that he remembers when he used to go along with the crowd amid songs of praise. We do not know for certain where he was or what the exact situation was.

For today: when you weep and others doubt your faith, you do not have to pretend to be strong. Tell God honestly what you feel, as the psalmist did, and remember that he encouraged himself to keep waiting on God.
exp.62:7:
My soul clings closely to God, that is, it stays close to him, following him closely and not letting go. At the same time he recognizes that God's right hand, his mighty hand, a sign of his power and care, has held him up. He holds on to God, but it is God who truly sustains him.

The title of the psalm attributes it to David, when he was in the wilderness of Judah. Many think he was fleeing from Saul or Absalom, though the text does not specify. He is in a dry and dangerous place, yet he remembers God in the night and rejoices under his protection. His enemies seek him to destroy him.

When you are weary or afraid, hold on to God with simple prayer and remember how he has helped you before. Your strength does not depend on how tightly you grip, but on the fact that he sustains you.
exp.105:40:
It says that God left Israel in the hands of the neighboring nations. The word "heathen" means peoples who were not Israelites. Those who hated them came to rule over them.

The psalm is a prayer of confession, written by an author who is not named. It reviews Israel's history: again and again the people turned away from God, followed idols, and disobeyed. Here the consequence is shown. God did not abandon them on a whim, but allowed them to suffer the fruit of their rebellion. Even so, the psalm recalls that God rescued them many times.

For today: when we turn away from God, sooner or later we feel the consequences. This is not meant to make us despair, but to return. If today something has power over you and pulls you away from God, confess it to Him honestly; He remains patient and ready to rescue.
exp.138:0:
This verse begins with a note for the choir director: it is a psalm of David, meant to be sung. Then the author addresses God and says that He has searched him and known him. "Searched" here means to investigate thoroughly, to look inside. God does not know him superficially, but completely.

The one speaking is David, or at least the title indicates so. He is praying and singing, not giving a lesson. The verses that follow explain that God knows his steps, his thoughts, and his ways. That is why the psalm springs from wonder, and at other points in the poem also from a desire to be guided by God.

For today: you do not have to pretend before God. He already knows you, with your fears and your failures. You can pray with sincerity, without embellishment, trusting that His knowledge comes together with care, not rejection.
exp.115:15:
The psalmist speaks with humility and gratitude. He says that he is the servant of the Lord, and he repeats it for emphasis. "Son of thy handmaid" means that he was born into a household of faith, where his mother also served God. "Bonds" are the chains or fetters: God set him free from them.

The author does not name himself in the text. Some think of David, but this is not certain. The speaker has been through a danger of death, and God rescued him. For that reason, in the verses around it, he promises to keep his vows and to offer a sacrifice of praise before all the people.

Today we can remember what God has delivered us from, whether a distress, a fear, or a bad habit. And instead of keeping it in silence, we can thank him and tell what he has done, serving him with joy.
exp.82:2:
These enemies of Israel make their plans with great cunning and in secret against God's people. "Consulted" means they gathered together to plan, and "take counsel together" means meeting to scheme something. "Thy hidden ones" are those whom God keeps and protects like a treasure.

The author is Asaph, or someone from his line of temple musicians. He lifts up an anguished prayer because several nations have joined together to destroy Israel. The verses that follow show that they want to erase even its name. For this reason Asaph asks God not to stay silent or still. Scholars do not agree on which exact historical attack is in view.

For today: when someone speaks or plans something against you in secret, you do not have to answer with the same cunning. Bring the matter to God in prayer with sincerity, trusting that you matter to Him and that He cares for you even when you cannot see what is being plotted.
exp.68:22:
The explanation says that the eyes of the enemies should be darkened so that they cannot see, and that their loins, that is, their waist or their back, should shake continually. The image is of people who are blind, weak, and unsteady, with no strength to hold themselves up.

The one speaking is the psalmist, David according to the title of the psalm, who suffers mockery and injustice because of his faithfulness to God. He prays in pain, for they gave him gall and vinegar. It is a psalm of lament and a cry for justice. The New Testament quotes this psalm in connection with Jesus (John 2:17; 19:28-29), and Paul quotes these words in Romans 11:9-10 when speaking of spiritual blindness.

Today we do not use this psalm to wish harm on others, since Jesus taught us to love our enemies. Rather, when we are hurt unjustly, we can be honest with God, hand over our pain, and let him judge with justice.
exp.17:14:
It says that when God rebuked, the deepest places of the sea were seen and the foundations of the earth were laid bare. The word for the deep places is rendered here as the channels of waters, and the foundations of the world are simply its base. The phrase about the blast of the breath of God's nostrils is a poetic image: God's strong breath, like a snort of anger, that stirs the waters.

David speaks here, giving thanks to God for rescuing him from his enemies and from Saul, according to the title of the psalm. He uses images of storm, earthquake, and the open sea to describe God's power in action. It is not a literal account but poetic language. The verses that follow say that God drew him out of many waters, that is, out of a great danger.

For today: when your problems feel stronger than you are, remember that no force, not even the depths of the sea, is beyond God's control. You can call on Him with confidence.
exp.97:2:
It says that God did not forget the promises he made to Israel. The phrase that is rendered "the ends of the earth" refers to the most distant places in the world.

The psalmist invites the people to sing a new song, because God has done something great. It is not stated with certainty which specific event is meant; some think of a deliverance of Israel, and others read it as pointing toward a final salvation. What matters is that God's work with Israel is seen before the nations.

For today: when you doubt that God will keep his word, remember what he has already done. Write down three things in which you have seen his faithfulness, and give him thanks out loud.
exp.18:2:
The verse says there is no "speech," meaning discourse or language, no words, and no voice heard with the ears. Creation speaks, but without human sound.

Here David speaks, in a psalm for the choirmaster. He has just said that the heavens declare the glory of God day and night. This verse makes clear that the message is silent. Some translators understand it differently: "There is no language where their voice is not heard," meaning that the message reaches all peoples. The Hebrew text allows both readings, and both fit with the next verse, where the message goes out through all the earth.

For today: take a few minutes to look at the sky, by day or by night, in silence and without your phone. Let creation remind you of the greatness and care of God.
exp.54:9:
It says the city is surrounded all the time, day and night, by the walls that protect it, but that inside, wickedness and suffering reign. "Iniquity" means injustice or wickedness, and "labor" here is understood as pain, distress, or trouble, not as employment.

David speaks, who according to the title of the psalm is distressed and cries out to God. He feels that violence and strife dominate the city. The verses that follow show that the most painful thing is a betrayal by someone close, not by an open enemy. It is not known with certainty which exact moment of his life he refers to, and scholars interpret it in different ways.

For today: strong walls do not guarantee peace if there is corruption and deceit within. Ask God to watch over your heart, your home, and your community from the inside, and when a betrayal hurts you, bring your pain to him in prayer, as David did.
exp.139:7:
The explanation says that David asks God not to grant the wicked what they desire, nor to let their schemes prosper, so that they do not become proud. A "wicked" person is someone who lives without respect for God. To "exalt themselves" means to become arrogant.

The one speaking is David, according to the heading of the psalm. He is surrounded by violent and deceitful people, and he has already placed his trust in God, whom he calls his strength and protector in the day of battle. So he begs God to stop the plans of those who attack him.

For today: when you feel that injustice is advancing, do not fill yourself with resentment or seek revenge. Bring your distress to God honestly, trust that He sees everything, and ask Him for wisdom and protection. He can restrain evil better than you can.
exp.103:0:
Here the psalmist speaks to himself and says: "Bless the Lord, O my soul." He recognizes that the Lord, his God, is very great. The phrase "thou art clothed" is rendered as "thou art clothed" in the verse above, and the word for "splendor" and "greatness" is captured by "majesty" in that verse. God appears as a king clothed in glory.

The psalm does not say who wrote it; some attribute it to David, but the text does not confirm this. The one speaking is a worshiper who looks at creation and praises God for it. The verses that follow show this: light, the heavens, the clouds, and the wind speak of his power. Since this is a psalm of praise, it begins by encouraging the heart itself to worship.

For today: before asking or worrying, take a moment to praise God. Go out and look at the sky or the plants, and give thanks aloud for what you see. This helps you remember who God is and to trust him more.
exp.117:6:
The Lord is on my side and counts himself among those who help me. So when the verse says I shall see my desire upon them that hate me, it means I will see them defeated, or that I can look at my enemies calmly because they did not overcome me. The phrase "among those who help me" means that God is my chief helper.

"Hate me" means to despise or reject someone.

The one speaking is a believer from Israel who went through a great distress, and God brought him out into a wide place, that is, into freedom. The psalm is a song of thanksgiving, and many believe it was sung at the people's celebrations. We do not know with certainty who wrote it or what exact situation he lived through. The verse that follows shows that his conclusion is to trust in God more than in people.

Today you can face opposition or rejection without living in fear. Pray with sincerity, trust that God sustains you, and let him take care of the outcome, without seeking revenge.
exp.48:3:
The explanation says that the psalmist will turn his ear to hear proverbs or wise sayings, and that he will then explain his dark saying with the music of the harp. The words "I will incline mine ear" mean "I will give attention" or "I will listen closely." "Examples" refers to proverbs or sayings that teach something. A "dark saying" is a deep truth, hard to understand at first sight.

The one speaking is a wise author, identified as one of the sons of Korah according to the title of the psalm. He has called everyone, rich and poor, to listen.
