Before teaching, he first listens with humility. His dark saying is the question of why he should not fear when the wicked prosper, which the following verses develop.

Today we can learn that, before speaking or advising others, it is good to listen to God with humility. When we are troubled by injustice or by the success of those who trust in their wealth, we can bring that doubt to God in prayer and in his Word, and there find peace.
exp.118:151:
He says the psalmist has known God's commands for a long time. "For a long time" is the sense of the phrase "of old." And "you founded them" means that God established them on a firm foundation, so that they do not change or come to an end. What God commanded remains forever.

The one speaking is the author of Psalm 119, a believer who loves the Word of God. We do not know for certain who wrote it. He is suffering, because people who have turned away from the law are persecuting him. In the midst of that pressure, he leans on what he has learned over the years. His experience confirms to him that God's Word is firm, and so in the verses that follow, he asks for help with confidence.

When everything around you changes or pressures you, return to the Word of God. Set aside a few minutes each day to read it. Over the years, you will discover that it is solid ground where you can lean.
exp.1:7:
God tells his king: "Ask me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and the farthest parts of the earth as your possession." "Inheritance" means what is passed down to you, and "possession" is something that belongs to you. "The nations" are the peoples and nations of the world, and "the farthest parts of the earth" are the most distant places in the world.

Here the anointed king speaks, quoting what the LORD said in the decree. The psalm shows the nations rebelling against God, while He establishes his king in Zion. For the Jews, it first referred to the king of David's line. The New Testament applies this psalm to Jesus, the Son of God (Acts 13:33; Hebrews 1:5).

For today: God invites us to ask. Pray for your family, your neighborhood, and other peoples, trusting that Christ reigns and wants everyone to know him. Ask him with faith and with a willingness to take part.
exp.111:5:
This verse says that the righteous person will not fall forever, meaning they will not be permanently overthrown. "Shall not be moved" means they will not be shaken or brought down for good. And "everlasting remembrance" means they will be remembered for a long time, with affection and respect.

Psalm 112 does not say who wrote it. It is a wisdom song that describes the person who fears God: generous, merciful, and managing their affairs with uprightness. This verse shows the result: a steady life and a good remembrance. It is a general principle of biblical wisdom, not a promise that the righteous will never face anything bad.

For today: live with integrity and generosity even when no one applauds you. Trust that God sustains the one who is faithful to him, and that the good you do leaves a mark that lasts.
exp.40:2:
He says that God cares for and sustains the sick person who is confined to bed. "Bed of languishing" is the bed where someone suffers. "Make all his bed" means that God arranges it and makes it comfortable, like someone who adjusts the pillows and sheets to bring relief. It is an image of tenderness and care.

David, or the psalmist, speaks in a Psalm that he dedicated to the chief musician. Earlier he says that God blesses the one who thinks about the poor and helps them. Afterward, the author confesses his sin, asks for healing, and mentions enemies who wish for his death. Some think he himself is sick, though the text gives no further details.

For today: if you are sick or tired, you can trust that God is with you and sustains you. And if you know someone who is suffering, visit them, help them, and make their burden easier to bear.
exp.35:4:
This verse says that God's faithful love is so great that it reaches to the heavens, and that his faithfulness reaches to the clouds. The word "mercy" here means a loyal love that does not abandon. "Faithfulness" speaks of God keeping his word.

The one speaking is David, according to the title of the psalm. First he describes the wicked person, who lies, plans evil even in his bed, and does not turn away from what is bad. Then David looks upward and sets that picture against the character of God. In contrast to a crooked world, God remains faithful and good.

For today: when you see injustice or feel discouraged, do not fix your gaze only on evil. Take a moment to remember how God has been faithful to you, and rest in the knowledge that his love is greater than any problem.
exp.48:12:
The explanation says that the way of those who trust in their riches and their fame is foolishness. Even so, their children and followers repeat what they said and approve of it. "Foolishness" here means folly, a lack of wisdom. "Their sayings" refers to their words or their way of thinking. "Selah" is a pause for reflection; its exact meaning is not entirely certain.

The one speaking is the psalmist, a son of Korah according to the title of the psalm. He teaches wisdom to everyone, rich and poor alike. He wants no one to be frightened or to envy the powerful, because wealth does not deliver anyone from death. The verses that follow show that God does redeem the life of the one who trusts in Him.

Today we also copy ideas without thinking: "success is having more." Before following what everyone repeats, ask yourself: does this serve me before God and for eternity? Seek the wisdom of God and trust in Him, not in your possessions.
exp.59:6:
God claims the regions of Israel as his own. Gilead and Manasseh were territories east of the Jordan. Ephraim is the strength of his head, like a helmet that protects. Judah is the tribe from which the scepter, or authority, comes. Here the word for ruler can also be understood as a staff of command.

God speaks, answering from his sanctuary, after a national defeat. The psalm is attributed to David and mentions battles against Edom. God affirms that the land and the tribes belong to him, and that promise encourages the people to ask for help with confidence.

For today: when you feel defeated or divided, remember that your life belongs to God, even when everything seems out of order. Pray with confidence, asking for his help, and let his word strengthen your hope before the situation changes.
exp.118:17:
This verse is a prayer. The psalmist asks God to open his eyes, not the eyes of his body, but the eyes of his understanding. He says that if God does this, he will be able to see the wondrous things in God's law, that is, the amazing and admirable things found in his teaching. The word "law" here refers to God's instructions in general.

The one speaking is the author of Psalm 119, whose name is not known for certain. He is someone who loves God's word. He has just asked to live by and keep the Lord's word. He then describes himself as a stranger passing through the earth, and for that reason he needs God not to hide his commandments from him.

Today we can pray this way before reading the Bible: "Lord, open my eyes." Reading alone is not enough; we need God to give us understanding. Read calmly and wait for him to speak to you.
exp.21:28:
This verse says that even the powerful people of the earth, those who have wealth and fame, will eat and worship God. All mortals will also bow down before him, including those who are going to die. It reminds us that no one can save his own life. Some understand "eat" as sharing in God's blessing; others see it as a table of fellowship.

David speaks in a psalm that begins with deep suffering, when he feels abandoned. Then his prayer turns to hope: God will reign over all nations. Christians often see here a foreshadowing of Christ, because Jesus quoted the opening of this psalm on the cross.

For today: do not trust your strength, your money, or your position to save you. Today you can humbly place yourself before God, give him thanks, and entrust your life to him, because only he gives and sustains life.
exp.146:10:
He says that God takes pleasure in, and is delighted by, the people who honor him with reverence and who trust in his mercy, that is, in his faithful love and his goodness. The phrase "takes pleasure" means that he is pleased with them and finds joy in them. "Fear" here does not mean being afraid, but honoring God and taking him seriously.

The psalmist, whose name is not known for certain, praises God for caring for creation, from the ravens to Jerusalem. Earlier he said that God is not impressed by the strength of a horse or by the swift legs of a man. What pleases him is not human power but a humble heart that waits on him.

Today we can stop relying only on our own strength, money, or abilities. When you face a need, pray with reverence and wait patiently for the goodness of God, knowing that he takes pleasure in those who trust in him.
exp.110:2:
This verse says that everything God does is glorious and beautiful, and that his righteousness, meaning his right and good way of acting, never comes to an end. The word "work" refers to everything God does: creation, his care, and his salvation.

The speaker is the psalmist, a person whose name we do not know. This psalm begins with "Hallelujah", which means "praise the Lord". He wants to thank God in the midst of the congregation of the upright. After saying that God's works are great, he explains why: they are beautiful, just, and worthy of being remembered.

For today: when you feel uncertain because everything is changing, remember that God does not change. Take a moment to write down three good things God has done in your life, and give thanks for them.
exp.117:26:
God is the Lord, and he has shown us his light: he has revealed his favor and his help. That is why the people are invited to bind the sacrifice with cords, up to the horns of the altar, that is, to the projections at the corners of the altar. The word about shining means that God made his light shine upon us.

This is the end of Psalm 118, a song of thanksgiving for a deliverance. The one speaking seems to be a leader of the people, together with the community, in a procession toward the temple. Scholars do not agree on what the exact occasion was. It was sung at the festivals, and the people came to the house of the Lord to give thanks with offerings.

For today: when God helps you, do not let it pass as if nothing happened. Give him thanks in concrete ways, with a sincere prayer, with time set apart for him, or with generous help for someone else.
exp.68:33:
This verse invites all of creation to praise God: the heavens, the earth, the seas, and every living creature that is in them. It is like a huge choir where nothing is left out.

David speaks, according to the psalm's heading. He was suffering greatly, surrounded by enemies and crying out to God. But by the end of the psalm his complaint turns into trust. He praises because he believes God hears the humble and does not abandon those held captive. Then he promises that God will care for Zion and Judah. Scholars debate whether the last part was added later, since it speaks of rebuilding cities.

For today: even in the middle of pain, you can praise God as an act of trust, without waiting for everything to be fixed. Today, when you look at the sky or hear the birds, join in that praise with a simple prayer of thanks.
exp.97:0:
He says we should sing to the Lord, that is, to the Lord, a new song, because he has done marvelous things. His right hand, a symbol of power, and his holy arm, which speaks of his pure and righteous strength, are what the text names as the source of that power. The text says that with this power he himself has brought salvation and victory.

It is a psalm of praise, and it does not say who wrote it. The author calls the people to celebrate. The verses that follow explain the reason: God has shown his salvation and his righteousness to the nations, and he has remembered his faithfulness to Israel. Some believe it speaks of a specific victory, and others that it also looks toward the final salvation. The text does not specify.

For today: when you feel tired or have no words, remember what God has already done for you, and give him thanks with a song, even a simple one. Praising with gratitude renews the heart.
exp.49:19:
It says this person would sit down calmly to speak badly of his own brother, and would throw accusations and disgrace against the son of his very own mother. The phrase "sat down" suggests he did it without hurry, as something habitual. "Disgrace" means bad reputation or slander. "Brother" can refer to a relative or to another member of God's people.

God is speaking in this psalm, which is attributed to Asaph. He is calling to account those who think of themselves as religious but live in injustice. He reminds them that his silence was not approval: they thought God was like them, but he tells them he will set everything before their eyes.

For today: take care with what you say about others, above all about your family and your community of faith. Before you comment on something negative, ask yourself whether it is true, whether it helps, and whether you would say it in front of that person. If you have spoken badly, ask forgiveness from God and from the one you offended.
exp.104:37:
The verse says that the Egyptians were glad when the Israelites left. The reason is that they felt a great fear of them. The word "fear" in the verse means a very strong sense of dread. After the plagues, the Egyptians were afraid of what might happen to them if the Israelites stayed.

Psalm 105 is a song of praise that remembers God's works with his people. The psalmist does not speak of Israel's strength, but of what God did: he struck down the firstborn, brought his people out with silver and gold, and cared for them so that none of them became sick. Egypt's fear shows that God was defending them.

For today: when you feel small before a big problem, remember that God can work in ways you do not expect. Trust that he cares for his own and give thanks for what he has already done.
exp.85:1:
David asks God to watch over his life. The word "holy" in this verse, as it appears in the King James Version, can also mean faithful and loyal to God, and some translations render it as "favored by God." "Preserve my soul" means "protect me, care for my life." A "servant" is someone who belongs to God and serves Him, and "trusteth" means putting all one's hope in Him.

The one speaking is David, in prayer. He feels troubled and in need, as the previous verse says. He does not present himself as perfect, but as someone who leans on God. The verses that follow show that he prays urgently, all day long, asking for mercy and joy.

For today: when you feel weak or distressed, pray simply. Remind God that you trust Him and ask Him to care for you. Speaking to Him honestly strengthens your faith and reminds you that you are not alone.
exp.19:0:
This verse begins with a note for the choir director: it is a psalm of David. Then it is a prayer or blessing: may the Lord hear you in the day of trouble or of struggle. "Trouble" means a hard situation, a serious problem. May the name of the God of Jacob defend you, meaning that God's power and character protect you.

It seems to be a song the people sang for their king before going into battle. Here the Israelites, or perhaps the priests, speak, wishing that God will answer their leader. Scholars do not know with certainty the exact moment it was used. It calls God the God of Jacob, a weak man whom God cared for and was faithful to.

Today you can pray this way for others: for your family, your pastor, or a friend in difficulty. When someone faces a hard day, do not only encourage them; bring them to God in prayer.
exp.73:5:
It says that the enemies, using axes and hammers, smashed all the carvings in the sanctuary. The "carved work" refers to the ornaments carved in wood, and "break down" means to tear apart or wreck. It is the picture of a beautiful work, made with care, ruined with blows in a short time.

The psalm is attributed to Asaph, or to an author from his circle, and it is a lament of the people before God over the destruction of the place of worship. Many connect it with the fall of Jerusalem and the temple, although the psalm does not say with certainty which moment it refers to. The speaker does not argue with the enemies but presents his pain to God and asks him to act.

For today: when you see that something precious to your faith is being damaged or lost, do not keep the pain to yourself. Bring it to God honestly, as the psalmist did, and trust that he remains faithful even when you do not understand what is happening.
exp.108:10:
It says that the creditor, that is, the person to whom money is owed, should take everything the man has. Here "catch" means to seize or carry off everything, as with a net. And "strangers," people who are not part of his family, should take the fruit of his labor.

The psalm is attributed to David. It appears in the middle of a prayer of complaint against a cruel enemy who persecuted the poor and showed no mercy. These phrases are called imprecations: harsh requests that justice fall on the wicked. Some believe David is quoting what his accusers were saying against him (vv. 6-19); others think it is his own cry. Scholars interpret it in different ways.

For today: when you feel anger over an injustice, bring it to God honestly instead of seeking revenge. And remember that Jesus taught us to pray for those who do us harm (Matthew 5:44).
exp.86:4:
It says that of Zion, the city of God, it will be said with joy: "This one and that one were born in her." That is, people from many nations will be counted as citizens of Jerusalem. The word "establish" means "will make her strong," and "the highest" is God himself, who holds her up and keeps her firm.

The psalm is a song of the sons of Korah, in honor of Zion. Here the psalmist speaks, and God himself seems to speak in the verses nearby. Rahab (a poetic name for Egypt), Babylon, Tyre, and Ethiopia were peoples who were sometimes enemies of Israel. The psalm presents them as people who come to know God. Some think it announces a future blessing for the nations.

For today: God opens his family to everyone, regardless of their origin or their past. Receive others with the same joy with which God receives them, and rest in the fact that he sustains his people.
exp.7:0:
It says that God, whom David calls "O Lord our Lord," has a name that is great and admirable in all the earth. His glory is so great that it is set "above the heavens," meaning it is above everything that has been created. The phrase "To the chief Musician upon Gittith" is a direction for the leader of the singing. The meaning of "Gittith" is uncertain: it could be an instrument or a tune, and it is not known for sure.

The one speaking is David, according to the title of the psalm. It is a song of praise, and the verses that follow show that he marvels at God when he looks at the heavens, the moon, and the stars. The text does not say at what exact moment he wrote it.

For today: before asking God for something, take a moment to praise him. Look up at the sky, give thanks, and remember that the great God of creation also hears you.
exp.48:0:
This verse opens with a dedication: the psalm is "to the chief Musician," that is, to the director of the singing in worship, and it was "for the sons of Korah," a group of Levites who served by singing in the temple. Then comes a call to everyone. "Hear this" and "give ear" mean "pay attention." "All ye inhabitants of the world" refers to all the people who live on the earth.

The one speaking is the psalmist, probably a poet from the sons of Korah. His name is not known. He calls all peoples, not only Israel, because he is going to speak about a theme that touches every person: wealth, death, and what truly gives security.

Today we can stop and listen with humility before chasing after what the world promises. Ask yourself: what am I really trusting in? God invites us to hear his wisdom.
exp.128:7:
Psalm 129:8 says that no one will greet the enemies of Zion with a blessing. In ancient times, a person passing by the reapers would often greet them with words like "The blessing of the Lord be upon you." Here, no one says that to them. The Lord's blessing is what the passerby would have wished upon the workers, and the verse shows that the enemies receive no such good wish from anyone.

Psalm 129 is a song of the pilgrims who went up to Jerusalem. It is spoken by Israel, who remembers how much they suffered and how God delivered them. The verses before it compare those who hate Zion to grass on a rooftop: it grows quickly, but it dries up without producing fruit. Here there is no harvest, no joy, and no blessing.

For today: we should not rejoice in the misfortune of others, but we should remember that whatever rises against God does not bear lasting fruit. Let us live so that our words are a blessing, and trust that God does justice.
exp.42:2:
Here the psalmist asks God to send out his light and his truth, as if they were guides leading him by the hand. He wants them to bring him to the holy hill, that is, to the place where God dwells, and to his tabernacles, which are his dwelling places or places of worship.

The one speaking is a distressed believer, perhaps far from the temple, who feels surrounded by deceitful and unjust people. It is not known with certainty who wrote it or at what exact moment. He feels abandoned, yet he still speaks to God with confidence and longs to worship him again with joy.

For today: when you do not know which way to take or you feel overwhelmed, ask God to guide you with his truth. Read it in his Word and seek his presence, without ceasing to wait on him.
exp.77:21:
Here is why God was displeased with Israel in the wilderness. The people did not believe God and did not trust in his salvation, that is, the help God gives to rescue and care for his people.

Psalm 78 is a psalm of Asaph that tells the story of Israel to teach the new generations. The psalmist remembers that God opened the rock and gave water, but the people doubted and asked whether he could also give them bread and meat. Their doubt was not a lack of evidence but a lack of trust, and God still sent them the manna.

Today we can remember what God has already done in our lives when new needs arise. If he helped us yesterday, we can trust that he will sustain us tomorrow. So instead of complaining, we can pray with gratitude and hope.
exp.70:2:
God is described as a secure rock where a person can always take refuge. The phrase "a firm place to dwell" means a solid place where one can settle down and be safe. "Where I may go continually" means a place one can keep coming back to. "Thou hast commanded" means "you have ordained" or "you have decided." The psalmist trusts that God has already decided to save him, because God is his rock and his fortress.

The psalm does not say who wrote it. The one speaking is an elderly person (later he speaks of his old age) who has trusted God since youth. Now he is surrounded by wicked and violent people, and he asks for help. That is why he seeks refuge in God, since he has no other safe place.

For today: when you feel fear or pressure, do not run to just anywhere. Make prayer your place of refuge, and return to God every day, not only in crises. Then, when the storm comes, you will already know the way to your rock.
exp.82:6:
This verse continues the list of nations that joined together against Israel: Gebal, Ammon, Amalek, the Philistines, and the inhabitants of Tyre. Gebal is uncertain: it may be the Phoenician city of Byblos or a region near Edom.

The one speaking is the psalmist Asaph, who prays to God on behalf of his people. The enemies, neighbors on every side, made an alliance to attack Israel. It is not known with certainty what specific event the psalm refers to, and scholars debate it. Asaph presents the problem to God as an attack against the people of God.

For today: when you feel surrounded by pressure or opposition, do not carry that fear alone. Bring honestly to God what you are facing, as Asaph did, and trust that He hears you.
exp.118:43:
Here the psalmist says that he will obey God's law every day, without stopping. "I will keep" means to fulfill and to guard with care. The phrase rendered in archaic wording means the same as "forever," for all eternity.

Psalm 119 is a long poem in honor of God's word. No one knows for certain who wrote it; the one speaking is a faithful person who has suffered mockery. In the verses before, he asks that God not take the word of truth out of his mouth. Now, relying on that trust, he promises to obey always. Afterward he says that he will walk "at liberty," that is, with freedom and without anguish.

For today: obedience is not lived out in one day of enthusiasm, but through daily decisions. Choose a simple habit, such as reading a few verses each morning, and ask God for help to be consistent.
exp.103:22:
This verse says that people go out to their work and to their labor in the field, and they do so during the day, until evening comes. The word "work" here means a person's task or daily occupation, and "labor" refers to the tilling of the land.

The psalm is a song of praise to God as Creator and sustainer of all things. It is not known with certainty who wrote it; many connect it with David, but the text does not state this. The psalmist describes the order of creation: at night the animals come out, and at dawn they rest while people go out to work. Human labor appears as part of God's wise design.

Today we can see our work, whether in the field, the office, or the home, as part of the order that God has set in place. At the beginning of the day, we can thank Him for the strength and the occupation, and work with honesty, knowing that He sustains us.
exp.118:24:
He says that the psalmist feels his soul clinging to the dust, that is, brought low, without strength, very close to discouragement or even death. The word "quicken" is an old word meaning "give me life" or "restore my strength." "Daleth" is just the name of the fourth Hebrew letter, with which this section of the psalm begins.

The one speaking is the psalmist, a believer who loves God's word. We do not know for certain who wrote it. He had been criticized by powerful people, and now, tired and sad, he does not seek a way out on his own: he tells God about his ways and asks for instruction. His hope rests in what God has said.

When you feel discouraged, do not stay silent or shut yourself away. Speak with God honestly and read his Word calmly, asking him to renew you inwardly. He knows how to lift up the weary.
exp.8:12:
He says David asks God for compassion ("Have mercy upon me"). He asks God to look at his suffering, caused by people who hate him. And he acknowledges that God is the one who "lifts him up from the gates of death," that is, who rescues him when he is about to die. "Trouble" means pain or distress, and "hate" means to despise or be against.

The speaker is David, according to the title of the psalm. He is praising God for having done justice and not forgotten the cry of the poor. Even in the midst of that praise, he asks for help in his present need. Afterward he promises to tell of God's praises "in the gates of the daughter of Zion," a poetic way of referring to Jerusalem.

For today: when you are suffering, you do not have to pretend to be strong. You can tell God honestly what hurts, asking for his help, and remember the times he has already sustained you.
exp.102:20:
It says that all the hosts of heaven, that is, the beings who serve God, should praise him. "Bless ye" means to speak well of God and acknowledge his greatness. "His ministers" are his servants, those who attend to him. And these do his pleasure, that is, what he desires.

The psalm is by David, who first addresses his own soul and then calls every created thing to praise God. He has just said that God's throne is in the heavens and that his kingdom rules over all. So he invites the angels, all his works, and finally himself once more. Some think "hosts" refers only to the angels; others believe it includes other heavenly beings. The text does not specify.

For today: praising God is not only singing, it is also obeying him. Today you can choose a small task that you know pleases him and do it with joy, as a way of blessing him.
exp.144:20:
He says the psalmist will use his mouth to praise the Lord, that is, to speak well of who God is and of what he does. He also wishes that all people, every human being, would bless his holy name. Here "bless" means to honor and give thanks. The phrase "for ever and ever" means without end.

This is the last verse of Psalm 145, which tradition attributes to David. The whole psalm speaks of God's greatness, goodness, and faithfulness. Before this closing, the psalmist recalls that God hears those who fear him, saves them, and cares for those who love him. That is why he ends with a personal decision to praise and with an invitation for everyone.

For today: before you ask for something in prayer, begin by giving thanks out loud for something specific that God has done in your life. And when you can, tell another person about it.
exp.36:3:
This verse invites us to find our joy and rest in God. "Delight thyself" means taking pleasure in God, rejoicing in him. And the promise is that God will give us the desires of the heart of those who seek him.

David says this in a psalm of wisdom addressed to people who grow anxious when they see the wicked prosper. Just before, he says that they will wither like the grass. Then he asks us to trust and to commit our way to God. The emphasis is on trusting, not on worry or envy.

For today: instead of striving for what you want, set aside a moment each day to give thanks and to get to know God better. As he takes the center, your desires gradually come into order. This is not a formula for getting everything you ask for, but an invitation to trust in his goodness.
exp.27:3:
This verse is a prayer asking for justice. The psalmist pleads with God to deal with the wicked according to what they have done. "Wickedness" means evil, and "their desert" means what they deserve for their actions. The idea of "the work of their hands" is repeated to stress that their deeds have consequences.

The psalm is spoken by David, according to its heading. He is distressed and cries out to God with his hands lifted toward the temple. He does not want to be treated like the wicked, who speak peace to their neighbors while keeping evil in their hearts. He asks God to do justice, rather than taking revenge himself. Afterward, the psalm says that God will tear them down because they ignored his works.

For today: when you are wounded by hypocrisy or injustice, do not repay evil with evil. Bring your pain to God in prayer and trust that he is a righteous judge. Ask him also to keep you sincere of heart.
exp.1:9:
Psalm 2:10 says that the rulers of the world should become wise and allow themselves to be corrected. The verse calls on them to pay close attention and reflect. To accept correction means to agree to be taught and warned. Those who govern or administer justice are the ones addressed.

In this psalm, the nations rebel against God and against the king he has chosen. The verses before this one show God giving that king the nations as his inheritance. Here the psalmist, whom many believe to be David, though the text does not say so, speaks to the rulers with a warning that is serious but also an invitation. Christians read this as a reference to Christ, the Son.

Today, all of us have some kind of authority, at home, at work, or in the church. Ask yourself: do I let myself be corrected? Listen to advice with humility, and remember that God is the supreme authority.
exp.95:0:
This verse invites us to sing to God a "new song," that is, a fresh, sincere praise filled with gratitude. The invitation is not only for a few people: it says "all the earth," meaning all the nations. The name of God here is "the Lord," and the old-fashioned form of the verb is simply the same call to sing that we would use today.

The psalm does not say who wrote it. It encourages Israel, and also the nations, to praise God. The verses that follow speak of announcing his salvation and of telling his wonders among the peoples. Some believe it was used in public worship, but that cannot be stated with certainty.

Today you can renew your praise: do not stop at habit alone. Think of something specific that God has done for you this week, and give him thanks with a song, a prayer, or by telling someone about it.
exp.77:0:
This verse opens a psalm with an invitation to pay attention. The word "Maschil" is probably a musical or literary term; many think it indicates a song of teaching or reflection, though this is not certain. "Asaph" is the name of the author or of his group of singers. "Law" here means teaching or instruction, and "incline your ears" means: listen carefully and humbly.

The one speaking is the psalmist, who addresses the people of Israel as a teacher. The verses that follow show that he wants to pass on what earlier generations told about the works of God. His purpose is that the people learn from history, remember God's faithfulness, and not repeat the mistakes of their fathers.

For today: set aside some time to truly listen to the Word of God, without hurry. And think of someone young, a child, a nephew, or a friend, to whom you can tell how God has helped you.
exp.129:6:
The people of God should hope in the Lord with confidence. "Hope" means to trust and to wait patiently. The name of God appears here as "the Lord," and the word for "redemption" means rescue and deliverance. The text affirms that with God there is mercy (love that forgives), and that his rescue is more than enough.

This is a psalm of ascent, sung by pilgrims going up to Jerusalem. The psalmist speaks from a place of deep distress and guilt (vv. 1-3). After confessing his own waiting, like the watchman who longs for the dawn, he encourages all Israel to do the same. His hope rests on the character of God, not on the merits of the people.

When you feel weary of waiting or burdened by your mistakes, remember that God's mercy never runs out. Come to him with sincerity, rest in his forgiveness, and wait for his answer with patience, like someone who knows the dawn will come.
exp.118:89:
This verse says that God's truth does not change with the passing of time. "Thy truth" can also be understood as your faithfulness: God does what he says. To show this, the psalmist points to the earth: God set it firm, and it abides, that is, it stays standing and endures.

The speaker is the author of Psalm 119, who is not named with certainty. He is someone who loves God's word and is going through a time of affliction. This psalm opens its section by speaking of the eternal word of God. Here the author uses the steady creation as proof that God is trustworthy.

Today, when everything seems to change and we feel insecure, we can lean on God's faithfulness. Each morning, when we see that the earth still stands firm, remember that God also upholds his promises, and bring him your worries with confidence.
exp.118:32:
He tells us that the psalmist asks God to teach him the way of his statutes, that is, his rules and teachings. He promises to keep them "to the end," meaning all his life. The Hebrew letter that opens this section of the psalm is called "He," and that is the name given to this section.

The speaker is the author of Psalm 119, a long poem in honor of God's word. We do not know for certain who wrote it. He has just affirmed his attachment to God's testimonies and said that he will run in his commandments. Now he recognizes that he needs help: it is not enough to want to obey, he must also be taught by God himself.

For today: before reading the Bible or making a decision, simply ask God to teach you and to give you a willing heart. Then commit to one concrete step of obedience, and keep practicing it faithfully.
exp.139:1:
This verse describes the enemies of David. It says they imagine mischief in their heart, that is, they plan harm inwardly, on purpose and not by accident. They are continually gathered together for war, which means they keep preparing and stirring up fights and conflicts, and they do it all the time, as something constant.

David is the one speaking, and the psalm is a prayer. He asks God to deliver him from violent and wicked people. The verses that follow compare their words to the poison of a serpent. The exact details of the situation are not stated, so we do not know who these enemies were in particular.

For today: when someone treats you badly or surrounds you with conflict, you do not have to answer in kind. Do as David did and bring your situation to God in prayer, asking him for protection and wisdom. And also examine your own heart, so that no plans that harm others come out of it.
exp.13:3:
This verse asks a rebuking question: do those who do evil understand nothing? It says they devour God's people as naturally as someone eats bread, and that they never called upon the Lord, that is, they never cried out to Him or sought Him.

The one speaking is the psalmist, David according to the title of the psalm. First the psalm describes how God looks down from heaven and sees a corrupted humanity. Here the focus falls on the oppressors, who take advantage of the weak without remorse. Then the psalm says that God is with the righteous, and that the poor find their hope in Him.

For today: if you are suffering injustice, trust that God sees it. And examine your own heart: do not live as if God did not exist, and do not use your power to take advantage of others. Instead, call upon Him every day.
exp.118:125:
It says that the time has come for God to act, because people have made his law void. The phrase "It is time to act" means it is the moment for God to intervene. The word "made void" is an old way of saying they have set his law aside, broken it, or spoiled it.

The one speaking is the psalmist, a servant of God who loves the Word. He has just asked for mercy and understanding. Now he grieves to see that many despise the commandments. It is not known exactly who wrote it or when, so it is best not to claim more than the text says. What is clear is that his grief leads him to pray rather than to seek revenge.

For today: when you see that what is good is despised, do not stop at complaining. Pray with humility, ask God to act, and begin by obeying him yourself, at home and at work.
exp.118:71:
The explanation says that God's teaching, the words that come from his mouth, is worth more to the psalmist than huge amounts of gold and silver. The word "law" here is not only a set of rules but all of God's instruction and guidance. Saying that God's word is more valuable than a great fortune is the point of the verse.

The speaker is the author of Psalm 119, who is not identified with certainty. He speaks after going through suffering, saying that he was brought low and that this helped him learn. He also contrasts his attitude with that of people whose hearts are hardened and insensitive. For him, God's law is a treasure that corrects him and guides him.

Today, before spending your best time and energy on money or achievements, set aside a fixed moment each day to read the Bible. Ask God to teach you, even in difficulties.
exp.48:11:
It says that a human being, even though he has riches and fame, does not stay in that honor forever. In the end he dies, just like the animals. "Perish" means to die or disappear. "Honor" is the prestige and the recognition that others give a person.

This psalm was written by the sons of Korah, and the author speaks as a teacher of wisdom. He addresses everyone and wants to remove the fear that comes from seeing the rich and powerful prosper. He reminds them that neither the wise nor the foolish escape death, and that they leave their possessions to others. Some understand the comparison with the beasts only as a reference to the fact that everyone dies, not as a claim that a human being is worth the same as an animal.

Today we can ask ourselves where we are placing our security. If we place it in money, status, or applause, it is something that does not last. Let us seek first what remains: loving God, caring for people, and living with humility and generosity.
exp.24:3:
This verse is a simple prayer. The psalmist asks God to show him his ways and teach him his paths. "Ways" and "paths" speak of the manner in which God acts and of the way he wants us to live. He is not asking only for information, but for direction for his life.

According to the heading, it is a psalm of David. It speaks in a time of pressure: he has enemies, he fears being put to shame, and he trusts in God. That is why, before asking for guidance, he declares that he waits on Him. His desire to learn is rooted in trust, not in carelessness.

For today: before making an important decision, pray this prayer calmly. Ask God to teach you his way, and study his Word with a willingness to obey, even when it is not the easiest thing. God guides those who trust him and is ready to teach those who are willing to learn.
exp.9:13:
It says that God does see what the weak suffer. "You have seen it" means that nothing escapes him. The poor person places himself in God's hands, and he is the refuge, that is, the protection, of the fatherless.

The psalmist speaks, traditionally attributed to David, although the psalm does not say so in its heading. He is distressed because the wicked seem to prosper and think that God is not paying attention. So he asks God to rise up, and in this verse he answers himself with confidence: God does see.

If today you feel abandoned or are going through an injustice, you can bring your burden to God in prayer, honestly. And if you know someone who is vulnerable, be a concrete form of protection for them.
exp.4:7:
David asks God here to guide him along the right path. The word "righteousness" in the verse refers to what is right in God's eyes. The phrase "because of mine enemies" means that his adversaries are watching him closely, and so he needs great clarity. The request "make thy way straight before my face" means: make the way plain and free of stumbling, so that I can see it and follow it.

The psalm is, according to its heading, spoken by David in a morning prayer. He has just said that God hates lies and deceit, and that he himself will come into God's house with reverence. He is surrounded by false people, and he does not want to answer them with their own weapons, but to walk as God commands.

For today: when you face unjust people or a difficult decision, do not respond with revenge or with trickery. Ask God for direction, seek his Word, and move forward step by step along the path he shows you.
exp.36:12:
It says that God laughs at the wicked person who plans to harm the righteous. It is not a cruel, mocking laugh but the laugh of someone who knows those plans will not succeed. The reason is that God sees that the wicked person's day is coming, that is, the time when he will receive the judgment he deserves. "He will laugh" is a human way of speaking to show that God is not frightened or out of control.

It is a psalm of David, written as the counsel of a man already advanced in years. It speaks to believers who are distressed to see the wicked seem to prosper and attack the good. The verses before it show the wicked person plotting and gnashing his teeth; the verses that follow say that his own sword will reach him.

When someone treats you unjustly, do not fill yourself with resentment or fear. Trust that God sees everything and acts in his own time. In the meantime, keep doing good with calm.
exp.87:14:
The explanation says that the psalmist is suffering and in great need. "Afflicted" describes someone struck down by pain. The word for needy or poor describes someone who lacks everything and depends on help. He feels that from his youth he has carried the terrors of God, that is, experiences of anguish that he perceives as coming from the hand of God.

The psalm is attributed to Heman the Ezrahite, though we do not know with certainty all the details of his life. It is a very dark prayer: there is almost no relief and no word of hope. Even so, the one speaking keeps crying out to the LORD, and at the start of the psalm he calls him "God of my salvation." His complaint arises from long suffering, perhaps illness or abandonment, and from feeling that God has drawn far away.

For today: if you are going through a long pain and see no way out, you can pray with complete honesty, without disguising what you feel. The Bible allows us to lament before God, and continuing to speak to him is already a form of faith.
exp.70:3:
Here the psalmist asks God, whom he calls "my God," to rescue him from wicked people. The "unrighteous" person is one who lives without regard for God. The "wicked" man is one who practices evil, and the "cruel" man is one who harms others with force or brutality. He asks to be delivered from the "hand" of such people, that is, from their power.

The psalm does not say who wrote it. The speaker is an older person who remembers how God has cared for him since his youth and even before he was born. He is facing a real threat and takes refuge in God, whom he calls his rock and his fortress. His request comes from trust, not from despair.

For today: when you feel that someone or something stronger than you is oppressing you, do not stay silent. Speak honestly with God and remember the times he has already helped you. That strengthens your hope.
exp.88:27:
He says that God promises to keep his mercy, that is, his faithful love and kindness, for ever with the person he is speaking of. He also affirms that his covenant, that is, the agreement or commitment he made, will be firm and will not be broken. The word "keep" means to hold on to and not let it be lost.

God is speaking, and the psalmist (Ethan the Ezrahite, according to the title) recalls the promise God made to David. God committed himself to sustain David and his descendants on the throne. The verses that follow clarify that the children could be corrected if they turned away from the law, but the covenant remained in force. Christians see in this promise a foreshadowing of Jesus, a descendant of David.

For today: when you fail or feel that everything is shaking, remember that God's faithfulness does not depend on your steadiness, but on his word. Trust in him and return to his way.
exp.105:34:
The explanation says that the people of Israel, instead of staying faithful to God, joined with the peoples of Canaan and adopted their customs. "Were mingled" means they lived closely together, without separating themselves. "Learned their works" means they copied their practices and their way of living and worshiping.

The psalmist, who is not named in this psalm, goes over the history of Israel to acknowledge the people's sins and to praise God's patience. Before this verse, Israel did not destroy the peoples as God had commanded. Afterward, that living together led them into idolatry, and the verses that follow even mention the sacrifice of children.

Today we can take care with the influences around us. This is not about isolating ourselves or looking down on anyone, but about being honest: what am I learning from my surroundings, from what I see and from my friendships? Let us ask God for wisdom to love everyone without losing our faithfulness to Him.
exp.105:32:
The explanation says that the people made Moses' spirit fill with bitterness and anger, and so Moses spoke without thinking, with impulsive words. The phrase "his spirit was provoked" means that his inner self was stirred up and exasperated.

The psalmist, who does not identify himself, reviews the sins of Israel in the desert. Here he recalls what happened at Meribah (Numbers 20), where the people complained for lack of water. Moses, tired of so much complaining, spoke in anger and struck the rock instead of speaking to it as God had commanded. The psalm shows that the people's rebellion had consequences even for their leader.

For today: when someone wears you out or provokes you, your anger does not justify speaking without control. Before you respond, pause and pray. Ask God for self-control so that your words do not lead you to disobey.
exp.34:15:
This verse describes cruel people who mock the psalmist. Those who "flatter" pretend friendship with sweet words; the "mocking jesters" are scoffers and clowns who laugh at others at the table. "Gnashing the teeth" is a gesture of rage and contempt. There are several ways to translate the Hebrew text, which is difficult, but the general idea is clear: they surround him with ridicule and hatred.

David speaks here, according to the title of the psalm. He asks God for help because people he treated like brothers, and for whom he prayed and wept, now rejoice in his misfortune and attack him without cause.

For today: if someone you trusted betrays you, you do not have to keep your pain silent. Bring it to God honestly, as David did, and trust that he sees what is happening and sustains you.
exp.59:8:
Here the speaker asks two questions: who will lead me into the strong city? Who will bring me into Edom? The strong city is a city protected by walls, and the question shows that a guide is needed for a difficult task.

The psalm is attributed to David, in a time of war. God had just promised victory over several neighboring peoples, but the people feel defeated and abandoned. Edom was a strong enemy, with cities that were hard to reach. Many understand that the question has no human answer: the answer is in the next verse, where trust is placed in God and not in people. Scholars discuss some historical details of the exact moment.

For today: when you face something that seems like a strong city, such as a big problem or an impossible situation, do not rely only on your own strength. Ask God to guide you, and walk with the confidence that He goes before you.
exp.72:20:
This verse says that the psalmist's heart became bitter, filled with irritation and pain. The explanation of the word that describes his heart being soured is that it refers to becoming bitter or filled with displeasure, which is covered in the verse itself. In biblical language, the innermost part of a person, their most private feelings, is the deepest place of the self. The sharp hurts he describes are like stabs: a piercing pain felt inside.

Asaph, or the author of the psalm, looks back. Earlier he felt envy when he saw the wicked prospering, and that embittered his soul. Now, after entering the sanctuary and understanding their end, he honestly acknowledges how much it hurt him and how deeply it affected him inwardly.

For today: when comparison or envy makes you bitter, do not hide it. Tell God sincerely what you feel, and ask Him to restore your perspective. He holds your hand even in the midst of your confusion.
exp.33:2:
It says that David invites others to join him in praising God. To "magnify" the Lord means to recognize and declare that God is great, not to make Him any greater than He is. To "exalt" His name means to lift it up or honor it. "Together" means side by side, at one time, with one mind.

David is speaking. The title of the psalm connects it to the time he pretended to be insane before Abimelech (in 1 Samuel the king is called Achish) and was able to escape. After that danger, he does not keep his thankfulness to himself: he calls others to rejoice together that the Lord delivered him.

For today: when God helps you with something, tell someone in your church or your family, and pray or sing together giving thanks. Praise grows stronger when it is shared, and it also encourages those who are going through hard times.
exp.57:10:
This verse says that when people see how God acts against wickedness, they will recognize two things: that doing what is right does bring a reward, and that there is a God who rules and judges here on the earth. The word "Then" points to the moment when God steps in.

It is a psalm of David, who cries out against unjust judges who handed down crooked rulings (vv. 1-2). It speaks in very strong, poetic language, with images of violence, such as washing one's feet in blood. Many read it as a dramatic way of saying that the righteous will see God's justice, not as an invitation to take revenge. David asks God to act, and he ends with hope.

For today: when you see injustice, do not despair or seek revenge. Keep doing what is right, and trust that God sees, judges with righteousness, and does not let your faithfulness go unrewarded.
exp.112:2:
This verse says that praise to God should reach every place and last the whole day. "From the rising of the sun to where it sets" means from east to west, from sunrise to sunset. "Lord" is the proper name of God in this translation, and "is to be praised" is an invitation: that his name be honored.

The psalm does not mention its author. It opens with a call to praise, which means "praise the Lord." It speaks to the servants of God, that is, to his people. The verses that follow give the reason: God is above all nations and above the heavens. For this reason, his praise is not limited to one place or one people. Some also see here a look toward the whole world.

For today: begin your day with a short prayer of thanks, and end it the same way. In this way, your morning and your evening remind your heart that God is worthy of praise.
exp.129:4:
He says the psalmist has waited for God with his whole being. "I wait for the Lord" is the name of God, the Lord. "My soul doth wait" means he waited from the heart, with his whole life and not only with words. And "in his word do I hope" means he trusts in what God has promised. The word "wait" here means to trust with patience.

This is one of the songs of ascent, which pilgrims sang as they went up to Jerusalem. It is not certain who wrote it. The speaker cries out from the depths, aware of his guilt. He has already recognized that no one could stand if the Lord kept a record of sins, but that with the Lord there is forgiveness. That is why he now waits with confidence.

For today: when you feel guilty or the answer is slow in coming, do not turn away from God. Read a promise from his Word, repeat it in prayer, and trust that his forgiveness and help are coming.
exp.118:30:
The psalmist says that he has clung, or held fast, to God's testimonies, that is, to his teachings and words. The verse's phrase "I have stuck unto thy testimonies" expresses this closeness. With that trust he prays: "put me not to shame," meaning that he should not be left in shame for having trusted in God.

The speaker is the author of Psalm 119, a believer who loves the law of the Lord. We do not know for certain who wrote it. In the verses nearby he says that he chose the way of truth and wants to turn away from falsehood. His request comes from a firm decision: to follow God, even though he may face pressure or mockery.

Today, we can hold fast to God's Word in our daily decisions, such as at work, in the family, or with money. Let us do so with humility, asking him to sustain us, because faithfulness does not depend only on our own strength.
exp.72:4:
It says that the wicked do not go through the difficulties and the struggle that ordinary people suffer. The words "human toil" refer to the normal burdens and struggles of life, and "plagued" refers to the blows or afflictions that others receive. This is how the psalmist seems to see them: free of trouble.

The speaker is Asaph, the author of this psalm according to its heading. He is confessing his inner struggle: he almost stumbled when he saw people without God prosper and live at ease. He describes what he was seeing, that is, his perception at that moment. Later in the psalm he understands things differently, when he enters the sanctuary of God.

For today: when you feel envy toward those who seem to live without problems, do not stop at what you see on the outside. Bring your restlessness to God in prayer, be honest with Him, and ask Him to give you His perspective.
exp.10:2:
This verse asks a hard question: if what holds everything up collapses, namely justice, order, and truth, what can a righteous person do? The word "foundations" refers to the firm bases of a house or of a society.

David speaks in a psalm of confidence. His friends, frightened, advise him to flee to the mountains like a bird, because the wicked attack the upright in secret. They believe all is lost. This question probably expresses their fear, and there is more than one way to understand it. David answers right away: the Lord still sits on his throne, sees everything, and tests the righteous.

For today: when everything seems to be falling apart, do not let yourself be carried away by panic. Keep doing what is right, and rest in the fact that God reigns and sees.
exp.140:5:
The explanation says that the judges or leaders of the wicked will be thrown down in rocky places, as if hurled from a cliff. Then they will hear the psalmist's words, which are "suaves," that is, kind and true.

The one speaking is the psalmist, who according to the traditional heading would be David. He asks God to keep him from evil and accepts correction from the righteous. This verse is difficult, and scholars interpret it in different ways. One common reading is that, when the power of the wicked falls, they will recognize that his words were true.

Today we can receive the gentle correction of other believers with humility, leave the judgment of the wicked in God's hands, and speak with gentleness, without revenge.
exp.98:8:
This verse invites everyone to lift up God's name in praise. "Exalt" means to raise up and honor someone as great. To bow down means to bend low or prostrate oneself in respect. The phrase "his holy hill" most likely refers to Zion, the place of worship in Jerusalem. The reason is simple: God is holy, unique, and perfect.

The psalmist speaks to the people of Israel. He has just recalled how God guided Moses, Aaron, and Samuel, and how God answered them. God forgave them, but He also held them accountable for their actions. His holiness joins mercy with justice.

Today, let us not take God lightly. Before praying or going to church, pause, quiet the voice of your heart, and recognize who He is. Worship Him with gratitude and with reverence.
exp.21:24:
What it says: The speaker says that his praise to God comes from God himself, and that he will offer it in the great assembly, that is, in the large gathering of the people. He also promises to fulfill his vows, which are the promises he made to God in difficult moments. He will do so before those who fear him, that is, those who respect and honor God.

Context: It is a psalm of David. It begins with a cry of anguish (the well-known "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?"), but from verse 22 onward it turns to thanksgiving because God heard the afflicted one. Here David promises to praise publicly. Christians see in this psalm a reflection of Jesus on the cross, although David first spoke of his own experience.

For today: When God helps you through a trial, do not keep your gratitude a secret. Tell what he did in your church or with your family, and keep what you promised. Your testimony can encourage others.
exp.118:167:
The explanation says that the psalmist has kept and cared for God's instructions, called here "commandments" and "testimonies" (what God has declared and taught). The reason he gives is that all his ways, that is, his whole manner of living, are before God: God sees everything.

Psalm 119 is a long poem in honor of God's word, and this is the last stanza of the eighth section, the one whose verses all begin with the same letter of the Hebrew alphabet (the following section is the final one). Tradition attributes it to David, though the text does not say so. The speaker is a believer who loves God's law and, even in the midst of difficulties, wants to live sincerely before Him.

For today: living with the awareness that God sees us does not have to cause fear, but sincerity. Before deciding something, ask yourself: "Could I do this with God at my side, openly?" That question helps us walk with honesty.
exp.106:27:
This verse says that people, when they are in serious trouble, cry out to God, and he delivers them from their distresses. The word "distresses" refers to a very strong kind of suffering, like feeling squeezed with no way out. The verse's wording "delivers" means he rescues them.

The psalmist is speaking of sailors caught in a storm at sea. They have lost control, and all their skill is of no use to them. It is one of several scenes in the psalm, where different people in danger ask God for help and he responds. The psalm invites us to give thanks for his faithful love.

When you feel you have no way out, do not wait until you have the perfect words. Cry out to God honestly, just as you are. He listens, and often he leads us to a place of rest, even when we do not always know how or when.
exp.17:9:
This verse says that God moved with great power and speed. "Rode" means to be carried on horseback, "cherub" is a heavenly being in God's service, and "wings of the wind" is an image of swiftness. It should not be understood as a literal description, but as poetry.

David speaks here in a song of thanksgiving after God rescued him from his enemies and from Saul. Earlier, David cried out in his distress (v. 6), and here he describes God's response with images of storm, fire, and darkness. Many understand the language to be symbolic and to show that God acts with majesty.

For today: when your problem feels bigger than you, remember that God hears and can act. Pray with confidence and wait on Him, even when you do not know how or when He will respond.
exp.1:3:
This verse says that God, who sits in the heavens, laughs at the kings who rise up against him. The word "shall laugh" does not speak of cruelty, but of how those human plans seem ridiculous to him in view of his power. The word "sitteth" means "dwells" or "lives," as in the verse above.

Psalm 2 does not say who wrote it, although the New Testament attributes it to David (Acts 4:25). Here the psalmist describes rulers who want to free themselves from God and from his "anointed," the king he has chosen. Many Christians see in that king a picture of Christ. God's laughter is not amusement, but a sign that no one can defeat him, and it sets up his response in the verses that follow.

For today: when you see powers or ideas that seem stronger than God, do not live in fear. Trust that he is still in control, and seek to submit to his authority instead of resisting it.
exp.9:2:
The verse says that the wicked person boasts about what his heart desires, as if his cravings were something worthy of applause. He also praises the greedy person, that is, someone who always wants more and takes advantage of others. The phrase "blesseth" here can be understood as "praises." The text adds that the Lord abhors that greedy person. Some translators understand the phrase differently: that the greedy person himself turns away from God. The original wording allows both readings.

The one speaking is the psalmist, perhaps David, though the psalm does not say so. He prays in distress because God seems far away while the proud oppress the poor and no one seems to stop them.

Today, it is wise not to admire someone who succeeds only by getting what he wants. Let us value character more than wealth or fame, and bring our cravings before God.
exp.118:19:
My soul is broken, meaning worn down and spent inside, because of a very strong longing. What he desires so intensely are God's judgments, which here mean his righteous decisions, his commands, and his way of governing. And he longs for them at all times, without pause.

The one speaking is the psalmist, whose name we do not know. In this psalm he praises God's law. A few verses earlier he calls himself a stranger passing through, and for that reason he needs God's guidance. Then he speaks of the proud who turn away from God and of the mockery he suffers.

Today we can ask God to grow in us a hunger for his Word, not only when everything is going well. One practical idea is to set aside a few minutes each day to read a passage and pray: "Lord, teach me to love what you say."
exp.30:9:
It says that grief and sighing have been wearing away his life. The word translated "enflaquecido" means he has grown weak. "Iniquity" means wickedness or guilt. The bones that are "consumed" express a deep exhaustion, one felt even in the body.

The title of the psalm attributes it to David, although it does not say at what exact moment he wrote it. The one speaking is distressed, rejected by neighbors and acquaintances, and threatened by enemies. Some understand that he suffers because of his own sin. Others think the Hebrew word can also mean affliction or the consequences of evil, which is why some translations say "affliction." Even so, in the psalm he trusts in God.

Today, if you are worn out by pain or guilt, do not hide it. You can tell God honestly how you feel, as the psalmist did, and trust in his mercy.
exp.117:3:
This verse invites those who fear the Lord, that is, those who revere him and honor him with respect, to declare out loud that his mercy endures forever. The word "mercy" here translates a Hebrew word that speaks of faithful, loyal love. The call to say it now is a summons to respond with praise.

The psalm does not say who wrote it. It seems to be a song of thanksgiving meant to be sung together in community, perhaps in the temple. It first calls Israel, then the priests (the house of Aaron), and then all who fear God. Some think it may also include people from other nations who worshiped the Lord, but this is not certain. Afterward, the psalmist tells how God rescued him from distress.

For today: do not keep your gratitude to yourself. When you remember how God has sustained you, say it out loud before your family or your church. That encourages others to trust.
exp.117:14:
This verse says that in the homes of the righteous there are songs of joy and victory, because God has acted with power. "Tabernacles" in the verse refers to dwellings or homes, since people once lived in tents. "Rejoicing" is joy expressed out loud. "Salvation" here means rescue or deliverance. "The right hand" of the Lord is a symbol of strength. "Doeth valiantly" means that he has done mighty deeds.

Psalm 118 is a song of thanksgiving. The one speaking has been attacked almost to the point of falling, but God helped him. Many think a king or leader speaks on behalf of the people, although no one knows for certain who he is. His testimony becomes a shared celebration among those who trust in God.

For today: when God helps you through a difficulty, tell it out loud to your family or your church. Giving thanks together strengthens faith and encourages others who are going through a trial.
exp.28:2:
This verse says that the voice of God is heard over the waters like thunder. He is called "the God of glory" because his greatness is seen in his power. The phrase "thundereth" means that the thunder is like his voice. "The many waters" could be the sea or the storm clouds; the text does not make this clear.

David writes this psalm as a song of praise. First he calls on the mighty ones (perhaps heavenly beings, though some think of powerful people) to give glory to God. Then he describes a storm as a sign of his power. The whole psalm shows how the voice of God rules over creation.

For today: when your life feels stirred up like a sea in a storm, remember that God is above the waters. Pause for a moment, acknowledge his power, and rest in the fact that he governs what seems uncontrollable to you.
exp.79:6:
The explanation says that the people ask God, called the one who has all power, to make them come back, that is, to bring them back to Himself and restore them. They ask that his face shine upon them, that he look on them with favor and kindness. They trust that in this way they will be saved, that is, rescued and made safe.

The speaker is the community of Israel, in a psalm of Asaph. They are suffering: they eat bread of tears, their neighbors despise them, and their enemies mock them. This same plea is repeated as a refrain in verses 3 and 19. Then they recall how God planted his people like a vine brought out of Egypt. Scholars do not agree on the exact time when it was written.

For today: when you feel defeated or far from God, do not stay only in complaint. Ask him sincerely to restore you and to look on you with kindness. Salvation depends on his grace, not on your own strength.
exp.13:5:
This verse speaks to the wicked and tells them that they mock the plan or the counsel of the poor. In the verse your reader sees, the word used is "shamed," meaning to put to shame or to treat with contempt. The reason is that the poor person trusts in God, and the Lord is his refuge. The mockers see that trust as foolishness.

The psalm is attributed to David. It describes people who live without God and oppress his people, and it compares them to those who devour bread without thinking. Here David speaks to these oppressors, and the verse that follows expresses his desire that God bring deliverance. Some explain "the counsel" as the plans or the trust of the poor in God; the text does not go into more detail.

Today we can keep trusting God even when others laugh at our faith or at our humble situation. We can also take care not to look down on those who have little, for God looks on them with kindness.
exp.108:3:
It says that, in return for the love the psalmist showed, others became his enemies. "Adversaries" are people who oppose and accuse. But he responds in a different way: "but I give myself unto prayer." Instead of returning attack for attack, he hands his pain over to God.

The psalm is spoken by David, according to its heading, although some scholars debate how it was used later. He is surrounded by lies and hatred without cause, and yet he remembers that he treated them with love. Further on, the psalm asks for strong justice against his accusers, something many readers find hard to understand.

For today: when someone repays you with evil for having done good, do not hold on to the pain or seek revenge. Bring it to God in prayer, tell him everything honestly, and ask him for peace and wisdom to respond well.
exp.53:6:
It says that God rescued the psalmist from every kind of distress or suffering. It also says that his eyes "saw his desire" over his enemies, meaning that he was able to look with satisfaction at how the threat that pursued him had ended. The expression is brief, and some translators add "I have seen the defeat of my enemies."

The title of the psalm attributes it to David, at the time when the Ziphites went to tell Saul where he was hiding. David asks God for help, and here he ends with gratitude, speaking like someone who has already seen the answer. Some think it is an early confidence, others that it is a testimony written afterward.

For today: when God sustains you in a difficulty, don't stop at the relief alone. Write down what He did and give Him thanks. And if someone has wronged you, trust God's justice instead of seeking revenge yourself.
exp.111:6:
The explanation says that the person who fears God is not frightened by bad news. The phrase "evil tidings" means bad news or reports of misfortune. A heart that is "fixed" is steady, firm and ready. His heart is calm because he trusts in the Lord.

This psalm is a poem of praise, and no one knows for certain who wrote it. It describes the one who fears God and lives with generosity, justice and good judgment, as seen in the verses before and after. This man's confidence does not come from never facing bad things, but from knowing in whom he rests.

When bad news arrives, before letting fear take over, stop and pray. Remember that God is still caring for you, and ask him for calm so that you can decide wisely and keep doing good.
exp.7:5:
It says that God gave human beings authority over everything He created. "The works of your hands" refers to all of creation. "You put all things under his feet" is a way of saying that everything was placed under his care and command.

David speaks here in a psalm of praise. He is amazed that the God who made the stars pays attention to humankind, which seems so small. The verses that follow name the animals of the field, the birds, and the fish. Some Christians also see a look toward Christ here, because the New Testament quotes this psalm in Hebrews 2.

Today we can see our work and our care for the earth as a task that God has entrusted to us. To rule is not to abuse, but to care humbly for what belongs to God.
exp.86:1:
It says that God loves the gates of Zion in a special way, that is, Jerusalem, more than all the other homes or cities of the people of Jacob (Israel). The word "dwellings" in the verse means places where people live. The gates were the place of gathering, of justice, and of entrance to the city, so naming them stands for the whole city and its people.

This psalm was written by the sons of Korah, Levites who served in the worship of the temple. They celebrate Jerusalem as the city that God himself founded and chose. The verses that follow say that even distant nations, such as Egypt (Rahab) and Babylon, will be counted among those who know God. Scholars discuss some details of that part, but the idea of a love that reaches beyond Israel is clear.

Today we can value the community where God gathers us. If God loves his people, we too can love the church, pray for it, and serve it with joy, even with its imperfections.
exp.113:5:
Here the psalmist asks the mountains and the hills a question, as if they could answer: "Why did you leap like rams and like little lambs?" The word "skipped" in the verse above is an old way of saying "leaped." It is poetic language: the mountains move with joy or fear, like animals that jump.

The psalm recalls Israel's departure from Egypt, the crossing of the sea and of the Jordan. It does not say who wrote it. The author speaks as someone celebrating what God has done. He asks creation itself to show that all of it responded to God. Some think it refers to the trembling at Sinai, but the text does not make this clear. The answer comes in the next verse: the earth trembles before the presence of the Lord.

For today: if even the mountains shake before God, we can draw near to Him with reverence and confidence. Today you can set aside a moment to pray, remembering that the mighty God also cares for you.
exp.118:34:
The explanation says that the psalmist asks God to lead him along the path of his commandments. The word "path" here means a narrow way, and "delight" means desire or pleasure. It is like saying: "Lead me by your commandments, because there is my joy."

Psalm 119 is a long poem in honor of God's Word. It is not known with certainty who wrote it; many attribute it to David, but others think of a later author. The speaker already loves God's law, but recognizes that he needs help to follow it. That is why, in the verses nearby, he also asks for understanding and a heart turned toward God.

For today: we can pray with humility, asking God to guide us, even when we want to obey him. Before making a decision, you might say: "Lord, lead me on your way, and change my desires if necessary."
exp.93:19:
Here the psalmist asks a rhetorical question: can God join himself to a corrupt government, to a "throne of iniquity" that frames mischief by a law? The verse's wording "shall ... have fellowship with thee" means that such a throne would be an ally of God. The explanation that follows describes how it invents injustices and uses the law as an excuse. The expected answer is: no, God never sides with that.

The psalm is a cry to God as judge of the earth. The one speaking sees rulers or judges oppressing the innocent, and he asks whether God allows it. The verses that follow show the abuse: they conspire against the righteous. But the psalmist also remembers that God's mercy held him up when he felt his foot slipping, and that God is his refuge.

Today we can trust that God does not approve of injustice, even when it is dressed in legality. When you see abuses, pray, act justly in what is yours to do, and rest in God as your refuge.
exp.68:0:
This verse begins with a note for the choir director: the tune is called "Shoshannim," and it is a psalm of David. Then comes the cry: "Save me, O God." The waters that reach up to the soul are an image of danger and distress, like someone nearly drowning. The word "soul" here can also be understood as life, or the neck.

The speaker is David, or so the title indicates. He is suffering greatly, surrounded by troubles and enemies, and already tired of asking for help. The verses that follow speak of mire, deep waters, and a voice hoarse from crying out. We do not know with certainty what exact moment of his life is meant.

For today: when you feel overwhelmed, you do not have to pretend to be strong. You can say to God in sincerity, "Help me, I can't go on." Scripture shows us that praying this way, with honesty, is an expression of faith.
exp.132:2:
This verse compares unity among brothers and sisters to the dew of Hermon, which falls on the mountains of Zion. It is an image of freshness and life. "There" refers to that place where there is unity, and the LORD commands the blessing, that is, he gives favor and good. Life forevermore can also be understood as life for ever, or a full and lasting life.

It is a song of ascents by David, the kind the people sang as they went up to Jerusalem. Here the harmony of God's people is celebrated. Hermon is a high mountain far to the north, and Zion is in Jerusalem; some think the image speaks of abundance, since the dew there was plentiful. Scholars debate the geographical detail.

When there is peace among brothers and sisters, God usually brings life to that setting. Today you can seek reconciliation with someone in your family or church: take the first step with a kind word.
exp.131:7:
This verse is a prayer. The people ask God to "arise," that is, to set out and go to his rest, the place where he would dwell. "The ark of your strength" is the ark of the covenant, a symbol of God's presence and power.

The psalm recalls when David wanted to find a place for the ark. The places named in the psalm are tied to his search, and scholars debate their exact identification. The speakers are the people, or a group of worshipers, who want God to dwell among them. Many think it was used when the ark was brought into the temple, though there is no certainty.

Today we can pray that God be the center of our lives, not an occasional visitor. Set aside a space in your day, even a brief one, to seek him, listen to him, and worship him, and ask him to reign in your home and in your heart.
exp.118:5:
