This verse says that the psalmist would not feel ashamed if he gave careful attention to all of God's commandments. The word "respect" is an old way of saying "give attention to" or "obey carefully." And "ashamed" means he would not be left in disgrace or with his face downcast.

The speaker is the author of the psalm, whose name is not stated with certainty. He is a believer who loves God's law. He has just said that he longs for his ways to be steady in obeying. Now he expresses that a life aligned with all of God's word does not end in disgrace, and so he goes on with praise and a request for help.

For today: do not choose only the commandments that are easy for you. Today, pick one specific area where you know God is asking something of you, and take one simple step to obey it, trusting in his help.
exp.78:10:
Let the groans of the prisoners reach God. The word that the source uses for "presence" means being before him. A groan is a cry of pain. The prisoners are captives, and those condemned to die are people sentenced to death. The psalmist asks that God, with his great power, care for and save those who are about to perish.

Asaph, or an author from his circle, speaks on behalf of the people of Israel. The psalm mourns the destruction of Jerusalem and the temple by enemies who killed and took captives. Many believe it reflects the fall of Jerusalem to Babylon, although the psalm does not give the exact date. The people acknowledge their sins and appeal to God's mercy.

For today: when you know someone who suffers injustice or confinement, pray for that person with confidence, knowing that God hears the groans. And, if you can, help in a concrete way.
exp.50:12:
David says that after being forgiven, he will teach the transgressors, those who turn aside from God's law and break it, the ways of the Lord. He hopes that sinners will turn back, that is, that they will return to God. The word "salvation" in the nearby verses is what the Hebrew-influenced wording points to as salvation, and I'm deleting any further comment on specific words.

I'll delete it.

The speaker is David, in a psalm of repentance. Tradition links it to his sin with Bathsheba and the confrontation by the prophet Nathan, although the text itself only indicates this in its heading. He has asked for cleansing and restoration, and now he promises to use his experience to help others return to God.

For today: if God has forgiven you and lifted you up, do not hide your story. Share it with humility and gratitude, without boasting, to encourage others to seek God. Your testimony can show that there is forgiveness and a way back.
exp.28:9:
He says that the Lord is seated as King over the flood, that is, over the great waters. He rules from his throne, and his reign is not temporary but lasts forever. The Hebrew word for "flood" appears almost only here and in the account of Noah, so some think it recalls that great deluge, and others think it speaks in general of the waters of chaos and danger.

It is a psalm of David, which describes a powerful storm as the voice of God. The waters, the thunder, and the trembling of the wilderness show his power. This verse is the conclusion: in the midst of all that uproar, God remains on his throne, calm and sovereign. What follows, strength and peace for his people, shows that his power protects.

For today: when life feels like a storm and everything overflows, remember that God still reigns. Ask him today for strength and peace, and trust that he has not lost control.
exp.68:6:
The psalmist says he has endured insults and scorn for God's sake. The quoted phrase about shame covering his face speaks of the embarrassment that shows on a person's face, like someone who lowers their eyes because of dishonor.

The psalm is traditionally attributed to David, according to its title, though some think another writer may have composed it in a similar situation. He is distressed and rejected even by his own family, because his faithfulness to God brings mockery upon him. Christians see in this psalm a shadow of Jesus, since the New Testament quotes parts of it (John 2:17; Romans 15:3).

Living faithfully to God can bring us criticism or misunderstanding. When that happens, do not lose heart: bring your pain to God honestly, as the psalmist did, and remember that He sees what you suffer out of love for Him.
exp.23:4:
He will receive the blessing from the Lord, the person whose hands are clean and whose heart is pure, described in the verse before. He will also receive righteousness from the God of his salvation. In plain modern English, "salvation" here means deliverance, and "righteousness" can be understood as being declared right by God or receiving his approval.

This is a psalm of David, probably sung in procession toward the sanctuary. It first asks who may draw near to God, and answers with inner and outer integrity. This verse shows the result: God himself blesses and gives salvation. The psalm then speaks of those who seek his face and announces the entrance of the King of glory.

Today we can approach God with sincerity, without pretense. You might pray this way: "Lord, cleanse me and teach me to live in truth." The blessing comes from him, not from how we appear.
exp.101:15:
This verse says that when the Lord has rebuilt Zion, that is, Jerusalem, his glory will be seen there clearly. The phrase "will build up" carries the sense of rebuilding, and "shall appear" means that he will show himself to all.

Psalm 102 is the prayer of a person in distress, who feels alone and weak. In the midst of his pain, he looks with hope toward Zion, which seems to lie in ruins. Many believe it reflects the time of the exile, but the text does not say so with certainty. The psalmist trusts that God will act on behalf of his people and that the nations will acknowledge him.

For today: when you feel that something in your life lies in ruins, remember that God knows how to rebuild. Pray with sincerity, wait with patience, and look to see his glory in what he restores, in his time and in his way.
exp.5:4:
This verse says that when a person dies, they can no longer remember or praise God. The psalmist asks God who will give thanks to him there, in the grave.

David, according to the title of the psalm, is the one speaking. He is sick, distressed, and surrounded by enemies, and he feels that God is far away. He asks to be rescued because of God's mercy. His argument is not that death is the end of everything, but that he wants to keep living so that he can give thanks to God. Scholars understand this language in different ways: as a poetic expression of pain, or as a reflection of how little was known at that time about life after death.

For today: when you are distressed, you can speak to God honestly, even with tears. Ask him for help, and also for a purpose: that your life, even in pain, may serve to give him thanks and praise.
exp.105:33:
They did not wipe out the nations that lived in Canaan, even though God had given them that command. Here, "destroyed" means to remove or drive those peoples out of the land. "Jehovah" is the name of God.

The psalmist reviews Israel's failures from the desert to the promised land. No one knows for certain who wrote it. He recalls this to confess that the people were disobedient again and again. The verses that follow show the result: they mixed with those nations, copied their customs, and worshiped their idols. Partial obedience opened the door to something worse.

For today: God asks us not to leave half-finished what He points out to us. If an influence, a habit, or a friendship pulls us away from God and we do not face it, it slowly changes us. Obey quickly, even when it costs you, and ask God for help.
exp.135:24:
It says that God feeds and sustains every living thing. The word "sustenance" means food, what is needed to live, and "all flesh" means every living creature, people and animals alike. Each time someone eats, God is at work, and the reason is his mercy, which lasts forever.

This psalm is a song of praise that was sung in community. A leader would say a line and the people would answer with the refrain: "for his mercy endureth forever." Earlier, the psalm recalls creation and Israel's deliverance from its enemies. Here it moves from the history of the people to the daily care of every creature. Then it closes by inviting praise to the God of heaven.

For today: the next time you eat, pause for a moment and give thanks. Recognizing that our daily bread comes from God's goodness makes us more grateful and more willing to share with those who have less.
exp.32:21:
This verse is a closing prayer. "Mercy" here means God's faithful and kind love. "Lord" is the name of God. The phrase "according as we hope in thee" means "just as we trust in you." It asks that God's love cover us to the degree that we entrust our lives to him.

The psalm does not say who wrote it. It speaks in the plural: it is the voice of God's people singing together. Earlier, the psalm praises God as Creator and protector of those who trust in him. Now, at the end, the people respond with a humble plea: "Give us your love, Lord, because in you we place our hope."

Today we can make this verse a simple prayer when we are worried. Instead of depending only on our own strength, we can say: "Lord, I trust in you; care for me with your love." Waiting on God is not doing nothing, but resting in the knowledge that he sustains us.
exp.2:7:
Salvation comes from the Lord alone, and his blessing rests on his people. Here the word for salvation does not refer only to good physical health, but to deliverance, rescue, and victory. The word "Selah" that closes the verse is of uncertain meaning; many believe it marked a pause for reflection or a moment in the music.

The speaker is David, according to the title of the psalm, at a time when he was fleeing from his son Absalom. He was surrounded by enemies, and many said God would no longer help him. Even so, he slept in peace and trusted in God. The psalm ends by acknowledging that deliverance does not depend on his army but on the Lord, and it asks for blessing on the whole people, not only on himself.

For today: when you feel surrounded by problems, pause and hand over to God what you cannot resolve. Rest in the knowledge that he is your help, and pray also for others, not only for yourself.
exp.78:3:
He says that God's people are "reproached," that is, humbled and shamed, by the nations that live nearby. They are also "scorned and derided": others laugh at them and treat them with contempt. Their neighbours, instead of showing compassion, mock them.

The speaker is the psalmist, Asaph or someone from his circle, speaking on behalf of the whole people. This psalm arose after a terrible attack on Jerusalem, when the temple was defiled and many died. Many scholars connect it with the destruction by Babylon, although the text does not say so clearly. After the pain comes the mockery, and the people bring it before God in prayer.

When you are humiliated or mocked, you do not have to keep the pain in silence. You can bring it to God honestly, as the psalmist did, and trust that he hears those who suffer.
exp.6:3:
David says that if he has repaid evil to someone who lived at peace with him, or has harmed the one who was his enemy without cause, then let God judge him. "Repaying evil" means returning harm for good. "At peace with me" refers to a friend or ally. The phrase in parentheses can be understood this way: he even rescued or helped his enemy. Another possible reading is that he plundered the one who oppressed him without cause; scholars read it both ways.

Context: David prays to God because someone is accusing him unjustly (the title mentions Cush the Benjamite, though we cannot be certain who he was). David declares his innocence and places his life and his honor in God's hands, the righteous judge.

For today: when you are accused without reason, do not defend yourself with revenge. Examine your heart honestly before God, and if you are innocent, entrust your cause to Him.
exp.26:12:
David says he would have lost heart, or given up, if he had not trusted that he would see the goodness of the Lord. "I had fainted" means "I would have fainted." "In the land of the living" refers to this life, here and now, in contrast with the grave. It is a phrase left unfinished, as if he did not want to think about what would have happened without that hope.

David speaks in a psalm of confidence, surrounded by enemies, false witnesses and cruel people. Earlier he asks for guidance and protection. Afterward he encourages himself to wait. We do not know exactly when in his life he wrote it, but it is clear that he was under real pressure.

For today: when everything feels heavy, remember how God has been good to you before. Write down three examples and go over them when you feel tired. That concrete hope can sustain you while you wait.
exp.110:6:
What it says: The psalmist affirms that everything God does is true and just. The word "judgment" here refers to justice, to what is right. And "faithful" means dependable: all his commandments are sure, and they can be trusted and obeyed without fear that they will fail.

Context: This psalm is a song of praise, and we do not know with certainty who wrote it. The speaker invites people to give thanks to God for what he did for his people Israel: he sustained them, remembered his covenant, and gave them a land. The following verses show that these works and commandments are firm forever.

For today: When you doubt what God asks of you, remember that he has been faithful in everything he has done. You can trust his ways even when you do not fully understand them, and obey him with the assurance that his word will not let you down.
exp.7:7:
This verse closes the list of creatures that God placed under human care. It speaks of the birds of the air, the fish of the sea, and whatever passes through the paths of the seas, that is, the routes or currents of the ocean. With this, the psalmist covers the sky, the land, and the water.

The speaker is David, according to the traditional title of the psalm. He looks at creation, perhaps at night, and is amazed that God, so great, gives frail humanity a place of responsibility. That is why the psalm begins and ends by praising the name of Jehovah.

For today: take care of what God has entrusted to you, such as your home, your animals, your community, and the environment where you live. Do it with gratitude and humility, not as an absolute owner, but as someone who answers to the Creator.
exp.118:114:
The psalmist says he is asking the "evildoers," that is, people who do wrong, to depart from him. The reason is clear: he has decided to keep the commandments of his God. The phrase "depart" means to go away from him, and "keep" means to hold to and obey the commandments carefully.

The one speaking is the author of the psalm, a believer who loves God's law. In the verses before this one he says he hates vain thoughts and that God is his hiding place and his shield. No one knows for certain who wrote it. Here it seems that bad company could lead him astray, so he sets a firm boundary to stay faithful.

For today: if you want to obey God, be careful about who you associate with and what influences you let in. Saying "no" respectfully to whatever pulls you away from God is not pride, it is wisdom. Ask God for the strength to stand firm.
exp.2:6:
David asks God to act: "Arise" and "save me." This is the language of prayer, asking God to step in. Then he recalls that God has already defeated the enemies. "Thou hast smitten upon the cheek bone" means striking the jaw, and "thou hast broken the teeth" shows that God took away the power of the wicked, like an animal that can no longer bite.

The title of the psalm places it when David was fleeing from his son Absalom. He was surrounded by people who attacked him and mocked him. Even so, he prays with confidence. Some think the past tense speaks of earlier victories; others think it expresses a faith so certain that it sees the help as already done.

When you face a situation that is bigger than you, pray sincerely and ask God for help. Remember how He has cared for you before. That memory will give you the calm to rest, even if the problem has not yet ended.
exp.19:4:
It says that the people will rejoice in the victory God gives to the king. It also says they will set up their banners in the name of God, and they ask that the Lord fulfil all the king's petitions.

This psalm is a prayer of the people for their king before he goes into battle. The speakers are the Israelites, who support their leader and trust that God will hear him. The verses that follow say that some trust in chariots and horses, but they trust in the name of the Lord. Many see it as a psalm that also points to the Messiah, though this is understood in different ways.

Today we can pray with that same attitude for our leaders, our families, and our brothers and sisters who face trials. Before trusting only in our own resources, let us support others with prayer and joy, believing that God can give the victory.
exp.54:7:
The explanation says that the psalmist would hurry to escape from the strong wind and the storm. The words "hasten" and "escape" in the verse are used to describe this rush to get away. The stormy wind and the tempest are an image of troubles that strike him and wear him down.

The psalm is attributed to David, although the text does not say at what exact moment he wrote it. It speaks with pain because he suffers betrayal and violence in the city, and so he longs to fly like a dove to the wilderness, far from everything. Some connect it with the rebellion of Absalom, but that is an interpretation, not something the psalm states.

It is natural to want to flee when everything becomes heavy. God is not troubled by your weariness; the psalm itself invites you to bring it to prayer. Rest, ask for help, and leave your burden with Him (v. 22).
exp.88:1:
The explanation says that the psalmist is convinced that God's faithful love (the "mercy") will keep being built up and will last forever, like a firm structure. And that God's faithfulness ("your truth") is as certain as the heavens themselves. "You will establish" means that God upholds it and confirms it there, where nothing can move it.

Ethan the Ezrahite speaks, the author of this maskil, that is, a psalm meant to instruct. He sings of God's faithfulness to the covenant with David, which is mentioned in the verses that follow. Later the psalm shows that this promise seemed to be shaking, but he holds fast to what God said.

For today: when your circumstances change, remember that God's love does not depend on them. Today, write down one of God's promises and repeat it in prayer, trusting that He is faithful.
exp.12:2:
David asks here that God would look at him and answer him. "Lighten my eyes" means giving him light, strength and hope, the way someone is lifted up out of exhaustion. The phrase about not sleeping the sleep of death speaks of not falling into death; it may refer to a real danger, or to a discouragement so deep that it seems to bring life to an end.

David wrote this psalm in a time of distress. He feels forgotten by God, filled with anxiety, and surrounded by enemies who boast over him. We do not know exactly what moment of his life this was, and scholars interpret it in different ways. But we see that he prays with sincerity, and he ends by trusting in God's mercy.

For today: when you feel without strength or without answers, do not hide your pain. Speak to God honestly, ask him for light to see your situation with hope, and remember his past faithfulness.
exp.118:96:
This verse is an expression of deep love. The psalmist says that he loves God's law, that is, His teachings and commands. The word "Mem" is the name of a Hebrew letter with which this section of the psalm begins. (Rewritten per instructions: the Hebrew-letter sentence refers to a word not in the verse, so it is deleted.)

The speaker is the author of Psalm 119, whose name is not stated with certainty. He speaks as someone who faces enemies who want to harm him. Even so, he does not rely on his own cleverness, but on the word of God, which gives him wisdom and firmness. His love for the law comes from what he has already lived through with it.

For today: set aside a few minutes in the morning to read a brief verse, and repeat it during the day, at work, on the road, or at home. In this way its message will stay with you in your decisions and worries.
exp.45:2:
It says the waters of the sea will roar and churn with great force, and that even the mountains will tremble because of their violence. "Roar" means they will make a loud, thundering noise, like a growl. "Churn" means they will stir up and become muddied. "Fury" means wild rage or untamed force. "Selah" is a pause or a musical marking; its exact meaning is not known for certain.

It is a psalm of the sons of Korah, temple singers, addressed to the chief musician. The author uses images of a natural disaster, with an angry sea and shaking mountains, to say that even if everything trembles, God remains a refuge and a strength. Then it speaks of the city of God, where calm reigns because He is in the midst of it.

When your life feels like a restless sea, pause, as the Selah invites, and remember that God is still with you. Tell Him your fear in prayer, holding nothing back.
exp.105:17:
It says that a fire was kindled among the rebellious group, and that the flame consumed the wicked. The word "company" in this verse refers to the group or gathering of people who joined together in opposition. Those described as "the wicked" are people who live without reverence for God. The verse recalls a real judgment upon those who rose up against his authority.

The psalmist reviews the history of Israel in order to confess the sins of the people and to praise the patience of God. This verse alludes to the rebellion of Dathan, Abiram, and their followers against Moses and Aaron (Numbers 16). There, a fire from God consumed 250 men who were offering incense. The psalm does not excuse the people; it shows how serious it is to challenge what God has established.

Today it invites us to examine the heart when we criticize those who serve or lead. It is not forbidden to voice an opinion or to correct with respect, but it is wrong to complain with pride or envy. Let us ask God for humility, and remember that he is just and patient.
exp.140:4:
The psalmist says that if a righteous person strikes him or corrects him, he will receive it as a kindness, like a fine oil that does not hurt the head. He also says that his prayer will keep rising for them in their calamities. Here, "smite" and "reprove" mean correcting with firmness. The end of the verse is difficult, and translators understand it in several ways.

David speaks, according to the title of the psalm. He has just asked God to guard his mouth and his heart from evil, and not to let him share in the pleasures of the wicked. For this reason he prefers the correction of a righteous person to the flattery of the wicked.

For today: seek out wise and faithful people who speak truth to you, and receive their corrections without becoming defensive. A rebuke given in love heals more than it seems, and empty flattery ends up doing harm.
exp.48:14:
It says that, unlike those who trust in their riches and end up in the grave like sheep, the psalmist trusts that God will rescue his life from the power of the grave. "But" is the plain word here, and "grave" translates the Hebrew word Sheol, the place of the dead. "Receive me" suggests that God will take him in or carry him along with Him. "Selah" is probably a pause for reflection, though its exact meaning is not certain.

The speaker is a wise man, a son of Korah, who reflects on why we should not envy the rich who trust in their money. No amount of money can buy eternal life. Scholars disagree about how much detail the author had about life after death, but he expresses a firm hope in God.

Today, when we feel envy or pressure to have more, let us remember that what is secure is not what we accumulate, but our relationship with God. Let us trust Him with our future.
exp.118:56:
This verse says that the psalmist decides that the most valuable thing in his life will be to obey God's word. "Cheth" is the name of the eighth letter of the Hebrew alphabet, with which each verse of this section begins. "Portion" means an inheritance, or what one receives as one's own share. "Keep" means to watch over and to fulfill.

The speaker is the author of Psalm 119, whose name is not known for certain. Here he speaks to God with sincerity. In the verses around it, he tells how he remembers God at night, seeks him with all his heart, and asks for mercy. He also examines his way and returns to God's commands. It is a decision made out of trust in God.

For today: before you begin the day, tell God in your own words that you want his word to be your treasure. Choose a teaching from the Bible and put into practice today one concrete action that obeys it.
exp.103:17:
This verse says that God made the high mountains as a home for the wild goats, and that the rocks serve as a refuge for the rock badgers. The hiding places and caves where the animals find shelter are the refuge in view here. As for the word translated "rock badgers," the original Hebrew refers to a small rock-dwelling animal, the hyrax, which some versions render differently. This is a translation point that is debated.

The psalm does not say who wrote it. It is a song of praise to God as Creator. The psalmist surveys creation and pauses at each creature, showing that God provided a fitting place for every one of them, from the trees and the birds to the animals of the rocks.

For today: if God cares for the smallest and most hidden animals, He also cares for you. You can trust that He knows where you need shelter, and you can give thanks for the places of rest He has given you.
exp.88:2:
Here God speaks and says that he made a covenant, that is, a solemn promise, with his "chosen one," who is David. "Swore" means that he bound himself by an oath. "Servant" indicates someone who serves him and belongs to him. What God promised is presented in the following verse.

The psalm is a maskil (a teaching song) by Ethan the Ezrahite. He celebrates God's faithfulness and recalls the promise made to David that his family and his throne would continue. Here Ethan quotes God's words to support his praise. Later the psalm shows tension, since reality seemed to contradict that promise, but it begins by affirming that God is faithful.

For today: when your circumstances make you doubt, remember what God has already promised and fulfilled. Praise him for his faithfulness, and trust that his word stands firm even when you cannot yet see everything.
exp.118:10:
The psalmist says he has kept God's words deep within his heart. The "sayings" are the words or teachings that God has spoken. "Keep" here means to treasure, like someone who hides something of great value. And he does it with a purpose: so that he would not sin against God.

Psalm 119 is a long poem in honor of God's law, and no one knows for certain who wrote it. The speaker seems to be a sincere believer, perhaps young, since the verse before asks how a young man can keep his way pure. The answer is to obey God's word, and this verse shows how: by carrying it within the heart.

For today: spend a few minutes each day memorizing one verse and repeat it throughout the day. When temptation or a difficult decision comes, that stored word can remind you what pleases God and help you choose well.
exp.17:7:
This verse describes God with images of fire and smoke, as if he were a warrior in great anger. The human-style phrases about his nose and mouth show his anger in a way we can picture. The fire here is one that destroys everything it touches. The glowing coals show intense heat, like embers burning.

David speaks in a psalm of thanksgiving for having been rescued from his enemies, among them Saul (as the psalm's heading indicates). He uses poetic and figurative language to say that God heard his cry and acted with power. It is not a literal description, but a way of expressing how real God's intervention was.

For today: when you feel trapped by distress, cry out to God with confidence. He sees injustice, he cares for you, and he is not indifferent to your pain.
exp.106:16:
This verse says that some foolish people suffered because they had followed a path of rebellion and because of their wickedness. The word "fools" refers to those who act without wisdom, ignoring God. "Afflicted" means that they went through pain and suffering as a consequence of their choices.

This psalm is a song of thanksgiving that invites all those rescued by God to give him thanks. Here the psalmist describes a group that, because of their own rebellion, fell into sickness and distress. The verses that follow show that, even so, when they cried out to the Lord, he saved them. Notice that the Bible does not say that every suffering is a punishment; here it speaks of a specific case.

Today it reminds us that our decisions have consequences. But there is also hope: if we recognize our error and cry out to God with sincerity, he is merciful and willing to rescue us.
exp.1:5:
It says that God himself has set his king in Zion, the mountain where he dwells and which is holy to him. "Yet" marks a contrast here: the nations rebel, but God answers with a firm decision. The phrase "my holiness" speaks of something set apart for God.

The one speaking here is God, who answers the kings of the earth who conspire against him. Zion was Jerusalem, the city of David. Israelites read it as the promise of a king from David's line. Christians also see it fulfilled in Jesus, and the New Testament quotes this psalm in that sense. The verses that follow speak of the Son and his inheritance.

For today: when the world seems to be drifting or set against God, you can rest in the knowledge that he still reigns. Entrust your fears to his king, Jesus, and not to human powers.
exp.17:20:
He says that David has followed and obeyed God's instructions. "Kept the ways" means living according to what God teaches. "Wickedly" means with evil intent, turning his back on God on purpose. He affirms that he did not turn away from his God in that way.

David speaks in a psalm of gratitude, after God rescued him from his enemies, including Saul, according to the psalm's heading. He does not claim to be perfect, since the Bible shows that he also failed. He speaks of his general loyalty to God, in contrast with those who pursued him without cause. Some readers see here a defense of his innocence against those accusations.

Today we can seek a life faithful to God, without boasting or pretending to be perfect. When we fail, let us return to Him with humility, trusting in His mercy, and keep walking with Him each day.
exp.37:10:
The explanation says that the people closest to the psalmist pulled away when he was suffering most. Here, "sore" means the wound, sickness, or affliction that marked him. "Lovers" are those who walked with him, and "friends" are his relatives or neighbors. All of them kept their distance.

The psalm is spoken by David, according to its title. He is ill, anguished, and feels guilt for his sin. He prays to God with sincerity, and he also suffers because his enemies take advantage of his weakness. His pain is physical, emotional, and also the pain of loneliness. Scholars do not agree on exactly what his illness was.

If today you feel abandoned in a trial, tell God everything, as David did. And if you know someone who is suffering, do not pull away: call them, visit them, or stand with them patiently and without judgment.
exp.102:16:
It says that God's faithful love, his mercy, has no beginning and no end: it goes "from everlasting to everlasting," that is, from forever and to forever. It rests on "those who fear him," which means those who respect and revere him with love. His righteousness, or his faithfulness to what is right and to his promises, reaches to "children's children," that is, to grandchildren.

David speaks in a psalm of praise. Just before, he says that human life is brief, like grass that the wind carries away. By contrast, God's love endures. The verses that follow make clear that this blessing is for those who keep his covenant and obey his commandments.

For today: even though our life is short and fragile, we can trust in a God who does not change. Live with reverence toward him, and teach your children and grandchildren by your example to trust in his mercy.
exp.134:0:
This verse begins with "Praise ye the Lord," a call to give praise to God. The psalmist then repeats the invitation: praise the name of the Lord, which is God's personal name. He addresses the servants of the Lord, that is, those who belong to him and serve him.

The psalm does not say who wrote it. It is a call to praise addressed to those who serve in the temple, as the following verses show, where he speaks to those who stand in the house of the Lord. Some think it was used in the public worship of Israel, but the text does not state this with certainty.

Today, praise is not only for special moments. If you consider yourself a servant of God, begin the day thanking him in your own words, remembering who he is and what he has done for you.
exp.143:7:
The explanation says that David's enemies speak empty and false things. The word "vanity" here means words without worth or truth. Their right hand, which should confirm their word, also lies: neither their word nor their oath can be trusted.

David, the king, speaks while asking God to rescue him from strangers, that is, foreigners or disloyal people. He calls them "great waters," an image of danger that overwhelms. His complaint is that these enemies are deceivers. After the cry for help, David promises to sing a new song to God, who has delivered him before.

For today: do not let yourself be intimidated by false words or empty promises. Put your trust in God, who is faithful. And make sure your own word is sincere: let your "yes" be yes.
exp.75:7:
This verse says that God caused his judgment to be heard from heaven. It is as if his voice of authority reached the whole earth, and the people responded with fear and fell silent, still, unable to move or speak. Here "still" means quiet, frozen in amazement.

The psalmist, a writer from Israel (the title attributes the psalm to Asaph), sings of God as the God of Jacob, who defends his people. The verses before it speak of armies halted by his rebuke, and the verses after it explain the purpose: God rises to judge in order to save the meek, that is, the humble and oppressed. It is often connected with a deliverance of Jerusalem, though which one is not known for certain.

For today: when you feel that injustice or the powerful have the last word, remember that God sees and judges with justice. Rest in him and live with humility.
exp.57:5:
David asks God to stop some wicked men. He compares them to young lions who tear others apart. Asking God to break their teeth and jaw teeth is asking him to take away their power to do harm. "Young lions" are strong and dangerous. Breaking means smashing or shattering.

The psalmist, traditionally David, speaks in a psalm of complaint against unjust judges or rulers (Psalms 58:1-2). Earlier he describes them as poisonous snakes that refuse to listen. It is poetic and forceful language, the prayer of someone who suffers injustice and leaves the matter in God's hands rather than seeking revenge himself.

For today: when you are hurt by the injustice or wickedness of others, bring your pain honestly to God. Ask him to stop the evil and bring justice, and trust that he will do it in his own time, without taking revenge yourself.
exp.21:15:
The psalmist says that cruel enemies surround him, like a pack of wild dogs, a gang of wicked people who have him cornered. "Pierced" means "bored through" or "run through." It speaks of wounded hands and feet. It should be noted that the Hebrew of this phrase is difficult, and some older and modern translations render it in another way, as "like a lion are my hands and my feet."

It is a psalm of David, written in a moment of extreme anguish, feeling abandoned by God. Christians have seen in this psalm a prophecy of the cross of Jesus, who quoted its first verse while he was being crucified. The verses that follow, about dividing up his garments, the Gospels connect with his crucifixion.

When you feel that everyone is against you and God seems far away, do as the psalmist did: tell God honestly what you feel. He can hear your pain without becoming angry.
exp.106:28:
He turns the storm into stillness. The source word meaning calm and tranquility is not available to the reader, so I'll render it directly. "Waves" are the waves of the sea, and "are still" means they settle down and grow quiet. It is not people who master the storm, but God, with his word and his power.

The psalmist speaks to the whole people redeemed by God. He describes sailors who, in the middle of a tempest, lose all their skill and cry out to the LORD. It is one of several scenes in the psalm, in which different people in danger are rescued. Many see here an image of the troubles of life in general, although the text speaks of a real storm at sea.

When you feel that your life is in a storm and you no longer know what to do, cry out to God with sincerity. He can give peace in the middle of the trial or calm the situation itself. Afterward, do not forget to give him thanks.
exp.65:15:
This verse is an invitation. The psalmist calls all who reverence and honor God to come and listen to what God has done for his soul, that is, for his innermost life. The verse is a call to gather and hear. The sentence explaining the old wording is removed because the verse itself uses the modern words "come" and "hear."

The speaker is the psalmist, who gives thanks after a time of distress. He had promised offerings to God if God helped him, and now he fulfills those promises. Scholars debate whether the speaker is an individual or the whole people, but here he speaks in the first person. He wants to tell how God answered him when he cried out.

For today: when God helps you through a difficulty, do not keep it secret. Simply tell other believers what God has done in you. Your testimony can encourage them and strengthen their faith.
exp.68:25:
They persecute the one whom you yourself have struck down, and they gossip about the pain of the one you have wounded, either mocking it or making it worse. The word "wounded" here means that you were the one who caused the injury. The word "gossip" in this verse is best understood as talking or commenting.

The one speaking is the psalmist, traditionally David, who is suffering greatly and crying out to God. He feels that his enemies take advantage of his fall and use it as an excuse to attack him even more. This is an imprecatory psalm, a prayer asking for justice. Some believe that "the one you struck down" is the psalmist himself; others see in it an image of the righteous sufferer, and the New Testament quotes other parts of this psalm in connection with Jesus.

Today, if someone is going through a hard time, do not add to their pain with gossip or cruelty. And if you are the one who is hurting, bring your anger and your pain to God in prayer, and leave justice in his hands.
exp.67:3:
This verse is an invitation to sing. Sing praises to his name means praising God with songs. To exalt means to honor him and lift him high above everything. The one who rides upon the heavens describes God as King over all creation. JAH is a short form of God's name, the LORD. And rejoice before him means to delight in his presence.

The psalm is attributed to David in its title, although some scholars debate how it was composed. Earlier, the psalm says that the wicked vanish like smoke and wax, while the righteous rejoice. Afterward, it shows why we should praise him: God cares for the fatherless and the widows, gives a home to the lonely, and sets prisoners free.

For today: when you are tired or worried, sing or listen to a song of praise and remember one concrete thing God has done in your life. Praising him does not ignore the problem; it reminds you who is greater than it.
exp.36:2:
This verse invites us to trust God and to do good. To "wait on the Lord" means to place your trust in the Lord, even when things are not yet clear. The promise is that the one who does this will "dwell in the land" in security, and "verily will be fed." That last phrase can be understood as being sustained, or also as enjoying the faithfulness of God. There are several possible translations.

David writes this psalm in his old age to encourage those who see the wicked prospering and feel tempted toward impatience or envy. Earlier he says that these evildoers will wither like the grass. Then he invites the reader to delight in God and to commit their way to him. "The land" refers especially to the land promised to Israel.

For today: when it bothers you to see others doing well by cheating, do not compare yourself to them. Choose one good and honest action today, and calmly entrust the outcome to God.
exp.69:4:
Here the psalmist says he is "afflicted," that is, suffering, and "needy," that is, in want and without resources. He asks God to hurry and come to him. He calls God "my help" and "my deliverer," and pleads: "make no tarrying," that is, do not delay.

The psalm is traditionally ascribed to David. It is a short, urgent prayer, very similar to the ending of Psalm 40. David is surrounded by enemies who mock him with cries of "Aha! Aha!" Earlier he asked that those who seek God would rejoice, and now he returns to his own need. The exact details of the situation are not known.

For today: when you feel without strength, do not wait until you have the perfect words. You can pray with sincerity, as David did: "Lord, I am in need, come quickly." Acknowledging your need before God is an act of trust, not of weakness.
exp.47:7:
This verse says that the people of Jerusalem had not only heard about the works of God, but now saw them with their own eyes. The city belongs to the Lord of hosts, which means the Lord of the powers of heaven. The verse's last word about making the city secure means that God will keep it firm. Selah probably was a pause for meditation, though its exact meaning is not certain.

This is a song of the sons of Korah, perhaps sung by the people gathered in the temple. Earlier, enemy kings were terrified before Zion and fled. Now the people acknowledge that what their ancestors told about God's protection was true. Scholars debate exactly which event is being remembered.

Today, do not live only on what others tell you about God. Write down the times He has sustained you and return to them when fear comes. Your faith grows when you remember and trust.
exp.34:7:
This verse asks that ruin come suddenly upon the enemy, before he expects it. The word "destruction" here means ruin or disaster. The net he hid to catch others would be the one that catches him, and he would fall into the very disaster he had prepared for someone else.

David speaks in this psalm, according to its heading. He is pursued by people who set traps for him without cause. He cries out to God for justice. This is the language of intense prayer, typical of Hebrew poetry, and not a personal desire for revenge. Many understand it as a request that God set right the wrong done.

For today: when you are treated unjustly, bring your pain to God in sincere prayer and do not take vengeance into your own hands. Trust that He sees and brings about justice, and let your heart, like David's, end up rejoicing in Him.
exp.147:2:
This verse invites the sun, the moon, and all the bright stars to praise God. The word "Praise" here is an older way of saying "give praise," and "stars of light" means stars that shine. It is poetry: the created world is addressed as if it could sing.

The psalm does not say who wrote it. It is a song of praise that calls all creation to honor God, beginning with the angels and then moving on to the heavenly bodies. The reason follows right after: God commanded, and everything was created. Here the sun and the moon are not gods, as other peoples worshiped them, but creatures that give glory to their Creator.

Today, when you see the sun, the moon, or the stars, take a moment to thank God. May the beauty of creation lead you to praise the Creator and to remember that your life is in his hands.
exp.16:7:
Here David asks God to guard him as one guards what is most delicate and precious. The part of the eye that we all protect by instinct is the pupil. The image of a bird spreading its wings over its chicks to give them shelter is what the second phrase is meant to evoke.

David speaks this prayer in the midst of a threat. He is surrounded by proud enemies who oppress him and seek to take his life. That is why he draws near to God with confidence, sure that He hears him. Scholars do not agree on the exact moment in David's life when he wrote it.

For today: when you feel fear or pressure, you do not have to face it alone. Pray with sincerity and ask God for His care. You can rest knowing that you are precious to Him, even when your situation looks difficult.
exp.93:22:
It says that God will make the evil of the wicked fall back upon themselves. The phrase "make it return" means "bring it back," and the injustice they commit is the wrong they do. The word meaning "cut down," as one cuts down a tree, means that God will eliminate them. Their own wickedness will be the cause of their fall.

The psalmist, whose identity we cannot know for certain, cries out to God in the face of oppression. The preceding verses speak of powerful people who gang up against the righteous and condemn the innocent. But he trusts that God is his refuge and his rock. This verse closes the psalm with the hope that God will do justice in his time.

When you suffer an injustice, you do not have to take revenge. You can entrust your case to God, pray sincerely, and keep doing good. He sees everything and is a secure refuge. Trusting does not mean becoming passive, but resting in the knowledge that final justice belongs to Him.
exp.80:4:
God established this feast as a testimony, a sign, for the people of Joseph, that is, Israel, when they went out through the land of Egypt. "Established" is the word the verse uses for "ordained," meaning appointed or set in place. The last sentence says that a language was heard that was not understood.

The psalm invites us to celebrate a feast with trumpets. The one speaking seems to be God, through a psalmist. It recalls the departure from Egypt. The phrase about "a language that I understood not" is interpreted in several ways: it may refer to the foreign language of the Egyptians, which Israel heard during their slavery, or to another idea that is not entirely clear.

Today: God wants us to remember with gratitude how he has delivered us. Once a week, write down something specific that God has done for you, and give him thanks for it.
exp.67:29:
The verse asks God to restrain the violent peoples. "Rebuke" means to hold back or check, and "the company of spearmen" refers to a crowd of soldiers. The "bulls" and "calves" are usually understood as powerful leaders and their followers, though some scholars interpret them differently. The phrase "with pieces of silver" may refer to tribute or an offering; the Hebrew text is difficult and is translated in several ways. In the end, God scatters those who delight in war.

The psalm is attributed to David, a song of victory that celebrates God as the defender of his people. Here the prayer is that, by the temple in Jerusalem, even hostile nations would submit and bring offerings. What follows shows Egypt and Ethiopia drawing near to God.

For today: when violence or injustice overwhelm you, pray for peace, trusting that God rules over all human power, and seek to be an instrument of peace yourself.
exp.90:6:
It says that even though many people may fall around you, a thousand at one side and ten thousand at the other, the danger will not reach you. The verse uses the wording of an older form of the text, so the reader should simply hold the verse as it appears above.

The psalm does not say who wrote it. It speaks of someone who trusts in God as their refuge, and it assures them that God protects them from dangers by day and by night, such as wars or plagues. The verses that follow say that this person will see the punishment of the wicked. It is poetry: it uses large numbers to show God's protection, not to promise that a believer will never suffer.

Today we can rest in God when there is frightening news or crisis. Trusting in Him does not remove every problem, but it gives us peace and the assurance that He cares for us. Pray and hand over your fears to Him each day.
exp.100:2:
Here it says he will set nothing wicked or evil before his eyes, that is, he will not look upon it with pleasure or take it as a goal. He rejects the conduct of those who turn aside, that is, those who leave the right path. The word "cleave" in the verse is an older way of saying "to stick to" or "to be drawn close." He does not want to be influenced by them.

David is the speaker, according to the title of the psalm. It is a kind of promise of how he wants to rule and live. Earlier he said he would walk with integrity within his house, and then he adds that he will not tolerate the wicked person or the slanderer. Scholars often see here a king's commitment to keep his household and his court clean, although we do not know with certainty at what point in his life he wrote it.

Today we can think about what we let in through our eyes: screens, networks, entertainment. We can calmly decide which things we will not look at or follow, and choose friendships that draw us closer to doing good.
exp.89:1:
It says that God existed before the mountains were born and before he formed the earth and the world. "From everlasting to everlasting" is an older way of saying "from forever and to forever," or "from eternity to eternity." God had no beginning and will have no end.

The title of the psalm attributes it to Moses, the man of God. Many read it as a prayer that contrasts God's eternity with human frailty. The verses that follow speak of man returning to dust and of a thousand years being to God like yesterday. His eternity is the reason he is a refuge for his people in all generations.

When life feels uncertain or fleeting, remember that you rest in someone who does not change and does not come to an end. Today, give God one specific worry and trust that he was already there before it and will still be there after it.
exp.135:16:
This verse says that God defeated powerful kings. "Smote" means that he struck them down and overcame them. "Mercy" here translates a Hebrew word that speaks of faithful love, a kindness that does not break. Each line of the psalm repeats that this love endures forever.

The psalm is a praise song sung by the people of Israel, probably in worship. It is not known for certain who wrote it. It recalls how God brought them out of Egypt, guided them through the wilderness, and gave them the land. The kings mentioned afterward, Sihon and Og, are understood as enemies who blocked their way. The people see those victories as signs of God's love toward them.

For today: when you face something that seems too big, remember how God has sustained you before. Write down three moments when he helped you, and thank him today, trusting that his love does not change.
exp.139:2:
They say the enemies of the psalmist have sharpened their tongues the way a serpent does, and that under their lips there is the poison of a viper. "Sharpened" means made sharp or given a point. The "asp" is a poisonous snake. "Selah" is a musical term or a marker for a pause, whose exact meaning is not known for certain; it is usually understood as an invitation to stop and reflect.

David speaks here, according to the heading of the psalm. He is asking God to deliver him from violent people who plan evil and stir up quarrels every day. In this verse he describes that their main weapon is words: slander, deceit, and lies that wound like a bite.

For today: words can wound or heal. When someone hurts you with their tongue, take your pain to God in prayer instead of answering in kind. And examine your own mouth as well, so that it speaks truth and kindness.
exp.15:6:
David says he will bless, that is, praise and give thanks to God, because God guides him with his counsel. "Reins" is an old way of speaking of the innermost part of a person, such as deep thoughts and feelings. Thus, even at night, in quiet, God instructs him from within.

In this psalm David speaks in confidence. He has just said that God is his inheritance and his greatest treasure. So, grateful, he recognizes that God also directs him. The verses that follow show the result: keeping God always before him, not being shaken, and living with joy and security. Some believe that "the night seasons" refers to times of calm reflection, although the text gives no further details.

Today, before going to sleep, you can set aside a few minutes to pray and to think on God's Word. In that silence, ask him to counsel you and thank him for his guidance.
exp.77:22:
This verse says that God gave a command to the clouds and opened the doors of heaven, as if the sky had windows or gates. Here the language is poetic, meaning that God acted from on high to care for his people.

The speaker here is the psalmist, called Asaph, who reviews the history of Israel in the wilderness. The people did not trust God or his salvation, which here means rescue. Even so, God provided manna, a food that fell from heaven. The following verse shows that, despite their lack of faith, God was generous.

For today: when you doubt that God will care for you, remember his past faithfulness. You can ask him for help with sincerity and thank him for what he has already given you, even if at times you have doubted.
exp.75:5:
He says that when God, the God of Jacob, rebuked the enemies, their war chariots and horses were brought to a standstill. "Rebuke" is a firm command that carries authority. The verse's wording on the horses and chariots means they were left unable to move or fight. Some translations say they were put into a dead sleep, or left stunned.

The psalm is attributed to Asaph, a temple singer. It celebrates a victory God won on behalf of Jerusalem (Zion). Many think of the defeat of the Assyrian army, but the psalm does not say so with certainty. The surrounding verses show warriors stripped of their strength and defeated, and the whole earth fearing God's judgment.

For today: when you face something that seems stronger than you, remember that no human force is greater than the word of God. Pray with confidence, do what is yours to do, and rest in the knowledge that he cares for his own.
exp.79:8:
It says that God prepared the ground for the vine he had brought out of Egypt. The phrase about clearing the way means that he removed the obstacles and made room for it. The phrase about causing its roots to take hold means that he made it send down deep roots, so the vine grew and filled the land. The vine represents the people of Israel.

It is a prayer by the psalmist Asaph, on behalf of the whole people. It remembers with gratitude what God did in bringing Israel out of Egypt and giving them the promised land. But it does so in a time of sorrow, for later it asks why God allowed the vine to be destroyed. Remembering the past gives it a foundation for asking for help.

For today: when you go through a difficult season, remember how God has cared for you before. That memory nourishes hope and encourages you to pray with confidence, asking him to make his face shine upon you again.
exp.6:16:
This verse says that the psalmist promises to give thanks and praise to God for his righteousness. The word "praise" here means to give glory, and the phrase "according to his righteousness" means in keeping with how just God is. "Will sing praise to the name" means singing to God himself, whom the psalmist presents as "the Most High," the one who is above all.

The psalm is attributed to David in its heading, although it mentions a man named Cush, and it is not known with certainty who he was. David asks God to deliver him from those who pursue him. The verses before this one show the wicked man falling into his own trap. Seeing that God judges with justice, David ends the psalm with praise.

For today: when you feel that something is unfair, do not stop at complaining. Hand the matter over to God, trust that he sees and judges rightly, and give him thanks today with a prayer or a song.
exp.26:1:
It says that when the wicked, those who troubled him, and his enemies came near to devour him, they themselves stumbled and fell. "Came near" is the sense of the verse's wording "came upon me." The phrase "to eat up my flesh" is an image of fierce attack, like wild beasts wanting to tear apart their prey. "Troublers" are those who cause distress.

David speaks, and he does so from the confidence he expresses at the beginning of the psalm: the LORD is his light and his strength. Here he recalls past experiences in which his adversaries attacked him and did not manage to overcome him. Scholars do not agree on the exact moment in his life when he wrote it, so it is not wise to claim a specific episode.

For today: when you face opposition or fear, remember the times God sustained you. Recalling his past faithfulness strengthens your trust for what lies ahead, without needing to think that everything will be easy.
exp.144:5:
This verse says that people will speak of the awe-inspiring power of God, and that the psalmist himself will tell how great he is. The word "terror" in the verse refers to something that causes fear and respect because of its strength, and the "mighty acts" are the powerful deeds of God. To "tell" means to relate or recount, to tell again.

The psalm is traditionally attributed to David, though some scholars debate how it was composed. The one speaking is a worshiper who praises God and joins a chorus that passes from generation to generation. After this verse, the praise moves toward God's goodness, justice, and mercy.

Today we can do the same: tell simply, to a child, a friend, or a coworker, something concrete that God has done in our lives. Our testimony can strengthen the faith of others.
exp.36:32:
This verse speaks of the righteous person, the one who has God's law in his heart. It says that the Lord will not leave him in the hand of the wicked man who lies in wait for him. And if they bring him to trial, God will not allow him to be condemned unjustly.

The psalm is by David, and he writes it as counsel for someone who is distressed to see the wicked seem to prosper. In this passage, the wicked man watches the righteous and seeks to kill him, but David affirms that God cares for his own. Some understand that this protection is fully fulfilled in God's time, not always immediately.

For today: if you face injustice, do not respond with revenge or with fear. Keep obeying God, pray, and trust that he knows your situation and will defend you in his time.
exp.70:4:
This verse says that God is the hope of the one speaking, and that from his youth he has trusted in Him. The word "trust" here means firm confidence, something a person leans on without fear. "Lord God" is the name of God, and "Lord" presents Him as the master and guide of his life.

The speaker is an older believer, since later he asks that God not abandon him in old age. The psalm does not say who wrote it. Some connect it with David, but this is not certain. He is surrounded by enemies, and so he prays to God as a rock and a fortress where he can hide. He remembers that God has cared for him all his life.

For today: when difficulty comes, remember how God has sustained you before. That memory feeds your trust and encourages you to keep praying with hope.
exp.26:7:
The psalmist says that his heart heard an invitation from God: "Seek ye my face." He answers: "Thy face, Lord, will I seek." The phrase "my face" refers to God's presence, to being near Him.

The psalm is traditionally attributed to David. It speaks in the midst of enemies and dangers, yet it trusts in God. Right after this, it asks that God not hide His face from him. His desire to seek God comes from both need and trust. Some understand that the heart is repeating what God says to him inwardly; others, that it is David's own longing.

Today, when you are afraid or under pressure, do not look first for solutions: seek God. Set aside a few minutes to pray and to read the Bible, and answer His invitation in your own words.
exp.33:0:
The verse begins with a note about the occasion when David wrote this psalm: when he pretended to be mad before Abimelech, and Abimelech drove him away, and he left. "He changed his behaviour" means that he altered his conduct and his appearance. Then David says: "I will bless the Lord at all times", that is, I will praise him always, and his praise shall continually be in my mouth.

David speaks after escaping a great danger. He was fleeing from King Saul and reached Philistine territory, where he was afraid and pretended to be mad to save himself (1 Samuel 21). Abimelech appears to be another name or title for King Achish. Even so, David acknowledges that God delivered him, and he resolves to praise him.

Today we can choose to thank God not only when everything goes well, but also after getting through moments of fear or failure. A good step is to write down one thing each day for which to give thanks.
exp.46:6:
This verse says that God is not king of one people only, but of the whole earth. For that reason it invites us to sing to him "with understanding." The original word (maskil) can mean singing with understanding, or it has also been taken to mean a psalm meant to instruct. Scholars explain it in both ways.

Psalm 47 is a song of praise, probably for the people of Israel in their worship. It speaks of God going up to his throne amid shouts and trumpets. We do not know with certainty the exact occasion on which it was used. The verses that follow show that even foreign nations join themselves to the God of Abraham.

Today we can sing or praise God without doing so out of habit or passing emotion. Before singing, think about what the words say. Ask yourself: do I believe this? Do I recognize God as King of my life? In this way our praise will be sincere and thoughtful.
exp.118:142:
This verse says that the psalmist went through times of suffering and great pressure. "Affliction" means trouble or hardship, and "anguish" is a tightness that squeezes the heart. He says these things "have taken hold on me," as if they reached him without his looking for them. Even so, God's commandments were his delights, that is, his joy and his comfort.

The one speaking is the author of Psalm 119, a psalm in honor of God's Word. We do not know for certain who wrote it. Earlier the psalmist describes himself as small and despised, that is, little valued by others. Even so, he does not forget God's law, because he sees it as just and true.

For today: when a difficulty comes, do not leave the Bible for later. Read a passage each day, even a short one, and ask God to give you comfort and direction in the middle of your problem.
exp.37:21:
The verse says: "Make haste to help me, O Lord my salvation." The word "health" here does not speak of being well in the body, but of salvation or deliverance. It is a cry asking that God not delay in intervening.

David speaks, according to the psalm's heading, which calls it a prayer for remembrance. He is suffering greatly: he feels guilty for his sin, is sick, and is surrounded by people who repay him evil for good. He ends with this urgent plea, after asking that God not forsake him or stay far away. Scholars debate exactly what illness or situation he was living through, and the text does not make it clear.

Today, when you feel weak or misunderstood, you can pray with this same honesty. You do not need beautiful words. Say to God: "Help me quickly, you are my salvation," and trust that he hears you.
exp.72:21:
It says the psalmist recognizes his own foolishness. "Ignorant" and "I did not understand" mean that he did not have the right perspective. Comparing himself to "a beast" is a strong way of saying that he thought and reacted without wisdom, like an animal that does not reason. And he admits it "before you," that is, in God's presence.

Asaph, the author of this psalm according to its heading, speaks. He had felt envy when he saw the wicked prospering, and his heart had grown bitter. When he entered God's sanctuary, he understood their final destiny. Now he repents of his complaint. Right away he remembers that God never let go of him.

For today: when life seems unfair to you, be honest with God and admit that you do not see everything. Acknowledging your limits does not distance you from Him; it draws you closer, because He keeps holding your hand.
exp.56:5:
They say that his enemies set a trap in his path, like a net to catch animals. His soul is "abatida," that is, deeply weighed down and discouraged. They also dug a pit in front of him, but they themselves fell into it. "Selah" is a word that probably invites a pause for reflection, though its exact meaning is not known for certain.

The one speaking is David. The title of the psalm places it when he fled from Saul and hid in the cave. He is surrounded by violent people, yet in the midst of danger he praises God and asks that his glory be exalted over all the earth.

For today: when someone harms you or you feel your way is being blocked, do not hide your weariness; bring it honestly before God. Then trust that He knows how to act with justice. Like David, even with a bowed-down soul, you can choose to sing to Him and wait for the new day with faith.
exp.118:175:
It says that the author feels like a sheep that has wandered off the path. For this reason he asks God: "seek thy servant." The phrase "seek thy servant" is the one that matters here, meaning "look for me, your servant," that is, his servant. It also says that, even though he has gone astray, he has not forgotten God's commandments, that is, his instructions.

This is the last verse of Psalm 119, a long poem that praises God's Word. It is not known for certain who wrote it; tradition has attributed it to David, but the psalm does not say so. The speaker loves God's law and, even so, acknowledges his weakness. He ends with humility, not with pride.

For today: you can love God and still stumble. You do not have to hide or pretend. Speak to God with sincerity, ask him to find you, and return to his Word. Jesus also spoke of a shepherd who looks for the lost sheep (Luke 15:4).
exp.72:11:
The explanation says that the wicked, although they live without respect for God, seem to be at ease and keep increasing their riches. The phrase "without being troubled like other people" means that they have no worries or problems, or that they live in calm. The phrase "they increased in riches" means that they managed to accumulate possessions.

The one speaking is the psalmist Asaph, according to the heading of the psalm. He is confused and nearly slips in his faith when he sees that the unjust prosper, while he strives to live with integrity and suffers. Later in the same psalm, he understands things differently when he enters God's sanctuary and sees their end.

Today, when it seems unfair to you that others do well without living rightly, do not stop at what you see. Tell God your complaint honestly, as Asaph did, and trust that He sees the whole picture.
exp.88:31:
It says that if the sons of King David rebel and abandon God's law, he will correct them. "Visit" here means to come and call to account. The "rod" and the "stripes" are images of discipline, like a father who corrects his children. "Iniquities" are wickedness or serious faults.

God speaks, as the psalmist Ethan the Ezrahite recalls, and repeats the promise he made to David about his descendants. God says he will not overlook the sin of his heirs. But the punishment is not a rejection: the following verse makes clear that he will not take away his mercy or break his covenant. His correction seeks to restore, not to destroy.

For today: if God corrects you, do not take it as abandonment. Examine your path, acknowledge your fault, and return to him, trusting that his faithfulness remains firm even though you have failed.
exp.10:5:
He says that God will bring judgment upon the wicked, like someone setting traps that fall from heaven like rain. The word "snares" refers to traps or nets. "Fire and brimstone" recalls the punishment of Sodom. "An horrible tempest" refers to strong, destructive winds. "The portion of their cup" means the share each person must drink; here, their fate.

David speaks in this psalm. Some were advising him to flee from danger, but he answers that he trusts in the LORD, who reigns from heaven and sees everything. God tests the righteous, but He hates the one who loves violence. This verse shows that injustice will not have the last word.

Today, when you see evil seeming to win, do not respond with revenge or fear. Trust that God sees and judges with justice. In the meantime, seek to live uprightly, knowing that He looks on the righteous with love.
exp.103:29:
He sends out his spirit, and living things are created. Through this, God renews the face of the earth, meaning its surface or appearance. It speaks of a life that springs up again and again.

The psalmist, who is not named in this psalm, praises God as the Creator and sustainer of all things. Earlier he spoke of the animals that depend on God's hand for their food. When God withdraws his breath, they die; when he sends it, there is new life. The psalm invites us to worship God for his constant care.

Today we can look at nature and at our own lives as God's daily gift. When you feel tired or without hope, ask him to renew your strength, and thank him for the breath of each day.
exp.118:143:
The explanation says that God's testimonies, that is, his teachings and commands, are righteous forever; they do not change with the times. That is why the psalmist asks for "understanding," meaning to grasp the word of God and not merely to know it. He says "I shall live" because that understanding gives him a full life, not just the continuation of breathing.

The author of Psalm 119 is speaking, though his name is not known for certain. He writes in the middle of affliction and distress, yet still finds joy in God's commandments. This verse closes the previous section, and right after it another begins in which he cries out to God with his whole heart.

Today we can read the Bible with a simple prayer: "Lord, give me understanding." It is not enough to read in a hurry; it is good to pause, think, and ask God for help to live out what we understand, especially in difficult times.
exp.24:18:
It says that David asks God to look upon his enemies, because they are many and they hate him with a fierce cruelty. The word "hate" in the verse means to despise deeply. "Cruel hatred" refers to a hatred that seeks to do harm, not just a simple dislike.

This psalm is attributed to David, who speaks in a time of great distress. He feels alone, troubled, and surrounded by adversaries. Before this verse, he also acknowledges his sins and asks for forgiveness. Afterward, he asks that God keep him and not let him be put to shame, because he has trusted in Him. The exact details of the moment in which he wrote it are not known with certainty.

When someone rejects you or treats you badly, you are not obligated to keep your pain silent. You can tell God honestly about it, ask Him for protection, and also examine your own heart, as David did.
exp.59:11:
It says that, with God's help, his people will do brave and mighty deeds. The word for these deeds refers to acts of great courage. The explanation of the verse's second action is that to tread down means to crush someone completely, that is, to defeat them thoroughly. The one who truly defeats the enemy is God, not the people.

The psalm is attributed to David, and it is connected with a war against Edom and other nations. Israel has just suffered a defeat and feels that God has left them alone. Even so, David asks for help. He says that human help is of no use. This verse closes the psalm with a declaration of trust.

When you face a big problem, do your part with courage, but do not rely only on your own strength or resources. Ask God for help, even if you have failed or feel far from Him. He can give you the strength to keep going and overcome what seems greater than you.
exp.118:135:
He says the psalmist wept so much that it was as if rivers of water ran from his eyes. The reason is that other people were not keeping God's law. It is a poetic way of expressing deep grief.

The one speaking is the author of Psalm 119, who loves God's word and stands up for it. We do not know for certain who wrote it. He suffers because of the wickedness he sees around him and the violence of the people he mentioned earlier. His weeping is not from pride or anger, but from sadness at seeing that what God says is being despised. Right after this, he acknowledges that God is just.

Today we can ask God for a tender heart. When we see injustice or indifference toward God, instead of criticizing harshly, let us pray with compassion for those people. Let us also examine our own obedience.
exp.118:61:
This verse says that the psalmist would get up in the middle of the night to give thanks and praise to God. "At midnight" means the middle of the night. "Judgments" are God's decisions and verdicts, and "righteousness" speaks of his uprightness. He praises God because his decisions are fair and good.

The author of Psalm 119 is not named with certainty; many think of David, but it is not known. It is someone who loves the law of God. Just before this, the writer says that the wicked have "robbed" him (they despoiled him or surrounded him with evil), yet he did not forget the law. His nighttime praise shows trust in the midst of pressure.

For today: when it is hard for you to sleep or you feel under pressure, use that moment to thank God in prayer. Think of something God has done well and give him thanks, even though your situation has not yet changed.
exp.39:9:
This verse says that the psalmist did not keep secret what God is and what God does. He did not hide God's righteousness in his heart, but spoke of God's faithfulness and his salvation. To hide something means to cover it or keep it out of sight, and a large crowd gathered together is what is meant by the great assembly.

David is the speaker, according to the title of the psalm. Earlier he has given thanks for having been rescued, and he says he delights to do God's will. Here he tells that he proclaimed it in public. Afterward, however, he acknowledges that troubles and guilt surround him, and he asks that God's mercy keep him. His testimony and his need exist side by side.

For today: when God helps you or teaches you something, do not keep it to yourself. Tell it humbly to a family member, a friend, or in your church. Your sincere testimony can encourage others, even if you are still going through difficulties.
exp.36:24:
It says that David, now old, remembers that in all his life he never saw a righteous person forsaken, nor his children asking for bread in the streets. The phrase "I have been young" is the same as "I was young," and "seed" means offspring, children and grandchildren, and "begging" means asking for charity.

This psalm is written by David and is attributed to his old age. He wants to encourage the faithful who become troubled when they see the wicked doing well. The nearby verses speak of God upholding the one who falls and caring for his steps. It is a personal observation, not an absolute promise: other passages in the Bible acknowledge that at times the righteous suffer need.

Today, when life seems unfair or scarcity frightens you, remember that God cares for his own. Keep doing good and be generous, trusting that He will sustain you, even in difficult times.
exp.30:11:
The speaker says he feels forgotten, as if he were already dead and no one remembered him. He also feels like a broken vessel, that is, a cracked or discarded jar that is no longer good for anything.

The speaker is David, according to the heading of the psalm. He is suffering greatly, with pain, weariness, and rejection from neighbors, acquaintances, and enemies. It is not known exactly which moment of his life is in view. Even so, the psalm does not end in complaint: shortly afterward he says, "But I trusted in you, O Lord."

When you feel forgotten or useless, do not hide that pain. Bring it honestly before God, as David did. What you feel is not always what God thinks of you. He remains your God even when people turn away.
exp.67:11:
The verse says that kings of armies fled in haste, defeated. Meanwhile, the women who had stayed at home divided the spoil, that is, the things the enemy left behind. The word "spoil" in the verse refers to goods taken after a victory.

This psalm is a song of David that celebrates God as the one who rescues his people and leads them to victory. Earlier, it speaks of women who announced the good news of the triumph. Some believe it refers to a specific battle, and others to the general history of Israel. It is not certain which is the case. What is clear is that the victory comes from God.

For today: God can give you the fruits of a battle you did not fight with your own strength. Trust him, serve wherever you are, even in the simple things of your home, and thank him for every blessing.
exp.130:0:
The explanation says that David comes before God with humility. "My heart is not puffed up" means that he did not fill up with pride. "Nor do my eyes look down on others" speaks of not looking at others with superiority. "I did not walk in great matters" means seeking things that are too big or too important for oneself, and "things too high for me" are matters that go beyond our ability to understand.

It is a "song of ascents," that is, one of the songs that were probably sung as people went up to Jerusalem, though scholars do not fully agree on the meaning of the term. David, king of Israel, is the speaker, and the title says so. It is a brief personal prayer, and at the end it invites the whole people to trust in the Lord.

For today: you do not need to have an answer for everything or pretend to be more than you are. Today you can hand over to God what you do not understand and rest in the knowledge that He does know.
exp.62:4:
It says that the psalmist's soul will be satisfied the way someone enjoys a rich feast. The words "marrow" and "fatness" in the verse are symbols of the finest food, as they were in that time. "Joyful lips" are lips that praise with gladness. God satisfies the deepest part of a person.
