The title of the psalm attributes it to David, when he was in the wilderness of Judah. Many believe he was fleeing from Saul or from Absalom, though the text does not specify. He was far from the temple and in a dry place, yet he found in God his true nourishment. His praise springs from having experienced that God's love is worth more than life.

When you feel empty or in a "wilderness," do not first try to fill yourself with things. Take a few minutes to remember what God has done for you and give thanks to him. That gratitude can satisfy your soul.
exp.118:105:
He says that the psalmist made a firm oath and confirmed it: he will keep God's righteous judgments, that is, God's just decisions and commands. The verse "I have sworn, and I will perform it" means that he reaffirmed it and made it firm.

The one speaking is the author of Psalm 119, a poem about God's Word. It is not known for certain who wrote it. He has just said that God's Word is a lamp to his feet, and that is why he decides to commit himself. Even so, in the next verse he acknowledges that he suffers greatly and asks God to revive him.

For today: a commitment to God is not just a feeling of the moment. You can decide on a concrete practice, such as reading a passage every day, and ask God for strength to keep it, especially when you are going through trials.
exp.147:7:
It says that even the forces of the weather call on us to praise God: the fire (perhaps lightning or flashes of lightning), the hail, the snow, and the vapour (mist or clouds). The stormy wind obeys God's word, that is, it does what he commands. "Fulfilling" means carrying out or accomplishing.

The psalm has no named author; it is a song of praise that calls all creation to honor the LORD. First it summons the heavens and then the earth, with the deeps, the mountains, the trees, and the animals. The verses before it remind us that God created everything and set in place an order that does not break. Scholars understand in several ways how things without voices "praise," and many see it as poetic language.

Today we can look at a storm not only with fear, but also remembering that God sustains creation. If the wind obeys him, we can trust him in our own storms and give him thanks.
exp.146:11:
This verse is an invitation to praise. It is addressed to Jerusalem and to Zion, which are names for God's city and his people. Both sentences say the same thing in different words: that the people should acknowledge their God and honor him.

The psalmist, whose name the text does not give, speaks to the people of Israel. Earlier he said that God is not impressed by the strength of the horse or of a man, but takes pleasure in those who revere him and trust in his mercy. Then he gives reasons to praise: he protects the gates of the city, blesses its children, and gives peace and food. Many believe it was written after the return from exile, though this is not certain.

For today: before asking for something, name three concrete things God has already given you, such as protection, family, or bread on the table, and thank him out loud.
exp.103:14:
This verse says that God gives three gifts from the earth: wine, which gladdens the heart; oil, which makes the face shine; and bread, which strengthens the heart. The phrase "make the face shine" speaks of a fresh and radiant appearance. "Strengthens" means that it nourishes and keeps a person alive.

The psalm does not say who wrote it. It is a hymn that praises God as Creator and caretaker of everything that exists. Earlier it speaks of the rain, the grass, and the animals; later, of the trees and the birds. The verse shows that God also cares for people with food and joy.

For today: the next time you eat, pause for a moment and give thanks to God. Recognizing that our daily bread is a gift helps us enjoy it with gratitude and without selfishness, and to share it with someone who has less.
exp.129:0:
The explanation says that the one speaking is in a very deep place, in great distress, and from there cries out to God. The phrase that heads Psalms 120 through 134 is a title that many believe means they were sung while going up to Jerusalem, though this is not known for certain. The word for the name of God shows up here, and crying out means asking for help with force.

The author does not name himself. The one speaking feels sunk down, and the verses that follow show that he thinks about his sins and his need for forgiveness. The depths may be guilt, pain or danger; the psalm does not give the details. What matters is that, even in that low place, he turns to God and does not keep silent.

For today: when you find yourself in the lowest place, do not wait until you feel better before you pray. Speak with God just as you are, with honest words and without ornament. He hears the cry of the one who comes to Him in humility.
exp.105:28:
This verse says that the people of Israel angered God by their actions, and because of this a plague came that killed many people. The word that describes their act is an old one meaning to provoke someone to anger or to make them angry. The word for the plague refers to the death of many people, in this case caused by a disease that spread widely.

The psalm is a prayer of praise and confession that recalls Israel's failures from Egypt to Canaan. Here it refers to the episode at Baal-peor, in Numbers 25, when the people joined themselves to the idolatry of Moab. The psalmist does not hide his people's sin; he acknowledges it honestly in order to highlight God's patience.

For today: let us not take lightly what displeases God. If we realize that we have drifted away, let us return to Him soon with humility, because his mercy remains open to anyone who repents.
exp.137:6:
Here the explanation says that although David goes through moments of distress, God will revive him and give him new strength. When his enemies become angry with him, God will stretch out his hand to restrain them. The word "hand" in this verse stands for power, and the right hand in particular is a symbol of strength. The phrase "save me" means God will rescue him.

The speaker is the psalmist, whom the heading attributes to David. He is giving thanks to God for answering him. Earlier in the psalm he says that God attends to the humble and looks on the proud from afar. He then adds that God will carry out his purpose in him. Some scholars debate the exact details of the time in which it was written, but the tone of confidence is clear.

For today: when you are in a difficulty, do not wait for it to pass before trusting God. Tell him simply, "I am in trouble, but I know you sustain me." Ask him for encouragement for today, and take the next step with humility.
exp.72:8:
The explanation says that the wicked speak without respect against God and also without restraint among people. "They set their mouth against the heavens" means that they dare to speak against God or to speak as if they were masters of what is holy. "Their tongue walketh through the earth" shows that their words go everywhere, opining, boasting and giving orders without limit.

The one speaking is Asaph, the author of the psalm. He is confused and nearly slips because he sees the proud prospering while he suffers. In the verses before, he describes their pride and violence. Here he shows that their arrogance reaches the heavens and the earth. Later, when he enters the sanctuary, Asaph understands what their end will be.

Today, before envying those who succeed with arrogant words, it is good to guard our own tongue. We can bring our doubts to God with honesty and speak with humility.
exp.148:1:
Psalm 149:2 says that the people of Israel should rejoice in God, who made them and formed them as a nation. "Maker" means Creator. The "children of Zion" are the inhabitants of Jerusalem, God's people. The word "joyful" in the verse means they should be filled with gladness. God is presented as King, that is, the one who rules and cares for his people.

The psalm does not say who wrote it. The speaker is a singer who invites the community to praise God with a new song. The verses that follow mention dancing, the timbrel (a hand drum) and the harp, and explain the reason: God takes pleasure in his people and honors the humble with salvation. Some believe it was written after a deliverance, but that is not certain.

For today: before asking God for something, take a moment to thank him because he made you and cares for you as your ruler. Rejoice in him, even if your day is difficult.
exp.108:28:
It says that those who speak evil of the psalmist and falsely accuse him should be clothed with shame, that is, with dishonor and disgrace. It asks that their own confusion cover them completely, like a cloak or mantle that they cannot take off.

The psalm is traditionally attributed to David, and it speaks from the middle of an unjust persecution. He is attacked with lies and hatred, even though he had answered his enemies with prayer. The psalm includes very harsh prayers against his enemies, known as imprecatory prayers. Here he trusts that God, and not his own revenge, is the one who will bring about justice. Christians often read it alongside Jesus' words about loving one's enemies.

When someone slanders you, bring your pain to God in sincere prayer, instead of repaying evil with evil. Ask him to defend the truth, and leave justice in his hands, while you continue to answer with kindness.
exp.72:18:
It says that the wicked, who seemed so secure and prosperous, collapse suddenly. The word for "destroyed" means ruined or laid waste, and the phrase for "in a moment" means in an instant. Their end comes quickly, and their fall is dreadful, filled with terror.

The psalmist Asaph speaks. He had felt envy when he saw the proud prospering, and he nearly stumbled in his faith. Everything changed when he entered the sanctuary of God, that is, when he sought God in worship and saw things from God's eternal perspective. There he understood their end.

For today: when you become discouraged seeing that unjust people seem to do well, do not dwell on envy. Bring your complaint to God in prayer and in fellowship with other believers. There you will recover perspective, and you will trust that God is just and has the final word.
exp.103:27:
He gives food to all his creatures. When he gives it to them, they gather it up; when he opens his generous hand, they are satisfied with good things. The phrase "they are filled with good" means they are filled up, eating until they are content. The creatures do not produce their own food by themselves; they receive it from him.

The psalm does not say who wrote it. It is a song of praise to the Creator for his care over all creation: the sea, the ships, the great sea monster, and all the animals. All of them wait on God, and he feeds them in their season. The verses that follow show that life depends on him: if he takes away his breath, they die; if he sends it forth, there is new life.

Today we can thank God before we eat, remembering that every meal comes from his hand. We can also trust that he will care for us day by day, and share with those who have less.
exp.118:90:
It says that all of creation still stands today because God ordered it so. The word for "ordinances" in this verse means his decrees or commands. Creation continues steady and firm. Everything that exists obeys God and serves him.

The one speaking is the psalmist, in Psalm 119, who praises God's law. The verses before this one say that God's word endures forever and that the earth remains firm. The author sees that the order of creation shows God's faithfulness. The verses that follow say that this same word sustained him in his affliction. It is not known with certainty who wrote it.

For today: when you feel insecure, look at creation and remember that God sustains all things faithfully. If he sustains the world, he can also sustain you. Trust his word today.
exp.58:0:
The verse begins with a note for the choir director: the song is to be sung to the tune called "Do Not Destroy," and it is a "Michtam" of David (a word whose exact meaning is uncertain). Then David prays: "Deliver me from mine enemies, O my God; defend me from those who rise up against me." "Defend me" means protect me and keep me out of danger.

David is the one speaking. The heading recalls the moment when Saul sent men to watch David's house in order to kill him (1 Samuel 19:11). David was innocent, but the king pursued him out of jealousy and fear. Some scholars believe the psalm arose from that night, although its use may also have been expanded later.

For today: when someone treats you unjustly or you feel afraid, you do not have to carry that anguish alone. Bring your situation honestly before God, as David did, and ask him for protection and wisdom to act rightly.
exp.0:4:
This verse says that the wicked will not be able to stand firm when judgment comes, nor will they have a place among the righteous. The phrase "shall not stand" means "will not hold up" or "will not come through it well." "Congregation" refers to the gathered community of God's people.

The psalm does not say who wrote it; no title appears, and scholars debate whether it was David or another author. It works as an introduction to the whole book of Psalms. It contrasts two paths: that of the righteous, like a tree well watered, and that of the wicked, like the chaff (the light husk) that the wind carries away. Interpreters discuss whether the "judgment" refers to a judgment in this life, to the end of time, or to both.

For today: do not lose heart when it seems that evil is winning. God has the last word. Seek to live rooted in his Word and in a community of faith, trusting that his justice is sure.
exp.104:9:
It says that God confirmed his promise to Jacob as a firm law, and to Israel as a covenant that does not end. The word "confirmed" in the verse above is the same idea: he made the promise stand firm. A "decree" is an official order or decision. "Everlasting" means eternal, lasting forever. The promise God made to Abraham and Isaac, he renewed with Jacob.

The psalmist, who is not named in this psalm, invites the people to praise God by remembering his faithfulness. He speaks of the promise of the land of Canaan, made when Israel was a small group of strangers. It is remembered so that the people will trust God, because he keeps what he says.

For today: when you feel small, without resources, or without direction, remember that God is faithful to his promises. Make a list of the times God has cared for you and give him thanks. This strengthens trust in him for whatever comes next.
exp.30:14:
He says that the whole of the psalmist's life, with its good seasons and hard ones, is in God's hands. "Times" refers to the moments and circumstances of his life. From there he asks to be delivered from those who hate and pursue him.

David is said to speak, according to the psalm's heading, though it is not known with certainty at what exact moment he wrote it. He suffers slander, fear and threats of death, since others gathered together to plan to take his life. Even so, he declares that he trusts in God and calls him "my God."

When you feel that your life is uncertain or that someone is harming you, you can say to God: "My times are in your hand." Hand over your worries to him, pray with sincerity, and trust that he continues to care for you, even when you do not yet see the way out.
exp.100:1:
He says that David resolves to act wisely on the path of a whole life, that is, without duplicity or hypocrisy. "I will behave myself wisely" means he will pay attention and act with prudence. "A perfect way" here speaks of a complete and sincere life, not of never failing. The verse's question, "O when wilt thou come unto me?", can be read as a question or as a promise; scholars interpret it both ways. "I will walk within my house with a perfect heart" means he will live this way in his home.

It is a psalm of David, who speaks as king and singer. After praising God's mercy and justice, he promises how he will govern and live. His commitment begins within his own house, and then extends to those around him.

For today: true integrity is tested at home, where no one applauds us. Today you can choose to be the same person in private as in public, speaking the truth and treating your family well.
exp.66:2:
It says that all the peoples, without exception, should praise God. The word "praise" here appears in the same form as in the verse your reader sees, so the sentence about the old form is removed. The word "peoples" refers to the nations and human groups of the earth. This phrase is repeated like a refrain throughout the psalm, which underlines its importance.

This psalm is a song addressed to the chief musician, to be sung with stringed instruments. We do not know for certain who wrote it. The speaker is God's people, who ask for his blessing so that, through it, his way and his salvation may be known among all nations. Universal praise is the goal of that blessing.

For today: when you ask for God's help, think of others too. Pray for people from other cultures and places so that they may come to know God. You can support a missionary work or share with someone close to you the good that God has done in your life.
exp.118:39:
The psalmist looks to God and declares how deeply he longs for God's commandments. To long after them means to desire them eagerly, the way someone who is thirsty longs for water. So he asks God to revive him and restore his strength, and he asks for this according to God's righteousness, that is, in keeping with God's uprightness and faithfulness.

The one speaking is a believer who calls himself a servant of God. The verses nearby show that he suffers mockery and shame, yet he trusts that God's word is good. This whole psalm praises the law of God. We do not know with certainty who wrote it or the exact time it was written.

For today: when you feel tired or discouraged, do not ask only for relief. Ask God to restore your delight in his Word. Set aside a few minutes each day to read it, and pray with this same verse: "Lord, give me life."
exp.117:0:
This verse is an invitation to give thanks to God. "Praise" means to praise or to thank, and the name of the Lord is the name the verse gives for God. "Mercy" here translates a Hebrew word (hesed) that speaks of faithful love, a kindness that does not give up. It says that God is good and that his love lasts forever.

It is a psalm of thanksgiving. The text does not say who wrote it. It seems to be a song meant to be said together in a community, since the verses that follow call on Israel and the house of Aaron, the priests, to repeat the same phrase. Many think it was used in celebrations at the temple, but this is understood in different ways.

For today: when everything changes, you can begin the day by remembering that God is good and that his love does not end. Say out loud one specific reason you give him thanks, even if your situation is hard.
exp.118:65:
Here the psalmist asks God to teach him good judgment, that is, discernment to tell right from wrong, and also wisdom. The reason he gives is that he has believed in God's commandments, meaning he trusts them.

The author of Psalm 119 is a believer who loves God's Word. We do not know for certain who wrote it. He comes from recognizing that God has been good to him (verse 65), and that before his suffering he had gone astray (verse 67). That is why he asks for discernment to follow God wisely.

For today: before making a decision, ask God for wisdom and look in his Word for what it says about the matter. Trusting his commandments helps you judge better what you face each day.
exp.67:26:
This verse describes a procession with representatives of several tribes of Israel. The phrase "their ruler" means that Benjamin went at the front, guiding or leading them. The "princes" are the leaders or chiefs of each tribe. Judah (south), Zebulun and Naphtali (north) are named, as a picture of the whole people gathered together.

David, the author of the psalm, praises God as the one who guides and protects his people. The psalm seems to recall a procession of worship, perhaps when the ark went up to Jerusalem, although scholars do not agree on the exact moment. That tribes from the north and the south are present shows unity before God. Why Benjamin is mentioned as the guide is not entirely clear.

Today we can learn that worshiping together has a special value. Even though we differ in background, character or temperament, God gathers us to praise him in unity. Make an effort to take part with your church and to value the brothers and sisters who are not like you.
exp.106:14:
This verse invites us to thank God for his mercy, which is his faithful and compassionate love, and for the wonderful works he does on behalf of people. "Praise" is an invitation to acknowledge and celebrate what God has done. "The Lord" is God's name. "Men" simply means human beings.

Psalm 107 does not say who wrote it. It seems to be addressed to those whom God rescued from various hardships. It speaks of those who sat in darkness, cried out to God, and were set free by him. That deliverance is the reason for the praise.

For today: think of a time when God sustained or helped you, and thank him today in simple words. Telling what you have lived through can also encourage others who are still in distress.
exp.87:0:
This verse begins with a musical note: it is a song for the sons of Korah, to be given to the chief musician, to be sung upon "Mahalath" (perhaps a melody or a theme of sickness or sorrow; this is not known for certain). The word "Maschil" probably means a teaching or a meditative song. Then the psalmist says, "O Lord God of my salvation," and states that he has cried out to God day and night.

The one speaking is Heman the Ezrahite, a wise man or musician mentioned in the Bible. He is suffering greatly, and the psalm is known for ending without a clear answer of relief. Even so, he begins by calling God his salvation.

Today we can pray with sincerity even when we are tired or without answers. If you are going through a dark season, keep speaking with God. Crying out to Him is already an act of faith.
exp.81:5:
He says that God himself spoke and called certain people "gods" and "children of the most High." The word "you" in the verse is the everyday plural, meaning "all of you." "Most High" is a title for God, meaning the highest of all. It does not mean they are gods in the true sense, but that they received a place of authority.

In this psalm, God judges the rulers and judges of his people, because they defended the poor poorly and favored the wicked. Many understand "gods" to refer to those human judges, though some think of spiritual beings. The following verses make clear that they will die like any man. Jesus quoted this verse in John 10:34-36.

If you have any kind of authority, at home, at work, or in church, remember that it is entrusted to you by God. Use it to protect the weak and act with justice, not for your own benefit.
exp.82:3:
The enemies of God speak among themselves and encourage one another: "Come, let us wipe out Israel as a nation, so that no one will ever remember its name." The phrase "let us cut them off from being a people" means to destroy them completely, until they cease to exist as a people.

It is a psalm of Asaph, a prayer of the people asking God for help. It speaks of neighboring nations that form a secret alliance against Israel (the verses that follow name Edom, Ishmael, Moab, and others). We do not know with certainty which historical moment it refers to; scholars have interpreted it in several ways. What is clear is that the psalmist presents the attack as an attack against God himself.

For today: when you feel threatened by forces greater than you, do not stay alone with the fear. Do what the psalmist did: tell God everything honestly and trust that he cares for his own.
exp.53:5:
The explanation says that the psalmist will offer a sacrifice "freely", that is, gladly and without anyone forcing him. It also promises to praise the name of the Lord, and gives the reason: because God is good. The phrase "I will freely sacrifice unto thee" simply means that he will offer sacrifice to God.

David speaks, according to the heading of the psalm. The people of Ziph had betrayed him to Saul, who was pursuing him. In danger, he asked God for help. In this verse he already responds with thankfulness, trusting that God sustains him. The freewill offering was different from those the law required, and it expressed sincere gratitude.

For today: we can thank God not only out of obligation, but with freedom and joy. Even in difficult times, it is worth remembering that God is good and giving him thanks through a prayer, an offering, or an act of service.
exp.101:3:
It says that the psalmist's heart is struck down and dried up, like grass that withers in the sun. His pain is so strong that he forgets to eat. "Smitten" simply means struck down, and "withered" means dried up, as the words of the verse itself show. "My bread" is a way of speaking about his daily food.

The title of the psalm presents it as the prayer of someone in distress who pours out his complaint before God. It is not known for certain who wrote it. Some think of someone in exile, but this is debated. It speaks from deep suffering and asks God to hear him soon.

For today: when pain takes away your appetite, your sleep, or your strength, do not hide it. Tell God honestly, as the psalmist does. And do not neglect your body: eat something, rest, and ask help from someone you trust.
exp.60:5:
He says God will give the king a very long life, adding day after day. The word "Thou wilt prolong" means "you will lengthen" or "you will give more." The phrase "and his years as many generations" shows years stretching out as if they span many generations, that is, a long life and a long reign.

The speaker is David, according to the psalm's heading, though scholars do not agree on the exact time. He feels far from home and weak, but trusts God as his refuge. After asking for help, he speaks of the king in the third person, perhaps of himself. Many Christians also see here a look toward the Messiah, whose kingdom has no end.

For today: our life is in God's hands, day by day. You can entrust him with your week, your health and your future, and ask him to sustain you today, knowing that he cares for every day he gives you.
exp.93:17:
This verse says that when the psalmist felt he was slipping or could no longer keep his footing, God's mercy held him up. "Slippeth" means that the foot loses its firmness. "Mercy" is God's faithful and compassionate love. "Held me up" means that he supported him and kept him standing.

The psalmist speaks in a psalm that asks God for justice against the wicked who oppress others. Earlier he had asked who would stand up for him, and he acknowledges that without the help of the Lord he would have been lost, brought down to silence, a way of speaking about death. We do not know with precision what situation he was living through; the text does not say.

For today: when you feel your spirit or your strength failing, do not wait until you are steady to turn to God. Tell him honestly, "I feel that I am slipping." Then remember the times he held you up, and trust that his love will hold you up again.
exp.36:8:
This verse sets two destinies side by side. "Evildoers" are those who do wrong, and "shall be cut off" means they will be cut down, like a tree that is felled. By contrast, "those that wait upon the Lord," that is, those who trust God patiently, "shall inherit the earth," meaning they will receive as their inheritance a secure and stable place.

David is the author, according to the psalm's heading, and he speaks like an older man who has seen life (v. 25). He counsels those who become upset when they see the wicked prosper. For the people of Israel, the land was God's promise and a sign of his care. The nearby verses call for calm and for not responding with anger or wrongdoing.

Today, when something unjust troubles you, do not repay evil with evil. Breathe, pray, and entrust the matter to God, trusting that he brings justice in his own time.
exp.17:28:
It says that David, with God's help, can overcome great armies and get past walls that seem impossible. The phrase about running through a troop means to defeat or scatter enemy forces. The phrase about leaping over a wall speaks of attacking and getting past the walls of a fortified city. The strength does not come from him but from God, who is the one by whom he runs and the one through whom he leaps.

The speaker is David, in a psalm of thanksgiving for having been rescued from Saul and all his enemies, as the heading of the psalm indicates. It comes right after saying that God lights up his darkness. Afterward he will say that God's way is perfect and that he is a shield for those who trust in him. David does not boast of his own weapons, but of his God.

Today, when faced with a problem that looks like an enormous wall, you do not have to face it alone. Do what is yours to do with courage, but lean on God, asking him for wisdom and strength, and trusting that he walks with you.
exp.118:88:
It says that God's word does not change or come to an end. "Settled" means that it stays firm and steady. "In heaven" speaks of a high and secure place, beyond the reach of human attacks. "Lamed" is just the name of a Hebrew letter, since this psalm is arranged according to the alphabet, and each group of verses begins with a different letter.

The speaker is the psalmist, whose name we do not know for certain. He had just said that he was nearly knocked down, but that he did not let go of God's commandments. Now, under pressure, he looks upward and remembers that God's word is firmer than his troubles. The verses that follow compare that firmness with the earth and creation, which still stand by God's order.

When everything around you is shifting or you feel weak, lean on what God has said. Read a passage of the Bible each day and repeat it in prayer, because his word remains firm even when your circumstances change.
exp.118:83:
This verse shows a believer speaking honestly to God. He asks how many days his life has, meaning that his time is short and fragile. He also asks when God will bring justice against those who persecute him. Here, "executing judgment" means correcting the injustice and setting things right.

The speaker is the psalmist, the author of this long psalm about God's law. We do not know for certain who he is. He is suffering, and shortly before he describes himself as a wineskin shriveled in the smoke: dried out and blackened. Even so, he does not forget God's word, and he asks God for help.

For today: when you suffer an injustice, you can bring your weariness and your questions to God without disguising them. Pray with honesty, keep obeying his word, and leave justice in his hands, without repaying evil with evil.
exp.93:20:
It says that there are wicked people who gather together in groups to attack the life of the righteous person. The phrase about gathering in groups means they come together as a group, organize themselves and agree with one another. And the phrase about condemning innocent blood means they declare guilty someone who has done nothing wrong, even at the cost of his life.

The psalmist speaks, though his identity is not known with certainty. He sees injustice among those who govern and judge, since they use the law to do harm. Before this verse, he tells how God's comfort brought joy to his soul amid many worries. Afterward he affirms that the LORD is his refuge and that God will do justice.

For today: when you see or suffer an injustice, do not keep your distress to yourself alone. Bring it to God, seek comfort and refuge in Him, and trust that He is the righteous judge. In the meantime, make sure you never join those who speak evil of others or accuse them without reason.
exp.55:0:
The explanation says that David, the chief musician, wrote this song to be sung to the tune "The Silent Dove in Distant Places." It calls it a "Michtam," a word whose meaning is not certain; some think it is a poem or a special kind of composition.

Then it cries out: "Be merciful unto me, O God," that is, "have pity on me." It says that the man would "swallow me up," meaning he wants to destroy him, and that he "fighting daily oppresseth me."

The one speaking is David. The title says he wrote it when the Philistines took him in Gath. Some believe it refers to the episode in 1 Samuel 21, though scholars do not fully agree. What is clear is that David was in danger and felt cornered.

For today: when you feel worn out by a pressure that never seems to end, do not wait until you are strong to pray. Say honestly, "Be merciful unto me, O God." He listens to the one who feels weak.
exp.141:6:
David asks God to bring him out of his confinement so that he can praise God's name. "Prison" can mean a real jail or a picture of distress and being shut in. "Bountifully" means generous and kind. He hopes that the righteous, that is, people who are faithful to God, will surround him and rejoice with him, because God will deal kindly with him.

The title of the psalm says it is a prayer of David when he was in the cave, probably fleeing from Saul, although it is not known with certainty which cave it was. He speaks with God from his loneliness, feeling pursued and without strength, but he declares that God is his hope and his portion.

For today: when you feel shut in by fear, sadness, or problems, pray sincerely and ask God for help. And do not isolate yourself: seek out brothers and sisters and friends of faith who will walk with you and encourage you while you wait for his answer.
exp.35:11:
It says that those who do evil have fallen into a place and were no longer able to get up. The phrase "workers of iniquity" refers to those who practice injustice. The word that is rendered "cast down" means pushed down with force. The verse describes a final and irreversible fall for those who live in wickedness.

David speaks here, according to the heading of the psalm. Before this, it contrasts the wickedness of the godless person with the faithful love of God, and asks to be protected from pride and from the hand of the wicked. This verse sounds like a confident view of the outcome: although the wicked may seem strong today, they will fall. Some read it as prophecy and others as a declaration of faith; the text does not specify the moment.

For today: when injustice discourages you, do not grow bitter or seek revenge. Trust that God sees and has the last word. In the meantime, ask Him to keep you humble and close to Him, and keep doing good with patience.
exp.62:3:
The explanation says that David wants to bless God, that is, to speak well of Him and thank Him, throughout his whole life. "Lifting up the hands in your name" was a way of praying and worshiping, raising the hands toward God with trust and devotion. It is like saying: "As long as I live, I will praise you and seek you in prayer."

The title of the psalm connects it with David when he was in the wilderness of Judah. Many believe it was while he was fleeing from Saul or from Absalom, but the text does not make this entirely clear. What we do see is that he is in a dry and difficult place, and yet he says that God's love is worth more than life itself. For this reason his praise comes from gratitude, not from comfort.

Today we can make praise a daily habit. Even if you are tired or going through a hard time, set aside a few minutes to pray, give thanks for something specific that God has done, and lift your heart to Him.
exp.85:10:
Here the psalmist asks God to show him how to live. Asking for direction for everyday life is what "teach me your way" means. "I will walk in your truth" means he wants to obey what he learns. To "unite my heart" means that his heart would not be divided or scattered. "Make my heart fear your name" does not mean being afraid; it means respecting and honoring God with reverence.

It is a prayer of David, according to the title of the psalm. He is in a time of distress and needs help. Before asking this, he recognizes that God is great and the only God. Afterward he promises to praise him, because God has been merciful and has delivered him. The exact details of his situation are not stated.

Today we can pray this way each morning: "Lord, teach me and unite my heart with you." Then choose one decision for the day and ask God what he wants from you in it.
exp.77:3:
This verse says that we will not hide from our children the teachings about God. On the contrary, we will tell them to the next generation: the praises of Jehovah (his works worthy of praise), his strength (his power), and the wonderful works he has done. "Hide" means to keep out of sight, and the old spelling of "to" is not a word you will see in the verse.

The psalm is spoken by Asaph, according to the title of the psalm. He is telling the history of Israel as a teaching in the form of a parable. What he heard from his fathers he now passes on to the people. The verses that follow explain that God commanded the parents to teach his law to their children, so that each generation would know him and keep telling it on.

For today: tell the younger ones, in simple words, something concrete that God has done in your life or in your family. You can do this at the table, on the road, or before bed, so that they too learn to trust in him.
exp.76:7:
Here the psalmist asks whether God's faithful love has come to an end for ever, and whether his promise has failed to hold from one generation to the next. The phrases "has his mercy clean gone" and "does his promise fail" are painful questions, not statements.

The speaker is Asaph, or someone from his group of singers, according to the title of the psalm. He is distressed, perhaps by a crisis facing the people, though the text does not say exactly what it was. He spends the night awake, remembering and wondering whether God has left him. Later, in verse 10, he decides to remember God's past deeds.

When you feel that God is distant, you do not have to pretend or keep your doubts to yourself. You can bring them honestly to God in prayer. Then, like the psalmist, remember what God has done before, both in your own life and in the Bible, so that your hope is strengthened.
exp.11:2:
It says that God will put an end to flattering, false words and to the proud tongue that boasts of great things. "Flattering" means praising people in order to deceive them or gain something from them. "Speaking great things" refers to speaking with arrogance, like someone who thinks they are powerful.

David speaks in prayer. He feels surrounded by false people who say one thing and think another, speaking with a double heart. The proud believe their words will win them the day and that no one can rule over them. But God answers that he will rise up for the poor and the oppressed and will keep them safe. So this verse is a promise of justice.

Today we can ask God to make us people of sincere speech. Let us avoid flattering people to get something, or boasting to impress them. If someone suffers because of lies or abuse, we can trust that God sees and acts, and we can speak truthfully and kindly in their defense.
exp.88:36:
This verse compares God's promise to David with the moon: just as the moon remains steady in the sky, the reign of his descendants will also be established forever. The moon is seen as a "faithful witness" that is always present in the sky. The word "Selah" is a pause or musical marking; its exact meaning is not known for certain.

The speaker is Ethan the Ezrahite, the psalmist, who recalls God's covenant with David. God had sworn that David's descendants and throne would endure. But the psalm turns painful, because in the verses that follow it seems that the fallen, humbled king contradicts that promise. Ethan presents this tension to God with honesty. Many Christians see in Jesus the final fulfillment of this promise.

For today: when your situation seems to contradict what God has promised, do not hide your confusion. Tell it to him honestly, but remember that his faithfulness is steadier than what you can see.
exp.135:17:
It says that God defeated strong kings, and that he did so because his mercy endures forever. "Slew" here means he defeated them in battle; "mighty" refers to kings with great strength and armies. The refrain "his mercy endureth for ever" is repeated in every line of the psalm.

The psalm is a song of praise of the people of Israel, probably sung in worship, with a leader and the congregation answering. It recalls how God brought them out of Egypt, led them through the wilderness, and gave them the land. The verses that follow name Sihon and Og, kings who opposed Israel's passage. For the psalmist, those victories show God's faithfulness to his people.

For today: when you face something that seems bigger than you, remember how God has cared for you before. Write down a few moments when he helped you, and thank him, trusting that his mercy does not run out.
exp.58:16:
He says that David addresses God as "my strength," that is, his power and his support. He promises to sing to him because God is his defense, and he calls him "the God of my mercy," meaning the God who treats him with kindness and compassion.

According to the title of the psalm, David wrote it when Saul sent men to watch his house in order to kill him. This is a tradition that the text itself points to. David is surrounded by enemies who lie in wait for him like hungry dogs, but he ends the psalm with confidence and praise, not with fear.

When you are in a difficult situation, do not wait for it to pass before giving thanks. You can begin the day by recalling out loud how God has cared for you before, or sing a simple song of praise to him. In this way your heart is fixed on who God is, and not only on the problem.
exp.103:8:
This verse speaks of the waters, which God set a boundary they cannot pass. "Thou hast set a bound" means "you set a limit for them." "Pass over" means "cross over." "Turn not again to cover the earth" means that they will not come back to flood the whole earth.

The one speaking is the psalmist, who praises God as Creator. The verses before recall how the waters fled at the voice of God, and He ordered the earth. Many readers see here an echo of creation and, perhaps, of the flood, although the psalm does not say this clearly. Then the psalm shows how God cares for the animals with springs of water.

For today: God sets wise and good limits, and His care is constant. When you feel that your life is overflowing with problems or worries, remember that God governs even the greatest waters. Speak to Him with confidence and rest in the knowledge that He sustains what you cannot control.
exp.63:8:
It says that when God acts against evil, all people will feel a deep respect before him. They will speak about what God did and understand that it was his work. Here, the word for "fear" means reverence and awe, not just fear. "His doing" refers to what God accomplished in carrying out justice.

David speaks, according to the psalm's title. He is distressed by enemies who attack with words, slander, and secret plans. He prays asking for protection. Before this verse, he says that God will strike them suddenly and that their own words will turn against them. Then the psalm ends with the joy of the righteous who trust in the Lord.

When you suffer because of injustice or hurtful words, bring your case to God in prayer and do not seek revenge. Trust that he sees everything. And when you see his work in your life, tell others about it with gratitude.
exp.93:10:
God knows perfectly what we think, even what no one else sees. And the verse declares that human thoughts are "vanity," that is, something empty, fleeting, and without lasting worth when they turn away from God. Paul quotes this verse in 1 Corinthians 3:20.

The psalmist speaks in the midst of injustice. Some wicked people oppress the weak and say: "The Lord does not see or understand" (vv. 6-7). The psalmist answers with questions: if God made the ear and the eye, how could he not hear and see? That is why this verse is a warning to those who think they are hidden, and a comfort to those who suffer.

Today, when you feel confused or worried, pray with complete sincerity: God already knows your thoughts. Ask him to replace empty thoughts with his truth, and trust that he sees every injustice.
exp.114:1:
This verse is a question that neighboring peoples asked with mockery. The psalmist asks God to act so that they will not laugh at his people. The phrase "the heathen" refers to the nations that did not know the LORD, and the word "now" suggests that, seeing their suffering, they thought their God had abandoned them.

The one speaking is the people of Israel, who pray to God. The exact date of the psalm and the specific situation behind it are not known for certain, and it is interpreted in several ways. What is clear is that they ask for help so that the name of God, not their own, will be honored. That is why the previous verse speaks of his mercy and his truth. The answer comes right after: our God is in the heavens and does whatever he pleases.

For today: when others doubt your faith or ask you where God is in your difficulty, do not despair. Pray with humility, ask that God be glorified in your situation, and trust that he still reigns.
exp.7:6:
It says that God placed under human care the domestic animals, such as the sheep and the oxen, and also the wild animals. "All sheep and oxen, yea, and the beasts of the field" refers to the animals living in the wild. "All of them" means that none of these is excluded from that charge.

The one speaking is King David, in a song of praise. He marvels that God, being so great, has given human beings such dignity and responsibility. The psalm begins and ends by praising the name of the LORD, so human dominion is not a cause for pride but for gratitude toward God.

For today: take care, with respect and kindness, of everything God has entrusted to you, whether animals, plants, or resources. To have dominion here means to manage as God would: with care, not with abuse.
exp.15:2:
David says that his greatest joy is found in the people who belong to God. "Saints" means those set apart for God, and "excellent" refers to those with a sincere and upright heart. "Delight" means affection or pleasure. The verse before this one says that his good comes from God, and this one adds that his good shows itself in loving the faithful. The translation of the first part is difficult, and some understand it this way: "my good does not depend on you, but on the saints," but the most common reading is the one explained here.

David speaks in a psalm of trust. He asks God for protection and declares that the LORD alone is his Lord. Then he turns away from those who follow other gods and from their offerings. That is why he chooses his companions from among the faithful people.

For today: look for friends who love God and value honesty. Take part in a church or prayer group, and let those people encourage you to keep following the Lord.
exp.138:10:
This verse says that if someone thought, "Surely the darkness shall cover me," the night itself would become light around them. The word "cover" means to hide or conceal. The phrase "about me" means "around me." The idea is that no darkness is able to hide a person from God.

The psalm is spoken by David, according to its heading. Earlier in the psalm he asked whether he could flee from God, by going up to heaven, going down to the grave, or going to the farthest edge of the sea. God is present in all of those places. Here the psalmist does not speak with fear but with wonder: God knows him completely and stays with him.

For today: when you feel lonely, confused, or in a hard night, remember that you are not outside God's sight. And if there is something you want to hide, bring it to Him honestly; His light not only sees, it also guides and sustains.
exp.92:3:
This verse says that God, who reigns from on high, is mightier than the noise of many waters and than the mighty waves of the sea. "Noise" here means a very loud roar, and "mighty" means strong or violent. The psalmist compares the roar of the sea with the power of God, and God is greater.

The psalm does not say who wrote it. It is a song that celebrates the Lord as the eternal King. The rivers and waters that lift up their voice are often understood as an image of forces that seem threatening: chaos, nations, or dangers. Some think of enemy powers; the text does not make this clear. Even so, God's throne remains firm.

When your troubles sound like enormous waves, remember that they are not greater than God. Today you can pray sincerely, tell him what worries you, and trust that he still reigns, even when everything around you is stirred up.
exp.11:7:
It says that the wicked are found everywhere, moving about freely, just when the most worthless and despicable people are placed in positions of honor. The phrase "walk on every side" means they prowl around or go in circles. "Exalted" means lifted up, raised to positions of importance. The "vilest men" are those of low conduct and no moral worth.

The psalm is attributed to David, and it is a prayer in times of lying, deceit, and oppression of the poor. The verses before it contrast the false words of people with the pure words of God, compared to silver refined seven times. Some understand the idea of the wicked surrounding the righteous as a threat against them; the Hebrew text is brief and allows for nuances.

When you see that injustice triumphs and that people without integrity are admired, do not lose hope. Hold on to the Word of God, which is firm and trustworthy, and try to live with honesty even when no one applauds you.
exp.129:3:
This verse says that God has forgiveness at hand, always available. "But" is the word that connects this line to what comes before it, and "that thou mayest be feared" means "so that you may be held in reverence." Here "fear" does not mean being afraid, but respecting God with awe and gratitude, because he forgives.

The one speaking is a believer who cries out to God from a very deep place, as the beginning of the psalm says. He knows himself to be a sinner and recognizes that, if God kept a record of our faults, no one could stand. That is why what sustains him is the hope in God's forgiveness, and why he keeps waiting for it with patience, like the watchman waiting for the morning. This is one of the psalms called "songs of ascents," which were sung when going up to Jerusalem, although we do not know for certain who wrote it.

When you fail, do not hide from God. Come near with sincerity, trusting that his forgiveness is close, and let that lead you to love and respect him more.
exp.70:15:
He says the psalmist will go in the midst of the mighty acts of the Lord. "Mighty acts" here means deeds of strength and power. "I will go" in this verse is like saying "I will present myself" or "I will walk in trust." And "I will make mention of thy righteousness, even of thine only" means that he will remember and speak of God's righteousness alone, not his own. The word "only" stresses that there is no other basis for trust.

The speaker is an elderly believer who looks back and sees how God has guided him since his youth. The psalm does not say who wrote it, so we cannot be certain. He is going through hardship, and so he asks that God not abandon him in old age. Even so, he decides to keep hoping and to keep speaking of what God has done.

For today: when you feel weak or tired, do not lean on your own merits. Remember how God has been faithful to you, and tell someone younger or your family about it.
exp.42:3:
He says the psalmist wants to draw near to God's altar, whom he calls "my exceeding joy," that is, the deepest source of his joy. There he will praise him with the harp, a stringed instrument. He repeats "my God" with affection and closeness. The verse's wording "Then will I go unto the altar" is an older form of expression, but its meaning is clear: "I will go" to the altar.

The psalm does not say who wrote it. The speaker feels far from the temple, oppressed by enemies and discouraged. He asks that God's light and truth guide him back into his presence. After this verse, he encourages himself to hope in God.

For today: when you are sad or tired, do not move away from God; draw near to him. Seek his presence in prayer, in the Bible, or with other believers, and praise him even when your spirits are low. He can restore your joy.
exp.48:18:
The explanation says that the rich and proud man of whom the psalm speaks, at his death, will join his ancestors, that is, he will go to the place of the dead. The phrase "he shall go to the generation of his fathers" is an old way of saying that he will be united with those who died before him. The phrase "they shall never see light" speaks of being left without the light of life; the verb is in the plural, and some understand it as "they", meaning those of that generation.

The psalm was written by a teacher of wisdom, among the sons of Korah, for those who are alarmed when they see rich people who trust in their possessions prosper. He reminds them that wealth cannot buy life, nor can it be carried into the grave.

For today: do not place your security in money, prestige, or applause. Ask yourself today what you are building that will last beyond this life, and entrust your life to God, who can indeed redeem the soul (v. 15).
exp.72:3:
The explanation says that, in the eyes of the psalmist, the wicked seem to suffer no pain when they die. The word "bands" refers to pains or sufferings that hold the sick person until death. So they die without anguish, and while they live, their strength (their body, their vigor) stays healthy and firm. Some translators understand the text differently, but the general idea is the same: they seem to have a calm life and a calm death.

The speaker is Asaph, or a psalmist from his group. He is confessing that he nearly lost his faith on seeing that the wicked prosper while he suffers. He feels envy, and for that reason he almost slipped. Later in the same psalm, he will understand their end when he enters the sanctuary of God.

For today: when you feel envy on seeing that others do well without caring about God, do not stay silent with that pain. Bring it to God honestly, as Asaph did, and seek his perspective. Appearances do not tell the whole story.
exp.87:13:
Here the psalmist asks God directly why He rejects him. The sense he has is that God has set him aside, and the question "why hidest thou thy face from me?" expresses his feeling that God has withdrawn and no longer looks on him with favor. Where the earlier verse says his prayer came early, before anything else, the wording conveys that his prayer reached God first, ahead of everything.

The one speaking is a sick and anguished man, identified in the title as Heman the Ezrahite. This psalm is unusual because it hardly ends in hope. He has prayed faithfully since youth, yet he still suffers and does not understand God's silence.

For today: if you are in a dark season, you can be honest with God. Bringing your questions and your pain to Him, without disguise, is also faith. Keep praying even when you feel no answer, and seek the support of other believers.
exp.118:87:
This verse is a prayer. The psalmist asks God: "Give me life again, according to your mercy." "Quicken me" means "restore my strength, courage, and life," so I have removed that phrase and the translation shows the verse's own wording instead. The "mercy" here speaks of God's faithful love and goodness. Then he promises that he will keep the testimony of God's mouth, that is, he will obey what God has said in his Word.

The speaker is the author of Psalm 119, a believer who loves God's law. We do not know with certainty who he was. In the verses before this one he says that he is being persecuted without cause and has nearly been overcome, but he has not abandoned God's commandments. For that reason he asks for help and renewal.

For today: when you feel tired or discouraged, ask God to renew you, trusting in his kindness and not in your own merits. And let his Word be your daily guide, even in difficult days.
exp.104:4:
This verse invites us to remember. "Remember" is the word the reader sees in the verse, and it means to keep in mind. We are asked to keep in mind the marvellous works God did, his wonders (astonishing and powerful deeds), and the judgments of his mouth, that is, the decisions and commands God declared, his words with authority.

The psalm does not say who wrote it. Part of it appears in 1 Chronicles 16, where it is linked with David, though there is no certainty about who composed it. The one speaking calls Israel, the descendants of Abraham and Jacob, to praise God. They recall their history: how God cared for his people and kept his covenant.

For today: take a few minutes and write down three things God has done in your life or in your family. Give thanks for them, and read that list again when you feel tired or full of doubt. Remembering strengthens trust.
exp.63:3:
The explanation says that the wicked shoot their arrows from hidden places against an honest person. "Shoot in secret" means to fire arrows unseen, and the one at whom they shoot is someone upright, with no deceit. They attack him suddenly, without warning, and feel no fear or shame for what they do.

The speaker is David, according to the title of the psalm. He is asking God to protect him from enemies who plot in secret. The verses before this one show that their arrows are bitter words: slander and accusations thrown out behind people's backs. The verses that follow say these men encourage one another, thinking that no one sees them.

For today: if someone harms you with gossip or criticism behind your back, do not answer in kind. Bring your pain to God in prayer, for He sees what is hidden. And guard your own tongue, so that it never becomes an arrow aimed at others.
exp.101:13:
What it says: God's servants feel such affection for Zion (Jerusalem) that they cherish even its stones and show pity for its dust. Here "pity" means tender grief and care for something dear that lies in ruins. The stones are the remains of its walls and buildings.

Context: The psalmist is a person in distress who prays in the midst of great anguish. Many believe he writes in a time of destruction or exile, though the psalm does not give the exact date. He asks that God arise and show mercy to Zion. His love for the city shows his faith: he trusts that God will restore what has fallen and that the appointed time has come.

For today: We can love the church and its people even when they appear broken or worn down. Instead of criticizing or withdrawing, let us pray and serve with tenderness, trusting that God knows how to raise up and rebuild what seems like dust.
exp.35:3:
It says that the wicked person does not even rest from his wickedness. "Plots wickedness upon his bed" means that, instead of sleeping in peace or thinking with uprightness, he plans evil while lying in his bed. "Sets himself in a way that is not good" means that he holds firmly to a crooked course of conduct. And "he abhorreth not evil" shows that he feels no revulsion toward what is wrong; it already seems normal to him.

The psalm is by David, and it begins by describing the wickedness of the ungodly person, who has no fear of God (v. 1). Then, in the verses that follow, the tone changes completely, and David praises the steadfast love, faithfulness, and righteousness of the LORD. This contrast makes the message stronger: human wickedness is deep, but God's love is greater.

For today: take care what you think about in the stillness of the night. Before you sleep, bring your thoughts before God and ask him to teach you to hate what is evil and to love what is good.
exp.57:4:
It says that the deaf serpent does not listen to the voice of the charmers, no matter how skillful the one who plays or sings. The "charmers" here refers to those who try to master the serpent with sounds or words. The "adder" is a poisonous viper. The image shows people who refuse to hear, even when they are spoken to with skill.

David (the psalm bears his name) speaks against unjust rulers or judges, who decree wickedness and lie. He compares them to poisonous, deaf serpents. It is not a mere outpouring of feeling: he cries out to God to stop their violence, because they will not let themselves be corrected by any person.

For today: when someone hardens his heart, do not wear yourself out trying to persuade him with more arguments. Speak with truth and love, but entrust the situation to God. And examine your own hearing: ask him to always keep you willing to listen to his correction.
exp.120:2:
He says that God will not let your foot slip or let you stumble and fall. A slippery place is a spot where one loses footing, a dangerous piece of ground. He also says that the one who keeps you, God himself, never falls asleep or becomes careless about you.

This is a song of ascents, one of the psalms the people sang as they went up to Jerusalem. Scholars debate who is speaking: it may be the traveler speaking to himself, or someone answering him with encouragement. The roads through the hills were hard and dangerous, so the promise of care was very concrete for someone walking them.

Today you can rest in the fact that God is not distracted and does not grow weary. When you feel fear about the future or about a difficult decision, pray and hand that worry over to him. Then sleep peacefully, because he remains awake, watching over you.
exp.39:7:
It says that David finds joy, not burden, in doing what God wants. The phrase "I delight" expresses that he takes pleasure in it. The innermost part of a person, the heart, is where God's law is not only written in a book but placed within him.

The verse is part of a psalm of thanksgiving for having been rescued. David says that God does not seek only sacrifices, but an obedient heart. The book mentioned may be Scripture. Hebrews 10:5-10 quotes these verses and applies them to Christ, who fulfilled the Father's will.

Today, instead of seeing obedience as an obligation, ask God to give you delight in his Word. Read a short passage each day and keep one phrase in your heart to put into practice.
exp.79:5:
He says that God allowed the neighboring nations to fight and quarrel over Israel, as people quarrel over something they are disputing. Moreover, the enemies laugh and mock the people among themselves. "Strife" means a dispute or quarrel.

The speaker is the psalmist Asaph, on behalf of the whole people. It is a prayer of lament: Israel is suffering, feels abandoned, and asks God how long this will continue. It is not stated with certainty what historical moment is meant; scholars have understood it in several ways. What follows is a cry for help: "turn us again," that is, restore us.

When you feel humiliated or mocked, you can bring that pain to God honestly, without pretending to strength. The psalm teaches us to complain before Him and to ask for His face, His favor, because only He can restore.
exp.29:11:
The psalmist, filled with gratitude, vows to sing praise to God and not remain silent. He calls his own soul, or the most precious part of his being, "my glory," which now joins in praise. "Lord" is the name of God, and "to you" is simply "to you." He promises to praise him forever.

The speaker is David, according to the heading of the psalm. Earlier he was in sorrow, and so he spoke of lament and of mourning clothes. God turned his sorrow into dancing and joy. This verse is the response: giving thanks out loud. Some understand it to refer to an illness or danger, but the text does not specify.

Today we can take a moment to remember something specific that God has done for us and thank him out loud or with a song. Let us not keep our gratitude in silence: telling it strengthens our faith and encourages others.
exp.71:0:
This verse is a prayer. The writer asks God to give the king his judgments, that is, his just way of deciding and governing. He also asks that God's righteousness be given to the king's son, who would be the heir to the throne. The title "A Psalm for Solomon" can mean "of Solomon," "for Solomon," or "about Solomon," since the Hebrew text allows several readings.

The one speaking is the psalmist, who intercedes for the king. It is not known with certainty whether David, Solomon, or someone else wrote it. The verses that follow give the reason: that the king would rule justly toward the afflicted and that there would be peace in the land. Many Christians also see in this a look ahead to Jesus, the perfect King.

For today: pray for those who hold authority, in your country, your workplace, or your family, that they would act justly and care for the weakest. If you have some authority yourself, ask God for that same justice.
exp.38:2:
David says that his heart burned within him. As he kept thinking and turning over his pain, it was as if a fire were kindled, and at last he could no longer keep silent and spoke.

David wrote this psalm and dedicated it to the chief musician, Jeduthun. He had decided to keep quiet and not sin with his words, especially in front of wicked people. But staying silent did not take away his pain; it built up inside him. Then he speaks, and what he says is not a complaint against others, but a prayer to God about how brief life is.

For today: when you feel that pain is burning inside you, do not keep it bottled up until it explodes, and do not unload it on others. Bring it to God in prayer with honesty. He can hear what you should not say to anyone else.
exp.106:26:
This verse describes sailors caught in a violent storm. They reel and stagger like drunken people, unable to keep their footing. The word "wits" here refers to their skill and experience; the phrase says that all their seamanship comes to an end, they are "at their wits' end." They no longer know what to do.

The psalmist speaks to the community that returned from exile or from dangers, inviting them to give thanks to God. In this section (vv. 23-32) he recalls those who cross the sea. The storm comes at God's word, and the sailors reach the limit of their strength. But the next verse shows the turn: they cry out to the LORD and He rescues them.

For today: there are moments when our experience, our plans, and our strength are not enough. It is not shameful to reach that point. It is the place where we can cry out to God with sincerity, trusting that He hears and can calm the storm.
exp.36:16:
What it says: The "arms" represent strength and power. It says that the power of the wicked will be broken, that is, destroyed. By contrast, the righteous, that is, those who live uprightly before God, are upheld by the Lord, who is called here by his covenant name. The Lord upholds them.

Context: This is a psalm of David, written in the tone of wise counsel. He encourages those who see the wicked prospering and feel anger or envy. He reminds them that this advantage does not last. The verses before speak of swords and bows that turn against the wicked, and the verses after promise care and an inheritance for the faithful.

For today: When you feel weak in the face of injustice, do not place your trust in human strength. Pray, do what is right even when it costs you, and rest in the knowledge that God upholds you.
exp.32:12:
This verse says that God looks down from heaven and sees all people, leaving no one out. The word "saw" is from an older form of the language; here the verse uses "beholdeth," which means he looks at or observes. "Sons of men" means human beings, all of humanity, not only one people.

Psalm 33 is a song of praise, and this text does not say who wrote it; tradition has attributed it to David, but that is not certain. The psalmist invites the people to praise God, who created the world and governs history. Before this verse he speaks of God's eternal plans and the blessedness of the people He chose. Now he reminds us that God also watches over everyone else.

For today: when you feel overlooked or alone, remember that God sees you. You can also look at others with more respect, because God sees them and values them just as He values you.
exp.109:1:
The explanation says that God himself extends the power of the King, whom David calls "my Lord." The "rod" is the scepter, the symbol of authority. That power goes out of Zion, that is, Jerusalem. And the King is commanded to rule in the midst of those who oppose him.

David writes this psalm and speaks of another whom he calls "my Lord." First the Lord promises him victory over his enemies. Jesus quoted the beginning of this psalm to show that the Messiah is more than a simple descendant of David, and the New Testament applies it to Christ.

For today: although it sometimes seems that evil is winning, Christ truly reigns. We can rest in his authority, pray with hope, and obey him without fear, trusting that his kingdom does not depend on our strength.
exp.143:6:
The explanation says that David asks God to stretch out his mighty hand from heaven to rescue him. "Rescue" means free, and "the great waters" is an image of dangers that nearly drown him. The "strange children" are foreigners, people who are outside of God and his people. The "arrows" are darts.

David, king of Israel, speaks in the middle of enemies who lie and do not keep their word. First he asks that God come down like a storm, with mountains smoking and lightning flashing. Then he promises to sing him a new song. Some think the psalm recalls past victories; the text does not make this entirely clear.

For today: when you feel sunk under problems or under people who deceive you, do not carry it alone. Pray openly, asking God for help, and decide to thank him ahead of time, even before you see the answer.
exp.29:7:
The explanation says that the psalmist, in his distress, does not stay silent or manage on his own. He cries out, calling loudly and urgently, and he makes his plea with humility, begging for help. He addresses God by two names: the personal name of God, and "Lord," which expresses that He commands and cares for His people.

The one speaking is David, according to the title of the psalm, which speaks of the dedication of the house, although it is not known with certainty what exact moment it refers to. Before this, he felt secure and thought nothing would shake him. Then God hid His face, that is, he felt that God's favor was gone, and he was deeply troubled. So he returns to God with pleas, and then asks for mercy and help.

For today: when you feel shaken, do not wait until you are strong to pray. Speak to God with sincerity, tell Him what you feel, and ask for His help. He hears us, and prayer reminds us that our security comes from Him, not from our circumstances.
exp.68:27:
This verse is a prayer in which the psalmist asks that his enemies be "blotted out" of the "book of the living." He also asks that they not be written alongside the "righteous," who are the people who are upright before God. It is strong language, speaking of being removed from the company of those who belong to God.

The speaker is David, or a psalmist who suffers injustice. He is worn out, mocked, and pursued, and he cries out to God for justice. The image of the "book" appears in other passages of the Bible, and scholars understand it in different ways: as present life or as life with God. For that reason there is no single certain explanation. This is a psalm of pain, and the next verse shows that the psalmist ends up trusting God.

For today: when you are hurt, you can bring your pain and your anger honestly to God, and leave justice in his hands, without taking revenge yourself.
exp.88:29:
This verse says that if the children of King David leave God's law and do not live according to his judgments (that is, his just decisions and commands), there will be consequences. Here "judgments" does not mean punishments, but the rules and teachings God gave to guide life.

God speaks in this psalm, which recalls the promise he made to David: that his family would reign forever. It is a firm covenant. But God makes clear that this promise does not remove responsibility: if the descendants turn away from him, they will receive correction, as the following verse says. God corrects, but he does not abandon his promise.

For today: God's faithfulness is no excuse for living carelessly. We can trust in his love and, at the same time, take his word seriously. Today, choose a biblical teaching you have neglected and put it into practice this week.
exp.104:20:
It says that the king of Egypt put Joseph in charge of his house, and as ruler over all that he owned. The phrase "he made him" is the sense here, and the word for ruler means one who governs and holds authority. Joseph went from being a prisoner to being the manager of everything.

The psalmist recalls the history of Israel to praise God. He speaks of Joseph, sold by his brothers and imprisoned in Egypt. The verses before this one say that God tested him until the appointed time arrived. Then the pharaoh set him free. The psalm shows that God was caring for his people even when everything seemed lost.

For today: when you go through a hard wait or an injustice, do not think that God has forgotten you. Stay faithful and responsible in small things, as Joseph did, and trust that God knows when and how to raise you up to serve others.
exp.37:20:
Here the psalmist begs God not to leave him alone or stay far from him. "Forsake" means to abandon or leave without help. "Be not far from me" asks God to stay close, present and attentive. It is a simple, direct cry, spoken with confidence: he calls him "LORD" and also "my God."

The psalm is attributed to David, and it is called a prayer to bring something to remembrance. It speaks of a man who suffers because of his own sins, from sickness or deep pain, and also from the attacks of enemies who hate him without cause. He says they repay him evil for good, even though he tries to do what is right. Scholars do not agree on the exact moment in his life when he wrote it.

When you feel alone, wounded, or misunderstood, do not keep silent. Tell God honestly: "Do not leave me." He invites us to pray this way, even in the midst of weakness.
exp.136:2:
It says that the Babylonians, who had taken the Israelites away as prisoners and destroyed their land, asked them to sing and be happy so as to entertain them. The word "wasted" in the verse means leaving someone ruined and with nothing. The phrase "sing us one of the songs" is simply asking them to sing. And "mirth" here refers to songs of joy meant to amuse.

It speaks of an Israelite exiled in Babylon, probably after the fall of Jerusalem (586 B.C.). His grief was deep: they missed Zion and had hung up their harps. The captors asked for sacred songs as if they were a show, and that hurt them. Scholars do not know exactly when the psalm was written, but it clearly comes out of the exile.

For today: when you are in pain, you do not have to pretend to be joyful to please others. God accepts your sincere lament. And take care that your praise is not a performance, but something that comes from the heart.
exp.107:6:
God speaks from his sanctuary, that is, from his holy place, and joyfully promises that he will divide Shechem and measure out the valley of Succoth. "I will rejoice" expresses the joy with which he makes this promise. "Divide" speaks of dividing the land in order to hand it over.

The psalm is attributed to David. After praising God, he asks for help and hears a divine answer. Shechem lies west of the Jordan and Succoth lies east of it, so together they represent the whole promised land. Some translations read "in his holiness" instead of "from his sanctuary." In either case, the idea is that the land belongs to God and that he is the one who distributes it.

For today: when you face a situation that seems uncertain, remember that God has the final word. Before deciding out of fear, pray, read his Word, and trust that he is able to fulfill what he has promised.
exp.68:13:
Here the psalmist asks God to pull him out of the mud so that he does not sink, and to rescue him from those who hate him and from the deep waters. "Mud" and "waters" are images of danger and distress. To be "sunk" means to be pulled down or swallowed up.

David is the one who writes, according to the title of the psalm. He is suffering mockery and rejection, even from respected people who used to sit at the city gate. After being humiliated, he prays to God and trusts in his mercy. Some see here a foreshadowing of Christ's suffering, and the New Testament quotes other verses from this psalm.

For today: when you feel yourself sinking into problems or criticism, do not stay silent. Ask God for help sincerely, and trust that his mercy is firmer than any mud.
exp.16:11:
The explanation says that David's enemies are like a hungry lion that wants to seize its prey, and like a young lion waiting hidden to attack by surprise. With the image of two lions, both open strength and the hidden trap are shown.

David is the one speaking, and he prays to God asking for protection. He is surrounded by proud men, hardened and insensitive, full of themselves, who seek to bring him down. We do not know with certainty what exact moment of his life the psalm reflects; some think of Saul's pursuit, but the text does not say so.

For today: not every danger comes head-on; sometimes evil is silent and well disguised. Ask God for wisdom to discern, and trust that He takes care of you, even when you do not see the threat.
exp.88:15:
This verse says that God's people are filled with joy all day long because of who God is, and that they are lifted up or raised high by God's righteousness, not by their own merits. The word "exalted" means lifted up, honored. "In thy name" refers to his character and to what he has shown of himself.

The psalm is written by Ethan the Ezrahite, according to its heading. Before this verse, it praises God because his throne rests on righteousness and justice, and because mercy and truth go before him. It speaks of a blessed people who walk in the light of God's face. Afterward, the psalm says that God is their strength, their shield, and their king.

For today: when you feel tired or insecure, do not place your joy in your achievements. Take a moment during the day to remember who God is: just, faithful, and merciful. Give thanks for that, and let that trust sustain you.
exp.114:12:
This verse says that God will bless all who revere and honor him. "Fearing the Lord" does not mean living in terror of him, but holding him in reverence and trust. The phrase "both small and great" means that no one is left out: neither the little ones nor the great ones, neither those of little importance nor those of much.

Psalm 115 is a prayer and song of the people of Israel, probably used in communal worship. It is not known with certainty who wrote it or at what exact moment. First it compares the living God with idols that can do nothing, and then it encourages the people to trust the LORD.
