This verse extends the promise to everyone who fears him, not only to Israel or to the priests.

For today: God does not measure people by their age, their position, or their achievements. You can draw near to him with confidence, whatever your situation. Today, place yourself in his hands with respect and gratitude, and remember that his blessing is for you too.
exp.119:3:
It says that the punishment for the lying tongue will be like sharp arrows shot by a strong warrior, together with glowing coals of juniper. The "arrows" are the sharp arrows of the mighty. The juniper is a shrub (some translate it as "broom bush") whose wood, it is understood, burns for a long time and gives very hot embers.

The one speaking is the psalmist, who cries out to God for having suffered lies and deceit. In verse 3 he asks what the deceitful tongue will receive, and here he answers: a sure and painful punishment. It is a pilgrim psalm, and the author feels surrounded by people who do not want peace. Some see the arrows and the coals as God's judgment; others see them as an image of how harmful false words are.

For today: lies wound and burn, so do not respond with deceit. Entrust your pain to God, ask him for justice, and take care that your own words are true and bring peace.
exp.108:5:
It says to set a wicked person over him as an accuser, and to let the adversary stand at his right hand. The word "wicked" refers to someone who lives without reverence for God. The phrase "at his right hand" means at his side, the place where the accuser would stand in a trial. The word "Satan" can also be translated as "accuser" or "adversary."

The speaker is the psalmist, traditionally David. They have repaid him with hatred and lies, although he answered them with love and prayer. These verses are a cry for justice, spoken out of pain. Some think that from here to verse 19 the psalmist is quoting the curses of his enemies against him; others believe these are his own words. Both readings are possible.

For today: when you are treated unjustly, do as the psalmist did: bring your pain to God with complete honesty and leave justice in his hands, without taking revenge. Jesus also taught us to pray for those who harm us.
exp.24:1:
This verse is a prayer of trust. David tells God that he places all his security in Him. He asks that he not be "ashamed," that is, humiliated or disappointed, as if trusting God had been a mistake. He also asks that his enemies not rejoice at seeing him fall.

The speaker is David, and this is one of his psalms. It begins by saying that he lifts up his soul to God, that is, that he presents himself before Him with his whole being. He feels threatened by enemies, although the text does not say who they were or at what exact moment he wrote it. The verses that follow affirm that whoever waits on God will not be confounded.

For today: when you feel pressured or fear that you will come out looking foolish, do not hold on to that fear. Bring it to God honestly, as David did, and ask Him to teach you His ways. Trusting does not mean denying fear, but bringing it to God.
exp.135:18:
This verse recalls that God defeated Sihon, king of the Amorites. The Amorites lived to the east of the Jordan River. The phrase "for his mercy endureth for ever" means that his faithful and constant love never ends.

The psalm is a song of praise that the people of Israel sang, probably in worship, with a choir answering after each verse. It reviews what God did: he created the world, brought Israel out of Egypt, and gave them a land. The victory over Sihon and Og took place before entering Canaan (Numbers 21). The psalm sees in that victory an act of God's faithfulness toward his people.

For today: remember the times God sustained you in situations that seemed impossible. Write them down and thank him. Remembering his past faithfulness strengthens confidence to face today's challenges.
exp.88:16:
This verse says that God himself is the glory of his people's strength. Their strength does not come from them, but from him. The image of the "horn" stood for power and victory, like the horn of a bull. The phrase "our horn shall be exalted" means that God will lift them up and give them dignity and strength. "Favour" is his goodwill, his pleasure in them.

The psalmist, called Ethan the Ezrahite in the title, sings praises to God and remembers his covenant with David. He speaks on behalf of the people of Israel. First he celebrates those who know how to praise God; then he says that the LORD is their shield and their king. Everything prepares the remembrance of the promise made to David.

For today: do not rely only on your own abilities. Recognize that your strength and your achievements are a gift from God's kindness, and thank him every day.
exp.104:12:
The explanation says that Israel's ancestors, namely Abraham, Isaac and Jacob with their families, went from one place to another, passing through different nations and kingdoms. The phrase "from one nation to another" means "from one people to another." They had no fixed home but lived as travelers, without land of their own.

The psalmist is recalling Israel's history in order to praise God for his faithfulness. God had promised them the land of Canaan, but they were few and foreigners. Even so, the next verse says that God did not allow anyone to harm them, and that he even rebuked kings on their account. The texts speak of episodes such as Abraham's dealings with Pharaoh and with Abimelech.

For today: at times we feel insecure, passing through, or without a clear direction. This verse reminds us that God cares for his people even on uncertain paths. We can trust that his promises still stand as we go forward.
exp.72:0:
It says that God is truly good to Israel, that is, to his people, and especially to "those who are clean in heart," those who seek him with sincerity and without duplicity. The word "truly" shows a firm conviction. "Asaph" is the name that appears in the heading of the psalm.

The one speaking is Asaph, or a psalmist connected with his name, and nothing more precise can be established. It begins with a truth that he holds clearly, but soon admits that he nearly stumbled, because he felt envy on seeing the wicked prosper. The psalm arises from that inner struggle.

For today: when life seems unfair and others prosper without caring about God, begin by remembering what you know of him: he is good. Say it in prayer, even when your feelings tremble. That truth can sustain you while you seek answers.
exp.106:7:
This verse invites people to thank God for his mercy, that is, his goodness and compassion, and for the wonderful works he has done on behalf of humanity. Its call to praise is addressed to the whole people of God, and it is meant to be spoken out loud by those who have received his care.

The psalmist has just described travelers lost in the desert who cried out to God and were led to a city where they could live. This is a refrain that repeats several times in the psalm, after each story of rescue. The verses that follow speak of hungry people being filled and prisoners being set free.

Today we can remember the times God helped us, even in small things. This week, write down three of them and give thanks for them out loud, perhaps sharing them with someone in your family or your church.
exp.142:0:
Here David speaks to God with simplicity and urgency. He asks God to hear his prayer and his pleas, that is, his supplications. He appeals to two qualities of God: his faithfulness to his promises, and his righteousness, his right and good way of acting.

The title says it is a psalm of David. The verses that follow show that he is distressed: an enemy pursues him and he feels as if he is in darkness. It is not known with certainty at what point in his life he wrote it; some connect it with the flight from Absalom, but that is only a possibility. Note that David does not rest on his own merits, but on the character of God.

When you are in trouble, pray with candor and trust in what God is like, not in how good you are. You can say: "Lord, you are faithful; hear me."
exp.45:9:
It says we should stop, be still, and recognize that God is God. "Be still" can also be understood as "stop struggling" or "let go." God promises that he will be exalted among all nations and throughout the earth.

The one speaking here is God himself, addressing a people surrounded by threats. The psalm describes a world in chaos, but also a God who stops wars, breaks the bow, and burns the chariots. Some think it refers to a historical event, others that it announces a final peace; the text does not make this clear. Its message is that God is in control and is a refuge for his people.

For today: when you feel distressed, take a pause of a few minutes, breathe deeply, and pray, saying: "Lord, you are God, I am not." Hand over that worry and trust that he still governs.
exp.106:20:
This verse is an invitation: that people would praise God for his mercy, that is, his faithful love and his compassion, and for the wonderful things he does for human beings. The phrase "children of men" is an old way of saying "people." "Lord" is the name of God.

The psalm does not name its author. It is a song of thanksgiving for those whom God rescued from various dangers. It speaks of people who cried out in their distress, and God sent his word, healed them, and delivered them from destruction. That is why the psalmist repeats this call to give thanks. This verse recurs as a refrain in other parts of the psalm.

Today we can remember the times God helped us, even when the help was simple. Take a moment this week to thank him out loud and, if you can, tell someone what he has done for you.
exp.85:14:
The verse says that God is compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love and truth. "Merciful" here means that he forgives and treats people with tenderness. "Mercy" is compassion that acts on behalf of the one in need. "Slow to anger" means that God is patient.

David speaks, according to the title of the psalm. He is surrounded by proud and violent people who pursue him and do not respect God. In the middle of the danger, David remembers what God is like, and with these words, which recall what God said about himself in Exodus 34:6, he supports his plea for help.

For today: when you are afraid or have failed, do not begin by looking at the problem, but at the character of God. Say to him in prayer: "You are patient, compassionate, and faithful," and then ask him for help with confidence.
exp.106:42:
This verse asks a question for each reader to consider: who is wise enough to remember and keep in their heart what they have just read? The phrase "keep these things" means holding them in mind and taking them seriously. The "lovingkindness" refers to the acts of faithful love and kindness of God toward his people.

The psalm does not say who wrote it. It is a song of thanksgiving that repeats how God rescued different groups: people lost in the wilderness, prisoners, the sick, and sailors caught in a storm. Each time they cried out, and he delivered them. This last verse closes the psalm by inviting us to reflect on all of that and to learn from it.

Today we can make a habit of remembering. Each week, write down one time when God helped you, even if it was small. That way, when hard days come, you will keep his faithfulness in mind and trust him more.
exp.24:6:
This verse is a prayer. The psalmist asks God not to remember the sins of his youth, nor his transgressions, meaning the times he rebelled against Him. Instead, he asks God to remember him according to His mercy, or compassion, and for His goodness.

The psalm is attributed to David, although some scholars debate how it was composed. The one speaking feels in need of guidance and forgiveness. Earlier he asked to be taught in God's truth, and afterward he acknowledges that God is good and teaches the humble. His confidence rests on the character of God, not on his own merits.

When your past weighs on you, you can pray with sincerity, without excuses, and lean on God's mercy. Ask Him for forgiveness and direction, and trust that He guides those who come to Him in humility.
exp.105:12:
It says that the people of Israel, soon after being rescued, were quick to forget what God had done. The phrase "they soon forgat" means they forgot very quickly. "His works" refers to God's miracles, such as parting the sea. "They waited not for his counsel" means they did not have the patience to wait for God's guidance and plan.

The psalmist reviews the history of Israel to acknowledge the people's sins and God's faithfulness. This verse comes right after crossing the Red Sea, when they sang songs of praise. But that faith did not last long: soon they craved things eagerly in the wilderness and put God to the test.

For today: when God helps you in a difficult moment, do not let it fade from your memory. Write down what He has done and go over it again when the next time of waiting comes. That will help you trust and not act in haste.
exp.135:15:
It says that God guided and cared for his people the way a shepherd looks after his sheep while they walked through the desert. "Led" means that he guided them, fed them, and protected them. And again and again the psalm repeats that his mercy (his faithful love and steady goodness) endures forever.

Psalm 136 is a sung prayer, most likely used in the worship of the people of Israel. The speaker recalls what God did: the departure from Egypt, the crossing of the sea, and the years in the wilderness. After this the psalm mentions the conquest of lands. Scholars do not know for certain who wrote this psalm or when it was first used.

When you go through dry or uncertain times, remember how God has cared for you before. You can write down three moments when you felt his help and give him thanks, trusting that his love does not run out.
exp.135:0:
This verse invites us to give thanks and praise to God for two reasons: He is good, and His mercy endures forever. The word "Alabad," which means "praise," and "Jehová," the name of God in the Old Testament, are not in the verse your reader sees, so they are left out here. The word translated as "mercy" here comes from a Hebrew word that speaks of a faithful, loyal love that does not abandon. Other versions translate it as "steadfast love" or "goodness."

It is the opening of a psalm that does not name its author. It seems to be a song for the people of Israel, perhaps used in worship at the temple. This is evident because every verse repeats the phrase "his mercy endures forever," like a response that the congregation sang. The psalm recalls what God did for his people: creation and deliverance from Egypt.

Today we can begin the day by remembering one concrete way God has been faithful to you, and giving him thanks out loud. In this way your confidence rests on his steady love, not on your changing circumstances.
exp.17:34:
God says he gave David the shield of his salvation (the word "salvation" here means rescue or deliverance). His right hand held David up, meaning his power kept him steady. And his gentleness, his goodness and kindness, made David great. Some translations say "your humility" or "your condescension," and this can be understood as God bending down with care toward him.

David speaks here, according to the psalm's heading, after the Lord rescued him from his enemies and from Saul. It is a song of thanksgiving. Before and after, he describes how God trained him for battle, strengthened him, and gave him victory. He acknowledges that he did not win alone.

For today: when you achieve something or come out of a trial, give thanks to God. Recognize his protection, his support, and his goodness, and do not rely only on your own strength.
exp.44:13:
She is brought to the king in richly embroidered clothing. Behind her come young virgins, her companions, who are also presented to the king. The phrase "following her" means the companions come after her in the procession.

This psalm is a song for a royal wedding. The writer first addresses the king and then the bride, and here he describes the wedding procession. Many read it as a poem for a king of Israel. The New Testament applies part of the psalm to Christ (Hebrews 1:8-9), and for this reason many Christians see in the bride a picture of the church. Others read it only as a wedding poem. Both readings are possible.

For today: God invites us to come before Him with a clean and joyful heart, not with outward appearances. And we can approach Him accompanied, encouraging others to walk with Him.
exp.108:26:
He says David wants his enemies to recognize that the help he receives comes from God. The word "hand" refers to God's power and action. "Done it" refers to his deliverance. The desire is that no one would think it was chance or human strength.

David speaks, according to the title of the psalm, in the middle of false accusations and mockery. He feels despised and asks God to save him for his mercy's sake, not because of his own merits. This psalm contains very harsh requests against his adversaries. Some see it as a cry for justice entrusted to God, and others read it with more caution, but the center here is that God shows himself as defender.

For today: when you face an injustice, instead of taking revenge, pray and entrust the situation to God. When help arrives, give him the credit so that others notice it.
exp.79:11:
Here the psalmist asks God a painful question. The phrase "you have broken down her walls" means that God tore down the walls or fences that protected the vineyard. Because of this, anyone who passes by the road can pick its grapes. The phrase "gather the harvest" means that they strip the crop.

The psalm is sung by an Israelite, perhaps on behalf of the whole people. The vineyard is an image of Israel, which God brought out of Egypt and planted, and which grew very large. Now the people are battered and plundered by other nations. The exact author and the historical moment are not certain, and several different periods have been proposed. What is clear is that the people cry out, asking for restoration.

For today: when you feel unprotected or mistreated, you can bring your questions to God honestly, as this psalmist does. Praying with sincerity is also an act of trust.
exp.135:19:
This verse says that God also defeated Og, king of Bashan, and that he did so because his mercy endures forever. Bashan was a fertile region east of the Jordan River.

It is part of a song of praise that the people of Israel sang, probably in worship. A leader would say each line and the congregation would answer: "his mercy endures forever." The psalm recalls how God brought Israel out of Egypt, led them through the wilderness, and gave them the land. Defeating Sihon and Og was seen as a sign of God's care for his people.

For today: remember the times God has sustained you in situations that seemed too big. Thank him by name, as the psalm does, and trust that his mercy does not run out in the face of new problems.
exp.143:13:
This verse asks that the oxen, which helped with plowing and hauling, be strong enough to do their work. It also asks that there be no breaking in, no going out, and no cries of alarm in the streets, that is, in the open spaces of the town. The meaning of "breaking in" and "going out" is not entirely clear: it could refer to an enemy raid or to people being led away, and the verse does not settle which.

The psalm is traditionally attributed to David. The speaker prays to God for protection from enemies and then for blessing on the whole people: healthy children, abundant harvests, and peace. It is a prayer for a quiet and prosperous life.

For today: ask God for peace and provision for your family and your community, and thank him for what you already have. Work faithfully, but remember that your true security lies in the Lord being your God.
exp.59:4:
It says that David asks God to rescue those whom He loves. The "beloved" are God's dear ones, His people. "Your right hand" is His right hand, a symbol of His power. "Hear me" is a plea, a short and direct prayer.

David, king of Israel, speaks in a psalm of lament after a military defeat. The earlier verses speak of hard blows and of a cup of staggering, that is, a suffering that left them reeling like drunkards. Even so, David remembers that God gave them a banner, a sign of hope. After this request, God answers and promises victory over the lands of Israel.

For today: when you feel defeated or confused, do not keep silent or try to manage alone. Speak with God honestly, ask Him for concrete help, and trust that He hears you as a beloved child.
exp.67:32:
It says that God rides upon the highest heavens, which have existed since ancient times. When He speaks, His voice sounds with strength and power. The phrase about His voice giving forth a voice of strength means that His voice is mighty, like thunder. The expression about the heavens of heavens refers to the very highest part of the sky.

It is a psalm of David, a song of victory that praises God as king and warrior. The verses before it invite Egypt, Ethiopia, and all the kingdoms of the earth to sing to Him. The verses that follow ask us to acknowledge His strength, for He gives it to His people. Scholars understand the exact historical context of the psalm in different ways.

For today: when you feel weak or face very great problems, remember that God reigns from on high and His voice has power. Take a moment to praise Him and ask for the strength that He gives to His people.
exp.96:8:
This verse says that the Lord is far above all the earth. "High" speaks of his supreme authority, and "exalted" means that he is honored and placed in the highest place. The "gods" are the idols and powers that people worshiped.

The psalmist, whose name is not given, speaks in the middle of a song of praise to God's reign. Earlier, the psalm says that the idols are put to shame, and that Zion rejoices because of God's judgments, that is, because of his righteousness. Then it invites those who love God to hate evil, because he watches over his own.

Today we can ask ourselves what things are taking God's place in our hearts: money, success, or the opinion of others. This week, put God first in one specific decision and trust that he is above all.
exp.96:11:
The explanation says that the righteous should rejoice in God and give thanks as they recall his holiness. "Rejoice" is the verb in the verse above. "Give thanks" is the verb in the verse above. "The remembrance of his holiness" refers to recalling how holy and perfect God is, and what he has done.

The psalm does not say who wrote it. It celebrates that the Lord reigns and judges with justice. The verses before it encourage those who love him to turn away from evil, and promise that God watches over his faithful people and delivers them from the wicked. This verse closes the psalm with an invitation to joy.

For today: when you feel tired or worried, remember how God has cared for you and been faithful. Write it down or say it aloud, and give thanks. Joy does not depend on everything going well, but on who God is.
exp.106:24:
This verse says that God spoke and, by his word, caused a strong storm wind to rise. That wind made the waves of the sea grow. "He commandeth" means that his order was enough. "Raiseth" means that he made it rise up suddenly. "Waves" are the billows of the sea.

The psalmist speaks to the community of Israel that has been rescued. In this psalm he gives thanks to God for different groups of people who cried out in their distress and were delivered. Here he speaks of the sailors, who see the power of God on the sea. This verse shows that the storm does not escape his control. Some understand this as a test meant to lead people to depend on God.

For today: when a storm comes into your life, remember that God still reigns over it. Cry out to him with confidence, for the one who commands the wind can calm you and sustain you.
exp.89:8:
It says that our life is growing shorter day after day, and that this happens under God's wrath. "We spend our years as a tale that is told" means that life passes as quickly as a sigh or a thought that crosses the mind. Other versions say "as a sigh."

The psalm is presented as "a prayer of Moses, the man of God." It speaks on behalf of the people, who experience human frailty before an eternal God. The verses before it speak of sins that God sees clearly. Many understand that the "wrath" is connected with death as a consequence of sin. Some link it to the desert, but that is not stated with certainty.

For today: since life is brief, it is worth living it with humility, asking God for forgiveness and using each day well. Today you can set aside a few minutes to pray and ask God what matters most.
exp.36:7:
It says to let go of anger and release resentment.

It is a psalm of David, written as advice from an older man to the one listening. Before this, it says not to be troubled by seeing the wicked prosper, and to be still before God and wait on him. Afterward, it explains that the wicked will disappear and that those who trust in the LORD will inherit the land. The anger here comes from the envy or injustice one sees.

When something unjust troubles you, do not respond with rage or revenge. Breathe, pray, and hand the situation over to God. Trusting that he will bring justice helps you avoid doing something you later regret.
exp.117:24:
The explanation says that the people urgently plead with God: "Save now." They also ask him to "send now prosperity," that is, to grant success and well-being. The phrase "I beseech thee" is an older way of saying "I earnestly ask you," and both are simple and direct pleas.

This psalm is a song of thanksgiving and celebration, and it seems to have been sung in a procession toward the temple. The speakers are the people and their leaders, who have just seen the hand of God in a deliverance. Even so, they keep asking for his help. The verses that follow bless the one who comes in the name of the Lord. In the New Testament, the crowd uses these words when welcoming Jesus (Matthew 21:9).

We can give thanks for what God has already done and, at the same time, keep asking him for help with what lies ahead. Today, before you begin your tasks, say to him sincerely: "Lord, save me and guide me this day."
exp.97:5:
This verse invites us to praise God with great enthusiasm. "Shout" means to cry out with joy, as when someone important is welcomed. The "trumpet" here is a ram's horn, the shofar, which made a loud sound. In this verse it joins the trumpets to greet the Lord as King.

This psalm does not say who wrote it; it simply presents itself as a psalm. It is a song of praise that invites everyone, not only Israel, to celebrate God for his salvation and his justice. Earlier the harp and singing are mentioned, and then even the sea, the rivers and the mountains join the celebration. It is a poetic image of all creation praising.

Today we can praise God wholeheartedly, without shame or routine. This week, choose a song that fills you with gratitude and sing it with your whole heart, alone or with your family, acknowledging Jesus as King of your life.
exp.11:0:
The chief musician's note at the start of this verse says "upon Sheminith." It probably indicates a type of melody or instrument, though no one knows for certain; some think it means "octave." Then David cries out, "Help, Lord." He says that no longer are there any godly men, meaning good and compassionate people, nor any faithful ones, meaning loyal and trustworthy people.

David is the one speaking, and he does so in prayer. He feels surrounded by deceit and falsehood, as the following verses show: people lie and flatter with a double heart. We do not know the exact moment in his life when he wrote it. His complaint is naturally exaggerated, as is typical of someone who is deeply hurt, and later God answers that he will indeed protect the weak.

For today: when you feel discouraged by the falsehood you see, bring your complaint to God with sincerity. And ask him to help you be a faithful and compassionate person toward those around you.
exp.9:1:
The explanation says that the wicked, in his pride, pursues and oppresses the poor. But it also says that these wicked people will be caught in their own traps. The words for schemes and traps refer to clever plans or deceits; the verse's "devices" is the word used for them here, and the sentence about being caught in them is simply about being trapped by one's own plans.

The speaker is the psalmist, probably David, though the psalm does not say so. The lament comes from asking why God seems far away while he sees injustice. He is distressed and sincere, and he presents to God what he sees: powerful people who abuse the weak and live as if God did not exist.

For today: if you see injustice or suffer it, you can speak frankly to God about what you feel, as the psalmist did. And do not repay evil with evil. Trust that God sees, and help the needy person near you, with your voice, your time, or your resources.
exp.84:5:
Here the psalmist asks God whether he will not give them new life again. "Giving us life" means reviving, restoring, bringing back strength. And "will rejoice in you" means that the people will find their joy in God himself, not only in things going well.

The people of Israel speak here, in the voice of prayer. It seems God had already shown them favor before (verses 1-3), but now they are living through a time of hardship that they feel as God's anger. It is not known with certainty which historical moment is described; many place it after the return from exile, although it is interpreted in several ways.

Today we can pray with this same confidence when we are weary or spiritually dull. Ask God to renew your heart, and remember that his work is not only to give you relief, but to restore to you the joy of being close to him.
exp.130:2:
This verse is an invitation. The psalmist tells all the people of Israel to put their hope in the Lord, the name of God. The word "hope" means to trust and to wait patiently. The phrase "from now on and forever" means that this trust is not only for today, but for the whole of life.

David speaks in this song of ascent, which was sung on the way up to Jerusalem. First he confesses his humility: he does not seek greatness or want to understand everything. He compares his soul to a weaned child, who no longer cries to get something, but rests quietly with his mother. Then he invites the whole people to live the same way.

Today we can let go of anxiety about what we do not understand or control. When something worries us, we can pray calmly: "Lord, you know more than I do; in you I rest."
exp.105:14:
God gave the Israelites what they asked for, but along with it he sent a wasting sickness that weakened them. The word used there means weakness or decline. Some understand it as a disease that wore them down, or as an emptiness within them.

The psalmist reviews the history of Israel and acknowledges the people's sins. Here he is thinking of the wilderness, when they complained about wanting meat and God gave them quail (Numbers 11). Many believe the psalm also recalls the plague that came afterward. The problem was not asking, but demanding impatiently and without trusting God's wisdom.

Today we can ask God sincerely, but also with humility. Before insisting on a desire, let us ask ourselves whether we trust that God knows what is truly good for us.
exp.9:12:
The psalmist asks why the wicked person despises God and shows him no respect. The answer is in his heart: he thinks God will not hold him accountable. "Inquire" here means to investigate, to call someone to account, and to judge. "Provoke" means to offend or to anger.

The speaker is the psalmist, probably David, although the psalm does not say so. He is watching the wicked oppress the poor and seem to go unpunished. That is why he cries out to God in pain, and shortly afterward he confesses that God does see the suffering, and that the fatherless and the poor can find refuge in Him.

For today: when you see injustice that goes unpunished, do not conclude that God does not notice. Bring your pain to him in prayer, trust that he sees and will judge with justice, and in the meantime help whoever is suffering near you.
exp.52:5:
The explanation says that the psalmist longs with all his heart for Israel's salvation to come out of Zion, that is, out of Jerusalem, where the temple stood. The word for salvation that appears here is an old term meaning deliverance or rescue. The phrase about bringing back the captivity means restoring the people and ending their suffering. When God does this, Jacob and Israel, names for God's people, will be filled with joy.

The psalm is attributed to David. It is almost the same as Psalm 14. Before this verse, the psalmist describes foolish people who oppress God's people and do not seek him. It ends with a prayer of hope: he knows that only God can rescue and restore. It is not entirely clear what captivity is meant; it could be oppression in general or the exile.

Today we can pray with hope in the midst of injustice or trials. God is still the one who restores, and we can wait with confidence that he will bring joy.
exp.73:12:
It says that God divided the sea by his great power and crushed the heads of the sea monsters in the waters. "Divided" means split open, and "crushed" means broke or smashed. Here the word that translates "sea monsters" can refer to great creatures of the sea or to serpents of the waters.

The speaker is the psalmist Asaph, or someone from his group, in a moment of national grief, probably after the destruction of the temple. He asks God for help and reminds him of his past deeds. Many think the parted sea points to the exodus from Egypt. The monsters may symbolize powerful enemies, but scholars understand this in several different ways.

When your problems feel bigger than you, do as the psalmist did: remember what God has already done and how he has sustained you. That remembrance can give you courage to keep praying with hope.
exp.111:2:
The explanation says that the person who fears God and delights in his commandments has abundance in his house. Here "wealth" means goods or property, and "riches" means resources or prosperity. It also says that his righteousness, that is, his upright and faithful life, does not come to an end but remains forever.

This is a psalm of praise, written in an acrostic style, and no one knows for certain who wrote it. The poet describes the life of the one who honors God. There are different ways to understand the wealth mentioned: some see it as material blessing, others as an image of fullness. The Psalms speak of general principles, not automatic promises, since the Bible also shows righteous people who went through need.

For today: value uprightness more than money. If God gives you possessions, manage them with generosity and honesty. What endures is not the bank account, but a faithful life.
exp.4:10:
This verse says that all who trust in God will have joy. They will sing with shouts of gladness forever, because God defends them. Those who love his name will also be full of happiness in him. The word "rejoice" means to be very glad, and the phrase "shout for joy" means they will sing or cry out with happiness.

The psalm is spoken by David, its author, according to the heading. He is praying in the morning. Earlier he described lying and rebellious people, with false words and deceitful flattery. Now the tone changes: in the face of wickedness, he reminds us that those who trust in God have reason to be glad. The next verse speaks of God as a shield that protects the righteous.

For today: when injustice or lies surround you, do not let them steal your courage. Begin your day trusting in God, tell him what worries you, and thank him for watching over you. His protection is a reason to be glad.
exp.26:0:
It says that God is David's light, that is, the one who shows him the way and drives away the darkness of fear. He is also his salvation, the one who rescues him. For this reason David asks: "whom shall I fear?" It is not a doubt but a declaration of trust. The phrase "the strength of my life" means a secure refuge and a source of strength. The word "afraid" means to feel fear.

David, the king of Israel, is the speaker. The title attributes the psalm to him, although we do not know with certainty the exact moment he wrote it. The verses that follow speak of enemies who attack him, like an army surrounding him. Even so, he trusts in God. It is a song of faith in the midst of danger.

For today: when you feel fear because of an illness, your work, or the future, do not deny it. Speak it in prayer and remember who God is: your light and your strength. Choose one worry today and hand it over to him simply.
exp.77:54:
This verse says that God drove out the nations that lived in Canaan to make room for his people. "He cast out the heathen" means that he drove them out. The phrase about dividing the land by measuring line refers to measuring the land and giving each family its share. In this way, the tribes of Israel were able to live in the houses and lands that had belonged to others before.

Psalm 78 was written by Asaph, and it is a song that recalls the history of Israel. First it speaks of the crossing of the Red Sea and God's guidance in the desert. Then the psalmist shows that, despite so much kindness, the people rebelled. He recalls what God did so that new generations would not repeat the mistakes of their fathers.

For today: remember the times God has cared for and provided for you. Being thankful for what we have received helps us not to forget it and to remain faithful. Today, write down three concrete things God has done for you and give him thanks.
exp.39:6:
It says the psalmist answers God with readiness: "Here I am, I come." He speaks of "the wrapping of the book," that is, a scroll, which was the form of ancient books. There, he says, something is written about him. It can be understood as God's law or God's plan for his life.

He speaks, according to the psalm's title, as David. He has just praised the wonders of God and recognizes that God does not seek only sacrifices, but open ears and obedience. The New Testament, in Hebrews 10:5-9, applies this passage to Christ. Some read it first as the words of David and others as a prophecy of Jesus; many see both.

For today: when God shows you something in his Word, respond as the psalmist did: "Here I am." Before doing religious things, offer him an attentive heart ready to obey.
exp.83:6:
They go on from strength to strength, gaining strength with every step. In the end, they appear before God in Zion, which is Jerusalem, where the temple stood.

The speaker is a psalmist, probably a Levite, who longs to be in the house of God. He speaks of the pilgrims who went up to Jerusalem for the feasts. The valley of Baca (which may mean "tears" or "balm"; it is not known for certain) was a hard place, but God turns it into a place of blessing. Some understand the phrase "from strength to strength" in another way, as "from wall to wall" or "from stage to stage."

For today: when the road becomes hard, do not rely on your own strength alone. Seek God steadily, and He will renew you at every stage until you arrive in His presence.
exp.100:6:
It says that the one who practices deceit will not live in my house, and that the one who tells lies will not remain steady before my eyes. The phrase about practicing deceit means acting with trickery or fraud. The phrase about not being established means that such a person will not be accepted or allowed to remain nearby.

David speaks here as a king, according to the title of the psalm. He promises how he will govern and how he will care for his household and his court. Earlier in the psalm he spoke of rejecting slander and pride, and of seeking out the faithful. Here he says he does not want near him those who live in falsehood. Some also see in this a reflection of the just rule of God.

Today we can guard the truth in our home, our work, and our church. That includes not lying ourselves and not surrounding ourselves with deceit. With humility, let us seek out people of integrity, and also strive to be such people ourselves, asking God to help us always tell the truth.
exp.90:0:
It says that whoever lives under God's protection, called here "the Most High" and "the Almighty," will find rest and security. A "refuge" is a place of shelter and safety, and "shadow" suggests a close care, like that of someone who covers us from the strong sun. To "dwell" and to "abide" speak of staying, not of passing by as a visitor.

This psalm does not say who wrote it. Some attribute it to Moses, because of its place next to Psalm 90, but this is not certain. It changes voice: first someone who teaches speaks, then the believer who declares his trust, and then God himself. Its purpose is to encourage the people to trust God in the midst of dangers.

For today: let us not treat God only as help for emergencies. Let us seek to live close to him every day, with a brief prayer in the morning and gratitude at night, so that his peace may sustain us when problems come.
exp.86:0:
This psalm is described as a song of the sons of Korah, a group of Levites who served in the worship of the temple. The phrase "His foundation" refers to the city of God, which is named in the following verse. The "holy mountains" are the sacred hills, that is, the hills of Jerusalem where God dwelt in the midst of his people. The city is founded on a place set apart for God.

The musicians of Korah speak here, singing in Israel. They praise Zion because God chose it and loves it. We do not know with certainty the exact moment it was written; some connect it with a victory or deliverance of Jerusalem, but that is a supposition. What is clear is that they celebrate that the city rests on God's choosing, not on its own strength.

For today: ask yourself what your life is founded on. The holy mountains speak of something firm because God sustains it. Build your family, your work and your faith on God and his word, and not on what changes.
exp.140:0:
The explanation says that David, in urgency, calls out to God and asks him to come quickly and listen to him. The phrases "I have cried to you" mean "I have called to you loudly," or with force. "Make haste to me" means "come quickly to help me." "When I call" means "whenever I call to you," that is, each time I call on you.

The title says it is a psalm of David, and that is how the text presents it. It does not say when exactly he wrote it. From the rest of the psalm, it is clear that David was under pressure from wicked people and wanted to be kept from sinning. Here it begins with a sincere and urgent prayer, before asking for concrete help.

For today: when you are pressured or afraid, do not wait until you have the perfect words. Speak with God right away and sincerely, like a child calling to his father. He hears you, and praying quickly can calm your heart before you react badly.
exp.118:20:
He says that God has rebuked the proud, that is, the arrogant who think themselves greater than God. He calls them "cursed" because they live under his judgment, and he gives the reason: they "err" from his commandments, that is, they turn aside from the path God set and follow their own.

The one speaking is the psalmist, a believer who feels like a stranger passing through the earth. He hungers for the Word of God and suffers the scorn of powerful people. That is why he remembers that God does not leave the proud unanswered. We also do not know for certain who wrote this psalm; tradition does not fully settle the question.

Today, when you see pride seem to prevail, do not grow bitter or turn away. Trust that God is just, and stay humble and faithful to his Word, even when others mock you.
exp.64:0:
It says that God is pleased with the praise offered to him in Zion, that is, in Jerusalem, where the temple stood. The word "waiteth" in the verse means that praise is ready and expected, waiting for God. "The vow" refers to promises made to God, which were then fulfilled with offerings or acts of thanksgiving. The phrase "To the chief Musician" is a note for the director of the singers.

The speaker is David, according to the title, although some scholars debate when and on what occasion he wrote it. It is a song of thanksgiving to be sung together as a community. The following verses show that God hears prayer and forgives the people's rebellions. That is why the praise springs from a God who is near and merciful.

Today we can make praise a sincere habit, not just a moment in church. And if you have ever promised something to God, such as serving, helping, or giving up a bad habit, pray and take a concrete step to keep it with gratitude.
exp.113:2:
The explanation says that the sea "saw" something and fled, and that the Jordan River turned back. The phrase about the sea seeing and fleeing is poetic language: the psalmist speaks of the sea and the river as if they were people who are startled before God. It refers to the parting of the Red Sea when Israel left Egypt, and to the Jordan held back when the people entered the promised land.

The psalm is an anonymous song of praise, probably used in the worship of God's people. It remembers the deliverance from Egypt and the entrance into Canaan. The verses that follow show that all creation trembles before the presence of the Lord, who had made Israel his sanctuary and his dominion.

For today: when you face an obstacle that seems impossible, remember that the God who turned back the sea and the river remains faithful. Trust him and take the next step in faith.
exp.146:8:
This verse says that God is the one who feeds the animals. "Beast" refers to animals in general, and "food" means nourishment or sustenance. It also mentions the young ravens, who "cry out," that is, they call for food with their squawking when they are hungry. God cares for them all.

The psalm does not say who wrote it. It is a song of praise, probably for the people of Israel, inviting them to sing to God. Earlier it speaks of how He sends clouds, rain, and grass. The psalmist presents God as the one who sustains creation day after day. Then the psalm says that God takes delight in those who fear Him and trust in His mercy, not in human strength.

For today: if God cares even for the young ravens, you can trust that He also cares for you. When you feel worried about what you need, bring it to God with thankfulness and trust, and work each day in faith.
exp.105:10:
It says that the waters of the sea closed over the Egyptians who were pursuing Israel, and none of them survived. "Á" is the old form of "a," and "no quedó uno" means that not even one escaped. The text recalls the end of Pharaoh's army in the Red Sea, called here "Bermejo."

This psalm is a prayer of praise and confession from the people of Israel. It does not say who wrote it. It reviews the history of the deliverance from Egypt, but it also acknowledges that the people soon forgot what God had done. The verse shows the complete rescue: the danger was left behind. Then the psalm tells how they believed and sang, but quickly forgot.

Today, we can remember the times when God helped us or delivered us from something that seemed impossible. Writing it down, giving thanks for it, and telling others about it helps us trust Him when new trials come, and keeps us from living with a short memory.
exp.91:14:
The explanation says that the righteous, even when they are already old and still bearing fruit, have something to proclaim: that the Lord is upright. The word "upright" means just, honest, not bent or twisted. "My rock" is like saying "my rock", the one who holds me up. And "there is no unrighteousness" means that in God there is no wickedness or deceit.

The psalm is a song of praise, a psalm for the Sabbath day. The psalmist speaks in the first person and compares the righteous to a tree planted in the house of God. We do not know with certainty who wrote it. The verse closes the psalm: the long life of the faithful serves as a testimony that God is trustworthy.

For today: when we go through difficult years or old age, we can calmly tell how God has sustained us. Your testimony of his faithfulness can encourage others, no matter your age.
exp.44:5:
It says that the throne of the King will last forever and that his rule is just. The "staff" was the scepter, a symbol of authority; here it is "a scepter of justice," that is, a rule that is upright and without abuse. And the text calls the King "God."

It is a wedding song for a king of Israel, and the one speaking is the psalmist, who praises him. Some believe it refers to a historical king; others see that the expression "O God" goes beyond a mere man. The New Testament quotes this verse in Hebrews 1:8 and applies it to Christ.

For today: trust that Jesus reigns with justice and that his kingdom does not end. When you see injustice, do not lose hope. Ask God to help you use your own authority, at home or at work, with justice and humility.
exp.58:7:
This verse says that God is not frightened by those who attack his servant. "You will laugh" and "you will mock" are human images: God looks calmly and with authority at his enemies. "The nations" means the peoples who do not follow him. The word "but," used here to begin the verse, is the one the explanation points out.

David speaks in this psalm. The title says that Saul sent men to watch his house in order to kill him. The enemies move about at night like dogs, surround the city, and speak with sharp words, thinking that no one hears them. David answers by saying that God does hear, and that he has not lost control.

Today, when someone speaks to you with malice or threatens you, remember that God hears everything. You can pray with honesty, hand over your fear to him, and wait on him without returning evil for evil.
exp.25:3:
He says the psalmist has not gathered with or made friends with people who lie. The phrase "vain persons" refers to people who are empty, deceitful, and live in falsehood. Those who "go in with dissemblers" are people who hide their true intentions, the hypocrites or pretenders. To "go in" with them means to join their company and their plans.

Speaking according to the title of the psalm, David is the speaker, though some scholars debate this. He asks God to examine him, because he feels sure he walks in integrity. He does not claim to be perfect: his confidence rests in God's mercy and truth. Avoiding wicked people shows that he desires to worship God with clean hands.

Today we can examine who we spend time with and what activities we take part in. This is not about looking down on anyone, but about not joining in deception, gossip, or crooked dealings. Ask God to examine your heart, and seek friendships that help you live with sincerity.
exp.21:26:
It says that people from every corner of the earth "shall remember," that is, they will recall God and turn back to him. "The ends of the earth" refers to the most distant places. "Shall worship" means they will bow down in respect. And "the families of the nations" means all the peoples, not only Israel.

David speaks in a psalm that opens with a cry of anguish ("My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?"). After his suffering, he moves into praise and sees that God's deliverance will reach many nations. The New Testament applies the opening of this psalm to Jesus on the cross, and many Christians see here a promise of his worldwide reach.

For today: do not limit your faith to your close circle. Pray for people in other countries and cultures, and generously support, with your money or your time, others coming to know God.
exp.70:22:
The psalmist says he will rejoice aloud when he praises God with music. He says that the old form of the word for sing psalms is not the point here; instead, his lips will sing, and his whole soul will too, because God has redeemed it, that is, rescued and set it free.

The one speaking is an older believer (see verses 9 and 18), who has trusted God since his youth. He has been through distress and enemies who wished him harm. The psalm does not say who wrote it, and this cannot be known for certain. At the end of his prayer, he looks back and promises to praise God for having saved and comforted him.

For today: praise is not just a sound, but a response of gratitude for what God has done. Today you can remember a time when God sustained you and thank him, singing or with a sincere prayer, even if you are tired or in the middle of a trial.
exp.32:1:
Praise the Lord with music. The word translated as "praise" carries the idea of celebrating with joy and giving honor. The verse names instruments with strings: the harp, the psaltery, and an instrument of ten strings. This last one had ten strings.

The psalm does not say who wrote it. Some traditions attribute it to David, but the text itself does not state this. The psalmist invites the righteous to rejoice in God. The verses that follow give the reason: the word of God is upright and his work is faithful. Praise grows out of knowing what God is like.

Today we can praise God with whatever we have: a guitar, a keyboard, or simply our voice. What matters is singing with sincerity and gratitude. Try this week to sing a song of worship and think about what it says about God.
exp.118:174:
He says the psalmist wants to keep living so that he can praise God. "Let my soul live" is a desire for life, strength and encouragement, not merely to keep breathing. "Judgments" means God's just decisions and teachings, his way of ruling and guiding. He asks that those words of God be his support.

The one speaking is the author of Psalm 119, a believer who loves God's law. It is not known for certain who wrote it. It comes from asking for help and saying that God is his delight. Right after, he admits he has strayed like a lost sheep, and so he seeks for God to sustain and find him.

Today we can ask God that his Word be our daily support. Before facing the day, read one verse and say a brief prayer of praise, acknowledging that you need his help to stay standing.
exp.101:14:
So the heathen shall fear the name of the Lord, and all the kings of the earth thy glory: this means that when God acts on behalf of Zion (Jerusalem), the nations and their rulers will regard the Lord with respect. "Fear" here means honoring and taking God seriously, not merely being afraid. "Heathen" refers to the peoples who are not Israel, and "glory" refers to God's greatness and power.

The psalm is a prayer of a afflicted person, who suffers and feels alone. It seems to have been written in difficult times for Jerusalem, perhaps during or after the exile, though this is not known for certain. The psalmist trusts that God will show mercy to Zion at the time He chooses, and that this work will be seen by the whole world.

For today: when you feel small or without strength, do not stop praying. God hears the cry of those in need, and what He does in your life can lead others to respect Him and come to know Him better.
exp.118:128:
He says that God's testimonies are wonderful, and that for this reason the psalmist has kept them with his whole being. "Pe" is the name of a Hebrew letter, since this psalm is arranged according to the alphabet. "Testimonies" are the teachings and commands through which God bears witness to his will. "Soul" means the whole person, his life and his heart. "Has kept them" means that he has obeyed them and also treasured them.

The speaker is the author of the psalm, a believer whose name we do not know for certain. He loves God's Word and sees it as something admirable, not as a burden. His obedience springs from admiration. The verses that follow say that the Word gives light and understanding to the simple.

Today we can read the Bible seeking to be amazed, not only to comply. Before reading, ask God to show you something admirable about Him. When you marvel, obeying becomes more natural and joyful.
exp.43:3:
It says that God is the king being spoken of, and asks him to command deliverances for Jacob. "Deliverances" here means salvation, victories or rescues. Jacob represents the people of Israel. It is a prayer that acknowledges God as the highest authority and asks him to act on behalf of his people.

The speaker seems to be the psalmist, speaking on behalf of the whole nation. He recalls how God gave the land to Israel, not by military strength, but by his favor. For this reason, he confesses his dependence on God here. The verses that follow say that he will not trust in his bow or his sword. Some believe the psalm was written in a time of defeat, but that is not certain.

For today: before seeking solutions with your own strength, acknowledge God as your king. Bring your needs to him and ask for his help, trusting that he can act better than your own resources.
exp.83:5:
They say that the pilgrims who pass through the valley of Baca, which means "weeping," turn it into a place of springs. Making it a spring means "transforming it into a fountain." Also, the rain fills the pools, that is, God blesses them with abundant water. Some translations read "blessing" instead of "rain"; the original text allows both ideas.

A psalmist, probably a Levite or a pilgrim, expresses his longing to be in the temple. He travels toward Jerusalem to worship. We do not know for certain where the valley of Baca was; it may be a real, dry place, or an image of the difficulties of the road. The verses nearby say that whoever trusts in God goes on "from strength to strength."

Today: when you go through a time of sorrow, keep walking with God. He can give you comfort and strength in the midst of pain, and even use your experience to encourage others.
exp.103:15:
The explanation says that the trees of God are full of sap, that is, the liquid that keeps them alive and green. It speaks especially of the cedars of Lebanon, large and famous trees, and affirms that God himself planted them. The name of God is the one spoken of in the verse as "the Lord."

The psalm does not say who wrote it. It is a song of praise to God as Creator and sustainer of all things. Earlier it spoke of the bread, wine, and oil that God gives to people. Afterward it speaks of birds and animals that find a home among the trees and the rocks. The cedars show that God cares even for what no one plants or waters.

For today: when you see a tree, a plant, or the rain, pause for a moment and give thanks to God. He sustains life and also cares for you. You can bring your daily needs to him with peace.
exp.32:10:
The explanation says that God's plans are not canceled or outdated. The word "counsel" means a settled purpose or decided plan, and "the thoughts of his heart" are his deepest intentions. What the Lord has purposed stands firm, no matter how many generations pass.

This psalm is a song of praise, and it does not say who wrote it; tradition often attributes it to David, but the text itself does not state this. Earlier, it speaks of God's creative word and of how he frustrates the plans of the nations that oppose him. This verse offers a contrast: human plans fail, but God's plans remain. Then the psalm celebrates the people God has chosen.

When your plans fall apart or the future worries you, remember that God keeps working with a firm purpose. You can rest in the fact that his goodness does not depend on your circumstances, and you can ask him to align your plans with his.
exp.87:12:
The explanation says that the psalmist, despite his pain, keeps crying out to God. The verse's word "prevent" is an old one, and the sentence that explains it has to be rewritten for a word that appears in the verse above. So "in the morning shall my prayer prevent thee" means that from early on, before the day begins, he is already praying.

It speaks of a man who suffers greatly. Psalm 88 is attributed to Heman the Ezrahite, and it is one of the few psalms that end without a word of relief. He feels close to death, abandoned and unanswered. Even so, he does not stop praying. His earlier questions about the grave and being forgotten show his anguish, and the ones that follow ask why God seems to be hiding.

For today: when you feel that God is silent, you do not have to pretend that everything is fine. You can bring him your complaint honestly, from early on, and keep on praying. Crying out is already an act of faith.
exp.118:108:
He says that the psalmist's life is always in danger. "My soul is continually in my hand" is an old expression meaning to live risking one's life, like someone carrying something fragile in the palm who could lose it at any moment. Even so, he says he has not forgotten the law of God, that is, his teachings and commands.

The speaker is the author of Psalm 119, who is not identified with certainty. Earlier he said he was very afflicted, and afterward he mentions that the wicked had set traps for him. He suffers persecution or threat, but instead of letting go of his faith, he clings to God's word and asks for help.

For today: when life feels fragile or fear presses on you, do not leave the Bible for later. Choose one verse, repeat it through the day, and bring it to God in prayer. He can sustain you when your strength seems small.
exp.61:8:
The explanation says that human beings, whether of humble standing or of high position, are like a breath: fragile and passing. "Vanity" means something that has no weight and does not last, like vapor. "Lie" here means that they cannot be relied upon to lean on. If they were placed on a balance, they would weigh less than that breath.

David speaks, according to the psalm's heading, and confesses that only in God does his soul find rest. Before this verse he invites the people to trust in God and to open their hearts to him. Afterward he warns against trusting in violence or in riches. Scholars debate when in his life he wrote it, so there is no certainty.

For today: do not place your ultimate security in money, in reputation, or in the opinion of others. Value them, but rest in God, and speak to him honestly about what you feel.
exp.104:25:
He sent Moses, whom he called "his servant," and Aaron, whom he had chosen. The word "sent" shows that God took the initiative. The words "á" and "al cual" are old spellings of "a" and "a quien," and these should be rewritten or removed.

Wait, I must correct my draft: the source-language words must not appear, and the old-spelling sentence explains a source-language form not present in the verse, so it must be deleted. Here is the final output:

He sent Moses, whom he called his servant, and Aaron, whom he had chosen. The word "sent" shows that God took the initiative.

The psalm is a song of praise that recalls God's works on behalf of Israel. It is not known with certainty who wrote it, and I will not claim otherwise. Before this verse, the people were growing in Egypt, and the Egyptians hated them. After this, the psalm recounts the signs and the plagues. Its purpose is for the people to remember that God keeps his covenant and rescues.

For today: when you face a difficult situation, remember that God often acts by sending and using people. Trust that he can call you and sustain you, and also thank him for those he has placed in your path to help you.
exp.118:165:
He says that the psalmist has confidently waited for God's salvation, and has obeyed his commandments. The word "health" here does not speak of physical well-being, but of salvation, that is, rescue and deliverance. "Have put into practice" means that he has practiced or carried out what God commands.

The speaker is the author of Psalm 119, a lengthy poem in honor of God's word. It is not known with certainty who wrote it. From what it says, he seems to be someone who suffers pressure and opposition, yet loves God's law. In the verses nearby he speaks of the peace of those who love that law and of his desire to please God in everything.

For today: wait on God without ceasing to obey him. Hope is not only waiting with folded arms; it is also living faithfully in the small things of each day, trusting that God will keep his promise.
exp.136:5:
He says the psalmist would rather be silent than forget Jerusalem. The phrase "let my tongue cleave to the roof of my mouth" means that his tongue would stop moving and he would be unable to speak or sing. The word "exalt" means to lift up or raise high. What he calls "chief joy" is what brings him the most gladness, the first thing in his heart.

He speaks as an Israelite in exile in Babylon, after Jerusalem had been destroyed. His captors asked him for songs of Zion, but he grieved for his homeland. Jerusalem was the place of the temple and of God's presence, so remembering it was sacred. The verses that follow express a very deep pain and a longing for justice.

For today: do not let your daily occupations or comforts make you forget what God loves. Set aside a moment each day to remember with gratitude what God has done and to pray for his people.
exp.16:3:
This verse says that the psalmist, in dealing with other people and their actions, has kept himself away from violent paths. He managed this by being guided by what God has said. "Works of men" refers to what people do, and "the destroyer" speaks of the one who acts with violence or wickedness.

David speaks, according to the psalm's heading, and prays to God in the midst of persecution by his enemies. He asks that God himself judge his cause and affirms that his heart is sincere. He does not say he is perfect, but that he has tried to be faithful and not to misuse his mouth.

Today, when the pressure of settings where others are deceived or harmed surrounds you, return to God's Word before you decide. His words can be your guide to avoid destructive paths, even when others follow them.
exp.24:13:
What it says: God's "secret" speaks of close friendship and trust, not of something mysterious or hidden. God shares his intimacy with those who fear him, meaning those who respect him and honor him with reverence. To them he makes known his covenant, which is his promise, his faithful commitment to his people.

Context: The speaker is David, in a psalm of prayer and trust. According to the traditional title, it is by David, though some scholars debate details of its origin. He asks for guidance, forgiveness, and rescue, and the verses that follow show that he feels lonely and troubled. Even so, he trusts that God teaches those who follow him.

For today: Draw near to God with humility and respect. Set aside time each day to read his Word and pray, asking him to help you understand his will. He makes himself known to those who seek him sincerely.
exp.98:6:
He spoke to his people from a pillar of cloud. They, for their part, kept his testimonies (the teachings and commands that bore witness to God's will) and the statute (the law or rule) that he had given them.

The psalmist calls us to praise God because he is holy. He remembers Moses, Aaron, and Samuel, men who prayed and received an answer. The cloud is mentioned in Exodus and in Numbers, when God spoke to Moses, and to Aaron and Miriam. The text does not make clear whether God spoke to Samuel in this way; the verse seems to refer mainly to the time of Moses and Aaron. Interpreters understand it in different ways.

God communicates with us, and listening to him includes obeying him. Today we can read his Word with attention and ask him for help to put into practice one concrete thing we learn this week.
exp.118:77:
This verse is a prayer. The psalmist asks that the proud, meaning those who think themselves superior, be put to shame, because they have attacked him with lies and without reason. The word "slandered" in the explanation means they falsely spoke badly of him. Instead of answering them with revenge, he says he will meditate, that is, think calmly and wholeheartedly, on God's commandments.

The one speaking is the author of Psalm 119, who is not identified with certainty. He presents himself as a servant of God who suffers attacks and contempt. Earlier he asked for comfort and mercy, and afterward he desires that those who fear God draw near to him and that his heart remain whole. His refuge is in God's word.

When someone speaks badly of you unjustly, you do not have to pay them back. Bring your case to God in prayer and fill your mind with his word. In this way your heart stays at peace and firm.
exp.76:0:
This verse begins with a note for the choir director: it is a psalm of Asaph, dedicated to Jeduthun, another musician of the temple. Then Asaph says he cried out to God with his voice, that is, aloud. He repeats "I cried unto God with my voice" to show his persistence. The phrase "and he gave ear unto me" expresses his confidence that God does listen.

Asaph speaks as a Levite, someone in charge of the music in worship. The verses that follow show that he is in a night of distress, without comfort and with a discouraged spirit. The text does not say exactly what his problem was; some think it was a personal crisis and others think it was a situation affecting his people.

For today: when you are overwhelmed, do not keep everything to yourself. Speak with God honestly, even aloud, and trust that he hears you even when you do not yet feel relief.
exp.24:0:
The explanation says David directs his soul toward God. The phrase "I lift up my soul" is an old way of saying: I place my whole being, my desires and my worries in your hands, and I look to you. The name of God in the Old Testament is the one written in the Hebrew text as the Lord, and this is not just a gesture of the mind but a complete surrender of the heart.

The one speaking is David, king of Israel, according to the title of the psalm. The verses that follow show that he is going through a difficulty: he has enemies and fears being put to shame. That is why he begins by seeking God before asking for anything. The text does not say exactly when he wrote it, so it is best not to invent the situation.

When worry comes, before speaking with everyone or turning the problem over and over in your mind, stop and pray. Give God your fears in simple words, and trust that he hears you.
exp.15:1:
Here David speaks to himself: his soul tells God that he is the Lord. Then he adds that his goodness does not reach God, meaning it is of no use to him and adds nothing to him. Some translations understand it differently: "apart from you I have no good thing." Both ideas fit the confidence of the psalm.

David prays for protection because he trusts God. He recognizes that God does not depend on how good he is. For that reason, in the next verse, he directs his love and his kindness toward the saints, the faithful people who live on the earth.

For today: God does not need our merits, but we can do good to others out of love for him. This week, help someone concrete, a brother or sister in the faith, and do it with gratitude, not to earn God's favor.
exp.77:41:
They did not remember God's power, the strength of his hand to act. Nor did they remember the day when God rescued them from their suffering, which here refers to the oppression and misery they endured under the Egyptians. Redeemed means that he set them free, either by paying a price or by a mighty act.

This is a psalm of Asaph, which reviews the history of Israel to teach the new generations. Before this, the psalmist tells how the people provoked God in the wilderness. Afterward, he recalls the signs in Egypt, such as the plagues. His purpose is to warn: forgetting what God has done leads to distrust of him.

For today: remember the times God helped you. Write them in a notebook and review them when you are afraid or doubting. Remembering his faithfulness helps you trust him today.
exp.68:24:
It says that the place where the enemies live should be left in ruins and empty. The words for their dwelling can be understood as their stronghold or their camp, and their tents are their homes. Ruined means destroyed and laid waste. Those who live there are the inhabitants.

David speaks here, according to the title of the psalm, while he suffers mockery and unjust attacks because of his faithfulness to God. It is a psalm of lament, and these words are a cry for justice to the Judge of all, not a personal desire for revenge. In the New Testament, Peter quotes this verse and applies it to Judas (Acts 1:20), so many also read it as a prophetic announcement.

For today: when you are wronged unjustly, do not take revenge. Bring your pain and your anger to God honestly, and leave justice to him, as Jesus taught, who also asked us to pray for our enemies.
exp.118:137:
This verse says that God's teachings, which he himself has commanded, are righteous and completely trustworthy. "Testimonies" means what God declares and teaches, that is, his Word. The phrase about commanding means that he has given them as a charge to be kept. "Righteous" means just and without error. "Faithful" means worthy of trust.

The one speaking is the author of Psalm 119, whose name is not known for certain. He is someone who loves God's Word. Shortly before, he wept because others did not obey the law. This section begins with the Hebrew letter Tzaddi, and it speaks of God's justice. The psalmist praises God even in the midst of pain and opposition.

For today: when you don't understand something or feel confused, return to the Bible and trust that God is just and faithful. Read one passage each day and ask him to help you obey it.
exp.44:3:
It says that the king, in the midst of his glory, moves forward successfully like someone riding on horseback, and what carries him forward is truth, humility, and justice. The words "be prosperous" in the verse mean "may things go well for you, may you advance successfully." "Terrible things" are deeds that cause fear and awe, because they show great power. "Your right hand" is his right hand, a symbol of strength.

The psalm is a song for a royal wedding. The poet addresses the king, and it is not known with certainty who he was. Some think of a king of Israel; the New Testament applies part of the psalm to Christ (Hebrews 1:8-9). For this reason many Christians see here the Messiah, whose kingdom is upheld in justice.

For today: true strength is not found in imposing oneself, but in living with truth, humility, and justice. This week, in a difficult decision or conversation, choose to speak the truth with humility and to treat others with justice.
exp.118:153:
Here the psalmist asks God for three things. "Plead my cause" means that God would take up his case, like a lawyer who speaks on behalf of someone. "Redeem me" means that God would rescue him and set him free. Asking to be made alive again means asking to be given life or to be renewed. "Your word" is God's promise.

The one speaking is the author of Psalm 119, a believer who loves God's law. He is going through affliction and perhaps opposition from wicked people, although the text does not say who they were. He does not claim a right on his own merit but rests on what God has promised. For that reason, in the verses nearby, he insists that he has not forgotten the Lord's law.

For today: when you feel weary or unfairly treated, pray with the promises of the Bible. Look for one that fits your situation, speak it back to God in prayer, and trust that he can give you renewed strength.
exp.32:5:
This verse says that God made the heavens by his word. "All the host of them" refers to the sun, the moon, and the stars, which the Bible sometimes calls by that name because of their order and their great number. The phrase about the breath of his mouth is like the breath of God; in the original language the word used can mean breath, wind, or spirit, and some see here a reference to the Spirit of God.

This is a psalm of praise, and the text does not name its author. It invites the righteous to sing to God. Before this, it speaks of his word being upright and his work being true. Afterward, it mentions how God gathers the waters of the sea. The psalmist wants everyone to recognize the power and goodness of the Creator.

For today: if God created the universe with his word, he can also sustain your life. When you feel fear or confusion, read his word and trust that what he says is firm and true.
exp.70:13:
He says that, whatever happens, the psalmist will never stop hoping in God. "Will hope" means to trust patiently, even when help is slow to come. "Will yet praise thee more and more" means he will praise God more and more each time, adding new reasons for gratitude to those he already had.

The psalm does not name its author; tradition links it to David, but this is not certain. The speaker seems to be already old (verses 9 and 18), surrounded by enemies who want to harm him. He has just asked God not to go far away and to help him soon. Even so, in the middle of his distress, he decides to keep his hope and his praise.

Today we can practice this in difficult times: besides asking for help, write down each day one thing for which to give thanks to God. In this way hope stays alive while the answer is on its way.
exp.115:6:
The psalmist speaks to himself and tells his soul to return to rest. The reason is simple: the Lord has been good to him. The word "rest" speaks of inner calm and security. The explanation also notes that one word is an older form of another, and that a word means something else in its original wording, but those points are not needed for your reader.

The speaker is the psalmist, whose name is not given. He came out of great distress: he felt close to death, brought low, and God rescued him. Some think it was a serious illness, but the text does not make this clear. After being delivered, he encourages himself to rest in the goodness of God, who is gracious, righteous, and merciful.

When anxiety unsettles you, do as the psalmist did: speak to your heart. Write down three good things God has done for you, and rest in them while you hand over what worries you today.
exp.64:12:
The explanation says that the open fields look as if they are clothed with flocks, and that the valleys are covered with wheat and other grains. Everything seems to sing and shout for joy.

"Pastures" are the flat grasslands where animals feed. "Flocks" are herds of sheep and goats. "Corn" is the cereal of the harvest. "Clothed" and "covered" are poetic images.

It is a psalm of David, a song of praise to God for His care of the land. Earlier it speaks of the rain and of a year crowned with blessings. Here the psalmist describes the result: pastures, harvests, and a creation that seems to celebrate. Some understand the song of nature only as poetic language.

For today: learn to see the food of each day as a gift from God, not as something automatic. Before eating, or when you see the field or the market, give thanks out loud. Gratitude protects us from anxiety and complaint.
exp.25:2:
This verse says that David keeps God's faithful love always before him, as if he were looking at it all the time. Here "lovingkindness" is his steadfast, faithful goodness. And "I have walked in your truth" means that he lives guided by what God says and by his faithful and just character.
