David speaks in a psalm where he asks God to examine him and judge him. He does not claim to be perfect; he explains that his conduct rests on God's love and God's truth. The verses that follow show that he separated himself from false people and from the wicked, and that he did not want to share their ways.

For today: before deciding something, remember how God has treated you with kindness and faithfulness. Let that, together with his word, guide your steps and your friendships, and not only your wishes of the moment.
exp.67:24:
This verse describes a procession with music. The singers walked at the front, those who played stringed or wind instruments came behind, and in the middle the young women advanced playing tambourines, which were small hand drums or frame drums.

The psalm is attributed to David, and it celebrates God as King who defeats his enemies and walks with his people. The verses before it speak of everyone seeing "the goings of God in the sanctuary," that is, his presence among them. This procession seems to be a public celebration of that victory. Scholars debate whether it describes a specific event, such as the moving of the ark, or a scene of worship in general. The text does not make this clear.

For today: praise is not only something personal, it is also communal. Each person had their place: singers, musicians, young women. Ask yourself what you can contribute to the worship of your church, with joy and without comparing yourself to others.
exp.109:2:
The explanation says that the people of the Messiah will follow him gladly, without anyone forcing them, when he shows his power. They come clothed in holiness. The second part is poetic: from the dawn, the King has youthful dew, an image of vigor and new life that is renewed every morning. Some understand this as referring to the King, others to his numerous people, like drops of dew.

David writes this psalm and speaks of "my Lord," someone greater than himself. Jehovah has given him authority as King and Priest. The verse shows how his people respond when he reigns: with willing devotion. The New Testament applies this psalm to Jesus.

For today: serve God out of love and not out of obligation. Each morning, offer him your day with joy and ask him for a clean and willing heart.
exp.50:11:
What it says: The speaker asks God to restore to him the joy of feeling saved. The word for "health" here means salvation, not just good physical condition. He also asks for a "free spirit," meaning a willing and generous heart that obeys gladly and not out of mere duty, and that keeps him steady.

Context: According to the psalm's heading, it is by David, after the prophet Nathan confronted him about his sin with Bathsheba. It comes right after asking for forgiveness and a clean heart. Now he asks not only to be forgiven, but also to recover the joy he had lost. Afterward he promises to teach others God's ways.

For today: If you feel guilty or spiritually dull, do not turn away from God. Confess honestly what you have done and ask him to restore the joy of his salvation. His forgiveness does not only erase guilt; it can also renew your spirit so that you serve him gladly.
exp.61:3:
He says that his enemies think only about bringing him down from his place of honor or dignity. They take pleasure in lies. With their mouths they speak well of him and even bless him, but inwardly, in the deepest part of the heart, they wish him harm. "Selah" is a pause or a musical indication; its exact meaning is not certain, but it invites the reader to stop and think.

David speaks, according to the title of the psalm, although some scholars debate the exact occasion. He feels attacked by false people who pretend to be friends. Even so, in the verses around it he repeats that God alone is his rock, his salvation, and his refuge.

For today: when someone treats you with a double face, do not live obsessed with their falseness. Hand your pain over to God, find your security in Him, and make sure your own words are sincere, matching what is in your heart.
exp.56:4:
This verse is a short prayer of praise. The psalmist asks God to be exalted, that is, lifted up to the highest place, above the heavens. He asks that his glory, which is his greatness and his honor, be seen across all the earth. The words "Be exalted" mean "rise up" or "show yourself great."

The title of the psalm attributes it to David, when he was fleeing from Saul and hid in a cave. He is surrounded by enemies he describes as lions, with words that wound like spears and knives. Even so, in the midst of danger, his attention turns back to God. This verse is repeated in verse 11, as a refrain of the psalm.

When you are pressed by problems or by people, do not let fear fill all your thinking. Pause and praise God, asking that his greatness be greater than your situation. That reminds you who is in control.
exp.39:14:
It says that those who mock the psalmist, who shout "Aha, aha" at him, should receive ruin as their payment for their insult. The word "desolate" in the verse means left in ruin and emptiness. "Shame" means a disgrace or dishonor, a humiliation brought on by insult. The phrase "aha, aha" is an expression of mockery, like saying "Ha, ha, how good!", celebrating another person's misfortune.

The psalm is attributed to David in its heading, although some scholars think the text was later used in other times of distress. He is surrounded by enemies who want his life and laugh at his fall. For this reason he asks God to deliver him soon. These words are a prayer of lament, not a plan for personal revenge: he hands the matter over to God.

Today, when someone mocks you or humiliates you, you can bring that pain to God honestly, and leave justice in his hands. Jesus also teaches us to pray for those who mistreat us.
exp.93:0:
The explanation says that the psalmist asks God to act. "Vengeance" here speaks of justice that sets wrong right, not of personal resentment. The phrase "shew thyself" means "let yourself be seen" and "act clearly and openly." The verse repeats "O God, to whom vengeance belongeth" to press the request with force.

The psalm does not say who wrote it. The speaker sees that the wicked oppress others and seem to get away with it, as the verses that follow show. For that reason he cries out to God as the Judge of the earth. He does not take justice into his own hands, but leaves it in God's hands.

When you see injustice, or suffer it, you can bring it to God honestly, even with pain and questions. Praying this way keeps you from filling up with bitterness or seeking to get even. Trust that God sees, judges with justice, and knows when to act. In the meantime, try to do good.
exp.144:14:
All living things look to God with hope, and he gives them their food just when they need it. The phrase about looking to him means trusting him and looking to God as the one who provides. The phrase about giving food in its season means at the right moment.

This is a psalm of praise, traditionally attributed to David. He celebrates the greatness and goodness of God. Before this, he speaks of God's eternal kingdom and of how he upholds those who fall. Afterward, he says that God opens his hand and blesses every living thing. The psalmist shows that God's care reaches all of his creation.

For today: when you feel anxious about what you need, remember that God cares for you. You can pray with confidence, work with responsibility, and give thanks for what you receive each day, even when it comes differently than you imagined.
exp.38:0:
The explanation begins with a dedication: the psalm is for the choirmaster, for Jeduthun, and it is by David. Then David says that he resolved to watch his conduct so as not to sin with his words. "I will keep my mouth" means he will hold his tongue so as not to speak too much. "The wicked" refers to the evil person standing before him, and "while" means "as long as."

David speaks here as one who suffers the presence of wicked people close to him. The verses that follow show that his silence did not relieve his pain, and in the end he had to pour out his heart before God. Jeduthun appears as one of the musicians in worship, although the psalm gives no further details.

For today: when someone treats you unjustly, restrain your words so that you do not answer in anger, but do not keep everything bottled up inside. Tell God honestly what you feel.
exp.77:56:
What it says: The people of Israel turned their backs on God and rebelled just as their ancestors had. "They turned back" here means they drew away or retreated. And "a deceitful bow" is a defective bow, one that looks good but fails when the archer uses it and the arrow goes off course.

Context: This psalm is a song of Asaph that reviews the history of Israel. God had given them the promised land, but they tested him and did not keep his commands. Before and after this verse, the psalm speaks of their high places and idols, which provoked God's anger. The psalmist wants the new generations to learn from the mistakes of the past.

For today: A bow fails exactly when we need it most. That is how we can be if our faith is only in words. Ask God to help you be faithful and to learn from the stumbles of the past.
exp.118:67:
It says that God is good and that he does good to people. For this reason, the one speaking asks him to teach him his statutes, that is, his rules and commands. The word "good" in the verse means something like someone who does good for others, so this describes God's kindness toward people.

The speaker is the psalmist, an author who is not named in this psalm. He admits that he had been going astray, that is, lost, and that suffering helped him return to God's word. Besides this, he is surrounded by proud people who make up lies against him. In the middle of this, he trusts that God is good and wants to learn from him.

For today: when you go through difficulties or injustice, before asking only that God change your situation, remember that he is good. Spend a few minutes each day reading his word and ask him to teach you how to live in a way that pleases him.
exp.143:12:
This verse asks that our storehouses be full, supplying every kind of grain, and that our flocks multiply by the thousands and tens of thousands. The storehouses are the places where grain is kept. The verse's wording about the animals means that the sheep and cattle have their young. The open ground or the streets of the town are where the flocks are seen.

It is a prayer of David, king of Israel. First he asks God to deliver him from lying enemies, and then he longs for peace and prosperity for his people. Some understand these phrases as a petition, and others as a description of what a blessed people would look like. The psalm ends by saying that the greatest happiness is to have the LORD as one's God.

For today: thank God for what He gives you, such as bread and work, and ask Him with confidence for what you need. But remember that His greatest blessing is not things, but knowing Him.
exp.67:19:
This verse says that our God is a God who saves. The phrase "He will save us" means that He will do it and has the power to do it. The phrase "rescue from death" speaks of delivering from death or from the dangers that threaten life. The name "LORD," the proper name of God, is tied to His faithfulness to His people.

The psalm is by David and celebrates God as a victorious king who accompanies his people. Earlier, the psalmist praises God because He cares for and blesses His own every day. Later, he announces that God will overcome His enemies. Thus this verse is a declaration of trust: the God who cares for us each day can also save in the most serious moments.

For today: when you feel fear because of an illness, a loss, or an uncertain future, repeat this verse in prayer. Trust that God sustains you today and that your final life is in His hands.
exp.37:4:
Here the psalmist describes his wounds in very strong words: they rotted and became infected. "Wounds" are open sores, "rotted" means they went bad, and "foolishness" refers to folly: acting without wisdom, apart from God.

David speaks, according to the title of the psalm, though we do not know with certainty which moment of his life it refers to. He is suffering in body and in soul, and he acknowledges that his sin and his folly weigh on him like a burden. Some believe the illness is real, and others think it is a picture of his anguish. Both readings are possible.

For today: do not hide what hurts you inside or your bad decisions. Bring them before God with honesty, as David does. Recognizing foolishness is the first step to receiving his forgiveness and healing.
exp.118:148:
Here the psalmist asks God to hear him. "According to your lovingkindness" means according to his goodness and faithful love. The phrase "quicken me" in the verse above is an older way of saying "give me life": renew me, strengthen me, or save me. "Judgment" here does not mean so much punishment as God's righteous decrees and his upright way of acting.

The speaker is the author of Psalm 119, whose name is not given. He had been praying since early morning and during the night watches, meditating on God's word. People surround him who persecute him and turn away from the law, and so he cries out for help and encouragement.

For today: when you feel weary or pressured, pray with confidence, not because of your merits but because of God's goodness. Set aside a quiet moment of the day to read his word and ask him to renew your strength.
exp.40:4:
The explanation says that the psalmist's enemies speak evil of him. With malice they ask when he is going to die, and they want his name to vanish and be forgotten. "Perish" means that no one remembers him, and that neither his reputation nor his family continues.

David, to whom tradition attributes this psalm, is sick, confined to bed. He has just said that God sustains the one who is ill, and he has asked God for mercy and healing, acknowledging his sin. While he suffers, those around him do not comfort him: some visit him with falsehood and then spread gossip. His illness becomes an occasion for mockery.

For today: when someone speaks badly of you in your weakest moment, do as the psalmist did. Do not answer with resentment; bring everything to God with sincerity, ask for his mercy, and rest in the fact that he sustains you, even when others turn their backs on you.
exp.59:0:
The explanation says this is a song for the chief musician, with the tune called "Lily of the Testimony" (Susan-Eduth). It is a "Michtam" of David, which seems to be a kind of poem, and it serves "to teach." The title recalls a war against the Arameans and a victory of Joab over twelve thousand Edomites in the valley of salt. Then David prays: "God, you have rejected us, you have scattered us, you have been angry; return to us." "Rejected" means cast off, and "scattered" means that you have spread them apart.

David, king of Israel, speaks in a moment of defeat and national disorder, although the title mentions victories. Scholars do not agree on how these two things fit together. Even so, he understands that without God nothing is secure.

For today: when you feel that everything is falling apart, you can speak to God honestly, without pretending. Ask Him to draw near and restore you, and remember that He can raise up what has fallen.
exp.123:3:
This verse uses the image of a great flood. It says that, without God's help, the waters would have covered them and the torrent would have passed over their soul, that is, over their whole life. The explanation of the word "would have" is about a situation that did not happen because of God.

It is a psalm of ascent, attributed to David, which the people of Israel sang, probably when going up to Jerusalem. It remembers a huge danger caused by enemies and celebrates that God delivered them. The exact historical details are not mentioned, so we do not know which moment it refers to.

When you look back and see problems that could have crushed you, take a moment to thank God for having sustained you, even if you did not notice it at the time. Remembering his past help strengthens trust to face what is coming.
exp.115:2:
The psalmist says he felt completely surrounded by the danger of dying. "The sorrows of death" are like ropes that bind him, and "the grave" (in Hebrew, Sheol, the place of the dead) seemed ready to seize him. "They compassed me" means "they surrounded me," and "they found me" shows that the distress caught him with no way out.

The author does not identify himself in the text, and scholars do not agree on who he was. He is someone who nearly died, perhaps from illness or from enemies, and now he gives thanks because God heard him. That is why, in verse 4, he calls on the LORD to deliver his soul.

When you feel that fear or pain surrounds you, do not wait until you are better before you pray. Cry out to God honestly, as the psalmist did. He listens to those who feel they have no way out, and remembering how he has helped you before strengthens your trust.
exp.115:16:
This verse says that the psalmist will offer God a sacrifice of thanksgiving, that is, an offering of gratitude, and that he will call upon the name of the LORD in prayer.

The speaker is a believer who has been rescued from a great danger, perhaps from death. He says that God has freed him from his bonds, as if he had been released from chains. For this reason he responds with public gratitude: he will fulfill his vows in the temple, in front of all the people. It is not known with certainty who wrote this psalm or what his exact situation was.

For today: when God helps you with something, do not forget it or keep it to yourself. Give thanks to Him with a sincere prayer and tell someone what He has done. That gratitude is an offering that pleases God.
exp.118:70:
It is good for the psalmist that he was brought low, because it led him to learn God's teachings. The word "afflicted" means brought down, troubled, or placed in a lowly condition. The "statutes" are the rules and instructions that God has given.

The one speaking is the author of Psalm 119, who loves God's law. We do not know for certain who wrote it. Here he says that proud people slandered him with lies, and that his heart was dull and unfeeling. Even so, he sees that his suffering bore good fruit: it drew him closer to God's word, which he values more than gold.

For today: when you go through a difficulty or an injustice, do not stay only in the pain. Ask God what He wants to teach you, and open your Bible with humility. He can use what is hard to shape you, even though suffering in itself is not good.
exp.131:3:
This verse says that someone vows not to sleep or rest. "I will not give sleep to my eyes" and "nor slumber to my eyelids" are two ways of saying the same thing: there will be no rest. "Slumber" is that drowsiness that closes the eyes.

The psalm recalls David's vow to God, whom it calls "the Mighty One of Jacob." David promised not to rest until he found a place for the presence of God, that is, a place for the ark. Many understand that the psalm speaks of this longing of David, though we do not know for certain who wrote the psalm or when.

For today: David put God before his own comfort. We can ask ourselves what good thing for God we have put off for later out of laziness or tiredness. Today you could set aside a specific time to pray or to serve, even if it costs you something.
exp.95:9:
This verse invites us to tell all the nations that the Lord reigns. The phrase "Say among the heathen" means "say among the nations." "Reigneth" indicates that God is King and exercises his rule. "The world also shall be established" means that he made it firm and stable, and so it will not be moved. Moreover, God will judge the peoples righteously, that is, in a straight and impartial way.

The psalm does not say who wrote it. It is a song of praise that calls Israel to proclaim the greatness of God to the whole world. Earlier, the psalmist asks for worship with offerings and reverence in the sanctuary. Afterward, all creation rejoices because its King governs with justice. Some read it as a song for worship in the temple, and others also see in it a hope for the future.

For today: when the world seems unstable or unjust, remember that God is still King. Rest in him and share that hope with someone who needs it.
exp.57:9:
The explanation says that the righteous will rejoice when they see God doing justice, and that they will wash their feet in the blood of the wicked. "Vengeance" here means fair punishment, not personal resentment. The "wicked" is the one who lives without respect for God. The phrase "he shall rejoice" and the verb "wash" are the older forms of the same wording. The image of washing one's feet in blood is very strong and poetic; it evokes a battlefield where evil has been defeated.

According to the title of the psalm, David speaks against unjust judges who harm the people with violence and lies. It is the language of Hebrew poetry, with exaggerated images, crying out to God for justice. It is not a command to kill, but a prayer that leaves judgment in God's hands.

Today, when you see injustice, do not take vengeance into your own hands. Pray, trust that God judges with justice, and keep doing good. Your hope is not in seeing the wicked suffer, but in knowing that God governs.
exp.73:18:
The explanation says that God should not hand over his dove to the beasts. The dove is a small, fragile, defenseless bird, and here it represents God's people. The beasts are cruel enemies. The word translated as "soul" in the verse means life itself. Those who are afflicted are those who suffer and are oppressed. The psalmist asks that God not forget them forever.

This is a psalm of Asaph, or of his group, written as a communal lament. It probably reflects the destruction of the temple and the mockery of the enemies, although scholars debate the exact moment. The people remember that God is Creator and Lord of all, and for that reason they dare to ask him for help.

For today: when you feel small or without strength, you can speak with God with complete sincerity. Ask him for help, remind him who he is, and also care for others who suffer.
exp.117:2:
This verse invites the priests, the descendants of Aaron, to declare out loud that God's mercy lasts forever. The word "mercy" here translates a Hebrew word (chesed) that speaks of faithful love, loyal and steadfast kindness.

This psalm is a song of thanksgiving used in the worship of the people. It calls different groups in turn: Israel, the house of Aaron, and those who fear the Lord. Many think it was sung in a responsive way, though we do not know for certain how it was used. The priests served in worship, so their voice carried special weight. Afterward, the psalmist tells how God answered him in his distress.

For today: no one is exempt from remembering God's faithful love. This week, say it out loud or share it with someone: "God has been faithful to me," and mention one concrete example.
exp.93:1:
Here the psalmist asks God to rise up as a judge who acts. Rising up here means standing to pass judgment. Giving a reward means handing out what is deserved, and the proud are those who think themselves superior to everyone, even to God.

The one speaking is a believer from Israel, whose name we do not know, who sees arrogant people oppress others and mock justice. The verses that follow show his pain as he asks how long this will go on. He does not take revenge on his own, but brings his cry to God, the only perfect Judge.

Today, when we see injustice or abuse, we can pray honestly and hand the matter over to God, instead of settling the score with our own hands. Praying this way helps us let go of bitterness and trust that he will do justice in his own time.
exp.118:136:
This verse declares that God is righteous and that his decisions are right. "Tzaddi" is the name of a letter of the Hebrew alphabet, with which this section of the psalm begins. "Lord" is the name of God, and "judgments" are his decisions and his way of governing, which are always correct.

The one speaking is the psalmist, who loves God's law. We do not know for certain who wrote it. He had come through a time of great weeping because the people did not obey God. Even in the midst of that pain, he does not accuse God; he acknowledges him as just. This psalm is organized according to the letters of the Hebrew alphabet, and each section begins with one of them.

When you see injustice or suffer yourself, you can tell God honestly what you feel, and at the same time declare that he is just. Trusting in his character gives you peace even when you do not understand everything that is happening.
exp.137:5:
Although God is very great and dwells on high, he pays careful attention to the humble person. The proud, on the other hand, he keeps at a distance; he does not draw near to them or treat them with the same closeness. The word "proud" here means arrogant, the one who feels superior to others.

The speaker is David, according to the title of the psalm. He is giving thanks to God with his whole heart. Earlier he says that even the kings of the earth will praise him. Then he confesses that if he passes through distress or enemies, he trusts that God will keep him safe. His message: the mighty God is also near to the lowly.

For today: when you feel small or in need, come before God with sincerity, without pretending to strength. Acknowledge your limits and ask him for help. He draws near to the one who trusts in him with humility.
exp.24:14:
He says that the psalmist keeps his gaze fixed on God all the time, that is, he trusts in him and depends on his help. The "net" is the trap that hunters use; here it stands for dangers, enemies, or problems that a person cannot get out of alone. He believes that the Lord will free him.

The psalm is traditionally attributed to David, according to its heading. He is going through a difficult moment: shortly afterward he describes himself as alone, afflicted, and with a distressed heart, and he also mentions enemies. The psalm is a prayer of trust in the middle of trouble. The verses before this one speak of God guiding and teaching those who fear him.

For today: when you feel trapped by a worry, a debt, or a bad decision, begin the day by turning your eyes to God in prayer before looking at your problems. Tell him simply where you feel stuck and ask him to show you the next step.
exp.120:6:
It says that God will watch over you from all evil, and that he will protect your soul, that is, your life and your whole being. Where the verse says "preserve," the word means to care for, watch over, and protect. "Evil" can include dangers, harm, and calamities.

This psalm was probably sung by pilgrims as they traveled up to Jerusalem. The speaker seems to encourage the traveler (or himself) by reminding him that God is his constant protector, like a shade that covers him from the sun. Interpreters debate whether there was one singer or several, but the message is clear: God cares for his people on the road.

For today: when you feel fear or uncertainty, pray and entrust your day to God. It does not promise that we will never have difficulties, but it does promise that nothing separates us from his care. Rest in the fact that he sustains your life and your soul, even in difficult moments.
exp.34:27:
This verse says that the psalmist will speak of God's righteousness and praise him all day long. The word "praise" is an old one, and it means the praise or commendation given to someone. "My tongue shall speak" means that he will use his voice to tell who God is and what he does.

The psalm is traditionally attributed to David. He is asking God for help because unjust people are attacking him and rejoicing in his misfortune. Before this verse, he prays that his enemies will be put to shame and that those who favor his cause will rejoice in God. At the end, he promises to respond with praise when God defends him.

For today: when you go through an injustice or a difficulty, do not let complaint be the only thing that comes out of your mouth. Choose each day to mention something good that God has done. You can thank him out loud in the morning or tell someone about it. In this way your trust grows, even while you wait for his answer.
exp.77:63:
Their priests were killed by the sword, and their widows could not mourn for them. The word "sword" here refers to death in war. That their widows did not mourn may indicate that the disaster was so great that there was neither time nor circumstance for grief.

The psalm is by Asaph, and it reviews the history of Israel to remember the people's unfaithfulness and God's patience. Many believe this verse alludes to the defeat at Shiloh, when the sons of Eli died and the ark was captured (1 Samuel 4). The psalmist presents that tragedy as the consequence of the people's rebellion.

Today we can take sin seriously without living in fear. God corrects, but He also restores, as the following verse shows. If anything in your life is drifting away from God, return to Him today.
exp.108:7:
It says that this man's life should be short and that another person should take his position. The word "office" here refers to his post or responsibility, and the verse uses the word "office" in the same sense. In Acts 1:20 Peter quotes this verse in connection with the replacement of Judas.

The one speaking is David, according to the heading of the psalm. He is crying out to God about an enemy who falsely accused him and repaid him evil for good. These words are a prayer of complaint, a kind of psalm that scholars call imprecatory. Some believe David is quoting what his accusers said against him; others, that these are his own desires for justice. There are different interpretations.

For today: when you are wronged unjustly, do not take revenge with your own hands. Bring your sincere pain to God and leave justice in his hands, remembering that Jesus taught us to pray for our enemies as well.
exp.77:62:
This verse says that fire destroyed the young men of Israel. "Young men" are the young male warriors or youths. "Maidens" are the unmarried young women, and "were not given to marriage" means that they never got to marry, so no one sang wedding songs for them. The "fire" can be understood as a war fire or as an image of destruction; the text does not make clear which.

The author is Asaph, who reviews the history of Israel in this psalm. He tells how the people rebelled again and again, and how God allowed their enemies to defeat them. He probably has in mind the defeat at Shiloh, when the ark was captured, though the text gives no further details. The grief is very great: young men, weddings, and joy are gone.

For today: sin has real consequences, and it affects even the youngest. But God does not abandon us completely; the psalm goes on to speak of his deliverance. If we have failed today, let us return to him sincerely.
exp.119:0:
This verse says that the psalmist cried out to God when he was in distress, and that God answered him. The title of the psalm is "A Song of degrees," and this phrase is also rendered as "a song of ascents" or "of the going up."

This is the first of the fifteen songs of ascents (Psalms 120 to 134). Many think that pilgrims sang them as they went up to Jerusalem, though this is not certain. The psalm does not say who wrote it. The one speaking suffers because of the lies and deceit of others, as the following verses show. He remembers how God had already helped him before.

For today: when you feel distress, for example from slander or injustice, do not carry it alone. Speak to God honestly, and remember the times he has already answered you. That strengthens confidence to keep going forward.
exp.20:9:
It says that God will remove from the earth the "fruit" of the king's enemies, that is, their children and descendants. "Seed" is another word for offspring. The verse speaks of a total judgment, one that reaches not only the enemies but also their lineage.

Psalm 21 is a psalm of David, which speaks of the king and gives thanks to God for his victory. Here it is addressed to the king or to God about those who oppose the divine plan. The language is harsh and typical of Hebrew poetry. Many Christians see in the king a sign of the Messiah. Some understand that the destruction of the offspring expresses the end of the evil they sowed, rather than a desire for revenge.

For today: do not take justice into your own hands. Entrust your pain over injustice to God, trust that he will judge with righteousness, and ask him to help you love those who harm you.
exp.80:9:
God presents himself as the LORD, the one who brought Israel out of Egypt. He tells them to open their mouths wide, and he will fill them. The phrase "I will fill it" is the same idea as the verse's own wording, so no note is needed here.

God himself is speaking, in a psalm of Asaph that was sung at a festival of Israel. He reminds them of his deliverance from Egypt and asks them for faithfulness, with no other gods. The image of the open mouth speaks of trust, like a little bird waiting for food. But the people would not listen to him.

Today we can stop looking for satisfaction in other things and come to God with trust and real need. Before rushing to our own resources, we can pray and listen to his voice, expecting that he will provide for us.
exp.31:8:
It says not to be like a horse or a mule, animals that have no understanding and must be guided by force. The "halter" is the rope tied to the animal's head, and the "bit" is the piece placed in its mouth. Without these, the animal does not come near its owner.

Here God speaks, or the psalmist quotes his counsel. It comes right after the promise that God will teach the way and watch over us. David, who has just described the pain of hiding his sin and the joy of being forgiven, invites us not to be stubborn. Some believe the psalm refers to his own experience, though the text does not say so in detail.

For today: when you sense that God is correcting or guiding you, do not wait until circumstances force you to act. Seek his direction with humility, listen to his Word, and obey promptly, like a child who trusts his Father.
exp.105:8:
He spoke sharply to the Red Sea, and it dried up. So the people of Israel went through the bottom of the sea as if they were walking through a desert, that is, over dry, solid ground. The deep waters are what is meant here by the depths.

This psalm is a song of praise and confession. The psalmist recalls the history of Israel: although the people did not understand God's wonders and rebelled by the sea, God saved them for the sake of his name. This shows that their deliverance depended on the faithfulness of God, not on the people's merit. Then the waters covered the Egyptians who were pursuing them.

For today: when you feel trapped with no way out, remember that God can open paths where you do not see them. Moreover, his help does not depend on our being perfect. Respond with gratitude and trust, not with rebellion.
exp.101:20:
The verse says that God acts, looks down from heaven and hears the groaning of the prisoners, with a purpose: that in Zion the name of the Lord be declared, and in Jerusalem his praise be proclaimed. When something is told, declared, or made known, it is shared through words. Zion and Jerusalem refer to the place where God's people gathered to worship him.

Psalm 102 is the prayer of a afflicted person, unnamed in the text, who suffers and feels close to death. Even so, the person looks beyond the pain and trusts that God will restore his people. The deliverance God gives does not end in relief, but leads to the praise of the nations.

For today: when God helps you through a difficulty, do not keep that testimony to yourself. Tell your family or your church, because your story can encourage others to trust in him.
exp.62:0:
David speaks to God in a personal way: "You are my God." He promises to seek him early, that is, first thing in the morning, at the start of the day. His soul and his body thirst for God, like someone in a dry land, worn out and weak, with no water. The phrase "early will I seek thee" means "I will rise early to look for you."

The title says that David wrote this psalm in the wilderness of Judah. The Bible records several times when he was there, fleeing from Saul or later from Absalom. The text does not say which one it was, and scholars debate it. What is clear is that, in a barren place far from the sanctuary, David feels more hunger for God than for water.

For today: when you feel tired or are going through a dry season, begin the day by speaking with God, even if with only a few words. Tell him honestly that you need him, and let him be your first source of strength.
exp.4:5:
The explanation says that God will bring an end to those who speak lies. "Destroy" means that God will cause them to perish. A "bloody and deceitful man" is someone violent who sheds blood, and "deceit" is the falsehood by which such a person takes advantage of others. "Abhor" means that the Lord rejects them with deep disgust. Lying and violence appear together as two faces of wickedness.

David speaks in a morning prayer. He is surrounded by enemies who slander him and set traps for him. Before this verse he has said that God does not love wickedness. Afterward, David contrasts his own attitude: he enters the temple trusting in God's mercy and asks him to lead him in righteousness.

For today: God values truth. If someone lies to you or harms you, you can hand that pain over to him without seeking revenge. And examine your own mouth: ask him to help you speak honestly, even in small things.
exp.21:8:
It says that God is the one who took the psalmist out of his mother's womb, that is, the one who brought him into the world. It also says that God made him trust, or hope, from when he was a nursing infant. The idea that matters most is the one found in the phrase "me hiciste confiar," which other translations render in the same sense, and this is the main point of the verse.

The verse is spoken by David, in a psalm of great suffering. People mock him and doubt that God will help him. Against those taunts, he remembers that God has cared for him since the beginning of his life. The New Testament connects this psalm with Jesus's sufferings on the cross, although David wrote it out of his own distress.

When others mock your faith or you feel alone, remember how God has cared for you from the very beginning. Write down some of the ways you have seen his help, and go back over them when doubt comes.
exp.70:6:
He says that this man's life has been like a strange sign or a wonder to many people. The word "wonder" refers to something that causes amazement or even dread. Even so, he affirms that God is his strong refuge, that is, a secure place where he can take shelter.

The psalm does not say who wrote it. The speaker seems to be an older person looking back over his whole life: God sustained him from birth and now he asks not to be abandoned in old age. Some believe the "wonder" speaks of sufferings that others watched with astonishment; others think it refers to how God cared for him. The text allows both readings.

Even when others do not understand your life or your trials, you can run to God. Today, when you feel watched or misunderstood, pray, saying: "Lord, you are my refuge."
exp.14:2:
He who can dwell near God does not use his tongue to speak ill of others, does not harm his neighbor, and does not accept or repeat an insult against him. "Backbiting" is speaking badly of someone to damage their reputation. "Reproach" is a disgrace or insult. "Accept" here can be understood as believing or passing along that gossip.

David writes this psalm answering a question: who may dwell in the presence of God, in his tabernacle and on his holy hill? The answer describes an honest and righteous character, not merely religious rituals. This verse shows that such integrity includes how we speak and how we treat others.

For today: before you share a comment or rumor about someone, ask yourself whether it is true, whether it is necessary, and whether it helps. If not, it is better to keep silent. And if others criticize someone who is absent, do not join in.
exp.53:2:
This verse says that strange and powerful people have risen up against David and want to take his life. What is serious is that they do not take God into account: they live as if he did not exist. "Life" here means life itself, and "Selah" is a pause or musical sign to stop and reflect; its exact meaning is not entirely certain.

David speaks in prayer. According to the heading of the psalm, the Ziphites, inhabitants of the region where he was hiding, told Saul where he was. Saul was pursuing him, and David felt betrayed and in danger. For this reason he cries out to God, asking for salvation and defense. Some understand "strangers" as people outside his tribe or without loyalty to him.

For today: when someone attacks you or fails you, bring your situation to God with sincerity. He sees what no one else sees. Ask him for help, trust in his justice, and do not respond with revenge.
exp.36:4:
This verse invites us to commit our way to God, that is, to place it in his hands and entrust it to him. "Way" refers to the whole of life: plans, decisions and worries. The idea of waiting on him means trusting with patience, and the promise that he will act means that God will work in his own way and in his own time.

It is a psalm attributed to David, written in the tone of counsel, almost like a father teaching his children. Its purpose is to calm those who become troubled when they see wicked people prospering. Before and after this verse, the psalmist urges us to do good, to delight in the Lord, and not to be upset by those who prosper in wickedness.

Today you can bring to God, in prayer, whatever worries you, and then keep doing what is right without despairing. Trusting is not sitting with your arms folded, but letting go of the need to control everything. This does not promise that everything will turn out as we wish, but it assures us that God is faithful and acts with justice.
exp.131:8:
The explanation says that God's priests were to be clothed with righteousness, that is, to live uprightly and not merely wear ceremonial garments. It also asks that God's people, the faithful ones set apart for him, be filled with joy.

This psalm is a prayer of the people of Israel, probably sung when the ark came to Jerusalem. It is not known for certain who wrote it. Here the people ask God to arise and dwell in his resting place, the place of his presence. The priests, who served before the ark, were to reflect the character of God, and the people could rejoice. The psalm then recalls God's promise to David.

For today: true worship joins an upright life with sincere joy. Today you can ask God that your way of treating others at home and at work be just, and praise him with gladness.
exp.58:10:
He says that David asks God not to kill his enemies outright, so that the people will not forget the lesson. He asks that God make them wander aimlessly, by God's power, and that He bring them low. The words "Slay them not" are a request not to finish them off at once. The phrase "our shield" is a picture of protection: God is the one who covers him in battle.

David speaks here in a moment of danger. The title of the psalm connects it to the occasion when Saul sent men to watch David's house in order to kill him. He trusts that God is his defense. He asks that God's justice be visible and lasting, not just a quick blow that is soon forgotten.

For today: when you are wounded or persecuted, do not take revenge with your own hands. Commit the matter to God, trust that He is your shield, and ask Him to act with justice in His own way and in His own time, while you keep a humble heart.
exp.43:0:
This verse opens with a note for the choir director: it is a psalm of the sons of Korah, and the word "Maschil" probably indicates a poem meant to instruct or to be meditated upon (its exact meaning is not entirely certain). Then the people say that they have heard with their own ears what their fathers told them: the works that God did in the times of old.

The speaker is the community of Israel, not a single person. The sons of Korah were Levites in charge of the music in worship. They recall, as the lines that follow show, how God gave them the land, not by their own strength. The psalm later turns into a lament over difficult times; we do not know with certainty at what historical moment it was written.

For today: tell your children, nephews, nieces, or friends how God has helped you. Those memories sustain the faith of others, especially when moments of doubt or difficulty come.
exp.32:16:
A horse is a vain thing for safety, meaning useless or deceptive. In that time the horse was a weapon of war, a symbol of military power. Even when it is great and strong, it cannot bring a true rescue. The word "rescue" here means saving someone, and the phrase "vain thing" is not about pride, but about something that does not do what it promises.

It is part of a psalm of praise. The psalmist calls the people to praise God, who created everything and watches over everyone. Before this, he speaks of the king and the army, and then shows that God's eye watches over those who fear him and wait for his mercy. It is not known with certainty who wrote it, since the text does not say.

For today: do your work well and use your resources wisely, but do not place your ultimate security in money, in your abilities, or in your plans. Put your trust in God, who cares for you.
exp.118:9:
He says the psalmist has sought God with his whole will, his affections, and his thoughts, not halfway. That is why he prays: "O let me not wander from thy commandments." Here "wander" means to go astray, to drift off the path without noticing, like someone who gets lost. The "commandments" are God's instructions.

The author of Psalm 119 is not identified with certainty; tradition has attributed it to David, but the text does not say so. It is in the section that begins by asking how a young person can keep his way pure. Here the poet answers with prayer: he desires to obey, but he acknowledges that he needs God's help so as not to stray.

We can seek God sincerely and still feel prone to wander. Today, before reading the Bible or beginning the day, pray with humility: "Lord, guide me, and do not let me turn aside from your path." Seek God with constancy and ask for his help every day.
exp.30:20:
The explanation says that David praises God because his steadfast love, his mercy, was something remarkable and out of the ordinary toward him, right when he was in a strong city, that is, a city with walls and defenses. "Blessed" means worthy of praise, and "the Lord" is the name of God.

The one speaking is David, in a psalm of prayer and thanksgiving. He had felt great fear, slander, and threats. In the verses that follow he admits that he thought God had abandoned him, but God heard his cry. It is not known for certain which city is meant; some think of a real place where he was protected, and others of an image of God's protection.

For today: when you go through pressure or criticism, stop and remember how God has cared for you before, and thank him out loud. That strengthens trust.
exp.68:8:
He says David was so filled with love and passion for God's house that this zeal wore him down from within. Zeal is a burning interest in something one loves. Reproaches are insults, and the verse speaks of people who spoke ill of God and looked down on him. The insults others hurled against God fell upon David, as though they were aimed at him.

The psalm speaks David's words in a time of distress. He suffers rejection, even from his own family, for being faithful to God. The Gospels cite the first part of this verse in connection with Jesus (John 2:17) and the second part in Romans 15:3, seeing in this psalm a reflection of his suffering.

For today: if you truly love God, you will sometimes feel the weight of mockery or rejection. Do not respond with pride or anger. Pray, stand firm, and let your love for God show itself with humility and mercy.
exp.67:20:
It says that God himself will defeat those who hate him and keep living in wickedness without repenting. The phrase about striking the head is an image of a decisive blow. The top of the head, the part that is struck, stands for the whole person, and the verse speaks of someone proud and self-assured who does not fear God.

This psalm is traditionally attributed to David. It is a song of victory, in which Israel celebrates that God cares for them, saves them from death, and overcomes their enemies. The verses that follow use very strong war language, typical of ancient poetry. Some read it as a promise of justice for the oppressed people.

For today: we do not have to take revenge or live with resentment. We can trust that God will do justice in his own time. It also invites us to examine our own hearts and leave sin behind before we become hardened.
exp.65:8:
He says that God is the one who keeps us alive and who did not let our feet slip. The word that appears in the verse for slipping is "moved," and that is the image: someone walking on dangerous ground who is kept steady by God. That image is about being kept from falling or failing.

The psalmist speaks on behalf of the people and calls the nations to praise God. He remembers that God kept them, even when he later mentions hard trials, such as being refined like silver. It is not known with certainty what exact moment he has in mind, and scholars interpret it in different ways.

Today we can thank God not only for the great miracles but also for the times he held us up without our noticing. Before you begin the day, take a minute to say to him: Thank you for holding me up.
exp.50:15:
This verse says that God takes no pleasure in animal sacrifices or burnt offerings, even though the speaker would be willing to give them. The "burnt offering" was an offering that was burned whole on the altar. The word "would give" here means "would offer."

The psalm is attributed to David after his serious sin, when he was confronted by the prophet Nathan (according to the psalm's title). He asks for forgiveness and cleansing. Here he recognizes that rituals, without a repentant heart, do not repair what sin has broken. The verses that follow make this clearer: what God values is a broken spirit and a humbled heart. Scholars debate how to connect this with the last verses, but the central idea is clear.

For today: when you fail, do not try to make up to God with religious activities or good works. Come to him sincerely, acknowledge your guilt, and ask him for forgiveness; he receives the humble heart.
exp.144:18:
This verse says that God makes real what those who fear him long for, that is, those who respect him and honor him with reverence. He also listens to their cry, that is, their call for help, and saves them. "Will fulfil" means that he will carry it out, and "will also hear" means that he listens as well.

This psalm is attributed to David and is a song of praise to the greatness and goodness of God. Here David describes what God is like toward his people: just, merciful, and close to those who seek him sincerely. The verses that follow add that God watches over those who love him. Many understand that the desires God fulfills are those of a heart that seeks to please him.

For today: when you are in trouble, pray sincerely and trust that God hears you. Ask him to shape your desires according to his will, and wait for his answer with patience.
exp.29:5:
David says that when everything was going well, he thought nothing and no one would shake him. The word "moved" here means shaken or made to fall. It was a calm confidence, but it rested on his good situation.

David speaks in a psalm of thanksgiving for being rescued from a serious trial. The heading connects it to the dedication of the house, though it is not known for certain which moment it refers to. The following verses show that God took away the favor he had felt, David was troubled, and he cried out again. So he learned that his strength came from God, not from his comfort.

For today: in good times, give thanks and remember that everything is a gift from God. Do not place your security in your health, your money, or your success, but in Him, who also sustains you in difficult days.
exp.19:1:
It says that God sends help to the believer from the sanctuary, the place where he was worshipped, and that from Zion, that is, Jerusalem, he upholds or strengthens him. The verse's "send thee help" simply means "to send you help"; "strengthen thee" means "to give you support and steadiness".

This psalm is by David and is addressed to the chief musician, to be sung in community. It seems to be a prayer of the people for their king before facing a conflict, perhaps a battle. Many think the people are speaking to the king, though the text gives no further detail. The sanctuary and Zion reminded people that God was near his people.

For today: do not face your struggles alone. Ask God to strengthen you, and let your community of faith pray for you. Also pray for others who are going through a hard day, and offer them your concrete support.
exp.47:6:
He says that God has power over the greatest forces. The "east wind" is a strong wind from the east, and the "ships of Tarshish" were large, sturdy ships, probably used for long trading voyages. It is not known for certain where Tarshish was. The verse shows that God can break what seems strongest.

The psalm is one of the songs of the sons of Korah, sung by the people who celebrate Jerusalem, the city of God. The verses before it tell how enemy kings saw the city, grew frightened, and fled. By comparing that fear to ships broken by the wind, the psalmist says that nothing can withstand God. Some see here a poetic image rather than a specific historical event.

For today: when something seems too big or too strong for you, such as a problem or a threat, remember that God is greater. Bring your fear to him in prayer and trust his care.
exp.7:3:
The explanation says that the psalmist asks, with wonder: what is a human being that God should remember him? To "be mindful of him" means that God thinks about him and keeps him in view. "That you visit him" means that God draws near to care for him. "Son of man" is another way of saying "human being," as in a poetic parallel.

The psalm is traditionally attributed to David, according to its heading. He looks at the sky, with the moon and the stars, and feels small before the greatness of the Creator. But right away he is amazed that this God, so great, takes care of people and gives them honor and responsibility over creation.

For today: when you feel small or unimportant, go out and look at the sky and remember that God knows you and thinks about you. Give him thanks, and faithfully care for what he has entrusted to you.
exp.144:7:
It says that God is "gracious," meaning compassionate and kind toward those who do not deserve it. He is also "full of compassion," because He is moved by our weakness. "Slow to anger" means that He does not become angry right away, but has great patience. And He is "of great mercy": His compassion is abundant and never runs out.

This psalm is attributed to David and is a song of praise. Earlier, the psalmist speaks of telling of God's mighty works to future generations. Here he recalls what God's character is like, something already said in Exodus 34:6. Then he declares that God is good to all.

For today: when you fail, do not run from God out of fear. Come near with sincerity, acknowledging your mistake, because He is patient and compassionate. At the same time, treat those around you with patience.
exp.108:20:
Here the psalmist asks God to act on his behalf. The phrase "do thou for me" means "work for me" or "treat me well." He does this "for thy name's sake," that is, appealing to God's reputation and character, not to any merit of his own. He asks to be delivered and gives the reason: God's mercy is good, that is, his faithful and compassionate kindness.

The one speaking is King David, according to the title of the psalm. He is surrounded by false accusations and by people who repay his good with evil. After asking for justice against his slanderers, he changes tone and turns to God with humility. He confesses that he is afflicted, needy, and with a wounded heart.

When you feel unjustly treated, do not rely on your own defense or your desire for revenge. Pray with sincerity, trusting in the kind character of God and leaving the outcome in his hands.
exp.51:4:
This verse says that God himself will bring down the wicked person the psalm is speaking about, for ever. It uses strong images: to "destroy" means to ruin completely, and to "take away" and "root out" are like pulling a plant up by its roots. "The land of the living" refers to this life, the place of the living. "Selah" is a pause to reflect, and its exact meaning is not known for certain.

The psalm is attributed to David, after Doeg the Edomite reported the priests to Saul (1 Samuel 22). David speaks to this man of deceitful tongue, who loved lies and evil. He trusts that God will bring about justice.

For today: we do not need to take revenge or live in bitterness over injustice. We can leave judgment to God and, in the meantime, take care with our words so that they are true and good.
exp.93:21:
What it says: The psalmist affirms that God has been his refuge, that is, a secure place where he can find protection. He also calls him "the rock of my refuge," an image of something firm that does not move. The word "But" marks a contrast with what came before.

Context: The speaker is a believer who watches rulers and unjust judges band together against the righteous and condemn the innocent. We do not know for certain who wrote it or at what exact moment. Faced with so much injustice, he does not trust himself or the courts, but God. The following verses say that God will respond to their wickedness.

For today: When you face injustice, slander, or treatment you do not deserve, run first to God in prayer. Tell him what you feel, rest in the fact that he sees everything, and avoid repaying evil with evil.
exp.71:6:
During this king's reign, it says, righteousness will flourish like a growing plant, and there will be abundant peace. The phrase about peace in abundance means a great deal of peace, more than is usual. The image of endurance "so long as the moon endures" is a poetic way of saying "forever," since the moon seems like something permanent.

This psalm is attributed to Solomon, though some understand it as a prayer for him. The speaker asks God that the king would rule with uprightness and care for the poor. Many Christians also see in it a look toward Christ, the perfect King, and others read it as an ideal for any ruler. Both readings are possible.

Today we can pray for those who govern, asking for justice and peace. And in our own circles, at home or at work, we can sow justice and honest dealing, trusting that God makes what is good flourish.
exp.120:1:
This verse says that a person's help does not come from the mountains or from any other created thing, but from Jehovah, the name of God in the Old Testament. He is the one who made heaven and earth. "Help" here means aid in a time of trouble.

This psalm is a "song of ascents," or pilgrim song, which the travelers probably sang as they went up toward Jerusalem. The speaker looks at the mountains and wonders where his help will come from. Scholars debate whether the mountains stand for dangers along the road or for places of false worship. In any case, the answer is clear: the help comes from the Creator, not from the creation.

Today, when you feel stuck with no way out, before rushing to look only for human solutions, take a moment to pray and say: "Lord, my help comes from you." Trust that the One who made everything also cares for you.
exp.40:11:
It says that God upheld the psalmist because he lived with integrity, that is, with a sincere heart and without duplicity. Furthermore, God set him "before your face," that is, in his presence, and that "forever." "Upheld" means that God kept him steady and did not let him fall.

The psalm is spoken by David, according to its heading. He is sick and surrounded by enemies, and even a close friend betrayed him (v. 9). He asks God for help and yet trusts that God sustains him. This verse is his expression of confidence. Some understand "forever" as a lasting fellowship with God in this life, and others also see a hope beyond death.

When you feel weak or betrayed, do not depend on your own strength. Try to live sincerely before God, and trust that He upholds you and keeps you close to Him.
exp.68:20:
It says that when the psalmist was hungry and thirsty, instead of help they gave him something bitter and unpleasant. The gall was a bitter substance, and the sour wine was a sharp, spoiled drink. In this way they mocked his need instead of relieving it.

The psalm is spoken by David, according to its title, in the midst of deep suffering. He feels alone, humiliated, and surrounded by enemies, and no one comforts him. The New Testament connects this psalm with Jesus, and the Gospels tell that they offered Him sour wine on the cross (Matthew 27:34, 48; John 19:28-29). Christians see in this a reflection of his suffering.

For today: when you feel lonely or misunderstood, bring your pain honestly before God. He knows your shame and understands your suffering. And you, be someone who offers comfort to those who suffer.
exp.32:7:
This verse calls all the people of the planet to fear God. "Fear" here does not mean living in dread, but honoring him with awe, recognizing him as God and taking him seriously. "The inhabitants of the world" means everyone who lives on the earth, without exception.

The psalm does not say who wrote it, though many attribute it to David; this is not certain. It is a song of praise. Before this verse it speaks of how God created the heavens with his word and set the seas in their place. Afterward it explains that what God says comes to pass, and that no human plan can overcome his. For this reason it invites everyone to revere him.

For today: when you feel small or insecure in the face of the news or your problems, remember who God is. Take a moment to admire his creation and place your worries in his hands, with reverence and trust.
exp.77:45:
It says that God handed over the crops of the Egyptians to insects that devoured them. The word "caterpiller" refers to a creature that destroys plants; here it means a plague similar to the locust. "Increase" means the harvest, and "labour" is what the farmer sowed and tended with effort. The old spelling of the verse's wording is not something you need to notice here.

The psalmist, Asaph according to the title, reviews the history of Israel to teach the new generations. Here he remembers the plagues of Egypt, when God freed his people from slavery. The purpose is that Israel would not forget the works of God or repeat the rebellion of their ancestors.

For today: Remembering how God has acted in the past strengthens trust in Him. Today you can write down some times when God helped you and tell them to your children or friends, to encourage them to trust in Him.
exp.30:2:
What it says: David affirms that God is his rock and his fortress, that is, a firm and secure place where he can take shelter. He says God will lead him and guide him "for your name's sake," meaning for the honor and character of God. To guide means to show the right way and to lead along it.

Context: David speaks in a psalm addressed to the chief musician. He is in a time of distress, asking for help and deliverance. The text does not say precisely what situation he was facing, and scholars interpret it in different ways. What is clear is that, even in danger, he remembers who God is and trusts in Him. Later he speaks of hidden nets and commits his spirit into God's hands.

For today: When you do not know which way to take or feel threatened, before looking for ways out, pause and say to God: "You are my rock; guide me." Resting in his faithful character gives you security to take the next step.
exp.118:55:
This verse says that the psalmist received something good because he had obeyed God. "This" points back to what he has just mentioned: the songs during his journey, the remembrance of God's name in the night, and the peace of keeping his law. The sentence can also be understood this way: "this belongs to me, because I have kept your commandments." Translators interpret it in several ways.

The speaker is the author of Psalm 119, a psalm devoted to God's Word. We do not know for certain who wrote it. He feels like a stranger or a traveler, and perhaps he is going through trials. Even so, he finds joy and comfort in God's teachings.

For today: obedience to God is not only a burden; it also brings comfort and companionship. Choose one teaching from the Bible and put it into practice this week. Then remember with gratitude how God sustained you.
exp.17:15:
He sent from above and took hold of me; he drew me out of many waters. The phrase "out of many waters" is the image of rescue from deep trouble, as in a flood that threatens to drown. The words "he took me" and "he drew me out" express God's personal action in lifting David up and bringing him to safety.

David, the king of Israel, speaks in a song of thanksgiving for God's deliverance from his enemies and from Saul (as the heading of the psalm indicates). The verses just before describe God acting with storm, lightning, and power over creation. The water here is a symbol of distress, not necessarily a literal flood.

For today: when you feel overwhelmed by problems, ask God for help with confidence. He can lift you up and sustain you, and afterward it is good to remember and give thanks for what he has done, as David did.
exp.78:1:
It says that the enemies left the bodies of God's servants unburied, so that the birds of the sky and the wild animals would devour them. "Saints" here means the faithful to God, his people. "Servants" are those who belong to him and serve him.

Asaph, or someone from his group of singers, speaks in a lament to God. The nations invaded Jerusalem, defiled the temple, and killed many people. Many believe it refers to the destruction of Jerusalem by Babylon (586 BC), although the psalm does not say so clearly. Leaving a body unburied was a great dishonor.

For today: when the pain is so great that you have no beautiful words, bring it to God honestly. This psalm shows that you can weep and bring your complaint before him, and that he listens to those who suffer.
exp.57:8:
It says that, before the pots can feel the heat of the thorns used as fuel, God will sweep away the wicked like a whirlwind. The words "both living, and in his wrath" probably mean that they will be taken while still full of life and anger; the Hebrew of this verse is very difficult and is translated in several ways. The image speaks of a swift judgment, before the pot has even had time to get hot.

David cries out to God against unjust judges who hand down violence instead of justice (vv. 1-2). He uses strong images, typical of Hebrew poetry, to ask God to stop their wickedness. It is a psalm of prayer, not an order to take revenge personally.

Today, when you see injustice, do not grow bitter or take revenge. Bring your pain to God honestly and trust that he judges with justice, in his own time.
exp.18:4:
The explanation says that the sun comes out each morning like a bridegroom leaving his bedchamber, full of joy, and like a strong man who delights to run his course. "Bedchamber" is the room or bed of the wedding. "Strong man" here means a very strong and brave man, an athlete.

It is a psalm of David, who praises God for his creation. The verses before it say that the heavens declare the glory of God without words. God placed in them a dwelling, that is, a place or tent for the sun. Then the psalm turns to speak of the Law of the LORD, which is perfect. In this way it links creation with the Word of God.

For today: each morning, when you see the sun rise, remember that God sustains you and is faithful. Begin your day with gratitude and joy, and open his Word so that it may guide you.
exp.109:6:
He says the victorious king will drink water from a brook while he is on the road, and for that reason he will lift up the head. "Lift up the head" means he will be encouraged, strengthened, or come out triumphant. The picture is of a warrior who does not stop in the battle: he takes a sip from the brook, is refreshed, and keeps moving forward.

This is a psalm of David about the Messiah, as king and priest. The verses before it speak of judgment on kings and nations. This last verse closes with a simple scene of rest and strength. Some think the brook speaks of God sustaining him on the way; others see it only as a picture of his victory. The text does not explain it further.

For today: even on long and difficult journeys, God gives us small refreshments to keep going. Stop to pray, rest, and receive his strength. Then lift up your head and continue with hope.
exp.31:10:
This verse invites the righteous to be glad and rejoice in the Lord, that is, in God. It also calls on all who are upright in heart, meaning those who live with sincerity before Him, to shout for joy. The verse speaks in the plural, addressing all of them together. The explanation's point about the wording is that the command is addressed to a group, not just one person.

Psalm 32 is attributed to David. He speaks after having confessed his sin and received forgiveness. Earlier in the psalm he warns us not to be stubborn like a horse or a mule, which need a bridle to be made to obey. He contrasts the sorrow of the wicked with the mercy that surrounds the one who trusts in God. That is why it ends with a call to joy.

For today: when you feel forgiven and upheld by God, do not keep that joy to yourself. Give thanks to God out loud or sing a song of praise today, even on a difficult day.
exp.55:4:
David says that every day his affairs cause him sorrow and pain. The word for "afflict" or "grieve" here means to bring sadness or distress. The word for "affairs" does not mean trade or business here, but his affairs or, in the Hebrew, his words, which is why other versions say they twist what he says. In addition, his enemies think only of doing him harm.

The speaker is David, and the title of the psalm links it to the time when the Philistines seized him in Gath. He is surrounded by hostile people who watch him and set traps for him. Even so, in the verses before this one he declares that he trusts in God and is not afraid of what a mere human being can do to him.

For today: when you feel misunderstood or pressured, do not hide your distress. Tell it honestly to God and, like David, choose to trust his word even while you still feel fear.
exp.4:6:
It says that the psalmist will enter the house of God, not because of his own merits, but because of the abundance of God's mercy. There he will bow down toward the holy place where God is present, and he will do so with fear, which here means reverent awe, not terror.

The speaker is David, according to the traditional heading of the psalm. He has just said that God hates wickedness, lying, and deceit. Set against those enemies, David presents himself differently: not because he is perfect, but because he trusts in God's mercy. He then asks God to lead him in the midst of his adversaries.

For today: when you come near to God, do not come presuming on how good you are. Come trusting in his mercy and in humility, and begin your prayer or your gathering with gratitude and reverence.
exp.23:8:
The psalmist asks the gates to lift up their heads, that is, to open wide, so that the King of glory may enter. It is a poetic image: the gates are treated as if they were people who must bow before a King. The phrase about everlasting doors speaks of gates that are ancient, firm and lasting. This verse repeats the previous verse, as in a song.

This is a psalm of David, probably sung in a procession toward the sanctuary. Many think it recalls the bringing of God's ark to Jerusalem, although the Bible does not state this with certainty. It has the feel of a dialogue: some ask for the gates to be opened, and others ask who the King is. The answer is that the LORD is strong and mighty.

For today: open the doors of your life, your decisions and your fears, so that God may enter and reign. He is not a distant guest, but the King who deserves a welcome.
exp.119:2:
Here the psalmist asks a question of the false tongue, that is, of lying and slander. He asks what gain or punishment awaits it: "What shall be given unto thee?" and "What shall be done unto thee?" It is a rhetorical question: the liar gains nothing worth having. The word "false" means that it lies in order to harm.

The one speaking is a believer who is far from home, surrounded by hostile people, while going up to Jerusalem (it is a song of ascents, and many believe it was sung on those journeys). He had cried out to God in his distress, and now he addresses those who slander him. The next verse gives the answer: their words will be like arrows and burning coals, that is, severe judgment. Where Meshech and Kedar were is debated, and they are perhaps used as images of hostile places.

For today: before you speak badly of someone or exaggerate the truth, remember that a lie brings no lasting gain. And if others lie about you, bring it to God in prayer, as the psalmist did.
exp.77:42:
This verse recalls that God worked signs and wonders in Egypt, specifically in "the field of Zoan." "Signs" are events that show God's power, and "wonders" are amazing works. Zoan was a region or city in the Nile delta, and it is linked with the area where Egypt's power was centered. The word "wrought" means that God carried them out on purpose.

The psalmist, Asaph according to the psalm's heading, tells the story of Israel to teach the new generations. He has just said that the people tested God and forgot how he had redeemed them. So he goes back over the plagues: they are clear evidence that God set them free and that they had no reason to doubt him.

For today: when you doubt God, remember what he has already done in your life. Write down the times he helped you and review them in difficult moments.
exp.39:12:
It says that David asks God to rescue him and to do so quickly. The words "Be pleased" translate the idea of asking God earnestly to do this, and "make haste to help me" conveys urgency. It is a short, direct, and sincere prayer, from someone who feels in great need.

The one speaking is David, according to the title of the psalm. He is surrounded by troubles and also weighed down by his own faults, which he describes as more numerous than the hairs of his head. He feels without strength, and yet he does not stop praying. The verses that follow show that he also has enemies who want to harm him. Some understand these troubles to be sufferings and others to be guilt; the text seems to join both things together.

For today: when you feel overwhelmed, do not wait until you have the perfect words. You can pray something simple, such as "Lord, help me, and do it soon." God is not troubled by an honest and urgent prayer.
exp.36:31:
This verse says that the wicked person watches the righteous one, like someone waiting for the right moment to attack, and looks for a way to take his life.

It is a psalm of David, already an old man, who advises believers not to be anxious or envious of the wicked who seem to prosper. In this passage he acknowledges that the righteous can indeed be persecuted. But he immediately adds that the LORD will not leave him in the hands of the wicked, nor allow him to be condemned unjustly.

For today: if someone treats you badly for doing what is right, do not respond with resentment or fear. Keep walking in God's way, pray, and trust that he watches over you and will bring about justice in his time.
exp.9:16:
What it says: The psalmist affirms that God hears the desire of the humble, that is, those who suffer and depend on Him. Also, God "prepares" or strengthens their heart and pays careful attention to their prayer. The phrase "thou wilt cause thine ear to hear" means that God bends His ear to listen.

Context: The speaker is the psalmist, probably David, though the psalm does not say so clearly. Before this, he cried out in distress over the injustice of the wicked who oppress the poor. Here the tone shifts to confidence: God sees the oppressed, and the next verse says that He will do justice for the fatherless and the poor.

For today: When you feel small or unjustly treated, pray with sincerity. God not only hears you, He can also give you calm and firmness in your heart while you wait for His answer.
exp.144:8:
This verse says that God is good to everyone, leaving no one out. "The Lord" is the name of God. "Tender mercies" are his acts of compassion and care. And "over all his works" means that his kindness reaches everything he has made, including people and creation.

This psalm is written by David, and it is a song of praise to God as king. Just before this, he has recalled that God is gracious, slow to anger, and great in mercy. Afterward, he invites all of God's works and his people to bless him and to speak of his kingdom. Some scholars debate how far that "all" reaches, but the text emphasizes the broad generosity of God.

For today: when you deal with someone difficult or very different from you, remember that God is also good to that person. Ask him to help you respond with kindness, patience, and respect, and give thanks for his goodness in your own day.
exp.17:4:
It says that David felt surrounded by death. The word that appears here refers to the place of the dead, the grave, which in Hebrew is called Sheol. "They surrounded me" means that they hemmed him in on every side. "The snares of death confronted me" means that the traps of death were already set in his path, like a net laid across the road. It is poetic language: it describes a danger so great that it seemed there was no way out.

David is the speaker, and the title of the psalm connects it with the day the LORD delivered him from all his enemies and from the hand of Saul. Here he recalls how desperate his situation was before he tells how God rescued him. The verses that follow show that he cried out and God heard him.

For today: when you feel cornered by fear, sickness, or problems, do not keep silent. Tell God honestly what you feel. David went through the darkest valley, and even there God heard him.
exp.114:13:
This verse says that God will increase his blessing on his people and also on their children. The word "increase" means to grow or add more. The promise does not stop with one generation but extends to the next.

Psalm 115 is a song of praise from Israel, probably sung together in community. The verses before it say that God remembered his people and blesses all who fear him, both small and great.
