Here it seems that someone, perhaps a priest or a leader, directs these words to the congregation as a blessing. Scholars are not sure of the exact occasion when it was used.

For today: trust that God cares for your family. Pray for your children, or for the young people close to you, and teach them to respect and love God through your daily example.
exp.125:3:
This verse is a prayer. The people ask God to "turn again" their captivity, that is, to restore them and bring them back to a state of blessing.

"South" refers to the Negev, a dry region where the streams nearly disappear, but when the rains come they suddenly fill with water.

The people of Israel speak in a pilgrimage song. The verses before it recall a joy over a restoration that God has already given them. Even so, here they ask for more. Some understand that they speak of the return from exile in Babylon; others, of a restoration still incomplete after the return. The text does not make this entirely clear.

For today: if you are going through a dry or difficult season, you can ask God for restoration with confidence. Remember what He has already done for you, and hope that He can renew what today seems empty.
exp.115:5:
It says that God watches over and protects the simple-hearted, a term that here refers to people who are plain, humble, and free of malice (some translations say "the simple"). The psalmist tells that he was brought low, that is, worn down, without strength and in great need, and that God helped him and rescued him.

The speaker is the psalmist, someone who came very close to death, amid distress and tears. He cried out to God asking that his life be delivered, and God answered. The verses that follow show his thankfulness and his rest. No one knows for certain who wrote it or what his exact situation was.

For today: when you feel without strength, you do not need to pretend to be strong. Come to God with sincerity, tell him your need as it really is, and trust that he cares for those who come to him with humility.
exp.8:13:
In this verse, the psalmist asks that God rescue him so that he may tell of all his praises. "The gates of the daughter of Zion" refers to Jerusalem, and "salvation" here means deliverance, that is, the rescue God gives. He wants to rejoice in it.

David speaks here, according to the title of the psalm. He was troubled by enemies who hated him, and he had just asked for mercy, saying that God lifts him up "from the gates of death." Now he contrasts those gates with others: the gates of Jerusalem, the public place where people gathered and where important matters were spoken of. He wants to move from the shadow of death to open praise.

Today we can remember what God has done for us and tell others about it: in the family, in the church, or with a friend. Giving thanks aloud strengthens everyone's faith.
exp.62:1:
This verse says that David longs to see God's power and greatness, just as he had beheld them before in the sanctuary, that is, in the place of worship. Seeing God's power in this way means he had experienced it up close.

David speaks in the psalm's heading that he is in the wilderness of Judah. He feels dry and weary, and for that reason his soul thirsts for God. Scholars do not agree on exactly when in his life this took place, but the text suggests he is far from the sanctuary and remembers with longing what he experienced there.

For today: when you find yourself in a season of weariness or hardship, thankfully remember the times when God seemed near to you. That memory can revive your desire to seek him again in prayer and in his Word.
exp.93:2:
This verse is a cry: the psalmist asks God how much longer He will allow the wicked to be joyful and to feel secure. The wicked are people who live without respect for God or for others. The phrase "triumph" here means they celebrate and rejoice, as if nothing will ever happen to them.

The author of the psalm is not identified. He speaks on behalf of God's people, who are suffering mistreatment and abuse (v. 5). Earlier he asked that God, as Judge of the earth, would act and do justice. His question comes from pain, not from doubt about who God is. He brings it directly to Him.

For today: when you see injustice seem to win, do not keep your anguish inside or take revenge. Speak it to God in prayer, honestly, and trust that He is the just Judge and will act in His time.
exp.95:12:
This verse says that all creation rejoices before the Lord, because he is coming to judge the earth. The text promises that God will judge the world with righteousness and the peoples with his truth, that is, with uprightness and without deceit.

This psalm is a song of praise that calls all the nations to worship God. It does not say who wrote it. The psalmist invites the heavens, the earth, the sea, and the trees to celebrate, because God's judgment is good news: he will set everything in order and correct the injustices.

For today: when you see injustice and feel that no one is correcting it, trust that God judges with perfect truth and righteousness. That lets you wait in peace and live honestly yourself, without taking revenge.
exp.36:23:
The explanation says that the person whom God guides may fall, but will not be left lying on the ground. "Utterly cast down" means knocked down and unable to get up. "Though he fall" speaks of stumbles, troubles or failures. The reason is that the Lord upholds him with his hand, like a father holding his child.

The psalm is attributed to David. It is spoken by an older man who advises believers not to fret or envy the wicked who seem to prosper. In the verses that follow, he says that in his long life he has not seen the righteous forsaken. It is a teaching of trust, not a promise that there will never be falls.

If today you stumble or fail, do not stay on the ground. Ask God for help, get up calmly, and take the next step, trusting that his hand does not let you go.
exp.101:26:
He says that God does not change and never ends. "But" means "yet": everything created grows old like clothing, but God remains "the same." "Your years will not run out" means that his life and his faithfulness have no end.

The psalm is the prayer of a person who is afflicted, weak, and feels that their days are running out (vv. 3-11). It is not known for certain who wrote it. Seeing his own frailty, the writer looks to God, who endures. For this reason the next verse promises that the children of his servants will live secure before him. The letter to the Hebrews (1:10-12) quotes this passage and applies it to Christ.

When you feel that everything is changing, that your strength is failing, or that the future is uncertain, rest in the fact that God remains the same. Today, bring him one specific worry and remember that his faithfulness does not depend on your circumstances.
exp.117:12:
He says that someone was pushed with great force so that he would fall, but God held him up. "Thou hast thrust" means "you pushed me," and "but" is the word that marks the turn to what God did. "The Lord" is the name of God. The speaker addresses his enemy, and he acknowledges that he did not get up by his own strength, but because God helped him.

The psalm is a song of thanksgiving for a victory. The one speaking seems to be a leader or king of Israel, although the text does not give his name, and some think the whole people are speaking. He was surrounded by enemies, swarming like bees, and he almost fell. After God saves him, he says that the Lord is his strength and his song.

Today, when a crisis, a betrayal, or a loss knocks you down, do not think everything is over. Ask God for help with sincerity, and when you get back up, give him thanks, also in front of others.
exp.36:21:
It says that those whom God blesses will inherit the earth as their possession, and those whom God curses will be cut off, like a tree that is cut down. Those "blessed by him" are the ones who belong to God and receive his favor; those "cursed by him" are the ones who remain under his judgment.

This is a psalm of David, who was already old (v. 25), and it offers wise counsel to those who become troubled when they see the wicked prosper. For this reason the psalm repeats: do not become impatient, trust in the Lord. In Israel, "the land" was God's promise to his faithful people. Jesus returned to this idea in Matthew 5:5, when he said that the meek will inherit the earth.

Today, when injustice seems to be winning, you do not have to envy or respond with wickedness. Trust that God has the final word, and in the meantime live with honesty and generosity.
exp.24:16:
It says that the psalmist's inner pain has grown very great. Words like "distresses" are sufferings that weigh down the soul, and "troubles" are deep afflictions and feelings of being overwhelmed. That is why he asks God: "bring me out", that is, free me from the burden that is pressing on him.

This is a psalm attributed to David. The one speaking feels alone, surrounded by enemies, and also aware of his own faults, since in the following verse he asks for forgiveness. Some believe it was written in a time of persecution, but the psalm does not say exactly which moment it was. What is clear is that he cries out to God with sincerity.

For today: when your heart is heavy, you do not have to pretend that you are fine. You can tell God in simple words what you feel and ask him for help. Also, seek out someone you trust who can walk with you in prayer.
exp.25:6:
The explanation says that the psalmist wants to come to God's altar for two things: to speak aloud giving thanks and to tell of all the Lord's wondrous works. To "publish with the voice of thanksgiving" means to proclaim gratitude openly, without hiding it. "Wondrous works" are the mighty and admirable deeds of God.

David speaks, according to the traditional heading of the psalm. He asks God to examine him and declares that he has avoided the company of the wicked. He wants to wash his hands in innocence and come before the altar with a sincere heart. His desire to worship springs from a life that seeks to be whole. Then he says that he loves the house of God, the place of his glory.

For today: do not keep your gratitude only in silence. This week, tell someone something concrete that God has done for you, or give thanks to him out loud in prayer. Speaking of his works strengthens your faith and encourages others.
exp.105:18:
It says that the people of Israel made a calf at Horeb (another name for Mount Sinai) and bowed down before it. "Molten image" refers to a statue made from melted metal poured into a mold. "Bowed down" means they prostrated themselves to worship it.

The psalmist reviews Israel's history to acknowledge the people's repeated sins, despite God's faithfulness. Here he recalls what happened in Exodus 32, when Moses was slow to come down from the mountain. The order of the psalm does not follow the events exactly: earlier it mentions Dathan and Abiram, which happened later. The author groups the examples to show a pattern of rebellion.

For today: it is easy to put things in God's place, such as money, success, or comfort. Ask yourself what gives you security and where you devote your best time. Return to God with humility and gratitude.
exp.17:27:
Here the psalmist says that God is the one who lights his lamp and who brightens his darkness. "Light" means to give light, and "darkness" refers to times of gloom, danger, or confusion. The lamp can represent his life, his hope, or his guidance. He does not trust in his own light, but in God's.

The one speaking is David. This psalm was written after God delivered him from his enemies and from Saul, as the title indicates. In the verses nearby, David speaks of God's justice, who saves the humble and brings down the proud. For this reason, his trust in God is not blind: he knows God's faithfulness.

Today, when you cannot see the way or feel distressed, you do not have to have all the answers. Ask God for light for the next step, and trust that He will guide you with patience and truth.
exp.42:0:
This verse is a prayer. The speaker asks God to be his judge and to plead his case. "Judge me" here means "do me justice," not "condemn me." "Plead my cause" means "defend my case." He also asks to be delivered from ungodly people, that is, people who do not honor God, and from a deceitful and unjust man. The word "iniquity" means wickedness or injustice.

Psalm 43 does not name its author. Many see it as a continuation of Psalm 42, but this is understood in different ways. The one speaking feels far from the temple, surrounded by oppression, and confused because God seems to have left him. Even so, he continues to trust God as his stronghold.

When someone treats you with lies or injustice, you do not have to respond with revenge. You can bring your case to God honestly, even with your doubts, and ask Him to be the one who brings justice and guides you.
exp.59:9:
Here the people acknowledge with pain that God seemed to have rejected them. He no longer went out with their armies into battle. Some versions read it as a question: "Wilt not thou, O God, which hadst cast us off?"

The heading of the psalm attributes it to David and connects it with wars against neighboring peoples. The one speaking is the king on behalf of the nation, after a defeat. Earlier he mentioned God's promises concerning Moab and Edom, but now reality looks different. That is why he cries out, "Give us help," because human help is not enough.

When you feel that God is far away after a failure, do not hide your pain. Bring it to him honestly, as this psalm does, and trust again that true victory comes only with God.
exp.21:14:
The explanation says that the strength of the one speaking has dried up like a broken piece of baked clay (a potsherd, a fragment of a broken pot). His tongue clings to the roof of his mouth from thirst and extreme weakness. And he feels that God has let him fall into the dust of death, that is, to the edge of the grave.

David speaks in a psalm of distress, surrounded by enemies who attack him like wild animals. He describes a total suffering, of body and of heart. The New Testament connects this psalm with the cross of Christ (Matthew 27:46; John 19:28), although scholars explain in different ways how it first applied to David.

For today: when you feel without strength, you do not have to pretend to be strong. You can tell God with complete honesty how you are, just as the psalmist did. He hears even the most weary cry.
exp.78:12:
This verse says that God's people, whom it compares to sheep that he cares for, promise to give him thanks and praise him forever. A "pasture" is a grassy field where the flock feeds and rests. The phrase "from generation to generation" means that children and grandchildren will also sing that praise, from one age to the next.

The psalm is spoken by the psalmist, Asaph or someone from his group, on behalf of all Israel. It arises from a great tragedy: enemies invaded the land, destroyed the temple, and left death and prisoners behind. After asking for help and justice in the earlier verses, it ends with a promise of trust: although they suffer today, they will again praise God.

For today: even in difficult times, we can choose to give thanks to God and teach others to do the same. Today you can thank God out loud for something specific and share with your children or someone close to you how God has cared for you.
exp.109:4:
The Lord who sits at the right hand of the chosen king will defeat the kings when the day of his righteous anger comes. "At your right hand" means at your side, the place of support and authority. "Strike through" means that he will wound them or overcome them. "Wrath" is his anger against wickedness.

This psalm is by David and speaks of the Messiah, whom David calls "my Lord." Jesus quoted it this way (Matthew 22:44). The psalm presents a king who is also a priest, and here the emphasis is that God backs his kingdom and will one day judge the powers that oppose it. Some understand this day as the final judgment; others see it as partly fulfilled in history.

For today: you do not have to fear the unjust powers of this world, because God has the last word. Trust in his justice, refrain from taking revenge yourself, and live with hope.
exp.88:50:
It says that God's enemies have mocked and taunted his "anointed one," that is, the king chosen by God. "They have dishonored the footsteps" refers to mocking every step he takes, perhaps his walk and his whole life, as if God had abandoned him. The verb here means to taunt or to throw the failure back in someone's face.

The one speaking is the psalmist, Ethan the Ezrahite according to the title of the psalm. He is distressed because David's kingdom seems fallen, even though God had promised that his line would endure. So he calls on God to keep his promises and lays before him the suffering of his people. It is not known with certainty which king or what exact moment is described.

For today: when you are mocked, or when it seems that God is taking his time, you can speak to him honestly, remind him of his promises, and keep praising him, as the psalm ends: "Blessed be the Lord forever."
exp.140:8:
Here David asks God to watch over him from the traps others have set for him. "Snares" and "gins" are traps, like the ones used to catch animals. "Workers of iniquity" are those who do evil. In other words, he asks for protection against the deceit and dangers that the wicked prepare.

The speaker is David, in a psalm of prayer. He feels surrounded by danger and by people who want to make him fall. So he looks to God, trusts in Him, and pleads that He will not abandon him. The next verse shows his hope: the wicked will fall into their own nets. Scholars do not agree on the exact occasion when he wrote it.

For today: when you feel pressure to fall into deceit, temptation, or bad advice, pray simply and ask God for wisdom to see the traps. Then step away from what you know is harming you.
exp.138:11:
It says that for God, darkness is not a hiding place. Where we see nothing, he sees everything clearly. The night shines before his eyes as the day does, and for him there is no difference between light and darkness. The phrase "hideth not from thee" means that darkness does not hide you or cover you from him.

It speaks King David, in a psalm where he reflects on how God knows him completely. Earlier he asked whether he could flee from God's presence, and he concluded that he could not. Even if he tried to hide in the darkness, that would not work. This knowledge of God then leads him to praise, as he remembers that God formed him.

For today: when you feel alone, confused, or in a hard night, remember that God sees you and stays with you. Speak to him honestly, without pretending, because nothing about you surprises him.
exp.85:16:
Here David asks God for "a token for good," that is, a clear sign of his favor and kindness. He wants those who hate him to see it and be ashamed, humbled as they realize God is on his side. He ends with a reason: God has already helped him and comforted him.

This is a prayer psalm attributed to David. He is in trouble and surrounded by enemies, and so he pleads with God. Earlier he recalled that the Lord is merciful, slow to anger, and abundant in mercy and truth. That is why he dares to ask. Some understand the "token" as a visible act of God's intervention; the text does not say exactly what it would be.

When you are going through a trial, remember how God helped you before and ask Him with confidence to sustain you again. His character does not change. Ask Him for help to trust Him, without seeking revenge on anyone.
exp.114:3:
This verse says that the idols of the other nations are made of silver and gold, and that they are "the work of men's hands." In other words, they are not living gods but objects made by people. "The work of men's hands" means something made and shaped by human beings.

The psalmist speaks on behalf of God's people. The nations mocked them, asking, "Where is their God now?" The people answer that their God is in the heavens and does whatever He pleases. Then they contrast the two: the idols look valuable, but they were created by human hands. We do not know with certainty the exact occasion on which the psalm was written; there are several opinions.

Today we can ask ourselves what things made by us, such as money, success, or image, we are treating as if they could save us. Let us put our trust in God, not in what our hands produce.
exp.129:5:
It says that the psalmist waits for God more eagerly than the night watchmen wait for morning. The people who guard the city while everyone else sleeps are the ones in view here. The phrase about the ancient spelling is only that. The comparison is repeated to give the idea force: the waiting is intense and sure.

It is a song of pilgrims, perhaps sung as they went up to Jerusalem. The one speaking is in a very hard situation, from the depths, and acknowledges his guilt. Even so, he trusts that God forgives. That is why his waiting is not hopeless but full of hope, and then he invites all of Israel to wait in the same way.

For today: when you are in a long night of guilt, fear, or trouble, do not just stare into the darkness. Wait for God as the watchman waits for the dawn, sure that the light will come. Pray with sincerity, read his word, and trust that his forgiveness and his help are real.
exp.41:5:
The psalmist tells God that he feels deeply discouraged. "Cast down" means sad and without strength. Even so, he decides to remember God, speaking of remembering you from the land of Jordan, the mountains of Hermon, and the hill Mizar.

The one speaking is a believer who once went with the crowd to the house of God and is now far away. The places he names lie to the north of Israel. The name of that hill is not known with certainty, and we also do not know for sure what situation he was living through.

Today, when you feel discouraged, do not pretend you are fine. Tell God how you feel, and deliberately remember what He has done for you. That remembrance can sustain your hope.
exp.111:8:
It says that the person who fears God gives generously and gives to the needy. "Dispersed" is like sowing with an open hand, without stinginess. "His righteousness endureth for ever" means that his good conduct is not forgotten or lost. "His horn shall be exalted with honour" uses the image of an animal's horn, a symbol of strength and dignity: God will give him honour.

The psalm does not say who wrote it, but it is a song of wisdom that describes the man who fears the LORD. His trust in God keeps him steady when there is bad news. His generosity is part of that life of faith. The next verse shows the contrast: the wicked man sees his honour and is filled with anger.

For today: practise generosity in a concrete way. Set aside part of what you have, even if it is little, to help someone in need. Do it with trust in God, without seeking applause.
exp.82:4:
They have said, in their hearts, that they agree with one another completely, as if they were one person. To plot something in secret is one way to describe what they are doing, and to form a binding alliance is another. The phrase "with one purpose" means that they are united, all pursuing the same goal. What is most serious is that by attacking God's people, they are setting themselves against God himself.

This is a psalm of Asaph, a prayer in the middle of a great threat. Several neighboring nations, which the following verses list, join together to wipe out Israel. Scholars do not agree on which exact historical event gave rise to it, so it is better not to claim one. The psalmist does not take revenge; he brings the problem to God.

For today: when you feel that many are rising up against you or against what is right, do not grow bitter or lose hope. Do as the psalmist did: tell God everything honestly, and trust that he sees what is being planned in secret.
exp.102:12:
This verse compares God's love with the tenderness of a good father. The word "pitieth" means to feel tenderness and show mercy toward someone in their need or weakness. God is the Lord, and "them that fear him" are those who respect him and honor him with reverence, not with terror.

It is a psalm of David, who praises God for his blessings. Earlier it speaks of the forgiveness that removes our sins as far as the east is from the west. Then it explains the reason for that compassion: God knows our frailty and remembers that we are dust, that our days are brief like grass.

For today: when you fail or feel weak, do not hide from God. Come near with confidence, like a child who knows his father understands him. And if you are a father or mother, let God's compassion teach you to treat your own children with tenderness.
exp.114:5:
This verse continues to describe the idols of the nations. It says they have ears, but they cannot hear, and they have noses, but they cannot smell. The words "they hear not" and "they smell not" in the verse above correspond to the wording of the original text, which uses an older form of the verb tense; today we would say simply that they do not hear and do not smell. They are figures made by human hands, with the shape of a body but without life.

The psalm does not say who wrote it. It seems to be a song of God's people, perhaps for worship, which contrasts the Lord, who is in the heavens and does as he pleases, with the idols of silver and gold. It mocks idolatry with seriousness in order to remind us that only God lives and answers.

Today we can ask ourselves where we place our trust: money, fame, work, or the approval of others. If those things cannot truly hear us or help us, let us turn again to prayer to the living God, who does hear.
exp.50:14:
It says the psalmist asks God to open his lips, so that his mouth may declare and proclaim God's praise. "Lord" here refers to God, and "shew forth" means he will speak openly and make it known. It is a humble plea: he cannot praise on his own and needs God to give him the words.

Traditionally, the title of the psalm attributes it to David, after his sin with Bathsheba and after the prophet Nathan confronted him. This is understood that way from the heading, which was added in the ancient tradition. After asking for forgiveness and cleansing, David longs for his mouth, once silenced by guilt, to praise God again with sincerity.

For today: when you feel far from God or ashamed, do not stay silent. Ask him simply to heal your heart and restore your desire to give thanks to him. He receives the one who comes broken.
exp.24:12:
The explanation says that the person who fears God will live with a soul at peace, enjoying the good things God gives. The word "dwell at ease" means that he will rest and live in tranquility. "His seed" means his descendants, children and grandchildren. "Inherit the earth" speaks of receiving the promised land as an inheritance and of living secure in it.

It is a psalm attributed to David. He prays to God with humility, acknowledges his sin, and asks for forgiveness and guidance. In the verses around it he speaks of the one who fears the LORD, that is, who reverences him and trusts him. God teaches him the way and shows him his covenant. The "earth" is understood above all as the promise to Israel; some also see it as an image of God's blessings in general.

For today: when you feel restless, seek God sincerely, confess what you have done wrong, and ask him for direction. His peace can sustain your heart, and your way of living can leave a good mark on your family.
exp.77:2:
The psalm says that the stories of God that the psalmist is about to tell are nothing new: the people have heard them, have understood them, and received them from their ancestors. "Known" here means they know them well. "Told" means they were passed on by word of mouth.

Asaph speaks, and in this maskil (a teaching song) he calls Israel to listen. He is going to review the nation's history, with its wonders and its failures. The verses that follow explain the reason: God commanded that each generation tell the next one his works, so that they would not forget them.

For today: think about who taught you to know God and give thanks for that person. Then look for an opportunity this week to tell a son, nephew, friend, or neighbor something specific that God has done in your life.
exp.97:3:
The explanation says that all the earth, that is, all the peoples and not only Israel, is invited to sing to God with joy. "Make a joyful noise" means to sing with delight. "Make a loud noise" means to do it out loud. "Rejoice" speaks of shouting praise with enthusiasm, and "sing praise" means singing psalms or songs of praise to God.

The author of the psalm is not named; the psalm is simply called a psalm, and we do not know with certainty who wrote it. It speaks to the people and to the nations, because God has shown his salvation and his righteousness, and has been faithful to Israel. What God has done is now seen by all the peoples, and that is why they are invited to celebrate.

Today we can praise God without waiting to feel perfect. Choose a moment this week to sing, alone or with your family, remembering something specific that God has done for you. Praise is born from remembering his goodness.
exp.77:55:
Yet they challenged and angered God Most High, and did not keep his decrees.

This verse says that the people of Israel tested God and made him angry. "Challenged" means they defied him, doubting his patience and his power. "God Most High" is a title that emphasizes that God is above all. "Decrees" refers to his commands and teachings, which they did not obey.

The psalm is written by Asaph, who recalls the history of Israel to teach the new generations. God had already brought them into the promised land, had driven out the peoples who lived there, and had given them an inheritance. Even so, the people repeated the rebellion of their fathers. The psalmist wants the people to learn from that mistake.

For today: let us not take God's goodness for granted. If he has given us peace, family, or work, let us respond with gratitude and simple obedience, not with distrust or indifference.
exp.36:1:
The explanation says that the wicked may seem strong, but their success does not last long. "Soon" means quickly, without delay. They will be cut down like the grass, which dries up right away. "They shall soon be cut down like the grass, and wither as the green herb" means that they will fade like a tender, green plant that quickly loses its freshness.

David writes this psalm, traditionally considered his, to encourage people who suffer when they see unjust people doing well. That is why it begins by telling us not to fret or be envious. Then it invites us to trust in God and do good. The tone is that of wise counsel, like a father speaking to his children.

When you see someone dishonest prospering, do not let envy or bitterness take control of you. Breathe, pray, and keep doing what is right. Place your trust in God, not in the appearances of the moment.
exp.87:3:
He says that the psalmist feels the same as those who are about to die. "The pit" is an old way of speaking of the grave or the place of the dead (in Hebrew, the "Sheol"). "Without strength" means that he no longer has any spirit or energy left to keep going.

The psalm is written by someone who suffers greatly and prays in anguish. The heading attributes it to Heman the Ezrahite, although there are different opinions about who he was and when he wrote it. It is one of the darkest psalms, because it almost never ends in relief. Even so, it begins by calling God "the God of my salvation," and for that reason it keeps crying out to Him.

For today: when you feel without strength, you do not have to pretend you are fine. You can tell God with complete honesty what you feel, just as this psalmist did. Praying this way is already a way of continuing to trust. And if the weight is very heavy, also seek out someone you trust who can walk alongside you.
exp.80:11:
God says that he let his people follow the stubbornness of their own hearts. The phrase translated here as "I gave them up" means "I let them go, I released them." The hardness of their hearts refers to a stubborn will that refuses to be corrected. Walking in their own counsels means they lived by their own ideas and decisions, not by God's.

The one speaking is God, through the psalmist Asaph, during a festival in which Israel remembered their departure from Egypt. God reminds them that he rescued them and offered them provision, but they would not listen to him. So he allowed them to continue on their own path. His words that follow show sorrow: he would have wanted to bless them and protect them.

For today: when God speaks to us through his Word and we ignore him again and again, we can grow hard. Today is a good time to listen to him with humility and obey, before our stubbornness guides us.
exp.127:3:
This verse sums up what the psalmist said before. The opening words are an old-fashioned way of saying "look" or "notice." The phrase about fearing the Lord does not mean living in dread, but respecting him, honoring him, and living in obedience to God. This is how the one who does so will be blessed.

Psalm 128 is a song of pilgrims, which the Israelites sang as they went up to Jerusalem. It describes the blessing of a family: fruitful work, a wife and children gathered around the table. The images of the vine and the olive trees speak of life, food, and joy in the home. It is not a mechanical promise that everything will always go well; it is a picture of how God often cares for those who trust him.

Today we can begin each day by recognizing God in everyday life: our work, our family, the shared table. Respecting him in small things opens the heart to value and give thanks for what he gives us.
exp.90:1:
Here the speaker declares with his own mouth what he believes about God: "I will say of the Lord". He calls him "my hope" and "my fortress", that is, his refuge and his secure place, like a stronghold. He ends with a decision: "in him will I trust". The word "shield" that appears later refers to a small shield.

The psalm does not say with certainty who wrote it, and some have attributed it to Moses, though this is not certain. In verse 1 the one who lives under God's care is spoken of, and here that person responds with a personal confession. Afterward the psalm describes dangers such as plague and snares, and God's protection against them.

Today we can do the same: before facing a problem, say aloud or in prayer: "Lord, you are my refuge, and in you I trust." Doing this each morning helps us place our trust in God and not only in our own strength.
exp.105:3:
The psalmist asks God: "Remember me, O Lord, with the favour that thou bearest unto thy people; visit me with thy salvation." The word "favour" in the verse means goodwill and kindness. "Salvation" here does not speak only of bodily health, but of deliverance, that is, God's rescue and help.

The author does not name himself. Earlier he praised God and called blessed those who live in righteousness. Now he prays as someone who longs to be counted among the people who receive God's blessing. Later the psalm confesses the sins of Israel, so this prayer springs from humility, not pride. Some think it reflects the time of the exile, but the text does not say so with certainty.

For today: pray with confidence, but without presumption. Ask God to keep you in mind because of his kindness, not because of your merits, and seek to stay close to his people.
exp.40:9:
Here the psalmist asks God to have compassion on him and to raise him up from the bed where he lies sick. He also says that afterward he will repay his enemies, that is, they will receive what they deserve. "Raise me up" means healing me and setting me on my feet again.

The psalm is attributed to David. He is ill, his enemies speak as if he were already about to die, and even a close friend has betrayed him. The image of lifting the heel against him is a picture of betrayal. Some understand the repayment as the justice of a king; others understand it as a human desire for revenge. Jesus quoted the preceding verse when speaking about Judas.

For today: when you feel weak or betrayed, ask God for compassion and strength, and leave justice in his hands, without taking revenge yourself.
exp.36:28:
This verse says that righteous people, that is, those who live uprightly and trust in God, will receive the land as an inheritance and will dwell in it forever. To inherit means to receive something as a gift and a lasting possession, not on the basis of one's own merit.

Psalm 37 is a poem by David, written in the tone of wise counsel. He speaks to people who suffer as they see the wicked seem to prosper. He reminds them that this advantage will not last and that God cares for his own. Some understand "the land" as the land promised to Israel; others also see it as a broader promise, fulfilled fully in the future.

For today: when injustice discourages you, do not become bitter or imitate those who do wrong. Keep doing good with patience, and trust that God is faithful to his promises, even if you have to wait a long time to see them fulfilled.
exp.102:17:
It says that God's mercy and justice are with those who "keep his covenant," that is, those who remain faithful to the relationship God made with his people. It is also with those who "remember his commandments to do them": not only do they remember them, but they practice them. The phrase "to do them" means carrying them out.

It is a psalm of David, which praises God for his forgiveness and compassion. Earlier, the psalm compares human life to a flower that the wind carries away, but it says that God's love lasts forever. This verse clarifies who enjoys that goodness: those who fear him, that is, those who respect him and trust in him. Afterward, the psalm shows God reigning over all.

Today, it is not enough to remember what God says. You can choose a teaching of the Bible that you already know and put it into practice this week, trusting in his mercy and not in your own strength.
exp.34:21:
The psalmist speaks to God with confidence and tells him that he has already seen everything that is happening. He asks God not to stay silent and not to be far from him. "Keep not silence" means "do not stay quiet; act or respond." "Be not far from me" is a plea to feel his closeness.

Context: David is the speaker, according to the title of the psalm. He is surrounded by enemies who speak with deceit, mock him, and say, "Aha, aha, our eyes have seen it!" as if they were celebrating his downfall. So David turns to God as his defender and asks him for justice. He no longer trusts in himself, but in the righteous judgment of the Lord.

For today: When you feel unfairly treated or very alone, do not keep your pain to yourself. Speak to God honestly, remind him that he sees everything, and ask for his closeness. Then leave the defense in his hands, instead of responding with revenge.
exp.93:6:
The explanation says that the wicked, while they oppress others, persuade themselves that God does not see them or take notice.

The psalmist speaks in the midst of great injustice. The powerful mistreat the widow, the stranger, and the fatherless, who are the most defenseless. He quotes what these oppressors say in order to show their foolishness. Right after, in the following verses, he answers them: he who made the ear and the eye, how will he not hear or see?

For today: when you see injustice, or feel forgotten, remember that God does see and does hear. Bring him your pain in prayer and, while you wait, do not look the other way: defend and help the one who suffers near you.
exp.108:25:
It says: "Help me, O LORD my God: save me according to your mercy." It is a direct plea for help. The word "mercy" here translates a Hebrew word that speaks of God's faithful love, his loyal kindness. The psalmist does not rest on his own merits, but on who God is.

The one speaking is the psalmist, traditionally identified as David, although the text gives no further details of the situation. He is weak from fasting, thin, and mocked. His enemies accuse him and shake their heads with contempt. He has prayed in pain, and now he cries out to God as his only way out.

For today: when you feel without strength or judged by others, do not wait until you are well to pray. Ask for help simply, and trust that God responds because of his goodness, not because of your perfection.
exp.41:7:
This verse says that God sends his faithful love (his "lovingkindness") during the day. And at night, the psalmist has a song that reminds him of God, along with a prayer addressed to the God of my life, that is, the God who gives and sustains his life.

The one speaking is a deeply discouraged believer, perhaps a Levite, far from the temple and far from home. He remembers God from the region of the Jordan and Mount Hermon. He feels covered by waves of anguish, and his enemies mock him. Even so, in the midst of his pain, he expresses his confidence that God has not left him.

For today: when you feel downcast, begin and end your day by remembering God's love. You can sing a song of praise or offer a simple prayer before sleeping.
exp.103:5:
This verse says that God covered the earth with the deep ocean, like someone wrapping it in a garment. The waters rose so high that they covered even the mountains. The word "deep" refers to the primeval, ancient waters. "It" refers to the earth, mentioned in the previous verse.

The psalmist praises God as Creator. The psalm does not name its author in the text; some connect it with David, but this is not certain. Many think the passage evokes the earliest moments of creation (Genesis 1:2, 9), although some also relate it to the flood. Interpreters explain it in different ways. The next verse shows that, at God's command, the waters withdrew and everything was put in its place.

For today: if God governs even the deepest and most chaotic waters, he can also hold steady your disordered moments. Today, in prayer, hand over the situation you feel is out of control, and trust that he sets limits and brings order.
exp.50:18:
This verse says that once God has shown his goodness, then the offerings presented to him will please him. "Sacrifices of righteousness" are offerings made with an upright heart. A "burnt offering" is the offering that was burned whole on the altar. Bullocks are young bulls that were offered in worship.

The speaker is David, according to the heading of the psalm, after acknowledging his sin. He has already said that God desires a broken spirit. Then he prays for Zion and for the walls of Jerusalem. Some think this last part was added later, but that is not certain.

For today: before any offering, service, or song, God looks at the heart. If you come to him with humility and sincerity, your worship truly pleases him.
exp.106:10:
This verse says that some people ended up in suffering because they rebelled against what God had said. Where the explanation notes that they rebelled, the meaning is that they opposed God and would not obey. The phrase about despising the counsel of the Most High means that they scorned the guidance of God, who is the supreme God.

The psalmist speaks to Israel, inviting them to give thanks to God for his love. He describes a group who lived in darkness, imprisoned and in chains. Here he explains the cause: their own rebellion. Even so, the psalm goes on to show that, when they cried out, God delivered them.

For today: when a counsel of God makes us uncomfortable, let us not reject it with pride. If we have ignored his guidance, we can return to him with humility and ask for his help, knowing that he listens and rescues.
exp.4:2:
This verse says that David speaks to God with confidence: each morning he cries out, and God hears him. The phrase about God hearing his voice means that God attends to his prayer. Presenting oneself before God is like standing before a king to speak with him. Waiting means he waits patiently and hopefully for the answer.

David is the one speaking in this psalm. He is asking God for help and calls him "my King and my God." The verses that follow show that he feels surrounded by wicked and deceitful people. That is why he takes refuge in a righteous God, who takes no pleasure in wickedness. The text does not say which exact moment of his life it refers to, so it is best not to claim it.

For today: before you begin your day, set aside a few minutes to pray. Tell God your burdens and plans, and then wait patiently, trusting that he hears you.
exp.48:5:
The verse describes those who believe their money makes them strong and protected.

The one speaking is a psalmist, a teacher of wisdom, who says he will use the harp to explain his "enigma," that is, a deep truth about life. He asks why he should fear when the wicked surround him. His answer begins here: the rich who trust in their money cannot buy their own salvation, as the following verses say. It is not known with certainty who wrote this psalm.

Today we can ask ourselves where our hearts rest. Having possessions is not wrong, but they cannot give us true peace or deliver us from death. It is best to trust in God first and to use what we have with humility and generosity.
exp.106:31:
It says we should magnify God and praise him publicly, in the midst of the whole community. "Exalt him" means lifting him up, speaking of his greatness. "Congregation of the people" is the gathering of all the people. "Assembly of the elders" is the group of leaders and senior members who guided and made decisions for the community, like a council.

Psalm 107 does not name its author. The speaker invites the redeemed of the LORD to give thanks. Earlier, the psalm recounts rescues: travelers who were lost, prisoners, the sick, and sailors caught in a storm. This verse closes the last account, that of the sailors whom God brought safely to harbor. Gratitude was not meant to stay private, but to be told before everyone.

For today: when God helps you with something, tell it. Share your testimony in your church or with your family, and give thanks also before the leaders. In this way others are encouraged to trust him.
exp.118:40:
This verse begins with "Vau", which is the name of a Hebrew letter. In this psalm, each group of verses starts with a letter of the alphabet. The psalmist asks that God's mercy, that is, his faithful love, come to him. He also asks for his salvation, meaning deliverance and rescue, according to what God has promised.

The psalm does not say who wrote it. The speaker loves God's law and faces mockery and contempt, as seen in the verse before and the verse after, where he mentions the one who shames him. For this reason he asks God for help and leans on what God has said.

For today: when you feel pressured or ashamed because of your faith, do not rely only on your own strength. Pray with the promises of the Bible, asking God to sustain you according to his word, and return to it every day.
exp.100:4:
The explanation says that whoever speaks badly of their neighbor in secret, slandering them behind their back, will not be tolerated. The same goes for the one with a haughty look, meaning the person who looks down on others with contempt, and the one with a proud heart, who is arrogant. "I will cut off" means to remove or eliminate from one's presence; "secretly" means done in a hidden and disguised way.

The one speaking is David, according to the title of the psalm, as a king who promises to rule with integrity. Before and after this verse, he declares that he will reject what is unjust, deceit, and lies, and that he will seek out faithful people to be near him. It is a commitment to care for his household and his kingdom. Some also see here an ideal that only God fulfills perfectly.

For today: avoid commenting on other people's faults behind their backs. If someone tells you a piece of gossip, do not repeat it; instead, speak well of that person or, if there is a real problem, talk about it directly with them and with humility.
exp.20:5:
This verse says that God has blessed the king permanently and has filled him with joy by being in his presence. "You have blessed him" means you gave him favor and good. "Made him" is an older way of saying "you made him." "With your face" means being near God, under his kind gaze.

This is a psalm of David, or dedicated to him, and it is a prayer of thanks for a victory. The people speak to God about the king, and they acknowledge that his strength, his long life, and his honor come from God. Many Christians also see here a look toward Christ, the ultimate King, although the text first speaks of a king of Israel.

For today: the greatest joy is not in what we accomplish, but in being close to God. Today, spend a few minutes praying quietly and thanking him for one specific blessing.
exp.34:18:
Here David asks God not to let his enemies mock him. Those who attack him without reason are called the "wrongful" ones. The old phrase for winking an eye, a gesture of mockery or spiteful complicity, as if saying "See, it turned out badly for him," is rendered in the verse above as wink with the eye.

David speaks in the middle of a time of persecution. He has suffered attacks and betrayals, and so he asks God, "How long?" In the verses nearby he promises to praise God publicly if he is rescued. Then he describes how his enemies speak deceit and laugh at his fall. Some scholars see this psalm as David's personal prayer; others point out that it has also served to express the pain of any righteous person who is mistreated.

For today: when someone treats you badly or mocks you without cause, do not respond with revenge. Tell God honestly what you feel, ask Him for justice, and trust that He sees what no one else sees.
exp.56:0:
David asks God for mercy, and he repeats the request to show how urgently he needs it. He entrusts his soul to God and compares himself to a small bird that takes shelter under its mother's wings. The phrase "I will make my refuge" points to finding safety and protection. He hopes to stay there until the storm has passed. The heading is a musical and occasional note, and the term "Michtam" has an uncertain meaning.

David is the speaker, and the heading says he was fleeing from Saul and was in a cave. The Bible records that he hid in caves during that pursuit (1 Samuel 22 and 24), though we cannot be certain which episode the psalm refers to. He writes out of fear, but also out of faith.

For today: when you feel cornered, do not wait until everything is resolved. Pray honestly, repeat your cry if you need to, and stay close to God while the difficulty passes.
exp.135:14:
He says that God defeated Pharaoh of Egypt and his army in the Red Sea. To overthrow means that God threw them down into the waters and drowned them. The Red Sea is the name used in the verse above, and scholars debate its exact location.

Each line ends by saying that his mercy endures forever.

This psalm is a song of praise that the people repeated together in community, with a constant refrain. No one knows for certain who wrote it. It recalls the departure from Egypt: God opened the sea, guided Israel, and defeated their enemies. The psalmist presents the deliverance as a sign of God's faithful mercy, which sustained his people.

For today: when you remember how God helped you in difficult moments, give him thanks out loud. Write down those occasions and review them when a new trial comes. In this way your confidence grows, because his mercy does not change or run out.
exp.118:63:
The verse says that the goodness and faithful love of God fill the whole earth, and so the psalmist asks him to teach him his statutes, that is, his rules and commands. The word "mercy" here speaks of loyal, compassionate love. The name of God used in this older version is the one rendered "Lord."

The speaker is a believer who loves God's law. Tradition does not agree on who wrote it, and many link it with David, but the psalm does not say so. It comes right after mentioning that he would rise at midnight to praise God and that he joins those who fear him. Now he looks at the world, sees God's goodness everywhere, and concludes that he wants to learn more from him. It is a psalm in which each section is arranged according to the Hebrew alphabet.

For today: When you notice God's goodness in everyday things, the sun, food, family, let that lead you to ask him, "Teach me." Spend a few minutes reading his Word with that humble attitude.
exp.69:2:
This verse asks that those who mock David be turned back in the shame they deserve. The phrase about being turned back means that they retreat, and the phrase about the shame they have brought on themselves means that it comes as a result of their offense. The words "Aha, aha" are a cry of mockery and scorn, like someone laughing at a person who is suffering.

David speaks in the middle of a time of distress. This is a psalm to call something to mind, that is, to remind God of his need. He is surrounded by people who wish him harm and mock him. For this reason he cries out to God asking for quick help, and he leaves the answer to those who insult him in God's hands.

For today: when someone mocks you or humiliates you, there is no need to take revenge. You can bring your pain to God with sincerity, ask him for help, and trust that he will do justice. Meanwhile, seek to keep your heart humble and full of hope in him.
exp.71:17:
It says that the Lord, the God of Israel, deserves to be praised, because he alone does wonderful things. "Blessed" means worthy of being praised and acknowledged. "Only" means that no one else can do works as great as his.

This psalm speaks of a just king, whose reign brings abundance and blessing to all peoples. Many read it as a prayer for Solomon, and Christians also see in it a sign of the reign of Christ. Verses 18 and 19 are a final song of praise. With them the second book of the Psalms ends. The closing line about the prayers of David seems to mark the end of that collection. Who wrote it is a matter of debate.

When you see something good in your life or in the world, do not credit it only to luck or effort. Stop for a moment and give thanks to God out loud.
exp.146:3:
This verse says that God knows how many stars there are and calls each one by its name. "He" refers to Jehovah, the Lord. The words "all of them" are an old way of phrasing "all of them" in the verse above, so they need no separate comment.

The psalm does not say who wrote it. It is a song of praise, and it was probably sung when the people returned from exile. Earlier, the psalmist speaks of a God who rebuilds Jerusalem, gathers the scattered, and heals those whose hearts are broken. Then he says that God's understanding has no limit. The stars show that the same God who governs the universe also cares for the wounded.

If God knows every star by its name, no detail of your life is lost to him. When you feel small, forgotten, or hurt, pray with confidence: the great God is also near, and he knows who you are.
exp.118:82:
The psalmist says he feels like a wineskin (a bag made from animal skin for holding wine or water) left in the smoke. With the heat and soot, the skin wrinkles, darkens, and dries out. That is how he feels: worn out and parched. Yet he adds that he has not forgotten God's statutes, that is, his commands and teachings.

The one speaking is the author of Psalm 119, who loves God's law. He is suffering, waiting for comfort, and being persecuted by proud people. We do not know who he was or the exact moment of his life. Some understand the image as weariness and pain; others as the passing of the years. In both cases, his faith remains firm.

When you feel worn down by trials, do not go silent or pull away from God. Tell him honestly how you feel, and hold on to a promise from his Word that you can repeat today.
exp.36:38:
This verse says that the salvation or deliverance of righteous people comes from God, not from themselves. It also says that God is their strength, that is, their refuge and support, when times of distress arrive, in other words, of difficulty and deep suffering. The name of God appears in this passage as the LORD.

This psalm was written by David, and in his old age he gives counsel to those who become troubled when they see the wicked prosper. For this reason he contrasts the end of the righteous, which is peace, with that of the wicked, which is destruction. Here David holds that true security is not found in circumstances, but in God.

When a hard time comes, do not rely only on your own strength or embitter yourself by comparing yourself with others. Pray, ask God for help, and lean on him step by step, with patience and trust.
exp.135:9:
He struck Egypt by taking the lives of its firstborn sons, and even in that, his mercy endures forever. "Struck" means hit or punished. "Firstborn" refers to the eldest children.

It is a psalm of praise that the people repeated, probably in worship, with the refrain "his mercy endures forever." After recalling creation, the psalmist remembers Israel's deliverance from slavery in Egypt, recounted in Exodus 11 and 12. That last plague was the blow that led to the people's departure. The text presents that judgment as part of God's faithfulness toward his oppressed people.

For today: when it is hard to understand God's judgment, remember that he is just and faithful. You can trust that God does not abandon those who suffer oppression, and give thanks for his past deliverances.
exp.137:4:
This verse says that the kings of the earth will sing about how God acts, because his glory is great. "The ways of the Lord" are his manner of working and of dealing with people. "Sing of" means they will sing about them, celebrating them.

David speaks here, according to the title of the psalm, and gives thanks because God answered him when he cried out and strengthened him. He imagines that even kings, when they hear the words of God, will acknowledge him. Right after this, he says that God attends to the humble and looks from afar on the proud. His glory is not only power: it also bends toward the poor.

For today: when God helps you in a difficult moment, do not keep it silent. Tell it and thank him with a song or a prayer. In this way others can see what God is like and be encouraged to trust him.
exp.104:7:
He remembers his covenant forever, that is, the solemn agreement or commitment he made with his people. "He remembered" means that he keeps it in mind and is faithful to it. "The word he commanded" is what he ordered and promised, and "a thousand generations" expresses a very long time, without any practical limit. Some understand the number literally, and others as a way of saying "forever."

The psalmist speaks to Israel, the descendants of Abraham and the children of Jacob, inviting them to praise God. He recalls how God cared for them from Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob onward. The psalm recounts the history of God's promises to encourage the people to trust and obey him.

For today: when you feel your circumstances are changing or your strength is failing, remember that God's faithfulness does not depend on you. You can rest in his promises and respond with gratitude and obedience.
exp.20:12:
It says the people ask God to show himself great by his own strength. "Be exalted" means "be lifted up, be recognized as great," and the verse's "power" refers to his might. At the end, the people promise to answer with song and praise for who God is and what he does.

This is a psalm of David, and it was probably sung by the people on behalf of the king. The verses before it speak of enemies who plan evil but do not succeed. This last verse closes the psalm with a prayer and a promise of worship. Some think it is a celebration after a victory; others think it is a prayer before battle. The text does not make this entirely clear.

For today: when you feel that evil or injustice surrounds you, do not rely only on your own strength. Ask God to act, and choose to praise him now, even before you see the answer.
exp.102:1:
Here David speaks to himself and commands himself to praise God with his whole being. To "bless" means to speak well of God, to give thanks to him, and to acknowledge who he is. "Benefits" are the good things God has done. David asks his soul not to forget any of them.

The psalm is written by David, according to its title. It begins with personal praise and then lists what God does: he forgives, heals, redeems, and crowns with kindness. We do not know with certainty at what point in his life he wrote it, and scholars do not agree. What is clear is that David speaks out of gratitude.

For today: set aside a few minutes and make a list of the good things God has done in your life. Thank him for them aloud or in writing. Remembering his benefits protects the heart from discouragement and ingratitude.
exp.22:1:
He says that God, like a good shepherd, makes his sheep lie down in grassy pastures of tender green. "Soft pastures" means gentle, fresh grass. "Lie down" means to recline or rest. "Still waters" are calm waters, where the sheep can drink without fear. "Will lead" means that he will care for and guide.

David speaks in the first person. He had been a shepherd of sheep before becoming king, so he knows this work well. He uses that image to express his confidence in God, who looks after him and gives him what he needs. Scholars do not always agree on when in his life he wrote it, and the text does not say.

For today: God wants to give us rest, not only to demand more of us. Today you can set aside a few quiet minutes to pray, read the Bible, and hand over your worries, trusting that he cares for you.
exp.77:50:
This verse recalls the last plague on Egypt: God struck down all the firstborn, the chief of their strength, that is, the eldest sons, the first fruit of each family's vigor. The tents of Ham refers to the homes of Egypt, since Ham is the ancestor the Bible connects with that land.

The psalmist (Asaph, according to the heading) reviews the history of Israel to teach the new generations. He tells how God judged Egypt, which oppressed his people, and then brought them out of slavery. The passage shows that God is both just and a deliverer. Some wonder about the severity of this plague; the Bible presents it as judgment after many warnings and a pharaoh who refused to yield.

For today: remember that God sees injustice and cares for his own. Trust that he knows how to deliver and guide, and do not forget to tell others what he has done for you.
exp.9:7:
He sits in the hidden places of the villages, like someone waiting for a chance. There, in secret, he kills the innocent. His eyes watch over the poor with patient and evil intent, waiting to strike when they are helpless. Hidden places and secret corners are the kind of places where a person can stay out of sight.

Psalm 10 is a prayer from someone who cries out to God on behalf of the oppressed. Tradition attributes it to David, though the text does not say so, and the exact situation behind it is not known for certain. The psalmist describes the wicked person, who believes that no one will see him or punish him. Further on, the psalm ends with trust that God does see and does defend the orphan and the poor.

For today: when you see injustice that seems to go unpunished, do not stay silent or lose heart. Pray to God, who does see, and look for ways to help those who are vulnerable near you.
exp.21:12:
It says that the enemies opened their mouths against the one speaking, like a lion that tears its prey and roars. The word "ravening" in the verse means seizing or preying on, and the image shows a fierce and violent threat.

David speaks in this psalm out of deep suffering. He feels abandoned by God and surrounded by enemies, whom he compares to strong bulls of Bashan, a region known for its good cattle, and now to a lion. Christians see in this psalm a foreshadowing of Jesus' sufferings on the cross, since he quoted its first verse. Some read it as a prayer of David and others as a prophecy; many accept both.

When you feel attacked or surrounded by criticism and pressure, you can do what the psalmist did: tell God with complete honesty about your fear and your pain, without hiding it.
exp.88:17:
The explanation says that the verse calls the Lord our defence, that is, our protection and safeguard. It also says that our king is the Holy One of Israel, that is, God himself. Here "defence" and "king" are used together. In several translations, the text can be understood this way: the defence and the king of the people belong to God. That reading is possible, though the phrase can also refer to a human king.

The psalm is attributed to Ethan the Ezrahite. The people celebrate God's faithfulness and remember his promise to David. The verses that follow explain why God is their defence: he chose and anointed David. Later the psalm turns sorrowful, as the people see the king fall.

Today we can rest in the knowledge that God cares for us. When you feel fear or pressure, pray, saying, "Lord, you are my defence," and trust in his protection.
exp.98:5:
This verse recalls three men from the history of Israel: Moses, Aaron and Samuel. Aaron was a priest, and Moses also appears here among the priests because of his service as mediator. Samuel was a prophet and judge. All of them called upon the Lord, that is, they called on him in prayer, and he answered them.

This psalm is a song of praise that does not say who wrote it. It exalts God as a holy, just and upright King. The psalmist recalls how God listened to these leaders, who were faithful to him and obeyed what he commanded. In this way he encourages the people to worship him.

For today: God still listens to those who seek him. You do not need to be a great leader; it is enough to pray with sincerity and obey his Word. Right now you can speak to him with confidence and wait on him.
exp.93:14:
It says that justice, which today seems twisted, will one day be set back in its place. "Judgment" refers to decisions and to fair government. "Returned to righteousness" means it will again become just. And "after it" means that all the upright in heart will go after it, following it. These are the sincere and honest people before God.

The psalmist speaks in the midst of injustice. The wicked oppress and seem to get their way. But he remembers that God does not abandon his people. The psalm does not say when or how this will happen; he trusts that God will act. Some read it as hope for the present, and others also as a final promise.

For today: when you see injustice, do not become bitter or seek revenge. Keep doing what is right with a sincere heart, and trust that God is a righteous judge who sustains you.
exp.68:23:
Here the psalmist asks God to let his anger fall on those who attack him. To "pour out" means to empty a container completely. The "fury of your anger" speaks of a very intense anger, and "overtake them" means that they cannot escape it.

The speaker is David, according to the psalm's title. He is suffering mockery and unjust persecution, and he cries out to God as a righteous judge. The verses that follow say that these enemies were adding pain to the one God had already struck. It is strong language, typical of the psalms that call for justice. The New Testament cites this psalm in reference to Jesus, though Christians interpret it in different ways.

For today: when you are hurt unjustly, do not hide your pain from God; bring it to him honestly and leave justice in his hands. In this way you avoid taking revenge yourself, and you can even pray for the one who wronged you, as Jesus taught.
exp.67:23:
The explanation says that the people saw how God moves forward, how he acts as King, and that this procession reached the sanctuary, the place of worship. "Goings" here means his steps, his works and his way of acting. "They" does not name who; the text that follows suggests it was the people, especially those who were in the procession.

The psalm is by David and celebrates victory and God's presence with his people. Earlier, God promises to rescue his own and to defeat their enemies. Afterward, the psalmist describes a procession: first the singers, then the musicians, and in the middle the young women playing timbrels.

For today: when you worship, remember how God has worked in your life and in the lives of others. Thanking him aloud, and even better in community, strengthens faith and reminds you that he is still King.
exp.36:19:
This verse says that the wicked, that is, those who live without respecting God, will come to a bad end. They are called "enemies of the Lord" because they stand against Him. The image of "the fat of lambs" probably refers to the fat that was burned completely on the altar, or to something that disappears quickly. Interpreters understand it in different ways. "They shall consume; into smoke shall they consume away" means that they will vanish without leaving a trace.

This psalm was written by David, already in his later years, to comfort the righteous who are troubled when they see the wicked prosper. Earlier, it promises that God watches over the upright and gives them a lasting inheritance. Afterward, it contrasts the wicked person who does not repay with the righteous one who gives generously.

For today: do not lose heart or envy the one who succeeds through injustice. Keep doing good with patience, and trust that God has the final word.
exp.71:14:
This verse says that the righteous king will live a long life. Gold will be brought to him from Sheba, a rich kingdom in southern Arabia. People will pray for him without ceasing and will praise him all day long. The sentence about the quoted words is removed, since the verse above uses "shall be given" and "shall be made" directly, and those phrases need no explanation.

It is a psalm of Solomon, or for Solomon, asking God for a king who will rule with justice. Earlier in the psalm, this king is described as caring for the poor and rescuing the weak from violence. For that reason the people honor him. Many Christians also see in this a look ahead to the Messiah, Jesus, although the psalm first spoke of a king of Israel.

For today: pray for those who govern and for the leaders you know, that they will care for the poor. And if you hold any position, even a small one, use it to serve with justice and compassion.
exp.15:8:
The explanation says that the psalmist's heart was filled with gladness, and that his glory rejoiced. Here "glory" probably refers to his soul or his innermost self, though some understand it as his tongue or his honor. It also says that his flesh, that is, his body, will rest secure, that is, confident and without fear.

The speaker is David, who has just said that God counsels him and keeps him always close at his side. His gladness springs from that trust. The New Testament (Acts 2) quotes the following verses and applies them to the resurrection of Jesus, although the psalm also expresses David's own confidence.

For today: when you feel fear or unrest, remember that God is at your side. Take a moment to thank him and to rest in his care, and let that trust bring you peace and joy.
exp.77:48:
He cast upon them the fierceness of his anger, wrath, and indignation, and trouble, by sending evil angels among them. It says that God let fall on the Egyptians the full weight of his anger: fury, rage, wrath, and distress. He did this through "evil angels," that is, messengers of judgment. Some understand these angels to have been destructive beings; others take the phrase to simply describe the harmful nature of the plagues. The text gives no further details.

Context: the psalm is by Asaph. It reminds Israel of God's works in the exodus, from the plagues of Egypt to the journey through the wilderness. It does so so that the people will not repeat the rebellion of their ancestors and will remember God's faithfulness.

For today: God takes injustice and oppression seriously, even when it may seem he is slow to act. Remembering how he delivered his people encourages us to trust his justice and not to harden our hearts. Today we can respond with humility, repentance, and gratitude.
exp.56:6:
The explanation says that the psalmist's heart is firm, prepared, and determined. "Ready" or "firm" is the meaning here, not "hurried." "I will compose psalms" means he will write and sing psalms, that is, songs of praise to God.

The title of the psalm attributes it to David, when he fled from Saul and hid in a cave. He is surrounded by enemies who laid a net for him and dug a pit, and his spirit is downcast. Even so, he decides to praise God. According to the psalm, the enemies fall into their own pit. Scholars do not agree on which cave it was exactly.

For today: when everything becomes difficult, do not wait until you feel better to pray or sing. Decide ahead of time to keep your heart firm in God. You can begin with a simple song or a prayer of thanksgiving, even in the middle of hardship.
exp.118:160:
Princes have attacked the writer, meaning rulers or people in authority, even though he has done nothing wrong. Even so, what truly moves him to reverence is God's word. The Hebrew letter name that opens this section of the psalm is not a word about wrongdoing; it is simply the name of the letter with which each verse in this part begins. The phrase "stood in awe" here means a deep reverence, not fear of being punished.

The one speaking is the psalmist, whose name is not known for certain. He writes under pressure and injustice, and the whole of Psalm 119 is a song of love for God's law. Here he sets two kinds of fear side by side: the human power that pursues him, and the authority of God, which weighs more heavily on his heart.

For today: when someone treats you unfairly, do not let that pressure rule your conscience. Ask what God says in his word, and decide from there, with calm and firmness.
exp.21:1:
The explanation says that the psalmist calls out to God all day and also all night, yet feels that God does not answer him. In both cases, it shows a constant pain.

The speaker is David, according to the title of the psalm. We do not know with certainty which moment of his life it describes. It is a prayer of anguish, sincere and without embellishment. Jesus quoted the first verse on the cross (Matthew 27:46), and for this reason many Christians also read this psalm as an early look at his suffering.

For today: when you feel that God is not answering, you do not have to pretend that everything is fine. You can tell him honestly what you feel, by day and by night, and keep speaking to him. Crying out is also a way of trusting.
exp.112:7:
He says that God not only lifts the poor and the needy out of their misery, but also gives them a place of honor alongside princes, that is, alongside the rulers or nobles of the people. The word for "needy" here means someone in want, and the "dunghill" was the heap of refuse where what was despised got thrown away. Setting them among princes speaks of dignity and acceptance.

This is a psalm of praise, which begins and ends with "Praise the LORD." We do not know for certain who wrote it. The one singing remembers that God, being very great and dwelling on high, bends down to look upon the humble. For this reason the people praise him. Afterward the psalm mentions the barren woman as another example of God's care.

For today: God values those whom the world overlooks. We can treat humble people with respect, give them a place at our table, and remember that our worth comes from the love of God, not from our position.
exp.17:26:
This verse says that God rescues humble people, that is, those who are afflicted and trust in Him. It also says that God brings down those with haughty eyes, that is, those who live with pride and think themselves better than others. The word the explanation discusses here, a word from the verse wording, means bringing down or removing pride.

David speaks, and according to the heading of the psalm he wrote it on the day the Lord delivered him from his enemies and from the hand of Saul. He is grateful and describes what God is like: He responds to each person according to their heart. With this verse he explains why God cared for him in the midst of so many dangers.

For today: if you are going through a trial, come to God with simplicity and without pretending to have strength. Acknowledge your need, and also examine your heart: if you notice pride, ask God to remove it before life teaches you the lesson the hard way.
exp.138:15:
It says that God saw the psalmist when he was still a very early form, that is, a life only just beginning to take shape. In the verse, all the days and parts of his life were recorded in God's book before any of them existed, and none of them was missing.

The text is spoken by David, according to the psalm's heading, and he praises God because God knows him completely. Earlier he said that his body was formed in a hidden place, a poetic expression that many understand as the mystery of the womb, though not everyone interprets it the same way. The "book" is an image, not a literal record.

For today: if your life seems small or confusing, remember that God has known you since the beginning and looks on you with care. You can bring Him your fears and decisions, trusting that you are not an accident to Him.
exp.134:2:
This verse invites us to praise the Lord, a shortened form of God's name, Jehovah. The reason is simple: God is good. It also calls for singing psalms to his name, "for it is pleasant," that is, agreeable and sweet. Some understand that what is pleasant is God's name; others, that it is the act of singing to him itself.

The psalmist calls God's servants, those who gather in the temple, to worship him. Then, in the following verses, he gives more reasons: God chose Israel as his own people and is greater than all gods. Who wrote the psalm is not known with certainty.

Today we can begin or end the day with a song or a prayer of thanksgiving, remembering something specific in which God has been good to us. Praise does not depend on how we feel, but on who he is.
exp.44:11:
The explanation says that the people of Tyre, a rich and famous city on the coast, will come with a gift to honor the queen. The phrase "shall intreat thy favour" means they will seek her goodwill, and "the rich among the people" are people with power and money. Even they will approach her with respect.

The psalm is a song for a king's wedding. The poet speaks first to the king and then to the bride. Here the bride receives honor and gifts from other nations. Christians have seen in this psalm an image of Christ and his people, and ancient Jews read it as a royal song. Interpreters do not fully agree, so it is wise to read it with humility.

For today: true honor is not gained through wealth or showing off, but through a life given over to God and faithful to him. If he honors you, you do not need to compete for anyone's applause. Serve with simplicity and let God decide the recognition.
exp.44:16:
It says that the king's name will never be forgotten. "I will make his memory to be remembered" means that his remembrance will stay alive from one generation to the next.
