For this reason, the peoples will praise him forever and ever, that is, without end. "Will praise" means that they will acknowledge him and honor him.

Psalm 45 is a song for a royal wedding. Here the psalmist speaks, addressing the king and promising him that his name will be remembered. Many Christians see in this king an image of the Messiah, and the New Testament applies part of this psalm to Christ (Hebrews 1:8-9). Others read it first as a song for a king of Israel in that time. Both readings have been held.

Today we can ask ourselves what name we want to leave behind. Living with faith and goodness leaves a memory that blesses others. And above all, we can give Christ the praise he deserves.
exp.138:8:
He says that even if someone took the wings of the morning, that is, traveled as fast as the morning light that spreads across the sky, and went to dwell in the uttermost parts of the sea, meaning the farthest point of the sea, even then they would not escape God. The phrase "wings of the morning" is poetic. It probably speaks of going toward the east, where the sun rises, and the sea would be the Mediterranean, to the west.

The psalmist is the one speaking, and the title attributes the psalm to David. He is not running away because he wants to hide from God out of fear. He reflects with wonder on how God knows him and accompanies him everywhere. Some believe it is a prayer of thanksgiving; others also see a desire to be examined by God.

For today: if you feel far away, alone, or in an unfamiliar place, remember that God is with you. Speak to him sincerely right there, without needing to go anywhere special first.
exp.39:2:
God, after rescuing the psalmist, put a new song in his mouth, a song of praise to our God. Many will see this, and it will lead them to fear the Lord, meaning to respect God with reverence rather than simple dread, and to trust in him.

The psalm is traditionally attributed to David. He has just described how he waited patiently, cried out, and God lifted him out of a deep pit and the mire, an image of profound distress. We do not know exactly what situation this was. His new song comes from having experienced God's help, and his testimony encourages others.

For today: when God helps you through a difficulty, do not keep the experience to yourself. Tell it with gratitude to someone, because your story can strengthen other people's trust in God.
exp.16:8:
The explanation continues the previous prayer. David asks that God hide him from the wicked who oppress him, that is, far from the sight and reach of those who mistreat him. His enemies surround him as someone who corners a person, with the intention of taking his life. The wicked here are people who are violent and unjust.

The one speaking is David, who prays to God in the midst of a real persecution. From the context, he feels surrounded and in danger. He asks for protection with tender images: to be kept as the apple of the eye and sheltered under the wings of God. The text does not say which exact moment of his life it refers to, and scholars do not agree on that.

For today: when you feel cornered by injustice or fear, you can do what David did. Tell God honestly what you are facing and ask him to care for you. Prayer does not deny the danger, but it places it in the right hands.
exp.34:19:
They do not speak peace. They do not talk in order to make things right again. Instead, against people who are calm and gentle, the ones the psalm calls "the meek of the land," they work out false words in their minds, lies dressed up to look like truth. The word "devise" here means they plan these things with care.

David is speaking, according to the title of the psalm, and he asks God for help because they attack him without cause. Earlier he promised to praise God in public, and now he describes those who hate him as hating him without cause. Later they mock him openly. The verse shows that their wrongdoing is not a simple misunderstanding but a plan of deceit.

For today: if someone accuses you with lies, do not answer with revenge. Bring your case honestly before God, keep seeking peace, and make sure your words are always truthful.
exp.26:9:
It says that even if a person's father and mother abandoned them, God would not. "Will take me up" means that God would welcome, look after, and receive them like someone who has no one else. It is an image of refuge and closeness.

The psalm is traditionally attributed to David. The speaker is in danger: enemies and false witnesses surround him. For this reason he asks that God not hide his face from him or leave him unprotected. It is not known with certainty at what exact point in his life he wrote it. Here it does not necessarily say that his parents abandoned him; it uses an extreme case to show that God's faithfulness is greater than any human support.

For today: if you feel lonely, rejected, or hurt by your family or by other people, you can approach God with confidence. Tell him honestly what you feel, and also seek a community of faith where his care can become visible.
exp.105:43:
Nevertheless he regarded their affliction, when he heard their cry: This verse says that God, despite everything his people had done wrong, looked upon them when they were suffering and listened to their cry for help. The phrase "nevertheless" means "even so" or "in spite of that." "Affliction" is a deep pain or distress, and "cry" is a call for help.

The psalm is a prayer of praise and confession; it is not known for certain who wrote it. The author reviews the history of Israel: again and again the people rebelled and suffered the consequences, but God did not abandon them. This verse is a turning point of hope: after punishment comes compassion, and the verses that follow speak of his covenant and his mercy.

For today: if you have failed and feel you are paying the consequences, do not turn away from God. Come to him sincerely and tell him what you are going through. He still listens to those who cry out to him.
exp.86:2:
It says that glorious and wonderful things are spoken about Jerusalem, the city God chose. The word "Selah" is a musical or pause marker; its exact meaning is not known for certain, but it seems to invite the reader to stop and meditate.

The psalm was written for the sons of Korah, Levites in charge of the music in worship. The author celebrates Zion as the place God loves, and where it is recognized that even foreign peoples, such as Egypt, Babylon, and Tyre, can be counted among those who belong to God. The following verses show this.

For today: God loves his people and has a place for everyone who seeks him. We can pause to give thanks that we are received into his family, and treat others with that same welcome, no matter where they come from.
exp.118:104:
The explanation says that God's word is like a lamp that lights the place where we step, and like a light that shows the way ahead. The image is of a light that gives clarity to what is right in front of us. The explanation also notes that this section of the psalm opens with the Hebrew letter Nun. The psalm is arranged by the alphabet, and this section begins with that letter.

The speaker is the psalmist, a believer who loves God's law. We do not know for certain who wrote it. Earlier, he said that God's words are sweet to him and that they gave him understanding to reject what is false. Later he says that he has committed himself to obey, even though he is suffering, and he asks God for renewed strength.

For today: when you have to decide something, do not wait to see the whole road. Read the Bible calmly, ask God for direction, and take the step that is shown to you clearly today. His light is usually enough for the next step.
exp.88:4:
This verse says that the heavens will praise God's wonders, and that his faithfulness will also be acknowledged by the saints gathered together. "Will praise" means to praise with joy. "Wonders" are his extraordinary works. "Faithfulness" here means that God keeps what he promises.

"The saints" may refer to the faithful people of God or to heavenly beings; it has been understood in both ways.

The psalm is written by Ethan the Ezrahite, according to its heading. It comes from remembering the covenant God made with David, promising him a lasting throne. For this reason the psalmist praises God: his faithfulness sustains that promise. Further on, the psalm shows pain, because that promise seemed not to be fulfilled.

For today: even though your situation may seem confusing, you can praise God for his faithfulness in the past. Remembering what he has fulfilled helps you to trust while you wait.
exp.144:6:
This verse says that people will remember the great goodness of God and share it with joy. "They shall abundantly utter the memory" means they will bring forth or declare the remembrance, as someone who lets it pour out in abundance. "The memory of thy great goodness" refers to the enormous number of good things God has done. And "shall sing of thy righteousness" speaks of celebrating with song that God is upright and faithful.

This is a psalm of David, and it is a song of praise. Here David speaks of what all generations will do: tell what God has done. A little earlier, he himself says he will speak of God's wonderful works. Then the psalm explains why there is so much to sing about: God is gracious, merciful, and slow to anger.

For today: when God helps you with something, write it down and tell someone about it this week, in your family or in your church. Remembering and sharing God's goodness strengthens the faith of others and your own.
exp.118:75:
Here the psalmist asks God that his mercy, that is, his faithful and compassionate love, would now come to comfort him. He does not ask for something made up by himself, but according to what God has already said to his servant, that is, according to his promises. The word "servant" refers to himself, someone who serves God.

The one speaking is the author of Psalm 119, whose name is not mentioned. He is suffering, and he acknowledges that God is just and faithful even in affliction. He is also slandered by proud people. For this reason he holds on to God's word as a source of hope and comfort.

When you are going through a difficult time, do not stay alone with your sadness. Look in the Bible for God's promises and bring them to him in prayer, trusting that he is faithful. You can say: "Lord, comfort me according to your word."
exp.106:15:
This verse says that God broke the gates of bronze and shattered the iron bars. These are images of very strong prisons, impossible for a person to open. The words "broke the gates of brass" and "cut the bars of iron in sunder" mean that he smashed them to pieces and split them apart.

The psalmist speaks to a people whom God rescued. In this psalm, several groups are described: people who were lost, imprisoned, or sick, who cried out to God and were set free. Here they are people who were in darkness and chains. The text does not say exactly which prison is meant; many think of the exile, although it may also be a general picture of any kind of slavery.

For today: if you feel trapped by guilt, a habit, or a fear that you cannot break, cry out to God with sincerity. He can open what you cannot. Then give thanks out loud and tell others what he has done.
exp.142:6:
It says that the psalmist asks God for a quick answer, because he feels drained of strength. The phrase that his spirit is fainting means that his courage is fading away. He begs that God not hide his face from him, that is, that God not turn away from him or leave him without his favor. He fears being counted among those who go down into the pit, that is, among those who are already dead or without hope.

The title of the psalm attributes it to David, and many read it that way, although some scholars have doubts. The one speaking is pursued by enemies and deeply discouraged. Earlier he remembered God's past works and stretched out his hands with a thirst for him. Now he cries out with urgency, yet he still trusts.

For today: when you feel drained of strength, do as the psalmist did. Remember what God has done, speak with him honestly, and ask for his presence. You do not have to pretend to be strong; you can tell him that you need him.
exp.50:5:
This verse says that God is not satisfied with what can be seen from the outside. He desires sincerity in the inward parts, that is, in the depths of the heart. And there, in the hidden part, God teaches wisdom to the one who lets himself be guided. The word "Behold" in the verse is a call to look and pay attention.

The psalm is spoken by David, according to its heading, after his serious sin with Bathsheba and against Uriah. He has just acknowledged his guilt and that he was born with a tendency toward evil. Now he understands that God wants total honesty, not appearances, and for that reason he asks to be cleansed and renewed.

For today: it is not enough to look good before other people. Take a moment to pray openly, telling God what no one else sees: your doubts, your mistakes, and your desires. Ask him to teach you and to cleanse you from within. He welcomes with grace the sincere heart.
exp.66:5:
This verse says that the earth will yield its harvest, and that God, who is our God, will bless us.

Psalm 67 is a prayer sung by the community of Israel. It asks for God's blessing so that all the nations will know him and praise him. Earlier, the psalm speaks of God as a just judge and as shepherd of the peoples. Many understand the harvest as a concrete sign of his care. Scholars do not fully agree on whether it refers to one specific harvest.

Today we can thank God for what we eat and for those who work the land. We can also remember that his blessings are not only for us: sharing with those who have less is a simple way of showing his goodness to others.
exp.68:29:
This verse says that the psalmist wants to praise God's name with a song and to magnify him with gratitude.

The speaker is David, according to the heading of the psalm. He is suffering, surrounded by enemies, and feels distressed, but he trusts that God will defend him. Before this verse he asks for justice; afterward he says that God takes more pleasure in a grateful heart than in a sacrifice of animals. Interpreters see here a praise that is born in the middle of pain, not after it.

For today: when you are going through a trial, do not wait until everything is fixed before giving thanks. Today, say aloud or sing a short word of praise to God, naming something he has done for you. That strengthens hope.
exp.80:15:
He would have fed them with the finest wheat, the very best of the harvest. "Fat of wheat" refers to the choicest grain, the finest flour. "Honey from the rock" speaks of wild honey found in the crevices of the rocks. "Satisfied" means that he would have left you completely content.

The one speaking is God, addressing Israel in this psalm of Asaph. He reminds them that he brought them out of Egypt, but they would not listen to him (vv. 8-13). That is why the "should have" expresses a wish that went unfulfilled: if Israel had obeyed, God would have given them victory and abundance. His words carry a sincere sorrow, like that of a father.

For today: obedience is not a burden but the path to what God wants to give us. Before thinking that his instructions limit us, let us remember that he wants to satisfy us with what is good. Today you can choose to listen to him in one concrete decision.
exp.131:12:
This verse says that God himself chose Zion, that is, Jerusalem, and wanted it as his dwelling. "Chosen" means that God made that decision by his own will. "Desired" means that he wanted it. "Dwelling" is a place to live.

The psalm seems to be a prayer of the people, recalling two promises of God: one to David about his throne, and another about Zion as the place of his presence. The verses before show that the promise to David had a condition: that his descendants keep the covenant. Here the focus is on the faithfulness of God. Scholars do not agree on the exact date when the psalm was written.

For today: God desires to be close to his people. You can live trusting that he seeks you not out of obligation, but out of love. Today, make room in your day to pray and to listen to him, as one welcomes a deeply beloved guest.
exp.127:1:
This verse says that when you eat what you have earned through your own labor, you will be happy and things will go well with you. The word "eat" in the verse is the same as the word "eat" you see there. "Happy" means joyful or blessed. "It shall be well with you" means you will enjoy well-being.

The psalm is a song of ascents, a song that pilgrims sang as they went up to Jerusalem. It does not say who wrote it. It sounds like a voice encouraging or blessing someone who respects God. The promise is for the one who fears the LORD, that is, the person who honors him and lives according to his ways. The psalm speaks of family, the table, and work, the everyday life of a home.

Today we can receive our work as a gift from God, not only as a burden. Before eating or getting paid, give thanks to God for what you have. God cares for those who live with honesty, even when not everything turns out as we hope.
exp.85:4:
This verse says that God is good, that he forgives, and that his mercy is abundant. That goodness reaches "all who call on you," that is, those who call out to him asking for help. The word "forgiving" means that he is willing to forgive. "Mercy" is compassion and faithful love toward someone who is in need.

The speaker is David, according to the title of the psalm, although some scholars think others may have used it later. It is a prayer of someone in distress, who cries out to God all day. Before this verse he asks for mercy and joy for his soul. Afterward he speaks of his anguish and of his confidence that God answers. Here David bases his request on what God is like.

Today, when you feel guilty or worn out, you can pray without fear. You do not have to get yourself ready first. Begin by remembering that God is good and forgives, and speak to him honestly, as David did.
exp.12:1:
Here David asks "how long?" two more times. "Take counsel in my soul" means turning his thoughts over and over, looking for a way out without finding one. The "sorrow in my heart" is a pain that stays with him every day. And "exalted" means that his enemy appears stronger and superior to him.

David speaks in prayer, in the middle of a long trial. He feels forgotten by God and pressed by an enemy. We do not know with certainty what situation he was living through, so it is better not to invent one. What is valuable is that the psalm, written to be sung, gives voice to the pain of God's people.

When worry keeps going around in your mind, do not hold it in or pretend to be strong. Speak it honestly with God, as David did. Praying this way is an act of faith: you keep turning to God even when you do not yet see an answer.
exp.67:8:
He says God poured out abundant rain on "his inheritance," that is, his people, who are like his treasured possession. When that people was exhausted and worn out, God refreshed them, giving them new strength and reviving them. The rain can be understood as literal provision or as God's generous care.

The speaker is David, in a psalm of praise. He recalls how God accompanied Israel through the wilderness and revealed himself at Sinai. The verses that follow say the people settled in the land and that God provided for the poor. Some scholars see here real rain in the desert; others see a general image of blessing. The text does not specify more.

For today: when you feel worn out, do not rely only on your own strength. Ask God to renew you, and remember the times he has already sustained you. Resting in him is not weakness; it is trust.
exp.118:95:
The explanation says that the psalmist has seen that everything that appears perfect in this world has a limit, an end. By contrast, God's command is extremely wide, without limits. The word "perfection" refers to what seems complete or ideal; to "see an end" is to discover its limits.

The one speaking is the author of the psalm, a believer who loves the Word of God. He has just said that he belongs to God and that wicked people are lying in wait for him. Faced with that pressure, he holds fast to the divine teaching. Some understand "commandment" as all of Scripture; others as God's will in general.

For today: do not place your ultimate hope in achievements, people, or ideas that have limits. Set aside a moment each day to read a Bible passage and ask yourself how to apply it in your work, your family, or your decisions. Its wisdom never runs out.
exp.52:1:
God looked down from heaven on the human race, to see whether anyone was truly wise and sensible, someone who really sought him. The verse describes God looking out from heaven to watch all people.

The psalm is by David, and it is almost the same as Psalm 14. It opens by speaking of the fool, who in the Bible is not someone without education but someone who lives as though God did not exist. David describes a corrupt world and shows that God does not look from a distance: he observes closely. The next passage says the result was sad, since no one was seeking him. Paul quotes these words in Romans 3.

Today, this verse invites us to ask ourselves whether we truly seek God or only remember him in times of crisis. We can set aside a moment each day to pray, read his Word, and ask him for wisdom, knowing that he is glad to be sought.
exp.34:25:
What it says: The psalmist asks that those who rejoice at his misfortune be put to shame and left in confusion. He asks that the shame cover them like a garment. The words "that magnify themselves against me" mean that they think they are better than others and treat him with arrogance.

Context: The psalm is attributed to David. He is being attacked by people who had once received his kindness and now celebrate his downfall. He does not take revenge with his own hands but appeals to God as a just judge. Psalms of this kind, called imprecatory psalms, honestly express deep pain and leave judgment in God's hands.

For today: When someone mocks or wrongs you, you can tell God everything you feel, without holding it in or taking revenge. Entrust your cause to Him and ask Him to do justice. In this way your heart finds rest, and you can end, as David did, by praising God.
exp.118:28:
Here the psalmist asks God for two things: that he be kept far from every "way of lying," that is, from a life built on deceit, falsehood, and bad choices. And he asks, "grant me thy law graciously," which in today's words would be: "give me, as a gift from you, the grace to know and live by your law."

The one speaking is a believer who loves God's word. The author does not name himself in the psalm. He is distressed, for earlier he says that his soul cleaves to the dust. So he prays with humility, knowing he needs help. Then he declares that he has chosen the way of truth, and his request shows a desire to remain faithful.

For today: ask God each morning to keep you from lying, including the small excuses you tell yourself. Then read a passage of the Bible and ask for the grace to put it into practice that day.
exp.105:38:
This verse says that the people of Israel defiled themselves from within by their own actions. "Defiled" means they were stained and made unclean before God. "Went a whoring" here does not refer only to sexual sin, but to being unfaithful to God, like someone who leaves their spouse for other loves.

Psalm 106 is a prayer that recalls the history of Israel. We do not know for certain who wrote it. The psalmist confesses the sins of the people, from Egypt to Canaan, to show that God was patient and faithful even though they failed. This verse closes the description of their idolatry and prepares the judgment that follows.

For today: what we do shapes us. If we place our trust and our time in things that take the place of God, little by little we move away from Him. Let us ask Him today to show us what we are giving the place that only He deserves, and let us return to Him with sincerity.
exp.149:2:
This verse invites us to praise God with musical instruments. The "trumpet" here refers to a horn or trumpet blown with force, like the shofar. The "psaltery" was a stringed instrument, something like a box with strings that were plucked with the fingers, and the "harp" was also a stringed instrument. The phrase "with the sound of" simply means "with the sound of."

The psalm does not say who wrote it. It is the last of the Psalms and closes the whole book with an outburst of praise. The speaker calls the whole people to praise God, in his sanctuary and for his mighty works. The instruments mentioned were in common use in Israel's worship.

For today: use what you have to praise God. You do not need to be a great musician; you can sing, play something, or simply give thanks out loud. Spend a few minutes today praising him with whatever you know how to do.
exp.107:0:
This verse says that David has a steady heart, ready to praise God. "Fixed" means prepared and determined. To "sing praise" means singing psalms, that is, songs of praise. "My glory" can be understood as his soul or the most precious part of his being, though some interpret it in other ways.

The one speaking is David, according to the title of the psalm. The verses that follow speak of awakening the harp and praising God among the nations. Many scholars note that this psalm joins parts of Psalms 57 and 60, but we do not know with certainty why it was put together this way. Even so, it expresses a determined praise, even in difficult times.

For today: before waiting to feel like it, decide to set your heart in order before God. Spend a few minutes each day singing, praying, or giving thanks, even when you are tired. Praise can also be a firm decision, not only a feeling.
exp.6:15:
It says that the harm someone plans against others will come back on that very person. The image is of a blow that lands right on the one who threw it.

David speaks in a psalm that the title attributes to him, and it mentions Cush, a Benjamite. It is not known for certain who he was or what the exact episode was. David feels persecuted and falsely accused, so he places his case in the hands of God, the righteous judge. The verses before this one use images of pregnancy and of a pit to show how evil turns back against its author.

For today: instead of seeking revenge, we can trust that God does justice. It also reminds us not to sow wickedness, because sooner or later it leaves its consequences.
exp.54:21:
We are told that we can hand over to God what weighs on us, and that he will sustain us. The word "cast" means to throw or lay something on someone; "burden" is any weight, worry or pain; "sustain" means that he will keep us standing firm. The "righteous" person is one who tries to live uprightly before God, and the promise is that such a person will not be left fallen forever.

The psalm is traditionally attributed to David. He is suffering the betrayal of someone close to him, who spoke with smooth words like oil but harbored war in the heart. We do not know with certainty which exact moment of his life it reflects. Even so, in the midst of that pain, David chooses to trust God and not to take revenge.

Today, when betrayal, pressure or fear wounds you, do not carry everything in silence. Pray honestly, name your burden and hand it over to God, even if you have to do so every day. He sustains the one who trusts him.
exp.93:5:
It says that the wicked kill the most defenseless people in society: the widow, the stranger, and the fatherless. The explanation of the word for stranger, which is an old printing error, is not needed here, since the verse above uses "stranger" directly. The phrase for taking life, which means murder, is covered by the verse's wording "slay" and "murder," so no separate note is needed.

The psalmist cries out to God, calling him the God of vengeance (v. 1), because the unjust oppress the people and mock, thinking that God does not see. The text does not say who wrote this psalm or at what exact moment, so it is not wise to claim either. What is clear is that God's law commanded care for widows, orphans, and strangers.

For today: God sees the vulnerable and cares about their fate. We can draw near to a widow, an immigrant, or a child without support, helping them in concrete ways and praying for justice.
exp.76:4:
He says the writer was thinking about the past. "Considered" means that he was reflecting on it or going over it carefully. "The days of old" and "the years of ancient times" refer to times long ago, perhaps his own past life or what God did for his people in earlier ages. Interpreters understand this in different ways.

The speaker is Asaph, or the author of this psalm that bears his name, in the middle of great distress. He cannot sleep and feels that God is far away. So he seeks comfort in memory, recalling how God acted before. The verses that follow show that he still has painful questions.

For today: when you are sad or confused, pause and calmly remember how God has helped you before. You can write those memories down and pray them. That does not erase the pain, but it strengthens hope.
exp.140:6:
It says that our bones are scattered at the mouth of the grave, like when someone breaks open and splits the ground, and the clods lie scattered everywhere. The word "cleaveth" means to split or open up; "grave" is the tomb or the place of the dead. It is a strong image of ruin and destruction.

The psalm is spoken by David, according to its heading, as he asks God for help in the middle of pressure from wicked people. The verse is difficult, and it is interpreted in several ways: some see it as a description of the danger the righteous were facing, others as the fate of the wicked. What is clear is that the next verse turns the gaze toward God: "But mine eyes are unto thee, O GOD the Lord."

For today: when you feel broken and without strength, do not stare only at the damage. Do as the psalmist did: lift your eyes to God, trust in Him, and ask Him to keep your soul.
exp.88:8:
This verse says that God rules over the sea when it is raging. "Raging" means violent force, and "waves" are the surging water. "Stillest" means that he calms them and makes them become still. When the waves rise up with force, God quiets them.

The psalm was written by Ethan the Ezrahite, according to its heading. It praises God for his power and for his faithfulness to the covenant with David. In the Bible the raging sea often represents chaos and the forces that threaten. For this reason the psalmist connects it with the defeat of Rahab, a poetic name that is sometimes linked to Egypt or to a monster of chaos. Interpreters explain this in different ways.

When your life feels like a stormy sea, remember that no storm is beyond God's control. You can pray with confidence, even before you see the calm.
exp.78:8:
Here the people ask God to help them and rescue them. They call him "our salvation," meaning the one who saves them. They ask him to act for the glory of his name, that is, for his honor and reputation. They also ask for forgiveness, asking God to cleanse them of their sins and to deliver them, so that he will be calm toward them and pardon them.

The speaker is Asaf, or a psalmist from his circle, speaking on behalf of Israel. Enemies had invaded the land, destroyed the temple, and killed many people. The verses before and after show grief, shame, and a plea that God not abandon his people. Scholars debate the exact moment being described, but the destroyed city fits the fall of Jerusalem.

For today: when you are in trouble, pray honestly. Acknowledge your failures, don't make excuses, and ask God to forgive and help you, trusting in his character rather than in your own merits.
exp.101:17:
The explanation says that what God has done will be put in writing for those who will live after us. And a people not yet born (the word "created" in the older wording means "to be created" or "to be born") will praise the LORD. Here "LORD" stands for the name of God, and the short form of that name is "JAH."

The psalm is the prayer of a person in distress, speaking to God out of suffering. The writer trusts that God will restore Zion (Jerusalem) and will hear those who have no one to help them. No one knows for certain who wrote it or exactly when; many think it reflects the time of exile or the period after it. Here the psalmist sees that God's help is not only for today but is a witness for future generations.

For today: tell your children, your friends, or your church how God has answered you. Write those answers down in a notebook. Your story may encourage someone who comes after you to trust and praise God.
exp.118:51:
He says that he remembered, O Lord, the righteous decisions and works that God has carried out from long ago, and this brought him comfort. "Judgments" here is not only punishment: it refers to God's just rulings, deeds, and decisions. "Of old" means from times past. The words "I remembered" and "I have comforted myself" are simply the verse's own wording, rendered directly.

The one speaking is the author of Psalm 119, whose name is not known for certain. He is suffering, and the proud mock him for his faithfulness. In the midst of that pressure, he does not look only at his problem, but recalls how God has acted with justice throughout history. Many understand this as a remembrance of what God did in Israel, though the text does not give concrete examples.

For today: when you feel wounded or misunderstood, take a few minutes to remember, in writing or in prayer, how God has been faithful in the Bible and in your life. That remembrance can give you calm and steadiness.
exp.51:3:
He says this person has come to love every kind of word that destroys. This is not a single lapse; it is something they love.

David speaks in this psalm. The title connects it to Doeg the Edomite, who reported the priests of Nob to Saul, according to 1 Samuel 22. David addresses this powerful man who boasted of his wickedness. Then he declares that God himself will judge him.

For today: examine what kinds of words you enjoy, such as gossip, mockery, or exaggeration that harms others. Ask God to help you speak with truth and love, and not to take pleasure in what wounds.
exp.10:4:
The explanation says that God examines the righteous person, like someone who tests a metal to see whether it is genuine. By contrast, God hates the wicked and the one who loves violence. The explanation's comment on the word "but" is dropped here, since the verse's wording is different. The phrase about hating is explained as meaning that God himself truly rejects the one who takes pleasure in doing harm.

This psalm is by David. It seems someone was advising him to flee from danger, because the foundations of justice were collapsing. David answers that God still sits on his throne and sees everything. The verses that follow speak of judgment on the wicked and of God's love for justice.

For today: when you are going through a trial or see injustice reigning, do not think that God is absent. He watches over you with care, and trials can reveal and strengthen your faith. Keep doing what is right and trust that God is just.
exp.118:22:
Psalm 119:23 describes powerful people who gathered and spoke badly about the psalmist, meaning they criticized or accused him. But he, calling himself "your servant," did not respond in anger. Instead he began to meditate, that is, to think calmly and carefully, on God's decrees, which are his rules and teachings.

The one speaking is the author of Psalm 119, whose name we do not know for certain. Earlier he asked God to take away the insult and the contempt, and he said he had kept God's testimonies. Afterward he states that those testimonies are his delight and his counselors. This suggests that when he was under attack, God's word guided him and sustained him.

For today: when you are criticized or treated unfairly, before you answer or defend yourself, spend a few minutes reading a passage of the Bible and praying over it. In this way your response will come from peace and truth, not from pain.
exp.33:1:
David finds his pride and joy in God, not in himself. The phrase "My soul shall make her boast" means that he feels happy and proud of God, and celebrates him. "The humble" are those who do not think themselves better than anyone else. They will hear his testimony and be glad.

David is speaking. The title of the psalm connects it to the time he pretended to be mad before the king of Gath so he could escape. First Samuel 21 tells the story with the name Achish, king of Gath; scholars explain the difference in name in different ways, and it is not certain what the reason is. David, rescued from a great danger, gives thanks and encourages others to praise God.

Today: when God helps you with something, do not keep it silent. Share it with humility with someone who is going through a difficulty. Your simple testimony can bring them encouragement and hope.
exp.148:4:
It says that the "faithful ones," that is, the people who are loyal and devoted to God, will rejoice because God honors them (in glory). It also says they will sing "upon their beds": in the place of rest, at night or in private.

The psalm does not say who wrote it. It is a song of praise for the people of Israel, celebrating that God delights in the humble and saves them. The verses that follow speak of swords and judgment on the nations. Scholars understand it in several ways: as a real victory, as language of spiritual battle, or as the hope of God's final judgment.

Today we can make the bed a place of gratitude. Before sleep, instead of going over worries, we can thank God for his care and sing to him, even if only in a quiet voice.
exp.139:5:
The explanation says that the psalmist speaks directly to God and declares to him, "You are my God." Then he asks God to hear him when he cries out. "Supplications" are pleas made out of real need. "Hear" means to pay attention with care, not merely to notice a sound.

The psalm is attributed to David, though we cannot be certain at what point in his life he wrote it. The one speaking feels threatened by violent and proud people who set traps for him, like a hunter who hides his nets. Before asking for help, the psalmist reaffirms his relationship with God. His request rests on that trust.

When you are under pressure or feel threatened, before listing your problems, remember who God is to you. Tell him sincerely, "You are my God." Then bring your needs to him simply. That trust does not remove the difficulty, but it gives you a firm place from which to pray.
exp.88:13:
The explanation says that God's rule rests on justice and judgment, that is, on what is upright and on deciding with fairness. The word for base or foundation of the throne is the support on which it stands. Also, mercy (compassionate love) and truth (faithfulness) go before his face, like servants who open the way for him and present him.

The psalm is by Ethan the Ezrahite, according to its heading. It praises God for his power over creation and for his faithfulness to the covenant with David. Earlier it speaks of the north and the south, Tabor and Hermon, as created by God. Then it says the people who know how to praise him are happy. Later the psalm complains that the kingdom seems fallen, but here it remembers what God is like.

For today: when life or the world seems unjust, remember that God governs with justice and goodness at the same time. Seek to imitate him: be firm in what is right, but treat others with compassion and honesty.
exp.105:29:
This verse tells how Phinehas, grandson of Aaron and a priest, stood up and "executed judgment," that is, he acted firmly to put a stop to a serious sin. Because of this, the plague that was punishing the people was stayed.

The psalmist looks back over Israel's history to remember their failures and God's patience. Here he speaks of Baal-peor (Numbers 25), when many Israelites joined in idol worship and immorality, and a plague came. According to Numbers, Phinehas acted with violence against one particular case of open defiance. The psalm recalls this as an act that God counted to him as righteousness.

For today: we do not copy his violence, but we can learn not to stay silent in the face of sin that harms others. We must act with humility, truth, and love, seeking to heal and restore, not to hurt.
exp.118:0:
He says that happy and fortunate are those who live with integrity, who walk according to God's teaching. The sentence about the word "Blessed" means joyful, favored. The phrase about the undefiled in the way does not speak of people without any mistakes, but of those whose conduct is sincere and whole. The letter that opens this section is the first letter of the Hebrew alphabet. The word "law" here means God's instruction.

Psalm 119 is a very long poem, organized according to the Hebrew alphabet, and all of it celebrates God's word. No one knows with certainty who wrote it; tradition attributes it to David, but many think it was another author. It speaks as someone who loves God's instruction and wants to teach that true happiness is found in it.

Today we can ask ourselves each morning: "How do I want to walk before God today?" Reading a passage of the Bible and obeying one specific thing is a good step to begin.
exp.118:157:
The explanation says that the psalmist looked at the transgressors, that is, people who deliberately betray or disobey God. Seeing them, he was grieved: he felt a deep sorrow, as if something were wearing him down from within. The reason is that they did not keep God's word.

The one speaking is the author of Psalm 119, a believer who loves God's law (no one knows for certain who he was). He is surrounded by enemies, but he does not turn away from God. His sadness is not pride or contempt. It comes from loving God and from grieving to see others ignore him. He soon asks the Lord for life and mercy.

For today: when you see indifference toward God, let compassion move you more than anger. Pray for those people, and ask God to keep you faithful and with a tender heart.
exp.110:1:
It says that the works of God are great, meaning admirable and powerful. It adds that all who take delight in them study and seek them out, that is, those who find pleasure in them and hold them in high regard. Whoever loves God desires to know what he does.

The psalm does not say who wrote it. The one speaking is a worshiper who promises to praise God with his whole heart, together with the company of the upright, those who live with sincerity. It is a psalm of praise that remembers what God has done: his glory, his justice, and his mercy. The verses that follow confirm this.

For today: spend a few minutes each day thinking about what God has done in creation, in the Bible, and in your own life. Write down one specific thing and thank him for it. In this way your heart will learn to seek out his works with joy.
exp.94:7:
Psalm 95:8 tells us not to become hard or stubborn before God. Hardening the heart means refusing to listen and obey. Meribah means "quarrel" or "strife," and Massah means "testing" or "trial." These are places in the wilderness where the people doubted God.

The psalmist calls people to worship, and then suddenly the voice changes: God himself speaks. He recalls what happened in Exodus 17, when Israel complained about lack of water and tested God, even though they had seen his works. It is a warning that worshipers should not repeat the rebellion of their ancestors.

For today: true worship includes a heart willing to listen. When difficulties come, instead of complaining bitterly, tell God what you feel and trust that he cares for you as a shepherd cares for his sheep. Obey today, without putting it off for later.
exp.117:10:
They surrounded me on every side. The enemies closed in on the psalmist from all directions. He says that they pressed in so there was no way out. Then he answers that, in the name of the Lord, he will break them, that is, defeat them. The Hebrew verb can be rendered in several ways, such as destroy or push away.

The speaker may be a king or the whole nation of Israel, and it is not known for certain which. It is a song of thanksgiving for a deliverance. The phrase is repeated to show that, although the threats were many, his trust was in God and not in princes or human strength.

When you feel surrounded by pressure, debts, or fears, do not trust only your own resources. Pray, place your situation in God's hands, and take the next step with the assurance that you are not alone.
exp.143:9:
This verse praises God as the one who gives victory and protection to kings. "Salvation" here means rescue or deliverance, not merely being healthy or well. To deliver means to set free or rescue someone from danger. The hurtful sword is a cruel blade, a picture of enemies who want to kill.

The speaker is the psalmist, whom the title of the psalm attributes to David, a king who lived through many wars. Before this verse, he sings a new song of thanksgiving, and after it he again asks to be rescued from lying enemies. His praise rests on what God has already done, and that gives him confidence to ask for help once more.

For today: when you face a threat or a great problem, remember how God has helped you before. Give thanks for that, and from that thankful memory, ask him with confidence to keep caring for you.
exp.115:1:
This verse says that God "inclined his ear" toward the one who speaks, meaning he gave attention with care, like someone who bends down to hear better. For this reason, the person promises to call upon him, that is, to cry out to God and trust in him, every day of their life.

The psalm does not say who wrote it. The speaker had come very close to death, surrounded by pain and distress, and cried out to God. God heard him and delivered him. This verse is his grateful response: if God heard me when I needed him most, I will keep turning to him always.

Today we can remember the times God helped us and let them become a reason to pray with more confidence. Write down an answer to prayer you have seen, and return to it when you feel weak.
exp.140:9:
David asks that the wicked be caught in their own traps, while he himself goes on his way unharmed. The explanation says the traps are the nets the wicked set for others. The phrase "whilst that I withal escape" is an old English way of saying "while I myself get away," meaning he will keep going, safe.

David speaks, according to the psalm's heading, in a moment of danger. The verses before this one show that he looks to God, trusts in Him, and asks for protection against the snares that have been laid for him. This verse closes the prayer with a wish for justice: that the harm others prepare will turn back on them. It has been understood as a prayer, not as personal revenge.

For today: when you find yourself surrounded by injustice or deceit, bring your case to God in prayer rather than taking revenge. Ask Him for protection, wisdom, and peace to go on with integrity, trusting that He knows how to do justice.
exp.96:7:
It says that Zion, that is, the people of God who live in Jerusalem, heard the news and was filled with joy. The "daughters of Judah" are the cities and villages of Judah. They rejoiced because of God's judgments, which here mean his righteous decisions and acts of rule, not only punishments.

The psalmist does not give his name, and we do not know for certain who wrote it. He speaks in the midst of a song of praise that presents God as King over all the earth. First, the idols are put to shame; then, people are called to love God and to hate evil. Zion's joy springs from seeing that God rules with justice.

Today we can rejoice that God does not ignore evil or abandon his own. When you feel weary of injustice, remember that God is the righteous Judge and give him thanks for it. That trust helps you live with hope and reject what is wrong.
exp.135:4:
This verse says that God made the heavens with understanding, that is, with wisdom and intelligence, not by chance. And each time, the people answer: "his mercy endures forever," which means that his faithful love and his goodness never run out.

Psalm 136 is a song of praise, probably used in the worship of the people of Israel, where a leader said one part and the congregation answered with the refrain. It is not known for certain who wrote it. Here the creation is remembered as a sign of God's care, and then the psalm goes on to his work in the history of Israel.

Today, when you look at the sky, let it remind you that God is wise and faithful. If you are going through something confusing, repeat the refrain in prayer: his mercy does not end, and his wisdom sustains even what you do not understand.
exp.44:7:
It says the king's garments smell of fine perfumes: myrrh, aloes, and cassia, which were very valuable aromatic spices. The phrase "ivory palaces" refers to palaces decorated with ivory, and "have made you glad" means they have cheered or delighted you. It is an image of luxury, beauty, and festivity.

This psalm is a song for a royal wedding. The author speaks to the king and describes him with honor, justice, and joy. The verses before it speak of an eternal throne, and for that reason the New Testament, in Hebrews 1:8, applies those words to Christ. Many read it as a picture of Christ, the King, and his people. Others place more weight on the historical king of Israel; the psalm does not name him.

For today: if Christ is a King worthy of honor and joy, let us give him the best of our lives, not the leftovers. Let our worship be sincere, and let our conduct leave a sweet fragrance of justice and love.
exp.31:3:
It says that while David kept silent about his sin, he felt God pressing on him without rest, day and night. "Thy hand was heavy" means that the weight of God grew heavier. "Moisture" is the freshness of a living plant, and "drought of summer" is the dryness of the summer heat. His strength dried up like a plant under the heat. "Selah" is probably a pause for reflection, though its exact meaning is not certain.

The speaker is David, according to the traditional heading of the psalm. He speaks of his experience when he kept his sin hidden and did not acknowledge it. We do not know for certain which offense he means, though many connect it with his sin with Bathsheba. The following verses show that he found relief in confessing and receiving forgiveness.

For today: if something weighs on your conscience, do not hide it. Speak with God honestly about it and trust in his forgiveness. If needed, also seek out a trusted person who will listen to you and pray with you.
exp.146:17:
He sends out his word, and the ice and snow melt. Then he makes his wind blow, and the frozen waters start to flow again. The words "sends out" and "blow" sound like future actions, but in the account they describe what God usually does each year when winter ends. "Flow" means that the waters run or glide freely.

The psalm is a song of praise, by an unknown author, addressed to the people of Israel. Earlier, the psalmist showed God's power in the extreme cold. Here he shows that this same God also brings the thaw with only his word. Then the psalm joins that word that governs nature with the word God gave to Jacob and Israel, that is, his law.

For today: if God can change the winter with his word, he can also soften difficult situations or cold hearts. Trust him and seek his word with patience.
exp.39:8:
The psalmist says he has proclaimed God's righteousness, that is, his right and faithful way of acting, before a great assembly. "Great congregation" is a large gathering of people, and the verse appears in the KJV. He affirms that he did not seal his lips or keep silent, and he calls God as his witness: "thou knowest."

The speaker is David, the author according to the title of the psalm. He has just given thanks because God rescued him, and he says he desires to do the divine will from the heart. Some Christians also read the preceding verses as words of Christ, because Hebrews 10 quotes them that way. Even so, the basic sense is gratitude that becomes public testimony.

When God helps you, do not keep that to yourself. Tell plainly and honestly what He has done, in your church, your family, or with a friend. Your testimony may encourage others to trust Him.
exp.64:4:
This verse says that God answers his people with awe-inspiring and righteous deeds. "Terrible things" means works that cause fear and wonder. "Salvation" is what the verse calls deliverance, the word "salvation" in the phrase "God of our salvation." "The ends of the earth" and "them that are afar off upon the sea" are the most distant places in the world. God is the hope of all of them.

The psalm is attributed to David, who praises God in the middle of worship. Earlier it speaks of sins that weighed heavily on him, but also of the forgiveness God gives, and of the joy of being near Him in His house. Then it describes God as creator who sustains the mountains and calms the seas and restless nations. Some think that "terrible things" refers to acts of deliverance; the text does not make this specific.

For today: when you feel guilty or overwhelmed, come to God with confidence. He forgives, listens, and is righteous. Speak with Him today and entrust to Him what weighs on you.
exp.2:3:
The writer says that the psalmist prayed aloud to the Lord (God), and that God answered him. The phrase in the verse about the mountain refers to God's holy mountain, that is, the place where God made his presence known. The word "Selah" is a pause or a musical marking; its exact meaning is not known for certain.

The title of the psalm attributes it to David when he was fleeing from his son Absalom. Many people were saying that God would no longer save him. Even so, David remembers that God is his shield. The "mountain" most likely refers to Zion, in Jerusalem, where the ark was, although David was far from there. God was not limited by distance.

When you find yourself surrounded by criticism or fear, pray sincerely, even aloud. You do not need perfect words. God listens, and his answer can bring a peace that lets you rest, even though the problems have not yet disappeared.
exp.104:5:
This verse is an invitation addressed to a special people. "Seed" means descendants, and the phrase "you all" is directed at them. It calls out to the descendants of Abraham and of Jacob, described as servants of God and chosen by Him.

The psalm does not name an author at this point, although part of it also appears in 1 Chronicles 16, where it is linked to David. The speaker urges Israel to remember the wonders of God. The reason is that God remembered His covenant, the promise He made to Abraham and to his children. Before asking them to remember, he reminds them who they are: a beloved and chosen people.

For today: before doing anything for God, remember who you are to Him. If you believe in Christ, the New Testament teaches that you also belong to the family of faith of Abraham (Galatians 3:29). Today, write down three good things God has done for you and thank Him for them.
exp.47:4:
They saw the city of God and were amazed. They were troubled, that is, they were filled with fear and confusion, and they fled in haste. The phrase "they hasted away" means "they hurried off." The phrase "as they saw it" refers to Zion, the city of God, which they looked upon.

It is a psalm of the sons of Korah, sung by God's people to celebrate his protection over Jerusalem. It is not certain which specific attack it recalls; some think of a historical deliverance and others of a general picture of how God defends his people. The psalmist wants the people to remember that God is their refuge.

Today we can remember that powers that seem enormous crumble before God. When you feel fear over a great problem, pray and rest in him as your refuge. His care is firmer than any threat.
exp.61:11:
This verse says that God is merciful and also just. The word "mercy" means kindness and compassion toward someone who does not deserve it. The phrase "renderest to every man" means that God gives each person what is due, and "according to his work" means according to what he has done, that is, according to his actions.

David speaks here, according to the title of the psalm, although some scholars debate the exact circumstances. He has said that his soul rests only in God. Now he warns others not to trust in violence, robbery, or riches, because true strength belongs to God. He closes by reminding them that God is both kind and just.

For today: if you are tempted to get ahead through deception, or to place your security in money, remember that God sees everything. Act with honesty, and trust in his mercy rather than in your own means.
exp.18:5:
This verse continues to speak of the sun. It says that it rises from one end of the sky, travels its path to the other end, and nothing is left free of its heat. The word "end" here means the far edge or limit, the "circuit" is its journey across the sky, and "hid" means that no one can stay outside its reach.

The speaker is David, according to the title of the psalm. First it shows that creation proclaims the greatness of God without words. Then, from verse 7 on, it moves to the law of the LORD. Many understand that the sun, which reaches everyone, prepares the comparison with the Word of God, which also gives light and life. That connection is an interpretation, not something the text states directly.

For today: when you feel the sun or see the sunrise, let it remind you that God faithfully cares for his creation. And just as the sun does not skip any corner, set aside a moment each day to read his Word and let it reach every area of your life.
exp.31:0:
It says that truly happy is the person whose wrongdoing God has forgiven and whose sins He has erased. The word "blessed" here means deeply happy and favored. "Transgressions" refers to wicked or twisted acts. The term "Maschil" seems to be a musical or literary label; its exact meaning is not known with certainty, and some think it indicates a psalm of teaching.

According to the title, David is the speaker. What follows shows that he speaks from his own experience: he kept his sin silent and suffered inwardly until he acknowledged it before God. Many connect it with his sin involving Bathsheba, but the text does not say so explicitly, so that is a possibility, not a certain fact.

For today: if there is something you carry on your conscience, do not hide it. Bring it honestly before God, trusting that He forgives and gives peace. True joy begins when we stop concealing and receive His forgiveness.
exp.85:6:
The explanation says that when the psalmist goes through a moment of pain or distress, he will call on God. And he will do it with confidence, because he already knows that God answers him. The word "trouble" means a situation of great pressure, suffering or fear. "I will call upon you" is the same as "I will ask you for help."

The speaker is David, according to the heading of the psalm. It is a prayer in the middle of a real need. Earlier, he remembered that God is good, forgiving and abounding in mercy. Afterward, he affirms that there is no other God like him. His confidence does not come from himself, but from how he knows God.

For today: when a difficult day arrives, do not wait until you feel strong to pray. Speak with God sincerely, remembering his goodness. You can say: "Lord, I am troubled, but I trust that you hear me."
exp.55:1:
David complains that his enemies pursue him without rest. The word "swallow" in the verse means that they press in on him relentlessly, giving him no breathing room. He says that many are fighting against him, and he addresses God as "most High," a title pointing to someone far above any enemy.

Context: David is the speaker, and the psalm's heading says he wrote it when the Philistines seized him in Gath. He was in real danger and felt alone, far from his people. Even so, he does not stop at the complaint: in the verses that follow, he says that when he is afraid, he trusts in God. Scholars debate which exact moment in his life the heading refers to, but the cry itself is clear.

For today: When you feel that your problems give you no rest, speak to God honestly, as David did. Tell Him how heavy what you face is, and remember that He is above all things, even what overwhelms you today.
exp.82:1:
What it says: The psalmist tells God to look at what is happening. The verse's word "tumult" means they make a great noise, like a stormy sea or an angry crowd. The phrase "lifted up the head" describes those who rise up with pride and defiance. Those who "hate thee" are the ones who oppose God and his people.

Context: Asaph, a worship leader in Israel, or perhaps someone from his family of singers, prays on behalf of the people. The verses that follow speak of nations plotting to destroy Israel. That is why the psalmist asks God not to remain silent. Scholars do not agree on which specific historical attack he has in mind.

For today: When you feel that evil makes more noise than good, do not pretend to be calm. Bring your concern to God honestly, and trust that he sees, hears, and acts in his own time.
exp.17:6:
When David describes God answering the cry of his servant, he says the whole earth shook. The words "was moved" and "trembled" mean that it shook with force. The foundations of the mountains are their deepest bases, and even these were shaken. The phrase "he was wroth" means that God was angry, not without cause, but at the injustice his servant was suffering.

The psalm's heading tells us that David speaks after being delivered from his enemies and from Saul. Remember that he was surrounded by distress and in danger of death. Here he describes, in poetic language of great force, how God's response was experienced. Many understand these as images to express the power of God, not necessarily a literal earthquake.

For today: when you feel surrounded by problems, cry out to God. He hears you and cares about what you suffer. Trust that he is not indifferent to your distress.
exp.58:11:
This verse continues the psalmist's prayer against his enemies. It says that their sins come from what they speak: their words, their pride, their curses and their lies. He asks that they be "caught," that is, trapped, by their pride. The word "speak" in this verse refers to the words they say.

David speaks, according to the title of the psalm, when Saul sent men to watch his house in order to kill him. His enemies lay in wait for him with words full of hatred and deceit. David cries out to God asking for justice, not for revenge of his own. His language is strong, typical of psalms that call for judgment, and it is understood as entrusting the matter to God.

Today we can take care of what comes out of our mouths, because words carry weight before God. And when someone slanders us, instead of responding in the same way, we can bring the matter to God in prayer and trust that He judges with justice.
exp.77:26:
This verse tells how God caused flesh to fall upon the people of Israel in abundance, as thick as the dust. He also sent feathered fowls, as many as the sand of the sea. It is a way of saying they were countless. "Flesh" here refers to quail, and the "feathered fowls" are birds that fly.

The psalm is written by Asaph, and it recalls Israel's history in the wilderness. It tells how God provided bread from heaven (the manna) and then meat, when the people complained and asked for food to their liking. The psalmist uses this as a lesson: God was powerful and generous, but the people distrusted Him. The verses that follow show that, even when they were satisfied, their hearts remained far from God.

For today: give thanks for what God already gives you, instead of complaining. Ask Him with confidence, but also ask Him for a grateful heart, because having everything we desire does not always draw us closer to God.
exp.105:44:
This verse says that God remembered his covenant, that is, the promise he made to his people. The explanation also says that he "repented," which here does not mean that he was mistaken, but that he changed the way he acted and had compassion. He did so according to the multitude of his mercies: his compassion is abundant.

The psalmist reviews the history of Israel: the people rebelled again and again and suffered the consequences. Even so, God looked upon their distress and heard their cry. At the end, the writer asks God to gather them from among the nations, so he probably speaks from a time of scattering or exile, though it is not known with certainty when.

Today, if you have drifted away from God, do not think there is no way back. His faithfulness does not depend on yours. Cry out to Him sincerely and trust in his mercy.
exp.48:9:
This verse says that death comes to everyone, no matter who they are. It shows that the wise die, just like the fool and the senseless, who are people who live without thinking about God. In the end, everyone leaves their riches to others. The word "perish" means that they end their life in this world.

The psalm was written by the sons of Korah, and the one speaking is a teacher who gives a lesson to all peoples. He wants no one to fear the rich or trust in money. The verses before explain that no one can pay to escape death. The verses that follow show that many dream of leaving their houses and names forever, but they do not achieve it.

Today we can ask ourselves what we trust in most: what we have or God. We can use our goods generously and seek what lasts, knowing that our life is in God's hands.
exp.68:14:
This verse is a prayer asking for help. The one praying uses the image of someone sinking: he asks that the force of the waters not drown him, that the deep not swallow him, and that the pit not close its mouth over him.

The psalm's title names David as the speaker, in a time of great distress. He is rejected, accused, and hated without cause. The waters and the mud are a picture of the suffering that surrounds him. Even so, he prays with confidence in God's mercy. This psalm is quoted later in the New Testament in connection with Jesus, although this particular verse is not quoted.

For today: when you feel that your problems are pulling you under, do not wait to get out on your own. Tell God honestly what you feel, as David did, and trust that his mercy is greater than your distress.
exp.134:13:
He says that the Lord will defend his people and do them justice. "Will judge" here means that he will act on their behalf, not that he will condemn them. The phrase "will repent himself concerning his servants" means that he will feel compassion for them and soften how he treats them. It is not that God makes a mistake, but that his heart is moved with tenderness toward those who serve him.

The psalmist calls people to praise God for his works and his faithfulness. He recalls how God gave the land to Israel and affirms that his name is eternal. This verse (which also appears in Deuteronomy 32:36) shows that God does not abandon his own. Afterward, the psalm contrasts the living God with the mute and blind idols.

For today: if you are going through an injustice or a hard moment, you can trust that God sees you and has compassion on you. Hand your situation over to him in prayer, without seeking revenge, and wait patiently for his help.
exp.64:8:
Here, the psalm says that God cares for the earth like someone who visits it with tenderness. He waters it and enriches it so that it bears fruit. The "river of God, which is full of water" is a poetic image of the abundant rain that comes from heaven; it does not refer to a literal river. "You prepare their grain" means that God provides the wheat and the food of the people, and "when you have so provided for it" means that he does so by preparing the earth in that way.

It is a psalm of David, a song of praise. Earlier it speaks of God as the one who calms the seas and the nations; here it moves to his simple daily care: the rain and the harvest. The people give thanks because their bread depends on that provision.

For today: when you eat or see it rain, offer a brief prayer of thanks. Recognizing that everything comes from the hand of God frees us from anxiety and makes us generous toward others.
exp.76:8:
These two painful questions are asked in this verse: Has God forgotten to be gracious? Has he, in anger, locked up his tender mercies? "Selah" is a pause, perhaps a moment to stop and reflect (its exact meaning is not entirely certain).

The one speaking is the psalmist, identified as Asaph in the title of the psalm. He is distressed and cries out to God at night. His pain leads him to doubt out loud. But notice that these are questions, not statements. Then he decides to remember God's works of long ago, and that is where his mood begins to change.

When you feel that God is far away, you can bring him your doubts honestly, without pretending. And afterward, like Asaph, take time to remember: write down or recall the times God helped you. That does not erase the pain, but it sustains hope.
exp.129:7:
It says that God himself will redeem his people, Israel, from all their sins. "To redeem" means to pay the price to set someone free, as was done for a slave or a prisoner. The important point is that it speaks of all sins, not just some of them.

This is a psalm of the "songs of ascent," which the people sang as they went up to Jerusalem. The psalmist speaks from a very deep place of distress and guilt (v. 1), but he waits on God the way a watchman waits for the dawn. He closes by encouraging all of Israel to trust in the Lord's mercy. Scholars do not agree on who wrote it or when.

For today: if something from your past weighs on you, do not expect to fix it alone. Bring it honestly to God and trust in his forgiveness. He does not tire of redeeming.
exp.70:12:
It says that the psalmist asks that his enemies be put to shame and brought to an end. "Let them be confounded and consumed" means that they should fail or come to their end. "Adversaries to my soul" refers to those who attack his life. "That seek my hurt" refers to those who want to do him harm. In the end, he asks that shame and confusion cover them like a cloak.

The one speaking is an elderly believer (verses 9 and 18 suggest this). The psalm does not name its author, and some have attributed it to David, but this is not certain. His enemies say that God has abandoned him and that no one will rescue him. For this reason he cries out to God. These words are a request for justice, not personal revenge; and right after, he decides to keep waiting and praising.

When someone hurts you or mocks your faith, do not take revenge. Honestly hand your pain over to God, ask Him for justice, and decide to keep trusting and praising Him.
exp.118:159:
The verse says that God's word is true from its beginning, and that each one of his righteous decisions lasts forever. Some translations say "the sum of your word is truth," meaning the complete whole. Both readings are possible. "Judgments" here means his righteous decisions, his rules and rulings.

The one speaking is the psalmist, a believer who loves God's law. He has just described how painful it is to see those who betray what God commands. Now, in the middle of that pain, he holds on to something firm: God does not change or contradict himself. He also asks to be made alive again, that is, restored in life.

When you see that the people around you change their minds with every trend, you can anchor yourself in the Bible. Before deciding something important, read it calmly and ask what it tells you, not what most people think.
exp.60:7:
He says the psalmist will praise God's name forever, meaning that his song of gratitude will have no end. Keeping his promises to God, probably made in times of distress, is the sense of the phrase that follows. And he will do this day by day, with steadiness.

The psalm bears the name of David, though some think another person wrote it on behalf of the king. It speaks of someone in trouble who cries out to God from afar, and then God gives him protection. The verses before this one ask for a long life for the king, and this closing part responds with thanksgiving. Opinions differ about the exact moment it was written.

For today: think of a promise you have made to God, such as prayer, service, or forgiveness, and keep it today. Let your gratitude be not just a feeling, but a daily habit.
exp.22:2:
He renews the strength and spirit of the one who is weary inside. "Restoreth" means to strengthen and to comfort. "My soul" refers to my whole self, my inner life. "Leadeth me" is "he leads me." "Paths of righteousness" are straight paths, the ones that please God. He does this "for his name's sake," that is, because his character is faithful and good.

The one speaking is David, who was a shepherd of sheep before becoming king. He uses that experience to describe God as a careful shepherd. He comes from speaking of pastures and quiet waters, and here he trusts that God also guides him morally. That guidance prepares him for the dark valley he mentions afterward.

Today, when you feel exhausted or lost, ask God to strengthen you and show you the right way. Then take the next obedient step you already know, trusting that he is faithful.
exp.19:2:
Here it is asked that God remember all your offerings and accept your burnt sacrifice, the sacrifice that was burned up completely. The fire that consumed the offering suggests that God received it.

Selah is a word whose meaning is uncertain; it probably indicates a pause or a moment in the music.

This is a psalm of David, sung by the people, who pray for the king before a battle. We do not know with certainty what the occasion was. The Israelites trust that God sees the offerings of their leader and will support him.

Today we can pray this way for our leaders, pastors, or family members who face trials. Moreover, let us remember that God does not forget what we give to him sincerely: our prayer, our service, and our obedience.
exp.35:8:
It says that God is the source of life, like a spring where fresh water rises up and never runs out. It adds that when we are in God's light, we can truly see. "Your light" helps us understand life, see what is good, and know Him.

David writes this psalm, according to its heading. Before this, he has contrasted the wickedness of the godless with the mercy of God, under whose wings His people take refuge. Afterward, he asks that God continue to show His goodness and protect him from the pride and violence of the wicked.

For today: when you feel dry or confused, do not look first for answers in other sources. Spend a few minutes praying and reading the Bible, asking God to give you life and clarity for the day.
exp.17:0:
This verse is the heading of the psalm and its opening line. It says it is a song of David, the servant of the Lord, addressed to the chief musician, that is, the leader of the singing in worship. David spoke it on the day the Lord rescued him from all his enemies and from Saul. The line "I will love you" expresses his devotion, and "my strength" names the Lord as the one who gives him power to stand.

David speaks here after many years of persecution, above all from King Saul, and also after wars with other peoples. This same song appears in 2 Samuel 22. Scholars do not agree on the exact time when he wrote it, but the text presents it as a deep thanksgiving for the deliverance received.

For today: when God sustains you through a difficulty, do not move on quickly. Write down how He helped you and thank Him with sincere words. In this way your love for Him grows from what you have lived, not only from theory.
exp.118:131:
He says the psalmist asks God to look upon him with kindness and show him compassion. "Look upon me" is a plea for God to turn his attention toward him and attend to him. "Be merciful unto me" means treating him with love and not according to what he deserves. He also appeals to how God usually acts, as God is accustomed to act toward those who love his name, that is, toward those who love Him.

The speaker is the author of Psalm 119, who cannot be identified with certainty. Earlier he says he desires God's Word so deeply that he opens his mouth and pants. Then he asks that God direct his steps and free him from the oppression of men. His plea comes from a heart that loves God's Word and feels its need.

Today we can pray with confidence, not presuming on our own merit, but relying on the character of God. When you feel weak or pressured, ask Him to look on you with mercy, remembering that He has been faithful to those who seek Him.
exp.67:14:
Bashan was a region east of the Jordan, famous for its high mountains and rich land. The psalmist calls it "the hill of God" and repeats that it is a high hill. Some think the expression means a majestic mountain; others, that it is a mountain that belongs to God. It is not entirely clear what the sense is.

The author is David, according to the heading of the psalm. It is a song of victory that celebrates God as King who protects his people. The following verses show the contrast: the great mountains like Bashan seem to look on with envy, but God chose Mount Zion, smaller, to dwell in it.

For today: God does not look at what is big or impressive, as we do. If you feel small or unimportant, remember that God can choose you and dwell with you. Seek Him, not recognition.
exp.146:9:
He takes no delight in the strength of a horse, which in those days was a symbol of military power. Nor is he pleased by the legs of a man, that is, by a soldier's speed or physical toughness. Here "pleasure" means something that gives him satisfaction, and "takes delight" means he is glad about it and finds joy in it.

The psalmist, whose name is not given, praises God as the Creator who cares for nature: the clouds, the rain, the grass, and even the ravens. If God sustains all of this, he does not depend on human strength. The next verse makes clear what does please him: those who fear him and trust in his mercy. Many believe the psalm was sung after the return from exile, but this is not certain.

For today: do not place your security only in your strength, your money, or your abilities. Work hard, but rest in God, trusting his goodness every day.
exp.106:35:
God makes the hungry settle in a place. The verse says he "maketh the hungry to dwell," meaning he gives them a home to live in. There they "prepare a city for habitation," that is, they build and set up a town where they can live. God turns a dry place into a home for people in need.

The psalmist praises God and recalls how the Lord rescues various people in trouble. Just before this, the text says that God can make a desert fertile, and also, because of the wickedness of its inhabitants, turn a fruitful land into a salty wasteland. Afterward, the people sow, plant vineyards, and are blessed. The psalm shows God's care and his justice.

When you are in need or in a difficult place, trust that God can provide for you and give you a fresh start. And if he helps you, respond with honest work, gratitude, and generosity toward others who are in need.
exp.107:1:
