What it says: David speaks to himself and to his instruments, as if commanding them to wake up. The lyre and the harp were stringed instruments used to praise God. "I will awake early" means that he himself will get up very early, at dawn, to sing. Praise will be the first thing in his day.

Context: This is a psalm of David. Just before, he says his heart is steadfast and ready to sing. Afterward he promises to praise God among the peoples, because his mercy is greater than the heavens. Many scholars note that this psalm joins parts of Psalms 57 and 60, though it is not known for certain why David or a compiler put it together this way.

For today: Try to begin your day with a few minutes of thanks to God, before the rush arrives. You can sing a song, read a psalm, or simply give thanks aloud. In this way you place your heart in Him from the morning.
exp.51:0:
The explanation says that David wrote this psalm, a maschil (probably a teaching song), for the chief musician. He speaks forcefully to a mighty man who boasts of his wickedness: "Why boastest thou thyself in mischief, O mighty man?" Then he sets that arrogance against something firm: the goodness of God endures continually.

David is the speaker. The title connects it with Doeg the Edomite, who told Saul that David had come to the house of Ahimelech the priest. That story appears in 1 Samuel 21 and 22, where Doeg later killed many priests. David rebukes that wickedness, but in the end he looks to God.

For today: do not take pride in power or in words that wound. And if you suffer because of the wickedness of others, remember that their power has an end, but God's goodness remains there every day. Today you can guard your words and rest in his faithfulness.
exp.98:1:
This verse says that God is great in Zion, that is, in Jerusalem, the mountain where the temple stood. To be "high above" means to be lifted up, placed far above everything else. So the Lord is above all the nations, not only Israel.

The psalm does not say who wrote it. It seems to be a song of praise for the people gathered in worship. Earlier it speaks of God seated among the cherubim, an image of the ark of the covenant, and then calls him holy, just, and a lover of righteousness. His greatness is not only power: it is also good and just character.

For today: when you feel small before your problems or before the powerful, remember that God remains high above all things. Take a moment to praise him, and trust that his justice is greater than any injustice you see.
exp.26:8:
This verse is a prayer of David asking that God not turn away from him. "Hide your face" means withdrawing his favor or nearness. "Put away in anger" is rejecting someone in wrath. "You have been my help" recalls that God has already come to his aid before. "Salvation" here means deliverance, that is, rescue and protection.

The speaker is David, according to the traditional title of the psalm. He is in danger from his enemies, but earlier he said he would seek the face of God. Now he begs that God not forsake him. The following verse shows his confidence: even if his own father and mother abandon him, God will take him in.

For today: when you feel alone or afraid, pray sincerely, as David did. Remember the times God helped you before and ask him to guide you. Your confidence rests on his faithfulness, not on your own strength.
exp.144:13:
This verse says that God, whom the Bible calls Jehovah, upholds all who fall and lifts up those who are bowed down, that is, those who are weighed down, crushed by the burden of life or of others. Falling can mean stumbling, failing, or collapsing.

Psalm 145 is attributed to David, and it is a song of praise. Earlier it speaks of God's eternal kingdom and his mighty deeds. Then it says that God gives food to all in due time. David shows that the King of the universe also cares for the weak and the weary.

For today: if you are going through a moment of falling, failure, or exhaustion, you do not have to get up alone. Speak to God honestly, ask him for strength, and seek the support of other believers. You can also be a hand that helps someone else up.
exp.139:11:
It says that David is confident that the Lord will defend the cause of the afflicted and do justice for the poor. The word "poor" here refers to those who live in need, without resources. The phrase "will maintain the cause" means that he will side with the one who suffers and act on their behalf.

This psalm is attributed by its title to David. He prays to God asking to be delivered from violent, deceitful, and slanderous men who set traps for him. Before this verse he asks that evil fall upon them, a strong kind of language typical of the psalms. Afterward, it ends with hope: the righteous will give thanks and will live in God's presence.

For today: if you are suffering an injustice, you do not have to take revenge. You can entrust your case to God in prayer, keep acting uprightly, and trust that he sees and will respond. And if you have the opportunity, help those in need.
exp.144:12:
This verse says that God's kingdom has no end. The phrase about the kingdom lasting through all ages means that it endures forever, in every era. The word for his authority refers to his rule as Lord and ruler, and the phrase about every generation means that his government reaches each generation without interruption, from parents to children.

The speaker is David, according to the title of the psalm, which is a song of praise. It follows from the call for everyone to speak of the glory and mighty works of God. Here it gives a reason: God's kingdom is eternal, unlike human kingdoms, which change and pass away. Right after, it shows how God reigns: he sustains those who fall and lifts up the oppressed.

For today: when everything seems uncertain, remember that God is still governing. Rest in the fact that his care does not depend on the times. And tell the younger ones how faithful he has been to you.
exp.135:23:
This verse says that God freed us from those who harmed us or oppressed us. "Rescue" means to bring someone out of danger or slavery. The reason given is that his mercy, that is, his faithful and compassionate love, endures forever.

Psalm 136 is a prayer sung by the people of Israel. It remembers how God brought them out of Egypt, led them through the desert, and gave them the land. After each statement, the people respond: "His mercy endures forever." The verses before this one speak of a time of low estate, a period of humiliation and weakness, in which God remembered them. Scholars debate exactly which enemies are meant, but the general sense is clear: God saved them.

Today we can remember the times God sustained us in difficult moments. Write them down and give him thanks, trusting that his love never ends.
exp.106:40:
It says that God lifts the poor out of their misery, that is, out of their state of need and humiliation, and sets them in a safe place. Furthermore, He causes their families to grow and multiply like flocks of sheep, which was a sign of blessing, abundance, and a future.

The psalm does not name its author. It is a song of thanksgiving addressed to those who have been rescued by God. The verses before it show that God can bring down the powerful who turn aside. Here we see the other side: God cares for the needy. The psalm ends by inviting the upright to rejoice and to reflect on the Lord's mercies.

If today you are going through scarcity or feel forgotten, remember that God sees the humble. Trust in Him, and in the meantime, help generously anyone who is in need, so that you may reflect His mercy.
exp.3:3:
This verse invites people to pause before they sin. "Stand in awe" means to be moved, to take God seriously, and it can also be understood as "be angry," according to other translations. "Commune with your own heart" is to reflect quietly, and "be still" means to calm down and stay quiet. "Selah" is probably a musical or meditative pause; its exact meaning is not certain.

David speaks, according to the heading of the psalm. He is distressed because some people stain his honor, love empty things, and believe lies. Even so, he trusts that the LORD hears him, and he calls his opponents to think and return to God with righteousness.

For today: when you feel anger or worry, do not act right away. At night, before sleep, speak honestly with God, examine your heart, and ask him for peace to decide well.
exp.68:34:
He says that God will protect Zion, that is, Jerusalem, and will build the cities of Judah again. His people will live there and receive the land as an inheritance. "Will save" means that God will take care of it and rescue it; "will rebuild" means that he will raise it up once more; "will have it as their own" means that they will hold it as their possession.

The one speaking is King David, according to the title of the psalm. He begins by crying out in great pain over his sufferings and his enemies. In the end, his complaint turns into praise, because he trusts that God hears those in need. Some think the final verses were added later, perhaps during or after the exile, but this is not known with certainty.

For today: even if your life or your surroundings lie in ruins, you can pray with sincerity and hope that God will restore what seems lost. He listens, and his faithfulness is greater than your situation.
exp.77:32:
This verse says that God caused the days of that people to be spent on empty things, with no fruit or purpose, and that their years were filled with anguish and fear. The word "consume" means that their days were running out. "Trouble" means suffering or affliction. The phrase "in vanity" speaks of emptiness, of a life that is spent without leaving anything lasting behind.

The psalm is written by Asaph, who recalls the history of Israel in the wilderness. Although God rescued them and performed miracles, the people kept sinning and did not trust him. This verse shows the consequences of that lack of faith. The verses that follow say that they sought God only when they suffered, and then forgot him again.

For today: do not wait for a crisis to draw near to God. Today you can give him your time with sincere trust, and so your days will have meaning and will not be lost in emptiness.
exp.7:8:
This verse repeats the praise with which the psalm begins. "Lord" is the name of God, and "our Lord" shows that we acknowledge him as our master and guide. "Name" here means everything God is: his character, his power, and his care. And it says that this greatness is seen "in all the earth."

The psalm is attributed to David, though the text gives no further details about when he wrote it. Earlier, the author speaks of creation: the sheep, the oxen, the birds, and the fish. He marvels that God has given human beings a place of care over them. That is why he ends with worship.

Today you can pause to look at creation, or even at your own life, and thank God out loud. In this way, wonder becomes prayer, and routine is filled with gratitude.
exp.103:21:
It says that when the sun rises, the animals of the night, such as the lions, withdraw and lie down to rest in their dens. The explanation of "gather themselves together" is that they come together or pull back, and "dens" are the shelters where they live.

The psalmist, an author whom tradition does not name with certainty, praises God for how he ordered creation. In the verses before, the night is the time of the wild beasts. Here the day arrives, and they draw away. Then people go out to work until evening. Everything has its time and its place, and the psalmist sees in this the wisdom of the Creator.

God placed a rhythm of work and rest in his creation. Today we can trust in that order: to work diligently during the day, and to rest without guilt when the time comes. Respecting that rhythm is a way of recognizing that God cares for everything and that we do not depend only on our own effort.
exp.8:9:
This verse says that those who know God's character, his name, will put their trust in him. The reason is that the Lord has never abandoned those who seek him.

David speaks here in a psalm of praise. He has just said that God judges with righteousness and is a refuge for the poor and the one who suffers. Then he calls people to sing and to tell of his works, because God remembers the oppressed. This verse joins both ideas: trust is born from having seen how God acts. Scholars debate the exact historical context of the psalm, so we cannot pin it down.

For today: when you doubt, remember how God has sustained you before, and read how he cared for others in the Bible. Knowing him better will help you trust, and seeking him in prayer is a good place to begin.
exp.8:1:
David says he will be filled with joy and gladness because of God. The old forms of the words "I will be glad" and "I will rejoice" appear in his text, and he promises to sing praise to God's name, calling him "most High," meaning the one who stands above all things and all people.

David, the king of Israel, speaks in a psalm addressed to the chief musician. The musical note at the start of the psalm seems to be a musical instruction, but its exact meaning is uncertain and is understood in several ways. David praises God because he has delivered him from his enemies and has defended his cause with justice, as the following verses show.

Today we can make gratitude a habit. Before asking for more, let us take a moment to remember what God has already done for us and thank him aloud, with a prayer or a song. In this way our joy rests in God, not only in our circumstances.
exp.90:12:
It says that whoever trusts in God will be able to tread on dangerous animals. The "basilisk" is a poisonous serpent; some translations say "asp" or "cobra," and the Hebrew term is of uncertain meaning. "Trample" means to step on with force, as a sign of victory. The "dragon" may be a large serpent or a sea monster. All of them are symbols of danger.

The psalm does not say who wrote it. First a narrator speaks, and then, in the following verses, God himself. It aims to encourage whoever lives under the protection of the Most High. The animals represent threats and enemies, and the promise is that God cares for his people in the midst of them. Some also read it as an image of victory over evil.

For today: when you feel afraid before a great problem, remember that you do not face it alone. Pray and trust that God is with you and sustains you, even when the road is hard.
exp.108:2:
He says that the enemies of the psalmist surrounded him with words full of hatred, like someone closing a ring around him. Furthermore, they attacked him "without cause," that is, without any just reason. "They fought against me" speaks of a constant attack, not just a passing argument.

The one speaking is David, according to the title of the psalm. He is crying out to God because deceitful and lying people accuse him unjustly. The verses that follow say that he showed them love and they repaid him with hostility, but he responded by praying. This is a psalm of lament, where help is asked of God.

For today: when someone attacks you with lies or contempt for no reason, you do not have to respond in kind. You can bring your pain to God honestly, as David did, and ask him for justice, peace, and a heart that does not fill with bitterness.
exp.107:5:
What it says: The psalmist asks God to rescue "your beloved," that is, his people, those whom God holds especially dear. He asks that they be saved with your right hand, a symbol of power. And he asks God to answer him, to hear him.

Context: David is said to be the speaker, according to the psalm's title. He has just praised God for his mercy and his truth, which are greater than the heavens. Now he moves from praise to petition, because his people face enemies. Right after this, God answers with a promise about the land of Israel. This psalm brings together parts of Psalms 57 and 60, which becomes clear when the texts are compared.

For today: Before asking for help, you can remember who God is: faithful and merciful. Praising him first strengthens your trust. Then bring your need, and the needs of your loved ones, to him simply, and wait for his answer.
exp.78:11:
The explanation says that God should bring back on the neighboring peoples, "sevenfold" (seven times over), the scorn with which they insulted him. "Into their bosom" means paying them back in the place closest to them for what they did. "Reproach" is an insult or disgrace. The anger centers on the fact that they offended God.

The speaker is the people of Israel, probably after Jerusalem and the temple had been destroyed and plundered (Psalm 79:1-3). The writer cries out to God for justice, because the nations mock: "Where is their God?" It is a prayer of pain, not an order for personal revenge. The cause is placed in God's hands.

For today: when you are hurt or when your faith is mocked, bring that pain to God honestly, instead of seeking revenge. You can ask him for justice, but remember that Jesus also teaches us to love and pray for those who harm us (Matthew 5:44). And like the psalmist, end your prayer with confidence and praise.
exp.31:2:
He says that when David stayed silent and would not speak of his sin, he felt his bones wearing away. "Waxed old" means they grew weak, as if they had aged all at once. "My roaring all the day long" speaks of a constant groaning, an inner pain that would not leave.

David speaks in this psalm, which he calls a "Maskil," a word usually understood to mean a song for instruction. He has just said that the one who receives forgiveness is happy. Now he remembers the time before he confessed: the silence weighed on him, and he felt God's hand upon him. Then he says he confessed his sin and God forgave him. The psalm does not say what that sin was, so it is not wise to claim it.

For today: when something weighs on your conscience, do not hide it. Speak with God honestly, without excuses, and trust that He forgives. If needed, also seek out a brother or a trusted counselor who can pray with you.
exp.91:5:
This verse says that the person who is brutish does not know, and the one who lacks understanding does not grasp "this." The words "brutish" and "fool" do not speak of low intelligence, but of someone who lives without taking God into account. "This" points to what follows: that the wicked spring up like the grass, but their end is destruction, while God remains on high forever.

The psalm is a song of praise, and its title connects it with the sabbath day. No one knows for certain who wrote it. The psalmist rejoices in the works of God and in his deep thoughts. He then points out that whoever does not live with reverence for God fails to understand that the prosperity of the wicked is temporary.

For today: when it seems the wicked are doing very well, do not be deceived by what you see. Ask God for wisdom to view life from his perspective, and trust that his justice is firm and enduring.
exp.87:11:
This verse is a painful question put to God. The one speaking wonders whether, in the darkness of death, anyone can know your wonderful works or your righteousness. The words "darkness" and "the land of forgetfulness" are poetic ways of naming the place of the dead, where no one remembers anything. "Wonders" means your amazing works.

The psalm is written by someone deeply distressed, ill, and feeling abandoned. The title attributes it to Heman the Ezrahite, though not everyone is sure of his identity. It is one of the darkest psalms, since it has almost no visible hope. Its questions aim to move God to act while the writer is still alive. Even so, the writer keeps crying out: "I have cried unto thee."

For today: when you feel without strength or without answers, you can be honest with God and bring him your hardest questions. Praying with honesty is also a form of faith.
exp.32:2:
It says we should sing to God a new song and do it skillfully and with joy. The phrase "sing unto him" means "sing to him," and "play skilfully with a loud noise" refers to playing instruments with strings and making a loud, joyful sound. Shouting for joy is a happiness so great that it is expressed aloud, almost like a cry of delight.

Psalm 33 does not say who wrote it; some traditions attribute it to David, but this is not certain. It is a call to praise directed to the righteous. The verses that follow give the reasons: the word of God is upright, his works are faithful, he loves justice, and the earth is full of his mercy. The "new song" may reflect renewed gratitude for what God does.

Today, do not wait for a perfect moment to praise. Set aside some time this week to sing to God sincerely, perhaps a song that comes from your heart, and prepare well to do it, with effort and joy.
exp.77:43:
God turned the rivers of Egypt into blood, along with their streams, that is, the canals and channels, so that the Egyptians could not drink water. This refers to the first plague, which is recorded in Exodus 7.

The psalmist, Asaph, reviews the history of Israel so that the children will not forget what God did. The verses before this one say that the people "did not remember his hand." That is why he recalls the signs in Egypt, in the region of Zoan, in the Nile delta. They show God's power in rescuing his people.

Today, take time to remember how God has helped you in difficult moments. Write down two or three examples and thank him in prayer. Remembering his faithfulness strengthens confidence when new trials come.
exp.147:0:
"Praise ye the Lord" is the opening of this verse, and it means "praise the Lord" (God). It is an invitation to give him glory. The call is that the praise should come "from the heavens" and "in the heights," that is, from everything that is above, in the place where God reigns. The words "praise ye" and "praise him" are older English forms of the call to praise.

The author of the psalm is not identified with certainty. He speaks as someone who calls all of creation to acknowledge God. The verses that follow invite the angels, the sun, the moon, and the stars. First the psalm calls on what is in the heavens, and then it moves down to the earth. The reason is that God is worthy, since he made all things.

For today: before asking God for something, take a few minutes to praise him. Look at the sky, give thanks for what you see, and remember that all creation honors him, and you can do so too.
exp.67:31:
It says that all the nations of the world, not only Israel, should sing and praise God. "Kingdoms of the earth" refers to the peoples and their governments. "Sing unto God" is the same as "sing to God." "Selah" is a Hebrew word that probably indicates a musical pause or a moment to reflect, though its exact meaning is not certain.

This psalm was written by David as a song of victory and praise. Shortly before, it speaks of God ruling over violent peoples and of Egypt and Ethiopia drawing near to Him. That is why the call opens to all nations: the God of Israel is worthy of worship from everyone. Interpreters differ on when this is fulfilled, whether partly in history or in the future.

For today: do not keep your praise only for your group or your church. Pray and sing asking that people from all peoples come to know God, and take a pause today to thank Him for who He is.
exp.95:6:
This verse calls all the families of the nations to acknowledge God. "Give" means "hand over" or "ascribe." The "glory" is the honor he deserves for who he is, and the "strength" is his power. It is not about giving him something he lacks, but about recognizing what already belongs to him.

The psalm does not say who wrote it. Part of it also appears in 1 Chronicles 16, where it is connected with David and the moving of the ark, although not everyone agrees on how the two passages are related. The psalmist speaks to all peoples, not only to Israel, and contrasts the Lord, creator of the heavens, with idols, which are nothing.

For today: before asking something of God, take a moment to acknowledge his power and his goodness. Tell him in your own words what you admire about him, and live that day trusting that he sustains your life.
exp.101:21:
It says that a time will come when people from many nations and governments will gather in one place with one purpose: to serve Jehovah, that is, the Lord. "Gathered together" means the people come together, and "kingdoms" are the countries along with their rulers.

The psalm is the prayer of someone deeply troubled, who feels weak and sees life slipping away. Even so, they lift their eyes and remember that God hears prisoners and those condemned to death, and that his work of rescue will be told in Zion. Scholars disagree about who wrote it and when; many think of the time of the exile, but this is not certain. The New Testament applies the end of the psalm to Christ (Hebrews 1:10-12).

For today: when your pain makes you see only what is immediate, remember that God is working in something larger than your situation. Pray honestly, and trust that he continues gathering a people to worship him.
exp.54:12:
Here the psalmist speaks directly to the one who betrayed him. He tells him that he was a man who was his equal, someone of his own standing and trust. He was his guide, a close counselor, and his acquaintance, a friend who was very well known to him and trusted.

David is said to be the speaker, according to the psalm's heading, though we cannot know for certain which exact episode he wrote about. He is distressed by the violence in the city. But what hurts him most is not a declared enemy, but the betrayal of a friend with whom he shared confidences and walked toward the house of God.

For today: if someone close to you has wounded you, do not hide that pain. Bring it to God honestly, as the psalmist did, and ask him for wisdom to forgive and to trust with prudence.
exp.46:1:
This verse gives the reason why everyone should clap and shout for joy to God. It says that the Lord Most High is "terrible," a word that here does not mean "evil" but rather stirs awe and reverence for his greatness. It also calls him a great King over all the earth, meaning that his authority is not limited to a single people.

This psalm was written for the chief musician, and it is attributed to the sons of Korah, who served in the music of the temple. The speaker invites all peoples to celebrate. It was probably a song of worship in community, which acknowledged God as ruler of all nations. Scholars discuss the exact occasion on which it was used.

For today: when you feel that the world is out of control, remember that God is still King. Praise him with gratitude and entrust your concerns to his care.
exp.68:12:
He says that, although others mocked him, the psalmist kept praying to God. He trusts that God answers "in the time of his good pleasure," that is, at the moment God considers right and favorable. He asks that God hear him because of his great mercy and the faithfulness of his salvation. "But" is the plain word here, and "salvation" is the word for deliverance.

The psalm is spoken by David, according to its heading, though this is debated. He is suffering mockery, rejection and accusations. The leading people of the city, those who sat at the gate, spoke badly of him, and even the drunkards made songs about him. He feels like someone sinking into deep waters, and that is why he cries out to God.

When you are criticized or feel alone, do not stop praying. Speak to God honestly, lean on his mercy, and trust that he knows when and how to help you.
exp.74:2:
The explanation says that the earth and all who live in it were "falling apart," that is, coming undone or melting, like something that loses its firmness. But God declares: "I bear up its pillars," meaning, I keep firm what holds the world up. "Selah" is a pause to reflect, and its exact meaning is not entirely certain.

The psalm is by Asaph, a temple singer. In the verse before, God promises to judge with uprightness when the time He has chosen comes. Here it seems God Himself is speaking, though some think it is the psalmist. In times of chaos and injustice, it is a reminder that God is still in charge.

When everything seems to be coming down, in your family, your work, or your country, remember that God still holds up what you cannot. Do today what is yours to do, with honesty, and rest in the knowledge that He sustains all things.
exp.123:6:
The explanation says that God's people felt like a little bird caught in a trap, and that suddenly the trap was broken and the bird could fly free. The snare is the net or cord used to catch birds. The hunters are the ones who set that trap. Note that the psalmist speaks of escaping and of the snare being broken, without boasting about his own strength.

This is a psalm of David, sung by Israel, probably after being delivered from a powerful enemy. The verses before it use images of a flood and of wild beasts. It is not known with certainty what exact danger it refers to, and several events could fit. What is clear is that the people acknowledge that God rescued them.

For today: when you come out of a situation that seemed like a trap, a debt, a bad decision, or a fear, do not credit it only to luck. Stop and give thanks to God, and trust that he is still your help.
exp.105:39:
This verse says that God was very angry with his people, Israel, and felt rejection toward what was his own. The phrase about his anger burning is an old way of saying that his anger blazed. "Inheritance" means his most cherished possession, that is, his people. "Abhorred" means he looked upon them with disgust.

The psalmist reviews the history of Israel: how many times the people failed and, even so, God rescued them. Here he recalls a very dark moment, when they worshiped the idols of Canaan and even sacrificed their sons and daughters. God's anger is not a whim: it is his rejection of injustice and of harm done to the innocent. Then came the consequence: they fell into the hands of their enemies.

For today: God grieves over what harms people. If something has taken God's place in your life, you can acknowledge it today with humility and return to him. The psalm goes on to show that God listens and has compassion.
exp.82:14:
He says that God should pursue his enemies like a strong storm and leave them terrified with a whirling wind. The explanation of what "terrify" means is removed here, since that word is not in the verse. "A whirling wind" is an wind that spins around with great force. These are images of a power that no one can stop.

This psalm is attributed to Asaph. It is a prayer for help: several neighboring nations form an alliance to destroy Israel (vv. 3-8). Asaph does not ask for personal revenge, but for God to act. The following verses show a deeper desire: that, put to shame, they would seek the name of the Lord. Scholars debate what the exact historical occasion was.

For today: when you feel surrounded by injustice, you can bring your distress to God in sincere prayer, instead of avenging yourself. And you can ask him that his justice bring about, even among your adversaries, a change of heart.
exp.95:4:
What it says: The psalmist states that the gods other peoples worship are idols, that is, empty things with no real power. By contrast, the Lord, the God of Israel, made the heavens. The contrast is between what has no power and the Creator of all things.

Context: This psalm is a song of worship, and the speaker invites Israel to proclaim God's glory among the nations. The verses before it describe him as one to be held in reverent awe above all gods. This verse gives the reason: the other gods did nothing, but God created the heavens. The psalm then invites all peoples to give him glory.

For today: Today idols can be money, success, or the approval of others. Ask yourself what thing in your heart has taken the place of God, and entrust it to him with confidence, for he does have the power to sustain you.
exp.39:5:
It says that God does not take pleasure only in offerings. The words that were rendered as offerings of animals and of grain are offerings in the sense of gifts brought to God. A burnt offering was what was burned up completely, and a sin offering was the offering made for sin. The phrase "mine ears hast thou opened" means that God gave him the ability to listen and obey. The phrase "burnt offering and sin offering hast thou not required" means that God was not asking only for that.

The one speaking is David, according to the title of the psalm. He has just thanked God for his wonderful works. Then he says, "Lo, I come," and expresses that he wants to do God's will. The rituals were good, but God was looking for an obedient heart. Hebrews 10 quotes this passage and applies it to Christ, and some read it that way in a deeper sense.

For today: do not be content with merely performing religious rituals. Before asking God for something, take a moment to listen to him in his Word, and ask him what he wants from you today.
exp.106:1:
This verse invites those whom God has rescued to speak up. "Redeemed" refers to people who were set free by the payment of a ransom. The explanation's wording about the enemy, that it can also be rendered as distress or oppressor, has no equivalent in the verse above, so that sentence is removed. Where the source says the phrase means "let them say it," it means that they should tell out loud what God has done for them.

The psalm does not say who wrote it. It opens by calling people to praise God for his goodness and his mercy that endures forever. The verses that follow speak of people gathered from all the lands, and of others who wandered lost in the wilderness. Many understand it as a song of the people of Israel returning from exile, though some read it more broadly, as applying to anyone rescued by God.

For today: if God has helped you through a difficult time, do not keep it to yourself. Tell a friend or your family. Your testimony may bring hope to someone who is still lost in their own wilderness.
exp.18:8:
This verse says that the fear of the LORD is clean and endures forever. "Fear" here is not a fear that paralyzes, but deep respect and reverence toward God. "Judgments" means his decisions and his rules, and the text affirms that they are true and altogether righteous, without error or injustice.

Psalm 19 is attributed to David. First it praises God for what creation shows, and then for his law. Here it uses several similar words (law, testimony, commandments, precepts, fear, judgments) to describe God's Word and its effects: it renews, gives wisdom, brings joy, and gives light. Afterward it will say that it is worth more than gold.

For today: when you have to decide something, do not look only at what suits you or at what people say. Ask yourself humbly what pleases God, and trust that his way is just even when it costs you.
exp.67:4:
It says that God cares for those left without protection: the orphans, who have no father, and the widows, who have lost their husband. A word from the verse, "father", is the key idea here: God is described as a father to the fatherless, and as the one who brings justice for widows. The phrase about God's dwelling place refers to the holy place where God lives, and it can be understood either as heaven or as his presence with the people.

It is a psalm attributed to David, which calls people to sing to God. The verses that follow speak of God leading his people through the wilderness. In that time, orphans and widows were often very vulnerable, and the Law of Moses commanded that they be cared for. The psalm shows that God himself takes on that role.

Today, if you feel alone or unprotected, you can come to God with confidence. And if he cares for them, he also invites us to help those who are in need near us.
exp.134:11:
He says that God gave the lands of those defeated peoples as an inheritance to Israel, his people. The word "gave" in the verse is the same as "gave" in English, and "inheritance" means a property that is received as an inheritance, not earned by merit, but given as a gift. The repetition of "for an inheritance" emphasizes that it was a secure and lasting gift.

The psalmist speaks in a song of praise addressed to God's people, probably gathered in the temple. He recalls what God did in bringing Israel out of Egypt and leading them into Canaan, defeating kings such as Sihon and Og. His purpose is to show that Jehovah is greater than any power, and that Israel received the land through God's faithfulness. The writings of Moses and Joshua tell that story in more detail.

Today we can remember that what we value most comes from God's grace, not from our own effort. That leads us to live with gratitude and humility, and to trust that he keeps what he promises.
exp.75:11:
This verse says that God "shall cut off the spirit of princes," meaning that he can break the pride and strength of rulers. The word "cut off" is like the way a cluster of grapes is harvested: God brings them down from their height. And "terrible" does not mean evil, but worthy of awe and respect, because no one can withstand him. The powerful leaders of the nations are the "kings of the earth."

This is a psalm of Asaph that celebrates God as the defender of Jerusalem (Zion). It speaks of a great deliverance from enemies, though the Bible does not make clear here exactly what that was. The psalmist invites the people to keep their vows and to bring offerings to God, who is owed reverence.

For today: even though the powerful sometimes seem untouchable, God remains greater. You can trust him when you feel fear in the face of injustice, and live with humility and gratitude, keeping what you have promised him.
exp.105:41:
This verse says that Israel's enemies treated them harshly. "Oppressed" means they mistreated them and ruled over them. "Broken" means they were left weak and defeated. "Under their hand" means they were under the power of their enemies.

The psalmist speaks in a psalm that reviews the history of Israel. It tells how the people turned away from God again and again, especially in the days of the judges. The verses before explain that God gave them over to other nations because of their rebellion. The psalm does not hide their failures, but it also shows that God saw their distress and heard their cry.

For today: our choices have consequences, and turning away from God often brings pain. But if you are going through a consequence like this, do not think that God has forgotten you. You can return to Him sincerely, because He hears the cry of those who humble themselves.
exp.44:6:
He says this King loved righteousness and hated wickedness. Therefore God, who is also his God, anointed him with the oil of gladness, that is, filled him with joy and honor above his companions. To anoint is to pour oil on someone to set them apart and honor them. Your reject means you firmly turned away from evil.

Psalm 45 is a song for a royal wedding. The psalmist addresses the king and praises his character, not only his power. The verse before calls him God and speaks of his throne forever. Hebrews 1:8-9 quotes these words and applies them to Christ. Some scholars think it was first sung to a king of Israel, and later read as a prophecy of the Messiah.

For today: Jesus joins love of justice with rejection of evil. We can ask him to help us love what is right in small things, such as honesty at work or at home, and to trust that true joy comes from God.
exp.40:8:
It tells of a very close friend, someone the psalmist trusted and who shared his table, who turned against him. The phrase "the man of my peace" refers to a friend with whom he had a good relationship. Lifting up the heel is an expression of betrayal, like someone raising a heel to kick or knock another down.

The psalm is spoken by David, according to its title, though we cannot be certain which moment it refers to. He is sick, confined to bed, and his enemies expect him to die. What hurts him most is that one of his friends betrays him. Jesus quoted this verse in John 13:18 when speaking about Judas.

For today: if someone close to you fails you, do not hide that pain. Bring it to God honestly, as David did, and ask him for mercy and for a heart that does not fill with bitterness.
exp.18:6:
The explanation says that God's teaching is complete and lacks nothing. The phrase in the verse that speaks of restoring the soul means that it restores, revives, and brings a person back onto the right path. "Testimony" is what God declares about himself and his will, and the verse's word for his testimony means that it can be fully relied on. The simple are the inexperienced, those who lack understanding, and God gives them wisdom.

David speaks here, according to the psalm's heading. Before this, he admired the sun and creation, which display the glory of God without words. Here he turns to the written Word, which reveals God with greater clarity. The verses that follow continue to describe its qualities: upright, pure, clean, and true.

For today: when you feel tired or confused, read a passage of the Bible calmly, even if it is short. Ask God to speak to you, and take one concrete step of obedience that day.
exp.87:7:
You have put my friends and companions far from me. You have made me something they find disgusting, a thing to be avoided. I feel shut in, trapped, with no way out.

The psalm is presented as the prayer of a man named Heman the Ezrahite, according to its title. He is very sick and has been suffering for a long time. It is a prayer without a happy ending: it does not finish with relief but in darkness. Even so, he keeps speaking to God and keeps calling out to him day after day. Some understand the cause to have been sickness; the text does not say more.

If you feel lonely, rejected, or without a way out today, you can tell God everything you feel, without dressing it up. The Bible makes room for honest pain. And if you know someone who is suffering, draw near to them instead of pulling away.
exp.39:16:
The explanation says the psalmist recognizes himself as afflicted and needy, yet trusts that the Lord thinks upon him, that is, that he keeps him in mind and takes an interest in his situation. He calls him "my help" and "my deliverer," and he asks him: "make no tarrying," that is, do not delay in acting.

The one speaking is David, according to the heading of the psalm. Earlier he gave thanks to God for having brought him up out of a pit of despair, and now he faces enemies who mock him. The psalm ends with a sincere prayer: he acknowledges his weakness, but he does not lose hope. Some think this last part of the psalm is a separate request, because it appears almost word for word in Psalm 70.

For today: when you feel weak or in need, do not pretend to be strong. Tell God honestly how you are, remind him that you trust in him, and rest in the knowledge that he keeps you in mind, even if the answer seems slow in coming.
exp.89:3:
This verse says that for God a thousand years are like a single day, the day of yesterday, which has already passed. It also compares them to a "watch in the night," which was each of the shifts into which the night was divided so that someone could keep watch, only a few hours long. In other words, a stretch of time that is very long for us is very short for God.

The psalm is titled "Prayer of Moses, the man of God." It is traditionally attributed to him, although some scholars debate its authorship. It speaks of God as eternal, existing before the mountains, while human beings are frail and fleeting. From this comes the prayer asking for wisdom to live well.

For today: do not live in haste or anxiety, as if time were slipping out of God's hands. He is eternal, and he holds your years in his hands. Make the most of each day with gratitude, and entrust your plans to him.
exp.119:5:
The explanation says that the psalmist has lived too long among people who do not want peace. The phrase "my soul hath long dwelt" means that he has lived or remained there for a long time, and he feels weary. "Hateth" means that they hate or reject peace.

This psalm opens the songs of ascents, which were sung as pilgrims climbed up to Jerusalem. The speaker is a believer troubled by lies and violence. He mentions Meshech and Kedar, distant places associated with peoples considered hostile. These are probably an image of his surroundings rather than a literal location. Scholars understand it in several ways. He then says that he desires peace, but they answer with war.

For today: if you find yourself living alongside people who stir up conflict, do not grow used to their spirit. Speak with truth and kindness, pray to God sincerely, and seek peace, without losing your own.
exp.111:3:
It says that for the upright, light shines even in the middle of darkness. The word "darkness" speaks of difficult times, and "upright" refers to those who live with honesty. "Gracious" means that someone treats others with kindness and patience; "full of compassion" means that someone feels for others and helps them; "righteous" means that someone acts with fairness. It is uncertain whether the subject of "is gracious" is God or the upright man; many see it as the righteous man, others as God, the source of that light.

The psalm is a poem of praise, with no author named. It describes what someone who fears God is like and what they receive, as Psalm 111 and the beginning of this one announce. The psalmist wants to show that a faithful life is blessed and leaves a mark on family and community.

For today: when you go through a dark situation, do not stop being honest and compassionate. That conduct can be a light for others, and God does not abandon those who follow him. Today, choose to help someone with your kindness.
exp.36:35:
It says that the wicked person, who seemed so powerful, disappeared. The word "yet" in the verse means "but," "passed away" means that he went by or was gone, and "lo, he was not" means that he could no longer be seen. The psalmist looked for him and did not find him.

The author is David, now older, who speaks like a wise teacher to people who are troubled to see the wicked prosper. Shortly before, he described seeing a wicked man greatly exalted, like a spreading green tree. Now he shows that this greatness did not last. Then he contrasts that ending with the peace that awaits the upright.

When injustice seems to be winning, do not despair or envy the one who prospers by doing wrong. What seems firm can disappear. Trust in God, keep doing what is right, and leave the outcome in his hands, because his justice is more certain than any human power.
exp.42:1:
The explanation says the psalmist speaks to God with honesty. He reminds God that God is his strength and his refuge, and yet he feels abandoned. "Rejected" means turned away or set aside. "Mourning" means dressed in grief, sad and heavy-hearted. "Oppression" means mistreatment or unjust pressure.

The one speaking is a believer who suffers because of deceitful and wicked enemies. We do not know for certain who wrote it or in what exact situation; many see it as connected with Psalm 42, and his longing to return to the temple suggests he is far from it. He asks for justice, and then asks for light and truth to be guided to the presence of God.

For today: when you feel abandoned, do not hide your questions. Bring them to God honestly, remembering who He is, and ask Him to guide you with His light and His truth.
exp.118:129:
It says that when someone begins to open God's Word, light already enters. "The entrance" can be understood as the beginning or the opening of his words; some translations say "the unfolding" or "the entrance." "Gives light" means gives light. "The simple" are ordinary people, without much training, who still need to learn and are open to teaching. God gives them understanding.

This verse is in Psalm 119, a long poem in honor of God's law. It is not known for certain who wrote it; tradition attributes it to David, but this is uncertain. The psalmist loves the Word, calls it wonderful, and desires to obey it. Here he recognizes that it guides and instructs him.

For today: read the Bible even if you feel you know little. Start with a short passage, ask God to teach you, and trust that He gives light step by step.
exp.65:1:
This verse invites us to sing about the glory of God's name and to make his praise glorious and worthy of him. "Sing forth" is a gentle command to sing. "Make his praise glorious" means to praise him with honor and wholehearted devotion, not in a cold or hurried way. God's name represents who he is, his character, and his works.

The psalmist calls the whole earth to join in worship. This is a psalm for the choir director, meant to be sung in community. The author does not identify himself in this psalm, so we do not know for certain who wrote it. The verses that follow explain the reason: God is powerful, his works are impressive, and everyone will recognize his greatness.

Today you can praise God with intention. Before you pray or sing in church, remember something specific that he has done for you, and express it with sincere gratitude.
exp.32:17:
This verse says that God looks on with careful attention those who fear him, that is, those who respect him and honor him with reverence. He also watches over those who hope in his mercy, meaning those who trust in his faithful love.

The phrase "behold" is an old way of saying "look" or "take notice." The "eye of the Lord" is an image: it speaks of God's care, not of mere surveillance.

This psalm is a song of praise, and the Bible does not say who wrote it, although some attribute it to David. Earlier, the psalmist says that neither a great army nor a strong horse saves a person. Afterward, he explains that God delivers from death and sustains in famine.

Today we can let go of the idea that our safety depends only on our own resources. In a moment of fear or need, pray calmly and trust that God sees you and cares for you.
exp.106:41:
This verse says that the righteous, that is, those who live with justice and honesty, will see what God does and will rejoice. But all iniquity, that is, wicked people, will shut their mouths: they will be left silent, with nothing to answer.

The psalm is a song of thanks to God for rescuing his people from different troubles. The text does not say who wrote it. Here the psalmist sums up what came before: God humbles the proud, lifts up the poor, and cares for families. Seeing this, the righteous rejoice, and the unjust have no way to defend themselves. The following verse invites us to think about these things with wisdom.

Today we can pay closer attention to God's works in our own lives and in the lives of others. Write them down, give thanks for them, and let joy grow, even when you see injustice. God is still watching.
exp.143:1:
This verse describes God with several images of protection. "My goodness" means that God is the source of kindness and faithful love. "Fortress" and "high tower" are safe places, hard to attack. "Deliverer" is the one who rescues, and "shield" is the one who covers us from danger. "Subdueth my people under me" means that God brings the people under control, putting them in order so that David can rule over them.

The speaker is David, king of Israel, in a psalm of praise. He has just mentioned that God trained him for battle. He recognizes that his victories and his authority do not come only from his own strength, but from God. Then he humbly asks why God pays attention to human beings.

For today: when you face pressure or conflict, do not rely only on your own ability. Before you act, take a moment to pray and trust God as your refuge, and then give your best effort with humility.
exp.132:1:
It says that unity among brothers is like the fine, fragrant oil that was poured over the head of Aaron. The oil ran down his beard and reached the edge of his robe. "Oil" is the ointment, and "garments" are the clothes. The image speaks of something abundant, that reaches the whole body and is enjoyed.

The psalm is attributed to David and is one of the songs of ascents, the kind that were sung when going up to Jerusalem, probably at the feasts. Aaron was the first high priest, and the anointing oil set him apart to serve God. Here it reminds us that the unity of the people is something holy and pleasing to God. Some think that "unity" refers to all the tribes united together.

Today, seek to be a peacemaker in your family or church: forgive quickly, speak with respect, and avoid gossip. Unity, like the oil, spreads out and blesses everyone.
exp.122:0:
The explanation says that the psalmist lifts his eyes toward God, who dwells in the heavens. The title "A Song of degrees" appears in several psalms (120 to 134). It is usually understood as "a song for ascending," meaning songs sung on the way up to Jerusalem, though not everyone is certain of its exact meaning. Lifting the eyes is a way of saying that a person seeks help and trusts in God.

The speaker is not identified with certainty. The one speaking feels despised, and then speaks in the plural, so it seems to be the voice of a people or community. The verses that follow explain that they look to God the way a servant watches the hand of his master, waiting for mercy in the midst of the contempt they suffer.

Today, when you feel ignored, humiliated, or without a way out, before seeking your own defense, lift your gaze to God. Tell him plainly what you feel, and wait patiently for his mercy.
exp.45:4:
He says that God dwells in the midst of the city of God, and therefore she will not be shaken. "Shaken" means moved or shaken with force. "When the morning appears" means at dawn, when the day begins. God will help her just in time.

The psalm was written by the sons of Korah, Levites who served in worship. It is a song for God's people in times of danger. The roaring waters, the trembling mountains, and the restless nations are images of chaos. Many think that "the city" is Jerusalem, and others see it as the people of God. The psalm does not say what specific event inspired it.

For today: when your world seems to tremble, do not look first at the storm, but at who is with you. Pray calmly, trust, and take the next step. God is never late; his help comes at his appointed time.
exp.101:1:
What it says: The psalmist asks God not to hide himself from him while he is suffering. To "hide the face" means to turn one's back or seem absent. "Incline your ear" is like bending down to listen closely. "Answer me speedily" is an urgent plea: "answer me quickly."

Context: The title of the psalm says it is the prayer of one who is afflicted and pours out his complaint before the LORD. It is not known for certain who wrote it. The one speaking is someone tired, sick, or deeply battered, who feels weak like smoke and dry grass, and so cries out with urgency.

For today: When you are distressed, do not wait until you have beautiful words. Speak to God honestly, tell him everything you feel, and ask him for help, trusting that he hears those who suffer.
exp.61:2:
Here David asks his enemies with firmness: "How long will you plot evil against a man?" He warns them that all of them will fall. "Imagine" means planning something harmful in secret. He compares them to a leaning wall and a fence about to collapse, which no longer have any strength and soon come crashing down.

David speaks here, and in this psalm he rests in God alone. His enemies want to pull him down from his position, and the verses that follow say they pretend to bless while cursing inwardly. We do not know with certainty which exact moment of his life he was living; some think of Absalom's rebellion, but the text does not say so.

When someone attacks you or speaks badly of you, do not spend your strength defending yourself with resentment. Rest in God, who is your refuge, and trust that what is false cannot stand forever.
exp.103:18:
It says that God made the moon to mark the times, that is, the seasons and the dates of the feasts, and that the sun knows when it must go down. "Sunset" is the moment when the sun sets. The word "times" can refer to the months or to the appointed feasts; the text does not specify which.

The psalm does not say who wrote it. It is a hymn of praise to the Creator, and many connect it with the account of creation in Genesis 1. Before this, it speaks of birds, goats and rabbits, and afterward of the night and the lions. Everything shows an order in which each creature has its place and its hour.

Today we can trust that God also orders our times. When we see the sunset, we can pause for a moment to thank him. And if we live in a hurry, we can learn to respect rest, since God himself set the rhythms of day and night.
exp.24:17:
Here the psalmist asks God to look upon his suffering and his weariness. "Affliction" is the pain and sorrow; "toil" here means distress, fatigue, or hardship, not a job. Then he asks for something deeper: that God forgive all his sins.

This is a psalm attributed to David. The speaker feels alone, surrounded by enemies, with an anguished heart. It is striking that alongside his pain he also mentions his guilt. It is not clear whether his suffering came from his own mistakes or from other causes, and scholars do not settle the question. Even so, he brings both burdens to God.

For today: when you are tired or hurting, speak to God with complete honesty. Tell Him your sorrow, and also acknowledge your failings, trusting that He listens with mercy.
exp.83:4:
It says that the man who finds his strength in God is happy and truly blessed. "Blessed" means deeply favored, with a profound joy. The phrase about having God's ways in the heart means that he carries God's paths within him, that is, the desire to follow him. The original is brief in this part, and some understand it to refer to the roads that lead to the temple.

This psalm was written by a son of Korah, one of the Levites who served in worship. It expresses a great longing to be in the house of God, in Jerusalem. Pilgrims traveled all the way there, and the psalmist says that his strength does not come from the easy road, but from God. The Valley of Baca (which perhaps means "weeping") is a difficult place, yet God turns it into a place of springs.

For today: when you feel tired, do not look first to your own strength. Before facing the day, take a few minutes to pray and read the Bible, and ask God to guide your heart.
exp.25:9:
It says that there are people who have wickedness in their hands, that is, who practice it and plan it. Their right hand, the hand of strength and action, is full of bribes, that is, money received to pervert justice.

David speaks, according to the title of the psalm. He asks God not to count him among sinners, and describes the kind of people he does not want to keep company with. He has declared that he loves the house of God and wants to walk in integrity. What follows shows that he does not consider himself perfect, for he asks to be redeemed and to receive mercy.

Today it invites us to examine our hands: what we do, accept, or stay silent about for money or convenience. We can choose friends and surroundings that draw us closer to honesty, and ask God for help to remain upright, without feeling superior to anyone.
exp.79:18:
This verse is a prayer. The writer asks God to "turn us again," that is, to bring us back to himself and restore us. "Cause thy face to shine" means showing his favor and kindness, as when someone looks at us with a smile. "And we shall be saved" means that we will be rescued and kept safe.

The psalm is a plea from Israel, the people of God, who are going through a time of suffering and defeat. The writer speaks on behalf of everyone. This same refrain is repeated earlier, in verses 3 and 7. Before this verse, help is requested for the one whom God strengthened. Interpreters understand this in different ways: it may refer to the people of Israel or to a king chosen by God.

Today we can pray with humility: "Lord, I cannot return to you by my own strength; draw me near and restore me." Recognizing our need is a good beginning.
exp.71:3:
This verse says that the righteous king will defend those who suffer. The verse's "shall judge" means that he will see that they receive justice. Those who suffer are the oppressed and mistreated. A person who is poor and in need is someone who has nothing to fall back on. "Break in pieces" means that he will stop and overcome the violent one who abuses the weak.

This psalm bears the name of Solomon, though the Hebrew heading can also be understood as "for Solomon," and scholars debate this. It is a prayer for the king, that he may govern with God's justice. Many Christians see here also a look toward Jesus, the perfect King, who cares for the poor and brings peace.

For today: God cares for those who suffer injustice, and we can imitate him. This week, help someone vulnerable: defend a person who is being mistreated, support a family in need, or pray for them faithfully.
exp.30:18:
This verse celebrates the goodness of God. The psalmist says that God has stored up good things, like a treasure, for those who fear him, that is, those who hold him in respect and reverence. He has also made them visible before the sons of men, that is, in plain view of everyone. Those who trust in God are the ones who wait on him.

The psalm is attributed to David, according to its heading. Earlier, he had been asking for help in the middle of distress, mockery, and lies from his enemies. Now, under that pressure, he praises God. The verses that follow say that God hides him and protects him from tongues that attack.

For today: when you are criticized or feel under pressure, do not look only at the problem. Remember that God keeps good things for those who trust in him. Thank him today for one concrete sign of his care.
exp.48:16:
The explanation says that when a rich person dies, they take nothing of what they gathered. Their reputation and honor do not go with them to the grave. The word "glory" here refers to their wealth, their standing, and everything that made them look important. "When he dieth" means "when he dies."

The one speaking is a psalmist, one of the sons of Korah according to the heading of the psalm. He speaks like a teacher of wisdom. He wants to encourage those who feel intimidated by powerful and wealthy people. Earlier, he affirms his hope: God will redeem his life from the power of the grave. In other words, his trust is in God, not in money.

For today: do not measure your worth or the worth of others by what they have. Invest your time in what lasts, such as your relationship with God, love for your family, and generosity toward others.
exp.135:11:
This verse says that God brought Israel out of Egypt with a "strong hand" and an "outstretched arm." These are images of power: a firm hand and an arm stretched out to act. The word "mercy" here translates the Hebrew term hesed, which speaks of loyal, faithful, steadfast love. What God did was not only strength, but love that does not give up.

It is a psalm of praise, probably sung in the worship of God's people. The text does not say who wrote it. A leader calls out and the people respond in each verse: "for his mercy endureth for ever." It recalls the exodus from Egypt, when God freed his people from slavery, just before they crossed the sea.

For today: when you feel trapped in something you cannot overcome, remember how God has acted before. Make a list of the times he helped you and give him thanks, trusting that his love remains firm.
exp.93:7:
Here the psalmist calls attention to those who act as if God pays no attention to anything. The "fools" he addresses are people without spiritual common sense, who do not think clearly. The urgent question "when will you become wise?" is a call to reflect and to stop deceiving yourselves.

The psalmist speaks in the midst of injustice: powerful people mistreat the widow, the stranger and the orphan, and they reassure themselves by saying that God does not see. So he answers them with clear questions: the one who made the ear and the eye, will he not hear or see? Some believe that the phrase "among the people" refers to Israelites who had become foolish.

For today: when you see injustice, or when you yourself are tempted to think that no one notices, remember that God sees and hears everything. Live with honesty and defend those who are vulnerable.
exp.70:9:
What it says: The psalmist tells us that his enemies speak evil about him. "They have spoken against me" means that they talk about him and make plans against him. "Those who lie in wait for my soul" are the ones who watch him, waiting for a chance to harm his life. "Take counsel together" means that they agreed with one another, making plans as a group.

Context: The one speaking is an older person who has trusted God since youth. The psalm does not give his name; some connect it with David, but this is not certain. In the verses that follow we see what his enemies say: that God has forsaken him. For this reason he asks God not to leave him in old age.

For today: When others speak badly about you or make you feel that God has left you, do not stay silent with that pain. Bring it to God in prayer, as the psalmist did, and remember his faithful care in the past.
exp.4:9:
David asks God to bring his enemies to nothing. "Destroy them" means to make their plans fail. "Let them fall by their own counsels" means that they fall through their own schemes or intrigues. "Cast them out" means to drive them away and reject them. The reason he gives is that their rebellions were not only against him, but against God.

David speaks, probably in a morning prayer, surrounded by lying and flattering people. The previous verse describes them in harsh words: they speak with deceit, and their mouths are like open graves. David does not take revenge himself; he places the matter in the hands of God, the righteous judge, and then contrasts their fate with that of those who trust in God.

For today: when someone treats you with injustice or deceit, do not respond with revenge. Bring your pain honestly before God, ask him for justice and wisdom, and trust that he cares for his own.
exp.94:4:
The explanation says that the sea belongs to God because he himself made it, and that with his hands he formed the solid land. The psalmist covers everything: seas and continents, what seems immense and what seems firm.

This psalm is a song of worship, probably meant to gather the people of Israel for worship. The speaker invites everyone to praise God. First he reminds them who God is: a great God, King over all, owner of the depths and the mountains. That truth prepares the invitation that follows: to come, to bow down, and to listen to his voice.

For today: when something feels too big for you, such as a problem, a fear, or an uncertain situation, remember that the sea and the dry land came from the hands of God. Before you worry, stop for a moment and worship him with confidence.
exp.142:4:
This verse says that the psalmist remembers the past. He thinks about "the days of old," that is, about what God did in earlier times. He thought slowly and attentively about God's works, and he considered the work of God's hands.

The psalm is spoken by David, according to its title. He is in a very dark moment: an enemy is pursuing him, he feels crushed, and his heart is troubled. In the middle of that pain, he does not just stare at his problem. He turns his attention back to what God has already done, and then he stretches out his hands in prayer.

For today: when you feel discouraged, pause and remember how God has helped you before. Write down three things He has done in your life or in His Word, and thank Him for them. This strengthens hope.
exp.110:9:
This verse says that wisdom begins when we respect God with reverence and awe. The word "fear" here does not mean living in dread, but taking him seriously and honoring him. "Those" refers to his commandments, mentioned earlier in the verse. "Praise" means the act of praising him. Whoever puts into practice what God commands has good understanding, and the praise of God never ends.

The psalm does not say who wrote it. It is a song of praise that recalls God's works: his faithfulness, his redemption of his people, and his covenant. After recounting all of this, the psalmist concludes that recognizing who God is, is the starting point for living well.

For today: before making an important decision, stop for a moment and ask yourself what pleases God. Then take one concrete step of obedience, even a small one. In this way wisdom stops being only an idea and becomes a way of living.
exp.41:6:
He says that sorrows come one after another, as if one deep were calling out to another deep. "Waterspouts" refers to cascades or rushing torrents of water that fall with force. "Waves" and "billows" are the waters of the sea or river rising up. The poet feels himself covered by all of them, like someone who is sinking.

The speaker is a faithful Israelite, probably a Levite, who is far from the temple in the region of the Jordan and Mount Hermon. He feels overwhelmed, perhaps by the oppression of his enemies. He uses the image of cascades and waves to describe his distress. Even so, in the verses nearby he speaks to his own soul and reminds himself that he must wait on God.

When you feel that troubles are coming in a chain, do not deny them. Tell God honestly how you feel, as the psalmist did, and remember that he is still your firm rock.
exp.43:21:
The explanation says that the people suffer a constant kind of death for being faithful to God. The sentence about the old wording is dropped, since the reader's verse does not contain it, and the slaughterhouse note is also dropped, since it explains a source-language word that does not appear in the reader's verse. They feel like sheep with no defense, treated as if their lives were worth nothing.

The psalm speaks for the people of Israel, or for a group among them, in the middle of defeat and persecution. We do not know for certain who the author is, since the psalm is attributed to the sons of Korah. They insist that they have not abandoned God, and that is why they do not understand their pain. Honestly, they bring their complaint before God.

For today: when you suffer without understanding why, do not hide your pain. Bring it before God with honesty, as this psalm does. Paul quotes this verse in Romans 8:36 and then affirms that nothing will separate us from the love of Christ.
exp.70:16:
He says that God has been his teacher since youth. "Youth" means the early years of life, and "taught me" is the phrase used in the verse. From that time until now, the person has declared God's wonderful works, that is, the amazing things He has done.

Psalm 71 does not say who wrote it. What we see is someone already advanced in years, who has trusted God all his life. He is surrounded by troubles and asks that God not forsake him in old age. Earlier he spoke of proclaiming God's righteousness all day long, and now he asks to remain alive so that he can speak of God to the new generations.

Think about what God has taught you since you began to believe in Him. Today, tell someone younger about it, such as a son, a nephew, or a friend. Your story with God can give them encouragement and hope.
exp.34:5:
Let their way be dark and slippery, places where a person loses their balance and falls. He also asks that the angel of the Lord pursue them. "Pursue" here means to go after them without giving them rest.

David speaks in this psalm. He feels attacked without cause: he says they spread a net for him and dug a pit for him "without cause." He cries out to God as his defender and entrusts his case to him. These words are a prayer of lament, intense and very frank. Some understand them as a plea for justice rather than a personal desire for revenge.

For today: when someone treats you unjustly, bring your pain to God with sincerity, instead of repaying evil for evil. Ask him for justice, and also for a heart free of resentment. Jesus taught us to pray even for those who persecute us.
exp.118:94:
Here the psalmist says that there are wicked people who watch him and wait patiently to harm him or to take his life. The way the verse is worded in the King James Version, "The wicked have waited for me," shows they have been lying in wait for him, like someone stalking their prey. But he does not respond with fear or with revenge: he says he will consider God's testimonies, that is, his teachings and commands, paying close attention to them and reflecting on them.

Psalm 119 is a long poem in praise of the Word of God. It is traditionally attributed to a believer going through trials, although the author is not named with certainty. In the verses nearby, he affirms that he belongs to God, that he has sought out his commandments, and that they have given him life. So, when faced with threat, he returns to what gives him steadiness.

For today: when someone threatens you, criticizes you, or makes you feel pressure, before reacting, stop and read and think about the Bible. It does not remove the problem instantly, but it gives you calm, wisdom, and direction to respond well.
exp.118:173:
Here the psalmist says that he has longed for God's salvation, meaning deliverance and rescue. He also declares that God's law is his delight, that is, his joy and pleasure. He does not see it as a burden, but as a source of gladness.

Psalm 119 is a long poem about the word of God. It is not known for certain who wrote it. Here we hear someone who loves the commandments, asks God for help, and shortly afterward admits that he has felt like a lost sheep. His desire for salvation and his joy in the law go together, and both come from depending on God.

Today we can ask God to teach us to delight in his word, not only to obey it. Try reading for a few minutes each day, praying simply: "Lord, help me to love what you tell me and to trust in your salvation."
exp.5:8:
This verse says that David is sure God heard him. The word "supplication" means a request made with humility. The phrase "will receive my prayer" means that God accepted it and did not ignore it. It repeats the same idea twice to give firmness to his confidence.

The one speaking is David, according to the title of the psalm. Before this, he was deeply distressed: he was weeping, sick in his soul, and surrounded by enemies. Suddenly his spirit changes, and he declares that God has already heard him. The psalm does not explain how that change came about, and it does not say that his problem was already resolved. What changed was his confidence in God.

When you pray in the middle of a difficulty, do not stay only in tears. Remember that God hears you, and rest in that, even if you do not yet see the answer.
exp.29:8:
Here the psalmist speaks to God with honesty, and almost "reasons" with him: if he dies, he will no longer be able to thank him. "The pit" is the grave, and "the dust" refers to the dead body. He asks what gain there would be for God, or for himself, in his death, if he could no longer praise God or tell of his faithfulness.

The words are said to be David's, according to the heading of the psalm. He had gone through a serious trial, perhaps an illness, and felt that God was hiding his face. That is why he cries out. His words reflect the Old Testament view of death, with little light on what comes after. Then God answers him and turns his weeping into dancing.

For today: you can be honest with God in your distress and ask him for help. And remember that your life is an opportunity to praise him and to speak of his faithfulness to others, today itself.
exp.18:9:
This verse compares the word of God to very valuable things. "More to be desired" means worth longing for. Fine gold is gold that has been purified, of the highest quality. The honeycomb is the wax structure where bees store honey. So God's commandments are worth more than great wealth and are sweeter than the purest honey.

The speaker is David, according to the heading of the psalm. First he praises God for creation and then for his law. He describes the word of God as upright, pure, and true. That is why he says it is more precious than what the world values most.

For today: before you seek money, success, or pleasure, ask God to give you a hunger for his Word. Read one passage each day, slowly, and ask yourself: "What does this teach me about God and about how to live?"
exp.106:25:
The explanation describes sailors in the middle of a storm at sea. The waves lift them so high that it seems they are rising up to the sky, and then they drop them down as if they were going into the deep. The depths of the sea are the sense of the words "they go down again to the depths," and the phrase about the soul being melted means that their courage runs out and they come apart from fear in the face of danger.

The author of the psalm is not known for certain. He speaks like a singer who invites people to give thanks to God for having rescued different groups of people in trouble. Here he presents the sailors. God himself allows the wind to raise the waves, and the purpose is to show that when no one can save themselves alone, the only thing left is to cry out to him, as the verses that follow say.

There are moments when life lifts us up and drops us down without control, and we feel we no longer have any strength. In those days there is no need to pretend that we are strong. We can do what they did: honestly tell God that we are frightened, and trust that he hears us.
exp.89:7:
This verse says that God sees all the wrong we have done. The words for our wrongdoing refer to our faults and sins, and our errors are our mistakes, including the ones we make without realizing it. The phrase about God's presence means that nothing stays hidden: everything is in plain view before God, as if it were under a bright lamp.

The psalm is traditionally attributed to Moses, according to its heading. It speaks on behalf of the people and reflects on how brief life is and how serious sin is. Many understand it to refer to God's discipline in the wilderness, although the text does not state this clearly.

For today: do not try to hide your failings from God. Bring them to him honestly, asking for forgiveness. The Bible teaches that God forgives the one who confesses sin (1 John 1:9). In this way we live with humility and with a clear conscience.
exp.134:17:
They that make idols become like them, and so does everyone who trusts in them. The phrase "are like unto them" means "will become like them." It is a strong statement: whoever trusts in something lifeless ends up spiritually deaf, blind, and mute.

This psalm is a song of praise from the people of Israel, probably for worship in the temple. The author is not known for certain. It compares the living God, who acts in history, with the idols of the nations, which are the work of human hands. The verses before this one describe those idols: they have mouths, eyes, and ears, but they cannot use them. Afterward, the psalm calls the whole people to bless the Lord.

For today: when we trust in money, fame, or success as if they were the most important things, we slowly become hardened inside. Today you can reflect on what you trust most, and turn back to pray to God, who does hear.
exp.141:3:
