He says that the psalmist looked to his right hand and watched closely, but no one recognized him or took his side. He had no place to take refuge, and no one cared what happened to him. In that time, the right hand was where the defender or helper would stand.

The title of the psalm attributes it to David, when he was in the cave, probably fleeing from Saul. He felt alone, pursued, and with traps hidden along his path. That is why he pours out his complaint before God with complete honesty.

When you feel alone or ignored, do not keep your pain to yourself. Tell it to God honestly, as David did. Even when no one else notices, God knows your way and can be your refuge, as the psalmist acknowledges in the following verse.
exp.118:120:
The psalmist says he has acted with uprightness and justice, and for that reason he asks God not to hand him over to those who oppress him. "Ain" is the name of a Hebrew letter with which this section of the psalm begins. Here, "judgment" means doing what is right and fair. "Oppressors" are those who abuse others.

The speaker is the author of Psalm 119, who cannot be identified with certainty. He loves God's law and lives among unjust and proud people. He has just said that he reveres God and fears his judgments. Now he asks for protection, not because he thinks himself perfect, but because he has tried to live according to the Lord's will.

For today: if you are suffering for trying to do what is right, do not lose heart. Keep acting with honesty and ask God to watch over you and give you strength. He hears those who trust in him.
exp.77:27:
This verse says that God caused the birds, the quail, to fall right in the middle of Israel's camp, all around their dwellings. The sentence that explains the wording of "let fall" and "dwellings" is rewritten here: the verse says God let the quail fall in the midst of the camp, and the dwellings are the tents where they lived in the desert. This way they had their food within reach.

The psalmist, Asaph, is telling the story of Israel to teach new generations. He recalls that the people, in the desert, asked for meat with a discontented and distrustful heart. God gave them what they asked for, but the psalm tells it as a warning, since it goes on to describe God's anger over their attitude (verses 29-31).

For today: before demanding something from God, let us examine our hearts. He is generous and gives us what we need, but it is wise to trust Him and be thankful, not to live complaining about what we do not yet have.
exp.141:0:
The explanation says that David, in a very difficult moment, prayed aloud to God. The word "Maschil" probably indicates a poem or song meant to teach, though its exact meaning is uncertain. "Cried" means to ask for help with strength, and "mercy" is compassion and favor that one does not deserve.

David is the speaker, and the heading says he prayed "when he was in the cave." It could have been the cave of Adullam or the cave of En-gedi, when he was fleeing from King Saul; the text does not specify which one. He was alone, pursued, and afraid, and the verses that follow speak of his distress and of hidden traps.

For today: when you feel trapped or overwhelmed, do not keep everything inside. Speak to God honestly, even aloud if you can. He hears you and does not tire of your cry.
exp.71:13:
This verse says that the righteous king will rescue the poor from deceit and violence. The word "redeem" here means to free, to rescue, like someone who pays to set another person free. The idea of their "blood being precious" means that their lives have great worth in his sight; he does not see them as disposable people.

The psalm is "of Solomon" or perhaps "for Solomon"; the Hebrew title can be understood in either way. It is a prayer for the king, asking that he rule with justice, especially on behalf of the weak. Many Christians also see here a picture of the perfect reign of Christ, though the psalm speaks first of a king of Israel.

For today: God values the lives of the vulnerable, and we can do the same. Think of someone who is being deceived, taken advantage of, or mistreated, and help them with a concrete action: accompany them, defend their cause, or support those who are helping them.
exp.104:13:
God did not allow anyone to harm the patriarchs. The word "wrong" in the verse means to offend or mistreat them. And because he cared for them, God corrected and punished kings who threatened them.

The psalmist praises God by recalling how he looked after Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob when they were few in number and lived as strangers. Many think he has in mind episodes like Abraham's dealings with the pharaoh and with Abimelech, in Genesis. The psalm does not say who wrote it, but 1 Chronicles 16 contains a similar passage and connects it with David. Its purpose is to encourage the people to trust God.

For today: even if you feel small, weak, or out of place, God cares for you. Trust in his protection, and instead of seeking revenge, rest in the knowledge that he defends his own.
exp.49:22:
He says that whoever offers praise as a sacrifice honors God, and that to the one who sets his way in order, that is, who arranges and directs his life carefully before God, God will show his salvation.

God himself speaks, in a psalm of Asaph. God rebukes those who carried out religious rituals but lived forgetting him and assumed God was like them. He warns them firmly, but ends with an invitation: what he seeks is not only outward offerings, but a grateful heart and an upright life.

For today: before you ask for something or fulfill your religious duties, begin the day by thanking God with sincere words. Then review one specific area of your life, such as how you treat others or your honesty, and put it in order before him.
exp.108:1:
It says that wicked and deceitful people have opened their mouths against the psalmist. "Wicked" describes someone who lives without respect for God, and "deceitful" describes someone who seeks to confuse others with falsehoods. They have spoken about him with a lying tongue, that is, they accuse him with lies.

The psalm is attributed to David, and the one speaking is a person attacked unjustly. In the verse before, he asks God not to remain silent, because his defense is in Him. The following verses say they surrounded him with hatred and attacked him without cause, even though he had shown them love and responded by praying. It is not known with certainty which exact moment in David's life is in view.

For today: if someone slanders you, you do not have to respond in kind. You can bring your pain to God with sincerity, ask Him for justice, and keep acting with integrity, trusting that He sees the truth.
exp.82:15:
It says the psalmist asks God to cover his enemies with shame, with the hope that they will end up seeking the name of the Lord. "Faces" refers to the whole person, and "shame" is being humbled. "Lord" is the proper name of God. To seek his name is to come to him and acknowledge him.

It is a psalm of Asaph, a prayer from Israel facing a coalition of nations that wanted to destroy it (verses 3 to 8). The people cry out because they feel threatened. This verse sounds harsh, but its goal is not only punishment: it asks that the enemies come to know God. Some understand this as a sincere turning to God, others as an acknowledgment forced by his power.

Today we can bring God our pain over injustice, without taking revenge ourselves. We can ask him for justice and also that those who hurt us come to know him.
exp.41:9:
He says the author feels a pain so deep that it is as if his bones were being broken. His enemies reproach him, that is, they insult and shame him, and every day they keep saying to him, "Where is your God?" That mockery aims to make him doubt that God is caring for him.

The speaker is a believer who is far from the temple and surrounded by oppression. The psalm is attributed to the sons of Korah, and no one knows for certain who wrote it or at what exact moment. We see a sincere man: he tells God that he feels forgotten, yet he still speaks to him and ends by encouraging his own soul to wait on Him.

Today, when someone mocks your faith or your pain makes you doubt, do not hide it. Tell God honestly how you feel, and remind your heart of what He has already done for you.
exp.88:33:
He says that God will not forget his covenant, that is, the solemn promise he made. Nor will he change or take back what he said with his lips. God affirms that his word is firm and that he does not go back on it.

In this psalm, the one speaking is God, and he says it in reference to David and his descendants. Earlier, God says that if David's sons rebel, he will correct them, but he will not take away his mercy from them. The covenant promised that David's throne would endure. Many Christians see the final fulfillment of this promise in Jesus, a descendant of David.

For today: when you feel you have failed or you doubt God, remember that his faithfulness does not depend on your perfection. Rest in his promises, return to him with sincerity, and trust that his word still stands.
exp.101:12:
It says that God will arise, that is, act, and show compassion to Zion, or Jerusalem. It affirms that the appointed time for that favor has already come. "Set time" here means a fixed moment, and "have mercy" means compassion that helps.

The psalm is the prayer of a person in affliction who feels weak like a shadow and dry grass. Many think it reflects the situation of the people in exile or after it, but the text does not give the exact date. The psalmist takes comfort because God remains forever, and for that reason he hopes for the restoration of Zion.

For today: when your strength runs out or the waiting grows long, remember that God is not limited by your short days. Pray with confidence, entrust your situation to him, and wait for his time, which is wise and faithful.
exp.9:5:
The wicked man speaks to himself and makes sure of it: nothing will shake him, now or ever. He thinks no disaster will reach him, because he feels secure and above all punishment.

Psalm 10 is the prayer of someone who sees an arrogant man prospering while he oppresses the poor. The verses before it say that this man does not seek God and lives as if God did not exist. The verses that follow show how his confidence serves him as an excuse to deceive and harm the innocent. The psalmist does not speak calmly about this, but brings his complaint before God.

Today we can ask ourselves whether, in our successes, we speak as if we did not need God. True security does not lie in believing that nothing will happen to us, but in trusting God, who sees and judges with justice.
exp.37:6:
This verse describes a very intense physical pain. "Loins" is the lower part of the back, the waist. "Irritation" here refers to a burning or inflammation that stings. The author says that this area is badly hurting and that his body finds no relief or improvement.

David speaks here, according to the title of the psalm, which calls it "a psalm of David, to bring to remembrance." He is sick and suffering, and he acknowledges that part of his affliction comes from his own sin and his folly, that is, his poor decisions. Some think the illness is literal and others that it is an image of suffering; the text does not make this entirely clear.

When you are worn out in body or in soul, you do not need to hide anything from God. David tells him everything, without pretense. You can do the same: honestly tell him where it hurts, ask his forgiveness if needed, and wait for his help.
exp.77:47:
It says God let hail fall on the animals of the Egyptians, and that the fire, probably lightning, killed their herds. Hail is the word for the frozen pellets that came down with the storm, and "cattle" and "flocks" are the animals the Egyptians raised. It recalls the seventh plague on Egypt (Exodus 9:22-25).

The psalm is attributed to Asaph. He reviews the history of Israel to teach the new generations. It tells how God freed his people through the plagues, while Egypt hardened its heart. The aim is that Israel remember the works of God and not repeat the rebellion of its ancestors (vv. 5-8).

For today: let us not take for granted what God gives us, nor harden our hearts when he corrects us. Remembering how he has cared for us helps us obey him with trust and humility, before stubbornness costs us dearly.
exp.146:5:
It says that God lifts up and honors the humble, that is, those who do not think themselves better than anyone else and depend on Him. On the other hand, the wicked, who live without respecting God and do evil, He brings down to the ground. In the verse, the word "lifteth up" means to raise or give a place of honor.

This psalm is a song of praise, and it is not known for certain who wrote it. The people are invited to celebrate a God so great that He counts and names the stars, yet who also pays attention to the brokenhearted. Before and after the verse, it speaks of His power over the sky, the clouds, and the rain. In this way it shows that the same God who governs all things also cares for the humble.

Today you can live with humility, without boasting or relying only on yourself. If you feel small or overlooked, remember that God sees you and knows how to lift you up in His time.
exp.138:19:
The explanation says that God's enemies speak against Him wickedly and use His name without respect. "Blasphemies" are words that insult or belittle God. "Taking his name in vain" means using it lightly, with lies, mockery, or falsehood. Some translations read this verse differently, because the Hebrew is difficult, but the general idea is the same.

David, or a psalmist in his tradition, speaks after reflecting on how near God is to him. Now he turns toward those who oppose God and him. He feels surrounded by violent people and wants to stand on God's side. His language is strong, fitting for an honest and raw prayer.

Today we can be careful about how we speak of God and with what attitude we use His name. We can also bring our anger at injustice to God in prayer, instead of taking revenge, and ask Him for a heart that defends His honor without hating people.
exp.34:1:
Here David asks God to act like a warrior getting ready for battle. The shield was a small protection, and the large shield that covered nearly the whole body was the kind a soldier could hide behind. To ask God to take hold of them is to ask Him to arm Himself. And "stand up for my help" is a plea that He come quickly to come to his aid.

David speaks in this psalm while he suffers attacks and persecution from enemies who hate him. He uses the language of war and of the courtroom: he asks God to be his defender. It is not a personal revenge, but a cry from someone who feels helpless and trusts that God is just.

For today: when you feel weak in the face of an injustice or a pressure, you can tell God honestly what you feel and ask Him for help. You do not have to fight alone; you can rest in the knowledge that He defends you.
exp.29:10:
God says he turned the psalmist's sorrow into joy. The words "mourning" and "sackcloth" in the verse above stand for a sad song of grief and a rough cloth worn in times of mourning or repentance. The word "dancing" stands for celebration, and "girded" means wrapped around or clothed. God took away the clothing of sadness and dressed him in gladness.

The one speaking is David, according to the heading of the psalm, which presents it as a song for the dedication of the house. He had been very sick, close to death, and he cried out to God asking for help. The verses before this one show his plea: the dead cannot praise. Now God has heard him and healed him. The verses that follow show his response: singing and praising without falling silent.

For today: if God has lifted you out of a hard time, do not keep it to yourself. Today, thank him out loud, or tell someone what he has done for you.
exp.128:2:
It says that Israel's enemies mistreated him as if they were farmers plowing a field. The words for those who plow and for the deep lines a plow leaves are the ones the verse itself uses, "plowers" and "furrows." The image suggests long, painful wounds across the back, like those of a slave who has been whipped.

The speaker is the people of Israel, as if they were one person remembering their history. This is one of the songs of ascents, meaning one of the psalms that were probably sung as people went up to Jerusalem (this is understood in several ways). The psalmist remembers years of oppression, but in the next verse affirms that God is righteous and has cut the cords of the wicked.

For today: if you have gone through long suffering, do not deny it. You can name it before God, and as you look back, recognize that the wounds did not have the last word. He sustained you.
exp.77:30:
God's anger fell upon the people of Israel and caused the death of the strongest among them and of the chosen young men. "Anger" is the sense of this word, meaning intense displeasure. The strongest ones are the most robust or the best fed. "Food" is the sense of the word for the meat they craved.

The psalm was written by Asaph, who recalls the history of Israel to teach the new generations. Here it refers to the time when the people, in the wilderness, asked for meat with a bad attitude, distrusting God (Numbers 11). God gave them the quail, but judgment came while they were still eating. The psalm shows that the problem was not the food, but a rebellious heart without trust.

For today: before asking something of God, examine your heart. Ask Him with trust and gratitude, and do not demand or doubt His goodness. Receiving what we desire does not always mean that we are right with Him.
exp.104:19:
This verse tells how the king of Egypt had Joseph brought out of prison and set him free. The old wording is understood this way: where it says "soltóle," the meaning is "let him go," and where it says "desatóle," the meaning is "set him free." The phrase "lord of the peoples" refers to the pharaoh, who ruled over many nations.

The psalmist, who is not named in this passage, reviews the history of Israel to praise God for his faithfulness. Here he remembers Joseph, sold as a slave and wrongly imprisoned. The text says that God's word tested him, meaning that it waited until what God had said was fulfilled. After that testing, God used the pharaoh to free him and place him in a position of responsibility.

For today: when your situation feels stuck, remember that God can act in his own time and use anyone to open doors. While you wait, keep being faithful and trust that he has not forgotten you.
exp.62:2:
It says that God's faithful love is worth more than life itself. "Lovingkindness" here translates a Hebrew word (chesed) that speaks of his loyal and constant goodness, the kind that does not abandon. That is why the psalmist says his lips will praise God: the praise is born from having experienced that love.

The speaker is David, according to the heading, when he was in the wilderness of Judah. It is not known with certainty at what exact moment this was; some think he was fleeing from Absalom or from Saul. He was in a dry and harsh place, thirsty in body, and yet his soul thirsted for God. He remembered how he had seen him in the sanctuary.

For today: when everything feels dry or uncertain, pause and remember how God has sustained you. Thank him out loud for his love, even if your circumstances have not changed yet.
exp.90:9:
This verse says that no harm will befall the person who trusts in God, and that no plague or disaster will come near their home. The word "befall" means something that arrives suddenly, and "dwelling" is the place where one lives.

Psalm 91 does not say who wrote it, and this is not known with certainty. It speaks of the one who makes God Most High his refuge and his dwelling place, that is, his safe place. The verse before explains the reason: "you have made the Lord your dwelling place." The promise rests on living close to God. Some read it as literal protection, others as spiritual security, since the Bible also shows believers who suffered.

For today: when you feel fear for your home or your family, make God your first refuge. Pray for your household every day and trust that his care sustains you, even in trials.
exp.134:20:
God is worthy of praise from Zion, the hill in Jerusalem, because he dwells there. "Blessed" means praised or worthy of honor. "Dwells" means lives or resides. "Hallelujah" means "praise the Lord" and closes the psalm with a shout of joy.

The psalmist calls the whole people to praise: Israel, the priests (the house of Aaron), the Levites, and those who fear God. This psalm recalls what God has done for his people and mocks lifeless idols. The author is unknown. Many believe it was sung in temple worship. Jerusalem was the place where God had placed his name and met with his people.

For today: do not wait until you feel perfect to give thanks. Take a few minutes to name aloud what God has done for you, and end with a simple "Hallelujah," either alone or with your family or your church.
exp.83:11:
This verse closes the psalm with a simple statement: the person who places their trust in God is happy, blessed. "Lord of hosts" is a title that speaks of God as the Lord over all power, in heaven and on earth. "Blessed" means fortunate, full of deep well-being.

The psalm is a song of the sons of Korah, Levites who served in the temple. The speaker is a believer who longs to be close to the house of God, perhaps far from it. After saying that one day in the courts is worth more than a thousand elsewhere, the psalm concludes that true happiness is not found in a place, but in trusting God himself.

Today, when something worries you, hand it over to God in prayer and say sincerely: "I trust in you." His care sustains you even when you cannot yet see the answer.
exp.118:16:
The verse says, "Deal bountifully with thy servant, that I may live, and keep thy word." That is, "be kind to me, for I am your servant." The speaker asks for life, and wants it in order to keep your word, that is, to obey it. "Gimel" is just the name of the third Hebrew letter, with which the verses of this part of the psalm begin.

The psalm does not say with certainty who wrote it. The speaker is a believer who loves God's law and feels like a stranger on the earth, as he says shortly afterward. He asks for God's goodness, but not merely for comfort: he desires to live in order to obey. His request joins life with obedience.

Today we can pray this way: "Lord, give me life and strength, not only for my own plans, but to live out what you say." At the start of the day, ask for his help to obey him in something specific: a conversation, a decision, or a temptation.
exp.123:2:
This verse says that if God had not been on the side of his people, their enemies would have swallowed them alive. "Swallowed" here means devoured, as when something is eaten in a single bite. The word rendered as "wrath" is a very strong anger, and the phrase "was kindled" means it flared up like a fire.

The title attributes the psalm to David and calls it a "song of ascents," which was probably sung when going up to Jerusalem, although scholars do not fully agree on its exact meaning. Here Israel remembers that it survived attacks from hostile men. The psalm does not boast of its own strength but thanks God for having delivered them. The images that follow, such as waters and torrents, reinforce the idea of an enormous danger.

For today: think of a difficulty you went through that seemed about to crush you. Take a moment to thank God, acknowledging that you did not get through it alone. That gratitude gives us humility and confidence for the future.
exp.56:7:
Here the psalmist speaks to himself and rouses his glory, that is, his soul or inner self, to praise God. He also calls on the psaltery and the harp, stringed instruments with which songs were sung. "I myself will awake early" means he will rise early, perhaps to begin the day with praise, or even waking the dawn with his music.

The title of the psalm attributes it to David, at the time he fled from Saul into the cave. That is why he speaks of nets and pits: he felt hunted and discouraged. Even so, his heart is steady and he resolves to sing. Commentators differ on whether "my glory" refers to the soul or to the tongue, but the idea is similar.

For today: when you feel weary or under pressure, do not wait for circumstances to change before praising God. Begin the day with a song, a prayer, or words of thanks, and remember that his mercy is great.
exp.11:3:
This verse shows the attitude of proud people who believe their words are their best weapon. They say: "With our tongue we will prevail; our lips are our own, so no one can command us." The phrase "we will prevail" means they will get their way and come out on top. The question "who is lord over us?" asks: "Who is our master, or who can give us orders?"

David cries out to God because there are almost no faithful people left around him. The speakers here are the liars and flatterers, who use pretty, deceptive words to take advantage of the poor. God answers that he will rise up to defend the oppressed, and that his words, unlike theirs, are pure and trustworthy.

For today: be careful with what you say, and do not use words to manipulate or crush others. Speak with truth, and trust that God hears those who suffer from unjust words.
exp.149:1:
This verse invites us to praise God for two reasons: what He has done and who He is. "Mighty acts" refers to His powerful works, His great and wonderful deeds. The phrase "according to his excellent greatness" means His abundant greatness, so immense that it cannot be measured.

The psalm does not say who wrote it; tradition does not point to a certain author. It is the last of the Psalms and closes the book with a great song of praise. God's people are called to praise Him in the sanctuary, with instruments and with everything they have. Here the reason is given: God deserves praise for His acts and for His character.

Today we can pause and remember something concrete that God has done in our lives. Then we can thank Him aloud, and also acknowledge who He is, great and worthy of trust, even when we do not understand everything.
exp.106:34:
This verse says that God can change a dry, empty place into a place full of water and life. The "standing waters" are pools or lakes, and the "springs" are sources where water rises up out of the ground. What seemed dead and hopeless becomes fruitful.

The psalmist speaks in a song of thanksgiving to God. Earlier he showed that God can also dry up the land when its people live in wickedness. Now he shows the other side: God gives life and, according to the verses that follow, helps the hungry settle, sow, and harvest. It is a psalm that praises his mercy.

For today: if you are going through a dry season, whether at work, in your family, or in your faith, do not lose hope. Pray, take the simple steps you can, and trust that God knows how to renew what seems lost.
exp.113:7:
This verse says that God turned a hard rock into a pool of water, and a stone into a spring. "Rock" and "stone" refer to firm, dry ground. The word "turned" means "changed" or "made into." In other words, from what is driest and hardest, God made water flow for people to drink.

The psalmist sings about Israel leaving Egypt. The verses before this one speak of mountains that leap and of the earth that trembles before the Lord. This last verse recalls that God gave water to his people in the desert (Exodus 17 and Numbers 20). We do not know who wrote this psalm; it is a song of praise from the people.

For today: when your situation feels hard and dry, remember that God can bring life where it seems impossible. Trust in Him, ask Him for help simply, and thank Him for the times He has already sustained you.
exp.118:46:
It says that the psalmist will find joy and delight in God's commandments, and that he already loves them. "I will delight myself" is an older way of saying "I will take pleasure in" or "I will be glad." The "commandments" are the instructions God gave to his people.

The one speaking is the author of the psalm, a believer whose name we do not know. This whole psalm praises God's word. Earlier he said that he walks in freedom and that he will speak boldly before kings. Here he gives the reason: he does not obey out of obligation, but because he loves what God says. His love comes first, and from it his joy grows.

For today: instead of seeing the Bible as a burden, ask God to teach you to take delight in it. Read a short passage each day, slowly, and ask yourself: "What does this show me about God?" Over time, your affection for his word can grow.
exp.90:7:
The passage says that whoever trusts in God will witness what happens to the wicked. "Wicked" refers to people who live without respect for God. "Reward" here means the payment or just consequence of their actions. Seeing it "with your eyes" suggests the believer watches from a place of safety.

This psalm does not say who wrote it. In this part, someone speaks to a person who trusts in God, and later another voice seems to answer. The verses before speak of dangers, plagues, and death all around, but with the promise that God protects whoever takes refuge in Him. The psalm aims to bring encouragement and confidence in times of danger.

For today: when you see injustice or danger around you, do not be consumed with worry or seek revenge. Rest in God, who is just and takes care of His own.
exp.29:9:
This verse is a short and sincere prayer. The psalmist asks God for three things: that he hear him, that he have mercy (that is, compassion and kindness that he does not deserve), and that he be his helper, the one who comes to his aid in his need.

The speaker is David, according to the title of the psalm. He is recalling a moment of serious danger, perhaps an illness, when he felt he was close to death. That is why he asks whether the dust could praise God. With this he expresses that he wants to live in order to keep giving thanks. The following verses show that God answered and turned his weeping into dancing. Scholars debate which exact situation he has in mind.

For today: when you feel without strength, do not wait until you have the perfect words. Pray simply, as David did: "Lord, hear me, have mercy on me, and help me." God invites you to speak to him this way.
exp.88:32:
God says that, even when he corrects his children, he will not stop loving them or stop keeping his word. "Lovingkindness" is his faithful and steadfast love. "Nor suffer my faithfulness to fail" means that he will not be unfaithful or fail to do what he promised. "Will I not utterly take from him" refers to the descendant of David mentioned earlier.

Here God speaks in a psalm that recalls the covenant with David. Before this, he warns that if David's descendants rebel, he will discipline them with the rod and with stripes, that is, with corrective punishment. But that discipline does not cancel his promise. There are different ways of understanding this passage, but many Christians see in it a foreshadowing of Christ, the descendant of David.

For today: when you fail, or feel that God is correcting you, do not conclude that he has abandoned you. Return to him with humility, trusting that his love and his faithfulness remain firm.
exp.104:35:
It says that God struck down all the firstborn of Egypt, that is, the first sons of each family. The phrase "the chief of all their strength" means that they were like the first fruits of that nation's vigor and future. "Struck" here means that this last plague was added to the earlier ones, and it was harsher than they were.

The psalmist recounts, in a spirit of praise, how God acted to free Israel from slavery. This psalm recalls the plagues of Egypt and the exodus, and shows that God kept the promise he made to Abraham. After this plague, Egypt let the people go, as the following verses say.

For today: this passage reminds us that God is faithful to his promises and that he sees oppression. When you feel trapped, trust that God still cares for his own. Remembering what he has done before can strengthen your faith and lead you to give him thanks.
exp.77:37:
This verse says that God is compassionate. Although his people deserved punishment, he forgave their sin and did not destroy them. Many times he held back his anger and did not let all of his wrath break loose. The word "forgave" in the verse is the key word here: it means to pardon guilt, and "iniquity" is the sin or guilt that was pardoned. Many times he turned his anger away, meaning that again and again he restrained his anger.

The psalmist, Asaph, reviews the history of Israel in the wilderness. Shortly before this, he says that the people flattered God with their words, but their hearts were not sincere or faithful to the covenant. Then he recalls that God knew we are frail, like a passing breath. Thus the psalm contrasts human unfaithfulness with the patience of God.

For today: do not use God's patience as an excuse to stay the same. Instead, let his mercy lead you to sincere honesty. Today, humbly confess one specific fault, and ask him that your heart and your words may go together.
exp.40:5:
He says that an enemy would come to visit the sick man, but he spoke with falsehood. Inside, he kept gathering wickedness, like someone storing up a pile of bad things in his heart. When he went out, he would go and tell outside what he had seen.

(These comments are dropped in favor of the verse's own wording: the sentences above are rewritten to match "to see me" and "he telleth it.")

The one speaking is David, according to the title of the psalm, although some scholars doubt the exact circumstances. He is sick and weak, and he acknowledges his sin before God. Meanwhile, those around him pretend to be concerned, but in reality they expect his death and wish that his name would disappear. The verses that follow show that they were murmuring against him.

For today: let us be sincere when we visit someone who is sick or suffering, and be careful not to repeat their troubles as gossip. If someone has betrayed you in this way, bring your pain honestly to God, as David did.
exp.110:3:
This verse says that God has made his wonderful deeds worth remembering. The words in the original that sound like "memorable" mean that they can be recalled. The word that means "gracious" in the original refers to someone who is kind and patient, and the word for "compassionate" describes one who feels for the person who suffers. God acts not only with power, but also with tenderness.

The psalm does not say who wrote it. The one speaking is a psalmist who praises God before the community of the upright. The verses that follow speak of provision for those who fear him and of the inheritance given to his people, so he probably has in mind what God did for Israel. Some think it refers to festivals such as Passover, but the text does not make this clear.

For today: write down, or count out loud, the times God helped you. Remembering his goodness strengthens your trust when difficult days come.
exp.58:15:
Whatever happens, David says he will sing with gratitude. "But" means "but," "I will sing" means "I will praise," and "refuge" is protection. He promises to praise God's strength and mercy in the morning, because God has been his shelter when he was in distress.

The speaker is David. The psalm's title places it at the time when Saul sent men to watch his house in order to kill him (1 Samuel 19). The enemies are compared to dogs that roam the city at night, searching for prey. Faced with that threat, David chooses to trust in God and not in his own strength. Some scholars think the psalm was later used in a broader way, but the title points to that moment.

Today we can begin the day by remembering how God has sustained us before. Before checking our phones or our worries, take a moment to give thanks aloud or with a song. That habit reminds us that God is still our refuge, even when the problem has not yet been resolved.
exp.84:7:
The psalmist says he is ready to listen closely to what the LORD God is going to say. And what God will speak is peace for his people and his saints, that is, those who belong to him and are faithful to him. The final warning is that they must not turn back to foolishness, living in a foolish way and turning away from God. The word translated as "salvation" in the nearby verses means deliverance or rescue.

The one speaking is a psalmist who prays on behalf of the whole people. He asks God to restore them and to show them his mercy, and then he falls silent to hear the answer. Many scholars think it reflects a time after a national hardship, but the psalm does not specify this, and it is interpreted in several ways.

For today: after praying, take a moment to be quiet and listen to God by reading his Word. His peace is not an excuse to return to foolishness, but a call to walk close to him.
exp.103:3:
God makes his angels spirits, that is, messengers who have no body, and his ministers, that is, his servants, like blazing fire. The Hebrew phrase can also be understood this way: "He makes the winds his messengers and fire his servants." Scholars have read it in both ways.

The one speaking is the psalmist, who does not name himself, and who praises God as Creator. Earlier he speaks of light, the heavens, the clouds and the wind; afterward, of the earth and the waters. Everything that exists, visible or invisible, obeys God. Hebrews 1:7 quotes this verse when speaking of the angels.

For today: if the whole universe serves God, you can trust that he also governs your life. Today, offer him your worries in prayer and ask him for a willing heart to serve him with joy, as his messengers do.
exp.139:9:
It says that burning coals will fall on the psalmist's enemies, and that God himself will cast them into the fire and into deep pits from which they will not be able to rise. The "wicked" are those who do evil, and the one who uses his tongue to do harm is the "slanderer." These are strong images of judgment, not a literal description.

The psalm is attributed to David, according to its title, and he is surrounded by violent people who slander him and set traps for him. He does not take revenge on his own. He asks God to do justice, and he trusts that God defends the afflicted and the poor, as the following verses say. Some scholars see here a poetic prayer, not a command to punish others.

For today: when someone wrongs you, do not hold on to resentment or seek revenge. Hand the matter over to God honestly, even with your pain and anger, and trust that He is just. Jesus also taught us to pray for those who do us harm.
exp.76:18:
It says that God opened a way through the middle of the sea, and that his paths passed through deep waters, yet no one could see his traces. In other words, God acted with power, but the way he worked remained beyond human reach.

The psalmist, Asaph according to the title, speaks in a moment of distress. He wonders whether God has forgotten him, and then he recalls the exodus. Many understand this to refer to the crossing of the Red Sea, although the text does not name it. The following verse shows that God led his people through Moses and Aaron.

For today: there are times when we cannot see God's footprints or understand what he is doing. Even so, you can remember how he has helped you before and trust that he is still guiding you, even when the path leads through waters that frighten you.
exp.62:6:
This verse says that David recognizes that God has been his help in difficult moments. Because of this, trusting in God, he says he will rejoice and sing in the shadow of your wings, an image of protection and care, like a bird that covers its young. "Help" here means aid in time of need. "Rejoice" means to be filled with joy.

The psalm bears the heading that David wrote it in the wilderness of Judah. Many think it was when he was fleeing from Saul, though others connect it with Absalom's rebellion; this cannot be known for certain. In any case, David was in danger and far from the temple, yet he remembers God in the night and finds in Him his rest and his joy.

You can do the same today: before going to sleep, remember how God helped you in the past. Give thanks for that, and let those memories give you confidence and joy to face your present problems.
exp.68:35:
It says that the children and descendants of those who serve God will receive the land as an inheritance. It also says that those who love God's name will live in it. "Seed" means offspring, and "inherit" means to receive something as one's own property from another.

David speaks here, according to the title of the psalm. He moves from an anguished cry to a hopeful song of praise. Earlier he asked for help amid mockery and suffering. Now he trusts that God will care for Zion and restore Judah. This verse closes the psalm with a promise to the faithful people: God will give them a secure and lasting home.

For today: loving God's name means living close to Him, even in hard times. You can trust that God does not forget His people or their children. Today, pray for your family and teach them by your example to trust in Him.
exp.118:13:
What it says: The psalmist affirms that he has rejoiced in following what God has declared, and that this joy is worth more than any treasure. "Testimonies" refers to the teachings and reminders that God gave about himself and his will. "Way" speaks of a manner of living.

Context: Psalm 119 is a long poem in honor of God's Word. No one knows with certainty who wrote it; tradition usually thinks of David, but the text does not say so. The one speaking is a believer who loves God's law. In the nearby verses he blesses God, asks to be taught, and recounts the Lord's judgments with his lips. His joy comes from knowing God, not merely from keeping rules.

For today: Spend a few minutes reading the Bible unhurriedly, asking God to teach you. Then write down something from what you read that brings you joy, and think about how to live it out that day. In this way you will learn to delight in his Word as a true treasure.
exp.102:0:
The explanation says that David speaks to himself and encourages himself to praise God with his whole being. To "bless" means to speak well of God, to thank him and to acknowledge his goodness. "My soul" refers to his entire person, and the inner depths, such as his feelings, are what is meant by the heart within him. The name of God that is blessed refers to everything God is.

The one speaking is David, according to the heading of the psalm. The text does not say when he wrote it. What follows shows his reason: God forgives faults and heals sickness, and so David does not want to forget his benefits.

For today: when you feel discouraged or distracted, do not wait until you feel like praying. Like David, talk to yourself and make a list of specific things you can thank God for today, with all your heart.
exp.73:3:
The enemies of God roared, shouting like wild beasts, in the middle of the places where his people gathered to worship him. There, right in those places, they set up their banners, that is, their flags or emblems, as a sign that they had won. The word "congregations" in the verse refers to places of gathering for worship, not necessarily to the synagogues of New Testament times.

The one speaking is the psalmist Asaph, or someone from his group, in a lament over the destruction of the sanctuary. Many think of the invasion of Babylon, but this is not certain. He asks God to remember his people and to act.

Today, when something sacred to you seems trampled, do not hide your pain. Bring it to God honestly, trusting that he does not forget his own.
exp.36:36:
Look closely at the person of integrity, the one who lives with uprightness and sincerity, and at the righteous. Their "end" is their outcome, how their story finishes. And that outcome is "peace." The word "integrity" describes someone whole, without duplicity.

It is a psalm of David, written from a life already well acquainted with hardship. He writes to encourage those who grow anxious when they see the wicked prospering. Earlier he recalls a wicked man who seemed as strong as a green tree, yet he passed away and was gone. Then he contrasts the two: the end of the wicked is ruin, while God upholds the righteous in distress. Some understand this peace as well-being in this life; others understand it also as hope beyond this life.

Today, when you are troubled that others seem to do well without honoring God, do not compare yourself to them. Remain honest and faithful today, and entrust your end to God, who gives true peace.
exp.138:14:
It says that nothing of my body was hidden from God, even though I was formed in secret. "Woven together" means joined or shaped with care, like a well-made fabric. The phrase "the lowest parts of the earth" is a poetic image of the hidden place where a life begins. Many think it refers to the mother's womb, but not everyone interprets it the same way.

The speaker is the psalmist, who according to the heading is David. He is praising God because God knows him completely, from before he was born. The nearby verses speak of God's wonderful works and his precious thoughts toward him.

For today: your life is not an accident or something without value before God. When you feel insignificant, remember that God knew you and cared for you from the beginning. And treat others with that same respect.
exp.94:10:
It says that God, angered by the rebellion of his people, made a solemn oath that that generation would not enter his "rest." "Therefore" means "for this reason." "Wrath" is a very strong anger, and "sware" means he made a firm promise. The "rest" was the promised land, with its peace and security.

Here God himself speaks, and the psalmist recalls what happened in the wilderness (Meribah and Massah, Exodus 17 and Numbers 14). The Israelites doubted God even though they had seen his works, and for that reason they did not enter the land. The psalm warns those who sing it: "Today if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts." The New Testament takes up this passage in Hebrews 3 and 4.

Today, let us not delay obedience or harden our hearts. If God speaks to us through his Word, let us respond with trust and humility, and so enjoy the rest that he offers.
exp.34:23:
Here the psalmist asks God to judge him according to his righteousness, that is, with perfect uprightness and without favoritism. The name of God is the Lord, and he asks that his enemies have no cause to mock him or celebrate his fall.

The psalm is spoken by David, according to its heading. He is surrounded by people who attack him without reason and who rejoice in his troubles. For this reason he cries out to God to see what is happening, not to remain silent, and to defend his cause. He does not ask to be declared perfect, but that God, who knows all things, would do justice.

For today: when you are treated unjustly, you do not have to take revenge or defend yourself at all costs. You can bring the matter to God honestly, ask him to examine your heart, and trust that his judgment is just and true.
exp.54:5:
Here the psalmist wishes he had wings like a dove so that he could fly far away and find rest. The old phrase "Oh that I had" is an older way of saying "I wish I had." The dove stands for something gentle and free, and he longs to escape from what weighs him down.

The psalm is attributed to David, and its heading presents it as a prayer in a time of distress. He speaks of fear, terror, and the betrayal of someone close to him (vv. 12-14). Many connect it with the rebellion of Absalom, but the text does not state this with certainty. What is clear is that he writes out of deep pain.

For today: wanting to escape when we are worn out is human, and it is not a lack of faith. But David does not stop at the wish; in the end he says, "Cast thy burden upon the LORD, and he shall sustain thee" (v. 22). Today you can bring your weariness honestly to God, and also seek healthy rest and the help of trusted people.
exp.63:2:
They say the wicked sharpen their tongue as a knife is sharpened, and use a bitter word as an arrow, that is, a harsh and cruel remark. The image is of words that truly wound. "Sharpen" is the word that matches "whet" in the verse, and "arrow" is what the bitter words are compared to. It is a picture of words that wound for real.

David prays to God because enemies surround him, gathering in secret to do harm. The following verses explain that they shoot their words in hiding at an upright person, and feel safe thinking no one sees them. David does not take revenge: he brings his complaint to God and asks for protection.

For today: if someone has hurt you with their words, or if you have hurt others, remember that the tongue can do great damage. Before you speak, ask yourself whether your words heal or wound. And if you have been hurt, bring it before God in prayer, trusting that he sees everything.
exp.138:13:
The psalmist says he wants to praise God because his works are "fearful," meaning awe-inspiring and worthy of respect, and also "marvelous." He himself is amazed at how God made him. The phrase "my soul knows it well" means he knows it very well, deep down within his being.

The speaker is David, according to the title of the psalm. He has just said that God knows him completely, that even the darkness cannot hide him from God. Then he recalls that God formed him in his mother's womb. His praise springs from knowing himself to be known and cared for since before he was born.

Today you can thank God for how you were made, even with your limits. When you feel of little worth, repeat this truth: God formed you with care and knows you completely.
exp.77:18:
This verse tells us that the Israelites spoke against God with a question full of doubt: "Can God furnish a table in the wilderness?" To "furnish a table" means to give them food, to prepare a feast. They were not asking in faith but in distrust, as if putting God to the test.

The one speaking is the psalmist Asaph, who reviews the history of Israel. He recalls that the people had seen God divide the sea and bring water out of the rock. Even so, in the wilderness they doubted that he could give them bread and meat. That is why the psalm says they tested God and that he was angered.

For today: when we pass through a time of scarcity or uncertainty, let us remember what God has already done for us. Instead of demanding from him or doubting his care, we can ask him with trust and humility.
exp.68:16:
This verse is a prayer. The psalmist asks God not to hide his face, that is, not to turn away or ignore him. He calls himself God's servant and explains why he cries out: he is in trouble, deeply pressed down by pain. So he pleads for God to hear him quickly, asking for a prompt answer.

The psalm is traditionally attributed to David, though some scholars think another voice may have written or adapted it. He feels like someone sinking in deep waters and a pit. He is surrounded by enemies who humiliate and accuse him. In the middle of that pressure, he does not rely on his own strength but on God's mercy.

For today: when you are overwhelmed, you do not have to pretend to be strong. You can speak to God honestly, tell him your distress, and ask for help simply, trusting that his mercy is good and that he hears you.
exp.77:19:
It says that God struck the rock and waters came out like streams that flowed with force. But the people, instead of giving thanks, asked whether God could also give them bread and meat. The word for "prepare" in the original is dropped here, since your reader's verse does not use it. The word for "rock" is also dropped, since the verse already says "rock." The word for water flowing in waves is likewise left out, because the verse already describes the streams overflowing.

The psalmist, Asaph, is recalling the history of Israel in the wilderness. He tells how the people doubted God even though they had already seen miracles. These words are what they said, and the psalmist presents them as a complaint full of unbelief. That is why the following verse says God became angry, because they had not believed or trusted in his salvation.

For today: when you face a new need, remember what God has already done for you. Instead of doubting his power, give thanks for his past help and trust that he can care for you again.
exp.91:12:
It says that the righteous are like trees planted in the house of God, that is, in the place where he is worshiped. The courts of the temple are the places where people gather to worship, and to flourish means to grow, to be full of life, and to bear fruit.

This psalm is a song for the Sabbath day. The one speaking is a psalmist who praises God for his faithfulness. The text does not say with certainty who wrote it. In the nearby verses it compares the fall of the wicked with the steady life of the righteous, who grow like the palm and the cedar, strong and long-lasting trees. The following verses add that this life keeps bearing fruit even in old age.

For today: seek to put down roots in a community of faith. Attending faithfully, praying, and serving alongside others helps you grow spiritually, even in difficult times, and to bear fruit throughout your whole life.
exp.24:10:
David asks God here to forgive his sin. He gives a surprising reason: he does not say "because I deserve it," but "for your name's sake," that is, because of who God is, because of his faithful and merciful character. He admits that his sin is great. The phrase "you will also forgive" can be understood as a request: "please, forgive."

This is a psalm of David, written as a prayer. Earlier it speaks of God guiding the humble and of his paths being mercy and truth. Afterward it speaks of those who fear him. Between those two ideas, David admits that he needs that forgiveness. Scholars do not agree on when in his life he wrote it.

For today: when you feel your failure is too great, do not hide the truth or lean on your own merits. Come before God honestly, trusting in his goodness, which is greater than your sin.
exp.88:42:
He says that God made the king's sword lose its edge, meaning that God left it without strength. The king was left without support at the most difficult moment.

This psalm is written by Ethan the Ezrahite, according to its heading. First it recalls God's promise to David of an enduring kingdom. Then, from verse 38 on, it complains because it seems that God has rejected his anointed and allowed his enemies to triumph. It is not known with certainty which specific defeat is meant. It is a sincere and painful prayer that calls God to account.

For today: when you feel your strength failing and God seems distant, you can speak to him with honesty, as the psalmist does. Bringing him your complaint and reminding him of his promises is an act of faith, not a lack of faith.
exp.68:30:
It says that praise and song please God more than a costly sacrifice. "Ox" and "young bull" were large animals offered in sacrifice. The phrase "that has horns and hoofs" describes a fully grown young bull, with well-formed horns and hooves, meaning an animal in good condition and of real value. The phrase "shall please the Lord" means that God will be pleased by it.

The psalm is spoken by David, according to its heading. He is suffering, surrounded by enemies and mockery, and he trusts that God will rescue him. He promises to thank God with songs. He does not reject the sacrifices the law commanded, but shows that God looks at the grateful heart, not only at the outward ritual.

For today: do not let your faith shrink to simply keeping customs. Even in a difficult moment, take a few minutes to thank God in your own words or with a simple song. He values a sincere heart.
exp.88:11:
It says God created the north and the south, that is, the whole earth from one end to the other. The mountains Tabor and Hermon, one to the west and the other to the north of the Jordan, appear as if they sang with joy over God's name. This is poetic language: all of creation praises its Creator.

This psalm is written by Ethan the Ezrahite. First it celebrates God's power over the sea, over Rahab (a monster that symbolizes chaos or pride) and over enemies. Then it recalls God's promise to David. Praising the Creator prepares the heart to trust his promises, even in difficult times.

Today, when you see a beautiful landscape, let it lead you to give thanks. If God holds up mountains and continents, he can also care for your life and fulfill what he has promised.
exp.142:10:
This verse is a prayer. The psalmist asks God to give him new life and to bring him out of his distress. The word "quicken" means to give life or to renew strength. He asks this "for thy name's sake," that is, for who God is and for his good reputation, and "for thy righteousness' sake," that is, because God is faithful and upright.

The heading attributes this psalm to David, although some scholars debate how such headings were used. The speaker is pressed by enemies and feels worn out and without a way out. So he takes refuge in God, asks for guidance to do his will, and presents himself as God's servant.

For today: when you feel overwhelmed by distress, do not rest your prayer on your own merits, but on the character of God. Say to him simply: "Lord, you are faithful and just; renew my strength and guide me." And ask him also to teach you to obey him in the middle of the trial.
exp.105:23:
This verse says that the people of Israel despised the land God had promised them. The word "yea" is an older way of saying "indeed" or "yes," and "pleasant land" refers to a land that is good, beautiful, and valuable. The reason was that they did not believe God's word, that is, they did not trust what he had promised.

The psalmist, whose name is not given, recalls in a prayer of confession the failures of Israel. He refers to the time when the spies returned from Canaan and the people were afraid to go in (Numbers 13–14). God had done miracles in Egypt and at the Red Sea, but even so they doubted. Moses interceded for them.

For today: when God gives you a promise and the path looks difficult, do not stare only at the obstacles. Remember what God has already done for you and trust his word, even when you are afraid. Taking a small step of faith is better than staying behind complaining.
exp.88:43:
This verse says that God brought to an end the brightness of the king, that is, his glory and splendor, and that his throne was thrown down to the ground.

The phrase "brought to an end" means "stopped" or "finished." "Thrown to the ground" means that his power was destroyed.

The one speaking is Ethan the Ezrahite, according to the title of the psalm. First he recalls God's promise to David of a lasting throne. Then he complains because it seems that God broke it: the king descended from David suffers defeat and shame. Scholars do not agree on the exact moment in history when this happened.

There are times when life seems to contradict God's promises. This psalm teaches us not to remain silent, but to bring our pain and our questions honestly before God, without ceasing to trust in his faithfulness.
exp.17:17:
They attacked him just when he was at his lowest point, beaten down and weak. But God was his support, that is, something firm to hold onto so that he would not fall. The word "prevented" in the verse means they came against him, and "calamity" refers to a time of pain, ruin, or distress.

David speaks here, according to the title of the psalm, after the Lord delivered him from his enemies and from Saul. It is a song of thanksgiving. It tells how God drew him out of "many waters," an image of danger, and brought him into a wide and safe place.

For today: when everything seems to be falling apart and problems arrive all at once, you do not have to hold on alone. Before acting out of fear, speak honestly with God and lean on Him. Afterward, remember and give thanks for how He has sustained you, as David did.
exp.148:8:
It says that God will carry out against the nations the judgment that has already been decreed, and that this act will be an honor for all his saints, that is, his faithful people. "Execute" means to carry out a sentence. The "judgment written" may refer to what God has already declared in his word. The psalm ends with "Praise ye the Lord," which means "praise the Lord."

The author is unknown. It is a psalm of praise for Israel, celebrating God as king and judge. The verses before it use images of war. Some see it as a historical victory of Israel; others see it as a hope in God's final justice. Many Christians caution that it does not justify personal violence.

For today: instead of taking revenge, trust that God will do justice in his time. Praise him while you wait, and let that hope help you forgive and do good.
exp.76:13:
This verse says that God is the one who works wonders, that is, deeds that amaze us and that only he can do. It also says that he showed his strength before the peoples.

The one speaking is the psalmist, traditionally called Asaph, although the text gives no further details. He is distressed and wonders whether God has forgotten him. To encourage himself, he decides to remember what God did before. That is why he soon mentions the redemption of Israel, when God brought out his people and opened the sea, although the psalm does not name the Exodus in this verse.

Today, when you feel discouraged, call to mind what God has already done in your life and in the history of his people. Write down those occasions, thank him for them, and tell them to others. Remembering his past faithfulness strengthens hope for the present.
exp.30:6:
It says the psalmist will be filled with joy and gladness because of God's mercy, that is, his faithful and compassionate love. The reason is that God was not indifferent: "you have seen my affliction" means that he looked upon his suffering, and "you have known my soul in adversities" means that he stood with him and understood him in his deepest pain. The word "rejoice" here is an older way of saying "be glad."

David speaks here, according to the title of the psalm, although some scholars debate the exact circumstances. It comes from trusting in God, rejecting empty idols, and placing his life in the Lord's hands. His joy is born of a deliverance he has already experienced, although in the verses that follow he again asks for help in his distress.

Today, when you suffer, remember that God sees you and knows you. Before everything is resolved, you can thank him once more for his past companionship and faithfulness.
exp.104:17:
It says that Joseph had fetters put on his feet and that his body was bound with iron. Fetters are rings of metal placed on the ankles so that the prisoner could not walk or escape. The phrase about his person means his own self, his body, and the expression about being placed in iron suggests that they bound him in chains. Some translators understand that the iron reached his neck, but the Hebrew allows several readings.

It is a psalm of praise that recalls God's works with Israel. The psalmist reviews the story of Joseph, sold by his brothers and imprisoned in Egypt. He tells it to show that God cared for his people even in suffering, for what seemed to be ruin was preparing the salvation of Jacob's family in a time of famine.

For today: when you go through an unjust or painful season, remember that God has not forgotten you. He remains faithful, and you can wait with confidence, because He can work in your process.
exp.101:27:
They say that the descendants of those who serve God will dwell securely, and that their children and grandchildren will be established and firm in his presence. Their dwelling in that verse means they will live with stability, as in a home. The word for descendants is "seed," and the phrase "established" means made firm and secure.

The psalm is a prayer of someone in affliction, whose author is not named. The writer feels weak and feels life fading away. But the writer looks to God, who does not change, while the heavens and the earth wear out like old clothing. Some think the psalm speaks from the time of the exile, but this is not certain. The verse closes the psalm with hope: since God endures, his people will also have a future.

Today, you can rest in the knowledge that your family and your future do not depend on what passes away. Pray for your children and for those who come after you, and live faithfully, trusting in the God who does not change.
exp.54:2:
This verse gives the reason David cries out to God. He does so because of the voice of the enemy, that is, their threatening words, and because of the oppression of the wicked, the evildoer who crushes him. The phrase "they cast iniquity upon me" means they load wickedness onto him, or accuse and attack him unjustly. The phrase "in wrath they hate me" means they threaten him with violent anger.

David speaks here, according to the title of the psalm, and he is distressed. The verses that follow speak of fear and terror of death. We do not know with certainty at what point in his life he wrote it; some connect it with the betrayal of someone close to him, but that is interpreted in various ways.

For today: when you feel threatened or pressured by hurtful words, you do not need to pretend you are calm. You can tell God with complete honesty what hurts you and what you fear, as David did, trusting that he listens.
exp.37:18:
It says that the psalmist's enemies are still alive, full of energy, and that more and more of those who hate him without reason are gathering. The phrase "they have multiplied" refers to their growing numbers. "Without cause" means that he gave them no reason to hate him.

The psalm is attributed to David, and it is a prayer from someone who is sick, weary, and aware of his sin. He feels close to falling, while his adversaries seem to be doing well. Even so, he does not hide his wrongdoing: he confesses it. The verses that follow show that some repay him evil for the good he does. The exact time when he wrote it is unknown, and scholars place it at different points.

When you feel weak and surrounded by unfair criticism, do as the psalmist did: be honest with God about your own failings, but do not let opposition make you doubt that He hears you. Bring everything to Him in prayer and ask Him not to stay far from you.
exp.42:4:
The psalmist speaks to himself. He asks, "Why are you cast down, my soul? Why are you disquieted within me?" To be cast down means to feel fallen and without strength, and to be disquieted means to be restless and troubled. Then he encourages himself: "hope in God," because he will yet praise Him, who is the health of his countenance and his God. God is his help and his God.

The one speaking is a believer who is far from the temple and feels oppressed by unjust people. For that reason he had asked that God send His light and His truth to guide him back into His presence. This verse is a refrain that is repeated in Psalms 42 and 43. Many believe that both psalms originally formed one single psalm, although this is not certain.

When you feel discouraged, do not ignore what you feel, but speak to your heart with truth. Remind yourself who God is, pray with sincerity, and wait on Him, even though you do not yet see the answer.
exp.17:38:
It says that God gave David strength, like someone tying a belt around him, to fight in battle. The explanation of the first quoted word, which means that he was surrounded or equipped with power, is left out because it refers to wording the reader does not see. The second quoted phrase means that God brought down, subdued, or put under control his enemies, so that they ended up beneath David's feet.

David, the king of Israel, is the speaker. This psalm is a song of thanksgiving, because the LORD delivered him from his enemies and from Saul, according to the title of the psalm. David does not credit the victory to himself, but to God. The verses before and after describe the battle with poetic and forceful language, typical of warfare in that era.

For today: when you face a difficult struggle, whether at work, in the family, or within yourself, ask God for strength before relying only on your own. And when you come through it, do not forget to thank Him.
exp.25:11:
It says that the psalmist feels secure on the right path. The phrase "My foot standeth in an even place" means that he stands on firm, level ground, that is, in what is upright and just. For that reason he promises to bless the Lord in the congregations, that is, the gatherings of the people, where worship is shared together. The Lord is the name of God.

The psalm is traditionally attributed to David, according to its heading, although some scholars debate its authorship. It grows out of a plea for God to defend him from corrupt people who accept bribes. He declares that he is determined to live with integrity and asks God for redemption and mercy. This verse closes the psalm with confidence and gratitude.

Today we can ask God for help to live honestly in our everyday lives, even when others cheat. Then, in church or in a faith group, we can give thanks publicly for being sustained. An upright life and praise go hand in hand.
exp.88:21:
It says that no enemy will be able to dominate or subdue King David, and that no wicked man will succeed in destroying him. The words about exacting and afflicting in the verse are the ones explained here: to exact upon someone means to subdue or rule over them, and to afflict means to break or crush them.

Here God speaks, as recalled by the psalmist Ethan the Ezrahite, remembering the promise he made to David. God chose him, anointed him, and promised to sustain him with his hand. This is part of the covenant with David, which Christians see fulfilled finally in Jesus, a descendant of David. The psalm then shows tension, because the people see that this promise seems not to be fulfilled.

For today: when you feel threatened or overwhelmed, remember that God sustains those he calls and is faithful to his word. Trust him, even when you do not yet see the answer, and ask him for strength to keep doing what is right.
exp.124:1:
It says that Jerusalem is surrounded by mountains, and that in the same way God surrounds his people, from now on and forever. The word "Lord" is the name of God. The image speaks of constant protection, which has no expiration date.

This psalm is a song of ascents, that is, one of the songs connected with the journeys up to Jerusalem. No one knows for certain who wrote it. The one singing speaks of the security of those who trust in God. Jerusalem is set among hills and valleys, and that image helped the people understand God's care, in the midst of pressure from unjust people.

For today: when you feel fear or instability, remember that your security does not depend on everything being calm, but on God being present all around you. Trust him today, and give him thanks for his care.
exp.136:1:
The explanation says that the Israelites exiled in the middle of Babylon hung their harps on the willows. Harps were instruments for singing and praising God. By leaving them hanging, they express that they had no heart for music. Some think the "willows" were poplars or trees that grow beside water; scholars do not fully agree.

The speaker is the people of Judah, carried captive to Babylon after the destruction of Jerusalem. They remembered Zion with pain. Their captors asked them for joyful songs as entertainment, and they felt that singing to the LORD in that place and under those circumstances was impossible.

Today, when you are going through grief or a trial, do not force yourself to pretend to be joyful. God accepts your silence and your tears. Bring your pain to him honestly, and let other believers accompany you until the song returns.
exp.63:0:
The chief Musician is the director of singing in worship, and the psalm is attributed to David. Then comes the cry: "Hear my voice, O God, in my prayer." He asks God to pay attention to his plea. "Preserve my life from fear of the enemy" means he asks for protection from the terror his adversary causes him.

The one speaking is David, or so the title indicates. It is not known for certain at what point in his life he wrote it. The verses that follow show that he is surrounded by people who plot in secret and wound with words, like knives and arrows. That is why he prays with urgency.

For today: when fear or unjust criticism troubles you, do not keep the anguish to yourself. Speak to God honestly, aloud if you can, and ask him to watch over your life and your heart.
exp.29:2:
Here David says that God brought him up from the "grave," which is the place of the dead (in Hebrew, Sheol). "You brought up my soul" means that he rescued him from death, or from something so serious that it seemed like the end. "Pit" is the hole in the ground where the dead are buried. God gave him life again.

David speaks in a song of thanksgiving. The title says it was sung at the dedication of the House, though we do not know for certain which one is meant, and scholars interpret it in several ways. Earlier he had cried out to God during an illness or serious danger, and God healed him. That is why he now praises God.

For today: when God brings you out of a hard trial, do not forget it. Take a moment to thank him aloud or in writing, and tell someone else what he did for you.
exp.43:17:
It says that the heart of the people was not turned back, meaning they did not abandon God inwardly. Nor had their steps, that is their way of living, strayed from the path of God.

The one speaking is the people of Israel, or their collective voice, in a moment of defeat and humiliation before their enemies. They complain because they feel they have been faithful and yet they suffer. It is not easy to know with certainty which battle the psalm refers to; scholars have interpreted it in several ways. What is clear is their pain and their confusion before God.

For today: when you suffer without understanding why, do not move away from God. You can be honest with Him, tell Him your pain, and keep walking beside Him, trusting that He hears you even in the darkness.
exp.39:3:
He says that happy and blessed is the one who puts his trust in the Lord, that is, in God. That person does not look up to the proud, meaning those who trust in themselves, nor to those who turn aside to falsehood, following what is untrue. The word "blessed" means truly happy and fortunate.

David is the speaker, according to the heading of the psalm. He has just given thanks to God because he was lifted out of a deep pit, an image of profound distress, and was given firm footing and a new song. After being rescued, he concludes that true happiness lies in trusting God and not in what the proud have to offer.

Today we might ask ourselves whom we look to for a sense of security: success, appearances, influential people? This week we can choose to bring a specific worry to God in prayer, and not admire or imitate those who succeed through deceit.
exp.104:40:
It says that God opened a rock and water came out of it in abundance. The water ran through dry places, as if it were a river. In other words, where there was only dryness and danger of dying of thirst, God gave life and relief.

The psalmist, who is not identified in this psalm, recalls God's works with Israel in the wilderness. He mentions the cloud, the fire, the quail and the bread from heaven. All of this is told to praise God, because he was faithful to the promise he made to Abraham. The accounts of the rock appear in Exodus 17 and Numbers 20.

When you find yourself in a dry season, lacking resources, strength or hope, remember that God has already cared for his people before. You can ask him for help with confidence and thank him for the times he has already sustained you.
exp.77:35:
The explanation says the people spoke sweetly to God, but they were not sincere. "Flattering" means praising or fawning over someone with pleasant words to win favor. "Lying with the tongue" means their words did not match what they felt inside.

The psalm is written by Asaph, and it reviews the history of Israel in the wilderness. When God corrected them, they would seek him and remember that he was their refuge and redeemer. But, according to the following verse, their heart was not upright nor faithful to the covenant. Even so, God showed mercy and did not unleash all his anger.

Today it invites us to examine whether our prayers and our songs are sincere. God does not seek only pleasant words in times of trouble, but an honest and faithful heart. We can come to him with truth, confessing our failures, because he remains compassionate and forgives.
exp.103:13:
This verse says that God makes the grass grow for the livestock and the plants that people cultivate and need. Hay is the grass or fodder for the animals. Beasts are the animals of the field. For the service of man means for the use and benefit of people. And bringing forth bread out of the earth means that food, such as wheat, comes from the ground thanks to God.

Psalm 104 is a song of praise to God as Creator. It does not say who wrote it; tradition links it to the psalm before it, which is attributed to David, but this is not certain. The psalmist surveys creation: waters, mountains, birds, animals, and crops. He shows that God cares for every living thing.

For today: before you eat, pause and truly give thanks. Remember that behind every meal there is rain, soil, and the work of many people, and that all of it comes from the hand of God.
exp.90:11:
It says that God's angels will carry his child in their hands, the way someone cares for a little child, so that he does not strike his foot against a stone. The first sentence of the explanation rewrites the word that appears in the verse above as "dash" and explains what that means: to stumble or fall while walking. It is an image of tender, attentive care.

The psalm does not say who wrote it, and some connect it with Moses, but this is not certain. Here the psalmist speaks, encouraging the one who trusts in God as a refuge. At the end of the psalm, God himself speaks and promises to deliver the one who loves him. Jesus quoted this verse when he was tempted, but he answered that we should not put God to the test (Matthew 4:5-7).

For today: trust in God's care in your daily paths, but do not act recklessly. Rest in his protection and, at the same time, use the wisdom he gives you.
exp.77:14:
He split open the rocks in the wilderness and gave them water to drink, as abundant as if it came from enormous depths. The reader's verse uses "clave" for split open and "rocks" for the stones; the explanation's comment on those words is rewritten to fit this verse: "split open" means broke or opened, and "rocks" are large stones. "Gave them" means he gave them water, and "depths" here refers to very deep and plentiful waters.

This is a psalm of Asaph, which recalls the history of Israel. It reviews what God did after the exodus from Egypt: the sea opened, the cloud, the fire, and the water in the desert (see Exodus 17 and Numbers 20).
