Its purpose is to teach new generations not to forget God's faithfulness, because the people, though they received so much, sinned again.

For today: God can provide what we need where it seems impossible. Remembering how he has cared for us before helps us trust and give thanks, instead of complaining. Today, write down three times when God sustained you, and give him thanks.
exp.33:12:
This verse calls for care over what we say. Keeping your tongue from evil means controlling the tongue so it is not used for harmful things, such as insults, gossip, or curses. Keeping your lips from speaking deceit means not using the mouth to lie or to mislead. Deceit is saying something false so that another person believes what is not true.

The speaker is David, who according to the psalm's title wrote it after escaping from Abimelech (the texts connect it with an episode in which he pretended to be insane). Here he acts as a teacher who calls the children to listen. He teaches them the fear of the LORD, that is, respect and reverence for God, and shows them that a good life includes an honest mouth.

Today, before you speak or write a message, ask yourself this question: "Is this true and helpful, or could it cause harm?" If it is not, it is better to stay silent or to change it. Ask God to watch over your words.
exp.98:7:
He says that God listened to his people when they sought him. He was a God who forgave, but he was also one who did not overlook evil and corrected it. The phrase "avenger of their deeds" here means that God judges and sets things right, not that he acts out of spite.

The psalmist speaks on behalf of the people and recalls Moses, Aaron and Samuel, who prayed and received an answer. God spoke to them from the pillar of cloud, and they obeyed. The "deeds" that were corrected are understood to be those of Israel, or perhaps those of these same leaders. The psalm aims to show that God is holy: merciful and just at the same time.

For today: you can draw near to God with confidence, because he hears you and forgives. But do not take his grace lightly; let his correction shape you and bring you closer to him.
exp.108:17:
He clothed himself with cursing the way a person puts on his clothes. It was so much a part of him that it covered him on the outside. Then the verse says the curse went into his body like water when it is drunk, and like oil that soaks down into the bones. The "bowels" are the deepest part of a person. In other words, the consequences of his wickedness marked him both outside and inside.

The psalm is attributed to David in its heading. He is crying out to God because enemies accuse him with lies and repay good with evil. Here he describes how the one who persecutes the afflicted and shows no mercy lives. It is a harsh psalm, and interpreters read it in different ways, but all of them see a cry for justice placed in the hands of God.

For today: what we repeat every day shapes us. If we clothe ourselves in hardness and resentment, that eventually soaks in deep inside. Let us ask God for a merciful heart and leave justice in his hands.
exp.53:4:
This verse says that God will make the evil that the enemies planned come back on them. The word "shall reward" carries the sense of repaying, so God is asked to return the harm to those who did it. The phrase "cut them off" is a plea for God to stop them or remove them from the way. All of this is asked "in thy truth," that is, by God's faithfulness and justice.

David is speaking. The title of the psalm connects it with the time the Ziphites told Saul where David was hiding. He was pursued by people who had no fear of God. For this reason he prays for justice, trusting that God is his helper. Some understand this language as a request for justice, not as personal revenge.

For today: when someone treats you unfairly, avoid taking revenge. Bring your pain to God with sincerity, and trust that he is just and faithful. Ask him to do what is right and to keep you from a vengeful heart.
exp.78:5:
Here the psalmist asks God to pour out his anger on the nations that do not know him and do not call on his name. "Nations" here means peoples or nations, and "kingdoms" refers to the governments of those nations. "Pour out" is an image of justice falling with force.

The speaker is an Israelite, probably speaking on behalf of the whole people, after the destruction of Jerusalem and the temple. It is not known with certainty which exact moment is described. The neighboring peoples mock them, and the people suffer. They cry out for justice, because those nations have devoured Jacob and laid waste his dwelling place.

Today we can learn to bring our pain and our indignation at injustice before God in prayer, instead of taking revenge with our own hands. We leave justice in his hands, and we also ask for mercy, as the psalmist does in the following verse.
exp.54:4:
He says the psalmist feels a very strong fear. "Fearfulness and trembling" describes a fright that shakes the whole body, and "horror hath overwhelmed me" means that this dread covers him completely, like a heavy blanket. "Are come upon me" means they arrived all at once, without him looking for them.

The title of the psalm attributes it to David, although it is not known with certainty at what point in his life he wrote it. The speaker is under pressure: an enemy threatens him, accuses him unjustly, and causes him anguish. Later he also speaks of the betrayal of a close friend. That is why, in the verses that follow, he wishes to escape flying like a dove.

For today: feeling fear is not a lack of faith. The psalmist does not hide his trembling; he puts it into words before God. When something overwhelms you, tell God honestly what you feel, and also seek out someone you trust to pray with you.
exp.98:2:
This verse invites everyone to praise God's name, which is "great and awesome." "Awesome" here does not mean something bad, but worthy of deep respect and wonder. The reason for the praise is that God is "holy," that is, unique, perfect, and distinct from all that has been created.

The psalm does not say who wrote it. It is a song that celebrates the LORD as king. Earlier it speaks of peoples who tremble before him and of his throne between the cherubim, an image tied to the ark of the covenant. Then it recalls that this king loves justice and righteousness, and that he has shown them to Israel. His power and his goodness go together.

For today: before asking anything of God, take a moment to admire him. Tell him in prayer who he is: holy, just, and near. That helps you live with reverence, trust, and humility.
exp.72:5:
It says that pride is like a necklace or a crown that the wicked wear, and that violence is like the clothing that covers them. In other words, their arrogance and their wrongdoing are visible on the outside, like an ornament they wear without shame. "Therefore" connects with what came before: since everything goes well for them, they fill up with arrogance.

The speaker is Asaph, the author of the psalm, who confesses that he almost stumbled when he saw the wicked prospering. He is not envious out of malice, but he is confused: he struggles to understand why things go so well for them. Later, in verse 17, he will understand better when he enters God's sanctuary.

For today: if you see that an unjust person is doing well, do not let bitterness carry you away, and do not imitate them. Bring your doubt to God in prayer, and trust that he sees everything with justice.
exp.34:16:
Here the psalmist asks God: "How long are you going to keep watching this?" He asks God to rescue his soul from the attacks his enemies are making on him. The word for "my darling," meaning the one thing he holds most precious, is his life, the most valuable thing he has, and the "lions" stand for those fierce enemies. The destructions are ruins or attacks that tear everything apart.

David is the speaker, according to the heading of the psalm. He is distressed because people he once helped now rejoice in his misfortune, gather against him, and slander him without cause. He feels like prey surrounded by wild beasts, and so he cries out to God, asking him to act.

When you feel attacked or unjustly treated, you can tell God with complete sincerity: "How long?" The Bible shows that praying this way is valid. Bring your pain before him instead of seeking revenge, and trust that he cares for you.
exp.43:1:
It says that God, with his own hand, drove out the nations that lived in the land of Canaan and planted his people there, as one plants a tree. The words "the heathen" in the verse above mean nations or peoples. The phrase "how thou didst afflict the people" means that he weakened or struck them down, and "cast them out" means that he drove them away.

The speaker is the community of Israel, in a song of the sons of Korah. They recall what their fathers told them about the conquest of the land. The verses that follow make the point clear: they did not win by their own sword or their own strength, but by God. Later the psalm shifts into a lament for hard times, so this remembrance serves them as a ground to lean on God.

For today: when you have achievements or face trials, remember what God has already done for you and your family. Give thanks without boasting, and trust that he is still your help.
exp.106:4:
They said these people were so hungry and thirsty that their strength and their spirit gave way. "Soul" here means the whole person, their life and their will to keep going. The word translated as "fainted" means they were growing weaker, almost collapsing. It was an exhaustion of both body and heart.

The psalmist speaks to Israel and calls those whom God has redeemed to give him thanks. He describes a group of people who were gathered from many lands and who wandered lost in the desert, with no road and no city to live in. Some think it recalls the exodus or the return from exile, but the text does not specify this. What follows is key: they cried out to the Lord and he delivered them.

When you feel empty and without strength, you do not have to pretend you are fine. You can tell God honestly what you are suffering. The verses that follow show that he hears the cry and leads toward a safe place.
exp.77:69:
He chose David as his servant and took him from the sheep pens where he looked after the flocks. The sheep pens were the places where the sheep were kept. David was a simple shepherd, and God chose him of his own free will.

Psalm 78 was written by Asaph, who reviews the history of Israel to teach the new generations. It tells how the people were unfaithful again and again, yet God remained faithful. Here the psalm reaches the point where God sets aside the other tribes, chooses Judah, and places David as the shepherd of the people. The next verse says that David cared for Israel with a whole heart and skillful hands.

For today: God does not look for what impresses people. He can call you and use you from your everyday work. Be faithful in small things, because that is often where God shapes character.
exp.73:19:
He says the psalmist asks God to "have respect unto the covenant," that is, to remember the promise he made to his people. The reason is that the dark places of the earth, the corners where no one sees or protects, are full of homes where cruelty rules.

The one speaking is Asaph, or someone from his circle, and he prays after an enemy destroyed the temple and mocked God. The people feel like a defenseless dove among wild beasts. That is why he does not appeal to their merits, but to God's faithfulness to his covenant.

For today: when you see injustice or feel without defense, pray relying on God's promises and not on your own strength. And if you can, be a light for whoever suffers in the darkness.
exp.21:27:
It says that the kingdom belongs to God and that He rules over all the nations. The original wording means "to rule" or "to govern." The word for "nations" refers to peoples and nations in general, not only to Israel. The name of God is the LORD.

The psalm is spoken by David, and it begins with a cry of anguish ("My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?"). After the pain, the psalm fills with hope: it declares that all the nations will turn to the Lord. Many Christians also see here an anticipation of Jesus on the cross and of the worldwide reach of the gospel.

For today: when the world seems out of control, remember that God is still the King. You can pray with confidence, knowing that your pain does not have the last word, and that He cares for all peoples and for you too.
exp.64:3:
It says that the person whom God chooses and brings near to himself, so that they may dwell in his courts, that is, in the courtyards of the temple, is blessed. There, those who are close to God are fully satisfied with the good things of his house.

The word "blessed" means fortunate or greatly favored by God. "Satisfied" means completely content. "Courts" refers to the courtyards of the sanctuary.

It is a psalm of David, sung by the people in praise of God. Just before this, the psalmist acknowledges that his sins weighed heavily on him, but God forgives rebellions. For that reason, being close to God is not something earned by oneself, but a gift of his grace. Afterward, the psalm celebrates God as savior and as a powerful creator.

For today: do not live far from God out of guilt or weariness. He forgives and invites you to draw near. Set aside a moment each day to pray and read his Word, and there receive a peace and satisfaction that nothing else gives.
exp.17:10:
It says that God surrounds himself with darkness, as if it were his hiding place and his tent. The image is of a place where someone withdraws out of sight, and of a covering that encloses him. That darkness is made of dense waters and clouds of the sky, like a dark storm that covers his presence.

David speaks in a song of thanksgiving for having been rescued from his enemies and from Saul (see the heading of the psalm). He uses poetic images of storm to describe how God came to rescue him. It is not a literal description of the weather, but the language of poetry that shows the power and mystery of God.

For today: there are times when we do not understand what God is doing and everything seems clouded over. This verse reminds us that darkness does not mean that God is absent. He continues to work and to care for us, even when we cannot see it. We can trust in him even without understanding everything.
exp.95:11:
This verse invites the field and everything in it to be filled with joy. It then says that the trees of the wood will overflow with gladness, that is, they will be full of delight. The words "let the field be joyful" call for the field to rejoice greatly. It is poetic language: the whole of creation is pictured as if it were singing for happiness.

The psalmist calls all the nations to worship God. He has just said that the LORD reigns and that he will judge with righteousness. For that reason the whole of creation joins in the praise, because the Lord comes to judge the earth with truth. We do not know with certainty who wrote this psalm or on what occasion it was first sung.

For today: the next time you see a tree, a field, or an open sky, pause for a moment and give thanks to God. Remember that He governs with justice, and let that trust bring back your joy.
exp.116:1:
It says that God's mercy toward us has been very great, meaning his love and kindness have reached us abundantly. It also says that the truth of the Lord, that is, his faithfulness and what he promises, endures forever. The name of God is the LORD, and the cry "Praise the Lord" calls people to praise God.

It is the shortest psalm in the Bible. The author is not identified, and we do not know who wrote it. The one speaking is the people of Israel, who invite all the nations to praise God. The "us" probably refers to Israel, and yet the invitation reaches all peoples. The reason is that God is faithful and merciful. Paul quotes this psalm in Romans 15:11.

When you have doubts or feel tired, remember how God has been faithful to you before. Write down three things in which you have seen his goodness and give him thanks today. Your thankfulness may encourage others to trust in him.
exp.128:4:
Psalm 129:5 says that all who hate Zion, that is, Jerusalem and the people of God who live there, will end up shamed and forced to turn back. "Hate" means to despise or dislike intensely, and "turned back" means that their plans fail and they have to withdraw in defeat.

The people of Israel speak as if they were a single person. They remember that they suffered greatly, like a field plowed across the back, but God is righteous and broke the ties of their oppressors. It is a psalm of the pilgrims who go up to Jerusalem. From the text it is not known with certainty who wrote it or at what exact moment it was written.

For today: when you feel attacked or looked down on for your faith, do not answer with hatred. Trust that God is just and acts in his own time. Rest in the knowledge that evil does not have the last word, and keep walking with hope and patience.
exp.147:13:
It says that God has given strength and honor to his people. The expression "exalted the horn" is an old one: the horn of an animal was a sign of power, so it means that God lifted up, strengthened, and gave dignity to his people. The word "near" means that Israel lives close to God, in relationship with him. The shout of praise "Hallelujah" means "praise the Lord."

This psalm does not say who wrote it. The psalmist invites all of creation, heavens, earth, young people and old, to praise God. At the end, the call is directed to the faithful of Israel, who have received his care in a special way. Many believe it was written after the exile, but this is not certain.

Today we can remember that everything good that strengthens our life comes from God, and not from ourselves alone. Before the day ends, think of one concrete way God has sustained you, and give him thanks out loud.
exp.135:7:
It says God made the sun to "rule" or govern the day. "Rule" here does not mean ruling harshly, but marking and ordering time with its light. The phrase "his mercy endureth for ever" is the refrain repeated throughout the psalm. "Mercy" can also be understood as faithful love or constant goodness.

This psalm is a song of praise from the people of Israel, probably used in worship, with a leader saying one part and the congregation answering with the refrain. It remembers God's works in creation and then in the history of Israel, such as the exodus from Egypt. It joins both things together: the same God who set the sun in its place cares for his people.

For today: each sunrise can be a reminder that God's goodness does not run out. As the sun rises, give thanks for one specific thing God has given you, and trust that his faithfulness will stay with you even in hard times.
exp.71:12:
He will show compassion to the poor and to the needy, that is, to the one who lives in want. The explanation also says that he "shall save the souls of the poor." Here the word "souls" means the lives, the whole persons, and not only a spiritual part. "Save" means to rescue from oppression and from danger.

This is a psalm of Solomon, or for him, according to the heading. It describes the ideal king, whose rule is just and who cares for the weakest. The neighboring verses speak of him delivering the afflicted from deceit and violence. Many Christians see in this king a picture of Jesus, although the psalm also speaks of a human ruler, and interpreters read it in different ways.

For today: if God has compassion on the needy, we too can do the same. This week, help someone in need in a concrete way, with your time, your attention, or material help.
exp.126:3:
It says that children born when one is young are like arrows in the hand of a warrior. An arrow that is well aimed travels far and serves to defend, and a strong soldier is the one who holds it. The phrase "children of the youth" means the children a man has during his own youth. Some believe it speaks of children who grow up while the father still has strength to guide them; others, that they are a protection in old age.

The psalm is headed as a song of ascents and is attributed to Solomon. It was probably sung when pilgrims went up to Jerusalem. Before this, it speaks of how work is in vain without God. Then it presents children as a gift from him. The gate was the place where the disputes of the city were settled.

Today: children are not a burden or a trophy, but a charge entrusted by God. Give them time, teach them the faith, and pray for them, so that they may go far and on a good course.
exp.104:14:
It says that God himself protected his people with a firm command: no one was to harm those whom he had set apart and those who spoke on his behalf. The words "anointed" refer to people chosen and set apart by God, and the wording here is the older form of the phrase. The command "touch not" means do not do them harm.

The psalmist recalls how God watched over Abraham, Isaac and Jacob when they were few and wandered as strangers among the nations (Genesis 12 and 20 tell of episodes like these). God defended his patriarchs, and the verses that follow show that he was already preparing Joseph. Praising God for his faithfulness is the purpose of the psalm.

For today: we can trust that God cares for his own, even when we feel small or vulnerable. And we should respect and care for those who serve God, without speaking ill of them carelessly, although we can examine their teachings in the light of the Bible.
exp.33:8:
This verse invites the saints, that is, the faithful people of God, to fear the Lord. Here fear does not mean being afraid, but respecting him, honoring him, and living in trust in him. The phrase "there is no want" means that they lack nothing they need.

David speaks in this psalm of gratitude. According to the psalm's title, he wrote it when he pretended to be mad before Abimelech and managed to escape (1 Samuel 21). After being rescued, he encourages others to trust in God. Some scholars see here a general promise, not a guarantee that the believer will never suffer.

For today: when you feel that something is lacking, pray and trust that God cares for you. Honor him in your daily decisions and ask him to give you what you need, including peace and wisdom, even in difficult times.
exp.72:17:
He says that God places the wicked in slippery places, that is, in slick spots where they have no firm footing. The verse says their apparent security is fragile and that they will end up falling into ruin.

The psalm is spoken by Asaph, its author. He felt envy when he saw wicked people prosper, and it hurt him and confused him. His answer came when he entered God's sanctuary: there he understood their end. His view changed when he looked at life from God's perspective, not only from what the eye can see. Interpreters disagree about when that fall happens, whether in this life or after it.

Today, when injustice troubles you or you envy the success of someone who lives without God, do not stay only with your comparisons. Stop to pray, open the Bible, and seek God's perspective. There you recover peace and trust that He is just.
exp.105:13:
The people of Israel, while in the desert, were overcome by a very strong craving, an appetite they could not control. The phrase "lusted exceedingly" means they longed for something with great intensity. The phrase "tempted God" means they put him to the test, doubting his care and demanding what they wanted. "In the desert" refers to the barren, uninhabited place.

The psalmist reviews Israel's history to confess the sins of the people and to remember God's patience. This passage alludes to the time after leaving Egypt, when they complained and asked for meat (Numbers 11). Although they had seen the Red Sea, they soon forgot the works of God. The following verse says that God gave them what they asked for, but with painful consequences.

For today: when you feel anxious about something God has not given you, do not demand it or doubt his goodness. Remember what he has already done for you, and bring your desire to him with confidence and humility, willing to accept his answer.
exp.91:3:
The explanation says that the psalmist is glad because of everything God has done. "For" simply means "because." "Hast made me glad" means that God gave him joy. "The works of thy hands" is a poetic way of speaking about everything God creates and does, and that is why the psalmist is filled with joy and sings.

Psalm 92 is a song of praise for the Sabbath, according to its title. No one knows for certain who wrote it. The one speaking is a worshiper who thanks God with music: harp, lyre, and the ten-stringed instrument, which had ten strings. The verses that follow say that God's works are great and that the fool does not understand them. For that reason this verse contrasts the joy of the believer with the blindness of the one who does not recognize God.

Today we can pause to notice what God does: creation, his daily care, the answers to prayer. If each night you give thanks for three specific things, your heart will learn to rejoice in him and not only in your troubles.
exp.101:6:
The explanation says the psalmist spends his nights unable to sleep. He feels like a bird alone on the top of a roof, without company, watching everything from a distance. The word "alone" shows a deep isolation.

The psalm presents itself as the prayer of a person in distress who is downcast and pours out his complaint before God. No one knows for certain who wrote it or at what exact moment. Many place it during times of exile or of ruin for Jerusalem, but this is understood in different ways. What is clear is that he suffers from his illness, from the mockery of his enemies, and from loneliness.

For today: if you spend nights without sleep and feel alone, you can speak to God with complete honesty, as this psalmist did. And also, seek out a trusted person and tell them how you feel. You do not have to carry your pain alone.
exp.104:10:
God spoke to his people and promised them the land of Canaan. A "cord" was the rope used to measure plots of land, so the phrase about the cord of your inheritance means that this land would be their measured portion, their inheritance. Notice that God speaks first to "you" in the singular and then switches to the plural, because the promise was made to the patriarchs and also to their descendants.

The psalmist is not named in the text; it is a song of praise that recalls the works of God. It goes over how God made a covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. It is told to encourage Israel to trust a God who keeps what he promises, even when those patriarchs were few and foreigners, as the next verse says.

Today we can learn to wait with patience. God promised and fulfilled, though it took generations. If you feel today that your prayers are taking a long time, remember that God is faithful and his timing is not always ours. Trust in him and give thanks for what he has already done.
exp.118:62:
The psalmist says that he feels joined to all the people who revere God and obey his commandments. Here "revere" does not mean being afraid, but honoring God with deep respect. The explanation's old-form words are rendered in the verse above: "fear" in the verse means this same reverent respect, and "keep" means to obey and hold to God's precepts. "Companion" means a close friend, someone who walks beside you.

The author of Psalm 119 is not identified with certainty. The speaker loves God's law, even when the wicked have attacked and robbed him. In the middle of that pressure, he does not abandon the Word, and now he says with whom he wants to walk: with those who share that same faith and obedience.

Today we can seek out and cherish friendships that bring us closer to God. It might be a church, a small group, or a faithful friend. Walking with other believers encourages us to stay firm when the atmosphere around us pushes us to forget what God says.
exp.108:16:
That wicked person grew used to cursing others, and he enjoyed doing it. For that reason, the curse ended up falling on him. And since he never wanted to bless or to receive a blessing, good stayed far from his life.

David is the one speaking in this psalm. He is distressed by enemies who accuse him falsely and attack him, and he asks God to do justice. Here he describes the conduct of his accuser: he showed no compassion and pursued a man who was suffering. The verses that follow show that his wickedness wrapped around him like a garment. Some readers see these requests as a cry for justice; others see them as words that Jesus invites us to go beyond by loving our enemies.

Today we can ask ourselves what habits of speech we are forming. Let us choose to bless, even when we are hurt, because what we sow with our words tends to grow in our hearts.
exp.43:15:
The explanation says that the psalmist's shame comes from the voice of the one who insults and dishonors him, and because of the enemy who seeks revenge.

The speaker is the people of Israel, or someone speaking on their behalf, in a time of defeat and humiliation. The exact historical situation is not known for certain. What stands out is that they cry out to God without having turned away from him, as the verses that follow say. They feel that they suffer even though they are faithful, and they tell God so honestly.

For today: when others criticize or humiliate you, you do not have to pretend it does not hurt. Bring your pain to God honestly, as this psalm does. Praying frankly helps you avoid answering with resentment, and reminds you that he sees your faithfulness.
exp.17:47:
He says that God is the one who rescues the psalmist from his enemies. The phrase "you lifted me above" means that God gave him the victory over those who attacked him. The "violent man" is a cruel and aggressive person, and God delivered him from that man. What had been a threat now rested under God's care.

David, the king of Israel, speaks in a song of thanksgiving that also appears in 2 Samuel 22. He wrote it after God saved him from Saul and other enemies. The verses that follow show that his praise reaches beyond Israel and that he acknowledges God's faithfulness to his covenant with him and with his descendants. Many Christians see in this a look toward Christ.

Today we can remember with gratitude the times God sustained us in the midst of injustice or pressure. Instead of boasting in our own strength, let us give thanks out loud, as David did, and trust that he will keep caring for us.
exp.43:2:
The explanation says that Israel's ancestors did not take the land of Canaan by their own military strength. Neither their sword nor their arm gave them the victory. It was God's right hand (his mighty hand), his arm (his power), and the light of his face (his favor and presence). The final reason is that God took pleasure in them, that is, he looked on them with delight and loved them.

The speaker is the people of Israel, in a psalm of the sons of Korah, the musicians of the temple. They remember what their fathers told them about the conquest of the land. They do this to acknowledge that everything was the work of God, and so to support their trust in him in the present, as the following verse shows.

For today: when you achieve something good, do not credit it only to your own effort. Give thanks to God, and trust him also in your current struggles, knowing that his love sustains what you cannot accomplish alone.
exp.88:51:
God deserves to be praised forever. "Blessed" means praised and honored. The word "Amen" is repeated here to affirm it with force: truly, so be it.

This verse closes Psalm 89 and also the third book of the Psalms. The psalmist, Ethan the Ezrahite according to the title, speaks out of pain. Enemies mock the anointed king, and it seems that God has forgotten his promises to David. Even so, the psalm ends in praise. Some think this closing line was added by those who arranged the book, but this is not known for certain.

When you feel confused or hurt, you can speak to God honestly and, even without having all the answers, choose to praise him. His faithfulness does not depend on what you feel today.
exp.36:30:
This verse says that the righteous person carries God's teaching inside the heart, not only in the mind or on the lips. That is why his steps do not slip or stumble. Here "slide" means to slip, to totter, or to lose one's balance while walking. The "law" refers to God's instruction or teaching.

It is a psalm of David, written as wise counsel for someone troubled by seeing the wicked prosper. Earlier it speaks of the mouth of the righteous, which speaks wisdom, and later of the wicked lying in wait for him. The message is that God upholds the one who is faithful to him, even amid threats.

For today: spend a few minutes each day reading a passage of the Bible and repeat it through the day. When a difficult decision comes, that word kept in your heart will give you firmness to walk with confidence.
exp.84:8:
It says that God's help and deliverance (in this text, the word translated as "salvation") are very near to those who fear him, that is, to those who honor him and remain faithful to him. The purpose is that God's glory, his presence and his honor, would dwell in the land of the people.

The psalm is spoken by a believer or a group of Israelites who asks God for restoration. Earlier they asked for mercy and heard a promise of peace for the people. Many think it was written after a time of hardship, although the text does not say which one. The verses that follow describe that restoration with images of mercy, truth, righteousness and peace.

When you feel far from God or in need, do not give up. Draw near to him with reverence and trust, and ask him to fill your home, your work and your community with his presence.
exp.63:6:
It says that God will respond to the wicked with an arrow. Their punishment will come suddenly, without warning. The word "wounds" here means blows or injuries, not diseases. Those who were plotting to harm others in secret will end up wounded by God's action.

The psalm is attributed to David, who cries out to God for protection from enemies who plot evil in secret and use words as weapons. They believe no one sees them. This verse marks a turning point: God, from whom they cannot hide, acts. The verses that follow say their own words turn against them, and that others, seeing it, will recognize the work of God.

When someone hurts you or plans evil against you, you do not have to take revenge. You can hand your pain over to God, trust in his justice, and ask him to guard your heart, so that you do not become like those who hurt you.
exp.91:13:
This verse says that righteous people will keep bearing fruit even in old age.

The psalm does not name its author; its title calls it a song for the Sabbath day. The writer praises God and compares the righteous person to the palm tree and the cedar, strong and long-lasting trees. These righteous people are "planted in the house of the LORD," that is, rooted in their relationship with God. The next verse gives the purpose: to declare that God is upright and faithful.

For today: old age does not have to be a useless stage of life. If we remain rooted in God, we can keep serving, praying, advising, and testifying to his faithfulness, regardless of our age or the limitations of the body.
exp.145:0:
The explanation says the psalmist begins with "Praise ye the Lord," which means "Praise the Lord." Then he speaks to himself: "Praise the Lord, O my soul." Here "soul" refers to his whole being, his entire self.

The text does not say who wrote this psalm. Some traditions connect it with the prophets Haggai and Zechariah, but this is not certain. The speaker encourages his own heart to worship God. The verses that follow explain why: he promises to praise as long as he lives, and he warns against trusting in powerful people, because people cannot truly save. God, however, is worthy of trust.

For today: when you feel tired or worried, speak to your own heart as the psalmist does. Before looking for help from others, take a moment to thank God aloud for something specific.
exp.21:13:
He says he feels drained of strength, like water poured out on the ground that cannot be gathered back up. His bones are out of joint, that is, out of their place, as if the body were coming apart. His heart is like wax melting inside him: courage and spirit are running out. The word "bowels" refers to the inner parts of the body.

It is a psalm of David, expressing the anguish of a righteous man surrounded by enemies, described as bulls and lions. Christians see here a prophecy of the cross, and the New Testament cites the opening of the psalm on the lips of Jesus (Matthew 27:46). Others read it first as David's own lament. Both readings recognize a deep suffering.

For today: when you are exhausted and without strength, do not pretend that you are fine. You can honestly tell God how you feel. This psalm shows that honest prayer, even from weakness, has a place before God.
exp.82:8:
The psalmist asks God to deal with Israel's enemies as he dealt with other peoples in the past. He mentions Midian, defeated in the days of Gideon, and Sisera and Jabin, defeated in the days of Deborah and Barak, beside the brook Kishon. The phrase "Do unto them" in the verse is simply "do to them," and "as unto" is simply "as to."

The one speaking is Asaph, who prays in a moment of great danger. An alliance of neighboring nations plots to destroy Israel (verses 3-8). The psalmist remembers that God had already rescued his people when it seemed impossible. This is not personal revenge, but a cry for justice and protection.

For today: when you feel surrounded by problems bigger than you, remember what God has done before. Pray honestly, leaning on his past faithfulness, and leave justice in his hands instead of taking it into your own.
exp.10:3:
This verse says that the Lord is in his holy temple and that his throne is in heaven. From there his eyes see, and his gaze examines the children of men. The eyes watching closely speak of a careful look, like someone narrowing their eyes to see clearly. "Throne" means the seat of a king.

David wrote this psalm. Some advise him to flee like a bird to the mountains, because the wicked attack in secret and the foundations seem to be collapsing. David answers with confidence: God has not lost control. His throne remains firm, and he sees what is hidden. Scholars debate whether the "temple" refers to heaven itself or also to the sanctuary in Jerusalem.

Today, when injustice overwhelms you and you feel that everything is falling apart, remember that God sees. Before fleeing in fear, pray and rest in the knowledge that he governs and knows your situation.
exp.77:24:
The text says the people ate what was called "bread of nobles," that is, the manna, a food so special that it seemed to be of high rank. Other translations say "bread of angels," because the Hebrew word can be understood in several ways. The phrase "to the full" means that God sent them food until they were satisfied.

The psalm is written by Asaph, who recalls the history of Israel in the wilderness. He wants to teach the new generations that God cared for them abundantly, even though the people tested Him and doubted Him. The manna was a daily and generous provision.

For today: We can remember with gratitude how God has sustained us in the past. Before complaining about what is missing, it is good to give thanks for what we have already received and to trust that God will keep caring for us, one day at a time.
exp.29:3:
This verse invites the "saints," that is, those who belong to God and are faithful to him, to sing praises to him. It also calls them to remember and give thanks for how holy he is.

The speaker is David, according to the psalm's title. He has just told how God healed him and rescued him from being near death. His personal gratitude now becomes an invitation to the whole people. He then explains that God's anger is brief, but his favor lasts a lifetime. It is not known with certainty what illness or danger he experienced.

For today: when God helps you through a difficult moment, do not keep your gratitude to yourself. Tell it, sing it, or share it with other believers, and remember how faithful God has been.
exp.69:1:
He says that David asks God to let those who want to take his life be ashamed and confused. He also asks that those who wish him harm be turned back, meaning that they retreat and fail in their plans. Wishing him harm means they long for things to go badly for him.

David is the one speaking. This psalm is a brief, urgent prayer, written in a time of danger, although we do not know exactly what the situation was. It begins by asking God to hurry and rescue him. Some scholars note that it is very similar to the final part of Psalm 40. David does not seek revenge on his own; he leaves the matter in God's hands.

For today: when someone hurts or threatens you, bring your pain honestly to God instead of taking revenge. Ask him to bring about justice and to give you peace while you wait.
exp.73:22:
This verse is a plea to God. The psalmist asks him not to overlook what his enemies are saying. The words "the tumult of those that rise up against thee" refer to noise, shouting, and agitation. The ones who rise up against you are those who oppose God. The verse says that this noise "increaseth continually," meaning it does not stop.

This psalm is attributed to Asaph, or to someone from his circle of singers. It appears that the temple was destroyed and the people are distressed. Scholars connect it with the fall of Jerusalem, although not all of them agree on the date. The psalmist does not take revenge on his own, but asks God to act and defend his name.

When you see mockery or violence against what is right, do not fill yourself with resentment. Bring your distress to God in prayer, with honesty, and trust that he sees and will act in his own time.
exp.118:54:
It says that the psalmist, during the night, remembered God's name, that is, who God is: his character and his faithfulness. And as a consequence, he kept his law, that is, he obeyed it. The verse's word "remembered" is the same as the one used in the verse itself.

The one speaking is the author of Psalm 119, a psalm in honor of God's Word, whose author is not identified with certainty. He feels surrounded by people who despise the law, and yet he finds comfort in God's commandments while he is a stranger in this world. The night can be a time of loneliness or anguish, but for him it is a moment to remember God.

For today: when night comes with its worries, before you toss and turn in bed, take a few minutes to remember who God is and some promise of his. That strengthens the heart to obey him the next day.
exp.126:2:
The explanation says that children are a gift from God, an inheritance that comes from his hand. An "inheritance" is something received as a gift, not something earned. "Something precious" refers to something of great value, and "the fruit of the womb" refers to children born. "Behold" is like saying: "Take careful notice!"

The psalm is headed "for Solomon," though some understand that it was written by him and others that it was dedicated to him. It is a song to be sung while going up to Jerusalem. It begins by saying that without God, human effort is not enough, and then presents children as his gift, not as a personal achievement.

For today: if God is the one who sustains the home, we can raise our children with gratitude and trust, not with anxiety. Today you can give them time, listen to them, and pray for them, remembering that they are a precious charge from God.
exp.77:15:
It says that God brought streams of water out of a rock, and that the waters flowed down in abundance, like rivers.

The speaker is Asaph, the author of this psalm, who reviews the history of Israel in the wilderness after leaving Egypt. He recalls how God cared for his people, guiding them with the cloud and the fire and giving them water. He does this as a warning, because the verses that follow show that, even with such care, the people sinned again and doubted God.

God provides even where it seems impossible. Today we can remember his past help in order to trust him, and thank him instead of complaining when trials come.
exp.25:10:
What it says: David affirms that, unlike the wicked, he will keep living with integrity, that is, with a sincere and upright heart. He does not boast of being perfect. He asks to be rescued and shown compassion, asking God for deliverance and mercy.

Context: The speaker is the psalmist, traditionally David. He has just asked not to be counted among the violent and the corrupt. Now he contrasts his way with theirs. His confidence is not in his own merits but in God sustaining him. The verses that follow speak of his firm footing and of praising God together with his people.

For today: Decide to be honest in small things, at work, at home, or with money, even when others cheat. And when you fail, do not hide: ask God for forgiveness and help. Integrity grows by walking each day under His mercy.
exp.45:10:
The explanation says that the Lord of hosts, that is, the Lord who rules over all the powers of heaven and earth, is with his people. "Is with us" means "is with us." The God of Jacob is our refuge, a safe place where we can be protected. "Selah" is a Hebrew word whose exact meaning is not known for certain; many think it invites a pause and meditation.

The psalm was written by the sons of Korah, Levites who sang in worship. It speaks of a time of great upheaval and war. The verses before it show God stopping the battles and calling everyone to recognize that he is God. This verse is the people's response: calm trust. It is repeated in verse 7.

When you find yourself surrounded by problems or frightening news, pause, as the Selah invites. Remember that God is with you, and run to him in prayer. He is a real refuge.
exp.118:147:
The psalmist says he opened his eyes before the night watches ended. He gave this up on purpose, so that he could think about what God has said.

The one speaking is the author of Psalm 119, who is not identified with certainty. He is in distress and is being pursued, as the following verses show. For this reason he cries out to God and trusts in his word. His meditation at night comes from need and hope, not only from routine.

For today: set aside a quiet moment, even a brief one, to read a promise of God and think about it. When you are worried and cannot sleep, instead of going over your fears again and again, slowly repeat a verse and speak with God about it in prayer.
exp.21:29:
The explanation says that the descendants of those who trust in God will serve him. "Posterity" means the children and the generations that come after. The second part, which in the older wording says that this descendant "will be counted by a generation of the Lord," is understood to mean that this line of descendants will be considered or recorded as belonging to the Lord. Some translators explain it differently, but the central idea is that faith passes on to future generations.

David speaks in a psalm of deep suffering. It begins with the cry "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?", a line Jesus quoted on the cross. At the end, the psalm moves from pain to hope: God will reign over all the nations, and his righteous work will be proclaimed to those who are not yet born.

For today: faith is passed on. Through your example, your words, and your prayers, you can tell your children, nephews, nieces, or young people close to you what God has done for you. Today, share with someone younger a concrete experience of God's faithfulness.
exp.72:19:
The explanation says that the prosperity of the wicked is like a dream: when one wakes up, one realizes it was not real. So when God "awakes," that is, when he acts, he will look down on their appearances, that is, the image of success and greatness they displayed. The word "despise" means to regard as worthless.

The speaker is Asaph, a psalmist who felt envy when he saw the wicked prospering. He was confused until he entered God's sanctuary and understood their end (vv. 16-17). Here he describes how fragile their situation is. Afterward he admits that his bitterness came from not understanding.

Today we can stop measuring our lives by what others seem to have. When you feel tempted to envy, pray and fix your gaze on what lasts forever: God's presence and his justice.
exp.108:4:
It says that those who received affection and help from David gave him back the opposite: they repaid him with evil for the good he did, and with hatred for the love he gave. "They set against me" means they paid him back and loaded it onto him. It is a complaint about a painful injustice.

The speaker is the psalmist, whom the title of the psalm attributes to David. He is surrounded by false accusations and baseless attacks, and he responds by praying rather than taking revenge. The verses that follow contain harsh requests against his enemy. Scholars debate how to understand them: some see them as a cry to God for justice, others as words of the accusers that the psalmist quotes.

When someone repays your kindness with harm, bring your pain honestly to God. Praying first helps you avoid answering with resentment and helps you trust that God is the just judge. Jesus also taught us to love our enemies and to pray for them.
exp.106:5:
This verse says that when people cried out to God in their distress, he delivered them from their troubles. The words "but" and "however" appear in the original wording, and the sentence that explains the old word and its meaning should be dropped. In other words, after being lost, hungry, and with no way out, they asked God for help, and he answered.

The psalm does not say who wrote it, although the author calls those who have been redeemed to give thanks. Here it describes a group of travelers lost in the desert, unable to find a city where they could rest. It is the first of several scenes in the psalm, where different people in trouble cry out to God and he rescues them. Some think of Israel's journeys; others think of various situations in life.

For today: when you feel lost or exhausted, do not wait until everything is resolved before you pray. Speak to God honestly, just as you are. The psalm reminds us that he hears the sincere cry and knows how to guide us, step by step, toward a safe place.
exp.31:4:
Here the psalmist says he told God about his sin without hiding anything. "Guilt" means wickedness or blame, and "transgressions" are the times he turned away from God on purpose. He chose to confess them to the Lord, and God forgave the guilt of his sin. "Selah" is probably a pause for meditation, though its exact meaning is not known for certain.

David is the speaker, according to the title of the psalm. Earlier it explains that while he kept silent about his sin, he felt worn out and dry inside, as if God's hand weighed heavily on him. When he confessed, relief came. The psalm does not clearly say which sin it refers to.

If something weighs on your conscience, do not hide it. Speak with God honestly and without excuses, trusting that He forgives. If needed, also ask forgiveness from the person you offended.
exp.77:13:
It says that God guided his people Israel during their journey through the wilderness. By day he led them with a cloud, and by night with a light like fire. The sentences that explained the old wording of the verse have been left out, because your verse uses different words.

Psalm 78 is a psalm of Asaph, a teacher or singer of the people. He reviews Israel's history to teach the children what God did for their parents: the wonders in Egypt, the crossing of the sea, and the guidance in the wilderness. His purpose is that the new generations trust God and do not repeat the disobedience of their ancestors.

God does not abandon those he guides. They had a visible sign day and night, and today we can trust that he also accompanies us in the clear times and in the dark ones. This week, when you are unsure which path to take, pray and remember a time when God sustained you. Tell someone younger about it.
exp.40:0:
This verse says that the person who "considereth the poor" is happy and blessed, meaning the one who thinks carefully about them, cares for them, and helps them. The word "blessed" in the verse means happy and favored. The "evil day" is a time of distress or trouble. The promise is that the Lord will deliver him in that difficult time.

The psalm is attributed to David and was addressed to the chief musician, to be sung in worship. The verses that follow speak of sickness and enemies, so David seems to be speaking from suffering. Some think it refers to a specific illness of his, but the text does not say so. Here compassion is presented as a path to blessing, without being an automatic guarantee that pain will never come.

Today we can look out for someone in need near us: a neighbor, a relative, or someone in the church. A visit, a meal, or a concrete act of help can be a simple way to practice this compassion.
exp.102:3:
This verse says that God redeems your life from destruction. The word "pit," a term that speaks of the grave, of death, or of mortal danger, is not used here. He also crowns you with loving kindness and tender mercies, that is, He surrounds you with goodness and compassion, like someone placing a crown on a beloved person.

The one speaking is David, according to the title of the psalm. He speaks to himself: "Bless the Lord, O my soul." He is grateful and encourages himself not to forget what God has done: forgiving, healing, rescuing, and caring. It is a song of praise that remembers the character of God.

For today: make a short list of the times God has sustained you or delivered you from something difficult. Read it aloud and give thanks to Him. Remembering His benefits strengthens faith when the hard days come.
exp.129:2:
This verse asks: if God were to keep a record of all our sins, who could stand? The implied answer is: no one.

The one speaking is a worshiper crying out from the depths, that is, from a situation of distress, perhaps aware of his own guilt. It is a psalm of ascent, which many believe pilgrims sang as they went up to Jerusalem. His hope appears right away: with God there is forgiveness.

For today: you do not need to come before God with a list of merits or hide your failures. You can come with sincerity, acknowledge what you did wrong, and trust in his mercy. Today, tell God honestly where you have fallen short, and receive his forgiveness with gratitude.
exp.50:16:
This verse says that what pleases God most is not animal offerings, but a broken spirit, that is, a person who acknowledges their sin and humbles themselves. "Broken and contrite" means deeply sorry, with a heart grieved by having failed. God does not reject someone like that.

The psalm is spoken by David, according to its traditional heading, after his serious sin with Bathsheba. He asks for forgiveness and cleansing. Before this, he says that God does not want only outward sacrifices. The verses that follow show that sacrifices are not despised, but they are worth something when they come from a sincere heart.

For today: when you fail, do not hide or try to make up for it with religious activity. Come to God with honesty, admit your wrong without excuses, and trust that He receives with tenderness the one who comes back sorry.
exp.143:11:
It says that the people desire their sons to grow strong, like plants that develop well from their youth. And that their daughters be like pillars at the corners, carved with beauty, like those of a palace. The phrase "carved corner stones" refers to stones or columns sculpted with skill. Some understand them to be corner pillars, others decorative columns.

David, king of Israel, speaks in a psalm of prayer. He has just asked to be rescued from enemies who lie and deceive. Then he describes what he longs for: a nation at peace, with healthy and steadfast families, abundance in the granaries, and no attack. Prosperous children are part of that blessing.

For today: pray to God for your children and for the young people you know, and help them with your example and your time. May they grow with firm roots in faith and with solid character, and may they be a support to their family and their community.
exp.88:6:
It says God is "terrible," meaning he inspires a deep and reverent awe, not that he is evil. The "assembly of the saints" is the group of heavenly beings or faithful ones who surround him, and interpreters debate who exactly is meant. In any case, even those closest to God honor him with great reverence.

It is a psalm of Ethan the Ezrahite. It praises God for his greatness and for his faithfulness to the covenant with David. It compares the Lord with any other heavenly power and concludes that no one is his equal. Later the psalm also expresses distress, because the promises seem not to be fulfilled.

For today: before asking God for something, take a moment to admire who he is. That reverence gives us peace, because the same God who is so great is faithful to his promises.
exp.71:8:
The psalmist says that distant peoples will bow down before this king until they touch the ground, and that his enemies will lick the dust. The phrase "they that dwell in the wilderness" is the wording of the King James Version, but some translations read "distant peoples" instead, because the original can be understood in more than one way. "Lick the dust" is a picture of total surrender and humiliation.

This psalm is a prayer for the king, and its title connects it with Solomon. It asks that he govern with justice and peace, and that his reign reach to the ends of the earth. Many Christians see in these words an anticipation of Christ, whose reign is perfect.

Today we can rest in the fact that Jesus reigns and that justice will have the final word. When you see injustice, do not lose hope: pray, do good around you, and trust in the King who one day will put everything in order.
exp.61:5:
He only is the rock, the salvation, and the refuge of the one who speaks. "Strong" here means a firm rock or a stronghold, and "health" means salvation or deliverance. "I shall not be moved" is an expression of trust: with God as my support, I will not fall or be left without a foundation.

The speaker is David, according to the heading of the psalm. He feels surrounded by people who want to bring him down from his position. They put on a show of kindness, blessing with their mouths, but inwardly they wish him harm. Facing that falseness, David keeps telling himself that his soul should rest in God alone.

When someone treats you with two faces, or you feel your stability wobbling, do not place your security in what other people think. Do as David did: speak to your own heart, tell God what you feel, and rest in the fact that he holds you up.
exp.37:0:
This verse is the opening of a prayer. David calls it a psalm "to bring to remembrance," and some think it serves to call to mind before God his suffering. He asks the Lord not to rebuke him or chasten him when he is angry. "Wrath" and "hot displeasure" are strong words for God's anger. To "rebuke" means to correct harshly.

David speaks from a very great pain. The verses that follow say that he feels the hand of God upon him, that his body is sick, and that he acknowledges his sin. It is not known exactly what illness or situation he was living through. Even so, he does not turn away from God: he prays to Him.

For today: when you fail or suffer because of your mistakes, do not hide from God. Come to Him with humility, acknowledge your guilt, and ask for mercy. He corrects His children, but He also listens and forgives.
exp.21:4:
It says that Israel's ancestors cried out to God for help, and he rescued them. They trusted in him and were not put to shame, meaning their hope did not turn out to be in vain. The word "delivered" means rescued or saved, and "were not confounded" means they were not left in shame or disappointed.

David speaks in a psalm of deep suffering. He remembers how God acted in the past with his people while he himself feels forsaken, scorned, and mocked, as the following verses show. His memory of God's faithfulness sustains his faith in the midst of pain. Christians also read this psalm with Jesus on the cross in mind, since he quoted it (Matthew 27:46).

When you are going through a difficult time, remember the times God helped you or others. Write those memories down and pray with them, so that your trust grows stronger even when you do not yet see the answer today.
exp.92:0:
It says that the Lord is King. He is "clothed with majesty," that is, with splendor and greatness, like a king in his royal robes. He is also "girded with strength," like someone who puts on a belt to be ready and strong. Moreover, he "made the world firm": he set it steady and stable, so that it will not be moved.

This psalm does not say who wrote it, so the author is unknown. It speaks as a worshiper who celebrates God's reign. The verses that follow mention rivers that lift up their roar; many understand these as images of chaos and of the forces that threaten, but God is above all of them.

When life or the news makes you feel that everything is moving, remember that God still reigns. Today, before facing your worries, pause for a moment and say to him: "You are King, and I trust in you."
exp.77:5:
This verse says that God wants His works to be known from one generation to the next. Those who live today tell their children, the children tell those who will be born after them, and they in turn tell their own. The phrase "might know them" means that the next generation should come to know them, and the phrase "declare them to their children" means that they should pass them on, so that the chain is never broken.

The psalm is spoken by Asaph, who in this psalm recalls the history of Israel. The verses before this one explain that God commanded that His law be taught to the children. The purpose, as the verses that follow make clear, is that they put their trust in God, do not forget His works, and keep His commandments, and not repeat the rebellion of their ancestors.

For today: tell the younger ones, in simple words, what God has done in your life and in His Word. It can be at the table, on the way somewhere, or before bed. Your personal testimony can plant trust in God.
exp.54:6:
The explanation says that the psalmist, full of fear, wishes to escape far away and live in the desert, a lonely place far from everyone. The phrase "I would certainly flee" is the wording behind the verse. The exact meaning of "Selah" is not known for certain; many believe it marks a pause for reflection or is a musical instruction.

Psalm 55 is attributed to David. He suffers because of violence and quarrels in the city, and because of the betrayal of someone close to him (verses 12-14). We do not know with certainty the exact moment of his life when he wrote it. His distress is so great that he longs to fly away like a dove.

For today: it is normal to want to escape when everything overwhelms us. There is no need to be ashamed of that desire. You can do what David did: honestly tell God about your fear. Later in the psalm he says: "Cast your burden upon the Lord, and he shall sustain you" (v. 22).
exp.114:15:
This verse says that the heavens belong to God, who is called Jehovah here, and that he has given the earth to human beings to live in and to care for. "Children of men" simply means humankind. "Given" does not mean that God stops being its owner, but that he entrusts it to us.

The psalm is a song of the people of Israel, probably meant for worshiping together. Earlier, it speaks of idols that can do nothing, and it calls people to trust in the true God. Here it contrasts the heavens, where God reigns, with the earth, where we live. Then it says that the dead do not praise, and that the living will. Scholars discuss how to understand that phrase, but the tone is one of gratitude.

Today, you can care with gratitude for what God has entrusted to you: your surroundings, your work, your family, and your time. And do it praising him as long as you have life.
exp.18:1:
This verse says that creation is never silent. Each day "utters speech," that is, it sends out a message, and passes it on to the next day. Each night "shows knowledge," that is, it makes known the knowledge of God to the night that follows. It is like a relay that never stops.

King David, the psalmist, speaks in a psalm dedicated to the chief musician, to be sung. He looks at the sky and recognizes that the order of time, with its days and nights, shows the greatness of the Creator. The verses that follow make clear that this message uses no human words or sounds.

For today: pause each day, in the morning or at night, to look at the sky and give thanks to God. Let what He has created remind you that He sustains your life faithfully and in good order.
exp.125:2:
The explanation says that the people acknowledge that God has done great things for them, and that is why their hearts are glad. "The Lord" is the name of God, and "we are glad" means that they feel full of joy. Earlier, other nations had said the same about them (v. 2); now they confirm it with their own words.

The people of Israel speak in a song that was sung when going up to Jerusalem. It recalls when God brought them back from captivity. Many understand this to refer to the return from Babylon, although the psalm does not say so with certainty. The psalm also asks for a greater restoration (v. 4), so it looks back with gratitude and forward with hope.

For today: remember what God has done in your life and give him thanks out loud. That gratitude strengthens faith when you are going through difficult times that are still unresolved.
exp.144:19:
The explanation says that God takes care of and protects all who love him. The word "preserveth" means that he watches over them, sustains them, and defends them. It also says that in the end God will destroy the wicked, that is, those who oppose him and practice evil without repenting.

This is a psalm of praise attributed to David. He exalts the greatness and goodness of God. Earlier he spoke of God being near to those who call on him in sincerity and hearing their cry. Here he contrasts two destinies: care for those who love God and judgment for those who persist in wickedness. Then David ends with praise.

For today: if you love God, you can rest in knowing you are not alone. Trust in his care, even in difficult times, and leave final justice in his hands instead of living with bitterness.
exp.79:3:
Here the psalmist asks God: "How long?" The word "smoke" in the sense of anger is an image: God is burning in wrath, like smoke rising from a furious nostril. What is striking is that this anger seems directed even against the prayer of his own people, as if God were not listening to it. Calling him "Lord God of hosts" presents him as the Lord with power over all things.

The speaker is an Israelite speaking on behalf of the whole nation, probably in a time of defeat and suffering. He mentions Ephraim, Benjamin and Manasseh, tribes of the north. The exact occasion is not known for certain; some have thought of the fall of the northern kingdom, but that is an interpretation.

Today, when you feel that God is taking his time, you can speak to him honestly, without pretending. This psalm shows that asking "How long?" is a way of continuing to trust, since the psalmist keeps addressing God.
exp.95:1:
This verse invites us to sing to God and to bless his name, that is, to speak well of him and to acknowledge who he is. It also asks us to proclaim his deliverance from day to day. Here "deliverance" does not mean bodily health, but rescue: the liberation and saving that God gives.

The psalm does not say who wrote it. It speaks of a worshiper who calls the whole people, and even the whole earth, to praise God. The verses that follow ask us to declare his glory among the nations, because the Lord is great and worthy of the highest praise. Some believe it was used in temple worship, but this is not entirely certain.

For today: each day, look for a simple way to thank God for his salvation. It could be a song at home or a brief testimony to someone. In this way your praise does not stay hidden away.
exp.17:19:
The explanation says that God has given David a reward that matches his righteousness. The phrase "has paid me" means "has repaid me" or "has rewarded me." The phrase "has returned to me" means "has given me back" or "has recompensed me." "The cleanness of my hands" speaks of a clean conduct, without violence or deceit.

David speaks here after being rescued from his enemies, among them Saul, according to the title of the psalm. He has just described how God brought him out into a spacious place. Here he does not claim to be perfect, but that he was faithful to God in the face of accusations and persecution. Some understand this as his integrity in that particular conflict, not as a total absence of sin.

For today: when people treat you unfairly, keep acting honestly and trust that God sees your heart. You do not need to take revenge or defend yourself with trickery; you can leave your cause in his hands.
exp.85:5:
This verse is a simple request: the psalmist asks God to hear him. He repeats the idea in two ways: "listen to my prayer" and "pay attention to the sound of my pleas." The word "pleas" points to requests made with humility and need. "Pay attention" means to give careful heed.

The psalm is presented as a prayer of David, though some scholars debate how it was put together. The speaker calls himself a servant and is in distress. Before asking, he reminds himself that God is good, ready to forgive, and abounding in mercy. He then declares that he will call on God in the day of his trouble, because he trusts that God answers.

Today you can pray with the same openness. You do not need polished words: tell God what weighs on you, first recalling what He is like, good and compassionate. That confidence helps you pray with hope, even when the answer takes time.
exp.118:72:
It says that God is our Creator: his hands made us and gave us shape. That is why the psalmist asks him, "make me understand," that is, give me comprehension and clarity. He promises that if God gives him that understanding, he will learn and keep God's commands. "Jod" is the name of a Hebrew letter; this psalm is arranged according to the alphabet, and each section begins with one letter.

The speaker is the author of Psalm 119, whose name is not stated with certainty. He is someone who loves God's word and has gone through suffering. Earlier he said that being humbled helped him learn. Now he appeals to God as his Maker: the one who formed him can also teach him how to live. Later he speaks of God having been faithful even when he afflicted him.

For today: if God made you, he also knows how to guide you. Before reading the Bible, ask him simply, "Lord, help me understand." Then decide to obey one specific thing you discover that day.
exp.104:28:
It says that God turned the waters of Egypt into blood, and that the fish died. Here the verse recalls the first of the plagues that God sent upon Egypt.

This psalm was written by an author whose name is not known for certain. It is a song of praise that reviews what God did for his people, from Abraham to the departure from Egypt. Egypt is also called by another name, which is linked to Ham, son of Noah. The psalmist recounts these signs so that Israel will remember that God cared for them and kept his promise. The plague shows God's power over the Nile, on which Egypt depended.

For today: when you feel that something you trust in, such as your work, your money, or your health, gives you complete security, remember that only God is firm. Give him thanks and put your trust in him first.
exp.21:6:
All who see me mock me; they make faces at me, they shake their heads, saying, and then they begin to speak with sarcasm.

The one speaking is the psalmist, David according to the title of the psalm. He is in deep pain and feels despised, like a worm. Even so, he speaks with God and tells him everything. Christians see here a prophecy fulfilled in Jesus on the cross, because the Gospels describe similar mockery (Matthew 27:39-43).

When someone mocks your faith or your pain, do not keep silent or harden yourself. Do as the psalmist did: bring to God what you feel. He does not mock you, and he can sustain you even when others despise you.
exp.118:164:
Those who love God's law, that is, his teaching and his commandments, live with great peace. The verse says that nothing causes them to fall in a lasting way. Some understand that they do not lack difficulties, but that they have no cause for falling or for shame.

The speaker is the psalmist, the author of Psalm 119, whose name is not known with certainty. In this psalm he praises God's word. Just before this verse he says he hates lies and praises God seven times a day. Then he expresses that he hopes for the salvation of the LORD and that he keeps his commandments. Thus, peace is born from loving and practicing what God says.

For today: when you feel anxiety or confusion, spend a few minutes each day reading a passage of the Bible and ask God for help to obey it in one specific thing.
exp.0:5:
This verse says that God knows well the way of people who live righteously; that is, he watches over them and knows where they are headed. By contrast, the way of the wicked comes to an end and ends in nothing.

Psalm 1 does not say who wrote it. It is a wisdom poem that serves as an introduction to the whole book of Psalms. It compares two kinds of people: the righteous, who is like a firm tree beside the water, and the wicked, who is like chaff, the light husk that the wind carries away. This verse closes the psalm with the final contrast.

Today we can ask ourselves what path we are following. We do not need to be perfect; it is enough to want to live close to God, to read his Word, and to trust that he watches over our course, even in difficult times.
exp.68:11:
The explanation says that the important or idle people who gathered at the city gate spoke against the psalmist. In addition, drunkards made songs mocking him. "Mock" means to wound with jeers or reproaches. The "cider" was a fermented drink, and "cider drinkers" refers to people who drink to excess.

The speaker is David, the author according to the title of the psalm, in a time of great suffering. He is criticized and ridiculed both by those who had authority, since public matters were handled and judgments made at the gate, and by ordinary people at their feasts. He had fasted and wept out of humility, and yet they mocked him. The Gospels apply other parts of this psalm to Jesus.

When someone criticizes you or mocks you, do not respond with bitterness. Do as the psalmist did: bring your pain to God in prayer and trust in his mercy.
exp.6:7:
God is the judge of all the nations. That is why David asks him to judge him too, "according to my righteousness, and according to mine integrity that is in me." Integrity here means living with a sincere heart, without duplicity. "Judge me" here is a plea that God examine his case and do him justice.

David speaks, according to the psalm's heading, while he is accused and pursued by his enemies (the text mentions a man named Cush, a Benjamite). David does not claim to be perfect. He affirms that he is innocent of this particular accusation and trusts that God, who searches the hearts, knows the truth.

For today: when you are falsely accused, do not defend yourself with bitterness. Come before God with sincerity, ask him to examine your heart, and trust that he does justice. And if he shows you a fault, acknowledge it with humility.
exp.61:6:
This verse says that everything David needs rests in God: his salvation (his deliverance) and his glory (his honor or dignity). It calls God "the rock of my strength," meaning a firm rock that makes him strong, and also his refuge, a safe place where he can shelter.

The psalm bears David's name, although the text does not say exactly when he wrote it. It is clear that he faces pressure and opposition from powerful people, and so he speaks to his own soul to remind it where its security lies. He then invites all the people to trust in the same way, and warns that putting one's hope in other people is fragile.

Today, when you feel fear or pressure, do not look first for security in money, people, or reputation. Stop and tell God honestly what you feel, pouring out your heart before him. Then rest in the fact that he is your firm refuge.
exp.112:0:
This verse begins with "Hallelujah," which in Hebrew means "praise Yah," that is, praise the Lord. It then calls on the "servants of the Lord" to praise. The verb "praise" is the ordinary word for giving praise to God. The "name of the Lord" stands for God himself: who he is and what he is like.

This is the opening of a psalm of praise. The text does not say who wrote it. The speaker invites all the people who serve God to worship him. It is one of the psalms that many Jews sang at their festivals, and the verses that follow ask that God be praised in every place and at all times.

For today: if you serve God, do not limit that service to tasks alone. Set aside a moment each day to thank him and praise him in your own words, even when your day is hard.
exp.131:13:
This verse shows God speaking about Zion, that is, Jerusalem. It says that this place will be his "rest," that is, the place where he stays and makes his home. "Forever" speaks of something lasting. God adds that he chose it because he has desired it: it was his own decision, born of his will.

The psalm recalls God's promise to David. Here God himself is speaking, according to the psalmist. Earlier it said that David's descendants would reign if they kept the covenant. Afterward it promises to bless the poor with bread and to clothe the priests with salvation. Scholars understand in several ways how the "forever" is fulfilled: in the temple, in David's kingdom, or in Christ.

For today: God desires to dwell among his people and close to you. You can set aside a few minutes each day to pray quietly, remembering that he wants to be with you, not only that you seek him.
exp.21:23:
This verse says that God did not look down on or reject the suffering of the one who is afflicted, nor did he turn his back on him. "Despised" means to treat as worthless, and "abhorred" means to feel disgust or revulsion. "Hid his face" means to ignore someone. On the contrary, when the poor man cried out, God heard him.

The psalm is spoken by David, and it begins with a cry of abandonment (the same one Jesus quoted on the cross). Here the tone changes: the psalmist has already been heard and calls all Israel to praise God. Many Christians see in this psalm a foreshadowing of Christ, although it also expresses David's own experience.

For today: when you feel small or ignored, pray with sincerity. God is not ashamed of your need. And since he does not hide his face, do not you turn away from those who suffer either.
exp.67:28:
