It says that, because of God's temple in Jerusalem, kings from other lands will come to bring him gifts. Gifts are offerings or presents, and the reason they come is the temple itself; it is what draws them near.

It is a psalm of David, a song of victory and of a procession toward the sanctuary. Some understand the temple to be the place where God reigns; others think it looks ahead to the time when Solomon would build the temple. The verses that follow speak of Egypt and Ethiopia drawing near to God, so the psalm announces that his glory will reach the nations.

For today: the God who cares for his people deserves our best. We can offer him our time, talents, and resources with gratitude, not out of obligation. Furthermore, our life of worship can be a witness that draws others to know him.
exp.103:31:
He looks at the earth, and it trembles; He touches the mountains, and they smoke. The explanation says that God is so powerful that a single look from Him is enough to make the earth shake, and a single touch from Him is enough to make the mountains smoke. The image recalls earthquakes and volcanoes, but the psalmist uses them as pictures of God's power over creation.

Psalm 104 is a hymn of praise to God as Creator. The author is not identified in the text; tradition often associates it with David, though this is not certain. Earlier, the psalmist speaks of how God sustains and renews life. Afterward, he responds with a personal commitment: to sing to God all his life and to rejoice in Him.

For today: when you feel small before your problems or before the force of nature, remember that God governs over all. This truth is not meant to frighten you, but to lead you to trust and to praise Him with joy, speaking with Him every day.
exp.118:44:
It says the psalmist will walk in freedom and openness, not feeling trapped or distressed, because he has earnestly sought God's commandments. The phrase "walk at liberty" means living in a spacious, safe and free place. "I have sought" indicates that he not only knows them, but has pursued them with effort.

The speaker is the author of Psalm 119, a long poem in praise of God's law. We do not know with certainty who wrote it. In the verses nearby he asks that the word of truth never be taken from his mouth, and he promises to keep it always. Here he presents obedience not as a prison, but as an open road.

Many people think that obeying God limits life. This verse invites us to see it the other way around: seeking his will frees us from guilt, lies and unnecessary burdens. Today you can read a passage of the Bible each day and ask yourself: "What concrete step can I take today?"
exp.118:42:
Here the psalmist asks God not to take "the word of truth" out of his mouth, meaning that it should never fail him when he needs to speak it with firmness. He says he has hoped in God's judgments, and God's decisions and righteous laws are the things in which he places his hope.

The one speaking is the author of the psalm, who is not identified with certainty. He belongs to the section of this acrostic poem about God's law that begins with the letter Vau. Earlier he asked for mercy and said he would answer those who shamed him. That is why he asks not to be silenced when he must speak of the truth.

For today: before speaking in an argument or under pressure, ask God for wisdom. Fill your mind with his Word so that, when the moment comes, you speak with truth, humility, and courage.
exp.48:17:
Although the rich man, while he lives, congratulates himself and calls himself blessed, people also praise him while things go well for him and he enjoys life. The phrase "when you do well for yourself" means that you give yourself a good life.

The psalm is a teaching of wisdom, and its heading attributes it to the sons of Korah. The author speaks so that believers will not feel envy or fear before the rich and powerful. Some understand that "you" is the people's praise directed at the rich man; others take it as a general statement. But the idea is clear: that applause lasts only a short time, because death comes for everyone.

Today, do not measure your worth or that of others by money, success, or applause. Seek first to be faithful to God, because his approval does endure.
exp.54:20:
He says there is a person whose words are soft and sweet, as smooth as butter and oil, yet there is hostility in his heart. His words seem kind, but they wound like knives. The words that describe his speech speak of pleasant and deceptive language, and the picture of war refers to an intention to do harm.

The speaker is David, although the psalm does not say exactly what moment of his life it refers to. He is hurt by the betrayal of someone close who broke their covenant of friendship (vv. 12-14, 20). So he cries out to God, and afterward he takes heart and casts his burden on Him.

Today we can learn not to be fooled only by pleasant words, but to look at actions as well. And if someone betrays us, we can bring that pain honestly to God and trust that He sustains us.
exp.54:11:
It says that the deepest pain does not come from an openly declared enemy. An insult from someone who hates us can be endured, and one could even hide from it. To "reproach" means to insult or shame someone in public. "Lifted himself up against me" means that he rose up with pride to attack me.

The one speaking is David, according to the title of the psalm, although we do not know with certainty the exact moment of his life. He is distressed by the violence and deceit in his city. What hurts him most is that the blow comes from a close friend, as the following verses show. Some think of Ahithophel, but the text does not say so.

Today, if someone close to us hurts us, it is natural that it stings more than an offense from a stranger. We can do as David did: tell God everything, without hiding anything. He listens and sustains the wounded heart, and he also helps us to forgive with wisdom.
exp.127:0:
This verse says that happy and blessed is the one who fears the Lord and walks in his ways. "A Song of degrees" is the title of the psalm; "blessed" means happy, truly content. "Fear the Lord" does not mean being afraid, but honoring him and taking him seriously. "Walk in his ways" means living each day as he teaches.

The psalm does not say who wrote it. It is one of the songs of the pilgrims who went up to Jerusalem; scholars do not agree on the exact meaning of the title. The following verses describe the blessing with images from everyday life: work, a wife, and children. They are pictures of general blessing, not automatic promises for every case.

For today: the happiness that God gives begins in everyday life. Before asking for blessings, ask yourself how you can honor him today in your work, your home, and your decisions, and take one concrete step of obedience.
exp.82:11:
This verse describes what Israel's enemies say: "Let us take for ourselves the pastures and the dwelling places of God as our inheritance." The word "dwelling places" can refer to the places where God dwells, such as the land of Israel or his temple. Some translations say "the pastures of God," so the exact meaning is understood in different ways.

Asaph prays in this psalm while several neighboring nations join together against Israel with a plan to destroy it. He asks God to act as he did in the past, when he defeated Midian in the time of the judges. Israel's enemies were also opposing God himself.

Today we can remember that when something that belongs to God is attacked, we do not have to respond with hatred or with our own strength. We can bring it to God in prayer with sincerity, trusting that he is just and defends what is his.
exp.64:10:
He says God "crowns" the year, meaning he crowns it like a king who rewards: he fills the whole year with his goodness. "Goodness" here refers to his gifts and provision. "Your paths drop fatness" means his paths overflow with abundance: the rain makes the land fertile and produces food in plenty. "Fatness" here means richness and fertility, not grease in a bad sense.

It is a psalm of David, a song of praise for the people of Israel. It thanks God for the rain, the harvests, and the care of the land. The verses before speak of how God waters and prepares the field; the verses after, of how the deserts, the hills, and the valleys fill with life. For the Israelites, rain and harvest were not automatic, but a gift from God.

For today: before eating, or at the end of a year of work, stop to give thanks. Recognize that what you have comes from the generous hand of God, and share with someone in need.
exp.35:0:
This verse says that David, the servant of the Lord, wrote this psalm for the chief musician. He states that the wickedness of the ungodly speaks to the heart, that is, it makes plain something very clear: that person has no fear of God. He does not respect God or take Him into account in the way he lives. The word "ungodly" means someone who lives as if God did not exist.

David speaks as an observer of the conduct of wicked people. The verses that follow show how that person deceives himself, speaks falsely, and does not want to do good. Some scholars translate the phrase differently, as "wickedness speaks to the ungodly person deep within his heart," and the meaning shifts a little. Both readings are possible.

Today we can ask ourselves whether our daily decisions take God into account. The fear of God, which is respect and trust in Him, protects us from deceiving ourselves and moves us to speak the truth and do what is good.
exp.138:2:
This verse says that God knows everything I do: when I walk and when I rest. "Path" is the way I travel, and "my lying down" refers to my time of rest. "Thou compassest" can be understood as God examining or watching closely. "Art acquainted with" all my ways is an old expression meaning that God knows well every one of my paths.

David is the speaker, according to the title of the psalm. He reflects with wonder on how well God knows him: his movements, his thoughts, and even his words before he speaks them. The verses nearby show that this is not a cold kind of knowledge, but the knowledge of someone who cares for him and protects him with his hand.

For today: you can live your daily life without pretending before God. He knows your tiredness, your decisions, and your routines. Speak with Him sincerely, knowing that He knows you and walks with you.
exp.39:13:
The explanation says David asks that those who seek to take his life be ashamed and confounded together. The verse's own word "together" covers this. It also asks that those who wish him harm be driven backward and put to shame. The phrase "cut her off" refers to ending his life.

David speaks, according to the psalm's heading. He has just thanked God for rescuing him in the past, but now he feels surrounded by troubles and acknowledges his own failings. With a weary heart, he cries out to God for help. It is a prayer of distress, yet made with confidence. Some scholars see in this psalm a foreshadowing of Christ, since the New Testament quotes part of it in Hebrews 10.

For today: when you feel attacked or overwhelmed, bring your distress to God honestly instead of seeking revenge. Ask him to defend your cause, and remember how he has helped you before.
exp.104:8:
God remembers his covenant forever, the one he made with Abraham. The explanation also speaks of the oath he swore to Isaac, meaning the solemn promise he renewed with him.

The psalmist speaks to the people of Israel and invites them to praise God for his faithfulness. He recalls that God promised the land of Canaan to Abraham, and that this promise passed to Isaac and then to Jacob. These promises are found in Genesis, for example in Genesis 15 and 26. The psalm wants the people to remember that their history rests on the word of God.

For today: God keeps what he promises, even when it takes generations. When you doubt that he sustains you, remember how faithful he has been in the past and trust his word. You can write down the promises of the Bible that encourage you most and review them in prayer.
exp.85:9:
It says that God is great and does marvelous things, that is, works that cause wonder and that no one else can do. It ends with a firm statement: the Lord alone is God. Its wording about "doer" refers to the one who makes or carries out something, and it is written in that sense in the verse.

The passage is spoken by David, according to the title of the psalm, and it is a prayer in a time of distress. Shortly before, he asks God to hear him because he is afflicted and in need. Before asking for help, he remembers who God is. After this verse, he asks to be taught to walk in the Lord's truth and promises to praise him with all his heart.

When you are worried, begin your prayer by remembering who God is, not only what you need. Think of something He has done in your life and give Him thanks. Looking at His greatness helps you see your problems with more confidence and peace.
exp.89:4:
It says that God carries people away like a flood of water, that is, like a river's sudden rush that comes with force and passes quickly. It also compares life to a sleep that fades when one wakes, and to grass that sprouts in the morning. The "carriest them away as with a flood" phrase describes a sudden flood.

Psalm 90 is attributed to Moses and is a prayer addressed to God. Moses contrasts the eternity of God with the brevity of human life. The psalm also connects that frailty with mortality and with the consequences of sin. Some scholars think it reflects the years in the desert, but that cannot be stated with certainty.

For today: since life is short, do not spend it on what does not matter. Today ask God for wisdom to use your time well, and devote it to loving, forgiving, and serving.
exp.49:14:
This verse invites us to ask God for help when we are in trouble. Asking for help means calling out to him or speaking to him directly. "Trouble" refers to a time of distress, pain or affliction. God promises to rescue, and the one who is rescued responds by giving him honor, that is, by acknowledging that he is the one who helped.

In this psalm God himself speaks, as judge of his people. He tells them that he does not need animal sacrifices, because everything belongs to him. What he desires is a grateful heart and faithfulness to his promises. Afterward, the psalm warns those who talk about God but live without obeying him.

For today: when a difficulty arrives, do not wait to solve it alone. Speak with God honestly, trust him, and when he helps you, thank him openly. A relationship with God is based on trust and gratitude, not on empty routines.
exp.117:5:
He says that God is on his side, and so he is not afraid of what other people might do to him. The expression "is for me" means that God supports and defends him. "I will fear" means "I will be afraid." The line does not deny that there are people who do harm, but affirms that their power has a limit when set against God.

The one speaking is a psalmist who went through a severe distress. Earlier he tells how he cried out to God, and that God answered him and brought him out into a wide place, that is, into freedom. Then he speaks of enemies and concludes that it is better to trust in God than in people. We do not know with certainty who wrote it or the exact situation; many see it as a song of thanksgiving of the people.

Today, when you feel fear of criticism, rejection, or a threat, pray sincerely and remember that God is with you. That helps you act with calm and courage.
exp.70:19:
He says that God, who let the psalmist go through many troubles and hardships, will give him life again and lift him up once more "from the depths of the earth." The depths of the earth are an image of the very lowest place: extreme danger, suffering, or closeness to death. It can be understood as a figure of pain, and some also see it as hope of rescue from death.

The psalm does not say who wrote it. It speaks as an elderly believer who has lived through long trials and asks God not to abandon him in old age. He wants to keep telling the next generation about God's works. So in this verse he remembers the difficult past and trusts that God will sustain him again.

For today: when you go through a dark season, remember how God has sustained you before. Write down one of those times and give thanks for it, asking him for strength to keep trusting.
exp.131:11:
This verse says that God promises David that his descendants will reign forever, on one condition: that they keep his covenant and his instructions. The word "keep" in the verse is the one that matters here, meaning to observe or fulfill; "testimony" refers to the commands God gives as a sign of his covenant; "covenant" is the agreement between God and his people.

Psalm 132 is a prayer of Israel that reminds God of the promise made to David. Here we hear God's answer: his promise still stands, but each generation must live in obedience. Christians often see its final fulfillment in Jesus, a descendant of David, although the kings of Israel were not always faithful.

For today: faith is lived out and also passed on. If we want our children to know God, let us teach them by our example and by his Word, trusting that God is faithful.
exp.22:4:
God says he prepares a table full of food for the believer, even while his enemies are watching. The word "prepare" here means to set in order and get ready. The "enemies" are those who cause distress or persecution. Anointing the head with oil was a gesture of honor and care toward a guest. A cup that is overflowing speaks of abundance, more than what is needed.

The one speaking is David, according to the title of the psalm. Earlier he described himself as a sheep guided by its shepherd. Here the picture seems to shift to that of a generous host. Some think this is a scene of hospitality; others think it continues the idea of the shepherd who prepares the pasture. In both cases, David trusts in God's protection in the midst of danger.

For today: when you face opposition or fear, do not think only about the problem. Give thanks for what God has already given you, and rest in the fact that he cares for you and sustains you.
exp.88:40:
Verse 41 says that all who passed by on the road plundered him, and that he became a reproach to his neighbors. The word "plundered" here is understood as stripping, robbing, or treating with contempt. "Reproach" means mockery or dishonor.

The psalmist, called Ethan the Ezrahite, speaks to God in pain. Earlier he recalled the promises made to David and to his descendants. Now he sees the king defeated and humbled, and feels that God has abandoned what was promised. It is not known with certainty what historical moment he has in mind; scholars have interpreted it in several ways. It is an honest prayer, not a complaint that rejects God.

For today: when you feel humbled, or it seems that God is not keeping his word, you can tell him so with sincerity, as this psalm does. Bring your pain to God and remember his promises, even when you do not yet see the answer.
exp.77:67:
It says that God did not choose the tribe of Ephraim, but the tribe of Judah. He also chose Mount Zion, and the text states that he loved it. "Chose" means that God made a free and deliberate decision. Mount Zion is the hill where Jerusalem and the temple later stood.

Psalm 78 was written by Asaph, who reviews the history of Israel to teach the new generations. He recalls how the people were unfaithful again and again, and how God was patient. Before this verse, God sets aside the tabernacle at Shiloh, where Ephraim had held importance. Afterward, the psalm goes on to the choice of David as the shepherd of the people. In this way it shows that God guides history according to his purpose.

For today: God acts out of love and grace, not because of human merit. You can trust that he leads your life with purpose, even when plans change.
exp.86:6:
The explanation says that those who sing and play instruments in Zion will declare that all their springs, that is, the source of their joy, their life and their blessing, are in her. "Players" are those who play instruments, and "springs" speaks of wells that give life.

This is the end of a psalm of the sons of Korah that praises Zion, the city of God. The psalmist says that God himself established her and that even people from other nations will be counted as born there. Who exactly is speaking in this verse is understood in several ways: it may be the worshipers in the temple, or all the peoples gathered in praise. Many Christians see here a shadow of God's family opened to all nations.

For today: ask yourself where you expect to draw your joy and your strength. God invites you to return to him as your spring, and to do so in community, singing and giving thanks together with other believers.
exp.22:5:
This verse says that goodness and mercy will accompany the speaker all the days of his life, and that he will live in the house of the Lord for long days. "Lord" is the name of God. "Mercy" means faithful, compassionate love. "Follow" conveys the idea of going behind, like accompanying closely. "Dwell" means "live" or "remain."

The speaker is David, according to the psalm's title, and he presents himself as a sheep cared for by its shepherd. He has just spoken of dark valleys, of enemies, and of God's provision. Now he concludes with confidence. "The house of the Lord" may refer to the sanctuary or to living near God; interpreters understand it in different ways, and many Christians also apply it to eternal life.

For today: when the day is hard, remember that God does not leave you alone. At the end of the day, write down one sign of his goodness that you have seen, and give him thanks for it.
exp.108:22:
He says that the one speaking feels his life slipping away, like the shadow that stretches out and vanishes as evening falls. He also feels shaken about like a locust, swatted away by someone's hand without being able to resist.

The speaker is David, according to the title of the psalm. He is being accused and attacked unjustly by people he had once treated with kindness. He finds himself weak, wounded inside, and without strength. For this reason he cries out to God and relies on God's mercy and on his name, not on his own merits.

For today: when you feel fragile, exhausted, or pushed aside, you do not have to pretend to be strong. You can tell God honestly how you are doing, just as David did. He hears those who feel like a passing shadow, and his mercy remains good.
exp.34:10:
False witnesses rose up against the psalmist, ready to lie about him. On top of that, they questioned him about things he had no knowledge of, as if he were guilty of something. The explanation here refers to the verse's wording: "They laid to my charge" means that they made accusations against him.

The psalm is spoken by David, according to its title. He is asking God to defend him from enemies who attack him without reason. Shortly before this, he praises God because he rescues the afflicted from those who are stronger. He then describes how he was repaid with evil for the good he had done, since he had prayed and fasted for them when they were sick. We do not know exactly when in his life this took place.

If someone accuses you unjustly, do not respond with revenge. Bring your case to God honestly, keep doing good, and trust that he knows the truth even when others distort it.
exp.88:3:
God promises to establish David's descendants forever and to uphold his throne through all generations. "Seed" means offspring or family line. "Build up" here means to establish and sustain. "Selah" is a pause or musical marking in the song; its exact meaning is not known for certain.

The one speaking in this verse is God, as quoted by the psalmist (Ethan the Ezrahite, according to the psalm's heading). He recalls the covenant God made with David and uses it to praise the Lord's faithfulness. Later in the psalm there is grief, because the kingdom seemed to have fallen. Many Christians see in this promise its final fulfillment in Jesus, a descendant of David.

For today: when everything seems uncertain, rely on God's promises more than on what you can see. He is faithful, and his word stands even as the years pass.
exp.104:3:
Psalm 105:4 invites us to seek the Lord and his strength, that is, his power and his help. The phrase "seek his face evermore" means to make it our aim to stay close to him, to live in his presence. The word "seek" does not describe a one-time action but something constant.

The psalm does not say who wrote it, but tradition connects it with the song of praise sung by King David when the ark arrived in Jerusalem (1 Chronicles 16 contains a very similar text). Here the people of Israel are called to sing and to remember the wonders of God, because he had been faithful to Abraham and to Jacob.

For today: before facing your day, set aside a few minutes to speak with God and to read his Word. Do not seek him only when you have problems, but as a daily habit of trust.
exp.4:11:
In Psalm 5:12, God is said to bless the righteous and to surround them with his favor, as if he put a shield all around them. The word "surround" is the one the verse uses here: he surrounds them with favor. "Favor" here means goodwill, kindness and grace toward them. Here "righteous" refers to someone who lives faithfully before God and trusts in him; it does not mean someone who is perfect.

The psalm is attributed to David in its heading. He prays in the morning while surrounded by enemies and by people who lie and act violently. He asks God for help and ends with confidence: those who take refuge in the Lord will rejoice. This verse closes the prayer with a promise of protection.

For today: when you feel surrounded by pressure, criticism or fear, begin the day praying as David did. Entrust your path to God and remember that his goodness covers you. This does not promise that there will be no difficulties, but it does mean you do not face them alone.
exp.120:0:
The psalmist says he will lift up his eyes to the hills and asks where his help will come from. "Song of ascents" is the title given to Psalms 120 through 134; the word "ascents" relates to going up. "Help" means aid in a time of need. It is a question, and the next verse gives the answer.

Many believe this song was sung by pilgrims climbing up to Jerusalem, a road surrounded by mountains and full of dangers. The hills could be seen with fear, or also as places of false gods; scholars understand it in several ways. In any case, the psalmist turns his gaze from the landscape toward God, his true protector.

When you feel fear or need, pause and lift your eyes. Instead of trusting only in your own resources or in what you see, say to God simply: "My help comes from you."
exp.65:13:
This verse continues the previous line: the psalmist will pay the vows that my lips uttered and my mouth spoke when I was in trouble, that is, in a time of great distress or suffering. A vow was a promise made to God, and here the person remembers that they made it with their own words.

The speaker may be the people or a single individual; the psalm moves from "we" to "I." It speaks after having passed through trials, described as fire and waters, and after having been rescued. Now he comes to the temple with offerings to fulfill what was promised. Some see in this a collective voice of Israel, others the voice of one believer.

For today: if in a difficult moment you promised something to God, do not forget it when things get better. Keeping your word, with gratitude and simplicity, is a way of honoring him and remembering his faithfulness.
exp.30:21:
The explanation says that the psalmist, in the middle of his anguish and distress, thought that God had hidden him from his sight. Here the sense of being hurried and pressed by trouble is conveyed by the verse's own words "in my haste," and the sense of being cut off is conveyed by "I am cut off from before thine eyes." But God did hear his voice when he cried out to him.

The psalm is spoken by David, according to its heading. He was under pressure, slandered, and surrounded by enemies. At that moment he felt that God was far away. Afterward he acknowledges that his feeling did not match reality: God had heard him, and for that reason he ends by praising him and encouraging others to trust.

For today: when you feel that God does not see you or has left you alone, do not keep silent. Cry out to him honestly, even with your doubts. Your feelings in a crisis can deceive you, but God remains attentive to your voice.
exp.104:18:
It says that Joseph went through the trial of slavery and prison until the time came when what God had said was fulfilled. The phrase "his word" can refer to Joseph's word, that is, what he foretold or his dreams, and "the word of the Lord" is what God had announced. The word "tried" means that he was tested or refined, the way gold is tested.

This psalm recalls God's works with Israel. The psalmist tells how God sent Joseph to Egypt, even by the road of suffering, to preserve his people. The verses that follow show the outcome: the king released him and put him in charge of everything. Some understand that the trial was for Joseph, others that the word of God proved that Joseph was faithful.

Today, when you wait for a promise from God and everything seems to go the wrong way, remember that waiting does not mean abandonment. God may be forming your character. Keep being faithful in small things while his time arrives.
exp.135:2:
This verse invites us to praise God as "Lord of lords," that is, the highest ruler, above any other power. The word "mercy" here translates the Hebrew term "hesed," which speaks of a faithful, loyal love that does not abandon. It says that this love lasts "forever."

It is a psalm of praise that was probably sung in the worship of the people of Israel. It seems to be a prayer led by a leader, and the people responded with the refrain "his mercy endures forever." Then the psalm recalls creation and the deliverance from Egypt. The reason is to give thanks for what God has done for his people.

Today we can remember that no authority, problem, or fear is above God. When you feel small or insecure, repeat this truth in prayer: his faithful love does not run out. Thank him for one concrete sign of his care this week.
exp.1:4:
What it says: God, after laughing at the kings who rebel, now speaks to them in anger. The word translated "vex" means to frighten them, leaving them terrified. "Wrath" and "sore displeasure" speak of his righteous anger at wickedness and rebellion. The phrase "shall he speak unto them" is an older way of saying "he will speak to them."

Context: The psalmist describes the nations and their rulers who want to free themselves from God's rule and that of his anointed, calling his authority "bonds." God is not alarmed by their rebellion; first he laughs, and then he answers them. Immediately he declares that he has already set his king on Zion. Many Christians see here a reference to Christ; the psalm first spoke of the king of Israel.

For today: No one can live against God without consequences. But his warning is also an invitation to return. Today you can ask yourself: is there any area of my life where I resist his direction? Surrender it with humility before your heart grows hard.
exp.32:11:
The explanation says that the people who have the Lord as their God are happy and privileged. The word "blessed" means happy, favored. The word "nation" and "people" refer to a nation. "Inheritance" is a very dear possession, something a person treasures and cares for. God chose his people to be his own.

The psalm is a song of praise, and the text does not say who wrote it, although tradition connects it with David. It comes after saying that human plans can fail, but God's plan remains. Here the psalmist first speaks of Israel, the people God chose. Then he remembers that God looks upon all of humanity.

For today: true happiness does not depend on a country's power or fortune, but on living under God's care. This week, instead of worrying about the news or about your own plans, take a moment to thank him for belonging to him and entrust your concerns to him.
exp.107:8:
God claims authority over the peoples who live around Israel. Moab, which was an enemy, is left as a humble basin for washing the feet. Throwing a sandal over Edom is usually understood as a sign of ownership or rule, though scholars explain it in several ways. Here the verse names the Philistines, and God says he will rejoice in his victory over them.

God speaks from his sanctuary, and the psalmist, David, repeats his promise to ask for help. God had already declared the lands of Israel and the tribe of Judah to be his. Then the psalmist acknowledges that he needs God to lead him against Edom, since without him the armies do not advance.

When you face something that seems very large, remember that God has the last word. Trust his promises, but walk with humility, asking for his guidance at every step.
exp.71:7:
It says that the king the psalm speaks of will have wide rule, "from sea to sea," that is, from one end to the other. "The river" probably refers to the Euphrates, and "the ends of the earth" means the most distant places. "Will rule" means that he will govern with authority.

This psalm is titled as belonging to Solomon, though some think it was a prayer by David for his son, the new king. The speaker asks God that the king govern with justice and peace. Over time, Christians have seen in it a picture of Jesus, the perfect King, whose kingdom has no borders.

For today: this verse invites us to trust that Christ reigns over all, even when the world seems disordered. We can pray for our leaders and live with justice and peace in our surroundings, knowing that his kingdom continues to grow.
exp.9:11:
This verse is an urgent prayer. The psalmist asks God to rise up and act, to "lift up thine hand," a way of speaking about God using his power to intervene and defend. He also asks that God not forget the poor, that is, the humble and afflicted who suffer injustice.

The one speaking is the psalmist, probably a believer who sees a wicked man oppressing the weak. That wicked man thinks God has forgotten and that he sees nothing. The psalmist does not accept that lie and brings it before God in prayer. Afterward he affirms that God does see the suffering and that the poor find refuge in him.

For today: when you see an injustice and feel weary, pray sincerely, as the psalmist did. Ask God to act, and ask him how you can help someone who is suffering near you.
exp.84:11:
This verse says that God himself will give what is good, and that the people's land will respond with its harvest. "The good" is everything that comes from his goodness: blessing, peace, and provision. The harvest is what the land produces, but it can also be understood as a life that flourishes under God's favor.

Psalm 85 is a prayer of the sons of Korah. It seems to have been written after God restored his people, though it is not known for certain when. The verses before it speak of mercy, truth, righteousness, and peace meeting together. Now the psalmist trusts that God will keep acting, and that his work will be seen in the people's daily life.

For today: trust that God is the source of all that is good, and at the same time do your part faithfully. Sow with honesty in your work and in your family, and wait with gratitude for God to give the growth.
exp.119:4:
Here the psalmist expresses his distress: "Woe is me" is a cry of lament. He says that he lives as a stranger, a sojourner, in Mesech and dwells among the tents of Kedar. "Sojourn" here means to reside as an outsider, without feeling at home. Mesech and Kedar were distant peoples, known for their harsh character.

The speaker is a believer surrounded by deceitful and violent people, as the preceding verses about the deceitful tongue show. He probably uses the names figuratively, since it is not clear that he literally lived there; many understand it as a way of saying that he feels himself among people hostile to peace. This psalm opens the songs of ascents, which pilgrims sang on their way to Jerusalem.

For today: if you feel out of place in settings of mockery or deceit, you are not alone. Bring your complaint to God honestly, and make an effort to remain a person of peace.
exp.73:17:
Remember this, the psalm says: an enemy has insulted the Lord, and a foolish people has spoken against your name. The words "insulted" and "spoken against" are the ones that matter here, meaning mockery and contempt directed at God.

It is part of a psalm of Asaph, a prayer of lament. It probably reflects the destruction of the temple and of Jerusalem, although scholars debate whether it refers to the fall before Babylon or to some other moment. The people cry out because they see that the name of God is being dishonored. Before asking for help, they remember that God is lord of the day, the night, and the seasons.

When you see people mocking God or the faith, do not respond with resentment. Pray honestly, remembering that God governs all things, and ask him to defend his name and to give you patience and trust.
exp.149:5:
It says that every living creature with breath should praise God. The word "Hallelujah" means "praise the Lord." The phrase "let it praise" is an old form of invitation or command: let everything praise.

The author of the psalm is not identified in this passage. It is the last of the psalms, and it closes the whole book with a great call to praise. Before this, the verses mention instruments: flutes, strings, cymbals. With this, the psalmist shows that worship can be joyful, varied, and shared by the whole people. Some understand "everything that has breath" as all people; others as all living creation. The text allows both readings.

Today, each breath can remind you that life is a gift. Before you start your day, pause, take a deep breath, and thank God out loud for one specific thing. In this way your breath becomes a small act of praise.
exp.138:12:
What it says: David states that God "possessed" his inmost parts, meaning that God formed him inwardly and belongs to him. In biblical language, the kidneys represent what is most intimate: emotions, thoughts, and conscience. The word for "covered" means the way one who protects and carefully shapes a baby in the womb does.

Context: David speaks in prayer. He has just said that there is no place, not even darkness, where he can hide from God. Now he remembers that God has known him this way since before he was born. His knowledge is not distant but that of a near Creator. This leads him to praise.

For today: If God formed you and knows you within, you do not need to pretend before Him. Today you can bring Him your fears and doubts with sincerity, trusting that your life has value from its origin.
exp.147:8:
This verse continues the list of created things that are called to praise God. Here appear the mountains and all the hills (the smaller rises of land), the fruit trees and all the cedars. Thus, from what is highest and most firm to what gives food, everything is invited to honor the Lord.

The psalm does not name its author. The one speaking is a psalmist who calls the whole universe to praise the LORD, first in the heavens (verses 1-6) and then on the earth. After the mountains and the trees, the list goes on to the animals and to the kings and peoples, until it reaches human beings. It is poetic language: we do not know whether the mountains literally "sing," but the whole of creation shows the greatness of God.

For today: the next time you see a tree or a mountain, pause for a moment and thank God for it. May creation remind you to praise him too.
exp.147:11:
This verse continues the list of those who are to praise God. The young men, the maidens, the old men, and the children are named, so that every age and both sexes are included.

The psalm does not name an author, and we do not know for certain who wrote it. The psalmist calls all of creation to praise the LORD: the heavens, the angels, the animals, the rulers, and here the ordinary people of every age. The reason is that the name of God alone is exalted, and his glory is above heaven and earth.

For today: praise is not only for adults or for those who are especially mature in faith. We can look for ways to worship together in the family and in the church, where children and the elderly sing, pray, and give thanks side by side, and encourage one another.
exp.9:9:
He crouches and lowers himself, like a wild beast ready to pounce, and says that many unfortunate people, that is, poor folk with no defense, fall by his strength. The word "unfortunate" refers to those who suffer from misfortune or injustice. Some translations render the Hebrew differently, but the general idea is the same.

The psalmist, traditionally attributed to David though the text does not say so, complains before God. He describes the wicked person as a lion or hunter who lies in hiding places to catch the weak in his net. He thinks God does not see and does not care what he does. That is why the psalm ends by asking God to rise up.

For today: if you see injustice, do not stay silent or believe that God is not watching. Pray with sincerity, as the psalmist did, and look for ways to protect or stand with a vulnerable person near you.
exp.125:0:
It says that when God brings his exiled people back, the joy will be so great that it will seem like a dream. The heading "A Song of degrees" is the title of a psalm that was probably sung by the pilgrims going up to Jerusalem. The phrase "turned again" means to bring back, and "captivity" refers to the exile or to the restoration of the people.

The speaker is the people of Israel, who remember with joy their return to Zion. Many think it refers to the return from Babylon, but the text does not say so with certainty. The verses that follow show laughter, praise, and amazement, even among the other nations, because they recognize that God acted.

For today: if you are going through a season of pain or waiting, remember what God has already done in your life and in his people. That feeds hope. And when restoration comes, do not forget to thank him with joy and praise.
exp.118:155:
It says that God has great mercies, that is, a very great compassion and love. For this reason the psalmist asks him: "give me life," which in today's language is "give me life" or "restore my strength." He asks that this life come "according to your judgments," that is, according to God's just decisions and his way of governing.

The one speaking is the author of Psalm 119, whose identity is not known for certain; some think of David, but the Bible does not say so here. He is surrounded by enemies and by people who despise God's law, and this grieves him. For that reason he does not rely on his own merits, but on the mercy of God.

For today: when you feel tired or under pressure, do not rely only on your own strength. Ask God to renew you, trusting in his mercy, and return to his Word to receive encouragement and direction.
exp.117:8:
This verse says that it is wiser and safer to place our trust in God than in rulers or powerful people. "To trust" here means to rely on, to take refuge in. "The Lord" is the name of God, and "princes" are leaders or authorities who hold power.

Psalm 118 is a song of thanksgiving. The one speaking was surrounded by enemies and saw God deliver them. We do not know for certain who wrote it; some think it is a king speaking, or the whole nation of Israel. From that experience it says: the powerful may fail, but God is faithful. This verse sits almost at the center of the whole Bible.

For today: respect your authorities and use the resources you have, but do not place your final hope in them. When you face a need or a difficult decision, first put your trust in God in prayer, and then act with wisdom.
exp.139:12:
The explanation says that righteous people will give thanks and honor God, and that the upright, that is, those who live with sincerity and honesty, will live close to Him. "Give thanks unto thy name" means recognizing who God is and what He does. "Dwell in thy presence" speaks of living under His care, in fellowship with Him.

This psalm is attributed to David. He is surrounded by violent and deceitful people, and he asks God to protect him. In the verses before, he trusts that God will bring justice to the afflicted and the poor. This verse closes the psalm with hope: after distress, those who trust in God end up thanking Him and staying close to Him.

When you go through injustice or hurtful words, don't stop at complaining. Walk with integrity, and take time today to thank God for something specific, trusting that He sustains you.
exp.51:8:
David says that he will praise God forever for what He has done. He also says that he will keep trusting in God's name, that is, in who God is, because His character is good. He will do this in the company of the "saints," who are the faithful, the people of God.

The psalm's title attributes it to David and connects it with the betrayal by Doeg the Edomite, who reported Ahimelech to Saul. David contrasts the wicked man who trusted in his riches with himself, who feels like a green olive tree, protected in the house of God.

Today we can thank God out loud, together with other believers, and trust in Him more than in money or in our own personal security.
exp.103:23:
This verse is an exclamation of wonder. It says that God's works are very many, and that he made them all with wisdom. The name of God in this translation is "the Lord." The good gifts and provisions that God gives are called "benefits"; the earth is full of them.

The psalm does not say who wrote it. It is a song of praise to God as Creator, who cares for his creation. Earlier, the psalmist describes how the animals hide when the sun rises, and how people go out to their work until the evening. Then he looks toward the sea and its creatures. Faced with such a well-ordered world, the writer can do nothing but marvel and worship.

For today: during the day, pause for a moment to notice something God has placed within your reach, such as food, rain, a tree, or the work you have. Give thanks for it. In this way, the routine becomes a reason for praise.
exp.60:6:
He says the king will remain forever in God's presence. And he asks that mercy and truth, that is, God's faithful love and his faithfulness, would watch over him and keep him steady. The phrase about preparing that they would preserve him sounds old-fashioned; it means "command that they guard him."

The one speaking is David, or a king of Israel, depending on how the psalm is understood. He cries out to God from a place of distress, far from home, and trusts that God has heard him. Here he prays for the king, whether himself or his descendant. Many Christians also see a look toward Christ, the eternal King, although that is an interpretation.

Today we can rest in the fact that it is not our own strength that sustains us, but the love and faithfulness of God. When you feel insecure, pray with confidence: "Lord, care for me with your mercy and your truth." Then give thanks each day, as the psalmist does.
exp.85:8:
The explanation says that all the peoples God created, not only Israel, will one day come before Him. To "bow down" means to lower oneself in respect and acknowledge that He is God. "Glorify" means to honor and praise His name. The word for "nations" refers to the peoples of the earth.

It is a prayer of David, who cries out to God on a day of distress and trusts that He answers. Before and after the verse, David says that there is no one like God and that only He is great. From that trust, he looks beyond his own need and hopes that all peoples will acknowledge their Creator. How and when this will happen, Christians understand in various ways.

For today: when you have problems, pray with confidence, but do not lose sight of the fact that God is the God of all. Ask Him to teach you to love people from other nations and to share His goodness with them.
exp.8:18:
This verse is a prayer. The psalmist asks God to act. The word for "Arise" is a way of saying "step in and show your power," so the request is for God to rise up and intervene. He asks that man not prevail, meaning that the proud human being should not think of himself as invincible or have the final word. "The heathen" are the nations, and "be judged in thy sight" means that God should examine them and bring about justice.

The speaker is David, according to the heading of the psalm. He has just given thanks to God for rescuing him from his enemies and for not forgetting the poor. Now he asks that God continue to act, and in the following verse he asks that the nations recognize that they are only human.

For today: when you see that human power seems to dominate everything and injustice is advancing, do not lose heart or take revenge. Bring your concern to God in prayer, trusting that he is the righteous Judge and that he does not forget those who suffer.
exp.17:13:
The explanation says that God launched his arrows, meaning his shafts, and with them scattered the enemies. He also sent lightning and destroyed them. The sentence that explains the word "arrows" (flechas) and the word for "scattered" can be dropped, since those words appear in the verse. The phrase "discomfited them" is rendered as making them flee in disorder, and "shot out" as launching them or making them fall.

David speaks in a song of thanksgiving after God rescued him from Saul and all his enemies. He uses images of storm, thunder, hail and fire to describe God's power. These are poetic figures: David does not say that literal arrows fell from heaven, but that God acted with great force to deliver him.

When you feel cornered by problems bigger than you, remember that God hears and can act on your behalf. Call on Him with confidence, and leave in His hands what you cannot resolve.
exp.57:0:
This verse begins with a note for the choir director: the tune is called "Do Not Destroy," and michtam is a word whose exact meaning is not known for certain. Then David asks a "congregation" with irony: do you really speak righteousness? Do you judge uprightly, O sons of men? The word "congregation" may refer to judges or rulers, though some understand it as "mighty ones" or even "gods," depending on the Hebrew.

David speaks like someone suffering from unjust decisions. The verses that follow show that these judges were doing evil in secret and committing violence. That is why the psalm is a complaint and a plea for God, the true Judge, to act.

For today: if you have authority, at home, at work, or in the church, ask yourself whether you judge with truth and without favoritism. And if you suffer an injustice, you can bring it to God honestly.
exp.80:10:
It says that the people of Israel did not listen to God's voice and would not obey him. "Would not hearken" means they paid no attention, and "would none of me" means they did not accept him or want him as their God.

Here God himself speaks, in a psalm of Asaph that recalls the deliverance from Egypt. God had asked them not to worship other gods, and he promised to give them more than they asked for. Even so, they turned away. Because of this, in the verses that follow, God lets them follow their own plans, and he laments what might have been.

For today: God does not only want us to know him, but to listen to him. Today you can choose one thing you already know he asks of you, and obey it with trust, without putting it off.
exp.96:2:
When God comes as King, a fire goes before him. That fire burns all around those who oppose him. Its picture of his holiness and power is a powerful one.

The psalm does not say who wrote it. It is a song of praise that celebrates that the LORD reigns. Earlier it speaks of joy for the whole earth, and then it describes lightnings and mountains melting. The fire is poetic language for God's presence, as at Sinai. It shows that his reign is just and that evil does not stand before him.

For today: you do not have to fear that evil has the last word. Trust that God is just, and it is your part to live with reverence, leaving judgment to him and bringing your wrongdoing to him with hope.
exp.6:1:
David says he fears that his enemy will catch him and take his life, like a lion that seizes its prey and tears it to pieces. And the worst part is that there is no one to rescue him.

To "tear my soul" means to take his life away by violence. To "deliver" here means to rescue or save.

David speaks in prayer to God. The title of the psalm mentions Cush, a son of Benjamin, but the Bible does not tell us who he was or what he did, so it is not known for certain. It appears that David is being accused and pursued unjustly. That is why he runs to God and, in the verses that follow, declares that his hands are clean.

For today: when you feel cornered, without help and afraid, do not keep your anguish to yourself. Speak to God with complete honesty, as David did, and place yourself in his hands. He is the deliverer who is never absent.
exp.45:0:
God is said to be our refuge and our strength, and one who is always ready to help us when we go through difficult times. At the beginning there is a note for the choir director: the psalm belongs to the sons of Korah, and the word "Alamoth" probably indicates a kind of music or voices, though its exact meaning is not certain.

The psalm was sung by the people of Israel in their worship. The sons of Korah were Levites devoted to the music of the temple. The verses that follow speak of a trembling earth, falling mountains, and roaring seas, images of extreme danger. The psalmist does not deny fear or problems, but affirms that God is firmer than all of that.

For today: when a crisis comes, before searching for a thousand solutions, pray and remember that God is near and is your refuge. Tell him honestly what you feel and ask him for help.
exp.36:0:
This verse asks us not to become angry or troubled over wicked people who seem to get away with what they do. "Fret" means to become agitated or upset inside, to be irritated. The "evildoers" are those who deliberately cause harm. "Envious" means wanting what others have, even when they got it by doing wrong. "Iniquity" means wickedness or injustice.

The psalm is attributed to David, according to its heading. He speaks as someone with experience and as a father giving advice. The verses that follow explain the reason: the wicked pass away quickly, like grass that is cut down. By contrast, the person who trusts in God and does good has a secure future. Scholars agree that it is a wisdom psalm, though it is not known at what exact moment in David's life he wrote it.

For today: when you see an unjust person prospering, do not feed resentment or comparisons. Hand that feeling over to God in prayer, and decide to do one concrete good deed today.
exp.70:0:
It says the psalmist trusts in Jehovah, that is, in the Lord. The verse's wording "in thee... do I put my trust" expresses the idea of trusting or taking refuge. The word "confused" is an old word meaning ashamed, defeated, or let down. So he prays: "Lord, in you I trust; let me never be put to shame."

The psalm does not say who wrote it; it has no title. The one speaking is a person who has known God for a long time and is now going through danger or attacks. That is why he asks to be rescued and calls God his rock, his stronghold, and his fortress, images of a safe place to which one can run again and again.

When you are pressed or afraid, you can begin your prayer as this psalmist does: by remembering in whom you trust. Tell God sincerely, "You are my refuge," and return to him every day, not only in times of crisis.
exp.75:2:
It says that God, in Zion, destroyed the enemy's weapons: the burning arrows of the bow, the shield, the sword, and all the equipment of war. "Arrows" here are the arrows themselves, and the war equipment means the weapons and the preparations for fighting. "Selah" is a pause or musical sign; the exact meaning is not known for certain, but it invites the reader to stop and reflect.

It is a psalm of Asaph, sung in worship, with stringed instruments. It celebrates that God defends his people from Salem (which many understand as Jerusalem) and Zion. It is not stated with certainty which victory is in view; some think of the defeat of the Assyrian army under Hezekiah, but this is an interpretation, not something the text affirms.

Today, when you feel that something stronger than you is threatening you, remember that God can disarm what seems invincible. Do your part with wisdom, but rest in the knowledge that the final victory belongs to him. Take your own pause and give him thanks.
exp.118:38:
The psalmist asks God to take away the shame or disgrace he so greatly fears. He gives the reason: God's judgments, that is, his decisions and his just way of governing, are good.

The one speaking is the author of Psalm 119, who cannot be identified with certainty. He is someone who loves God's law and lives among mockery or pressure. He comes to this point after asking God to turn his eyes from vanity and to confirm his word. It is not clear what kind of shame he means: it may have been the mockery of others or the fear of failing God. Interpreters understand it in both ways.

For today: when you fear shame or what others will say, bring that fear to God in prayer. Trust that what he says is good, even if others laugh, and ask him for the strength to follow him.
exp.90:2:
This verse promises that God will rescue you from hidden traps and from diseases that destroy. A "snare" is a trap for catching birds, and the "fowler" is the one who sets it. The "noisome pestilence" refers to a deadly epidemic or disease that sweeps everything before it.

The psalm does not say who wrote it. Some attribute it to Moses and others to David, but this is not certain. Here someone speaks to the one who trusts in God. The verses before it speak of living under the protection of the Most High and saying, "My God, in you I will trust." The promise grows out of that trust, and the images that follow, of feathers and wings, show God's care.

Today, we can begin each day by handing over to God our dangers, both hidden and visible. Trusting does not mean there will never be difficulties, but that we do not face them alone. Rest in his care.
exp.81:3:
This verse commands rescuing the person who suffers and the one who lacks what they need. "Deliver" means pulling someone out of danger or oppression. The "afflicted" are those beaten down by pain or injustice. "The wicked" are those who live without respect for God and trample on others. The request is to take the weak out of their hands.

The speaker is God himself, who in this psalm presides over a kind of court. He addresses certain rulers or judges who were meant to represent his justice. He rebukes them because they favored the wicked and neglected the poor. Some scholars think these are human judges; others think they are spiritual beings. It is understood in several ways.

For today: if you have a voice, influence, or resources, use them on behalf of someone vulnerable. You can accompany a person who has been mistreated, report an abuse, or support a needy family, without expecting anything in return.
exp.75:9:
Even human anger and violence end up serving to bring praise to God. This verse says that people's fury and violence, even when they don't intend it, can result in God being glorified, and that God sets a limit on the rage that does not serve his purposes. Other ways of rendering this verse exist, but the central idea is that God is in control.

The psalm is a song by Asaph that celebrates a victory of God in Zion. It speaks of God rising up to judge in order to save the humble. The point is that no king or enemy stands above him. It is not known with certainty which historical event it refers to.

For today: when you have to endure the anger or injustice of others, trust that God has the last word. Hand over your pain, resist the urge to take revenge, and ask him to bring something good out of the situation.
exp.146:16:
He casts out his ice like crumbs or morsels, and no one can withstand his cold. The phrase about "morsels" refers to small bits of ice or hail. The question "who can stand?" means "who can stand before his cold?" It is a rhetorical question: the answer is that no one can.

The psalm does not say who wrote it. It is a song of praise, probably from Israel after the exile (though this is interpreted in several ways). It praises God because he governs nature by his word: he sends snow, frost, and ice, and then, by his word, melts them. That same God also spoke his word to Israel.

For today: when you feel small before things you cannot control, remember that the same God who sends the winter also brings it to an end. Trust in him and rest in his care.
exp.142:7:
Here the psalmist asks God to let him hear his mercy (his faithful love and kindness) as soon as morning comes. He says he has trusted in Him and begs Him to show him the path he should walk. "Lift up the soul" means giving to God the deepest part of oneself, with complete dependence.

The psalm is attributed to David, although the text does not detail when he wrote it. He is seen as distressed, pursued by enemies, with his spirit low and feeling close to death. That is why, before asking for direction, he asks for comfort: he first needs to remember that God loves him.

For today: begin your day with a few minutes of silence, remembering God's love before looking at your problems or making decisions. Then say to Him simply: "Lord, I trust you; show me the next step today." God tends to guide those who first rest in His care.
exp.75:6:
He says that God is worthy of awe and reverence. "Awesome" does not mean evil but overwhelming, someone before whom one trembles with reverence. The question "who may stand before you?" means that no one can remain standing in front of God when his anger is stirred. "When you begin to be angry" indicates that it is enough for Him to start acting for everything to come to a halt.

The psalmist, identified as Asaph, sings of a victory that God gave Israel in Jerusalem (Zion). The strongest soldiers were left powerless, and the chariots and horses were left motionless. Scholars do not agree on which exact battle is being remembered. The author wants the people to see that salvation came from God, not from weapons.

Today, you can remember that God is greater than any problem or person who intimidates you. Trust in Him with humility and respect, knowing that He cares for the meek.
exp.8:11:
This verse says that God, when he calls to account for blood that has been shed, remembers the victims. "Demanding the blood" means that God, as a just judge, requires an answer for lives taken by violence. And he does not forget the cry of the poor, that is, of the humble and oppressed who ask for help.

The speaker is David, in a psalm of thanksgiving after a victory over his enemies. He praises God because he is a righteous judge and does not abandon those who seek him. He invites everyone to tell of his deeds. Then, in verse 13, he asks for mercy in his own affliction, trusting that God will hear him as well.

Today you can know that no unjust suffering goes unnoticed by God. If you suffer, or see others suffer, pray with confidence, without holding on to resentment or seeking revenge, and act with compassion toward those in greatest need.
exp.146:12:
He has made the bars of your gates strong, that is, the bolts or bars that secure the gates of the city. It also says that he blessed the children who live within it. "Strengthened" means he gave firmness and protection.

The psalmist calls Jerusalem, also called Zion, to praise God. We do not know for certain who wrote it or at what exact time. Some think it was after the return from exile, when the walls were rebuilt, but not everyone agrees. What is clear is that the people give thanks to God for his protection, for peace, and for the care of families.

Today we can recognize that our safety and our home depend on God, not only on our own efforts. A practical idea: before you close the door of your house at night, thank God for your family and place them in his hands.
exp.118:100:
The psalmist says here that he kept away from every evil path. Holding back his feet means that he stopped himself, that he did not let his steps carry him where he should not go. He did this with a clear purpose: to keep your word, that is, to obey what God says.

Psalm 119 is a long poem in honor of God's Word. The speaker is a believer who loves the law of the Lord, though we do not know for certain who wrote it. In the verses around it, he says that meditating on the Word gave him understanding, and that obeying it was sweeter to him than honey. His obedience grows out of delight in God, not from mere obligation.

Before making a doubtful decision, stop and ask yourself: "Does this agree with what God teaches?" If the answer is no, hold back your steps. Reading the Bible every day will help you recognize those paths in time.
exp.94:6:
He says that the Lord is our God, and that we are the people he cares for, the way a shepherd cares for his pasture and his sheep. The word "pasture" refers to the grassy land where the flock feeds. "The sheep of his hand" means that he guides and sustains us personally. Then the sentence is left open: "To day if ye will hear his voice," that is, "if today you will listen to his voice."

It is a psalm of worship, used to invite the people to praise God. First it calls them to bow down before the Creator, and here it gives the reason: God not only made everything, he also cares for his people. The closing phrase sets up a warning that continues in verse 8, about not repeating the hardness of heart that was shown at Meribah and Massah.

For today: trust that God cares for you like a good shepherd, and answer him without putting it off. Today, in prayer or while reading his Word, listen with a willing heart and obey whatever he shows you.
exp.94:2:
This verse says that the Lord is a great God and a great King, above all gods. "All the gods" refers to the gods that other peoples worshiped; the psalmist affirms that none of them compares with the God of Israel.

The psalm is a song of worship, and no one knows for certain who wrote it. It invites the people to come to God with joy and praise. This verse gives the reason: "For..." It tells them why it is worth singing to him. The verses that follow show his greatness: the earth, the mountains, and the sea belong to him.

For today: when your problems, fear, or money weigh more than everything else, remember who God is. Before asking him for something, take a moment to praise him for his greatness. That helps you see your worries from his real size, not your own.
exp.70:8:
The explanation says that the psalmist asks God not to push him away or leave him when old age comes and his strength is spent. To push away means to set aside, to reject. To leave alone means to abandon someone, leaving them without help. The word "spent" is an older way of saying "is used up."

It is a prayer psalm from an elderly person. It does not say who wrote it; some connect it with David, but this is not certain. The one speaking has trusted God since his youth and calls him his strong refuge. Now he fears being left alone, because his enemies say that God has already forsaken him. That is why his plea is so urgent.

For today: if you feel tiredness, age, or weakness, you can pray honestly, without shame, and ask God to sustain you. We can also keep company with and visit the elderly in our family or church, so that they do not feel forgotten.
exp.108:11:
He says that no one should show kindness to this man, and that no one should feel compassion for his fatherless children. The word translated here as "mercy" means kindness and help toward someone who is suffering. The phrase "extend mercy" means "to treat with kindness."

The speaker is David, according to the title of the psalm. He is crying out to God because enemies falsely accused him and repaid his love with hatred (vv. 2-5). These verses are a very harsh prayer against an adversary. Some believe David is quoting what his accusers were saying against him (v. 6 onward), but others read it as the prayer of David himself. There is no certainty.

For today: when we are wounded, we can be honest with God and hand over our pain and our desire for justice. But Jesus asks us to go further: to love our enemies and pray for them (Matthew 5:44).
exp.78:4:
Here the psalmist asks God: "How long?" He asks whether his anger will last forever and whether his jealousy, which is his firm love for his people and his holiness, will keep burning like fire.

Someone from the nation of Israel speaks, probably after Jerusalem was attacked and destroyed. There are dead left unburied and mockery from the neighboring peoples. It is not known with certainty which invasion is remembered; many think of the fall of Jerusalem to Babylon. The people feel they are suffering under God's discipline and beg him to intervene.

For today: in pain, you can bring God your most sincere questions, even the "How long?" Praying honestly is not a lack of faith; it is continuing to seek God when everything seems dark.
exp.37:17:
He says that the psalmist openly acknowledges his guilt. To declare something means to state it aloud, to confess it. His sin is his wrongdoing or failing. To be sorry is to be filled with distress, with deep sorrow. He does not hide his error: he admits it and grieves over it.

The text is attributed to David according to the heading of the psalm, although some scholars consider it a prayer that anyone who suffers might pray. He is sick, weak, and surrounded by enemies who rejoice at his fall. In the midst of that pain, he does not defend himself or blame others for everything, but acknowledges his own sin before God.

Today, when we fail, we can stop making excuses and speak with God honestly. Telling him plainly what we did, feeling the weight of it, and asking for forgiveness opens the way to healing and to a renewed heart.
exp.9:14:
Psalm 10:15 says that God should break the power of the wicked, that is, take away the strength with which he does harm. The reference to the "arm" stands for strength and the ability to oppress, and the verse itself names it: "Break thou the arm of the wicked and the evil man." Then the psalmist asks that God seek out the wickedness of the evil man until none is found, meaning that God examine it and bring it into the light until it is put to an end. The verse "seek out his wickedness" sounds like a confident request.

The psalmist, traditionally identified with David (though this psalm does not say so), speaks in prayer. He sees that the wicked oppress the poor and the orphan, and that they say in their hearts that God will not call them to account. For this reason he cries out to God as a just judge, and immediately afirms that God is an eternal King who hears the humble.

For today: when you see injustice and it fills you with anger or discouragement, bring it to God in prayer instead of taking revenge. Trust that He sees everything, and ask Him how you can help those who suffer.
exp.30:4:
He says that the psalmist places his spirit, that is, his whole life, into God's hands. The word "commit" means handing something over so that another will take care of it. He gives as his reason that God has redeemed him, which means rescued or delivered. He also calls God the God of truth, because he is faithful and does not fail in what he promises.

David speaks here, according to the heading of the psalm, and he is in a moment of danger. The verses before it speak of a hidden net, that is, a trap set by enemies. The verses that follow show that God has seen his affliction. The Gospels tell that Jesus quoted these words on the cross (Luke 23:46), and Stephen expressed something similar as he died.

When you feel fear or have no control over a situation, make a simple prayer: "Lord, into your hands I place this." Remembering how God has helped you before helps you trust again.
exp.71:15:
It says that a handful of grain, sown on the tops of the mountains, would produce so much fruit that its heads of grain would sway with a rustling sound, like the cedars of Lebanon. And the people of the cities would grow in number and strength, like the grass of the field. The phrase "shake" describes the movement of the heads of grain in the wind. It is an image of abundance springing from something very small.

This psalm is attributed to Solomon. It is a prayer for the king, and it describes what a just government would be like: it defends the poor and brings peace and prosperity. Many Christians also see here a promise that points to the Messiah, although the psalm speaks first of a king of Israel.

For today: do not despise what is small. God can make a kind word, a prayer, or an act of justice grow more than you imagine. Sow in faith, and trust that he gives the fruit.
exp.37:2:
This verse says that David's body is sick and without relief, and he feels this as a consequence of God's anger. His body is the "flesh" here, and "soundness" means health. It also says there is no peace in his bones, that is, he feels a deep discomfort, and he attributes it to his sin.

David speaks in a psalm meant to call something to remembrance. He is suffering greatly and connects it to his guilt before God. Earlier he asked that God not rebuke him in his anger. It is not known with certainty whether his illness was literal, figurative, or both, and scholars interpret it in different ways.

Today, when the weight of a wrong takes away our peace, we can do what David did: bring our sin honestly before God, ask for forgiveness, and seek his help, instead of carrying it in silence.
exp.1:2:
This verse records the words of the rebellious kings. The "bands" were the leather straps that tied oxen together under the yoke, and the "cords" were the ties that bound them. They say, "Let us break their bands asunder, and cast away their cords from us," that is, they do not want anyone to rule over them.

The speakers are the kings and rulers of the earth, mentioned in the previous verse. They join together against the LORD and his anointed, the king chosen by God. Many Christians also see here a reference to Christ. They see God's commands as an oppressive burden. The following verse shows that God is not alarmed by this rebellion.

For today: sometimes we feel that obeying God is a chain that limits us. Ask him to help you see it as a path of care, and not as a restraint. Speak with him honestly about whatever you find hard to let go of.
exp.82:5:
This verse begins to name the peoples who joined together against Israel. The "tents" here are the dwellings or camps of these peoples, so it speaks of Edom, the Ishmaelites, Moab, and the Hagarenes. The Hagarenes were descendants of Hagar, and they are sometimes linked with the Ishmaelites.

The psalm is by Asaph, and it is a prayer to the Lord. He asks for help because several neighboring nations banded together to destroy Israel completely. It is not known with certainty which historical moment is in view; there are different opinions. What is clear is that the psalmist sees this attack as hostility against God himself, since these nations had conspired against him as well.

For today: when you feel surrounded by opposition, you are not alone. Do as Asaph did: name your fears honestly before God, and rest in the fact that he cares for his people.
exp.82:13:
This verse uses two images: a fire that burns a whole mountainside and a flame that consumes the thickets, that is, the brush and the dense undergrowth. It is a comparison with the way God might act against his enemies: quickly, completely, and with no way to stop it.

The speaker is Asaph, in a psalm of prayer. Israel's neighboring nations have joined together to destroy it and take possession of the place where God is worshiped and the land itself. Asaph asks God to intervene. The language is poetic and forceful, and the psalm ends with the desire that they would seek the name of the LORD.

When you feel threatened or unfairly treated, bring your cry to God instead of taking revenge yourself. You can speak to him with complete honesty, and leave justice in his hands, asking that even your adversaries might come to know him.
exp.8:10:
This verse is an invitation to sing praises to the Lord, who dwells in Zion, that is, the place where God was present among his people. It also calls on the reader to declare his doings among the peoples, that is, among the nations.

David speaks here, according to the title of the psalm. He has just said that God is a refuge for the poor and never forsakes those who seek him. So, after acknowledging his faithfulness, he invites everyone to celebrate it. Then he reminds us that God does not forget the cry of the afflicted.

For today: when God helps you through a difficult moment, do not keep it to yourself. Tell a family member, a friend, or your church, and thank him with a song or a prayer. Your testimony can encourage others who are distressed today.
exp.14:0:
This verse is a question put to God: who may live near Him? "Tabernacle" was the sacred tent where God was worshiped, and "holy hill" refers to the holy place where God was present. "Abide" and "dwell" speak of being welcomed and remaining in fellowship with Him.

The psalm is attributed to David, and he himself raises the question. The exact occasion on which he wrote it is not known for certain. The verses that follow give the answer: the person who lives with integrity, practices righteousness, speaks the truth, and does not harm their neighbor with words or actions.

Today we can ask ourselves whether our daily lives show what we say we believe. This week, try to be honest in your words and not to speak badly of anyone behind their back. God looks for a sincere heart, not merely an outward religious appearance.
exp.105:45:
He made those who had carried them away captive to feel pity for them. Pity means feeling sorry for someone who suffers and treating them with kindness. Captives are people taken prisoner and carried off to another land. Although they were a people who had been punished, God moved the hearts of their captors to ease their situation.

The psalmist reviews the history of Israel: their rebellions and God's patience. The verses before say that God saw their distress, heard their cry, and remembered his covenant. That is why verse 47 turns into a prayer asking God to gather them from among the nations. It is not known with certainty which exact moment is meant; many connect it with the exile in Babylon.

Today we can trust that God can work even in the hearts of those who press us or treat us badly. When you are in a difficult situation, cry out to God sincerely and trust in his goodness, even if the problem arose from your own mistakes.
exp.105:6:
Our forefathers in Egypt did not grasp the wonders God performed. They did not remember the abundance of his kindness, that is, his goodness and compassion. Instead of trusting him, they rebelled by the sea, the Red Sea, as we call it today.
