The one speaking is the psalmist, who tells Israel's history as a confession. He says "we sinned along with our fathers," because he identifies himself with the sin of his people. He recalls that, when the Egyptian army came, Israel doubted God (Exodus 14). Even so, the next verse shows that God saved them for the sake of his name.

For today: when a difficulty comes, remember what God has already done for you. You can write down some of his help and thank him, so that you can trust him when you cannot see a way out.
exp.33:15:
This verse says that God sets himself against those who do evil. In the King James wording, "the face of the Lord is against them," which means that his attitude and his presence stand in opposition to them, and "to cut off the remembrance of them from the earth" means that, in the end, their memory disappears and they leave no lasting legacy.

The psalm is traditionally attributed to David, who wrote it to thank God for delivering him, according to the psalm's title (1 Samuel 21). David encourages others to trust in God. This verse contrasts with the ones before and after it: God watches closely over the righteous and hears them, but he opposes those who persist in wickedness.

Today we can remember that what we do leaves a mark. If we seek peace and do good, we live under God's care. Before acting wrongly to get ahead, it is wise to ask ourselves what kind of memory we want to leave behind.
exp.32:0:
The explanation says that those who live rightly before God (the "just" and "upright") should rejoice in the Lord. "Rejoice" means "be glad." "The Lord" is the name of God. Here "comely" means that praise suits them well, is fitting and pleasant for those who are sincere.

This psalm has no title in this version, so we cannot know for certain who wrote it; tradition attributes it to David, but this is not certain. It is a call to the community of God's people to praise with music, as seen in the following verses: harp, psaltery, and a new song. The reason is that God is faithful and powerful.

Today, before worrying about your problems, take a few minutes to thank God aloud or with a song. Sincere praise changes your focus and reminds you who He is.
exp.72:27:
The explanation says that for the psalmist, the best thing in life is to be close to God. Therefore he has placed his hope in the Lord God, that is, he trusts in Him completely. And the result is that he will be able to declare, or proclaim, all of God's works. The word "draw near" speaks of personal closeness, and "good" means what is best and most valuable.

The speaker is the psalmist, called Asaph according to the title of the psalm. He had felt envy on seeing the wicked prosper and nearly lost his faith. Upon entering God's sanctuary, he understood that turning away from Him leads to ruin. This verse closes the psalm with his decision to stay close to God.

For today: when you feel envy or feel confused by what others have, spend a few minutes in prayer and thanksgiving. Then tell someone about something good God has done for you.
exp.8:6:
This verse says that the Lord reigns forever, while the nations and the wicked pass away. "Will endure" means that he does not change and does not come to an end. "Has prepared his throne" means that his throne is already set in place, and he uses it for judgment, that is, for doing justice.

David speaks in a psalm of praise. He has just seen how God defeated powerful enemies, and how their cities and their memory were lost. Against that downfall, David stresses that God remains firm. The verses that follow explain that his judgment is fair and that he protects the poor and the one who suffers. Scholars do not agree on which specific victory David had in mind.

For today: when you see injustice or abusive power, remember that no one reigns forever, only God. You can bring your distress to him in prayer and trust that he will do justice in his time, while you keep acting with honesty and kindness.
exp.112:8:
God gives a home to the woman who could not have children, and she lives happily as the mother of a family. The woman who could not have children is the one the verse calls "the barren woman." "Hallelujah" means "praise the Lord."

The psalm is anonymous and calls God's servants to praise him. It shows that God looks on the humble: he lifts up the poor and turns the sorrow of the woman without children into joy. It recalls the song of Hannah in 1 Samuel 2. It is believed that this psalm was sung at the feasts of Israel, though the details are debated.

If you feel that your longings have gone unanswered, do not keep silent: bring them before God and praise him for who he is. He sees those whom others overlook. Also notice who is alone around you, and walk alongside them.
exp.48:19:
It says that a person who receives honor, that is, who has wealth, fame, or a good position, but does not understand what truly matters, is like the animals that die. "Á" is the old form of "a," and "perecen" means that they die and come to an end. The comparison does not despise the human being; it warns that without understanding one lives as though only this life exists.

The psalm belongs to the sons of Korah. The one speaking is a wise teacher who addresses all peoples, rich and poor. He reflects on death, which reaches even the powerful, and on false trust in money. This verse closes the psalm with a conclusion. Some scholars see here only a warning about death; others see a hope in God, as in verse 15.

Today we can ask ourselves what we value most: what others admire or what God considers valuable. Ask God for understanding to live with humility, gratitude, and hope, and not only to accumulate or to appear important.
exp.123:1:
This verse follows the idea of the previous one: if the Lord had not been on our side when men rose up against us, things would have ended very badly. "Being on our side" means being for us, supporting and defending us. "Rose up" speaks of a real attack or threat.

It is a song of pilgrims, and the title attributes it to David. Here all of Israel speaks together, since the psalm invites the people to say this aloud. They remember a time when enemies attacked them and they had no strength to resist. The text does not say what that moment was, so it is better not to invent it. What can be seen is gratitude for having been rescued.

For today: think of a difficult situation you came out of and acknowledge that God was with you, even if you did not notice it at the time. Thank Him in prayer and tell someone about it, as Israel did, so that others too may be encouraged to trust in Him.
exp.21:30:
Here the explanation says that some "will come," that is, people of future generations, and they will tell a people not yet born the righteousness that God did. The phrase "that shall be born" in the verse above carries the same meaning. "Righteousness" here refers to his faithful and upright acts, to what God did to save.

The speaker is David, according to the title of the psalm. He began crying out in pain, feeling abandoned, and ends by praising God because he was heard. That is why the ending looks forward: what God did must not be kept silent, but passed on from generation to generation. Christians often see here an echo of Jesus, who quoted the beginning of the psalm on the cross, although the text does not say so in those words.

For today: think of a time when God helped you and tell it to a son, a nephew, or a younger friend. Your simple testimony can strengthen their faith.
exp.118:149:
They draw near who pursue wickedness; they are far from your law, says the psalmist. The people who oppress him are close to doing evil, yet far from God's law. The contrast is clear: they come close to wrongdoing and move away from the Word of God.

The one speaking is the psalmist, whose name is not given in this psalm. He is going through opposition and prays at night, meditating on the words of God. He asks God for help and reminds him that he himself stays close to the law. In the following verse he affirms that God is near, and this brings him comfort in the face of his enemies.

For today: when someone treats you unjustly, do not let bitterness take hold of you. Draw closer to God, read his Word, and pray. In this way you will have wisdom and peace, even when others walk far from what is right.
exp.33:10:
Here the speaker calls to the young: "Come, ye children, hearken unto me" means, in plain words, "come, children, listen to me." He promises to teach them the fear of the Lord, that is, a reverent respect for God that includes trust and obedience, not only fear.

The psalm is attributed to David, and its heading connects it with the time he pretended to be insane before Abimelech and escaped. Now delivered, David gives thanks and speaks like a teacher, almost like a father or a wise man. After telling how God cared for him, he wants others to learn to live trusting God. The verses that follow show that this teaching is practical: guarding the tongue and turning away from evil.

Today you can be a humble learner: seek God in his Word and listen to mature people in the faith. Recognizing God in everyday life, for example by speaking honestly, is a simple way of living out that reverence.
exp.25:1:
David asks God to examine him completely. "Test me" means to put him to the test, and "search me" means to explore him thoroughly. The sentence that explains the old word "kidneys" is rewritten: the word "reins" in the verse refers to the innermost parts of a person, the feelings, desires and hidden thoughts. The word "heart" refers to the mind and the will. It is like saying: "See me from the inside, Lord."

David speaks in a psalm where he defends his integrity, that is, his desire to live uprightly. He does not claim to be perfect. Rather, he trusts in God and wants Him to confirm that his life is sincere. The following verses say that he relies on God's mercy and truth, and that he turns away from falsehood.

For today: pray with honesty and ask God to show you what is within you: motives, fears, pride. Do so without fear, because He examines in order to heal and guide, not to destroy you.
exp.49:4:
God commands that his "saints" be gathered before him, that is, his people set apart for him. They are those who made a covenant with him "by sacrifice." The words "Gather" and "gather together" in the verse are the ones the reader sees, so "Gather my saints together unto me" is the phrase to rely on.

In this psalm, by Asaph, God himself speaks. He appears as a judge who comes with fire and tempest, and he calls the heavens and the earth as witnesses. He summons his people, not to condemn outsiders, but to examine their faithfulness. The covenant by sacrifice probably recalls the covenant at Sinai, though some understand it more broadly. What follows shows that God desires sincere hearts, not only rituals.

For today: being part of God's people means commitment, not merely religious custom. Today you can ask yourself humbly: "Do my life and my obedience match what I say I believe?"
exp.78:2:
The explanation says that the enemies killed so many people in Jerusalem that their blood ran like water, and that no one was left alive to bury the dead. It was a great shame for a body to be left without burial, meaning without a proper and dignified burial.

The psalm is spoken by Asaph, or by someone from his group of singers, on behalf of the people. Jerusalem had been invaded and the temple defiled. Many believe it refers to the destruction by Babylon in 586 B.C., although the psalm does not state this clearly. It is a prayer of grief, which lays before God what has happened.

For today: when suffering is so great that there are no beautiful words, you can be honest with God. This psalm shows that prayer can also be weeping, telling God about the pain and asking for his help. We can also stand with those who suffer, so that they are not left alone.
exp.21:25:
The explanation says that the meek will eat and be satisfied. Those who seek the Lord will praise him, and then it promises: "your heart shall live for ever," meaning there will be courage and lasting life. "Satisfied" means full and content. The phrase "to the Lord" points to praising him, and "seek him" means they look for him.

David speaks in a psalm that begins with an anguished cry and ends with hope. After his suffering, he rejoices that God did hear the afflicted one and he shares this in the great congregation. Some see here a meal of thanksgiving offering; others also read it as a greater promise, reaching all the nations. Christians often see in this psalm a foreshadowing of Christ.

Today: if you are going through need or pain, keep seeking God with confidence. And when he helps you, tell of it and share what you have with others who suffer.
exp.139:10:
This verse says that the person who speaks evil, who slanders and lies, will not stand firm or have a stable life. "Evil speaker" refers to someone who uses their tongue to harm others. The phrase "evil shall hunt" gives the idea that evil itself will pursue the violent person until it catches him and brings him down. A "violent man" is someone who does harm without reason.

David is the speaker, according to the title of the psalm. He is surrounded by enemies who use poisonous words and plan violence against him. Instead of taking revenge, he places his cause in God's hands, trusting that wickedness will turn back on those who sow it.

For today: take care with your words. Gossip, mockery, and lies may seem powerful, but they destroy trust and destroy you as well. If someone harms you with their tongue, do not answer in kind; entrust it to God and seek to speak with truth and kindness.
exp.54:0:
This verse opens with a note for the choir director: the song was to be played "on Neginoth," which probably means with stringed instruments. The word "Maschil" seems to indicate a poem or song of instruction, though its exact meaning is uncertain. Then David prays: "Give ear to my prayer, O God, and hide not yourself from my supplication," that is, do not turn away or ignore me when I plead with you.

David is the speaker, according to the title. The verses that follow show that he is distressed by the threat of enemies and by the oppression of wicked people. Scholars do not agree on the exact moment in his life when he wrote it, so it is better not to claim a specific event.

For today: when you are troubled, you do not have to hide your feelings or polish your words. You can speak to God honestly, ask him to listen, and tell him what weighs on you, trusting that he wants to draw near to you.
exp.114:6:
The explanation says that the idols have the shape of a body, but cannot use it. They have hands, but they feel and touch nothing. Their hands cannot take hold of anything. They have feet, but they do not walk, and they cannot make a single sound with their throat. They are lifeless figures.

The psalm is a prayer and song of the people of Israel. It is not known for certain who wrote it. It clearly mocks the idols of the nations, made of silver and gold by human hands. Then it calls Israel to trust in the LORD, who does hear, help, and protect. The verses that follow say that whoever trusts in them becomes like them.

Today we may not worship statues, but we can still put our trust in things that cannot save us: money, success, or the opinions of others. Ask yourself what you rest on when you are afraid. Carry that burden to God in prayer, because he does hear you and care for you.
exp.88:35:
It says that the descendants of David will last forever. "Seed" means offspring, his children and heirs. And his throne, that is, his reign, will be as steady as the sun, which always appears before me, that is, in plain sight of God.

Here God is speaking, as recalled by the psalmist Ethan the Ezrahite. He is repeating the promise God made to David: that his family would always reign. God swears by his holiness that he will not lie. But the psalm then shows a crisis: the king seems rejected and defeated. For that reason the author reminds God of his promise. Many Christians see in Jesus, a descendant of David, the fullest fulfillment of this promise.

For today: when your situation seems to contradict what God has promised, you do not have to hide your pain. You can bring it to God in prayer, relying on his faithfulness, which does not depend on what you see.
exp.92:1:
This verse says that God's throne is firm, secure, and well established, and that God has no beginning. "Since then" means from always, from before creation. "Eternally" is an old way of saying "forever": God exists forever, without beginning or end.

The psalm does not say who wrote it. It is a song that celebrates God as King. Earlier, the psalmist speaks of his strength and of a world that does not move. Later, he speaks of rivers and seas that roar. Many understand those waters as an image of forces that threaten and frighten, although the text does not fully explain this. Even so, God is more powerful.

For today: when everything around you seems to be moving, as in a crisis or a frightening piece of news, remember that God reigns and does not change. You can pray like this: "Lord, you remain on the throne; in you I rest."
exp.93:4:
The explanation says that the wicked are crushing God's people and making those who belong to him suffer.

The sentences that explain the meanings of the quoted words are removed, since the verse above uses different wording.

The speaker is the psalmist, a believer whose name is not given in this psalm. He cries out to God as a just Judge. He sees that the wicked boast, speak harshly, and take advantage of the weakest, such as the widow, the foreigner, and the fatherless. He thinks God does not see it. The psalmist does not take revenge; he brings his complaint to God honestly.

When you see injustice or suffer because of it, you can tell God sincerely what hurts you. Praying this way is not a lack of faith, but trust that he does see. And ask yourself too whom you can help today.
exp.47:13:
This God is the one who has proven faithful to his people, and he says he is our God forever, with no end date. The phrase "for ever and ever" means without limit, and "he will be our guide" means he will lead us like a captain or leader. "Even unto death" can be understood as meaning he will guide us throughout our whole life. Some translators read a different expression in the original here, which is why other versions say "beyond death" or "forever."

The psalm is a song of the sons of Korah that celebrates Jerusalem (Zion) as the city where God protects his people. Before this verse, the psalmist invites the reader to walk around the city, count its towers, and look at its walls, so they can tell the next generation what God has done. The walls remind us that true security is God himself.

For today: when you feel fear about the future, remember that you do not walk alone. Tell your children or other young people how God has cared for you, so that they too may trust in his guidance.
exp.65:0:
This verse begins with a note for the choir director: it is a song, a psalm to be sung. Then it calls on people to shout to God, that is, to cry out to him with enthusiasm and joy, the way people shout to honor a king. And it is not just for a few: it invites "all the earth." The word "á" with an accent mark is an old way of writing "a."

The psalm does not say who wrote it. The one speaking is a worshiper who invites all the nations to celebrate God. The verses that follow speak of his mighty works, and then the psalm mentions the deliverance of Israel. Some think it was written for a festival at the temple, but this is not certain.

Today we can begin the day with sincere praise, even if it is brief. Before asking God for something, you can thank him out loud for one specific thing he has done in your life.
exp.16:4:
This verse is a prayer. The speaker asks God to hold his steps steady, that is, to keep him firm on the ways of God. Keeping steady means not stumbling or losing balance. The meaning is: "Lord, hold me up so that I do not wander off or fall."

The Psalm is introduced as a prayer of David. David speaks in the middle of being pursued by enemies. Earlier he has said that God tested his heart and found no wickedness, and that he kept himself from violent ways. Now, aware of his weakness, he asks for help to stay firm. His integrity is not pride, but dependence on God.

For today: do not rely only on your own willpower. Each morning, ask God to uphold you in difficult decisions, and seek his Word to know which way to walk.
exp.77:53:
He brought them to the land he had set apart for himself. The words for "borders" or "boundaries" are no longer in the verse, so the sentence about them is removed, and the sentence about "sanctuary" is adjusted to match the verse's wording. The phrase "this mountain" can point to Canaan in general or to Mount Zion; scholars understand it in both ways. The phrase "his right hand" speaks of his power.

The psalm is by Asaph. It reviews the history of Israel: the departure from Egypt, the wilderness, and the arrival in the promised land. It does this to remind new generations how much God cared for his people, even though they were often unfaithful to him.

For today: remember how God has guided you in the past. If he cared for you in the wilderness, he can also lead you to a place of rest. Give him thanks today and trust in him.
exp.114:16:
The dead no longer remain in this world to praise God with their voice. The Lord is the one who is praised. Going down into silence is a poetic way of speaking about death, about the grave, where there are no more words or singing.

This psalm was sung by the people of Israel, probably in a moment of worship, remembering that their God is real and alive, unlike the mute idols mentioned earlier. The psalmist speaks from the perspective of the Old Testament, where praise is tied to present life. That is why the next verse says: "But we will bless the Lord from this time forth and for evermore." Some understand that the verse does not deny life after death, but emphasizes the urgency of praising while we are alive.

Today we can give thanks and praise God without putting it off. Today you have a voice, breath and time: use them to give thanks, pray and sing to him, and encourage others to do the same.
exp.14:4:
This verse says that the person who lives uprightly does not lend money to someone in need while charging unfair interest, nor accepts bribes to harm an innocent person. Charging unfair interest is usury, and taking a bribe to pervert justice is what the verse calls reward against the innocent. Whoever lives this way, the psalm says, "shall never be moved," meaning they will have a firm and secure life.

This is a psalm of David. It answers the question of the first verse: who may dwell in God's presence? The answer is a list of honest conduct. In Israel, the law of Moses asked people not to exploit a poor brother with abusive loans. This verse closes the list.

For today: be honest with money. Do not take advantage of others' need, even when it is easy or suits you. And if someone offers you a benefit for keeping silent or bending the truth, say no.
exp.131:5:
It says: "We heard of it at Ephratah; we found it in the fields of the wood." The word "found" here is the same as "we found it." "It" seems to be the ark of the covenant, the symbol of God's presence.

The psalm recalls David's vow not to rest until he found a place for God. Here the people speak, telling how the ark was heard of and then found. Ephratah may refer to the area of Bethlehem or to the tribe of Ephraim; it is not entirely clear. "The fields of the wood" probably alludes to Kiriath-jearim, where the ark stayed (1 Samuel 7:1-2), though this is debated.

For today: God lets himself be found by those who seek him with a whole heart. Just as David would not rest until he gave God a place, we can give him real space in our week, through prayer and reading his Word, without putting it off until later.
exp.10:0:
It says that David, who wrote this psalm for the chief musician, has put his trust in God. That is why he is puzzled that people would tell him, "Flee as a bird to your mountain." The source's comment on the wording of the verse (the old forms of certain words) is not applicable to the reader's verse, so it is left out.

David speaks against advisers who, out of fear, suggest he escape because the wicked are threatening those who are upright. It is not known with certainty when in his life he wrote it; some connect it with his flight from Saul, but that is a guess. What is clear is that he answers with faith: his refuge is not a mountain, but God.

For today: when fear or alarming advice pushes you to give up or to flee from everything, stop and pray first. Ask yourself where your trust is placed. You may make wise decisions, but do so from the assurance that God sustains you.
exp.70:7:
This verse expresses a wish: that the mouth of the one speaking would be full of praise to God, and that they would speak of his glory all day long. "Let it be full" means "let it be full" in the sense of "may it be full." "Glory" refers to the greatness and splendor of God.

Psalm 71 does not say who wrote it. It speaks of a person who is now old and has trusted in God since birth. They have lived through difficult times, and there are enemies lying in wait. So, before asking for help in old age, they remember how God has always sustained them and resolve to praise him.

For today: when you feel pressured or afraid, begin by remembering how God has cared for you. You can thank him aloud for three specific things each morning, and let that gratitude fill your conversations throughout the day.
exp.17:41:
He says David crushed his enemies completely. He uses two images: the dust that the wind carries away without a trace, and the dirt of the streets that is thrown out or trampled. These are poetic comparisons to show a complete victory.

The speaker is David. This psalm is a song of thanks to God for rescuing him from his enemies and from Saul (as the heading indicates). The language is poetic and deliberately exaggerated, to exalt what God did. The verses before this one say that his enemies cried out and God did not answer them, and the verses that follow speak of how God made him head over nations.

For today: not everything we face is an enemy of flesh and blood. We can thank God for the times he sustained us in our struggles and trust that he is our refuge. Rather than seeking revenge, let us learn to hand over to God what is beyond us and to acknowledge his help with gratitude.
exp.58:2:
He says David sees his enemies as hunters lying in wait, watching for a chance to take his life. The word "lie in wait" means to watch in secret in order to attack. "They are gathered" is the same as "they have gathered together." "The mighty" are powerful and violent men. David declares before God that they have not attacked him because of any fault or sin of his.

The psalm speaks, according to its heading, when Saul sent men to watch David's house in order to kill him (1 Samuel 19). David does not claim to be perfect, but in this case he is innocent of what he is accused of, and so he turns to God as his defender.

For today: when you are attacked or treated unfairly, do not carry the distress alone. Bring your situation honestly before God, ask him for protection, and also ask him to examine your heart, trusting that he sees the truth.
exp.103:25:
It says that in the sea there are ships that go back and forth, and also a great sea creature called the leviathan. God made it to play in the sea. "Ships" are large vessels. "Leviathan" is a Hebrew word for an enormous creature of the sea; some think it refers to a whale or a sea monster, and others see in it a symbol of the chaos that God rules over. "Play" means to enjoy oneself.

The psalmist, who is not named in the text, praises God as Creator. He is surveying creation: the earth, the sea, the animals. His wonder reaches to the greatest and most mysterious things in the ocean, and it shows that God cares for and governs everything with wisdom.

For today: do not fear what seems enormous or out of control, because God made it and sustains it. Also, enjoy creation and give thanks to him; even the awe-inspiring can be part of his joy and his care.
exp.94:5:
This verse is an invitation to come together and worship God. We worship God because he made us.

The psalm does not say who wrote it, although some traditions attribute it to David. The one speaking calls the people to worship. Earlier, the psalm reminded us that everything belongs to God: the mountains, the sea, and the land. Then it reminds us that we are his people, like sheep in his hand, and warns us not to harden our hearts as Israel did at Meribah and Massah.

For today: before you begin the day, take a moment to bow your heart, and if you can, your body too, to acknowledge God as your Creator. Give him thanks and listen to his voice with a willing heart.
exp.65:2:
Say to God that his works are impressive, so powerful that they cause awe and reverence. Here "terrible" does not mean evil but astonishing. The phrase about enemies does not speak of them lying out of wickedness; rather, faced with his great power, they pretend submission or give in to his strength. Other translations say "submit themselves" or "bow down."

The psalmist invites the whole earth to praise God. It is not known with certainty who wrote it. It is a song for the choir director, probably for the worship of the people of Israel. Further on it recalls God's works, such as the deliverance at the Red Sea (v. 6), and celebrates that God is greater than any adversary.

Today we can praise God not only for what we feel but for what he has done. Before asking for something, take a moment to remember and thank God aloud for one of his works in your life, and so your trust will grow.
exp.146:1:
He says that God is the one who lifts up and builds Jerusalem again. He also says that he will gather together the outcasts of Israel, that is, the exiles, those who were driven out and scattered far from their land. The words "build up" and "gathereth together" show a God who rebuilds and brings his people back together.

The psalm does not say who wrote it. It is a song of praise, and many connect it with the return from exile in Babylon, though this is not certain. The psalmist calls for singing because God restores what was broken. The verses that follow show that this same God heals wounded hearts and knows every star by its name.

For today: if you feel far away, scattered, or with your life in ruins, you can trust that God knows how to rebuild and bring together. Bring what is broken before him in prayer, and praise him even while you wait.
exp.34:20:
They opened their mouths wide against him, in a sign of mockery and of delight at his misfortune. "Aha, aha!" is an expression of laughter or triumph. With "our eye has seen it" they claim to have watched him fall or make a mistake, and they celebrate it.

The speaker is David, according to the title of the psalm. He is being attacked by people who once received his kindness but now hate him without cause. They rejoice in his fall and speak with deceit. For this reason, in the next verse, he leaves his case in God's hands, for God truly sees everything and can judge with justice.

When someone mocks you or rejoices in your hard time, there is no need to answer them in the same way. You can bring your pain to God honestly, as David did, and trust that he sees the truth and defends those who suffer unjustly.
exp.148:3:
The explanation says that God rejoices and takes delight in his people. Its comments on the wording must be adapted to words that appear in the King James verse. "Takes contentment" is best rendered by the verse's own phrase "taketh pleasure," so the explanation's point is that God is pleased and satisfied with them. "Beautify" is already in the verse, so it can be explained as adorning or making beautiful, and the word "salvation" in the verse can be understood as deliverance, victory, or well-being. The "meek" are those who do not think themselves superior and who trust in God.

The psalm is a song of praise, and no one knows for certain who wrote it. It calls Israel to celebrate its Creator and King with dancing, music, and singing. This verse gives the reason for that celebration: God himself delights in his people and cares for those who are simple. The verses that follow speak of joy and also of struggle, though commentators explain this in different ways.

For today: remember that God does not merely tolerate you, but takes pleasure in you when you live with humility. Today, before asking him for anything, thank him and praise him for who he is.
exp.104:42:
This verse says that God led his people, Israel, out of Egypt, and that he did it amid joy and singing. The word "chosen" refers to those whom God picked to be his own. The joy in the verse is a happiness that shows and is celebrated.

The psalmist, who is not named here, reviews the history of Israel to praise God. He remembers the exodus and the water God gave in the desert. He says God acted because he remembered the promise made to Abraham. Some scholars think the joy refers to the immediate departure from Egypt, and others to the celebration afterward; the text does not make this clear.

For today: when you remember how God has cared for you, let that memory turn into gratitude. Write down one thing God has done for you this week and give thanks for it out loud.
exp.44:0:
This verse opens with a note for the choir director: it is a song for the sons of Korah, set to the tune called "Shoshannim" (which is usually understood to mean "lilies"), a maschil (a teaching poem) and a song of loves. Then the author says that his heart is overflowing with a good matter, that is, it is full of it. He says he dedicates his works to the King, and that his tongue is like the pen of a very swift scribe, that is, a quick and skilled writer.

The one speaking is the poet, who composes a song for a royal wedding. The verses that follow praise the king and his glory. Many Christians see in him an image of Christ; others read it first as a song for a king of Israel. It is not known for certain which king it was.

For today: when your heart is full of gratitude toward God, do not keep it inside. Express it in your own words, a prayer, a letter, or a song, and offer it sincerely.
exp.48:6:
This verse says that no person, however rich or powerful, can save another from death. Nor can anyone pay God the price to set that person free. The explanation describes "redeem" as buying someone's freedom back, and "ransom" as the payment made for it.

The speaker is a wise man who writes this psalm to teach everyone. He does not fear the evil days, even though people surround him who want to harm him. He looks at those who trust in their wealth and feel secure. He reminds them that riches cannot buy eternal life. The text implies that only God can deliver the soul (v. 15).

Today we can ask ourselves what we truly trust in. Money helps, but it does not give lasting peace or save the soul. We can rest in God, who does deliver, and use what we have with humility and generosity.
exp.0:2:
The explanation says that the person who loves God's word is like a tree planted by streams of water. Because it always has water, it bears fruit in its season, its leaves do not wither, and what it does goes well. The word "prosper" speaks of getting ahead, and not necessarily of wealth. Saying the leaf "does not wither" means that it does not fade or dry up. "Beside" is simply "beside" or "by."

Psalm 1 does not say who wrote it; it serves as an introduction to the whole book of Psalms. Setting out two paths, the way of the righteous and the way of the wicked, it invites the reader to choose. The tree stands in contrast with the chaff, the light husk of the grain that the wind carries away. The Psalms show that the righteous also suffer, so this is a general picture of a stable life, not a promise that there will never be trouble.

For today: find a moment each day, even a brief one, to read the Bible and think about it calmly. In this way your roots draw near to the water, and in dry times you will have something to hold on to.
exp.50:8:
This verse is a prayer. The speaker asks God for two things: that he would hide his face from his sins, meaning that he would not look at them in order to condemn him, and that he would blot out all his iniquities, as someone wipes a page clean until no trace remains. Iniquities means the wrongs and offenses committed.

It is part of Psalm 51, which the title attributes to David, after the prophet Nathan had exposed his sin (2 Samuel 12). It speaks with grief and repentance. It makes no excuses; it acknowledges guilt and trusts in God's mercy. The nearby verses speak of cleansing, joy, and a new heart.

For today: when you fail, do not hide from God or justify yourself. Come before him honestly, confess what you have done, and ask for forgiveness. He promises to cleanse and restore those who approach him with humility (1 John 1:9).
exp.79:16:
He says the people ask God for his hand of protection and help to rest upon "the man at your right hand," that is, someone placed at his side in a place of honor and power. He also calls him "the son of man," that is, a human being, whom God "strengthened," an older word meaning he made firm and established for his service.

Israel speaks in a psalm of lament. The nation, compared to a burned and destroyed vine, suffers under God's judgment. Scholars disagree about who this "man" is: it may be the king of Israel, the people themselves, or a figure pointing toward the Messiah. Many Christians see here a shadow of Jesus, but the text does not make this entirely clear.

For today: when you feel broken, pray asking for God's hand and not only for relief. Like the people, who promise "we will not turn back from you," ask him to uphold you and keep you close to him.
exp.106:37:
This verse says that God blesses his people, and that they grow greatly, meaning they have many children and much prosperity. The phrase about not letting their livestock decrease means that God does not allow their animals, which were their wealth, to diminish. Here "livestock" refers to the herds.

The psalm does not say who wrote it. It is a song of thanksgiving that invites those redeemed by the Lord to give him thanks. Here the psalmist reminds the hungry that God led them to a place where they could settle, sow, and harvest. All the progress is credited to God's blessing. But the next verse shows that there are also times of sorrow and loss.

For today: when you have provision and growth, recognize that it comes from God and give thanks. Use what you have with generosity, and trust him also in difficult times.
exp.99:2:
It says that we should acknowledge, that is, accept and be clear about, that the Lord is God. He made us; we did not make ourselves. We are his people and the sheep he tends in his pasture. The words "presence" and "to" are the modern forms, since old wording of this kind is no longer used today.

The psalm is sung by a worshiper who invites all the inhabitants of the earth to praise God. It is thought that it was used in worship at the temple, since it speaks of entering through its gates and courts. This verse gives the reason for praise: who God is and who we are before him.

For today: when you feel pressure to prove your worth, remember that you did not make yourself. God created you and cares for you like a shepherd. Thank him today for something specific that you have received from his hand.
exp.78:6:
The explanation says that the enemy nations have devoured Jacob, that is, the people of Israel, and have laid waste their dwelling place, which may refer to their land, their homes, or the temple. The words "devoured" and "laid waste" in the verse are the ones that carry this sense of total destruction, meaning brought to an end and left in ruins.

The speaker is Asaf, or a psalmist from his line, who cries out to God after the invasion of Jerusalem. The exact moment is not known with certainty; many connect it with the destruction by Babylon. The people suffer, yet they acknowledge their own sins and ask for mercy, not only for vengeance.

When pain crushes you, you can bring it to God honestly, without pretending to be strong. Ask Him for justice, but also examine your heart and ask for His forgiveness and help. He hears those who cry out to Him.
exp.93:13:
It says that God will not abandon his people or leave alone his "inheritance," that is, the people who belong to him, his cherished possession.

The one speaking is the psalmist, probably in the midst of injustice and oppression at the hands of wicked people. We do not know with certainty who wrote it or the exact moment in which it was written. Before this, he speaks of God correcting and teaching the one he loves, and giving rest in difficult times. Afterward he promises that justice will return and the upright will follow it. Thus this verse is the reason for his hope: God is faithful.

For today: when you feel alone or unfairly treated, remember that God has not let go of you. You can pray sincerely and keep doing what is right, trusting that He is still with you, even in the middle of correction or waiting.
exp.115:9:
The explanation says that the psalmist believed in God and therefore spoke, even while he was deeply afflicted. "I believed" speaks of trust in God. "I spoke" can mean confessing his faith, praying, or telling what God has done. "Greatly" means very much. His suffering was deep, but his faith did not stay silent.

The one speaking is the psalmist, a man who was rescued from a deadly danger and now gives thanks to God. We do not know his name or the exact situation. The verses around it show that, in his distress, he even said in haste that "all men are liars." Afterward he acknowledges how good God has been to him. Paul quotes this verse in 2 Corinthians 4:13 to speak of faith that is expressed.

For today: when you are going through a hard moment, do not keep your faith silent. Speak with God honestly and, when you can, tell someone you trust how God has sustained you.
exp.21:20:
This verse is a cry for help. The speaker asks to be saved from the mouth of the lion, an image of a fierce and deadly enemy. He also asks to be rescued from the horns of the wild oxen. The original word probably refers to wild bulls (buffaloes or aurochs), strong and dangerous animals, not to the mythical one-horned beast of later legend.

David speaks in a psalm of deep suffering. He feels surrounded by enemies, described as dogs, lions, and wild bulls. The verses before this one ask God not to stay far away. From here the tone shifts: the psalm moves toward a promise to praise God before the congregation. The New Testament quotes this psalm in connection with Jesus on the cross, although David wrote it out of his own distress.

When you feel that problems surround you, you can cry out to God honestly. Ask him for help, and then choose to thank him and tell others what he does.
exp.134:14:
This verse says that the false gods of the neighboring nations are nothing more than objects made of silver and gold. They are not living or powerful beings; they are the work of human hands.

The psalmist, within a song of praise for God's people, first exalts the Lord as eternal and faithful, the one who cares for his servants. Then he sets this living God against the idols of the nearby peoples. The verses that follow say the idols have mouths, eyes and ears, but they do not speak, see, or hear. The contrast is meant to encourage Israel to trust in Jehovah alone.

Today we may not carve statues, but we can place our trust in money, success, or the things we build. Ask yourself: what thing made by human hands gives me more security than God does? Surrender it to him today in prayer.
exp.27:1:
Here David asks God to hear him. "Pleas" are requests made out of real need, and "cry out" means calling out with force. "Lifting up the hands" was a way of praying, showing that one hopes for everything from God. "Thy holy oracle" is the holy place where God was understood to be present.

David speaks in a moment of distress. He feels that if God keeps silent, he would be like those who have gone down to the grave. He is also troubled by the wicked, who speak peace while hiding evil. Scholars do not agree on the exact situation he was living through, so it is best not to invent details.

For today: when you feel overwhelmed, do not keep your prayer to yourself. Speak to God honestly and with all your heart, even if all you can say is "Hear my voice." He invites his people to cry out to him.
exp.107:10:
The psalmist says that God seems to have rejected his people and no longer goes out to fight alongside their armies. Some translations read this as a question: "Wilt not thou, O God, who hast cast us off?" It is a sincere lament, not a cold accusation.

The psalm is attributed to David and joins parts of two other psalms (57 and 60). After declaring that God rules over Moab, Edom, and Philistia, the people face a fortified city and feel that without God they cannot advance. Their defeats make them think that God has withdrawn. Scholars do not agree on which specific battle is in view.

For today: when you feel that God is far away, do not remain silent or pretend. Bring your complaint to him honestly, as the psalmist did, and ask for help, because the next verse shows that hope is born from exactly this.
exp.105:2:
It says that those who act with uprightness and justice are happy. "Blessed" means happy, favored. "Keep judgment" means they live with good sense and obey what is right. "At all times" shows that they do not do this only when it suits them, but always.

The psalmist, who does not name himself, begins by praising God for his goodness and his everlasting mercy. Then he acknowledges that no one can count all his works. This psalm later goes on to recount the failures of Israel, so this verse works as an ideal. Afterward, the author asks God to remember him and include him among his people, as someone who needs help to live this way.

Today we can practice justice in small and steady ways: paying what is fair, speaking the truth, treating everyone well, even when no one sees us. And when we fail, we can ask God for his help, as the psalmist did.
exp.105:1:
It says that no one can fully describe God's mighty acts or tell all the reasons to praise him. It is a rhetorical question: the answer is that no one can. The first quoted word refers to deeds of power or feats, and the second refers to the reasons why God deserves to be praised.

The psalm does not say who wrote it. The author calls people to praise God for his goodness and his enduring mercy. Then he recalls how God cared for Israel and how the people were unfaithful to him. That is why the question expresses wonder: God is so great that words fall short.

Today we can praise God without waiting to understand everything. This week, write down three concrete things God has done for you and thank him out loud. Even if you cannot tell it all, you can begin to give thanks for what you do see.
exp.119:6:
He says the psalmist is a person of peace, yet as soon as he speaks, others respond with fighting. "Peaceable" means that he seeks peace and harmony. The phrase "when I speak" simply means "as soon as I speak." "They are for war" speaks of hostility, perhaps harsh words or actions against him.

The one speaking is the psalmist, a believer who feels far from home. This psalm opens the songs of ascent, songs associated with going up to Jerusalem. Meshech and Kedar are distant places, known for their warlike or unfriendly peoples. Many understand them as images of a hostile environment, not necessarily his actual location. He suffers because he lives among people who hate peace.

Today, even when we seek peace, we are sometimes misunderstood or attacked. We can pray and not respond with the same harshness. Speak with truth and kindness, and leave in God's hands what you cannot control.
exp.70:17:
This verse is the prayer of an elderly person. He asks that God not abandon him now that he has reached old age and has gray hair. He wants God to sustain him until he can tell the next generations about God's power, that is, God's strength, and God's mighty acts to those who will come after him.

The psalm does not say who wrote it; tradition connects it with David, but that is not certain. The one speaking has trusted God since his youth and has proclaimed God's faithfulness all his life. Now, in old age, he faces distress and does not want to finish his life without leaving a testimony to the younger generation.

For today: think of one concrete way to tell someone younger what God has done in your life, such as a child, a nephew, or a friend. And if you are older, remember that your testimony still has great value.
exp.131:4:
This verse completes a promise that began earlier: David will not rest "until I find out a place for the Lord". The word "habitation" means a place to live, and "the mighty God of Jacob" is a title of God, meaning the powerful God who cares for his people.

The psalm recalls David the king's vow to find a place for the ark of the covenant, which represented God's presence. That is why he gives up his own house and his sleep. The verses that follow mention Ephrathah and "the fields of the wood", places that are probably connected with the ark, although scholars explain them in various ways.

Today we can ask ourselves what place we give God in our daily lives. Perhaps it means setting aside a fixed time each day to pray and read the Bible, before other things take up all of it.
exp.33:20:
It says that the wickedness of the wicked ends up destroying them. The word "slay" here means that it brings them to ruin or death. "Hate" means they are hostile toward the righteous, and "desolate" means ruined or left in emptiness. Thus those who hate the righteous will not escape the consequences of their attitude.

David speaks, and the tradition of the psalm's heading connects it to the time he pretended to be mad before Abimelech in order to escape. He gives thanks to God for delivering him and teaches others to trust. The verse contrasts the end of the wicked with that of the righteous, whom God cares for in the midst of his many troubles. It is a general principle of wisdom, not a promise that everything will happen immediately.

Today you can rest when someone treats you unjustly or with resentment. You do not need to take revenge; hand the matter over to God and keep doing good. Trust that He is just and sustains you, and take care that your own heart does not fill with hatred.
exp.38:6:
It says that, after reflecting on how short life is, the psalmist asks himself: "What do I wait for now?" And he answers at once: "My hope is in you." The word "vanity" in the earlier verses means something fleeting, like a breath.

The psalm is spoken by David, according to its title. He is troubled by his sin and by the frailty of life. He has seen that working hard and piling up riches gives no security, because no one knows who will end up with them. So he turns his eyes back to God, and right away he asks for forgiveness for his rebellions.

For today: when you feel that life is passing quickly or that your efforts give you no security, pray this simple prayer: "Lord, my hope is in you." Hand over your worries to him and ask him to be your firm support, more than your achievements or your possessions.
exp.89:14:
The explanation says that the people ask God for a joy that is as great as the time of suffering they went through. "Make us glad" is the idea of the verse. "According to the days" means "in proportion to the days." "The years in which we have seen evil" refers to years of misfortune and pain.

This psalm is traditionally attributed to Moses. The one speaking is the people of God, who recognize that life is brief and that sin brings hardship. Some think it refers to the years in the wilderness, but the text does not say so with certainty. After speaking of affliction, the psalmist pleads that God will again show his goodness.

For today: you can bring your pain to God honestly, without pretending that everything is fine. Ask him for hope and joy, trusting that he can give meaning even to the difficult times you have lived through.
exp.44:1:
He says this king is more beautiful than any other man. His words are full of grace, that is, kind and pleasant to hear. That is why God has blessed him forever. "Fairer" means that his beauty stands out above others; "therefore" explains the reason for the blessing.

The one speaking is the psalmist, a Levite from the sons of Korah, who writes a wedding song for a king. He speaks directly to the king, with a heart overflowing. Jews and Christians have read it in several ways: as a song for a king of Israel and, in the New Testament (Hebrews 1:8-9), applied to Christ, the perfect King.

Today we can notice that God's blessing is joined to words full of grace. Before you speak, ask yourself: "Does what I am about to say give life and help others?" Ask Jesus to teach you to speak as He does.
exp.117:19:
It says there is a gate that belongs to God, and that only the righteous pass through it. "Lord" is the name of God, and "righteous" refers to those who live uprightly and trust in Him. The gate speaks of access to his presence, to the place of worship.

The psalm is a song of thanksgiving. The one speaking seems to be a leader or a people who was severely disciplined by God, but not handed over to death. Now he comes to the temple to give thanks. The verses that follow speak of the stone the builders rejected that becomes the chief cornerstone, and the New Testament applies it to Jesus. Some interpreters see the gate as the temple in Jerusalem; others see it as a broader image of access to God.

For today: when God corrects you or rescues you from a difficult moment, do not turn away in shame. Come near with gratitude and humility, and thank him in prayer for his care.
exp.58:5:
They return every evening. Here the explanation is simply describing the enemies coming back each evening. They make a noise like barking dogs, and they go around the city looking for their prey. It is an image of constant threat, repeated every night.

The psalm is spoken by David, and its heading places it at the time when Saul sent men to watch David's house in order to kill him (1 Samuel 19). That is the tradition of the heading, although some scholars think the psalm was later used in other situations. Dogs in that time were street animals that roamed looking for food, not pets. David describes his fear and asks God for help.

When you feel that your troubles come back every night, like barking that never stops, do what David did: honestly tell God what you are afraid of. He does not mock your fear; the psalm ends with confidence that God is your refuge and your strength.
exp.147:4:
This verse invites all of creation to praise the name of the Lord. The reason is simple: God spoke, gave a command, and everything that exists began to exist. The word "created" is the key idea here. The verse shows that God is the origin of all things and that his word has power.

The psalm does not say who wrote it. The psalmist calls the heavens, the sun, the moon, and the stars to praise God, as if the whole creation could sing. This is poetic language that shows everything exists to honor its Creator. Then the psalm also calls the earth and its people to join in that praise.

Today we can remember that our lives are not an accident. God knows us and gave us existence. This week, when you look at the sky, a tree, or the sunrise, pause for a moment and give thanks to God out loud for having created it all.
exp.6:5:
What it says: The psalmist asks God to act. "Rise up" and "lift yourself up" are ways of saying: "Get into action, step in." "Wrath" and "anger" speak of God's indignation against injustice. "Those who oppress me" are the people who are crushing him. And "awake the judgment you have commanded" means: carry out the justice that you yourself have established.

Context: According to the psalm's title, David speaks, though a man named Cush is mentioned, and we do not know with certainty which specific event it refers to. He is being falsely accused and persecuted. Earlier he declares that, if he were guilty, he would deserve punishment. Since he claims to be innocent, he leaves his case in the hands of God, the righteous judge. That God seems "asleep" is poetic language from someone who feels that help is slow in coming.

For today: When you are treated unjustly, do not take revenge. Bring your case to God honestly, examine your own heart, and trust that he will do justice in his time.
exp.17:8:
He bowed the heavens and came down, the explanation says, like someone stooping to descend, and it describes him reaching down to the earth. Beneath his feet there was a thick, dark cloud. Here the word "darkness" means dense storm clouds. The picture shows a God so great that the sky bends before him.

David speaks here, giving thanks to God for having rescued him from his enemies and from Saul, according to the heading of the psalm. To describe how God answered his cry, he uses poetic language: trembling, smoke, fire and storm. It is not necessarily a literal account of an event, but a way of saying that God intervened with power.

When you feel alone or surrounded by problems, remember that God is neither far away nor indifferent. He hears the cry of his children and can come down into your situation. Call on him with confidence, even when you cannot see how everything will turn out.
exp.101:5:
He says that the psalmist feels like a lonely bird in an empty place. The "pelican" and the "owl" in the desert and among the ruins (the "solitudes") were birds associated with abandoned places. Some translations use other birds, because the Hebrew is not entirely certain about which birds are meant. What is clear is the image: loneliness and abandonment.

The one speaking is someone deeply distressed, who prays before God. The title of the psalm presents it as "the prayer of the afflicted." He is sick, without appetite, worn out from so much groaning, and surrounded by enemies. We do not know with certainty who wrote it or the exact moment it was written, but his pain is real and he expresses it without pretense.

When you feel alone or abandoned, do not hide it. Tell God honestly, as the psalmist did. And also seek out a trusted person who can accompany you.
exp.5:2:
It says that David's soul is greatly troubled, meaning deeply distressed and shaken within. Then he asks God, "How long?" It is an unfinished question, left hanging, like someone so weary from suffering that he can hardly find words. "Troubled" means stirred up, filled with fear and pain. The name of God here is the LORD.

David speaks in a prayer of lament. He is sick, weak, and feels that God is correcting him in anger. Earlier he already mentioned that even his bones trembled. We do not know with certainty what illness or trouble he was living through, and scholars understand it in different ways. What is clear is that he suffers in body and soul, and he turns to God.

For today: when pain weighs you down, you do not have to pretend to be strong. You can say to God honestly, "I am very troubled. How long?" The Bible shows that praying this way is not a lack of faith, but trust that God hears.
exp.30:13:
The explanation says that, although everything seems to be going wrong, the psalmist decides to trust in the Lord. "But" marks a contrast: despite what came before, he declares firmly: "You are my God." It is a personal statement of faith. "Lord" is the name of God, and "trusted" means he placed his security in Him.

The one speaking is David, according to the title of the psalm, though we do not know with certainty at what point in his life he wrote it. He feels forgotten, like a broken vessel (a shattered jar that no one wants anymore). He hears mockery, feels fear, and knows that his enemies plan to kill him. In the middle of that anguish, his faith holds on to God.

For today: when you feel lonely or afraid, do not wait until you feel better before you trust. Say out loud: "You are my God," and bring your specific problem to God in prayer.
exp.118:141:
This verse says that God's righteousness does not change or come to an end: it is everlasting. And his law, that is, his teachings and commands, is the truth, something firm that one can trust. The word for the purity of the verse before this one is explained elsewhere, and it means very purified, without any mixture of error. (The sentence about that earlier word is deleted, as it refers to wording outside your verse.)

The one speaking is a psalmist, who calls himself a servant of God. He feels small and looked down upon, and he goes through affliction and distress. Even so, he does not forget the word of God. Scholars do not agree on who the author was, so we cannot state it with certainty. What we do see is that, in the middle of his pain, he leans on what God has said.

For today: when everything around you seems uncertain or unfair, return to the Bible. Read a passage each day and remember that God and his truth do not change, even though your circumstances do.
exp.113:6:
It says that the whole earth trembles when God makes his presence known. The phrase "in the presence" is an older way of writing "before him," that is, in front of Him. He is called "the God of Jacob" to remind readers that he is the God who joined himself to his people and remained faithful to them, not a distant god.

The psalmist speaks in a song of praise that recalls Israel's departure from Egypt. Before this verse he asks poetic questions of the sea, the Jordan, and the mountains, as if they were frightened people. Then the verse gives the answer: they tremble because God is present. Afterward, the psalm recalls how God brought water out of the rock in the desert. This is poetic language, not a scientific description.

For today: God remains greater than any obstacle that seems impossible to you. When you face a "sea" or a "mountain" in your life, pray by remembering that God has cared for his people, and trust that he can also care for you.
exp.76:6:
Here the psalmist asks a painful question: Will God reject me forever? Will he no longer show me his love? The sentence explaining the quoted wording is removed, since the reader's verse uses "cast off" and "favourable" directly, and I'm translating the sense of the question as it stands.

The author is Asaph, according to the title of the psalm, though some think it expresses the distress of the whole people. He is in a night of affliction, without comfort. He remembers God's past and his songs from earlier times, but now he feels silence. His questions are not cold unbelief but a sincere lament. Later in the psalm, he looks again at God's works and finds hope.

For today: when you feel God far away, do not hide your doubts. Bring them to him in prayer with honesty, and remember what God has done before. Feeling his absence does not always mean he has left you.
exp.13:0:
It says that the fool, deep in his heart, thinks or decides that God does not exist or does not matter. "Fool" here does not speak of little intelligence, but of someone who lives without moral wisdom. The verse says they have become corrupt, and that their deeds are hateful to God. It affirms that this attitude goes together with a crooked way of living.

It is a psalm of David, addressed to the chief musician, that is, the leader of the singing in worship. David speaks with grief about human wickedness. Scholars debate exactly which situation it refers to. The text stresses that denying God is more a matter of the heart and of conduct than of logic.

Today we can ask ourselves whether, even if we believe in God with our words, we live as if he were not watching. A good practice is to begin the day by asking him, "Lead my decisions," and then to act with honesty.
exp.105:26:
God swore that, because of the people's rebellion, their descendants would fall among the nations and be scattered across different lands. The word "seed" means descendants, "nations" are the non-Jewish peoples, and "scatter them" means to disperse them.

The psalmist reviews Israel's history to acknowledge the people's sins. Here he recalls when they grumbled against God in the wilderness and would not obey him. God spoke with solemn judgment. Many think the psalm was written when Israel already lived in dispersion, so this warning helps him understand their history. That is not entirely certain.

For today: constant complaining hardens the heart and draws us away from God. When you notice that you are grumbling, stop and pray with gratitude. Listening to his voice in time is always better than suffering the consequences of ignoring it.
exp.118:79:
This verse is a prayer. The psalmist asks that his heart be "sound" (in the King James wording, whole, sincere and without duplicity) in God's statutes, which are his laws and teachings. And he adds the reason: so that he will not be "ashamed," that is, disappointed and humiliated.

The one speaking is the author of the psalm, who is not named. He is someone who loves God's law and suffers slander from proud people. Earlier he has asked that the proud be put to shame; now he asks that he himself not be. His security is not in defending himself, but in being faithful to God within.

Today we can pray this same verse. Rather than merely appearing devout, it is good to ask God for a sincere heart that obeys his Word in truth. When someone speaks ill of us, we can rest in the knowledge that God sees our heart and sustains us.
exp.30:19:
It says that God protects those who trust in him, as someone hides them in a private and safe place, in his presence, close to him. He keeps them from the proud arrogance of others, that is, from the pride and abuse of people. Here the shelter is like a tent or refuge, and the attacks are quarrels, accusations, and words that wound.

David is the one speaking in this psalm, although some scholars point out that the text does not make clear every exact moment of his life. He feels attacked by lies and contempt. Before this verse he asks that lying lips be silenced, and he praises the goodness that God keeps for those who honor him. Afterward he gives thanks, because God cared for him even when he thought he was lost.

When you are criticized or spoken badly of, do not spend all your strength defending yourself. Pray, rest in God's presence, and let him be your refuge and your defender.
exp.118:47:
This verse says that the psalmist will lift up his hands toward God's commandments, which he loves, and that he will quietly reflect on God's decrees. "Lifting up the hands" can be understood as a gesture of prayer, respect, or devotion; scholars interpret it in different ways. To meditate is to reflect slowly and carefully. Decrees are God's instructions or rules.

The speaker is the author of Psalm 119, a believer who loves God's law, and we do not know with certainty who he was. He has just said that he will speak of God's teachings even before kings without feeling ashamed. Now he adds that his love for the Word shows itself both in attitude and in thought.

For today: set aside a few minutes each day to read a passage of the Bible, think about it unhurriedly, and pray, asking God to help you put it into practice.
exp.38:10:
God says that when a person sins, he corrects him with punishments. That correction makes what seemed great and valuable wear away, like clothing eaten by a moth. For this reason the psalmist concludes: "surely every man is vanity," that is, we are frail and passing. "Selah" is probably a pause for meditation, although its exact meaning is not certain.

David speaks, according to the title of the psalm. He suffers an affliction that he sees as God's discipline, and so he keeps silent. Even so, he asks God to remove his blow and hear his prayer, for he feels like a stranger passing through the earth, as his ancestors did.

For today: when God corrects you, do not defend yourself or despair. Acknowledge your frailty, stop trusting in your achievements, and cry out to God with sincerity. His correction seeks to bring you back to Him.
exp.54:17:
It says that God rescued the psalmist and gave him peace in his soul, even though there was a battle against him. Here "redeem" means to deliver or rescue. The phrase "many were against me" means that there were many who were attacking him. The peace it mentions is not only calm on the outside, but inner rest.

The psalm is spoken by David, according to its title, although some scholars are not sure of the exact moment. He is hurt by the betrayal of someone close to him, who broke his covenant (v. 20). Surrounded by enemies, he chooses to pray evening, morning, and noon, trusting that God hears him.

For today: when you feel attacked or betrayed, do not wait for the problem to pass before seeking God. Pray every day, at several moments, and ask him for peace for your heart. He can care for your soul even in the middle of the struggle.
exp.8:17:
It says that God does not forget the poor forever. Even when it may seem that no one sees them, their hope will not come to an end. Where the source phrase speaks of perishing forever, the sense is that their hope will not be lost completely or permanently.

The one speaking is David, according to the heading of the psalm. He is giving thanks to God because he has carried out justice against the wicked. The verses before this one speak of nations that live forgetting God. This verse sets up a contrast: while they forget God, God does not forget the needy. Then David asks God to rise up and judge. The word for "hell" in this version translates the Hebrew term that is usually understood as the place of the dead.

For today: if you are going through hardship or feel overlooked, do not lose hope; pray with confidence and seek God. And if you have the means, help someone in need, so that they feel they are not alone.
exp.144:3:
This verse says that each generation will tell the next what God has done. The word "tell" here means to recount or relate. The "mighty acts" are God's powerful deeds, his acts of strength and deliverance. And "declare" means they will make it known openly.

This psalm is attributed to David, and it is a song of praise. He has just said that he will bless God every day and that his greatness cannot be measured. Now he thinks beyond his own life: the praise should not end with him. The psalmist then speaks again in the first person, saying that he too will speak of that greatness.

For today: tell someone younger, or someone close to you, about a time you saw God at work in your life. It can be at home, at church, or in a simple conversation. In this way faith passes from one generation to another.
exp.76:12:
He says that God's way, that is, his manner of acting and guiding, is holy, pure, and set apart from all evil. For this reason the psalmist asks: "Who is so great a God as ours?" The question expects no answer, because the answer is clear: no one. Some translators read this verse differently, understanding its key word as "the sanctuary" rather than "holy," and the explanation notes that this reading is also possible.

The speaker is Asaph, or a psalmist from his tradition, who is distressed and full of doubts. To keep from sinking into sadness, he decides to remember what God did before, especially when he rescued Israel from Egypt. Remembering that history restores his confidence.

For today: when you feel overwhelmed, make a list of the times God helped you before. Read it back to him in prayer and thank him. Remembering his past faithfulness strengthens faith to face what you do not understand today.
exp.50:17:
Here the psalmist asks God to act with kindness toward Zion, that is, Jerusalem, and to rebuild its walls. The words "do good" in the verse above carry the same sense of God acting favorably and generously toward the city. The walls represent protection and security for the city.

The psalm is attributed to David, after his serious sin with Bathsheba. After asking for forgiveness and confessing his brokenness, he ends by praying for the whole people. Some scholars think these final verses were added later, perhaps in the time of the exile, when the walls lay in ruins. This is not certain, and it is interpreted in several ways.

For today: when God restores us, our prayer does not stop with ourselves. We can ask that God also care for and strengthen his people, our church, and our community.
exp.23:6:
It says the gates should lift up their "heads," that is, open wide and completely, because the King of glory is about to enter. "Lift up yourselves" means "be lifted up," and "everlasting doors" suggests ancient, firm, and lasting gates. This is poetic language: the gates are imagined as people welcoming the King.

The psalm is attributed to David. After asking who may go up to the mountain of the LORD, the song moves into a celebration with questions and answers. Many believe it was sung in a procession, perhaps when the ark arrived in Jerusalem, but the text does not say this with certainty. Some Christians also see here a foreshadowing of Christ as King.

For today: open your heart to God without reservation. Examine whether there is any "door" still closed, such as a grudge, a habit, or a fear, and give it to Him, for He seeks to enter where He is welcomed with sincerity.
exp.117:22:
It says that what happened comes from God, not from chance or human effort. And what God has done causes wonder in those who see it. "It is marvellous in our eyes" means that it seems admirable and extraordinary to them. "The Lord" is God's name, and "from the Lord" means that it comes from him.

The speaker is the psalmist, probably together with the people, in a song of thanksgiving after being rescued. The verse before speaks of the stone that the builders rejected and that became the main cornerstone, the one that holds up the corner of the building. Scholars debate whether that stone represents Israel, a king, or another person. The New Testament applies this image to Jesus.

For today: when a painful situation changes for the better, take a moment to recognize the hand of God and give him thanks, instead of attributing everything to luck or to your own effort.
exp.105:16:
The verse tells how the earth opened and swallowed up Dathan, and covered the company of Abiram. "Swallowed up" means that the earth devoured them. "Company" is the group of followers who were with them.

The psalmist reviews the history of Israel in the wilderness. He remembers how the people rebelled against Moses and Aaron, whom he calls the holy one of the LORD. This is told in Numbers 16. There Korah is mentioned most of all, although this psalm names only Dathan and Abiram. The psalm aims to show God's faithfulness and the stubbornness of the people.

For today: envy and pride can lead us to rebel against the authority that God has placed. Before criticizing or dividing, examine your heart. Ask for humility, and learn to respect with gratitude those who serve faithfully.
exp.118:4:
This verse expresses a sincere wish: that the life of the one speaking were well directed and steady in keeping what God commands. The phrase "O that" is simply a way of saying "how I wish" or "I long that." "My ways were directed" refers to the way he lived, his decisions and habits, following a good course. "Statutes" are God's instructions or rules. "Keep" here means to hold to and practice, not just to look at.

The psalmist speaks in the first person, and tradition does not always identify him with certainty; some think of David, but the text does not say so. He has just said that God commanded that his precepts be kept diligently. He recognizes that he does not always manage this, and he longs for more consistency. He then adds that in this way he would not be put to shame, and he would praise God with an upright heart.

For today: instead of pretending you have everything figured out, tell God honestly where obeying is hard for you. Ask him for help, and take one concrete step this week, such as reading his Word every day.
exp.20:2:
This verse says that God went out ahead to meet the king with good things, like someone going out to welcome him. "Going out to meet" means going to receive someone. The "good blessings" are good and abundant favors. The "crown of fine gold" is a crown of pure gold, a sign of honor and authority.

It is a psalm of David, written for the choir director. Here the people, or David himself, gives thanks to God for what he did for the king: he granted what he asked and honored him. Some think it speaks of a specific victory, and others also see a look toward the Messiah. Scripture does not fully make this clear.

For today: Recognize that the good you have comes from God's hand, who often goes ahead of your needs. Today, before asking for something, take a moment to thank him for one specific blessing.
exp.118:97:
He says that God, through his commandments, gave the psalmist more wisdom than his enemies have. The reason is that those commandments are everlasting for him: they are always with him, and they are never taken away or lose their force. The phrase "they are everlasting to me" can also be understood as "I always have them with me," and translators read it in both ways.

The one speaking is the author of Psalm 119, a poem that praises God's law. We do not know with certainty who wrote it. This section opens with the Hebrew letter Mem, and in it the author says how much he loves the law and meditates on it all day long. The verses that follow show that this meditation gives him more understanding than his teachers and the elders.

For today: set aside a few minutes each day to read and think about the Bible. That way, when facing difficult decisions or people who pressure you, you will have God's guidance more present and clear.
exp.141:4:
David says that he cried out to God and declared to him: "You are my hope." He also says that God is his "portion," that is, his inheritance, the most valuable thing he has. "The land of the living" refers to this life, while we are still alive here.

The title of the psalm connects it to David when he was in the cave, probably fleeing from Saul. He felt alone, pursued, and with no one to defend him. Some scholars think of the cave of Adullam and others of the cave of En-gedi; the text does not fully clarify this. Even so, in the middle of his fear, David directs his pain toward God.

When you feel alone or without a way out, you can speak honestly to God. You do not need perfect words. Tell him simply, "You are my hope," and remember that he is your refuge today as well.
exp.101:19:
It says that the LORD looked down from his holy place to hear the groaning of the prisoners and to free those condemned to death. "Groaning" is a deep cry of pain. "Free" means to let go and set at liberty. "Condemned to death" refers to people who had no human way out left. The "á" with the accent is simply the way the word "a" is written in older spelling.
