Psalm 102 is the prayer of someone who is afflicted, feeling weak and alone. Then the psalmist looks to God, who reigns forever, and hopes that he will restore Zion. The "prisoners" may be the exiles or the oppressed of Israel. Many think of the captivity in Babylon, but the psalm does not state the author or the date with certainty. What is clear is that this deliverance is recorded so that future generations will praise God.

For today: when you feel that your cry is getting lost, remember that God hears the groaning. Pray with confidence and, if you can, help someone who is suffering injustice, illness, or confinement.
exp.136:6:
The explanation says the people ask God not to forget what the descendants of Edom did when Jerusalem fell. They were shouting "rase it, rase it, even to the foundation thereof," meaning "tear it down completely, down to its base," that is, to the very bottom of the buildings.

It was spoken by an Israelite exiled in Babylon, after the destruction of Jerusalem in 586 B.C. Edom, a neighboring people and a distant relative of Israel, rejoiced in its misfortune. The psalmist does not take revenge on his own; he leaves his pain in God's hands. It is an honest prayer full of wounds, and the verses that follow are even harsher. Some see in it a cry for justice, not an example to imitate.

Today we can bring God our pain and our anger with sincerity, and entrust justice to Him, rather than repaying evil for evil (Romans 12:19).
exp.117:4:
The psalmist says that, in a time of great distress, he called out to JAH, a short form of God's name (Jehovah, the Lord). God answered him and set him in a large place, meaning he brought him out into a wide, open, free space, in contrast with the narrowness of distress. The word "distress" also suggests a narrow place with no way out.

The one speaking is a believer from Israel who gives thanks publicly. This psalm invites the whole community, including the priests (the house of Aaron) and those who fear God, to repeat that his mercy endures forever. It is not known for certain who wrote it or in what exact situation; some think of a king or a leader of the people. What follows shows his confidence: he will not fear what man may do to him.

For today: when you feel trapped or without a way out, speak with God honestly, without waiting to feel better first. He listens and knows how to give you room and rest in his time.
exp.147:5:
This verse says that God made the heavens, the stars and the waters above, and that he keeps them in place forever. He also set over them a fixed order or decree that will not pass away. The phrase about what is "broken" or "violated" or "will cease to be kept" is an old way of explaining that this order will never be overturned, so that rewrite is deleted here as not needed for the reader's verse.

The psalm does not say who wrote it. The author calls all of creation to praise the LORD, from the heavens down to the earth. Earlier in the psalm it says that everything was created by his command. Here the verse gives another reason for praise: God not only created, but also gives order and stability. Some understand this "decree" as the laws of nature; others understand it as God's firm decision over every created thing.

Today we can trust that the God who maintains the order of the universe also cares for your life. When you feel that everything is changing or falling into disorder, remember his faithfulness and praise him, because what he upholds does not fall.
exp.80:6:
It says that God heard the cry of his people when they were in distress and rescued them. He answered them "in the secret place of thunder," that is, from a hidden but powerful place, as if behind the storm. It also says that he "tested" them at the waters of Meribah. "Selah" is a pause or a musical indication; its exact meaning is not certain.

Here God himself speaks, reminding Israel how he brought them out of Egypt and freed them from the heavy burden. Meribah refers to the place where the people complained about lacking water (Exodus 17). God reminds them of his faithfulness to ask them to listen to him and not follow other gods.

For today: when you are in trouble, call on God, and when you go through trials, remember how he has helped you before. Let that memory lead you to trust in him and obey him, instead of complaining or looking for support in other things.
exp.103:24:
It says the sea is great and has very wide boundaries. In it live countless fish, and also creatures both small and large. The word for "boundaries" here means limits or shores, and "beasts" refers to living creatures in general, in the sense of all that has life. "So is this great and wide sea" is an older way of speaking; today we would say "this great and wide sea," matching the wording of the verse above.

The psalmist speaks to God with praise. The psalm celebrates all of creation: the heavens, the mountains, the rivers, and the living creatures. After looking at the earth and human work, it now looks at the sea and marvels at the wisdom of God. This psalm does not name its author in the text, although some connect it with David.

Today we can pause to observe creation, whether it is the sea, a river, or a garden, and give thanks to God. That pause reminds us that He cares for all things, and that He will also care for us.
exp.128:5:
It says the enemies of Zion will be like the grass that grows on the rooftops. There the soil is very thin and the sun dries it out quickly, so it withers before it grows and is good for nothing. The ropes of the yoke are the cords that bind the oxen to the plow, and the sheaves are bundles of cut grain.

This psalm is a song of pilgrims, sung by Israel. The people remember that they were oppressed from their youth, but that God, who is righteous, delivered them. So they pray that those who hate Zion will not prosper. It is a prayer about the justice of God, not a personal revenge.

For today: when wickedness seems strong, do not lose hope. What has no root in God does not last. Place your trust in what He sustains, and leave justice in His hands without becoming bitter.
exp.73:0:
He says the psalmist asks God in pain, "Why have you rejected us forever?" He speaks of God's anger as smoke that rises, that is, as a wrath that burns. He calls the people "the sheep of your pasture," that is, the sheep of the grassland that God cares for. "Maschil" probably indicates a psalm meant for instruction or meditation; its exact meaning is not entirely certain.

The psalm is attributed to Asaph, or to his group of singers. It seems to have been written after a great destruction of the sanctuary, although it is not known for certain whether it refers to the fall of Jerusalem in 586 BC or to another event. The people suffer and do not understand God's silence.

For today: when you feel that God is far away, you can bring him your questions with honesty. Praying sincerely, even with pain, is also an act of faith, because you keep coming to him.
exp.66:3:
This verse invites all the nations to be filled with joy and to sing for gladness, because God governs the peoples with justice. The word "equity" means impartial justice, without favoritism. "Shepherd" means that God guides and cares for the nations the way a shepherd cares for his sheep. "Selah" is a word that probably indicates a pause for reflection, although its exact meaning is not certain.

It is a psalm of praise, whose author is not named in this text. The writer asks for God's blessing on Israel, but with a greater purpose: that his way and his salvation be known throughout the earth. That is why the joy is not only Israel's, but the joy of all peoples.

For today: when you see injustice in the world, pause and remember that God is a righteous judge and a faithful shepherd. Trust in Him, and ask Him that your life also reflect his justice toward those around you.
exp.38:7:
Here the psalmist asks God to forgive him and to rescue him from all his rebellions, that is, from his sins and acts of disobedience. He also asks that he not be allowed to become a scorn and a public shame before the fool, the person who lives without taking God into account.

The psalm is traditionally attributed to David. He is suffering under a severe discipline from God, which he calls a plague. After reflecting on how brief and fragile life is, he places his hope in the Lord alone. He recognizes that his suffering is tied to his sin, and so he asks for forgiveness and relief.

For today: when you fall short or go through trials, do not hide or make excuses. Come to God honestly, acknowledge your sin, and ask him for forgiveness and help. He restores the humble heart.
exp.80:14:
The explanation says that, if Israel had obeyed, those who hate God would have submitted to him. "Haters" are those who hate him, and "would have submitted" means they would have yielded before him. The phrase "their time would have been forever" can be understood in two ways: that Israel's blessing would have lasted forever, or that the punishment of the enemies would have been permanent.

God himself speaks in this psalm, in a song for a feast of Israel. With sorrow, he recalls that his people would not listen to him. That is why the verse speaks of what could have been but was not: God wanted to protect them and give them abundance.

For today: obedience to God is not a burden but a path of care. Think of an instruction from God that you have put off, and take one small step today to attend to it.
exp.118:36:
Here the psalmist asks God to turn his eyes away from what is empty, false, and of no lasting worth. He also asks God to give him life, encouragement, and strength to walk as God teaches.

The author of Psalm 119 is someone who loves God's word, though no one knows for certain who wrote it. Just before this, he asked that his heart be turned toward God's testimonies and not toward greed. He recognizes that his eyes and his heart can go after worthless things, and that is why he depends on God's help.

Today we live surrounded by images and messages competing for our attention. We can pray this verse when we begin the day and decide what we will look at and listen to. It may be wise to cut back on whatever distracts us and set aside a few minutes to read the Bible, asking God to revive us.
exp.120:3:
It says that God never falls asleep or gets distracted. The explanation of the verse's wording (the words that show he does not nod off even briefly and does not sleep at all) has been rewritten above, and the verb choices are left aside here, so the sentence is simply that his watchfulness has no breaks or lapses. "Keeps" means he cares for, protects, and watches over. "Israel" refers to God's people. In other words, God's care has no pauses and no neglect.

This psalm is a "song of ascents," which pilgrims probably sang as they climbed up to Jerusalem. It is not known for certain who is speaking: some think it is one person encouraging himself, and others see a group answering one another. The road was dangerous, with slippery ground, strong sun, and uncertain nights, and the psalm reminds them who is looking after them.

For today: when you have insomnia, fear, or worries about your family, remember that you need sleep, but God does not. Before you go to bed, bring to him in prayer what you cannot control, and rest in the knowledge that he is still awake, caring for you.
exp.111:1:
This verse says that the children and descendants of the person who fears God will have strength and influence in the land. A word that appears in the verse above, "seed," means offspring, that is, children and grandchildren. "Mighty" can be understood as strong, respected, or influential. And "the upright" are people who live with honesty and faithfulness to God.

This psalm does not say who wrote it. It opens with a call to praise the Lord, an invitation to give God glory. It is a wisdom poem that describes what the life of someone who honors the Lord and loves his commandments looks like. It is a broad picture of blessing, not an automatic promise for every case. Believers have understood this in different ways.

For today: if you want to leave a good inheritance to your children, begin by living with honesty and love for God in front of them. Your daily example speaks more loudly than your words.
exp.64:7:
The explanation says that people who live in the farthest parts of the earth feel awe and respect for the great works of God. The word "dwellers" refers to the people who live there, and "afraid" here means they stand in reverent wonder. It also says that God makes the "outgoings of the morning and evening" sing with joy, that is, the dawn and the dusk, where the sun rises and sets.

It is a psalm of David, a song of praise. Earlier, it speaks of God's power over the mountains, the seas, and even the tumult of the peoples. Afterward, it celebrates how God cares for the earth with rain and harvests. Many understand that the psalm joins the order of creation with God's daily care.

For today: begin and end your day giving thanks to God. A sunrise or a sunset can remind you that his care is constant and that it deserves your joy.
exp.74:0:
The verse opens with a note for the choir director: it was to be sung to the tune "Al-taschith," and it is a psalm of Asaph. Then it says: "We give thanks to you, O God, we give thanks to you, because your name is near." That is, God shows himself present and close. The phrase about telling of his wonders means that people speak of the great works God has done.

Asaph was a musician and worship leader in Israel. Here the people give thanks to God together as a community, and the verses that follow show God speaking as a just judge. It is not known with certainty what situation the psalm was written in; some think of a national crisis, but that is a guess.

Today we can begin the day by thanking God for something specific he has done, and telling it to another person. Recalling his works out loud strengthens faith, especially when everything seems uncertain.
exp.65:10:
It says that God allowed his people to fall into a net, like a trap where one becomes caught. It also says that he laid affliction upon their loins, that is, a heavy burden or painful pressure on the waist and back, as a sign of oppression and strain.

The psalmist speaks on behalf of the people, using "us." He looks back and acknowledges that they went through hard trials, but he understands them as part of the refining work God was doing, as silver is refined. Scholars do not agree on the exact historical situation he had in mind. What is clear is that the psalm ends in gratitude, for God brought them out into a place of abundance.

For today: when you feel trapped or burdened, do not think that God has gone away. You can bring your distress to him honestly, trust that he is still at work, and remember how he has sustained you before, so that you can wait with hope.
exp.118:53:
It says that God's teachings became songs for the psalmist in the place where he lived as a foreigner or passing through. The words "statutes" in the verse refer to God's instructions and commands. "House" here means a home or dwelling place, and "pilgrimage" refers to his wandering life, as a traveler.

The speaker is the author of Psalm 119, who is not named with certainty. Some think of David, but this is not certain. He is in a difficult time: the wicked abandon God's law, and this fills him with horror. In the middle of that pain, he remembers God's righteous works from the past and finds comfort. His words become music to his heart.

For today: when you feel far from home, tired, or surrounded by things that do not reflect God, memorize a verse and repeat it or sing it quietly. God's Word can give you company, encouragement, and peace along the way.
exp.131:16:
It says that God will make David's power grow again, like a shoot that comes up anew. "Horn" was an image of strength and victory. "I have ordained a lamp" means "I have prepared a lamp" for his anointed, that is, the chosen king. The lamp speaks of life, light and the continuation of his line.

Here God speaks in response to the prayer of the people, who remind him of his promise to David. "There" refers to Zion, or Jerusalem, where God chose to dwell. Many Christians see in this verse a announcement of Jesus, the Anointed One or Messiah, a descendant of David. The Jews of that time thought first of the kings of the Davidic line.

For today: when everything seems extinguished or without a future, trust that God keeps his promises. He can kindle a light where there seemed to be no hope. Pray, reminding him of what he has said in his Word.
exp.15:4:
Here the psalmist says that God himself is his inheritance, the best thing he possesses. The "portion" is the part that falls to a person; the "cup" speaks of what is given to drink, his daily provision; the "lot" is the land or inheritance that fell to him. He says that God is enough for him and that God keeps firm what belongs to him.

The psalm is spoken by David, according to its heading. It comes after rejecting those who serve other gods and after declaring his affection for the faithful people. After saying that he will not take part in their offerings, he affirms that his true inheritance is the Lord. The verse that follows speaks of the measuring lines by which the land was divided out.

For today: when you feel that something is missing, remember that having God is more than anything else. Before asking for more, give thanks for what you already have in Him, and let that assurance calm your longings.
exp.146:7:
This verse says that God is the one who covers the heavens with clouds, who prepares rain for the earth, and who makes grass grow on the mountains. The phrase "makes the mountains produce grass" means that He sustains nature.

The psalm does not say who wrote it. It is a song of praise, and the psalmist invites the people to sing to God with the harp. God is presented as the one who cares for the humble and also for the animals. The rain and the grass show His daily care, not only His great works. Interpreters connect it with the return of the people from exile, but this is not certain.

Today, when you see clouds, rain, or plants growing, take a moment to thank God. Remembering that He cares for the small and everyday things helps us trust that He will also care for you.
exp.11:6:
The verse says that God will care for his people and protect them forever. The word "keep" means to protect, to watch over with firmness. The phrase "this generation" refers to the wicked people of that time.

The psalmist, David, prays in a time of injustice, when the wicked oppress the poor and lie without shame. In the verses before, God himself answers and promises to rise up on behalf of the weak. His words are compared to silver refined seven times, that is, completely trustworthy. There is a note: some scholars believe that "you will keep them" refers to the poor, and others to the words of God. Both readings fit the passage.

When injustice or wickedness surrounds you, rest in God's promise. He does not abandon those who trust in him. Hold fast to his Word, which is firm and pure.
exp.41:0:
Speaking of the deer's longing: just as a thirsty deer pants and eagerly seeks the streams of water, so the psalmist's soul cries out for God. "To the chief Musician" was a direction for the one leading the singing. "Maschil" probably indicates a psalm of instruction or meditation, though its exact meaning is not certain. "Panteth" here means that the deer gasps and longs intensely.

The speaker is an Israelite believer, and the title attributes the psalm to the sons of Korah, a group of Levites in charge of music in worship. From what follows, he seems to be far from the temple, suffering and mocked by others who ask him: "Where is your God?" His desire for God is born of pain and of longing to worship him.

For today: when you feel dry or tired inside, do not pretend you are fine. Tell God honestly that you need him, and seek his presence in prayer, in his Word, and in the company of other believers.
exp.93:9:
This verse asks a question that already carries its answer. God is the one who corrects the nations, so he will certainly rebuke them. And he is the one who gives human beings knowledge, so he knows everything. Here "chastiseth" means to correct or discipline, and "knowledge" means understanding or wisdom.

The psalmist cries out to God, the Judge of the earth, because the wicked crush the weak and say that God neither sees nor notices. So he calls those who think this way "fools" and shows them their error with logical questions: the one who made the ear hears, and the one who formed the eye sees.

For today: when you see injustice or feel that no one notices your pain, remember that God sees and knows. Commit your situation to him with confidence and do not take justice into your own hands. And if he corrects you, receive it as care, not as rejection.
exp.56:1:
David says here that he will cry out, that is, call out for help with force, to God, whom he calls "most high," the one who is above all things. He also describes him as the God "that performeth all things for me." Some translations render this idea in other words, and the sense is of one who brings about what he intends on David's behalf.

David speaks. The title of the psalm says he wrote it when he was fleeing from Saul and hid in a cave. His life was in danger and he had no place to find protection. For this reason he takes refuge in God, under the shadow of his wings, an image of care and protection.

For today: when you feel cornered or without a way out, do not wait until everything is resolved before you pray. Speak to God honestly and trust that he is working on your behalf, even when you cannot yet see how.
exp.142:11:
In this verse David asks God to act in his mercy (his love and compassion) and to bring his enemies to an end. The word that was used for "destroy" in the older wording means to make something vanish, the way the wind scatters a cloud. In place of that, the reader can think of the verse's own word "destroy": David is asking God to wipe out those who attack his life and his peace. At the end, David gives the reason for his request: "I am thy servant," that is, someone who belongs to God and obeys him.

The speaker is David, according to the title of the psalm. He is distressed, pursued, and feels weak. Earlier in the psalm he asked God to teach him God's will and to guide him. Some think he wrote this during the pursuit by Absalom or by Saul, but this is not certain.

For today: when you feel attacked or overwhelmed, do not rely only on your own strength or your own righteousness. Pray with humility, seek God's will, and trust in his mercy, remembering that you belong to him.
exp.80:7:
The explanation says that God calls his people to listen to him with attention. Here the verse's own wording stands in for the older phrasing: God wants to speak to them seriously, as a solemn warning and a testimony against them if they fail. The unfinished phrase is left open, like a longing: may Israel be willing to listen.

The one speaking is God himself, within a psalm by Asaph that was sung at Israel's festivals. He recalls how he freed them from slavery in Egypt and cared for them in the desert. After so much care, he now asks for faithfulness: that they not worship other gods. What follows in the text shows that his warning comes from love.

For today: before asking God for something, set aside a few minutes to listen to him, reading his Word quietly. Ask yourself what he is saying to you and which things are occupying the place that belongs to him alone.
exp.145:4:
This verse says that the person who has the God of Jacob as their help, and who places their hope in the Lord their God, is happy and blessed. "Happy" here means deeply content, someone whom God favors. The name "the Lord" is God's personal name, and "the God of Jacob" calls to mind the God who remained faithful to that family despite their failures.

The one speaking is the psalmist, who praises God. The verses just before warn us not to trust in princes or in human beings, because they die and their plans come to an end. Then the psalm shows why God can be trusted: he created everything, he is faithful, he does justice, he gives bread to the hungry, and he frees prisoners.

For today: when you face a need, pray first and place your hope in God, without ceasing to value the help of other people. They may fail, but God does not.
exp.73:10:
Here the psalmist asks God why He is not acting. "Withdrawing the hand" means not using it, and "the right hand" is the hand of power. "Hiding it in the bosom" means keeping it tucked inside one's clothing, against the chest, like someone who folds their arms and does nothing.

The speaker is Asaph, or someone from his group of singers, speaking on behalf of the people. It is a lament: the temple has been destroyed and the enemies mock the name of God. The people feel left without prophets and without answers. Even so, the following verse reminds them that God is still their King.

We can be honest with God when He seems silent. Praying with doubt and pain is legitimate. And, like the psalmist, it helps to remember what God has already done before, in order to sustain hope.
exp.51:6:
It says that someone did not make God his refuge and his strength. Instead, he put his trust in having much money and possessions, and he remained firm in doing evil. The word translated here as "strength" in the source means a secure place or protection, but since that word does not appear in the verse you are reading, there is no need to explain it further. The phrase about remaining in his wickedness means that he kept on in it and did not change.

The psalm is spoken by David, according to its title, which connects it with Doeg the Edomite, who reported the priests to Saul (1 Samuel 22). The righteous repeat these words as a mockery when they see the wicked man fall. It is a contrast: he trusted in his riches, but David trusts in God, like a green olive tree in the house of God.

Today we can ask ourselves where our hearts truly rest. Money helps, but it cannot give us peace or protect us from everything. We can work diligently and, at the same time, place our trust in God and in his mercy.
exp.58:13:
The explanation says that the enemies of the psalmist return at evening, bark like dogs, and go around the city. In the verse your reader sees, "at evening" corresponds to the phrase about returning in the evening, and "go round about the city" describes them circling. Going around the city means they are circling, searching for something. In that time, the city's dogs were often street dogs, and they roamed at night looking for food.

David is the speaker. The title of the psalm connects it to the time when Saul sent men to watch his house in order to kill him. Some understand the verse as a wish that his enemies keep going around without achieving anything. Others read it as a description of his threat. Both readings show his distress and his need for help.

Today, when you feel that problems surround you at night, bring them honestly before God. You do not have to take revenge. Like David, you can wait for the morning singing that God is your refuge.
exp.67:22:
He says that God's people will see a victory so complete that their feet will be stained with the blood of their enemies, and even the dogs will lick up that blood. "Will be dyed red" means it will be colored red. It is a strong image, typical of war in the ancient world, to say that evil was utterly defeated.

The psalm is by David, and it is a song of victory that celebrates God as King who delivers his people. Earlier it speaks of God striking down his enemies, and afterward it describes a procession of praise in the sanctuary. Some understand this scene as a historical event of war, and others as poetic language about God's final triumph. The text does not make clear which is the exact case.

For today: you can rest in the knowledge that God does not let injustice have the last word. Trust Him when evil seems strong, and instead of seeking personal revenge, let God judge, while you keep praising Him with hope.
exp.14:3:
The person who lives uprightly does not admire someone who is worthless because of their wickedness; instead, they honor those who respect God. Furthermore, if they have made a solemn promise (an oath) and that promise turns out to cost them dearly, they keep it anyway and do not back down.

This psalm is by David. It answers the question of the first verse: "Who may dwell in your holy hill?" It describes the character of the one who can be near God. This verse shows that such a person has clear values: they know whom to respect and they are faithful to their word, even when it costs them.

Today we can learn to keep what we promise, even when it is no longer convenient for us. It is also wise to choose carefully whom we admire: to value people who are honest and humble, rather than those who only have success, fame, or power.
exp.106:30:
This verse is an invitation to give thanks. To "praise" means to recognize and celebrate the good that God does. "Mercy" is his faithful, compassionate love. "Wonderful works" are his amazing deeds. "Children of men" simply means people, humanity in general.

The psalmist is not speaking of his own story, but calls on everyone God has rescued to praise him. In this passage he describes sailors caught in a storm who cry out to God, and he calms the waves and brings them safely to harbor. It is one of several pictures of people rescued in the psalm. Many understand that the storm also illustrates other difficulties of life.

For today: when a difficulty passes, do not stop at relief alone. Write down one thing in which God helped you and give thanks for it out loud, or tell someone in your church or family about it.
exp.71:9:
It says that kings from distant lands will come to honor the king with gifts. "Tarshish" was a distant region, probably to the west, by the sea, though its exact location is not known. "Sheba" and "Seba" were peoples of the south, and scholars debate where they were located. The words "gifts" and "tributes" refer to presents that show respect and submission.

This is a psalm attributed to Solomon, or dedicated to him, that asks God for a just king. It describes a wide reign full of peace. The verses that follow explain the reason: this king protects the poor and the afflicted. Many Christians see here a sign pointing to Jesus Christ, the righteous King.

For today: if Christ is worthy of honor, we can give him our best, and serving those in need is one way of honoring him.
exp.37:3:
It says that David's sins have covered him completely, like water rising higher than his head. It also compares them to a very heavy load that he can no longer bear. The wrongs and failings he committed are what the verse speaks of; the verse says they have become heavier.

The psalmist, whom the title attributes to David, speaks in a time of physical suffering and distress. He feels that God is disciplining him for his sin. We do not know exactly what his fault or his illness was, and scholars understand it in several ways. What is clear is that his conscience crushes him.

For today: do not carry the guilt alone. Acknowledge it honestly before God and ask Him for forgiveness. The Bible promises that He forgives those who come to Him with humility, and that Jesus invites us to bring Him our burdens.
exp.79:0:
The opening line is a note for the choir director: "Shoshannim Eduth" seems to indicate a tune or type of song, and its exact meaning is uncertain. Then the psalmist cries out to the Shepherd of Israel, who cares for his people as a flock. "Joseph" here stands for the whole people. "Between the cherubim" recalls the ark of the covenant, where God's presence was felt. "Shine forth" is a plea: that God would reveal himself and act.

The speaker is Asaph, or someone from his group of musicians, speaking on behalf of the people. From the verses that follow (Ephraim, Benjamin and Manasseh), it seems the northern tribes were suffering a crisis. Scholars do not agree on the exact historical moment. What is clear is that they are asking for help and restoration.

For today: when you feel lost or without strength, pray with sincerity. God is a shepherd who listens, and you can ask him to guide you and restore you.
exp.68:15:
It says the psalmist asks God to hear him and to look upon him with attention. He asks this because God's mercy is "lovingkindness", that is, good and kind. His "tender mercies" are God's compassion and tenderness toward those who suffer. He asks that God look upon him according to the greatness of that compassion, not according to his own merits.

The psalm is traditionally attributed to David, according to its heading, though some scholars debate how some of the details fit. He is surrounded by enemies and feels as if he is sinking into mud or deep waters. His distress is so strong that he can only lean on the character of God, not on his own strength.

When you are overwhelmed, pray with sincerity and rest on how good God is. You do not need to present a perfect argument; it is enough to come near, trusting in his compassion.
exp.83:1:
The writer says the psalmist longs with great intensity to be in God's temple. The word "longeth" here names a good and strong desire, not greed. The "courts" are the open areas of the sanctuary where people gathered to worship. The phrase "my flesh" refers to the body: his whole being, inside and out, sings with joy to the living God, the God who is real and present.

This psalm was sung by the sons of Korah, a family of Levites who served in worship. The speaker feels far from the sanctuary and misses it. The text does not make clear with certainty where he was or why, and scholars interpret it in various ways. What is clear is his deep love for being close to God.

For today: cultivate a desire to seek God, not merely out of duty. Set aside a moment during the week to pray, sing, or meet with other believers, and ask Him to renew your hunger for Him.
exp.81:7:
It says that the psalmist asks God to rise up, that is, to act, and to judge the earth with justice. The reason is that all the nations belong to Him. The word "inherit" means that He will receive them as His own. "Nations" means peoples or nations.

In this psalm, God appears in the midst of an assembly and rebukes unjust rulers who did not defend the poor or the fatherless. He calls them "gods" because of the authority they held, but reminds them that they will die like any human being. Some understand this to refer to human judges and others to spiritual beings. The final verse is the psalmist's prayer: that God Himself would set things in order.

For today: when you see injustice and feel weary, pray with confidence, because God is the true Judge. And if you have any authority, even a small one, use it to care for the weak.
exp.69:0:
The explanation says that David asks God for urgent help. "Come quickly" is what the request means, "deliver me" means rescuing him from danger, and "hasten to help me" is a plea that God not delay in coming to his aid. The heading dedicates it to the chief musician, the leader of singing in worship, and it includes the words "to bring to remembrance," which probably indicates a psalm meant to call a need to God's attention. Its exact sense is not entirely certain.

David is the speaker, although the psalm does not say at what exact moment of his life he wrote it. He feels threatened by enemies who seek his life, as the verses that follow show. This psalm is very similar to the final part of Psalm 40 (verses 13 to 17), and it is not known with certainty which one was written first.

When you are in a tight spot, you do not need an elaborate prayer. You can simply say to God: "Help me, and quickly." He hears the honest cry of someone who admits that they cannot manage alone.
exp.34:4:
They are like chaff, the light outer husk of the grain that separates when it is winnowed. The wind carries it away without any effort. The psalmist asks that the angel of the Lord act against them.

The psalm is spoken by David, according to its heading. People pursue him without cause, they set traps for him, and they repay good with evil. So he cries out to God as to a defender in a court case and in a battle. This kind of prayer is called imprecatory: it asks that God do justice, not that David take revenge.

For today: when someone treats you unjustly, do not take revenge. Bring your pain to God honestly and trust that he judges better than you do. Then ask him also for a heart free of resentment, as Jesus taught about praying for those who persecute us.
exp.115:0:
The explanation says that the psalmist loves God because God listened when he cried out for help. "Lord" is the name of the Lord. "Supplications" are requests made with need and humility. The phrase "he hath heard my voice" shows that God was not far away or indifferent, but attentive to his cry.

The psalm does not say who wrote it. The one speaking is a person who came very close to death and was delivered, as the following verses show: "the sorrows of death" and "the pains of the grave." His love springs from gratitude. Some think the psalm was sung in worship to give thanks to God, but this cannot be stated with certainty.

Today we can calmly remember the times God sustained us, even in simple ways. Taking a moment to thank him in prayer, in our own words, helps our love for him grow and helps us trust him more in the difficulties ahead.
exp.106:22:
This verse speaks of sailors and merchants who travel the sea in ships. "They that go down to the sea in ships" is an old way of saying they board their ships and set out to sail. "That do business in great waters" means they work and trade out on the ocean or the great seas.

Psalm 107 is a song of thanksgiving for the people of Israel. Its author is not known for certain. Here the psalmist presents several groups of people whom God rescued: travelers in the desert, prisoners, the sick, and, in this case, sailors. The verses that follow show that, in the middle of a storm, they saw the power of God.

For today: even in your daily work, God is present. If you pass through a storm of problems or uncertainty, cry out to Him, and afterward do not forget to thank Him and tell what He has done for you.
exp.143:4:
Here the psalmist asks God to come down from heaven and act. "Bow your heavens" is an image: as if God opened the sky and leaned toward the earth. "Touch the mountains, and they shall smoke" recalls when God came down on Mount Sinai and the mountain smoked (Exodus 19:18). Mountains are a symbol of what is firm and powerful, yet before God they tremble.

David speaks, according to the title of the psalm. He has just acknowledged that human beings are frail, like a shadow that passes. For this reason he does not trust in his own strength. He is in the middle of dangers and enemies, and he asks that God intervene with power.

For today: when you feel small before a great problem, you do not have to pretend to be strong. Acknowledge your weakness and ask God to intervene. He is greater than any mountain you face.
exp.43:9:
This verse says that God made his people turn back before the enemy, and that those who hated them carried off their goods for themselves. The phrase "they plundered us" is an old way of saying "they robbed us," and the words "those who hated us" refer to the people who had hatred toward them.

The psalm is a complaint from the people of Israel, speaking together as a whole. They had been defeated in battle, and they did not understand why, since they remembered the victories God had given them before. The psalm does not mention any specific sin, so the people feel they are suffering without knowing the reason. Scholars do not agree on which particular defeat is meant.

For today: when you feel that God is silent in the middle of a loss, you can tell him honestly what you feel, as this psalm does. Praying with sincerity, without pretending, is also faith.
exp.30:3:
It says God will rescue the psalmist from a hidden trap. The "net" is like the kind used to catch birds or animals: it was set out of sight to snare someone without warning. The word for a place of safety and firm protection, where one shelters from danger, is a stronghold. The word for "quickly" appears in the verse before it, meaning "soon."

The speaker is David, according to the psalm's heading. He is in distress, surrounded by enemies who set traps for him with deceit. For that reason he asks for help and declares that God is his rock and his fortress. Shortly after, he will say: "Into thy hand I commit my spirit," words that Jesus also spoke on the cross (Luke 23:46).

Today, when you feel that someone is deceiving you or that life is setting traps for you, do not rely only on your own cleverness. Speak to God honestly, ask Him for wisdom, and take refuge in Him. He is a safe place, even when the road becomes hard.
exp.118:66:
This verse says that before going through a time of suffering or affliction, the psalmist was lost, straying from the right path. Now, by contrast, he keeps God's word. The word "straying" means having wandered off the way, like a sheep that gets lost. "Afflicted" here refers to being troubled or tested, not only to feeling shame.

The speaker is the author of Psalm 119, a believer who loves God's law. We do not know for certain who wrote it or what his exact affliction was. In this section (the letter Teth) he says that God has dealt well with him, and then mentions that the proud attacked him with lies. He sees that this pain, in some way, drew him closer to God.

For today: when you go through a difficulty, ask God what He wants to teach you. Sometimes trials bring us back to the path and make us value His word. Take a moment to read the Bible and thank Him for how He has guided you.
exp.82:9:
It says that those enemies died at Endor and were left like dung on the ground. A heap of rubbish or manure is the picture here. It is a harsh image: their bodies were left lying there, with no honor at all.

The speaker is Asaph, or a psalmist from his group, who prays to God when several nations join together against Israel. He asks God to do now what He did before with Midian, Sisera, and Jabin. Endor does not appear in the account in Judges of that battle, so it is not known for certain which detail is meant.

For today: when you feel threatened, remember that God has already defended His people before. Bring your fear to Him in prayer, trust His justice, and do not take revenge on your own.
exp.43:5:
Here the psalmist says that he does not put his trust in his weapons. The "bow" and the "sword" stand for military strength and human resources. He says it is not they that will save him. The words "will not trust" and "shall not save me" show that his hope lies somewhere else.

The speaker is a psalmist who represents the whole people of Israel, and the psalm is attributed to the sons of Korah. It is not known with certainty in which battle it was written. First, the people remember that God is their king and that he gave them victories. Then they say that God kept them safe and that for this reason they will glory in him always. The victory is credited to God, not to weapons.

Today we can work and prepare ourselves with effort, but without placing our hearts in money, studies, or our abilities as if they were what saves us. When you face a great problem, do what is yours to do and entrust it to God, trusting that he sustains your life.
exp.100:5:
He says that the one speaking will look with favor upon the faithful and honest people of the land, so that they may live near him. Whoever strives to walk in an upright way (a life without duplicity, not one without mistakes) will be the one who serves him. The faithful are those who are loyal and trustworthy.

It is a psalm of David, according to its heading, and it speaks as a king who promises to govern with righteousness. Before and after this, it rejects liars, the proud, and slanderers. Here it shows the positive side: surrounding oneself with people worthy of trust so that his house and his government may be just.

For today: when choosing friends, partners, or coworkers, look for people who are faithful and sincere, and make an effort to be a person of integrity yourself. Honesty protects homes, churches, and work.
exp.149:3:
He says we should praise God with varied music. The "timbrel" was a small hand drum, a percussion instrument. The "pipe" is a wind instrument. The "strings" are stringed instruments, and the "organ" was probably not the church organ we know today, but a simple wind instrument, perhaps a pipe with several tubes.

This is the second-to-last psalm of the book, a closing full of joy. We do not know for certain who wrote it. The psalmist invites the whole people to praise God in his sanctuary, for his mighty deeds and his greatness. The instruments mentioned were the ones used in Israel's worship.

For today: God gladly receives praise expressed in many ways. Use with joy the gifts you have, whether singing, playing, or simply giving thanks, and offer them to God without comparing yourself to others.
exp.34:6:
It says that David was attacked without reason. His enemies hid a net for him and dug a pit, as one does to catch an animal. Here "my soul" means his life, himself. "Without cause" means that he had done them no wrong.

In this psalm David speaks as one crying out to God. He feels hunted by people who set traps for him in secret, even though he had treated them well. For that reason he asks God to be his defender. The verses that follow ask that the trap prepared for him fall back on them. It is strong language, fitting the prayer of a wounded man who leaves justice in the hands of God.

For today: when someone treats you unjustly or speaks badly of you without reason, bring your pain to God honestly. Ask him for justice and protection, and do not take revenge on your own. He sees what is hidden.
exp.65:17:
This verse says that if the psalmist had held onto evil in his heart, approving it and keeping it close, the Lord would not have listened to him. The phrase "looking at iniquity" means dwelling on it with pleasure and without wanting to let it go. The word "hear" in the verse carries the same sense, so the meaning is simply that God would not have heard him.

The speaker is the psalmist, perhaps King David, though the text does not state this with certainty. He invites those who fear God to listen to his testimony. He had cried out to God, and in the verses that follow he rejoices that God did answer him. In other words, his heart was sincere before the Lord, with no attachment to sin.

For today: before you pray, ask God to show you whether there is something you are protecting or excusing. Confess it honestly. God does not demand perfection, but He does ask for a heart willing to return to Him.
exp.58:8:
In this verse, David, faced with a powerful enemy, decides to place his hope in God and not in himself. The word "strength" refers to the enemy's strength, though other translations read it as "my strength," and scholars debate which reading is original. "Defence" means a safe refuge, like a high tower where no one can reach you.

David speaks, according to the psalm's heading, when Saul sent men to watch his house so they could kill him. The verses before describe enemies who speak with words like knives and believe no one can hear them. David answers that God does hear and is above all things.

When someone stronger than you threatens or pressures you, do not just stare at their power. Pause, pray sincerely, and remember that God is your refuge. Then take the next step calmly, trusting that you are not alone.
exp.117:1:
This verse invites Israel, the people of God, to declare aloud that the Lord's mercy endures forever. The phrase "let them say" conveys the idea of saying it now, without delay. Here "mercy" speaks of God's faithful and steadfast love, the kind that never gives up and never grows weary.

The psalm begins with a call to praise God. It seems to be a public invitation, perhaps used in the worship of the people. It then mentions the house of Aaron, the priests, and those who fear the Lord, that is, those who hold him in reverence and trust. Some believe it was sung in alternating parts, but the text does not say so with certainty.

Today we can do the same: declare aloud, with other believers or in prayer, how God has been faithful to us. Remembering his mercy in difficult days strengthens our faith and gives us hope.
exp.113:3:
The explanation says that the mountains skipped like rams and the little hills like lambs. It is poetic language: it pictures all of creation moving with joy or awe. The hills that are described are small hills, and the verb describes quick leaps, like those of young animals full of life.

The psalmist, a poet from Israel who is not named, recalls the time when God brought his people out of Egypt. He mentions the sea that fled and the Jordan that turned back. Many understand that the mountains that leap may recall earthquakes at Sinai, although the text does not make this clear. The idea is that all of nature responded to the presence of the Lord, and that is why the psalm goes on to ask the sea, the Jordan, and the mountains why they moved.

If even the mountains tremble before God, we too can draw near to him with reverence and joy. Today, before you pray, pause and remember something God has done for you. Let it fill you with wonder and gratitude.
exp.106:29:
This verse says that when the storm settles, the sailors rejoice because the waters have become still. Then God brings them to the harbor they wanted to reach. The waves grew calm and there was peace, so the sailors could rest.

Psalm 107 does not say who wrote it. It speaks of people whom God rescued from various dangers, and this section describes those who traveled by sea. When they cried out in their distress, God stilled the storm. The psalm calls for giving thanks for his mercy, and the verses that follow ask that he be praised before the people.

For today: when you go through a crisis, cry out to God sincerely. He can calm the storm or guide you through it to a safe place. Afterward, do not forget to thank him and tell others what he has done for you.
exp.139:8:
They say that those who surround me on every side be overtaken by the harm their own words were meant to cause. "Let the mischief of their own lips cover them" is a picture: the evil they spoke will fall on them like a burden or a cloak. "Lips" refers to what they say.

David is the one speaking, according to the title of the psalm, although some scholars debate certain details of its authorship. He is surrounded by violent and deceitful people. In the verse before, he gives thanks that God protected him on the day of battle. Now he asks for justice: that the evil planned against him turn back upon those who planned it.

For today: when someone speaks badly of you or slanders you, you do not need to take revenge. You can bring your pain honestly to God, as David did, and trust that He will do justice. Watch your own words too, because they have consequences.
exp.21:18:
Here the psalmist asks God not to stay far from him. He calls him "my strength," meaning "you are my strength," and begs him to hurry to help him. The word "haste" in the verse is simply a call to come quickly. It is an urgent cry from someone who feels alone.

The psalm is attributed to David in its heading. He is surrounded by mockers and enemies, and his suffering is extreme. The verses before this one describe how his clothing is divided among others, and the New Testament connects that scene with the crucifixion of Jesus (John 19:23-24). After describing his distress, David turns again to ask God for help.

Today, when you feel alone or without a way out, you can pray honestly and without embellishment: "Lord, do not stay far from me, help me quickly." God is not bothered by your urgency. Speaking with Him in the middle of pain is a way of trusting Him.
exp.44:9:
She is told to listen closely, to look carefully, and to pay attention. She is also asked to leave behind her own people and her father's house. "Hearken" means "listen"; "incline thine ear" means "pay attention with humility." This is not a rejection of her family, but an invitation to begin a new life.

This psalm is a song for a royal wedding. The speaker seems to be the poet, who addresses the bride. It was customary for the wife to leave her home to join the household of her husband. Many Christians see here a picture of Christ and his Church, and the New Testament applies the psalm to the Son in Hebrews 1:8-9. Others read it only as a poem for a king of Israel.

For today: following Christ means listening to his voice and being willing to let go of what holds us back, such as habits, fears, or loyalties that compete with him. Today you can set aside a few minutes to listen to him in his Word and ask him what you should leave behind.
exp.84:0:
He says God was kind to his land. "Favourable" means gracious, kind, willing to help. The phrase "thou hast brought back the captivity of Jacob" means that God brought his people back from exile or slavery. Jacob here stands for the whole nation of Israel. At the beginning there is also a note for the choir director: it is a psalm for the sons of Korah, a family of musicians in the temple.

The sons of Korah speak here, singing on behalf of the people. They recall what God has already done in order to ask him to act again. Many think it refers to the return from Babylon, but the psalm does not say so clearly, so we cannot be sure. The verses that follow speak of forgiveness and of God calming his anger.

When you are going through a difficulty, remember the times God helped you before. Giving thanks for the past strengthens your trust and encourages you to pray with hope for what you need today.
exp.4:8:
The explanation says that the enemies of the psalmist are not sincere. Honesty is the sense of the first word quoted, their inward part is their heart and inner self, and wickedness is their corruption. Their throat is like an open grave: from it come death and rot. The last phrase means they will flatter, speaking with pleasant but false words.

David speaks, according to the traditional title of the psalm, in a morning prayer. He feels surrounded by liars who want to harm him. First he asks God to guide him, and then he asks God to judge those enemies. Paul quotes this verse in Romans 3:13 to speak of human wickedness in general.

For today: guard your words and be wary of empty flattery. Ask God to let your mouth speak the truth with love, and entrust to him the offenses of those who lie.
exp.103:19:
It says that God is the one who brings on the darkness, and so night comes. When that happens, the wild animals of the forest come out and move about. The word "creep" here means they move about in every direction, and "forest" refers to the woods or hills, not necessarily a tropical jungle.

This is a psalm of praise that does not say who wrote it. It celebrates God as Creator and caretaker of everything that exists. The psalmist surveys creation: mountains, moon, sun, night. It shows that every creature has its time and its place, and that all of this depends on the order God set in place.

For today: the night, which sometimes frightens us or leaves us weary, is also under God's care. You can rest knowing that he upholds the world, even when you cannot see anything. Today, before sleeping, thank him for the day and entrust your worries to him.
exp.119:1:
The psalmist here asks God to rescue him, that is, to save him and protect him. His soul, or in other words his whole life, is threatened by lying lips and deceitful tongues, words that speak of people who lie, deceive and slander. A deceitful tongue is one that is tricky and false.

The one speaking is a believer living in distress. The verse before this one says that he has already called out to the Lord and that the Lord answered him. This is the first of the songs of ascents, which pilgrims probably sang as they went up to Jerusalem. We do not know for certain who wrote it or what the exact situation was, but the pain of living surrounded by deceit is clearly felt.

For today: if someone has hurt you with lies or gossip, do not answer with more hurtful words. Bring your pain honestly before God, ask him to defend you, and take care that your own mouth always speaks the truth.
exp.52:0:
This verse begins with a musical note: it is for the choir director, "upon Mahalath" (probably the name of a melody or an instrument; it is not known for certain) and it is a "Maschil," which seems to be a song of instruction. It says that the fool, that is, the one who acts without wisdom or fear of God, thinks in his heart: "The fool hath said in his heart, There is no God." Because of this they became corrupt and did abominable iniquity. "There is none that doeth good" describes a wickedness that is very widespread.

David, the psalmist, speaks as a teacher. He wants to show that denying God is not just an idea, but an attitude that affects behavior. This psalm is very similar to Psalm 14. Paul quotes similar words in Romans 3.

For today: examine your heart. Sometimes we do not deny God with words, but we live as if he did not see us. Ask him to give you wisdom and humility to obey him.
exp.138:23:
This verse is a prayer. The psalmist asks God to look into his life and see whether there is any wicked way in him, that is, any crooked or harmful conduct. He also asks God to lead him in the way everlasting, the way of God, which lasts forever and leads to true life.

The speaker is David, according to the heading of the psalm (some scholars debate how that attribution should be understood). Earlier he spoke of his rejection of the wicked, and now he turns toward himself. Instead of considering himself righteous, he invites God to examine his own heart. Some understand "the way everlasting" as God's ancient and tested path.

For today: sincerely ask God to show you attitudes or habits that harm you, such as pride, resentment, or lying. Pause in silence, listen, and be willing to change with his help.
exp.118:130:
It says that the psalmist opened his mouth and drew in deep breaths, because he longed for God's commandments. The image is of someone breathing hard and panting, like a person who is very thirsty or very hungry. Opening the mouth and panting is a picture of urgent need.

The one speaking is the author of Psalm 119, a believer who loves God's Word. We do not know for certain who wrote it. He has just said that God's testimonies are wonderful and that his word gives light to the simple. Now he expresses how much he needs it. Right after this, he asks God for mercy and for guidance in his steps.

For today: do not see the Bible only as a duty, but as food the soul needs. Before reading it, ask God to give you a hunger for it, and set aside a few quiet minutes to listen to him.
exp.146:15:
He sends the snow, and the snow falls soft and white, like wool. He also scatters the frost like ashes.

It is a psalm of praise. We do not know for certain who wrote it. It seems to be addressed to the people of Israel, and many place it after the return from exile, although this is debated. The psalmist praises God because he cares for his people and also rules over nature. The same word of God that gives peace and food also commands the winter and then melts it.

For today: when cold or difficult seasons arrive, remember that God is still in charge. Thank him for ordinary daily blessings, and trust that he also knows how to bring the thaw.
exp.83:2:
This verse says that even small birds, like the sparrow and the swallow, find a safe place to live and to raise their young, close to the altars of God. The title "Lord of hosts" speaks of God as the Lord of all power. The psalmist calls him "my King and my God," with personal affection.

The one speaking is an worshipper from the sons of Korah, who served in the work of worship. He feels a deep longing to be in the house of God. Scholars debate whether the birds literally nested near the sanctuary or whether this is only a poetic image, but the meaning is clear: he desires that same place of rest.

Today we can remember that God offers us a spiritual home, no matter how small or weary we feel. Seek a moment of prayer or of gathering with other believers today, and rest in his care.
exp.49:21:
It says that God calls the attention of those who live as if He did not exist. Consider this carefully is what the phrase means. To forget God is to live without keeping Him in mind. The verse speaks of God tearing someone apart like a wild beast that seizes its prey, and no one being able to rescue them from His judgment.

God Himself speaks in Psalm 50, a psalm of Asaph. Before this, He rebukes people who keep religious practices but live in wickedness: they slander their own brother and think that God, by remaining silent, approves of what they do. His silence was patience, not approval. This warning is a merciful alert before judgment, and the next verse offers a path of gratitude and obedience.

Today, do not mistake God's patience for indifference. Examine how you speak about others and, if there is something to correct, ask forgiveness and change today.
exp.18:12:
He says David asks God to hold him back, to restrain him, so that he does not fall into presumptuous sins, that is, sins committed deliberately, with arrogance and defiance. He asks that these sins not have dominion over him, that they not rule him like a master. If God keeps him, he will be upright (blameless, with a sincere heart) and will be cleared of great transgression, which is a serious sin against God.

David, the psalmist, speaks here after praising God's law. He recognizes that there are errors he cannot see, and now he also fears the sins he could commit knowingly. He calls himself God's servant because he submits to God. Some think the presumptuous sins might also refer to proud people, but the more common understanding is presumptuous sins.

For today: ask God each morning to hold you back from the temptations you already know, and stay away from situations where you usually give in.
exp.118:123:
Here the psalmist asks God to deal with him according to his mercy, that is, with his love and kindness, and not according to what he deserves. He also asks God to teach him his decrees, which are God's laws and commands. Calling himself God's "servant" means that he recognizes himself as someone who belongs to God and obeys him.

The one speaking is the author of Psalm 119, whose identity we do not know for certain. He feels pressed by proud people who treat him with violence. His eyes grew tired from waiting for God's deliverance, which here means his salvation or help. Even in that distress, he asks not only to be rescued but also to learn.

Today we can do the same: when we are in trouble, let us trust in God's mercy and not in our own merits. And let us also ask him to teach us his way, seeking to understand his Word every day.
exp.24:7:
It says that God is good and upright, meaning that his character is kind and also just. Because of this, he himself teaches sinners the right way. The word "sinners" here describes people who have gone astray and need guidance. The promise that he will teach them means that God does not leave them lost.

This psalm is attributed to David. Before this verse, he asks God not to remember the sins of his youth or his rebellions, but to deal with him according to his mercy. Now David relies on what he knows about God: because he is good, he dares to hope that God will correct and guide him. Afterward, the psalm speaks of the humble who receive direction.

For today: if you have failed, do not run from God. Come near with humility, acknowledge your mistake, and ask him to show you the next step. His goodness invites you to return, not to hide.
exp.97:6:
This verse invites the sea to roar, along with everything in it, and also invites the world and all its inhabitants. The explanation of the old word that means to roar or make a great noise has to go, since the reader's verse does not contain it. The sea's fullness refers to everything that fills the sea: its waters, its creatures, its vastness.

The psalm does not say who wrote it. It is a song of praise that calls everyone to celebrate God as King. Earlier, harps and trumpets are used; here the whole of creation is added. The reason appears afterward: God comes to judge the earth with righteousness and uprightness.

Today we can remember that praise is not only a matter for Sunday or for music. When we see the sea, a landscape, or our everyday life, we can pause and give thanks to God for his greatness and for his justice, which gives us hope.
exp.107:3:
This verse says that God's faithful love is immense, higher than the heavens, and that his truth or faithfulness reaches up to the clouds. The word "mercy" here means his steadfast love, which never gives up. "Thy truth" means that God keeps what he promises and can be trusted.

David speaks, according to the title of the psalm. He is full of encouragement and resolves to praise God early in the day, with music, before all the peoples. Many scholars note that this psalm joins parts of Psalms 57 and 60. After praising, David asks God for help for his people.

For today: when you feel small or guilty, remember that God's love is greater than your failures. Begin the day by thanking him for his faithfulness, and ask him for help with confidence.
exp.77:40:
They kept turning away from God again and again, and they put Him to the test. The explanation says that the people of Israel repeatedly turned away from God and tested Him again. The verse's phrase "tested God" here means provoking God or putting Him to the test with distrust, as if demanding that He prove His power. The phrase "limited the Holy One of Israel" means they set limits on Him, placing restrictions on what He could do: they thought God could only help them in a certain way. "Holy One of Israel" is a title of God that highlights His purity and greatness.

The psalm is by Asaph, a leader of worship. It recalls Israel's history in the wilderness to teach new generations. It wants them not to repeat the rebellion of their ancestors, who forgot God's miracles in Egypt, even though He had cared for them with patience.

For today: when we pray, let us avoid telling God how and when He should act. Let us remember what He has already done for us and trust that His help can be greater than we imagine.
exp.91:7:
It says that, unlike the wicked, who pass away quickly, God is the Most High forever. "Lord" is the name of God, and "most high" means that he is above all things and all people, with nothing able to surpass him. The phrase "but thou" marks a contrast.

This psalm is a song of praise, and the one speaking is the psalmist, whose identity is not known for certain. He has just said that the wicked grow like the grass, that is, quickly and without firm roots, but they end up destroyed. In contrast to that passing reality, he focuses on the fact that God reigns forever, and so he trusts that justice will come.

For today: when it seems that wicked people are doing well, do not lose heart or become bitter. Remember that God is still on his throne. Rest in the knowledge that he has the last word, and keep doing good with patience.
exp.115:7:
The explanation says that God has rescued the one speaking from three dangers: death, tears, and stumbling. Rescued means saved or brought to safety. The verse itself puts it this way: for you have delivered my soul from death, my eyes from tears, and my feet from falling. In other words, God saved me from dying, took away my weeping, and kept my feet from falling.

The speaker is a psalmist who does not name himself, and tradition does not identify him with certainty. He had been deeply distressed, brought low, and close to death. God lifted him up. Now he speaks to his own soul, tells it to rest, and remembers the good things God has done. Right after this, he vows to keep living faithfully before God.

For today: think back to the times God held you steady in hard moments. Write them down and thank him for them. Remembering his faithfulness helps you rest and trust when new trials come.
exp.45:5:
The explanation says that the nations "raged," meaning they made a great deal of noise, like roaring with fury. The kingdoms "were moved," that is, they staggered and lost their firmness. But when God "uttered his voice," the earth "melted": everything came undone before his word. Human noise is loud, but the voice of God is more powerful.

This psalm was written by the sons of Korah, Levites who served in the worship of Israel. They speak on behalf of God's people, who face threats from nations. What sustains them is not an army, but that God is in the midst of his city. That is why they sing with confidence: "The Lord of hosts is with us."

For today: when the news, crises, or fears make a lot of noise, remember that God is still greater. Before you become anxious, pause, pray, and trust that he is with you and sustains you.
exp.104:0:
This verse invites us to give thanks and praise to God, to call on his name, and to tell everyone what he has done. Praise means to commend and honor. Calling on his name means appealing to him with confidence. Making his deeds known means letting them be seen and shared. The peoples are the nations, or people in general.

The psalm does not say who wrote it. Its first verses appear in 1 Chronicles 16 in a song of David when the ark was brought to Jerusalem, though some scholars think it was a later composition. The speaker calls Israel to remember God's faithfulness throughout their history: the promises to Abraham, Joseph, and the exodus.

Today we can do this: this week, tell someone one specific thing God has done in your life. It can be in a simple conversation, without preaching. And before you do, thank him yourself first in prayer.
exp.21:0:
This verse begins with a note for the choir director: the tune is called "Aijeleth Shahar," which is usually understood to mean "the doe of the dawn," though this is not certain. Then David cries out to God, asking why he has been abandoned. Here "salvation" means rescue or help, and "roaring" is a cry for help. The verse says that God seems far from his deliverance and from the words of his desperate cry.

David speaks here in a moment of deep anguish. The exact circumstances he was living through are not stated, and scholars understand them in several ways. Jesus quoted the first line on the cross (Matthew 27:46), and for this reason many Christians also read this psalm as a foreshadowing of Christ's suffering.

For today: if you ever feel that God is far away, you can tell him so honestly. This psalm shows that sincere prayer, even with questions and pain, is still prayer. Keep speaking to God; do not turn away from him.
exp.26:2:
It says that even if an army camps around David to attack him, his heart will not fear. And even if war breaks out against him, he will keep trusting "in this." The phrase about the camp means that an army sets up its camp to surround someone.

The one speaking is David, in a psalm of confidence. He has just said that God is his light and his salvation, and that his enemies stumbled and fell before. So his courage is not pride: it rests on what God has already done. Scholars discuss what "in this" refers to: perhaps that God is his light and strength, or his desire to dwell in the house of the Lord, which comes next.

Today, when something frightens you, remember how God has cared for you before. Write those times down and go over them in prayer. Your confidence will grow as you look at who He is, not at how big your problem seems.
exp.36:6:
It tells us to be still before God and to wait for him calmly.

The author is David, according to the heading of the psalm. He writes as an older man with experience, to comfort those who feel that the unjust are winning. The verses nearby promise that God will bring about justice in his time and that the wicked will not last.

For today: when it bothers you to see someone dishonest doing well, do not feed envy or anger. Take a few minutes to pray, hand your worry over to God, and keep doing what is right, trusting that he knows when and how to act.
exp.84:10:
This verse paints two movements that meet: from below, truth springs up from the earth like a plant growing from a seed; from above, righteousness looks down from heaven, like someone watching with care. "Salvation" in that time meant rescue, and "good" refers to the good things God gives.

The psalm was written by the sons of Korah. It seems the people of Israel are praying after a restoration, perhaps after the return from exile, though this cannot be known with certainty. They ask God to renew his favor and trust that he remains near those who fear him. Many Christians see here a foreshadowing of Christ, but that is a reading made in light of the New Testament.

For today: practice truth in small things, being honest and faithful, and trust that God sees and acts with justice. Your sincerity can be a seed in which God makes something good grow.
exp.108:27:
Here the psalmist says that, even though others curse him, he trusts that God will bless him. The phrase "let them arise, but let them be ashamed" means that his enemies may rise up against him, but they will end up in shame. And "your servant," that is, he himself, will rejoice. The word "but" simply means "but."

The psalm is spoken by David, according to its heading. He is being falsely accused and attacked with words of hatred, even though he has treated them with love. He does not take revenge on his own, but cries out to God and asks Him to be the one who answers and saves him.

For today: when someone speaks badly of you or treats you unjustly, you do not need to strike back. You can bring your pain to God in prayer, ask Him to defend you, and trust that His blessing outweighs any harsh word against you.
exp.10:1:
The explanation says that the wicked have already prepared their weapons. They have bent the bow and set the arrow on the string, ready to shoot. The wording "bend their bow" means that they pulled the bow taut. "Make ready" means that they got everything set. "Arrow" refers to the shafts they shoot. "Shoot at" means to wound with arrows. They do this "privily," in secret, against "the upright in heart," people who are sincere and honest.

David speaks, though we cannot know exactly at what moment of his life he wrote it. His friends, out of fear, advise him to flee to the mountain like a bird. They describe the danger, but David has already declared that his trust is in the LORD. Later he will say that God sees everything from his throne.

For today: when you feel that wickedness or injustice surrounds you, do not let fear alone guide you. Recognize the danger honestly, but pray and rest in the fact that God sees what is hidden and nothing escapes him.
exp.82:12:
It says the psalmist asks God to make his enemies like whirlwinds and like chaff, that is, dry leaves and straw that the wind carries off without direction. The image is of something light and without strength, unable to stand firm.

The speaker is Asaph, or a psalmist from his tradition. He prays for Israel, which faces an alliance of nations that wants to wipe it out and take over the dwelling places of God. He recalls ancient defeats, such as those of Oreb, Zeeb, Zebah and Zalmunna, Midianite leaders defeated in the days of the judges. It is a prayer of cry, not a command for personal revenge.

For today: when you feel surrounded by injustice, bring your complaint to God in prayer instead of taking revenge yourself. He is the defender of his people and can act with justice.
exp.33:17:
This verse says that God is very near to those whose hearts are broken by pain. "Those who are broken-hearted" are people who carry deep wounds, and "those who are crushed in spirit" are people who are humbled and downcast on the inside. "Saves" means that God rescues them and holds them up.

The psalm is attributed to David, and its heading connects it to the time he pretended to be insane before Abimelech in order to escape. It speaks from the experience of having been delivered from danger. Earlier it says that God hears the cry of the righteous, and then it acknowledges that the righteous person goes through many troubles, but God stays with them in them.

Today, if you are going through a sorrow, you do not have to pretend to be strong. You can speak to God honestly, weep before Him, and also seek the support of trusted people. God does not move away from the one who suffers; He draws near.
exp.49:13:
This verse invites us to offer God gratitude and praise as if they were a sacrifice, and to fulfill the promises we have made to Him. "Offer" means to present something to God; "vows" are solemn promises made to God; "Most High" is a title of God that emphasizes that He is above all.

God Himself speaks here, addressing His people. First He makes clear that He does not need animals, because the whole world belongs to Him. What He seeks is not merely a ritual, but a grateful and faithful heart. Then He invites them to call on Him in distress, and He warns those who speak of His covenant without truly living it.

For today: before asking God for something, take a moment to thank Him sincerely. And if you have promised Him something, such as serving, forgiving, or changing a habit, make an effort to keep it honestly.
exp.61:1:
He alone is David's firm rock, his salvation, and his secure refuge. The explanation of "fortress" here means a rocky height or stronghold, a place where a person is safe. "Health" means salvation or rescue, not merely good physical condition. The phrase "I shall not be greatly moved" means that although he may stumble, he will not fall completely or be destroyed.

David is the speaker, and the psalm's heading directs it to Jeduthun, a musician of the temple. David is under pressure, since the following text speaks of people who plot against him, want to bring him down from his position, and speak lies with their mouths while cursing inwardly. Therefore he affirms that only in God does his soul rest. It is not known with certainty at what exact moment of his life he wrote it.

When someone criticizes you, betrays you, or makes you feel insecure, you do not have to rest all your worth on the opinions of others. Stop, pray, and place your trust in God as your firm foundation. He can hold you up even when you stumble.
exp.91:1:
This verse says it is good to proclaim God's faithful love when the day begins, and his truth or faithfulness when night comes. "Lovingkindness" here speaks of his constant and loyal goodness, and "faithfulness" refers to the fact that God is trustworthy and keeps what he promises.

Psalm 92 presents itself as a song for the Sabbath. It does not say who wrote it; the title only connects it with the Sabbath. The one speaking is a worshiper who is grateful, because God has gladdened him through his works. Praising in the morning and in the evening suggests a whole life surrounded by thankfulness.
