For today: begin your day by remembering one sign of God's love and end it by reviewing a promise he has kept. You can do this with a short prayer, a song, or by writing it in a notebook. In this way your trust grows, whatever kind of day you have.
exp.32:15:
This verse says that no king is saved by his large army. Nor does a brave man escape danger by being very strong. "Being saved" here means being rescued from defeat or death. "Brave" refers to the strong warrior.

Psalm 33 is a song of praise, and the text does not say who wrote it. It invites the people to praise God because He created everything and rules over all the nations. Before this verse, the psalm says that God looks upon all the inhabitants of the earth and knows their works. Afterward, it says that the horse, a symbol of military power, is not enough to save. God watches over those who fear Him and hope in His mercy.

Today we can make plans, work, and prepare well, but without placing our final trust in money, position, or our own strength. When you feel afraid, pray and rest in God, who takes care of you.
exp.88:30:
It says that if the sons of King David break God's statutes and do not keep his commandments, there will be consequences. The word "break" here means to treat as common what is holy, to despise it, or to defile it. "Statutes" are the rules God establishes. The sentence is incomplete and connects with the following verse, where God says how he will respond.

God is speaking, as recalled by the psalmist Ethan the Ezrahite. God had promised David a lasting line of descendants and a throne (2 Samuel 7). Here he makes clear that this promise does not ignore sin: his descendants will be corrected if they rebel. But verse 33 adds that God will not withdraw his mercy or break his word.

For today: God loves us like a faithful father, and so his correction seeks to restore us, not destroy us. If today you neglect what God asks of you, do not hide or lose heart; return to him sincerely, trusting in his mercy.
exp.114:10:
This verse calls on "those who fear the Lord" to trust in Him. "Fear" here does not mean being afraid, but honoring God with reverence and love. The idea that "he is their help and their shield" means that God comes to their aid and protects them like a shield in battle.

This psalm is a song of praise from God's people, probably used in worship, with voices answering one another. First it speaks to Israel, then to the priests (the house of Aaron), and then to all who fear the Lord. Some think it includes foreigners who worshiped the God of Israel, but the text does not make this clear. Set against silent idols, the psalm affirms that only God truly helps.

Today, when you feel fear or pressure, remember that God cares for you. Before relying only on your own strength, pray and hand that specific problem over to Him.
exp.43:16:
All this has come upon us, yet we have not forgotten you, and we have not failed to keep your covenant.

The one speaking is a psalmist, probably on behalf of all Israel, in a time of defeat and mockery from their enemies. We do not know for certain when in history it was written. They do not understand why they are suffering when they have been faithful, so they bring their complaint to God with sincerity. Some believe the verse does not speak of perfection, but of not having abandoned God for other gods.

When you suffer without understanding why, you can speak with God honestly, without pretending. Bringing him your pain and your questions is also a way of remaining faithful to him.
exp.58:1:
It says that David asks God for two things: to deliver him and to save him. It speaks of people who "obran iniquidad," that is, who practice wickedness, and of violent men, people who seek to shed blood. The phrase about violent men refers to people who are cruel and ready to kill.

According to the psalm's heading, David speaks at a time when Saul sent men to watch his house in order to kill him. That reference appears in 1 Samuel 19:11. David does not defend himself with his own strength but cries out to God. The following verses insist that he had done nothing wrong to deserve that persecution.

For today: when you face injustice or threat, you can pray sincerely and ask God for protection, without repaying evil with evil. Bring your situation before Him with confidence, and also seek prudent and safe help if you need it.
exp.54:15:
It says that, faced with pain, the psalmist decides to turn to God. Calling out for help, loudly and urgently, is what the verse describes. The name of God used here refers to the God of the covenant with Israel. The closing words express confidence that God will rescue him.

The speaker is David, according to the psalm's heading. He suffers because a close friend, someone with whom he shared confidences and worshiped in the house of God, betrayed him. Some readers think of Ahithophel, during Absalom's rebellion, but the psalm does not give the name, so this is only a possibility. Facing that betrayal, David does not rely on himself but turns to God.

For today: when someone hurts you or fails you, before seeking revenge or shutting yourself in with your pain, speak with God. Tell him honestly what you feel, and trust that he sustains you.
exp.4:3:
This verse says that God takes no pleasure in wickedness, and that the one who keeps doing evil cannot live near Him. The phrase "dwell with you" means staying as a guest, being in His house and in His company. The word "wicked" here refers to someone who persists in doing evil, not to someone who stumbles and repents.

David speaks, praying in the morning, surrounded by enemies who lie and cause harm. Before asking for help, he remembers what God is like: just and holy. His trust rests on the fact that God does not side with wickedness or leave it unanswered.

For today: when you see injustice or feel hurt, begin your day praying as David did. Place your trust in the just character of God, and ask Him also to cleanse your own heart, so that you may live near Him with sincerity.
exp.104:33:
He spoke, and swarms of locusts came, along with young locusts, in numbers beyond counting. The explanation of "young locusts" here translates a Hebrew word that is commonly understood as a kind of young locust or grasshopper still in its growing stage; the exact meaning of the term is debated. What matters is the picture: a huge plague that came at the mere word of God.

The psalmist recounts what God did for Israel in the days of Moses. This passage recalls the plagues on Egypt, when the pharaoh refused to let the people go. The psalm wants Israel to remember God's faithfulness, his power, and his care for the promise made to Abraham.

For today: when you feel small in the face of enormous problems, remember that God does not need great resources; his word is enough. Trust in him, pray with calm, and give thanks for what he has already done in your life.
exp.33:6:
The angel of the Lord settles in around those who revere him and honor him with awe, and he rescues them. "Encamps around" means he surrounds them on every side. "Fear" here does not mean being afraid, but trusting and obeying with reverence.

The speaker is David. The psalm's heading links it to a time when he escaped a serious danger. He gives thanks because God heard him and set him free. Some understand "the angel of the Lord" as an angel sent by God, and others as God's own presence. In both cases, the message is that God watches over his own.

Today, when you feel fear or feel alone, remember that God cares for you. Pray sincerely and trust him. This does not promise that there will be no problems, but it does mean you do not face them alone.
exp.48:7:
This verse says that buying a life back from death costs too much. "Redemption" means ransom, the payment that sets someone free. "Their soul" refers to the life of any person. The phrase "ceaseth for ever" indicates that no human being can pay that price. The neighboring verses use the words "to God" and "wealth," which we would say today as "to God" and "goods."

The psalm is attributed to the sons of Korah. The speaker is a teacher who gives a lesson to everyone. He wants no one to fear the rich or trust in money, because before death we are all equal. Interpreters debate how to understand the psalm's final hope, but the idea here is clear.

For today: do not place your security in your money or your achievements. They are useful, but they cannot save you. Rest in God, who can indeed redeem your life.
exp.71:19:
Here it says that the prayers of David, the son of Jesse, are finished. The word "finished" here is the plain sense of "are ended" in the verse. This is a brief note that closes a collection of psalms, not a new message.

This line was probably written by the person who gathered the psalms, not by David himself. It closes the second book of the Psalter (Psalms 42–72), after the praise that ends Psalm 72. Some psalms of David appear later, in other books, so the line is understood as the close of an earlier collection. Scholars explain this in several ways, and it cannot be said with certainty what the exact reason was.

Today it reminds us that a person's prayers come to an end, but God keeps working. David prayed with honesty, with complaints and with praise. We can imitate him: speak to God sincerely and leave the outcome in his hands.
exp.8:2:
David rejoices and gives thanks because his enemies were turned back. Words such as "turned back" mean that they were forced to retreat, and "perish" means that they will be destroyed. All of this happens "at thy presence," that is, in the presence of God. The point is that the enemies did not fall on their own, but because God was present.

David speaks in a psalm of praise addressed to the chief musician. It follows his declaration that he will praise God with his whole heart. He then says that God sat on his throne as a righteous judge. The title of the psalm is uncertain, and scholars interpret it in several ways. David attributes his victory to God, not to his own strength.

For today: when a difficulty is resolved, do not credit it only to your own effort or to luck. Stop and give thanks to God by name, and trust that he also knows how to do justice in what still worries you.
exp.104:22:
This verse tells how the people of Israel, represented by Jacob, came to live in Egypt. "Ham" is another name for Egypt, since it is linked to Ham, son of Noah, whose descendants are associated with that region. The word "sojourned" is an older way of saying "stayed" or "lived for a time." Jacob was not the owner of that land, but a stranger who lived there as a guest.

The psalmist recalls Israel's history to praise God for his faithfulness. Earlier, the psalm speaks of Joseph, whom God led to a position of authority in Egypt. Afterward, his family arrived there. The text then shows that God made them grow, and that over time the Egyptians changed their attitude toward them.

For today: even when you feel like a stranger in a new or difficult place, God continues to guide your story. Trust that he can care for you and carry out his purpose in you.
exp.106:21:
This verse invites us to give thanks to God in an active way. "Let them sacrifice the sacrifices of thanksgiving" means offering God gratitude as if it were an offering, and "declare his works with rejoicing" means telling with joy what He has done. The word "rejoicing" refers to a joy that is expressed out loud.

The psalmist speaks to the people of God, especially to those who were rescued from sickness and ruin. This psalm repeats that different groups, such as those who were lost, imprisoned, sick, or at sea, cried out to God and He delivered them. That is why he calls them to respond with gratitude. In Old Testament times, thank offerings were part of that response.

Today we can thank God in concrete ways: think of something He has done for you and tell it to a family member or a friend, or give Him thanks in prayer with joy and without rushing.
exp.77:44:
It says that God sent upon the Egyptians a mix of flies that bit them and troubled them greatly, and also frogs that brought them ruin. Some understand that these were swarms of several different kinds of flies; the Hebrew text does not specify which ones.

The author is Asaph, a psalmist who recounts the history of Israel. He remembers the plagues of Egypt to show that God delivered His people with power. The psalm wants the new generations not to forget what God did, nor to repeat the rebellion of their ancestors. Here the fourth plague and the second are recalled, though not in the same order as in Exodus.

For today: remembering with gratitude how God has worked in our lives and in history helps us trust Him when we face difficult situations. It also invites us not to harden our hearts when God speaks to us.
exp.105:24:
This verse says that the people of Israel complained quietly, inside their tents (the tents where they lived in the desert), instead of listening to what God was telling them. "Murmured" means to complain with discontent.

The psalmist recalls Israel's history after leaving Egypt. When the spies returned from Canaan, the people were afraid, rejected the promised land, and did not trust God (Numbers 14). Because of this, God left them in the desert. The psalm does not clearly name its author, and it seeks to help the people learn from their mistakes and praise God for his patience.

For today: quiet complaining can slowly harden the heart. When you feel the urge to murmur, stop and read God's Word. Tell him honestly what you feel, and ask him for help to trust him and obey him.
exp.17:3:
David says he felt surrounded by the danger of death, as if deadly sorrows were closing in on him. "Floods of ungodly men" are waves of wickedness, like a swollen river that frightens and sweeps a person away. The word "ungodly" in this verse translates a Hebrew term that speaks of wicked people or of something worthless.

David, king of Israel, is the speaker. The title of the psalm says he sang it when God delivered him from his enemies and from the hand of Saul. Earlier he praised God as his rock and refuge; now he describes how serious his situation was. Some believe he is using poetic images, not only literal facts.

For today: when you feel that your problems are drowning you, do not deny them. Tell God honestly, as David did. He listens and can be your refuge.
exp.134:16:
They have ears, but they cannot hear; there is no breath in their mouths. The word "breath" here means breath or breathing. In other words, they look like people, but they are dead and lifeless.

The psalmist praises the LORD and mocks, with seriousness, the idols of the nations. They are only silver and gold, made by human hands. Set against them is the living God, who hears, speaks, and acts. The psalm then says that those who make them and trust in them become like them: without life or response. It then calls the whole house of Israel to bless God.

Today, idols can be money, success, or the approval of others. Ask yourself: what do I trust most? What cannot hear you or save you does not deserve your heart. Speak today to the God who does listen.
exp.8:16:
The explanation says that those who live in wickedness and forget God will end up in the "hell" of the verse. The Hebrew word is "Sheol," which in the Old Testament usually means the place of the dead, the grave. Some understand it only as death, while others also see in it a judgment beyond death.

David sings this psalm to thank God for having delivered him from his enemies. The verses before show that the wicked fall into their own traps. What follows reminds us that God does not forget the poor or the needy. It is a song of trust that God does justice.

For today: do not live as if God did not exist. Set aside a moment each day to remember him with a simple prayer. And if you suffer an injustice, do not become bitter or seek revenge; trust that God sees, and that he will do justice in his time.
exp.122:1:
Psalm 123:2 says that just as servants and maidservants fix their eyes on the hand of their master or mistress, waiting for a command, help, or provision, so the people look to God. The word "look" here means to wait attentively. "Until he has mercy" means until God acts with compassion and helps them.

It is a song of ascents, a psalm that was probably sung on the way up to Jerusalem, though this is not known for certain. The speaker is God's people, or someone speaking on their behalf, who suffer mockery and contempt from proud and comfortable people. They have no power to defend themselves, so they turn their eyes to God.

When you feel despised, tired, or without a way out, you do not have to solve everything alone. Pause, pray sincerely, and wait on God with confidence, attentive to his guidance, while you keep faithfully doing what is yours to do today.
exp.104:39:
The explanation says that the people of Israel asked for food in the desert, and God brought quails, birds that covered the camp. He also filled them with "bread of heaven," which is the manna.

This psalm is a song of praise that remembers God's works with his people, from Abraham to the exodus from Egypt. The author does not name himself in this psalm. Here he reviews the journey through the desert: God covered them with a cloud, gave them light with fire, food and water. He did all this because he remembered his promise to Abraham. The accounts of the quails and the manna appear in Exodus 16 and Numbers 11.

For today: when you have a need, bring it to God with confidence. Then remember how he has cared for you before; giving thanks for what you have received strengthens faith for the future.
exp.88:37:
It says that God rejected and despised his "anointed," that is, the chosen king of Israel, and that he was angry with him. The word for "cast off" means to throw aside, and "abhorred" means to treat as of little worth. An "anointed" one is someone set apart by God with oil for a mission.

The one speaking is the psalmist, identified as Ethan the Ezrahite. The verses before recall God's promise to David: his descendants and his throne would last forever. But now it seems everything has collapsed. Scholars think it may describe a defeat of the kingdom of Judah, although it is not known with certainty when. The psalmist does not hide his confusion; he brings his complaint honestly before God.

For today: when what you are living does not match what God has promised, you do not have to pretend. You can bring your pain and your questions to him in prayer, without ceasing to trust his faithfulness.
exp.87:15:
He says the psalmist's pain is so great that he feels it as a wave of God's anger passing over him. The word "fierce" in the verse names the intensity of that anger. The "terrors" are the overwhelming fears that break a person down, leaving him without strength, as if he had been cut apart.

The one speaking is a man in deep affliction, identified in the title of the psalm with Heman the Ezrahite. He has suffered for much of his life and feels that God has withdrawn from him. This psalm is especially striking because it almost never ends with visible hope; it is an honest prayer from the darkness. Even so, it begins by addressing God as the God of his salvation, and it goes on praying.

For today: if you are going through suffering you do not understand, you do not have to pretend you are fine. You can tell God exactly what you feel, even if it sounds raw. Praying honestly, even without answers, is also a form of faith.
exp.75:0:
He says that God is not unknown to his people. In Judah and in Israel he is known, and his name is honored as great. At the beginning there is a musical note: "To the chief Musician" was the director of the singing, and "Neginoth" seems to refer to stringed instruments. "Asaph" is the name of the Levite to whom the psalm is attributed, or of his group of singers. "Song" indicates that it was sung.

The psalmist speaks as part of the worship of the people. The verses that follow mention Salem and Zion, that is, Jerusalem, and speak of broken weapons. Many think it celebrates a deliverance from enemies, although the psalm does not say with certainty which event it refers to.

Today we can move from knowing about God secondhand to a real experience of God. When we give thanks out loud for what he has done in our lives, his name becomes great among those around us as well.
exp.100:7:
He says that, every morning, the speaker will remove the wicked from the land. "I will destroy" means to put an end to their influence, and "root out" means to pull up completely by the roots, the way someone pulls up a weed. The goal is to cleanse "the city of the Lord" of all who practice wickedness.

This is a psalm of David, and here he speaks as a king. Earlier he promised to surround himself with faithful and honest people, and to keep away liars and cheats. That is why this verse describes his commitment to govern with justice. Some understand it as the task of judging and correcting; it is not a license for personal violence. Jesus later taught love for enemies.

For today: every morning, ask God to help you remove from your life and your home whatever is unjust or dishonest, beginning with your own heart, and to choose your companions wisely.
exp.33:4:
They looked to him, and were radiant: and their faces were not ashamed. This verse says that those who looked to God, that is, who put their attention and their trust in Him, received light. The idea of being made bright means they were filled with clarity, joy, and hope. And the idea that their faces were not ashamed means they were not left humiliated or let down. Some translations render the verb as a command ("Look to him and be radiant"), and both readings are possible.

The speaker is David. The heading of the psalm connects it to the moment when he pretended to be insane before Abimelech in order to escape. After being delivered, David invites others to praise God and tells what he himself experienced: he sought God, and God heard him and rescued him from his fears.

For today: when you feel fear or shame, do not just keep staring at the problem. Spend a few minutes praying, reading the Bible, and remembering how God has helped you before. Looking to Him brings light and peace to the heart.
exp.43:25:
It says that the people ask God to act: "Arise" is a way of saying "step into action." "Help us" means to come to our aid, and "redeem us" means to rescue us, to set us free. They ask this "for thy mercies' sake," that is, for the love and compassion of God, not on the basis of their own merit.

The psalm is a lament and a plea from the community of Israel. They have suffered defeat and humiliation, and yet they say they have not forsaken God. The verses before this one describe them as feeling far away from him, brought down to the dust. It is not known with certainty what historical event it refers to, and scholars have interpreted it in several different ways.

For today: when you feel without strength, you can speak to God honestly, even with pain. Ask him for help by relying on his goodness and not on your achievements. Praying this way is itself a form of trust.
exp.36:26:
It says we should turn away from evil and practice good. The promise is that by doing so we will dwell for evermore, that is, have a secure and lasting life.

It is a psalm of David, already an old man, speaking from his experience: he never saw the righteous forsaken. He writes to encourage those who see the wicked prosper and grow discouraged. The verses that follow explain the reason: God loves what is right and cares for his own. Some understand "for evermore" as lasting in the promised land and through their descendants; others take it as a hope that looks toward eternal life.

Today, before deciding something, ask yourself: "Does this take me away from evil, or bring me closer to doing good?" Choose one concrete step, such as being honest at work or helping someone in need, and trust that God cares for those who walk uprightly.
exp.46:7:
This verse says that God rules over all the nations. "Reigneth" here means that God exercises his reign, and "the heathen" are the non-Jewish peoples, that is, the nations of the world. "Sitteth" is the verb for sitting: God is seated on his holy throne, like a king who governs with authority and purity.

The psalm is a song of praise, attributed to the sons of Korah. It invites all peoples to celebrate God as King. The verses before it call for singing with understanding, that is, grasping what is being sung. The verses that follow show leaders of the nations joining the people of the God of Abraham. Interpreters debate on what occasion it was sung, and this is not known with certainty.

For today: when the world seems confused or unjust, remember that God remains on his throne. Trust in him and worship him with your mind and your heart.
exp.118:91:
It says that, if God's law had not been his joy and his delight, the psalmist would already have died in the middle of his suffering. "Delight" means something that is greatly enjoyed. "Affliction" is pain, anguish, or trial. "Perished" means destroyed or dead.

The one speaking is the author of Psalm 119, a psalm about God's word. It is not known for certain who wrote it. He is seen suffering, perhaps from mockery or persecution. Earlier he speaks of God sustaining the earth and creation with faithfulness. Then he says that God has given him life, that is, has restored his life and strength.

For today: when a trial comes, do not wait until you are broken to seek God. Read his word regularly, even a little each day. Then, when pain arrives, you will have a firm place to lean and to receive comfort.
exp.104:36:
He brought them out with silver and gold, and among their tribes there was not one who stumbled. The psalmist recalls the story of the exodus to praise God for his faithfulness. Before this, the psalm tells of the plagues. The gold and silver are connected with what the Egyptians gave them when they left (Exodus 12:35-36). That there was no one who stumbled may be a literal description of God's care, or a way of stressing that they came out whole and strong. Interpreters understand it in different ways.

For today: when you remember how God has sustained you in the past, your confidence grows for the future. Write down today one or two times when God cared for you, and give him thanks. That grateful remembrance helps you walk with hope, even if the road is still long.
exp.58:6:
The explanation says that the psalmist's enemies speak without restraint. They pour out words with violence. Their lips are like swords: their words wound like weapons. And they do it with confidence, thinking "who hears?", meaning they believe no one sees them or will judge them.

The psalm's title presents David speaking when Saul sent men to watch his house in order to kill him. That is the situation the title sets out, although some scholars think the psalm was later used in a broader way. David cries out to God for protection, and in the verses that follow he trusts that God sees everything and does not stay silent in the face of wickedness.

For today: when someone hurts you with words, slander, or mockery, do not simply carry the pain alone. Bring it to God honestly. He does hear and He does see. And take care with your own words too, because they can wound as well, and God hears them.
exp.39:15:
This verse asks that all who seek God be filled with joy and gladness in Him. The phrase "those who love your salvation" means those who love the salvation that God gives. They should keep saying: "May the Lord be magnified!" The word "magnified" means lifted up and honored.

David speaks here, according to the heading of the psalm. He has just asked for help because he has enemies who want to harm him. Even so, in the midst of danger, he also asks that those who trust in God have joy. Then he describes himself as "afflicted and needy," but he trusts that God is thinking of him. Some interpreters see here a contrast between the enemies and the faithful.

For today: when you are in trouble, do not look only at your need. Take a moment to give thanks and to say out loud that God is great. Praising in the middle of difficulty strengthens confidence.
exp.16:10:
They have now surrounded us wherever we go: they follow close behind and have surrounded him. The phrase in the verse about their eyes being set means they watch him closely with the intent to harm him.

David speaks here in a prayer for help. He feels cornered by proud and violent people, whom he compares to a lion lying in wait. Some scholars think this refers to the time when Saul was hunting him, but the psalm does not say so clearly. What is certain is that David does not defend himself alone: he cries out to God to deliver him.

For today: when you feel surrounded by pressure, criticism, or injustice, do not carry that weight alone. Speak to God honestly, tell Him what you feel, and ask for protection and wisdom. He listens to those who trust in Him.
exp.82:17:
This verse says that everyone should recognize that God's name is Jehovah, the personal God of the covenant, and that he alone is the Most High, meaning the highest and supreme one, above all the earth.

It is part of a psalm of Asaph, a prayer in the middle of a crisis. Several neighboring nations had joined together to destroy Israel. The psalmist asks God for help and asks that his enemies be humbled. Notice that the goal is not only their defeat, but that they come to seek and know God.

For today: when you face problems or people who harm you, pray that God be recognized above all things. Trust that he is in control, and ask him that his glory be what matters most, not your revenge.
exp.54:19:
He lifted his hand to attack those who lived at peace with him, and in doing so he broke the agreement he had made. The "those at peace" are the ones who were his friends or allies, with no intention of harming him. "Broke his covenant" means he failed to keep his promise of loyalty.

The one speaking is David, though the psalm does not say with certainty at what point in his life he wrote it. Some connect it with the betrayal by Absalom or by Ahithophel, but this is an interpretation, not something the text states. David suffers because the one who hurts him is someone close, someone he trusted. Even so, he trusts that God hears him and delivers him.

Today, if someone close to you fails you or breaks their word, it is natural for it to hurt. You do not have to pretend it did not happen. Bring that pain honestly before God, as David did, and ask him for wisdom and peace to act without revenge.
exp.121:5:
This verse invites us to pray for the peace of Jerusalem. It says that those who love that city will prosper, meaning things will go well for them and they will live in blessing. The word "pray" is what the verse is asking readers to do, and "prosper" refers to being in well-being and security.

It is a psalm of David, one of the songs of ascent that pilgrims sang as they went up to Jerusalem for the festivals. Here the psalmist rejoices over the city where the people gathered to worship the LORD and where the throne of justice stood. He invites everyone to wish peace on that place, so important to the faith of Israel.

Today we can apply this principle by praying for the peace of the places where God has placed us: our church, our family, our city, and our country. Loving a place and its people means asking for them and seeking their good through concrete actions.
exp.101:22:
He weakened my strength along the way, and shortened my days. "Weakened" means that he brought the psalmist low or made him suffer. "Way" refers to the course of his life. It is a poetic way of saying that he feels weak and believes he has little time left.

This psalm is the prayer of a person in distress who pours out his heart before God. Its heading describes it as the complaint of one who is afflicted. We do not know with certainty who wrote it. Many think it reflects the pain of Israel in exile, but it is interpreted in several ways. Although he is weary, the psalmist looks toward the restoration of Zion and the praise of the nations. Then he asks God not to let him die halfway, remembering that God is eternal.

When you feel your strength running out, do not stay silent or pretend to be strong. Speak with God honestly, as the psalmist does, and remember that your passing life is in the hands of One who remains forever.
exp.49:7:
God says he will not rebuke his people for their sacrifices or their burnt offerings. "Burnt offerings" were offerings that were burned whole on the altar. The phrase "before me" means that God saw them being offered continually. In other words, the problem was not that the offerings were lacking.

Here God himself speaks as judge, addressing Israel, "his people." He wants to correct them, but not because of a lack of rituals. In the verses that follow he explains that he has no need of animals, since everything belongs to him. Many understand the rebuke to be aimed at the heart: they offered without gratitude or obedience.

For today: it is not enough to carry out religious duties, such as going to church, giving, or singing, if the heart is far from God. Today you can ask yourself: "Am I worshiping with gratitude and obedience, or only going through the motions out of habit?"
exp.118:27:
This verse says that the psalmist's soul melts away because of sorrow and distress. "Melteth" means that the soul wears away or is worn down, and "heaviness" here is a deep pain, a weight on the heart. That is why he asks God to strengthen him, to hold him up according to what God has promised in his word.

The one speaking is the author of Psalm 119, whom we do not know for certain. He is someone who loves God's law and is going through hard times. Earlier, he told God about his ways and felt that God answered him. Now, without hiding his weariness, he asks for strength and for more teaching to keep walking in the path of truth.

For today: when anxiety wears you out, speak to God honestly, without dressing anything up. Then look for a promise in the Bible, read it slowly, and ask him to sustain you with it.
exp.118:127:
He says the psalmist considered all of God's commandments good and right, in every matter of life. For that very reason, he firmly rejected every false path.

The author of Psalm 119 is a believer who loves God's law. It is not known with certainty who wrote it. Just before this, he says that people have set aside the law, and yet he loves it more than pure gold. His faithfulness stands out against a setting that disregards God.

Today we might ask ourselves: do I accept God's Word only where it suits me? Choose one area, such as work, money, or the way you speak, and decide to follow what God teaches, even if others do not.
exp.0:0:
He says that the person who turns away from bad influence is truly happy and blessed. "Blessed" means happy, favored. "Man" is the word for the person. The "counsel of the wicked" refers to the ideas of those who live without God. "Path of sinners" is their way of life, and "seat of the scornful" is the place of those who mock what is good. There is a progression here: walking, standing still, and sitting down.

Psalm 1 serves as a doorway into the whole book of Psalms. It is not known for certain who wrote it. Its purpose is to show two paths: that of the righteous, who loves God's law, and that of the wicked. The verses that follow explain where true happiness comes from.

Today: be careful about who you spend time with and what voices you listen to, whether friendships, social media, or television. Choose a healthy influence, and set aside a few minutes each day to read the Bible.
exp.8:5:
The explanation says the enemy can no longer keep destroying: his ruins and devastations (the destructions) have come to an end. The cities he tore down were left so wrecked that even their memory vanished. The Hebrew text is difficult and is translated in several ways. Some understand that the enemy himself was left in ruins forever.

The one speaking is the psalmist, whom tradition identifies as David. He is giving thanks to God because God defended his cause and acted as a righteous judge against the nations that attacked him. The verse celebrates that the power of the oppressor is not eternal, while God does endure and reign with justice.

For today: if you suffer from an injustice, do not think that the one who does harm will have the last word. Hand your cause over to God, trust in his justice, and refrain from taking revenge yourself.
exp.68:9:
It says that the psalmist wept and humbled himself with fasting, that is, he stopped eating in order to seek God in sincere sorrow. But instead of receiving respect, people mocked him. "Reproach" means shame or insult. "Chastened my soul" means humbling oneself through deep grief.

The psalm is spoken by David, according to its title. He is suffering because of his love for God and his house, and even his own family rejects him. His prayers and his grief over sin and the dishonor of God's name become a reason for mockery. The New Testament quotes parts of this psalm in connection with Jesus (John 2:17; Romans 15:3).

Today we can remember that living with sincerity before God sometimes brings mockery or misunderstanding. Even so, we should not stop praying or seeking him. He sees our heart and draws near to those who suffer for love of him.
exp.81:0:
It says that God himself is present in an assembly and there passes judgment. An "assembly" or court is the gathering described. The word for "gods" in the verse is understood in several ways here: human judges and rulers, or spiritual beings under God's authority. Scholars do not agree.

The psalm is by Asaph, a Levite responsible for the music in worship. Here the writer describes God as the supreme Judge who examines those who ought to dispense justice. The verses that follow show the reason: they were judging unjustly, favoring the wicked, and neglecting the poor, the fatherless, and the afflicted.

For today: if you have some authority, at work, in the family, or in the church, remember that God is watching you. Use it justly, without favoritism, and take special care of those who have less voice or fewer resources.
exp.131:0:
A Song of degrees: this verse opens the psalm with a prayer, in which the people ask God to remember David and all his troubles. The phrase "Song of degrees" is a heading; it is usually understood as a song of ascent, sung when going up to Jerusalem. The word "remember" does not mean that God forgets, but that he acts by recalling his promise. "Troubles" refers to David's labors and cares.

The one speaking is the psalmist, probably on behalf of the whole people; no one knows for certain who wrote it. The verses that follow recount David's oath to find a place for the Lord. Many think the psalm was sung around the temple and God's covenant with David, but scholars debate the exact date.

For today: when you pray, lean on God's faithfulness and his promises. Also remember the effort of those who served God before you, and give thanks for them.
exp.21:10:
It says the one speaking pleads with God not to stay far away from him. He feels that suffering is already upon him and that no one else can help him. The word "trouble" means a very great distress or pressure, and "near" shows that the danger is immediate.

It is a psalm of David. Here he cries out to God from a moment of great pain, surrounded by enemies, whom he later describes as bulls and lions. Just before this, he remembers that God cared for him from the time he was born, and that is why he dares to ask for help. The New Testament connects this psalm with the sufferings of Jesus on the cross, and many Christians read it that way too.

When you feel alone and without support, you can do as David did: remember how God has cared for you before, and say to him sincerely, "Be not far from me." God is not troubled by your cry; he hears it.
exp.106:17:
Some people, the passage says, became so ill that they could not stand any food. Their soul "abhorreth" all food, meaning they felt disgust and revulsion toward eating. Losing their appetite in this way left them nearly without strength, brought to the very edge of death, that is, close to dying.

The psalmist speaks to the community that returned from exile or distress, and calls them to give thanks to God. Here he describes those who suffered because of their rebellion and wrongdoing. Many understand that the sickness is a consequence of their wrong path, although the text does not say that all suffering is punishment. Then the psalm shows that they cried out to God, and he healed and delivered them.

When you are without strength or have strayed from the right path, do not wait until you feel better to pray. Cry out to God honestly; he hears, forgives, and can restore you.
exp.55:2:
It says that when David feels afraid, he decides to place his trust in God. He does not deny the fear; he acknowledges it. "What time I am afraid" means "when I am afraid," and "I will trust" means "I lean on you." The trust here is a decision, not the absence of fear.

The one speaking is David. The title of the psalm connects it with the moment the Philistines seized him in Gath. It is known that he was surrounded by enemies and was asking God for mercy. Scholars debate which exact episode of his life is meant, so it is best not to claim more than the text says.

For today: when you feel afraid, do not wait for the fear to leave before you trust. Tell God honestly what you fear and hand over that specific worry, even if your heart is still trembling.
exp.17:39:
This verse says that God gave the psalmist complete victory over his enemies. The phrase about giving the back of the neck is an old expression, and the word "neck" here means the back of the neck or the nape. To show the enemy's neck means the enemy flees defeated and turns his back. The verse also speaks of the psalmist bringing to an end those who hated him.

The psalm is traditionally attributed to David, according to its heading, and he sings it after God rescued him from Saul and other enemies. It is a song of gratitude: he credits the strength and the triumph to God, not to himself. The language of war was natural for his time and for his role as king.

For today: when you get through a difficulty, do not take all the credit for yourself. Gratefully recognize that God sustained you. And remember that for the Christian, the main struggle is not against people but against evil; in that struggle God also gives strength.
exp.27:8:
This verse is a closing prayer. The psalmist asks God to save his people and bless his inheritance, that is, those who belong to him as something precious. He also asks God to shepherd them, meaning to care for and guide them the way a shepherd leads his sheep, and to lift them up and sustain them forever.

The title of the psalm attributes it to David. He has just given thanks because God heard his cry, and he calls God his strength and his shield. After speaking of his own experience, he turns to intercede for the whole people. Some understand "his anointed" as King David; others also see in it a look toward the Messiah.

For today: when God helps you, do not stop at giving thanks for yourself. Learn to pray for your family, your church, and your community, asking that God would care for them and guide them.
exp.118:45:
The psalmist says he will speak of God's testimonies, that is, of his teachings and commands, even before kings, and that he will not be ashamed. To be ashamed here means to feel embarrassment or fear of being humiliated for what one believes.

The speaker is the author of Psalm 119, whose name is not known with certainty. This whole psalm celebrates God's word. Earlier, he says he will keep the law and walk in freedom, because he has sought God's commandments. His confidence comes from loving and practicing what God has said. Afterward, he goes on to speak of delighting in them and meditating on them.

For today: if you know God's word well and live by it, you will be able to speak about your faith with more calm and courage, even before people in authority. Begin by reading and meditating on the Bible each day, and share what you believe with respect and sincerity.
exp.13:2:
They are all gone aside, the explanation says: they all turned away from the right path. "Gone aside" means they veered off course, and "become filthy" means they had spoiled morally. The verse insists that there is none who does good, not even one.

David writes this psalm after speaking of the fool, who lives as though God did not exist. God looks down from heaven seeking anyone who seeks him, and the result is grim. It is strong language describing the general condition of humanity. Some read it as a description of the wicked who oppress God's people, and Paul quotes it in Romans 3 to show that all of us need God.

Today, this verse invites us to humility. We are not good on our own, so we can ask God for forgiveness and help each day, and treat others with compassion.
exp.118:134:
Here the psalmist asks God to make his face shine upon him, that is, to look on him with approval and favor. He calls himself God's "servant," like someone who belongs to God and obeys him. He also asks God to teach him his "statutes," which are the rules and teachings of God.

The one speaking is the author of Psalm 119, a believer who loves God's law and lives among pressures and people who oppress him. Earlier he asked to be redeemed from the violence of men. Afterward he weeps because others do not obey God. His plea comes from a heart that longs for God's nearness and for living the way he wants. The text does not say who the author was.

For today: before opening the Bible, pray with this same desire. Ask God to show you his grace and to teach you. In this way you will read not only to know more, but to know him and obey him with confidence.
exp.115:18:
The psalmist says he will keep his promises to God in the courts of the temple, in the midst of Jerusalem. The courts are the open areas around the temple where people gathered to worship. Vows are promises made to God.

The speaker is a believer who was rescued from death or from a great danger (verses 3 and 8). We do not know his name; some think of David or of a king such as Hezekiah, but this is not certain. In gratitude, he does not want to keep his thankfulness secret. He wants to express it publicly, with the people gathered in Jerusalem. This psalm is connected with the Jewish festivals of thanksgiving.

When God helps you, do not keep your thanks to yourself in silence. Tell what He has done, fulfill what you promised, and give thanks together with other believers in your church. Your testimony may encourage someone else.
exp.17:30:
These two questions expect no answer, because the answer is obvious: no one is God apart from the Lord, and no rock is firm apart from our God. Here the word "rock" means a secure and firm refuge. In this way, the psalmist affirms that only the Lord is the true God and the true security.

David is speaking, and the psalm places him on the day the Lord delivered him from his enemies and from the hand of Saul. After telling how God rescued him, David sings his gratitude. Earlier he said that God's way is perfect and his word is pure, refined like metal in the fire. Here he confesses that his strength did not come from his army.

For today: when you feel that your security rests in your work, your money or your own strength, remember that all of these can fail. Today, name the thing that worries you and give it to God in prayer, trusting that he is indeed firm.
exp.3:7:
The explanation says that the speaker lies down calmly and sleeps in peace. The reason is that only the LORD gives him security.

The psalm bears the name of David, and many think he wrote it in a time of distress and opposition, although the text does not give the exact moment. Others doubt that God can help, and ask who will show them good. David, by contrast, already has in his heart a joy greater than that of those who have abundant harvests.

Today, before you sleep, you can hand God your worries, one by one, in prayer. Your security does not depend on everything being resolved, but on who takes care of you while you rest.
exp.36:37:
This verse says that those who rebel against God and do evil will be destroyed together. "Transgressors" are those who break God's law. The phrase "together" means all of them at once, and "the end of the future" refers to what lies ahead, the final outcome. So the future of the wicked is cut off.

The psalm is by David, in his later years, and works as wise counsel. The verses before it speak of the wicked person who seemed strong and then suddenly was gone. David encourages the faithful not to envy the wicked, because their prosperity does not last. In contrast to that end, the righteous have peace.

For today: when it troubles you to see that unjust people seem to be doing well, do not grow bitter or imitate them. Keep doing what is right and trust that God has the last word.
exp.81:2:
This verse commands us to defend the poor and the fatherless, and to do justice to the one who suffers and the one who lacks what is needed. "Defend" means to protect and to speak on behalf of someone. "The afflicted" is the one who suffers, and "the needy" is the one who lives in want.

God speaks in this psalm of Asaph. He stands in the midst of the gods, a term that is understood in different ways: some think they are human judges or rulers, others that they are spiritual beings. In any case, God rebukes them because they judged unjustly and favored the wicked. Their duty was to care for the weakest.

For today: if you have any influence, in your work, your family, or your church, use it to help those who have no voice. You can accompany a vulnerable person, speak up for them with truth, or support those who defend them.
exp.128:6:
It says that the grass on the rooftops is so poor that the reaper cannot fill his hand with it, nor can the one who binds the sheaves fill his arms. The word "filleth" is an old form of "filled." A sheaf is a bundle of cut stalks or grass tied together. In other words, that grass yields no harvest at all.

This is a psalm of the pilgrims who went up to Jerusalem. Israel speaks, remembering how it has been greatly oppressed since its youth, yet God has sustained it. Here the enemies of Zion are compared to grass without root on a roof: it grows quickly, but it dries up and is good for nothing. The verses that follow show that no one wishes them a blessing.

For today: do not lose heart when you see evil seem to prosper. What has no root in God bears no lasting fruit. Work to root your life in Him, and do not be carried along by the apparent success of others.
exp.83:9:
It says that one day in the courts (the courtyards) of the temple is worth more than a thousand days somewhere else. The author would rather be a doorkeeper, or simply stand at the entrance of God's house, than live comfortably among wicked people. The word "preferred" in the verse expresses this choice.

This psalm was written by the sons of Korah, Levites who served in the temple. The speaker deeply longs to be in God's presence, perhaps because he lives far from Jerusalem, though the text does not make this clear. Earlier the psalm prays for the king, and then it declares that God is sun and shield, and that he gives good things to those who walk with integrity.

For today: ask yourself what places and companions fill your time. Set aside a moment each day to be with God, even if it is brief, and value it more than any comfort.
exp.30:8:
Here the psalmist asks God to have mercy on him because he is going through great distress. He says that his eyes, his soul, and his inner being have been worn down by grief, that is, they have been drained by sorrow. The inner being is the innermost part of a person, the seat of his deepest feelings.

The one speaking is David, according to the heading of the psalm, although it is not known with certainty at what point in his life he wrote it. He suffers because of enemies, because of the rejection of his neighbors, and also because of his own failings. Even so, earlier he had said that God saw his affliction and held him up.

Today, when pain wears you down inside and out, you can pray honestly, without pretending to be strong. Tell God how you feel and ask for his mercy. He does not grow weary of listening to you.
exp.131:2:
Here David promises that he will not enter his house or lie down in his bed. The words "dwelling of my house" refer to his home, and "couch of my bed" refer to the bed where he rested. It is a strong way of saying that he will allow himself no comfort or rest.

The psalm is a song of ascents, one of those sung while going up to Jerusalem. The one speaking here is the psalmist, who recalls David's oath to the LORD, "the Mighty One of Jacob." David wanted to find a place for the Lord, that is, a place where the ark would rest. The verses that follow make this clear: he would not sleep until he had accomplished it. It is a solemn vow, not a command from God.

For today: David put God before his own comfort. We can ask ourselves what place God holds in our priorities. We do not need to make extreme vows, but we can give God time and attention before rest or our own affairs.
exp.135:1:
This verse invites us to give thanks to God, whom it calls "the God of gods." That expression does not say that there are many true gods. It is a way of saying that God is above everything people worship or fear. "Mercy" here means faithful love, a kindness that does not abandon. "For ever" means that it never comes to an end.

Psalm 136 was written to be sung together as a community, and the text does not say who its author was. Probably a leader would say a line and the people would answer: "for his mercy endureth for ever." It remembers God's goodness in creation and in the deliverance of Israel. The neighboring peoples worshiped many gods, and so this song affirms that the Lord is superior to all of them.

When your problems or fears feel enormous, remember that God is greater and that his love does not change. Today you can thank him for one concrete sign of his faithfulness in your life.
exp.124:2:
It says that the power of the wicked will not remain forever over the land God gave to the righteous. "Rod" is the staff of the one who rules, and here it stands for oppressive dominion. "Lot" is the inheritance or portion that fell to the people, and "lest the righteous put forth their hands unto iniquity" means that the righteous should not feel tempted to do wrong to get out from under the oppression.

It is a song of pilgrims who went up to Jerusalem. The writer (we do not know his name) encourages the people: God surrounds them as the mountains surround the city. They probably lived under foreign rule, though scholars do not agree on the exact time.

For today: when you suffer injustice, trust that God sets a limit on evil, and do not respond by doing the same. Wait on Him and keep acting with uprightness.
exp.50:13:
This verse is a prayer. The psalmist asks God to deliver him from bloodguiltiness, which in the original Hebrew is literally "bloods," referring to guilt for shedding blood. "Salvation" is the word used for deliverance. He promises that once he is forgiven, his tongue will sing of God's righteousness.

According to the psalm's title, David wrote it after the prophet Nathan confronted him about his sin with Bathsheba. That event involved adultery and the death of Uriah. David does not defend himself; he asks for forgiveness and cleansing. Some think "bloods" points to the death of Uriah, though others see it in a broader sense.

For today: when you fail, do not hide or justify yourself. Speak to God honestly and ask for his forgiveness. Forgiveness is not only personal relief; it also opens your mouth to praise God and to help others through your testimony.
exp.135:6:
He says that God made the great lights, that is, the great lamps of the sky: the sun, the moon, and the stars, which are named in the verses that follow. And after naming this work, the psalm repeats that his mercy endures forever. Here "mercy" translates a Hebrew word that speaks of faithful and steadfast love.

Psalm 136 is a song of praise that the people of Israel sang, probably in worship, with a refrain that everyone answered. The author is not identified. First it celebrates God as creator and then as the deliverer of his people. By ordering the heavenly bodies, it sees in creation a sign of God's constant care.

For today: each time you see the sun rise or the moon at night, offer a brief prayer of thanks. Let that habit remind you that God sustains you with faithful love every day.
exp.147:12:
This verse invites everyone to praise the name of the Lord. The reason is that his name alone is exalted, meaning nothing and no one compares with him. His glory, or his greatness and splendor, is above the earth and the heavens.

The author of the psalm does not name himself, and we do not know who he was. He calls all of creation to praise God: first the heavens, then the earth. Here he speaks to people: kings, judges, young men and maidens, old men and children. No one is left out. Then the psalm mentions the people of Israel, whom God strengthened. The phrase "raised up the horn" is an image of strength and victory.

Today we can remember that God is greater than anything that worries us or that we admire. Before asking him for something, take a moment to thank him and praise him. That puts everything in its proper place and gives us peace.
exp.125:5:
It says that the one who goes out to sow while weeping, carrying the precious seed, will return with joy and bring in his sheaves, which are the bundles of harvested grain. The explanation of the verse before it, which speaks of the south, and of a great joy, has been left out because those words do not appear in the verse your reader sees.

This is one of the psalms of ascent, which the people of Israel sang. It speaks from the community that remembers the joy of returning from captivity and asks God to restore them fully. It is not known with certainty whether it refers to the return from Babylon or to some other situation; scholars understand it in several ways. Sowing with tears paints a hard season that God can turn into a harvest.

For today: if you are doing good in the midst of pain, such as praying for a child, serving while tired, or persevering through difficult work, do not give up. Keep sowing in faith, and trust that God knows how to bring forth fruit in its time.
exp.101:18:
This verse says that God looks down from the height of his sanctuary, that is, from his holy place in heaven. The Lord looks out from the heavens to behold the earth. "Looked" speaks of a close, attentive gaze, not a distracted one. "LORD" in the preceding context is a short form of God's name.

The psalm is written by someone deeply afflicted, who feels alone and weak. Although it is not known with certainty who the author was, the psalm speaks of people in captivity and of the restoration of Zion. Many relate it to the time of the exile, but this is interpreted in several ways. The author comforts his own pain by remembering that God does see and hear, and that this will be told to future generations.

For today: when you feel alone or without a way out, remember that God sees you. Speak to him honestly in prayer, without hiding your pain. He does not despise the plea of the one who suffers.
exp.102:15:
It says that when the wind passes over the flower of the field, it dries up and disappears, and the place where it stood no longer remembers it. "Perished" means it ceased to exist. "Its place knows it no more" is a poetic way of saying that no trace of it remains.

The one speaking is David, who praises God in this psalm. He has just said that God knows we are frail, dust, and that our life is short like grass. But the next verse turns the thought: although a person passes away quickly, the mercy of the LORD lasts from age to age for those who fear him.

For today: our life is brief, and we do not control time. Instead of being anxious about that, rest in a compassionate God who knows you and endures. Live today with gratitude, and care for what truly lasts: your relationship with Him and love for others.
exp.45:8:
He makes wars stop throughout the whole earth. Breaking the bow, cutting the spear, and burning the chariots are images of destroying the weapons of that time. "Chariots" refers to war chariots. It is a picture of peace that God imposes, disarming those who fight.

It is a psalm of the sons of Korah, sung by God's people. It speaks of trust in the middle of danger: the earth shakes and the nations are in turmoil. Some think it recalls a deliverance of Jerusalem, but the text does not say which one. The psalmist invites us to look at what God does, and then God himself speaks: "Be still."

Today, when you feel that conflicts or fears surround you, pause for a moment. Pray and remember that God has final control. Trusting in him is not passivity, but resting in his power while you seek peace with others.
exp.121:4:
The explanation says that in Jerusalem stood the thrones or seats where justice was administered, that is, the courts. They were "the thrones of the house of David," because the descendants of King David governed and judged from there. "Judgment" here means deciding with justice, not only punishing.

This is a psalm of pilgrimage, attributed to David, which the Israelites sang as they went up to Jerusalem to worship. The speaker rejoices at arriving in the city. Jerusalem was the center of the unity of the people, of the worship of God, and of just government. That is why, in the verses that follow, the speaker asks to pray for its peace.

For today: worship and justice go together. We can pray for those who govern and judge in our country, that they may act uprightly. And in our own home or work, we can decide with justice and honesty, remembering that God sees everything.
exp.77:46:
This verse says that God destroyed the vines of the Egyptians with hail, and their sycamore trees with frost. Here "frost" is the word for a severe icy storm, and the sycamore trees are fig-bearing trees that grew in those fields. To say God "destroyed" them means he completely ruined those plants.

Asaph wrote Psalm 78, and he reviews the history of Israel to teach the new generations. Here he remembers the plagues of Egypt, when God rescued his people from slavery. The hail struck the Egyptians' crops, and this showed that God had power over nature. Asaph tells this so that Israel would not forget what God did or begin to doubt him again.

For today: remember the times God has cared for you or carried you through. Write them down and tell them to your family. Recalling his faithfulness strengthens your trust when hard times come.
exp.88:9:
He says that God completely defeated Rahab, as one defeats someone who is dead, and that with his strong arm he scattered his enemies. "Broken" means that he crushed him, and "scattered" means that he made them flee in every direction. Rahab here is not the woman of Jericho, but a poetic name for a sea monster, a symbol of chaos and arrogant power. Some connect it with Egypt.

The psalm is by Ethan the Ezrahite. It praises God as Creator and unmatched King. Earlier it speaks of God calming the raging sea; here it shows that he also overcomes everything that seems threatening. Then it affirms that heaven and earth belong to him.

For today: when you feel that a problem is too big or chaotic, remember that God has already shown himself to be stronger. Pray with confidence and rest in the fact that he still governs.
exp.118:121:
Here the psalmist asks God to stand as his surety, that is, to guarantee him, to back him up and defend him. He asks that God do what is good for his servant. And he pleads that the proud, the arrogant, not oppress him, meaning that they not crush him or trample him down. The psalmist calls himself God's servant, someone who serves God.

Psalm 119 is a long prayer about God's word. It is not known with certainty who wrote it. The one speaking is a believer who loves God's law, yet he feels the pressure of powerful and arrogant people. He says he has tried to act justly, and for that reason he does not want to be left alone before those who oppress him.

For today: when you feel pressured or unfairly treated, do not let yourself become bitter. Bring your situation to God honestly, keep acting with uprightness, and trust that he stands with you.
exp.112:1:
The explanation says that the name of God is to be blessed, that is, praised and honored with gratitude and respect. Here "name" stands for God himself: who he is, his character, and his works. The words "from this time forth and for evermore" mean that this praise has no pause and no end: it begins today and continues through all eternity.

This psalm begins with the call "Praise the Lord," which means to praise the Lord. The psalmist calls on the servants of the Lord, the people who belong to him, to praise him. It is not known with certainty who wrote it. It belongs to the psalms of praise that were sung in Israel, and Jewish tradition used them at the festivals. The following verses show that God deserves praise in every place and at every time.

For today: begin or end your day by saying aloud a phrase of thanks to God, no matter how you feel. In this way you train the heart to bless him from now on.
exp.75:8:
He says that God rose up to judge, and that He did so with a purpose: to rescue all the humble of the earth. The humble are those who do not abuse or force their way over others, and very often they are the oppressed. "Selah" is probably a pause for meditation, though its exact meaning is not known for certain.

This is a psalm of Asaph, a song of praise to God for a great victory. The text does not say with certainty what historical event gave rise to it; some think of the defeat of the Assyrian army before Jerusalem, but that is only a guess. The psalmist shows that God's judgment is not only punishment; it is also salvation for the humble.

For today: if you suffer an injustice, you do not have to take revenge. Trust that God sees, and that He knows how to rise up on behalf of the humble in His time.
exp.30:7:
He says that God did not hand the psalmist over into the hand of his enemy, that is, did not leave him trapped or without a way out. The word "shut up" here means to hand over or leave captive. Instead, God set his feet in a large room, meaning in a wide, open and safe place where he could move about freely.

The psalm is spoken by David, according to its heading, although some scholars think the text reflects a more general experience of those who are persecuted. He looks back and gives thanks for how God cared for him in affliction. It is striking that the psalm goes on with strong laments, so gratitude and pain live side by side in the same prayer.

For today: when you feel cornered, remember the times God opened a way for you. Thanking Him for what He has already done does not deny your present pain, but it helps you trust that He is still caring for you.
exp.28:0:
This verse is an invitation to acknowledge who God is. The word "Give" means "ascribe" or "attribute" the honor due to him. "Mighty ones" can refer to powerful beings of heaven, such as angels, or to people with authority; scholars understand it in several ways. It calls us to give God the glory, that is, the honor he deserves, and to recognize his strength.

David, the king and psalmist, speaks and addresses the mighty ones, calling them to bow before God. The verses that follow describe the voice of God over the waters and in the storm. In this way, the psalm shows that God's power stands above all human or natural power.

For today: before you ask or complain, begin your prayer by acknowledging who God is. Take a moment to thank him and to marvel at his greatness. That helps you remember that no problem is greater than he is.
exp.121:2:
It says that Jerusalem was built as a compact city, with its parts well joined together and in order. Many believers see both ideas at once.

The psalmist speaks, and the title attributes the psalm to David. It is a song of ascents, that is, a song of pilgrims who went up to Jerusalem for the festivals. He rejoices at going to the house of the LORD and describes the city he sees on arriving. All the tribes went up to it to praise God together.

For today: the church too should be a place of union. We can seek unity with other believers by serving, praying, and worshiping together, even when we think differently about secondary matters.
exp.103:34:
The explanation says that the psalmist wishes that sinners and the wicked would disappear from the earth. Then he speaks to himself: "Bless the Lord, O my soul", meaning, praise him with your whole being. Praise the Lord is the call to praise God together.

The psalmist, who is not named in the text, has celebrated God as the Creator and sustainer of all things. At the end, he thinks about the evil that harms that good creation. Many understand this wish as a cry for wickedness to come to an end, not as personal hatred. Some also see it as a call for sin to be taken away.

For today: when evil hurts you, do not fill yourself with resentment. Ask God to bring about justice and to change hearts, and turn back to praising him. Begin the day by saying: "Bless the Lord, O my soul."
exp.138:5:
It says that God's knowledge of us is too wonderful for the human mind. "Knowledge" here means knowing or understanding, not science in the modern sense. What a person is able to grasp is what the verse calls "attain." The psalmist admits that he cannot fully understand it, because it is so high, meaning it is far above him.

The speaker is David, according to the heading of the psalm. He has just acknowledged that God knows him completely: when he sits, when he walks, even his words before he speaks them. God surrounds him and cares for him with His hand. Faced with this, David is amazed. He immediately asks where he could flee from God, and discovers that He is present everywhere.

For today: when you do not understand everything God does or knows about your life, do not be anxious. You can rest in the fact that an infinitely wise One knows you and cares for you. Answer Him with trust and worship, not fear.
exp.118:6:
The explanation says that the psalmist promises to praise God with an upright heart, that is, sincerely and without duplicity, when he has learned God's righteous judgments. Here "judgments" does not mean punishments, but God's just decisions and standards. The praise grows out of learning.

The speaker is the psalmist, probably a believer who loves God's law. We cannot know for certain who wrote it. It comes from a desire for his ways to be firm and from not wanting to be put to shame. He knows he needs to learn in order to obey, and so he asks God not to abandon him.

For today: when you read the Bible, do not study only to know more. Ask God that what you learn will lead you to thank him honestly. After reading, take a moment to thank him for something specific you have seen of his righteousness.
exp.36:27:
Here the explanation says that God loves what is just and right, and that he never abandons his "saints," that is, those who are faithful to him and belong to him. They will be cared for forever. By contrast, the "seed" of the wicked, that is, their descendants, will be "cut off," an old word meaning uprooted and removed.

This is a psalm of David, written as wise counsel, perhaps in his old age. It encourages those who become troubled when they see the wicked doing well. The message is that such prosperity does not last, and that God sustains the faithful. The verses that follow speak of inheriting the land, a promise very important for Israel. Some understand the words "forever" more broadly, as an eternal hope.

For today: when injustice discourages you, do not become bitter or imitate the one who does wrong. Keep doing good calmly, trusting that God cares for you and sees everything.
exp.28:4:
It says that the voice of God is so powerful that it can break the cedars, which were the largest and strongest trees in the region. The word "breaketh" means to split or shatter. The cedars of Lebanon were famous for their height and hardness, so the example shows that nothing in creation can withstand the word of the Lord.

This is a psalm of David, written as praise. It describes a storm moving from the sea toward the mountains, and the psalmist presents it as a sign of God's power and glory. Some think it refers to a real storm; others think it is a poetic image. In either case, the purpose is to invite the people to worship God.

Today we can remember that the God who sustains creation also cares for us. When something great intimidates you, pray with confidence: no difficulty is stronger than his voice.
exp.12:0:
This verse is the cry of someone who feels abandoned by God. The repeated "how long" shows that the pain has already lasted far too long. "Hide thy face" means feeling that God has turned away or is no longer looking on us with favor. "To the chief Musician" is a note addressed to the leader of the singers.

The title attributes the psalm to David. It is not certain when he wrote it. The verses that follow speak of anguish, thoughts that go around and around, and an enemy who seems to be winning. It is a sincere prayer, offered in the middle of trouble, within a song the people used in worship.

When God seems silent, you do not have to pretend you are fine. You can tell him honestly what you feel, even your doubts and your weariness. Praying like this is also an act of faith, because you are still speaking to God and not walking away from him.
exp.21:5:
What it says: The speaker feels as small and despised as a worm, and feels that people no longer treat him as a person. He is mocked and looked down on, and feels that people despise him and reject him.

Context: This is a psalm of David, speaking about his own suffering. Just before, he recalls that God delivered his ancestors who trusted in Him, and by contrast he feels that he is not being rescued. The verses that follow show people mocking his faith. The Gospels quote parts of this psalm at the crucifixion of Jesus, and many Christians also read it as a prophetic view of his suffering.

For today: If you feel humiliated or worthless, you can tell God so with complete honesty, as David did. Praying honestly, even in pain, is a way of continuing to trust in Him.
exp.113:4:
Here the psalmist speaks to the sea and to the Jordan River as if they were people, and asks them: "What happened to you? Why did you flee and turn back?" It is a poetic question. The phrase "turned back" means that the Jordan drew back and stopped flowing forward.

The psalm recalls when God brought Israel out of Egypt. It remembers the sea that opened and the Jordan that stopped so the people could cross (Exodus 14 and Joshua 3). The author is not known for certain. He asks as if teasing with affection, and the answer comes in the next verse: the earth trembles at the presence of the Lord.

For today: if all creation acknowledges God, we too can trust Him. The seas and rivers that seem to block our way are no greater than God. Today you can bring that obstacle to Him in prayer and remember how He has helped you before.
exp.25:7:
Here David says he loves the place where God dwells. The phrase "the habitation of your house" refers to the place where God makes his presence known among his people. The "tabernacle" was the tent of worship, and "glory" speaks of God's bright and powerful presence. In other words, the psalmist declares his affection for being near God.

The title of the psalm attributes it to David, though some scholars debate this. The speaker asks God to examine him and affirms that he has tried to live with integrity. Just before this verse he washes his hands in innocence before coming to the altar, and afterward he asks not to be counted among the wicked. His love for God's presence goes hand in hand with a desire for a clean life.

Today we can cultivate that same love for God's presence. Set aside time to pray, read the Bible, and meet with other believers, not out of obligation, but out of delight. And ask God to cleanse your heart so you can draw near with sincerity.
exp.5:3:
This verse is an urgent prayer. "Return" asks God to come near again, as if he had drawn away. "Deliver my soul" means rescue the life, or the whole person. "Mercy" is his faithful, compassionate love, not something the psalmist has earned.

The psalm is attributed to David, according to its title, though we cannot know with certainty the exact moment it was written. He is sick, distressed, and worn out from weeping. He feels that God is silent and fears he may die. Many think he also suffers from discipline or from enemies, but the text does not make this entirely clear.

For today: when you feel without strength, do not pretend to be fine. Speak to God honestly, even in tears. Ask for help leaning on his mercy, not on your merits, and keep praying even when you do not yet see the answer.
exp.18:10:
What it says: The psalmist speaks of God's commandments and judgments, which he calls "them." He says that through them God warns him, or corrects him. He also affirms that keeping them brings a great reward, that is, a great blessing or good.

Context: David is traditionally named as the author in the psalm's heading, though some scholars debate his authorship. He has just praised God's law as more precious than gold and sweeter than honey. Here he calls himself God's servant in humility, and right after this he asks forgiveness for hidden faults and protection from pride.

For today: Read the Bible not only to learn more, but to let yourself be corrected by it. This week, ask God to show you one specific area where you need to change, and take one small step of obedience. That reward is often peace, clarity, and closeness with God.
exp.9:17:
This verse says that God will act as judge in favor of the fatherless and the poor, so that the mortal, weak human being will no longer carry on violence. "To judge" here means to do justice, to defend the one who has no one to defend him. "That" simply introduces the result God brings about: the oppressor will no longer be able to keep harming.

The psalmist, traditionally attributed to David (the psalm itself does not say so), cries out to God in the face of the wickedness of the oppressors. At the end of the psalm he finds calm by remembering that the LORD is King forever, that he hears the desire of the humble and prepares their heart. His confidence is that oppression will not have the last word.

For today: when you see injustice against the weak, pray with confidence that God sees them, and act concretely. You can help a needy child, accompany a widow, or support someone poor with your time or your resources.
exp.85:11:
It says that the one speaking wants to praise God with his whole being, holding nothing back. The phrase "glorify" means recognizing how great and valuable God is and speaking of Him that way. The words "for evermore" show that this praise will not be passing, but a decision for a whole lifetime.
