It is a prayer of David, according to the title of the psalm. He is in trouble: proud people and violent men surround him, looking for a way to harm him. Even so, just before this verse he asks God to teach him His way and give him a steady heart. Then he gives the reason for his praise: God has rescued him from a danger of death, described as a deep pit.

For today: before asking for more, thank God for something specific that He has already done in your life. Say it aloud, sincerely and without rushing, even if your situation is still difficult.
exp.118:60:
The psalmist says that bands of wicked people have plundered him, yet he has not forgotten God's law. The word "bands" refers to groups or gangs, and "wicked" describes those who live without respect for God. The verb "robbed" can also be understood as "surrounded" or "bound," since the original can be translated in several ways.

The speaker is the psalmist, whose identity is not certain. In this psalm he praises God's word in the midst of pressure and opposition. Earlier he said he examined his life and turned back to obey; later he tells how he would rise at midnight to give thanks to God. His faithfulness does not depend on everything going well.

When you are treated unfairly or lose something, keep a verse in your heart and repeat it. In this way, instead of becoming bitter, you can respond with confidence and gratitude to God.
exp.84:9:
This verse uses a very beautiful image: four qualities of God meet together and embrace like friends. Mercy is the love that forgives; truth is his faithfulness and honesty; righteousness is doing what is right; peace is harmony and complete well-being. Kissing was a greeting of affection and reconciliation.

The psalm was written by the sons of Korah, probably after the people returned to their land, though it is not known with certainty which return that was. The people ask God for restoration and then say they will listen to what he says about peace. The verse describes how God will bring that salvation: without giving up his righteousness or his mercy.

For today: you do not have to choose between being firm and being compassionate. When you must correct or forgive someone, seek to speak the truth with kindness, and pursue what is right with a desire for peace.
exp.46:5:
This verse repeats the command to sing four times: twice to God and twice to our King. The word "sing" is a direct invitation, in the plural, to offer praise. Today we would write "to God" rather than the older form. The repetition shows insistence and joy, as if to say: "Don't stop praising him!"

It is a psalm of the sons of Korah. We do not know with certainty who composed it or on what occasion it was used. The speaker calls all the peoples to rejoice that God is King. The verse before it speaks of God who "went up" with shouting and "with the sound of a trumpet," an image of a king being proclaimed. Some think it was sung in worship in the temple; this is understood in several ways.

For today: make praise a habit. Even on a difficult day, sing or give thanks to God aloud, remembering that he reigns and cares for you.
exp.88:26:
God says that he will make his chosen one his "firstborn," that is, the son with the place of greatest honor and inheritance. He also says he will make him "higher than the kings of the earth," meaning with more authority and dignity than any other ruler.

Here God speaks, recalling the promise he made to David that his family would reign forever (2 Samuel 7). David was not the oldest son of his household, yet God honored him as if he were. Many Christians see that this promise is fully fulfilled in Jesus, called "firstborn" in Colossians 1:15-18. Others read it first as a promise for David's dynasty.

For today: God is faithful to his promises, even when they take a long time or seem impossible. If you feel small or unimportant today, trust that God can lift up and honor the one he chooses. Rest in his word and wait with patience.
exp.143:3:
It says that the human being is like a breath, something empty and fleeting. The word "vanity" here does not speak of pride but of breath or vapor, something that lasts only a very short time. His days are like a shadow that moves and soon disappears.

David is the speaker, according to the traditional heading of the psalm. He is a warrior king who gives thanks to God for his protection and is amazed that the great God would pay attention to someone so frail. Then he asks God to intervene and deliver him from his enemies. His weakness leads him to trust in God.

For today: Remembering that life is brief helps us avoid living with arrogance or anxiety. We can devote our days to what matters and trust in God, who truly cares for us.
exp.135:20:
It says that God gave the land of the kings Sihon and Og to the people of Israel as an inheritance, and that he did so because his mercy endures forever. The word "gave" appears in the verse as is, and "inheritance" means property received as a gift of family, not earned through merit.

This psalm is a song of praise sung by the community, most likely in the worship of Israel. It recalls creation and the deliverance from Egypt, and then the victory over these kings on arrival at the promised land (Numbers 21). After each remembrance, the people respond: "his mercy endures forever." In this way they acknowledge that everything was the work of God, not only of his strength.

For today: remember what you have received without deserving it, such as an opportunity, a person, or help in a difficult moment. Give thanks to God by name and trust that his mercy continues to accompany you today.
exp.13:1:
The explanation says that God, from heaven, looks down on all of humanity, like someone leaning over to observe carefully. He looks for someone "understanding," that is, wise and sensible, who seeks Him. Here "understanding" does not mean being highly educated, but having the wisdom to recognize God.

David writes this psalm after describing the fool, who says in his heart that there is no God. In the Bible, a fool is someone who lives as if God did not matter. David shows that this attitude leads to corruption and injustice, even against God's people. The verses that follow say that God finds no one who seeks Him as he should.

Today we can remember that God watches us with care and desires that we seek Him. Ask Him for wisdom today, and seek His guidance in your decisions.
exp.139:0:
This verse begins with a note for the choir director: it is a psalm of David, meant to be sung. Then David prays for help. "Deliver me" means "save me" or "rescue me." "Preserve me" means "protect me." He asks to be kept safe from wicked and violent people.

David is the one speaking, and he does so with a sincere prayer. The verses that follow describe his distress: there are people who plan harm, stir up quarrels, and wound with words, like serpents with venom. The Bible does not say here at what exact point in his life he wrote it, so we do not know with certainty what situation he was facing.

For today: when someone hurts or threatens you, do not carry that weight alone. Speak to God honestly, ask Him for protection and wisdom, and trust that He hears you. Prayer does not remove your responsibility to act with prudence, but it gives you peace.
exp.50:4:
This verse says that David recognizes himself as a sinner from the very beginning of his life. "I was shapen in iniquity" and "in sin did my mother conceive me" are strong expressions meaning that his inclination toward wrong goes back to the start. He does not accuse his mother of having done anything wrong.

The psalm is attributed to David, after the prophet Nathan showed him his sin with Bathsheba. He makes no excuses but confesses his guilt before God. Scholars understand this verse in several ways: as language of exaggeration to express his deep need, or as a reference to the sinful condition that all of us inherit.

Today, instead of justifying ourselves with phrases like "that's just how I am," we can humbly acknowledge our need and ask God to cleanse and transform us, trusting in his mercy.
exp.87:1:
The explanation says that the psalmist asks God to let his prayer reach Him. The word "come" in the verse, as in "Let my prayer come before thee," is the phrase being explained, meaning that he asks God to let it reach His presence. "Incline thine ear unto my cry" means "pay attention to me." "Cry" is a shout for help made out of pain.

The speaker is Heman the Ezrahite, according to the title of the psalm. He is suffering greatly and feels close to death. This psalm is very unusual, because it has almost no relief and no visible hope. Even so, he does not stop praying, and he calls God "the God of my salvation," that is, of my deliverance. There are several opinions about exactly who this Heman was, so it is best not to claim more than that.

Today, if you are going through a dark season, you can pray honestly, without dressing up your words. God is not offended by your pain. Speak to Him just as you are, even if you do not yet see an answer.
exp.43:7:
They say the people want to boast in God, and not in themselves, at all times. "Boast" means to feel proud and glad about someone. "Praise" means to commend or extol. "Selah" is a Hebrew word that probably indicates a pause to reflect or sing; its exact meaning is not entirely certain.

It is a psalm of the sons of Korah, sung by the people of Israel. It remembers with gratitude the victories God gave in the past and declares that they do not trust in weapons. However, the following verses change in tone: now they suffer a defeat and do not understand why. So this praise is spoken in the middle of confusion. The exact battle they had in mind is unknown.

We can praise God even when we do not understand what we are going through. Today, when something goes well, let us thank God instead of relying only on our own strength; and when something goes wrong, let us keep drawing near to Him with sincerity.
exp.88:0:
The explanation says the author will always sing of God's mercies, that is, his faithful love and his goodness. It also promises that from one generation to the next he will speak of God's truth, that is, his faithfulness and his keeping of what he has said.

The word that appears in the title of this psalm probably indicates a poem or song meant to teach, although its exact meaning is not entirely certain. Another term is explained as meaning "known to all."

The speaker is Ethan the Ezrahite, named in the title of the psalm. The verses that follow explain his reason: he remembers the covenant God made with David, and that God's love and truth are as firm as the heavens. The psalm then shows grief because that promise seems not to be seen fulfilled, but it begins with praise.

For today: think of one concrete example of God's faithfulness in your life, and this week tell it to a child, a friend, or someone in your family. In this way faith is passed from one generation to another.
exp.63:1:
Here David asks God to hide him and keep him safe. "Secret counsel" refers to the plans people make in private, behind closed doors. "Wicked" describes people full of evil, and "conspiracy" is a group that gathers to do harm. "Workers of iniquity" are those who practice injustice.

The psalm is attributed to David, and its heading directs it to the chief musician to be sung. David speaks in fear, because his enemies attack him with sharp words and in secret. The verses that follow compare their tongues to a sword and their words to arrows. It is not known for certain at what exact moment of his life he wrote it.

When someone slanders you or plots something against you, you do not have to carry that fear alone. Do as David did: tell God honestly what you feel and ask him for protection. Then avoid responding with the same bitterness, and leave your defense in his hands.
exp.118:14:
The psalmist says he wants to think calmly and carefully about God's commands. The verse's phrase "I will meditate in thy precepts" means to reflect slowly, turning it over in the mind. The phrase "have respect unto thy ways" means to look closely at how God acts and how he wants us to live.

The speaker is the author of Psalm 119, a psalm in honor of God's Word. We do not know for certain who wrote it. Earlier the psalm says he speaks of God's judgments with his lips and that he delights in his testimonies more than in riches. Now he moves from speaking to thinking: he loves the Word from the inside, not only outwardly.

For today: set aside a few minutes each day, without rushing or looking at your phone, to read one short verse. Ask yourself what it teaches you about God and what change it calls you to make. Then repeat it to yourself during the day.
exp.17:22:
The explanation says that David was sincere and upright before God, and that he kept watch over his own wickedness. "I was blameless" means that he acted with a whole heart, without duplicity. "I kept myself" means that he stayed alert so as not to fall into the evil that was within him.

David speaks in this psalm of thanksgiving, after God delivered him from his enemies and from Saul, as the heading of the psalm indicates. He does not claim to be perfect; the Bible itself shows his failings in other passages. He is referring to his general faithfulness to God, and interpreters understand this passage in different ways, but almost all read it as a testimony of loyalty.

For today: honestly recognize where you tend to stumble, and ask God for help to watch over that weak point. Integrity is not having no failures, but walking sincerely with God and guarding against whatever draws us away from him.
exp.36:20:
This verse compares two kinds of people. The wicked person borrows and does not repay; he is someone who uses others and does not keep his word. The righteous person, by contrast, "shows mercy," that is, he is compassionate, and "gives," meaning he shares generously. Here "wicked" means a person who lives without respect for God or for others.

It is a psalm of David, written as wise counsel for those who are troubled when they see the wicked prosper. David asks them to trust in God, because the one who acts with evil does not endure, while those who belong to God are upheld, even in difficult times. The verses nearby speak of that promise. Some scholars see here a contrast of character rather than a rule for every case.

For today: keep your commitments and debts with honesty, and look for a concrete way to help someone in need this week, even if it is small.
exp.117:7:
This verse says that it is better to place our hope in God than in people. The word "trust" here means to rely on, take refuge in, and lean on someone. The name "the Lord" is God's name in the Old Testament.

The psalm does not clearly name its author. The one speaking has been through great distress, surrounded by enemies, and was rescued by God. So he tells what he has learned: God was with him when people could not or would not help. The verses that follow speak of rulers, that is, people with power, and yet he says God is a better refuge.

Today we can be thankful for the help of family, friends, and authorities, but without making them our only support. When you feel pressured or alone, before looking for human solutions, pray and hand your worry over to God. He never fails.
exp.123:7:
Our help comes from God. "Help" here means aid in a time of danger. "The name of the Lord" refers to who he is, his character and his power. And he is described as the one "who made heaven and earth," that is, the Creator of everything, who has no rival.

It is a psalm of ascent, attributed to David, which the pilgrims sang as they went up to Jerusalem. The people of Israel remember that they came close to being devoured by powerful enemies. They compare themselves to a little bird that escaped the hunter's trap. They acknowledge that they were not saved by their own strength, but by God. This verse is the conclusion of that song of praise.

For today: when you face a problem that is bigger than you, do not trust only in your own resources. Before you act, bring the matter to God in prayer, and remember that the One who holds up the universe also cares for you.
exp.36:14:
This verse says that the weapons the wicked prepared to do harm will turn back against them. The sword they drew to wound others will end up wounding them, and their bow, which they meant to shoot with, will be broken and left useless. The phrase "shall enter into their own heart" means that the evil they planned will fall back on them.

The speaker is David, who writes a wisdom psalm to encourage the righteous. The verses just before describe the wicked who attack the poor and the needy. David wants to calm those who are troubled to see the evil apparently getting their way. God sees everything and has a time to act.

Today we can leave justice to God and not take revenge. If someone wrongs us, instead of becoming bitter or repaying evil with evil, we can pray, keep doing what is right, and trust that God cares for his own.
exp.104:31:
It says that God changed the rains of Egypt into hail and into fire that fell like flames. Instead of water that gives life to the fields, the rain became a blow and destruction. "Flames" refers to burning fire or lightning.

The psalmist recalls the plagues of Egypt within a song of praise for the works of God. He wants the people of Israel to remember how God cared for them and freed them from slavery, keeping his promise to Abraham. This plague appears in Exodus 9, where the hail comes together with fire. The details of exactly how it happened are not explained beyond what the text says.

For today: God is faithful to his own and hears the oppressed. We can trust that no injustice is indifferent to him, and respond with gratitude, remembering his works in our lives.
exp.84:4:
Here the psalmist asks, with pain, whether God will stay angry with his people forever. He asks whether his anger will last through many generations. This is not an accusation but a sincere cry.

An Israelite speaks on behalf of the whole people. The earlier verses recall that God had already forgiven and restored them before. Now, facing a new hardship, they ask God to renew his favor. The exact moment is not known for certain; some think of the return from exile, others of the difficulties after they came back.

For today: when you feel that God is far away or that your mistakes weigh too heavily, you can bring that question to him honestly. Remember how he has helped you before, and ask him with confidence to renew you. He invites us to pray sincerely, not with pretense.
exp.118:84:
The explanation says that some proud people, the "proud ones," have set traps for the psalmist. The picture of "digging pits" is that of hunters who hide a hole so that the prey falls into it. It then clarifies that these people "do not live according to your law," meaning they do not live in line with what God commands.

The speaker is a faithful believer, perhaps an older man who is suffering persecution. We do not know with certainty who wrote it or the exact moment it was written. He feels squeezed, like a wineskin (a leather bag for wine) hanging in the smoke, but he does not forget God's word. He asks God to do justice.

For today: when someone treats you with malice or sets traps for you, do not answer in kind. Hold fast to God's Word, pray with sincerity, and let Him take care of justice.
exp.65:6:
He rules by his power forever; his eyes watch over the nations. Let not the rebellious lift themselves up. Selah.

The explanation says that God governs with his power and will do so forever. The phrase "rules as Lord" means that he gives commands as Master. Where it says his eyes watch over all the nations, the picture is of someone standing high and keeping careful watch over everything below. The rebellious, those who oppose God, will not triumph. "Selah" was probably a musical pause or a moment for reflection, though this is not known with certainty.

The psalm is a song of praise from Israel, and no one knows for sure who wrote it. It recalls when God opened the Red Sea and the Jordan River. The people invite everyone to see what God has done, and from this they conclude that God still governs and cares for his people.

For today: when you see injustice or feel insecure, remember that God is not distracted. He sees everything and remains Lord. Trust in him and respond with gratitude and humility.
exp.108:15:
This verse gives the reason for the psalmist's complaint: that wicked man never remembered to be compassionate. On the contrary, he pursued a person who was afflicted, poor, and crushed in spirit, to the point of wanting to kill them. "Needy" and "crushed in spirit" are words that describe someone hurt on the inside.

The psalm is spoken by David, according to its title, and he asks God for justice against an enemy who accuses him falsely and repays good with evil. Such strong prayers are called imprecatory psalms. Some understand that David is quoting the words of his accusers, though this is interpreted in several ways.

For today: God takes notice of how we treat those who suffer. Today you can show compassion to someone fragile, and when you are wounded, hand your pain over to God instead of taking revenge.
exp.90:4:
This verse says that whoever trusts in God does not need to live in fear. The terrors of the night are the dangers that come in the dark, such as perils, threats, or sudden frights. The arrow that flies by day represents the attacks that come in broad daylight. Thus the verse covers the whole of time: night and day.

The psalm does not say who wrote it, and this is uncertain; some have attributed it to Moses, others to David. It is spoken by someone who encourages trust in God as a refuge, and the image of a bird that covers with its wings shows his care. The verses that follow speak of pestilence and death, which were very real dangers for the people. The psalm does not promise a life without pain, but the assurance of being under God's care.

Today, when fear takes away your sleep or troubles you during the day, stop and pray. Hand your worry over to God and remind yourself that he is your refuge.
exp.54:13:
Here the psalmist remembers what his relationship with a very close friend used to be. They shared their confidences with tenderness, sweetly, and even walked together toward the house of God, that is, the temple, to worship in company.

The one speaking is David, according to the heading of the psalm. He is distressed, and what hurts him most is not the attack of an open enemy but the betrayal of someone intimate, a companion he once trusted. The Bible does not say with certainty who that person was; some think of Ahithophel, but that is an interpretation and not something confirmed in the text.

For today: if someone close to you has wounded you, do not hide your pain. Bring it honestly before God, as David does, who ends by saying: "But I will call upon God." Also value and care for the friends who walk with you in faith.
exp.114:17:
We, the people of God, say that we will bless and praise him from now on and forever.

The psalm declares that the Lord is the true God, unlike the idols. The speaker is the people of Israel, who sang this together as a community. The verse before it says that the dead do not praise God; this contrasts with the living, who can do so as long as they have life. Scholars understand that phrase in different ways, but the general sense is to make use of life to praise.

Today we can decide to thank God every day, even with a short prayer in the morning. As long as we have life, we have the opportunity to praise him with our words and with our conduct.
exp.30:0:
David says that the psalmist, David, places all his trust in God. To say that he has waited on God means that he has trusted in God and leaned on him. The request "let me never be ashamed" means that he should not be left ashamed or let down. He asks to be rescued "in your righteousness," meaning because God is faithful and upright. The heading "To the chief Musician" is a note for the one leading the singing in worship.

The title attributes the psalm to David, and the one speaking is someone in danger or distress. The text does not specify the exact moment of his life it describes, and scholars interpret it in different ways. What is clear from the verses that follow is that David describes God as a rock, a fortress, and a stronghold, images of a secure refuge.

For today: when you feel pressured or afraid, begin your prayer by remembering who God is, as David does. Tell him in your own words, "In you I put my trust." Then bring him your specific situation and wait for his help with patience.
exp.77:57:
This verse says that the people of Israel angered God with their high places, which were elevated places where they worshiped, and with their carved images, that is, idols or sculpted images. The phrase "provoke to jealousy" means to stir up God's jealousy, as when someone who is loved is betrayed by another love.

The psalm is written by Asaph, and it reviews the history of Israel to teach new generations. Here it recalls how the people, after entering the promised land, became like a bow that fails just when it is needed. This leads to the judgment that follows: God left Shiloh, where the tabernacle was.

For today: examine what things in your heart occupy the place that belongs only to God, such as money, success, or the approval of others. Ask Him for help to return to Him with sincerity, not merely with religious habits.
exp.77:70:
He took David from following the ewes that had just given birth, that is, the ewes with small lambs, which need very gentle care. He called him to be the shepherd of Jacob, that is, the people of Israel, whom the Bible calls his inheritance, that is, his most cherished possession.

This psalm is by Asaph, a temple musician. It reviews the history of Israel, with its failures and God's faithfulness. At the end it tells how God rejected Shiloh and chose Judah and David. It shows that God guides his people with kindness, even using ordinary people.

For today: God does not look at prestige, but at the heart and at faithfulness in small things. If you care patiently for what is entrusted to you, whether your family, your work, or your church, God can prepare you for something more. And if you lead, do so with care and tenderness.
exp.96:0:
He says that God is King and that He already reigns. For that reason the whole earth should be filled with joy, even the most distant places. "Lord" is the name of God, and "reigneth" means that He exercises His authority as sovereign. The "isles" represent the coasts and distant lands, that is, peoples who perhaps have never heard of Him.

This psalm does not say who wrote it. It is a song of praise that celebrates God's rule over the whole world. The verses that follow describe it with clouds, fire, righteousness and judgment. His reign is powerful and also just, so it invites joy and not only fear.

For today: even when the world seems disordered, you can rest in the knowledge that God is still King. Today, when facing a specific worry, pause and thank Him because He governs with justice, and let that trust restore your joy.
exp.24:20:
The explanation says that the psalmist asks God to be guarded by integrity and uprightness, that is, by living honestly and doing what is right. And it gives the reason: "for I wait on thee," meaning he has placed his trust in God and keeps waiting for his help. Here, waiting is not passivity but trusting with patience.

Tradition attributes the psalm to David. It speaks from a difficult moment: he has many enemies who hate him violently, and he fears being put to shame. That is why he asks for protection and deliverance. His integrity is like a shield, and his hope is placed in God. Some scholars point out that the psalm is an acrostic poem, and that the final verse, about Israel, extends the prayer to the whole people.

Today we can ask God to keep us from acting wrongly when we are under pressure or hurt. When someone treats us unjustly, the temptation is to respond with deceit or resentment. We can pray this verse and choose to be honest, trusting that God cares for us.
exp.117:25:
It says that the one who comes in the name of the Lord is blessed, that is, with his authority and his favor. The name of God is the word "Lord" in the verse. Then those who are in the temple, the house of the Lord, answer with a blessing toward those who arrive. The word "you" in "we have blessed you" refers to the ones who arrive; it means the same as "we have blessed them."

This psalm is a song of praise, and it was sung at Israel's festivals. It seems that a procession arrives at the temple and the priests or the people receive it with this blessing. No one knows for certain who speaks in each part; some see it as a song sung back and forth. In the New Testament, the crowd greets Jesus with these words as he enters Jerusalem (Matthew 21:9), and Christians see him as the one who comes in the name of the Lord in the fullest way.

For today: when someone arrives at your church or your home, welcome them with a word of blessing and not with indifference. And remember that you too come to God with confidence, because he receives you.
exp.105:25:
This verse says that God "lifted up his hand" against the people of Israel. That expression was like raising the hand to make a solemn oath. The word "overthrow" means to cause them to fall, and here it means they would die in the wilderness.

The psalmist reviews the history of Israel. After leaving Egypt, the people refused to enter the promised land, did not trust God's word, and grumbled in their tents (Numbers 14). As a result, that generation did not enter the land. The psalm confesses these sins, but it also remembers God's mercy.

For today: constant complaining can gradually wear down our trust in God. When you feel the urge to grumble, stop and remember what God has already done. Then speak to him honestly in prayer and obey what he has shown you.
exp.91:4:
This verse says that God's works are vast and wonderful, and that his thoughts are very deep, hard to fully grasp. The word "how" in the verse means "to what great extent," and "Lord" is the name of God. "Deep" speaks of something that cannot easily be measured.

This psalm is a song for the Sabbath day. The one speaking is a worshiper, whose name is not known for certain. It comes from praising God with music and rejoicing in what he has done. Right after, it contrasts that admiration with the foolish person, who does not understand God's ways, especially why the wicked seem to prosper for a time.

For today: when something does not make sense, pause and remember what God has already done. Praise him, and trust that his thoughts are deeper than yours, even though you do not yet understand them.
exp.117:20:
It says that the one speaking gives thanks to God for two reasons: because God heard him when he cried out, and because God himself became his salvation. The word "health" here does not speak only of being well, but of rescue, victory and deliverance. "You were my health" means "You became my salvation."

The psalmist comes to the gates of the temple to give thanks publicly after having been delivered from a great danger. It is not known with certainty who is speaking: it could be the king or the people represented by one voice. The psalm continues with the rejected stone that becomes the chief cornerstone, an image the New Testament applies to Jesus.

Today we can remember the times God helped us and thank him aloud, without waiting for everything to be perfect. Praying with gratitude reminds us that we are not alone and strengthens our trust.
exp.48:8:
No one can pay a price so that another person lives forever on this earth and escapes death. The word that the verse renders as "corruption" in the King James Version refers to the grave, and in the original language it can also mean "the pit" or "decay." To "redeem" means to rescue by paying a price.

The psalm is attributed to the sons of Korah, and it reads like a lesson in wisdom for everyone. It speaks against those who trust in their riches. Even when they are wealthy, they cannot buy more life. The wise and the foolish die alike, and others inherit what they leave behind. Some interpreters see here a hope beyond death, which appears in verse 15.

Today, do not place your final security in money, success, or possessions. Use them with generosity and humility, and entrust your life to God, the only one who can rescue you from death.
exp.118:109:
The explanation says that wicked people set a trap for the psalmist, yet he did not turn away from God's commandments. "The wicked have laid a snare for me" means that they set a trap for him, like the kind used to catch animals. The wicked are people who live without respect for God. The word "yet" means "but."

The one speaking is the author of Psalm 119, whose name the text does not give. Some connect him with David, but there is no certainty. Shortly before, he speaks of his life being in danger, a phrase that suggests constant risk. Even so, he does not forget God's law. Afterward he says that the Lord's testimonies are his inheritance and his joy. His faithfulness does not come from fear but from loving God's word.

For today: when someone pressures you or sets a trap to make you act wrongly, remember what God has said and ask him for help. Decide ahead of time which path you will follow.
exp.24:11:
This verse asks who the person is who fears the Lord, meaning someone who respects and honors God with reverence and trust, not with terror. The answer is a promise: God himself will teach that person the way they should choose, that is, the best decision for their life.

The psalm is attributed to David, who prays for guidance and forgiveness, acknowledging that his sin is great. Earlier in the psalm he speaks of God's mercy toward those who keep his covenant. Afterward he promises rest, blessing for children, and closeness with God. In this way David shows that God guides with tenderness even those who recognize their failures.

Today, before making an important decision, pray with humility, asking God to give you wisdom. Read his Word, listen to wise counsel, and walk with a willingness to obey, trusting that he knows how to guide you.
exp.94:0:
This verse invites everyone to come and praise God with joy. Here the wording "come" appears as the verse does in English, and "let us sing" tells us to join together in song. "Let us make a joyful noise" describes a gladness that is sung out loudly and with strength. "The rock of our salvation" means the rock that saves us, since "salvation" here refers to being rescued, not to physical health. God is described as a firm and secure refuge.

The psalm does not say who wrote it. It sounds like a song for the people of Israel to sing together, perhaps when they gathered to worship. The one speaking calls the others to join in. The verses that follow give the reason: the Lord is a great God and a King above all. Then the psalm shifts to a warning not to harden the heart.

For today: before you begin your day, or when you feel insecure, take a moment to sing or give thanks to God aloud. Remember that He is your firm rock, even when everything around you is shaking.
exp.118:12:
He says that the psalmist has declared with his own lips all the decisions and teachings that God has spoken. "Judgments" does not refer only to punishments, but to God's just verdicts and decisions, that is, what He has said is right. The word "declared" means told, spoken out loud.

Psalm 119 is a long poem in honor of God's Word. It is not known for certain who wrote it; tradition does not say. The one speaking is a believer who loves God's law. First he kept the Word in his heart, and now he shares it with his mouth. What is inside comes out.

For today: do not keep what you learn from the Bible only to yourself. This week, share with someone, your family or a friend, a verse that has helped you, and tell them why.
exp.37:8:
It says that David speaks to God with complete sincerity: everything he longs for lies open before God, and even his sighs, those wordless groans, are not hidden from him. "Desires" here can be understood as deep longings, and "is not hidden from you" means that God sees and knows them.

The psalm is attributed to David, and its heading calls it a prayer for remembrance. He suffers in body and soul: sickness, weakness, distress and loneliness, since his friends have drawn away. Many understand that he also suffers because of his sins (vv. 3-4), though the text does not detail what his exact situation was.

For today: when you are so tired or wounded that you cannot find words, do not stay silent before God. Bring him your longings and even your sighs. He understands them, even when no one else notices, and he listens to you with care.
exp.38:12:
It says that the psalmist asks God to turn his punishing gaze away from him, so that he may recover his spirit and his strength before he dies. The phrase that is rendered "spare me" means "turn away from me" or "give me a little relief." "Recover strength" means "rejoice" or "recover breath." The word for "be no more" means "pass away," that is, die.

The psalm is traditionally attributed to David, according to its heading, though some read it in a more general way. He is suffering God's discipline for his sin and feels that life is brief and fragile. He calls himself a stranger, because he knows he is only passing through. His request is honest and desperate, not an accusation against God. Some scholars debate the exact tone of this line, but all recognize his pain.

For today: when you feel exhausted or corrected, you can speak to God with complete sincerity. Ask him for relief and strength, and remember that your life is in his hands.
exp.80:13:
It says that if the people had obeyed, God would have defeated their enemies very quickly. "In a moment" means "in an instant," almost without effort. "Brought low" means to bring down or subdue. "Turned my hand" speaks of acting with power against the adversaries.

The one speaking is God, through the psalmist Asaph, during a feast of Israel. God reminds them how he delivered them from Egypt, but they would not listen to him. So he left them to follow their own counsel. Here he expresses his grief: "Oh, that my people had listened to me!" It is a promise that went unfulfilled because of their disobedience.

For today: God does not force anyone, but he invites us to obey him because he wants to bless us. Before deciding something important, ask yourself whether you are listening to his voice in the Bible and in prayer. Many struggles become lighter when we walk with him.
exp.8:4:
It says that God sternly corrected the nations that opposed him, defeated the wicked, and blotted out their name completely. "You rebuked" means that God confronted them with authority. The phrase about blotting out is best rendered as "you blotted out their name," which is the wording your verse uses, so the idea of erasing something that has been written down is already in the verse itself. The phrase "forever and ever" stresses that their downfall was final.

David, the king of Israel, speaks according to the title of the psalm. He is thankful because God defended him from his enemies and acted as a just judge. It is not known with certainty which exact victory is in view. It is a song of praise, not of personal revenge.

For today: when you feel that injustice is winning, remember that God sees and judges with justice. Instead of taking revenge, entrust your cause to him in prayer and give thanks for the times he has already sustained you.
exp.76:19:
It says God guided Israel like a shepherd leads his sheep, using Moses and Aaron as his helpers. The word "leddest" means "led". Sheep do not know the way, but they trust the one who leads them.

Psalm 77 is written by Asaph, who is troubled and wonders whether God has forgotten his people. To encourage himself, he remembers the exodus: the crossing of the Red Sea, with a storm and footprints no one saw. This verse closes the psalm with a note of calm. God acted with power, but also with tenderness, and he did it through human leaders. Some scholars observe that the psalm ends briefly, without giving a complete answer to the initial distress.

When you cannot see the way or feel God's footprints, remember how he has cared for you before. He still leads, often through ordinary people he places beside you. Give thanks for them today.
exp.118:23:
This verse says that God's teachings, called "testimonies," are a delight to the psalmist. The word "delight" refers to deep pleasure or joy. In addition, those teachings are his "counselors," that is, they guide him and tell him what to do when he has to make a decision.

The one speaking is the author of Psalm 119, whose name is not mentioned in the text. Before this verse, he tells how he is criticized and how even rulers speak against him. Facing that, he does not sink into bitterness, but meditates on what God has said. The Word gives him comfort and direction in the midst of pressure.

For today: when you face criticism or doubts, before asking everyone for their opinion, set aside a few minutes to read a passage of the Bible calmly. Ask God to show you what to do, and let his Word be your first counselor and your joy.
exp.118:163:
It says that the psalmist praises God seven times a day. The reason is "the righteous judgments" of God, that is, God's fair decisions and commands. Here the word "judgments" does not speak of punishment, but of his rules and his upright decisions. The number seven can mean an exact amount or, as many understand it, something constant and complete: praising often, throughout the whole day.

The one speaking is the author of Psalm 119, a very long psalm in honor of God's Word. We do not know with certainty who wrote it. It comes from someone who loves the law, hates lies, and finds joy and peace in the Word, even in difficult times.

For today: choose several fixed moments of the day, for example when you wake up, at midday, and when you go to bed. Stop for a minute, remember something good that God has said or done, and give him thanks.
exp.68:2:
Here the psalmist says he is worn out from crying out to God. His throat is hoarse from shouting for help, and his eyes have grown weak, almost dim, from looking and waiting for God to answer. "Weary" means that his strength is spent, and his voice has broken and become rough.

David speaks, according to the title of the psalm. He is in very great distress, which he describes as water rising up to the neck and mud where there is no place to set the foot. Besides this, many hate him without cause. Some believe it is a prayer from a time of persecution, but the psalm does not pinpoint an exact moment in his life.

For today: if you feel tired of praying and see no answer, you are not alone. The Bible allows us to be honest with God about our exhaustion. You can keep waiting for him, even with little strength, and tell him honestly how you are.
exp.17:40:
The explanation says that David's enemies cried out for help, but no one rescued them. Even when they called on the Lord, He did not answer them.

David speaks here in a psalm of thanksgiving for having been delivered from Saul and all his enemies. He describes the victory God gave him. The enemies in view are those who attacked him with hostility, and their cry seems to be desperation in the moment of judgment rather than sincere repentance. Other passages in the Bible show that God hears the humble person who turns to Him from the heart, so this verse is best understood within that context.

For today: do not wait for a crisis to seek God. Cultivate a daily relationship with Him, in humility and obedience, so that in the difficult day your cry comes from trust and not only from fear.
exp.79:10:
It says that the vine God planted grew so large that its branches reached the sea, and its shoots reached the river. The words for "boughs" and "branches" refer to young limbs and sprouts that spread out. "The sea" is the Mediterranean, and "the river" is usually understood to be the Euphrates, though it is interpreted in several ways.

The psalmist, Asaph or someone from his circle, prays to God in a time of national distress. He compares Israel to a vine brought out of Egypt and planted in the promised land. He recalls its great prosperity in order to ask God to restore it, since its walls are now broken down and others are devouring it.

For today: when you go through a difficult season, remember what God has done before. That memory can sustain your prayer and your hope, because the One who made you grow can care for you again and restore you.
exp.118:73:
It says that those who respect and honor God, "those that fear thee," will be glad when they see the psalmist. "Fear" here does not mean being afraid, but revering God. He explains the reason for that gladness: his hope has been placed in God's word.

The one speaking is the author of the psalm, who is not identified with certainty. He is in the section marked with the letter Jod, where he asks for understanding. He speaks of his suffering, since in the following verses he acknowledges that God afflicted him justly. His firm hope in the midst of trial can encourage other believers.

When we trust in God's Word during a difficult moment, our lives can become a testimony that encourages others. Today you can read a Bible passage each day, hold fast to its promises, and share with someone in your church how God sustains you.
exp.65:3:
All the peoples of the world, from every nation, will worship God and sing to him. To "worship" means to recognize God as God and to honor him with the whole heart. The word "thee" in the verse is the old form of "you," addressed to God. The word "Selah" appears many times in the Psalms; it probably marks a pause for reflection or a moment in the music, although its exact meaning is not known for certain.

Here the psalmist speaks, inviting everyone to praise God. Earlier, the psalm speaks of the Lord's wonderful works, and afterward it recalls how God opened the sea and the river for his people. It is a song of thanksgiving for the salvation God has given and a hope that all will acknowledge him.

Today, we can praise God without shame, at home, at work, or in church, remembering specific things he has done for us. In this way our praise becomes a testimony to others.
exp.5:0:
This verse begins with a note for the choir director: the psalm was to be played on stringed instruments (Neginoth) and set "upon Sheminith," a phrase that may indicate a low-pitched melody or an eight-stringed instrument; no one knows for certain. Then David prays to God: "O Lord, rebuke me not in thine anger, neither chasten me in thy hot displeasure." To rebuke is to correct with severity, and to chasten is to discipline.

David speaks out of suffering. The verses that follow show that he is weak, sick, and troubled. He does not say exactly what his sin was or what his illness is, and scholars understand this in several ways. Even so, he feels that God is correcting him, and he begs for mercy.

When we suffer or feel guilty, we can come to God honestly, without pretending to be strong. It is better to bring Him our pain and ask for mercy than to run away from Him.
exp.114:9:
The explanation says that the descendants of Aaron, that is, the priests, must trust in the Lord. The reason is that God himself is the one who helps and protects them like a shield. "Trust" is a command in the plural: it means putting one's security in God. "Shield" speaks of protection in the midst of danger.

The psalm contrasts God with idols, which are the work of human hands and cannot do anything. For this reason the psalmist calls on three groups: Israel, the house of Aaron, and those who fear the Lord. It seems to be a song of praise for worship, perhaps with voices answering one another. The priests were guides of the people, so their trust was very important. We do not know with certainty who wrote it or on what occasion it was sung.

Today, if you are called to guide others, at home, in church or at work, do not rest only on your own experience or your strength. Say to God with sincerity: "You are my help and my shield," and trust in him before you decide.
exp.138:16:
This verse says that God's thoughts are very precious to the one speaking, and that they are so many they cannot be counted. The word "precious" means of great value, and the word "sum" refers to the total of those thoughts.

The one speaking is David, according to the title of the psalm. He has just remembered that God saw him and cared for him from before he was born, when he was formed in a secret place, a poetic way of speaking of the mother's womb. Thinking about this, he marvels that God has thought so much about him. He then says that if he tried to count them, they would be more than the sand.

For today: when you feel forgotten or without worth, remember that God knows you and thinks about you. Take a few minutes to thank him for something specific in your life, as a sign of his care.
exp.76:9:
The explanation says that the psalmist recognizes his pain and doubts as something like a sickness that afflicts him. For that reason he decides to remember the years of the right hand of the Most High, that is, the times when God acted with power on behalf of his people. The right hand is the symbol of strength. Some translations understand the phrase differently: that his weakness is to think that God has already changed.

The one speaking is the psalmist, traditionally associated with Asaph. He is distressed and asks whether God has stopped being merciful. Before this verse he asks very honest questions, and here his focus begins to shift: he moves from complaint to remembrance.

For today: when you doubt or feel abandoned, do not hide your questions from God. But write down or recall the times He helped you before. That memory can sustain your faith.
exp.49:2:
This verse says that God will come and will not keep silent. Before Him there will be a fire that consumes, and all around Him, a very strong storm. The fire and the storm show his holiness and his power.

It is a psalm of Asaph, a Levite in charge of the music in Israel's worship. Here God himself appears, calling the whole earth and presenting himself as judge of his people. The verses that follow explain that he does not come to condemn the sacrifices, but to correct a religion made only of rituals, without a faithful heart.

For today: God is not indifferent or silent before what we do. Today you can examine your heart honestly and ask yourself whether your faith is sincere, not just a habit. Draw near to him with humility, trusting in his mercy.
exp.97:7:
This verse says that all of creation joins in praise. The rivers "clap their hands," that is, they applaud, and the hills are filled with joy together. It is a poetic image: nature celebrates the way a crowd would.

The psalmist calls everyone to praise God as a king. First he invites people with trumpets, then the sea and the world, and now rivers and hills. The reason appears right away: the LORD has come to judge the earth with righteousness and equity. This is figurative language; it does not mean that the rivers have hands, but that everything created rejoices because God will set things in order.

Today we can praise God with joy, without waiting to feel perfect. Going out for a walk, looking at a river or a hill, and giving thanks reminds us that He is just and that His judgment is hope for the world.
exp.106:13:
He brought them out of the darkness and the shadow of death, meaning out of a situation so gloomy it seemed to be the very edge of death. He also broke their bonds, which were the chains or fetters that kept them imprisoned.

The psalmist invites those whom the Lord has rescued to give thanks. The verses before this one speak of people who suffered because of their rebellion, cried out to God, and he delivered them. Some think of the return from exile; others see a general description of several rescues. The text does not specify a single situation.

For today: if you feel trapped by sadness, a habit, or guilt, do as they did: cry out to God with sincerity. And when he helps you, do not keep it quiet; tell what he has done and give him thanks.
exp.9:0:
Here the psalmist asks God why he seems far away and hidden just when he is needed most. It is not a cold accusation but a sincere cry. "Trouble" means a time of distress or hardship. The phrase "you hide yourself" expresses the feeling that God does not let himself be seen or act.

The speaker is the psalmist, traditionally identified with David, though this psalm does not carry his name and some doubt it. He sees the wicked oppressing the poor, and it seems no one stops them. So he asks with pain. After the verse, he himself describes the arrogance of the wicked man and little by little returns to trusting that God does see and does bring justice.

For today: when you feel that God is far away, you do not need to pretend. You can tell him honestly what you feel, as the psalmist did, and keep praying even when you do not understand. The Bible shows that this sincere cry is also faith.
exp.57:6:
They say the wicked should melt away and vanish like water that runs off and is lost. It also asks that when the wicked bend their bow to shoot their arrows, the arrows be cut in pieces and unable to do harm. Some translators understand the last part in other ways, because the Hebrew is difficult.

David speaks in a psalm of lament. He is indignant at unjust judges and rulers who decree violence instead of justice. He asks God to stop their power, like someone asking for the teeth of a lion to be broken. It is poetic and forceful language, typical of someone crying out for justice.

For today: when you see injustice, do not take justice into your own hands or let yourself be filled with bitterness. Bring your pain to God honestly, trust that he judges with righteousness, and in the meantime act with justice and mercy wherever you can.
exp.77:4:
God himself established a testimony and a law among his people. The testimony is his teachings and commands that bear witness to who God is. God commanded the parents to pass on his word to their children.

The psalm is by Asaph, a worship leader in Israel. It speaks on behalf of the people and asks that what God has done not be kept from the coming generation. It recalls Israel's history, with its victories and also its failures, so that the young may learn to trust God and not repeat the mistakes of their ancestors.

For today: faith is not inherited on its own; it is taught. If you have children, nephews, nieces, or young people nearby, look for a simple moment this week to tell them something God has done in your life or what his Word says.
exp.121:0:
It says that David felt great joy when others invited him to go to the temple, which here is called "the house of the Lord" (the Lord is the name of God). The phrase "song of ascents" probably means a song of the pilgrimages, that is, a song for the travelers who went up to Jerusalem. Its exact meaning is not entirely certain.

The psalm is spoken by the one singing it, and the heading attributes it to David. It is a psalm of pilgrimage: the people traveled to Jerusalem for the feasts and to worship God. Here the emotion of going together, as a community, toward the place where God was worshiped is remembered.

For today: when someone invites you to gather with others to pray or worship, do not see it as a burden. Try to receive it with joy, as an opportunity to draw close to God and to encourage yourself alongside other believers.
exp.102:8:
God does not spend his life fighting with us or holding a grudge. The explanation says that the words "will contend" mean to argue, complain, or bring a legal case. The phrase "will keep his anger" means that he does not keep his anger burning forever. His discipline is real, but it is not his final attitude toward his people.

David speaks here, according to the heading of the psalm. He is praising God and reminding himself of his blessings. Shortly before, he recalls how God made himself known to Moses as "merciful and gracious, slow to anger." This verse explains that kindness: God corrects, but he does not condemn forever those who come to him with reverence.

If you have failed and feel that God is still angry with you, bring him your sin honestly. Confess, make right what you can, and rest in his forgiveness. His mercy is greater than your guilt.
exp.105:11:
After seeing how God saved them at the sea, the people of Israel believed what God had said and sang his praise. The word "á" is an old form of "a," so the phrase is not in the verse above; I will not comment on it.

The psalmist, an author who is not named in the text, looks back over Israel's history to acknowledge the people's sins. This verse recalls the crossing of the Red Sea (Exodus 14–15), when they sang to God. But the psalm tells it to show a contrast: their faith did not last long, for they soon forgot what God had done, as the following verses say.

It is easy to believe and praise God when we see his help clearly. The challenge is to keep trusting when hard days come. A good practice is to write down what God has done for you and review it often, so that your faith depends not only on the moment, but on his faithfulness.
exp.38:4:
It says God gave human beings a very brief life. "Short span" means that our days are numbered and pass quickly. Compared with the eternity of God, a person's age is like nothing at all. "Vanity" does not speak of pride, but of something fleeting, like a breath. "Selah" is a pause for reflection; its exact meaning is not certain.

The psalm is spoken by David, according to its heading. He is distressed, and his heart burns within him. He had kept silent, and now he prays and asks God to help him understand how short his life is. He does not say this in bitter hopelessness, for in the end he concludes: "My hope is in you."

Today, this truth invites us to live with calm and wisdom. We do not have to worry about accumulating things that will not last. You can begin the day by asking God: "Teach me to use my time well," and placing your hope in Him.
exp.30:15:
Here the psalmist asks God to look upon him with favor and kindness. The phrase "Make thy face to shine upon thy servant" is an older way of speaking about God's favor, like when someone smiles at you with affection. A "servant" is someone who belongs to God and serves him. He asks to be saved, not because he deserves it, but because of God's mercy, that is, his compassionate love.

The speaker is David, according to the heading of the psalm, though it is not known with certainty when he wrote it. He is surrounded by enemies and persecutors, and yet he says that his life is entirely in God's hands. Then he prays not to be put to shame.

Today, when you feel pressured or unfairly treated, you can pray simply: "Lord, look on me with favor and help me for your kindness' sake." Rest in the knowledge that your days are in God's hands.
exp.146:13:
This verse says that God is the one who brings peace to the borders of his people, meaning the limits of their land. It also says that he feeds them until they are satisfied with the very best of the wheat. The word "borders" in the King James wording of this verse means the boundaries or edges of their territory. The phrase about the finest of the wheat refers to the best and most abundant grain, the finest part of the harvest.

The psalmist calls Jerusalem to praise God. We do not know for certain who wrote it, and many think it was written after the return from exile, when the walls were rebuilt. He remembers that God protected the gates, blessed the children, and now gives peace and food. All of this is the reason for praise.

For today: peace and daily bread are gifts from God, even though we work for them. Today you can thank him before eating or at the end of the day, and calmly entrust him with your concerns for your family, your work, and your safety.
exp.49:6:
God tells his people to listen closely. He says he is going to speak and to bring a serious charge against Israel, that is, to present an accusation as in a court case. And he reminds them who he is: "I am God, even your God," the same one who made a covenant with them.

In this psalm, by Asaph, God appears as a judge who calls his people together. The heavens announce his righteousness. He does not rebuke them for lacking sacrifices, since they were offering them, but because their religion had become merely external, without a sincere heart. The verses that follow show this.

For today: before we speak or ask for something, let us learn to be quiet and listen to God. He does not seek only religious acts, such as attending or giving, but a sincere relationship. We can ask him humbly: "Lord, is there something in my heart that you need to correct?"
exp.96:9:
This verse says: "You who love God, hate evil. He watches over the lives of his faithful ones and rescues them from the power of the wicked." The words "hate" and "deliver" mean to reject firmly and to rescue. The word "saints" here refers to the people who are faithful to God, and "souls" refers to their lives.

The psalm does not say who wrote it. The speaker invites the people to celebrate that God reigns over the whole earth and is above every so-called god. Earlier, Zion rejoices because of God's judgments, that is, his justice. Afterward, light and joy are promised to the righteous. Love for God shows itself in rejecting what he rejects.

For today: if you love God, firmly reject something wrong you have been putting up with, such as gossip, dishonesty, or a harmful habit. Do it trusting that God watches over you and sustains you.
exp.19:6:
Some trust in chariots, and some in horses, which were the greatest military strength of those times. But God's people say that they will remember the name of the Lord, that is, they will recall him and call upon him. Here "name" refers to his character and his power.

This is a psalm of Israel before a battle. It seems that the people and the priests pray for the king, the anointed one, asking that God would keep him safe. The verses that follow show the contrast: those who trusted in weapons fell, but those who trusted in God rose up. It is not stated exactly which war it was; scholars interpret it in various ways.

Today we have our own chariots and horses: money, work, connections, or plans. These are not bad in themselves, but they should not be our final security. Before you decide or worry, stop and remember who God is and how he has cared for you.
exp.2:0:
This verse is the heading and the first cry of the psalm. David tells God that his enemies are many and that many are rising up against him. "Fleeing from before" means he was escaping from Absalom. "Have increased" means they have grown in number.

David, king of Israel, is the speaker. According to 2 Samuel 15 to 18, his son Absalom rebelled and drew away the support of the people, and David had to leave Jerusalem. The psalm's title ties it to that moment, though some scholars debate whether the title was added later. What we can see is a father wounded, in danger, and not knowing how everything would end.

Today, when you feel that problems or criticism are growing, you do not have to pretend to be strong. You can tell God honestly how heavy it weighs on you. David began by praying, and the verses that follow show that this is where he found confidence.
exp.38:5:
The explanation says that human beings live as if among shadows: they do not see clearly what truly matters. The phrase about being restless in vain means that a person stirs and strives after things that do not last. The word about heaping up means that a person piles up riches or possessions, yet does not know who will gather them, that is, does not know who will collect or enjoy them after death.

David speaks here, according to the heading of the psalm, and he does so with sincerity before God. He is reflecting on how brief life is and asks the LORD to teach him to see it as it really is. For this reason, at the end, he turns his gaze to God and says that his hope is in Him.

For today: before you strive to gain more, ask God what is truly valuable. Use your time and your possessions wisely, and place your hope in Him, not in what you accumulate.
exp.67:17:
God rises up on high like a victorious king. "Thou hast led captivity captive" means that he defeated the enemies and left them without power. Then he receives gifts from men, even from the rebellious, so that he may dwell among them.

The psalmist, David according to the title, celebrates a triumphal procession of God toward his holy mountain, Zion. He remembers when God was with his people at Sinai. The verses that follow praise God for saving. Paul quotes this verse in Ephesians 4:8 and applies it to Christ, but he changes "received" to "gave gifts." Scholars explain that difference in several ways.

For today: God does not turn away from the rebellious; he wants to dwell among them. If you feel unworthy, draw near to him with confidence and humility.
exp.146:4:
This verse says that our Lord is great and has great power. It also says that his understanding has no limit, meaning that his wisdom cannot be measured or counted.

The psalm does not say with certainty who wrote it. It is a song of praise, probably from Israel after the restoration, although this is interpreted in several ways. Earlier, it speaks of a God who heals broken hearts and counts the stars, calling them by name. Afterward, it says that he lifts up the humble. The psalmist joins God's enormous power with his tender care.

Today, when you feel small or confused, remember that the God who knows every star also knows your pain. You can bring him your worries with confidence, because his power and his wisdom have no limit, and he cares for you.
exp.49:10:
God says that he knows all the birds of the mountains, that is, that not one of them escapes his notice. He also says that the wild beasts of the field are his, meaning that the animals that roam free belong to him and are under his care. The word "wild beasts" refers to the animals that live free out in the fields.

Here God himself speaks, in a psalm of Asaph. He addresses his people, who were offering sacrifices thinking that in this way they were giving him something he needed. God corrects that idea: everything already belongs to him, and he does not depend on our offerings as if he were hungry.

For today: we do not need to buy God's favor with things or by keeping rituals. He is not a needy God. What he looks for is a grateful and sincere heart. Today you can thank him, trust him, and obey him, knowing that he cares for you as he cares for the birds.
exp.118:103:
Through God's instructions, the psalmist has gained understanding and wisdom. For this reason he now firmly rejects every way of living that is false. "Gained understanding" means he has grown in comprehension, and "hate" here means he rejects it with strong conviction. A "false way" is any way of living built on deceit or on untrue ideas.

The speaker is the author of Psalm 119, a long poem honoring God's word. We do not know for certain who wrote it. Here he says that God himself taught him, and that God's words are sweet to him, like honey. His love for the truth comes from that experience, and this prepares what follows: the word as a lamp on the path.

For today: read the Bible slowly and ask God to help you see where you have accepted deceptive ideas or habits. Let his truth guide you in one concrete decision this week.
exp.54:16:
The explanation says that the psalmist will pray three times a day: in the evening, in the morning, and at noon. The verse's words "will I pray, and cry aloud" mean that he will speak to God with strength, from the depths of his heart. And he trusts that God "shall hear my voice," that is, that God will listen to him.

The one who speaks is David, according to the title of the psalm, though some scholars debate the exact moment. He feels distressed because people close to him have betrayed him and there is violence around him. For this reason he cries out to God and not to his own strength. The verses that follow show that God gives him peace in the midst of the conflict.

For today: choose three moments of the day, even if they are brief, to speak with God. You do not need perfect words. Tell him honestly about your worries, and trust that he listens to you.
exp.70:18:
This verse says that God's righteousness reaches to the highest heights, meaning that it is enormous and has no limits. The one speaking praises God for the great things he has done and asks, "Who is like you?", meaning that no one can be compared to him.

Psalm 71 is the prayer of a person who is already old and has trusted in God since youth. The text does not say who wrote it, so we do not claim that with certainty. This person asks that God not forsake them in old age, so they can tell the coming generations what God has done. They speak out of distress, but also out of hope.

For today: think of a time when God helped you and tell someone younger, such as a child, a nephew, or a friend. In this way your experience can strengthen the faith of others.
exp.141:2:
When David's spirit was worn down and drained within him, the explanation says, God knew well which way he was going. "Path" is the road or direction of his life. It also says that while he was walking, others secretly laid a snare for him, meaning a net or trap set to catch him.

David speaks in a prayer he made while he was in a cave. From the title of the psalm and other accounts, it is commonly thought that he was fleeing from King Saul, though it is not known for certain which cave it was. He felt alone, hunted, and surrounded by danger, and so he pours out his complaint before God with complete honesty.

For today: when you feel weighed down, or suspect that someone is trying to harm you, you do not need to explain everything in fine words. Tell God what you feel. He knows your path, including the dangers you cannot see, and he does not leave you alone in them.
exp.17:35:
It says that God gave the psalmist a wide and secure path. The phrase "Thou hast enlarged my steps under me" means that God made room for him to walk without stumbling. The phrase "my feet did not slip" means that his feet did not give way or slide out from under him.

The words are spoken by David, according to the psalm's title, after God rescued him from his enemies and from Saul. It comes from a scene of war: God teaches him to fight, gives him protection, and holds him up. David recognizes that his stability and his victories do not come from his own strength, but from God's help.

For today: when you face a difficult situation, do not rely only on your own strength. Ask God for firmness to take the next step, and then take that step with confidence. Afterward, thank him for what held you up.
exp.88:41:
It says that God himself gave strength and victory to the king's enemies. The phrase "raising the right hand" means lifting up power, making someone triumph. The "adversaries" are those who oppose. And "made to rejoice" means that the enemies celebrated when they saw him fall.

The psalm is written by Ethan the Ezrahite, according to the title. First it recalls God's promise to David: that his throne would be firm. But now, in this complaint, it sees the king defeated and humbled. So it calls out to God, as if saying: "You promised one thing, and it seems another is happening." Scholars often connect it to a national defeat, though the exact moment is not known with certainty.

For today: when life seems to go against what God has promised, you can tell him so honestly in prayer. The Bible shows that it is possible to weep and to protest, without ceasing to trust that God remains faithful.
exp.28:3:
This verse says that when God speaks, his voice has power and also splendor. In this version, the word "power" means strength, and "glory" speaks of his greatness and his beauty. It is a voice that not only commands, but also shows who he is.

This psalm is attributed to David and is a song of praise. The psalmist calls people to worship God and then describes his voice as thunder over the waters, which shakes the cedars of Lebanon. The phrase "the voice of the Lord" is repeated seven times in the psalm. Many see here a storm, though others think it is a poetic way of speaking of God's power in general.

Today, before you make decisions or when you are troubled, pause for a moment to listen to his Word. If his voice has such strength, you can trust that his promises have it too.
exp.34:11:
He says David received evil in return for the good he had done. The phrase "They rewarded me" is in view here, meaning they paid him back. The phrase "to the spoiling of my soul" means to sink it, to leave it without spirit, to destroy it from within. His enemies were not only ungrateful, but they sought his ruin.

David speaks here, according to the title of the psalm, though some scholars think the language can also express the cry of any righteous person who is persecuted. He is asking God to defend him. The verses that follow show that, when those people were sick, he fasted and prayed for them as if they were his brothers. Even so, they repaid him with false accusations.

When someone answers you with evil after you have done them good, do not stay in bitterness. Bring your pain to God, as David did, and ask him to defend you. Keep praying for that person and keep doing good, without repaying evil with evil.
exp.47:1:
The explanation says that Mount Zion is beautiful and is a cause of joy for the whole world. The word the verse uses for its setting, "situation," is understood here as a high and lovely hill. "Sides of the north" can refer to the northern part of the mountain, or perhaps to a place in the north; scholars interpret it in several ways. "The city of the great King" refers to Jerusalem, where God reigns.

It is a song of the sons of Korah, Levites who served in the worship of the temple. They praise Jerusalem because there God has shown himself as protector. The verses that follow speak of kings who gathered against the city and failed.

Today we can remember that the most beautiful things in our lives are not places or things, but the presence of the God who cares for us. Take a moment today to thank him from the heart.
exp.121:3:
This verse says that the tribes of Israel were going up to Jerusalem. They were the tribes "of the Lord," that is, belonging to the Lord, whose name is Jehovah. They went up according to the testimony given to Israel, that is, the command God gave them, to give thanks to his name.

This is a psalm of pilgrimage, attributed to David. The speaker remembers with joy the journey to the city. The tribes went together, as one people, to worship. The law required the Israelites to appear before God at the great feasts (Deuteronomy 16:16).

For today: praise is best when it is done together. Try not to worship alone, but to gather with other believers. Go with gratitude, not out of habit, and with the goal of honoring the name of the Lord.
exp.49:8:
God says he does not need the animals his people offer him. In other words: "I will not accept, as though I needed them, the bulls from your house or the goats from your pens."

God himself speaks in this psalm of Asaph, as a judge calling his people. He does not rebuke them for failing to offer sacrifices, since they were offering them. The problem was thinking that God depended on their offerings, as if those gifts gave him something he lacked. The verses that follow show that every animal already belongs to him.

For today: God cannot be bought with religious activities. Before giving, serving, or fulfilling duties, offer him a grateful and sincere heart. Everything we have already belongs to him.
exp.118:158:
Look, Lord, at how much I love your commands; give me life again according to your faithful love. The word "quicken" is an older word meaning "give me life," "renew me," or "restore my strength." "Faithful love" is God's steadfast love, which helps us even though we have not earned it.

The one speaking is the psalmist, in Psalm 119, a long poem about loving God's Word. The author does not name himself in the text. Here he feels surrounded by persecutors, and it grieves him to see people who scorn what God has said. So he does not boast of his merits but asks God for help, relying on his mercy, not on his own strength.

For today: when you feel tired or discouraged, do not wait until everything is in order before you pray. Tell God honestly that you want to obey him, and ask him to renew you by his mercy. Then take one small step: read a passage of the Bible and put it into practice today.
exp.93:3:
This verse is an anguished question put to God. It asks: how long will those who do evil keep speaking with arrogance and boasting about what they do? Hard things are proud, cruel, or insolent words. To boast means to take pride, to feel proud of their wickedness. Injustice is unfairness or evil.

The one speaking is the psalmist, whose name we do not know. He is crying out to God as the judge of the earth because he sees the wicked oppressing the people, the widow, the foreigner, and the orphan, and it seems that no one stops them. This is not a lack of faith; it is an honest lament.

Today we can bring our pain at injustice to God without hiding it. To pray with sincerity is to trust that he sees and judges with justice. And we can also help the vulnerable people near us.
exp.84:1:
He says that God forgave the guilt of his people and "covered" all their sins, meaning that he no longer held them against them. "Iniquity" is wickedness or guilt. "Selah" is a pause or musical marker; its exact meaning is not known for certain, but it invites the reader to stop and reflect.

This psalm was written for the sons of Korah, a group of Levites in charge of the music in worship. The speaker recalls how God was good to his land and restored the fortunes of Jacob, probably by bringing the people back after a time of punishment or exile. Scholars debate the exact date. This memory of forgiveness gives him grounds to ask God for new help.

For today: when you remember how God forgave you before, let that strengthen your confidence to come to him again. Give thanks today for one specific occasion of his mercy and rest in it.
exp.70:14:
It says that the psalmist will speak of God's righteousness and his salvation all day long. The word translated here as "health" is not only about physical well-being; in older language it means "salvation," that is, the deliverance God gives. The word "publish" means he will make it known openly. It adds that he does not know the number of them: God's works are so many that they cannot be counted.

The speaker is an older believer who has trusted God since youth and now faces enemies who want to harm him. Even so, he does not stay in fear. After asking for help, he decides to keep hoping and to praise more. Some think the author is David, but the psalm does not say so, so this is not certain.
