Today we can make it a habit to write down or tell others, each day, one specific thing in which we saw God's faithfulness. In this way gratitude grows, even in difficult times.
exp.48:15:
This verse tells us not to be afraid or envious when we see someone become rich or watch their household grow in fame and luxury. The phrase "the glory of his house" refers to his prestige, his possessions and his standing. The word "afraid" here can mean not to be intimidated or overwhelmed with anxiety.

The one speaking is a psalmist who teaches like a wise person. The sons of Korah present this psalm, which reflects on why the rich seem to have the advantage. He answers that wealth cannot defeat death, and that God will take care of his life. Some understand the phrase "when he takes me" as hope beyond death; others understand it as God's protection.

Today, when you compare your life with the success of others, remember that money is not the most secure thing. Trust in God, who gives true peace and hope.
exp.36:15:
It says that the little a righteous person has is worth more than the great wealth of many wicked people. What matters is not the amount, but how it is obtained and whether God blesses it.

The psalm is attributed to David in its title, and it is a wisdom poem. It addresses those who become troubled when they see the wicked prospering. The verses around it show that the wicked use violence against the poor, but their own weapons will turn against them. By contrast, the LORD upholds the righteous and cares for their inheritance.

For today: when you are tempted by envy at the success of someone who acts wrongly, remember that honesty with little is worth more than unjust gain. Trust that God sustains you, and choose to be faithful in what is small.
exp.105:36:
It says that the people of Israel offered their own sons and daughters as sacrifices to "devils." In the original, that word refers to false spirits that were thought to stand behind the pagan idols. "Sacrificed" here means they killed their children as an offering. The phrase further on about being unfaithful to God describes spiritual unfaithfulness toward him.

The psalmist is not standing in the middle of the scene. He looks back and confesses the sins of Israel from Egypt to Canaan. He wants the people to recognize their guilt and to depend on God's mercy. The verse before explains the path: they mixed with the nations, learned their customs, and ended up serving their idols.

For today: evil almost never begins all at once; it begins with small concessions. Be careful with whom you mix, what you copy, and to what you give your time and your heart. No modern idol deserves the most precious thing you have, and God always forgives the one who returns to him.
exp.68:19:
The explanation says that the mockery and contempt of others have broken his heart from within. A public offense that humiliates a person is what the word "reproach" means here. Being full of anguish and sorrow is what the phrase "full of heaviness" describes. He hoped that someone would feel pity and stay with him, but no one came. He looked for comforters and found none.

Speaking, according to the title of the psalm, is David, while he suffers from being rejected and attacked unjustly, even by his own people. He has already asked God to draw near and deliver him. The New Testament quotes parts of this psalm when speaking of Jesus; for example, the vinegar in the following verse appears at the cross.

When you feel alone and no one comforts you, do not hide your pain. Tell it to God honestly, as the psalmist did. And if you can, be the person who stays with someone who is suffering.
exp.36:10:
The explanation says that the meek, that is, the humble and patient people who do not let anger or revenge carry them away, will inherit the earth. "Shall delight themselves" means they will enjoy and take great pleasure in it. The "abundance of peace" speaks of a full peace, not merely the absence of problems.

It is a psalm of David, written as counsel for those who are troubled when they see the wicked seem to prosper. David tells them not to be angry or envious, because the success of the wicked does not last long. Those who wait on Jehovah have a firmer promise. Jesus repeated this idea in Matthew 5:5.

When someone treats you unjustly, or you see others get ahead through trickery, do not respond with resentment. Trust in God, act with humility, and seek peace. That inner calm is already a foretaste of what God promises.
exp.96:1:
God is surrounded by cloud and darkness, that is, there is something in him that is mysterious and that we cannot fully see or understand. But his throne, that is, his rule, rests on righteousness and judgment. Here "judgment" means right decisions, made with truth and fairness. "Habitation" means base or foundation.

The psalm does not say who wrote it, so its author is unknown. It is a song that celebrates God as King over all the earth. The verses around it speak of joy and also of fire and lightning, images that recall his power and holiness. The cloud brings to mind how God revealed himself on Mount Sinai, although the psalm does not make this clear.

For today: even when we do not understand everything God allows, we can trust that his character is just. When answers are lacking, rest in the knowledge that his rule is never arbitrary or unjust.
exp.49:3:
This verse says that God will call the heavens and the earth as witnesses to judge his people. The word "call" here means to summon or gather together. God does not judge in secret, but with all of creation present.

Here the psalmist, Asaph, describes God coming from Zion with glory, fire, and a storm. Those whom God calls are his people, the ones who made a covenant with him through sacrifices. Later in the psalm, God rebukes a religion made up only of outward rituals, without a sincere heart or obedience.

For today: it is not enough to carry out religious practices on the outside. Today you can ask God to examine your heart, and seek to live with gratitude, truthfulness, and obedience, not just with customs.
exp.104:6:
He is the Lord our God, the God of Israel, and his decisions are not limited to one place. His righteous acts, like the ones he carried out in Egypt, are his judgments, and they also include the laws he gave to his people. His rule reaches to all the nations.

The psalmist calls God's people, the descendants of Abraham and Jacob, to remember what God has done. The psalm reviews Israel's history to show that God was faithful to his covenant. The verses that follow say that God remembers his covenant forever. It is not known for certain who wrote the psalm; it is traditionally attributed to David, but the text does not say so.

For today: when you feel small or insecure, remember how God has helped you before. Write it down, thank him for it, and trust that he governs with justice and faithfulness, even when you do not understand everything.
exp.106:33:
He says God turns a fertile land into salt-ground, that is, barren, where nothing grows anymore. The reason the verse gives is the wickedness of those who live there. "Barrenness" refers to soil full of salt, which keeps crops from growing.

Psalm 107 was written by an anonymous psalmist, and he calls the redeemed people to give thanks to God in the congregation. After telling how God rescues the lost, he shows that He also governs nature. He can turn the desert into springs and springs into desert. Here the verse speaks of judgment, and the following verses show His mercy. Interpreters take this as poetic language, not as a rule that every drought is punishment.

For today: do not take blessings for granted. Live with gratitude and obedience, and remember that God can restore even what seems lost.
exp.60:3:
Here David says he wants to live near God all the days of his life. "Tabernacle" is the sacred tent where God was worshiped, and "abide" means to stay there, not merely to visit. The image of God's "covert of thy wings" shows God as a bird that shelters its young under its wings. "For ever" expresses a desire for constant nearness.

The speaker is David, or a king of Israel, according to the psalm. He feels far away and his heart is weak, perhaps from distress or a threat from enemies. We do not know the exact situation for certain; some connect it with his flight from Absalom, but this is not sure. Even so, he remembers that God has been his refuge and his strong tower.

When you feel fear or weariness, do not shut yourself in alone with your problems. Make prayer a place to rest, remembering how God has cared for you before.
exp.47:5:
It says that trembling took hold of those kings right there, and that they felt a pain like that of a woman giving birth. The phrase "took hold" in the verse above is the same idea as "seized," meaning fear came upon them and gripped them. The image speaks of a sudden fear, strong and impossible to control.

The one speaking is the psalmist, probably on behalf of God's people who sing about Jerusalem, called here the city of God. The kings gathered, saw the city, and fled in terror. It is not stated clearly which historical event is meant; some think of a specific military defeat, and others of a general picture of God's power protecting his people.

For today: when you feel that the powers of this world are too great, remember that God is greater. You can rest in his care, ask him for help with confidence, and not let fear make your decisions for you.
exp.35:1:
Here "flattereth himself" means to flatter oneself, to deceive oneself with pleasant thoughts about oneself. The wicked person looks so good to himself that he does not recognize his wickedness, until it is found to be hateful. The Hebrew of this verse is difficult, and some translations say that he thinks he is safe from his sin being discovered and rejected.

David, who calls himself the Lord's servant, describes the wicked person here. He says that the one who does not fear God lives deceived. Later in the psalm, David contrasts this dark picture with the faithful love of God.

For today: do not trust your own opinion of yourself. Ask God to show you what you do not see, and listen with humility when someone corrects you with kindness.
exp.47:12:
It says the people should look carefully at Jerusalem's defenses and its palaces. A "bulwark" was a low outer wall or rampart that protected the city. "Mark ye well" means paying close attention with care and gratitude. The purpose is to tell it to the children and grandchildren, to the generation that follows.

The psalm is a song of the sons of Korah, a hymn of praise to God for Zion, his city. The speaker invites the faithful to walk around the city and look at its towers, walls, and palaces. It is not only the architecture that is admired: it is recognized that God watches over it. Interpreters debate what historical occasion the psalm was written for, and the text does not make this clear.

For today: do not let God's blessings pass by without noticing them. Remember how He has cared for you, and tell your children, nephews, or younger friends about it. A simple conversation about what God has done can strengthen their faith.
exp.135:3:
It says that only God does great wonders, things no one else can do, and that his mercy, that is, his faithful and compassionate love, never ends. "Alone" here means the one and only. The word "mercy" in this verse translates a Hebrew term that speaks of a loyal love which keeps its promises.

This psalm is an invitation to praise, probably sung in Israel's worship, with a refrain that repeated "his mercy endures forever." The verses before it call God "God of gods" and "Lord of lords," showing that he is above all power. The psalm then recalls creation and the deliverance from Egypt.

For today: when you feel small before your problems, make a list of the wonders God has done in your life and pray them back to him, saying, "Your mercy endures forever." Remembering with gratitude strengthens trust.
exp.68:4:
This verse says that the psalmist speaks to God with honesty. He acknowledges that God knows his foolishness, a word that points to folly or mistakes made without wisdom. He also admits that his sins, that is, his faults, are not hidden from God.

The psalm is written by David, according to its heading, although some scholars debate how the details fit together. Here he is suffering, weary from crying out, surrounded by enemies who hate him without cause. Even so, he does not declare himself perfect. He says he is not guilty of what they accuse him of, but he does recognize that he has shortcomings before God. Then he asks that his situation not bring shame to those who trust in the Lord.

Today we can pray without disguises. If someone treats us unjustly, there is no need to pretend we are perfect. We can say to God, "You know me," confess what we need to correct, and ask him for help with humility.
exp.35:2:
The explanation says that what comes out of the mouth of this wicked person is evil and deceit. "Wickedness" here means injustice or evil, and "deceit" means lies or trickery. The phrase "he hath left off to be wise, and to do good" means that he stopped being wise and acting with goodness, because he did not wish to. It was not that he could not, but that he would not.

David, whom the title calls the servant of the Lord, describes what someone is like who lives without the fear of God. He does this to show how serious that path is and, right after, to contrast it with the greatness of God's love, which reaches to the heavens (verse 5).

Today we can take care with our words and ask ourselves whether they are honest and good. We are also invited to listen to God and to be willing to learn and to do good, rather than hardening our hearts.
exp.68:7:
It says that the speaker feels like a stranger or outsider to his own family. "Estranged" would mean kept at a distance or treated as foreign to them. "The children of my mother" are his brothers. And "a stranger to" means that he also feels foreign to them. The relationship is broken.

The one speaking is David, the author of the psalm. He suffers mockery and rejection "for your sake," that is, because of his devotion to God and to God's house, as the following verses say. His faithfulness costs him even the affection of his family. The New Testament quotes this psalm and applies it to Jesus, who was also rejected by his brothers (John 7:5; John 2:17).

If someone feels misunderstood or rejected by their family because they follow God, they are not alone. They can bring that pain honestly before God, keep loving with patience, and not abandon their faith.
exp.72:22:
Despite the doubts and bitterness the author felt, God never turned away from him. The phrase meaning "even so" is simply the verse's "nevertheless." The words that say God "held" him by the hand mean that God grasped him firmly, like someone who holds another person so they do not fall. The right hand was a symbol of strength and protection.

The speaker is Asaph, the psalmist. He had envied the prosperity of the wicked and felt wounded inside. He admits that his thoughts were foolish, that he was like a beast, meaning without understanding. Even so, in that difficult moment, he discovers that God had been sustaining him all along.

For today: when you feel confused or envious, do not keep your thoughts to yourself. Tell God honestly. Remember that his support does not depend on whether you always understand or feel strong, but on his faithfulness.
exp.147:3:
It says that everything that is in the heights should praise God. The quoted phrase meaning "praise him" is rendered here simply as the verse's own wording. "Heavens of heavens" is a Hebrew way of speaking of the highest heavens, the farthest that one can imagine. "The waters that be above the heavens" recalls the ancient idea of waters above, as in Genesis 1:7. It is not known precisely how they imagined them; there are several interpretations.

The psalmist, who is not named, calls all creation to praise the LORD. First he calls the angels, the sun, the moon and the stars, and then the heavens and the waters. The reason is given afterward: God commanded, and everything was created. Everything exists by his word and depends on him.

For today: if even the farthest heavens praise God simply by existing, you too can do so. Today, when you look at the sky, pause for a moment and give thanks to God for creating everything and for caring for you.
exp.113:1:
When the people left Egypt, God made them something very much his own. The sentence that speaks of "consecrated inheritance" means set apart for him and belonging to him. The word for the place where he rules is simply the place where he governs. The Hebrew text speaks of Judah as his sanctuary, which is why many Bibles translate it that way.

The psalmist is not identified. He remembers the exodus from Egypt in order to praise God. This psalm is part of the group of songs of praise that Jews sang at Passover. It means that the deliverance was not only escaping slavery, but coming to belong to God and living under his care.

For today: God does not rescue you only so that you are free, but so that you live close to him. Today, place your home, your work and your decisions under his command, and ask him to reign over them.
exp.142:2:
Here the psalmist tells what he is suffering. An enemy has pursued him without rest, has knocked him down until he lies on the ground, and has forced him to live in darkness, like those who have already died. "Lying on the ground" speaks of being defeated and without strength; the phrase about making him dwell refers to the enemy having made him live there in darkness.

The text says it is a psalm of David, although scholars do not agree on the exact moment in his life when he wrote it. The one speaking is a believer who is exhausted and distressed and who prays to God. Before describing his pain, he acknowledges that no one can come before God without needing his mercy.

For today: when you feel crushed or without hope, you do not have to pretend to be strong. You can tell God with complete honesty how you feel. Praying honestly is a first step toward remembering that He remains faithful.
exp.55:7:
He says that God has counted every time David wandered from one place to another. He asks God to keep his tears in his bottle, a small vessel or flask, and asks whether everything is not already written in God's book. The word "wanderings" can also be understood as "flights" or "roamings"; translators understand it in several ways.

David speaks as one hunted by enemies who watch him and wait to take his life. The title of the psalm connects it with the time when the Philistines seized him in Gath. So his prayer mixes fear, grief, and trust that God is on his side.

Today we can pray sincerely when we suffer. Our tears do not go unnoticed by God. If you are going through a season of distress, tell him everything with confidence, remembering that he sees you, knows you, and cares for you.
exp.44:8:
It says that among the women who attend the king in his palace are daughters of kings, who are honored companions. And at his right side, the place of greatest honor, stands the queen, adorned with gold from Ophir, a gold famous for its fine quality. The phrase about the right hand refers to the place of greatest honor beside the king, and the word "honourable" points to women of high standing and dignity.

This psalm is a song for a royal wedding. The poet speaks to the king and describes the ceremony with admiration. Many Christians see here a picture of the Messiah, and the New Testament applies part of the psalm to Christ (Hebrews 1:8-9). Some see it as a symbol of the Church, the bride of Christ. Others read it mainly as a historical poem about a king of Israel. Both readings are possible.

For today: God gives us a place of honor at his side, not because of what we have, but by his grace. Live with gratitude and simplicity, knowing that you belong to him.
exp.28:7:
This verse says that the voice of God is so powerful that it shakes the entire wilderness. The phrase "shaketh" means to make the ground tremble or be stirred. Kadesh, also spelled Kadesh-barnea, is a desert region; its exact location is debated, but it is thought to have lain in the south, toward the border of Canaan. The psalm moves across the land from north to south: Lebanon in the north and the wilderness in the south.

It is a psalm of David, according to its title. He speaks as a worshiper and describes a strong storm as an image of the power of God. The verses before it speak of Lebanon and of fire; the verses that follow speak of all creation praising God in his temple. Neighboring peoples attributed storms to their gods, and the psalm declares that it is the Lord who reigns.

For today: when you find yourself in a "wilderness" of loneliness or uncertainty, remember that the voice that shakes the earth also cares for you. Pray with confidence and reverence.
exp.114:0:
It says the glory belongs not to us, but only to God. The explanation's note about the old spelling of "to" is not needed here, so it is omitted. "Give glory" means to honor or to acknowledge as great. The psalmist asks that God be honored for his mercy (his love and compassion) and for his truth (his faithfulness, which keeps what he promises).

The psalm does not say who wrote it. It seems to be the voice of the people of Israel, praying in the face of mockery from other nations who ask, "Where is their God?" The verses that follow answer that God is in the heavens and does whatever he pleases. Scholars do not agree on the exact time when this psalm was used.

Today we can practice this prayer when we receive praise or an achievement. Instead of seeking applause, we can say, "Lord, thank you, all of this comes from you." In this way we remember that whatever is good in our lives springs from his goodness.
exp.88:5:
This verse asks a question that already contains its answer: no one in heaven can be compared with the Lord. The words "compared" and "likened" mean being able to be set alongside someone as an equal, and "the sons of the mighty" are powerful beings of heaven, that is, the angels or heavenly beings. Some scholars believe it refers to them, and others understand it differently.

The psalm is written by Ethan the Ezrahite. It recalls God's promise to David: a throne that will last forever. Before speaking of that promise, it praises God for his greatness and his faithfulness. If God is incomparable, his promise can be trusted.

Today, when something seems greater than your faith, remember that nothing and no one compares with God. Praise him for who he is and trust his promises, even when your situation seems uncertain.
exp.147:9:
This verse calls the animals to praise God: the wild beasts and the domestic animals, the creeping things, and the flying fowl, that is, the birds that fly. The word "beasts" here refers to the animals of the field, and "all cattle" seems to include the other animals of the earth.

Psalm 148 is a song of praise, and it does not say who wrote it. The psalmist invites all of creation to praise the Lord: first the heavens, then the earth. After mentioning fire, snow, mountains and trees, he names the animals, and later kings and all the people. In this way, all of creation, from the greatest to the smallest, has a place in this praise.

Today, when you see a bird, a dog or any animal, let it remind you of God's greatness. Take a moment to thank him for his creation and join in its praise.
exp.105:15:
They envied Moses in the camp, and Aaron, whom the Lord had set apart. The psalmist says that some of the people, while they were in the camp, became jealous of Moses and Aaron. Here the word "envied" means jealousy or rivalry, not a good zeal. He calls Aaron "the saint of the Lord" because God had set him apart for the priesthood.

The psalmist reviews the history of Israel to remember how many times the people rebelled, even though God was faithful. This event is connected with Numbers 16, when Korah, Dathan, and Abiram challenged the leaders whom God had appointed. The verses that follow mention the judgment that came upon them.

For today: when it bothers us that God uses others or gives them a place that he did not give us, it is wise to check envy in time. We can ask God for a grateful heart, and pray for those who lead us instead of criticizing them.
exp.62:10:
It says the king will rejoice because of what God has done. It also says that whoever swears by Him will be praised or have cause to glory, and that liars will be silenced. The word "but" in this verse introduces a contrast, and "swear by him" means to make a truthful commitment in God's name. The silencing of liars means their false words will no longer have any power.

The psalm is attributed to David, when he was in the wilderness of Judah, pursued by enemies. Many understand "the king" to be David himself; some believe it may have been written later. He trusts that God will do justice, and so he ends with hope rather than personal revenge.

Today you can rest in the knowledge that God sees lies and injustice. In the meantime, strive to be a person of honest word, one who keeps what you promise and does not answer deception with deception.
exp.9:6:
The explanation says the wicked person's mouth is full of curses, lies, and deceit. Fraud is a trick or a swindle. Mistreatment is abuse or oppression. "Under his tongue" suggests he keeps harm ready to use, like something hidden that later comes out in his words.

This is a psalm of prayer and complaint, traditionally attributed to David, although the text itself does not say so. The psalmist describes the wicked person who thinks he is untouchable and oppresses the poor and the innocent. He speaks this way to ask God to see the injustice and act, as the rest of the psalm shows.

For today: take care with your words. Ask yourself whether what you say helps or hurts, and whether it is true or is manipulation. And if you suffer from the unjust words of others, you can bring it to God with honesty, trusting that He sees and brings justice.
exp.32:19:
This verse says that our soul has waited for God with patience and trust. "Waiteth" means that it has stayed trusting in him. Furthermore, it affirms that God is our help (the one who comes to our aid) and our shield (the one who protects us like a defense in battle).

Psalm 33 is a song of praise, and here the people of God speak together, which is why it says "our." Earlier, it spoke of how God cares for those who fear him and wait for him, rescuing them from death and giving them life in times of famine. Then the people answer with confidence: their joy comes from having placed their faith in the name of God.

When you face a need or a difficult wait, remember that God does not leave you alone. Speak with him, rest in his care, and keep trusting, even when the answer takes a while.
exp.11:5:
God's words are completely pure, with no lie and no mixture. He compares them to silver refined in a furnace, purified seven times, a way of saying that they are perfect and complete. The word "pure" means free from stain or deceit.

David cries out to God in the middle of people who lie, flatter, and oppress with their words, saying: "With our tongues we will prevail." In contrast to those empty words, God promises to rise up on behalf of the poor and needy. The verse sets false human words against the promise of God, which is certain. Some scholars understand the furnace to be a clay crucible, although the Hebrew expression is not entirely clear.

When lies, pressure, or empty promises surround you, return to the Bible. What God says is firm and trustworthy. Before deciding something important, read it and ask that his word, not the voices around you, be your guide.
exp.76:11:
The verse says that the psalmist resolves to think carefully about everything God has done and to speak about his deeds. To reflect on something is to go over it again in the mind and the heart; "work" and "deeds" refer to God's actions on behalf of his people.

The speaker is Asaph, or someone from his group of singers, according to the title of the psalm. He is distressed and feels that God is far away. For this reason he calls his suffering "my sickness" (others translate it as "my pain" or "my weakness"). His decision is to look back and remember what God did before, especially in the history of Israel. Then comes a song of praise to the greatness of God.

For today: when you feel confused or tired, write down three things God has done for you or for your family. Go over them in prayer and tell them to someone else. Remembering his faithfulness strengthens faith.
exp.124:3:
This verse is a prayer. The psalmist asks God: "Do good, O Lord, to those who are good and to those who have an upright heart." The word "upright" here means sincere and honest, without duplicity inside.

This psalm is one of the songs the pilgrims sang as they went up to Jerusalem. The one speaking is God's people, who live under pressure from wicked people. He has already said that God surrounds them as the mountains surround Jerusalem. Now he asks that God bless the faithful, while those who turn aside will receive his judgment. It ends with peace for Israel.

For today: it is not enough for our actions to look good. Ask God for a sincere heart, and trust that he sees and cares for those who try to live with integrity, even when injustice surrounds them.
exp.17:29:
This verse says that God's way, that is, the manner in which he acts, is perfect, without error or wickedness. The word "tried" describes gold or silver that has been purified by fire, free of impurities. His word is pure and worthy of trust. And God is a shield, a protection, for all who put their hope in him, that is, all who trust in him.

David speaks here, according to the heading of the psalm, after being delivered from his enemies and from Saul. He looks back and recognizes that God sustained him in dangers and battles. His earlier words about the lamp and the walls show that his victory came from God, not from his own strength.

For today: when you do not understand what is happening in your life, remember that God does not make mistakes and that his word stands up under testing. Seek refuge in him through prayer and Bible reading before relying only on your own plans.
exp.77:11:
This verse says that God did astonishing things in the sight of Israel's ancestors, in Egypt. "Marvellous things" are miracles, deeds that only God can do. The "field of Zoan" refers to the region of Zoan, an Egyptian city that many identify with Tanis, though not all scholars agree. The plagues and the deliverance took place there.

This is a psalm of Asaph that reviews Israel's history as a teaching for the children. It comes after saying that the people forgot God's works and did not keep his covenant. That is why the psalmist recalls what their fathers saw with their own eyes, to show that their disobedience had no excuse.

For today: take time to remember what God has done in your life and in your family. Write it down or tell it to someone, so that in difficult times you do not forget his faithfulness.
exp.60:0:
It says this is a psalm of David, directed to the chief musician, that is, the one in charge of the music in worship. The phrase "upon Neginah" indicates it was sung with stringed instruments. Then David asks God: "Hear my cry, O God", meaning listen to my cry for help, and "attend unto my prayer", which means pay attention to my prayer. It is a simple and direct plea.

The speaker is David, and the psalm presents itself as a song for worship. The following verses show that he feels far away, with his heart faint, and that he needs protection. Some believe he wrote it while fleeing from Absalom, but the text does not say so with certainty, so this cannot be asserted.

Today we can pray with that same frankness. There is no need to have beautiful words: when you are tired or worried, tell God honestly what you feel, trusting that he hears you.
exp.47:0:
He says that the Lord is great and deserves to be praised very much. That praise is given in "the city of our God," that is, Jerusalem, and on "the mountain of his holiness," where the temple stood. "A Song and Psalm for the sons of Korah" is the heading: a song composed or directed by a group of Levites who served in worship.

The one speaking is the psalmist, together with the people who worship. The sons of Korah were musicians and gatekeepers of the temple. The psalm celebrates God as king and protector of Zion. Scholars do not agree on the exact event that prompted it; some think of a deliverance of Jerusalem from enemies, but the text does not state this clearly.

Today we can begin our prayer and our day by recognizing who God is before asking him for anything. Praising him together with other believers reminds us that he is greater than our problems.
exp.73:15:
The explanation says that God owns the day and the night. "Prepared" is an old word that means to make ready, set in place, or put in order. So God is the one who prepared and placed the moon and the sun, the lights that mark our days and nights.

This psalm is a prayer by Asaph, or by someone from his group of singers. The people are suffering because their enemies destroyed the temple, and the psalmist feels that God is far away. So he remembers God's power in creation and in history, as a sign that He still remains King. Scholars offer several interpretations of exactly who the leviathan was, but it speaks of God's power over frightening forces.

For today: when everything seems to grow dark, remember that even the night belongs to God. You can pray with confidence, knowing that He still governs.
exp.134:6:
This verse says that God governs nature. He makes the clouds rise from the farthest reaches of the earth, and he made the lightning that accompanies the rain. He brings out the winds from his storehouses, as if he kept them in cellars and released them when he chooses.

The one speaking is the psalmist, directing Israel in a song of praise, probably for worship in the temple. Earlier he said that the LORD is greater than all gods, and here he demonstrates it: the neighboring peoples attributed rain and wind to false gods, but the psalm declares that everything comes from God. Then it recalls how he acted in Egypt.

For today: when you see a storm or feel the wind, remember that nothing escapes the hand of God. Trust that the one who cares for the weather also cares for your life.
exp.55:9:
David says he praises God for his word, that is, for what God has said and promised. He repeats the phrase using two names: "God" and "the LORD" (the name of the Lord, meaning the faithful God of the covenant). "Praising his word" means celebrating that God is trustworthy and keeps what he promises.

David speaks, according to the title of the psalm, when the Philistines held him captive in Gath. He is afraid and surrounded by enemies, but he remembers that God counts his wanderings and keeps his tears. So, in the middle of danger, he chooses to trust and not to fear what man may do to him.

For today: when you are afraid or crying over something, do not wait until everything gets better to praise. Choose a promise from the Bible, read it aloud, and thank God for it. In this way your heart is strengthened by what God has said, not by what you feel.
exp.34:26:
It says that those who support the righteous cause of the psalmist should sing and rejoice, and keep repeating: "Let the Lord be magnified." "Exalted" means praised and lifted up. "Jehovah" is the name of God. "Peace" here can also be understood as well-being or prosperity. "Servant" is one who puts himself at the service of God.

David speaks, according to the title of the psalm. He is being persecuted and slandered by enemies who mock his fall. Earlier he asked that they be put to shame. Now the tone changes: his loyal friends celebrate, and all the glory belongs to God. The psalm ends with David promising to speak of God's righteousness all day long.

For today: when God helps you through a difficulty, do not stay silent. Share with others what he has done and thank him out loud. In this way your joy becomes praise, and others are also encouraged to trust him.
exp.4:0:
This verse opens with a note for the choir director: it is a psalm of David for the chief Musician. The words that follow are uncertain; some believe they refer to flutes or other wind instruments, but there is no certainty. Then David asks God to listen to him. Asking God to consider his meditation means asking him to pay attention to what David thinks and feels inwardly, even what he cannot express well.

David, the king of Israel, speaks in a tone of pleading. From what follows in the psalm, he feels surrounded by deceitful and violent people, and he turns to God as his King. The explanation does not say at what exact moment of his life he wrote it.

For today: when you cannot find words, pray anyway. God attends to what you say as well as to what you think in silence. Bring your concerns to him honestly today.
exp.45:6:
This verse says that the Lord of hosts, that is, the Lord who commands all the powers of heaven, is with his people. It also says that the God of Jacob is their refuge, that is, their safe place. "Selah" is a word that probably invites the reader to pause and reflect, although its exact meaning is not entirely certain.

The psalm was written by the sons of Korah, temple singers. It speaks of a world full of chaos: nations roaring, kingdoms shaking, and the earth trembling. In the midst of that, the psalmist affirms that God is in the midst of his people and therefore they will not be moved. This verse repeats that confidence, like a refrain.

For today: when you feel afraid because of the news, the economy, or your family, pause, as the "Selah" invites, and repeat this phrase in prayer: "God is with me." His presence does not remove all problems, but it does give you a secure place to rest.
exp.50:3:
David acknowledges that his sin, in the end, is an offense against God. "Against thee, thee only, have I sinned" means that God is the one chiefly wronged. "Done this evil in thy sight" refers to what God saw all along. "Be justified when thou speakest" means that God is right when he judges. "Be clear when thou judgest" means that his judgment is pure and without error.

David speaks in a psalm of repentance. Tradition links it to his sin with Bathsheba and against Uriah, after the prophet Nathan confronted him (2 Samuel 12). Although he hurt other people, here he confesses that the gravest thing is having disobeyed God. He justifies nothing and blames no one else.

For today: when you fail, do not make excuses or compare yourself with others. Come before God with sincerity, acknowledge your fault without evasion, and ask him for forgiveness. His justice and his mercy receive you when you are honest.
exp.89:15:
It says that God's servants ask that his work be clearly seen among them, and that his glory, that is, his greatness and power, reach their children as well. "Servants" are those who live in service to God. "Work" refers to what God does, such as his care, his deliverance, and his faithfulness.

This psalm is a prayer attributed to Moses, according to its heading. It speaks on behalf of the people, who feel fragile and passing, and who have been through years of pain. After acknowledging that life is brief, they ask God to show them his favor and that what he begins will not be lost to the next generation.

For today: pray that your children, nephews, nieces, or young people close to you will truly see God at work. Besides asking for it, tell them simply how God has helped you, so that they may come to know his faithfulness.
exp.105:9:
This verse says that God delivered his people from those who hated them and pursued them. "Enemy" and "adversary" are two ways of naming the same thing, and that repetition stresses that the deliverance was complete. "Saved" and "redeemed" describe what God did for them. "Hand" here means power or control.

The psalmist reviews the history of Israel. He remembers the exit from Egypt, when God opened the Red Sea before the Egyptian army that was chasing them. The psalm is a confession: it acknowledges that the people failed, yet God saved them for the sake of his name, that is, because of his own faithfulness and character.

For today: when you feel cornered by a problem you cannot solve, remember how God has helped before. Recall his works and trust that his faithfulness does not depend on your strength.
exp.131:1:
He tells us that David made a solemn vow to the LORD. He made a promise to God, whom here he calls "the mighty God of Jacob," that is, the powerful God who protected and sustained the people of Israel. The phrase "how he sware unto the Lord" is in an older style; today we would simply say that he swore an oath to the LORD.

The one speaking is the psalmist, whose identity we do not know for certain. In this pilgrim song he asks God to remember David and all he suffered. What follows shows the promise: David would not rest until he found a place for the Lord. Many understand this to refer to preparing a place for the ark, but the psalm gives no further detail here.

For today: God values commitments made with sincerity. Before promising Him something, think carefully, and when you do, keep it faithfully, trusting that He is strong enough to sustain you.
exp.3:1:
David speaks to "the sons of men," that is, to people who are important or powerful. He asks them how long they will turn his glory into shame, that is, into disgrace. He also asks how long they will love what is empty and seek after what is false. "Selah" seems to be a musical pause or a moment for reflection, though its exact meaning is not known for certain.

David prays to God in the midst of distress and then turns to those who dishonor him. Many think he is referring to slander against him, perhaps during a time of opposition, but the psalm does not state the exact occasion. What matters is that David trusts that God hears him.

Today we can ask ourselves what empty things we are loving and what lies we are believing or repeating. If someone slanders us, we can bring it to God in prayer and also take care with our own words, seeking the truth.
exp.102:10:
The explanation says that God's mercy is as great as the distance between the heavens and the earth. "Made great" means that he made it enormous, abundant. "Mercy" is his compassionate love that forgives and helps. "Those who fear him" are those who respect him and honor him with reverence, not those who live in terror.

The psalm is attributed to David, who praises God with his whole being. The verses before it remind us that God does not treat us as our sins deserve. Then it compares his forgiveness to the distance between the east and the west, and to a compassionate father. David wants us to remember the blessings of God.

When you feel unworthy because of your failings, lift your eyes to the heavens and remember that God's mercy is greater than your error. Come to him with humility and confidence, and ask him for forgiveness with sincerity.
exp.72:16:
It says that the psalmist was confused until he went into the house of God. There he came to understand what the end of the wicked would be. "End" means the final outcome, the ultimate fate. "House of God" is the holy place where God was worshiped.

The one speaking is Asaph, according to the heading of the psalm. He had envied the prosperity of the wicked and it seemed unfair to him that they lived at ease. Thinking about this was a heavy burden, a weight that wore him down. It is not known exactly what he experienced in the house of God; many believe that, in worship, he regained God's perspective and saw that the success of the wicked does not last.

When something seems unfair to you and weighs you down, do not stay turning it over alone. Seek God in prayer, in his Word, and in worship together with other believers. There your questions find a clearer place and your heart is set in order.
exp.38:8:
The psalmist says that he stayed silent and did not complain. "I was dumb" means that he became silent and did not speak. The reason he gives is that God himself was the one who allowed or sent what was happening to him. His silence is not indifference, but an attitude of accepting that God is in control.

The psalm is spoken by David, according to its heading. He is suffering a affliction or punishment that he connects with his sin, as the following verses show. Earlier he had struggled with the urge to speak, but now he surrenders to God. He asks forgiveness for his rebellions and trusts that his hope is in the Lord. Some think his illness was physical; the text does not specify.

When you are going through a difficulty, before you complain or blame others, stop and speak with God. Ask him to examine you, acknowledge what needs to be corrected, and trust that he can sustain you. Keeping silent before God is not resigning yourself without hope, but resting in him.
exp.101:0:
It says that this is the prayer of a person who is humble and in need, who is going through great distress and opens his heart to God. The phrase about pouring out his complaint means expressing his pain freely, holding nothing back. Then he asks with confidence: "Hear my prayer, O Lord, and let my cry come unto you."

The title of the psalm does not give the author's name; it only speaks of someone afflicted. For that reason, it cannot be said with certainty who wrote it. The verses that follow describe deep suffering, and many think it might reflect the pain of Israel in a difficult time, though this is understood in different ways.

Today you can be honest with God when you feel downcast. You do not need elegant words; it is enough to tell him how you really feel, trusting that he listens.
exp.104:1:
This verse invites us to sing to God and to speak of everything he has done. "Sing unto him" means to sing to him. "Psalms" are songs of praise. "Wondrous works" are God's amazing deeds, such as when he cared for, rescued, and guided his people.

Psalm 105 is a song of thanksgiving. Who wrote it is not clear from this passage; part of it also appears in 1 Chronicles 16, where it is connected with David. The psalm recalls how God was faithful to Abraham, to Joseph, and to Israel. For that reason it calls the whole people to praise him and to tell others what God has done.

Today you can write down each week something good God has done for you, and then sing it in prayer or share it with a friend or your family. In this way your gratitude grows, and others are encouraged to trust in him.
exp.50:1:
Here David asks God to wash him "throughly" from his iniquity, that is, thoroughly and completely, until he is truly clean. "Iniquity" refers to his guilt or wrongdoing, and "sin" to having failed before God. The image is that of washing a garment that is badly stained.

David speaks after having taken Bathsheba, and after the prophet Nathan had shown him his wrong, as the heading of the psalm indicates. He does not say this to make excuses: he acknowledges his guilt and turns to God's mercy, not to his own merits.

For today: when you fail, do not hide or justify yourself. Go to God with honesty and ask for forgiveness. He does not only forgive; he also cleanses the heart and renews it. Confessing is the first step to starting again.
exp.106:36:
The explanation says that the people whom God settled in a place that was once dry and empty now sow fields, plant vineyards, and gather an abundant harvest. The phrase about yielding fruit means that they produce a great deal. It is the image of a people who passed from hunger to provision.

The psalm does not name its author. It is a song of thanksgiving that invites those whom God rescued from various distresses to give thanks to Him. In this part, the psalmist shows that God can turn a desert into springs of water and give a home to the hungry. The verses that follow remind us that there are also times of pain and oppression, and that God remains attentive.

When God gives you a new beginning, work with diligence and gratitude. Sow, take care of what you receive, and acknowledge that the provision comes from Him.
exp.141:1:
It says that David was going to tell God everything, holding nothing back. The word "poured out" here means emptying completely, like someone tipping over a cup. "Complaint" means a sincere complaint or outcry.

David is the one speaking, and the heading says he prayed in a cave. Tradition connects this with his flight from Saul, although the text does not specify whether it was at Adullam or En-gedi. He felt cornered, with traps along his path and no one to defend him. That is why he cries out to God aloud, asking for mercy.

For today: you do not need to polish your words to pray. When you are distressed, tell God honestly what you feel, in detail and without fear. He already knows your path, and he invites you to pour out your heart in his presence.
exp.105:35:
It says that the people of Israel worshiped the idols of the nations of Canaan, and that those idols ended up being their downfall. The word "snare" can also be understood as a trap or a cause of falling. "Served" here means that they gave worship and obedience to them.

The psalmist, whose name the text does not give, reviews the history of Israel to acknowledge the people's sins and the patience of God. Before this verse, Israel did not obey the command to keep apart from the peoples of Canaan, but mixed with them and learned their customs. That led them into idolatry and, afterward, into much worse evils.

For today: what we put in place of God, such as money, success, or the approval of others, seems to help us at first but ends up binding us. Today you can ask yourself what thing occupies the place of God in your heart, and sincerely surrender it to him in prayer.
exp.85:15:
The explanation says that David asks God to look on him with kindness and to have compassion on him. He asks for strength for his servant, which is himself, and for protection for the son of God's maidservant, an expression that presents him as someone who belongs to God's household. To keep or protect means to watch over and defend.

The one speaking is David, according to the heading of the psalm. He is surrounded by proud and violent people who do not respect God and seek to take his life. For that reason he relies on what he knows of God: that he is merciful, slow to anger, and abundant in truth. He calls himself the son of God's maidservant, perhaps remembering that his family already served the Lord, although the text does not explain this in detail.

Today, when you feel weak or under pressure, you can pray simply: "O turn unto me, and have mercy upon me; give thy strength unto thy servant." You do not need to pretend to be strong. Rest on the character of God, who is compassionate and faithful, and ask him to sustain you one day at a time.
exp.106:12:
The explanation says that as soon as the people cried out to God in their trouble, he rescued them from their difficulties. Words like "as soon as" and "the moment" are the idea behind the phrase, so the reader can see that the help came right after the cry for help. To cry out means to ask for help loudly and urgently. The word "distresses" in the verse refers to hardships and suffering.

The psalm is a song of thanksgiving, and no one knows for certain who wrote it. Here it speaks of people who rebelled against God's word and suffered the consequences; they fell, and no one helped them. The psalm repeats this pattern: trouble, crying out, and deliverance. In this way it invites the people to recognize God's mercy.

For today: when you feel trapped, whether by your own mistakes or by other causes, do not wait to get yourself in order first. Come to God sincerely and ask him for help. Then give thanks out loud for what he does.
exp.34:3:
Here David asks God that his enemies be put to shame and confusion. "Seek after my soul" means they want to take his life. "Be turned back" means that they fail and retreat in their plans. "Devise my hurt" means they plan to do him harm.

David speaks, or the psalmist who identifies with him, in the midst of unjust persecution. The verses before this one show God as a warrior who takes up shield and spear to defend him. It is an imprecatory psalm, that is, a prayer that asks for justice against the wicked. Scholars debate how these requests should be read, but all agree that David leaves vengeance in God's hands.

For today: when someone treats you unjustly, bring your pain and anger to God in sincere prayer, instead of taking revenge yourself. Ask him to do justice and to care for you.
exp.102:21:
This verse calls everything God has made to praise him. "Bless" means speaking well of God, acknowledging his greatness, and giving him thanks. "Ye" is the old way of saying "you." "Dominion" is the place where God rules, which covers the whole universe. At the end, the psalmist includes himself: "Bless the Lord, O my soul."

The speaker is David, according to the title of the psalm, although some scholars debate how it was composed. Earlier he has invited the angels and the heavenly hosts to praise God, because they obey his voice. Now he widens the invitation to all creation. The psalm began with his soul praising God, and it ends the same way, like a complete circle.

Today, before asking God for anything, take a moment to bless him. Name aloud three things he has done for you, and join in the praise of all creation.
exp.68:17:
The psalmist here asks God to draw near to him, to rescue his life and free him from those who attack him. Redeem it means to rescue, like someone who pays to free a person who is held captive or in danger. The phrase because of mine enemies points to the reason for his plea: he is surrounded by those who oppose him.

The psalm is traditionally attributed to David, although some scholars think it may have been written by someone else in a similar situation. He is distressed, humiliated, and surrounded by people who despise him. He feels alone, because no one comforts him. So he cries out to God with urgency and trusts in his mercy.

For today: when you feel lonely, rejected, or weighed down, you do not have to pretend to be strong. You can say honestly to God, "Draw nigh unto my soul." Praying this way is an act of trust, because we believe that he hears us and that his compassion reaches us even when no one else responds.
exp.35:9:
This verse is a prayer. The psalmist asks God to continue extending his mercy, that is, to keep giving it and not withdraw it, to those who know him. This mercy means his faithful love and his goodness. He also asks for his righteousness, which here means his help and his acting uprightly on behalf of the upright in heart, that is, sincere and honest people before God.

The psalm is written by David, according to its title. It first speaks of the wickedness of the ungodly, then praises the love of God and his provision as the source of life and light. After that praise, it asks that God continue to care for his own and keep them from the pride and violence of the wicked, as the following verses say.

Today we can pray this verse with confidence. Instead of depending on our own strength, let us ask God to sustain us, and seek to live with a sincere heart, without duplicity, before him.
exp.56:8:
It says that the psalmist promises to give thanks and praise to God before the peoples, and to sing about Him among the nations. "I will praise thee" is an older way of saying "I will praise you," and "I will sing unto thee" means singing about who God is. His praise will not be only private, but public and open to everyone.

The title of the psalm attributes this song to David, when he fled from Saul and hid in a cave. He is in danger, but his heart is steady and he resolves to sing from the morning. His confidence rests on the mercy and the truth of God, which according to the psalm reach up to the heavens. His desire is that the glory of God be known throughout the earth.

Even in difficult times, we can choose to praise God and speak of His goodness to others. You can begin this week by telling someone something specific that God has done for you, or by singing a song of thanks in the middle of your worry.
exp.131:6:
The explanation says that the people will go to the house of God, to his dwelling place, and there bow down in worship before the place where God rests. The word "tabernacles" means his dwelling place or sanctuary. "Bow down" means "bow down in worship." The "footstool" is like a small bench beneath the throne; it is an image that God is King and his presence is near.

This psalm recalls David's desire to find a place for the ark of the LORD. Here the community speaks, remembering that longing: the ark was heard of in Ephrathah and found in the fields of the forest (probably Kiriath-jearim, although some interpret it in other ways). Now the people respond with determination: we will go to worship where God has chosen to dwell.

Today we can take worship seriously. Before going to church or praying alone, prepare your heart and bow inwardly, acknowledging that God is great and deserves our reverence.
exp.26:3:
This verse says that David has one great desire: to live close to God all his life.

David, the king of Israel, is the speaker, according to the title of the psalm. He is surrounded by enemies and war, but he is not afraid. His confidence does not come from his own strength, but from being near to God. He then says that God will hide him in the day of trouble and set him high upon a rock. Scholars do not agree on the exact time when he wrote it.

For today: in the midst of your worries, set aside time each day to be with God, without asking him for anything. Read a psalm, give thanks, and look at who he is. That habit will give you peace and steadiness when problems come.
exp.118:172:
He says the psalmist asks God that his hand, that is, his power and his help, would be ready to come to his aid. The explanation says "Help" means aid in a time of need. The reason he gives is: "for I have chosen thy precepts." He decided, of his own will, to follow God's ways.

The speaker is the author of Psalm 119, a long poem in praise of God's Word. We do not know for certain who wrote it. It is clear that he is someone who loves God's law, but he also faces pressure and opposition in other verses. That is why he asks for help, not trusting in his own strength, but in the hand of God.

Today we can pray like this: "Lord, I choose to obey you, but I need your help." When you face a difficult decision and want to do what is right, ask God for strength. Choosing his way is our part; holding on to it is the work of his grace.
exp.144:1:
David says that he intends to bless God every day, without missing a single one, and to praise his name for ever and ever, that is, throughout his whole life and without end. To bless here means to speak well of God and to give thanks to him. The name stands for everything God is, his character and his works.

David, king of Israel, speaks in a psalm of praise. He had already called God his God and his King, acknowledging that there was a King above him. His decision to praise comes from the fact that God is great and beyond our full understanding, and that each generation should tell its children about his works.

For today: choose a fixed moment of the day, for example when you wake up, and say out loud one specific thing you are thankful to God for. Praise becomes a habit when we practice it daily, not only when we feel well.
exp.79:12:
It says that God's vineyard, which is the people of Israel, was destroyed by a wild boar from the forest and eaten up by the animals of the field. The word for the boar is one that a reader of the King James Version will already recognize from the verse itself, so the wild boar is simply the "boar out of the wood" in the text. The verb "waste" in the verse means that the vineyard was ruined or badly damaged, and "devour" means that it was eaten up, the way livestock graze on grass.

It is part of a prayer by the psalmist Asaph, offered on behalf of the whole people. Israel is compared to a vine that God brought out of Egypt and planted, but now its walls are broken and enemies plunder it. The text does not say with certainty which invasion the psalmist has in mind; some think of Assyria, which destroyed the northern kingdom. The psalmist asks God to return and care for his vineyard.

For today: when you feel vulnerable or see everything falling apart, you can do as the psalmist did: speak to God honestly, remind him that you belong to him, and ask him to come back and care for you and restore you.
exp.118:92:
The writer says that the psalmist will never forget God's commands, because through them God gave him life. "To quicken" means to give life, to revive, or to restore strength. "Commands" here refers to God's instructions in general, not just a list of rules.

The speaker is the author of Psalm 119, a long psalm in honor of God's Word. We do not know for certain who wrote it. He speaks from a place of affliction: in the verse before, he says that without God's law he would already have perished. Besides this, the wicked are lying in wait for him. His gratitude springs from having been sustained in the midst of suffering.

For today: when you go through a hard season, do not put off God's Word until later. Read a passage each day, remember what God has already done for you, and thank him. In this way, what gave you encouragement yesterday will help you remember his faithfulness tomorrow.
exp.50:0:
This verse begins with a note explaining the occasion of the psalm: David wrote it after his sin with Bathsheba, when the prophet Nathan came to confront him. Then David prays: "Have mercy upon me, O God." He asks for compassion according to God's mercy and according to the abundance of his tender mercies. He asks that his transgressions be blotted out, that is, removed as one erases a written debt. The tender mercies are acts of compassion.

David, king of Israel, speaks here. According to 2 Samuel 11 and 12, he had committed adultery with Bathsheba and planned the death of her husband, Uriah. Nathan showed him his guilt, and David repented. The psalm springs from that brokenness. It is addressed "to the chief Musician," since it was given to the director of music in worship.

For today: when you fail, do not hide or make excuses for yourself. Come to God honestly and rest on his mercy, not on your merits. He is able to forgive and restore.
exp.34:2:
It says David asks God to take up the spear and go out against those who pursue him. He also asks for something deeper: that God would say to his soul, "I am your salvation," that is, "I am your deliverance" or "I am your rescue." The word for "salvation" here does not speak only of the body, but of being rescued.

David speaks in a psalm where he feels attacked and accused by enemies. He uses images of war (shield, spear) to ask that God himself would defend him. Some understand the "spear" as a poetic image, not as a literal weapon in God's hands.

Today, when you feel pressured or unjustly attacked, do not only ask that the situation change. Ask God to assure you of his presence and his care. Praying this way gives you peace, even before you see the answer.
exp.131:17:
It says that God will cover the king's enemies with shame, as one who clothes them in confusion. On the other hand, the crown of the anointed king will flourish, that is, his reign will prosper and shine. The words "clothe" and "cover" convey the same idea as "put upon," and "but" is the word that sets the enemies' shame against the king's flourishing crown.

In this psalm, the people remember the promise God made to David: that his descendants would reign and that Zion would be the place where God would dwell. Here God himself speaks, answering the prayer of the people. Christians often see in "my anointed" a sign that points to Christ, although the psalm first speaks of the kings of David's line.

For today: when you feel attacked or unfairly treated, do not rush to take revenge. Trust that God knows how to keep his promises and defend his own. Pray with patience, keep doing good, and let him take care of putting each thing in its place.
exp.77:71:
He cared for and guided God's people with an upright heart and with skillful hands. "Feed" here means to give food and look after them, the way a shepherd looks after his sheep. "Integrity" means honesty and sincerity. "Skill" means ability, the know-how to do a task well. So the verse joins two things: good character and good ability.

The psalm is written by Asaph, a Levite in charge of the music in worship. He reviews the history of Israel, its failures, and God's patience. At the end, he tells how God chose David, a simple shepherd of sheep, to shepherd his people. This verse sums up how David ruled, although the Bible also shows that he made serious mistakes.

For today: if you care for others, at home, at work, or in church, good intentions are not enough. Ask God for a sincere heart, and also make the effort to learn and do your task well.
exp.138:3:
This verse says that God knows what I am going to say even before the words leave my mouth. "Not yet a word is on my tongue" means that I have not yet spoken it. "You know it completely" means that God knows it whole, with nothing missing.

The one speaking is David, according to the heading of the psalm. He is amazed that God knows him inside and out: when he sits down, when he gets up, his thoughts and his ways. For him, this is not a threat but a cause for wonder and worship, as seen in the verses that follow.

For today: when you pray, you do not need to pretend or search for perfect words. God already knows what you feel and what you want to say. Speak to him honestly, and rest in the fact that the One who knows you so well also cares for you.
exp.80:8:
There shall be no foreign god among God's people, that is, no god other than the true one. Nor should they bow down before any strange god. The word "no strange god" in the verse means a god from other peoples, one that does not belong to Israel. The phrase "shall bow down" in older wording means to bend low or prostrate oneself in worship.

Here God himself speaks, in a psalm that was sung at a festival of Israel. He reminds them that he rescued them from Egypt and cared for them in the wilderness. Because he set them free, he asks for their faithfulness and that they listen to him. The text that follows sadly says that the people did not want to hear him.

Today we may not carve idols, but we can put money, success, or the approval of others in the place of God. Ask yourself honestly: what thing has more control over me than God does? Hand it over to him in prayer and listen again to his voice.
exp.118:1:
It says that those who keep God's "testimonies" are happy and blessed, that is, his teachings and commands, which bear witness to what he is like. "Blessed" here means happy, favored by God. And "seek him" means they pursue him, desire him, and follow him sincerely, "with the whole heart," without duplicity.

Psalm 119 does not say who wrote it; tradition often attributes it to David, but this is not certain. It is a poem that praises God's Word, and each group of verses begins with a letter of the Hebrew alphabet (here, Aleph). The author speaks as someone who loves the law of the LORD and wants to live according to it.

Today we can join obedience and desire. It is not only about following rules, but about seeking God wholeheartedly. You can set aside a few minutes each day to read the Bible, ask God what he is like, and ask for his help to live out what you read.
exp.72:9:
This verse is difficult and is understood in several ways. "His people" may refer to the crowd that follows the wicked, or even to God's own people, who turn back to look at their success. A full cup is a cup filled to the brim, and to be drained to the dregs means they drink it down or draw out every last drop. It may speak of abundance or of suffering.

The speaker is Asaph, a psalmist who nearly loses his faith on seeing that the arrogant prosper. The verses around it show his complaint: these men despise God and yet they do well. Later, in verse 17, his outlook changes when he enters God's sanctuary.

For today: if it discourages you to see the unjust doing well, do not keep turning it over on your own. Bring your confusion to God in prayer and ask him for his perspective.
exp.136:3:
The explanation has two parts. First, the captors ask: "Sing us some of the songs of Zion," that is, songs the people sang in worship to God. Then comes the psalmist's reply, in the form of a question: how can one sing to God in a land of strangers, that is, a foreign country that is not one's own?

The speaker is an Israelite exiled in Babylon, after Jerusalem was destroyed (in 586 B.C.). His conquerors ask him for music as entertainment, mocking his grief. For him, the songs of Zion are sacred, not a show. Interpreters do not agree on whether the question expresses an inability caused by sorrow or a refusal to profane what is holy; perhaps both.

Today we can learn that worship cannot be manufactured. In times of pain, it is honest to bring God our silence and our sadness, and to trust that He receives them, without pretending to a joy we do not feel before others.
exp.16:5:
David says here that he prays to God with confidence, because he is sure that God will answer him. "I have called upon thee" means that he has called out to God; "incline thine ear unto me" is a way of asking him to pay attention, like someone who leans close to hear better; "my speech" refers to his prayer or his cry.

The psalm is titled "Prayer of David." He speaks in the midst of people who attack him and harm him (the following verses speak of enemies). Earlier he said that he has kept away from violent paths by following God's word. Now he asks to be heard and protected. Scholars do not agree on the exact moment in his life when he wrote it.

For today: when you are in trouble, pray without fear or evasion. God is not distant; you can speak to him with sincerity and trust that he hears you, and you can base your prayer on the desire to keep following his ways.
exp.16:12:
David asks God to rise up as one who steps into action. To go out to meet the enemy before he attacks, and to bring him down, are the images here. The sword is the picture of God's power to deliver him from the wicked.

David speaks in a prayer of distress. Violent men surround him, watch him, and compare him to a lion ready to seize its prey. He does not defend himself with his own hands but hands the matter over to God. Some understand the sword as a symbol of divine judgment, not necessarily a literal weapon.

Today we can bring God our fears and the injustices we suffer, instead of seeking revenge. You can pray sincerely, "Lord, defend me and keep me from evil," and trust that He acts with justice and in His own time.
exp.118:21:
Here the psalmist asks God: "Remove from me reproach and contempt." "Reproach" is public dishonor or insult, and "contempt" is when others look down on him as someone without worth. The reason he gives is that he has kept God's testimonies, that is, his teachings and commands.

The one speaking is the author of Psalm 119, whose name is not known with certainty. He suffers mockery and attacks for following God's word. The following context says that even princes spoke against him, but he kept meditating on God's laws and saw them as his counselors.

For today: if you are criticized or mocked for living with integrity and faith, bring that pain to God in prayer. You do not need to defend yourself with anger. Stay faithful, seek his Word, and let it give you security and guidance.
exp.135:25:
This verse invites us to give thanks to God, who here is called "the God of heaven." The word "give thanks" means to praise, to be grateful, and to joyfully acknowledge what God is. "Mercy" here translates a Hebrew word that speaks of faithful love, a kindness that does not give up. And "for ever" means that it never comes to an end.

It is the last verse of Psalm 136, a song of praise that was surely sung in the worship of the people of Israel. A leader probably spoke each line, and the people answered: "for his mercy endureth for ever." The psalm remembers creation, the deliverance from Egypt, and God's daily care. The author is not known with certainty.

Today we can do something simple: before going to sleep, remember three concrete things in which God was faithful to you that day, and give thanks for them, repeating: "His mercy endures forever."
exp.111:7:
Psalm 112:8 says that the heart of the righteous person is firm and well established, and for that reason he is not afraid. That calm lasts until he sees his desire fulfilled over his adversaries: seeing them defeated or the situation resolved, the thing he longed for.

Psalm 112 is a poem of praise that does not name its author. It describes the person who fears God and the blessing he lives in. This verse shows his inner security: it does not depend on the news he hears, but on trusting the Lord. The verses that follow contrast the generous righteous person with the wicked, who is consumed with anger when he sees him.

For today: when bad news arrives or you feel threatened, before you react, remember what you have trusted in and pray. A steady trust in God helps you keep your calm and continue doing good, without repaying evil with evil.
exp.59:1:
He says God made the earth tremble and split it open, as if he had made cracks in it. Now the psalmist asks him to heal those breaches, meaning the ruptures or cracks, because the earth is staggering and about to fall.

The speaker is David, or a psalm written in his name, in the middle of a difficult war. His people had suffered defeats and felt rejected by God. The trembling earth is probably an image of the nation shaken and divided. Some think it could also have been a real earthquake, but the text does not make this clear.

For today: when your life or your family feels broken and unstable, do not hide your pain. Bring it to God honestly, acknowledge that only he can heal what is broken, and ask him for steadiness to keep going.
exp.27:4:
They do not pay attention to what the Lord does, nor to the work of his hands, that is, to his creation and to his acts in history. For this reason God will tear them down and not raise them up. The explanation of the verse's wording: "not regard" means they pay no attention and give no value to it. Here "build them up" is the opposite of tearing down: to sustain and make prosper.

David speaks, according to the traditional heading of the psalm. He is crying out to God in a moment of distress and asks not to be treated like those who speak peace with their mouths but keep evil in their hearts. This verse explains why God judges them: they live ignoring God. Afterward, the psalm moves to praise because God heard his plea.

For today: make a habit of pausing to notice what God does in your life and in the world around you, and give thanks for it. A life attentive to God becomes more humble and firm.
exp.143:5:
He says that God should send lightning and arrows to scatter and confuse the enemies. "Scatter them" means to make them vanish or drive them apart. "Confuse them" means to fill them with terror and disorder. It is a prayer asking God to act with power, the way a storm does.

David speaks here, according to the psalm's heading, while facing enemies who lie and deceive. Earlier he has acknowledged that human beings are frail, like a passing shadow, and for that reason he asks God to reach down from the heavens. He uses storm imagery to say that only God can deliver him. Interpreters see poetic language here, not a literal scene.

For today: when you feel small before people or problems that are bigger than you, do not rely on your own strength alone. Bring your need to God honestly and rest in the fact that he can act on your behalf.
exp.112:4:
This verse asks a question that needs no answer: is there anyone comparable to the LORD our God? It says that He has set His dwelling place high above, meaning that His place of dwelling is very high. The word "high" in this sense means lifted up, placed at the very top. The thought continues into the next verse: although He is so high, He bows down to look.

Psalm 113 is a song of praise, and no one knows for certain who wrote it. It was sung in Israel, and Jewish tradition uses it at the festivals, such as Passover. It invites all the people to praise God everywhere, and then shows why: God is great, yet He cares for the humble.

For today: if God, being so great, looks upon the small, you can speak to Him with confidence. Today, bring Him a concern of yours in simple words.
exp.83:8:
The explanation says the psalmist asks God to look upon him with favor. He calls God "our shield," that is, the one who protects and defends us. "Your anointed" is someone whom God chose and set apart for a task, usually the king. He asks that God turn his eyes upon him with kindness.

The psalm was sung by pilgrims who went up to the temple in Jerusalem, and it is attributed to the sons of Korah. It is not known for certain who the "anointed" is: many think it is the king of Judah, while others believe it may point to the Messiah. The one speaking loves the house of God and, in the midst of his need, prays for his ruler and for the people.

Today we can pray for those who lead us, in the church, the family, or the country, asking that God look upon them with favor and guide them. And we can remember that, if God is our shield, we can rest in his care.
exp.41:4:
Here the psalmist speaks to himself and asks: "Why are you so sad and troubled, my soul?" The explanation of "cast down" and "disquieted" needs no separate comment, since both words appear in the verse above. Then he gives himself a command: to hope in God, for he will yet praise him. The phrase about "the help of his countenance" refers to the salvation or help that comes from being near to God.

The speaker is a believer who suffers and feels far from the temple. Some of his enemies mock him, asking where his God is. The title links the psalm to the sons of Korah, Levites who served in worship. We do not know exactly the circumstances in which he wrote, but he mentions the region of the Jordan and Hermon, far from Jerusalem.

For today: when sadness overwhelms you, do not ignore it or deny it. Speak to your heart with truth, remember what God has done, and pray with hope, even though you do not yet see the change.
exp.15:3:
It says that those who rush after other gods will gather sorrows. The phrase about serving with great eagerness means they do it with much zeal. The "drink offerings of blood" were liquid poured out in a pagan rite, joined with blood. The speaker vows not to take part in those rites, not even to speak the names of those gods.

David is the speaker, according to the psalm's heading. He writes it as a prayer of trust in God. Earlier he said that the LORD is his Lord and that he rejoices with the faithful people. Here he draws a contrast: others chase after idols, but he holds fast to God. Later he will say that the LORD is his inheritance and his portion.
