For today: idols can be money, fame or pleasure, things that promise a great deal and leave you empty. Today you might ask yourself where you put the most effort, and ask God to truly be your first love and your greatest treasure.
exp.77:23:
It says that God caused manna to fall from heaven like rain to feed Israel in the desert. The poem calls this manna "grain of heaven," that is, bread or grain that comes from above. The word "gave them" in the verse is a poetic way of saying that the food did not come up out of the earth but was a gift from God.

Psalm 78 is a poem by Asaph that reviews the history of Israel to teach new generations. The psalmist remembers that God cared for the people even though they doubted him and did not trust in his salvation. In this way he highlights God's goodness in contrast to human distrust.

Today, this verse invites us to trust that God knows how to sustain us, even when we cannot see how. We can give thanks for what we receive each day and ask him to help us believe in him more than in our fears.
exp.34:8:
Here the psalmist says that his soul will be filled with joy and gladness in God.

David is the one speaking, according to the title of the psalm. He is being pursued by enemies who, without cause, set traps for him and falsely accused him. He asks God to defend him, and in this verse he promises to respond with joy when God delivers him. His gladness is not placed in the defeat of his enemies, but in the Lord himself.

When someone treats you unjustly, do not let bitterness be the only thing that fills your heart. Entrust your case to God and remember how he has cared for you before. Rejoicing in him, even before you see the resolution, gives you peace and hope.
exp.71:16:
It says that the king's name will last forever, as long as the sun exists. To "endure" means to continue without end. It also says that all nations will be blessed through him and will call him "blessed," that is, happy and favored by God.

This is a psalm attributed to Solomon (the title can also be understood as "for Solomon"). It is a prayer for the king of Israel, asking for justice, peace, and prosperity. The words sound like God's promise to Abraham to bless all nations. Many Christians see here a foreshadowing of Jesus, the perfect King; others read it first as a prayer for the kings of David's line.

For today: place your trust in the kingdom of God more than in fame or passing success. Live so that your life is a blessing to others, not only to yourself.
exp.59:3:
God has given a banner to those who fear him, that is, to those who honor and respect him, a banner to lift up. That banner was a signal for gathering together, and here it is linked with the truth. Some translators understand the final word differently, but the underlying idea is the same. The word "Selah" seems to be a pause for meditation.

David speaks on behalf of the whole people. Israel has just gone through a hard defeat, and the psalm describes it as an earthquake and wine that makes them stagger. In the midst of that pain, David remembers that God has not left them without direction.

For today: when you go through a crisis, do not stay fixed on the blow alone. Gather with other believers and hold firmly to the truth of God, for he himself has given it to you as a banner.
exp.25:0:
David asks God to judge him, that is, to examine his life and vindicate him. He says he has walked in his integrity, a word that means honesty and uprightness of heart. He also affirms that he has trusted in the Lord, and that for this reason he will not be moved, that is, he will not fall or stumble.

David is the speaker, according to the heading of the psalm. It is not known with certainty when he wrote it. He seems to be praying in the face of accusations or pressure, and he appeals to God as a righteous judge. He does not claim to be perfect: in the verses that follow he asks God to test him, and he acknowledges that God's mercy is always before his eyes.

Today we can pray sincerely and say to God, "Look at me as I really am." Ask him to examine your motives, and walk with honesty, trusting in his mercy and not in your own perfection.
exp.73:16:
He says that God is the one who set the limits or borders of the whole earth, and also the one who created the seasons: summer and winter. The word "borders" means limits. Some understand these limits as the coasts and regions of the world; others understand them as the order God gave to nature. In both cases, the world is under his hand.

This psalm is written by Asaph, or by someone from his group of singers. It is a prayer of lament: the sanctuary has been destroyed and the people are suffering. Before asking for help, the author recalls who God is: the Creator who governs the day, the night, the rivers, and the seasons. The verses that follow ask God to act against the enemies.

When your life passes through a difficult season, remember that God governs the times. Pray with confidence, knowing that your situation is not beyond him.
exp.68:10:
He says the psalmist put on sackcloth, a coarse cloth used as a sign of grief and repentance. Even so, the people mocked him and he became a "proverb," that is, someone spoken of with contempt or used as an example to laugh at.

The psalm is attributed to David in its heading. He suffers because of his zeal for God: it grieves him that God's name is dishonored. He fasts, weeps, and prays, but others mock him. Even those who sit at the gate, where the affairs of the city were handled, speak against him. The New Testament cites this psalm in connection with Jesus, although this particular verse is not quoted.

Today: if your sincere faith draws mockery, do not lose heart. Do as the psalmist did: bring your pain to God in prayer and trust in his mercy.
exp.77:66:
The explanation says that God rejected the "tabernacle of Joseph," that is, the place of worship and leadership of the northern tribes, and that he did not choose the tribe of Ephraim (the strongest of them) to be the center of his people. The word for "rejected" means that he set it aside, and "tabernacle" here refers to the sacred tent, which was at Shiloh, in Ephraim's territory.

The psalm is by Asaph, and it reviews Israel's history to teach new generations. Earlier, the people were unfaithful, and God allowed the sanctuary at Shiloh to fall. Afterward, God acted and chose Judah, Zion, and David. Many understand that the psalm shows that God's favor does not depend on pride or on a tribe's fame.

For today: do not take God's favor for granted because of your history, your family, or your church. Keep a humble and faithful heart, trusting that God guides with wisdom and grace.
exp.126:0:
It says that if the Lord is not in the building of a house, the builders' labour is wasted. And if the Lord does not protect a city, it does no good for the watchman to stay awake keeping guard. The words for "build" and "keep" in the verse are the ones in this verse, so no comment is needed on them. "In vain" means "without result."

The heading "A Song of degrees" probably refers to a song for going up to Jerusalem, though it is understood in several ways.

The heading says "for Solomon," and this can be understood as meaning he wrote it or that it was dedicated to him; scholars do not fully agree. It is a pilgrim song, the kind sung by those who went up to Jerusalem for the feasts. The speaker is a wise person who wants to remind the people that everything depends on God: the house, the city, and the family. The verses that follow speak of children as a gift from God.

Work hard, but do not depend on yourself alone. Before you begin your work, your home, or a project, pray and entrust it to God. In this way you can rest with greater peace, knowing that he cares for what you cannot fully control.
exp.43:6:
This verse says that God was the one who protected his people from their enemies, and the one who put to shame those who hated them. Some older words: "guarded" means protected or cared for; "shamed" means defeated and humiliated; "hated" is the same as despised.

The psalm presents itself as a prayer of the people of Israel, and it is attributed to the sons of Korah. It is not known for certain which war they had in mind. Before this verse, the people confess that their victory did not come from their own bow or sword. Afterward, the tone shifts: they feel that God has let them fall into defeat. So they recall their past victories while asking for help.

For today: recognize that what you have overcome was not only through your own strength. Give thanks to God for the times he cared for you. That memory can give you confidence when you are going through a difficult season and do not understand what is happening.
exp.50:2:
It says that David openly admits his guilt. The explanation of the first quoted word is that it means he accepts what he did and does not hide it. The second word refers to acts of defiance against God, such as deliberately ignoring his commands. It adds that his sin is "ever before" him: he cannot forget it, and it weighs on his conscience constantly.

The speaker is David, king of Israel. According to the title of the psalm, he wrote it when the prophet Nathan came to confront him after his sin with Bathsheba. Here he no longer justifies or excuses himself. He asks God for forgiveness and recognizes that the problem is his own, not the result of circumstances.

For today: when you fail, do not hide or look for excuses. Name your mistake honestly before God, without dressing it up. That honesty is the first step toward receiving his forgiveness and truly beginning to change.
exp.52:4:
The explanation says that the wicked, who did not fear God, were suddenly filled with terror even where there was nothing to fear. God scattered the bones of those who encamped to attack his people. The phrase "set up camp" in the source means they placed their army to lay siege. The word translated as "rejected" means that God turned them away. That is why they were put to shame.

David speaks in this psalm, which is very similar to Psalm 14. He describes corrupt people who ignore God and oppress his people. Here he affirms that God himself defeats them. We do not know for certain which historical event he has in mind; some think of a specific victory of Israel, others of a general principle of justice.

For today: when you feel surrounded by injustice or by people who hurt you, do not despair. Trust that God sees and that he has the last word. Bring your cause to him in prayer, without seeking revenge, and wait on him.
exp.138:22:
Here the psalmist asks God to examine him and know him from within. Asking God to "search me" and "try me" is like asking Him to look over his heart, just as gold is tested to see whether it is pure. "Know my thoughts" means that God should look deeply into what he thinks and feels, even the things hidden from others.

The words are spoken by David, according to the title of the psalm. He had just said that he hates the enemies of God, a strong expression that many interpreters understand as passionate loyalty to God. After speaking with such firmness, David does not consider himself beyond question: he invites God to check whether his motives are truly clean.

For today: before you judge others or defend your own reasons, pray this prayer sincerely. Ask God to show you your hidden attitudes, such as pride, resentment or fear, and let yourself be corrected and guided by Him.
exp.3:6:
It says that God gave the psalmist a joy in his heart greater than that of those who have abundant harvests. "Grain" is wheat or barley, and "new wine" is the juice of the grape, the freshly made wine. In other words, his joy is greater than the joy of a full harvest.

The psalm is attributed to David, and the text presents it as a prayer in a time of distress. Some around him doubt and ask who will show them good. He, however, asks God for the light of his face, his favor. Scholars do not agree on what the exact situation was, so it is wise not to claim more than the text says.

For today: true joy does not depend on what I have in the pantry or in the bank account. When you feel insecure, ask God for his presence before anything else. His nearness gives a joy and a peace that circumstances cannot take away.
exp.8:8:
It says that God is a safe place for the poor, that is, the oppressed or needy, and that he is especially a refuge "in the time of trouble," when life becomes hard. A "refuge" means a place of protection and rest. "Lord" is the name of God in the Old Testament.

Psalm 9 is by David, according to its heading. Before that, he celebrates that God reigns forever and judges with justice and righteousness. So the one who suffers injustice can trust: the Judge of the world has not forgotten him. Then the psalm says that God does not abandon those who seek him. Some scholars see here a concrete victory of David, although the psalm does not give all the details.

For today: when you feel pressure, fear, or injustice, do not carry everything alone. Offer a simple and sincere prayer, telling God what is happening to you, and remember that he is just and near.
exp.6:4:
Here David makes a very serious oath. He says that, if he truly is guilty of what he is accused of, then let his enemy chase him and overtake him, trample him down, and leave his honor lying in the dust. "Soul" here means his life. "Honor" means his dignity and good name. "Selah" is probably a pause for reflection, though its exact meaning is not certain.

David, the psalmist, is the speaker. The title of the psalm connects it with Cush the Benjamite, though we do not know for certain what event it refers to. Someone was accusing him unjustly, and David brings his case before God, confident that his hands are clean.

Today, when we are falsely accused, we can pray with sincerity, asking God to examine our hearts. If there is guilt, we acknowledge it; if there is not, we rest in the knowledge that God is a just judge.
exp.4:4:
It says that the foolish, that is, those who live with arrogance and without taking God into account, will not be able to stand in his presence. God hates those who practice wickedness. Here "workers of iniquity" means doing evil as a habit. The word "hates" expresses a strong rejection of evil and of those who cling to it.

David speaks, according to the title of the psalm, although some scholars debate this. It is a morning prayer. He feels surrounded by liars and violent people, and he brings his case before God. He trusts that God is holy and just. That is why, in verse 7, he contrasts his own situation: he enters God's house only by divine mercy, not by his own merits.

Today we can begin the day praying sincerely, asking God to guide and cleanse us. If there is injustice around us, we can trust that God sees it, and seek to live with humility, supported by his mercy.
exp.118:113:
This verse says that God is the place where the psalmist hides and also the protection that covers him, like a shield. The word "hiding place" in the verse means a refuge or a safe place. In addition, it says he has put his hope in God's word, that is, he has trusted in God's promises and in what He has said.

Psalm 119 is a long poem that praises God's word. Tradition attributes it to a believer who loves the Lord's law, although the text does not say who wrote it. Here the speaker rejects empty thoughts and wants to obey God, and soon he asks to be kept away from the wicked. His trust in God gives him security against the pressure of those who do evil.

Today, when you feel fear or pressure, you can take refuge in God by reading a promise from the Bible and praying with it. In this way your hope rests on something firm.
exp.99:4:
This verse gives the reason to praise God: he is good. His mercy is his faithful love and compassion, and it lasts forever. His truth is his faithfulness: he does what he says. And this does not change: it remains firm through all generations, that is, from parents to children, century after century.

This is the closing verse of Psalm 100, a psalm of praise or thanksgiving. No one knows for certain who wrote it or on what exact occasion. It seems to be an invitation to Israel to enter the temple to worship. The verses before it say that God made them and cares for them like a shepherd caring for his sheep.

For today: when you feel that everything is changing or that you have failed, remember that God is still good and faithful. Today, thank him for a specific example of his goodness in your life.
exp.103:32:
The explanation says that the psalmist will sing to Jehovah, that is, to God, for as long as he lives. The word for "sing" here is an old term meaning to sing psalms or songs of praise, and the phrase for "as long as I live" simply means "while I am alive." It is a personal promise to worship God without stopping until the end.

Psalm 104 is a hymn that praises God as Creator. It speaks of the earth, the water, the animals, and the seasons. It does not say with certainty who wrote it, although it is traditionally associated with David. After admiring creation, the psalmist responds with a commitment: not just to think about God, but to sing to him. Then he asks that evil disappear, and he blesses the Lord again.

For today: make gratitude a daily habit. You can choose a moment of the day, perhaps when you wake up or while you walk, to sing or thank God for something you see in his creation. In this way your praise does not depend on your mood, but becomes part of your life.
exp.37:11:
This verse describes enemies who were very active. "They that seek my life" means they wanted to take his life. "Lay snares for me" means they set traps for him. "They that seek my hurt" means they were after his harm. "Speak mischievous things" refers to their speaking evil and lies. "Imagine deceits" means they plotted deceptions, and they did it all day long.

David speaks in a psalm of lament, which tradition presents as a prayer of remembrance. He is sick, weak, and suffering because of his sin. Furthermore, his friends and relatives pulled away from him. In that moment of weakness, his enemies take advantage to attack him. Afterward, he keeps silent and does not answer, and he places his trust in God.

For today: when people attack you with lies or make you feel alone, there is no need to defend yourself with anger. You can speak to God honestly and entrust your cause to him.
exp.139:6:
This verse says that God is the strength that saves the psalmist. The phrase "the strength of my salvation" means "my strength that gives me salvation," and in the verse above it is the phrase "the strength of my salvation." "Thou hast covered my head" means that God protected him, the way a helmet protects the head. "The day of battle" refers to the day of fighting or danger.

The psalm is spoken by David, according to its title. He is surrounded by proud and violent people who have set hidden traps for him. Before this verse he has already asked God for help, and here he remembers that God has watched over him in past dangers. That gives him confidence to keep praying.

For today: when you face a big problem, remember the times God helped you before. Tell Him about it in prayer, thank Him, and trust that He is still your protection now.
exp.128:0:
The explanation says that the people of Israel recall with pain that they have suffered greatly since their earliest days. The title "A Song of degrees" is a note about the psalm's heading; many believe it was sung as the people went up to Jerusalem, though this is not certain. The word "afflicted" means oppressed, troubled, or pressed into hardship.

Israel speaks as a people, as if one person were remembering its history. The phrase "from my youth" probably refers to its beginnings, such as the slavery in Egypt, though some understand it more generally. The psalmist invites everyone to say it together, and the next verse makes clear that, despite the pain, they were not overcome.

Today, you can remember your past sorrows without hiding them, but also look at how God sustained you. Telling your story with honesty and gratitude can strengthen your faith, and sharing it with other believers can encourage them as well.
exp.18:3:
The explanation says that the message of creation reaches the whole earth. The word rendered "line" is understood as a measuring cord, and here it suggests that its reach extends everywhere. "To the end of the world" means to the farthest corner. It then says that God set a dwelling place, a tent or home, in the heavens for the sun.

The author is David, who writes a song of praise. The verses before it say that the heavens speak without audible words. Here it is shown that this silent testimony reaches all peoples. Some translate "line" as "voice," as the New Testament quotes it in Romans 10:18. Scholars explain this in different ways.

For today: when you see a sunrise or the night sky, stop for a moment and give thanks to God. Creation reminds you that He is powerful, orderly, and near, and invites you to trust in Him.
exp.67:12:
It says that, although you lay among the broken pots (pieces of cracked clay, or perhaps the dirty corners where old things are thrown away), you will become like the wings of a dove covered with silver, with feathers that shine like yellow gold. It is an image of beauty and honor after humiliation.

It is a psalm of David that celebrates God as the one who gives victory to his people. It comes after a won battle, and the women who stayed at home divide the spoils. The verse is hard to translate, and scholars understand it in several ways: some see the restored people, others the women who divide the plunder.

For today: if you are going through a time of shame, loss, or abandonment, remember that God can transform your story. Trust that he knows how to restore dignity and beauty, even if you cannot see it yet.
exp.89:12:
Here the psalmist asks God to "return," that is, to come back with kindness toward his people. The question "how long?" expresses a cry of weariness and pain. "Let it repent thee" means to relent, to change his mind about his anger, and "servants" are those who belong to him and serve him.

This psalm is presented in its title as a prayer of Moses, the man of God. Many see it as a prayer of the people in difficult times, perhaps in the wilderness, although this cannot be asserted with certainty. It speaks of human frailty and the weight of the consequences of sin. After acknowledging this, the people now ask for compassion.

For today: when you go through a long and painful season, you can be honest with God. Asking "how long?" is not a lack of faith. Bring him your weariness, acknowledge your need, and trust that his mercy is greater than your affliction.
exp.102:7:
It says that God is compassionate and kind. "Merciful" means that he feels compassion for the one who suffers or fails. "Gracious" means that he treats people with tenderness and not with harshness. "Slow to anger" means that he does not grow angry quickly, but gives time and patience. And "plenteous in mercy" affirms that his compassion is abundant, not scarce.

It is a psalm attributed to David, who addresses himself: "Bless the Lord, O my soul." Earlier it mentions that God made his ways known to Moses. This verse recalls how God described himself in Exodus. Then David explains that God does not deal with us according to what we deserve.

For today: when you fail, do not run from God out of shame. Come near with sincerity, trusting in his patience. And try to be slow to anger with those around you, as he is with you.
exp.3:4:
It says that, instead of acting wrongly, we should bring God offerings of righteousness, that is, offerings made with uprightness and sincerity. And in addition, we should trust in the Lord, who is the name of God.

David speaks in a night prayer. Some attack him and shame him. He calls them to calm down, to leave sin behind, and to reflect in silence. Many believe that "sacrifices of righteousness" refers to offerings made with a sincere heart, not merely to fulfill a ritual. Scholars do not fully agree on the details of the exact situation.

Today we can approach God with honesty, not only with religious customs. When something troubles us, before reacting with anger, let us pray calmly, correct what is wrong, and place our trust in God.
exp.118:78:
It says that the psalmist asks that those who honor God and know his testimonies return to be with him. The words "turn" and "return" are what this asking means. "Those who fear you" are those who respect God with reverence and love. "Testimonies" are the teachings and commands through which God makes his will known.

The one speaking is the author of the psalm, who suffers slander from proud people. He feels alone and rejected, so he asks God that the faithful draw near to him again. We do not know for certain who wrote it or at what exact moment, but the tone is that of someone wounded who seeks spiritual companionship.

For today: when you feel criticized or alone, look for friends who love God and his Word. They will encourage you to remain firm. And you can be the one who draws near to another who needs it.
exp.118:140:
This verse says that the psalmist feels small and looked down upon. The word "despised" means that others see him as someone of no worth and reject him. Even so, he declares that he has not forgotten God's commandments. His worth does not depend on what others think, but on his faithfulness to God's word.

Psalm 119 is a long meditation on God's law. Tradition is not unanimous about who wrote it, and the text does not say so with certainty. The one speaking is a believer who suffers contempt and sees his enemies forget God's words. His zeal for the truth wears him down, but his love for it remains firm.

Today, when you feel ignored, underestimated, or rejected, do not stop holding on to God's Word. Set aside a few minutes each day to read it and remember it. It reminds you who you are before God, even when others do not value you.
exp.65:14:
It says that the psalmist will offer God burnt offerings, that is, animals burned completely on the altar as a sign of total surrender. Fatlings are well-fed, carefully chosen animals; the aroma of the smoke rising from the offering as it burns is what the verse describes as the incense of rams. It also mentions bullocks and male goats. "Selah" is probably a musical pause or a moment for reflection, though its exact meaning is not certain.

The speaker is the psalmist, perhaps the king or someone from the people; we do not know for certain who. He had promised God offerings in a time of distress, and God heard him. Now he fulfills his vows in the temple, with public thanksgiving.

Today we do not offer animals, but we can still keep what we promised God in difficult moments. Think of some promise you made to him, of service, of change, or of commitment, and fulfill it with joy. God deserves our best, not what is left over.
exp.84:12:
It says that righteousness will walk ahead of God, like someone clearing the way, and that God's steps will then be set on a path. In plain language: wherever God acts, righteousness goes before him and marks out the route. The phrase "shall set us in the way of his steps" can be understood in two ways: that righteousness prepares the path God travels, or that his steps serve as a guide for us. Scholars translate it in several different ways.

It is a psalm of the sons of Korah, probably written after the people returned from exile or after a time of hardship. The psalmist asks God to restore Israel and, in the closing verses, describes with hope what that time will be like: truth, righteousness, peace and fruit on the land. The exact details of the historical situation are not entirely clear.

For today: before looking for quick results, make sure that righteousness and honesty go before you in your decisions. In this way we follow the steps of God.
exp.107:7:
God claims as his own the lands and tribes of Israel. Gilead and Manasseh were regions and tribes east of the Jordan. Ephraim is the strength of my head, that is, like a helmet that protects and gives strength. Judah is my lawgiver, meaning the tribe from which government would come, like the king's scepter.

This psalm of David repeats a promise that God gave from his holiness. David cites it to ask for help, for he wants to be delivered and to overcome his enemies. Many understand that, in saying "mine," God affirms that he rules over the whole territory and the people. The text does not explain more details about the exact moment.

For today: when you feel insecure or divided, remember that your life belongs to God. If he is owner of all things, you can pray with confidence and wait for his help, even in difficult struggles.
exp.67:7:
God's presence made the earth tremble, and the heavens poured down water. Even Mount Sinai, so great and firm, trembled before Him. The phrase "poured down" means that water was falling drop by drop, like rain. The word for "a" in this sentence is an older form, and "that Sinai" points to the mountain where God spoke with Israel.

The speaker is David, in a song that recalls how God led his people through the desert after bringing them out of Egypt. Many understand that it refers to what happened at Sinai, although the psalm uses poetic language rather than giving a detailed account. What matters is that the same mighty God cared for the lonely, freed the prisoners, and provided rain and sustenance for his weary people.

Today we can remember that God is great and yet near. If you feel tired or alone, pray with confidence: the God before whom the earth trembles is also the one who cares for you.
exp.40:3:
Here the psalmist asks God to show him compassion and to heal him. Mercy means showing kindness to someone who does not deserve it. The soul refers to the whole person, his life and his being. He acknowledges that he has sinned against God, and so he does not ask for help with pride, but with humility.

According to the heading, the psalm is by David. He is sick and surrounded by enemies who wish for his death, and even some who visit him pretend to be friends. Some think his illness is related to his sin, but the text does not make this clear. What is certain is that he cries out to God with sincerity.

For today: when you are suffering, do not hide your failings or your pain. Speak to God with honesty, confess what you know you did wrong, and ask Him for His forgiveness and His help. He listens to the humble heart.
exp.102:14:
It says that the life of a human being is short and fragile, like the grass of the field. "His days" refers to the time we live. "Flourishes like the flower of the field" shows that we may look beautiful and strong for a moment, but soon we pass away. The word that follows, which in the source appears as the age-long word, means "always" or "forever."

David speaks here, according to the title of the psalm. He praises God for his forgiveness and his care. Just before this verse it says that God, like a compassionate father, knows that we are dust. Afterward, the psalm contrasts our brevity with the mercy of the LORD, which lasts forever toward those who fear him.

Today you can remember that your time is limited, and so it is best not to live with pride or anxiety. Trust in the love of God, which never ends, and use it to live each day with humility, gratitude, and purpose.
exp.104:23:
God made the people of Israel grow very much while they lived in Egypt. He made them more numerous and stronger than the Egyptians, who were their enemies. "Increased" means that he made them grow in number, and "greatly" means very much. "Ham" is Egypt, a poetic name for the land.

The psalmist, whom the text does not name with certainty, recalls Israel's history to praise God. He wants to show that God kept his promise to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. Even in a foreign land, God cared for his people and made them grow. That growth, however, stirred up the rejection of the Egyptians, as the following verse says.

For today: even if you are going through a difficult season or feel far from home, God can still be at work in your life. Trust that he keeps what he promises, even when you cannot yet see it.
exp.49:20:
It says that God saw this person's wrongdoing and did not respond right away. So she thought God was just like her, someone who approves of evil or does not care. But God says, "I will reprove you," which means "I will rebuke you" or "I will accuse you." He also promises to set those faults before your eyes, that is, to make you see them clearly.

In this psalm by Asaph, God himself speaks as judge of his people. Earlier he has said that he does not want only sacrifices, but a sincere heart. Here he addresses the one who uses his mouth to lie and slander, even against his own brother. His silence was not permission, but patience.

For today: if God does not correct something right away, do not take it as approval. His patience is an invitation to change. Examine how you speak about others, leave behind gossip and lies, and ask for forgiveness sincerely.
exp.117:17:
It says that God disciplined the writer very severely, but did not allow him to die. The phrase about being corrected harshly is rendered simply as "chastened me sore," and "given over" here means being handed over to death.

The psalm is a song of thanksgiving. The one speaking had gone through great distress and was rescued. Some think a king is speaking, others that it is the whole nation of Israel; this is not known for certain. He sees his suffering as God's correction, not as abandonment. For that reason, right after, he wants to enter through the gates of the temple to give thanks.

For today: when you go through a hard season, do not assume God has left you alone. He may use difficulties to teach you and still hold you up. Today, give thanks for something you got through, and tell someone about it to encourage them.
exp.82:0:
This verse is a cry to God. The psalmist asks him not to stay silent, not to keep quiet, and not to stand still. "Keep not thou silence" and "be not still" mean: act, speak, step in. At the beginning it says "A Song or Psalm of Asaph," which indicates that this is a song attributed to Asaph, a musician and leader of worship.

The one speaking is Asaph, or someone from his family or group of singers. There are different opinions about when it was written. The next verse explains the reason: enemies of Israel are making plans in secret against God's people. The psalmist feels in danger and asks God not to stand idly by.

For today: when you feel that God is silent in the face of injustice or a threat, you can speak to him honestly, as Asaph did. Praying with frankness is not a lack of faith; it is trusting that he hears and can act.
exp.118:7:
The speaker commits to obeying God's laws. "Statutes" are the instructions or rules God gave. "I will keep" means to observe and take care to follow. Then he prays: "O forsake me not utterly," that is, "do not abandon me completely." It joins a promise with a prayer.

The speaker is the psalmist, a believer who loves God's word. The author is not named in the text. At the close of the Aleph section, which is the first eight verses, he expresses his desire to walk without shame. He knows that promising is easy, but keeping one's word is hard. For that reason he asks for God's help and does not trust only in his own strength.

Today we can imitate this attitude: sincerely decide to obey God and, at the same time, ask him for help each day. For example, at the start of the morning, read a verse and pray: "Lord, I want to do this today; do not let go of my hand."
exp.54:18:
God will hear and bring them down at once. He is the eternal God, who has reigned from before time began. "Afflict them" means that he will knock them down or bring them low. "Selah" is probably a musical pause or an invitation to reflect. "They do not change" means that they do not change their conduct, and "fear God" means to respect him with reverence.

David is the speaker, according to the title of the psalm, although some scholars debate the exact moment. He feels betrayed by someone close to him, who pretended peace with gentle words but kept war in his heart. That is why he prays evening, morning, and noon, trusting that God hears him.

Today, when someone wounds you or betrays you, do not carry the pain alone. Pray with perseverance and entrust justice to God, who is eternal and does not change. Also ask him that your own heart not grow hard or stop fearing him.
exp.80:3:
This verse explains why the feast should be marked with song and the sounding of the trumpet. The people do not celebrate out of mere human custom, but because God, the God of Jacob, commanded it for Israel. The old words used for this kind of command simply mean a fixed rule or required practice.

The psalm seems to be an invitation to keep a solemn feast, probably at the new moon. First the psalmist speaks, calling the people to praise. Later, God himself speaks and recalls how he brought Israel out of Egypt. Scholars do not agree on exactly which feast is meant. What is clear is that praise is joined to the remembrance of deliverance.

For today: set aside a regular time to give thanks to God, not only when you feel like it. Singing, praying, or reading the Bible together as a family can help you remember what God has done for you.
exp.1:10:
Here it says we should serve God with deep respect, "fear", that is, with reverence, knowing who He is. But it also tells us to rejoice, yet with trembling, that is, with a humble and serious joy. The words "serve" and "rejoice" in the older wording are forms that mean "serve" and "rejoice" today.

This psalm is usually attributed to David. It speaks of kings and nations that rebel against God and against His Anointed. First it describes God's power, and then the psalmist calls the rulers to reconsider, to accept correction, and to submit to God. At the end, a blessing is promised to those who trust in Him. Many Christians see here a reference to Christ.

Today we can live our faith without coldness or carelessness. Before we pray or work, let us remember that God is great and good, and let us serve Him with gratitude and seriousness.
exp.113:0:
This verse recalls the time when the people of Israel, also called "the house of Jacob," went out of Egypt. Here the word "strange" does not mean wild or cruel. It means that they spoke a foreign language, that is, a people of unfamiliar speech.

The psalm does not say who wrote it. It is a song of praise that celebrates the exodus, the deliverance from slavery. The following verses say that God made Judah his sanctuary and Israel his dominion, and that even the sea and the Jordan yielded to his presence. It is believed that the people sang it to remember what God had done for them.

For today: remembering how God has helped us in the past strengthens trust. You can write down some moments when you felt his help and give him thanks, especially when you face a difficult situation.
exp.87:8:
The explanation says the pain has left the writer without strength: his eyes are weak and worn out from so much weeping. Even so, he has cried out to God every day. The word for "grew weak" means that his eyes became dim or faded. The phrase "I have called" means "I have called upon you." Stretching out the hands is a gesture of prayer and of asking for help.

This psalm is written by a man named Heman the Ezrahite, according to the heading. It is a very dark prayer: he feels rejected by God, abandoned by his friends, and trapped in his suffering. It is unusual, because it offers almost no words of comfort. Even so, he keeps speaking to God and addresses him as the LORD, the God who saves.

For today: when you are tired and have no answers, do not stop praying. You can tell God everything you feel, honestly. Continuing to cry out is also a way of faith.
exp.17:18:
It says that God brought David out into a large place, that is, into a place of freedom and relief, after he had been pressed in by his enemies. "He brought me forth" means that God brought him out, "he delivered me" means that God rescued him, and "because he delighted in me" means that God took pleasure in him and loved him.

David speaks, according to the heading of the psalm, "in the day that the LORD delivered him from the hand of all his enemies, and from the hand of Saul." It is a song of gratitude. He remembers that when everything seemed closed in and his enemies were stronger, God was his support and rescued him.

For today: when you feel cornered by a difficulty, remember that God knows how to bring his children out into a large place. Speak with Him, trust in His care, and when relief comes, give thanks aloud, as David did.
exp.70:21:
The psalm promises to praise God with music. The instruments named in the verse are stringed instruments of the kind played in worship. "Your truth" refers to God's faithfulness, that he keeps what he has promised. "Holy One of Israel" is a title that stresses that God is pure and set apart from everything else, and that he has bound himself to his people. Singing psalms is the act of praising God in song.

The psalm does not say who wrote it. Tradition has linked it to David, but this is not certain. The one speaking is a person already advanced in years (vv. 9, 18) who has gone through many troubles and enemies. Now, confident that God will raise him up again, he responds with gratitude and praise.

For today: when you remember how God sustained you in hard times, do not keep that silent. Put on a song of praise, or tell someone what God has done for you. Giving thanks with words and music strengthens your trust for whatever comes next.
exp.138:6:
Here the psalmist asks two questions: "Where can I go from your Spirit? Where can I flee from your presence?" He is not really looking for a place to hide. It is a poetic way of saying that there is no place where God is not present. "Spirit" here refers to the Spirit of God, and "flee" means to escape or run away.

The psalm is attributed to David, although some scholars debate its exact authorship. The speaker is amazed that God knows him completely: He surrounds him, cares for him, and places His hand upon him. This knowledge is so great that he cannot fully grasp it. Then he reflects that he cannot get away from God.

If you feel lonely, ashamed, or far from God today, remember that He has not lost sight of you. You can speak to Him honestly, anywhere, because His presence goes with you and sustains you.
exp.94:1:
This verse invites us to come near to God with gratitude and joy. The words "come before his presence" describe approaching someone important with respect, and the verse says to do so with thanksgiving and singing with enthusiasm.

It is a psalm of worship for the people of Israel, and the speaker calls the community to gather. The text does not say who wrote it. The verses that follow give the reason: the Lord is a great God, King above all gods, and in his hand are the deep places of the earth and the strength of the hills.

For today: before asking God for anything, begin your prayer with thanksgiving. Take a few minutes to thank him for specific things, or sing a song that reminds you who he is. That shifts your focus and your heart.
exp.27:5:
It says that David praises God because he heard his cry. "Blessed" means worthy of praise. "Supplications" are requests made out of need and pleading. It is a simple thanks: God did not ignore his prayer.

In this psalm David speaks after asking God for help and asking for justice against the wicked, who did not respect the works of the Lord. Here the tone shifts from pleading to gratitude. David seems to trust that God has already heard him, and so, in the verses that follow, he calls him his strength and his shield. Some interpreters see here an answer already received; others see a firm confidence before the result is seen.

Today, when you pray, do not stop at asking. Take a moment to thank God for hearing you, even if the answer is not yet visible. Giving thanks strengthens your trust and reminds you that you are not speaking into emptiness.
exp.79:2:
This verse is a prayer. "Turn us again" means restore us and bring us back to you. "Cause your face to shine" is asking God to look on us with kindness and favor. And "we shall be saved" means that if God looks on us in this way, we will be rescued.

The one speaking is Asaph, or perhaps a group of musicians who carried his name, speaking on behalf of the whole people of Israel. The psalm describes a people in suffering, who see God as a shepherd who seems distant. Scholars do not agree on the exact moment in history when it was written. This same plea is repeated in verses 7 and 19.

For today: when you feel far from God or in great difficulty, do not wait to get yourself in order first. Pray simply: "Lord, bring me back to you and look on me with your favor." Salvation comes from him, not from our own strength.
exp.68:26:
Here the psalmist asks God to let the guilt of his enemies grow, that is, to let the punishment for their wrongdoing fall on them. He also asks that they not be counted among the righteous or receive God's forgiveness. The word "iniquity" here can mean both the sin itself and its consequences.

The speaker is a suffering man, traditionally David, who is persecuted without cause and feels abandoned. It is an imprecatory psalm: a harsh cry that leaves justice in God's hands. The New Testament quotes this psalm in connection with Jesus.

Today, when you are unjustly wounded, you can bring your anger and your pain honestly to God, instead of taking revenge. Then, following Jesus, pray also that your enemies will change and find his mercy.
exp.73:4:
In former times, a man gained a reputation according to how much he raised his axe against the thick timbers, that is, against the large trunks of the trees. "He became famous" means that he was valued or admired for that work. The Hebrew text is difficult, and some translations understand it as describing enemies destroying the temple as if they were woodcutters.

The speaker is the psalmist, identified as Asaph (the title of the psalm). He probably laments the destruction of the sanctuary, perhaps by Babylon, though it is not certain which exact event he describes. The enemies boast of their strength while they tear apart what was holy, and the psalmist asks God for help.

For today: when you see people mocking what is holy, or it seems that evil is winning, do not keep silent or lose heart. Bring your pain to God honestly, trusting that he sees everything.
exp.53:1:
David asks God to listen to him. "Hear my prayer" is a direct plea for God to pay attention to his cry. "Give ear to the words of my mouth" means that God should attend to what David says, his words and his petition. The phrase "words of my mouth" here simply means what David speaks, not complicated arguments.

David speaks in a moment of danger. According to the heading, the Ziphites, people of that region, told Saul where David was hiding. Saul was pursuing him, and David felt betrayed and threatened. That is why he prays with urgency, asking to be saved and defended.

For today: when you feel pressured or misunderstood, do not keep your anguish to yourself. Tell God with simple, sincere words what you feel and what you need. You do not need a perfect prayer; it is enough to speak to Him with confidence, knowing that He listens.
exp.111:4:
The verse says that the good and upright person shows compassion to others and lends generously. He also manages his affairs with wisdom and good judgment. "Compassion" here is kindness that becomes concrete help, and "discretion" means prudence and uprightness when making decisions.

Psalm 112 is a poem of praise that describes the person who fears the LORD and delights greatly in his commandments. No narrator is identified, and the text does not say who wrote it. Its purpose is to show what a life that honors God looks like: blessing, stability, and a confidence that does not break at bad news.

For today: if you have the opportunity, help someone with a loan or a favor without humiliating them, and at the same time manage your money with order. Generosity and good management go hand in hand.
exp.95:3:
The explanation says that the Lord is great and deserves to be praised above anyone else. The phrase "greatly to be praised" points to the fact that he is worthy of praise more than anyone. The word "feared" here does not mean something bad, but rather that he commands awe and reverence because of his power and holiness. "Above all gods" means that no other god can be compared to him.

The psalm does not say who wrote it. It is a song that calls the whole people to worship God and to tell his wonders among the other nations. The next verse gives the reason: the gods of the peoples are idols, but the Lord made the heavens. Some scholars connect it with worship celebrations in Israel, but that cannot be stated with certainty.

Today we can remember who God is when we feel that other things, such as money, success or fear, have control over us. Begin the day by praising him, and say out loud: "You are greater."
exp.55:3:
He says the psalmist praises God for his word, that is, for what God has said and promised. Since he has put his trust in God, he does not fear what mere humans can do to him. Mere humans are weak and limited.

According to the title of the psalm, David speaks at the time when the Philistines held him captive in Gath (1 Samuel 21). Enemies pursue him, watch him, and want to kill him. Even so, in the middle of real fear, he chooses to trust. Notice that he does not deny that he is afraid: he says, "I will trust in God."

For today: when you feel afraid, do not pretend it is not there. Read or remember a promise of God, praise him for it, and hand over that worry to him. Trusting means deciding to lean on him, even with fear.
exp.40:7:
The explanation says that the enemies of the psalmist talk among themselves about his illness. The phrase "evil disease" is an old way of putting it that can be understood as a terrible wickedness or sickness, and "cleaveth fast unto him" means that it has taken hold of him and holds him fast. They are sure that, since he "lieth" in bed, he will never rise again. In other words, they give him up for dead.

The speaker is David, according to the title of the psalm. He is sick and weak, and those who visit him pretend affection, but inwardly they wish him harm and then talk about him outside. These are their words, not God's. The following verse speaks of the betrayal by a close friend, and David ends by asking God to raise him up.

For today: do not let the words of others define your future when you are going through a trial. Bring your pain to God with sincerity, as David did, and trust that his mercy has the final word.
exp.46:3:
It says that God himself decides which inheritance or land falls to his people. The first sentence of the explanation is about the verse's words "our inheritance," which refers to the possessions received as a portion. "The excellency of Jacob" refers to the most valuable thing Israel had, namely the promised land and the privilege of being God's people. And all of this flows from the fact that God loved them. The word "Selah" was probably a musical pause or a moment for reflection, though this is not known for certain.

It is a psalm of the sons of Korah, a song of praise that proclaims God as King over all the earth. The people speak in the first person: they acknowledge that what they have was not obtained by their own strength, but because God gave it. The psalm then continues with shouts of joy and trumpets.

Today we can rest in the knowledge that God cares for our lives and for what we are given to live through. Instead of complaining or comparing ourselves with others, we can give thanks for what we have received, knowing that it comes from a God who loves us.
exp.83:0:
This verse has a heading and an exclamation. The heading says the psalm is for the chief musician, or leader of the singing, to be performed with "Gittith," and that it belongs to the sons of Korah. No one knows for certain what Gittith means; it could be an instrument, a melody, or a reference to the city of Gath.

"How lovely" means beloved, beautiful, worthy of affection. "Tabernacles" are the dwelling places where God lives, that is, his temple.

The sons of Korah were Levites who served in the worship and singing of the sanctuary. The speaker expresses a deep longing to be in God's presence, in the place of worship. We do not know exactly when he wrote it, since some think he was far from the temple and others that he visited it as a pilgrim.

Today we can cultivate a delight in being with God. Set aside a moment each day, and also gather with other believers, to pray and sing with joy, not out of obligation but out of love.
exp.100:0:
The explanation says David will sing to God about two things: mercy and judgment. "Mercy" means kindness and compassion; "judgment" means justice, doing what is right. He repeats "I will sing" to show that his song is praise directed to the LORD, the name of the Lord.

The title attributes the psalm to David, the king of Israel. Here he speaks as someone with authority who commits himself before God to govern well. The following verses show that he wants to live with integrity, first in his own house. Some think it is a kind of promise about his reign, although the psalm does not say exactly when he wrote it.

For today: if you have any responsibility, whether in your home, at work, or in the church, seek to balance compassion with justice. And before demanding anything of others, praise God and ask him for help to live with a sincere heart.
exp.55:8:
David says that when he prays with all his strength, his enemies draw back. The phrase about enemies being turned back means they will have to withdraw. The word about crying out means calling for help at the top of one's voice. And the phrase about God being for him means that God is on his side.

The psalm's title says David speaks at the time when the Philistines seized him in Gath. He was frightened, he was fleeing, and he was weeping. Even so, he did not stay in fear: he remembered that God sees his tears and keeps count of them. From that trust comes his praise in the verses that follow.

Today, when you feel fear or pressure, speak with God honestly. Tell him what you feel, and remember that he is with you. Prayer does not erase the problem at once, but it reminds you that you are not alone and helps you to trust in the middle of difficulty.
exp.55:10:
The psalmist says he has put his trust in God, and so he will not be afraid. The sentence about what man can do to him refers to the harm that other people might try to do to him.

The title of the psalm connects it to David, at the time when the Philistines seized him in Gath. The speaker is a man under pursuit, surrounded by enemies. Earlier he has said that God is on his side, and afterward he promises to give thanks because God has watched over his life. His courage does not come from feeling strong, but from trusting God.

When someone makes you feel afraid, whether through a threat, a criticism, or an injustice, remember what God has promised and say to him with sincerity: "In God I trust." Fear may come, but it does not have to rule over you.
exp.67:33:
It says we should recognize and declare that God is strong. "Ascribe" means giving God the credit, acknowledging that the power is his. His "excellency" speaks of his greatness and splendor, which are seen in a special way over Israel, his people. And his strength is "in the clouds," that is, far above everything human.

The psalm is a song attributed to David. It calls all the kingdoms of the earth to sing to God, who reigns over the ancient heavens and whose voice is powerful. It is a psalm of victory and praise. It ends by showing that this awesome and majestic God is also the one who gives strength to his people.

Today we can begin the day by acknowledging in words that strength comes from God and not only from ourselves. When you face a difficult task or feel weak, say in prayer: "Lord, power belongs to you; give me strength for today." In this way you turn anxiety into trust.
exp.7:4:
He says that God made human beings "a little lower than the angels," that is, a little below them, but "crowned them with glory and honour." Honour means brightness, respect and dignity. The Hebrew word translated "angels" can mean God, gods, or heavenly beings; for that reason some versions translate it as "a little lower than God." Interpreters understand this in several ways.

The speaker is David, according to the heading of the psalm. He looks up at the sky at night and feels small before the greatness of God. He is amazed that the Creator remembers people and gives them such worth and responsibility, as the following verses show.

For today: even when you sometimes feel small or unimportant, God has given you dignity. Treat others, and yourself, as someone precious before Him, and take responsible care of what He has entrusted to you.
exp.72:23:
It says that God has been the guide of the psalmist, leading him with his counsel, that is, with his wisdom and direction. The verse says "Thou shalt guide me," and it also promises that afterward, at the end, God will receive him "to glory." Some understand this as honor and blessing; others, as life with God after death. Scholars interpret it in both ways.

The speaker is the psalmist Asaph, according to the heading of the psalm. He had felt envy on seeing the wicked prosper, and he nearly stumbled. He acknowledges that he was foolish, but that God never let him go: he took him by the hand. From that confidence this verse arises.

When you feel confused because life seems unfair, do not cling to your own reasons. Ask God for his counsel, read it in his Word, and take the next step with confidence, knowing that he holds you by the hand.
exp.17:25:
This verse says that God responds to each person according to the way they live. To the one who has a clean heart, God shows himself pure and trustworthy. With the crooked person, the one who is twisted or wicked, God shows himself firm and hard in his judgment. Some translate it as God showing himself cunning, and the idea understood is that God thwarts the plans of the wicked.

David speaks here, after being delivered from his enemies and from Saul. It is a song of gratitude. He acknowledges that God was faithful to him, and he describes how God deals with people according to his character. He does not say that David was perfect, but that he sought to honor God.

For today: live with sincerity before God, without duplicity. If you make a mistake, confess it and ask forgiveness. God is neither unjust nor changeable; whoever seeks him with honesty finds him near.
exp.54:22:
God says he will bring the violent and deceitful down into the pit of destruction, the grave. "Bloody" men are those who seek to harm or kill others. "Shall not live out half their days" means they will not even reach the midpoint of a long life; their end will come before its time. The verse closes with a personal decision: "but I will trust in thee."

The speaker is David, in a psalm of distress. A close friend betrayed him, with gentle words but cruel intentions. David asks God for justice rather than taking revenge himself. Scholars do not agree on the exact moment in David's life, so it is better not to state it with certainty.

When someone betrays or deceives you, do not carry the resentment alone. Bring your pain to God in prayer, leave justice in his hands, and choose to trust him one day at a time.
exp.118:80:
Caph is the name of a Hebrew letter with which this section of the psalm begins. "Fainteth" means that the soul grows weak and worn out. "Salvation" here means rescue or deliverance, not good health of the body. The psalmist says he is worn out from waiting for God to rescue him, but he keeps trusting in what God has promised.

The speaker is the author of the psalm, and we do not know for certain who he was. The verses that follow show that he suffers, that he feels forgotten, and that he asks: "When wilt thou comfort me?" Even so, he does not stop holding on to God's word.

For today: when you are tired of waiting for an answer, do not keep your weariness to yourself. Tell God honestly, and keep reading his word. It can sustain your hope while help is on its way.
exp.52:2:
This verse says that all of them have turned away from God's path. The phrase "they had turned back" means they turned their backs on God, and "corrupted" means spoiled, rotted from within. The closing words, "there is none that doeth good, no, not one," stress that no one escapes this condition on their own.

David writes this psalm, a song meant to teach. It speaks of the fool who denies God in his heart, and it shows God looking down from heaven to see whether anyone seeks him. It is nearly the same as Psalm 14. Then it speaks of those who oppress God's people and the judgment that comes upon them.

For today: be humble and do not think yourself better than others. We all need God's mercy. This invites us to seek him sincerely every day and to thank him for his grace.
exp.102:13:
This verse says that God knows very well what we are made of. "Frame" is our nature, our way of being, with its limits and weaknesses. "Remembereth" means "remembers," and "dust" reminds us that we are fragile and passing, made from the earth.

The psalm is attributed to David, who praises God for his forgiveness and tenderness. Just before this, it compares God to a compassionate father. This verse explains why God treats us with such patience: he knows our frailty. What follows speaks of how brief human life is, like the grass or the flower of the field.

Today, when you fail or feel weak and tired, do not hide from God. Come before him honestly, trusting that he understands you and receives you with compassion, not contempt.
exp.73:7:
The explanation says the enemies thought in their hearts: "Let us finish them off once and for all." And they burned all the places where the people gathered to worship God. The word for these places, which the verse above calls "synagogues," refers to meeting places or places of worship. Here the translation uses that word, though the underlying term can mean places of sacred assembly.

It is a psalm of Asaph, a lament of the people before a great disaster. Many connect it with the destruction of the temple in Jerusalem by the Babylonians, but some think of another invasion; it is not known with certainty. The people cry out to God because the enemy wants to erase their faith and their identity.

Today, when you feel that something precious in your faith is under attack or falling apart, you can do what the psalmist did: do not stay silent, but bring your pain honestly before God and remind him, with confidence, that he remains faithful.
exp.5:7:
It says that the one speaking tells the wicked to depart from him. "Depart" is the same as "go away"; "workers of iniquity" are those who practice wrongdoing; "weeping" is their crying. The reason is that God has heard his weeping.

The speaker is David, according to the psalm's heading. He came out of nights of pain, weariness and tears, surrounded by those who troubled him. He was possibly sick or distressed, though the psalm does not give all the details. Suddenly the tone changes: it moves from complaint to confidence, because he feels that God has heard him.

For today: when you weep before God, do not think that your tears are lost. He hears them. That assurance can give you courage to step away from harmful influences and to rest, even though the situation has not yet changed.
exp.107:12:
It says that, with God's help, his people will do brave and mighty deeds. The word "valiantly" in the verse refers to acts of great courage. The word "tread down" means to trample under foot, that is, to defeat completely. So the verse states that God himself will defeat the enemies.

The speaker is David, in a psalm of prayer and trust. This psalm joins parts of Psalms 57 and 60. Before this, the people had felt that God had left them and that he did not go out with their armies. Even so, he asks for help, because human help is deceptive, and he ends by trusting that the victory will come from God.

Today you can face your struggles without relying only on your own strength or your own plans. Do your part with effort, but pray and rest in God. If you feel weak, remember that the final victory does not depend on you, but on him.
exp.21:11:
The explanation says that the speaker feels surrounded by powerful and violent enemies, compared to strong bulls. Bashan was a region east of the Jordan River, known for its rich pastures and sturdy cattle. Being "surrounded" means encircled, with no way out.

This psalm is attributed to David, and the one speaking is in deep distress. He has just recalled that God has been his God since he was born, and he pleads that God not go far away, because no one else is helping him. Afterward he will describe his enemies as lions and his own exhaustion. Christians also see in this psalm an image of Jesus' suffering on the cross, since he quoted its first verse.

When you feel surrounded by problems bigger than you are, do as David did: do not hide your fear. Tell it to God honestly and remind him, and remind yourself, that he has always sustained you.
exp.102:4:
He says that God fills the life of the one who trusts in Him with good things, and that this goodness renews one's strength, as if a person became young again and strong like an eagle.

Some explanation of this phrase's wording is needed here. The verb meaning to fill someone until they are content is used in the verse, and the reader can take it as satisfying. The word for mouth, as used in the verse, can be understood as the person's desire or appetite, though some scholars render this word differently, as your years or your life. For this reason not all versions read this phrase the same way.

It is a psalm of David, who praises God and speaks to himself so as not to forget His benefits. Before this, it mentions forgiveness, healing, and rescue. Afterward it recalls that God defends the oppressed and that He made Himself known to Moses and to Israel.

Today we can take up gratitude. Every day, write down three good things you received from God. That habit renews the spirit and reminds us that He continues to care for us.
exp.90:8:
This verse says that you have made the Most High God your home, your place of safety. The phrase "which is my refuge" sounds like a voice confessing: "The Lord is my refuge." Then it speaks to you directly: you have made him your "habitation," meaning the place where you live.

The psalm does not say who wrote it; some connect it with Moses, but this is not certain. Here there seems to be a change of voice: someone declares their trust in God and encourages another person to do the same. It is written for those who live in danger and need to know where to rest.

Today you can live close to God every day, not only in times of crisis. Before starting your day, pray, read a passage of the Bible, and hand over your worries to him. In this way your trust will have roots when trials come.
exp.108:14:
He says that the sins of that wicked man should always be present before God, so that God would wipe from the earth even the remembrance of his name.

The one speaking is David, according to the title of the psalm. He is crying out to God against an enemy who was falsely accusing him and persecuting the weak. These words are a harsh prayer, not a personal act of revenge: David asks God for justice. Some scholars believe that verses 6 to 19 are what David's accusers were saying, and others that they are his own request. There is no complete agreement.

For today: when you are wronged unfairly, do not take revenge. Bring your pain to God honestly and trust that He is just. And remember that Jesus taught us to pray for our enemies as well.
exp.90:3:
The verse says that God covers the one who trusts in him, like a bird that protects its young under its feathers and wings. There the person is safe. Two old words: one is a light shield carried on the arm, and the other is the larger protector; together they show complete protection. Here "his truth" means his faithfulness, that is, that God keeps what he promises.

This psalm does not say who wrote it, although tradition has connected it with Moses. At the start, the believer declares that God is his hope and his stronghold; then a voice assures him that God will deliver him from snares and disease. The images of bird, shield and fortress speak of refuge for the one who trusts.

For today: when you feel fear or insecurity, do what the psalmist did: tell God in your own words that you trust him, and remember that his faithfulness is your protection, even when you do not understand everything that is happening.
exp.88:23:
It says that God promises to accompany his servant with his truth (his faithfulness) and his mercy (his steadfast love). "Horn" is an ancient image of strength, power and victory, like the horns of a bull. To be "exalted" means to be lifted up and honored. So, by God's name and authority, his power will grow.

God speaks in a psalm attributed to Ethan the Ezrahite, which recalls the promise made to David that his descendants would reign. God assures him of protection against enemies and firmness in his reign. Many Christians also see here a look ahead to Jesus, a descendant of David, although the psalm speaks first of the king of Israel.

Today we can trust that strength does not depend on us alone. If you walk with God, his faithfulness and his mercy accompany you through trials. Today, ask him to sustain you and trust in his character, not in your own strength.
exp.118:154:
It says that salvation is far from wicked people, because they do not seek God's commands. The word translated here as "salvation" does not refer only to bodily health, but to rescue, deliverance, or being set free. The "wicked" are those who live without taking God into account. Their "statutes" are the rules and instructions that God has given.

The one speaking is the psalmist, whose identity is not known with certainty. He is afflicted and persecuted, yet he remains faithful to God's law. He asks for help and for rescue. In this verse he contrasts his situation with that of the wicked: he seeks God and hopes to be delivered, while they do not even seek him.

For today: if you desire God's help and guidance, seek him sincerely. Set aside time each day to read the Bible and to ask him what he wants to teach you. In this way your trust in him will grow, even in the midst of trials.
exp.48:2:
This verse says that the one speaking will share words of wisdom, and that what he considers deep in his heart is understanding. The word "wisdom" means knowing how to live well, and the word "understanding" means grasping things clearly. The speaker is not boasting; he announces that what he is about to say is worth listening to.

It is a psalm for the sons of Korah, a group of musicians and temple servants in Israel. The author calls out to everyone: rich and poor, important and ordinary. He wants to teach something for all people, and he does so with music and with a riddle, that is, a deep teaching about trusting God in hard times and about the limits of riches.

For today: before you speak or advise others, let the truth first settle in your heart. Meditate, pray, and think carefully, so that your words bring light and not just opinion.
exp.9:15:
This verse says that the Lord is King forever and ever, without beginning or end. It also says that the nations (the "heathen") who occupied his land were destroyed or disappeared. Here the word "heathen" means pagan peoples, not people in general.

The one speaking is the psalmist, probably David, although the text does not say so with certainty. He has spent the whole psalm complaining about the wicked who oppress the poor and the fatherless. Now, with faith, he declares that God reigns and that he has already acted before against the unjust. This gives him confidence that God will also hear the humble.

When you see injustice and it seems that the wicked are winning, remember that God is still King. You can pray with confidence, hand over your pain to him, and in the meantime defend with kindness the one who suffers.
exp.18:0:
The explanation says that the heavens, with everything we see in them, speak of how great and glorious God is. In the verse, the word "declare" means tell or announce. "Firmament" is the vast space of the sky, and "sheweth" here means shows or makes known. What has been created is like a work of art that reveals the hand of the artist.

The one speaking is David, king of Israel, in a psalm dedicated to the chief musician, the leader of the singing in worship. The verses that follow explain that this testimony is silent, yet it reaches everywhere, day after day and night after night. Then the psalm turns to speak of God's Law, showing that God reveals himself both in creation and in his Word.

Today, when you look at the sky, the sunrise or the stars, pause for a moment. Let it lead you to thank God and to trust in his power and care.
exp.117:11:
The explanation says that the enemies surrounded the psalmist like a swarm of bees, loud and threatening. But their attack did not last long, like the fire of thorns, which burns hot and fast and then goes out. The phrase "they compassed me about" means "they surrounded me," and "I will destroy them" here is understood as "I will destroy them" or "I will drive them back," always in the name of the Lord.

Psalm 118 is a song of thanksgiving for a victory. The speaker seems to be a leader or king of Israel, surrounded by nations or enemies. Jewish tradition sang it at the festivals. No one knows for certain who wrote it or which battle it had in mind. The verses that follow show that the victory came from God, not from the speaker's own strength.

When troubles surround you and seem many, do not trust only in your own strength. Pray, remember that God sustains you, and move forward in faith. Many pressures make a great deal of noise, but they do not always last.
exp.88:38:
It says that God seems to have set aside the covenant he made with David, his servant. The word for breaking is not used here, so I will simply say that the covenant was rendered void, and the phrase about the crown being profaned by being cast to the ground means that the royal dignity was thrown down to the dust and treated as worthless. The words about walls being broken down and shame appear in the verses that follow, and they speak of fortifications torn apart and of disgrace.

The one speaking is the psalmist Ethan the Ezrahite, according to the title of the psalm. First he recalls God's promises to David, that his throne would endure. Then, in this part, he looks at reality: the king is humbled and defeated, and it is not known with certainty at what historical moment this happened. He does not deny God, but brings his complaint to him honestly.

For today: when what you are living through seems to contradict God's promises, you do not have to pretend. You can pray with sincerity, even with pain, and continue to rely on the one who is faithful.
exp.134:9:
This verse says that God defeated many nations and took the lives of powerful kings. The word "smote" means that he struck them down or conquered them, and "great nations" means peoples or nations. It continues the list of God's acts on Israel's behalf.

The psalm is a song of praise, and it is not known with certainty who wrote it. It invites God's people to worship him by remembering what he did: the deliverance from Egypt and the conquest of the promised land. The verses that follow name two of those kings, Sihon and Og. The psalmist wants Israel to remember that the victory came from God, not from their own strength.

For today: when you face something that seems too big, remember what God has already done. Recalling his faithfulness in the past strengthens trust and fills the heart with gratitude. You can write down today three moments when God helped you.
exp.38:11:
Here the psalmist asks God to hear him. The phrase "hold not thy peace at my tears" means "do not ignore my weeping." He says that he is a "stranger" and a "sojourner," a person passing through who has no place of his own, and he adds that his fathers were the same.

The psalm is traditionally attributed to David, according to its heading. He is suffering under what he feels to be God's discipline for his sin, and he reflects on how brief and fragile life is. His weeping is sincere, and he comes to God not with pride but with humility. Some understand "stranger" to also speak of his complete dependence on God.

For today: if you feel like you are just passing through, weak, or in pain, you can weep before God without pretending to be strong. He does not despise your tears. Remembering that this life is brief helps us to trust Him more and to live with humility.
exp.2:2:
He says that God protects David on every side, like a shield that surrounds him. "Glory" here means that God is his honor and his true pride. "Lifter up of my head" means that God raises him up, encourages him, and restores his dignity when he is downcast.

The speaker is David, the king of Israel, while he flees from his son Absalom, who rebelled against him. Many have turned against him, and some even say that God is no longer going to save him. In the face of those voices, David answers with the word "But": although everything seems lost, God is his defense. Shortly afterward he sleeps in peace because he trusts in Him.

When you find yourself surrounded by criticism, fear, or pressure, do not stay alone listening to what others say. Tell God what you feel, and remember who you are in Him. His care surrounds you, even when you cannot see it.
exp.58:9:
It says that God, who is full of mercy and kindness, will go out ahead of the psalmist to help him. The word for "will go before me" is an old word that means "will come before" or "will arrive first." And the phrase about letting him see his desire upon his enemies means that God will allow him to see how his adversaries end up, that is, he will see God's justice acting upon them.

The psalm's heading says David speaks here when Saul sent men to watch his house in order to kill him. He is surrounded by violent people and places his trust in God as his defense. Some scholars understand his "desire" to be the fulfillment of justice, not simple personal revenge.

For today: when you feel attacked or unfairly treated, trust that God is already going ahead of you. Bring your distress to him in prayer, ask him for justice, and also for a heart free of resentment, and rest in the knowledge that he works in his own time.
exp.86:5:
God says he will keep a record of all the peoples, like a census, and when he writes down people from foreign nations he will say, "This one was born in Zion." The word "count" here means that he will tally or register them, and "Selah" is a musical pause or a moment to reflect; its exact meaning is not certain.
