The psalm was written by the sons of Korah to celebrate Zion, the city of God. Rahab (a poetic name for Egypt), Babylon, and other nations that were once enemies or far away appear here as included. Some see in this a reference to scattered Jews, and others see foreigners who become part of God's people.

Today it reminds us that before God, belonging to him matters more than our origin or our past. Welcome with kindness anyone who may seem distant, because God can also count them as his own.
exp.110:8:
This verse says that God sent redemption, that is, deliverance and rescue, to his people. It also says that he established his covenant, his solemn promise, forever. And it declares that his name is holy and reverend. The word "reverend" here does not mean evil, but rather it inspires reverent awe, like something worthy of wonder and respect.

The psalm does not say who wrote it. It is a song of praise that remembers the works of God. Many think of the deliverance from Egypt, although the text does not make this clear. Earlier it speaks of his faithful works, and then it says that the fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom.

Today, we can remember how God has been faithful and be freed from our burdens. That leads us to live with gratitude and respect, taking him seriously without being afraid of him, because his promises do not change.
exp.85:3:
David asks God to fill his inner life with joy. "Soul" here means his whole being, his person and his emotions. A "servant" is someone who serves God with humility. "Lift up my soul" means that he directs toward God his whole heart, his desires and his trust.

The psalm is presented as a prayer of David. The one speaking is in a time of distress, surrounded by difficulties, and so he cries out to God all day long. His words nearby show that he trusts God to be good, forgiving and attentive. He asks for joy because he knows that only God can truly give it.

For today: when you feel burdened or sad, before seeking relief in other things, pray honestly and bring God your thoughts and emotions. Ask Him for joy, and remember who He is: good, near and merciful.
exp.70:5:
It says that God has cared for and supported the author since before he was born. Being "supported" means being held up and sustained. The phrase about the womb refers to the mother's body before birth. God is the one who brought him out into the light, and for this reason he promises that his praise will always be directed to Him.

The psalm does not say who wrote it. The one speaking is an elderly person, who looks back over his whole life and asks to be rescued from wicked and violent people. Before making his request, he recalls that God has been his hope since his youth. His confidence rests on a long history with God, not only on the moment of difficulty.

For today: when you face a problem, take time to remember the times God has held you up, even in things you did not notice. Write them down and thank Him for them. Remembering His past faithfulness strengthens trust for the present and turns worry into praise.
exp.143:2:
This verse asks a question full of wonder: what is a human being, that God knows him and takes account of him?

David speaks in this psalm. First he praises God as his rock, his refuge, and his deliverer in battle. Then he pauses to think about how small a human being is, whose days pass like a shadow. His wonder comes from seeing that a God so great would care for someone so frail. Some readers see here an echo of Psalm 8.

For today: when you feel small or unimportant, remember that God knows you and cares for you. Give thanks for his care and trust in him, instead of relying only on your own strength.
exp.104:26:
It says that Moses and Aaron announced God's signs and carried out his wonders, that is, astonishing miracles, in Egypt. The name "Ham" is another way of writing Cam, the name the psalm uses as a poetic synonym for Egypt. "They shewed his signs among them" can be understood as meaning that they spoke and displayed those signs among the Egyptians.

The psalmist praises God by recalling the history of Israel. Here he relates how God sent Moses and Aaron to Egypt, where his people were mistreated. After this verse the plagues begin to be named, such as the darkness and the water turned into blood. The purpose is to thank God for his faithfulness.

For today: God acts even when evil seems to dominate. We can trust that he keeps his promises, and remembering what he has done in our lives helps us give him thanks and wait with patience.
exp.131:9:
It says that God should not reject his "anointed," that is, the chosen and consecrated king to govern his people. The request rests on the memory of David, called God's servant. "Turn not away the face" means not turning your back on him or withholding your favor.

The psalm is a prayer of the people, perhaps when the ark was being brought into the temple. They ask that God dwell among them and bless the king. They rely on the promise God made to David: that his descendants would reign. Scholars debate which king they had in mind, but many Christians also see here a sign pointing to Jesus, the Anointed descendant of David.

For today: when you pray, do not rely on your merits, but on God's promises and on the work of Christ. You can draw near with confidence, because God is faithful to what he has promised.
exp.100:3:
This verse says that the person with a crooked heart, that is, the one who leans toward evil and lies, will not have a place near the one speaking. "Froward" means bent away from what is good, so the word refers to a heart turned aside from righteousness. The phrase "I will not know a wicked person" means that he will have no fellowship or friendship with such a person, not that he is unaware the person exists.

It is a psalm of David, and many read it as his statement of purpose in ruling. He promises to live with integrity in his house and to surround himself with faithful people. That is why he says he will not tolerate wickedness in his close circle, either in conduct or among his advisers.

For today: be careful about whom you associate with and whom you give influence over your life. This does not mean despising anyone, since Jesus dealt with sinners. It means not letting evil teach you its ways. Begin by examining your own heart and asking God to cleanse it.
exp.34:0:
David asks God here to be his defender. The word "plead" means to take up a cause, the way a lawyer or a warrior takes the side of someone. "Them that strive" and "them that fight" refer to those who attack him and oppose him. It is as if he were saying: "Lord, take my side and stand against my enemies."

David is the speaker, and the title identifies this as one of his psalms. He feels attacked and pursued, and he does not trust in his own strength but cries out to God. The verses that follow use images of war, such as the shield and the spear, to ask for help. It is not known with certainty at what exact moment of his life he wrote it, and several situations have been suggested.

When someone treats you unjustly, you do not have to respond with revenge. You can bring your pain to God in prayer, with sincerity, and ask him to be your defender while you seek to act with honesty and peace.
exp.133:0:
It says that everyone who serves God should praise him. "Song of degrees" is a title repeated in several psalms and probably indicates songs of ascent, though its exact meaning is not known for certain. The word for "behold" means "look" or "pay attention." "Bless" means to speak well of God, give him thanks, and acknowledge his greatness. The phrase "you who stand by night" refers to those who served through the night in the temple.

It is the last of the songs of ascent. The author is not named. It seems that someone is calling to the guards or priests who looked after the temple at night. Perhaps the pilgrims encouraged them as they departed. The following verses seem to bring the reply, with a blessing for them. Some believe it was sung as a dialogue.

For today: even in quiet, tired hours, or when no one sees you, your work and your prayer can be praise. Today, before going to sleep, give thanks to God out loud.
exp.65:9:
God says that he put his people to the test. The words "proved" and "tried" mean to examine something thoroughly. The comparison is with silver: it is heated in the fire until it melts and its impurities are removed. In this way the people were purified and showed what they really were. Where the explanation comments on the wording, it refers to the phrase "thou hast tried us," which means "you put us to the test."

The psalmist speaks together with the whole people, in the first person plural. He praises God because God sustained them and delivered them from great dangers. The verses that follow speak of a net, oppression, fire and waters, and of being brought out into abundance. It is not known with certainty which historical moment is described, and scholars interpret it in different ways.

For today: when you go through a difficulty, do not immediately think that God has abandoned you. You can ask him to use that trial to strengthen your faith and remove what is unnecessary. Trust that he accompanies you and will bring you through.
exp.15:9:
He says that God will not leave the soul of the one speaking in the grave (in Hebrew, Sheol, the place of the dead). "Your holy one" refers to someone faithful to God. "Corruption" is the decay of the body after death. In other words: God will not leave him abandoned in death.

David writes this psalm as a prayer of trust. He keeps God always before him, and that is why he feels secure; even his body rests in peace. In the New Testament, Peter (Acts 2) and Paul (Acts 13) apply this verse to the resurrection of Jesus. Scholars debate how much David was thinking of himself and how much of the Messiah, but the apostles see it fully fulfilled in Christ.

For today: when you face fear or loss, remember that death does not have the final word for those who trust in God. Set the Lord before you each day, and rest in his promise of life.
exp.71:1:
It says that the king will rule God's people with justice, that is, in an upright and correct way. He will also treat the "afflicted," who are the poor, the humbled, or the mistreated, with "judgment," meaning with good discernment and fair decisions. The word "judge" here means to govern and defend what is right, not only to condemn.

The psalm carries the heading "For Solomon." It can be understood as a prayer for Solomon or as something he wrote, and it has also been read as a hope for the perfect king who would come. The speaker asks God to give the king his own justice, so that the people may live in peace and the weak may be protected.

Today we can pray for those who govern, asking that they act with justice. And each of us, in our work, family, or church, can treat with respect and fairness those who have less voice or less power.
exp.67:9:
The explanation says that God's people, called "your congregation" (your flock), have lived and settled in the land He gave them. And that God, out of pure goodness, has cared for the poor and provided them with what they need.

The psalm is by David, a song of praise to the God who delivers and accompanies His people. Earlier it speaks of Sinai and of the rain that refreshed the weary land. Some understand "therein" as the land of Israel; others understand it as the "inheritance" mentioned before. The central point is that God sustains His weak and needy people.

For today: if you have what you need, remember that it comes from God's goodness, not only from your own effort. That invites us to share generously with those who have less, because God himself cares for the poor.
exp.143:0:
This verse is a song of praise. David blesses the Lord, whom he calls "my rock," that is, his firm and secure refuge. He says that God "teacheth my hands to war" and "my fingers to fight," acknowledging that his skill in fighting comes from God. To "bless" means to praise or to be thankful for.

The title attributes the psalm to David, king of Israel, a man who lived through many battles. Here he does not boast of his strength or his training, but gives the credit to God. The following verses call God his fortress, his shield, and his deliverer. Shortly after, he humbly asks why God pays attention to human beings. Some scholars think the psalm was composed in times of war, but this is not certain.

Today we can recognize that our abilities, such as work, study, or patience, are a gift from God. Before facing a challenge, we can pray, giving thanks and asking for wisdom, instead of relying only on ourselves.
exp.77:58:
This verse says that God heard the idolatry and rebellion of Israel, was filled with anger, and firmly rejected them. The phrase meaning "he heard it" is rendered as "when God heard this," and the word for "became angry" is rendered as "he was wroth." The word "abhorred" here expresses a very strong rejection, not hatred without reason.

Psalm 78 is a poem by Asaph that reviews the history of Israel. It aims to teach new generations not to repeat their parents' mistakes. Here the psalmist speaks of the time when the people worshiped in high places (places of idolatrous worship) and with carved images. As a consequence, God left Shiloh, where the tabernacle stood, and allowed the ark to fall into enemy hands.

For today: God grieves when we give our hearts to other things. Examine honestly what holds first place in your life, and return to God with humility; he forgives those who repent.
exp.95:2:
It says we should tell all the nations how great and glorious God is, and speak of his wonders before all peoples. "Tell" means to recount or announce. The nations or peoples that were not Israel are the ones meant here. "Glory" is his greatness and his admirable character.

It is a psalm of praise. The one speaking is the psalmist, who is not identified here; the tradition in Chronicles connects it with David, though scholars debate this. It invites Israel to sing and also to share with other peoples who the LORD is. The verses that follow give the reason: the gods of the nations are idols, but the LORD made the heavens.

For today: think of something concrete God has done in your life and tell it this week to someone who does not know him. You don't need a speech; a simple testimony, shared with gratitude and without pressure, is enough.
exp.49:12:
God asks a question that already contains its answer: will I eat the flesh of bulls, or drink the blood of goats? The answer is no. The goats in question are full-grown ones. The word "or" is not a problem in this verse.

God himself is speaking, addressing his people in this psalm of Asaph. He does not rebuke the sacrifices themselves, which he had commanded, but the idea that he needed them as food. Every animal and the whole world already belong to him. What God is looking for is a thankful heart, one that keeps what it has promised and trusts in him.

For today: do not treat your religious practices, such as going to church, giving, or singing, as if they were doing God a favor. Come to him with sincere gratitude, keep what you have promised, and call on him in your hard moments.
exp.137:3:
It says that all the kings of the earth will praise the Lord and give thanks when they hear the words that come out of his mouth. The word "shall praise" is the same idea as "will give thanks" or "will acknowledge," and the word "words" here means sayings or promises.

The psalm is written by David, according to its title. He gives thanks to God because God answered him when he cried out and gave him strength. From that personal experience, he looks further and hopes that even the rulers of the world will acknowledge God. The verses that follow say that God takes notice of the humble. It is not known with certainty when or how this would happen; some see it as a hope for the future.

For today: when God helps you, do not keep the testimony only to yourself. His Word can reach any person, no matter their position. Share humbly what God has done in your life, and pray for those who govern.
exp.81:4:
They do not know, nor do they understand. They walk on in darkness, that is, without moral light to guide them. The "foundations of the earth" are the bases that hold up order and justice in society, and here they are shaking because those who should protect them are failing.

God speaks in this psalm of Asaph, presenting himself as judging in the midst of the rulers. Many understand these rulers to be human judges or governors, though some scholars interpret them as spiritual beings. He accuses them of defending the wicked and of abandoning the poor and the fatherless. When justice is corrupted, the whole social order weakens.

For today: if you have any authority, even a small one, in your family, your work, or your church, use it with justice. Ask God for light, and defend those who have less voice or less power.
exp.140:3:
David asks God not to let his heart turn toward what is evil. He prays that God will not allow him to be drawn into wicked deeds together with those who practice wrongdoing. The "delights" are the pleasures or feasts of those people, and to "eat" of them means to take part in and enjoy their way of life.

David is the one speaking, according to the title of the psalm. He is in distress and prays with urgency, like incense rising to God. Earlier he asked God to guard his mouth; now he asks that God guard his heart as well. He recognizes that he can be tempted, and that he cannot rely on himself alone. The exact details of his situation are not known for certain.

For today: do not rely only on your own willpower. Ask God each day to guide your desires, and stay away from settings and friendships that make what harms your faith look appealing.
exp.118:119:
The explanation says that the psalmist's body trembles out of reverence toward God. "Flesh" refers to his whole physical being, and the word rendered "trembleth" conveys that he shivers, that a chill runs through him. "Judgments" are God's just decisions and rulings, and "I am afraid" expresses a deep respect, not a hopeless terror.

The speaker is the author of Psalm 119, a believer who loves God's word. He has just seen that God rejects the wicked and those who turn away from his commands. That leads him to take God seriously. Later he will ask for protection against those who oppress him, so his fear and his trust go together.

Today we can ask God for a heart that takes him seriously. Before justifying a bad decision, stop and think: "How does God see this?" That reverence draws us close to him and protects us.
exp.72:10:
This verse shows what the wicked say with arrogance. They ask, "How doth God know?" and "Is there knowledge in the most High?" In other words, they act as if God does not see or notice anything. The phrase "in the most High" refers to God, who is in heaven.

The writer is Asaph, who is confused and nearly slips in his faith because he sees the wicked prospering. Here he describes how they speak: with pride, mocking God. Some scholars think verse 10 is obscure and is interpreted in several ways, but the general idea of this verse is clear: they deny that God calls them to account.

For today: when injustice seems to win and God seems not to see, do not doubt His knowledge. Bring your confusion to Him in prayer, as Asaph did, and trust that He sees everything and judges with justice.
exp.74:6:
It says that God is the one who judges and decides the fate of people: some he brings low, and others he lifts up and honors. No one rises or falls by pure chance.

The psalm is by Asaph, a singer in the temple. It speaks in the middle of a celebration to God, and it rebukes the proud who boast of their power (raising the horn was an image of arrogance). It reminds them that rising does not come from any point on the map, but from God. Then it speaks of the cup of judgment that the wicked will drink. Some scholars think the psalm relates to some national deliverance, but this is not known with certainty.

For today: if you receive an achievement, thank God for it with humility and do not boast. If you have to wait or you are ignored, trust that God sees and judges with justice.
exp.48:1:
This verse says that the message of the psalm is for everyone, regardless of their position. The common people are the ordinary folk, and those of important family are the highborn. In the Hebrew original, the phrase resembles "sons of Adam and sons of men," meaning people of humble condition and people of high rank. Rich and poor are placed together, on the same level, before the same teaching.

The speaker is a psalmist, and the psalm is attributed to the sons of Korah, a family of Levites who served with music in worship. He calls all the peoples because he is going to share a reflection on wealth and death, something that affects every person. He himself says he will speak with wisdom and with music of the harp.

For today: listen to the Word of God with humility, no matter how much you have or how much you lack. Before God, neither your money nor your position gives you an advantage, and we all need his wisdom.
exp.16:13:
David asks God to rescue him from people who live only for this world. The old text speaks of those whose bellies are filled with your hidden treasure; the word for filling means satisfying, and the little ones are their young children. These men have plenty: they eat well and leave an inheritance to their children. But their only reward is this present life.

David speaks out of distress, pursued by violent enemies who lurk like lions. Some think he means Saul and his men, but the psalm does not say so clearly. His contrast comes right after: he hopes to see God's face in righteousness.

Today we can ask ourselves what we truly seek. It is not wrong to have possessions, but it is wrong to live only for them. When you see those who ignore God prospering, do not become bitter; place your hope in being with Him, who satisfies the soul as nothing in this world can.
exp.21:22:
You that fear the Lord, praise him. The verse calls everyone who honors and respects God to praise him. The word "fear" here does not mean being afraid, but deep reverence and respect. The phrase "glorify him" means to recognize and proclaim how great he is. The word "seed" means descendants, so the whole people of Israel, the children of Jacob, are called to praise God and to respect him.

David speaks here, according to the title of the psalm. After describing very great suffering, he turns to praise. He invites the congregation to join him, because God did not despise the afflicted one or hide his face from him, but heard him when he cried out. Christians see in this psalm a foreshadowing of Jesus, who quotes its first verse on the cross.

Today, when God helps you through a difficulty, do not keep your gratitude to yourself. Tell your family or your church, so that others may also trust in him.
exp.115:12:
It says that the psalmist will answer God's goodness by lifting "the cup of salvation," that is, the cup of salvation or deliverance, and calling on the name of the Lord. "The Lord" is the name of God, and "call upon" means to call on him with thankfulness and trust. "Salvation" here does not speak only of good physical health, but of rescue.

The one speaking is a believer who was delivered from a serious danger, perhaps from death (vv. 3-8). He had grown discouraged and said that every person is a liar. Then he asks how he can repay God. His answer is not to give something great, but to receive with gratitude and worship. Some think the cup refers to a drink offering or to a thanksgiving meal; this is not certain.

For today: when God helps you, do not walk past it. Take a moment to thank him out loud and, if you can, tell others about it.
exp.67:5:
This verse says that God gives a home to those who are alone and sets prisoners free. "Living in families" means living together with others, in a house. "Chains" are the shackles placed on the feet. A "dry land" is parched, lifeless ground. The "rebellious" are those who refuse to submit to God.

King David speaks in a song of praise. Just before this, he has called God "a father to the fatherless and a defender of widows," and then he recalls how God led his people through the wilderness. Many understand that he is celebrating God's care for the weak and the deliverance from Egypt, though scholars debate which exact moment he has in mind.

For today: if God cares for the lonely, we can care for them too. Invite someone who is alone to your table, or visit a person who is alone, an elderly neighbor or a newcomer to the country. In this way you reflect the heart of God.
exp.37:7:
He says the psalmist is very weak and broken, like someone beaten until they have no strength left. "Broken" means crushed or worn down. "Roared" means crying out or groaning with force, like a roar of pain. "Disquietness of my heart" speaks of deep unrest and anguish within.

The psalm is said, in its heading, to be by David, described as a prayer of remembrance. He is sick and feels that his suffering is tied to his sin and to God's discipline. He also feels alone and exhausted. Scholars agree that it describes both physical and emotional pain, though it is not known with certainty what illness he had.

For today: when pain overwhelms you, do not hide it or disguise it. Tell God honestly, as David did. He already knows your sigh and listens to you.
exp.110:0:
It says that the one writing wants to praise God with his whole heart, that is, with sincerity and holding nothing back. The words "Praise ye the Lord" are the opening call to praise. The phrase "in the assembly of the upright" refers to the gathered group, and "the upright" are the honest and just people who seek to live well before God.

The psalm does not say who wrote it; the text gives no name for the author. It is a song of praise in which the writer speaks in the first person, and then it gives the reasons for praising: God's works are great and beautiful, and his righteousness endures. It seems meant to be sung together with the gathered people, although the exact occasion is not known.

For today: do not praise God only when you are alone. Seek out a group of believers, take part in your church's gathering, and praise with sincerity, remembering something specific that God has done for you.
exp.135:13:
It says that God made Israel pass through the middle of the Red Sea, which we call today the Red Sea. "Made pass through" means that he led them to the other side. The quoted phrase "á" is just an old way of writing "a," so that sentence is deleted. Each verse ends by repeating that God's mercy is forever, that is, his faithful love never runs out.

This is a psalm of praise, and it is not known for certain who wrote it. It remembers creation and the history of Israel, above all the departure from Egypt, told in Exodus 14. The people sang this psalm to remember that God had rescued them and that his care does not change.

When you feel trapped, with no way out, remember how God has cared for you and for others before. Write down today one occasion when he helped you and give him thanks, trusting that his mercy still stands firm.
exp.54:10:
It says that inside the city there is injustice and harm done to others. Offenses are wrongs or abuses. Deceit and trickery are lies and schemes used to gain an advantage. And the open squares are the wide streets and public places where people gather and do business. In other words, wickedness does not stay hidden: it is out in the open, in the center of everyday life.

The psalm is spoken by David, according to its title, although some scholars debate at what point in his life he wrote it. He is distressed and asks God to restrain the wicked. He sees violence and corruption in the city, and his pain grows because, as the following verses say, the betrayal comes from a close friend.

For today: when you see injustice or deceit around you, do not keep it silent or let it turn you bitter. Bring it honestly before God, as David did, and ask him to keep you honest in your own dealings.
exp.118:139:
Your word is very pure, like gold or silver that has been refined by fire until it is free of all impurity. That is why the psalmist, whom it calls your servant, loves it. His love grows from seeing that this word is clean and trustworthy.

Psalm 119 is a long poem in honor of God's law. No one knows for certain who wrote it. The one speaking feels surrounded by enemies who forget God's words, and in the verses that follow he describes himself as small and despised. Even so, his love for Scripture does not change.

When you feel pressed down or little valued, return to the Bible. Read it calmly each day, not out of obligation, but because in it you find a pure and firm truth that sustains you.
exp.127:5:
It says that whoever fears God will receive a very great blessing: living long enough to see his grandchildren, and seeing peace upon the people of Israel. In this older wording, the verb shown here as "see" means to live to see, and the phrase "children's children" refers to grandchildren.

This is one of the "songs of ascents," which the people sang as they went up to Jerusalem. No one knows for certain who wrote it. It speaks to a man who honors God and describes a blessed life: work, family, and community. It ends with a wish for peace for the whole people, not only for one household.

Today we can value family and pray to God for peace in our community. A life that honors God is not lived for oneself alone. Today you can pray for your children, your grandchildren, and your church or country, and seek peace with those around you.
exp.73:1:
Here the psalmist asks God to remember his people, whom he bought and set free long ago. "Congregation" is the community of Israel. The phrase about the rod of God's inheritance refers to the tribe or people who belong to God as his own possession. The word about redeeming means that he rescued them, as when he brought them out of Egypt. It mentions Mount Zion, where God dwelt in the temple.

The one speaking is Asaph, or someone from his group of singers. It is a lament from a people who feel God is far away, probably after the destruction of the sanctuary. Scholars debate whether it refers to the fall of Jerusalem in 586 BC or to another event. That is why it reminds God of what he has already done.

For today: when you feel abandoned, pray by remembering God's past works and his faithfulness. Ask him honestly, without hiding your pain, resting on what he has already done for you.
exp.144:16:
God is righteous in all his ways, and in everything he does, meaning in the way he governs and acts. The verse also says he is merciful, that is, compassionate and kind, in all his works.

This psalm is attributed to David and is a song of praise to the greatness of God. Earlier, the psalmist speaks of how God provides food for all living things. Afterward, he says that God is near to those who call on him sincerely. In this way, the verse joins his righteousness and his mercy as the basis for that nearness.

For today: when you don't understand what is happening in your life, remember that God does not stop being righteous or kind. You can pray sincerely, trusting that he hears you and cares for you, even when you do not yet see the answer.
exp.134:8:
It says that God sent signs and wonders into the midst of Egypt, aimed at Pharaoh and all his servants, that is, his attendants and officials. "Signs" are acts that show God's power, and "wonders" are marvels beyond the ordinary. Here the plagues that came before Israel's departure are recalled.

This psalm is a song of praise addressed to God's people and to those who serve in his house. No one knows for certain who wrote it. The psalmist reviews what God did in creation and in the history of Israel. Remembering Egypt, and then Sihon, Og and Canaan, helps him show that the Lord is greater than any human power.

For today: when you face something that seems stronger than you, remember what God has already done. Make a list of the times he helped you, and trust that he continues to care for his own.
exp.77:6:
This verse says that God wanted his people to learn three things: to place their trust in him, not to forget what he has done, and to obey his commandments. To "keep" his commandments means to carry them out and take care of them. The "works of God" are his mighty actions on behalf of Israel.

The speaker is the psalmist, called Asaph in the title of the psalm. He is telling the story of Israel. He explains that parents were to teach the law to their children, and they to their own, so that each generation would know God. Then he mentions that many before them failed: they were rebellious and forgot God, as the tribe of Ephraim did in battle.

For today: at home or in your church, tell how God has helped you. Sharing your experiences with God with your children, nephews, nieces, or young friends helps faith pass from one generation to the next so that it is not forgotten.
exp.84:6:
Here the people ask God to let them see his mercy, that is, his faithful love and his compassion. They also ask for "salud," a word from an older usage that here means salvation: rescue, help, and restoration. It is a short and sincere prayer, offered with empty hands.

The psalm is written by the sons of Korah and speaks on behalf of God's people. They seem to have lived through a difficult time, perhaps after a restoration that never fully satisfied them, and they feel that God is angry. Scholars do not agree on the exact date. So they ask whether his anger will last forever and beg him to give them life again.

Today we can pray this way when we feel far from God: without excuses, trusting in his mercy and not in our own merits. Ask him to show you his love, and wait for his answer, because he speaks peace to those who fear him.
exp.91:11:
The righteous person, the one who lives uprightly before God, says the explanation, will prosper and be seen as beautiful and strong, like a palm tree. They will also grow like a cedar of Lebanon, a tall, firm, and long-lasting tree. The explanation of "flourish" means they will bear fruit and live with vitality. The "righteous" are those who try to live according to God's will.

The psalm is a song of praise, and its heading associates it with the Sabbath day. We do not know with certainty who wrote it. The author thanks God for his faithfulness and contrasts the fleeting fate of the wicked, who sprout like grass and wither, with that of the righteous, who remain. The following verses explain the secret: they are planted in the house of the LORD.

For today: if you want a firm and fruitful life, seek to be well rooted in God through prayer, his Word, and the community of faith. In this way you can bear fruit even in difficult times and throughout the years.
exp.26:5:
God says he will lift up the psalmist's head above his enemies who surround him. "To exalt" means to raise up, to give honor. Therefore, the psalmist vows to offer sacrifices with joy in the house of God, that is, offerings made with gladness. To sing psalms means to praise with music.

Tradition says David is speaking, according to the heading of the psalm. He is surrounded by dangers, but he trusts that God protects him, as he said before: God hides him in his tabernacle and sets him high upon a rock. His confidence is not pride but faith. Even so, in the next verse he asks God for help, which shows that confidence and sincere prayer go together.

Today, before your problem is resolved, you can begin to give thanks and sing to God. Choose a song of praise or a psalm, and express your trust to him in the middle of what you are facing.
exp.8:14:
This verse says that the enemy nations fell into the same pit they had dug. They also got caught in the net they had hidden for others.

David is speaking here, giving thanks to God for rescuing him from his enemies. He describes how the harm they planned against him turned back on themselves. The verses that follow say that in this way God made himself known as a just judge. Some read this as a particular historical event, and others as a general principle; the text does not give more detail.

For today: do not repay evil with evil or set traps for anyone. If someone wrongs you, entrust your cause to God and trust that he is just. Better to seek to do good, because evil tends to come back on the one who plans it.
exp.101:8:
It says the psalmist eats ashes as if they were bread and mixes his tears into what he drinks. It is a picture of deep sorrow: the grief is so great that everything tastes bitter to him. Weeping means crying, and the phrase "as if" conveys that this is an image rather than a literal act.

Psalm 102 carries the heading "A prayer of the afflicted." No one knows with certainty who wrote it. The speaker is sick, alone, and mocked by his enemies, and he feels that God himself has let him fall. Some think it also reflects the pain of Israel in exile, though this is understood in different ways. Further on, the psalm turns toward trust in a God who endures forever.

For today: when pain takes away your appetite and your strength, do not hide it. Bring it honestly before God, as this psalmist does. He does not conceal his weeping; he turns it into prayer, and God hears him.
exp.24:19:
He asks God to watch over his life and rescue him from danger. "Keep my soul" means "protect my life." "Let me not be ashamed" means that he should not be left humiliated or disappointed. The reason he gives is simple: "I put my trust in you." His trust in God is the reason for his plea.

It is a psalm attributed to David, written in a time of distress. He acknowledges his sins, speaks of enemies who hate him with violence, and seeks refuge in God. The exact details of his situation are not mentioned, so we do not know which moment of his life it refers to.

When you feel threatened, pressured, or afraid of falling short, make a sincere prayer like this one. Tell God what you feel, acknowledge your failures, and place your trust in Him. You do not have to pretend to be strong: you can ask Him to watch over you and sustain you.
exp.88:12:
It says that God has an arm full of courage, a strong hand, and a right hand (his right hand) lifted up or exalted. In the Bible, the arm and the hand represent the power with which God acts. The right hand was a symbol of authority and victory.

The psalm is written by Ethan the Ezrahite, according to its title. It praises God as Creator and king, before recalling the promise made to David. The verses before speak of God founding the world, and the following ones say that his throne rests on righteousness and justice. Thus, his strength is neither violent nor capricious, but good and faithful.

For today: when you feel weak or facing a great problem, remember that God's power is joined to his justice, mercy, and truth. You can pray with confidence, knowing that your life is in strong and good hands.
exp.32:9:
The explanation says that God undoes the plans of the nations and makes the projects of the peoples fail. The phrase about making them "of no effect" means that He cancels them and leaves them without result. The word for "nations" here refers to nations or peoples, and the plans referred to are schemes and strategies, sometimes with bad intent.

This psalm is a song of praise, and it is traditionally attributed to David, although the text itself does not say so. The psalmist invites everyone to honor God, because He created the world by His word. Then he sets human plans, which can fail, against God's counsel, which stands forever. His purpose is to give confidence to the people who follow Him.

Today we can rest when we see injustice or human plans that seem unstoppable. We can do what is right, pray, and trust that God has the final word.
exp.36:13:
This verse describes the wicked as if they were at war: they draw the sword and string the bow. The word that was translated as "drawn out" means they pulled back the bowstring, ready to shoot. Their aim is to attack the poor, the needy, and those who live uprightly.

This is a psalm of David, written as wise counsel for those who suffer injustice. Earlier, the psalmist said that the wicked plot against the righteous, but that God laughs, because he sees that their day is coming. Then he promises that the sword will turn against them and their bow will be broken. His purpose is to calm the anguish of believers.

Today, when you see abuse or injustice, do not fill yourself with resentment or fear. Hand your pain over to God, keep living with integrity, and, if you can, help the person who is being mistreated.
exp.49:9:
God says that every animal of the forest belongs to him, and also the thousands of animals that roam the hills. Nothing in nature is foreign to him.

In this psalm, which is attributed to Asaph, God himself speaks, like a judge before his people. He does not rebuke them for neglecting the sacrifices, since they were offering them. The problem was thinking that God needed them, as if he depended on their offerings. He reminds them that everything already belongs to him, and that what he seeks is a grateful and obedient heart.

For today: what we give to God, whether time, money, or service, does not meet any need of his. We should give it with gratitude and sincerity, recognizing that everything we have comes from him, and not as an attempt to buy his favor.
exp.6:10:
This verse says that God is the judge of the righteous, that is, of those who try to live well, and that he is also angry with the wicked every day. The word "wicked" refers to someone who lives without respect for God. Being angry means being stirred to indignation at wrongdoing. Some translations say that God is angered each day, or that he is a righteous judge.

David speaks here, crying out to God because he is being pursued and falsely accused. He does not defend himself through revenge, but places his cause in the hands of the Judge who knows the depths of the heart. The verses that follow show that God calls people to change before he acts.

For today: when you feel treated unjustly, do not carry the bitterness alone. Pray, entrust your case to God, and examine your own heart, trusting that he judges with truth and with justice.
exp.106:6:
This verse says that God led his people along a straight road, that is, a safe path without detours, so that they would arrive at an inhabited city. The phrase "led them forth by the right way" means that he guided them on a path that was correct and secure, and "a city of habitation" refers to a place where people could live, with houses, food, and rest.

The psalm is written by an unnamed author. It speaks to those who have been rescued by God. Before this, it describes people lost in the wilderness, hungry and thirsty, who cried out to God. Many understand it as a memory of Israel in the desert, though it can also apply to any traveler who has been rescued. For that reason the psalmist invites them to give thanks.

For today: when you feel lost or without a way out, cry out to God with sincerity. He can guide you step by step, even if the path is not the one you imagined. Then remember to thank him for what he has already done.
exp.40:10:
Here David says that he will know God is pleased with him when his enemy cannot mock him or celebrate his fall.

The phrase "I will know" in the verse is the key idea, and it means "I will know" in the sense of finding out for sure. To be "pleased with" someone means that God takes delight in him. And "triumph over me" means that his enemy does not gloat at his misfortune.

David speaks as one who is sick and weak, surrounded by people who wish him harm. Even a close friend, with whom he shared his table, betrayed him. So he asks God for mercy and hopes that God will raise him up. Some see here a foreshadowing of Judas, since Jesus quoted verse 9 (John 13:18).

For today: when someone wounds you or rejoices in your fall, do not sink into revenge. Hand your pain over to God, trust in his mercy, and remember that his favor is worth more than the opinion of your enemies.
exp.88:7:
This verse is a question full of wonder: no one compares with the LORD, the God of hosts, that is, the one who rules over all the powers of heaven and earth. It says that he is mighty and that his faithfulness, or truth, surrounds him like a constant company.

Psalm 89 is a prayer by Ethan the Ezrahite. It praises God for his greatness and for his faithfulness to the promise made to David. Before and after this verse it speaks of the heavenly beings and of God's rule over the sea and his enemies. Later the psalmist complains because the condition of the kingdom seems to contradict that promise.

For today: when your problems seem enormous, remember who God is. Say to him in prayer, "No one is like you," and trust that his faithfulness surrounds you, even when you do not understand what is happening.
exp.33:16:
This verse says that when the righteous cry out to God, he hears them and rescues them from all their troubles. "Cry" means to call out for help, with urgency and great feeling. The phrase about God delivering them is the same idea: he took them out of danger and set them free.

David speaks in this psalm. According to its heading, he wrote it when he pretended to be mad before Abimelech and managed to escape. That is why he speaks from his own experience of being rescued. The verses that follow also make clear that God is near to those who are broken in heart, and they say that the righteous go through many hardships. So being delivered does not mean that there will be no suffering, but that God sustains and rescues his people in the middle of it.

Today, when you are in distress, do not keep quiet or bear it alone: speak honestly with God. He hears you, even though help may come in his own time and in ways you did not expect.
exp.1:8:
It says that the king chosen by God will defeat the nations that rebel. "Breaking them" means smashing them; "rod of iron" is a scepter or staff of firm authority; "dashing them in pieces" means shattering them. The image is that of a clay pot smashed into a thousand fragments: nothing can withstand its power.

The one speaking is the Son, the anointed king, who declares the decree of the LORD: God has given him the nations as his inheritance. The psalm shows earthly kings rebelling against God, and it ends with a call to them to understand and submit. Christians see Jesus Christ here, as the New Testament does (Revelation 19:15). Some scholars think it first spoke of the kings of Israel.

For today: do not trust in your own power or resist God. He offers correction before judgment, so today you can humble yourself, listen to him, and serve him with reverence and joy.
exp.19:3:
This verse is a prayer of blessing: it asks that God would grant someone what their heart desires and bring all their plans to fulfillment. "Grant thee" means "give you," and "counsel" here means the purpose or plan that someone has thought out.

It is a psalm of David, and it seems that the people are speaking on behalf of the king before going into battle. They offer sacrifices and ask for help from the sanctuary. Some scholars believe these are the voices of the people or of priests; the text does not make this entirely clear. The king's desire is joined to trust in the God of Israel.

For today: we can pray this way for others, asking that their plans be aligned with God's will and succeed. Before asking, it is good to commit our desires to God so that He may purify and guide them.
exp.108:8:
It says that the enemy the psalmist speaks of should lose his life, so that his children are left without a father and his wife without a husband. It is a very harsh request. "Fatherless" means children without a dad, and "widow" is a woman whose husband has died.

The psalm is attributed to David, who complains to God about someone who falsely accuses him and repays his kindness with hatred. These words are a prayer that calls for justice in strong language, a kind of cursing prayer. Some believe David is quoting what his accusers say against him, while others see it as his own request. Interpreters do not fully agree.

For today: when you feel anger over an injustice, bring it honestly to God instead of seeking revenge. Then remember the words of Jesus: love your enemies and pray for them.
exp.134:12:
It says that the name of Jehovah, that is, his character and everything he is, endures forever. "Memorial" here means the remembrance of who God is and what he has done, and that remembrance passes from parents to children, "from generation to generation." It is like saying that God will never be forgotten or stop being known.

It is a psalm of praise, written by an author we do not know. It invites God's people to praise him in the temple. Before that, it recalls how God gave victory over kings such as Sihon and Og and gave the land to Israel. Then it says that God will care for his people and mocks the idols, which are made by human hands.

For today: when you go through difficult times, remember what God has done and tell it to your children or to someone younger. In this way faith is passed on from one generation to another.
exp.64:5:
It says that God is the one who keeps the mountains firmly in place by his power. "Setteth fast" means that he holds them up and keeps them secure. "Strength" is his might. "Being girded with power" uses the image of someone fastening a belt to get ready for action; that is, God is clothed in strength, ready to act.

This psalm is attributed to David and is a song of praise and thanksgiving. Earlier, the psalmist speaks of the blessedness of being near God and of his listening to his people. Afterward, he speaks of God calming the seas and the restless nations. Here we see the God who sustains creation and therefore can care for his people.

For today: when you feel that everything is shifting and nothing is secure, remember that the God who keeps the mountains firm can also hold you up. Take a moment today to thank him for his strength and to hand over the worry that weighs on you most.
exp.79:7:
It says that God brought a vine out of Egypt, which represents Israel, and planted it in another land. To make room for it, He drove out the nations, that is, He removed the peoples who lived there. The image shows God as a careful farmer.

The one speaking is the psalmist, on behalf of the people, in a prayer of lament. Israel is suffering, its neighbors mock it, and it asks God to restore them. Remembering what God did before is the basis for asking for His help now. It is not known with certainty when exactly the psalm was written.

For today: when you go through a difficult season, remember how God has sustained you before. That memory can give you courage to pray with confidence, asking Him to restore you, because He does not abandon what He has planted.
exp.95:10:
The heavens are invited to rejoice, and the earth is glad. Everything God has made is called to celebrate. The sky rejoices, the land takes delight, and the sea roars loudly, along with everything that fills it. "Fulness" means all that fills the sea: fish, waves, and creatures. It is poetic language that shows a joy filling the whole universe.

The psalmist calls all nations to worship God, who reigns and governs with justice. We do not know for certain who wrote it or when. The following verses explain the reason for the joy: God comes to judge the earth with righteousness and truth. For the psalmist, that judgment is good news, because God will set things in order.

Today we can rejoice because God is just and has not lost control, even when we see injustice. Take a moment this week to look at the sky or nature and thank God for his care and his justice.
exp.101:4:
The explanation says that the psalmist's pain is so great that he cannot stop groaning, and from so much suffering he has become thin. The image of the bones clinging to the skin is vivid: the bones show through, almost without flesh, because his grief has taken away his appetite and his strength. A groaning is a deep cry, like a lament that rises from the soul.

The heading of the psalm presents it as the prayer of someone in affliction who feels himself fainting and pours out his complaint before God. No one knows for certain who wrote it or at what exact moment; some think of an exile, because of the later mention of Zion. Here he describes his loneliness and his illness with very raw images, hiding nothing.

For today: when pain wears you down, you do not have to pretend to be strong. You can tell God honestly how you feel, and also take care of your body: eat, rest, and seek support from someone you trust.
exp.91:6:
It says that the wicked grow quickly and look prosperous, like grass that sprouts everywhere, but their end is to be destroyed forever. The words "wicked" and "workers of iniquity" refer to those who live without respect for God and to wrongdoing and injustice. The idea of being destroyed here speaks of a final, definitive end.

The psalmist, in a song of praise for the day of rest, admires the works and the deep thoughts of God. He says that the foolish person does not understand that the prosperity of the wicked is temporary. The following verse contrasts this with God, who is the Most High forever.

When you see that those who do evil seem to be doing well, do not become discouraged or envy them. Their success is like grass: it lasts only a short time. Trust that God sees everything and acts with justice in his own time, and seek to live close to him.
exp.68:21:
It says that the table of the enemies, that is, their food, their comfort and their peaceful life, should become a trap for them. Words like "snare" and "trap" in this verse mean something that catches an animal, and something that makes a person stumble and fall. And the blessings or security they count on would end up being the cause of their downfall.

The psalmist speaks, David according to the title, who suffers mockery and abandonment. No one comforted him, and they gave him gall and vinegar. It is a prayer of pain that asks for justice, with very strong language. The New Testament cites parts of this psalm in relation to Jesus, and Paul quotes this verse in Romans 11:9-10 speaking of the hardness of Israel.

For today: when someone wounds you, you can be honest with God about your pain and leave justice to Him. Jesus also taught us to pray for our enemies, so ask that God do justice with mercy.
exp.138:7:
This verse says there is no place where God is not. If the psalmist went up into heaven, he would find God there. If he went down to the "abyss," which in the original is Sheol, the place of the dead, God would be there too.

The one speaking is David, according to the title of the psalm. He is amazed that God knows him completely. His question, "where can I flee?", does not seem to arise from fear but from wonder at a God so near. Some also read it as comfort.

For today: when you feel alone, far away, or in a dark moment, remember that God is with you. You can speak to him right there, without needing to go to some special place.
exp.21:19:
Here the speaker asks God to save him from death. "The sword" represents a deadly danger. "My soul" means "my life." "The dog" refers to cruel enemies who surround him. "My darling" is an old expression for "my precious life," the only one he has (some versions say "my lonely life").

This is a psalm of David. He suffers, and his enemies surround him like animals. The previous verse speaks of dividing his garments, something the Gospels connect with the crucifixion of Jesus. For this reason many Christians read this psalm as a prophecy about Christ, although it also expresses David's real pain.

For today: when you feel alone and surrounded by problems, do not keep silent. Speak to God with sincerity, ask him for help, and trust that he hears you, as David did.
exp.17:24:
He says God responds in the same way He sees our heart. To the one who shows mercy, God shows mercy. To the upright man, that is, the honest one with a sincere heart, God shows Himself upright, that is, just and faithful. It is not a mechanical exchange, but a truth about God's character.

David speaks here, in a song of thanksgiving after God delivered him from his enemies and from Saul (according to the heading of the psalm). He looks back over his life and recognizes that God was faithful to him. The verses that follow keep the same pattern: God is pure with the pure and firm against the crooked.

For today: show mercy to the one who failed you, and live with sincerity in what is hidden. In this way you will trust that God is faithful and just with you, even when you do not always understand how or when He responds.
exp.57:2:
The explanation says that the wicked turned away from God very early, as if their evil path had begun before they were born. "Estranged" means to be alienated or become a stranger, and "go astray" means to lose one's way. Furthermore, from childhood they speak lies. It is exaggerated, poetic language to show how deeply rooted their wickedness is.

David writes this psalm troubled by injustice. The judges or rulers of his time claimed to administer justice, but in reality they acted with violence. Some understand that he speaks of leaders of Israel, and others of judges in general. This verse describes their heart, which is twisted from the root.

For today: recognize that all of us have an inclination toward evil and need God's grace. Before pointing at others, ask him to cleanse your heart and help you always speak the truth.
exp.142:9:
David asks God to teach him to do what pleases Him. The reason is simple: "for thou art my God." He asks that God's good spirit lead him into a land of uprightness, that is, to a level, safe, and just place or path.

The word "spirit" is the one the translation uses for God's inner guidance; the phrase "land of uprightness" refers to a place or way that is level, secure, and just.

David speaks, according to the title of the psalm, in the midst of great distress. His enemies pursue him and he feels cast down. Before asking to be delivered, he prays to know the right way. Some understand "good spirit" as the Holy Spirit, and others as the kind direction of God; both ideas fit the psalm.

For today: when you are in trouble, do not ask only that the difficulty end. Ask God also to teach you what to do and how to live. Set aside a moment each morning to pray with this line and to listen to His Word, ready to obey.
exp.89:5:
The explanation says that human life is like grass: in the morning it sprouts, looks fresh and grows, but at evening it is cut down and dries up. The phrase in the verse that means "in the morning" and "in the evening" refers to the beginning and end of a single day, and "is cut down" means that it is mown or cut off. The image speaks of how brief and fragile our life is.

Psalm 90 is traditionally attributed to Moses, although some scholars debate this. It is a prayer addressed to God, who is eternal, in contrast with our frailty. Earlier, it says that a thousand years in God's sight are like yesterday. Then the psalmist acknowledges that sin and God's judgment are tied to this reality of death.

For today: since life is short, do not take it for granted. Today you can ask God for wisdom to use your time well, be reconciled with someone, forgive, or set aside a moment to pray. Living with humility before God helps us value what truly matters.
exp.45:3:
This verse speaks of a river whose channels, that is, its streams, bring joy to the city of God. That city is the sanctuary, the holy place where the Most High dwells. The word "tabernacles" in the verse recalls God's dwelling among his people.

The psalm was written by the sons of Korah, Levites who served in worship. Before this, the text describes chaos: mountains that tremble and seas that roar. Here the tone shifts: in the middle of the uproar a calm river appears. Jerusalem has no great river, so many understand this image symbolically, as God's presence and care that give life and peace.

For today: when everything around you is shaking, do not look for your calm only in fixing your circumstances. Draw near to God in prayer and in community, and let his presence be your constant source of joy and security.
exp.43:11:
He says God gave his people away like someone who sells something and gets nothing for it, "for nothing," that is, free of charge. "You did not profit from their price" means that God did not even ask a good price or make any gain; it seems that his people were worth little to him. It is very strong language, born out of pain.

The one speaking is the people of Israel, or their voice in prayer, after a military defeat. They feel abandoned, though they believe they have not been unfaithful (vv. 17-18). It is not known with certainty which battle is meant; scholars have interpreted it in several ways. The psalmist does not stay silent but brings his complaint to God.

For today: when you feel that God has left you, do not hide your pain. You can speak to him honestly, even with hard questions. The Bible shows that praying with sincerity is also faith.
exp.13:6:
"Oh, that the salvation of Israel would come out of Zion!" the psalmist says. Here the word "salvation" means deliverance or rescue, and the phrase "Oh that" expresses a strong longing, like "Oh that!" In the wording of this verse, "when the Lord bringeth back" refers to the moment when the Lord restores his people who are in captivity. Then Jacob and Israel will be filled with joy.

Tradition attributes the psalm to David. Before this, it speaks of foolish people who ignore God and oppress the poor. It ends with a cry of hope. Some think that "captivity" refers to the exile; others, to any kind of oppression. The text does not fully make this clear.

Today, when you see injustice or feel trapped, you can pray with confidence and wait on God. He knows how to restore, and joy will come from his hand.
exp.8:3:
It says that God defended the psalmist and did him justice. "You have maintained my right and my cause" means that God took up his case and settled it in his favor. "You sat on the throne" is "you sat on a throne," like a judge who passes sentence with justice.

David speaks, according to the psalm's title, although some scholars debate details of its origin. He has just seen his enemies turn back and fall. That is why he sings with gratitude, recognizing that the victory was not his alone: God, as a just Judge, intervened and set things in order.

For today: when you suffer an injustice, you do not have to take revenge or prove your innocence at all costs. You can entrust your cause to God in prayer, trusting that he judges with justice. While you wait, keep acting with honesty and give thanks for what you have already seen of his faithfulness.
exp.86:3:
This verse says that God mentions famous nations, some of them even enemies of Israel, as if they were people who know him. Rahab here is not the woman of Jericho, but a poetic name for Egypt. "Palestine" refers to Philistia. About each people it is said: "this man was born there," that is, they were counted as born in Zion.

It is a psalm of the sons of Korah that celebrates Jerusalem, the city of God. Here God speaks, and he announces something surprising: people from distant lands, and even rivals, will be registered as part of his city. Interpreters see it as a promise that God will open his family to all the nations.

For today: no one is so far away that God cannot receive them. We can welcome with joy those who seem different or distant, remembering that God also calls them to know him.
exp.117:13:
It says that God is the strength of the one speaking and also the reason for his song.

The speaker is a believer in Israel who gives thanks after finding himself surrounded by enemies, as if they were bees. He feels they pushed him to make him fall, but God held him up. Some think the king or a leader is speaking, and others that the whole people are speaking; the text does not make this clear. The verse is part of a celebration, and right after it come songs of victory in the homes of the righteous.

When you face pressure or fears, do not rely only on your own strength. Ask God to hold you up and, when he helps you, do not forget it: give him thanks with a prayer or a sincere song.
exp.148:0:
It says we should praise God with enthusiasm. "Hallelujah" means "praise the Lord." "Sing" is a command to everyone: "sing." "A new song" speaks of fresh praise, one that comes from the heart for what God is doing today. "The saints" are God's faithful people, and "congregation" is their gathering together.

The psalm does not say who wrote it. The speaker invites Israel to praise its Creator and King, as the verses that follow show, mentioning dancing, the tambourine, and the harp. Many think it was sung at the people's gatherings, perhaps after a victory or deliverance, but this is not known for certain.

Today we can renew our praise. A famous or perfect song is not required. This week, thank God for something specific he has done in your life and sing it or say it in your own words, ideally together with other believers.
exp.79:9:
The vine, which represents Israel, grew so large that its shadow covered the mountains. Its branches were as great as the cedars, the tall and majestic trees, as if God himself had planted them.

The psalm is a prayer by Asaph, a singer of the people, in a time of national distress. The exact date is not known with certainty. It remembers how God brought Israel out of Egypt and established it in the land, but now the people are weakened and their hedges are broken down. So it cries out to God, asking him to restore them.

For today: when you pass through a season of weakness, remember what God has already done in your life. Recall his past faithfulness and ask him with confidence to give you strength and growth again.
exp.51:7:
What it says: The psalmist compares himself to a green olive tree, strong and fruitful, growing in the house of God. He says he trusts in God's mercy, that is, in his goodness and faithfulness, always and forever. The word "but" in the verse marks the contrast with what came before.

Context: According to the psalm's heading, David wrote it when Doeg the Edomite told Saul that David had come to the house of Ahimelech (1 Samuel 21–22). Earlier in the psalm, David speaks of a powerful man who trusted in his riches and his wickedness. Now he contrasts that man's end with his own trust in God. The green olive tree suggests life and security, not a tree uprooted.

For today: When money, status, or injustice seem to win, decide today to put down roots in God. Pray, gather with others, and remember his mercy, because there your soul finds firmness and life.
exp.57:3:
Their words and deeds, the explanation says, are harmful, like the poison of a serpent. They are also like a viper that pretends to be deaf and refuses to listen. It is an image of people who deliberately reject every correction.

David is the one speaking, according to the title of the psalm. He is crying out to God about the judges or rulers who ought to do justice but act with violence and lies. The verses that follow ask God to break their power, and the picture of the snake that does not hear the charmer shows their stubbornness. Interpreters debate whether the psalm speaks of corrupt judges or of enemies in general, but the central idea is the same.

For today: examine whether you too close your ears when someone corrects you with love. Ask God for a heart willing to listen, and trust that he does justice when you cannot.
exp.147:6:
It says that all of creation should praise the LORD, including the most mysterious or fearsome parts of the earth. The word "dragons" comes from a Hebrew word that can refer to great sea monsters, serpents, or creatures of the sea. The "deeps" are the depths of the waters. In other words, even the greatest and least known things in the ocean are called to praise.

The psalmist, whose name we do not know, invites the heavens and the earth to praise God, because He commanded and everything was created. For the people of Israel, the sea and its monsters were frightening, but here they appear as creatures under God's authority, not as rival powers.

Today we can remember that nothing that frightens us is outside God's control. When you feel fear in the face of the uncertain, return to praising Him, trusting that the same Lord who governs the deeps watches over you.
exp.134:18:
The explanation says that the people of Israel and the descendants of Aaron, the priests, should praise God. "Bless" here means to speak well of God, to acknowledge him and to give him thanks. "House" means family or descendants. "Lord" is the name of God. The words "bless" and "to" in the verse as your Bible prints them are the usual forms; the older spellings are not used today.

The psalmist calls the whole people to worship, group by group: Israel, the priests, the Levites, and those who fear God. Just before, he mocks the idols, which have ears but do not hear. In contrast, the true God does hear and act, which is why he deserves praise. The author of this psalm is unknown.

For today: do not leave praise only to others. This week, thank God out loud for something specific, alone or with your family, remembering that he does hear you.
exp.92:4:
This verse says that what God has declared is very sure and dependable. "Testimonies" are his words and commands, what God makes known about himself. It also affirms that holiness is fitting for his house, meaning it belongs to it and suits it.

The psalm does not say who wrote it. Before this verse, it speaks of rivers and seas that roar, an image of chaos and of forces that seem threatening. In the face of that, God reigns with greater power. Many understand "his house" as the temple, though others think it includes all his people. The psalm seeks to bring calm to those who live amid storms.

Today, when everything seems to move like waves, lean on the Bible as on a rock. Read it every day and ask God to help you live with reverence and purity, because his word does not change.
exp.72:13:
The explanation says that the psalmist felt he was suffering without rest. "Plagued all the day long" speaks of constant blows or trials, and "chastened every morning" means that each day began with pain and correction. Today we would say: "All day long I suffer, and every morning begins with a new difficulty."

The speaker is Asaph, the author of this psalm. He is pouring out his heart to God because he sees the wicked prospering while he, who has tried to live with integrity, feels that he only receives troubles. It is a sincere complaint, not a final rebellion. Later, when he enters God's sanctuary, his perspective changes (v. 17).

For today: when you feel weary of suffering and believe that doing what is right does no good, do not hide your pain. Speak it to God honestly, and seek his presence, prayer, and the fellowship of faith. There, many times, what we cannot understand with our eyes alone becomes clear.
exp.21:2:
It says that God is holy, that is, completely pure and set apart from everything else. And it says that God "dwells," or is present, in the midst of the praises of his people. "Yet" is a word meaning "but." It is like saying: "Even so, you remain holy."

David speaks in the middle of a very deep pain. He feels abandoned, and his prayer seems to receive no answer. Even so, instead of accusing God, he remembers who God is. Then he looks at the history of Israel, where their ancestors trusted and God delivered them. Christians also read this psalm thinking of Jesus on the cross, who quoted its first verse.

When you feel that God is silent, do not wait until you feel better to praise him. Remember who he is and what he has done before. Praising in difficulty is a way of trusting that he is still good and faithful.
exp.126:1:
It is useless to get up very early, to go to bed very late, and to eat "bread of toil", that is, bread earned with great anguish and effort. The word "in vain" means "without result" or "without benefit". "Going to rest late" means going to bed very late. The verse ends by saying that God gives sleep to his beloved.

It is a psalm of ascent, which tradition attributes to Solomon, though some dispute this. The speaker teaches a people who were climbing up to Jerusalem. It comes after a house and a city that rise up in vain without God. Then it speaks of children as a gift from God. The message: everything depends on his blessing.

Working diligently is good, but we should not live anxiously, as if everything depended only on us. Tonight, hand over your worries to God and rest. Sleeping well can be an act of trust that he cares for what you cannot control.
exp.81:6:
They whom he called "gods" and "sons of the Most High" are not immortal. They will die like any human being and fall as tyrants fall, that is, cruel or abusive rulers. The word "but" in the verse marks the contrast, and "like one of the princes" can be understood as "just like any other powerful ruler."

In this psalm God himself speaks, judging in the midst of the "gods." Many understand them to be human judges or rulers who were meant to defend the weak but did not. Others think of spiritual beings; the Bible allows different readings here. In either case, God strips them of the appearance of greatness and reminds them that their authority is borrowed and limited.

For today: if you have any power, whether in your home, your work, or your community, use it with justice and humility, because you will answer to God. And if you suffer abuse, trust that no human power is eternal and that God remains the righteous judge.
exp.34:12:
The explanation says that when those people were sick, David did not rejoice. On the contrary, he put on sackcloth, a rough cloth used as a sign of grief, and he fasted to humble himself before God. The phrase about his prayer returning to his bosom can be understood in several ways: that he prayed with his head bowed toward his chest, or that his prayer, so sincere, seemed to return to his heart without receiving an answer. Scholars interpret it in both ways.

The speaker, traditionally David, feels unjustly attacked. People he had cared for now accuse him with lies and repay good with evil. He recalls his kind treatment of them to show that his complaint is just.

For today: pray sincerely even for those who have hurt you. You do not have to pretend it doesn't hurt, but you can choose to bless and not repay evil with evil.
exp.56:3:
David says he feels surrounded by enemies as dangerous as lions. The people he describes are full of rage, and the verse calls them "the sons of men" whose teeth are spears and arrows, and whose tongue is a sharp sword. In other words, the harm he faces comes both from real threats and from cutting words.

David speaks here, according to the psalm's heading, when he fled from Saul and hid in a cave. He lived under constant threat. Even so, both before and after this verse, he trusts that God will send his mercy and truth, and that his glory is above everything.

Today this can help you when you feel attacked by criticism, gossip, or pressure. You do not have to pretend it doesn't hurt. Tell God honestly what you feel, as David did, and then remember who he is: higher than any threat and faithful to his promises.
exp.22:0:
It says that the Lord, the God of the covenant, cares for his people the way a shepherd cares for his sheep. The heading "A Psalm of David" indicates that it is attributed to David. The name "Lord" is written here in capital letters, the way it appears in the verse itself. "I shall not want" means that under his care, nothing needed will be lacking.

The speaker is David, who was a shepherd of sheep in his youth before becoming king. He knew well the work of leading, feeding, and protecting. He uses that image to speak of his personal trust in God. The text does not say at what exact moment of his life he wrote it, so it is best not to claim it. The verses that follow explain how he is cared for: rest, water, and guidance.

Today, when you feel fear about what is to come, repeat this verse in prayer. Remember that God knows you and cares for you. In this way you can trust him and take the next step with more calm.
exp.104:16:
God sent a man, Joseph, ahead of his people to prepare the way for them. What is striking is how he sent him: Joseph was sold as a servant, that is, as a slave.

The psalmist praises God by recalling the history of Israel. He looks back to Genesis, when Joseph's brothers sold him and he ended up in Egypt. The psalm shows that, even behind that injustice, God was directing events and caring for his people during the famine.

For today: when we go through unjust or painful situations that we do not understand, we can remember that God is able to work even in them. This does not mean that evil is good, but that God does not lose control. We can keep trusting him and acting faithfully, as Joseph did, while we wait.
exp.130:1:
Here the psalmist says that he has calmed his soul and brought it into stillness. He compares it to a weaned child, that is, a child who no longer cries or demands his mother's milk. The phrase "I have behaved myself" means that he has settled down and put himself in his place with humility.

The speaker is David, according to the heading, in a song of ascents, a song for pilgrims going up to Jerusalem. Earlier he said that he had no pride and did not pursue things too great for him. At the end he calls all of Israel to hope in the LORD. Some understand that the child rests content simply because he is with his mother, not because of what he receives.

Today, when questions that you cannot solve trouble you, do not struggle to control everything. Pause, pray calmly, and rest in God himself, even though you do not yet have all the answers.
exp.19:5:
It says that the one speaking now knows with certainty that God takes care of his "anointed," that is, the person God chose and set apart for a mission. The phrase is rendered in English as "anointed" as it appears in the verse. God will hear him from heaven, his holy place, and will respond with the power of his right hand, a symbol of strength and victory, to save.

It is a psalm of David, or dedicated to him, and many think it was sung before the king went out to war. The people pray for him in the preceding verses. Here, the voice speaking (perhaps the people, or a priest or Levite, though this is not certain) expresses confidence that God will answer.

For today: when you face something difficult, pray with confidence and rest in God rather than in your own resources. And pray also for those who carry responsibilities, such as your leaders and your family.
exp.43:18:
It says that God crushed or broke them "in the place of dragons," that is, a desolate and wild place, and covered them with "the shadow of death," a darkness as deep as death itself. "Broke" means to strike until something is shattered. The "dragons" may be jackals or desert creatures, depending on how the verse is translated.

The speaker is the people of Israel, or a representative of them, in a prayer of complaint. They feel defeated and humiliated, though they affirm that they have not abandoned God.
