It is not known with certainty which historical defeat the psalm refers to; scholars have interpreted it in several ways.

For today: you can be honest with God when you suffer and do not understand why. The Bible allows you to pray with questions and pain without ceasing to trust in Him. Tell Him honestly what you feel, and keep walking close to Him.
exp.87:2:
This verse says that the author is full of suffering, so worn down by so much trouble that he feels he can no longer go on. The reader should know that "full to the limit" describes his soul being overfilled with hardship. His life drawing near the grave indicates that he feels at the edge of death.

The one speaking is Heman the Ezrahite, to whom this psalm is attributed. We do not know for certain what his exact situation was; it could have been illness, loneliness, or a great affliction. What stands out is that, even so, he begins by calling God the God of my salvation and cries out to Him day and night. This psalm is quite unusual because it almost never ends in relief.

For today: when you are exhausted by pain, you do not need to disguise it. You can speak to God with complete honesty, as Heman did, and keep praying even when you do not yet see an answer.
exp.32:20:
It says that our heart rejoices in God, because we have put our trust in his holy name. The word "therefore" in the verse is not a separate word for the reader to look at; the joy comes from what has just been said. "Name" refers to everything God is: his character, his faithfulness, and his power. "Holy" means that he is pure and set apart from everything else.

The psalm does not say who wrote it. Here the people of God speak together, using "we." Before this, the psalm recalls that God rescues from death and gives life in times of hunger. Our soul waited for the Lord, and he is our help and our shield. So the joy has a firm reason. Then the psalm closes with a prayer asking for his mercy.

For today: when you feel worried, say aloud one occasion when God helped you. Then give thanks for it. In this way your joy will rest in who God is, and not only in what is happening around you.
exp.124:4:
It says that those who turn aside onto crooked paths, that is, those who leave God to follow their wickedness, will end up with the evildoers. The crooked ways are the twisted paths, and practicing injustice means they commit wrong. Even so, the psalm closes with a blessing: peace upon Israel.

It is a psalm of pilgrimage, the kind sung while going up to Jerusalem. The psalmist, whose name is not given, trusts that God protects his people, as the mountains surround the city. He asks for good for the upright and warns that God does not overlook those who abandon their way. It ends with peace for the faithful people.

For today: do not get used to small detours, because one crooked step leads to another. Ask God for an upright heart and seek the company of people who encourage you to obey him. His peace protects the one who remains in him.
exp.21:7:
The explanation says that those who mock the sufferer repeat: "Let him commit himself to the Lord; let God deliver him and save him, since he delighted so much in him." Where the source quotes a word meaning "commit yourself" or "trust," I have rewritten the comment to match the wording of the verse your reader sees.

David speaks here, feeling humbled and reduced to the lowest of creatures. His mockers laugh at his faith, as if God had abandoned him. It is a bitter mockery, yet it reveals that he did trust in God. The New Testament shows similar words directed at Jesus on the cross (Matthew 27:43), so many Christians see in this psalm a foreshadowing of his suffering.

For today: when others mock your faith, or when your situation seems to say that God is not listening, do not remain silent. Do as the psalmist did: bring your pain honestly to God and keep trusting that he is your God.
exp.103:20:
The young lions roar as they chase their prey, and in truth they are asking God for their food. The verse says the young lions roar as they chase their prey, and that they seek their food from God. The word for roaring is "roar" as it appears in the verse, and the animal they hunt is the prey, the creature they catch to eat.

The psalmist is not identified with certainty, since this psalm does not give a clear author in the text. It is a hymn of praise to God as Creator. Here it describes the night, when the wild beasts come out, and then the day, when the animals rest and people go out to work. The poet shows that God cares even for the strongest and most feared creatures.

For today: if God provides for the lions, you can trust that He also cares for you. Work with effort, but recognize that your daily bread comes from Him, and give thanks for every meal and every day.
exp.68:3:
They who hate me without cause are more than the hairs of my head. He says his enemies are more numerous than the hairs of his head. They hate him without cause, that is, without a just reason. They attack him without any reason, and he says they are strong and powerful. In the end, he says he must restore what he never took, that is, bear guilt or losses that are not his own.

David speaks, according to the title of the psalm, in the midst of deep suffering. He feels sunk as in waters and mire, weary from crying out. Even so, the next verse shows that he does not claim to be perfect, for he acknowledges his own failing before God. The New Testament quotes this psalm in connection with Jesus, who was hated without cause (John 15:25).

For today: if you are accused or treated unjustly, do not hide your pain from God. Tell him honestly, acknowledge what you yourself need to correct, and trust that he sees the whole truth.
exp.88:47:
This verse asks two questions: is there anyone who can live forever without dying? Can anyone rescue himself from the power of the grave? Both questions expect the same answer: no. "Grave" is the tomb, the place of the dead. "Selah" was probably a pause for reflection, though its exact meaning is not certain.

The psalmist, called Ethan the Ezrahite, prays in sadness. It seems that David's kingdom is going through a great humiliation, and it appears to him that God has forgotten his promise. So he remembers that life is short and fragile, and he asks God to act with mercy.

For today: recognizing that our life is brief helps us live with humility and not put off what matters. We can also be honest with God in pain, without pretending to be strong, and ask him to sustain our hope.
exp.142:8:
The explanation says that the psalmist asks God to rescue him from those who attack him. The phrase "I flee unto thee to hide me" means "I take refuge in you," like someone running to a place of safety. Where the explanation refers to the name of God, it is Lord, and "quickly" in the sense of "soon" is set aside here.

The speaker is David, according to the traditional heading of the psalm. He is distressed, almost without strength, and feels that his enemy is oppressing him. He does not ask only to escape, but also to learn to obey God, as the following verses show. Some scholars debate the exact moment in his life when he wrote it, and this is not certain.

For today: when you feel cornered, do not first run to defend yourself with your own strength. Make prayer your first refuge, tell God honestly what weighs on you, and also ask him for wisdom to act rightly.
exp.118:115:
Here the psalmist asks God to uphold him according to what God has promised in his word. He says that this is how he will live, that is, he will have the strength to keep going. He also asks that God not let him be ashamed, meaning that he not be left in disgrace for having placed his hope in Him. The word "uphold" in the verse means to hold up or support, so that is what the psalmist is asking God to do.

The speaker is the author of Psalm 119, a believer who loves God's law and lives surrounded by wicked people. Shortly before, he said that God is his hiding place and his shield, and that he would turn away from evildoers to obey God. Now he admits that he cannot stand firm by his own strength. He needs God to hold him up.

When you feel weak or under pressure, pray with this verse. Look for a promise of God in the Bible, ask Him to uphold you according to it, and keep trusting Him one day at a time.
exp.117:23:
This verse says that the day the Lord has made is a reason for joy and gladness. "Lord" is the name of God. The phrase about being filled with joy means that we will be overflowing with happiness, and the word for celebrating means that we will celebrate with gladness. The "day" refers to a special moment in which God acted.

Psalm 118 is a song of thanksgiving from the people of Israel, probably sung in the temple during festivals. Shortly before, it speaks of the stone that the builders rejected that became the cornerstone, an image of how God lifts up what others despise. The verses that follow ask for God's salvation and bless the one who comes in his name. Scholars do not agree on who exactly is speaking: it may be the king or the whole people.

For today: as you begin your day, pause for a moment and thank God for something specific he has done for you. Choose to rejoice in him, even if the day brings difficulties.
exp.90:5:
This verse continues to speak of the dangers that can threaten us. A pestilence is a disease that spreads and kills many people; a mass death is a destruction that falls on great numbers at once. One threat comes in the darkness, without anyone seeing it coming, and the other at midday, in full view of everyone. In other words, at any moment God watches over the one who trusts in him.

The psalm does not say who wrote it. One tradition attributes it to Moses, but this is not certain. First someone speaks, encouraging the one who trusts in God, and later it seems that God himself answers. It uses images of a bird that protects its young and of a soldier with a shield to give security in times of fear.

For today: when you feel afraid for your health or for things you cannot control, pray with this psalm and rest in God. Trusting him does not mean being careless, but living with peace while doing your part with prudence.
exp.118:85:
He says that all of God's commandments are trustworthy and true. For that reason the psalmist complains that he is being persecuted without cause, that is, without reason or fault on his part. He ends with a simple cry: help me. In this older wording, the word "commandments" refers to all of God's instructions, not only the Ten.

The one speaking is the author of Psalm 119, a person who loves God's law. We do not know with certainty who wrote it. Here he suffers because of proud people who set traps for him and do not live according to God's law. Even so, he remains faithful and asks for help.

When people treat you unjustly, do not stay alone with the pain. Trust that God's word is firm, keep obeying it, and tell him sincerely: help me. He hears that cry.
exp.118:26:
Here the psalmist asks God to give him understanding so that he may grasp the way of his precepts, that is, the manner of living that God teaches. And he promises that, once he understands, he will speak of God's wonders, that is, of his marvelous works.

The one speaking is the author of Psalm 119, whose name we do not know for certain. He has just said that his soul cleaves to the dust, an expression that many understand as deep sadness or weariness. In that low state he does not seek escape, but asks that God teach him. Then he mentions the anxiety that weakens him and asks to be strengthened.

When you feel burdened, ask God to help you understand his Word, not merely to read it. Read a passage slowly, pray for light, and then tell someone about the good that God has shown you.
exp.96:10:
This verse says that God prepares light and joy for those who live with integrity. The image of "sown" suggests a seed placed in the ground: the full fruit is not yet visible, but God has already planted it and it will grow. The righteous person is one who seeks to live as pleases God, and the one with an upright heart is sincere inside, with no double face.

The psalm does not say who wrote it. It celebrates that the LORD reigns and is greater than all false gods. The verses before it encourage those who love God to reject evil, and remind us that he watches over his faithful ones and delivers them from the wicked. This verse gives the reason for that confidence.

For today: even if you are going through dark days now, keep doing what is right with sincerity. God does not forget your faithfulness, and you can wait in peace for his light and his joy to grow in his time.
exp.36:11:
The wicked person plots against the righteous one, with evil intent. The word "plotteth" means to scheme and prepare a hidden plan to do harm. The phrase "gnasheth upon him with his teeth" is an image of rage and hatred: clenching the teeth in fury against someone.

This is a psalm of David, written as wise counsel, perhaps in his old age. It is meant to encourage the faithful who suffer because of the wickedness of others. Earlier, the psalm assures us that the wicked will soon pass away. Later, it says that God laughs at them, because he sees that their day of judgment is coming. That laughter is not cruelty; it shows that their plans will not triumph over God.

Today, if someone attacks you or treats you unjustly, you do not have to answer with hatred or fear. Do what is right, pray, and trust that God sees everything and cares for you.
exp.17:2:
He says that David will call upon the Lord, because God is worthy to be praised, and that in this way he will be saved from his enemies. "I will call upon" means that he will call out or ask for help. "Worthy to be praised" means that God deserves all our thanks and honor. "So shall I be saved" speaks of being rescued or protected from danger.

The speaker is David, king of Israel. He wrote this song after God delivered him from all his enemies, including King Saul, who pursued him for years. Before this verse, David had already called God his rock, his fortress, and his refuge. Afterward, he recalls the moments of distress when he felt death close at hand.

For today: when you are afraid or facing trouble, do not start by looking for ways out on your own. Speak with God, thank him for who he is, and trust that he sustains you, even when the answer takes a while.
exp.28:10:
This verse says that God will give strength to his people and bless them with peace. "Peace" translates the Hebrew word "shalom," which includes tranquility, well-being, and being whole, not merely the absence of conflict.

The psalm is attributed to David. It is a song that describes a powerful storm as the voice of the Lord, shaking mountains and forests. After showing that enormous power, the psalm ends with tenderness: the God who reigns over the flood uses his power to sustain and bless his own, forever.

For today: when you feel weak or anxious, remember that the almighty God is on your side. Say to him simply, "Lord, give me strength today and your peace." Then take the next step with confidence, knowing that you do not carry it alone.
exp.135:12:
This verse says that God divided the Red Sea into parts. The old name for the sea here is "the Bermejo," which is simply another name for the Red Sea. "Mercy" here translates a Hebrew word that speaks of faithful, unbreaking love. That is why the line is repeated: his love endures forever.

Psalm 136 is a song of praise that the people of Israel sang, probably in worship, with one voice leading and everyone responding. It remembers creation and the deliverance from Egypt. This verse recalls the moment when God rescued his people from slavery, as told in Exodus 14.

For today: when you feel trapped, with no way out, remember how God has been faithful before. Make a list of the times he helped you and thank him for them; this strengthens trust for the present.
exp.94:8:
The explanation says that Israel's ancestors put God to the test in the wilderness. "Tempting" here does not mean enticing to evil, but putting to the test, doubting him, and demanding proof. "Proving" means the same thing. Even so, those people saw his work: they witnessed God's miracles and care with their own eyes.

The psalmist calls the people to worship God, and at this point God himself seems to speak, recalling what happened at Meribah and Massah, where the people complained for lack of water (Exodus 17). The text goes on to warn that that generation did not enter the promised rest. Its purpose is that readers not repeat that hardness of heart.

For today: seeing God's faithfulness in the past should strengthen our trust, not our complaints. When difficulties come, remember how God has helped you before, and respond with faith and obedience instead of doubt.
exp.89:9:
This verse says that a human life normally lasts about seventy years, and that if someone has great strength, it may reach eighty. Even so, those years bring weariness and pain. The phrase "is soon cut off" means that life ends quickly, and "we fly away" means that we pass by fast, like someone who is gone in a flash.

The title of the psalm attributes it to Moses, the man of God. Here he speaks on behalf of the people. He acknowledges that God is eternal and that we are frail. He also connects the brevity of life with sin and with the seriousness of God's judgment. Some think he wrote it during the years in the desert, but that is not certain.

For today: do not assume you have plenty of time. Think of a decision you have put off, such as forgiving someone, praying, or giving time to your family, and begin today, asking God for wisdom to use your days well.
exp.71:18:
This verse is a final act of praise. It says that God's glorious name should be blessed, that is, praised and honored, forever. It also asks that the whole earth be filled with his glory, so that everyone sees and acknowledges his greatness. "Amen, and Amen" means "so be it, truly."

This psalm closes the second book of the Psalms. It is dedicated to Solomon and is traditionally attributed to David, though some understand it as a prayer for Solomon. It describes a righteous king whose reign blesses the nations. For this reason Christians also read it with Jesus in view. At the end, the one speaking turns the focus to God, not to the king.

For today: before you ask God for things, take a moment to praise him. Then pray that his goodness reaches your family, your work, and your community, and that your life honors him.
exp.1:6:
Here the king whom God has placed on Zion speaks. He says he will declare the decree, that is, the official decision of God: "the Lord hath said unto me, Thou art my Son; this day have I begotten thee." The word "begotten" here means giving origin, and "this day" points to the day God presents him as king.

The psalm begins with the nations rebelling against God. Then God responds with firmness, and now the anointed king speaks. In Israel, the Davidic king was called God's son because of his closeness to God and his delegated authority. The New Testament applies this psalm to Jesus (Acts 13:33; Hebrews 1:5), although scholars debate how it was originally understood.

For today: when the world seems confused or hostile, remember that God has already placed his King. You can rest in Christ and submit your decisions to him.
exp.76:5:
He says that in the middle of the night the psalmist remembered the songs he used to sing. He thought about them with all his heart, and his spirit searched and asked insistently, trying to understand what was happening to him.

The psalm is attributed to Asaph, or to someone from his group, according to its title. He is distressed and can neither sleep nor speak. He remembers earlier times, when he felt God close and sang to Him with joy. Now those memories lead him to painful questions: whether God has abandoned him forever.

When you go through a difficult night, do not hide your doubts. Remember what God has done before, pray with sincerity, and bring your questions before Him. Remembering His faithfulness can sustain you while you wait for answers.
exp.72:24:
It says that no one in heaven compares to God, and that on earth there is nothing the psalmist wants more than Him. The phrase "apart from you" means the same as "besides you." It is a question that already carries its answer: no one.

Asaph, the author of this psalm, speaks here. He was deeply troubled because he saw the wicked prospering, and he nearly stumbled in his faith. Upon entering God's sanctuary, he understood that the wicked have no secure future. Then he acknowledges that God held him by the hand and that God is his true treasure, far more than any success.

For today: when you feel tempted to envy someone who seems to have everything, stop and ask yourself what you desire most. Tell God honestly: "You are my greatest good." Spending time with Him in prayer and Bible reading helps set the heart on what cannot be lost.
exp.19:7:
It says that those who trusted in their own strength bowed down and fell, while God's people stood firm. "Bowed down" here means they collapsed or gave way, like someone who falls down defeated.

It is a psalm of victory, attributed to David and connected with the king of Israel. It seems to have been sung when the people went out to war, and in this verse it speaks with confidence, as if the outcome were already secure. The verse before it contrasts those who trust in chariots and horses with those who remember the name of the LORD.

For today: when you face pressures, such as debts, illness, or a difficult problem, do everything that is your responsibility, but do not place your security only in your own resources. Take a moment to pray and remember how God has sustained you before. That helps you stay firm.
exp.80:0:
This verse begins with a note for the choir director: the psalm is by Asaph and is to be sung "upon Gittith," which was probably a kind of melody or instrument; no one knows for certain. It then calls us to sing to God, our strength, and to celebrate with a shout of joy, that is, with great gladness, to the God of Jacob.

Asaph was a musician and leader of praise in Israel. This psalm seems to have been meant for the feasts of the people, as the verses that follow show, speaking of the new moon and the solemn day. The people gather to worship and to remember what God has done for them.

For today: before facing your tasks, take a few minutes to sing or listen to a song of praise. Thank God for the strength he has given you this week, and do it with courage, even if you are tired.
exp.28:6:
This verse says that when God speaks, his voice has tremendous power, like flames of fire that scatter or burst forth. The word "divideth" here means that the voice of God throws off or splits the flashes of fire. Many understand it as an image of the lightning of a storm, although the text does not fully make this clear.

This is a psalm of David. In it he praises the Lord by comparing his voice to a great storm that moves from Lebanon to the wilderness of the south. Each time he repeats "the voice of the Lord," he shows that all creation is under his authority. At the end, those in his temple respond by giving him glory.

For today: when you feel small before problems or fear, remember that the voice of God is more powerful than any storm. Take a moment to listen to him in his Word and respond to him with gratitude and worship.
exp.33:13:
This verse gives three simple instructions: turn away from what is wrong, do what is good, and actively seek peace. "Turn away" means to go far from something, not to stay close to what harms you. "Pursue it" means to go after peace with steadiness, like someone who does not give up until they reach it.

The psalm is written by David, and its heading connects it to a time when he pretended to be out of his mind before Abimelech in order to escape. After giving thanks to God for rescuing him, David teaches others how to live. The verses before this one speak about guarding the tongue, and the verses after it say that God watches over the righteous and opposes those who do evil.

Today we can put this into practice like this: when a conflict arises at home, at work, or online, do not respond in anger. Take the first step toward peace with a kind word or a sincere apology, and do something good for that person.
exp.118:29:
This verse says that the psalmist made a decision: he chose to live in truth, that is, in the way of God. "Judgments" here means God's just decisions and standards, not a punishment. "I have laid before me" means that he keeps them always in view, like a guide so as not to get lost.

The one speaking is the author of Psalm 119, who cannot be identified with certainty. Tradition attributes it to David, but this is not known. He comes out of a moment of distress and asks God for strength and to keep him away from falsehood. Here he responds with a decision of his own: he not only asks for help, he also chooses.

Today you can do the same: before making a difficult decision, stop and ask what God's Word says about it. Choose the truth even when it costs you, and ask God to sustain you.
exp.30:5:
It says that David rejects those who put their trust in empty and deceptive things, such as idols or false promises. "I have hated" means he firmly turns away from such things. "Vain things that cannot help" are things that promise much but give nothing. Instead, he waits on the Lord, that is, he trusts in God and looks to him.

The speaker is David, according to the title of the psalm. He is in a time of distress, surrounded by enemies and traps. Shortly before, he said that God is his stronghold and placed his spirit in God's hands. Here he explains whom he trusts and whom he does not. Afterward he gives thanks that God rescued him and set him in a wide place.

Today we can ask ourselves where we place our hope when we are afraid: in money, in fame, or in our own plans. God invites us to trust in him, because he keeps his promises.
exp.44:10:
It says the king will delight in the beauty of the bride, and that she should honor him with respect, because he is her lord. "Desire" means that he takes pleasure in her; bowing down means bowing as a sign of honor and submission.

This psalm is a wedding song for a king of Israel. The psalmist speaks as a poet and addresses the bride, who comes from another people and must leave her home to begin a new life. It is not known with certainty which king it was. Many Christians also see in it a picture of Christ and his people, and Hebrews 1:8-9 quotes part of this psalm to speak of the Son.

For today: if we follow Christ, true honor begins in the heart. Today you can hand him one concrete decision and say to him simply, "Lord, in this I want to obey you."
exp.17:37:
It says the king completely defeated his enemies. "I have wounded them" means "I struck them down," and "that they were not able to rise" shows that they were left without strength to keep fighting. "They are fallen under my feet" is a picture of total victory, like a conqueror standing on the ground he has won.

It is David speaking, according to the title of the psalm, after he was delivered from his enemies and from Saul. It is a song of thanksgiving. In the verses nearby he makes clear that he did not win by his own strength: God girded him with strength and made the way wide before him. The victory is a gift from God.

For today: do not take this verse as permission to trample on others. Use it to trust that God gives strength in difficult struggles, such as fear, injustice, or bad habits, and to thank him for every step forward.
exp.118:37:
He says the psalmist asks God, "Stablish thy word", meaning that God would make firm and fulfill what he has promised. He calls himself "thy servant", someone who belongs to God and serves him, and he adds "who is devoted to thy fear", that is, he reveres God and honors him with awe.

The one speaking is the author of Psalm 119, a long psalm that praises God's law. We do not know for certain who wrote it. It follows on from asking that his heart not be turned toward greed, nor his eyes toward vanity, and from asking to be revived. Now he pleads that God would uphold his promises, for he desires to live faithfully and trusts that God will not fail him.

For today: when you feel weak or doubt what God has said, pray honestly and lean on his promises. Read them, memorize some of them, and ask him to make them firm in your life, while you keep living with reverence and obedience toward him.
exp.67:1:
The explanation says that God's enemies disappear before Him, just as smoke is scattered by the wind and wax melts in the fire. "Wicked" refers to those who live with their backs turned to God and oppose Him. "Perish" means they will be destroyed or cease to exist. The idea is that before the presence of God, evil cannot hold its ground.

David writes this psalm as a song for the choir director. It begins by recalling when the ark of the covenant was set in motion (Numbers 10:35), and the people asked God to rise up against their enemies. It is a song of victory and confidence. What follows shows the contrast: the righteous rejoice and sing.

For today: when you see injustice seeming strong, remember that it does not have the final word. Trust that God acts in His own time, and in the meantime, choose joy and praise instead of fear or bitterness.
exp.103:6:
The explanation says that the waters covering the earth ran off when God rebuked them. His voice, compared to thunder, made them hurry away. "Rebuke" is a strong command, and "hurried away" means they left in haste. The psalmist shows that the water obeys God like a servant.

The psalmist sings to God as Creator. Just before this, verse 6 says the waters covered the mountains. Here he recalls how God brought order to creation and set limits for the water. Many connect this with the third day of creation in Genesis 1, though the psalm is poetry and does not aim to give a scientific account. Some also see a reference to the flood, but the context points more toward creation.

When your problems feel like they are covering you like deep waters, remember that God has authority over them. Trust that He sets limits on what seems to be overflowing. Pray calmly and hand over your worry to Him.
exp.112:5:
This verse follows the question in the previous verse: "Who is like the LORD our God, who has exalted his dwelling, who humbleth himself to behold the things that are in heaven and in the earth?" The phrase "humbleth himself to behold" means that God, being so great, bends down or lowers his gaze to see what is in heaven and on earth. Nothing lies outside his attention.

The psalmist calls God's servants to praise him. This psalm celebrates that God is highest, yet he is not far away. His greatness does not make him indifferent. That is why the next verse says he raises the poor from the dust. The author is not known with certainty, and the psalm was used in Israel's worship.

For today: if God stoops to look upon all that he has made, he also sees you. You can pray with confidence, even when you feel small or overlooked. And you can imitate his humility by noticing those whom others ignore.
exp.114:2:
This verse says that our God is in the heavens, that is, that He reigns with sovereignty and authority above all things. The phrase "he hath done whatsoever he hath pleased" means that God acts according to His will, and nothing can stop Him. The explanation of the old-fashioned wording is removed here, since the word "pleased" in the verse above already conveys the same idea of deciding what to do.

The psalm is a prayer of the people of Israel. No one knows for certain who wrote it or when. The nations mocked them, asking: "Where is their God?" The people respond by asking that the glory belong to God alone, and then they contrast God, who acts, with idols, which are made by human hands and cannot speak or see.

For today: when everything seems uncertain or others mock your faith, remember that God still reigns. Trust in Him, pray with humility, and give Him the glory.
exp.122:3:
Our soul is weary and overwhelmed by the mockery of those who live at ease and by the contempt of the proud.

This is one of the psalms sung by pilgrims going up to Jerusalem. The speaker is the faithful people, or someone speaking on their behalf. The text does not say precisely who was despising them or at what exact moment, and scholars have understood it in several ways. What is clear is that, looking to God as a servant looks to the hand of his master, they ask for mercy because they can bear it no longer.

For today: when you feel humiliated or ignored, do not hold on to the pain or answer with resentment. Bring it honestly before God, as this psalm does, and wait for his mercy.
exp.118:162:
The psalmist says he feels a deep rejection toward lying. "Hate" and "abhor" are two strong words meaning to detest and to regard with disgust. In contrast, he says he loves God's law, that is, his teaching and his commandments.

The one speaking is the author of Psalm 119, a believer who loves God's Word. We do not know for certain who wrote it. He had been persecuted without cause by powerful people, and even so he revered God more than them. In the face of injustice and false accusations, he holds fast to God's truth and finds in it joy and peace.

For today: when you have to choose between a comfortable lie and a difficult truth, remember that loving God's Word helps you reject deception. Practice honesty in small things, such as excuses, exaggerations, or promises you do not intend to keep.
exp.20:11:
What it says: The verse says that God will make his enemies flee. It uses the image of an archer getting his bow ready. The strings are the bowstring. God aims the arrows "against their faces," that is, straight at them, and the enemies turn and run.

Context: This psalm is by David, and he sings it as king. He thanks God for the victory and trusts that God will also defeat those who plot evil against Him and His people. The verse before it says those schemes will not succeed. It is poetic language; many also see in it a look toward the Messiah, although interpreters understand it in different ways.

For today: We do not have to take revenge or live in fear before injustice. We can hand over to God what threatens us, pray, and keep doing good, trusting that He is just and has the final word.
exp.87:6:
It says that the weight of God's anger fell on the psalmist like something crushing him. The verse's wording suggests a burden that does not move. The waves are the swells of the sea: one after another they strike him and push him under. The word "Selah" was probably a musical pause or a moment for reflection, though this is not known for certain.

The speaker is a man in extreme suffering. The psalm is attributed to Heman the Ezrahite. He feels abandoned, near death, without friends and without comfort. It is one of the darkest psalms, because it almost never ends with visible hope. Even so, it begins by calling on God as "the LORD, God of my salvation."

Today, if you are going through a dark season, you can pray honestly, without pretending to strength. This psalm shows that you can bring your pain to God even when nothing makes sense. Continuing to cry out is already a form of faith.
exp.38:3:
Here the psalmist asks God to let him understand how long life lasts. "My end" is the close of his life, and "the measure of my days" is how many days he has left. "Let me know how fleeting I am" means: let me grasp how brief and passing my time on this earth is.

The psalm is traditionally attributed to David, together with the musician Jeduthun, according to its heading. He was distressed and had wanted to keep quiet, perhaps so as not to speak wrongly in the presence of the wicked, but his pain grew until he had to voice it. He does not ask to know the date of his death, but to see his life with realism, as something brief before God.

Today we too can ask God to teach us to value our time. Remembering that life is short helps us set priorities on what matters: loving, forgiving, and living with trust in God.
exp.89:2:
It says that God turns human beings back to dust, that is, to death, and that the word meaning "crushed" means undone, reduced to nothing. Then God calls out: "Return", or in other words, "turn back to me". Some understand that both phrases speak of death; others understand the second as a call to repentance.

It is part of a prayer attributed to Moses, the man of God. He compares God, eternal and a refuge for all generations, with human life, which is short and fragile. The following verses say that a thousand years for God are like a yesterday. For this reason the prayer seeks humility and wisdom.

Today we can remember that life is brief and is not in our hands. Instead of living with pride or putting off what matters, we can turn back to God each day, ask Him for forgiveness, and place our trust and our priorities in Him.
exp.72:15:
The explanation says that the psalmist tried to understand why the wicked seem to prosper while he suffers. He tried to think it through and reason it out, but it proved to be a heavy task, tiring and painful.

Asaph, the author of this psalm, was confused and nearly lost his footing in faith when he saw the unjust prospering while he felt punished every day. His reasoning alone did not bring him peace. The answer would come in the next verse, when he entered God's sanctuary and saw the end of the wicked.

Today, when something seems unjust to you, do not simply keep turning it over in your head. Bring your doubt to God honestly, pray, worship, and seek his perspective. There, many times, what reasoning alone cannot achieve becomes clear.
exp.16:14:
He says that the psalmist, because he is right with God, hopes to see his face, that is, to be in his presence. And that he will be satisfied when he awakes, that is, when he wakes up, and will be like God, which is what the words "with thy likeness" mean. Some understand that waking as the dawn of each day; others, as the resurrection after death. The text allows both readings.

The psalm is spoken by David, according to its title, while his enemies pursue him. He describes them as people who live only for this life, full of riches and inheritances. In contrast, David does not seek to fill himself with things, but with God himself.

For today: before seeking that something fill you, begin the day by asking God that his presence be your greatest joy. Things run out, but being with him gives a satisfaction that does not depend on what you have.
exp.70:20:
It says that God will increase the greatness of the one speaking and that he will comfort him again. "Thou shalt increase my greatness" means that God will give him more honor, dignity, or importance. "Thou shalt comfort me again" means that he will encourage him once more, after a time of sorrow.

The psalm does not say who wrote it. The voice is that of a person already elderly (verses 9 and 18) who has gone through many troubles and has suffered at the hands of enemies. Even so, he has trusted in God since his youth. For this reason he speaks with hope: he believes that the God who has sustained him all his life will raise him up again. Afterward, he promises to respond with praise and song.

When you go through a hard time, remember how God has cared for you before. You can ask Him for comfort with confidence, trusting that He will lift you up in His time, and in the meantime give Him thanks.
exp.12:3:
Here David asks God to act quickly. He fears that his enemy will say, "I have prevailed against him," and that his adversaries will rejoice if he falls.

David speaks, although the psalm gives no details about his situation. He is weary, living with daily anguish and feeling forgotten. He asks God for help so that he will not fall or die. Later in the psalm, there is a change: David decides to trust in God's mercy and sing to him.

Today, when you feel pressured or criticized, you can bring your fear to God with complete honesty. You do not have to pretend to be strong. Ask him to sustain you, and choose to remember his past goodness, as David did.
exp.118:166:
This verse says that the psalmist has kept, with his whole being, God's "testimonies," that is, his teachings and commands, which are like witnesses of what God wants and what God is. The phrase "I have loved them" is an older way of saying the same thing. And "exceedingly" means very much, with the whole heart.

The one speaking is the author of Psalm 119, a believer who loves God's word. We do not know for certain who wrote it. Earlier he spoke of the peace of those who love the law and of his waiting for God's salvation. Here he shows that his obedience comes from love, not only from duty. He also says that his life is open before God.

For today: do not see the Bible only as a list of rules. Ask God to help you love it, and read a passage each day calmly, ready to put it into practice.
exp.76:16:
It says that the clouds poured down torrents of water, that the sky thundered, and that God's lightnings flashed everywhere. "Went abroad" means they moved back and forth, like swift arrows. It is an image of a huge storm, showing God's power.

The psalmist Asaph speaks in a moment of distress. Feeling weak and full of doubts, he remembers what God did when he rescued his people. The neighboring verses allude to the crossing of the sea, though here the storm is described in poetic language, and we do not know whether it is a literal memory of a specific event. The text does not make this clear.

For today: when your situation seems bigger than you, call to mind what God has done before. Remembering his power and his faithfulness can bring back your calm and confidence, even when you cannot yet see the way forward.
exp.23:2:
Here the psalm asks two similar questions: who has the right to come near to God? "The hill of the Lord" is Mount Zion in Jerusalem, where the sanctuary stood. "His holy place" refers to that place set apart for God, his holy temple.

The psalm is attributed to David. First it says that the whole earth belongs to God, the Creator. Then it asks who may enter before so great a God. It was probably sung when people went up to the sanctuary, but the exact occasion is not known for certain. The answer follows right away: clean hands and a pure heart, not lying or deceiving.

For today: God does not look for outward religious appearance, but for sincerity. Before you pray or go to church, ask yourself calmly: is there something I should confess or correct? Come near with humility, trusting in his forgiveness.
exp.115:10:
He says that the psalmist, in a moment of distress and emotional haste, declared that all people are liars. The words "in my haste" carry the sense of alarm or desperation. The word "liars" speaks of someone who cannot be trusted.

The speaker is the psalmist, a man who was deeply troubled and who was rescued by God. We do not know with certainty who wrote it or what his exact crisis was. From the context, he recognizes that he spoke out of panic, perhaps disappointed in people. Then he turns his gaze back to God and asks how he can thank Him for His blessings.

When you are hurt or disappointed, be careful about the conclusions you draw in haste. Be honest with God about your disappointment, but do not let that moment define your view of everyone. Trust in God, who is faithful, and respond with gratitude.
exp.28:1:
This verse invites us to give God the honor he deserves for who he is. The word "give" means "ascribe" in the sense of acknowledging something as belonging to him, and the phrase "the glory due unto his name" points to the praise that his character calls for. "Worship" here calls for a humble bowing before him. The "glorious sanctuary" can be understood as the place of worship. Some translations speak of worshiping him "in the beauty of holiness," and the Hebrew text allows both ideas.

It is a psalm of David, who speaks as a leader of praise. He calls on the "sons of the mighty," who may be heavenly beings or powerful people; interpreters understand this in different ways. He then describes the voice of God over the waters and the storm, to show that his power is greater than that of anything created.

For today: before you bring a request in prayer, take a moment to acknowledge who God is and to give him thanks, with humility and without rushing.
exp.131:10:
This verse says that God made a solemn promise to David, and that he will not change it. He promised that one of David's descendants, "of the fruit of your body," that is, one of his sons, would reign after him. The word "sworn" means that God made the promise with a firm commitment. The word "set" means to place someone on a throne.

The psalmist is praying that God would remember David and bless the king of his time. He cites God's promise as the basis for asking for help. The psalm does not say who wrote it. The verses that follow make clear that the promise depended on his sons keeping the covenant. Christians see in Jesus the final fulfillment of this promise.

God is faithful to his word. When we pray, we can rely on his promises, and we can also respond to his faithfulness by obeying him with confidence.
exp.91:2:
This verse names three musical instruments used to praise God. The first was an instrument of ten strings, the second another stringed instrument, and the harp was played with a gentle, soft sound, meaning a calm and pleasant melody. It continues the idea of the previous verse: it is good to praise God.

The psalm presents itself as a song for the Sabbath day. It is not known for certain who wrote it. The speaker is a worshiper who invites others to sing by day and by night, because God has been faithful and has acted in his life. The verses that follow explain that his joy comes from the works of God.

For today: use whatever you have at hand to praise God, whether a guitar, a song, or your voice. You do not need perfect talent. What matters is thanking him from the heart, in the good days as well as the difficult ones.
exp.105:7:
It says that God saved his people despite their rebellion, and he did it for the sake of his name, that is, for who he is and for his faithfulness. His purpose was that everyone would come to know his power.

The psalmist speaks on behalf of the people of Israel and acknowledges that, just like their ancestors, they too have sinned. He recalls how the Israelites, when they came to the Red Sea, did not trust God, and yet he rescued them. It is a prayer of confession that remembers their history.

When you fail, do not think that God has already shut the door on you. His help does not depend on your being perfect, but on his faithful character. Confess your mistake honestly, and trust that he can lift you up and show his power in your life.
exp.36:25:
The explanation says that the righteous person is always merciful and generous. The word "lendeth" means that he gives or helps with what he has. "Seed" means descendants: children and grandchildren. In this way, his children also receive blessing and, in turn, become a blessing to others.

This psalm is by David, now an old man. He speaks like someone who has lived a long life and has seen how God cares for his own. He writes to encourage those who become troubled when they see the wicked doing well. His words are a general observation about life, not a promise that there will never be difficulties.

For today: practice generosity even when you have little. Help someone with your time, money, or a kind word, trusting that God cares for you. Also, your example teaches your children to live with an open heart.
exp.24:15:
This verse is a simple and sincere prayer. The speaker asks God to look upon him closely and to have compassion on him. The reason is that he feels alone and troubled. "Look at me" does not mean only to see, but to focus on someone in order to help them. "Mercy" means compassion that acts to help. "Afflicted" means suffering and in need.

This is a psalm attributed to David. He speaks with confidence in God, but also with pain: he mentions distress, enemies, and sins. Shortly before, he says that his eyes are always on the Lord, because He frees him from the net. So his loneliness does not drive him away from God, but leads him to pray. Scholars do not agree on the exact moment in his life when he wrote it.

When you feel lonely or overwhelmed, you do not have to pretend to be strong. You can say to God, in simple words, "Look at me, help me." He listens to that honest prayer.
exp.67:30:
This verse says that important people, such as princes or nobles, will come out of Egypt to honor God. Ethiopia, also called Cush, will quickly stretch out its hands toward Him. The phrase about hands being stretched out quickly is usually understood as reaching out eagerly in prayer, surrender, or offering. Some scholars read it differently, but the central idea is the same: they draw near to God in haste.

The psalm is a song of David that celebrates God as a mighty King, protector of the weak, and conqueror of His enemies. In context, kings bring gifts to the temple in Jerusalem. It is announced that distant nations, even powerful ones, will one day acknowledge the Lord. Afterward, all kingdoms are invited to sing to Him.

For today: God wants people from every nation to know Him. Pray for people from other cultures and welcome them with kindness, for God invites them too.
exp.46:2:
He says that God will place the peoples and the nations under the rule of Israel, as one who puts them beneath his feet. "Subdue" means to bring under control or authority. "Nations" refers to the peoples who were not Israel. It is language of victory, used in the ancient world to speak of a conquering king.

It is a psalm of the sons of Korah, sung by the people of Israel in worship. It celebrates God as King over all the earth. Many understand that it recalls the victories God gave Israel when they entered the promised land. Some also read it as a hope for the final reign of God. Interpreters explain it in various ways.

For today: trust that God has the last word over anything that seems stronger than you. When you face pressure or injustice, do not respond with pride or violence, but with praise and hope, because the great King still reigns.
exp.98:3:
This verse says that the King, who is God, delights in what is just. His power is not harsh or arbitrary, because it is joined to righteousness. "Judgment" here means fair decisions, and "righteousness" is what is right and correct. God establishes what is upright, and in Israel, called "Jacob," he acted with justice.

The psalm does not say who wrote it. It is a song of praise to the Lord as the holy King, who reigns from Zion, that is, Jerusalem. The people praise him because his greatness is holy. Then it mentions Moses, Aaron, and Samuel, who prayed and received an answer. In this way it reminds us that God is just and also near.

For today: if God loves justice, we can trust that he sees what is crooked. It also invites us to practice honesty and to treat others fairly at work, in the family, and in the church.
exp.37:13:
He says that the psalmist acted like someone who does not hear and who has no words of defense in his mouth. Here the word "reproofs" refers to replies or answers meant to correct or respond to his accusers. Where the explanation quoted "fui," the ordinary word is "was." He chooses not to answer.

The psalm is spoken by David, according to its title. He is sick, weighed down by his guilt, and surrounded by enemies who set traps for him and tell lies about him. Instead of returning attack for attack, he keeps silent. The verses that follow explain the reason: he waits on God and trusts that God will answer. Some scholars think his silence also reflects humility in acknowledging his own sin.

Today, when someone criticizes you or speaks badly of you, you do not always have to defend yourself right away. Before you respond, pray and entrust the situation to God. Sometimes silence, held in trust in Him, is the wisest answer.
exp.149:4:
He tells us to praise God with cymbals, which are two metal plates that are struck together to make a loud, bright sound. The words "resounding" and "joyful" in the source describe sounds that ring out strongly and a happiness that is visible and celebrated. The phrase "praise him" is repeated for emphasis, and the short form of God's name is part of the verse's exclamation.

Psalm 150 is the final psalm in the book of Psalms. We do not know for certain who wrote it. The psalmist invites all the people to praise God in his sanctuary, using every kind of instrument. The verses before it name trumpets, harps, flutes, and strings, and the verse that follows widens the invitation: everything that has breath should praise the Lord.

Today we can praise God wholeheartedly and without shame. If you feel your faith growing cold, sing or play music that honors God, and thank him for something specific from your day. Praise does not depend on having talent, but on a grateful heart.
exp.72:1:
Here the psalmist says that he came close to falling. "But as for me" marks a contrast with what he has just affirmed: that God is good to those who are pure in heart. "Slipping" and "losing footing" are images of someone who loses their balance on a dangerous path. He speaks of his faith, not of a physical fall: he almost lost his trust in God.

The speaker is Asaph, the name that appears in the title of the psalm. He is usually understood to have been a Levite dedicated to the music of worship, although it is not known with certainty which Asaph wrote this psalm. He nearly stumbled because he felt envy when he saw that the wicked were doing well and seemed strong and at ease.

For today: when you see others doing well even though they live without God, do not keep your confusion to yourself. Bring it to God in prayer, as Asaph did, and remember that He remains good and upholds your steps.
exp.91:8:
This verse repeats with force that the enemies of God will perish. The word "scattered" means driven apart and broken up, like smoke or mist that vanishes. Those who work iniquity are people who live by doing wrong without turning back from it.

Psalm 92 is a song of praise. The psalmist speaks and marvels that the wicked seem to flourish, springing up like grass, but their success lasts only a short time. In contrast, God is exalted forever. Afterward, the psalmist trusts that God will strengthen him.

For today: when you see injustice seem to win, do not lose hope or respond with revenge. Commit the situation to God, keep doing good and praise Him, trusting that He is just and has the final word.
exp.28:5:
He makes them also leap like a calf: the mountains jump like young calves, that is, like little bulls that skip about. Lebanon and Sirion, high mountains in the north of Israel, shake like young wild oxen. An old word in the verse probably stands for an animal of the wild ox kind, not a creature of legend. Sirion is another name for Mount Hermon (Deuteronomy 3:9).

The psalm is by David, a song of praise. It describes a storm that moves across the land, and through it shows that the LORD governs creation. The mountains and the cedars seemed firm and imposing, but at his voice they tremble. The verses before and after continue that same storm.

For today: if what seems greatest and most secure trembles before God, you can bring him your fears. Respect his voice, and rest in the knowledge that he is in control.
exp.65:12:
He says that the one speaking will enter God's house, that is, the temple, bringing burnt offerings. A burnt offering was an animal that was burned completely on the altar as an offering. He also promises to pay his vows, that is, to keep what he promised God.

Here the psalmist shifts from the voice of the people ("you brought us into the net") to a personal voice ("I will go in"). The verses before describe hard trials, and God brought them out into abundance and relief. His response is public thanksgiving. Scholars debate whether the psalm was written by a king or by a worshiper speaking for the people.

For today: if in a difficult moment you made a promise to God, do not forget it when the trial has passed. Keep it with gratitude, and not out of mere obligation.
exp.98:4:
Exalt the Lord our God, that is, honor him and lift him up, and worship at his footstool. The verse uses the word "worship" for bowing low or falling prostrate, before the footstool of his feet, an image of a stool placed beneath a king's throne. The reason is simple: he is holy, that is, unique, pure, and set apart from all evil.

The psalm does not say who wrote it. Here the psalmist calls the people to worship God as a just King who loves righteousness. Some understand the footstool of his feet as the ark of the covenant or the temple; others as the whole earth. Then the psalm recalls Moses, Aaron, and Samuel, who prayed, and God answered them.

Today, before asking God for something, take a moment to worship him. Bow in silence or on your knees, and acknowledge who he is: holy, just, and near to those who call on him.
exp.77:39:
This verse says that the people of Israel provoked God many times while they walked through the desert. The word "grieve" in the verse above conveys the same idea: they caused him sorrow and anger. "Desert" refers to an empty, dry place, the same wilderness.

The psalm was written by Asaph, who recalls the history of Israel to teach the new generations. He reviews how God brought the people out of Egypt and how they, even after seeing miracles, rebelled again and again. Before this verse we see God's patience, who kept forgiving and remembered that we are frail. Afterward the cause is explained: they forgot what he had done for them.

For today: when you go through dry seasons, do not forget what God has already done for you. Remember his past help and trust, instead of complaining, knowing that he is patient and merciful.
exp.105:37:
It says that the people of Israel killed innocent children, their own sons and daughters, offering them as sacrifices to the idols of Canaan. With that blood, the land was "polluted," that is, stained and seen as unclean before God. "Fornicated" is used here in a figurative sense: they abandoned God to follow other gods.

The psalmist, whose name the text does not give, looks back sadly on the history of Israel. He acknowledges the people's repeated sins, even though God had rescued them. The verses that follow show that God was angry, but the psalm also speaks of his mercy at the end.

Today we do not offer children to idols of stone, but we can sacrifice the well-being of others for money, success, or comfort. Let us ask God to show us which things have taken his place in our hearts, and to make us defend life and care for the most vulnerable.
exp.17:5:
It says that, in great distress, the psalmist asked Jehovah, that is, God, for help. The words "I called" and "cried" mean calling out and shouting for aid. The word "Á" is an old way of writing "to", so I have left out that note. God heard him "out of his temple," that is, from his holy place in heaven, and his cry reached his ears.

It is David who speaks. The title of the psalm presents him singing to God after being delivered from his enemies and from Saul. Before this verse, he describes his danger with images of death: sorrows, floods, and snares. Afterward, he describes God answering with power, making the earth tremble. Some think the "temple" is heaven; others think it is the sanctuary in Jerusalem.

For today: when you are distressed, do not stay silent or alone. Speak to God honestly, even if all that comes out is a cry. He hears, and your cry truly matters to him.
exp.118:64:
The explanation says that God has dealt well with the psalmist, who calls himself God's "servant," and that he has done so according to what he promised. "Teth" is not part of the message: it is the name of the Hebrew letter with which the verses of this section begin, because the psalm is built as an alphabetic poem. "According unto thy word" means "according to what you said." The word "unto" is an older way of saying "to."

The speaker is a believer who loves God's teaching. We do not know for certain who wrote this psalm; tradition has assigned it to different people, but there is no agreement. In the nearby verses he speaks of having gone through humiliation and of having strayed before. Now he looks back and recognizes that God dealt well with him, even in the difficulties.

For today: remember the times when God was faithful to you and thank him for them. That gratitude strengthens trust when difficult times come.
exp.44:14:
This verse describes the bride's attendants, who arrive at the king's palace in the middle of a celebration. The phrase "shall they be brought" means they will be led or escorted. To enter the palace is to be received with honor, joy, and delight.

Psalm 45 is a wedding song for a king, and the author speaks as a poet celebrating the occasion. At first it was thought to refer to a king of Israel, but Christians also read it as an image of Christ and his church, and the New Testament applies part of the psalm to the Son (Hebrews 1:8-9). Some scholars see only a royal wedding, while others also see a prophetic meaning.

For today: come near to God with thankfulness, not with fear. If Christ invites us into his house, we can enter with joy. You can also accompany others toward him, inviting them kindly.
exp.23:5:
These verses say that the people described before (those with clean hands and a pure heart) are the ones who seek God. "Generation" here means a group or type of people, not a period of time. "Seek his face" means to desire to be close to Him and to truly know Him. "Selah" is a pause or musical sign; its exact meaning is not known for certain.

The psalm is attributed to David and was sung in worship. It asks who may go up to the mountain of the Lord, and answers with the character of the one who draws near to God. This verse closes that answer. Afterward, the psalm celebrates the entrance of the King of glory. Many think it relates to bringing the ark to Jerusalem, although the text does not clearly state this.

For today: seeking God is not just feeling emotion; it is living with sincerity. Today, before you pray, ask Him to show you something you need to correct, such as a false word or a broken promise, and decide to obey Him.
exp.115:4:
The explanation says God is "gracious", that is, kind and compassionate toward the one who suffers. He is also "righteous", that is, upright and faithful in everything he does. And he is "merciful": he is moved by our need and treats us better than we deserve. The verse joins these three qualities without setting them in conflict.

The one speaking is a psalmist who came close to death. He felt surrounded by pain and distress, and then he cried out to God, asking him to deliver his life. This verse is his response after being rescued: he tells what he discovered about the character of God. We do not know for certain who wrote the psalm or what the exact situation was.

For today: when you are distressed, pray sincerely, even with only a few words. And when the difficulty passes, remember and give thanks for how God was good to you, so that your trust in him may grow.
exp.106:32:
He says that God has power over nature. He can cause rivers and springs of water to dry up and turn into a wasteland.

The psalmist is not speaking only about the weather. He invites the people whom God rescued to thank him publicly. It shows that God also acts in judgment: the next verse says that fertile land becomes salty because of the wickedness of its inhabitants. But the psalm does not end there, because afterward God turns the wilderness into pools of water. It is not known with certainty who wrote it or when, although many connect it with the return from exile.

For today: when you go through dry seasons, do not lose your trust. God governs even what seems lost, and he can change the desert into a spring. Live with humility, gratitude, and hope.
exp.89:0:
This verse presents the psalm as a prayer of Moses, called "man of God," that is, a man close to God who served him. It says that the LORD has been our dwelling place, a secure place where people can find shelter, throughout all generations.

The speaker is Moses, or so the heading of the psalm indicates. It is not known with certainty when he wrote it. Many think it recalls Israel's years in the wilderness, a time of travel and vulnerability. That is why it begins by remembering that God, and not a place, was their true home.

Today you can come to God as your dwelling place when you feel fear, change, or weariness. If He cared for his people through the generations, He can also sustain you. Take a moment today to tell him in prayer: "Lord, you are my dwelling place."
exp.145:6:
It says that God does justice for those who suffer abuse or injustice, gives food to those who are hungry, and sets prisoners free. The phrase "Lord" is the name of God. The phrase about setting prisoners free can be understood as freeing those who are locked up or bound by oppression; the text gives no further details.

The psalm does not say who wrote it. It is a song of praise that invites trust in God and not in human rulers, as seen in the verses before it. The author presents God as a faithful Creator who cares for the most vulnerable: the blind, the fallen, the foreigners, the orphans, and the widows.

For today: if God cares for those who suffer, we too can do the same. We can pray for those in need and help with something concrete, such as sharing food or standing up for someone treated unfairly, trusting that God is still our hope.
exp.87:10:
This verse is a question the psalmist puts to God: will anyone declare your faithful kindness in the grave, or your faithfulness in destruction? The word for destruction here refers to the place of ruin, that is, death. The word lovingkindness is God's steadfast, faithful love, and faithfulness is his reliability.

The one speaking is the author of Psalm 88, a man in deep suffering, sick and feeling that God is far away. It is one of the darkest psalms, because it hardly ends with hope. His questions express his anguish; at that point in the Old Testament, the idea of life after death was still unclear.

For today: when you feel without strength, you can speak to God with complete honesty, even with your doubts. He invites us to pray without disguises, and the psalmist, despite everything, kept crying out.
exp.74:3:
This verse is a warning to two kinds of people: the foolish, who act without wisdom, and the wicked, who live without respect for God. The phrase "do not be proud" means "do not fill yourselves with pride or think you are more than you are." The image of "lifting up the horn" comes from animals that raise their horns with force; here it speaks of boasting and of acting with arrogance.

The one speaking seems to be God himself, according to the verse before, where he says he will judge with righteousness and that he holds the earth firm. Some interpreters think the psalmist is the one speaking, but the message is the same: God governs, and no one should boast as if they were the owner of everything.

Today we can examine our hearts when we feel superior because of our achievements, money, or position. A simple practice is to thank God for what we have, remembering that everything comes from him.
exp.88:44:
He says that God has cut short the king's youth, meaning that his strength and vigor have faded early. The phrase quoted in the source, which is an old way of saying "you have covered him with shame," corresponds to the verse above, so no separate note is needed. "Selah" is probably a pause for reflection, though its exact meaning is not certain.

The speaker is the psalmist, called Ethan the Ezrahite. He is confused and hurt. God had promised David an enduring throne, yet now the king descended from David appears defeated and humiliated. It is not known with certainty which historical moment is in view. For that reason the psalmist brings his complaint to God with honesty.

For today: when you feel that life has burned out, or that God does not seem to keep his promises, you do not have to pretend. You can bring your complaint to him sincerely, remembering that he remains faithful.
exp.118:69:
It says that the hearts of the proud have become fat and insensitive, like the fat of an animal. The word "fat" here means that their hearts have become dull and hard, unable to feel or respond. In contrast, the psalmist says he finds joy and pleasure in God's law.

The one speaking is the author of Psalm 119, a believer who loves God's Word. The proud have invented lies against him, but he does not defend himself with anger. He prefers to draw near to God and to his teachings. The image of the heart made fat speaks of someone whose conscience no longer feels or responds to God.

Today we can ask ourselves whether our heart is sensitive or hardened. When someone treats us badly, instead of filling us with bitterness, we can open the Bible and seek in it comfort, direction and joy. Reading it with delight keeps the heart tender before God.
exp.105:5:
This verse is a confession. The psalmist says that his people sinned together with their ancestors. He uses three expressions that are close in meaning: "we have sinned," "we have committed iniquity" (doing what is crooked and unjust), and "we have done wickedly" (living without respect for God). Together they show that the wrongdoing was serious.

The one speaking is an Israelite who prays on behalf of the whole people. It is not known with certainty who wrote the psalm or when. Earlier, he asked that God remember him and save him. Then he goes over the history of Israel, beginning with the rebellion in Egypt and at the Red Sea. He acknowledges that he is no better than his fathers.

For today: before asking God for help, we can be honest with Him. Admitting our mistakes, without excuses or blaming others, opens the way to His forgiveness and mercy.
exp.118:116:
He says the psalmist asks God to hold him up, like someone who needs support so as not to fall. If God holds him up, he will be safe, that is, kept secure and protected. And he promises that he will always delight, or find joy, in God's statutes, which are his commands and teachings. The sentence about the old wording is removed, since the reader's verse uses "I will have respect unto thy statutes" and the idea of taking pleasure in them is already conveyed in the text.

The one speaking is the author of Psalm 119, a man who loves God's law. Earlier he turned away from the wicked and decided to obey. Then he remembers that God rejects those who go astray. His request comes from knowing that, by himself, he cannot stay firm. We do not know for certain who wrote it.

For today: do not trust only in your own willpower. Every morning, ask God to hold you up, and read a passage of the Bible looking for joy, not just duty.
exp.6:6:
The explanation says that David asks God to present himself as King and Judge, and that the assembly of the peoples gather around him. The phrase "congregation of the people" means a crowd gathered together, and "for their sakes" means "for the sake of them." "Return thou on high" is a request: that God return to his high place, the throne of judgment, to rule with justice.

David speaks in prayer, unjustly accused and pursued by enemies, according to the heading of the psalm, which mentions Cush, a son of Benjamin. We do not know with certainty who Cush was. David does not seek revenge, but appeals to the court of God, the Judge of all nations.

For today: when you suffer an injustice you cannot put right, do not carry the resentment alone. Bring your case honestly before God, examine your own heart, and trust that He knows how to judge better than you do.
exp.30:22:
It says that all who belong to God, "his saints," should love him. "Saints" here means those who belong to him and are loyal to him. "Faithful" refers to people who trust God and stand firm in him. "Preserveth" means that he protects and watches over them. And "plentifully rewardeth the proud doer" means that God gives the arrogant person who acts with pride what he deserves, with complete justice.

David speaks here, according to the traditional heading of the psalm. He has just come out of a severe distress. He thought God had rejected him, but God heard his cry. Now, grateful, he encourages others to love God. The exact details of his situation are not stated clearly.

For today: when you feel that God has drawn away, keep crying out to him. Then remember and tell how he answered you. That memory strengthens your love and your trust, and it also encourages other believers.
exp.45:1:
The explanation says that, because God is our refuge and strength, we should not be afraid even when everything that seems firm is shaken. The word meaning moved from its place, and the phrase meaning carried away, are simply describing mountains being uprooted and thrown into the sea. The deepest part of the ocean is the image of a total disaster, as if the mountains fell to the bottom of the sea.

It is a psalm of the sons of Korah, a family of musicians and singers in the worship of Israel. What the word at the start of the psalm's musical directions means is not known for certain; it may be a musical instruction, perhaps for high voices. The psalm sings of the confidence of God's people in the face of any threat, natural or human.

For today: when something shakes you, such as an illness, a crisis, or a loss, remember who your refuge is. Before you decide, pray and repeat this verse. The text does not promise that there will be no tremors, but that God remains with you in them.
exp.143:8:
The explanation says the psalmist wants to sing a new song to God, accompanied by musical instruments. The "psaltery" was a stringed instrument, similar to a harp, and the "ten-stringed instrument" was one with ten strings.

David speaks here, as both king and warrior. He is surrounded by lying enemies and by dangers that he compares to "many waters." Before singing, he asks God for help. Yet he already speaks with faith, like someone who trusts that God will answer. Some understand that the song is new because it springs from a new deliverance he expects to receive.

When you are going through a difficulty, do not wait until it passes to praise God. You can pray sincerely and, even with tears, sing to him with confidence. Praise reminds you that God remains faithful and that you are not alone.
exp.76:3:
It says that God kept the author's eyes open, as if he would not let him sleep. He was so distressed that he could not even speak.

The one speaking is the psalmist, traditionally associated with Asaph, although the psalm's title attributes it to his group. He goes through a night of pain and seeks God without feeling comfort. Interpreters do not agree on whether he speaks of a personal crisis or of the situation of the whole people. In either case, he honestly expresses his discouragement and his doubts.

When pain leaves us without words and without sleep, we do not have to pretend strength. We can come before God in silence, just as we are. It is a good moment to remember, as the psalmist does right away, what God has done before, and to ask someone we trust to pray with us.
exp.93:11:
It says that the person whom God corrects and teaches from his law is happy, or blessed. Where the wording of the verse has "blessed," the sense is happy or favored. Here "chastenest" speaks of correcting or disciplining, like a father who shapes his child, not of revenge. "Teachest" means instructing.

The psalmist, whose author is not named in the text, cries out to God as judge over the injustice of the wicked. Before this verse, he recalls that God sees and knows everything. Afterward, he explains that correction brings calm in difficult days, while the wicked fall into their own pit. God does not abandon his people.

For today: when you go through correction or hardship, ask yourself what God wants to teach you through his Word. Read it with humility, trusting that his correction comes from his care and not from his rejection.
exp.72:7:
The explanation says the wicked "se sueltan," meaning they mock everything and laugh at what is good. They speak with malice about how to oppress others, and they do it with arrogance, that is, with pride, looking down on others. The phrase about speaking of violence can be understood as boasting about oppression or planning it with words. Some translators understand it as "they mock" or "they speak with malice about oppression."

The speaker is Asaph, a psalmist who nearly loses his faith on seeing the proud prosper. In this psalm he honestly describes his envy and confusion. Later he understands, when he enters God's sanctuary, that their end is not as secure as it appears.

For today: let us watch our words. Speaking with contempt or harshness may seem like power, but it does harm. If it troubles you to see proud people succeed, bring your complaint to God honestly, as Asaph did, and ask Him for a longer view.
exp.79:17:
It says that if God strengthens and saves them, the people will no longer turn away from him. They ask him for life: "you will give us life" means that God will renew them and make them revive. Then they will call upon his name, that is, they will pray to him and acknowledge him as their God. The word "quicken" is the same as "give life" here, and "we will go back from thee" means "we will turn away from you."

The psalmist speaks on behalf of Israel, God's people, who are going through great destruction. He compares Israel to a burned and ruined vine. Earlier he asked that God's hand be upon the man of your right hand, and it is not known with certainty who this is: some think of the king, others of the people themselves. What is clear is that the people cry out for restoration.

For today: when you feel weak or have failed, ask God to renew you, and commit your heart to keep praying and seeking him every day.
exp.82:16:
They are asking that God's enemies be put to shame, confused, and destroyed. "Humiliated publicly" describes being shamed in front of others; "very disturbed or frightened" describes being deeply shaken; "losing respect and honor" means being stripped of standing and dignity; and the word for "perish" means to come to an end or be destroyed.

It is a prayer by Asaph, a psalmist connected with the temple. Israel is surrounded by nations that joined together to wipe out its name (verses 3-5). Asaph asks God for help. Although it sounds harsh, the verse before it asks that they seek God, and the verse after it says they should know that God alone is the Most High. Some understand that the ultimate goal is for them to acknowledge God, not merely to suffer.

For today: when you feel attacked or unfairly treated, do not take revenge. Bring your complaint honestly to God, as Asaph did, and ask him for justice. Also pray that those who harm you will come to know him and change.
exp.104:2:
This verse invites us to take pride, in the good sense, in the holy name of God. The word "glory" here means to rejoice in Him and boast of Him, not of ourselves.
