The phrase "to the Lord" is the same as "to the Lord" in the verse you are reading, and the word "seek" speaks of those who desire Him and follow Him. The promise is that those who seek God have reason to have a glad heart.

The psalm does not say who wrote it in this passage, but it is a song of praise for the people of Israel. It calls us to remember what God has done for them: His works, His wonders, and His faithfulness to His covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. The verses around it repeat the same idea: sing, speak of God, and seek Him always.

Today we can set aside a few minutes each day to remember something specific that God has done for us and to thank Him out loud. Seeking Him this way fills our hearts with joy, even on difficult days.
exp.72:26:
Those who turn away from God, it says, will end up lost, that is, without a true life or future. The word "perish" speaks of ruin and destruction. "Going a whoring" here does not refer only to sexual sin, but to being unfaithful to God, like a husband or wife who betrays their commitment. "Cut off" means that God will set them apart or remove them.

The speaker is Asaph, a psalmist and worship leader. He came close to slipping when he saw the wicked prospering. When he entered God's sanctuary, he understood how they end. This verse contrasts the fate of those who turn away with the peace of the one who stays close to God.

For today: when you feel envy seeing others prosper without God, do not turn away. Pray, go to church, or open the Bible, and draw closer to Him. Being with God is the true good.
exp.146:2:
This verse says that God heals people whose hearts are crushed by pain, and that he binds up their wounds like someone who tenderly cares for an injured person. Those who are broken in heart are those who suffer deep sorrow. To bind up means to wrap or tie a wound so that it can heal.

The author of the psalm is not identified in the text; it is a song of praise. Many connect it with the return of the people after the exile, because it speaks of God building Jerusalem and gathering the scattered, but this is an interpretation. The same God who counts the stars and calls them by name also cares for the wounded.

Today, if you are going through a loss or a disappointment, you can bring your pain to God honestly, without pretending to be strong. And you can seek support from people you trust, because God often heals through others.
exp.3:2:
He says that God has set apart in a special way his "godly" one, that is, the person who is devout, who reveres him and is faithful to him. "Know therefore" is an invitation to hold this as certain. And since God has set him apart for himself, the psalmist affirms that the Lord will hear when he calls to him.

David speaks in the middle of distress. His opponents damage his honor and cling to falsehood. Earlier he asked them "how long?", and now he warns them that God cares for those who belong to him. Some think the "godly" one refers to David himself, and others to every faithful believer. Both readings fit the psalm.

For today: if your life is given over to God, you are not alone when you are criticized or slandered. Before defending yourself in anger, pray with confidence. God knows you, cares for you, and hears you.
exp.118:52:
He says that the psalmist felt great dread, a kind of trembling within, when he saw wicked people turning away from God's law. The word "horror" can also be understood as indignation or deep distress. The "wicked" are those who live without reverence for God, and "forsake" your law means that they abandon it or despise it.

The speaker of Psalm 119 is a believer who loves God's word. We do not know for certain who wrote it. He had been mocked by the proud, but he did not turn away from the law. His pain is not pride: it grieves him to see others despise what for him is life. Then he remembers God's judgments and is comforted.

For today: we can grieve over the evil around us without becoming hard or proud. That grief can lead us to pray for others and to hold more tightly to God's Word.
exp.23:3:
This verse answers the previous question: who may draw near to God? It says it is the person with clean hands and a pure heart, that is, someone whose conduct and intentions are honest. They have not given their soul to emptiness, which means empty or false things, such as idols or whatever is not worth pursuing. Nor have they sworn deceitfully, that is, they have not made promises with a lie.

The psalm is attributed to David and seems to be a song celebrating God's presence on the mountain of the LORD, probably Jerusalem. Some think it was sung in a procession toward the sanctuary. First it recalls that God owns all creation, and then it asks what kind of people may stand before Him. The answer focuses on integrity, not only on rituals.

Today we can examine whether our actions and our thoughts are in agreement. A good practice is to keep what we promise and to ask God to cleanse our motives before we pray or serve.
exp.20:0:
This verse says that the king rejoices in the strength that God gives him, and that he is greatly glad because of the salvation God grants him. The word "salvation" here does not mean being in good health, but deliverance or rescue, that is, the victory and freedom that come from God. The phrase about the chief musician shows that the psalm was handed to the leader of the singing for worship.

The title attributes it to David, and the psalm speaks of the king in the third person, while the people address God directly. The verses that follow mention blessings and a crown, which suggests a celebration of a victory. Some see it as a song for a historical king of Israel, and others also read it as looking forward to the Messiah. Interpreters do not fully agree.

For today: when something goes well, do not place your joy only in your own effort. Give thanks to God, recognize that strength and help come from Him, and celebrate with gratitude.
exp.122:2:
The explanation says that the people ask God for compassion, and they repeat the request with urgency. The reason is that they are "exceedingly filled with contempt," that is, completely worn out from being treated with scorn and looked down upon. God is the Lord, and mercy is his kindness and help toward those who suffer.

This psalm is a song of ascents, a song the people of God would sing, probably while going up to Jerusalem. It speaks in the plural, "we." These are people humiliated by proud and mocking people, as the following verses say. No one knows with certainty who wrote it or the exact moment, but its cry is clear.

For today: when you feel despised or ignored, you do not have to pretend to be strong. You can lift your eyes to God and tell him honestly that you are tired. Ask him for his compassion and wait on him, trusting that he sees you.
exp.134:19:
This verse calls two groups to praise God: the house of Levi, and those who fear the Lord. "Bless" means to speak well of God, to thank him, and to acknowledge his greatness. To "fear" the Lord means to respect and honor him with reverence and trust.

An unnamed psalmist invites the whole people to praise. First he calls Israel, then Aaron, then Levi, who were the priests and helpers of the temple. Finally he adds anyone who fears God. Some think this last group also includes people from other nations who believed in him, though this is not certain. Shortly before, the psalm mocks idols, which cannot speak or see.

For today: no one is left out of praising God. Today, whatever your work or your story, thank God out loud for something specific.
exp.134:3:
What it says: The psalmist gives a reason to praise God: the Lord (called here "JAH," a short form of his name) chose Jacob, that is, the people of Israel, for himself.

Context: The speaker invites those who serve in the temple, in its courts, to sing and praise. It is not known with certainty who wrote the psalm. The praise rests on what God has done for his people and on the fact that he is great above all gods, as the following verses say.

For today: Many Christians see in this verse an invitation to remember that God seeks us first. Today you can thank him in prayer, without boasting, because your worth does not depend on your achievements, but on the fact that he loves you and calls you his own.
exp.33:3:
The psalmist tells of something that happened to him: he sought God, and God heard him. Moreover, God rescued him from all his fears. "Sought" here means turning to God with sincerity, drawing near to Him in search of help. "Heard me" means that God paid attention and answered. The word "delivered" means He rescued him, that is, He set him free from danger.

This psalm is attributed by its title to David, at a time when he was fleeing from King Abimelech (also called Achish in 1 Samuel 21). David was in great danger and fear. After being rescued, he invites others to praise God with him, and he shares his testimony to encourage the humble.

When you feel fear, do not carry it alone. Speak with God honestly, as the psalmist did, and trust that He listens. Then tell others how He helped you; that strengthens the faith of everyone.
exp.66:4:
This verse repeats an invitation: that all the peoples praise God. The word "praise" here is the same as the verse's own wording, so we can say simply that the verse calls for all the people to praise God. "Peoples" refers to the nations and to all people, not only Israel.

Psalm 67 is a prayer sung by the people of Israel. It does not say who wrote it. First they ask for God's blessing, and then they explain why: so that all the nations may know God. The nearby verses say that He judges with equity, that is, with justice and impartiality, and that He guides the nations like a shepherd.

For today: when you ask something of God, also think about how your life can show His goodness to others. Pray for people from other countries or cultures, and share with joy the good things God has done for you.
exp.118:86:
What it says: The psalmist tells us that his enemies almost brought him down, that is, that he came close to falling or being destroyed. Yet even so, he did not abandon God's commandments. "To bring down" means to knock someone flat or ruin them. "Almost" shows that the situation was very serious.

Context: We do not know for certain who wrote this psalm; tradition ascribes it to a man faithful to God's law, perhaps David, though this is not certain. He speaks in the midst of persecution. Earlier he says that the proud dug pits for him, that is, traps, although he had done them no harm. That is why he asks for help and then pleads that God would revive him, that is, restore his strength and courage.

For today: When you feel close to falling under pressure or injustice, do not let go of what God has taught you. Hold on to his Word, tell him honestly that you need help, and take one small step of obedience today.
exp.145:9:
The Lord will reign forever; he is your God, O Zion, for all generations. Praise the Lord.

The explanation says that the Lord, Jehovah, will be King forever. There will be no time when he stops ruling. It speaks to Zion, that is, the people of God, and reminds them that their God reigns from generation to generation. The closing words of the psalm, "Praise the Lord," close the psalm as an invitation to praise.

The psalmist, whose name is not given, praises God for how he acts: he opens the eyes of the blind, lifts up those who have fallen, and cares for the stranger, the fatherless, and the widow. He ends by saying that this God is the true King, far more trustworthy than human rulers, whom the psalm warns against earlier.

Today we can rest in the fact that God is still on the throne, even when the world seems unstable. When you feel worn out or worried about the future, remember that his care does not change. And you can imitate his heart by helping someone who is alone or in need.
exp.71:4:
This verse says that the king will be honored and respected for as long as the sun and moon endure, that is, for a very long time, from generation to generation. The phrase "they shall fear" is in an older form, and here "fear" means to hold someone in deep respect.

This psalm is titled "of Solomon" and is a prayer for the king that he will rule with justice, care for the poor, and bring peace. Some believe David wrote it with his son in mind. Many Christians also read it as an early look ahead to the perfect reign of Christ, since no human king has lasted as long as the psalm describes.

For today: reverencing God is not about being afraid, but about recognizing that his justice and his care for the weak last forever. We can live today in a way that teaches that same reverence to those who come after us.
exp.87:17:
He says that God has put his friends and companions far from him. Those who knew him are no longer near. "They hide in the darkness" means they have vanished from his sight, and he is left alone. "Hast put far" is "hast put away." "Acquaintances" are the close people who used to be around him.

The one speaking is a psalmist, named Heman the Ezrahite in the psalm's heading. He is suffering greatly, perhaps from a serious illness or deep distress; the text does not say exactly which. It is the darkest psalm in the Bible, because it ends without a single word of relief. Even so, he keeps speaking to God and calls him "God of my salvation" at the beginning.

If you are going through a season of loneliness or pain, you do not have to pretend that everything is fine. You can tell God honestly what you feel, as this psalmist did. Also, seek out someone you trust and give them the chance to walk alongside you.
exp.66:1:
This verse says that God blesses us "so that" all peoples may know his way and his salvation. "Way" refers to the manner in which God acts and to his will. "Salvation" is the word that here means saving or rescue.

The psalmist speaks on behalf of the people of Israel, probably within community worship, since it is a song meant for music. First he asks for mercy and blessing, and then he states the purpose: that this blessing reach all the nations. Scholars do not agree on the exact date or the occasion on which it was written, so it is best not to claim more than the text says.

For today: when God blesses you, do not think only of yourself. Ask him how you can use what you have received, through your testimony, your generosity, or your prayer, so that others may come to know his love.
exp.38:9:
The psalmist asks God to take away his blow, that is, the strike or punishment that God has sent him. He says that under the weight of the hand of God he feels consumed, that is, spent and finished, as if God's hand were fighting against him. The word for "blow" here speaks of a wound or affliction, not necessarily of an epidemic.

The psalm is spoken by David, according to its title. He is suffering an affliction that he recognizes as God's discipline for his sin, and for that reason he had earlier asked to be freed from his rebellions. He had kept silent, and now he cries out. The verses that follow show that he sees himself as frail, like a traveler passing through life.

Today we can speak to God honestly when we suffer. There is no need to pretend to strength. We can acknowledge our faults, ask for relief, and trust that He hears our tears, even when we do not always know why we go through the trial.
exp.144:2:
What it says: The psalmist declares that God is great and deserves to be praised greatly. "Greatly to be praised" means worthy of the highest praise possible. "Unsearchable" means that his greatness cannot be fully explored or measured; we would never finish understanding everything God is.

Context: The psalm is attributed to David in its heading. Before this verse he promises to praise God every day and forever. Afterward he says that each generation will tell the next about God's works. It is a psalm of gratitude and wonder, rising from knowing God closely as King and as a personal God.

For today: At the start of your day, take a minute to thank God for something specific he has done for you. Then tell someone close to you, such as a child, a friend, or a relative, what God has done in your life. In this way, praise becomes a daily practice and is shared with others.
exp.43:19:
This verse begins a conditional statement: "If we had forgotten the name of our God," that is, if we had stopped honoring him, or "stretched out our hands to a strange god," meaning, if we had prayed to other gods. Lifting up the hands was a gesture of prayer and worship.

The psalmist speaks on behalf of the people of Israel, who are suffering defeat and humiliation. He does not understand why God let them fall when they had been faithful to him. So he says, in effect: "If we had failed, it would make sense, but that is not what happened." Scholars do not agree on the exact date or the historical occasion of the psalm.

For today: when you suffer without understanding why, you can be honest with God, as the psalmist was, and still hold on to him. God knows your heart and is not offended by your honest questions.
exp.102:2:
This verse says that God is the one who forgives all our wrongdoings and the one who heals all our sicknesses. The word "all" emphasizes that his forgiveness and his care are not partial or half-finished.

Here David speaks, encouraging himself to praise God. He tells his own soul not to forget any of the Lord's benefits. This verse is the first item in the list of those benefits. Some understand the healing as physical, others also as healing of the heart and of life; the text does not explain how or when God heals.

For today: make a short list of the times God has forgiven you or helped you, and thank him for them. Remembering his benefits helps us trust him, especially when we ask for forgiveness or feel pain.
exp.107:4:
This verse is a prayer asking that God be exalted, that is, honored and lifted up on high. The psalmist wishes that God's glory, his greatness and his beauty, may be seen above the heavens and throughout all the earth.

The psalm is attributed to David. It joins parts of two other psalms (the 57th and the 60th). Here David praises God among the nations for his mercy and his truth. Then, in the verses that follow, he asks for help and salvation, and he recalls God's promises concerning the land. First he worships, and then he presents his need.

Before asking God for something, you can pause to tell him how great he is. Praying this way reminds you that he is greater than your problems. Today, before you bring him your burdens, tell him in your own words: "Lord, be exalted in my life."
exp.123:4:
This verse says that, if God had not been on their side, the proud and violent waters would have passed over them. "Soul" means the whole person, their life. "Proud" means haughty and arrogant, and here it describes a furious, overflowing flood.

It is a psalm of David, sung by the people of Israel, probably as they went up to Jerusalem. They remember a great danger, when powerful enemies attacked them with fury. We do not know with certainty what exact moment it refers to. They use the image of a flood to say how close they came to being swept away. Then they praise God for having delivered them.

When you go through a crisis and come out ahead, do not credit it only to your own strength. Stop to thank God and remember how he sustained you. That memory will give you confidence for the trials that come.
exp.88:45:
Here the writer asks God how long He will seem absent. The phrase about hiding means that God appears to have turned His face away and is not answering. The phrase about His wrath burning like fire expresses the fear that God's anger will never end.

Psalm 89 is attributed to Ethan the Ezrahite, according to its heading. First it recalls God's promise to David of an everlasting throne. But now that king has been humbled and his kingdom seems to lie in ruins. Many think it speaks of a national defeat, although the psalm does not say exactly when it happened. The psalmist does not doubt God; he cries out to Him honestly in the midst of his pain.

For today: when God seems silent, do not hide your pain. You can bring sincere questions to Him in prayer, and at the same time remember His promises and His faithful character, even when you do not understand what is happening.
exp.138:20:
Here the psalmist asks God whether it is not natural for him to reject those who hate you. "To hold in hatred" means to reject firmly, and "I am moved" means that he is filled with indignation or grief. He says that he takes God's side against those who despise him.

David speaks here, according to the title of the psalm. He has just acknowledged that God knows him completely. He sees that there are violent people who insult God's name, and he sides with the Lord. Many understand this "hatred" as intense language of loyalty, not as permission for revenge. Right after this, he asks God to examine his heart.

For today: you may feel sorrow or rejection in the face of evil and of mockery against God, but let God search your heart. Jesus taught us to love our enemies and pray for them, so reject sin without ceasing to desire good for people.
exp.71:5:
He says the righteous king will come with kindness, like rain falling on freshly cut grass, or like the dew that gently moistens the ground. The mown grass is the cut-down field, dry and wounded, which needs water to sprout again. The word for the rain's falling means it comes down drop by drop, gently.

This psalm is connected with the name of Solomon, though the heading can also be understood as "for Solomon" or "of Solomon." It is a prayer for the king that he will rule with justice, care for the poor, and bring peace. Many Christians see here a look toward Christ, the perfect King. That is a Christian interpretation, not something the text says in those words.

For today: when someone is hurt or worn out, they do not need pressure or harshness. You can be like that gentle rain, with kind words, concrete help, and patience. And if you are tired yourself, you can ask God to refresh you.
exp.43:22:
It says the people ask God to respond. "Awake" is a strong cry: they ask him to act, as if he were asleep. "Do not reject us forever" means that he not abandon them for good. God does not actually sleep; this is how they see it in their pain.

The words are spoken by the people of Israel in a psalm of the sons of Korah. They are suffering defeat and persecution, and they say this is happening even though they remain faithful. It is not known with certainty what historical moment it refers to. What matters is that they dare to tell God honestly what they feel.

For today: when you feel that God is silent, do not pretend you are fine. Tell him honestly about your pain and your questions, and keep praying. The Bible shows that God receives that cry without turning it away.
exp.6:11:
It says that God gives a chance before acting. The phrase "if he turn not" means "if the wicked person does not repent and change his way." Then God appears as a warrior who sharpens his sword and has his bow bent and ready. These are images of divine judgment.

David writes this psalm when he is being pursued and unjustly accused. He does not take revenge but brings his case before God, the righteous judge. Some scholars debate who "he" is in this verse, but most understand it as God, who warns before punishing.

For today: when you feel injustice, do not take revenge. Hand your case over to God. And if you yourself have strayed, remember that his patience is an invitation to return to him.
exp.20:7:
It says that God's power will reach all who oppose the king and hate him. "Reach" here means that God will find them, so that no one can escape. The "right hand" is the hand on the right side, a symbol of strength. Some understand that the verse speaks to the king, and others that it speaks to God, and the phrase allows both readings.

This is a psalm of David in which the people celebrate that God gave the king the victory. The verses before it speak of blessing and trust in God. This verse begins to describe how God will deal with the king's enemies, using strong images of judgment. Many Christians also read it looking toward Christ, the ultimate king.

For today: we do not have to take revenge or live in fear of those who harm us. We can trust that God sees injustice and is the one who judges with justice, and we can ask him to help us forgive and to do good.
exp.114:7:
This verse says that those who make idols, and those who trust in them, end up becoming like them. "Everyone who trusts in them" means anyone who places their hope in those figures. In plain modern English: "Those who make them become like them, and so does everyone who trusts in them."

The psalm is a song of praise from the people of Israel. The author is unknown. It compares the idols of the nations, made of silver and gold, with the living God. The verses before this one show that the idols have mouths, eyes, and hands, but they cannot feel or act. Many understand that whoever gives themselves over to them also becomes insensitive to God. Afterward, the psalm calls Israel to trust in the LORD, their help and their shield.

Few of us carve statues today, but we can trust in money, success, or fame. Ask yourself: "What do I rely on when I am afraid?" Bring that burden to God in prayer, because He does listen and He does help.
exp.77:36:
This verse says that the people's heart was not sincere toward God. The word "right" in the verse means honest, rightly directed toward him. The phrase "stedfast in his covenant" means they did not remain faithful to the commitment God made with them. They spoke well of God, but inwardly they were not with him.

Here the psalmist Asaph is speaking, reviewing the history of Israel in the wilderness. When God punished them, they remembered him and said the right words, but they were empty words. Even so, the following verses show that God was compassionate, forgave, and remembered that they were frail.

For today: it is not enough to say beautiful things in prayer or in church. Ask God to heal your heart and help you be sincere with him, including when you are not in trouble. His mercy encourages you to return with honesty.
exp.94:9:
God says that for forty years he was grieved with that generation. "It is a people that do err in their heart" means that their hearts wandered, turning aside again and again. And "they have not known my ways" means that they did not learn to walk as God wanted, even though they saw his works.

In this psalm, the psalmist calls people to worship God, and then God himself speaks. He recalls Israel in the wilderness, at Meribah and Massah, where the people doubted and tested the Lord. Those forty years were the time of the march through the desert, and that generation did not enter the rest that had been promised. It is a warning for those who listen today.

For today: do not grow used to hearing God with a closed heart. When you feel doubt or complaint, do not harden your heart; instead, answer quickly, pray sincerely, and ask him to teach you his ways.
exp.68:18:
God knows well what the one who prays is suffering. A public humiliation is a shame that is seen by others, and the words for it in the source explain it as contempt and mockery from other people. The psalmist also says that all his enemies are in God's sight, meaning that God sees them and nothing escapes him.

The psalm is attributed to David. He is distressed, surrounded by people who attack him without reason, and he feels that no one comforts him. For this reason he asks God not to hide his face and to rescue him. The verses that follow, about gall and vinegar, are later cited in the Gospels in connection with the suffering of Jesus.

When you feel humiliated or misunderstood, you do not need to explain everything with perfect words. Bring your shame before God as it is, with honesty. He already knows it, and you can leave both your pain and those who hurt you in his hands.
exp.118:161:
The psalmist says that he rejoices at God's word, and that his joy is like that of a soldier who finds great spoil after a battle. The word for the goods taken after defeating an enemy, the spoil of war, is what the verse calls "spoil."

Psalm 119 is a long poem in honor of God's law. No one knows for certain who wrote it. The speaker faces pressure, since he says that rulers have persecuted him without cause. Even so, he is not defeated: he marvels at God's word and sees it as a treasure.

For today: when hard days come, read the Bible not only out of duty, but looking for a treasure. Ask God to show you something that encourages you, and write it down to remember it.
exp.47:2:
This verse says that God has made himself known in the houses and strongholds of Jerusalem as a secure place to take refuge. Here "palaces" refers to the city's towers and fortifications, and "refuge" means firm protection. People have seen that there God watches over and defends.

It is a psalm of the sons of Korah, a group of Levites who led the praise in the temple. They sing in honor of Jerusalem, called Zion, but above all in honor of God, the great King who dwells in it. The following verses tell that enemy kings gathered together, saw the city, and fled in fear. The psalm does not say exactly what event it refers to, and some scholars connect it with an episode in Israel's history, but there is no certainty.

For today: when you feel fear or pressure, remember that your security is not in your walls, your money, or your plans, but in God. Seek him first in prayer.
exp.118:57:
He says that the psalmist sought God with his whole being. "I begged" means asking with humble pleading, and "your presence" is literally "your face," a way of speaking about seeking God's favor and nearness. He asks for mercy, that is, compassion and kindness he does not deserve, and he asks for it relying on what God has already promised in his word.

The speaker is the author of Psalm 119, a psalm about God's law; tradition is not unanimous about who wrote it. This section begins with the Hebrew letter Cheth. He has just said that his portion, the most valuable thing he has, is God and his word. Afterward he will tell how he reviewed his way and returned to God's testimonies. His plea comes from a life that wants to obey.

Today you can come before God with sincerity, without pretense, and ask him for mercy based on his promises. Before you pray, read a passage of Scripture and pray using those same words.
exp.118:59:
The psalmist says that he acted quickly and without delay to obey God's commandments. The word "made haste" is the English rendering of the verse, and "delayed not" means that he did not hold back or put it off for later. Keeping the commandments means obeying them and taking care to follow them.

The speaker is the author of the psalm, whose name is not known with certainty. In the verses before this one he sought God with his whole heart, asked for God's mercy, examined his life, and returned to God's teachings. Here his decision turns into immediate action. Afterward he mentions that the wicked attacked him, but he did not forget God's law.

When you know what God asks of you, do not postpone it. If you need to ask forgiveness, help someone, or give up a bad habit, take a small, concrete step today, trusting in God's mercy.
exp.75:3:
He says God is glorious and powerful. "Glorious" means admirable, full of splendor. The "mountains of prey" are the mountains where lions and other animals hunt for their prey; so the psalmist compares God with those mountains of predators and says that He is even more majestic. Some translations say "mountains of prey" or "everlasting mountains," and scholars debate the exact meaning of the expression.

The psalmist, within a song of God's people, celebrates a great victory in Jerusalem (Salem and Zion). God broke the weapons of the enemies. The Psalm does not say with certainty which specific battle it remembers; some think of the defeat of the Assyrian army, but this is a guess. What is clear is that the people recognize that the victory came from God, not from their own weapons.

For today: when you face a problem that seems bigger than you, remember that God is stronger than any threat. Pray with confidence and give Him the glory for whatever He resolves.
exp.97:4:
It says we should sing praises to Jehovah, that is, to God, accompanying ourselves with the harp. The verse repeats "with the harp" for emphasis: the music should accompany the singing with joy and with a clear voice.

The psalmist calls everyone to celebrate, because God remembered his mercy and his faithfulness toward Israel, and even distant nations saw his salvation. We do not know with certainty who wrote this psalm or when, but it is a song of praise that invites the whole world to acknowledge God as King. The following verses add trumpets and even the sea joining in the song.

Today we can praise God with our voice and with music, without holding back and with gratitude. This week, put on a song that speaks of what God has done for you and sing it from the heart, alone or with your family.
exp.49:0:
This verse presents God as the supreme Lord. The phrase "mighty God" means that there is no one above Him. "Lord" is the proper name of God in the Old Testament. "Called" means that He summoned everyone to gather. God speaks, and His call reaches the whole earth, "from the rising of the sun unto the going down thereof," that is, from east to west.

It is a psalm of Asaph, a Levite in charge of the music and praise in Israel's worship. Here the psalmist does not speak; rather, it announces that God Himself speaks. The verses that follow describe Him as a judge who comes from Zion, with fire and tempest, to call His people to account. The psalm is about sincere worship, and not only about rituals.

Before speaking, it is good to be silent and listen. God does not need our appearances; He seeks an honest heart. Today we can set aside a few minutes to read His Word attentively and let it speak to us.
exp.77:61:
He let his people fall to the sword, meaning they were killed in battle. He was angry with his inheritance, which is his people, the ones he had himself chosen as his own possession.

The speaker is Asaph, the psalmist, who reviews the history of Israel. Just before this verse he recalls that the people rebelled again and again. Here he describes a military defeat, probably the one in the days of Eli, when the ark was captured by the Philistines (1 Samuel 4). Scholars do not agree on every detail, but the psalm presents it as the result of the people's unfaithfulness.

For today: God does not take the sins of his people lightly, but his discipline is never the final word. The same psalm goes on to speak of how God awoke and restored them. If today you feel the consequences of your mistakes, return to him with humility and trust in his mercy.
exp.118:93:
He says that the psalmist belongs to God and asks him to take care of him. His reason is that he has sincerely sought the Lord's commandments. "Save me" means protect me, care for me, and rescue me. "Sought" speaks of a constant effort to know and obey, not of mere curiosity.

The speaker is the author of Psalm 119, whose name we do not know for certain. He is going through affliction and the threat of wicked people, as the following verses show. Earlier he said that God's law was his delight and gave him life. For that reason he comes near to God with confidence, as someone who already belongs to him.

For today: when you feel fear or pressure, begin your prayer by remembering that you belong to God. Then ask him for his care and keep reading his Word faithfully. His protection does not depend on your merits, but seeking him keeps your heart close to him.
exp.144:10:
This verse says that those who belong to God speak of the glory of his kingdom and of his power. The words "they shall speak" and "talk" are an invitation to tell, in our own words, who God is and what he does. The word "strength," in the sense of his power and his might, is the idea behind the verse's call to speak of God's power.

The psalm carries the heading "A Psalm of praise of David," and the text presents it that way. The one speaking praises God and calls others to do the same. In the verses before, God is good to all, and his works and his faithful ones bless him. Here the faithful people of God, that is, his people, share with others why God deserves praise. The next verse clarifies that they do this so that everyone may know his mighty deeds.

Today we can tell a family member, a friend, or a coworker something concrete that God has done in our life. A long speech is not needed. A simple and sincere testimony of his goodness and his power is enough.
exp.67:27:
It says that God himself has decided to give strength to his people. Then the psalmist asks him: "confirm," that is, establish, sustain, and bring to its goal, what you have already begun to do in us. "Ordained" here means decreed or commanded. Some older translations read "Command, O God, your strength," and scholars debate which reading is most likely.

The speaker is the psalmist, probably David, according to the heading of the psalm. He has been describing the tribes of Israel gathered in procession to worship, with Benjamin, Judah, Zebulun and Naphtali. Then he looks toward the temple in Jerusalem and the submission of the nations. He recognizes that Israel's strength comes from God, not from its armies.

For today: do not depend only on your own strength. This very day, pray like this: "Lord, finish what you began in me," and trust that he will sustain your way.
exp.77:1:
He says the psalmist will speak using a parable, that is, a teaching in the form of a story or wise saying. He also promises to tell of things hidden from long ago, that is, truths kept secret or guarded for a long time, which he now wants to make known.

Asaph speaks, and the psalm is called a maskil, which is probably a poem meant to instruct. He calls Israel "my people" and invites them to listen. He will recall God's history with them: his miracles, and also the failures of the people. The verses that follow explain that these teachings were passed from parents to children, so that no one would forget what God did. Matthew 13:35 quotes this verse, but scholars understand it in different ways.

For today: think about who taught you to trust God and what story of his faithfulness you can tell. Today, share with a son, a nephew, or a friend an experience of how God helped you.
exp.43:12:
It says that God allowed his people to become a disgrace before the nations around them. "Scorn" is cruel mockery, and "derision" is laughter meant to humiliate. "Those who surround us" are the nearby nations. In other words, the people living around Israel laughed at it and looked down on it.

This psalm is a lament of God's people, written by the sons of Korah. It is not known with certainty during which exact defeat it was written; several proposals have been made. The people remember the victories of the past, but now they suffer and do not understand why God allows it. Even so, they say they have not forgotten his covenant (vv. 17-18). It is an honest prayer in the midst of pain.

When you suffer humiliation or mockery and do not understand why, you can tell God honestly what you feel. The Bible shows that praying this way is not a lack of faith; it is continuing to come to Him.
exp.67:16:
God has a vast army at his service. The word "chariots" refers to vehicles of war, and here the psalm speaks of thousands upon thousands of angels. Most important is that the Lord is in the midst of them, just as he was on Mount Sinai when he gave the law, and now he is in his holy place.

It is a psalm of David, a song of victory. It is used to remember how God led his people, from Sinai to Jerusalem. The high mountains of Bashan seem to compete with God's mountain, but God chose his own mountain. Some understand it to be Zion; the text does not make this completely clear. The psalm celebrates that God reigns and protects.

For today: when you feel fear or see very great problems, remember that God is not far away or alone. His presence is greater than any threat. Pray with confidence, knowing that the Lord is near you.
exp.137:1:
He says David will bow down in worship toward the temple, that is, the sanctuary of God. He will give thanks for God's mercy (his faithful love) and for his truth (his faithfulness in keeping what he has promised). He explains that the Hebrew-based wording means "I will bow down." And "your word" means your promise. According to the text, God has exalted his word and his name above all.

David speaks here, the one who said earlier that he would praise God with his whole heart. The "temple" may have referred to the tabernacle, since in David's time the temple of Solomon did not yet exist. Some understand "the gods" to be idols, judges, or powerful beings. Afterward David recalls that God answered him when he cried out.

For today: before asking for something, take a moment to thank God for his faithfulness to you. Think of one of his promises that has been fulfilled in your life and give thanks for it sincerely.
exp.120:4:
The verse says that God is your keeper, that is, the one who looks after you and protects you. It also calls him your shade, standing at your right hand. In that hot climate, shade was a relief and a place of refuge. The right hand was the side where a defender stood, right beside you.

This psalm is a song of ascents, probably sung by pilgrims climbing up to Jerusalem along difficult roads. It is not certain who is speaking: it may be a traveler talking to himself, or one voice answering another. Either way, it expresses confidence that God watches over the people and over each person on the road.

Today, when you feel tired or exposed, remember that God is at your side. Say to him in prayer, "Stay with me today," and trust that he does not leave you alone.
exp.27:6:
This verse says that God is the strength and protection of the one speaking. A shield is what covers and defends from danger. The word "trusted" in the verse means the same as "hoped," in the past tense. "I am helped" means "I received help." That is why his heart rejoices and he wants to thank God with a song.

The one speaking is David, according to the title of the psalm. Earlier he cried out to God for help in distress, and in the verse before this one he blesses God because God heard his plea. This verse is his response of gratitude. Afterward, his praise extends to the whole people: he asks that God care for them like a shepherd.

For today: when you go through a difficulty, pray with confidence and then don't forget to give thanks. Write down how God helped you, or sing him a song. Remembering his past help strengthens your trust for what lies ahead.
exp.51:2:
Here David tells Doeg that he preferred evil over good, and lies over speaking what is right. This is not a slip or an accident, but a preference of the heart. "Selah" is a pause or musical marker; its exact meaning is not known for certain, but it invites the reader to stop and reflect.

David speaks in this psalm, which according to its title arose when Doeg the Edomite reported to Saul that David had been with the priest Ahimelech. His report, told with harmful intent, led to a great slaughter of priests (1 Samuel 22). David confronts a powerful man who boasts of his wickedness, and he trusts that God's mercy endures.

Today we can ask ourselves what we truly love. Sometimes a half-truth, a piece of gossip, or an exaggeration seems to give us an advantage. Let us ask God for a heart that loves what is good and speaks the truth, even when it costs us.
exp.36:39:
This verse says that God himself helps and rescues those who trust in him. The reason for the help is simple: they trust in God.

This is a psalm of David, who is now an older man and speaks from experience. He writes to encourage the righteous who suffer as they see the wicked seem to prosper. The verses before this one say that the wicked will be destroyed and that God is a stronghold in times of trouble. This verse closes the psalm with a promise of hope.

For today: when you feel that injustice is winning or that you see no way out, do not despair. Pray, keep doing what is right, and wait on God with patience, trusting that he cares for you.
exp.106:11:
He says God humbled the hearts of those rebels through hard labor. The word "broke down" means to humble, to bring down pride. "With labour" refers to weariness and suffering. In the end they stumbled and fell, and no one came to help them. They were left alone in their need.

This psalm is sung by the people whom God rescued. It is not known with certainty who wrote it. Here a group is described who suffered imprisonment and darkness for rejecting the words of God. According to the psalm, their pain was connected with their rebellion. But the psalm does not say that all suffering is punishment. The verses that follow show that, when they cried out, God delivered them.

For today: if you notice that your pride has left you alone and worn out, do not stay silent. Acknowledge your mistake and cry out to God today. He still listens, and he has the power to break chains.
exp.101:10:
The psalmist says that his days are like the shadow of the evening, which stretches out and soon disappears. He also says that he has withered like the grass, which fades under the heat.

The one speaking is a sufferer who, according to the heading, pours out his complaint before God. He feels consumed by suffering and thinks that God himself has let him fall. It is not known with certainty who wrote it; the closing verses suggest that he also grieves over the situation of Zion, Jerusalem.

For today: when you feel weak or it seems that life is slipping away from you, imitate the psalmist and tell God everything with sincerity. Then look, as he did, to God, who endures forever and has compassion.
exp.77:33:
This verse says that when God punished the people of Israel and some of them died, then they sought him. They became eager and diligent to find him. But their searching came from fear and pain, not from sincere love.

The one speaking is Asaph, the author of the psalm, who reviews the history of Israel in the wilderness. He wants to teach the new generations that the people sinned again and again, even after seeing God's miracles. The following verses show that their repentance was shallow: they flattered him with their mouths, but lied to him with their tongues.

For today: let us not seek God only when a crisis comes. We can ask him to give us a sincere heart, so that we draw near to him also in the quiet days, with gratitude and faithfulness, and not only out of necessity.
exp.137:7:
God will carry out what He has promised and begun in the psalmist's life. "Will perfect that which concerneth me" means that God will bring His purpose for him to completion. "Thy mercy" is His faithful, kind love, which never runs out. "The works of thine own hands" refers to the person himself, whom God has made and cares for. That is why the psalmist trusts that God will not abandon him halfway through.

The speaker is David, according to the psalm's heading, although some scholars debate his exact authorship. Before this verse, he gives thanks to God and acknowledges that God looks after the humble, and that He sustains him in distress and in the face of his enemies. Verse 8 is his conclusion, full of confidence and, at the same time, a humble prayer.

For today: when you feel unfinished or weary, remember that your worth does not depend on your strength. Hand your plans over to God in a simple prayer, and trust that He is still at work in you.
exp.85:12:
This verse says that David gives thanks to God because his mercy, that is, his compassionate love, has been very great toward him. It says that God has delivered his soul, that is, rescued him, from the lowest hell. The Hebrew word behind "hell" is Sheol, which can mean the grave or the place of the dead, and here it speaks of a deadly danger.

The speaker is David, according to the title of the psalm. He is praying in a time of distress, since the next verse mentions proud enemies who pursue him. Before this verse he asks to be taught by God and promises to praise him. His gratitude for what he has already received gives him confidence to ask for more help.

For today: calmly remember the times when God sustained you in difficult moments. Write them down and give thanks for them. That remembrance strengthens your faith when new trials come.
exp.79:1:
The explanation says that the people are asking God to show his strength and power on behalf of the tribes of Ephraim, Benjamin, and Manasseh. "Stir up thy strength" is a poetic way of saying "act with your power." "Come and save us" is a plea for God himself to come and rescue them.

The speaker is Asaph, or perhaps a group of singers who bear his name, praying for the whole nation of Israel. These three tribes appear together, and it is possible they marched near the ark in the wilderness (Numbers 2). The psalm does not say exactly what the disaster was, but it is clear they were in distress and needed God to restore them.

Today we can pray with this same sincerity. When we feel weak or in crisis, there is no need to pretend to strength: we can ask God to act, and trust that he cares for his people like a good shepherd.
exp.19:8:
The explanation says that the people ask the LORD to save them, and that the king hears them when they call. Others understand the king to be the king of Israel, and they take the verse as a request that God save the king and that the king hear them.

It is the final part of a psalm of David, which the people sing before a battle. The verses before it contrast those who trust in chariots and horses with those who trust in the name of God. It ends with a simple prayer for help.

For today: before looking only to human resources, practice calling on God first. When you face pressure or a difficult decision, offer a short, confident prayer, knowing that he hears those who call on him.
exp.125:4:
This verse says that those who sowed in tears will afterward reap with joy. "Sow" is to scatter seed in the ground; "reap" is to cut the harvest; "joy" is a very great gladness. The sorrow of the time of sowing is not the end of the story.

This psalm is a song of Israel's pilgrims. It seems to recall the people's return after the captivity, though some think it speaks of a restoration that is still incomplete. That is why they pray, "Turn again our captivity," like the streams of the south, which fill with water after the rain. They speak with gratitude and hope at the same time.

For today: if you are doing good with effort, through prayer, or in pain, do not think it is being lost. Keep sowing in faith, and trust that God knows how to bring forth fruit in its time, even if it is not always the way you expect.
exp.114:11:
This verse says that God has not forgotten his people. "Hath been mindful" means that he keeps them in mind and acts on their behalf. That is why he promises to bless Israel as a whole and, in a special way, the descendants of Aaron, the priests.

Psalm 115 is a song of God's people. It contrasts the living God with the silent idols of the nations. Before this verse, the psalmist calls Israel, the priests, and those who fear God to trust in him. Here the community answers with confidence: God will bless them. It is not known with certainty who wrote the psalm or exactly when it was sung.

For today: when you feel forgotten or are going through a hard time, remember that God keeps you in mind. Trust in him and give thanks for the blessings you have already received.
exp.144:11:
The explanation says that God's people speak of his mighty works and of his kingdom so that everyone may know them. To "make known" means to announce or tell. His "mighty acts" are the powerful deeds of God. His "glorious majesty" is his greatness and splendor. The "sons of men" are all human beings, not only Israel.

This psalm is titled "Praise of David." The speaker invites the faithful to bless God. The verses before this one ask that the holy ones speak of the glory of the kingdom, and this verse gives the purpose: that others should know it. The verses that follow explain why that kingdom deserves to be proclaimed: it is eternal and it sustains those who fall.

For today: tell someone, this week, one concrete thing God has done for you or your family. No sermon is needed; a sincere and simple testimony is enough.
exp.112:6:
He takes the most humbled person and lifts them up. "Dust" and "dung" speak of the lowest, dirtiest, and most despised places in society. A "needy" person is someone who lacks what is basic. God does not ignore the one nobody sees; he lifts that person out of there and gives back their dignity.

It is a psalm of praise, which begins and ends with "Hallelujah." We do not know for certain who wrote it. The speaker invites the people of Israel to praise God because he is very great, and yet he stoops down to look at the weak. The verses that follow say that he seats them with princes and gives children to the barren woman, examples of how God changes desperate situations.

For today: if you feel small or forgotten, remember that God sees you. And if you have more resources, imitate his heart: set aside time to help and dignify someone in need.
exp.89:16:
This verse is a prayer. It asks that the light, that is, the favor and goodness of the Lord our God, be upon us. It also asks that God would make the work of our hands succeed, which here means giving our labor order, direction, and good results. And the request to make it last means that it would be firm and enduring.

The Psalm is titled "Prayer of Moses, man of God." Although many attribute it to him, there is no complete certainty about who wrote it. The one who prays acknowledges that human life is brief and fragile, and that God is eternal. After speaking of affliction and hard years, it ends by asking for God's favor so that the effort of his people will not be in vain.

For today: before you begin your work, your studies, or your household tasks, pray this verse. Do your part with care, and ask God to give meaning and lasting fruit to what you do, trusting that he is able to do it.
exp.101:9:
It says the psalmist's suffering comes "because of" the anger and wrath of God. He feels that God first lifted him up, that is, set him high or showed him favor, and then cast him down, like someone who throws something far away. "You lifted me up" sounds like a blessing; "you have cast me down" sounds like rejection.

It is a psalm of lament, titled as the prayer of one who is afflicted. No one knows with certainty who wrote it. Some see it as coming from the time of exile, but that is an opinion. The one speaking is sick, alone, and mocked by his enemies. He interprets his pain as discipline or rejection by God. Even so, he does not stop praying, and a few verses later he declares that God remains forever.

For today: when pain makes you feel abandoned, you can tell God honestly what you feel, without disguising it. But do not let your feelings have the last word; remember that God is still faithful.
exp.103:12:
He waters the mountains from his upper chambers, and the earth is satisfied by the fruit of what he has made. The explanation says God waters the hills from his "chambers," an old word meaning the high rooms, that is, the heavens, from which the rain comes. Because of what God does, the earth is satisfied, meaning it is well provided for and full of life.

It is a psalm of praise, and it is thought that an unnamed psalmist wrote it. It sings of creation step by step. Earlier it speaks of springs for animals and birds; then it speaks of bread, wine, and oil. The point is that God cares for everything he has made, not merely sustaining it from a distance.

For today: the next time it rains or you eat, stop and thank God. Recognizing that everything comes from his hand frees us from anxiety and makes us more generous toward others.
exp.109:5:
This verse describes the Messiah as a judge who acts over the nations. "He shall judge among the heathen" means he will pronounce judgment among the peoples. "He shall fill the places with the dead bodies" is a strong image of total defeat for those who oppose God. "He shall wound the heads" speaks of breaking rebellious rulers or leaders. Some translators understand "the heads" as a single chief over many lands.

Psalm 110 is by David, who speaks of a Lord greater than himself: the King and Priest whom God establishes. The verses before it speak of God's oath and the day of his wrath. The New Testament applies this psalm to Jesus. The images of war are ancient poetry showing that God's justice will overcome evil.

For today: we do not have to take revenge or despair in the face of injustice. We can trust that Christ will judge with justice, and in the meantime live in peace, forgiving and doing good.
exp.47:3:
This verse tells how the kings of the earth gathered together, probably to attack Jerusalem, and then they passed by together. The phrase can be understood in two ways: that they went on past without accomplishing anything, or that they withdrew in defeat. The words "lo" serve to draw attention, as if saying: "Take notice!"

It is a psalm of the sons of Korah, a song of praise to God and to Zion, the city where He is known as a refuge. It is not known with certainty which attack is meant; some connect it to a specific threat against Jerusalem, while others read it in a more general way. The following verses show that, on seeing the city, the kings were troubled and fled.

For today: the powers that seem enormous do not have the last word. When you face a pressure that frightens you, remember that God remains your refuge, and seek His protection in prayer.
exp.55:12:
He says that God rescued the psalmist's life from death and kept his feet from stumbling or falling. The purpose is that he may walk before God in the light of the living, that is, enjoy life under God's watchful eye and care. "Rescued" in this sense means saved from danger, and a fall refers to a stumble or ruin.

The psalm is spoken by David, according to its heading, when the Philistines seized him in Gath. He was surrounded by enemies and afraid, but he chose to trust in God. In the verses before, he promises to fulfill his vows and to offer praise. Here he gives thanks because God saved him, or because he is certain that God will. Interpreters understand it in both ways.

When God cares for you in a difficulty, do not take it as something ordinary. Thank him with your words and live in a way that honors him, walking with honesty and trust each day.
exp.30:17:
This verse is a prayer that lying lips would be silenced. It speaks of people who say harsh and cruel things against the righteous, with pride and contempt. "Silenced" here means made mute, so that they can no longer keep speaking.

The one speaking is David, according to the heading of the psalm. He is distressed and feels that others slander him and reject him. He does not defend himself with revenge, but asks God to act. The verses that follow show his trust: God keeps and protects those who fear him, and hides them from hurtful words as in a safe refuge.

For today: when someone speaks badly of you unjustly, do not repay them in kind. Bring your pain to God in prayer, ask him to defend the truth, and rest in the knowledge that he cares for you.
exp.77:38:
He remembered that human beings are frail. "Flesh" speaks of our weakness and that we are mortal. "A wind that passeth away, and cometh not again" is like the wind: it passes and does not return. The word "remembered" means that God kept this in mind as he dealt with his people.

This psalm was written by Asaph, who reviews the history of Israel to teach the new generations. It shows that the people failed again and again in the wilderness, but God was patient and forgave them. This verse gives one reason for that compassion: God knows our frailty. Some understand "a wind that cometh not again" only as the brevity of life; one should not press the text beyond what it says.

Today, when you fail, do not use God's mercy as an excuse, but do not sink into shame either. Come to him with sincerity; he knows what we are made of.
exp.60:4:
This verse says that God heard the promises the psalmist made to him. "Vows" are solemn commitments or promises made to God. "Heritage" is an inheritance, something valuable received as a gift. "Those who fear your name" means respecting and honoring God with reverence, not being afraid of him as one would fear an enemy.

The psalm is attributed to David in its heading, though some think he wrote it while far from home, perhaps in a time of distress. It is not known for certain when it was written. He cries out to God from a difficult place and remembers that God has been his refuge. Now he trusts that God answers and blesses those who are faithful to him.

For today: when you are in difficulty, remember that God hears you and cares for his people. Keep faithfully what you have promised him, and trust that he sustains those who honor him.
exp.68:31:
It says that the humble, that is, those who do not think themselves superior and acknowledge their need, will see what God does and be glad. Then it invites them: "seek God," that is, draw near to him with sincerity, "and your heart shall live," that is, the weary or discouraged spirit will be lifted up and receive new life.

The one speaking is King David, according to the title of the psalm. He is suffering, surrounded by enemies and mockery, and he has cried out to God in distress. Even so, he promises to praise him with songs and trusts that God hears those in need. This verse is like a bridge: what David is going through, he wants other humble people to see and be encouraged by.

For today: when you are discouraged, do not shut yourself up in your sadness. Seek God with simplicity, in prayer and in reading the Bible, and stand beside others who suffer. He can revive your heart.
exp.26:10:
Here the psalmist asks God to show him how to live. Asking God to teach his way means asking for instruction to walk as pleases God. A plain path is a straight, just, and safe road. Because of mine enemies means he asks this because of those who watch him and attack him.

The speaker is David, according to the traditional title of the psalm. He is surrounded by enemies and false accusations, and he feels that he could be left alone, even if his father and mother forsook him. For this reason he asks not only for protection but also for direction. He knows that under pressure, one wrong step would be dangerous.

For today: when you face pressure or injustice, before you react, pray asking for guidance. Read the Bible with humility, and choose to do what is right, even when others act wrongly.
exp.34:22:
Here the psalmist asks God to act. "Stir up yourself and wake up" is poetic language: it does not mean that God is sleeping, but that the author feels God is slow to intervene. "My judgment" and "my cause" refer to his defense: he wants God to examine his case and bring him justice. He calls him "my God and my Lord," with personal trust.

David speaks, according to the psalm's heading. He is surrounded by enemies who accuse him without reason, mock him, and say: "our eyes have seen it." He does not seek revenge on his own, but appeals to the just Judge, asking that God not stay silent or stay far away.

For today: when you are treated unfairly or slandered, you can tell God sincerely what you feel, even that he seems to be taking his time. Hand your cause over to him in prayer instead of taking revenge, and trust that he sees and judges with justice.
exp.31:1:
This verse says that the person is happy whose guilt the Lord does not count against them, and who does not live with deceit in their heart. The word "blessed" means happy, favored. To "count" or "impute" something means to record it against someone's account. "Iniquity" means wickedness or sin. "Guile" means deceit or fraud; here it speaks of falseness of heart.

The speaker is David, in a psalm of instruction. The verses that follow show that he spent a time keeping his sin hidden and suffering inwardly. His joy comes after he stopped concealing it and received God's forgiveness. The New Testament quotes this passage in Romans 4:7-8.

For today: if there is something you are hiding, bring it honestly before God. He offers forgiveness, and living without pretense brings rest to the heart.
exp.146:19:
He has not done this for any other nation. Only to Israel did he make known his word, his laws, and his "judgments," which here mean his just decisions and commands. The phrase "they have not known them" speaks of the peoples who did not receive that revelation. "Hallelujah" means "praise the Lord."

The psalmist, whose name is not stated with certainty, calls the people of Israel to praise God. He praises him for caring for his people and for governing creation by his word, which melts the ice and makes the waters flow. The verses before this one say that God spoke to Jacob. This verse emphasizes that Israel received a special privilege, and for that reason it was to respond with gratitude.

Today we can see the Bible as a gift, not as something ordinary. If you have access to the Word of God, read it with gratitude and share it with others with humility, without feeling superior.
exp.17:48:
David says that, for all that God has done for him, he will give thanks before other peoples and sing praises to his name. Here, "to give thanks" does not mean admitting sins, but recognizing and publicly declaring who God is and what he has done. The "nations" referred to are peoples or nations that were not Israel.

David, king of Israel, speaks at the end of a psalm of gratitude. God had delivered him from his enemies, including Saul, according to the psalm's heading. After describing that deliverance, David responds with thanksgiving. The New Testament quotes this verse in Romans 15:9, applying it to the idea that the nations too should praise God.

For today: when God helps you with something, do not keep it to yourself. Tell a friend, your family, or your church, and give thanks through a song or a prayer. Your testimony can encourage others to trust in him.
exp.118:41:
It says that when someone mocks or insults him, the psalmist will have an answer: that he has placed his trust in God's word. The word "reproacher" refers to someone who dishonors, offends, or shames another. "Answer" means he will be able to reply with firmness.

The speaker is the author of Psalm 119, whose name is not known for certain. He is someone who loves God's law and suffers mockery or pressure because of it. He has just asked for God's mercy and salvation according to God's promise. That is why his answer to his critics rests on that promise, not on his own merit.

Today, when someone mocks your faith, you do not need to argue in anger. You can answer calmly and simply that you trust in God and in what he has said. To do that, read his Word often and keep it in your heart.
exp.103:10:
It says that the springs and streams that God sends give drink to all the animals of the field. "Give drink" means to give water to drink. "Quench their thirst" means to calm or put out their thirst. The "wild donkeys" are untamed burros that live in dry places and do not depend on any owner.

This psalm is a song of praise to God as Creator. It is not known with certainty who wrote it, because the text does not say. The psalmist contemplates how God set limits to the waters and then turned them into springs of life. Even the freest and most distant animals receive his care.

For today: if God takes care of a wild donkey on the mountain, you can trust that he also takes care of you. Today, as you drink a glass of water, give thanks to God for what he gives you each day, and rest in the knowledge that he knows what you need.
exp.95:7:
This verse invites us to give God the honor he deserves for who he is. Its call to give the glory due to his name means recognizing his greatness, not inventing it. It also asks us to bring an offering, and to come into his courts, the open grounds of the temple where the people gathered to worship.

The psalm does not say with certainty who wrote it. It is a song of praise that calls all the families of the nations to worship, not only Israel. The verses that follow give the reason: the Lord reigns, sustains the world, and will judge with justice. That is why worship is a response to his character.

Today we can prepare our hearts before going to church or praying. Instead of arriving in a hurry, think about who God is and give him something concrete: sincere thankfulness, your time, or generous help to someone in need.
exp.137:0:
This verse says that David wants to praise God with his whole heart, that is, with sincerity and without holding anything back. The source's quoted phrases are not in the verse your reader sees, so I have left out the sentence that explains an old form of wording. The verse also says he will sing praise "before the gods." That phrase is understood in several ways: it may refer to the false gods of the nations, to rulers, or to heavenly beings. Scholars do not agree on the exact meaning.

The speaker is David, according to the heading of the psalm. The verses that follow show that he gives thanks because God is faithful and kind, and because God answered him when he cried out to Him. His praise comes from gratitude for what God has done.

Today we can praise God sincerely, even when there are people or ideas around us that do not honor Him. Today you can thank Him out loud for a prayer that He has already answered.
exp.109:3:
God himself makes a solemn oath: he will not change his mind. He declares that the King of this psalm is also a priest, and that he will be one forever. "After the order of Melchizedek" means that his priesthood is like that of Melchizedek, not like that of the Levitical priests. "Will not repent" means that God will not take back what he has said.

David writes this psalm, and Jesus cites it as a reference to the Messiah (Matthew 22:43-45). Melchizedek was king of Salem and priest of God Most High in the days of Abraham (Genesis 14). The psalm joins two offices that in Israel were almost always kept separate: king and priest. Hebrews 5 through 7 explains this verse by applying it to Christ.

For today: your relationship with God does not depend on your own consistency, but on a priest who lives forever and an oath that God does not break. When you feel you have failed, come to Jesus in prayer with confidence.
exp.104:11:
This verse says that when God made his promise of the land of Canaan, the descendants of Abraham were very few in number and lived there as strangers, without land of their own. "Few men in number" means they were a small group, and "strangers" means they did not belong to that place.

Psalm 105 is a song of praise that remembers God's works with his people. It is not known for certain who wrote it, although a part of it also appears in 1 Chronicles 16 and is connected with David. The psalmist wants to show that God was faithful to his covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, even when everything seemed weak and without a future.

For today: if you feel small, without resources, or out of place, remember that God does not need great numbers to fulfill his promises. Trust in his faithfulness and give thanks for what he has already done in your life.
exp.35:6:
This verse says that God's mercy is something precious and admirable. Here "excellent" means outstanding, of great worth. The word "lovingkindness" is his faithful love and goodness. "Put their trust" means that people seek refuge and protection. The image of "under the shadow of thy wings" reminds us of a bird that covers its young.

The speaker is David, according to the heading of the psalm. Before the verse, it contrasts the wickedness of the godless with the greatness of God: his mercy, his truth and his justice are vast, like the heavens and the mountains. Then it says that God cares for all, both people and animals. After that it speaks of the abundance and the life that are found in God.

For today: when you feel insecure, tired or guilty, do not hide from God, run toward Him. Today, in prayer, hand over that specific worry to Him and rest in His care, trusting that His love is greater than your problem.
exp.118:48:
This verse begins with "Zain," which is the name of the seventh letter of the Hebrew alphabet. This section of the psalm is an acrostic poem, and every verse in this group begins with that letter. The psalmist asks God to remember the promise He made to him, since he has placed his hope in it. Here, "hope" means to trust and wait with firm confidence.

The speaker is the author of the psalm, who calls himself God's servant. No one knows with certainty who wrote it. He is in the middle of affliction and the mockery of proud people, yet he loves God's law. Asking God to remember does not mean that God forgets; it is a way of praying with confidence, relying on what He has already said.

Today we can do the same: when you are tired or discouraged, look for a promise in the Bible, read it in prayer, and tell God that you trust in it.
exp.73:11:
The explanation says that God has been the king of his people from long ago, from the very beginning. In other words, God is a king who rescues and brings salvation in the midst of the earth, in full view of everyone.

A psalmist from the family of Asaph speaks here. The people are probably suffering because the temple has been destroyed and because their enemies are attacking them; it is not known with certainty what exact moment in history is reflected. After complaining to God, the psalmist changes tone with this "but" and remembers who God is, recalling his great deeds of the past, such as the opening of the sea.

For today: when everything seems to be going wrong, do as the psalmist did. Tell God honestly what you feel, and then remember what he has done before. That memory can sustain your hope.
exp.145:2:
This verse advises us not to put our trust in princes, that is, in rulers and powerful people, nor in any "son of man," which means any human being. The reason is that there is no help in them, and here "help" means salvation or certain aid. A person cannot truly save us.

The psalmist, whose name the text does not indicate, begins by praising God with his whole being. Then he contrasts human beings with God: a man dies, his breath departs and he returns to the earth, and his plans come to an end. By contrast, happy is the one who waits on the God of Jacob.

We can respect and value our leaders and those who help us, but without placing in them the hope that belongs only to God. When a human promise fails, let us remember that God remains faithful.
exp.41:8:
Here the psalmist speaks to God with complete honesty. He calls him "my rock," that is, his firm and secure refuge, yet he feels that God has forgotten him. Being in mourning means dressed in grief, sad and heavy-hearted. The oppression of the enemy is the mistreatment of those who attack him.

The speaker is a writer from the people of Israel, probably a Levite, who is far from the temple and suffers mockery from his enemies. Scholars do not agree on the exact details of his situation. Even so, in the verses nearby he remembers that God gives him mercy by day and song by night, and at the end he encourages himself to wait on God.

Today, you can tell God what you truly feel, even your doubts and your pain. Praying with honesty is not a lack of faith; it is continuing to draw near to Him, the Rock, while you wait for Him to sustain you.
exp.34:13:
The explanation says that David treated his enemies as if they were a friend or a brother. He walked about with sorrow, bowed down heavily, like one who mourns the death of his mother.

The passage is spoken by David, in a psalm where he asks God for help against people who attacked him without reason. When they were sick, he fasted and prayed for them with sincere sorrow. Even so, they repaid his good with evil. It is not known with certainty what moment of his life he is referring to.

For today: we can pray and show compassion even toward those who have hurt us. This does not mean approving of the wrong they do, but trusting that God is just and keeping a tender heart, free from bitterness.
exp.103:11:
It says that, beside the springs and streams that God made flow between the mountains, the birds of the sky make their nests. Among the branches they sing, or lift up their voices, that is, they make their song heard. "They shall have their habitation" means that they live there; "which" refers to the streams of the previous verse.

The psalm is a hymn of praise to God as Creator. It does not say who wrote it; tradition links it with David, but the text itself does not claim this. The psalmist looks at nature and shows how God cares for all his creatures: he gives water to the animals and the birds, and then food to the earth and to human beings.

For today: if God cares even for the birds and their song, he also cares for you. Take a pause today to notice something of creation, such as a tree, the song of a bird, or the rain, and give thanks to God for his daily provision.
exp.57:1:
They don't only fail when they judge; in their hearts they plan evil. The word "Yea" in the verse means "indeed" or "in fact," and the verse says they work wickedness. "Ye work wickedness" means they do injustice. "Ye weigh the violence of your hands" describes those who, like someone weighing goods on a scale, measure out violence across the earth instead of justice.

David speaks in this psalm, which carries a heading that includes a word whose exact meaning is uncertain, perhaps a musical or literary term. He addresses an assembly, and some scholars think these are unjust judges or rulers; others read the word as "gods" and understand it differently. He rebukes them because they pervert justice and harm others.

For today: injustice begins in the heart. Before you act, ask God to examine your motives, and seek to treat with justice and honesty those who depend on your decisions, whether at home, at work, or in the church.
exp.120:7:
It says that God will watch over all your movements: "your going out and your coming in" is a way of speaking about everything you do, when you leave home and when you return, at the start and at the end of your tasks. "Will keep" means to protect and watch over with care. And that protection is not temporary: it is "from now on and forever."

This psalm is one of the "songs of ascents" or "songs of the steps" (Psalms 120–134), which many understand as songs of the pilgrims who went up to Jerusalem. No one knows for certain who first said it aloud: some read it as a dialogue, where one person expresses fear and another answers with this promise. It is the end of a psalm that insists that God does not sleep and cares for his people.

Today, before leaving home or when returning from a hard day, you can pray with this verse and remember that your daily life is in God's hands.
exp.118:170:
