This verse says that the psalmist's lips will be so full of praise that they nearly overflow, like a pot running over. The reason is that God teaches him his statutes, that is, his laws and commands. The verb in the verse, "when thou hast taught me," expresses this teaching as something God does for him.

The speaker is the author of Psalm 119, a long poem in honor of God's word. We do not know with certainty who wrote it. Here, in the section "Tau," he asks that God hear his cry, give him understanding, and set him free. His praise comes from learning, not only from feeling.

For today: when you read the Bible, ask God to teach it to you and not just read it out of obligation. Then thank him aloud for what you have learned. In this way your reading becomes sincere praise, and your heart is filled with gratitude.
exp.136:0:
The explanation says that the exiled Israelites sat down beside the rivers of Babylon and wept as they remembered Zion, that is, Jerusalem, the city of God. "There" points to the place of exile, and "remembered" means "when they recalled." The sorrow comes from longing for their homeland and their life of worship.

The speaker is the people of Israel, or a poet speaking on their behalf, after being taken captive to Babylon. This probably happened after the destruction of Jerusalem in 586 BC. The psalm does not say who wrote it. The "rivers" may have been the Euphrates and its canals, though the text gives no further detail.

When you are far from what you love or going through a loss, do not hide your pain. You can weep honestly before God, remember his promises, and seek the support of other believers. Sincere weeping can also be a form of prayer.
exp.5:5:
He says that David is worn out from so much groaning. Each night he weeps so much that his bed is soaked, as if it were flooded. Here, the bed, or the place where he rests, is what he drenches with his tears. It is an exaggerated and very expressive way of speaking about deep pain.

The one speaking is David, according to the title of the psalm. He is distressed, and the text does not state exactly the cause: it may be an illness, the pressure of his enemies, or the awareness of his sin. The nearby verses speak of suffering and of adversaries. He cries out to God asking for mercy, and in the end he finds that God has indeed heard his weeping.

Today it teaches us that we do not need to hide our pain before God. We can bring him our tears honestly, trusting that he hears them, even when we do not yet see the answer.
exp.73:2:
"Lift up your feet" is a way of asking God to come and walk toward the ruins, that is, to draw near and see what has been destroyed. "Desolations" means places that have been laid waste or left in ruins, and "perpetual" here seems to indicate something that has lasted a long time or appears to have no end. The psalmist asks that God look at the damage the enemy has done in the sanctuary.

Context: The speaker is Asaph, or someone from his group of singers, speaking on behalf of the people. The temple or place of worship has probably been attacked and destroyed. Scholars debate which exact moment is in view, perhaps the fall of Jerusalem. The people feel abandoned, yet they still speak to God with confidence.

For today: When you see ruin or injustice in what you love, do not silence it or carry it alone. Bring honestly to God what you see and ask him to act.
exp.117:21:
It says that the builders threw away a stone because they considered it useless, but that very stone ended up being the most important one in the building. The word translated as "refused" means rejected, and the quoted phrase about "the head stone" refers to the main stone at the corner, the one that holds and joins the walls together.

This psalm is a song of thanksgiving, probably sung at a festival in the temple, when the people enter through the gate. The one speaking seems to be someone who was rejected and then rescued by God. It is not known for certain whether it refers to Israel, to a king, or to another person; it has been interpreted in several ways. The New Testament applies this verse to Jesus, who was rejected by many and exalted by God.

For today: if someone has rejected you or you feel without value, remember that God can give you an important purpose. Trust in Him and thank Him, without holding on to resentment.
exp.82:10:
It says that God should treat Israel's enemies, their leaders and their princes, as he treated four Midianite leaders long ago: Oreb and Zeeb (the princes) and Zebah and Zalmunna (the kings). Those men were defeated in the days of Gideon (Judges 7–8). Military commanders are the heads of the army, and rulers are the ones who govern.

Asaph, the psalmist, speaks in a prayer of distress. Several neighboring nations had joined together to destroy Israel and wipe out its name (vv. 4-8). Asaph is not seeking personal revenge; he asks God to act as he did in the past. Scholars do not agree on which specific attack the psalm had in mind.

For today: when you feel threatened or overwhelmed, remember what God has already done before and bring it to him in prayer with confidence. But leave justice in his hands, and do not take it into your own.
exp.134:4:
The psalmist says he knows from experience that the Lord is great. "I know" speaks of a personal conviction, not a mere idea. He also affirms that our Lord is above all gods, meaning he stands above anything people worship or fear.

The psalm is a call to praise, probably addressed to the people of Israel gathered for worship. The speaker encourages others to praise because God is good and chose Israel. Then he gives reasons: God rules over creation, the clouds, the lightning, and the winds. God is compared with the gods of the nations, which do not have that power.

Today, when you feel small before problems, pressures, or things that compete for your heart, calmly remember what God has done for you. Say to him in prayer: "I know that you are great." That confidence helps put everything in its place.
exp.93:16:
The explanation says that if the Lord had not been his help, his soul would very soon have dwelt in silence. "Soon" means quickly, right away. "Would have dwelt" is the rendering of the old verb form. The "silence" probably refers to the grave or the place of the dead, as in Psalm 115:17. Some understand it as a death that was near; others as an anguish so great that it would have left him without a voice.

The one speaking is the psalmist, a believer who sees injustice and wickedness all around him. He has just asked who will defend him against the wicked. Here he answers with confidence: only God has sustained him. The text does not say who the author is or describe his exact danger.

For today: when you feel weak or have no one to defend you, remember how God has sustained you before. Thank him for that help and ask him to sustain you today as well. You do not have to carry everything alone.
exp.67:34:
It says that God commands respect and reverence because of his greatness, and that from his sanctuaries, that is, from the places where he is worshiped, he himself gives strength and power to his people. "Terrible" here does not mean evil, but worthy of awe and reverent fear. Strength is the energy to keep moving forward. It ends with praise: "Blessed be God."

This is the end of Psalm 68, attributed to David. It is a song of victory that recalls how God guided and defended Israel. Earlier, the psalmist invites everyone to acknowledge the strength of God, whose power is in the heavens. Some scholars see in the psalm a liturgical celebration, but its exact occasion is debated.

When you feel weak or tired, do not rely only on your own resources. Pray and acknowledge God as your source of strength, and end by giving thanks to him, as the psalmist does: "Blessed be God."
exp.9:3:
It says that the wicked person, through his pride (the "haughtiness of his face" is an attitude of arrogance that shows in his expression), does not seek God. In all that he thinks and plans, God simply does not count. Here "wicked" means the ungodly person, and "thoughts" refers to his schemes and calculations.

The psalm does not say who wrote it. It is a prayer of lament: someone sees the proud oppressing the poor and asks why God seems silent. Here the psalmist describes the root of the problem: the wicked person lives as if God did not exist. In the verses that follow, his false security is visible: he believes nothing will reach him.

For today: pride draws us away from God without our noticing. A good practice is to begin the day by asking God for direction before making plans, and to acknowledge with humility that we need him in every decision.
exp.103:9:
God is the one who causes the springs to rise and makes them flow like streams. These waters do not stay still: they pass through the middle of the hills, finding their way between them. The word "springs" here refers to the places where water comes up out of the ground.

The psalm is a song of praise to God as Creator. We do not know for certain who wrote it; some traditions connect it with David. The verses before it speak of how God set limits for the waters, and the verses after it show that this water satisfies the animals and the birds. The psalmist rejoices that God not only created the world but continues to care for it.

Today, the next time you drink water or see rain fall, give thanks to God for this daily care. You can also show gratitude by taking care of water and not wasting it.
exp.72:6:
It says that the prosperous wicked are so well fed and full of riches that their eyes are even seen bulging with fatness. The phrase "Their eyes stand out with fatness" speaks of abundance and comfort. "They have more than heart could wish" means that they get far more than they could ever desire, that is, everything their hearts long for.

The author is Asaph, who nearly stumbled in his faith when he saw the proud prospering while he suffered. He is describing what he saw, not what God approves. Later, when he enters God's sanctuary, he understands what their end will be (v. 17).

When you see unjust people doing very well, do not let envy or bitterness take hold of you. Bring that pain honestly to God, as Asaph did, and ask Him for a longer view: true riches are being close to Him.
exp.58:14:
They say the psalmist's enemies wander back and forth, like stray dogs, looking for something to eat. And if they are not satisfied, they complain and snarl. Here "grudge" is understood as protesting with anger. Some translations say they "spend the night" without being filled.

David speaks in this psalm, according to its heading, when Saul sent men to watch his house in order to kill him. He is distressed and asks God for justice. He uses the image of dogs that prowl the city at night. It is strong language, typical of psalms that cry out for justice, and the contrast comes right after it.

For today: when injustice or hostility surrounds you, do not keep staring at the restlessness of those who attack you. Do as David did: hand your distress over to God, and decide to praise him in the morning, because he is your refuge.
exp.93:8:
This verse asks two simple questions. God placed the ear in the human being and formed the eye, so it is reasonable to think that He himself hears and sees. The word "planted" is used here in the sense of "set in place" or "put there with care." The word "fools" refers to people who are foolish or senseless.

The psalmist speaks in the midst of a situation of injustice. The wicked were oppressing the people and saying, "The LORD does not see or understand." The author responds firmly and calls them to reason. If the Creator made the senses, He cannot be blind or deaf. The psalm does not say clearly who wrote it or at what exact moment.

When you feel that no one sees your suffering or your effort, remember that God sees you and hears you. Bring your prayer to Him with confidence. And if you are tempted to act in secret, remember that He sees that too.
exp.17:44:
This verse says that the foreigners or enemies lost their strength and were filled with fear. The word "fade away" means that they grew weak and lost heart. "Close places" refers to their hiding places or strongholds, the places where they felt safe. They came trembling out of there.

David is speaking, near the end of his life or after being delivered from Saul and his enemies, as the title of the psalm indicates. He is grateful because God gave him victory and set him as the head of nations. The "strangers" who once pretended loyalty now surrender in fear. David credits everything to God, his rock.

Today we can remember that no opposition is as strong as it seems. When you face pressure or people who intimidate you, trust in God as your refuge, act with integrity, and let Him take care of defending you.
exp.148:5:
The verse says that God's people will have high praises in their mouth and a two-edged sword in their hand. The first refers to words that exalt God, the second to expressing them with the voice, and the third to the mouth. A two-edged sword is one that cuts on both sides.

The psalm does not say who wrote it. It is a song of praise for Israel, celebrating that God takes pleasure in his people and honors the humble. The verses that follow speak of judgment on the nations, which is why there are images of war. Some understand this as a historical or future event, and others take it as symbolic language for spiritual struggle. The Bible says that the word of God is sharper than any two-edged sword (Hebrews 4:12).

Today you can keep praise and the word of God together: sing with gratitude, and lean on the Scriptures when you face difficulties, trusting that God brings about justice.
exp.78:0:
It says that foreign nations invaded the land that belongs to God. They defiled the temple, which was a holy place, and left Jerusalem in heaps of ruins. The nations that did not follow the God of Israel are the ones who came in, and the land is the inheritance God gave to his people.

It is a psalm of Asaph, a musician and worship leader of the people. The one speaking expresses the grief of the community before a terrible destruction. Many think of the fall of Jerusalem to Babylon, in 586 B.C., but the psalm does not say so clearly, so this cannot be stated with certainty. What we do see is a prayer born out of suffering.

When the pain is very great, do not silence it or disguise it. Bring it honestly before God, as this psalm does. He can hear your complaint and sustain you.
exp.98:0:
The explanation says that this verse declares the LORD reigns as King, and that for this reason the peoples tremble. He is seated above the cherubim, heavenly beings who represent his throne, and the earth shakes before him. The word for "reigns" means that he is reigning, and the phrase for "be moved" means "shake" or "tremble."

The psalm does not say who wrote it. It is a song of praise for the people of Israel, probably used in worship. The cherubim are mentioned above the ark of the covenant, where God was understood to be present. The verses that follow highlight that God is great in Zion (Jerusalem) and holy. Some understand the trembling as reverent respect; others understand it as the fear of those who oppose him.

Today we can remember that God governs, even when the world seems disordered. This invites us to pray with reverence and to trust that he is holy and just.
exp.141:5:
Here the psalmist asks God to hear him. The word "cry" in the verse means a call for help, and where the explanation says "brought very low," it means he is deeply downcast and in great pain. He says his persecutors are stronger than he is, so he admits he cannot save himself and asks God to deliver him.

The title of the psalm attributes it to David, when he was in the cave. Some think of the cave of Adullam and others of the cave of En-gedi, and this cannot be known for certain. He feels alone, without shelter, and pursued. For this reason he prays sincerely, without hiding his weakness.

For today: when you feel without strength before a problem, do not wait until you are strong to pray. Tell God honestly that you cannot do it alone. Ask him for help, and also seek out people of faith who can walk with you.
exp.118:150:
This verse says that God is near to those who seek him, and that everything he commands is true, meaning it is firm and worthy of trust. "Lord" is the name of God, and "commandments" refers to his instructions and his word.

The one speaking is the psalmist, a believer whose identity we do not know for certain. He is surrounded by people who pursue him, who draw close to wickedness and turn away from God's law. In the midst of that pressure, he does not focus on his enemies, but on the fact that God is present and his word does not fail. That is why he can ask for help with confidence.

For today: when you feel alone, pressured, or surrounded by people who live differently, remember that God is near. Before deciding what to do, read a passage of the Bible and pray sincerely, relying on what God has said.
exp.55:6:
This verse does two things: it asks a question and makes a prayer. David asks whether the wicked will get away with their wrongdoing, and right after that he asks God, in his righteous anger, to bring down the peoples who are attacking him. The word "iniquity" means wickedness or injustice. "Fury" is intense anger. "Peoples" here refers to nations or hostile groups.

The one speaking is David. According to the psalm's title, he wrote it when the Philistines seized him in Gath. His enemies watch him, pursue him, and want to take his life. He feels cornered, and he entrusts his cause to God.

For today: when you feel that someone is treating you unjustly, do not take justice into your own hands. Tell God honestly what you feel and leave judgment in his hands. He sees everything and knows how to act better than we do.
exp.6:9:
This verse says that David trusts God to be his protection, like a shield that covers him in danger. The word "saves" means delivers or rescues, and "upright in heart" refers to sincere people who seek to live honestly before God.

David speaks in this psalm while he is falsely accused and pursued. The title mentions a man named Cush, of the tribe of Benjamin, but we do not know for certain who he was or exactly when this happened. David does not defend himself with revenge; instead, he places his cause in God's hands, the righteous judge who knows the innermost heart.

When someone treats you unfairly, you do not have to repay evil with evil. You can pray sincerely, examine your heart, and rest in the knowledge that God cares for you and will bring about justice in his time.
exp.88:22:
God says that he himself will defeat the enemies of the king he has chosen, and he will do it "before his face," that is, in plain view of this king. To "beat down" means to crush or completely overcome, and "those who hate him" are the ones who hate him. To "plague" here means to strike and defeat.

The one speaking is God, recalling the promise he made to David and his descendants (2 Samuel 7). The psalmist, Ethan the Ezrahite, repeats that promise. Later in the psalm he complains because it seems God is not keeping it. Many Christians also see in this a sign pointing to Jesus, the descendant of David.

For today: when you face opposition or injustice, you do not have to defend yourself with resentment or with your own strength. Trust that God cares for his people, pray with patience, and keep doing good while he acts in his own time.
exp.105:21:
This verse recalls that God did wonderful works in the land of Ham, a poetic way of naming Egypt (Ham was a son of Noah, and Egypt is associated with his descendants). The Red Sea is the sea mentioned at the end of the verse, and the word "terrible" means that these works caused great awe and fear.

The psalmist is reviewing the history of Israel. First he tells how the people forgot God and worshiped a calf of metal, even though they had seen his miracles in Egypt and at the sea. It is a confession: God was faithful, but the people were forgetful. Then he mentions that Moses interceded for them.

For today: when you feel tempted to forget God, remember what he has already done for you. Write down your experiences of help and the gifts you have received, and review them in difficult moments to strengthen your trust.
exp.104:32:
It says that God struck the vines and the fig trees of Egypt, and broke the trees throughout its land. "Struck" means hit or damaged, and "land" means territory or region. This is the plague of hail, which destroyed the crops and the trees.

The psalmist recalls the plagues of Egypt within a song of praise that reviews God's works on behalf of Israel. According to the account in Exodus, Pharaoh refused to release the Hebrew people. The psalm wants Israel not to forget how God kept his promise and rescued his people from slavery.

For today: when we remember how God has sustained us in the past, our confidence for the present grows. Write down a few occasions when you saw his help and give him thanks. It is also a call not to harden our hearts when God speaks to us.
exp.111:0:
It says that the man who respects God and finds great joy in obeying his commandments is happy and blessed.

The word "Hallelujah" means "praise the Lord." "Blessed" means happy, fortunate in the deepest sense. "Fear" here does not mean being afraid, but revering and honoring God.

This psalm does not say who wrote it; some believe it was the same author as Psalm 111, because both are alphabetic poems that begin with "Praise ye the Lord." Psalm 111 speaks of how good God is, and this one speaks of how the person who honors him lives. The verses that follow describe his blessings: family, possessions, and a lasting righteousness.

Today we can ask ourselves whether God's Word is for us only a duty or a joy. A practical idea: read a passage of the Bible each morning and ask God to teach you to delight in what he asks of you.
exp.21:9:
From before he was born, the one speaking was placed into God's hands. "Womb" and "belly" both refer to the mother's body, where the child is carried. "I was cast upon thee" means he was entrusted to God's care, like a baby laid in safe arms. And from the beginning, God has been his God.

The speaker is David, in a psalm of deep suffering. His enemies mock his faith and tell him that if God loves him, let God save him. He answers by recalling that his trust is not new: God has sustained him from the very beginning. Christians also read this psalm with Jesus on the cross in mind, since He quoted its first verse.

For today: when you feel alone or mocked for believing, remember how God has cared for you since the beginning of your life. Write down three moments when you have seen Him faithful, and use them to pray with confidence.
exp.43:10:
He says that God left his people like sheep ready to be eaten, that is, defenseless before their enemies. The word "scattered" stands for being spread out among foreign nations, and "heathen" refers to the foreign nations themselves. The verse speaks of defeat and of living far from home.

The psalm is a communal lament by the sons of Korah. The people speak in the plural after a military defeat. What hurts is that they have remained faithful (vv. 17-18) and yet they suffer. Scholars do not agree on which battle or period is meant, so it is wise not to claim more than the text says.

For today: when you suffer without understanding why, you can bring your complaint to God with sincerity, without pretending. The psalm shows that honest prayer, even painful prayer, is also faith. Say it with confidence and seek support in your community.
exp.121:8:
It says that the psalmist, out of love for the temple, where God dwells among his people, desires and pursues what is best for Jerusalem. "I will seek thy good" means that he will work and pray for its well-being, its peace, and its prosperity. "The Lord" is the name of God in this ancient translation.

This is a "song of ascents," and the title attributes it to David. It was a song of pilgrims who went up to Jerusalem for the festivals. The speaker rejoices in arriving at the city and, after praying for its peace, ends with this commitment. His motive is not merely patriotic: Jerusalem was the place where the people worshiped God.

For today: think about your local church or your community of faith. Like the psalmist, seek its good through concrete actions: pray for it, serve with joy, help maintain unity, and treat fellow believers with love.
exp.99:0:
This verse invites all the people of the world to sing to God with joy. The heading "A Psalm of praise" tells us what kind of song this is: one meant to give thanks and honor God. The word "Make" in the verse is an older way of saying "sing," and the word "joyful" shows that the praise should come from a glad heart. "All ye lands" means the invitation is not just for one people, but for everyone.

The author is not named in this text. It was written for worship among the people of Israel, probably to be sung when coming before God. The verses that follow give the reason: the Lord is God, he made us, and he cares for us as a shepherd cares for his sheep. Some think it was used in the temple, but the text does not say so for certain.

Today you can begin your day by thanking God with a song, even a simple one. Remembering that he cares for you helps your praise to be sincere and joyful.
exp.88:34:
This verse says that God made a solemn oath, backed by his own holiness, that he will not fail David. "Once have I sworn" means he said it in a firm and definite way, and "I will not lie" means that he will not break his word.

Psalm 89 recalls the covenant God made with David, in which he promised that his descendants and his kingdom would endure. In these verses God himself is speaking, as the psalmist quotes him. Although the people are going through a difficult situation, the psalmist holds on to this promise. Many Christians see its final fulfillment in Jesus, a descendant of David.

For today: when it is hard to trust, remember that God backs his promises with his own character. Write down a biblical promise you need and repeat it in prayer, trusting that God is faithful even when you do not yet see the answer.
exp.108:21:
This verse says that the speaker feels "afflicted," meaning brought low and suffering, and "needy," meaning poor and without resources. It adds that his heart is "wounded within him": a deep, inner pain, not merely something seen on the outside.

The psalm is attributed to David, although some scholars debate when and under what circumstances he wrote it. The speaker is pursued by people who slander him and speak evil of him. For this reason he turns to God and asks for help "for your name's sake," trusting that the Lord's mercy is good. The verses that follow describe his weak and worn-out body.

For today: when you are wounded inside, you do not have to pretend to be strong. You can tell God honestly how you feel, as the psalmist did, and rest in the knowledge that his mercy is good.
exp.147:1:
This verse invites all the angels to praise God. The word "praise ye" means "praise him" in the plural, and the "ye" refers to the angels as a group. The "hosts" may refer to the armies of angels who serve God. Some think it also includes the heavenly bodies, although the text mentions them separately in the following verse.

The psalmist, whose name is not known for certain, calls all of creation to worship God. He begins with the highest things, the heavens, and then moves down toward the earth. The reason is that God himself made them, and he deserves to be honored by everything that exists.

For today: if the angels, who are always in God's presence, praise him, we too can do so. Today, before you begin your tasks, take a moment to thank God out loud, joining that praise that never stops.
exp.118:31:
He says that the psalmist will run, that is, will obey eagerly and quickly, along the path of God's commandments. He will do so when God enlarges his heart. To enlarge means to give it room, freedom, joy and understanding, so that obeying is not a burden. Some also understand it as giving it encouragement or courage.

The speaker is the author of Psalm 119, a psalm about loving God's law. We do not know for certain who wrote it. It comes right after he declares that he has chosen the truth and holds fast to God's testimonies. Here he recognizes that he needs God's help to obey with joy. Right after, he asks: "Teach me" and "Give me understanding."

For today: instead of obeying only out of duty, ask God each day for a willing and joyful heart. Read his Word in prayer, and trust that he can give you the desire to follow him.
exp.77:25:
He caused the east wind to blow in the heaven, and by his power he brought in the south wind. The first wind is the one the verse names as the east wind, and the second is the south wind, both of which are the names the King James Version uses. With these winds, God guided the quail toward the people, as the next verse tells.

The one speaking is the psalmist Asaph, who reviews the history of Israel in the wilderness. He wants the new generations to remember how God cared for his people with manna and meat, and how they, even so, complained and distrusted him. It is a call not to repeat that unbelief.

For today: God governs even what seems to be only nature, such as the wind, and he knows how to provide. When you doubt his care, remember how he has sustained you before, and thank him instead of complaining.
exp.18:11:
It says that no one can notice all of their own faults. The word translated "errors" refers to sins committed without realizing it or through carelessness. The word for "hidden" means that a person does not see them in himself. The psalmist asks God to cleanse him and free him from those hidden faults.

David speaks here, having just praised creation and God's Law as more precious than gold. As he looks into that Law, like a mirror, he sees himself and recognizes that his heart has corners he does not know. That is why he asks for help, and then asks to be kept from pride.

For today: do not believe you are the best judge of yourself. Read the Bible with humility, ask God to show you what you do not see, and listen calmly when someone you trust corrects you with love.
exp.133:1:
It says we should lift up our hands in the sanctuary and praise God. The verse's wording "lift up" carries the sense of raising, and "bless" means to speak well of God, give thanks, and honor him. The sanctuary is the holy place of the temple. Lifting up the hands was a gesture of prayer and worship. Some translators understand "in the sanctuary" as "toward the holy place," and others as "in holiness"; both ideas fit.

This psalm is a song of ascents, a song of those who went up to Jerusalem. It seems to speak to the servants who guarded the temple at night. Exactly who is speaking is not certain: it could be a group encouraging the guards, and the ending would be their reply. This is how the change in the last verse is understood, where someone blesses from Zion.

For today: even in quiet or tiring tasks, take a moment to lift your hands or your heart and give thanks to God.
exp.145:8:
This verse says that God watches over the strangers, that is, those who live far from their homeland and have no one to defend them. He also upholds the fatherless and the widow, people without protection in that time. The word "turneth upside down" means that God overturns or frustrates the path of the wicked, that is, of those who live in wickedness.

The psalmist praises God and calls us to trust in Him, not in rulers (verse 3). This psalm does not name an author or a precise situation. It shows God as a just King who defends the weak, and it ends by saying that He reigns forever.

Today we can imitate God's heart by caring for those who are alone or vulnerable: an immigrant, a child without support, a widow. A visit, a concrete act of help, or a word of encouragement reflects His care.
exp.17:33:
This verse says that God is the one who trains the psalmist's hands for battle. Thanks to that help, his arms have such strength that they can bend a bow of steel. The word "broken" here is better understood as "bent" or "drawn tight." Some versions say "bronze" instead, and the original can refer to that metal.

The psalm is spoken by David, according to its title, after God rescued him from his enemies and from Saul. He gives thanks and recognizes that his victories did not come only from his own skill. Both before and after the verse, he speaks of the strength, the shield, and the support that God gave him.

For today: if you have a difficult task, prepare yourself and make your best effort, but recognize that God is the one who gives the ability and the strength. Pray and give thanks for each accomplishment.
exp.118:111:
He says that the psalmist turned his heart, that is, his will and his desires, toward keeping God's commands. The idea is that he deliberately set himself in that direction. "Statutes" are God's instructions or rules, and "always" means without stopping, and "to the end" indicates that he will keep doing so until the close of his life.

The speaker is the author of Psalm 119, a poem in honor of God's Word. We do not know for certain who wrote it. He had just said that the wicked laid traps for him, but he did not turn aside. For him, God's teachings are like an inheritance, a source of joy. That is why he decides to obey with firmness.

For today: obeying God does not happen by chance, but by decision. Choose one concrete action that God asks of you, such as forgiving, being honest, or setting aside time to read the Bible, and ask Him for help to remain steady.
exp.77:51:
This verse says that God brought his people out of Egypt the way someone brings their sheep out of the pen, and led them through the wilderness the way a shepherd guides his flock. The explanation of "but" and "brought out" has been left out, since those words do not appear in the verse you are reading. The image is one of care and direction.

Asaph wrote Psalm 78, recalling the history of Israel to teach the new generations. Earlier, the psalm spoke of the plagues on Egypt, including the death of the firstborn. Here the tone changes: the same God who judged Egypt tenderly cares for his people. Then comes the crossing of the sea and the arrival in the promised land.

For today: even when you pass through a "wilderness," a hard or uncertain season, you can trust that God guides you like a good shepherd. You may not see the whole road, but he does know it. Give him your worries today and follow his direction step by step.
exp.53:0:
The explanation says that this psalm is a song for the choir director, with stringed instruments (Neginoth), and that it is a "maschil," a word that probably indicates a teaching or meditative song. The Ziphites, people from Ziph, told Saul where David was hiding. Then David asks God: "Save me by your name," that is, by who you are, and "defend me" with your power, or grant me justice.

It is David speaking, pursued by King Saul. According to 1 Samuel 23:19 and 26:1, the Ziphites betrayed him on two occasions. David was alone, fleeing, and betrayed by people close to him. We do not know with certainty on which of the two occasions he wrote it.

For today: when you feel betrayed or without a way out, do as David did and pray with sincerity. Ask God for his help, trusting in his character and not in your own strength.
exp.118:117:
He says that God "trodden down" — that is, trampled or rejected — those who turn away from his commands ("statutes"). The reason is that their "deceit," meaning the crooked path they follow, is "falsehood": it promises something it does not deliver and has no foundation.

The one speaking is the psalmist, who prays to God and asks for help to remain steadfast. It comes from asking for support and hope. Now he looks at those who abandon the Word and sees that their path ends badly. This leads him to love God's testimonies more and to take his holiness seriously.

For today: when something promises you happiness or success by turning you away from what God teaches, remember that it may be a deceit. Ask God, as the psalmist did, to sustain you, and seek his Word every day to tell what is true from what is false.
exp.114:4:
This verse describes what the idols of the nations are like. They have mouths, but they cannot speak; they have eyes, but they cannot see. They look like people, for they have shape and a face, but they have no life.

The psalm does not say who wrote it. It is a song of the people of Israel, probably for worship in community. The neighboring nations asked where the God of Israel was. The psalm answers that He is in the heavens and does whatever He pleases, while the idols are the work of human hands, made of silver and gold.

Today there may be different "idols": money, fame, success, or anything we trust more than God. Ask yourself: what is it that promises help but cannot answer me? God does hear, see, and act; you can bring Him your burdens in prayer today.
exp.63:7:
This verse says that the wicked will end up harmed by their own words. What they used to attack others will turn back against them. The phrase about their tongues falling upon themselves can be understood as their lies and slander bringing them down. The idea of those who see it fleeing away means that people who witness this will be struck with awe and a sense of reverent fear.

The speaker is David, or so the title of the psalm indicates. He prays to God asking for protection from people who plot evil in secret and use words like arrows. In the verses before this one, God answers with his own arrow. Afterward, people recognize the work of God, and the righteous rejoice in him.

For today: you do not need to take revenge with words on someone who wronged you. Hand the injustice over to God, guard your own tongue, and trust that he knows how to bring about justice in his time.
exp.88:19:
God says that he found David, his servant, and anointed him with his holy oil. "Found" means that he came upon him and chose him. "Anointed him" is "I anointed him": he poured oil on him to set him apart as king. The oil is called "holy" because it was dedicated to God.

Here God is speaking, recalling what he said in a vision to his faithful ones, according to the psalm. The author, Ethan the Ezrahite, remembers God's promise to David and to his family. He does this to rely on that promise while living through difficult times. What follows shows that God would support David with his hand and his arm.

For today: God does not choose by outward appearances or by human strength. If you feel small or not capable enough, remember that God can call you, set you apart for a purpose, and sustain you while you carry it out. Trust his calling, not only your own abilities.
exp.47:11:
This verse invites people to walk around Zion, that is, Jerusalem, and to go all the way around her to count her towers. "Walk about" is the same as "walk around," and "go round about her" means to go all the way around her. The towers were part of her defenses and also part of her beauty.

It is a psalm of the sons of Korah, a song of praise. We do not know for certain who is speaking, but it seems to be a voice encouraging the people to look at the city with close attention. Earlier, the psalm praises God and his righteousness. Afterward, it asks readers to notice her walls and palaces so they can tell the next generation about them. The city serves as a sign that God cares for his own people.

For today: take a pause to remember how God has sustained you. Write down, or tell someone younger, one of those experiences, so that their faith may also grow and trust in God.
exp.37:16:
Here David says he is about to fall. The phrase "about to" is what it means to be on the verge of something, and "limp" here means to stumble, to falter, or to give way out of weakness. His sorrow, whether from guilt, sickness, or anguish, is always before him and does not let him rest.

The one speaking is David, in a psalm of lament. He suffers because of his sin and with a body and spirit that are broken, and enemies surround him who take advantage of his fall. Even so, he says he waited on God and that God will answer. Scholars debate whether the physical suffering was a literal illness or a poetic way of speaking.

For today: when you feel on the verge of falling, do not hide your pain. Bring it honestly before God, as David did, and trust that He hears you and can hold you up even when you feel weak.
exp.77:34:
This verse says that the people of Israel remembered that God was their rock, meaning their stronghold and a secure place. They also remembered that the Most High God was their redeemer, the one who rescued and set them free. The word "remembered" is simply the verb "remembered," as in the verse itself.

The psalm is written by Asaph, who reviews Israel's history to teach the new generations. Here he describes how the people, in the middle of the wilderness and its punishments, turned back to seek God when they suffered. But the next verse shows that this remembering was shallow: they flattered Him with their mouths, yet their hearts were not sincere.

For today: it is not enough to remember God only when trouble comes. We can cultivate a sincere relationship with Him every day, thanking Him for what He has done and seeking Him with our hearts, not only with words.
exp.138:21:
The psalmist says he hates, with a complete hatred that holds nothing back, those who oppose God, and he counts them as his enemies. The verse's wording "I hate them" and "I count them mine enemies" conveys this directly, and "perfect" in the verse means complete, without reservation.

The psalm is attributed to David. He has just said that God knows him completely. The verses before this one speak of people who blaspheme and misuse God's name. His reaction is one of wounded loyalty toward God. Right after this, he asks God to search his heart, as if to make sure his anger is not pride or personal revenge. Scholars debate how to understand such strong language.

For today: Jesus teaches us to love our enemies. We can reject evil firmly, while asking God to examine our hearts and free us from resentment.
exp.77:31:
It says that, in spite of everything God had done and the punishment that fell on them, the people kept on sinning. They "believed not," which means they did not trust him, even though they had seen his power. The "wondrous works" are God's miracles.

Psalm 78 is a poem of Asaph that goes back over Israel's history to teach the next generations. Just before this, it speaks of the manna and the quail in the wilderness. Here the psalmist points out that not even after judgment did the people change their hearts. Afterward, they only looked for God when they were suffering.

For today: it is not enough to remember what God has done; we have to trust him every day. Think of a time when God helped you, and instead of doubting when the next difficulty comes, thank him and obey him with confidence.
exp.64:6:
This verse says that God calms the roar of the sea and the crashing of its waves, and that he also calms the tumult of the peoples. "Tame" means to quiet something, the way one calms a wild animal. "Nations" is the word for peoples or nations.

The psalm is a song of David, addressed to God in praise. Earlier it speaks of God as the one who sets the mountains firm by his power. Then it speaks of his care for the earth with rain and harvests. The stormy sea and the restless nations are placed side by side: God reigns over both. Some believe the sea represents chaos, but the text does not fully explain this.

When your life or the world seems like a restless sea, remember that God is still in control. Pray with a calm heart, give him your worry, and trust that he can bring peace.
exp.24:21:
In this verse, David asks God to rescue and free the whole people of Israel from their troubles and sufferings. To "redeem" means to rescue or set free, the way someone pays to bring another person out of a difficult situation.

This psalm is a prayer attributed to David. Throughout the text he speaks of his own fears, his enemies, and his sins, and he asks for forgiveness and guidance. At the end, in this last verse, he stops thinking only about himself and prays for the whole people. Some scholars think this closing line may have been added so the psalm could be used in community worship, though this is not certain.

For today: when you pray for your own needs, do not stop there. Include your family, your church, and your community as well, asking God to rescue and sustain them.
exp.105:47:
This verse is a closing expression of praise. It says: "Blessed be the Lord God of Israel from everlasting to everlasting." The first phrase, "from everlasting to everlasting," is the same idea that the King James Version uses here, so no further explanation of an old word is needed. The verse then asks all the people to say "Amen," and the word "Amen" in the verse means "so be it." The final line of the verse, "Praise ye the Lord," calls the people to praise him.

The psalm reviews the failures of Israel and the patience of God with them. The psalmist is not identified with certainty. Before this verse, the psalmist prays that God will gather them from among the nations. This verse also closes the fourth book of the Psalms, and many scholars think it is a final blessing that marks that division.

For today: even after we recognize our failures, we can end our prayer by praising God. His faithfulness does not depend on us. You can say "Amen" today to one of his promises, together with other believers.
exp.107:2:
It says that the psalmist promises to praise God not only in private but in public, before the peoples and the nations, that is, also before those who do not know the Lord. To sing a psalm means to sing praises to God, often with instruments. Jehovah is the name of God that many Bibles today translate as "the Lord."

David speaks, according to the title of the psalm. His heart is steadfast and determined to worship, and his praise comes from what the following verse says: God's mercy and truth are enormous, higher than the heavens. This psalm brings together parts of two other psalms of David (Psalms 57 and 60); scholars understand it as a prayer of trust before asking God for help.

For today: do not keep your gratitude only to yourself. This week, share with someone, in words or in a song, something concrete that God has done for you.
exp.51:1:
This verse says that this man's tongue plans to do harm to others. "Mischiefs" are wicked schemes meant to hurt people, and "deviseth" means he plots and prepares them with cunning. The "sharp razor" is a razor honed to a fine edge; that is how cutting and treacherous his tongue is, because it cuts while it deceives.

David is the speaker, and he is addressing Doeg the Edomite. According to the title of the psalm, Doeg told Saul that David had been to the house of Ahimelech. The story appears in 1 Samuel 21 and 22, where Doeg ended up taking part in the killing of the priests of Nob. David confronts him because he boasted of his wickedness.

For today: our words can wound like a razor, even when they sound kind. Before speaking about someone, ask yourself whether what you are about to say is true, whether it helps, and whether you would say it to their face. Ask God for an honest tongue.
exp.118:132:
This verse is a prayer. The one speaking asks God to direct his walk according to his word. To "order my steps" means to guide, to put every step of life in order. The word that the old text renders as "have dominion" points to a sin that rules over a person like a master. So he asks that no sin be his master.

The speaker is the psalmist, the author of Psalm 119, a poem that praises the law of God. We do not know with certainty who wrote it. Earlier in the psalm he longs for God's commandments and asks for mercy. Later he asks to be delivered from the violence of men. We see someone who loves God but feels his need for help.

For today: before deciding something important, pray with this verse and look in the Bible to see what God says. Ask him that his word, and not your habits or your impulses, would direct your steps.
exp.43:8:
The verse says that God has cast off his people and put them to shame. To be cast off is to be rejected or set aside, and to be put to shame is to be humiliated. Besides this, God no longer "goest not forth with our armies," meaning he does not go with them into battle, and that is why they lose.

The people of Israel, or a representative speaking for them, are voicing a community lament. First they recall past victories that God gave them. Now, with a painful "but," they describe a defeat they cannot understand. The psalm does not clearly explain the cause, and interpreters place it in different periods of Israel's history.

For today: you can be honest with God when you feel he is far away or you do not understand your situation. The psalmist does not stay silent or pretend; he brings his pain to God himself, and that is also faith.
exp.68:1:
It says the psalmist feels caught in deep mud, with no firm place to put his feet. He has come into very deep waters, and the current has covered him completely. The sentence that explains the old word for thick mud and the word for flooded or drowned is removed here, and the phrase about bottomless depths is simply translated as "bottomless depths of water" in the sense of places without a floor.

David, according to the title of the psalm, is the one speaking. He uses images of water to describe extreme distress: enemies who hate him without cause, weariness from so much prayer, and eyes worn out from waiting. This is not a literal description but poetic language of suffering. Some Christian readers also see here a foreshadowing of the sufferings of Christ, because the New Testament quotes parts of this psalm.

For today: when you feel there is nothing to lean on, do as the psalmist does and cry out to God honestly, without pretending to be strong. Tell him exactly how you feel, and also ask for the help of trusted people.
exp.65:16:
It says the psalmist asked God for help out loud, with his mouth, and then praised him with his tongue. The phrase "he was extolled" means "he was exalted" or "he was praised." The word "cried" points to a sincere and urgent plea. So it joins two things: asking and praising.

The one speaking is the psalmist, who invites all who fear God to listen to what God did for his soul. It comes from offering sacrifices in thanksgiving. The verses that follow explain that God heard him, and that a heart that holds on to evil is not heard. Some think he speaks on behalf of the people, others that he speaks personally; the text allows both readings.

For today: when you pray, don't stop at asking. When God answers, give him thanks out loud, and tell others to encourage them in their faith.
exp.16:6:
The verse says that God can show his faithful love in an astonishing way, that is, his mercy. David asks him to do this for those who trust in him. "Marvellous" means wonderful and extraordinary. God's "right hand" is a symbol of his power and his protection. "Them that rise up against them" are those who oppose God's people, and so oppose God himself.

The speaker is David, in prayer. He feels surrounded by enemies and appeals to God's justice. Earlier he asked to be held up so that he would not slip, and later he asks to be kept like the apple of God's eye. His confidence rests on the fact that God hears and saves.

For today: when you feel pressured or threatened, do not stay silent or rely only on yourself. Bring your need to God honestly, and ask him to show you his care. Trusting him is not a vague idea; it is resting in someone who has already proven himself faithful.
exp.143:14:
They are called happy, or blessed, the people who live under that blessing: abundance, peace, and security. But the most important point comes at the end: truly happy is the people whose God is the Lord, that is, Jehovah. "Happy" means very joyful and blessed by God.

Psalm 144 is attributed to David. He asks God for protection in war, and then he describes what a blessed people would be like: full granaries, large herds, fruitful work, and no attacks. Some scholars think these verses describe what David hopes for, not only what already exists. The final verse places God as the source of all that blessing.

Today we can enjoy and be thankful for what God gives us, such as work, bread, and peace, without making these things our goal. This week, before you eat, thank God for Himself and not only for His gifts.
exp.77:60:
He allowed his "strength" and his "glory" to be carried off as prisoners by the enemy. These words refer to the ark of the covenant, the symbol of God's presence and power. In the verse, the word "delivered" is the one given, and "captivity" means being taken prisoner.

The psalm is by Asaph, who reviews the history of Israel. Before this, the people had provoked God with idols and disobedience. For this reason God left Shiloh, where the tabernacle was, and the Philistines captured the ark (1 Samuel 4). It is understood as God's judgment for the sin of the people, though some also see it as a lesson about not trusting in religious symbols.

For today: do not confuse religious things with a living relationship with God. Objects, temples and customs do not protect us if the heart is far from Him. Examine your heart with humility, return to God sincerely, and trust in his mercy, which always offers restoration.
exp.106:18:
The explanation says that when these people were in great distress, they cried out to God for help, and he rescued them from their troubles. The verse's word for "trouble" refers to a very strong pain and desperation; "distresses" refers to their sufferings. Here "saveth" means "rescued."

Psalm 107 is a song of thanksgiving, written by an author who is not named. It invites those whom God has rescued to give thanks. Here it speaks of "the foolish," people who suffered because they followed their own rebellion and poor decisions, to the point of nearly dying. But the verse marks a turn: in their worst moment, they cried out, and God answered.

For today: if you are suffering, even because of your own mistakes, do not wait until you have put yourself in order before you pray. Speak to God honestly, just as you are. He hears the cry of anyone who turns to him, and his mercy is available.

sum.79: In this psalm, Asaph pleads with God, the Shepherd of Israel, to awaken his power and show his face again, because the people live in tears and mockery. Israel is described as a vine that God planted, which grew greatly, but is now destroyed. The people ask to be restored so that they can call on his name once more.
sum.51: David speaks to a powerful man who uses his tongue to deceive and destroy, and who loves evil more than good. God will tear him down, and the righteous will see his fall, because he trusted in his riches rather than in God. David, by contrast, compares himself to a green olive tree in the house of God, trusts in God's mercy, and promises to praise him forever.
sum.45: The psalmist says that God is our refuge and strength, so we should not fear even when the earth shakes and the nations are in turmoil. God is present in the midst of his city and protects it. He brings wars to an end and invites us: "Be still, and know that I am God."
sum.123: This psalm of David says that if Jehovah had not been on Israel's side when their enemies rose up against them, they would have been swallowed alive, as if swept away by a flood. But God did not hand them over, and they escaped like a bird from the snare. Therefore, their help is in the name of Jehovah, the maker of heaven and earth.
sum.78: In this psalm by Asaph, the people mourn because foreign nations invaded Jerusalem, defiled the temple, and killed many of God's servants. They ask for forgiveness for their sins, ask for help for the sake of God's name, and ask for justice against their enemies. They end by trusting that, like sheep in God's pasture, they will praise him forever.
sum.149: Psalm 150 is a final call to praise God in his sanctuary and for his mighty deeds and his immense greatness. It invites people to do this with every kind of instrument: trumpet, harp, flute, strings, and cymbals. It ends by saying that everything that has breath should praise the Lord.
sum.30: David asks God to rescue him from his enemies, and he takes refuge in Him as his rock and fortress, even though he feels weak, rejected, and surrounded by fear. He places his life in God's hands and trusts that God hears him. In the end, he praises God's goodness and encourages the faithful to be strong and take heart.
sum.120: This psalm teaches that our help does not come from the mountains, but from God, the Creator of heaven and earth. He watches over us without ever falling asleep. He is like a protective shade, and he guards our lives, our going out and our coming in, today and forever.
sum.137: David praises God with his whole heart for his steadfast love and his faithfulness, because God answered him and gave him strength when he cried out. He declares that even the kings of the earth will praise God when they hear his words. God looks kindly on the humble, protects those in distress, and does not abandon the work of his hands.
sum.44: The psalm is a wedding song written for a king. It praises his beauty, his righteousness, and his power, and says that God has anointed him and that his throne is eternal. Then it speaks to the queen, inviting her to leave her father's house, and promises that the king's name will be remembered and praised forever.
sum.18: The psalm says that the heavens, day and night, declare the glory of God without words, and that the sun travels its path in full view of everyone. It then praises the law of the Lord, which is perfect, gives wisdom, brings joy to the heart, and is worth more than gold. For this reason David asks to be cleansed of his faults and for his words to please God, his rock and redeemer.
sum.92: Psalm 93 declares that the LORD reigns, clothed in majesty and strength, and that his throne has been secure since long ago. Even though the rivers and the waves roar mightily, God is mightier than all the waters. His words are sure, and his house deserves holiness forever.
sum.124: This psalm says that those who trust in God are secure, like Mount Zion, and that God surrounds his people the way the mountains surround Jerusalem. God will not let wickedness rule over the righteous forever, so that they will not fall into evil. The psalmist asks for good things for the upright, and warns that those who turn aside toward wickedness will meet the same end as the wicked.
sum.20: In this psalm, the king rejoices because God gave him what he asked for, crowned him with honor, and granted him long life. Because he trusts in the Most High, he will not be shaken. Those who plan evil against God will not prevail, and the people end by singing and praising the power of Jehovah.
sum.3: In this psalm, David cries out to God in his distress and asks him to hear him. He confronts those who dishonor him and love lies, and he urges them to calm down, turn away from sin, and trust in the Lord. Although many people look for good in other things, David finds in God a greater joy, and he is able to lie down and sleep in peace.
sum.95: The psalmist calls the whole earth to sing a new song to the LORD, and to declare his glory and his wonderful works among all the nations. He is great and worthy of praise, while the gods of the nations are nothing but idols, for the LORD made the heavens. All of creation rejoices because he is coming to judge the world with righteousness and truth.
sum.140: David calls out to God urgently and asks that his prayer rise up like incense. He asks God to guard his words and his heart so that he will not join in with wicked people. He accepts correction from a righteous person as a kind of healing balm, though some of the verses in the middle are hard to interpret. He trusts God to rescue him from the traps set by the wicked.
sum.146: The psalmist calls on people to praise God because he heals the brokenhearted, gathers the scattered people of Israel, and cares for all of creation: the stars, the rain, the animals, and even the winter. God takes delight in those who fear him and put their hope in his faithful love, and he blesses Jerusalem with peace, while to Israel he gave his word.
sum.108: David asks God not to stay silent while deceitful people full of hatred repay his love with evil, and he cries out for severe judgment on his enemy. Then, distressed and weak, he pleads that God would save him according to his mercy, and he promises to praise God because He stands up for the poor.
sum.61: David says that his soul rests in God alone, because God is his rock, his refuge, and his salvation, even when his enemies attack him with lies. He invites the people to trust God at all times and to pour out their hearts to Him. He warns that people and riches do not give real security, because strength and mercy belong to God, who repays each person according to what they have done.
sum.107: David sings with a steady heart, praising God among the nations, because his mercy and his faithfulness are immense. Then he recalls God's promise about the land and the neighboring nations, and he admits that he needs help in his distress, since human rescue is unreliable. He concludes by trusting that victory will come only with God.
sum.66: The psalmist asks God to be merciful to his people and to bless them, so that his ways and his salvation may be known throughout the earth. He invites all the nations to praise God, because He judges with justice and guides the nations. He ends by saying that the land will yield its harvest and that all people will honor Him.
sum.143: David praises God as his rock and his protector, the one who trains him for battle. He acknowledges how fragile human beings are. He asks God to rescue him from enemies who speak lies, and he promises to sing a new song to God. He ends by wishing for strong families, abundant fields, and peace, and he declares happy the people whose God is the LORD.
sum.131: This psalm recalls how David vowed not to rest until he found a place for God to dwell, and it asks that God not forget his anointed one. God responds that he promised to keep David's throne secure if his descendants keep his covenant. He also chooses Zion as his dwelling place, where he will bless the people, save his priests, and give victory to his king.
sum.144: In this psalm, David vows to praise God every day, because he is a great King, good, compassionate, and slow to anger. Each generation will tell of his works, and his kingdom lasts forever. God lifts up those who have fallen, provides food for everyone, is near to those who truly call on him, and watches over those who love him.
sum.36: David urges people not to become impatient or envious of the wicked who seem to prosper, because their success does not last. He invites readers to trust in God, do good, be gentle, and let go of anger. He promises that God upholds, cares for, and saves the righteous, and that they will inherit the land.
sum.87: In this psalm, Heman cries out to God day and night from deep anguish, feeling close to death, alone, and rejected by those he knows. He asks whether the dead can praise God, and even so he keeps praying and asking why God hides his face. It is an honest psalm that ends in darkness, without an answer, but with the faith to keep crying out.
sum.63: David asks God to hear him and protect him from enemies who use bitter words like arrows and plot evil in secret, believing no one sees them. But God will strike them suddenly, and their own words will turn against them. Seeing this, people will fear God, and the righteous will rejoice and trust in him.
sum.52: The psalm says that the fool says in his heart that there is no God, and that humanity has become corrupt, with no one doing good. God looks down from heaven seeking anyone who seeks him, and those who oppress his people end up filled with terror and put to shame. In the end, the psalmist longs for the salvation of Zion, when God brings his people back and Israel rejoices.
sum.6: David runs to God in the middle of those who are pursuing him, and asks God to judge him. He insists that he has not repaid evil with evil. He trusts that God is a fair judge who protects the upright, and that the wickedness of the wicked will turn back on themselves, like someone who falls into the pit they dug. He ends by praising the LORD, the Most High.
sum.46: The psalm calls on all the peoples to clap their hands and sing to God with joy, because He is the Most High and the great King over all the earth. He is praised as the one who cares for His people, Jacob, and who reigns from His holy throne. At the end, the leaders of the nations join together with the people of the God of Abraham.
sum.29: David praised God because he healed him and rescued him from death when he cried out to him. He remembers that, although he felt secure in his prosperity, when God hid his face he was shaken and again asked for help. The psalm teaches that weeping lasts only a short time, and that God turns sorrow into dancing and praise.
sum.69: In this psalm, David asks God to come quickly to rescue him, and he asks that those who seek to harm him and mock him be put to shame. He also wishes that those who seek God will rejoice and praise him. David acknowledges that he is distressed and in need, but he trusts that God is his help and deliverer.
sum.32: This psalm invites the righteous to praise God with music and new songs, because his word is upright and by it he created the heavens and the sea. God watches over all the nations, frustrates the plans of the peoples, and no one is saved by a large army or great strength. He cares for those who wait on him, and they trust in him and rejoice in his mercy.
sum.110: The psalmist promises to praise God with his whole heart, together with the upright, because his works are great, beautiful, and just. God is gracious and merciful, takes care of those who fear him, always remembers his covenant, and has redeemed his people. The psalm ends by saying that the fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom.
sum.142: David prays to God out of distress: an enemy is pursuing him, and he feels as though he is dead in the darkness. He remembers the works of God, stretches out his hands thirsting for Him, and acknowledges that no one is righteous before God. He asks for mercy, for guidance to do God's will, and for deliverance, trusting that God will bring him out of his distress.
sum.129: In this psalm, the author cries out to God from a place of deep distress and admits that no one could stand before Him if He kept a record of sins. But there is forgiveness with God, and so the psalmist waits for Him eagerly, the way a watchman waits for the morning. He invites Israel to trust, because with God there is mercy and abundant redemption.
sum.67: David invites us to sing to God, who rises up against the wicked and cares for orphans, widows, and the lonely. He led his people out of the wilderness with power and provision. God dwells on his holy mountain, fills us with blessings every day, and saves us from death. In the end, all the nations are called to praise the God who gives strength to his people.
sum.85: In this psalm, David prays to God out of his distress, asking him to listen, to watch over him, and to give him joy. He does this because God is good, ready to forgive, and abundant in mercy. He acknowledges that there is no other God like him and asks him to teach him his way. Facing proud enemies, he trusts that God will help him and comfort him.
sum.77: Asaph calls the people to tell their children the works of God, so that they will put their trust in him and not be rebellious like their parents. He recounts how God rescued them from Egypt, led them, and fed them in the wilderness, even though they doubted and sinned again and again. God, in his compassion, disciplined them and forgave them, and in the end he chose Judah, Mount Zion, and David as shepherd.
sum.88: The psalmist praises God for his faithfulness and his power over creation, and recalls the promise of an eternal throne for David and his descendants. Then he complains that God seems to have rejected his anointed one and allowed him to be humiliated. He ends by asking God to remember his promise, and even so he blesses him.
sum.139: David asks God to rescue him from violent and deceitful people, who set traps for him and speak with venom. He trusts that God is his protector and asks that God not let the wicked prosper, and that their own evil fall back on them. He is confident that God defends the afflicted, and the righteous will praise him.
sum.76: In Psalm 77, Asaf cries out to God in a night of distress, finds no comfort, and wonders whether God has forgotten him forever. Then he decides to remember God's works and wonders from the past, such as the redemption of his people through Moses and Aaron. In this way he finds hope by meditating on the greatness and faithfulness of God.
sum.119: In this psalm, the author cries out to God in his distress and recalls that God answered him. He asks to be rescued from lying lips and deceitful tongues, which will be punished severely. He feels out of place, living among people who hate peace: he seeks peace, but they want war.
sum.101: In this psalm, a person in great distress and loneliness cries out to God, describing their pain, their weakness, and the mockery of their enemies. But they remember that God endures forever, that he will show mercy to Zion, and that he hears the prisoners and the lonely. Although all things come to an end, God does not change, and his servants will have a secure future through their descendants.
sum.2: David wrote this psalm while he was fleeing from his son Absalom, surrounded by many enemies who said that God would not save him. Even so, he trusts that the LORD is his shield, that He hears him when he cries out, and that He sustains him, so he can sleep without fear. He ends by asking for help and affirming that salvation comes from God, and His blessing is for His people.
sum.40: David says that the one who cares for the poor is blessed, because the LORD sustains them in the day of trouble and in sickness. Sick himself, he pleads for mercy and confesses his sin, while his enemies wish for his death, and even a close friend has betrayed him. Still, he trusts that God will raise him up and sustain him, and he ends by blessing the LORD.
sum.5: David prays to God in pain, asking that God not rebuke him in anger and that he show mercy to him. He is weak and full of distress, and he weeps every night, but he begs God to heal him and save him. In the end he trusts that God has heard his prayer and that his enemies will be put to shame.
sum.98: Psalm 99 presents the LORD as a holy and just King who reigns above the cherubim and is great in Zion. It recalls that Moses, Aaron, and Samuel called on him, and that he answered them, spoke to them from the pillar of cloud, and was a God who forgave but also corrected. For this reason the people are called to exalt him and worship him.
sum.59: In this psalm, David acknowledges that God had rejected them and broken them apart after a defeat, and he asks God to restore them and save them. God answers with promises: the land and the neighboring peoples belong to him. David concludes that human help is worthless and that victory will come only with God.
sum.37: David, sick and weighed down by his sin, pleads with God not to punish him in anger. He suffers pain, loneliness, and attacks from his enemies, but he keeps silent and waits on the Lord. He confesses his guilt and ends by crying out that God would not abandon him and would hurry to help him.
sum.102: David urges himself to bless God with his whole being and not to forget his benefits: God forgives, heals, redeems, and renews. He is compassionate, slow to anger, and abounding in mercy; he removes our sins as far as the east is from the west, and he remembers that we are frail as dust. His love lasts forever, and all creation should praise him.
sum.75: God is renowned in Judah, and his dwelling is in Salem and Zion, where he broke the weapons of war. The strongest warriors were overcome at his rebuke, and no one can withstand his anger. God rises up to judge in order to save the humble, and for this reason people are called to keep their vows and to honor him with offerings.
sum.25: David asks God to examine him and judge him, because he has tried to live with integrity, trusting in God's mercy and faithfulness. He has kept away from wicked people and deceivers, and he loves being in God's house to give thanks. He asks that he not be counted among sinners, and he promises to keep walking in uprightness.
sum.11: David cries out to God for help because faithful people seem almost gone, and everyone speaks to one another with lies and flattering words. God answers that He will rise up to protect the poor and the oppressed. His words are pure, like silver refined in a furnace, and His people can trust that He keeps them safe.
sum.134: The psalmist calls on God's servants to praise him, because he is good, he chose Israel, and he is greater than all the gods. He recalls his power over creation and how he rescued his people from Egypt and gave them the land. Idols made of silver and gold cannot speak, see, or hear, so Israel should bless the LORD.
sum.121: David rejoices when he is invited to go to the house of Jehovah. He remembers Jerusalem as a city that is well united, where the tribes go up to praise God and where the thrones of justice are. He then asks for prayer for the peace of Jerusalem, and promises to wish good for it for the sake of his people and the house of God.
sum.93: In this psalm the author asks God, the Judge of the earth, to act against the wicked who oppress the weak and believe that God does not see them. He reminds them that the one who made the ear and the eye does hear and does see. He trusts that God comforts him, sustains him, and is his refuge.
sum.147: The psalmist calls on all of creation to praise the LORD: the angels, the sun, the moon, the stars, the heavens, the sea, the storms, the mountains, the animals, and every kind of person, from kings to children. All of them should praise him because he commanded and everything was created, and his name alone is exalted. It is also emphasized that he strengthened his people Israel, who are close to him.
sum.109: God invites the Lord of David to sit at his right hand while he subdues his enemies, and gives him authority from Zion. His people follow him willingly, and God swears that he will be a priest forever, in the manner of Melchizedek. He will judge kings and nations, and in the end he will lift up his head.
sum.7: David praises God because his name is great throughout the earth and his glory is set above the heavens. Looking up at the moon and the stars, he is amazed that God would remember human beings, whom he honored and entrusted with caring for creation: the animals, the birds, and the fish. He ends by repeating his praise.
sum.38: David decides to keep quiet so that he does not sin with his tongue, but his pain grows until he ends up speaking to God. He acknowledges that life is brief and fragile, confesses that his hope rests only in the Lord, and asks Him for forgiveness, relief from his punishment, and to hear his tears, for he feels like a stranger passing through before Him.
sum.71: This psalm is a prayer for the king, asking that God would give him justice and that he would rule with righteousness, defending the poor and the afflicted and rescuing them from violence. It describes a reign of peace and abundance with worldwide reach, where all nations serve him and his name is blessed. It ends by praising God, the only one who does wonders.
sum.89: Psalm 90 is a prayer attributed to Moses. It says that God is eternal and a refuge for his people, while human life is brief, like grass, and is marked by sin and the anger of God. For this reason, it asks for wisdom to number our days, for compassion, for joy, and for God to establish the work of our hands.
sum.83: The sons of Korah express their deep love for the house of God and their strong longing to be in its courts. They say that happy are those who trust in God and seek Him, because He gives them strength on the journey, even through hard valleys. A single day near God is worth more than a thousand anywhere else, because He is sun and shield.
sum.65: The psalmist invites all the earth to praise God for his mighty works, such as when he opened the sea for his people. He recalls that God tested them with hard trials and then brought them out into a place of abundance. He vows to offer sacrifices to him and gives thanks because God heard his prayer and did not take away his mercy.
sum.82: In this psalm, Asaph asks God not to stay silent, because several nations have secretly joined together to destroy Israel and take its land. He prays that God will stop them, as he did with enemies in the past. His final desire is that they will come to recognize that Jehovah alone is the Most High over all the earth.
sum.104: The psalm calls people to praise God and remember his wonderful deeds. It recounts how he kept his promise to Abraham: he cared for his people, used Joseph, sent Moses with the plagues, brought them out of Egypt, and gave them the land of Canaan. In this way, they could obey his laws.
sum.70: In Psalm 71, an elderly person asks God to rescue them from their enemies and not to abandon them in old age, because they have trusted in Him since their youth. They promise to tell future generations about His deeds and His righteousness. The psalm ends with confidence that God will lift them up again, and they sing His praises with joy.
sum.141: David prays to God from a cave, feeling alone, hunted, and with no one to defend him. He pours out his distress with complete honesty, acknowledges that God is his refuge and his hope, and asks to be rescued from enemies who are stronger than he is. He ends by trusting that he will once again praise God surrounded by the righteous.
sum.94: The psalmist invites the people to sing and worship God with joy, because He is the great King, the creator of the earth, the mountains, and the sea, and we are His sheep. He then warns: if you hear His voice today, do not harden your hearts as your ancestors did in the desert, who did not enter His rest.
sum.113: This psalm recalls the time when God brought Israel out of Egypt and made them his holy people. The sea opened, the Jordan turned back, and the mountains leaped like young animals. All of creation trembles at the presence of the God of Jacob, who even made water flow from the rock.
sum.73: In this psalm, Asaph cries out to God because enemies have destroyed and burned the sanctuary, and the people feel abandoned. Even so, he remembers that God has been their king from of old, the creator and owner of everything. Because of this, he begs God to remember his covenant, defend his cause, and not let the afflicted be put to shame.
